Madrid versus Latin America: Where is housing more affordable?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:30:18 UTC
22:30:18 KST

Homes cost more per square metre in Madrid than in several major Latin American cities, but lower wages in those cities can make renting even less affordable.
For the price of one square metre of housing in Madrid, you can buy almost two in central Mexico City and nearly three in Buenos Aires, Bogotá or São Paulo. But higher property prices do not necessarily mean a heavier burden on local wages.
The key question is how much of their income locals need to spend to afford a home.
If you compare rents with wages, the gap shrinks and in some cases even flips.
In the Madrid region, renting an 80-square-metre flat at December 2025 asking prices would have absorbed 71% of the average gross salary advertised on InfoJobs that year, according to a study by Fotocasa and InfoJobs.
In Buenos Aires, a two-room apartment comes to almost 80% of an average worker's income.
And in parts of the Santiago metropolitan area, anyone on the minimum wage can end up spending between 78% and 96% of their take-home pay on the rent for a small flat.
These measures illustrate the pressure on incomes, although differences in flat sizes, geographical coverage and wage definitions mean they are not directly comparable.
A commonly used affordability benchmark is to spend no more than 30% of income on rent. Taking Spain's modal salary (the most frequently recorded salary, rather than the average), which was €16,520 in 2024, and dividing it by 12 gives approximately €1,377 a month before tax. Applying that benchmark leaves about €413 a month for rent.
At that price, searches on housing portals found nothing available in Madrid. The closest option was €500 for a flat of barely 30 square metres.
The exercise produces virtually the same result in Barcelona. For €500, you can find somewhere noticeably larger than in the national capital, but the search returned just three homes.
How much housing costs in Madrid
Existing homes in Madrid were advertised at an average of €6,471 per square metre in August, according to property website Idealista. This is 2.2% more than a year earlier and below the April peak of €6,619. The slowdown has not reached the cheapest districts: in Villaverde, the borough with the most affordable homes per square metre, prices have jumped 25% in a year.
Rents, meanwhile, show no sign of hitting a ceiling. In September, they set a record of €23.4 per square metre a month, 4.8% more than a year ago. A study by InfoJobs and Fotocasa, comparing advertised salaries with asking rents for an 80-square-metre home, put the cost at 71% of gross pay in the Madrid region in 2025, compared with a national average of 50%.
The Madrid regional government has not designated any “stressed” housing areas under Spain's Housing Act, which allows rent limits in those areas. Other regions, including Catalonia, the Basque Country and Navarre, have used the mechanism.
The national government has also sought to intervene. After parliament rejected two housing decrees on 2 October, the cabinet approved replacement measures on 6 October, including rental contract extensions, limits on annual rent increases and protection against evictions for vulnerable households. The new decrees still require parliamentary ratification.
Madrid versus other Spanish cities
Madrid is not the most expensive provincial capital for buying a home, although it is for renting. According to Idealista, in August San Sebastián was more expensive: €6,680 per square metre versus Madrid's €6,471. Behind them came Palma (€5,835) and Barcelona (€5,440).
For rentals, Madrid led the way with €23.4 per square metre in September, ahead of Barcelona (€20.1) and Palma (€19.6), while the national average was €15.1.
At the same time, Madrid’s asking house prices rose 2.2% in the year to August, the smallest increase among the cities compared here. Seville (11.5%) and Bilbao (10.6%) recorded the largest increases.
Barcelona, a cap Madrid does not have
Barcelona has been officially designated a stressed housing area since 2024.
According to the Catalan Land Institute (Incasòl), the average rent on new contracts was €1,137 a month in the first quarter of 2026, 4.7% less than two years earlier.
The latest asking-rent figures also show a contrast: rents in Barcelona fell 0.8% in the year to September, while in Madrid they rose 4.8%.
Supply remains contested. In the first quarter, 8,156 contracts were signed in Barcelona, 17% fewer than in the same period of 2024.
The regional government counters that the number of active contracts for regular residential rentals across municipalities with rent caps has increased by 20,994 since the measure was introduced. Idealista's spokesperson argues that advertised supply is falling most sharply in the most heavily regulated markets.
Housing costs still stretch wages across Spain
San Sebastián, the priciest provincial capital for buying, has seen advertised rents fall by 2.5% in a year. In Bilbao, advertised rents are down 0.3%, although sale prices are up 10.6%. The city has been declared a stressed area until October 2028.
In Valencia, which, like Madrid, has no declared stressed areas, rents are just 0.5% below their all-time high. Meanwhile, Seville's sale prices, despite a rise of 11.5%, remain 12% below the 2007 peak, when prices reached €3,322 per square metre.
Palma has seen the sharpest rent increase among the cities compared here, with prices up 7.3% to €19.6 per square metre. The Balearic Islands are the most expensive region in which to buy (€5,595 per square metre).
Despite these differences, renting remains expensive relative to wages. According to InfoJobs and Fotocasa, renting an 80-square-metre home at the end of 2025 would have absorbed 76% of the average gross salary advertised on InfoJobs in Barcelona province, 72% in Madrid province and 64% in the Balearics.
Latin America compared: Lower prices, but homes still out of reach
Mexico City is the most expensive Latin American city surveyed in Deutsche Bank’s Mapping the World's Prices 2026 report, which compares 69 cities worldwide. City-centre homes cost €3,441 per square metre, followed by Rio de Janeiro (€3,264), Santiago (€2,507), São Paulo (€2,397), Bogotá (€2,329) and Buenos Aires (€2,328).
These figures are below Madrid’s August asking price of €6,471 per square metre, although the comparison mixes Latin American city centres with Madrid’s city-wide market.
The picture changes when you set rents alongside minimum wages. In Madrid, an 80-square-metre flat at Idealista's average asking rent costs about €1,872 a month, roughly 1.3 times the minimum wage, equivalent to €1,424.50 gross a month when spread over 12 payments. In Mexico City, the average rent for a two-bedroom flat of 65 square metres is about 2.3 times the monthly minimum wage.
In Buenos Aires, the rent on a two-room, 50-square-metre flat also exceeds twice the minimum wage, and in Bogotá the average asking rent is about 2.1 times the monthly minimum wage.
The flat sizes differ, but the figures illustrate how lower prices can still leave housing beyond a low-paid worker’s reach.
Five cities, five housing crises
Behind these affordability pressures lie different policies and housing conditions. Mexico City and Colombia limit annual rent increases, while Argentina has relaxed rental rules. The following examples show how these approaches sit alongside the pressures on local incomes.
Mexico City: Rising rents despite limits on increases
Asking rents rose 9.6% in the year to June, more than double inflation, according to the Inmuebles24 index.
A two-bedroom flat costs an average of 21,921 pesos (€1,069) a month. Nearly two million people, one in four inhabitants, live in rented housing, according to the city government.
Buying is even further out of reach. A calculation by the financial publication 'Expansión' estimates that a monthly income of around 85,800 pesos (€4,187) is needed to buy a 60-square-metre home, almost nine times the 2026 minimum wage.
To improve affordability, the city already has a rent cap. The Supreme Court has upheld a rule limiting annual increases in agreed rents to the previous year's inflation. For 2026, that cap is 3.69%.
But it only applies to existing contracts. Meanwhile, the indices compiled by property portals track flats coming onto the market.
Buenos Aires: Rents after deregulation
Argentina took the opposite path. Javier Milei's decree scrapping the Rent Act came into force at the end of 2023, allowing rental terms to be negotiated freely.
Following deregulation, the supply of rental flats in the capital surged. Advertised supply in Buenos Aires is now 3.4 times greater than at the low point in February 2023.
Asking rents rose 19.2% in the first eight months of 2026, below estimated inflation of around 21.5%.
A two-room flat costs 886,527 pesos (€516) a month, close to 80% of what the average employed worker in Argentina earns, 1,104,227 pesos (€643), according to Indec, the national statistics office.
Buying is another story. A two-room flat on the market costs around €116,000 on average. According to a calculator by the Argentine daily La Nación, buying a 50-square-metre flat, depending on the neighbourhood, requires between six and 35 years of a person's entire income.
São Paulo: Rent weighs on low-income households
São Paulo has the highest asking rents of any Brazilian state capital, at 65.36 reais (€11.2) per square metre in August, according to the FipeZAP index. Asking rents rose 5.74% in 12 months, outpacing inflation at 4.22%.
Asking prices for houses in July were above 12,000 reais (€2,042) per square metre.
High rents are also the largest component of Brazil’s housing deficit. An estimated 5.77 million households in Brazil, representing 7.4% of the total, needed better or more affordable housing in 2024, with high rents the biggest reason.
In South America's biggest economy, 3.59 million low-income households spent more than 30% of their income on rent in 2024, accounting for nearly two-thirds of the country’s estimated housing deficit.
The state of São Paulo accounts for 26.9% of those households.
Bogotá: Rent limits in a tight market
In Colombia, a 2003 law limits annual rent increases to the previous year's inflation, setting the 2026 cap at 5.10%. Monthly rent cannot exceed 1% of the property's value either. Even so, the market is highly strained.
Bogotá’s rental vacancy rate is just 1.9%, and an average apartment was advertised in the first quarter at 3.76 million pesos (about €1,035) a month. That is more than double the 2026 minimum wage of 1,750,905 pesos (about €482), following a 23% increase.
The minimum-wage rise also pushed up the maximum permitted price of social housing. That ceiling is tied to the minimum wage and has risen 76% in four years. At the start of the year, the government published a draft decree to stop minimum-wage increases from automatically raising that price ceiling.
Santiago de Chile: 11 years' income to buy a home
A Chilean family on an average income would have to spend everything it earns for 11.4 years to buy a home at the average price, according to a late-2024 estimate from the Chilean Chamber of Construction. Beyond five years, the indicator classifies housing as unaffordable.
Renting also puts pressure on low-paid workers. In metropolitan municipalities such as Independencia or La Florida, a two-bedroom flat of under 50 square metres costs between 345,000 and 421,000 pesos a month, according to Fundación SOL. That absorbs roughly 78% to 96% of the take-home minimum wage used in its study.
Informal housing adds another layer to the crisis
In Latin America, between a fifth and a quarter of the urban population lives in informal settlements, according to CAF, citing UN-Habitat and ECLAC. More than 30% of the urban population lives in inadequate conditions, according to the housing yearbook produced by CAF and the Lincoln Institute.
The crisis also affects people who have built their own homes in neighbourhoods without basic services.
In Madrid, aside from exceptions such as the Cañada Real settlement, the problem is mainly one of affordability: there are homes available, but often at prices wages cannot support.
Across the cities examined, the common challenge is the gap between housing costs and what people earn. Lower prices alone do not make a home affordable if rent still consumes most of a worker’s income, leaving little for other essentials.

The Uzbek President’s Son-In-Law Secretly Acquired a UAE Passport While Serving as a Top Security Chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:30:00 UTC
22:30:00 KST

The Uzbek President’s Son-In-Law Secretly Acquired a UAE Passport While Serving as a Top Security Chief
Leaked records show the Uzbek leader’s son-in-law, Otabek Umarov, covertly acquired Emirati citizenship – an explicit legal breach of his position at the time as deputy head of presidential security. He then went on to obtain millions in luxury Dubai real estate.
Banner:
Zuzanna Michalak/OCCRP
Key Findings
Leaked documents show the Uzbek president’s son-in-law, Otabek Umarov, obtained Emirati citizenship in April 2023 while serving as deputy presidential security chief – a direct violation of a ban on second passports for officials in that position.
Leaked property records reveal Umarov, who left his post in 2024 to be made a top Uzbek Olympic official, later acquired 13 luxury Dubai apartments valued at around $7 million in early 2025 – a portfolio previously owned by his tycoon brother.
Uzbek officials are not required to disclose their income declarations to the public, so the Dubai real estate portfolio represents the first luxury assets that reporters have confirmed Umarov holds in his own name.
At the 2023 UN climate change conference in Dubai Otabek Umarov watched in the wings as his boss, Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, met with his United Arab Emirates (UAE) counterpart.
Sporting a crisp navy suit and tie, Umarov at the time was the second most important official charged with protecting the Uzbek president. Perhaps more importantly, he was –– and remains –– married to Mirziyoyev’s youngest daughter, and is widely seen as an influential behind-the-scenes power broker.
But on that December day in Dubai, Umarov carried a potentially career-ending secret: seven months earlier, he had covertly obtained an Emirati passport requiring his sworn fealty to the state led by the man his father-in-law was talking to, President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.
Under UAE law, foreigners can only obtain citizenship through a nomination by a royal court or senior official, and requires swearing an oath of allegiance to the Emirates.
Uzbek military law governing the security post Umarov occupied at the time prohibited his second citizenship, and would have served as possible grounds for discharge from active duty.
Nonetheless, Umarov remained in his post for 18 months after obtaining his UAE passport.
He was relieved of his position in November 2024 — officially "in connection with his transfer to another position" — and immediately appointed to serve under his father-in-law as first vice president of the Uzbek National Olympic Committee.
And Umarov's ties to the UAE extend beyond dual nationality.
Dubai land records obtained by reporters from OCCRP and RFE/RL’s Uzbek Service show that Umarov owns around $7 million worth of Dubai real estate.
The 13-property portfolio that Umarov acquired was previously owned by his tycoon younger brother, Oybek Umarov, according to leaked Dubai land records from previous years. Oybek Umarov has kept a low public profile while building a fortune across a range of sectors during Mirziyoyev's time as prime minister and, later, president.
Uzbek officials are not required to disclose their income declarations to the public, making the Dubai real estate holdings the first luxury assets that reporters can confirm in Otabek Umarov’s own name.
A screenshot from the Emirates News Agency (WAM) showing Oybek Umarov (circled) at the COP28 climate summit in Dubai.
It is not clear if Otabek Umarov bought the properties or his brother gifted them to him. Neither responded to requests for comment.
Otabek Umarov has publicly displayed opulent tastes, including luxury watches like a limited edition Richard Mille timepiece valued at up to $1.9 million, though he has never publicly explained his access to such wealth. Public commercial registries show no record of him owning private companies during his time as deputy presidential security chief.
However, Uzbek and international outlets including OCCRP have reported that Umarov did far more than guard the president, describing him as a “gray cardinal,” or a behind-the-scenes deal maker, who has wielded broad influence across the country's affairs.
An Instagram post showing Otabek Umarov displaying one of his luxury watches.
Multiple sources previously told OCCRP and RFE/RL’s Uzbek Service that while Umarov was still a top presidential security officer, he was also a hidden partner on lucrative Uzbek projects with the Abdukadyr family, who built a trading monopoly in Central Asia on what a former associate alleged was a vast bribery and smuggling operation
While Umarov's name did not appear on any of the paperwork related to the Abdukadyr family, reporters independently corroborated his personal connection to individuals the sources described as proxy owners of companies involved in these projects.
Leila Seiitbek, a human rights advocate and campaigner who researches corruption in Central Asia, told OCCRP that both Umarov’s UAE passport and real estate portfolio raise security concerns.
“For the man [then] responsible for the president's personal security, it's also a loyalty and counterintelligence problem – precisely why most states, including Uzbekistan's own military law, treat foreign citizenship in this category of position as disqualifying,” Seiitbek said.
OCCRP sent requests for comment to Umarov and the Uzbek presidential administration about his UAE citizenship and Dubai properties but did not receive a response in time for publication.
Oybek Umarov, the Uzbek presidential security service, and the UAE government did not respond to requests for comment.
Family Connections
Umarov married Mirziyoyev’s youngest daughter, Shakhnoza Mirziyoyeva, in 2007, when the future Uzbek president was serving as prime minister under the autocratic regime of Islam Karimov.
Mirziyoyev took power following Karimov's death in 2016, pledging greater transparency and rule of law compared to his predecessor’s dictatorial rule.
To the outside world, Mirziyoyev presents himself as a reformer who has transformed what was one of the region's most isolated nations into a country open for business on the international stage.
Credit: Igor Kovalenko/Anadolu Agency/Anadolu via AFP
Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev during a press conference in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on January 27, 2023.
But at home, he has continued the country’s tradition of concentrating power in the hands of insiders and relatives, including his elder daughter, Saida Mirziyoyeva, who now heads her father's administration.
Among those was Umarov, who for a majority of Mirziyoyev's tenure had served as deputy head of the presidential security service, a body responsible for the safety of the president and his family.
His tenure ended in late 2024 amid a high-level reshuffle within the security service several weeks after a shooting rocked the highest levels of the government.
In the early hours of October 26, 2024, two gunmen opened fire on a Range Rover on the outskirts of the Uzbek capital, Tashkent.
Inside the vehicle was Komil Allamjonov, former information-policy chief to the president and a close advisor to Saida Mirziyoyeva. Allamjonov and his driver were unhurt.
While prosecutors never implicated Umarov in Allamjonov’s shooting, regional analysts and media have reported a behind-the-scenes rivalry between the two men.
On November 25, 2024, amid a wider purge in the security apparatus, Umarov was formally relieved of his position in the presidential security service and appointed first vice president of the Uzbek National Olympic Committee under his father-in-law, one of several official sporting executive positions he holds to this day.
Otabek Umarov (standing) at a General Assembly of the Uzbek National Olympic Committee in 2024.
Following a closed-door trial, a military court in February 2025 convicted 10 men over the plot, sentencing several of them to two decades or more in prison – including a former head of internal security in the presidential security service.
An Oath to the Sheikhs?
Over the years, Umarov has built close ties with ruling elites in the UAE, traveling frequently in the country for international sporting events or informal meetings with members of the ruling royal families.
A 2019 instagram post shows him posing with a line of gold-robed Emiratis at the wedding of Crown Prince of Dubai Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum. Later that year, images show Umarov hosting the prince for lunch during a falconry trip to Uzbekistan.
A 2019 Instagram post showing Otabek Umarov (circled) posing at the wedding of Dubai Crown Prince Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum.
Whether friendships such as these may have helped pave the way for Umarov’s UAE citizenship is not known. But such passports are a rare and exclusive commodity which money alone can’t buy: Candidates can’t apply for the navy blue document adorned with a golden falcon, they must be nominated by senior UAE officials or rulers.
Reporters were unable to establish who nominated Umarov for UAE citizenship. But copies of Umarov’s UAE passport and residence permit obtained by reporters show that he was granted citizenship in April 2023, while he was still serving as Mirziyoyev’s deputy head of presidential security.
Nominees are subject to general requirements, such as “taking the oath of allegiance and loyalty to the UAE” and committing to “abide by the UAE’s laws,” according to the country’s citizenship and passport law.
These nominations are submitted for certain categories of foreigners, including “investors, doctors, scientists, specialists, inventors, intellectuals, talents and artists (and their families), [and] individuals with creative talents.”
It’s not clear under which category Umarov was nominated.
OCCRP independently confirmed the authenticity of Umarov’s citizenship records.
OCCRP sent inquiries about Umarov’s to both the UAE Foreign Ministry and UAE Federal Authority for Identity, Citizenship, Customs and Port Security but did not receive responses in time for publication.
While Umarov was barred from holding a second citizenship under Uzbek military law governing his presidential security post, having a foreign passport does not automatically trigger criminal penalties or fines.
But Uzbek law does list “voluntarily acquiring a passport of a foreign state” as possible grounds for revocation of one’s citizenship. The government does not recognize dual citizenship of its nationals.
Uzbek Military Law on Second Passports
Serving in the Uzbek Presidential Security Service is classified as active military duty, and Article 29 of Uzbekistan’s law on military service lists 11 criteria that represent grounds for discharge from active duty. The acquisition of citizenship of another country is the last one on that list.
A senior Uzbek Interior Ministry official told reporters in 2021 that if authorities confirm an Uzbek national’s second passport, a warning is issued to renounce their foreign citizenship within a certain window of time.
"If a person does not renounce their foreign citizenship within the given period, their Uzbek citizenship will be terminated by presidential decree,” the official, Dilshodbek Murodbekov, said, while adding that the individual would not face criminal or civil penalties.
Brother’s Dubai Buying Spree
Known for financial secrecy and low taxes, Dubai is where many of the world’s rich and powerful go to buy what they cannot explain at home.
The 2024 Dubai Unlocked investigation by OCCRP and partners mapped some 800,000 Dubai properties and found them studded with sanctioned politicians, alleged criminals, and “politically exposed persons” (PEPs) — public officials or their family members or associates.
Dubai property records and recent service-charge bills reveal that Umarov is among those with substantial real estate holdings in the UAE.
The 13-property portfolio that Umarov acquired had previously been owned by his brother, though reporters could not establish exactly when and how it came into Umarov’s ownership. The properties are split between two of Dubai's showpiece developments.
Eleven of these apartments are located in Jadeel, a low-rise cluster inside Madinat Jumeirah Living, a resort district of palm tree-lined walkways and Arabesque facades that faces the sail-shaped Burj Al Arab skyscraper across the water.
View of the beach in front of the Burj Al Arab in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, on November, 2022
Umarov's apartments in the complex are adjacent to one another, in effect occupying an entire floor.
Two other apartments that Umarov owns in his name are located in Emaar's Fountain Views towers in Downtown Dubai, steps from the Dubai Mall, with the Burj Khalifa and its fountain below.
His brother Oybek Umarov, 40, initially acquired them in a string of purchases made between 2021 and 2022.
He bought the two Downtown Dubai apartments in late 2021, and seven of the Jadeel units on a single day in June 2022, according to leaked Dubai real estate data obtained by OCCRP. He bought the remaining four Jadeel units weeks later.
At some point in 2025, Umarov became the listed owner of each of these properties, land registry records and recent service-charge bills confirm.
As a former senior official, Umarov falls under the UAE’s official definition of a PEP, and under UAE laws, any property or bank transactions he is involved in should be subject to scrutiny by real estate agents and financial institutions linked to these dealings, anti-money laundering experts told OCCRP.
A transfer of ownership, however, would not require the involvement of a bank or real estate agent or necessarily trigger checks on the origins of a PEP’s wealth, they said.
A Brother’s Wealth
Oybek Umarov became an early shareholder in Orient Finans Bank, one of Uzbekistan’s largest private banks, in 2010 when he was 24 years old. He also became a shareholder of Orient Group, a conglomerate with major investments across multiple sectors in Uzbekistan that has also received lucrative government contracts.
Corporate records have tied Oybek to numerous other Uzbek companies, from cement and metalwork to a Tashkent five-star hotel and a run of food ventures and gyms under the brand name OU7, which is widely associated with Otabek Umarov.
Neither Otabek Umarov nor Oybek Umarov responded to requests for comment about the Dubai real estate portfolio.
Whatever Umarov’s reasons for accepting Emirati citizenship, his secret second passport doesn’t appear to have dimmed his patriotism.
The president’s son-in-law was the country’s most prominent official when Uzbekistan’s soccer team took to the pitch in the United States this past summer.
“As the first country from Central Asia to reach the World Cup, this was a monumental milestone for our entire nation,” Umarov, 42, wrote in an op-ed, adding that Uzbekistan “is taking its rightful place among the world’s leading sporting nations.”
The team crashed out of the tournament after losing all three group stage games, but not before Abbosbek Fayzullaev had scored Uzbekistan's first-ever World Cup goal.
When Umarov posed for a photograph with his wife at the tournament final between Spain and Argentina, Uzbek bloggers noticed something expensive fastened to his wrist: another special edition Richard Mille timepiece, this time worth a modest $370,000.

Pezeshkian urges young talents to turn expertise into solutions

Pezeshkian urges young talents to turn expertise into solutions
TEHRAN – President Masoud Pezeshkian has stressed the important role of talented and capable young people in addressing the country’s challenges, saying society today needs individuals who can draw on their scientific knowledge, expertise and capabilities to help solve people’s problems and offer practical solutions to societal challenges.
Pezeshkian made the remarks on Wednesday at the closing ceremony of the third edition of a national competition titled "Rahi Sho" - literally meaning “Get Going”.
“If you are determined and make sustained efforts, there is no problem in the country that we cannot solve,” the president said, addressing young talented people.
He expressed confidence that Iran would be able to overcome the difficult circumstances created by its adversaries with dignity and resilience.
The Rahi Sho competition is a national annual initiative focused on addressing real-world industrial and technological challenges. It provides university students and graduates in engineering, medical sciences and basic sciences from across the country with an opportunity to work on actual industrial projects, gain a better understanding of their areas of professional interest, expand their networks, and develop a clearer picture of their future career paths.
Top-performing teams are eligible for a range of incentives, including elite-status points, cash prizes, admission to post-competition growth and acceleration programs, research grants, and opportunities to be introduced to various industrial sectors. The initiative also offers other forms of support aimed at facilitating participants’ entry into industry and contributing to the development of a knowledge-based and technology-driven economy.

How AI turned Anwar Sadat into an unlikely Gen Z icon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:29:06 UTC
22:29:06 KST

Breadcrumb
How AI turned Anwar Sadat into an unlikely Gen Z icon
Anwar Sadat, assassinated 45 years ago this week, has found an unlikely new audience among young Egyptians, as artificial intelligence transforms the former president into a social media hero for a generation born decades after his death.
AI-generated videos and images of Sadat have spread across Egyptian social media around the anniversary of the 1973 October War, depicting him confronting or mocking Israeli leaders and celebrating Egypt's crossing of the Suez Canal.
Other viral images place contemporary Egyptians themselves into the war, dressed as soldiers, riding tanks or appearing to storm the Israeli Bar Lev Line, effectively allowing users to digitally insert themselves into one of the defining events of modern Egyptian history.
The phenomenon has become particularly associated with Sadat, who was president during the war and was assassinated by Islamist militants at a military parade commemorating it on 6 October 1981.
Egyptian media have described Sadat as the "hero of the scene" in the latest wave of AI-generated content, with videos placing him in fictional encounters with former Israeli prime minister Golda Meir and defence minister Moshe Dayan.
But the trend appears to be doing more than simply producing patriotic memes.
Egyptian journalist Sami Abdel Radi said this week that Sadat had become a "trend" among a new generation, including teenagers aged between 14 and 20 who never experienced his presidency.
According to Abdel Radi, some young Egyptians encountering the former president through social media have subsequently begun searching for his speeches and footage of prominent Egyptian military commanders from the 1973 war.
Gen Z discovers the October War
The AI trend exploded around Monday's anniversary of the war, which Egypt officially commemorates as a military victory over Israel.
Egyptian social media users have shared prompts allowing others to generate their own October War images, while Egyptian outlets have published guides showing readers how to create AI pictures placing themselves alongside soldiers and military equipment from 1973.
Some of the resulting images deliberately imitate old photographs, giving users the appearance of having personally taken part in the crossing of the Suez Canal more than half a century ago.
The trend represents a striking change in how younger Egyptians encounter a conflict that has traditionally been remembered through school textbooks, state television, war films and annual official commemorations.
Egyptian media have increasingly discussed AI and short-form video as a new vehicle for transmitting memories of the war to Gen Z, whose members have no personal memory not only of the conflict but of Sadat himself.
The fascination with Sadat also predates this week's anniversary.
Earlier this year, schools in the southern province of Minya experimented with an AI-generated interactive version of the former president, allowing pupils to encounter a digital Sadat while learning about the October War.
A new version of Sadat?
The online revival nevertheless presents a highly selective version of one of Egypt's most consequential and controversial modern leaders.
Sadat succeeded Gamal Abdel Nasser in 1970 and oversaw the October 1973 surprise attack on Israeli forces in the occupied Sinai Peninsula, initially achieving dramatic Egyptian advances across the Suez Canal.
The war remains central to Sadat's reputation in Egypt and paved the way for negotiations that eventually resulted in Israel returning the Sinai Peninsula to Egyptian sovereignty.
Sadat later became the first Arab leader to visit Israel and signed the 1978 Camp David Accords and the 1979 Egyptian-Israeli peace treaty, securing the eventual return of the occupied Sinai Peninsula.
The separate peace was widely viewed as a betrayal at home and across the Arab and Muslim world, particularly with the Palestinian question unresolved, and saw Egypt suspended from the Arab League and isolated from much of the region.
His domestic legacy was equally as complicated.
His economic "infitah", or open-door policy, contributed to major social and economic changes, while cuts to subsidies triggered the 1977 bread riots.
In September 1981, weeks before his assassination, Sadat ordered the arrest of more than 1,500 political opponents and critics from across Egypt's ideological spectrum.
Much of that complexity is absent from the AI-generated Sadat circulating online.
Instead, the figure emerging on Egyptian social media is overwhelmingly Sadat the wartime president: confident, charismatic and triumphant, confronting Israel at a moment when Egypt was capable of dramatically altering the regional balance.
That image stands in stark contrast to Egypt's position today, with Cairo economically reliant on Gulf investment and billions of dollars in US support, and criticised for a cautious regional posture even as Israel's genocide in neighbouring Gaza has generated widespread anger among Egyptians.

Temporary protection for Ukrainians in Lithuania extended until 2028, but there is an exception
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

16:27:55 EEST

Temporary protection for Ukrainians in Lithuania extended until 2028, but there is an exception
Kyiv • UNN
Lithuania has extended temporary protection for Ukrainians until March 2028. Those liable for military service must confirm that they left the country legally or provide grounds for doing so.
The Lithuanian government has extended temporary protection until March 2028 for Ukrainian citizens fleeing the war. LRT reports this, writes UNN.
Details
It is noted that this time a condition is being introduced for the provision of temporary protection. If a person is subject to conscription for military service in Ukraine, they must provide proof of having completed it.
Proof will be considered a lawful crossing of the border when leaving Ukraine, an exit stamp in a passport, or an official document confirming exemption from military service or completion of such service.
This requirement will not apply to persons who were granted temporary protection in any European Union (EU) state before 4 August this year, or who applied for this status in Lithuania before that date but whose applications have not yet been decided.
Under the rules in force until now, temporary protection was valid until 4 March next year; however, the Cabinet of Ministers has extended it for another year.
According to the Ministry of the Interior, 52,000 people hold valid residence permits in Lithuania based on temporary protection.
After the start of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the EU activated an emergency protection mechanism for Ukrainians, granting them the right to live, work and receive assistance in the bloc, which consists of 27 countries. However, this year, taking into account Kyiv’s request to help locate persons liable for military service, the EU announced that from now on this measure would not apply to people arriving in the bloc who are subject to conscription into the army.
Currently, about 4.4 million Ukrainian refugees live in the EU under temporary protection status. Their largest communities are in Germany, Poland and the Czech Republic. According to the EU, adult men account for about 27% of all Ukrainians who currently have EU protection, women for 43%, and minors for 30%.
Last year, the EU said it sought to move away from the current system by giving Ukrainians the opportunity to reside legally in the bloc for longer or by providing assistance to those who wish to return home when conditions improve.

Iran parliament votes to criminalise interviews with 'hostile' foreign media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:27:42 UTC
22:27:42 KST

The bill passed 174 to six despite cabinet opposition, carrying penalties of up to two years in prison, fines and flogging for Iranians who speak to outlets designated as hostile by the Intelligence Ministry. The bill has not yet become law and faces Guardian Council review.
Iran's parliament voted 174 to six on Tuesday to pass an article banning Iranian nationals from giving interviews to or participating in discussions with media outlets designated as "hostile" by the Intelligence Ministry, or with outlets owned, managed or funded by operatives connected to countries classified as adversaries of the Islamic Republic.
Violations of Article 22 of the bill on "countering the penetration of intelligence services and foreign governments or entities" carry sixth-degree penalties under the Islamic Penal Code, including imprisonment of more than six months up to two years, fines, 31 to 74 lashes, deprivation of social rights and other restrictions.
The bill classifies foreign governments into two tiers: a "level 1 government" is a state formally designated as hostile under Iranian law or by decision of the Supreme National Security Council.
"Level 2" is defined as a state that has planned or carried out actions aimed at damaging Tehran's political, defence, security, economic, social or cultural interests.
The list of level two governments is to be drawn up by the Intelligence Ministry and the IRGC intelligence organisation, then approved by the Supreme National Security Council.
A proposal by Tehran MP Alireza Salimi to exempt government officials from the scope of Article 22 was also approved at the same sitting.
President Masoud Pezeshkian's cabinet had formally opposed the bill. At its 22 August meeting, the cabinet said the legislation had "serious flaws," including restrictions on scientific activity, the acceleration of elite emigration and negative consequences at national and international level.
First Vice-President Mohammad Reza Aref had warned of consequences for science and technology. Presidential legal deputy Majid Ansari said "criminalising broad and general categories in this bill could harm citizens' rights."
Parliament also passed Article 20 of the same bill, under which anyone who accesses unpublished official information by virtue of their job may not share it with a foreign agent without prior authorisation. The penalty is four to 10 years in prison and a permanent bar from the post through which the information was accessed.
The legislation follows months of hardline rhetoric from Iranian officials against Persian-language broadcasters outside Iran.
On 26 August, armed forces spokesman Abolfazl Shekarchi accused BBC Persian, Iran International and Radio Farda of links to US and Israeli intelligence organisations and said their staff could be placed in the Islamic Republic's "military targets bank".
Following the parliamentary vote, the bill still needs further approval to become law. The Majlis must complete its examination of remaining articles before sending the text to the Guardian Council, which reviews legislation for compatibility with Sharia and the constitution.
If the Guardian Council raises objections and the Majlis insists on its position, the Expediency Council makes a final ruling.
The parliament that passed the article emerged from elections in which turnout was reportedly at around 41%, the lowest since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.
Turnout in Tehran was around 24%. The leading candidate in the capital won some 598,000 votes, compared with more than 1.6 million for the leading Tehran candidate in the 2016 elections.

====================================================================================================

Netanyahu is guilty: His Palestinian strategy was a failure, and October 7 was the price - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:25:46 UTC
22:25:46 KST

The approaching election should not be reduced to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s criminal trial, judicial reform, or a coalition partner. It is about October 7, what led us there, what happened on that day, and what has happened every day since.
When we go to vote, the question we must focus on is what has happened to Israel during the years (since 2009) in which Netanyahu has dominated its politics.
And yes, October 7 stands above everything else.
It was the greatest security catastrophe in Israel’s history. Hamas overran Israeli communities and military positions, murdered about 1,200 people, and abducted 251 into Gaza. The IDF and intelligence services made catastrophic mistakes and must be held accountable. But ultimate responsibility cannot be outsourced to generals.
October 7 was not only an intelligence failure. It was the catastrophic culmination of a political strategy. Since returning to power in 2009, Netanyahu has been determined to prevent the emergence of a Palestinian state alongside Israel. In my view, almost everything else followed from that strategic choice.
A Palestinian state meant dealing with the Palestinian Authority and confronting the issues of borders, settlements, Jerusalem, and occupation. Netanyahu wanted none of that. Instead, Palestinian division served Israeli policy.
In 2019, Netanyahu worked to bring Qatari money into Hamas-controlled Gaza as part of a strategy of maintaining the separation between Hamas in Gaza and the Palestinian Authority in the West Bank. The logic was clear: A divided Palestinian polity made a negotiated Palestinian state far less attainable. Israel could then continue saying there was no Palestinian partner.
But strategies have consequences.
The consequences of Netanyahu's Palestinian strategy
GAZA REMAINED isolated and heavily restricted for years. More than two million people lived in an enclave with extraordinarily limited movement and economic opportunity.
Long before October 7, youth unemployment in Gaza had exceeded 60%. Universities and colleges continued producing educated young people for an economy incapable of absorbing them. A generation grew up with few prospects and little exposure to the world beyond Gaza.
None of that excuses Hamas. Poverty, occupation, and hopelessness do not justify murdering civilians or taking hostages. Hamas made its own decisions and bears responsibility for its crimes.
But responsible Israeli strategy should have asked a different question: What kind of Gaza were we creating on the other side of the fence?
Instead, Israel convinced itself that Hamas could be deterred, contained, and periodically weakened while the Palestinian political question was indefinitely postponed.
That conception exploded on October 7. The tragedy is that even now the larger lesson has not been absorbed.
The Israel-Hamas War formally ended with the October 2025 ceasefire. The American-led Board of Peace subsequently developed a framework intended to remove Hamas from governing Gaza, introduce a Palestinian technocratic administration, deploy new Palestinian police and an international stabilization force, begin reconstruction, and accompany Hamas’s disarmament with phased Israeli withdrawal.
A year later, implementation remains stalled because of Netanyahu. He has rejected important elements of the American plan and insisted that Israel will not withdraw until Hamas is fully disarmed, while the Board of Peace framework envisages phased, reciprocal implementation.
The result is precisely the vacuum Israel should fear: Hamas remains in control of much of the Palestinian population while the legitimate Palestinian alternative remains largely unable to take over.
We are again preserving the conditions we claim to oppose.
AND NOW look at the West Bank.
OCHA (United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs) documented 925 checkpoints, road gates, and other movement obstacles by the end of 2025 – the highest number in 20 years – restricting the movement of 3.4 million Palestinians.
Settlement expansion has accelerated dramatically. In July, the government approved funding for 34 additional settlements, bringing the number established during Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s tenure to more than 100.
Settler violence has also intensified. There have been more than 1,380 settler-related incidents of settler terrorism in the first seven months of 2026 alone. Just this week, more than 100 settler terrorists attacked the Palestinian village of Jalud, burned homes, and even injured Israeli soldiers who had arrived to facilitate a Palestinian family’s return.
Are we reproducing in the West Bank the same strategic failure that preceded October 7?
Millions of Palestinians living without a political horizon. Expanding settlements. Land increasingly inaccessible to Palestinians. Movement increasingly restricted. A weakened Palestinian Authority. Growing violence and despair. And Israeli ministers openly declaring that a Palestinian state will never exist.
You cannot permanently deny millions of people any prospect of freedom and then assume that military superiority alone will keep Israel safe.
October 7 should have taught us that.
Instead, Netanyahu’s political survival has increasingly depended on empowering precisely those forces that want to make Palestinian statehood impossible.
Itamar Ben-Gvir moved from the extreme margins of Israeli politics to become national security minister. Smotrich became finance minister and minister in charge of life in the occupied West Bank. Netanyahu did not create Israel’s far Right, but he legitimized it and placed it at the center of government because he needed its votes.
The consequences reach far beyond the Palestinian issue.
Reservists and their families have carried an extraordinary burden through years of war, while the government has continued trying to preserve broad military exemptions for haredi (ultra-Orthodox) men.
The economy has shown impressive resilience, but Israel has accumulated enormous war costs, greater debt, and reduced fiscal room for education, welfare, health, and infrastructure.
Public education is overcrowded and unequal. Welfare services are crashing. The health system is suffering from highly qualified medical personnel deciding to build their lives elsewhere.
And Israel’s international standing has collapsed to levels that should alarm anyone who cares about this country’s future. Some international criticism is unfair and hypocritical. Some ignores Hamas and the threats Israel faces. But Israel is a small country dependent on alliances, trade, technology, investment, and American support. International legitimacy is not a public-relations luxury. It is a strategic asset.
Netanyahu is unquestionably one of the most skillful political survivors in Israel’s history. But political survival is not national strategy. His great strategic failure was the belief that preventing Palestinian statehood would protect Israel from the risks of peace.
Instead, it helped preserve the conflict itself. And unresolved conflicts eventually send us their bill. October 7 was the most terrible payment.
The question now is whether we are preparing the next one in the West Bank.
ISRAEL NEEDS a completely different vision – one based not on permanently controlling Palestinians but on reaching a political settlement that enables Israel eventually to live in peace with all of its neighbors. That is not naive idealism. It is a strategic opportunity.
Across the Middle East, hundreds of billions of dollars in infrastructure, energy, transportation, technology, and trade are being planned. IMEC – the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor – could eventually connect India through the Gulf and the Middle East to Europe.
Israel sits geographically at the heart of that possibility. Imagine Israel connected by rail, energy, technology, and commerce to Saudi Arabia, the Gulf, Jordan, Egypt, Europe, and India. Imagine Israeli young people growing up seeing the Middle East not only as a source of threats but as a region of opportunity.
That future will remain incomplete as long as the Israeli-Palestinian conflict remains unresolved.
The choice ahead is therefore much larger than Netanyahu. It is between continuing to manage an increasingly unmanageable conflict and finally deciding where Israel wants to go.
A secure Israel. A democratic Israel. An Israel in which citizens share responsibility. An Israel with functioning schools and public institutions. An Israel integrated economically and diplomatically into its region. And an Israel that has ended its conflict with the Palestinian people and can finally live in peace with all of its neighbors.
That is the strategic vision Israel has lacked for far too long. On October 27, we must decide that Netanyahu has to pay the bill for his failures. On October 27, we are sending Netanyahu home – out of control over our future!
The writer is the Middle East director of the International Communities Organization and the co-head of the Alliance for Two States.

====================================================================================================

Israel’s election must address children without family support - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:25:46 UTC
22:25:46 KST

On October 27, we will all head to the polls and decide who will lead the State of Israel in the years ahead. The election campaign will, of course, focus on security, the economy, and the cost of living.
But there is another issue that should concern anyone seeking the trust of Israel’s citizens: What do they intend to do for the children and young adults who have no safe home to return to, no family member to catch them when they fall, and no family support network to stand by them in times of crisis?
For most children in Israel, even during the most difficult periods, family is the first line of defense. When school closes, when a crisis occurs, when they need money, advice, a hug, or simply somewhere to come home to, there is someone to turn to.
Children and young adults without family support do not have that layer of protection. When the public system fails to be there for them, there is no other system waiting to take its place. That is precisely why their well-being cannot remain a marginal matter relegated to “social services.” They are, in the most direct sense, the responsibility of the state.
The past several years have taken a heavy toll on children and adolescents in Israel. The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted frameworks, interrupted continuity of care, and deepened feelings of loneliness and uncertainty for many. Before the system had even had a chance to recover, war arrived, plunging an entire society into a prolonged reality of loss, anxiety, and upheaval.
But the same crisis does not affect everyone equally.
A child surrounded by a functioning family may still be deeply affected, but there is someone there to try to hold them together. A child without family support may find themselves coping simultaneously with a national trauma and their own personal trauma, without the consistent adult who is supposed to be by their side.
It is precisely in times like these that the state must become more stable, not less. It must guarantee a framework that does not disappear, continuity in therapeutic relationships, and meaningful adults who can accompany a child over time. For these children, continuity of care is not merely a professional provision in a treatment plan. It is a substitute for the continuity that a family would otherwise provide.
Every change of placement, every therapist who leaves, and every prolonged wait for assistance forces a child who has already learned that adults tend to leave them to start all over again: to rebuild trust, retell their story, and once again ask whether the person in front of them will disappear too. This is not merely a question of service quality. It directly undermines the treatment’s ability to succeed.
At the heart of this system are social workers, alongside the care and educational teams who are with these children every day.
It is easy to talk about national programs, therapeutic models, and reforms. But ultimately, for a child in distress, the “welfare system” is a person. It is the social worker who answers the phone. The counselor who is there at night. The staff member who notices that the child has stopped eating, has not shown up for school, or has withdrawn into their room. The adult who stays, even after the child has tested them again and again to see whether they can truly be trusted.
That is why staff shortages, burnout, and high turnover are not merely workforce problems within a government ministry. When there is no one there to care for a child, there is no care.
We cannot build a policy that expects professionals to handle some of the most complex and extreme situations in Israeli society while simultaneously accepting a reality in which they are difficult to recruit, difficult to retain, and burdened with ever-growing workloads. We cannot expect the welfare system to function as society’s emergency room while funding and operating it as though it were a secondary service.
There is also a fundamental flaw in the way the state views spending on children and young adults at risk. Care, guidance, housing, education, and mental health support are sometimes treated as expenditures that can be cut when more urgent priorities arise. But a child does not stop needing help simply because the budget has run out.
When support is not provided in time, the problem does not disappear. It usually becomes more severe, more deeply entrenched, and far more costly to address.
A young person entering adulthood without a family and without guidance does not suddenly acquire, at age 18, the tools that others have spent years learning at home: how to manage money, whom to call after losing a job, where to sleep when housing falls through, who can help with applying to school or university, and who will be there when life becomes complicated.
Reliance on families after finishing school
Most young people in Israel continue to rely on their parents long after they finish school. Yet the very young people who have no parents to rely on are often expected to become independent faster than everyone else.
This is an absurdity the state must correct. The state’s responsibility toward a child without family support does not end on the day that child legally becomes an adult. It ends when that young person has a genuine chance to stand on their own.
After everything we have been through in recent years, there should no longer be any need to explain what national resilience means. We have learned that resilience is not built solely through defense systems, weapons, and physical protection. It is also built through a society’s ability to support those who have been harmed within it and help them rebuild their lives.
Social services are not an act of charity that the state extends to the vulnerable. They are national infrastructure.
A strong country is not measured solely by its ability to defend its borders. It is also measured by what happens to a child for whom no one but the state bears responsibility.
That is where the election campaign should begin as well. Not with yet another general declaration about “strengthening the welfare system,” but with commitments that can be measured and funded: a long-term national plan to address trauma and emotional distress among children and adolescents; meaningful action to strengthen the social-work workforce and halt burnout and attrition; investment in the salaries and working conditions of frontline care and education staff; and multi-year funding that guarantees children and young adults without family support continuity of care and guidance as they make the transition to independent adulthood.
Having worked in Israel’s welfare system for many years, and now leading an organization that cares for children and young adults without family support, I know that Israel does not lack professional expertise. The professionals know the problems, and they know many of the solutions. What is missing is a national decision to give these issues the place they deserve among the country’s priorities.
On October 27, we will elect the people who will determine the budgets and priorities for the years ahead. Before we enter the voting booth, we should ask them: What are you committing to do for the children for whom the state is the last line of support?
They themselves are not yet able to vote.
That is precisely why the responsibility is ours.
The writer is the CEO of SOS Children’s Villages Israel. She previously held a leading role in Israel’s National Program for Children and Youth at Risk (360) and has extensive senior management experience in the welfare system.

Chicago Jewish theater drops Naomi Ragen play, says actors feared repercussions of working with her
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:25:42 UTC
22:25:42 KST

Naomi Ragen, the New York-born Israeli novelist and playwright known for her portrayals of Orthodox Jewish women in crisis, says the cancellation of a planned Chicago revival of one of her plays represents a “return to McCarthyism” in the American cultural scene.
Ragen, 77, has revealed that a Jewish arts company in Chicago has shelved plans to revive her 2001 play Women’s Minyan. In a post shared with her thousands of followers on Facebook, Ragen included an email from the company’s artistic director saying that she had been inundated by messages from actors, directors and designers who feared that working with a “pro-Zionist Jew/Israeli” like Ragen could damage their careers.
Ragen told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency that Chicago-based Arts Judaica first approached her in July with a request to stage her play about a haredi woman trying to flee her abusive marriage. Elayne LeTraunik, the company’s artistic director, told Ragen they intended to stage 13 performances next March.
Happy to collaborate, Ragen asked for a contract. She heard nothing until this week when she received a reply from LeTraunik, saying she “must sadly withdraw my intent to do the show.”
LeTraunik’s email continued: “People were seeing you were a pro Zionist Jew/Israeli, and I was bombarded with actors, directors, and designers who were actually afraid that doing a show with you as playwright would hurt their careers. I have never faced this before, and I was stunned by all the accusations of ‘genocide’ flying around.”
The episode contrasts with Arts Judaica’s stated mission: Its website says that “American audiences need Jewish stories on stage more than ever.”
“In the past I have done plays about suicide bombers and never had a peep from anyone,” LeTraunik told Ragen. “This world is getting insane. Perhaps once all this dies down (if it ever does), I will try again. I am so sorry.”
Born in New York, Ragen emigrated to Israel in 1971 and settled in Jerusalem. In addition to best-selling novels like Sotah and The Sacrifice of Tamar, she regularly writes opinion pieces sharing her hawkish views on Israel. On her website and on social media, she shares dispatches from her “Israel War Diary,” expressing strong support for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and IDF military action against Hamas. She has also spoken against what she describes as a worldwide “climate of hatred, fear, and intimidation.”
Some people, she said, have suggested the play was canceled because she is a right-wing Zionist. “Are we now back to McCarthyism, where you have to check the political credentials of an artist [before deciding] whether or not to promote their work?” she said.
“I thought all the progressives were against McCarthyism. Now we’re back there where I have to pass some kind of political test in order to have my work shown.”
LeTraunik told JTA she could never have predicted the pushback or the cancellation when she first approached Ragen. “This situation is one I have never faced before after a lifetime in theater,” she said.
“Since the play has nothing to do with politics, I didn’t anticipate any problems,” she continued. “But unfortunately, people had done research on Naomi and felt so triggered by her politics that it appeared that there were concerns from would-be actors, etc., and even the person who had offered to put up some of the funding was not comfortable.
“As for me, I am almost 80 years old, [a] lifetime American and Jew, and I have long decided not to get involved in the current political turmoil. I just want to do interesting theater.”
Ragen not angry at LeTraunik, has 'sympathy for her'
Ragen told JTA that while it is “strange to get such a response from a Jewish venue,” particularly one whose mission statement includes Holocaust education, she is not angry at LeTraunik.
“I have only sympathy for her,” she said. “I think all these Jewish cultural organizations are now under fire and what we need is not to criticize them because they’re not brave enough, but to understand the pressures they’re under.”
Earlier this month, the Anti-Defamation League published a report alleging “the systemic exclusion and marginalization of Jewish and Israeli artists across American cultural life.” In its examination of museums, publishing and live entertainment, the ADL said it found that Jewish, Israeli and Zionist artists have “faced growing scrutiny, organized protest activity, online targeting, event disruptions, reputational campaigns and, in some cases, cancellations or institutional distancing.”
Ragen said her play, originally commissioned by Habima, Israel’s national theater, has previously been staged in the United States. She is not taking the cancellation personally, she said, but as a symptom of a far greater problem.
“You had a situation in Germany in 1938 where you couldn’t produce a Jewish play or any play which didn’t toe the Nazi line,” she said. “Are we going back to that?”
In her conversation with JTA, Ragen called on “American Jews and good people” to “be a little brave,” adding: “It’s not time to build another Holocaust museum - it’s time to wake up, smell the coffee, and put your money and your time and your effort where your mouth is.
“If you are a person who wants to promote Holocaust education, well, you’re living in the middle of it.”

2026-10-07
13:25:18 UTC
22:25:18 KST

More than 75 senior retired US military leaders and legal experts rejected allegations that Israel committed genocide in Gaza in an open letter released Wednesday, on the third anniversary of Hamas’s October 7, 2023, massacre.
The letter, organized by the Jewish Institute for National Security of America (JINSA), concludes that the genocide allegation is unsupported by the facts and does not meet the legal definition of genocide.
Among the signatories are former senior US military officers who commanded American forces in combat. Drawing on their military and legal experience, they argue that civilian casualties, however severe, do not in themselves establish the specific intent required for a finding of genocide.
According to the signatories, Israel has neither demonstrated an intent to destroy Palestinians as a group nor conducted its military campaign in a manner consistent with such an intent.
“Accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza is obscene,” JINSA President and CEO Michael Makovsky said. “It egregiously distorts the truth, the facts, and the law.”
Makovsky said the former commanders and lawyers who signed the letter understand both “the realities of war” and what he described as the unprecedented measures Israel has taken to limit civilian casualties.
Signatories point to IDF measures to protect civilians
The letter cites a series of measures taken by the IDF during the war, including advance warnings, evacuation instructions, protected corridors, tactical pauses, legal reviews of potential targets, and decisions to cancel strikes when civilians were present.
Those precautions, the signatories argue, have at times required Israeli forces to relinquish tactical advantages and expose their own personnel to greater risks.
The letter does not dismiss the scale of Palestinian civilian suffering in Gaza. Instead, the signatories say their own experience commanding American forces has taught them that civilian harm can occur even when militaries seek to comply with the laws of armed conflict.
“There is no perfect attack; there are only those in which commanders use all available information to make hard decisions and their best judgment to comply with legal obligations and protect civilians,” they wrote.
The signatories also distinguish between statements made by Israeli political officials and the conduct of the IDF. They condemn inflammatory rhetoric by Israeli politicians but argue that such statements cannot, by themselves, substitute for evidence of genocidal intent in the conduct of military operations.
‘The precedent established today’ could affect US forces
The letter also frames the debate as having implications beyond Israel.
The signatories warn that lowering the threshold for defining genocide could incentivize adversaries to embed military forces among civilians, exploit the resulting casualties, and then characterize otherwise lawful military operations as genocidal.
“The precedent established today will shape the conditions under which American forces fight tomorrow,” the letter states.
They call on those making genocide allegations to apply the Genocide Convention according to its legal requirements and to distinguish between civilian suffering caused by warfare, possible violations of the laws of armed conflict, and the separate and specific crime of genocide.
Misapplying the standard, they argue, risks rewarding adversaries who deliberately place civilians in danger while undermining the ability of the United States and its allies to defend themselves.
“Protecting civilians and preserving the ability of our nation to defend itself requires us to defend the truth when the laws of war are being distorted to make false charges of genocide,” the letter concludes.

Former IDF Southern Command chief reflects on security situation three years after Oct. 7 attacks

Across Israel on Wednesday, people are marking three years since the brutal Hamas terrorist attack on Gaza border communities and other parts of the country on October 7, 2023, a date that remains deeply etched in the national consciousness.
Maj.-Gen. (res.) Tal Russo, who commanded the IDF Southern Command from 2010 to 2013, reflected on Israel’s situation three years later and said he still struggles to understand what happened that day. Russo said both the military and the state collapsed on October 7, adding that he had already seen early signs of erosion and arrogance years earlier.
Russo made the remarks in an interview with Gideon Oko and Amichai Attali on 103FM Radio.
Describing what he saw as the attack unfolded, Russo said: "I looked at the television and couldn’t believe it. I told myself: They’ll sweep them away any minute, they’ll clear this up any minute, but I didn’t understand the collapse of the security systems; the state collapsed."
"Only the heroism of civilians, police officers, soldiers, volunteer organizations - that is what stopped it. There was no state; the IDF wasn’t there," Russo added. "For three years I have been frustrated and unable to fully process it because so many things happened that led to that moment. Have we learned anything from it? Some things yes, but many things no."
Russo: State commission of inquiry could help prevent same mistakes in future
He also addressed the debate over establishing a state commission of inquiry, saying it could help Israel understand the circumstances behind the failure and prevent a similar breakdown in the future.
"Everything consists of internal investigations by the military and various bodies. It is important to establish a state commission of inquiry in order to assign the tasks in an orderly manner. It would have been better if this had happened closer to the event, but it will certainly improve things," Russo added.
He also reflected on the scale of the October 7 attack.
"When I try to define October 7, there isn’t even a word in Hebrew to understand the scale of the disaster, the failure, the massacre. I still haven’t found the appropriate word for the greatest tragedy that has happened to the State of Israel," Russo added.
Speaking about Hamas, which Russo said he knows well, he described how Israel’s approach to the terrorist organization changed over time.
Russo: Hamas went from 'enemy' to 'partner'
"Hamas in my time was an enemy," he said. "Afterward it became a partner; I didn’t understand that. For me, it was clear that you don’t talk to it and don’t do anything with it. It was a relatively weak organization. After that, it grew, received money from us, and developed," he said.
Russo concluded by saying that he had already identified signs of erosion in Israel’s approach to Hamas during his time in command.
Russo said, "I am troubled by the erosion of all kinds of things, through the arrogance of commanders and politicians: as though we control things, it is inexplicable arrogance. This is not something I am saying in hindsight; I saw this arrogance, and it frustrated me."

US Man Bought Plutonium From Russia and Sold It Online Across America

US Man Bought Plutonium From Russia and Sold It Online Across America
A Massachusetts man bought plutonium from Russia and resold the radioactive material online to dozens of customers across the United States and abroad, according to the US Attorney’s Office for the District of Massachusetts on October 5.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Jacob D. Miller, 44, pleaded guilty to illegally importing nuclear material after operating an online store that offered plutonium and other hazardous substances. Between late 2020 and March 2025, Miller sold plutonium to at least 67 customers in the US, Canada, Japan, and Switzerland.
According to The New York Times, Miller purchased the plutonium from a seller in St. Petersburg, Russia. The material was advertised through his online business, Collect The Periodic Table, which he had operated since 2017 and which specialized in samples of chemical elements.
Among the products Miller offered was plutonium-239 sourced from an old Soviet smoke detector, according to court records. Individual samples were sold for around $500 and shipped from Miller’s home in South Hadley, Massachusetts.
Plutonium-239 is a radioactive isotope used in nuclear reactors and nuclear weapons. Federal law restricts the import, possession, and transportation of nuclear material, while plutonium is prohibited from being sent through the US mail without authorization.
Federal authorities searched Miller’s home on April 8, 2025, finding radioactive and hazardous substances, six firearms, ammunition, and explosive materials. He has remained in custody since his arrest the following day.
Prosecutors said Miller also sold thallium, a highly toxic metal, to approximately 71 customers. In April 2025, Minnesota resident Stuart Hanmer purchased two five-gram portions of thallium from Miller. Hanmer was later charged with killing his neighbor, Cody Ernst, whose body was found to contain a lethal concentration of the substance.
Miller had previously come under scrutiny for selling radioactive material. In 2014, Massachusetts radiation regulators discovered that he was selling depleted uranium on eBay. Miller subsequently told authorities that he would stop selling radioactive substances.
Federal prosecutors said Miller later told FBI agents that he had been trying to make money quickly from the sales.
In addition to illegally importing plutonium, Miller pleaded guilty to mailing hazardous materials, illegally possessing ammunition and explosives, and possessing child sexual abuse material. The illegal importation of nuclear material carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison. Miller is scheduled to be sentenced on January 21, 2027.
Earlier, Russian soldiers were found to be systematically smuggling weapons from the war zone in Ukraine and reselling them on Russia’s black market and darknet platforms. An investigation by independent outlet Verstka documented assault rifles, machine guns, grenade launchers, and sniper rifles being diverted from the front into illicit supply chains.

Ukraine Identifies Five People Linked to Illegal Crimea Excavations and 14 Removed Artifacts
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) has identified five individuals allegedly involved in unauthorized archaeological excavations in temporarily occupied Crimea and published information on 14 Ukrainian cultural artifacts it says were removed during the excavations.
The information was published on HUR’s War&Sanctions portal under its “Stolen Heritage” section on October 7.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, Russian authorities have been conducting large-scale unauthorized archaeological work at and around the ancient city of Tauric Chersonese since 2020–2021 as part of the “New Chersonese” project. In July 2024, an archaeological park and museum-temple complex bearing the same name was opened as part of the project.
HUR said construction of the complex involved extensive interference with the site’s historical and archaeological environment, with building work significantly damaging and destroying parts of its cultural layer.
Ukrainian intelligence identified four people it says were involved in implementing the project: Natalia Solovyova, director of the Rescue Archaeology Center at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute for the History of Material Culture; Ivan Yesin, director of the My History Foundation for the Support of Humanities; Maksim Zhukalov, the so-called deputy governor of Sevastopol; and Larisa Shepko, a professor at the Department of World History at the so-called Donetsk State University.
HUR also named Nadezhda Milikhina, a junior researcher at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute for the History of Material Culture. According to the agency, she served as deputy to Russian archaeologist Alexander Butyagin during the State Hermitage Museum’s unauthorized Myrmekion archaeological expedition in temporarily occupied Crimea.
HUR noted that in 2024, the Prosecutor’s Office of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea and the city of Sevastopol notified Butyagin of suspicion over the deliberate and unlawful partial destruction of a cultural heritage site. In 2026, the charges were changed to violations of the laws and customs of war. He was detained in Poland in late 2025 before being released and transferred to Russia in April 2026 as part of a prisoner exchange.
Ukrainian intelligence also published information on 14 cultural artifacts it says were taken from the ancient city of Myrmekion during the expedition. Among them are a coin from the reign of Bosporan King Sauromates II, dating to 180–196 AD, and a black-glazed one-handled kantharos dating to 370–350 BC.

Dutch museum returns ancient vase to Sicily after provenance investigation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:24:04 UTC
22:24:04 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
The Allard Pierson Archaeology Museum in Amsterdam has voluntarily returned an ancient vase to Sicily on Wednesday after research raised questions about its provenance, according to broadcaster NOS.
The Centuripe pyxis, a third-century B.C. storage vessel depicting a wedding scene watched by the Greek god Apollo, had been part of the museum’s collection for nearly 30 years.
The museum bought the vase from a Swiss dealer at the Tefaf art fair in Maastricht in 1997. Its provenance documents and an export license were missing.
The seller claimed the vase had been in private Swiss ownership before 1970. But a roll of film Sicilian researchers discovered in 2016 showed the vase among objects handled by grave robbers in Centuripe, Sicily.
The film also contained a wedding photograph dated 1976, contradicting the claimed timeline of Swiss ownership.
“Clearly, things did not go by the book,” said Rogier Kalkers, who leads provenance research at the museum.
Kalkers said restitution was not legally mandatory because stricter rules introduced in the Netherlands in 2009 do not apply retroactively.
“There has been a grey area for museums, collectors, and dealers for forty years,” he said.
“We want to take responsibility and therefore distance ourselves from it,” said the museum.
An Italian delegation, including Sicily’s heritage minister, Carabinieri officers and a representative of the Italian Embassy, attended the handover.
“This is not a conclusion, but a stepping stone to joint follow-up research,” said Kalkers.
