3 years after Oct. 7, Israeli troops hold positions deep inside Gaza, but has Hamas been eliminated? i24NEWS embeds with the IDF to find out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:23:52 UTC
22:23:52 KST

- i24NEWS
- Israel-Hamas war
- Inside Gaza: The IDF’s mission three years after October 7
Inside Gaza: The IDF’s mission three years after October 7
Inside Gaza’s buffer zone, IDF officers say Hamas is rebuilding during the ceasefire, while displaced Israelis still fear returning home
Three years after the October 7 massacre, Israeli troops are no longer in bases overlooking Gaza from the border.
Dozens of outposts are now positioned throughout the Gaza Strip, well beyond the fence Palestinian terrorists breached to attack Israel’s southern border communities. The geography of Gaza has drastically changed over the past three years, but Israel’s central security question remains: Has Hamas been stripped of the ability to pose a threat to Israel?
During an IDF embed, i24NEWS visited Israeli positions inside the buffer zone in Gaza. Since the October 2025 ceasefire framework, Gaza has been divided by the Yellow Line, with Israeli forces controlling an estimated 63% of the Gaza Strip.
The U.S.-backed Board of Peace is intended to oversee Gaza’s transition, including Hamas’s disarmament and an eventual Israeli withdrawal. Those steps remain unfinished.
On the ground, the deputy commander of the Gaza Brigade described the immediate task in defensive terms.
“Our main mission right now is to defend and be ready for future possible developments.”
He said troops had dismantled most of the terror infrastructure in the area now controlled by the IDF, with nearly every building holding some sort of weaponry.
“I can't describe the feeling of getting into a house and then a different house, and every one of them has ammunition in it, has a tunnel going from it to another building next door.”
i24NEWS went inside one tunnel underneath what used to be the town of Shejaiya, less than 800 meters away from Israel’s Nahal Oz. The tunnel is equipped with infrastructure built beneath Gaza over the course of years, including toilets, potable water, and lighting illuminating the cold concrete walls.
According to officers briefing i24NEWS, the military has destroyed the vast majority of tunnels in the areas it controls. However, a substantial percentage of the tunnel network in areas under Hamas control is believed to still be intact, with the military unable to provide an exact estimate of the surviving network. The officers said Hamas is using the ceasefire to rebuild, regroup and rearm.
“If most of their resources wouldn't go underground, and they wouldn't have embedded themselves inside the population, and they would invest in, I don't know, making this place a different place, it would have looked completely different,” the deputy commander said.
The military also says that Hamas continues to test Israeli defenses near the Yellow Line, including by sending children toward different positions to observe troops’ responses.
“You have to understand: it's a fanatical organization in a survival mode,” the deputy commander said. “They will do absolutely anything they can to try and survive this time. And our mission is not to allow that thing.”
For Israeli residents across the border, knowing Hamas still has some capabilities is what prevents them from returning home.
“I really, really, really miss my home. I miss the kibbutz. But I can’t return because I don’t feel safe,” says Rona Epstein, an IDF staff sergeant who grew up in Kfar Aza.
Epstein lost five family members in the October 7 attack. Three years later, the prospect of returning home remains tied to a larger question: whether she can feel secure while Hamas remains across the border.
“I was growing up here believing in peace, believing that I’m safe and nothing like that would ever, ever happen. But we have discovered: no matter how big our army is, it doesn’t matter … They can still break the border. They could still do it again. And they wish to do it again,” says Epstein.
Three years after the massacre, security for families from Kfar Aza will also depend on the lessons drawn from the failures of October 7 and the policies put in place to prevent future threats. The measure of progress will be whether those changes give them reason to feel safe enough to return.

NATO’s top generals gather in Kiev
The NATO Military Committee, the bloc’s highest military authority, has gathered in Kiev despite Ukraine not being a member.
The visit comes just a day after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Ukraine’s NATO membership “is not on the table as we speak,” noting that accession would require unanimous backing.
Kiev’s potential NATO membership has been one of the central issues of the Ukraine conflict. Moscow has long opposed the US-led military bloc’s eastward expansion and has made Ukrainian neutrality a key condition of any settlement, arguing that NATO’s presence there would pose a direct threat to Russian national security.
Ukraine made joining NATO a foreign policy priority following the Western-backed Maidan coup in Kiev in 2014 and later enshrined the objective in its constitution. In September 2022, Vladimir Zelensky demanded “accelerated accession.” As recently as July, he argued that Ukraine’s membership would be “entirely natural.”
NATO continues to officially describe Ukraine as being on an “irreversible path” toward entry. However, former Ukrainian commander-in-chief Valery Zaluzhny, who now serves as Kiev’s ambassador to the UK, said in August that he saw no realistic prospect of it happening.
In a video address on Wednesday, Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, the chair of the NATO Military Committee, announced that he and military representatives from all 32 member states had arrived in Kiev. It is the committee’s first such visit to Ukraine in eight years.
“We are here in full strength with a clear message: the bond between NATO and Ukraine is stronger and stronger,” Dragone said.
According to the NATO official, the delegation discussed Ukraine’s military priorities with the country’s top brass, as well as lessons from the conflict that could be used to strengthen the bloc’s preparedness for “current and future threats.”
Despite being outside the organization, Ukraine has developed extensive military ties with NATO. The bloc says its members provide the overwhelming majority of military assistance received by Kiev and has pledged to continue support.

End of the Brexit era? Burnham's pivot back to Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:22:24 UTC
22:22:24 KST

The writer is a professor of politics at Queen Mary University of London and the co-author of European Politics – a Comparative Introduction.
ISTANBUL
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham surprised everyone – including many of his Cabinet colleagues – when, in his speech to the Labour Party’s annual conference, he unexpectedly reopened the question of the UK’s relationship with the EU.
Brexit, he declared, had “done more harm than good,” and, if we wanted to “restore a higher level of growth and prosperity,” then we needed a “clear path … into the rest of the century.” Accordingly, he continued, he would soon “take the opportunity … to lay out to the country what … the different options are” after which he would “see if we could find consensus around one which will give us clarity about our position, and the future of the continent we live in.”
In so doing, Burnham broke a taboo that has, since 2016, effectively condemned the majority of the UK’s center-left politicians to going no further than promising, just as his predecessor Keir Starmer did, to “make Brexit work” – largely out of fear of appearing to want to renege on what Leave campaigners still insist on calling the “will of the people” as expressed in the 2016 referendum.
Following the polls and the money
That Burnham’s words did not trigger a backlash amongst “the people” (or, tellingly perhaps, a detailed defense of Brexit’s benefits by its advocates) is testament to the fact that a majority of Brits have, since early in 2021, been telling pollsters that the decision the country came to 10 years ago was the wrong one. Currently, some 57% of voters, including 23% of those who voted Leave, agree, while some 55% say they want to rejoin the EU. And Burnham’s decision arguably makes even more electoral sense when one realizes that around eight out of 10 voters whose support he needs for Labour (or else to vote tactically at the next election so as to keep the Conservatives and Reform UK out of office) support rejoining the EU.
Just as importantly, his intervention makes economic sense. Indeed, it is likely that the research suggesting Brexit has done severe damage to the UK’s trade, growth and public finances is (along with this shift in public opinion and the concern that the USA is no longer such a reliable ally) one of the main reasons why Burnham has, after just 10 weeks in the job, concluded that more has to be done to reverse or at least further mitigate the colossal act of self-harm that Brexit constituted.
Under Starmer, the Labour government was pursuing a series of incremental moves to reduce the trade friction created by the UK’s departure. But no economist thinks that this strategy – much like the various trade deals the UK signed with other countries under the Conservatives – will add much more than a fraction of a percent to its GDP. In truth, the only move that will make more than a marginal difference will be joining not just the customs union (just like Türkiye) but the single market too. Yet to do that without going the whole hog and rejoining would mean the UK becoming, in the jargon, a “rule-taker” – something such a large economy with a particularly deep attachment to its sovereignty would probably find it impossible to accept both in principle and in practice.
The smart money is on Burnham inserting into Labour’s next election manifesto a commitment not to rejoin per se but to opening negotiations on a new, closer relationship with the EU, with any deal that might be arrived at being subject to a referendum.
High price of re-entry
Winning such a vote, however, is far from a racing certainty, especially if it were to involve full membership. That is because the current member states would almost certainly refuse to grant the UK most of the opt-outs and the budget rebate that it enjoyed before it formally left in 2020 – and current polling suggests that support for rejoining among the British electorate drops significantly once they are presented with that scenario.
Moreover, this assumes that every EU member state (and, under the rules, it really would have to be every member state) would welcome the UK back into the fold, and that cannot be guaranteed.
For one thing, European governments will worry about the possibility that any decision on the part of the UK to rejoin could be reversed by a future Eurosceptic government. For another, any deal would need to be negotiated with an EU whose largest members, France and Germany, might at that stage be run by two far-right parties (the French RN and the German AfD) whose affection for and affinity with Britain are, to say the least, questionable.
Against that, we should remember that Britain is still a relatively rich middle power with an outsized diplomatic and defense presence. And the positive reaction to Burnham’s opening gambit by France’s current president, Emmanuel Macron, is a reminder that many European politicians and publics would, whatever the obstacles negotiations might throw up, be happy to see the UK finally admitting to itself that, in an increasingly unstable economic and geopolitical environment, being inside the EU is the safest place to be.

Sovereignty incomplete unless state controls decisions on war, peace: Lebanese premier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:20:34 UTC
22:20:34 KST

Wasim Saifeddine and Ikram Kouachi
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said Wednesday that the country’s sovereignty could not be complete unless decisions on war, peace and national security were placed exclusively in the hands of state institutions.
Salam made the remarks at the opening of an exhibition marking the 100th anniversary of Lebanon’s Constitution at the National Library in Beirut.
He stressed the need to complete the implementation of the Taif Agreement and continue the process of building state institutions.
Salam said the Taif Agreement affirmed that Lebanon is “a final homeland for all its citizens, Arab in identity and affiliation,” and that its system is a “democratic parliamentary” one based on the separation, balance and cooperation of powers.
He added that the agreement introduced key principles into the preamble of the Constitution that have since become part of the very definition of the Lebanese state.
But the most important aspect, he said, was that Taif established a road map for completing the process of state-building.
The agreement states that “abolishing political sectarianism is a fundamental national objective” and calls for achieving it through a phased plan, Salam said.
“There is no meaning to popular sovereignty if there are multiple sources of authority outside the institutions that represent the people, and there is no meaning to the rule of law if the law does not apply to everyone,” he said.
“State sovereignty is not complete if sovereign decisions, such as decisions on war, peace and national security, are made outside its constitutional institutions,” he added.
The Taif Agreement was signed by Lebanese political forces in the Saudi city of Taif in 1989 under the sponsorship of Saudi Arabia and other Arab countries, ending Lebanon’s 15-year civil war.
The agreement redistributed political powers among Lebanon’s religious communities in an effort to strengthen political participation.
It transferred some powers of the presidency to the Council of Ministers and Parliament and established equal political representation between Christians and Muslims.

MPs back age verification plan for online adult services ads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:19:49 UTC
22:19:49 KST

MPs back age verification plan for online adult services ads
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Dutch MPs have backed a plan to introduce compulsory age verification for websites advertising sexual services, to protect children from exploitation.
An amendment tabled by opposition parties JA21 and ChristenUnie would require website operators to check the identity and age of anyone whose image is used in an advert, by comparing photo ID with a photo taken when the order is placed.
The vote went against the advice of justice minister David van Weel, who said he “did not disagree” with the principle of the amendment but questioned if it was the most suitable way to change the law.
Van Weel advised MPs to wait until the cabinet produced its own plan after consulting the Council of State and checking whether the amendment complied with European law.
“The amendment is the fastest way to change the law, but sometimes you end up cutting corners,” he said. The Senate still has to vote on the law.
The child protection organisation CKM said it was pleased the amendment had been passed, after earlier attempts to solve the problem through a voluntary agreement failed.
Voluntary approach failed
An investigation by CKM found that 80% of minors in cases of exploitation and abuse were advertised on legitimate websites.
Major adult services sites signed a covenant eight years ago with the police and prosecution service in which they pledged to alert the authorities to signs of abuse.
The agreement followed the conclusion of a notorious abuse case in Valkenburg, Limburg, in which a 16-year-old girl was forced to have sex with 29 men in a hotel room after another man had posted her details online.
Shamir Ceuleers, head of the CKM, told Nieuwsuur: “These are basically victims of human trafficking. They might not be advertised as underage, but there are enough signs in these adverts that something isn’t right.”
He pointed out that MPs had been trying for five years to make websites legally liable for checking the contents of adverts before they were put online because it was clear self-regulation was ineffective.
“Parliament has been asking for regulation by law since 2021, and with good reason,” he said. “The Valkenburg case is brought up every time, but even today there are underage children [advertised] online and that is unacceptable.”

OpenAI releases findings on hundreds of math problems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:19:41 UTC
22:19:41 KST

Yasin Gungor
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
US artificial intelligence company OpenAI has published hundreds of mathematics research papers produced by an unreleased AI model, making the findings available for examination while warning that some may contain errors.
The collection, released Tuesday on the code-sharing platform GitHub, contains 722 manuscripts grouped into 372 sets of related results. These can include a main finding, supporting arguments or alternative proofs.
The model attempted approximately 4,000 research problems during testing, according to the company.
OpenAI said the published results were at different stages of verification.
For many results, the company also released proofs written in Lean, a programming language that enables computers to check whether mathematical arguments follow logically. It plans to add more as they become available.
OpenAI published 10 summaries of the model’s reasoning and estimates of the computing power used. It said the average result required computing power equivalent to roughly three hours of ChatGPT Pro “thinking.”
The company said it consulted the independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence at the Institute for Advanced Study on how to present and share the research.
"This is an important event for mathematics, with consequences both for mathematics and for the mathematical community that extend far beyond the individual results," the group said, stressing its advisory role did not amount to an endorsement of the results
“Making this work public is a first step. This release is the beginning, not the completion, of the process of human understanding and the incorporation of the work into mathematical knowledge,” it added. “The future of mathematical research cannot consist only of understanding results produced by AI labs.”

Consensual relation turns sour: Woman cannot use ‘strong-arm tactic’ against man
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:19:20 UTC
22:19:20 KST

NEW DELHI: Supreme Court has held that a criminal prosecution cannot be reduced to a “strong-arm tactic” to force a person to marry by lodging a case of rape after consensual relations did not fructify in nuptial ties. It quashed criminal proceedings against a man which were initiated by his girlfriend after the relationship turned sour after three years of courtship.A bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran said consent allegedly under fear or misconception cannot be loosely inferred to fasten criminal liability on one of the parties when both admittedly had a consensual relationship and the other party willingly permitted a physical relationship. It said that a consensual relationship spread over three years has eventually ended with a criminal case lodged against the man in this case and it cannot be allowed.“Even on a bare reading of the complaint, there is no clear assurance or a promise made of marriage, since the specific allegation is that they entered into a physical relationship after courtship, fully knowing the consequences, but alleged to be under the pretext of marriage; clearly an afterthought.
The respondent (the woman) is a well-educated woman, who entered into a consensual relationship and carried it on for three years, allegedly on the pretext of marriage, which never fructified. She categorically states that she would drop the charge if he marries her. A criminal prosecution cannot be reduced to a strong-arm tactic,” the bench said.Referring to the apex court’s earlier order, the bench said there must be adequate evidence to show that at the initial stage itself, the accused had no intention whatsoever of keeping his promise to marry the victim. It said there may be circumstances when a person having the best of intentions is unable to marry the victim owing to various unavoidable circumstances.“In order to come within the meaning of the term “misconception of fact”, the fact must have an immediate relevance. Section 90 IPC (Consent given under fear or misconception) cannot be called into aid in such a situation, to pardon the act of a girl in entirety, and fasten criminal liability on the other, unless the court is assured of the fact that from the very beginning, the accused had never really intended to marry her,” the bench noted.In this case, the girl met the accused at an academy, wherein both were enrolled. Admittedly, they fell in love and their family members also talked to each other. On an understanding that they would be married, he used to visit her house, where she lived with her mother and brother. When nobody was at home, they entered into a physical relationship, which continued thereafter for about three years. Admittedly, the physical relationship continued for three years unabated and later they separated.
The marriage proposal mooted by both the families also fell through, upon which the complaint was raised.After examining the complaint, the bench said, “We are unable to find any criminal culpability on the appellant who entered into a consensual relationship with the respondent, whose consent cannot be said to be coerced or obtained on a misrepresentation.”

Former German top spy placed under formal arrest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:19:20 UTC
22:19:20 KST

Former German top spy placed under formal arrest
KARLSRUHE, Germany, Oct 7 - A judge of Germany's Federal Court of Justice issued a formal arrest warrant against a former spy chief accused of buying secret documents and using them in an analysis for a foreign intelligence service, the Office of the Federal Prosecutor said on Wednesday.
The case of 80-year-old August Hanning, detained on Tuesday over suspected espionage and attempted treason, has shocked the German intelligence community and lawmakers, and could emerge as one of the biggest leaks of classified documents in Germany since the end of the Cold War.
It has also raised concerns that foreign intelligence agencies could cut Germany off from important information.
Federal prosecutors have not identified the foreign intelligence service, and it is unclear whether Hanning's alleged analysis reached its intended recipient.
Der Spiegel news magazine reported late on Tuesday that investigators were pursuing a possible connection to Azerbaijan. It reported Hanning had been in contact with an agent from the country. Azerbaijan on Wednesday denied any connection.
Hanning on Tuesday did not respond to a request for comment.
"While it is true that he was in possession of confidential documents, the allegation that he passed on information contained therein to the detriment of Germany, let alone for payment, is incorrect," his lawyer told German newspaper Die Welt on Wednesday.
A judge at the Federal Court of Justice in the southwestern city of Karlsruhe issued the arrest warrant, federal prosecutors said.
The official warrant allows authorities to keep Hanning in custody.
Azerbaijan's Media and Broadcasting Council issued a statement saying the allegations were groundless disinformation.
"The malicious intent of the forces behind this disinformation operation is to damage Azerbaijan-Germany relations," the council said.
A senior Azerbaijani government official told Reuters that Baku had contacted German intelligence services through official channels and had been told that the case had no connection to Azerbaijani intelligence.
CHIEF OF STAFF IN CUSTODY
Hanning was head of the BND, Germany's foreign intelligence service, from 1998 to 2005.
Prosecutors allege that in 2010 Hanning agreed to pay for confidential information from an official identified as Manfred D, who served as chief of staff to successive BND heads prior to his retirement in March this year.
His position potentially gave him access to some of Germany's most current intelligence at the time that prosecutors say documents were being siphoned from the service.
Manfred D. was detained on Tuesday and also placed under formal arrest on Wednesday.
Prosecutors on Tuesday said that the investigation centered on suspicion that Hanning received approximately 2,000 documents from D. through June 2022. "Some of these documents were classified," a spokesperson for the prosecution service said.
It is still unclear what level of secrecy the potentially leaked documents had.
Marc Henrichmann, head of the parliamentary committee that oversees the intelligence services, said he was "pretty stunned" by the case.
But he downplayed comparisons to the 1970s case of East German spy Guenther Guillaume, secretary of Chancellor Willy Brandt, who eventually stepped down over the affair.
"I find (that comparison) a bit of a stretch at the moment, because we don't even know exactly what happened there yet," Henrichmann told public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk. REUTERS

China's Golden Week reveals cautious consumer spending despite travel surge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:18:00 UTC
22:18:00 KST

China's Golden Week: Travel surges, but spending stays soft
October 7, 2026
Ya Xi just returned to Shanghai on a red-eye flight after her Golden Week trip to Southeast Asia. "I can stay up all night for a cheaper ticket," she told DW.
She was among the 31.19 million passengers who traveled during the 13-day holiday period that followed the Mid-Autumn Festival on September 25 and China's National Day on October 1.
Many of them spent their budgets more cautiously this year.
"I earn less this year, so I'm lowering my budget for this year's Golden Week," said Xi, who is in her mid-20s. "I spent 5,000 yuan (about €660) on my flight, which was the largest expense of my trip."
Golden Week is viewed as a barometer of the Chinese economy with Beijing using it as an opportunity to showcase the world's second-largest economy's spending power. State media, for instance, reported a record-breaking 25.204 million passenger trips on China's railway network on October 1.
However, early data indicated more moderate spending per traveler and broadly flat passenger traffic, according to Citigroup analysts. Traffic volume during the first four days of the holiday rose just 0.1% year over year, far below the 3.5% increase seen during this year's Labor Day vacation.
Selective spending among younger consumers
Lizzi C. Lee, a fellow on the Chinese Economy at the Asia Society Policy Institute, told DW that Chinese consumers are becoming increasingly selective.
"My read is that people are willing to get out and spend. They're just being much more careful about how much and what they spend on," Lee said.
But being cautious doesn't mean staying frozen, she added. "They'll spend on travel, concerts, restaurants, experiences, and tech… if they think it's worth it, they'll economize pretty aggressively elsewhere."
Xi's Golden Week trip followed this pattern, paying more for significant experiences and economizing elsewhere: "Eat, drink, and be merry," said Xi, indicating she was willing to spend more on food. For example, she set a 200-yuan (about €26) budget for each meal.
Guo-Chen Wang, an associate research fellow at the Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research, told DW that the budget-travel trend among Chinese visitors was ongoing.
"The number of trips is increasing, butconsumption remains strained, as I saw in past years," Wang said.
The Chinese government attempted to boost Golden Week spending by providing coupons worth more than 310 million yuan (€41.2 million). Wang remained unconvinced about the effectiveness of such a measure: "That's an old solution to an old problem."
A sign of China's weak domestic demand
It isn't the first Golden Week to see weak consumer demand. During last year's holiday season, the average spending per trip was 911.04 yuan (around €121), the lowest in three years, according to Reuters.
"Beijing still believes the low spending was due to consumers' reluctance [to spend]," Wang said. "In fact, we think Chinese consumers are unable to spend."
While savings kept increasing in Chinese banks, Wang said the vast majority of the savings are held by a small proportion of the population. "In other words, the majority of Chinese people don't have savings."
"The fundamental issue is the wealth gap in Chinese society," he said. "I don't know whether Beijing really neglected this problem or was simply unwilling to face it."
A recent International Monetary Fund publication, Toward a New Economic Growth Model for China, once again noted that China's domestic demand has been weak since the pandemic, when the property market correction began.
Lee, however, saw weak spending during this Golden Week as a confidence problem.
"Theproperty downturnhas hit household wealth, income and job expectations are still pretty soft, and several years of weak prices have trained people to wait for discounts and hunt for value," she told DW.
Tightened cross-border rules played a limited role
Weeks before the Golden Week, China's tightened travel restrictions took effect on September 15. The new restrictions ban citizens from leaving the country if they are deemed to pose a risk to national as well as industrial or technological security.
Wang expected Chinese tourists to turn to domestic travel under the new rules, but the outcome did not match his expectations. "The volume of travel abroad is in fact growing, though not by much," he said.
Lee said she saw little evidence of a broad chilling effect on ordinary outbound tourism, with the Golden Week numbers serving as a "useful reality check."
"The September rules give authorities more room to verify travel purposes and ask for additional information in some cases," Lee said. "They still leave plenty of room for ordinary overseas tourism."
Mi Tang in Taipei contributed to this article.

Finnish public broadcaster's teletext service turns 45
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:16:47 EEST
22:16:47 KST

Yle is marking 45 years of its teletext service on Wednesday. The tech is delivered directly through televisions capable of displaying it, without the need for a modem or subscription.
The service was initially aimed at people with hearing difficulties — but it soon became a source of news and information for an audience of millions. The primitive-looking but colourful blocky text and images are page-based, meaning that each section and subsection are assigned page numbers, which viewers punch in with a remote control.
Teletext was first seen in the UK in 1974, when the BBC began offering the service.
Finland got its first glimpse of the technology when Yle debuted its teletext service on 7 October 1981. It is still available on televisions as well as the internet.
A very limited amount of Yle News in English content is also on teletext, beginning on page 190.
The medium revolutionised the way information was distributed — well before the internet became a way of life.
Yle's teletext continues to offer up-to-date news, sports scores, weather information and much more.

Used car prices fall in Q3, while demand for fuel-efficient vehicles grows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:16:28 UTC
22:16:28 KST

DETROIT — Used vehicle prices are forecast to fall more than previously expected this year, as high gas prices and broader inflationary costs hit Americans' pocketbooks.
Cox Automotive on Wednesday lowered its forecast for the company's Manheim Used Vehicle Value Index, from a 2% increase to a rise of only 0.2% for the year. That slight increase would mark the third consecutive year of relatively flat pricing after large increases and then declines during the pandemic.
The lower forecast follows a 1.95% decline in the index from July to September, including a 0.6% decline last month compared to a year earlier. September marked the first time since March 2025 that the monthly index hadn't been higher than a year earlier.
"As we enter Q4, interest rates are rising, consumer sentiment is falling, and yet a wealth effect from strong and sustained financial-asset growth is providing some offsetting cushion. Many metrics we watch are converging back toward pre-pandemic norms, but the road to get there has been anything but smooth," Cox Automotive's chief economist, Jeremy Robb, said in a release
The historical average for the Manheim index is about a 2.3% year-over-year gain. Non-adjusted wholesale used-vehicle prices fell 1.2% year over year in September and 1.3% from August as depreciation accelerated in the third quarter, Cox said.
The index is a closely monitored gauge for used vehicle prices that tracks the pricing of used vehicles sold at Manheim U.S. wholesale auctions. Retail prices for consumers traditionally follow changes in wholesale costs.
Cox noted electric vehicle sales and off-lease volume continued to grow, reshaping used-vehicle market dynamics as EVs and smaller, fuel-efficient vehicle values increased during the quarter. That compares with poor performances of large trucks and SUVs, the company said.
"The first half of the year actually showed more appreciation than usual, even in the face of higher fuel prices. But with the conflict in the Middle East ongoing, diesel prices at record highs, and interest rates climbing rapidly, increasingly worrying both businesses and consumers, wholesale prices have felt the sting," Robb said.
The juxtaposition in smaller, fuel-efficient cars and larger vehicles occurred as the national average of gas in September was $4.33 per gallon. That was 50 cents higher than the previous September record of $3.83 set in 2023, according to AAA.
Cox said retail demand for used vehicles is relatively healthy, but the pricing changes seem to be signaling dealers have hit a ceiling on what they can charge consumers.
The average listed price of a used vehicle was $27,239 as of August, according to Cox. That compares with new vehicles at an average price of more than $50,000.
The majority of U.S. consumers purchase used vehicles since they're more affordable than new models.

CIA Red Cell warns Israel risks civil war, state collapse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:10:14 UTC
22:10:14 KST

Breadcrumb
Secret CIA assessment warns Israel risks civil war, state collapse
A secret CIA assessment has warned that Israel could face civil war or state collapse, according to a report by US investigative outlet Drop Site News.
The assessment, apparently prepared by the CIA's "Red Cell" unit, found that years of Israel's genocide on Gaza and wars in Lebanon and Iran had deepened political, economic and social divisions within the country.
Drop Site reported that the assessment comes ahead of Israeli Knesset elections scheduled for 27 October, with the country facing a series of mounting internal crises—including economic pressures, rising military spending and the return of soldiers after three years of fighting with some suffering from severe psychological trauma.
The assessment also highlighted Israel's conscription crisis and deepening divisions between secular and religious Israelis, with exemptions for ultra-Orthodox Haredi men from military service remaining a major source of political and social tension.
Drop Site quoted a source familiar with the assessment as saying its conclusions should be taken seriously rather than viewed merely as a hypothetical scenario.
The source added that its authors were experts on Israeli affairs who believe Israel is approaching the possibility of genuine internal conflict.
Israel was also facing growing international isolation and declining support in the United States, the source said, adding that its increasing status as a "quasi-pariah state" could contribute to its potential disintegration.
What is the CIA's Red Cell?
The CIA's Red Cell was established in the immediate aftermath of the 11 September 2001 attacks to challenge conventional thinking within the US intelligence community and examine alternative or unexpected scenarios.
Then-CIA director George Tenet created the unit to test assumptions that had prevented US intelligence agencies and policymakers from anticipating the attacks.
Rather than producing conventional intelligence assessments, the Red Cell uses "alternative analysis" to challenge prevailing assumptions, identify vulnerabilities and consider unlikely outcomes.
The approach was subsequently adopted more widely across the US intelligence community following intelligence failures surrounding the 11 September attacks and the Iraq war.
According to the Stimson Center, senior US policymakers have received distinctive Red Cell reports several times a week examining assumptions underlying existing policies and considering unexpected consequences.
The method is intended to challenge established thinking and reduce the risk of policymakers being caught off guard by developments that fall outside conventional intelligence assessments.
The Red Cell approach has since also been adopted outside government, including in the business and cybersecurity sectors, to anticipate emerging threats, technological disruption and other unexpected developments.
Its reported assessment of Israel comes as the country approaches a closely watched election following three years of a genocidal war on Gaza and growing political divisions over the government's current policies.

Relief of queen of Poland-Lithuania, Bona Sforza, unveiled at Bari castle in Italy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:10:00 UTC
22:10:00 KST

A bas-relief honouring Bona Sforza, the 16th-century ruler of Lithuania and Poland who was also Duchess of Bari, Naples and Rosano, was unveiled Wednesday at the Swabian Castle in Bari, Italy.
The marble and bronze bas-relief, featuring gilded and enamelled elements, was created by Lithuanian sculptor Jonas Gencevičius. It was installed in the castle courtyard as a symbol of cultural cooperation between Lithuania and Italy.
The work replicates an image of Bona Sforza displayed in the Renaissance Garden at the Palace of the Grand Dukes of Lithuania in Vilnius. Gencevičius based it on an engraving depicting Bona as a young woman, shortly after her marriage to Sigismund I the Old.
The unveiling was accompanied by the signing of a cooperation agreement between the Palace of the Grand Dukes of Lithuania and the museum of Bari’s Swabian Castle. The event was part of Lithuania’s cultural season in Italy.
“Today in Bari, Lithuania is, in a sense, paying tribute to Bona Sforza and repaying a debt to her,” Vydas Dolinskas, director of the Palace of the Grand Dukes of Lithuania Museum, said in a statement. He said Bona had made major contributions to Lithuania’s state and society and helped strengthen Lithuanians’ historical memory and pride.
The project was launched at the initiative of Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda and carried out in cooperation with the Lithuanian Embassy in Italy, the Palace of the Grand Dukes of Lithuania and the Apulia regional directorate of national museums. The Foreign Ministry provided partial funding for the bas-relief.
Nausėda said Bona Sforza had a major influence on life in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania during the 16th century, contributing to major reforms and the spread of culture.
“This memorial will remain for centuries and testify that this person, this woman, had a huge influence on life in Lithuania in the 16th century,” Nausėda said. “She contributed to fundamental reforms and to the spread of culture in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania.”
The president described the bas-relief as a symbolic marker of Lithuania’s ties with Italy that would help strengthen the relationship in the future.
“From today, every visitor to Bari Castle will be able to read the title so dear to us Lithuanians, ‘Magna dux Lituaniae’, on the commemorative bas-relief as well,” Nausėda said. “It will remind us all that Vilnius and Bari are linked by a partnership tested by centuries and based on shared European values, both today and for the future.”
The Palace of the Grand Dukes said Lithuanian Ambassador to Italy Dalia Kreivienė and Lithuania’s honorary consul in the Apulia region, Giuseppe Saraceni, played an important role in bringing the project to completion.
Bona Sforza was born in 1494 at Vigevano Castle in northern Italy, the daughter of Milanese Duke Gian Galeazzo Sforza and Isabella of Aragon, a princess of Naples.
In 1517, she became engaged at the initiative of the Holy Roman Emperor, and the following year married Sigismund I at Wawel Castle in Krakow. She became grand duchess of Lithuania and queen of Poland. After her mother’s death, she inherited the duchies of Bari and Rosano in southern Italy.
Bona returned to Italy in 1556 and settled at Bari Castle. She died the following year after being poisoned. She was buried in the Basilica of St Nicholas in Bari, where part of a Renaissance monument featuring a sculpture of the kneeling ruler remains in the apse.
Bona was an educated and politically active ruler known for her diplomacy, administrative and economic reforms, support for urban trade, and promotion of Renaissance culture and art in Lithuania.
She also sought to secure the future of her children and the Jagiellonian dynasty. Her only son, Sigismund Augustus, was elevated to grand duke of Lithuania as a child and recognised as heir to the Polish throne.

One of Zippel's most strategic functions stands out as providing direct logistics support to the German Armed Forces.
German media reported that the sale of Zippel to Chinese Cosco could risk logistics lines toward Germany's eastern border in the event of a possible military conflict and was vital for the NATO defense alliance.

UK Conservative leader pledges to abolish inheritance tax on family homes
BIRMINGHAM, Oct 7 - The leader of Britain's opposition Conservatives, Kemi Badenoch, pledged on Wednesday to abolish inheritance tax on family homes and let couples pass on an additional £1 million ($1.3 million) without incurring the levy if the party wins power.
The Conservative Party, which has spent more time governing Britain than any other party, now sits third in opinion polls after years of political chaos and infighting in the aftermath of the 2016 vote to leave the European Union.
On the final day of the Conservative Party conference, Badenoch put tax cuts and growing the economy at the heart of her speech, framing the next election as a "battle for the soul of this nation" and contrasting her economic vision with that of the governing Labour Party.
Badenoch said she would like to abolish inheritance tax entirely when the British government can afford it, which is currently 40% of an estate's value over £325,000, or above £500,000 if a home is given to a direct descendant.
"I believe the people who work hard and save should be rewarded for that effort," Badenoch said.
BADENOCH SAYS WORK TO DO TO RESTORE TRUST
Polling suggests a cut in or abolition of inheritance tax would be broadly popular. Inheritance tax is regularly named in polls as Britain's most disliked levy even though only about 5% of wealthy estates pay the levy.
At its current level, the tax is expected to raise about £14.7 billion by 2030/2031, as rising property prices, particularly in London, mean a greater proportion of people are liable to pay it, according to research by the House of Commons.
In the speech, Badenoch cast herself as a champion of lower taxes and government spending compared to the state-directed economic plans of Prime Minister Andy Burnham's Labour Party.
Badenoch said Burnham's policies would make Britain "poorer" and accused him of wanting to spend "money we don’t have on things we can't afford".
She also proposed to cut employer National Insurance social security contributions from the current rate of 15% to 7.5% for 21- to 24-year-olds to help them find work.
Badenoch admitted there was "still a lot of work to do" to restore public trust in her party.
"People are looking through the shop window, they like what they see, but not enough of them are buying yet," she said. "We need to fix that." REUTERS

NASA’s Webb finds signs of Mars-sized worlds smashing together
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:09:15 UTC
22:09:15 KST

NASA’s Webb finds signs of Mars-sized worlds smashing together
- Date:
- October 7, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope is giving astronomers a glimpse of the kinds of violent collisions that may have shaped our own solar system, including the giant impact thought to have created the Moon. By studying 21 rare “extreme debris disks” around young stars, researchers found that their dust can reveal the scale and intensity of planetary collisions.
- Share:
Scientists think one of the most important events in the early solar system was a colossal collision between the young Earth and a Mars-sized body known as Theia. The impact likely vaporized huge quantities of rock and hurled material into space. Some of that debris eventually came together to form the Moon, where NASA's Artemis program is returning humans, preparing for Mars, and shaping the future of space exploration.
That ancient impact dramatically altered Earth. Now, astronomers are using NASA's James Webb Space Telescope to investigate young star systems that appear to be experiencing similarly violent events. By studying these systems, researchers can estimate how energetic the collisions were and learn more about how rocky planets form and evolve.
The team's findings published Oct 1. in The Astrophysical Journal.
Webb Targets Rare Extreme Debris Disks
The material surrounding a star changes significantly over time. Young stars begin with a juvenile, gas-rich protoplanetary disk where forming planets can reside. As the system matures, that environment develops into a gas-poor debris disk.
During its years of operation, NASA's retired Spitzer Space Telescope studied these debris disks and identified an unusual category known as extreme debris disks. These systems contain exceptionally large amounts of warm dust close to their stars, roughly in the same region where rocky planets orbit in our own solar system.
Kate Su of the Space Science Institute in Boulder, Colorado, led a team of astronomers that used Webb to investigate these unusual systems in greater detail.
Theoretical models suggest extreme debris disks should be relatively common, but observations tell a different story. Based on data gathered so far, scientists estimate that only about 1% of young stars display observable signs of this stage. Our own solar system may also have passed through such a phase while it was forming.
Even though these systems are uncommon, the researchers assembled a sample of 21 extreme debris disks. Five came from archival Spitzer observations, and 16 were studied with Webb. Of the Webb sample, 12 disks were newly observed, while four were follow-up observations of systems previously examined by Spitzer.
"This is the first time we have gathered enough systems to truly understand this subclass that we call extreme debris disks," said Su, lead author of the paper. "Before Webb, we had limited information. We knew that they are weird and very different from the typical cold debris disks that we know, like Vega and Fomalhaut. Now that we have more data, we can pin down what these disks represent for planet formation and evolution."
Dust Reveals the Nature of Planetary Collisions
The researchers confirmed that extreme debris disks have three defining characteristics. Their dust grains are smaller than those found in protoplanetary or more typical debris disks, they contain unusually high concentrations of warm dust, and their brightness changes irregularly over time. Webb and Spitzer revealed these features through mid-infrared spectra.
To understand what might be producing these unusual traits, the researchers examined the minerals present in the disks. Their analysis showed that the systems could be divided into two broad groups: silica-rich disks and silica-poor disks.
On Earth, volcanic glass such as obsidian is an example of silica-rich material. The silica-poor mineral forsterite, meanwhile, can be seen as green sand grains on certain beaches in Hawaii.
Whether a disk is rich or poor in silica can reveal important information about the collision that created its debris. The distinction may also help explain why some of the disks fluctuate more dramatically in infrared brightness.
"To just see their mid-infrared emission and beautiful spectral features with Webb, which allowed us to identify their compositions, was the most exciting thing for me," said Agnes Kospal of Konkoly Observatory in Budapest, Hungary, and a coauthor of the study. "We have no other way to study these planetary embryos directly because they are too small."
Mars-Sized Worlds May Be Smashing Together
Roughly one-third of the disks in the sample are silica-rich. The researchers say these systems likely formed after extremely energetic collisions between Mars-sized bodies. Such impacts would be powerful enough to vaporize a substantial amount of rocky material.
The other two-thirds are silica-poor. These systems appear to result from lower-energy collisions, including grazing impacts between Moon-sized objects.
The researchers also found an important age difference between the two groups. Silica-rich disks have only been identified around stars younger than 300 million years. Silica-poor disks, however, occur around stars spanning a much wider range of ages and tend to show stronger changes in brightness.
The team suggests that this variability may come from the rapid evolution of newly created debris. Changes in the material's orbit, along with additional collisions, could cause the infrared brightness to rise and fall over time.
The findings may also help scientists reconstruct the history of our own solar system, which could have passed through more than one extreme debris disk phase.
"How rocky planets formed and giant planets evolved are part of the broader story of the solar system's formation. It's all one story," said Su. "Our work on extreme debris disks helps us bring together the big picture of what we currently understand."
Clues to the Collision That Formed the Moon
Computer simulations suggest terrestrial planets, including Earth, should emerge within the first few hundred million years after a solar system begins forming.
That timeline matches the ages of the silica-rich extreme debris disks observed so far. It is also consistent with estimates that Earth and the Moon formed roughly 100 million years after the Sun, with the Moon likely being the result of a collision between Earth and a Mars-sized object.
Scientists are also interested in whether the Sun may once have passed through a silica-poor extreme debris disk phase.
If the older silica-poor disks and their seemingly random periods of changing infrared brightness are caused by orbital instability, the pattern would be broadly compatible with the Late Heavy Bombardment hypothesis for our solar system.
Under that scenario, the giant planets shifted significantly from their original positions. Their movement disturbed the orbits of smaller objects, setting off catastrophic collisions and producing brief periods filled with large amounts of dust, similar to what astronomers now observe in extreme debris disks.
"Of course, there's many things we still don't know about these disks," said Attila Moor of Konkoly Observatory, a coauthor of the study. "We expect no silica-rich systems among older extreme debris disks. We only have three disks in our sample that fit that age criteria, so it'll be nice to observe more of these systems to confirm our hypothesis."
The James Webb Space Telescope is the world's premier space science observatory. Webb is solving mysteries in our solar system, looking beyond to distant worlds around other stars, and probing the mysterious structures and origins of our universe and our place in it. Webb is an international program led by NASA with its partners, ESA (European Space Agency) and CSA (Canadian Space Agency).
Journal Reference:
- Kate Y. L. Su, Attila Moór, Ágnes Kóspál, George H. Rieke, Antranik A. Sefilian, Renu Malhotra, Ilaria Pascucci, Alan P. Jackson, Péter Ábrahám, Nicholas P. Ballering. Extreme Debris Disks: Insights into Violent Collisions in Planet Formation and Destruction. The Astrophysical Journal, 2026; 1010 (1): 1 DOI: 10.3847/1538-4357/ae88fe

Plasan turns a Jeep Gladiator into a 12-seat troop carrier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:09:10 UTC
22:09:10 KST

- Plasan and ASFIR 4X4 unveiled Stormer, a Jeep Gladiator-based special operations vehicle designed to carry up to 12 people and over 1,000 kg of payload.
- The companies will display the vehicle at the AUSA annual meeting in Washington but did not disclose price, production plans or customers.
Israeli armored vehicle maker Plasan and off-road equipment specialist ASFIR 4X4 have unveiled Stormer, a light tactical vehicle for special operations forces built on a Jeep Gladiator pickup and designed to carry up to 12 people and more than 1,000 kg (2,200 pounds) of payload.
The companies will show Stormer at the Association of the U.S. Army annual meeting in Washington, D.C., at booth 2407. They did not disclose a price, production plans or any customers.
Stormer starts as a commercial Jeep Gladiator powered by a 3.6-liter, 280-horsepower gasoline engine and an eight-speed automatic transmission. Plasan reinforced the chassis and driveline, including upgraded Dana axles, to handle the heavier loads, and added a modular roll-over protection frame that keeps the crew area open for all-around visibility. The companies say the vehicle is designed to be carried by aircraft for rapid deployment.
The rear platform can be set up for carrying troops, cargo, casualty evacuation, weapons or mission equipment such as radar, counter-drone systems, communications gear and an electric winch. A three-position folding rear door lets troops get in and out quickly and can hold a stretcher for casualty evacuation. The vehicle also has a 24-volt electrical system, blackout driving lights, a communications console and several antenna mounts for customer-installed systems.
Plasan said building on a commercial vehicle with widely available parts is meant to make Stormer simpler to maintain and support over time.
“STORMER was developed to address a growing operational requirement for a rapidly deployable platform capable of carrying larger teams and mission equipment without compromising mobility,” said Moshe Elazar, chief executive of Plasan.
“Our collaboration with Plasan enabled us to transform a proven commercial 4×4 platform into a practical and highly capable tactical solution,” said Tzachi Oz, chief executive of ASFIR 4X4.
Plasan, based at Kibbutz Sasa in northern Israel, is best known for armor. Its kitted protection hulls have been fitted to thousands of U.S. military vehicles, including Oshkosh M-ATV and Navistar MaxxPro mine-resistant vehicles, and its North American subsidiary supplies cab components for the U.S. Army’s Joint Light Tactical Vehicle. The company also builds its own SandCat protected vehicle family, which it says is in service on five continents. ASFIR 4X4, based in Tel Adashim, makes off-road accessories and components, including underbody protection for the Jeep Gladiator.
Stormer is unarmored, unlike the SandCat. Israeli outlet Ynet previously reported on a nine-seat, Gladiator-based combat vehicle called Barak from Plasan and an off-road engineering partner, with a payload of about one ton. Plasan has not said how Stormer relates to that vehicle.
Commercial pickup-based troop carriers are already in U.S. service. The U.S. Army’s Infantry Squad Vehicle, built by GM Defense on a Chevrolet Colorado chassis, carries a nine-soldier squad.

Palestinian killed in Israeli settler attack during olive harvest, officials say
BURQA, West Bank, Oct 7 - A Palestinian was killed on Wednesday during an Israeli settler attack while Palestinians were harvesting olives near the village of Burqa in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, the Palestinian health ministry said.
The attack came amid mounting violence from militant Israeli settlers during the Palestinian olive harvest, which has seen settlers fire live ammunition at farmers, attack journalists, and damage the trees.
The Israeli military said both soldiers and settlers had opened fire in Wednesday's incident. It said soldiers were responding to a report of a Palestinian throwing a rock at a settler but did not say why the settlers were in the area.

'FOR US, THE OLIVE TREE IS LIFE'
The olive harvest, which runs from October to November, has come amid a surge of violence in the West Bank, where Israeli settlers have killed at least 30 Palestinians this year, according to the Palestinian Authority.
It has also reported that more than 45,000 trees, including more than 26,000 olive trees, were cut down or damaged across the West Bank during the first half of 2026.
The olive trees bear great significance for Palestinians, representing their connection to the land as well as providing a vital source of income, amid mounting economic pressures.
"For us, the olive tree is life," said Tayseer Al-Sheikh, a 64-year-old Palestinian farmer, from the outskirts of Rantis village, northwest of Ramallah.

For Al-Sheikh, the loss is not measured merely by the number of trees or the quantity of oil produced, but also by the changing relationship of people to their land.
"In the past, everyone used to come to the olives, young and old. Today, many people are afraid to reach their lands," he told Reuters. REUTERS

French wine harvest set to hit historic low

Historic lows expected for French wine harvest after record summer heatwaves
With its wine industry hit by a swathe of summer heatwaves, France is set to see this year's harvest hit a historic low. The total harvest is down 14 percent below the 2021–2025 average, according to estimates published Wednesday by the ministry of agriculture.
At around 35 million hectolitres the total harvest would be down two percent on a mediocre 2025 yield and 14 percent below the 2021–2025 average, according to estimates published Wednesday by the ministry of agriculture.
According to the International Organisation of Vine and Wine (OIV), which tracks global statistics on wine production and consumption, France had already recorded last year its lowest production since 1957.
This latest decline is down not just to hot weather, which has been slightly mitigated by recent rainfall, but also a reduction in cultivated areas -- pared back 1.9 percent in the past year.
Some southern areas, already battered by the heat in 2025, have nonetheless seen production rise this year, notably Bordeaux.
There, despite a five percent decrease in cultivated areas production is set to come in up 10 percent on 2025, albeit still 11 percent below the 2021-2025 average.
Read moreClimate crisis pushes French winemakers to bet on warmer future in Brittany and Normandy
For the southwest the rise is around 12 percent, essentially a return to the previous four-year average.
The Champagne region fared less well as growers had to harvest exceptionally early after the extreme heat sped sugar buildup -- and hence natural alcohol production.
The harvest there wrapped up in September for the first time with production down by half on last year and the five-year average.
In Champagne, producer Claude Mandois reported harvesting three-quarters of an average yield in terms of volume although "in terms of quality visually and in terms of taste we had an exceptional harvest."
In Burgundy and the Beaujolais region, production is projected to be 30 percent lower than the five-year average.
"It's a level of heterogeneity I've never experienced before," said Jerome Despey, chairman of the wine advisory board at the public agency FranceAgriMer and a winegrower in the southern Herault department.
In the south, "we’ve seen that vines have been more resilient to the climate," he said, with previous intense heat spells causing growers to adapt vineyard management practices such as largely leaving leaves to protect the grapes.
Southern regions also benefited from May rainfall.
The ministry and the industry emphasised overall the "excellent health" of the harvest, free of fungi and other moisture-related diseases.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

The king and the cobbler: How Illi Gorlitzky built the language of the Israeli stage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:08:33 UTC
22:08:33 KST

A young actor stepped onto a Tel Aviv stage in 1964 to play both a majestic monarch and a penniless, drunken shoemaker, inadvertently changing the course of Israeli show business forever.
As the dual lead in the monumental musical King Solomon and Shalmai the Cobbler, Illi Gorlitzky didn’t just star in a hit; he helped anchor a high-caliber, Broadway-style theatrical language for a young nation still figuring out its cultural voice.
Gorlitzky, a towering pillar of the Israeli stage, screen, and Hebrew song, died this week at the age of 91.
His passing marks the twilight of a pioneering generation of founding artists who seamlessly blended classical theater, popular music, and everyday Hebrew culture into a singular national identity.
To understand Gorlitzky’s impact is to look back at the golden era of Israel’s performing arts.
Gorlitzky starred alongside Yona Atari in 'Solomon and Shalmai'
Starring alongside the brilliant Yona Atari, his performance in Solomon and Shalmai – set to the sophisticated translations of poet Natan Alterman and the lush melodies of composer Sasha Argov – became a runaway phenomenon that played over a thousand times.
“It was a display the likes of which had never been seen in Israel before, and rarely since,” recalled musician Hanan Yovel in a moving tribute. Yovel noted that Alterman himself had attended the dress rehearsal in absolute agony, convinced the play would be a catastrophic failure.
“Illi calmed him down and promised him he was wrong. Illi, of course, was right. He was a massive star – in my eyes, second only to God.”
Gorlitzky and Atari became an iconic comedic duo, later extending their stage chemistry to the wildly popular revue Bargain Market.
Across seven decades, Gorlitzky’s versatility knew no bounds. He won three prestigious Kinor David awards, moving effortlessly between high-brow theater at the Cameri and popular satirical acts with legends like Yossi Banai, while starring in landmark Israeli films such as Three Days and a Child, Scouting Patrol (Sayarim), and Tuvye and His Seven Daughters.
Yet, for all his effortless charm on stage, Gorlitzky’s most enduring legacy may be the battles he fought when the house lights went down. He was a rare breed in show business: a profound intellectual who possessed a sharp mind for practical, legal, and financial realities.
Recognizing that early Israeli performers had virtually no legal safety nets, Gorlitzky transitioned from star to labor pioneer.
First director of Israeli Union of Performing Artists, Eshkolot co-founder
Gorlitzky became the first director of the Israeli Union of Performing Artists (IUPA) and co-founded Eshkolot, the country’s primary organization responsible for securing and distributing royalties to performing artists.
“He was our Theodor Herzl and David Ben-Gurion rolled into one,” said veteran entertainer Tuvia Tzafir. “He was a visionary entrepreneur who thought of the public good.”
At a time when copyright and intellectual property were barely recognized in Israel, Gorlitzky single-handedly built the framework that ensured generations of future actors and musicians could make a dignified living from their craft.
Even as the years advanced, Gorlitzky stubbornly refused to look backward.
On the eve of his 80th birthday celebration at the Cameri Theater in 2015, he was asked for his perspective on a lifetime of achievements. His response became the definitive mantra of his later years: “I miss tomorrow.”
He lived with his eyes fixed on the horizon, famously quoting the philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein to describe his philosophy on life: “Don’t always live on the barren heights of cleverness; drop down sometimes into the green valleys of silliness.”
He followed that thought by invoking Dante: “It is love that moves the sun and the other stars.”
“That tells you everything about Illi,” noted one long-time media colleague, remembering a performer who was as comfortable discussing philosophy as he was dancing a light-footed tap routine on a television variety show.
Gorlitzky leaves behind his devoted partner of recent years, Anat Globus, a senior editor at Channel 12 News, who captured the heavy quiet left by his absence: “My man went his own way this morning. The house is empty. It is sad.”

Turkey sending technical, defensive support to Saudi Arabia to help fight Houthis, officials say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:08:32 UTC
22:08:32 KST

Turkey is sending mainly defensive and technical support to Saudi Arabia to help it fight Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis, two officials said on Wednesday, after the NATO member and Pakistan pledged to act on the collective defense commitment of their newly formed alliance.
Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member constituted an attack on all. They have been working to set the parameters of the new alliance and have held political and military meetings in response to the Houthi attacks.
On Monday, the countries said they had agreed to move immediately to implement their collective defense commitments and ensure the "rapid deployment" of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.
Turkey condemned Houthi attacks, vowed to help Saudis
Turkey, which has NATO's second-largest army and a robust defense industry, has condemned the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, voiced willingness to help meet Riyadh's technical military needs, and agreed to join a Saudi-led coalition to ensure navigational safety in the Red Sea.
A Turkish official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the support expected from Turkey was only in the form of military equipment, intelligence sharing, and weapons systems, adding that no other form of deployment had taken place as part of the alliance so far.
Drone operators, fine-tuning defensive measures
Officials have said that Turkish support for Saudi Arabia — including air defense systems — would largely be in a bilateral capacity for now, as Turkey's parliament has not officially ratified the joint pact. The amount and nature of the support would increase after ratification, they have said.
A US official briefed on the matter said that Turkey had so far decided to send capabilities that were broadly defensive, including strategic planning support and help with logistics. The official said the assistance included drone operators and help with fine-tuning defensive measures, as well as intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, speaking to state media after a meeting of the Mecca alliance in Riyadh, said the sides had discussed what support to provide Saudi Arabia to help its defensive capabilities.
"We had our Defence Minister and Chief of General Staff with us, and they especially provided very fruitful views on military issues, operational issues, and technical matters," he said on Monday.
Pakistani and regional officials have said Ankara and Islamabad have provided Saudi Arabia with military equipment that the kingdom is using in Yemen.
This week, Yemeni government forces with Saudi-led coalition air support launched a counter-offensive to recapture strategic territory near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, an international shipping route for energy exports and other trade.
Officials had told Reuters last week that Saudi Arabia was planning an offensive against the Houthis, with options being considered including a coastal push to secure the Red Sea shipping route or an assault on multiple fronts.

Father of 3: The first child benefit should be very generous in Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:08:00 UTC
22:08:00 KST

Father of 3: The first child benefit should be very generous in Estonia
Director Madis Ligema, who recently became a father for the third time, told ETV that while money does not necessarily motivate people to have children, more generous benefits could increase the number of births in Estonia.
"The benefit for the first child in particular should be massive to encourage people to have that first child because once you have the first, then the second and third — and perhaps even a fourth — will follow," Madis Ligema said.
Economist and Family Foundation supervisory board member Raul Eamets, however, stressed the importance of supporting families having a third child.
"When people are planning a third child, it actually means a kind of qualitative change in their living arrangements because it means needing an extra room or a larger car, as three child seats won't fit in every car. Why is the issue of a third child so important? Half of Estonia's children live in families with three or more children," Eamets explained.
Parental benefit and a fixed percentage of GDP
As one way of increasing the birth rate, Eamets suggested extending parental benefits to parents who stay at home: "There are certainly parents, whether fathers or mothers, who do this, but we have taken that option away from them. I, for example, really liked Heido Vitsur and Indrek Neivelt's proposal that if you have decided to raise children full time, you receive the Estonian median wage — their proposal was €500 per child, so if you have three children, that would be €1,500," Eamets said.
Member of the European Parliament Jana Toom (Center Party) said Estonia should make supporting families with children a national priority and allocate a fixed share of the budget to it.
"Our child benefits are shamefully low. We have an extraordinarily high percentage of children living in relative poverty and outright poverty," said Toom, a mother of five. "We need to develop a national policy specifically focused on children and allocate a certain percentage of GDP to it, just as we do with defense," Toom said.
Inconsistent support measures rob people of certainty
According to Elin Järvsaar, editor-in-chief of "Pere ja Kodu," stability in benefits is important to parents, while constant changes to legislation discourage young people from becoming parents.
"More important than the amounts is a sense of security. In recent years, we have made a great many changes to the system of family benefits and allowances. That provides no sense of security whatsoever — up and down, back and forth, the rules keep changing," said Järvsaar, a mother of four. "The system has been made so complicated and it gives me no confidence that I will have support for 18 years. Even if parental benefits or other benefits are extremely generous, I know that four years from now they could be completely different and I don't dare take that step," Järvsaar explained.
Raul Eamets agreed that the demographic problem requires a long-term agreement similar to that on national defense. "Family policy and demographic issues are every bit as important as security, meaning that we need a consensus across society and across party lines. By now, I think all parties have realized that this is a problem, but what we need now are decisions that extend beyond election cycles and strategic decisions. One coalition raises benefits, the next lowers them — I completely understand women wondering how they can dare take those risks under such circumstances. Otherwise, we will simply die out," Eamets said.
A total of 9,240 children were born in Estonia in 2025, a record low. During the discussion, Eamets predicted that the number of births could fall below 9,000 this year.

Judge signals support for Booking’s two-day office rule
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Judge signals support for Booking’s two-day office rule
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
An Amsterdam judge has signalled she is likely to back Booking.com in its attempt to make staff work at least two days a week in the office, the Financieele Dagblad has reported.
The travel platform faced off against its works council (an elected employee body whose consent is needed to change working conditions) over whether it is reasonable to require in-office presence at that rate for all its workers.
“Two days is really very little, I’m just telling it like it is,” the judge said during Tuesday’s hearing. For over three years, Booking has held the two-day-a-week rule as a recommendation, but now wants it enforced as a mandatory measure.
The headquarters, on Amsterdam’s Oosterdok, cover more than 65,000 square metres. Booking agreed in 2016 to pay €270 million for the building and its land-use rights, according to filings by its parent company with US regulators. The average attendance rate by staff is 27%, according to the FD.
Dozens of employees sat in on the hearing. The company told the court that making office attendance mandatory was a “small step”, and argued that working only from home can harm staff’s mental health.
The works council disagreed, and one employee told the court he commutes an hour to the office, only to sit on Zoom meetings all day with colleagues in other countries.
The council also spoke about mental wellbeing and said that making office days compulsory could harm staff by taking away their autonomy. A lawyer for the council also noted that Booking is economically thriving regardless of low office attendance.
But the judge seemed to lean towards the arguments of the business. “You might think Dutch judges are strange, but we find working 40% of the time in the office perfectly normal,” she told the courtroom, where the audience was partly international.
The two sides have been given a week to reach an agreement. If they fail, the court will rule at the end of October.

X-Bow to develop booster for future U.S. Navy interceptor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:05:57 UTC
22:05:57 KST

- X-Bow Systems won a prototype agreement worth up to $69.7 million to develop a solid rocket motor booster for a next-generation U.S. Navy weapon.
- The deal funds tooling for a Luling, Texas, line able to build up to 500 motors a year, with initial Navy capability planned for early fiscal 2031.
X-Bow Systems has won a prototype agreement worth up to $69.7 million to develop and qualify a solid rocket motor booster for a next-generation U.S. Navy weapon, and to tool a production line in Luling, Texas, that can build up to 500 motors a year, the Albuquerque, New Mexico-based company said on October 7.
The agreement, administered by U.S. Army Contracting Command at Rock Island Arsenal, covers a $50.4 million Phase 1 development effort lasting 12 months and a $19.3 million Phase 2 qualification option. The government obligated $50 million at award to fund Phase 1 in increments. X-Bow did not name the weapon the booster is intended for.
The company said the Navy program replaces single-purpose interceptors with a common design, including variants that fit more interceptors into each launch system. The U.S. Navy plans to field an initial capability in early fiscal 2031.
“To be the Arsenal of Freedom, we must first break the decades-old bottleneck in solid rocket motor production,” said Jason Hundley, founder and chief executive of X-Bow Systems. “This award is a clear signal the Pentagon is investing in advanced manufacturing to solve that problem, and we are ready to deliver the affordable, mass-producible propulsion our nation needs.”
Solid rocket motors are the propellant-filled engines that launch most U.S. missiles and interceptors. X-Bow makes them partly through additive manufacturing of the propellant, and it will run the program across its facilities in California, New Mexico and Texas, using a design approach it calls Modular Motor Architecture. The rate tooling for the Luling line is funded under the new agreement.
The award is the sixth new propulsion program X-Bow says it has been selected for in 2026, across the U.S. Navy, the U.S. Army and the Missile Defense Agency. The company also says it recently completed its first major production contract, delivering more than 2,100 rocket motors.
In July, the Missile Defense Agency gave X-Bow an $11 million contract to develop a high-performance solid rocket motor, saying it wanted to widen an industrial base that relies on two primary manufacturers, Northrop Grumman and L3Harris’ Aerojet Rocketdyne. In 2024, X-Bow received prototype agreements to build the Mk 72 and Mk 104 motors used in the U.S. Navy’s Standard Missile family.
X-Bow’s Texas site has grown alongside those contracts. The company finished installing a full production version of its additive manufacturing system at Luling in November 2025, and in May 2026 it earned certification for full production operations there. The U.S. Air Force Test Center had awarded it a four-year, $191.3 million motor manufacturing contract in September 2025.
The 12-month Phase 1 effort covers booster development, with the government holding the option to fund qualification in Phase 2.
