PROFILE - Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai: Chemists who made molecules choose a side
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:33:04 UTC
21:33:04 KST

Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai spent decades investigating why chemistry, and life itself, often favors one molecular “hand” over its mirror image.
Their separate discoveries eventually revealed how a tiny initial imbalance could be amplified until a chemical reaction overwhelmingly produced one molecular form.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the French and Japanese researchers the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry on Wednesday “for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis.”
The two scientists will share the 12 million Swedish kronor (around $1.2 million) prize equally.
Their work addresses a fundamental feature of chemistry known as chirality. Some molecules exist in two forms that contain the same atoms but are mirror images of one another, much like a person’s left and right hands.
These forms, known as enantiomers, can behave very differently when they interact with living organisms. One may have the intended therapeutic effect in a medicine, while its mirror image may be ineffective or cause unwanted effects.
Living organisms are overwhelmingly “homochiral,” meaning biological molecules tend to use only one of the two possible forms. Proteins, for example, are constructed almost exclusively from one form of amino acid, while DNA relies on sugars with the opposite orientation.
For more than a century, chemists struggled to explain how such uniformity could arise, and how it might be recreated without relying on living systems.
“Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously,” Nobel Committee for Chemistry Chair Heiner Linke said. 
Henri Kagan: Pioneer of asymmetric catalysis
Born in Boulogne-Billancourt, France, in 1930, Kagan studied at the Sorbonne before earning his doctorate from the College de France in 1960.
He spent nearly four decades at Universite Paris-Sud, now part of Paris-Saclay University, and became one of the leading figures in asymmetric catalysis, the use of catalysts to favor one molecular mirror image over another.
Among his influential early contributions was the development of DIOP, a specially shaped molecule known as a chiral ligand. When combined with a rhodium catalyst, it enabled chemical reactions to produce a high proportion of a desired enantiomer.
The approach influenced generations of chemists and encouraged the development of numerous related catalysts used in asymmetric hydrogenation and other reactions important to pharmaceutical manufacturing.
Kagan’s Nobel-recognized breakthrough came in 1986, when he demonstrated what became known as a nonlinear effect.
Scientists had generally expected the “handedness” of a reaction’s product to correspond directly to that of its catalyst. Kagan showed that the relationship could instead be nonlinear: even a modest imbalance in the catalyst could produce a substantially greater excess of one mirror-image product.
The finding provided chemists with both a practical method of amplifying molecular asymmetry and a new way to examine how catalysts interact during reactions.
Now 95 and a professor emeritus, Kagan had already received many of chemistry’s leading honors, including the 2001 Wolf Prize in Chemistry and the Franklin Institute’s 2005 Bower Award. He was also elected to the French Academy of Sciences and appointed a Knight of the Legion of Honor. 
Kenso Soai: A reaction that copies itself
Soai was born in Hiroshima, Japan, in 1950 and earned his doctorate in organic synthesis from the University of Tokyo in 1979 under prominent chemist Teruaki Mukaiyama.
He later worked with stereochemistry specialist Ernest Eliel at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill before joining the Tokyo University of Science in 1981. He became an associate professor in 1986 and a full professor in 1991.
Building on the broader idea of asymmetric amplification, Soai pursued an even more ambitious objective: creating a reaction in which a chiral product catalyzes the production of more of itself.
This process is known as asymmetric autocatalysis. Once a small amount of one molecular form appears, it accelerates the creation of additional molecules with the same handedness, strengthening the initial imbalance with each cycle.
In 1995, Soai published the first reaction with the potential to become homochiral. By 2003, he had demonstrated a reaction beginning with non-chiral materials that produced only one of two possible mirror-image molecules.
“Other than life itself, no one had previously achieved this feat,” the Royal Swedish Academy said.
The process became known as the Soai reaction and remains one of organic chemistry’s best-known demonstrations of how an almost imperceptible imbalance can grow into near-total molecular uniformity. 
From drug development to life’s origins
Kagan’s nonlinear effects showed that molecular asymmetry could be amplified. Soai then demonstrated a self-reinforcing chemical system capable of producing and reproducing one molecular orientation.
Together, their findings reshaped scientists’ understanding of how chirality is created, strengthened, and transmitted.
The discoveries have helped chemists design more selective reactions for manufacturing medicines, fragrances, and advanced materials. They have also provided a laboratory model for investigating how life on Earth may have come to rely on only one mirror-image form of many essential molecules.
More than 40 years after Kagan’s decisive experiment and three decades after Soai’s landmark reaction, the Nobel Prize recognizes two researchers whose work taught chemistry how to choose a side.

Exclusive: Iraq revises PMF law to curb powers after US pressure
Unknown

Breadcrumb
Exclusive: Iraq revises Popular Mobilisation Forces law to curb powers after US objections
Iraq is preparing to send a revised Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) law to parliament after removing provisions that angered Washington and drew opposition from Sunni and Kurdish parties, sources told The New Arab.
The bill, frozen in parliament last year, has undergone extensive changes under Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi aimed at reducing the PMF's powers and preventing it from becoming an oversized security institution.
Sources said the key amendments would restrict the PMF's freedom of movement, keep its forces away from cities and prevent it from rivalling the Iraqi army in weapons and organisation.
The changes have been backed by Zaidi and a majority of leaders in the ruling Shia Coordination Framework, according to the sources.
Despite the restrictions, the PMF would remain an independent security institution outside the defence and interior ministries, with its own chief of staff and operations command reporting directly to the prime minister as commander-in-chief.
The new legislation would replace the PMF law passed in 2016 during Iraq's war against the Islamic State group.
An earlier version was approved by the cabinet in February 2025 and received two readings in the Iraqi parliament but failed to pass amid US objections and opposition from Sunni and Kurdish blocs.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had warned that the legislation risked entrenching Iranian influence and empowering armed groups that undermine Iraqi sovereignty.
The previous draft included controversial provisions granting the PMF chairman ministerial rank and giving the organisation 16 departments and directorates, including its own military academy.
It also provided PMF personnel with financial privileges comparable to the Iraqi army and annual funding for weapons and development.
Ahmed al-Khazali, a member of parliament's Security and Defence Committee, told The New Arab that the revised bill was in its final stages and would reach parliament soon.
He said the amendments were "simple and limited" and would not affect fighters' interests, adding that parliament intended to pass the legislation after a legal review.
Military expert Sarmad al-Bayati said the law would protect PMF fighters while placing clearer limits on commanders and distinguishing the official force from publicly pro-Iran armed factions operating under the banner of the "Islamic resistance".
The PMF, an umbrella organisation comprising around 70 armed factions, was formally incorporated into Iraq's security apparatus in 2016. However, individual factions have continued to retain their own fighters, political and ideological affiliations, and areas of influence.

"Thousands of pretrial detainees have lost hope of being released," the organisation wrote in a statement on Monday.
The strike follows repeated attempts by detainees to engage with authorities to end the violations, which include physical assault and denial of medical care.
Some detainees have died as a result of the abuse, the NGO said.
FEDA was set up earlier this year by families of political detainees to push for the release of people wrongfully imprisoned, and press for improved detention conditions and fair trials.
Tens of thousands of political detainees are thought to be held in Egyptian prisons, including journalists, rights activists, protesters, academics and political figures.
Many are held in pre-trial detention for prolonged periods. Others are serving long sentences handed down following trials that rights monitors consider unfair.
FEDA called on authorities to release all detainees held indefinitely in pre-trial detention and immediately halt violations against political prisoners.
It urged the public prosecutor to organise urgent visits to prisons where tensions are particularly high.
Journalists detained
Egyptian authorities were condemned by dozens of international organisations last week after security services detained six journalists from independent fact-checking platform Matsadaash.
Lawyers for the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights have said the journalists were subjected to "various forms of torture and mistreatment, including beatings, electrocution, forced stripping, and threats made against their families.
The interior ministry has denied the claims, calling them "an attempt by those concerned to evade the charges attributed to them".
One of the journalists has been detained for 15 days pending investigation on charges of joining a "terrorist group" and spreading disinformation. Investigations into the other five are ongoing.
The government has accused the website of being affiliated with the "terrorist Muslim Brotherhood".
The latest arrests bring the number of journalists detained in Egypt to 26, according to EIPR.

The Greens may yet win in Holborn and St Pancras – but what happened to the party set to ‘replace’ Labour? | Andy Beckett
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:30:39 UTC
21:30:39 KST

Only a few months ago, in the spring, there was a sense of giddy possibility about the Greens. Zack Polanski’s radical new leadership felt fresh and dynamic, especially compared with those of the other parties. Former Labour supporters, in particular, were switching to the Greens in huge numbers, Green candidates were winning across the country, and the party was second behind Reform UK in some national polls.
Like Reform, the Green party presented itself as a revolt against a failed status quo. Unlike Reform, the Greens’ urgent stance on the climate crisis gave them a potent moral authority: even many people who did not support them believed that the Greens were right about the most universal issue.
After an unprecedentedly hot summer, some of that authority and momentum remains. Last week, at the party’s bustling conference in Brighton, impressive-sounding statistics about the party’s growth this year – along with modern icons of Green success, such as Hannah Spencer, victor of February’s Gorton and Denton byelection – were presented to determinedly cheering delegates in crammed halls.
This week, in the high-profile London constituency of Holborn and St Pancras, where Polanski hopes to succeed Keir Starmer in Thursday’s byelection, the usual cheery squads of Green activists have been striding back and forth between wealthy streets and council estates, distributing thick bundles of a party newspaper with the front-page headline “Greens close in!”. Given the party’s recent election record, Polanski’s populist appeal and the possibility that some of the many local leftwing voters may see the contest as a low-risk way to warn Andy Burnham not to follow Starmer’s premiership rightwards, a Green win is not impossible.
But, even if it happens, the problems the party has accumulated since the spring will not have gone away. For some voters, the novelty of Polanski’s leadership has faded. For others his style, more radical and provocative than previous Green leaders, has allowed the party to shift to extreme positions, particularly on Israel, with the Brighton conference passing a motion (which the Jewish Polanski neither supported nor opposed) that “Zionism is racism”.
Meanwhile, Burnham’s confident, sometimes iconoclastic start as prime minister has removed Polanski’s unique selling point as a good communicator who does not accept the usually conservative terms of British political debate. In his conference speech, Polanski admitted: “Now I get asked, isn’t your job done?”
The idea that one of the Greens’ main purposes is to shift Labour leftwards and towards bolder climate policies, and that that approach is yielding results, was everywhere at Brighton, from mutually encouraging chats between activists in the queues to upbeat contributions from the main stage.
It’s not a role that should be dismissed as minor. The Greens’ influence over Labour – both undermining Starmer in record time by taking so many votes from his party and creating political space for Burnham’s coup and governmental refresh – has arguably been a sign of Britain belatedly catching up with other European democracies, such as Spain, where centre-left parties have long been forced to be bolder by more leftwing ones. After decades of Labour paying most attention to forces to its right, the Greens’ important place in Labour’s calculations makes a refreshing change.
And yet, being an influence rather than a definite national rival – the Greens are now about 20 points behind Labour in some polls – is undeniably a comedown. During Polanski’s first months as leader, he regularly said he wanted the Greens to “replace” Labour. Partly because of that apparent possibility, the Greens attracted respected leftwing strategists such as Michael Chessum and James Meadway, who had worked under Jeremy Corbyn’s leadership and became disillusioned by Labour under Starmer.
At some leftwing gatherings last spring, those who hadn’t switched to the Greens could feel a bit over-cautious and old-fashioned. It’s possible that the rightwing media even encouraged this shift, giving Polanski plenty of coverage, in order to divide the left and prevent Labour from ever holding sole power again.
With Labour’s electoral future now looking more promising, one of the Greens’ leaflets in Holborn and St Pancras modestly presents Polanski as “a strong voice … to keep Labour in check”. In his Brighton speech, Polanski said: “Vote Green and watch Labour move.” It’s a typically pithy and clever line: explaining the mechanics of politics to voters, and treating them like grownups, in ways that party leaders rarely do.
But it may not be an inspiring line for more tribal Greens who decided decades ago that Labour, and alliances with Labour, were not for them. Another Green conference theme was “Real hope. Real change.” It sounded defensive, and too similar to Labour’s conference theme the previous week: “Hope again”.
The Greens do still hold the initiative on some issues: advocating rent controls, wealth taxes, an end to fiscal conservatism, and more radical climate policies, with Labour expected soon to allow a limited expansion of oil and gas drilling in the North Sea. There are also signs of the Greens positioning themselves as the party of the most disadvantaged, such as asylum seekers, benefits claimants and transgender people – groups that Burnham’s less judgmental government may treat better than Starmer’s did, yet probably within limits set by Labour’s considerable number of socially conservative supporters.
“We will always stand with … everyone who is under attack,” said Polanski in Brighton, a statement that could be seen as too vague, impractical and idealistic. Yet if this country is to become a more truly representative democracy – a possible upside of the current political fragmentation – why shouldn’t the most vulnerable effectively have their own party? The most privileged have had the Tories for centuries.
The astute political analyst Rob Ford suggests that the Greens’ poll decline “may not matter much” if the party still campaigns effectively and attracts strong support from the dozens of relatively youthful, highly educated and diverse urban constituencies. Thursday’s byelection will test that theory.
Yet either way, there is something disturbing about a party with such a crucial cause having to face a reduction in status. The Greens’ drift back towards the political margins reflects not just their own mistakes, but the reluctance of many Britons to face up to climate realities. As with Extinction Rebellion, it’s more comfortable to call them extremists and ignore what they say.
- Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist

Lithuanian firm brings Ukraine-proven drones to London
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:30:06 BST
21:30:06 KST

A Lithuanian manufacturer whose loitering munitions and reconnaissance drones are in Ukrainian service is bringing its full range to London this week, including a counter-drone interceptor built to shoot down Shahed and Lancet types, according to Granta Autonomy.
The company began supplying uncrewed aircraft to the Ukrainian front immediately after the full-scale invasion and says it is one of only a handful of suppliers to have remained continuously active since, changing its equipment to keep pace with the battlefield. Ukrainian forces now operate a full battery of its systems funded by European defence ministries, among them the X-Wing loitering munition and the Hornet XR reconnaissance drone.
The newest product is the Black Wasp, a vertical take-off interceptor engineered to counter Shahed, Geran and Lancet drones. It reaches 320 kilometres an hour with a climb rate of 30 metres a second, uses the company’s machine learning flight control system for automated flight, precision tracking and terminal guidance, and integrates with radar networks for three-dimensional targeting telemetry.
The X-Wing combines vertical take-off with fixed-wing efficiency to reach 70 kilometres with more than 45 minutes of loiter, carrying a four-kilogram anti-armour or fragmentation warhead and using machine targeting for navigation and strike where satellite signals are denied. The Hornet XR is a hand-launched reconnaissance aircraft weighing 3.2 kilograms, with more than three hours of endurance, a 70-kilometre control link and a deep-stall recovery for landing.
Gediminas Guoba, chief executive and founder, said: “Our team regularly tests our solutions on the frontlines alongside military operators. The new Black Wasp and X-Wing demonstrate our commitment to scalable, EW-resistant architecture. Paired with our Hornet XR, the X-Wing allows a single ground station to control a pair of ‘sensor’ Hornets alongside up to 30 ‘shooter’ X-Wings, creating a complete, highly effective kill chain that outpaces complex and costly alternatives.”
That last claim is the one to examine closely on the stand. One operator running two reconnaissance aircraft and thirty strike aircraft from a single ground station describes a quite different arithmetic from the one Western forces are used to, where each airframe generally requires its own crew, and it is the arithmetic that has made Ukrainian drone units effective against far better equipped formations.
The company also builds two-axis stabilised micro-gimbals in Lithuania to European standards, with dual electro-optical cameras offering up to 40 times zoom. The 180-gram NightScout carries a thermal camera for surveillance work, while the 135-gram SOLO is built for loitering munitions, and three-axis gimbals are due in the first quarter of next year.
Granta is exhibiting at Apex Europe at The Magazine in London on Wednesday and Thursday.

How the most everyday things become perilous under occupation
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:30:00 EEST
21:30:00 KST

"When I dream about going back, I'm scared I might say something in Ukrainian": how everyday things become perilous under occupation
Russian occupying forces make Ukrainians afraid of the simplest things: their language, books and national symbols, and their own beliefs. People living under occupation can be tortured for having a tattoo of the Ukrainian flag, fined for listening to Ukrainian music, and imprisoned for "discrediting the Russian Armed Forces". Driven into a corner by interrogations, searches and harassment, people often have no choice. Nothing must betray their Ukrainian identity or their connection to their pre-war lives in Ukraine.
Things that were once part of everyday life have become fraught with risk, turning their owners into obvious targets for the Russian military. That is why under occupation, Ukrainian history textbooks are buried in the ground, flags are hidden in preserving jars, and books are burned in furnaces.
Here we bring you the stories of three Ukrainian teachers from the occupied territories. The Russians have taken away their homes, but not their identity. These women tell us about the things they have lost and their attempts to find themselves again.
Svitlana: burying
Svitlana picked up the blue-and-yellow flag from the ground. It was stained with oil and still bore tyre tracks from Russian military vehicles.
"They drove over it," she sighs. The flag had flown outside the school where Svitlana had spent her entire life: first as a student, then in her first and only job, and eventually as headteacher. She used to ask the school's star students to raise the flag on the tallest flagpole in the village.
Svitlana tucked the flag under her jacket. She did not yet feel she was holding something that could provoke anger and violence from the Russians. These were the early weeks of the occupation of her village in Luhansk Oblast. She still thought of herself as one who belonged there, on her own land.
"I took it because it felt like something very dear and sacred. Something I had to protect," she says.
Svitlana's school, now packed full of Russian soldiers and reeking of unwashed bodies, was becoming unrecognisable. Russian military vehicles were dug in among the chestnut trees and flowerbeds in the school grounds.
Svitlana hurried home and stuffed the flag into a bottom drawer, covering it with clothes. Why did she hide it? She doesn't know. It didn't occur to her to hide her son's military uniform in the same way.
During the first few weeks of the occupation, Russian soldiers would often go into people's homes in Svitlana's village, but mostly to ask questions rather than conduct searches. They were not yet turning drawers inside out. A month later, uniformed men carrying assault rifles entered every house on Svitlana's street.
Outside her house, before she could even get inside, Svitlana was met with blows and shouts. "You're one cocky headteacher! You took the flag from the school!" Then things went flying out of the chest of drawers: first the top drawer, then the middle one. Her daughter-in-law was screaming and retching with fear. They found the military uniform. They took Svitlana's husband to the school, forced him to call their son, beat him up, and dumped him by the roadside.
After that, Svitlana's daughter-in-law begged her to bury the flag. She kept saying that next time they would all be killed because of it.
The place Svitlana chose for the flag was not in the vegetable garden, but between the house and the cellar. Somehow it seemed safer there. The soil in the village was black as tar, soft and yielding. Vegetables grew there in abundance. But now, instead of the seeds she had sown in that soil for decades, Svitlana was planting a jar that contained a blue-and-yellow flag.
"I hope it's still there," she says today, a note of doubt in her voice. Since she left her home and fled, the house has been damaged by attacks. The school has been hit too. The village is now in the grey zone, an active combat area.
"There is no village anymore," Svitlana was eventually told at a Ukrainian government institution.
"But I want to go back," she says wistfully. "To dig up that flag. I went on a trip for Teachers' Day recently. My colleagues had flags with them. And I thought: why haven't I bought one for myself yet, so I can travel around Ukraine with it? Maybe it's because deep down, I know I already have one?"
Natalia: hiding
"My parents built our house," says Natalia, a teacher of Ukrainian history from Kherson Oblast. "I was little. I watched the house grow before my eyes like a mushroom. I know every stone and every pipe that remains of it."
Natalia taught at a school not far from her home, in a neighbouring town half an hour away. She took great care over her appearance, wearing dresses and heels to work and styling her long hair in soft curls. "After all, a teacher is the face of the school," she explains.
On the first day of the full-scale war, Natalia locked the door of her rented apartment and went back to her village. She wanted to get through the hardest times together with her mother and sister.
Then the Russian occupation began.
"Up until autumn 2022, our little village had been quite far away from the main fighting. People stopped driving because their cars were being seized. The village was quiet and relatively calm, apart from regular raids by Russian soldiers. I realised that someone who taught Ukrainian history might also be of interest to them. So I had to make sure there was nothing in my behaviour, appearance or words that would attract their attention."
So she tied her hair back. She wore an old headscarf and trousers that concealed her figure rather than accentuated it. "I didn't care what my skin looked like, or whether a grey hair had appeared, or a new wrinkle. Under occupation, your goal is to stay alive," Natalia says. "I did my best to look like an ordinary, poorly educated person. You become grey, almost levelled with the ground, cowed into a life of growing vegetables and flowers and cooking. I stopped speaking Ukrainian. No social media posts, no likes, nothing. You don't exist."
Natalia had been doing some research about a soldier she knew who was killed in action in Donbas back in 2014, and had a folder full of material, poems and portraits. She buried it in the garden near the blackberry bushes. She used plenty of plastic wrap, plastic bags and tape: she knew it would all be lying in damp soil. She hoped it wouldn't be there for long.
She kept moving the Ukrainian history textbooks she used with her students further and further away. At first they were in a wardrobe. When the searches began, she hid them near the house so she could get them out for lessons. Then she moved them to the shed. Then to the cellar.
She buried some things further away from the house as her fear steadily grew. Did this new reality surprise her? "Not at all," she says. "This is life under occupation. I'd read about it a lot, and now I was living through it myself."
She left her work chats, and after every lesson she would delete the platform she was using to continue teaching Ukrainian history despite the risk to her life. Now she was doing it secretly, online.
"I worked on the first floor. Only my family knew I was teaching. The desk was by the window, and the window was open because there was no electricity. The sun was the only source of light. You're teaching a lesson and you hear a boom. You count: one, two, three, four… I thought I'd never get rid of that habit. Do you know what I was afraid of? That my students might see me covered in blood."
When the Russians blew up the Kakhovka Hydroelectric Power Plant, Natalia's village began to sink underwater before her eyes. As the water rose, she rushed to retrieve her documents and books from their hiding places. She was certain the flood wouldn't reach the first floor. She and her family fled to another village. When she returned, she carried everything that had survived out into the yard. "I don't know what I was thinking. There were Russian soldiers all over the place, and there I was, drying books outside," she recalls.
Natalia fled the occupation with her elderly mother, her sister, three cats and three dogs. They had neither the strength nor the space to take books.
She continued to teach online at her school from a city in Ukraine's south. She bought new Ukrainian history textbooks, choosing the same ones she had left behind at home. She no longer has to bury them in the ground or carry them down to the cellar. She doesn't even put them on a bookshelf. "For a teacher, they're like spoons in a kitchen," she says, laughing for the first time since our conversation began. "They should always be to hand."
Oleksandra: burning
"You're asking whether I had a bookshelf at home?" says Oleksandra. "I had over a thousand books on my 'shelf'!" Oleksandra, her husband and their 14-year-old daughter used to live in Luhansk Oblast. She taught Ukrainian language and literature at the village school and, like everyone else in the village, had a plot of land and plenty of work to do "on the land".
Oleksandra's home library was meticulously organised, the books arranged in neat rows. She loved late evenings, when the house fell quiet and she could settle down with a book: "I'd sit down intending to read for a couple of minutes, then finish at five in the morning and realise I wasn't going to get any sleep that night."
The Russians seized her village in February 2022, and within a few months they'd turned the school into a Russian one, clearing out everything to do with Ukraine and putting up Russian flags and portraits of Putin. Oleksandra packed the things she'd accumulated over her years of teaching into a box and took them home. She refused to collaborate with the occupying authorities.
A young teacher was arrested in a neighbouring district. Oleksandra heard that he had been accused of being a Nazi and that banned items and books had apparently been found in his possession. What books, you might ask? Well, it turned out to have been ordinary patriotic literature.
Oleksandra went over to her bookcase. There were several dozen Ukrainian books which had suddenly become dangerous for her to possess. She moved them behind the tightly-packed rows of Russian classics, worrying that she might have missed something.
She was right to worry. During the first search, six armed soldiers spread out through the rooms. Two went straight to the bookcase. They leafed through the Russian literature. In another room, Oleksandra's 14-year-old daughter was explaining why Crimea was shown as part of Ukraine on a map in her textbook. The soldiers were looking for flags. They called Oleksandra a Nazi and said there was no way she didn't have something buried somewhere.
It was a warm night. Her daughter was asleep in her bed now. Oleksandra laid several dozen books out in front of the furnace. Something was gnawing away at her inside. She began to cry. Maybe she should hide them after all, she thought. But how?
"Besides, I didn't know where or how they would search. What if they asked, 'What have you been digging up there?' I had doubts. I was afraid. And I didn't want my child worrying that we had something hidden," she recalls.
It was all done between midnight and 4 am, so that no one would see the smoke and the furnace would be cool by morning. They cut things up and fed the pieces to the flames. A camouflage net they hadn't yet managed to deliver to the Ukrainian military. Children's blue-and-yellow flags she had rescued from the school. Clothes and combat boots she'd been given by soldiers in recognition of her years of volunteering. And the books – they went in whole. The furnace burned as it always did, as reliably as ever. There was no smell. Only ashes remained.
Oleksandra has never asked her husband where he scattered them.
"The next time they searched, they rummaged through everything and pulled everything out. It was a good thing I'd burned the books. But I didn't feel any relief, because they could come up with any excuse for another search. One time they said my husband was a grenade launcher operator and they were looking for a grenade launcher. Another time they said he was a tank crewman. Were they hoping to find a tank? I had no idea what they would come up with next.
They said I was a traitor to the motherland and was facing 12 years in prison. Every day I'd wake up and keep looking out of the window until after five in the evening. The attacks weren't as frightening as waiting for them to come back."
Russian soldiers harassed Oleksandra for three months. They would come to search the house and interrogate her once a week, sometimes twice. She lost 13 kg (27 lb) over that period.
Since leaving for Ukraine's west, she has had a recurring dream: she comes back to her house, of which only the walls remain, and searches for her books. "In the dream, I'm scared because I have to speak Russian – God forbid I say anything in Ukrainian – and I know it's still occupied. I wonder whether the books are still there, because there's been snow and rain. But they're in my bookcase… I wake up and can't remember whether I found them."
Oleksandra has promised herself that she will never collect books again. The ones she burned would be impossible to replace anyway. One of the books she treasured most, about the defence of Donetsk Airport, is no longer in print. Others were rare self-published editions. One of the authors, a serviceman, has been killed in action. Oleksandra managed to contact another one on Facebook. He is serving in the military.
Despite the promise she made to herself, whenever her daughter asks to go to a bookshop, Oleksandra never says no. She always buys something. In her new involuntary temporary home, one constant from her old life has remained: reading.
***
What happened to Oleksandra, Natalia and Svitlana is far from unique.
Freedom House's Freedom in the World 2026 report has rated the occupied territories of Ukraine as the least free in the world. With a score of 1 out of 100, Ukrainians living in Russian-occupied territories have fewer political rights and civil liberties than people in Syria, North Korea, Belarus or Turkmenistan.
By comparison, Freedom House rated the part of Ukraine under Kyiv's control as Partly Free, giving it a score of 51 out of 100.
Between February 2022 and January 2024, the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine documented the policy of imposing Russian identity and suppressing expressions of Ukrainian identity in the occupied territories. Russian armed forces have detained people who openly expressed their Ukrainian identity and subjected them to violence.
Teachers have been required to follow the Russian curriculum, use the Russian language, and teach history in a way that justifies Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The report documented the removal from educational institutions of literature deemed "extremist" or "portraying the ideology of Ukrainian nationalism", including comics, textbooks, and literature about the Holodomor The Holodomor was a man-made famine in Soviet Ukraine which lasted from 1932 to 1933 and claimed the lives of millions of Ukrainians .
A report by the same organisation on the human rights situation in Ukraine between June and December 2025 stated that people living under occupation had begun switching to Russian in public spaces when Russian soldiers were nearby. A woman living in occupied Kherson Oblast said that displaying Ukrainian flags or symbols was prohibited. Another woman reported that a Russian soldier had come to her apartment and questioned her about watching a Ukrainian TV channel.
Ordinary objects and everyday actions have become evidence of a crime, forcing people who are trying to survive under occupation to dig graves in which to bury their own past and identity.
Nadiia Shvadchak

The Jaguar Type 01: a £150k gargantuan getaway vehicle utterly useless in the city
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:29:24 UTC
21:29:24 KST

The cutting-edge car du jour, even while very few will ever buy one, is a good index of what the world’s coming to. It’s a dress-for-the-job-you-want principle, on wheels: drive for the world you want to inhabit.
That’s why when Tesla launched the Model X with a bioweapon defence mode (2016!), we should have been much more worried than we were, and it’s why the Jaguar Type 01 Grand Tourer EV has a lot to say.
“A new era,” the heritage carmaker calls it, and it’s not wrong. But having test-driven the era (just with my eyes and imagination, rather than the car itself), I would like to return it to the showroom and choose pretty much any other era.
Its gigantic size alone makes it look as if it wants to wage war on the future. The whole point of the electrification revolution in motoring was that we could wean ourselves off energy profligacy and on to elegant sufficiency.
If you counteract all that with a car too wide (2 metres) and too long (5.2 metres) to fit into any UK car parking space, whatever advances you’ve made with aerodynamics cannot overcome the fact that you are hulking around something that looks more like a tank than a car, the atmospherics underscored by the glassless tailgate and 23-inch wheels.
To unpack that a bit, you can’t see into the back at all, the preference for all the other glass is blackout, and the wheels on a Toyota Hilux, the Chad warlord’s vehicle of choice, are between 16 and 18 inches.
All the aluminium in the world (73% of the car’s makeup) can’t put a dent in the 2.5-plus-tonne weight, and they’ve bust their own balls to reduce the drag coefficient only to arrive at one (0.23) easily bested by any average electric saloon (0.21).
The look it’s going for, according to the literature, is “monolithic”, but it’s a thin line, isn’t it, between an immutable colossus and a menace, so attempts have clearly been made in the design to introduce a note of friendliness.
It comes in peace, the Jaguar 01 GT; you can tell by the rounded nose, and the body design creating the visual illusion of a front-to-back taper. If it were in a cartoon, it would be driven by the heroes not the villains, but they’d be heroes with no domestic life who knew how to handle themselves. They wouldn’t be The Incredibles.
Traditionally, the Jaguar was driven by a guy in his 50s, wanting to signal to the world that he could afford a car that cost roughly half his salary. That’s what the company is now trying to steer away from, preferring buyers who are “rich, urban, very design literate, very technology literate”, according to Rawdon Glover, Jaguar’s MD.
Some texture on that 50-year-old of yesteryear, whose type I knew well: my uncle had a Jaguar. Its paintwork was maroon, its interior a buttery leather, which meant we all knew he was earning a tidy packet, and we weren’t allowed to bring our dog for Christmas in case he scratched it. That, in a nutshell, was the personality type, which – I posit – was bad enough.
Jag Persona #0.1 is different: he doesn’t want your social admiration, he wants you to jump out of your skin and get your children indoors at his approach, which you’ll see before you hear and only fleetingly, as he races from 62mph to 112mph in four seconds.
He wants you to know he has 150 grand in spare change (ticket price is £120,000 but the extras make that unlikely), and “urban” my aunt Fanny, there is no city situation in which this is a useful car. Regular city driving would be unbearable, given its width, and its standout features of power and agility (three engines, one at the front, one on each rear wheel) are best conceived for a getaway vehicle. Considering its gargantuan size, it doesn’t even have much space – only four seats and boot space that a Skoda Octavia would look at and laugh.
And yet, on the plus side, it comes in “London red”, inspired by our mansion blocks and doubledecker buses, our postboxes and room 32 of the National Gallery. These are all different reds, by the way, but then so are red trousers, yet their message is always the same: “I am the kind of person who would wear red trousers.” So if you see one, just think of that person and make them worse, times a thousand.

The latest figures on the ongoing high school protests across France revealed Wednesday that over 1,000 people have been injured since the start of the mobilization, while 30,000 students are unable to attend classes.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray told the National Assembly that 215 students and 88 education staff members have been injured since the protests over learning conditions began in mid-September.
Geffray noted that the vast majority of the student injuries were "due to reckless behavior or mortar fire," according to broadcaster BFMTV.
He also stressed that a "little less than half" of the injured education staff members were principals or deputy principals who were "deliberately targeted" in many cases.
"We have never seen this before," Geffray explained.
According to figures from Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu's office cited by Le Figaro, a total of 715 police officers or gendarmes were also injured.
Geffray further told the National Assembly that 24 high schools were set on fire or vandalized to an extent that they cannot reopen immediately.
“As a result, 30,000 high school students are unable to attend classes in person,” Geffray said, describing it as “enormous harm” to their education.
He added that several hundred other schools were also damaged seriously, with an estimated cost of at least €20-30 million ($22-33 million).
Use of grenades suspended during mobilizations
Meanwhile, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told broadcaster RTL that the police use of stun grenades would be suspended during student mobilizations, notably after a 15-year-old protester's hand was blown off earlier.
“I asked yesterday that these grenades no longer be used as part of the high school students’ movement,” he said.
Nunez also announced that 18 investigations were launched by the IGPN, France’s police oversight body, following acts of violence on the sidelines of the mobilizations.
“These judicial investigations are ongoing and will determine whether or not these actions were proportionate,” he stressed.
While underlining that a police response is needed in the protests, he reiterated that there must be proportionality.
“You do not manage a high school students’ movement in the same way as you manage a movement of adults," Nunez added.
He said President Emmanuel Macron also asked him and Geffray, following a meeting held Tuesday, to show more empathy and provide more explanation regarding their approach.
"The president recalled the need to maintain order and intervene whenever there is serious violence, while asking us to act with the greatest proportionality,” Nunez further noted.
According to the Interior Ministry figures, 6,547 people have been arrested since Sept. 28. 
Classes fully or partially suspended at over 500 schools
The Education Ministry also said classes were fully or partially suspended at 459 schools Wednesday, according to BFMTV.
A total of 891 of the country’s 3,700 high schools had classes “fully or partially suspended, for all reasons combined” on Tuesday, according to the Education Ministry.
The High School Students’ Union and the Student Union called for blockades to continue Wednesday, as well as for new marches Thursday, for an “Act IV” in Paris and other cities.
Mobilizations continued across France on Wednesday, with students gathering and blocking the entrances of several schools across Nice, Paris, and Lyon.
A total of 11 people have been injured in the Lyon region since the start of the day, as 21 educational institutions were affected.

No systemic risk to financial markets: VP Yılmaz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:27:50 UTC
21:27:50 KST

Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz spoke at the parliament on Oct. 7, 2026. (AA Photo)
There is no systemic risk to Türkiye’s financial markets and public funds will not be used to cover losses stemming from the ongoing fund crisis, Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz has said.
Addressing parliament on Oct. 7 on the fund investigation, Yılmaz said 131 funds currently in liquidation account for 4.6 percent of all funds and 7.7 percent of total portfolio value.
“The problem emerged in a limited area,” he said.
Yılmaz said Türkiye’s capital markets remain fundamentally sound and that the liquidation of troubled funds would strengthen rather than weaken the market.
He said the government would protect investors’ rights, ensure the orderly functioning of markets and implement any necessary measures without delay.
“Another fundamental point I would like to emphasize is that Treasury resources will not be used for private losses incurred during this process,” he said.
He noted that investment funds, particularly high-risk hedge funds, are not covered by the state guarantees that apply to parts of the banking system.
He said the liquidation process would be carried out on a fund-by-fund basis, with investors’ claims primarily being met through each fund’s own assets.
“As a principle, investors’ rights will be met through the resources of the relevant fund. In the liquidation process, resources currently held by the funds themselves will be used first,” he said.
Yılmaz added that additional resources would come from the recovery of excessive or unfair gains and from proceeds generated through the sale of assets removed from the system.
“Resources recovered from those who obtained excessive or unjust gains, as well as proceeds from the sale of assets taken out of the system, will also be used,” he said.

Pranas Domšaitis Gallery of the LNMA invites where the summer never ends  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:26:45 UTC
21:26:45 KST

On Thursday, 8 October, at 6:00 PM, the Pranas Domšaitis Gallery of the Lithuanian National Museum of Art (Liepų St. 33) Klaipėda opens Where the Summer Never Ends, an exhibition by American photographer Andy Sweet. Documenting the vivid life of Miami Beach, Sweet captured imagery of his immediate surroundings that powerfully reflects much broader complexities of the American social landscape from the late 1960s through the late 1970s. Exuding summer heat, his photographs capture profound shifts in American society – from the Jewish traditions permeating daily life and the emerging LGBTQ+ community to ongoing racial and ethnic segregation.
Following its 2024 debut at the Radvila Palace Museum of Art of the LNMA, the exhibition arrives in Klaipėda inviting viewers to soak up the warmth of Miami Beach’s sun-drenched views.
‘Audiences in Klaipėda are always enthusiastic about photography exhibitions, so we are delighted to present Andy Sweet’s work in our city for the first time. Living in a port city, no one can remain indifferent to coastal beachscape views,’ says Skaistė Marčienė, Director of the Pranas Domšaitis Gallery.
‘The people immortalized in Sweet’s photography also include Jewish Holocaust survivors from Lithuania – making this exhibition, in a sense, a homecoming. We owe a debt of gratitude to the artist’s family; these photography and video works have now entered the LNMA’s permanent collection and will remain accessible to the future generations. I am delighted that the exhibition arrives in Klaipėda. I believe the views of Miami Beach will take on a new life in our coastal city, reminding their viewers that summer continues regardless of a season,’ the exhibition curator Ugnė Marija Gausmanė presents the event.
The photographer who preserved the ancient colours of Miami Beach
In 1977, after earning his MFA from the University of Colorado, Andy Sweet (1953 – 1982) embarked on a photography career. Together with colleague Gary Monroe, he conceived The Miami Beach Photographic Project. Between 1977 and 1982, Sweet worked daily recording the swiftly changing world of Miami Beach. The town comes back to life in the bright-colour giclée prints made from his analogue photographs, accompanied by a video footage discovered in the artist’s family home in 2021.
In his MFA thesis, he wrote: ‘I want my pictures to reflect truth … that is why I work exclusively in colour. It is not the colours that matter most in each frame – they are only the means to enhance the potential of the media, which already absorbs a lot of reality by itself, to show even more.’
The drive to capture authenticity shines through the artist’s emphatic lens as he turns it at diverse communities of Miami Beach. The daily lives of elderly Jewish residents, together with drag performers, and other local figures come together to create a vivid portrait of a town in the midst of transformation.
An ode to the capital of sun and fun – and to its people
The photographer never distanced himself from his subjects: his images of everyday life speak to universal human desires: the need to belong to a community or simply to feel needed. Among his most striking subjects were elderly Jewish residents who had resettled to Florida’s South Beach from colder places across the United States. At the time South Beach was home to the largest in the country community of the Jewish retirees, including the Holocaust survivors of Eastern Europe and among them, of Lithuania. The scenes of their life, captured on the oceanfront, on city streets, and at local gatherings, evoke the sense of a vibrant ‘American Shtetl’, seamlessly weaving Jewish traditions into the rhythm of local life.
When in 1977, Miami became one of the first American cities to pass anti-discrimination protections to LGBTQ+ community, growing numbers of the community residents started moving to Miami Beach. This particular community contributed significantly to preserving the area’s historic architectural heritage, most notably, its iconic Art Deco buildings.
The exhibition Where the Summer Never Ends will run at the Pranas Domšaitis Gallery through 14 March 2027, inviting viewers to experience the artist’s deep love to his hometown and its people. Exhibition tours and educational activities will offer audiences a deeper look into the stories behind these vivid, colourful frames. For additional information please visit the LNMA website and social media channels.

Reform clears its own officials of breaking party funding laws despite police investigation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:26:34 UTC
21:26:34 KST

Reform UK has cleared two senior officials of breaking laws that ban foreign donations, despite the matter remaining under police investigation.
The party published a 27-page report of an internal inquiry by its legal secretary and general secretary, finding that Dan Jukes, Nigel Farage’s press adviser, and James Orr, its head of policy, had not breached funding rules.
Party sources said they intended to pursue legal action against the undercover reporting group Verbatim, whose footage led to the investigation and was broadcast by Channel 4 News.
Police have been investigating potential offences under electoral law since the broadcast in early September, saying they would widen an existing special inquiry relating to donations made to Reform. Jukes and Orr will remain suspended by the party while the police inquiry continues.
Jukes and Orr were filmed talking about a scheme in which a US donor paid for three polls with favourable narratives for Reform, costing more than £30,000. Donations from overseas sources are not allowed under political funding laws.
Jukes also discussed the idea of the US donor giving £500,000 to Reform through his UK-based son. The men they thought were father and son were undercover reporters.
Farage later met the undercover reporters as would-be donors over lunch in Clacton, and did not object when the idea of the scheme was explained to him. He later said he had not been listening.
In its internal report, Reform said it did not excuse the “foolish” way in which Jukes and Orr discussed donations with an overseas donor. But it said the party had not commissioned the £30,000 polling from the US donor, as Jukes was a contractor rather than a staff member.
Orr was recorded suggesting that the US businessman could pay for opinion polling to help with the party’s campaigns, which would “technically be a donation in kind” but “the reality is we could easily get away with it”.
However, the internal report found that because Reform did not make any payment for the polls or directly arrange for them to be carried out, “the payments made to JL Partners were therefore not donations to Reform UK within the meaning of the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000”.
In relation to discussions about the £500,000, which was never handed over, the report said it found no evidence that Orr or Jukes knowingly entered into or acted in furtherance of an arrangement to facilitate an impermissible donation.
The report said: “Nothing was agreed, no donations were made and no formal position was presented to the party’s finance team, and nothing was accepted. The party’s procedures for checking the identity of a donor and the source of funds were never engaged, because nothing reached them.”
Orr had also told the undercover reporter: “If there’s a non-trivial chance of you guys directly giving a … five or six-figure sum, then we could do a lunch with Nigel.” The report said “the words used were unwise” but concluded that “they were not a price”.
It also dismissed an incident in which Jukes discussed other purported foreign donors who had given money through their children, which would be against the rules. Jukes insisted “he simply invented circumstances for the purposes of not derailing the conversation” and that it was “foolish, loose talk” without foundation.
The investigation “found no basis for the suggestion that any supporter of the party has given in the way described”. As a result of the episode, which overshadowed Reform’s conference in early September, the party said it would bring in rules that the party treasurer’s office must be informed in writing of proposed donations and that no meetings with proposed donors should take place until background checks had been carried out.
A Reform spokesperson said: “Following the allegations raised by Verbatim Investigations and Channel 4 on 3 September, Reform UK commissioned a comprehensive internal investigation.
“The investigation examined all relevant evidence, including witness interviews, documentary records and electronic communications.
“Having concluded the review, the investigation found no evidence that any laws were broken. Reform UK takes its obligations on governance and conduct extremely seriously.
“We consider that the production company – Verbatim – acted unlawfully and will be taking the appropriate legal action in due course.”
Jukes told the Telegraph, which first reported the findings of the internal investigation: “I welcome the finding of this investigation, which crucially has found I did not break the law, as I have maintained from the outset.
“I am also considering all appropriate legal remedies in relation to any false and damaging statements made about me.
“For now, I will continue to take a break from politics to pursue other opportunities.”
A spokesperson for Verbatim said: “We note that this report is an internal one authored by Reform’s own barrister and general secretary, and that a police investigation remains ongoing. We are confident in our journalism, which speaks for itself.”

====================================================================================================

Interlaken vs Innsbruck: How Europe’s adventure travel hotspots compare for a winter holiday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:25:44 UTC
21:25:44 KST

These Alpine adventure destinations offers snow-covered slopes, unique hotels and local delicacies. But between Interlaken and Innsbruck, where should you choose to travel this winter?
Winter in Europe means time for outdoor adventures – often on the slopes. Few destinations offer quite the same combination of skiing, snowboarding, chilly winter hikes and other activities like in the continent’s Alpine resorts.
In central Switzerland, between Lake Thun and Lake Brienz, Interlaken sits in the heart of the Bernese Oberland region of the Swiss Alps. Despite the lower temperatures, the year-round resort surprisingly offers accessible hikes and kayak routes during the colder season.
While around 370 kilometres to the east, Innsbruck makes an equally strong claim for holidaymakers’ attention. The capital of Austria’s Tyrol state, it’s also regarded as the “capital of the Alps”, though Grenoble in France is another contender for that title.
So, with the winter upon us, where will you choose for your next adventure getaway?
Both Interlaken and Innsbruck share an Alpine setting and a serious appetite for outdoor pursuits, but each offers adventure travellers surprisingly different experiences – and not just skiing.
Interlaken, Switzerland
Interlaken is replete with lakes, mountain villages and the Bernese Alps with glaciers.
The winter landscape, especially the snowparks, broad pistes and vast downhill runs, can be explored with a pair of skis. And the Interlaken Holiday Region has five areas dedicated to skiing and snowboarding: Beatenberg-Niederhorn, Brienz-Axalp, Diemtigtal, Habkern, and Aeschi-Aeschiried.
The latter two are especially popular during very snowy winters. In Habkern, a single ski lift connects to its four pistes – each of varying difficulty. While in Aeschi-Aeschiried, skiing and snowboarding activities overlook Lake Thun and the Niesen peak.
Another way to enjoy the region’s panoramas is on two wheels through Interlaken’s trails – even during the winter.
The town’s bike-friendly infrastructure makes leisurely rides a breeze. Although snow and ice can make outdoor cycling a challenge in winter, cyclists need not fret. “Winterlaken” by Yellow Velo offers an easygoing two-hour e-bike tour guided by a professional to Interlaken’s old town, 13th-century castle ruins and the traditional town of Bönigen.
Another way to make tracks in the Interlaken snow is through the town’s extensive network of hiking routes – the region features 220 kilometres of winter trails. Come rain or snow, the trails are maintained to still be hikable during the winter. The circular Aeschi hike is always in view of the Niesen, Switzerland’s highest pyramid-shaped peak.
On neighbouring Lake Brienz, just east of Interlaken, it’s also possible to kayak and surf ski across its turquoise waters during winter. Surrounded by snowy peaks and equipped with a dry warm suit, lake-cruisers can go on a half-day tour through the calm waters in the heart of the Bernese Oberland.
Interlaken’s accommodation offerings range from properties perched thousands of metres above sea level, wellness hotels, as well as various camp sites where visitors can spend their nights in camper cans, caravans, mobile homes, tents or bungalows.
Within Switzerland, the region receives train connections every 30 minutes to and from major towns like Bern, Zürich, Geneva and Basel. It is also part of the country’s national road network, making car travel easy, too.
While Interlaken doesn’t have its own airport, the nearest is around 50 kilometres away in Bern or 135 kilometres away in Zürich.
Innsbruck, Austria
Winter in Innsbruck means speedy toboggan runs amid mountain landscapes, groomed slopes and ski tours through snow-covered Alpine valleys.
Taking its name from the River Inn, the Austrian city is home to Tyrol’s highest toboggan run. Situated in the Kühtai ski resort, and at an altitude of 2,127 metres above sea level, this 2,020m-long route takes roughly 45 minutes to ascend before the swift descent starts. When the sun goes down, the tobogganing doesn’t have to end as the run is floodlit well into the night.
Innsbruck is also home to the Bergisel Ski Jump, a 50m-high sports facility and landmark designed by Iraqi-British architect Zaha Hadid as part of a remodelling project.
While popular among ski-jump enthusiasts, visitors can also go to take in the sights from the viewing terrace, and also take in the scenery while dining at Bergisel Sky, a floor-to-ceiling glass-windowed restaurant.
For the skilled skier, almost 40 cross-country trails offer yet another way to explore the Innsbruck landscape. At the cross-country ski centre in Rinn, the Panoramaloipe trail winds through fields towards Judenstein, which is 900 metres above sea level. The free to ski trail also includes a diagonal and skating track.
After working up an appetite, skiers and tobogganers can head to the Graf Ferdinand Haus for a place to indulge in the “hot stone” dining concept and unwind over meat or cheese fondue (perhaps both?) or Graf Ferdinand's spare ribs. The mountain hut is open from December to April and also features a sun terrace – ideal for views of the surrounding mountains.
The region also offers an array of unique places to stay – from farmers renting out apartments for visitors to experience Tyrolean country life up close to mountain lodgings at various altitudes with spectacular views.
Unlike its Swiss counterpart, Innsbruck has its own airport, served by around 50 airlines. Lufthansa, Icelandair, British Airways, easyJet and Finnair are among the carriers operating flights to and from the city.
While on ground, Innsbruck has a dedicated coach terminal. Austrian, German, Italian and Swiss coaches, as well as trains, are also connected to the city's main train station. Train connections from Vienna run 20 times a day, twice daily from Venice and once daily from Frankfurt.

21:25:38 KST

TOKYO, October 7. /TASS/. High energy prices will likely persist for some time, even if the war involving the US, Israel, and Iran ends in the near future, International Monetary Fund (IMF) Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned.
"In addition, natural gas supply from the Gulf remains severely impaired, reflecting more-limited LNG transport options for as long as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains threatened," Georgieva said.
"This has uneven impacts across the world, with Asia and Europe particularly hard-hit. And, to quote from Game of Thrones, winter is coming. Price pressures may build further as countries replenish reserves and demand rises with the approach of the Northern hemisphere cold season."
"Even if the war in the Gulf were to end soon, the problem of high energy prices would likely persist for some time," the IMF chief added. "Brent futures, for example, now predict high oil prices through 2027. Higher energy prices are pushing up inflation, policy rates, and benchmark yield curves."
Georgieva noted that the average price per barrel of oil has remained above $100 for an extended period. According to her, the high cost of diesel fuel and other petroleum products is "due to a global shortfall in refining capacity."

Tallinn Airport sets record for September, but winter traffic expected to fall

2026-10-07

21:25:00 KST

Tallinn Airport sets record for September, but winter traffic expected to fall
Tallinn Airport reported it handled nearly 356,000 passengers in September, up 13 percent on the same month last year — the busiest September in the airport's history.
In the first nine months of the year, the airport reported serving a total of 2.89 million passengers, up 12 percent on the same period last year.
Despite the record, the airport expects a decline in numbers over the winter.
Tallinn Airport spokesperson Aet Härmaorg told ERR the past 12 months have all been records on the month, adding the "all-time record was exceeded in four months: May, June, July and August 2026."
Scheduled flights operated from Tallinn to 41 destinations in September. Passenger growth was driven primarily by no-frills carrier Wizz Air, which has expanded significantly in Tallinn over the past year.
In September, the airline carried 16 percent of all Tallinn Airport passengers and offered connections to nine destinations. airBaltic remained the airport's largest airline, with a market share of 27 percent. In total, 22 airlines operated scheduled and charter flights from Tallinn to more than 50 destinations during the month.
Scheduled flights accounted for 90 percent of passengers, while charter flights accounted for 10 percent. Antalya, Turkey, was the main charter destination, with holiday destinations in Greece and Montenegro also proving popular.
While winter is the off-season, there is a winter travel season, starting September, to destinations in Egypt.
Warsaw was the most popular direct destination for scheduled flights in September, followed by Helsinki, Riga, Stockholm and Frankfurt.
The number of aircraft movements also rose, by 5 percent compared with September last year. There were 4,031 landings and take-offs in total, averaging 134 aircraft movements per day.
Eero Pärgmäe, commercial director at Tallinn Airport, said the passenger records show the summer schedule was exceptionally dense. "The growth that Wizz Air started at the end of last year is still carrying us," Pärgmäe told ERR.
Nonetheless, some developments will lead to a fall in numbers over winter. "airBaltic has said it is cutting its schedule due to the restructuring it is currently carrying out. And the second thing is that, since the price of aviation fuel remains exceptionally high, most carriers have said that the high fuel price is hurting them and they will be scaling back their schedules in winter," Pärgmäe went on.
"If we look at next year, we are moving toward last year's level or even a little below," he added.
Passenger numbers also rose at Estonia's regional airports, which fall under the Tallinn Airport umbrella. Together, they served 9,078 passengers in September, compared with 8,191 in September last year. Tartu Airport took in 4,847 passengers, Kuressaare Airport 3,008 and Kärdla Airport 1,111. Pärnu Airport served 104 passengers and Ruhnu Airfield eight.
Tallinn Airport also says it expects higher passenger numbers during the busy school holiday travel period, October 21-November 4. For this reason the airport recommends arriving at the terminal at least two hours before departure time, as check-in, security screening and passport control can take longer than usual. Passengers arriving by car should allow extra time to find a parking space too.

Ukraine's General Staff reports damage to Samara oil station and Astrakhan gas processing plant supplying Russian forces
The General Staff has reported that the Samara oil pipeline control station and Astrakhan gas processing plant, which help meet the needs of the Russian Armed Forces, sustained extensive damage in strikes.
Source: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on Telegram
Quote: "As a result of the 2 October strike on the Samara oil pipeline control station in Prosvet, Russia's Samara Oblast, damage to 11 RVS-20,000 tanks, three RVSPK-50,000 tanks, a section of pipelines and an automated oil product loading station has been confirmed…
As a result of the 4 October strike on the Astrakhan gas processing plant in Astrakhan, Russia's Astrakhan Oblast, damage to elements of two gas treatment units, U-172 and U-272, as well as the secondary distillation unit U-1731, has been confirmed."
Details: The General Staff said both facilities targeted in the strikes contribute to meeting the needs of the Russian Armed Forces.
The Samara oil pipeline control station is a major hub for receiving, storing and blending oil. It is where Urals crude, which accounts for up to 50% of Russia's total oil exports, is produced.
The Astrakhan gas processing plant is one of the world's largest producers of gas sulphur, which is used to manufacture explosives and gunpowder. The facility has a designed capacity to process up to 12 billion cubic metres of formation gas per year and produces up to 3.5 million tonnes of technical sulphur annually, accounting for about 50% of Russia's total production.
Background: On 2 October, Ukraine's defence forces struck oil facilities in Russia's Samara and Volgograd oblasts, causing large fires.

F-1: Singapore Grand Prix — sprint history, race schedule
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:24:33 EEST
21:24:33 KST

F-1: Singapore Grand Prix — sprint history, race schedule
Kyiv • UNN
The Singapore Grand Prix will take place on October 9–11 in a new sprint format at the grueling Marina Bay circuit.
This weekend, from October 9 to 11, the 2026 Singapore Grand Prix will take place — the most grueling and hottest round of the Formula 1 season, which will be held in a sprint weekend format for the first time in history. Spectators can look forward to three days of uncompromising racing on the iconic Marina Bay circuit, where drivers lose up to three kilograms over the race distance, UNN reports.
Details
The first night race in F1 history will become a sprint weekend in 2026 — Marina Bay under the floodlights, with the opportunity to score points throughout all three days.
The Singapore race is the most physically demanding of the entire year: humidity exceeds 90%, temperatures rise above 50 °C, and there are almost two hours of uninterrupted concentration without a single break. The combination of the sprint format and a circuit where the appearance of the safety car is practically guaranteed makes this weekend one of the most strategically unpredictable of the entire season.
The Marina Bay circuit
"Marina Bay" is F1's first night race and the most physically demanding one. The circuit's defining features are narrow street corridors, numerous 90-degree corners, and constant braking and acceleration. Drivers complete 62 laps in hot and humid conditions under artificial lighting, making Singapore one of the most physically exhausting races of the season.
Drivers lose up to three kilograms over the race distance and describe the final 20 laps as a test of sheer willpower. As a result of the circuit's redesign in 2023, four corners along the waterfront were removed, but 19 remained, most of them merciless 90-degree street corners.
The circuit runs counterclockwise. Overtaking is formally possible at three corners — 1, 7 and 14 — but in practice, fighting for position in Singapore is extremely difficult, making a good qualifying result, a strong start and a successful strategy crucial.
The speed at the slowest corner is 75 km/h, while at the fastest it is 275 km/h. The probability of a safety car appearance is 100%, and teams will take this factor into account when developing their strategies.
The lap record at the Singapore circuit belongs to Lewis Hamilton — 1:33.808 (2025).
History of the Singapore sprint
The 2008 Singapore Grand Prix became the first night race in the history of the World Championship, and its inaugural running went down in history for all the wrong reasons. On September 28, 2008, Flavio Briatore ordered Nelson Piquet to crash into a wall so that Fernando Alonso would have the ideal strategy and be able to win the race.
At the 2008 Singapore Grand Prix, Fernando Alonso started only 15th after problems in qualifying and made an unusually early pit stop. Soon afterward, his teammate Nelson Piquet Jr. deliberately crashed the Renault, bringing out the safety car at precisely the moment that perfectly played into Alonso's strategy. As a result, the Spaniard surged through the field and won the first night race in F1 history.
For almost a year, everything looked like nothing more than a strange coincidence. But after being released by Renault, Piquet revealed that the crash had been planned. The investigation established that Flavio Briatore, technical director Pat Symonds and Piquet had conspired to arrange an intentional crash to help Alonso.
The consequences were serious: Briatore received an indefinite ban, Symonds a five-year ban, Renault a suspended two-year disqualification, while Piquet avoided punishment in exchange for cooperating with the investigation.
Singapore is famous for the fact that as soon as the winner takes the checkered flag, fireworks are launched. They fill the city's skyline and create an exceptionally spectacular celebration that not only looks fantastic on television but also adds a special flair to the spectacle.
The winners emerge from their cars against a backdrop of bright, saturated colors exploding across the night sky behind them. This has become such an important event for the race organizers that there are even fans who film the spectacle as a separate event.
Fireworks are launched both beside the circuit and over the water in Marina Bay, and similar post-race fireworks displays have since become a common feature at several other night races, including those in Bahrain, Abu Dhabi and Las Vegas.
Race format
The 2026 sprint format is an exciting stress test: the physical demands equivalent to two races packed into one weekend at the most demanding circuit of the season. Safety cars appeared in the vast majority of races in Singapore, so strategy teams view a stoppage as an inevitability to be planned for, rather than an opportunity. Under the floodlights, the cars run in cooler evening air than during a daytime race, but the humidity never lets up.
Ahead of the event, Andrea Kimi Antonelli (Mercedes) leads the drivers’ standings with 302 points. George Russell (Mercedes) is second with 236 points. At the same time, Mercedes confirmed that Russell will start from the grid due to a power-unit replacement.
If Andrea Kimi Antonelli has a clean weekend and finishes around the top three in both racing sessions, his lead over Russell could increase to nearly 100 points with six rounds remaining in the season.
The main question in the drivers’ standings is who will finish the season in second place. As noted, Russell currently holds that position, but a number of drivers are breathing down his neck, including Ferrari racers Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton, reigning world champion Lando Norris of McLaren, and Max Verstappen, who secured Red Bull’s first win of the season in Malaysia.
Interestingly, Verstappen has never won in Singapore, and throughout the event’s history he has led on this circuit for only three laps.
Schedule:
-  Friday, October 9: 11:30–12:30 — first practice, 15:30–16:14 — sprint qualifying; 
-  Saturday, October 10: 12:00–13:00 — sprint, 16:00–17:00 — qualifying.  
It should be noted that the race itself will take place at 20:00 local time (15:00 Kyiv time) on Sunday, October 11. First and foremost, this late time is intended to allow it to be broadcast during prime time in Europe, while it also offers the additional benefit of somewhat cooler conditions on the track.
The Setanta Sports Ukraine+ television channel will broadcast live the qualifying session, sprint, and the Singapore Grand Prix race itself in Ukraine.
