What to use to shoot down jet-powered drones: experts explain how Ukraine is adapting weapons to new threats
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:24:23 EEST
21:24:23 KST

What to use to shoot down jet-powered drones: experts explain how Ukraine is adapting weapons to new threats
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainian defense companies are increasingly adapting weapons that have already been developed to new tasks instead of developing systems from scratch. Experts explained why the speed of such modifications is critical in the war against Russia.
Ukrainian defense companies operate in a low-profile mode and are in no hurry to say what weapons and modifications they are developing. New solutions often become known only at the testing or deployment stage. One such project could be a new configuration of the FP-1/FP-2, which Quantum WIY Industries presented as part of the cooperation between Quantum Systems and Fire Point. What this could offer Ukraine and why the ability to quickly modify existing weapons is critical in the technological race with russia was examined by UNN.
Details
Most Ukrainian defense companies operate under an extremely high level of secrecy. On the one hand, this is connected with the need not to provide information to the enemy so that it does not have time to develop countermeasures… Therefore, when information about a development that had never previously been publicly announced suddenly appears, this does not mean that it literally emerged yesterday. Companies often work in parallel on a large number of different projects, some of which never reach serial production
Concept of a possible FP-1/FP-2 modification with eight SPYS interceptor drones. Image taken from the Drone Wars X account.
In the case of the FP-1/FP-2 modification, the concept involves placing four SPYS interceptor drones under each wing of the unmanned aerial vehicle—eight in total. The main advantage of this configuration is the ability to launch the interceptors from the air.
Under the concept, the FP-1/FP-2 could deliver the SPYS drones to the required area and altitude without using up the interceptors’ own resources flying from a ground launch point. Aviation expert Valeriy Romanenko explains that this approach would expand the area in which the interceptors can be used.
As for the concept under which the FP-1 and FP-2 could serve as carriers for interceptor drones and launch up to eight interceptors against jet-powered drones, it is generally interesting. Why? First, because it sharply increases the operational range of such drones. They do not need to expend fuel climbing and flying over a fairly long distance. Essentially, the airborne platform lifts them to a considerable altitude
Interception of the "Geran-5"
It should be noted that during the presentation of the SPYS interceptor in July, WIY Drones stated that it was capable of hitting targets moving at speeds of up to 600 km/h. To this end, the company worked, among other things, on a head-on interception algorithm. In September, the first confirmed use of SPYS against the Russian jet-powered strike drone "Geran-5" emerged.
Interception of the Russian jet-powered UAV "Geran-5" by a SPYS drone. Video: WIY Drones.
This Russian jet-powered UAV has become a new threat to Ukrainian cities: it is significantly faster than earlier modifications of the "Geran," making it more difficult to intercept. The "Geran-5" has a tubular fuselage and, in terms of its characteristics, already more closely resembles a cheap cruise missile than a classic long-range drone, said Fabian Hoffmann, a senior research fellow at the Norwegian Defence Research Establishment.
As a senior engineer at one of the defense companies told The Kyiv Independent on condition of anonymity, the "Geran-5" flies approximately 150 km/h faster than the jet-powered "Geran-4." This also changes the very logic of interception: instead of chasing the target from behind, the interceptor must be brought toward it head-on, which significantly complicates the task.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, the "Geran-5" can carry a warhead weighing approximately 90 kg. The Chinese turbojet engine for such a drone is estimated to cost approximately $40,000, while the entire aircraft costs about $115,000. By comparison, older piston-powered modifications could cost around $30,000.
At the same time, Russia is rapidly scaling up its use of jet-powered drones. Yurii Ihnat, head of the Communications Department of the Air Force Command, notes that on some days, jet-powered drones may account for up to two-thirds of all drones launched by Russia. Production volumes are also growing—the enemy is already capable of producing around 3,000 Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones per month.
The problem for Ukraine lies in the difficulty of intercepting them. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine is currently shooting down around 57% of jet-powered attack drones, calling this figure “significantly lower than necessary.” That is why finding new means of countering such targets is now becoming one of the key tasks for Ukraine’s defense industry.
“We are already seeing information that at least five manufacturers have proposed their solutions for countering jet-powered attack drones. At least 50 more Ukrainian companies are developing solutions to counter such targets. But if we are talking specifically about mass deployment, we will probably not see it any earlier than another three to four months from now. After the development stage, time is needed to scale up production, train personnel and, among other things, select appropriate tactics for their use,”
However, even after effective countermeasures against jet-powered drones emerge, the technological race will not stop: Ukraine will find a way to shoot them down, while Russia, in response, will try to improve its weapons once again.
“This means that, likewise, once interceptors have been developed and the percentage of jet-powered drones shot down reaches approximately 90–95%, we will see the enemy very quickly try to improve its solution. We are talking about several months. We will see the next stage in terms of speed. In other words, it will no longer be 400–650 km/h, but probably 750–800, perhaps even 900 km/h, which is, in principle, comparable to the speed of conventional cruise missiles,”
In fact, this concerns the ongoing evolution of systems that have already been created: a platform initially developed for one task can perform new functions as the adversary changes. In conditions where new means of attack and countermeasures against them emerge at intervals of several months, the ability to rapidly modernize existing weapons is a key condition for not losing the technological race to the enemy.
“I believe that Fire Point is demonstrating a very sound approach in this case—not simply creating a separate drone for each task, but using existing platforms and seeking new ways to employ them. This makes it possible to adapt more quickly to changes in the battlefield situation,”

EU agrees to sanction over 1,600 people and entities linked to Russia's war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:23:12 UTC
21:23:12 KST

The EU will soon add over 1,600 names, including 77 lawmakers who stood for election in the occupied territories of Ukraine, to its Russia sanctions. The decision comes amid an unsettling rise in hybrid attacks.
The European Union has agreed the single largest expansion of its sanctions list against Russia, adding 1,646 names in one go.
The deal, sealed on Wednesday by ambassadors in Brussels, covers 743 individuals and 826 entities accused of supporting Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Separately, it targets 77 lawmakers who stood in the Russian-occupied territories of Ukraine for the widely discredited State Duma election in September.
Ambassadors wrapped up the agreement after several weeks of deliberations and legal scrubbing, which was particularly intensive given the sheer number of names.
It will be formally approved on Monday when foreign ministers gather in Luxembourg. The targeted people and entities will then be made public.
Sanctions entail a travel ban, an asset freeze and a prohibition on providing funding.
Member states were keen to close the agreement to portray a united front amid a rapid succession of hybrid attacks, some attributed to Russia. Work has already begun on new listings in response to the drone incident at the Leipzig airport in Germany.
Another reason to project unity is last month's contentious decision to remove two high-profile oligarchs, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, from the blacklist.
Usmanov's removal, at France's request, was tied to a prisoner release with Azerbaijan brokered by the Turkic states, which have long lobbied in the billionaire's favour. One French citizen has been released while a second remains in prison.
In exchange for the painful concession, the EU extended the sanctions list for an unprecedented three years. In total, the blacklist will soon cover almost 4,650 names.
Earlier this week, High Representative Kaja Kallas celebrated the three-year renewal but admitted it is unlikely that Usmanov and Fridman will be included again.
"Countries are free to put forward names that should be included in the sanctions list. But in the end, it is up to the member states to decide," Kallas said.
"And I do not see this on these two persons happening any time soon."
Brussels is still grappling with the aftermath of the Usmanov saga and the precedent it might have set for the common foreign policy, which relies on unanimity.
As the bloc prepares to admit new members, the European Commission has proposed using the so-called passerelle clause to move from unanimity to qualified majority voting on issues such as sanctions, thereby avoiding the multiplication of vetoes.
But the clause creates a textbook Catch-22: it requires unanimity to end unanimity.

Kremlin responds to French ballistic missile launch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:22:54 UTC
21:22:54 KST

Kremlin responds to French ballistic missile launch
Russia views France’s nuclear-capable missile launch as a “loud and clear message” and will take “all necessary measures” to protect itself, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said.
The French military test-fired a submarine-launched M51.3 ballistic missile on Tuesday, in an exercise in the Atlantic Ocean watched by French President Emmanuel Macron. The weapon, a new variant of France’s 16-year-old M51 missile family, was launched without a warhead and splashed down in the North Atlantic, “hundreds of kilometres from any coastline,” according to the French military.
In a video message, Macron described the test as “a new demonstration of the credibility of our deterrence,” and “a clear message… for wherever it must be received.”
Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Peskov said: “Problems should be resolved through dialogue, not demonstrative missile launches.”
“Europe has become obsessed with plans to militarize the European Union,” he continued. “This is bad because they are building their defense and security identity on confrontation with the Russian Federation. This is a dead end. As history has shown, this leads to nothing good.”
“Against the backdrop of such aggressive actions and such plans, Russia is on alert,” Peskov added. “We are taking all necessary measures to ensure our national security at the strategic level.”
Outside the US, France possesses NATO’s only independent nuclear arsenal, which Macron is currently modernizing and expanding. France plans to spend €7.4 billion ($8.3 billion) on nuclear deterrence in 2026, while its updated military program adds €36 billion to overall defense spending through 2030. Much of this money will be spent on multi-year submarine, missile, and warhead contracts, but a substantial sum will go toward Paris’ controversial “forward deterrence scheme.”
Under this scheme, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, Germany, Greece, the Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Sweden, and the UK will potentially host French nuclear weapons on a temporary basis and take part in French nuclear exercises.
Russia, which possesses the world’s largest nuclear arsenal, cannot view the deployment of atomic weapons on its borders “as anything other than a step toward escalating tensions,” Peskov said on Tuesday. Peskov was responding to the Lithuanian parliament’s vote to remove a constitutional ban on hosting nuclear weapons on its soil. Although Lithuania has not signed on to France’s “forward deterrence” plan, Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas has expressed interest in hosting American nukes in Lithuania.

Three years of genocide: How Israel destroyed education in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:19:40 UTC
21:19:40 KST

- More than 20,000 students have been killed since October 2023
- Nearly 98% of Gaza’s school buildings have been damaged, according to UNICEF
- 700,000 children have missed nearly three years of formal, in-person schooling
Even in war, education remains a fundamental right for every child.
Yet three years into Israel’s genocide in Gaza, thousands of school-age children have been killed along with hundreds of education workers, while tens of thousands more have been deprived of regular schooling.
Despite a partial resumption of learning for the academic year that began Sept. 19, approximately 200,000 children in Gaza remained without access to structured education, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).
The scale of the devastation is also evident in the destruction of Gaza’s schools: 98% of school buildings have sustained damage, according to UNICEF.
More than 93% require major rehabilitation or full reconstruction, while approximately 81% were directly hit, it said.
According to figures from Gaza’s media office, 165 educational institutions were completely destroyed, while 392 were damaged as of April.
An August assessment by Save the Children found that 86% of kindergartens it surveyed had been destroyed, damaged or were inaccessible because they were located behind the Israeli military-controlled “yellow line.”
The destruction and disruption have kept hundreds of thousands of children out of classrooms.  
Some 700,000 children aged 4-17 missed formal, in-person schooling for almost three consecutive academic years, UNICEF reported.
By September, approximately 495,000 preschool and school-aged children were enrolled in UN- and partner-supported learning spaces. Another 70,000 reportedly attended community-led and private spaces.
Even with those efforts, 200,000 children still lacked access to any structured learning, according to the UN. 
Deaths and injuries
More than 20,000 students have been killed since October 2023, according to a Gaza Government Media Office report. To put that toll in perspective, attending one funeral every day for 20,000 deaths would take nearly 55 years.
Palestinian Education Ministry figures recorded 1,379 university students killed and 3,017 wounded. 
In the same period, 830 teachers and 194 university professors and academics were killed, the report further said. 
The ministry’s broader June tally recorded 802 school staff killed and 3,291 injured, alongside 246 university staff killed and more than 1,493 injured. 
Destruction of schools and universities
A UNESCO-backed assessment published in November 2025 examined 21 higher education institutions across 38 campuses.
22 campuses were completely destroyed and 14 damaged, affecting 95% of campuses assessed. 195 of 206 buildings assessed were destroyed or severely damaged and non-operational.  
620 specialised laboratories and facilities were destroyed or severely damaged and unable to operate.  
Infrastructure damage was estimated at $373.25 million. School buildings continue to house displaced families, limiting the space available for teaching. OCHA documented two UN schools serving as shelters in Al Bureij in September.  
Financial losses and recovery challenges
Preliminary estimates attributed to Gaza’s Government Media Office put direct education sector losses at approximately $4 billion.
The Education Cluster had received only 13% of the $170.8 million requested under the 2026 occupied Palestinian territory Flash Appeal, OCHA reported in September. The appeal covers Gaza and the West Bank.
Teacher shortages, disrupted pay, insufficient classrooms and supplies, rubble and explosive hazards continue to hinder learning.  
UNICEF warns that prolonged disruption is eroding literacy and numeracy skills, while trauma and economic pressure increase the risks of permanent dropout, child labour and early marriage.  
Almost all of Gaza’s 1.2 million children need mental health and psychosocial support, according to the agency.
Since Oct. 8, 2023, Israel’s genocidal war on the Gaza Strip has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others, while around 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure has been destroyed.

Scientists identify ancient Egyptian crocodile whose skull is missing its nose like the Sphinx
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:18:48 UTC
21:18:48 KST

A skull found nearly a century ago has helped Egyptian and European researchers revise part of the crocodile family tree, shedding light on the Mediterranean's prehistoric wildlife and revealing an unexpected connection to the Great Sphinx.
Scientists have identified a new crocodile genus from a 45-million-year-old Egyptian fossil after using CT scans to re-examine a skull recovered nearly a century ago.
The fossil comes from the Mokattam Formation, the same limestone formation from which the Great Sphinx was carved. Like the monument, the skull is missing the tip of its snout.
Researchers from Egypt, the UK, Sweden and Germany have named the animal Herugavialis cairensis. The findings were published in Royal Society Open Science.
The animal was first described in 1927 as Tomistoma cairense, placing it in the same genus as the living false gharial, which has a long, narrow snout.
But the new examination revealed differences in the skull's structure and the animal's evolutionary relationships. Among its distinctive features were raised, projecting eye sockets.
Those differences prompted the researchers to place the species in a separate genus, changing a classification that had stood for almost a century.
Paul Burke of the Swedish Museum of Natural History led the study, co-led by Philip Mannion of University College London.
Mannion said in a statement that the resemblance between the fossil's missing snout tip and the Sphinx's absent nose helped inspire the name, which honours the Egyptian god Heru.
About 45 million years ago, much of the region lay beneath shallow seas. Herugavialis lived alongside at least two other species of long-snouted crocodiles.
The animal belonged to a group whose only surviving members are the Indian gharial and false gharial. Fossils show that their relatives once had a far wider distribution, with more than 40 species recognised.
The researchers suggest that cooling and falling sea levels reduced suitable habitats around the Mediterranean, while later warming may have allowed their diversity to recover.
Studying more fossils could help explain how these ancient crocodiles spread around the Mediterranean and why they later disappeared from the region.

Who will govern Gaza? The battle over its post-war future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:14:51 UTC
21:14:51 KST

Breadcrumb
Who will govern Gaza? The battle over its post-war future
Khan Younis, Gaza Strip - A year after a US-brokered ceasefire halted Israel’s full-scale war on Gaza, the Palestinian technocrats appointed to govern the territory remain in Cairo, waiting for Israel to allow them to enter.
Palestinian analysts say the delay is a symptom of a deeper problem over Gaza’s future, with those chosen to govern the territory still unable to enter, while Israel continues to control the conditions for its governance and reconstruction.
The National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, chaired by Ali Shaath, a civil engineer and former deputy minister in the Palestinian Authority (PA), was formed in January under UN Security Council Resolution 2803.
It was endorsed by US President Donald Trump's 20-point plan and authorised a Trump-led Board of Peace to oversee Gaza's transition until the end of 2027.
Hamas dissolved its governing body in July to make way for the committee, but Israel has still kept it out. Israeli forces, which were to hold 53 per cent of Gaza behind the so-called yellow line under the ceasefire's first phase, now control around two-thirds of the territory.
Mohammed Daraghmeh Abu Allan, a researcher on Israeli affairs, argues that Israel has framed its demands, from disarmament to the destruction of the last Hamas tunnel, “in terms that can never be shown to be met,” allowing it to hold a long-term buffer zone and defend Israeli communities from inside Gaza.
"Israel's acceptance of the Gaza administration committee is conditional on guaranteeing the Israeli military's freedom of action across the entire Gaza Strip, including assassinations and thwarting any immediate threat," he told The New Arab.
"These are the very reasons Israel uses to reject any real solution in Gaza."
A Palestinian committee kept out
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected Trump’s plan in August, saying Israel would not withdraw until Hamas was fully disarmed.
Abu Allan sees Hamas's decision as an attempt to strip Israel of its main argument for keeping the committee out. On the other side, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar dismissed it as a ploy to copy Hezbollah's arrangement in Lebanon.
Meanwhile, the Board of Peace said it would judge Hamas by its actions, insisting on "one authority, one law, and one weapon".
Writer and political analyst Iyad al-Qarra expects the status quo, with Israel holding 70 per cent of the Strip and the committee stuck outside it, to last at least until the end of the year and until the shape of Israel's next government is clear.
“Hamas deserves credit for stepping back from government, but Shaath’s committee has done very little. They’ve spent months talking without actually getting anything done,” he told The New Arab.
Abu Allan is harsher still, describing the Board of Peace as “aligned with Israel's goals,” given its failure to take practical steps in Gaza since the ceasefire and its silence over what he calls Israeli crimes, assassinations, and the siege.
The committee, he says, is "nothing more than an amorphous body with no real existence, which is why Israel may accept dealing with them as governing bodies in Gaza".
The Palestinian Authority's road back?
Saeed Abu Rahma, a researcher on conflict affairs, argues that the end goal should be a unified Palestinian political system with Gaza inside it, on the road to statehood, rather than a separate entity called the Gaza administration.
"It is hard to imagine rebuilding the Palestinian political system without [the PA], and equally hard to imagine Gaza without any link to the Authority, whether direct or indirect," he explained.
Ramallah's position rests on the same premise, according to Munther al-Hayek, a Fatah spokesman and member of the movement's Revolutionary Council, who tells The New Arab that the PA accepted the Board of Peace and its committee “reluctantly,” given the scale of the catastrophe, for the sake of ending the genocide.
"The best solution from the start was for Hamas and the occupation to allow the [Palestinian] Authority to take up its responsibilities in Gaza, but that did not happen," he adds
"Now, we have few alternatives other than accepting that the national committee that emerged from the Board of Peace handles the recovery phase, provided that the Palestinian Authority takes over the entire reconstruction file according to the plans already prepared."
Al-Hayek sees elections as the way to reunite Gaza and the West Bank under the Authority's legal jurisdiction. PA President Mahmoud Abbas has set legislative elections for 28 November, the first since 2006, when a Hamas victory triggered the split that ended with the movement taking over Gaza in 2007.
Israel holds its own general election on 27 October, and the Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research has warned that the month between the two votes leaves almost no time for a new Israeli government to set its policy, making a postponement close to inevitable.
Al-Hayek still hopes any new government will be less damaging than Netanyahu's, whose far-right ministers, Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, he says, have left Palestinians with nothing.
Abu Allan, however, expects no such change, arguing that Israel will not accept the PA's return to Gaza because it would join the West Bank and Gaza in a single entity that could become the nucleus of a Palestinian state, and that only Washington could shift that position.
"Neither Hamas, nor the Authority, nor the Palestinians as a whole, nor even the Arab and Islamic states, nor even the European Union has the tools to confront Israel in its drive to keep Gaza outside any Palestinian governance or administration," he says.
Al-Qarra also rejects the idea that Hamas has lost its base, arguing that Fatah has suffered as much in the West Bank, where Israel has expanded settlements and checkpoints and stepped up killings.
“Gaza’s future,” Abu Allan says, “will depend less on who is in charge and more on the deal between the different parties over who governs, who pays for reconstruction, who provides security, and who ultimately gets to make the political decisions.”
A political and security vacuum
For human rights activist Hussein Hammad, the absence of the PA, or of any unified and internationally accepted government, leaves Palestinians to face the war machine and collapse alone, a view widely shared among Gaza's elite and public alike.
"This administrative vacuum obstructs the organisation of relief operations, prevents strategic recovery plans from being drawn up, and turns the Strip into a chaotic environment where needs collide with scarce resources," he says.
The situation in Gaza is dire; an estimated 1.98 million people, 94 per cent of Gaza's population, need shelter and basic household assistance, according to a Shelter Cluster survey led by the Norwegian Refugee Council, while the global hunger monitor IPC says more than 1.2 million people face acute hunger.
He also warns against sidelining UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, which he says is “the only logistical backbone” capable of distributing aid on the scale of the disaster. Already hit by Israeli bans on its operations, the agency laid off 600 staff and cut Gaza salaries by 20 percent in January to cover a $220 million shortfall.
The organisations filling the gap, from the World Food Programme and UNICEF to Arab institutions and local charities, lack UNRWA's staff, databases, and premises, Hammad says, and in his experience in the field they cover less than 10 per cent of actual needs.
Reconstruction has barely begun, with the Board of Peace unveiling a $2.45 billion plan in September to start rebuilding, a fraction of the $71.4 billion in needs over the next decade estimated by the EU and UN in April.
Abu Allan says there will be no reconstruction without disarmament, a position he says Israel and the Board of Peace share, and that Israel wants Gaza to remain "a place that drives life out" to advance a displacement project now back on Israeli campaign platforms.
Defence Minister Israel Katz said in September there was "no real solution for Gaza in the end without this migration," and analysts have warned that Israel's exit rules at the Rafah crossing are designed to ensure that more Palestinians leave than return.
Even Fatah, which has staked its return on the transition, expects it to drag on, with al-Hayek predicting that the Board of Peace's mandate, due to end in 2027, will be extended because nearly a year has passed without anything being done.
He also rules out any real improvement without an immediate and comprehensive end to the war, warning that after three years every coping mechanism, among residents and relief institutions alike, has been exhausted. A lasting administration, he argues, “can only spring from Palestinians' own free will”.
"Whoever ends up running Gaza cannot be a body imposed by tanks or by international resolutions detached from reality," he says.
Mohamed Solaimane is a Gaza-based journalist with bylines in regional and international outlets, focusing on humanitarian and environmental issues

Laws, pledges or an iron grip? How the EU, US and China are reining in AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:14:04 UTC
21:14:04 KST

The US, China and the EU are taking sharply different approaches to regulating artificial intelligence. Here is how the world's biggest economies are tackling the technology, and what is at stake.
Pressure is growing worldwide to rein in the most powerful artificial intelligence systems, and the world's three top AI heavyweights are answering in three very different ways.
The worries are much the same everywhere, starting from AI-powered cyberattacks, threats to national security and chatbots linked to children's suicides. The responses, it seems, are significantly different.
The EU has bet on binding rules, though it has already loosened some of them under pressure from industry. The US relies on voluntary promises and executive orders meant to keep its AI boom going. China is building its own rulebook under tight state control while rejecting calls to slow down.
Here is how each is going about it.
EU: "The world's first comprehensive rules on AI"
The European Union adopted its AI Act in 2024, which Brussels calls the "world's first comprehensive rules on artificial intelligence".
The Act regulates AI based on a four-tier risk framework, with rules escalating according to the threat level the AI system poses, going from those posing limited to no threat — such as video game elements and spam filters being able to operate freely — all the way to unacceptable systems with wide-reaching powers being outright banned such as social scoring, emotion recognition and manipulation.
But European companies, fearing the rules would stifle innovation as they race to catch up with US and Chinese rivals, lobbied hard and later won a delay as part of the AI Omnibus bill on rules covering high-risk systems, thanks in part to the Commission’s shift to the right following the EU elections.
Amid growing global calls for control, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said last month that the AI rules put "Europe in the position to shape global efforts".
She also said she would invite the main frontier labs "for a discussion on how we can support ongoing industry efforts to pace the frontier”.
European firms have been more wary of slowing down, fearing it could be an attempt by US giants to lock in their dominance.
The EU has other tools to regulate AI.
In August, ChatGPT became the first AI chatbot added to the EU's list of very large digital services subject to greater legal scrutiny under its online content rules known as the Digital Services Act.
Brussels last month also proposed forcing companies to make AI companions and chatbots safe before children use them.
The EU Kids Act calls for banning AI chatbots from "simulating interpersonal relationships in ways that create emotional dependency," the EU said, following a spate of suicides worldwide linked to children's interactions with such assistants.
US: 'Super intelligence'
Nearly two years into his second term, President Donald Trump has built his AI policy almost entirely from voluntary industry pledges and executive orders intended to sustain an AI boom that is powering the US economy.
On his first day back in office, Trump scrapped his predecessor Joe Biden's 2023 executive order requiring developers of the most powerful AI systems to share safety test results with the government and directing federal agencies to set guidelines for privacy to prevent algorithmic discrimination.
In July 2025, the White House unveiled an "AI Action Plan" listing more than 90 measures to speed up development, ramp up investment in infrastructure and deregulate the US sector as a whole.
An accompanying executive order titled "Preventing Woke AI in the Federal Government" requires federal agencies to buy only models deemed ideologically neutral.
The order was issued without any formal methodology to assess their neutrality other than sharing their platform’s technical documentation with the US government, something Dario Amodei’s Anthropic and Elon Musk’s xAI were all too happy to do especially given the latter’s history of controversial incidents.
Congress, politically divided and heavily lobbied by Big Tech, has yet to pass a federal AI law and is out of session until after the midterm elections in November.
Trump has tried to block state AI laws, but Congress has repeatedly refused to override them, and state laws are taking effect nationwide including California’s AI Transparency Act.
This year, the release of AI models capable of powerful cyberattacks shifted the focus to security. A June executive order set up a voluntary system for developers to give the government up to 30 days of early access to their most powerful models.
With voter anxiety growing, the heads of America’s six largest AI companies signed a White House accord on September 29 pledging independent audits and board-level oversight of cutting-edge models.
The pact allows the companies to self-regulate and carries no penalties should they fail to comply, though Trump called it "morally binding”.
The same day, Trump ordered federal agencies to replace the term "artificial intelligence" with "super intelligence" in official communications.
The latest figures show that AI infrastructure and investment make up roughly a fifth to a third of overall US economic growth at the moment, equal to .45 to .97 percentage points to overall US growth at of 2.1% to 2.3% in 2026, according to the Peterson Institute for International Economics.
China: 'Always under human control'
China already has a complex, evolving set of rules on how AI is used, including by children.
Regulations on AI companion chatbots took effect in July, aiming to curb emotional dependency and banning the creation of digital clones of real people without their consent.
President Xi Jinping said this summer that AI should be "always under human control", calling for more "laws and regulations, technological monitoring, early warning, and emergency response systems”.
Premier Li Qiang has also warned that the world risks "losing control" of frontier technologies such as AI if governments are too slow to regulate them.
However, "a general pause or deliberate slowdown in AI development remains outside the mainstream Chinese policy posture," Oxford China Policy Lab analysts wrote in September.
Some in China see calls to slow progress as hard to justify, "particularly given their perception that US measures such as export controls have already constrained China's AI development for years," they said.
China censors and controls AI-generated content much as it does other online information. And last month, its spy chief warned that AI could endanger national security.
"Hostile forces" are abusing generative AI to "fabricate political rumours and spread harmful information," Minister of State Security Chen Yixin said.

Drug target could block brain inflammation linked to Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:13:35 UTC
21:13:35 KST

Drug target could block brain inflammation linked to Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s
Scientists have found a way to dramatically reduce inflammation in human brain tissue using a drug-targetable receptor linked to Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, brain injury, and more.
- Date:
- October 7, 2026
- Source:
- University of Birmingham
- Summary:
- Blocking a receptor called P2X7 significantly reduced inflammation in human brain tissue, revealing a potential new treatment strategy for neurological and psychiatric disorders. The discovery could help researchers repurpose existing drugs for conditions including traumatic brain injury, Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, depression, and schizophrenia.
- Share:
Scientists may have found a new way to reduce harmful inflammation in the brain by targeting a receptor that can already be blocked with existing drugs.
The research, published in Brain and led by Professor Nicholas Barnes at the University of Birmingham, identifies the P2X7 receptor as an important driver of neuroinflammation. When researchers blocked this receptor, inflammation in human brain tissue was significantly reduced.
The findings could eventually have implications for a wide range of neurological and psychiatric conditions in which inflammation is thought to play a role. These include traumatic brain injury (TBI), Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, depression, and psychosis.
Blocking a Key Driver of Brain Inflammation
To investigate the receptor, the researchers used live cultures of human brain cells along with slices of brain tissue collected during neurosurgery. They focused on the P2X7 receptor, which helps trigger inflammatory signaling.
The team found that P2X7 receptors promote the release of cytokines, proteins that help regulate inflammatory responses. When the researchers used a specific antagonist to block the receptor, the inflammatory response in human brain tissue dropped significantly.
Professor Nicholas Barnes from the College of Medicine and Health at the University of Birmingham and corresponding author of the paper said: "This exciting discovery marks a major step toward repurposing existing therapeutics to combat neuroinflammation at its source. The identification of this receptor could have far-reaching implications for some of the most debilitating and widespread brain disorders such as Alzheimer's Disease, Parkinson's and Multiple Sclerosis, or inflammation-linked psychiatric conditions like schizophrenia and depression."
Studying the Brain's Immune Cells
A major part of the work involved microglia, immune cells that help coordinate the brain's response to injury and inflammation.
To study how these cells react to inflammatory signals, the researchers developed a method for converting a type of white blood cell into microglia. This process mirrors a cellular transformation that has recently been identified as occurring naturally in the brain during human aging.
The team started with human peripheral monocytes collected from blood samples and converted them into microglia-like cells. These cells provided a way to examine how human microglia may respond to inflammatory signals.
When the researchers applied the P2X7 receptor antagonist, they were able to interfere with signals released by microglia as the cells became damaged and died.
Professor Barnes said: "Studying human microglia has long been a major challenge: once removed from their native brain environment, they rapidly lose their defining characteristics, likely due to the absence of critical regulatory signals. Our approach involved the use of monocyte-derived microglia which provide a powerful, scalable, and virtually unlimited platform for studying human microglial biology with unprecedented precision."
From Lab Models to Human Brain Tissue
After identifying the response in the lab grown microglia-like cells, the researchers tested whether the same findings could be reproduced in human brain tissue obtained through neurosurgical procedures.
The successful results in human tissue strengthen the case for further investigation and could eventually lead to clinical trials in people with neurodegenerative diseases or traumatic brain injury.
Professor Barnes said: "Having identified the response in the human monocyte-derived microglia, this provided the impetus to translate these findings with human brain obtained following neurosurgical procedures. This successful translation means the next stage for this research is the development of clinical trials in patients with neurodegenerative conditions and patients with TBI where there are no effective pharmacological treatments to reduce the neuroinflammation and arising damage."

France suspends use of stun grenades against protesters
October 7, 2026
France is suspending the use of stun grenades at student-led protests as people report allegations of police brutality at demonstrations that have widened over the weeks.
"I am suspending their use in the high school student protests until the facts of the incident have been clarified," Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told RTL radio broadcaster on Wednesday.
He emphasized that the suspension was "only for the high school student protests" and for "just long enough to understand what happened."
Nunez announced the measure to curb growing anger after reports of serious injuries to teenage protesters drew public anger.
French regional newspaper La Voix du Nord reported this Monday that a 15-year-old had his hand and a part of his lower arm blown off after picking up a police stun grenade that then detonated during protests.
Last week, a 14-year-old student in northwest Paris was hit in the jaw as a tear gas canister was fired during protests, with the officer having been charged on Tuesday.
French prime minister to deliver speech
Wednesday's order comes before an address by Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu to protesters later Wednesday evening.
The demonstrations are also taking place at a difficult time for the French government as it tries to rein in its debts while facing demands to spend more on public services.
How long have students been protesting in France?
Protests first began mid-September in the Paris region after students began mobilizing against perceived inequalities in the education system.
From the outset, pupils said teaching, facilities and opportunities for advancement weren't as good for students in disadvantaged neighborhoods — despite the promise of France's national motto of "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity."
Demonstrations then spread to all parts of the country, including smaller towns with high schools.
On Tuesday, trade unions joined student protests. The Interior Ministry said nearly 256,000 people took part in protests nationwide on Tuesday.
Protests turned violent in Paris, where small groups of protesters clashed with riot officers at a city square toward the end.
More than 6,500 people have been arrested over the course of the last two weeks, most of them minors.

====================================================================================================

UK hopeful of deal with EU on Made in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:09:31 UTC
21:09:31 KST

U.K. Minister for Intergovernmental Relations and European Relations Hamish Falconer arrives to attend the weekly government Cabinet meeting at No. 10 Downing Street in London on Sept. 1, 2026. | Leon Neal/Getty Images
BRUSSELS — Britain is hopeful of doing a deal with the European Union to avoid British businesses being hit by new Made in Europe trade rules, the minister in charge of talks has said.
European Relations Minister Hamish Falconer told POLITICO’s Brussels Playbook Podcast it was “overwhelmingly in both sides’ interests” to strike an agreement on the proposed controls.
“For Europe to be more competitive and able to weather some of the shocks that we’re all talking about, we need to do it together,” he said. “I think that’s such an overwhelmingly powerful case that I am sure we will come to a sensible position on all this.”
Advertisement
Brussels is in the process of updating its trade rules to favor EU producers over those outside the bloc — and London fears some of its businesses will be locked out.
The U.K. has urged the EU to guarantee that British producers won’t be affected. Brussels says it can’t give those guarantees now as the rules are still working their way through the bloc’s cumbersome legislative process.
Yet in the event a deal isn’t reached, London believes its Brexit trade deal, the Trade and Cooperation Agreement (TCA), could force Brussels to think again.
“Our arrangements in terms of how we trade are underpinned by the TCA. That’s a strong arrangement between us which is independently overseen,” Falconer said.
“It provides lots of protections to both sides. Our basic position to our friends is, look, I don't think European competitiveness is enhanced by putting further impediments in the way of our industrial base.”
There are those in Brussels who agree. In-house lawyers at the EU Council have advised member countries that the bloc’s plans for the Industrial Accelerator Act could violate the union’s international trade deals, according to documents seen by POLITICO.
Advertisement
Falconer suggested the U.K. wanted a “straightforward” and “unfussy” arrangement where U.K. goods were simply counted as being of Union origin under the IAA.
But the minister wouldn’t be drawn on whether success at the upcoming U.K.-EU summit demanded an agreement on Made in Europe — as London had previously briefed.
That meeting is meant to sign off talks on agri-foods, youth visas, and emissions trading — as well as act as a launchpad for further negotiations.
“I don’t wanna get ahead of the discussions. I used to be a diplomat; there’s no discussion or negotiation that is made easier by publicly broadcasting it,” Falconer said.
The bigger reset
The minister rejected suggestions the EU was demanding the U.K. raise tariffs on Chinese cars in exchange for guarantees on the IAA. He stated that he was “surprised” at reports to that effect, adding: “That’s not the kind of conversation that I’m having with my European counterparts.”
Yet a landing zone may be emerging. EU officials and diplomats have previously indicated that reference could still be made to the subject at the meeting — perhaps in the form of a political declaration.
Advertisement
Falconer, who was in Strasbourg on Wednesday for his first European Parliament plenary, confirmed that he would be discussing “future options with European partners” — following Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s suggestion the U.K. could rejoin the EU, or at least its customs union or single market.
He is using the visit to meet with Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič, as well as European Parliament President Roberta Metsola. Of the EU institutions debating the industry act, Parliament is pushing for the strictest line on the Made in Europe rules.
Asked what options he was personally pushing for when it came to the future U.K.-EU relationship, Falconer wouldn’t be drawn, revealing only that Burnham would “say more” in a speech scheduled for around “the time of the summit.”
The meeting still has no officially announced date, though Nov. 20 is the latest in a string of days widely rumored to have been penciled in by diary officials in Brussels and London.
“I have a date in mind, but I don’t want to say it just yet,” Falconer told the podcast. “We will agree that with our friends, and you’ll be the first to know.”

Cuttlefish named ‘Fish of the Year’, though not really a fish
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:09:24 UTC
21:09:24 KST

The cuttlefish (or sepia) has been named Flemish 'Fish of the Year' by the Flemish Agro and Fish Marketing Centre, though it is really a cephalopod like squid and octopus. It is currently the most commonly landed fish-like species in our ports. “We often associate cuttlefish with southern cuisine, but it is caught in large numbers by our own fishermen,” says Hilde Crevits, Flemish Sea Fisheries Minister (Christian democrat CD&V).
Cuttlefish named ‘Fish of the Year’, though not really a fish
The Flemish fisheries sector hopes this award will help to raise the profile of a species that is still underappreciated.
The cuttlefish is a species of cephalopod with 10 arms, which it uses to swiftly seize its prey. Hidden beneath its mantle is an internal calcareous skeleton.
Cuttlefish are also true masters of camouflage: in the blink of an eye, they can adapt the colour, pattern and texture of their skin to their surroundings, for example to hide.
The species has a short life cycle (1 to 2 years) and can reproduce rapidly, meaning that populations naturally have a greater capacity to recover than others.
The cuttlefish is found across much of the Atlantic Ocean, from southern Norway to the waters off the coast of West Africa.
Where and in what numbers cuttlefish are found can vary considerably from year to year. This is mainly due to changes in seawater conditions. As a result of climate change, the species appears to be occurring in an increasing number of locations.
Economic importance
In 2024, landings rose by 25 per cent to 2,248 tonnes. This accounted for 19 per cent of total Belgian landings.
Within the landings of cephalopods (cuttlefish, squid and octopus), cuttlefish was by far the most important species, accounting for 79 per cent. This made cuttlefish the most commonly landed species in Flemish ports.
And in the kitchen?
Cuttlefish has a firm texture and a slightly nutty flavour. It is ideal for grilling, frying or using in stew.
Fresh cuttlefish, squid and octopus are (for the time being) used relatively rarely in our kitchens. Only 6.3 per cent of Belgians ever buy fresh cuttlefish, squid or octopus. Many are familiar with frozen calamari, which are imported from Asia.

JAKARTA, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- Indonesia's foreign exchange reserves stood at 146.3 billion U.S. dollars at the end of September 2026, down slightly from 146.5 billion dollars at the end of August, Bank Indonesia said on Wednesday.

Kenyan soccer league in limbo after play-off abandoned amid chaos
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:08:28 CST
21:08:28 KST

NAIROBI, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- The delayed start of the 2026-27 Kenyan Premier League faces further uncertainty after a promotion-relegation playoff was abandoned because of crowd trouble on Tuesday.
The second leg between Kariobangi Sharks and Mombasa United at the Ulinzi Sports Complex in Nairobi was halted in the second half following a pitch invasion.
Amid the continuing uncertainty, a parliamentary committee has called for the establishment of a normalization committee to take over the administration of Kenyan football.
The proposal is aimed at addressing persistent leadership disputes, financial issues and controversies surrounding the governance and regulations of the delayed domestic league.
United entered the match with a 2-1 advantage from the first leg in Mombasa the previous week and extended its aggregate lead inside the opening minute.
Sharks responded by scoring twice to lead 2-1 at halftime and level the tie at 3-3 on aggregate.
The match took a dramatic turn midway through the second half when referee John Sulwe awarded United a controversial penalty. Sharks players confronted the official following the decision before fans invaded the pitch, with the referee struck amid the ensuing disorder.
Sulwe was escorted from the field to safety by military and private security personnel stationed at the venue.
Both teams eventually left the pitch, and the match was abandoned after the referee was deemed unable to continue.
Tuesday's developments mean the start of the new Kenyan Premier League season, already delayed by two months, could be postponed further.
United and Sharks had agreed to a two-legged playoff following mediation overseen by the Football Kenya Federation (FKF) three weeks earlier, with both clubs laying claim to the 18th and final place in the top flight.
United argued that it had earned promotion from the National Super League after finishing third in the standings under amended 2025 league rules allowing three teams to be promoted and relegated.
Sharks maintained that it was entitled to a promotion-relegation playoff after finishing 17th in last season's Premier League under 2019 regulations.
The club argued in court that the 2025 amendments had not been introduced through the proper legal process, leaving the 2019 rules in effect.
Sharks had successfully obtained a High Court injunction postponing the start of the league until the matter was heard and determined.
However, a mediated agreement reached at the end of last month cleared the way for the two teams to contest the playoff.
The delayed start of the Premier League has also raised concerns over whether the national team, the Harambee Stars, will be adequately prepared for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON), which Kenya will co-host with Uganda and Tanzania.
The continental tournament, known as Pamoja AFCON 2027, is scheduled to run from June 19 to July 17, 2027.
Tuesday's incident is the latest in a series of problems to affect Kenyan football and has intensified calls for changes to its administration under FKF President Hussein Mohammed.
At the start of the current international break, the national team staged a strike over unpaid allowances ahead of its 2027 AFCON qualifiers.
Last-minute efforts allowed the team to train only once before a 1-1 draw against Eritrea in Nairobi, followed by a 1-0 defeat to Guinea in its subsequent Group D qualifier.
The team also drew 0-0 with Rwanda in a friendly on Monday.
Despite automatically qualifying for Pamoja AFCON 2027 as co-host, Kenya's recent form has raised questions over its readiness for the tournament.
The parliamentary committee also raised concerns over the FKF's handling of the national team's preparations.
"Further, concerns have arisen regarding outstanding payments to Harambee Stars players and allegations that the work permits for the team head coach, Benni McCarthy, and his technical staff are yet to be approved," it said.
The committee said the situation risked undermining player welfare and morale, disrupting football development and affecting the country's preparations for upcoming international competitions. ■

LANZHOU, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- Fourth-grader Zeng Hanyang steadied the remote control and guided his drone toward the goal as classmates cheered during preparations for a drone football match.
Zeng, a student at No. 1 Primary School in Baiyin District, Baiyin City in northwest China's Gansu Province, has been learning drone football since last year. The sport has grown increasingly popular among young students across Gansu, with schools training pupils for local and higher-level competitions.
"I like to play drone football," Zeng said, adding that his teacher also showed him how to assemble drones before matches.

Nearby Baiyin Road Primary School in Lanzhou has offered drone football courses for several years. Its students won third prize in the drone football event at the World Robot Contest finals in January 2025.
Youth science-and-technology sports such as drone football remain popular across the province. The Youth Science and Technology Sports and Aerospace Model UAV Education Competition, held in Linxia City in June, drew 318 teams from 13 cities and prefectures and more than 5,000 athletes and coaches, officials said.

Hungary's inflation rises to 1.6 pct in September
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:08:16 CST
21:08:16 KST

BUDAPEST, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- Hungary's consumer price index (CPI) rose by 1.6 percent year-on-year in September, accelerating from 1.3 percent in August, according to data released Wednesday by the Hungarian Central Statistical Office (KSH).
Food prices fell by 1.3 percent year-on-year, or 4.6 percent excluding food and beverage-serving services. Meanwhile, prices of electricity, gas and other fuels declined by 4 percent, the data showed.
Service prices remained a major source of upward pressure, rising by 4.9 percent year-on-year. Prices of alcoholic beverages and tobacco products increased by 3.3 percent, while consumer durable prices rose by 1.2 percent. Motor fuels increased by 6.9 percent.
Core inflation, which excludes volatile items such as food and energy, eased slightly to 1.9 percent year-on-year in September, according to the data.
Janos Nagy, macroeconomic analyst at Erste Bank, said the headline inflation figure was below both the bank's forecast and market consensus, while the slowdown in core inflation was a particularly favorable development.
However, he warned that the inflation outlook could become less favorable, as higher energy prices are already feeding into domestic producer prices and could gradually reach consumers. Rising global food prices and developments in the exchange rate of the Hungarian forint could also influence future price pressures, he said.
Erste Bank expects Hungary's average inflation rate to stand at 1.8 percent in 2026, before rising to 3.0 percent in 2027. ■

KABUL, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- Afghanistan's Ministry of Public Health has signed a memorandum of understanding with Save the Children International to strengthen healthcare delivery across two provinces, the ministry announced in a statement on Wednesday.
Valued at 1,668,876 U.S. dollars, the agreement will extend essential health services to 65,263 residents in southern Kandahar and northern Faryab provinces, according to the statement.

IMF chief warns high energy prices may persist even after Gulf conflict ends
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:07:57 CST
21:07:57 KST

SINGAPORE, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- International Monetary Fund (IMF) Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said on Wednesday that even if the conflict in the Gulf were to end soon, high energy prices would likely persist for some time.
"Brent futures, for example, now predict high oil prices through 2027," she said in the curtain-raiser speech for the 2026 Annual Meetings of the IMF and the World Bank Group, which will take place from Oct. 12 to 18 in Bangkok.
"So far, the energy price shock has been large but contained thanks to energy efficiency, fuel-source diversification, reserve releases, supply chain agility, and the usual organic demand and supply response," Georgieva said.
Nonetheless, despite a shaky recovery in flows out of the Gulf, oil prices remain around 100 U.S. dollars a barrel, reflecting risks, high transport costs and other factors.
"Add to this a crack spread of about another 100 dollars per barrel due to a global shortfall in refining capacity, and we get retail prices of diesel and other refined products at record highs," she said.
Natural gas supplies from the Gulf also remain severely impaired, reflecting more limited liquefied natural gas (LNG) transport options for as long as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains threatened, Georgieva said.
The disruption is having uneven effects around the world, with Asia and Europe particularly hard-hit, she noted.
"Price pressures may build further as countries replenish reserves and demand rises with the approach of the Northern hemisphere cold season," Georgieva said. ■

Why do Hong Kong’s Election Committee polls matter as nominations open?
The South China Morning Post examines who is running, what to watch for and how the committee will choose the city’s next leader
The nomination period opened on Wednesday for elections to the 1,500-member body responsible for choosing Hong Kong’s next chief executive and 40 lawmakers.
Hopefuls from at least four subsectors submitted their nomination forms on the first day.
The South China Morning Post explains the significance of the Election Committee polls, who signed up on the first day and what to watch for.
What is the Election Committee and why is it important?
Wednesday marked the start of a two-week nomination period for the 2026 Election Committee Subsector (ECSS) Ordinary Elections, scheduled for November 22.
Up to 982 subsector representatives will be elected to the city’s top electoral college. They will join 362 ex officio members and 156 members nominated by designated bodies. Together, the 1,500 members will be responsible for nominating and selecting the chief executive next March and electing 40 of the Legislative Council’s 90 members in 2029.

Poland to review Paramount takeover of TVN through acquisition of Warner Bros
Unknown

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Poland will examine whether Paramount Skydance can take control of TVN, one of the country’s leading broadcasters, following its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, which owns TVN.
The review is being conducted under a law that requires state approval for ownership changes of companies designated by the government as strategic and protected from takeovers deemed to threaten the national interest. TVN was added to the list in 2024, following reports of its possible sale.
Minister Aktywów Państwowych zajmie się przejęciem TVN przez grupę Paramount Skydance#PAPinformacjehttps://t.co/FxxDnozx9i
— Polska Agencja Prasowa/Polish Press Agency (PAP) (@PAPinformacje) October 6, 2026
Paramount Skydance’s $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, one of the largest mergers in the global media market, brings together major US media assets including Paramount’s CBS and MTV and Warner’s HBO, CNN and Discovery Channel.
After the deal was completed on Tuesday, Poland’s state assets ministry told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that, because the acquisition would give Paramount Skydance indirect control of TVN, the new owner must notify the ministry of the takeover.
The ministry then has 90 days to “conduct an administrative investigation into this matter to verify the impact of the transaction on security or public order in Poland”.
The ministry can either approve the change of ownership or block the new owner from controlling TVN. In the latter case, the state assets minister, Wojchech Balczun, may order the sale of TVN’s shares.
“I assure you that it will be an entirely substantive and objective administrative procedure, carried out in fulfilment of a statutory obligation, and nothing more,” Balczun told broadcaster Kanał Zero on Tuesday.
The procedure is necessary because the Polish government added TVN and another large private broadcaster, Polsat, to its list of strategic companies in December 2024, bringing them under state protection against takeovers considered aggressive or contrary to the national interest.
That move came amid reports that Warner Bros. Discovery was considering selling TVN and that a businessman linked to Hungary’s then-Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, an ally of Poland’s conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, was seeking to buy it.

To jest odpersonalizowana procedura administracyjna, która wynika z ustawy o kontroli… pic.twitter.com/jp3J9zC0jh
— Ministerstwo Aktywów Państwowych 🇵🇱 (@MAPGOVPL) October 7, 2026
Prime Minister Donald Tusk said at the time the move was intended to protect the broadcaster from hostile foreign takeovers and prevent foreign interference in Poland’s media and elections.
TVN, which was originally founded in 1995, has been in American hands since 2015, when it was bought by US broadcaster Scripps, which was in turn acquired by Discovery in 2018.
The station, which is known for taking a liberal position on many issues, has long been a target for Polish conservatives. In 2021, the then-PiS government passed a law that would have forced Warner Bros. Discovery to sell its majority stake. However, that was vetoed by then-President Andrzej Duda.
Poland is adding the country’s two largest private TV stations, Polsat and TVN, to its list of “strategic companies” under special protection.
That allows the government to block the sale of the firms to owners from “hostile states”, says PM @donaldtusk https://t.co/TwK9IFRPrs
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 11, 2024
Some in Poland have expressed fear that Paramount could push TVN in a more conservative direction, as it has been accused of doing with other media outlets it has acquired, notably US broadcaster CBS.
Paramount’s owner, David Ellison, is a Trump ally, as are PiS and Poland’s current president, Karol Nawrocki.
On Sunday, the Journalists’ Association, a Polish organisation representing journalists, called on TVN’s management to establish an editorial independence council similar to those being created at CNN and CBS under the settlement deal that paved the way for the merger in the US.
Media reports claim that President Trump tried to persuade Poland's defence minister to leave the government and form a coalition with the right-wing opposition.
We outline what is known so far and how the government, including PM @donaldtusk, has reacted https://t.co/m04H8VgoSF
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 5, 2026
In July, Reporters Without Borders (RSF) also raised concerns about the potential impact of the merger on TVN’s editorial independence, citing the new ownership structure and the risk of political interference.
The NGO called for guarantees protecting the channel as a condition of approval for the takeover from the European Commission. The EU executive, however, approved the deal in July without imposing such conditions, following an antitrust review.
The commission’s approval covered the entire European Union, meaning that national competition authorities have no grounds to challenge the deal, Tomasz Chróstny, head of Poland’s consumer protection authority UOKiK, told news service Wirtualna Polska before the transaction was completed.

1st Lt. Hilal Aydın
Türkiye’s Naval Forces have graduated their first female maritime patrol aircraft pilot after Navy 1st Lt. Hilal Aydın successfully completed her flight training.
Aydın, who serves at the Naval Air Command in Kartepe, northwestern province of Kocaeli, made history by becoming the first woman to qualify as a maritime patrol aircraft pilot in the Turkish Naval Forces.
Aydın said she had grown up surrounded by military life because her father served as a noncommissioned officer in the Turkish Armed Forces, adding that she had dreamed of becoming a soldier from an early age. She applied for pilot training in 2022.
After successfully completing a rigorous selection process and flight training, Aydın graduated as the Turkish Naval Forces’ first female aircraft pilot.
Now serving under the Naval Air Command in Kartepe, Aydın spoke about her journey from pursuing a military career to becoming a pilot, while also offering advice to young people seeking to pursue similar careers.
Recalling that she had always wanted to become a soldier since childhood, Aydın said that after graduating, she served aboard the TCG Gemlik as an operations and electronic warfare assistant officer and communications officer.
Aydın expressed she takes great pride in pursuing the same profession with Sabiha Gökçen, the first Turkish female fighter pilot.
“I believe she is one of the finest role models for every young woman who aspires to become a pilot and dreams of pursuing this career. Had I not become a pilot, I would have wanted to continue serving aboard our ships, just as I did when I first embarked on my military career,” she noted.

Minimum wage dispute set for nationwide vote

Unknown Publisher

Minimum wage dispute set for nationwide vote
Swiss voters are likely to have their say on the relationship between collective labour agreements and cantonal minimum wages.
A coalition of trade unions and political parties has submitted more than 100,000 signatures against plans to override cantonal minimum wages.
+ Swiss cantons push on with minimum wage despite national setback
The Federal Chancellery will decide whether the referendum on the bill recently passed by Parliament can go ahead once the signatures have been verified. Given the number submitted, however, this is expected to be little more than a formality. If the referendum is confirmed, voters are likely to head to the polls in either February or June 2027.
Opponents have described the move as an “attack on low-paid workers”. Under the new law, generally binding sector-wide collective labour agreements could take precedence over statutory minimum wages set by cantons or municipalities. In cantons and cities where minimum wages have been approved but have yet to come into force, tens of thousands of workers would not benefit from them.
Cantonal minimum wages are currently in place in the cantons of Geneva, Neuchâtel, Basel City, Jura and Ticino. However, Jura, Basel City and Ticino are not affected by the bill, as existing provisions already allow generally binding collective labour agreements to take precedence there. Several cities have also introduced local minimum wages, including Zurich, Winterthur and Lucerne.

German ex-spy chief arrested for treason: What we know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:04:51 UTC
21:04:51 KST

German ex-spy chief arrested for treason: What we know
Former top spy August Hanning led the Federal Intelligence Service from 1998 to 2005 and later worked at Germany’s Interior Ministry.
The man who led Germany’s intelligence agency from 1998 to 2005 has been arrested on suspicion of espionage and attempted treason, according to the country’s federal prosecutor’s office.
The office announced on Tuesday that August Hanning, 80, was arrested and faces charges including “treasonous espionage, obtaining state secrets, attempted treason” through contact with foreign intelligence services.
The office has not specified which country or countries Hanning is accused of working for.
Citing unnamed sources, however, German news outlet Der Spiegel reported that Hanning was in contact with an Azerbaijan intelligence agency representative. In 2025, prosecutors also accused Hanning of ties with Israeli spies in a separate case which ultimately led them to the ex-intelligence boss’s alleged espionage for other agencies.
If found guilty, treason carries a maximum sentence of life imprisonment in Germany.
German news outlet Deutsche Welle described Hanning’s arrest as Germany’s “biggest espionage scandal of the century”.
Here’s what we know:
Who is August Hanning?
Born in Nordwalde, Westphalia, western Germany, in 1946, Hanning served as the head of the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005 and later moved to work in the Federal Ministry of the Interior, before working as a state secretary until 2009.
He later worked as a private consultant.
German media showed pictures of Hanning being taken from his red-brick house in Norwalde, close to Munster, to a bulletproof vehicle by masked officers on Tuesday morning.
What do prosecutors allege?
They claim Hanning used classified intelligence to “draft an analysis” for a foreign intelligence service and kept “close contact” with another foreign spying service for “several years” while he was working as a private consultant.
They say that in 2010, Hanning came to an agreement to receive confidential information from his former bureau chief – who was in office until March this year and is named only as “Manfred D” – and was preparing to provide an “analysis” of it to a foreign power in exchange for money. It is unclear if the analysis was duly shared.
However, Hanning is also alleged to have passed on potentially sensitive political information, partly based on information provided by Manfred D, to a contact representing a separate foreign intelligence service.
Manfred D was also arrested on Tuesday and charged with aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage.
“Both suspects are believed to have agreed, in the spring of 2010, to have Manfred D continuously transmit valuable intelligence from the Federal Intelligence Service to Hanning in exchange for remuneration,” a statement from the prosecutor’s office said.
Over the years, Manfred D provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, “many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the Federal Intelligence Service for internal purposes, particularly for executive intelligence briefings”, it added.
“Hanning was to capitalise on said information in the context of his private consulting services, which he had since been offering,” the prosecutor’s office said.
The alleged espionage by Hanning and Manfred D was uncovered during an investigation into a separate kidnapping case involving German businesswoman and steakhouse chain heiress, Christina Block.
In that case, Hamburg prosecutors accused Block of arranging the kidnapping of her two youngest children in 2023 due to a custody dispute. Prosecutors said Hanning put Block in touch with a private Israeli espionage firm to carry out the abductions. The former spy chief and a police officer were accused of accepting more than 100,000 euros ($112,000) from Block in exchange for returning her children from Denmark, where they were living with her ex-husband. The trial is ongoing.
What do we know about the alleged documents that were passed on?
Little detail is available about the contents of the 2,000 documents, but German news outlet Suddeutsche Zeitung reported that a number of them related to Iran’s nuclear programme and the Russian military.
It added that other materials were highly sensitive and classified as secret by allied intelligence agencies in other countries.
What has the government said?
Marc Henrichmann, chairman of the parliament’s intelligence oversight committee, said in a statement to the AFP news agency that Berlin would not “tolerate the betrayal of secrets”.
“Whoever allies themselves with the enemies of our liberal democracy will be found out,” he said, adding that Hanning’s alleged actions would amount to “trampling his official duties underfoot”.
The current head of the BND, Martin Jaeger, told the German Rheinische Post newspaper that the agency had “quickly carried out extensive internal investigations” into the former chief before federal prosecutors took over the case.
“For the BND and for me, there are no compromises when it comes to internal security,” Jaeger said, adding that it had “not called into question any of my aims or any of my priorities”.
Have there been similar spy scandals in Germany before?
Yes.
In 2023, a high-ranking German intelligence officer, identified as “Carsten L”, was charged with high treason when prosecutors alleged he had obtained classified intelligence on the war in Ukraine and the Wagner mercenary group and shared it with Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB). His case is ongoing.
In 1974, West German Chancellor Willy Brandt was forced to resign following revelations that an East German spy had worked as his close aide for nearly two years.

NASA says Russia, China could join Artemis Accords if they align with principles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:04:09 UTC
21:04:09 KST

Beril Çanakcı
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Russia and China could one day join the US-led Artemis Accords on space exploration if they come to share its principles, but they do not today, NASA's deputy administrator said Wednesday.
"If one day, Russia and China were like-minded in those principles, which we don't see them as that right now, then there would be a possibility to join the Artemis Accords," Matt Anderson told reporters at the International Astronautical Congress in Antalya.
Anderson said the 76 countries that have signed the accords share a "common bond" built on agreed principles for safe, transparent, and responsible activity in space.
Moscow and Beijing are instead leading a rival effort, the International Lunar Research Station, which plans a joint research base on the Moon. Some countries belong to both groups. Some signatories' academic institutions also work with the Chinese-led project.
Asked whether that was a concern, Anderson said: "What sovereign nations do is up to them." Signing the accords does not stop countries from pursuing their national interests, he added.
Anderson spoke a day after co-chairing a closed-door meeting of the accords' members with Maj. Gen. Roberto Melgar Sheen, director of Peru's space agency, CONIDA. Anderson said just over 40 countries attended.
Melgar Sheen said participants reached agreement on space debris. They also discussed debris on the lunar surface.
"The first step to stop space debris, or to deal with space debris, is to stop creating it," Anderson said.
Asked about concerns over weapons in space, Anderson said the accords cover civil space activities. He said military matters belong with each country's national security bodies.
"For us in the United States, that's United States Space Force and United States Space Command. What the Artemis Accords is focused on is that civil space sector," he said. "Nobody wants kinetic fighting in space. We are about peaceful exploration."
Anderson also said students from member countries will be able to attend a new US Space Academy, a four-year civilian university. US President Donald Trump ordered its creation in August, and Anderson said the first students are expected in the summer of 2028.
He said member nations are eager to contribute to NASA's planned Moon base. Contributions could range from small satellites known as CubeSats to engineers on US industry teams building landers and rovers.
Germany will host the accords' next annual workshop in 2027, Anderson said.
Melgar Sheen said this year's workshop in Lima, the first in Latin America, used simulations and tabletop exercises to test principles such as non-interference, interoperability and data sharing. He said Peru hopes to take part in future lunar missions, possibly alongside other Latin American countries.
"We firmly believe that the future of lunar and deep space exploration must be guided by transparency, sustainability, interoperability, and inclusivity," he said.
Launched in 2020 by the US and seven other countries, the Artemis Accords are a nonbinding set of principles for the peaceful exploration of the Moon, Mars, and beyond. They are based on the 1967 Outer Space Treaty. Türkiye signed in August.
The accords are tied to NASA's Artemis program. Its Artemis II mission carried astronauts around the Moon in April, the first crewed lunar flight in more than 50 years.
