Webb finds a surprising atmosphere on a scorching lava world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:58:25 UTC
20:58:25 KST

Webb finds a surprising atmosphere on a scorching lava world
- Date:
- October 7, 2026
- Source:
- University of Chicago
- Summary:
- The James Webb Space Telescope has found strong evidence that the rocky lava world HD 3167 b has an atmosphere, despite circling its star every 24 hours under extreme heat. The surprising discovery could help scientists understand how rocky planets retain atmospheres and what the young, molten Earth may once have looked like.
- Share:
For scientists searching for life beyond Earth, rocky planets with atmospheres are among the most promising places to investigate. An atmosphere is essential for maintaining liquid water on a planet's surface. Yet among the more than 6,300 exoplanets cataloged thus far, most are not rocky, and only a small number of known rocky planets appear to possess atmospheres.
Now, researchers have added another world to that short list. In a study published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, a team led by University of Chicago scientist Brandon Park Coy reports evidence of an atmosphere surrounding HD 3167 b, a rocky super-Earth located 154 light-years away in the constellation Pisces. The intensely hot planet, classified as a "lava world," completes an orbit around its star in only one Earth day.
"What's so surprising is that the closer a rocky planet orbits its star, the harder it should be to have an atmosphere, because it's bombarded by stellar wind and gets more high-energy photons from the star. But it seems that many of these lava worlds do," explained Edwin Kite, UChicago associate professor of geophysical sciences and co-author of the study. "These planets are too hot for life, but by studying them, we can say something about the processes that matter for other rocky worlds."
In the Q&A below,Coy, a graduate student in Kite's group and first author on the study, explains why atmospheres on lava worlds are scientifically valuable, how researchers detected evidence for this one, and what they hope to learn next.
What was the goal of the survey that found this atmosphere-bearing exoplanet?
One of the driving questions that the James Webb Space Telescope is being used to answer is whether planets orbiting stars much smaller than the sun have atmospheres. It appears that most of those terrestrial planets don't -- they're just bare rock.
But surprisingly, we've found evidence that the majority of lava worlds -- similar in composition to Earth and Venus but much, much hotter -- might have atmospheres. Five terrestrial planets found with atmospheres, including the one described in this study, have been ultra-hot.
This planet, however, is the coldest lava world found so far with evidence of an atmosphere. This is interesting because we're trying to understand the temperature transition between planets with and without atmospheres.
The result is the first from a program led by Megan Weiner Mansfield, PhD'21, who's now at the University of Maryland. The goal of the program, which is looking at 10 ultra-hot lava worlds, is to see if there's a critical temperature over which you start seeing planets with atmospheres.
"We're interested in studying these kinds of planets because we think early Earth might have looked a lot like a lava world." -- Study author Brandon Park Coy
How can you tell if an exoplanet has an atmosphere?
Right now, directly looking at Earth-like planets for signs of life is out of reach. Instead, we can use the Webb telescope to detect light in the mid-infrared wavelength range to estimate the temperature of exoplanets, which can tell us if they might have atmospheres.
There are two primary ways that we study exoplanets. One is called transit, when the planet goes in front of the host star. Another called secondary eclipse, which is the method we used for this study, is when the planet passes behind its star, and we can measure how much light is lost. That difference tells us how much mid-infrared light comes from the planet itself, which essentially tells us how hot the planet is.
If a planet doesn't have an atmosphere, its star-facing, day side should be as hot as theoretically possible based on how reflective its surface is and its distance from the star. But an atmosphere would help redistribute heat from the day side to the night side. We see this happen on Venus -- there's almost no difference in surface temperature between the day and night sides, or between the poles and the equator. If a planet has an atmosphere, it might also have clouds that reflect incoming starlight and cool the dayside. So if a planet's day side is cooler than the maximum possible, it likely has an atmosphere.
The subject of this study, HD 3167 b, is noticeably cooler than its expected maximum, providing strong evidence that it has an atmosphere.
What do you think HD 3167 b's atmosphere is made of?
These lava worlds are so-named because the surface facing their star is likely melted rock. We think that HD 3167 b might have a silicate-rich composition, with a similar mixture of minerals that make up Earth's mantle. Before this study, we expected that any atmosphere on these ultra-hot planets would be composed of vaporized rock, but we're starting to see evidence that some might have heavier gases like carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, or water in their atmospheres.
The makeup of HD 3167 b's atmosphere is still up in the air. That's one reason we're so interested in getting new observations.
Why is this result important?
Because the four other lava worlds found to have atmospheres are in the ultra-hot regime, it raises questions about whether there's a critical transition temperature when silicate atmospheres start becoming very thick. Is there a temperature where these planets form silicate cloud decks that might reflect incoming radiation to space and cool its day side? This relatively cooler planet helps us better characterize and nail down this transition.
Despite how inhospitable they are for life, we're also interested in studying these kinds of planets because we think early Earth might have looked a lot like a lava world. We think that very early in the solar system's history, when the terrestrial planets formed, they were extremely hot due to the energy from all of the planetesimal collisions. Earth had what's known as a magma ocean stage with an entirely liquid surface. This result gives us a window into studying what conditions may have been like in Earth's first couple of million years.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Chicago. Original written by Maureen Searcy. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Brandon Park Coy, Qiao Xue, Megan Weiner Mansfield, Jason D. Eastman, Anjali A. A. Piette, Tyler Fairnington, Cole Smith, Michael Zhang, Eliza M.-R. Kempton, Jacob L. Bean, Xuan Ji, Peter Gao, Jegug Ih, Daniel D. B. Koll, Rafael Luque, Jaume Orell-Miquel, Edwin S. Kite. Evidence for an Atmosphere on the Ultra-short-period Super-Earth HD 3167 b. The Astrophysical Journal Letters, 2026; 1005 (2): L77 DOI: 10.3847/2041-8213/ae7f23

Kulbergs reveals how he will choose Latvia’s next coalition partners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:58:24 UTC
20:58:24 KST

The United List (AS) will choose as its next coalition partners those political forces that agree to implement changes, Prime Minister and candidate to continue in the post Andris Kulbergs (AS) told journalists on Wednesday at Riga Castle following a meeting with President Edgars Rinkēvičs.
Kulbergs said the coalition must be capable of implementing changes with full commitment, without fearing them, while also explaining them to the public. He acknowledged that the changes would not be comfortable for everyone but stressed that they are necessary for the country.
In the prime minister’s view, voters have clearly voted for change, and willingness to implement it will determine the choice of coalition partners.
Speaking about the structure of the government, Kulbergs said the number of ministries should not be an end in itself. In his view, the focus should be on achieving the greatest impact and economic benefit while using as few resources as possible. As examples, he mentioned governments consisting of 14, 12 or 11 ministers.
President Rinkēvičs, meanwhile, stressed that he had not drawn any red lines during consultations with the political forces but had instead set out three key principles.
The first is an unchanged course on national defence, security and foreign policy, including spending 5% of gross domestic product on security and defence and continuing support for Ukraine. Rinkēvičs said he had heard fairly broad support for this course during consultations, with the possible exception of one political force, which he did not name.
As his second principle, the president highlighted effectiveness rather than the size of the coalition. He stressed that the candidate for prime minister and his political force, the United List, had been given a strong mandate.
Rinkēvičs said the public would primarily hold the prime minister accountable because a large part of society had placed its trust in him. How that mandate is implemented is now a task for the prime ministerial candidate, the president noted.
As his third principle, Rinkēvičs said he wanted the coalition to be formed with the aim of governing for the full four-year electoral cycle.
 The next elections will take place in 2029, when European Parliament and municipal elections are scheduled, followed by the Saeima election in 2030.
Rinkēvičs stressed that there are effectively two years until the next election cycle in which much can be accomplished without worrying about how social media, experts, journalists or particular groups in society might react.
The president also acknowledged that changes may initially be unacceptable to certain sections of society or professional groups. He said he had heard from the parties that they were prepared to work on such changes.
Speaking about the formation of the coalition, 
Rinkēvičs also referred to Kulbergs’ list of priorities and whether political forces would agree to them.
The president said that when he met Kulbergs and the United List on the first working day after the election, they discussed their vision for the work ahead. He said he had heard proposals from AS aimed at putting public finances in order and creating a more efficient state administration.
Rinkēvičs stressed that this would require a broad package of measures.
He acknowledged that reducing the number of ministries is currently seen as a symbol of efficiency, but increasing the efficiency of public administration is a much broader process. Rinkēvičs explained that ministries themselves are not the largest institutions, while the systems under their supervision are often extensive. Therefore, subordinate institutions and their functions must also be reviewed.
In his view, merging ministries will only be effective if accompanied by a review of functions and the entire administrative system.
At the same time, Rinkēvičs noted that, from the perspective of the political distribution of posts, merging ministries or reducing their number would also reduce the size of the Cabinet and therefore have political consequences.
The president stressed that other parties had also expressed readiness during consultations to begin by merging ministries. However, there are differing views on what the future structure should look like, and more specific solutions will have to be found through political negotiations.

‘There will be no Tel Aviv’: Egyptians threaten Israel following Smotrich Sinai comments

20:58:14 KST

Egyptian media channels widely aired threats against Israel, Tel Aviv, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu this week as they reacted angrily to Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s warning Monday that Israel would destroy Sinai if Egypt attacked Israel, delivered during an interview with the haredi (ultra-Orthodox) news site Hashtiblach.
“What will cause Egypt not to attack us? They know that if they attack, there will be no Sinai,” Smotrich told the channel. “It won’t happen again. There is no [Menachem] Begin.”
Then-prime minister Menachem Begin made peace with Egypt by signing the historic Egypt-Israel Peace Treaty on March 26, 1979. Under the treaty, Israel agreed to withdraw its forces and civilians from the Sinai Peninsula in phases, while Egypt regained full sovereignty over the territory, and the two countries established security arrangements governing their forces in the peninsula.
“At least half of Gaza under tomorrow morning, and the same thing with Lebanon, up to 8, 9, [or] 12 kilometers that are ours. Guys, it won’t be [yours], you’re not coming back. Why? Because you started with us, and that’s the price of war,” Smotrich said.
Though his threat made clear that such an action would only be taken if Egypt attacked Israel, in the wider context of Israel’s post-October 7 security, his words were poorly received in Egypt. Egyptian parliamentarian and journalist Mustafa Bakri described the minister as an “extremist Zionist… thug” and insisted that Cairo could “crush” Israel’s military.
“[Smotrich] thinks Egypt is an open playground. I wish you would read how we crushed your army, you ignorant fool – the ones who did it once are capable of repeating it again.
“The Egyptian army is ready to confront and crush anyone whose soul dares to tamper with national security,” Bakri wrote. “You will surely be taken prisoner, and we’ll throw you in the mental hospital in Khanka. Don’t you dare overstep again, you madman [he said, addressing Smotrich].”
Egyptian TV host: Israel would pay 'heavy price' if it attacked
Egyptian TV host Ahmed Moussa, on Ala Mas’ouleety [Egyptian nightly talk show broadcast on the satellite channel Sada El Balad], also commented on Smotrich’s remarks, responding by insisting that “all 120 million Egyptians would die defending Egypt, and Israel would pay a heavy price if it took any step threatening Egyptian national security.”
Moussa noted Egypt’s success in the Yom Kippur War, during which more than 200 Israeli soldiers were taken prisoner by Egyptian forces, saying that this time there would be no hostages to exchange.
“If you act recklessly, there will be no Israel. You cannot get near an inch of Sinai, and what happened in 1967 will not be repeated with Egypt.”
“We are advocates of peace, but some extremists in the Zionist entity do not want peace. Egypt is a strong country. The war criminal says he will take Sinai. This is harassment and a threat to Egypt. We know what the lesson of 1973 was like for you,” Moussa said.
“You are an illegitimate state. We brought you back with the prisoner exchange, and after that there will be no prisoner exchange because there will be no prisoners.”
'There will be no Tel Aviv, there will be no Ben-Gurion Airport'
Amr Adib, on MBC Egypt, insisted that Cairo had actively worked to defend the border with Israel from any instability, and if the IDF attacked, “There will be no Tel Aviv, there will be no Ben-Gurion Airport, and there will be no Netanyahu.”
“Before you decide to finish us, you will be finished,” he said. “Before you throw us into the sea, you will be in the sewer.”
Egyptian political science professor Hamed Fares told Sky News Arabia that Smotrich’s comments reflected a form of “political adolescence” and demonstrated, in his view, the minister’s ignorance of the region’s power dynamics.
Fares added that he believed Smotrich’s comments, which he described as a “redline” for Egypt, reflected the finance minister’s efforts to maintain a hardline image ahead of the upcoming elections.
Fares said that by portraying neighboring countries as unstable, Smotrich was seeking to create a perceived need for territorial expansion on national security grounds.

Over 400 bereaved partners of IDF soldiers left mourning since Oct. 7, GFIDF reveals on anniversary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:58:01 UTC
20:58:01 KST

Since the start of Israel's war against Hamas, 412 fallen IDF soldiers left behind a bereaved partner or significant other, the organization "A Partner Left Behind" (GFIDF) revealed on Wednesday, the third anniversary of the October 7 massacre.
From the establishment of the organization in 1998 until October 7, only around 500 bereaved partners of killed soldiers had been recorded.
Over a quarter of the soldiers in question, 118, were killed on October 7, 2023. Another 23 bereaved partners faced the death of their significant others only in the last year.
While the oldest recorded bereaved partner was 60 years old, only 4% were over the age of 32. The youngest bereaved partner was 16, with over half (57%) being 21 or younger.
Bereaved partners lose their envisioned future
"Bereaved partners have lost not only the person they loved but also the future they had envisioned together," GFIDF CEO Attorney Adi Alon Sheinberg stated.
"Because they had not yet married, their place within the circle of bereavement is often not fully acknowledged - a fact that only intensifies the difficulty of coping with the loss," she added.
Only 8% of fallen IDF soldiers left behind a bereaved significant other, the organization reported.
"The pain remains; at the organization, we support bereaved partners by providing a therapeutic safety net and a warm community, enabling them to return to a full life - living alongside their grief rather than in its shadow," Sheinberg said.

Ammunition Hill hero and defense innovator Yaki Hetz passes away at age 80
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:57:55 UTC
20:57:55 KST

Yaakov (Yaki) Hetz, a decorated veteran of the battle for Jerusalem’s Ammunition Hill and an Israel Defense Prize laureate, has died, the Ammunition Hill memorial center announced on Facebook on Tuesday.
Hetz, who fought with the 66th Battalion during the Six-Day War, received the Medal of Courage for his actions in the battle and lit a torch at the state ceremony marking Israel’s 69th Independence Day.
Hetz (Haimovitch) was 21 when he fought at Ammunition Hill, becoming one of the figures most closely associated with the historic battle to liberate Jerusalem. After his platoon commander, Yoram Eliashiv, was hit, Hetz took command and continued leading his comrades under heavy fire. He was awarded the Medal of Courage for his bravery and conduct during the battle.
During the fighting, Hetz and fellow soldiers Yehuda Kendal and David Shalom helped overcome a fortified Jordanian bunker that blocked the Israeli advance. After a grenade failed to put the position out of action, the three gathered approximately 20 kilograms of explosives and detonated them against the bunker. The blast brought down a wall and part of the roof, clearing the way forward.
Hetz received a special commendation for his actions at the Battle of the Chinese Farm
Hetz also fought in the Yom Kippur War. Forty years later, he received a special commendation for his actions at the Battle of the Chinese Farm, where he risked his life to rescue wounded soldiers.
His story, however, did not end in the trenches of Ammunition Hill. He later worked in defense development and innovation, contributing to advanced weapons systems at Rafael Advanced Defense Systems.
Among his contributions was the idea that led to the development of the Maoz system, an advanced attack drone used by IDF soldiers. The concept grew out of his experience at Ammunition Hill and his determination to give future soldiers capabilities that he and his comrades had lacked in 1967.
In 1982, Hetz received the Israel Defense Prize for his defense work. In 2017, he was selected to light a torch at the official Independence Day ceremony.
Alongside his military and technological achievements, Hetz dedicated himself to remembrance, education, and preserving Israel’s heritage. For decades, he shared the stories of the soldiers who fought for Jerusalem, meeting generations of young people and recounting the battle and the experiences of his comrades.
Hetz published his autobiography in 2023, three years before his passing
In 2023, he published his autobiography, Baptism of Fire, describing the battle from his own perspective.
His bravery is commemorated at Ammunition Hill’s Six Day War Museum, which preserves the history of the war, the battles for Jerusalem’s liberation and reunification, and the personal stories of those who fought. His testimony and life story form part of the heritage passed on to visitors and future generations.
For Ammunition Hill, Hetz was much more than one of the battle’s heroes. He was an inseparable part of its community, belonging to the generation of soldiers who transformed a battlefield into a living center of remembrance, heritage, and education.
“Yaki Hetz was an inseparable part of Ammunition Hill, not only as one of the heroes of the battle for Jerusalem’s liberation and reunification, but also as a man who devoted his life to action, creation, and passing on our heritage to future generations,” said Menachem Landau, chairman of the board.
“Yaki was a man of many talents, with vast knowledge, a youthful spirit, and boundless curiosity. To us, he was much more than a soldier and a hero of Israel; he was one of the family, a partner on our journey, and a dear friend. His bravery is commemorated in the hill’s Six-Day War Museum, but his legacy lives far beyond the museum’s walls. Today we bid farewell to a man whose life story is intertwined with that of a united Jerusalem, and whose memory will continue to accompany us and future generations.”

Ukraine adds Kyiv trains, prepares pontoon crossings after Russian bridge attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:57:19 UTC
20:57:19 KST

Ukraine's state railway, Ukrzaliznytsia, has added 18 Kyiv City Express shuttle runs between Vydubychi and Darnytsia for 5–9 October, while the government has begun preparatory work on temporary crossings over the Dnipro River after Russian strikes disrupted bridge traffic. Minister for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport Mykola Kalashnyk outlined the backup plan in an interview with Suspilne on 3 October.
About 600,000 vehicles cross the Dnipro in Kyiv each day, making the river crossings critical to movement across the capital, Kalashnyk said. Russia's attacks on the Southern and Northern bridges have disrupted traffic, with the Southern Bridge fully closed to cars and metro on 2 October and restrictions introduced on other crossings. The risk of further damage is heightened by Russia's upgraded jet-powered Geran-4, which now carries a specialized warhead designed to cut through bridge structures and power-line supports, according to presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov.
Jams, restrictions, and extra trains
On 6 October, large traffic jams formed between Kyiv's left and right banks, with the heaviest queues on approaches to the Southern Bridge, Obozrevatel reported. The jams followed Russian strikes that cratered the Northern Bridge.
Green-line metro trains resumed carrying passengers between the banks during the yellow threat level on 4 October, Radio Svoboda reported. Under the current restrictions, traffic on the Southern and Podilskyi bridges is stopped in certain directions for at most the first 15 minutes after an air alert begins.
14 dead in Pryluky, two each in Kyiv, Kremenchuk, and Oleksandriia: Russia’s night of 70 missiles
The additional Kyiv City Express shuttles run during the busiest hours, 06:00–09:00 and 16:00–21:00. Together with scheduled suburban and regional trains, they bring the number of peak-hour runs between the banks to up to six, Ukrzaliznytsia said.
Pontoons first, tunnel later
Kalashnyk said the government plans to build several backup crossings over the Dnipro. The sites have already been chosen, and he named a combination of earth embankments and pontoon crossings as measures that can be built quickly. He said construction could take up to three months and that the backup crossings should provide at least 50% of the capacity of the existing bridges. The government is also considering quick-build concrete structures and, in the longer term, a tunnel under the Dnipro, he told Suspilne.
Volodymyr Kreidenko, deputy head of the parliamentary committee on transport and infrastructure and an MP from the Servant of the People party, proposed reversible traffic across the bridges: "in the morning from the left bank to the right, in the evening from the right to the left." He also suggested hubs near the bridges where people could take a bicycle or e-scooter, and passenger ferry crossings, Radio Svoboda reported.
Andrii Koretskyi, an associate professor in the department of bridges, tunnels and hydraulic structures at the National Transport University, cautioned that temporary crossings cannot substitute for a permanent bridge.
"The only alternative to a bridge is a bridge as a permanent structure," he told Radio Svoboda.
He said a tunnel under the Dnipro is technically possible but "not a quick solution at all." He pointed to the scale involved: where the Irpin River requires spanning a few dozen or, in places, a few hundred meters, the Dnipro within Kyiv is "roughly 400 to 1,500 meters" wide.

They survived October 7. Now they’re divided over who should rule Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:57:07 UTC
20:57:07 KST

They survived October 7. Now they’re divided over who should rule Israel
For residents of Israel’s Gaza Envelope, the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023, was not an abstract national trauma. Communities close to the Gaza border were among the first to come under assault, and residents spent hours locked in safe rooms, hiding from gunmen and rocket fire. Three years later, that shared experience has produced sharply different political conclusions among people living in the same region.
Michal Koren Kariv, a 50-year-old filmmaker from Kibbutz Mefalsim, remembers that morning all too well. As Hamas launched its deadly assault on communities across southern Israel, her family remained inside their home as armed militants reached the area. They spent hours in a protected room without electricity, unsure of what was happening outside.
When the family was finally able to leave, Koren Kariv says she saw devastation on a scale she had never witnessed before. The experience, she says, fundamentally changed her relationship with the state.
“I no longer believe anything,” she said. “Simply nothing.”
Accountability is a must
For her, the coming election is largely about the demand for a state commission of inquiry into October 7, an investigation that would establish what went wrong, who knew what and when, and which decisions or institutional failures contributed to the disaster. She says she plans to vote for those who promise to get to the bottom of those failures.
“I believe that whoever was prime minister when the attack occurred must bear political responsibility. Netanyahu was the head back then, so he should have resigned. I am not saying I won’t be voting for a right-wing party. All I am saying is that Netanyahu should not be prime minister.”
Koren Kariv says she has never voted for Netanyahu’s Likud, but she has never been in the so-called “anti-Bibi camp,” simply because she acknowledges the positive things Netanyahu has done for the country. She also recognizes that the current government has invested heavily in rebuilding the southern communities.
Shortly after the attacks, the Israeli government established the Tkuma administration to oversee reconstruction and recovery in communities damaged or evacuated after the massacre. Government figures show a multibillion-shekel reconstruction program covering housing, infrastructure, education, community services, and economic recovery.
Koren Kariv acknowledges that the Gaza Envelope has received substantial investment since the attack, including new construction, educational funding and a stronger military presence. But she draws a distinction between rebuilding communities physically and addressing the political and institutional failures she believes preceded the attack.
“The question here is not simply whether houses have been rebuilt or money has been allocated. I want to know why the country was so unprepared, whether warnings were missed and who should have acted differently. So my conclusion is therefore not that the state has done nothing. Rather, that reconstruction cannot substitute for an investigation into the failures that preceded the attack.”
Tilting towards the right
A few kilometers away, Sami Danieli, a 65-year-old former security officer from the religious moshav of Shibolim near Sderot, drew a very different lesson from October 7.
Unlike many other communities in the Gaza Envelope that experienced direct infiltration by militants, his moshav was relatively protected. Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad reached its outskirts but did not enter. Residents nevertheless sheltered as rockets fell, and Danieli says he lost close friends in neighboring communities that bore the brunt of the attack.
Even before October 7, Danieli had voted for National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who supports the expulsion of Palestinians and promotes settlement activity in the West Bank and Gaza. The events of October 7 did not weaken that support. They reinforced it.
“If I could vote for Ben Gvir twice, I would do so,” he said.
“I don’t believe there can be peace with Hamas, and that’s why Israel needs to take a tougher approach in its security policy.”
Ben-Gvir has said he would pursue a tougher security policy if he were given the defense portfolio following the election. As national security minister, he has already pursued a series of hardline measures towards Palestinians. These include worsening conditions for Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails, backing legislation imposing the death penalty for people convicted of terrorism, and distributing thousands of firearms to Israelis living in areas considered vulnerable to Palestinian attacks.
Danieli says he supports those measures. He remains firmly behind the right-wing bloc headed by Netanyahu and rejects claims that the current government bears responsibility for Israel’s failure to prevent or decisively end the war.
Instead, he points to anti-government protests and other factors that he believes constrained Israel’s ability to defeat Hamas.
“The anti-government protesters were the ones who weakened the country with their demonstrations. Then, when the war happened, total victory was not achieved partially due to the restrictions imposed by the Americans [under the Biden administration – ed.] and partially because of ammunition shortages.
“Netanyahu’s performance during the war was excellent though. Not very good – it was excellent.”
Danieli also gives the government credit for the reconstruction effort in the south.
“Government assistance reached the region and funds were provided, but of course there will always be people who will say that this is not enough,” he said.
“I believe that much of the criticism is coming from residents who are politically motivated. Eighty percent of them have a political agenda and this anti-Bibi bias prevents them from seeing the truth. This is why I don’t want the left to come to power. The right-wing must stay and rule,” he added.
Uncertainty prevails
Polling, however, shows that the hopes of Danieli might not materialize.
Reuters’ polling tracker, updated in late September, showed the centrist Yashar party led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot narrowly ahead of Likud in the polling average. The aggregate projected 66 seats for parties opposed to Netanyahu and 48 for parties supporting him, while also noting that the anti-Netanyahu camp did not have an obvious coalition path to the 61-seat threshold.
Individual polls by Israeli television channels and news outlets have produced different results. A Kan survey reported in late September put Yashar at 23 seats and Likud at 21, with the two main blocs each projected at 52 mandates.
A Times of Israel poll published on October 1 likewise found Netanyahu’s bloc ahead but still short of the 61 seats required to form a government on its own. Likud and Yashar were tied for first place among individual parties.
Israel uses nationwide proportional representation. Parties must pass a 3.25% electoral threshold to enter the Knesset, and a governing coalition requires the support of at least 61 of the parliament’s 120 members.
For the residents of the Gaza Envelope, however, the numbers on a polling chart tell only part of the story.
They lived through the same morning, heard the same rockets and waited behind the same locked doors for help to arrive. Yet, three years later, their memories of October 7 have taken them in opposite political directions.
Koren Kariv sees the election as a test of accountability, a chance to establish why the state failed and who should answer for it. Danieli sees it as a test of resolve, an argument for maintaining the political course he believes offers the strongest security.
Three years on, the communities closest to Gaza are no longer simply asking how they survived October 7. They are asking what the country should become because of it. And when they enter the voting booth, those two questions will lead them to very different answers.

The Zionist Regime; One Spark Away from Collapse from Within
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:56:03 UTC
20:56:03 KST

Prolonged wars, economic pressure, political disputes, and rising social discontent have pushed Israeli society into a phase whose consequences are being warned about even in American security circles.
 
According to a confidential report attributed to the US Central Intelligence Agency, experts at the agency have warned about the possibility of civil war or political collapse in the occupied territories. This report, prepared under the title "Infiltration from Within," examines a set of pressures that, if simultaneous, could confront the political and social stability of the Zionist regime with a serious crisis; from the increase in military costs and economic pressure to the mental and psychological problems of forces returning from war, the dispute over Haredi military service, and Benjamin Netanyahu's effort to preserve power.
 
The aforementioned report also refers to the rise in food prices and the costs that Israeli society has incurred as a result of warmongering policies. The issue is not just the rising price of goods; rather, the increase in living costs has occurred under conditions in which a significant portion of the regime's financial resources is spent on military operations and covering security costs. Under such circumstances, war is no longer merely a matter related to the battlefield and has directly entered the daily lives of citizens.
 
This is precisely the point at which a security crisis can turn into a social crisis. A society that, for a short period, is willing to tolerate economic and social pressures under the influence of a wartime atmosphere, if it feels that the war has become prolonged, costs have increased, and there is no clear prospect for its end, will gradually raise other questions: What are these costs for? Who is responsible for the continuation of this situation? And have the continuation of current policies really created more security?
 
In the Zionist regime, these questions are also tied to an older fissure; the fissure among different groups of society over the extent of participation in the military and security project. The dispute over Haredi military service is a clear example of this issue. Under normal conditions, such a dispute might be considered merely a political or legal controversy, but when a regime is engaged in a prolonged war and repeatedly sends a large part of its forces to the field, the feeling of discrimination in the distribution of the burden of war can become a factor in intensifying social divisions.
 
On the other hand, the return of military forces from a long period of conflict can itself have widespread social and psychological consequences. Mental pressures, exhaustion, psychological damage, and the difficulty of returning to normal life are not issues that disappear with the end of a military operation. The more the scope and duration of the conflict increase, the more the number of individuals who return to society with such an experience also increases. Therefore, part of the cost of war may manifest itself when the battlefield is no longer at the center of media attention.
 
Alongside all these factors, the political crisis also persists. Netanyahu's performance and his effort to preserve his political position is one of the main axes of internal disputes in the Zionist regime. The important issue is that when the political fate of a politician becomes tied to the continuation of a security crisis, the boundary between security decision and political expediency can become ambiguous for public opinion. In such a situation, every new military decision may, in addition to security consequences, also acquire a political interpretation.
This situation becomes even more significant especially on the eve of elections. Elections in any society can intensify political disputes, but in a society that is simultaneously facing economic pressure, casualties, military exhaustion, and social divisions, electoral competition can become a ground for the emergence of deeper fissures. For this reason, the warning about the possibility of a "spark" forming is important; because major social crises do not always necessarily begin with one big dispute. Sometimes a collection of small and accumulated disputes needs only one incident to turn into a widespread crisis.
The more important point is the issue of the Zionist regime's increasing isolation on the international stage. Over the past decades, this regime has obtained an important part of its power not only from military capability, but from the political and economic support of America and extensive relations with Western countries. Therefore, any sign of a reduction in this support can have psychological and political effects beyond a diplomatic dispute. A society that sees itself as losing external backing may also fall into doubt about its leaders' ability to manage the future.
Of course, the possibility of political collapse or civil war should not be taken to mean its definite occurrence. The Zionist regime still possesses powerful military, security, and political structures and has considerable ability to manage crises. But the important issue is that the set of pressures that existed separately in recent years are now becoming simultaneous. It is this very simultaneity that can turn a potential vulnerability into a real crisis.
In fact, the main point of weakness may lie not at the borders, but within society. A regime can respond to a missile attack, a military operation, or external pressure with security tools, but confronting public distrust, the erosion of social capital, division among different groups, and dissatisfaction with political performance is far more difficult.
The importance of this report lies precisely here. This time, the discussion is not just about the failure of an operation or a setback on a specific battlefield; the discussion is about the capacity of a political structure to withstand accumulated pressures. If economic pressure, war-induced exhaustion, social divisions, political crisis, and reduced foreign support intensify simultaneously, even a limited incident can become the starting point of a larger crisis.
The Zionist regime has for years tried to present an image of power, cohesion, and permanent security. But if this image erodes from within society, an issue arises that cannot be solved with military power. Perhaps the greatest threat to this regime will ultimately not be an attack from outside; rather, it will be the very fissure that has gradually expanded from within.
And it is precisely for this reason that today's issue is not only how much military capability Israel has on the battlefield; the more important issue is how much capacity Israeli society has to tolerate the continuation of this situation. If this tolerance reaches its endpoint, one spark can ignite a crisis whose containment will be very difficult for the political structure of the Zionist regime.

Lithuania extends protections for Ukrainians, adds condition for potential servicemen

20:55:00 KST

Lithuania’s government has extended temporary protection for Ukrainians fleeing Russia’s war through March 2028, while introducing a new requirement for some people subject to military service in Ukraine.
Under the new rules, Ukrainians subject to military service will have to provide proof that they have fulfilled their military obligations to qualify for temporary protection.
Acceptable proof will include evidence of a lawful departure from Ukraine, an exit stamp in a passport, or an official document showing that the person is exempt from military service or has completed it.
The requirement will not apply to people who were granted temporary protection in any European Union country before August 4, or who had applied for temporary protection in Lithuania by that date but had not yet received a decision.
Under the previous rules, temporary protection in Lithuania was due to expire March 4 next year. The government has now extended it for another year, through March 2028.
The Interior Ministry said about 52,000 people currently hold valid Lithuanian temporary residence permits based on temporary protection.
The EU activated temporary protection for Ukrainians after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, allowing those fleeing the war to live, work and receive social benefits in the 27-member bloc.
This year, following a request from Kyiv for help with personnel needed for the war effort, the EU said temporary protection would no longer apply to people arriving in the bloc who are subject to military service in Ukraine.
Under Ukraine’s wartime laws, men ages 23 to 60 are generally prohibited from leaving the country.
About 4.4 million Ukrainians currently live in the EU under temporary protection, according to EU data. Germany, Poland and the Czech Republic host the largest Ukrainian communities.
Adult men account for about 27% of Ukrainians currently receiving temporary protection in the EU, while women account for 43% and minors for 30%.
The EU said last year that it wanted to move away from the current temporary protection system by offering Ukrainians options for longer-term legal residence in the bloc or assistance to those who wish to return home when conditions allow.

From Qeshm to Tabas: exploring Iran’s remarkable geodiversity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:54:16 UTC
20:54:16 KST

From Qeshm to Tabas: exploring Iran’s remarkable geodiversity
TEHRAN - Iran can be described as a land of remarkable geological diversity, where high mountain ranges, deserts and plains, caves, rock formations, salt domes, valleys, springs, coastlines and erosion-shaped landscapes coexist across its vast territory. This diversity is the result of Iran’s complex geological history and the processes that have shaped the country over millions of years, from the movement and collision of tectonic plates to folding, faulting, volcanic activity, sedimentation and erosion.
International Geodiversity Day, observed on October 6, provides an opportunity to draw attention to this lesser-known dimension of the Earth’s natural heritage. It is also a reminder that protecting nature goes beyond conserving plant and animal species. Rocks, soils, water, minerals, fossils, caves, mountains and landscapes are all part of the planet’s natural capital and geological memory.
Protecting geodiversity, therefore, means safeguarding the history of the Earth, the resources upon which human societies depend, and the foundations of life in the future.
The importance of geodiversity extends far beyond the aesthetic value of natural landscapes. Every geological feature can tell part of the Earth’s history and provide researchers with valuable information about climate change, ancient environments, the formation of mountains and sedimentary basins, and even major events in the history of life. Geological structures are also closely linked to groundwater resources, soils, mineral deposits and the formation of habitats. For this reason, conserving geodiversity is an integral part of protecting a country’s natural capital.
One of the most distinctive examples of Iran’s geological diversity can be found in the south of the country, on Qeshm Island, where tectonic and erosional processes have created a remarkable collection of geological formations and landforms. The UNESCO Global Geopark of Qeshm lies in the southern Zagros Mountains, an area whose geological characteristics have been shaped by the collision of the Arabian and Eurasian plates. The Namakdan salt dome and salt complex, Namakdan Cave, Stars Valley and Chahkooh Canyon are among the area’s most prominent geological features. UNESCO describes Namakdan Cave, with its multicolored galleries and salt crystals, as one of the outstanding elements of Qeshm’s geological heritage.
In northwestern Iran, the Aras UNESCO Global Geopark offers a different picture of the country’s geological diversity. The region contains a wide range of rocks dating from different geological periods, including Paleozoic and Mesozoic carbonate rocks, igneous rocks and sedimentary deposits. One of the geopark’s most important geosites is the Alibashi area, which contains rock and fossil sequences associated with the Permian-Triassic boundary and is internationally significant for the study of one of the major events in Earth’s history. The Aras Geopark was added to UNESCO’s Global Geoparks Network in 2023, with around 30 geosites identified across the area.
Central Iran is home to the Tabas UNESCO Global Geopark, another major expression of the country’s geodiversity, known for the extent and variety of its geological features. The inclusion of Tabas alongside Qeshm and Aras on UNESCO’s list of Global Geoparks demonstrates that Iran’s geological diversity is not confined to a particular region or type of landscape. Valuable examples of the country’s geological heritage can be found across a wide range of environments and regions.
Geoparks, meanwhile, are not simply areas established to display geological features or serve as tourism destinations. The Global Geopark concept seeks to link the conservation of geological heritage with education, research, sustainable tourism and the participation of local communities. In Qeshm, for example, UNESCO has emphasized the connection between natural heritage conservation and sustainable livelihoods, including activities related to geological heritage and tourism. In Aras, geological heritage forms part of a broader natural and cultural heritage landscape encompassing a range of natural and historical attractions.
The mountains, caves, valleys, deserts and geological formations found across Iran contain part of the country’s natural memory and stand as records of the Earth’s evolution. Once destroyed, many of the processes and geological evidence accumulated over millions of years cannot be recreated.
Identifying and documenting geosites, protecting them, raising public awareness and promoting responsible tourism can therefore help turn this lesser-known natural asset into a more prominent component of the country’s broader efforts to conserve its natural heritage.

A Film Found in Britain May Turn Out to Be the First Sound Film in History
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:50:26 EEST
20:50:26 KST

A Film Found in Britain May Turn Out to Be the First Sound Film in History
Kyiv • UNN
Till the Bells Ring was shown in Edinburgh in 1926 with synchronized dialogue. The film may be the first sound feature-length film.
For nearly a century, the film "The Jazz Singer" was considered the world's first feature-length film with synchronized dialogue (the so-called "talkie"), which cemented English's status as the first language of cinema. However, a chance discovery threatens to overturn our understanding of film history: it has emerged that the title may have belonged to another film, released a year earlier—a movie made in Glasgow and written in Scots. The Guardian reports, UNN writes.
Details
The discovery was made by historian and self-proclaimed "film buff" Mark David Jacobs. He was researching material for a book about the first wave of British talking cinema when he came across the story of the film Till the Bells Ring.
The 45-minute feature film, with dialogue and synchronized sound throughout, was first shown in Edinburgh in October 1926—one year before "The Jazz Singer," starring Al Jolson, was released in New York, causing a major sensation and going down in film history.
This was the beginning of what we today regard as modern cinema. At the time, it was an entirely new art form, and if Britain had embraced it, the history of cinema might have been completely different, with the Americans not gaining such an advantage or establishing such dominance
Till the Bells Ring was created by Scottish playwright Graham Moffat. It is a domestic comedy set in Glasgow. The film featured Moffat's troupe of six actors, which toured the country, including his wife Margaret and daughter Winifred. The author himself called the language of the film "lowland braid Scots"—a term for the simple Scottish dialect spoken in central and southern parts of Scotland.
At the time, the film was advertised as "a super-sound picture… about the life of a Victorian family," and after its premiere it was described as a cinematic milestone. In a review, the Edinburgh Evening News wrote that even America had not attempted anything similar, while the synchronization between the images on screen and the Scottish dialogue was so perfect that it might have seemed as though the viewer were listening to a stage version of the comedy.
However, according to Jacobs, the film was quickly forgotten. "It is part of the broader history of British cinema, which has been astonishingly neglected. I think that if it had been regarded as a purely Scottish production, it might have survived or been found earlier. But it was placed in the category of British cinema, and there is not much sense that the history of British cinema is worth researching at all," he said.
There is no evidence that the film was ever shown publicly again after its week-long run at Edinburgh's Poole’s Synod Hall, on the site of which the Traverse Theatre now stands. Moffat died in 1951 without making another film.

Europe’s ability to buy gas before winter limited by Asia’s LNG price premium
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:47:37 UTC
20:47:37 KST

MOSCOW, October 7. /TASS/. Europe faces constraints on its ability to purchase LNG on global markets as regional gas prices lag behind Asian prices, which command a premium for suppliers, ahead of the heating season, according to a TASS analysis of key gas indices in the two regions.
Asian spot LNG prices based on the JKM index have consistently exceeded prices at Europe’s most liquid hub, the TTF in the Netherlands, since the second half of September. On average, gas prices on the Asian market have been 8% higher than in Europe over this period. This currently makes the Asia-Pacific region a more attractive and profitable destination for LNG suppliers.
Against this backdrop, Europe is still falling short of last year’s record LNG import levels. Meanwhile, European Union countries continue injecting gas into their underground storage facilities ahead of winter, although the pace of stockbuilding will soon slow significantly. The warm weather seen at the beginning of the month will give way to more typical fall temperatures by the end of the week.
As of October 5, Europe’s underground gas storage facilities were 72.83% full, 15.13 percentage points below the five-year average for that date, compared with 82.9% a year earlier. This remains the lowest level for that date since records began in 2011. EU storage facilities contain around 79.8 bln cubic meters of gas, 11.7 bln cubic meters less than a year ago and the lowest level since 2013. Gazprom has forecast that European gas storage levels may not even reach 75% and that the region faces a difficult fall-winter season.
TASS reported earlier that Europe risks entering the heating season with record-low gas reserves. By the traditional start of the fall-winter period, EU countries may have their storage facilities only 70-75% full, which would be the lowest level ever recorded at the start of the heating season.
Under European Commission requirements, EU countries must ensure that their gas storage facilities are 90% full at some point between October 1 and December 1 each year. A 10% flexibility is permitted if storage-filling conditions are difficult. Thus, net injections into European storage facilities ahead of the 2026-2027 fall-winter period must total at least 68 bln cubic meters to meet the storage target. However, in hopes of a very warm winter, the European Commission is prepared to lower the target to 80% this year.

Russia's jet-powered attack drones could eventually reach 800–900 km/h, and intercepting them will demand new piloting skills—so Ukraine has asked the makers of its interceptor drones to build simulators to train the crews, a senior Air Force officer told a parliamentary commission on 6 October, Suspilne reported.
Russia keeps modifying its jet Shaheds faster than Ukraine can field the drones meant to catch them, and Kyiv is now preparing crews for speeds its interceptors have never faced—a sign the air war is shifting from a contest of volume to one of raw speed.
The speed Russia hasn't reached yet
Colonel Yurii Cherevashenko, deputy commander of Ukraine's Air Force, told the commission that Russia's jet drones fly at around 600 km/h today but could eventually reach 800–900 km/h—speeds he said have not been recorded so far. That range sits near the cruising speed of a commercial airliner.
Ukraine just caught a Geran-5 at 425 km/h—the jet drone that has often outrun Ukrainian interceptor drones since January
Intercepting such targets will take specific piloting skills, Cherevashenko said. When an interceptor and its target move at roughly the same speed, he noted, the pilot barely perceives the difference in their speeds. To train for that, Ukrainian interceptor-drone makers have been tasked with building simulators where crews can practice against high-speed targets.
Where Ukraine stands now
Ukraine already downs 85% to 90% of Russia's slower, propeller-driven drones, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, but the jet models remain a tougher problem—Ukrainian interceptors scored their reportedly first kill of a jet-powered Shahed in November 2025. In a 28 September evening address, Zelenskyy put the jet-drone interception rate at about 57%, lower than required. Days later, he said Ukraine is testing five interceptor-drone models and could be producing about 400 of one of them by the end of October. Asked when jet-drone interceptors would arrive at the scale needed, Cherevashenko answered: "Not before the end of November."

Investigators estimate the two stole and potentially passed on more than 2,000 secret documents between 2010 and 2023. Federal investigators say it is unclear how much information was stolen and to whom it was sold.
Hanning ran the BND, Germany's foreign intelligence service, from 1998 until 2005 before becoming state secretary at the Federal Interior Ministry and then entering private business as a security adviser.
The issue has raised serious questions about the trustworthiness of Germany's intelligence agencies and shocked politicians into action as they claim not enough is being done to ensure high-ranking officials do not abuse their experience when transitioning to jobs in the private sector.
Who was Hanning selling data to?
Although it is currently not known who Hanning's potential customers were, Germany's weekly Der Spiegel magazine on Wednesday named Azerbaijan as one. The Azerbaijan Media and Broadcasting Council vehemently denied the accusation, calling it "unfounded" and adding, "The malicious intent of the forces behind this disinformation operation is to damage Azerbaijan-Germany relations."

Kenya Ebola case exposes gaps in border screenings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:44:14 UTC
20:44:14 KST

Kenya Ebola case exposes gaps in border screenings
NAIROBI/DAKAR, Oct 7 - By the time Kenya's first Ebola patient was whisked to a hospital by relatives straight after landing at Nairobi airport, he was already exhibiting some classic symptoms - fever, chills, muscle pain and bleeding beneath the skin.
Two days later he was dead, leaving public health experts to piece together how he had managed to transit through three countries and evade layers of screening meant to stop the ongoing outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo from spreading to neighbouring states.
Details about the man, a Kenyan national whose identity has not been made public, remain scant, but Kenyan officials have confirmed he travelled overland from the city of Beni, in northeastern Congo, to Uganda's capital Kampala, where he stayed one night before flying to Kenya.
The itinerary required traversing the border between Congo and Uganda, which has been closed since May.
The man would also have had to pass through multiple airport temperature checks - in Nairobi and Entebbe - and fill out at least two digital forms intended to flag any potential exposure to Ebola in Congo.
The case underscores the lapses in border screening systems in Africa and beyond that depend on effective implementation and honest disclosure on the part of travellers, according to health experts and officials who spoke to Reuters.
"This underlines the need (to strengthen) screening procedures, including know-how on posing the 'right' questions," said Thomas Paerisch, a public health specialist recently deployed to Congo with medical charity Medecins Sans Frontieres.
A POROUS BORDER CROSSING
Kenya's Health Minister Aden Duale said on Tuesday the man had been living in Congo for seven years and fell ill there about a month before arriving in Nairobi, though it is unclear when exactly he became infected with Ebola.
An itinerary shared by the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention showed his recent travels included a domestic flight in Congo across three Ebola-affected provinces before he moved by road from Beni to Kampala.
Uganda closed its border with Congo in late May to limit the spread of Ebola after recording several cases linked to individuals who had crossed from Congo. Ugandan authorities declared the country Ebola-free in late July.
But a Ugandan health ministry source involved in Ebola preparedness efforts acknowledged that the porous nature of the border made it impossible to make the closure watertight.
Ugandan government spokesperson Alan Kasujja said Kampala was not to blame.
"Leave Uganda out of this conversation. We don't have Ebola here," he said in a post on X.
A health ministry statement on Tuesday said the man had "normal temperature" when he was screened at Entebbe airport. Kenyan authorities have also said he could have taken medication to mask his symptoms when he was screened at Nairobi airport.
"We are trying to retrieve the digital form he would have filled out at Entebbe airport when he went through the thermal scanning process to see what he declared in that form. The form includes questions about recent health problems but also whether a traveller was recently in DRC," Dr. Richard Mugahi, a senior Ugandan health official, told Reuters.
"We are also going through airport security camera footage to see if we can identify the driver who dropped him at the airport so we can trace any contacts here."
Duale, Kenya's health minister, said on Wednesday 57 contacts of the dead man had been listed, including 10 who had been quarantined. "Efforts to trace the rest have been intensified," he said.
A dedicated gate for screening passengers arriving from Congo and other countries potentially linked to the Ebola outbreak has now been set up at Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, Duale added.
SYMPTOMS HARD TO DETECT
The current Ebola outbreak, Congo's worst on record, has infected more than 8,000 people and killed more than 4,000. It is caused by the rare Bundibugyo species, for which there is no known treatment or vaccine.
Experts said early symptoms may be hard to detect and medication including paracetamol can foil temperature checks.
Infrared thermometers used in airports measure surface rather than core body temperature, which can cause them to miss some infections, said Kamran Khan, an infectious disease physician and professor at the University of Toronto.
Screening also involves health declarations and visual assessments, but travellers may choose not to disclose symptoms.
Rose Tchwenko, DRC Country Director at Prosper Global, flew from Kinshasa to Nairobi last month and said border surveillance measures at both airports were very limited.
Before boarding, she was asked to fill out an online form about her health status and any symptoms to generate a QR code. On arrival, she underwent a temperature check and handed over the QR code. "The whole process takes less than two minutes, then you leave. Since then, no one has contacted me to check if I have developed symptoms." REUTERS

Rural women lead efforts to restore mangrove forests
TEHRAN – Rural women in southern Hormozgan Province are taking an active role in restoring mangrove forests and protecting the Shour–Shirin–Minab International Wetland, one of the country’s ecologically important coastal habitats.
In the village of Tiab, local women have been trained to collect mangrove seeds, prepare soil, raise seedlings and manage nurseries as part of an initiative designed to link environmental conservation with sustainable livelihoods.
The project was implemented by Mashgh Afarinesh Va Toseye Paydar with support from the GEF Small Grants Programme (SGP) of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and funding through the ICCA-GSI. It was carried out in cooperation with the Provincial Natural Resources and Watershed Management Organization, UNDP reported.
Training sessions and practical workshops equipped participants with the skills needed to establish and maintain a small-scale mangrove nursery. The initiative subsequently resulted in the establishment of Tiab’s first women-led mangrove nursery, with a capacity of around 1,500 seedlings.
The nursery has provided a practical means of contributing to ecosystem restoration while creating an opportunity for local women to generate supplementary income through environmentally sustainable activities.
For those involved, the work has also created a strong personal connection with the environment.
“We nurtured these seedlings with our own hands, just like our own children,” said Mehri Zarei, a member of the Tiab Women’s Green Nursery. “Planting each mangrove felt like giving birth to hope all over again. When I placed the roots into the mud, I felt as if I was becoming a mother once more, this time, to the Earth.”
The project has also promoted cooperation among communities in the region. Women from Tiab have shared their experiences with groups in neighboring villages, including Chah Sahari, where similar activities have been introduced.
The exchange has enabled the participating communities to share practical knowledge on mangrove seed collection, irrigation and nursery management, helping build local capacity for long-term conservation.
The experience in Tiab highlights the role that community-led initiatives can play in addressing environmental challenges while strengthening rural livelihoods. By involving women directly in conservation and restoration activities, the project has helped turn local participation into a practical tool for protecting one of southern Iran’s valuable coastal ecosystems.

Justina Shiroka Pula: Kosovo’s new president, elected during a crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:40:21 UTC
20:40:21 KST

Justina Shiroka Pula: Kosovo’s new president, elected during a crisis
An academic, former minister and a compromise choice, Pula was voted in by parliament amid protests.
Kosovo’s election of a new president has brought an end to heightened tensions in parliament and possibly on the streets.
On Tuesday, protests against the convictions of former Kosovo Liberation Army leaders coincided with a midnight deadline to elect a president.
Ultimately, the ruling Vetevendosje Movement (LVV) and opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo (PDK) reached an agreement on her candidacy, clearing the way for a parliamentary vote.
Lawmakers elected Justina Shiroka Pula to the country’s top office in the first minutes of Wednesday, close to the constitutional deadline, averting new early parliamentary elections that could have pushed the country into a deeper crisis.
The 81 votes she secured – one more than the two-thirds, 80-vote threshold required – were the result of a pragmatic compromise.
The parties also agreed to adopt amendments changing the legal framework governing the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, the Hague-based court established to try former Kosovo Liberation Army leaders for alleged war crimes – an issue demonstrators had been urging politicians to address.
After a prolonged period of political deadlock, none of Kosovo’s political parties appeared willing to take responsibility for triggering another election.
“I see the election of Justina Shiroka Pula as a mix of political necessity and the need to stabilise institutions,” Donika Emini, a research fellow at the University of Graz’s Centre for Southeast European Studies, told Al Jazeera.
Kosovo had already been in a prolonged political limbo, she said, with election fatigue and increasing public dissatisfaction with the political elite.
After the Specialist Chambers verdict and 20 days of protests, including violent incidents in Pristina on the night before the presidential vote, “going into yet another election would have carried a high political cost for everyone,” Emini said.
“I see this as more than a temporary fix, but I wouldn’t read it as proof that the underlying polarisation has been resolved.
“It was, above all, a politically necessary compromise to restore institutional functioning.”
Who is Shiroka Pula, Kosovo’s third woman president?
Shiroka Pula’s election extends the run of women leading Kosovo. The 73-year-old is the country’s third female president, after Atifete Jahjaga and Vjosa Osmani.
Born in Pristina in 1953, Shiroka Pula brings to the presidency a career spanning academia, public institutions and politics.
After graduating from the University of Pristina’s economics faculty, she completed postgraduate studies in the theory and policy of economic development at the Faculty of Economics in Zagreb, then in Yugoslavia. She later earned a doctorate, researching the relationship between demographic investment and Kosovo’s economic development.
After a brief period working at the National Bank of Kosovo, Shiroka Pula began a long academic career back at the University of Pristina, rising from assistant lecturer to professor and heading the department of management and informatics.
Last December, she became the first woman to be elected head of the Kosovo Academy of Sciences and Arts, known by its Albanian acronym ASHAK.
Her path to the presidency, however, has not been solely academic.
Shiroka Pula served as Kosovo’s minister of energy and mining from 2008 to 2011. She was then a PDK member of parliament from 2011 to 2014.
That record means she should not be portrayed simply as a non-partisan academic, Emini said.
“She has a substantial political and institutional background,” Emini told Al Jazeera. “She was minister of energy and mining from 2008 to 2011 and a PDK member of the Assembly from 2011 to 2014.
“She has also had a long academic career and has worked extensively with civil society, which in Kosovo had an extensive state-building role for a long period of time,” Emini added.
The combination gives Shiroka Pula a strong understanding of Kosovo’s political and institutional landscape, as well as experience that could allow her to act as a counterbalance between institutions.
Her name was already acceptable to different political actors and was seen as less confrontational than other prospective candidates, according to Emini.
“The outcome was driven by urgency, but it also opens an opportunity to move Kosovo out of a long period of institutional paralysis,” she said.
Unlike the previous presidential arrangement, Shiroka Pula begins her term with backing from the ruling LVV and the PDK, giving her a broad political base from the outset.
But the extent of her political room for manoeuvre will depend on the relationships she develops with the Democratic League of Kosovo (LDK) and other opposition parties, as well as on the team she assembles in her office.
“The question is less whether she has that experience and more whether she will have the political courage and institutional backing to use it independently,” Emini said.
Hopes for a ‘more coordinated’ leadership
Kosovo’s president has limited formal executive powers. Yet the office carries political and diplomatic weight: The president represents the country at home and abroad, helps safeguard institutional continuity, and can mediate when relations between political parties are blocked.
Shiroka Pula’s academic, institutional and international exposure may also make her an appealing figure to Kosovo’s international partners, Emini said. But her influence will depend on how she uses the political and diplomatic space offered by the office, and on her relationship with the government.
Historically, Kosovo’s presidents have at times played a more active foreign policy role than the constitutional division of responsibilities might suggest, depending on the individual and on their relationship with the prime minister.
“I hope this presidency will bring a more coordinated foreign policy among the president, the prime minister and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs,” Emini said. “The tensions between the previous president and the government showed how costly poor inter-institutional coordination can be, including on important processes such as Kosovo’s Council of Europe membership.”

Russia Is Building Tanks From the Parts Bin—and Rebuilding 360 T-72s a Year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:39:35 UTC
20:39:35 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
Russia Is Building Tanks From the Parts Bin—and Rebuilding 360 T-72s a Year
Russia is replenishing its battered tank fleet faster than previously believed, upgrading roughly 360 stored T-72s a year and assembling T-80UE-1s from old turrets, recovered hulls, and previously damaged vehicles.
Russia’s defense industry appears to have increased the rate at which stored T-72A tanks are converted into modernized T-72B3Ms to roughly 360 vehicles per year, according to Defense Express, citing OSINT researchers Jompy and T-90AK on October 7.
That figure is notable because previous estimates suggested Russia could upgrade around 200 T-72As annually at Uralvagonzavod.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russia’s T-72 rebuild rate almost twice what was expected
If the newer estimate is accurate, Moscow is processing its Soviet-era tank reserves at nearly twice the previously assumed pace.
The T-72B3M upgrade involves significantly more than simply returning old vehicles to working condition. The modernization includes an improved fire-control system, Relikt explosive reactive armor, and the more powerful 1,130-horsepower V-92S2F engine, bringing stored T-72As closer to the standard of Russia’s current frontline main battle tanks.
Defense Express notes that the higher conversion rate changes calculations about how long Russia can continue drawing on its remaining T-72A reserve.
Earlier estimates suggested the available stock could keep Uralvagonzavod occupied for roughly another four years, but a faster rebuild tempo would consume those reserves considerably sooner unless additional vehicles are found elsewhere.
T-80UE-1s are being pieced together from existing stocks
Russia is reportedly taking an even more unconventional approach to the T-80UE-1. According to the OSINT findings cited by Defense Express, Russian industry still has a stock of T-80UD turrets that can be installed on restored hulls from damaged or decommissioned T-80B and T-80U tanks.
By combining those available components, Russian factories can effectively produce additional T-80UE-1s without manufacturing an entirely new tank from scratch.
There is currently no reliable estimate for how many such vehicles Russia can assemble each year.
The T-80UE-1 itself is not a new design. The modernization program dates back to the 2000s and originally involved upgrading T-80BV tanks with the fighting compartment of the T-80UD, the 1A45 fire-control system, and the 9K119 Refleks guided-missile complex.
At the time, the project proved too expensive for large-scale production, and only a few dozen vehicles were reportedly built. Defense Express argues that Russia’s willingness to return to the concept now reflects the pressure created by years of heavy armored-vehicle losses and the need to extract additional combat-ready tanks from whatever usable Soviet-era components remain available.
What Russia does with its remaining T-72As
It remains unclear whether Moscow intends to convert every available T-72A into a conventional T-72B3M or reserve part of the fleet for other programs.
One possibility highlighted by Defense Express is Russia’s Shturm project, which envisions unmanned or remotely operated combat vehicles based on the T-72 chassis.
If that program moves beyond experimentation into larger-scale production, some stored T-72As could be diverted away from traditional tank modernization.
The broader picture is therefore somewhat contradictory for Russia. Its defense industry appears capable of restoring and modernizing old armor at a faster pace than previously estimated, but much of that output increasingly depends on finite Soviet-era reserves, recovered vehicles, and combinations of existing components rather than newly manufactured tanks.
Earlier, Russia’s new Shturm robotic assault tank reportedly suffered repeated communication failures during its debut at the Tsentr-2026 strategic military exercise before getting stuck in mud—even after a human driver took control of the vehicle.

Berlin und Paris: Diesel-Versprechen an Trump erfordert keine neue Freigabe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:39:29 UTC
20:39:29 KST

Berlin und Paris: Diesel-Versprechen an Trump erfordert keine neue Freigabe
Die Äußerungen deuten darauf hin, dass Europas Zusage, Treibstoff aus den Reserven bereitzustellen, weniger großzügig ausfällt als zunächst angenommen.
BRÜSSEL — Deutschland und Frankreich teilten am Mittwoch mit, dass sie Dieselvorräte freigeben werden, die bereits im März im Rahmen der G7-Zusage zugesagt worden waren. Damit bleibt unklar, ob darüber hinaus noch weitere Bestände freigegeben werden, wie zwei mit der Angelegenheit vertraute Diplomaten gegenüber POLITICO sagten.
Die Äußerungen deuten darauf hin, dass Europas Versprechen an US-Präsident Donald Trump von vergangener Woche, Millionen Barrel des Kraftstoffs freizugeben, weniger großzügig war, als zunächst angenommen.
Die G7-Länder haben sich am Freitag dazu verpflichtet, in den nächsten 20 Tagen eine „erhebliche“ Menge Diesel freizugeben, um die weltweiten Preise zu senken. Zuvor hatten hochrangige Vertreter der Trump-Regierung damit gedroht, ein Exportverbot für den Kraftstoff zu verhängen, sollten die europäischen Länder ihre Reserven nicht freigeben.
Advertisement
In einem Treffen hinter verschlossenen Türen räumten die Länder am Mittwoch ein, dass die Freigabe keine neuen Barrel Diesel umfassen würde, so die beiden Diplomaten. Stattdessen handele es sich um Barrel, die bereits im Rahmen einer umfassenderen europäischen Verpflichtung zugesagt worden waren, zwei Drittel davon Raffinerieprodukte. Diese Vereinbarung wurde im März, wenige Wochen nach Ausbruch des Krieges im Iran, von der Internationalen Energieagentur (IEA) vermittelt.
Die genauen Mengen, die die beiden Länder freigeben werden, sind noch unklar. Sie werden jedoch einen Teil der verbleibenden Bestände ausmachen, für deren Freigabe im März eine Zusage gemacht wurde, wie die Diplomaten und ein Sprecher der deutschen Regierung bestätigten.
Von den zugesagten 2,65 Millionen Tonnen Öl, Diesel und Jet-Fuel hat Deutschland bislang nur 600.000 Tonnen auf den Markt gebracht. Inwieweit Frankreich seine Zusage, 14,6 Millionen Barrel freizugeben, bereits erfüllt hat, bleibt unklar. Doch das Land hat erklärt, dass es von dieser Zusage noch mindestens 8 Millionen Barrel übrig habe, die es im Rahmen der jüngsten Bemühungen freigeben könne, wie zwei weitere Diplomaten gegenüber POLITICO sagten.
Die Länder, die über einige der größten Vorräte an raffinierten Erdölprodukten in Europa verfügen, wurden von der Trump-Regierung dafür kritisiert, dass sie ihren im März zugesagten Anteil noch nicht vollständig bereitgestellt haben. Deutschland führt dies laut einem Dokument, das POLITICO vorliegt, auf die schwache Nachfrage nach den Barrel zurück.
Es ist unklar, ob sich die Länder letztendlich dazu entschließen werden, zusätzliche Barrel bereitzustellen. Ein europäischer Beamter erklärte am Montag gegenüber POLITICO, dass die neue Zusage „zwangsläufig“ eine erneute Freigabe impliziere. Wie zwei weitere mit der Angelegenheit vertraute Personen sagten, wird heute eine außerordentliche Sitzung der IEA stattfinden.
Dieser Schritt erfolgt vor dem Hintergrund der Verunsicherung in anderen Mitgliedsländern darüber, wer wann wie viel bereitstellen würde. Einige osteuropäische Länder wie Bulgarien äußerten zudem Bedenken, dass der Abbau der Reserven zur Bekämpfung der Preise sie im Falle einer Versorgungskrise verwundbar machen würde, so die Informanten.
Advertisement
Eine Sprecherin des Bundeswirtschaftsministeriums bestätigte am Dienstag, dass Berlin keine neuen Barrel freigeben werde.
„Die G7 hat die IEA gebeten, die zügige und vollständige Umsetzung der für März 2026 eingegangenen Verpflichtungen zu überwachen“, sagte die Sprecherin gegenüber POLITICO. „Vor diesem Hintergrund und unter Berücksichtigung der bereits erfüllten Verpflichtungen sollen die Verpflichtungen durch eine koordinierte Freigabe von 100 Millionen Barrel über die IEA umgesetzt werden.“
Sie fügte hinzu, dass „zum jetzigen Zeitpunkt keine weiteren Mengen“ freigegeben würden.
