Ukraine Spoofs Two Russian Ballistic Missiles Mid-Flight, Sending Them Into Dnipro River
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:39:19 UTC
20:39:19 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Spoofs Two Russian Ballistic Missiles Mid-Flight, Sending Them Into Dnipro River
Earlier this year, Ukraine used an electronic warfare system to divert two Russian ballistic missiles from a key government site in Kyiv, causing them to crash into the Dnipro River, according to The Wall Street Journal on October 7.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The missiles were traveling toward the Ukrainian capital at hypersonic speeds when they were disrupted by radio signals generated by the Ukrainian electronic warfare unit Night Watch, which operates the domestically developed Lima system.
Around the same time, navigation applications on phones across Kyiv began showing users as being located in Peru—an effect linked to the false positioning signals generated during the operation, according to WSJ.
Night Watch uses Lima to interfere with satellite navigation relied on by Russian drones, guided bombs, and missiles. The system can transmit signals across a range of roughly 120 miles, or 193 kilometers, according to a member of the unit who uses the call sign Alchemist.
Rather than physically destroying an incoming weapon, electronic warfare can jam its navigation or use spoofing to feed its guidance system false positioning information, potentially forcing it away from its intended target.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Night Watch also says it used a similar method against a Russian Kinzhal hypersonic missile in November 2025. The system reportedly transmitted false navigation data that caused the missile to change course and ultimately fail while traveling at high speed.
Lima systems are deployed across Ukraine as part of a wider electronic warfare network designed to disrupt Russian precision-guided weapons. Ukrainian personnel told WSJ that the equipment can also interfere with friendly drones, requiring coordination between electronic warfare teams and Ukrainian UAV operators.
An officer with Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces said electronic warfare suppresses between 70% and 95% of radio-controlled Russian drones detected in the sector where his team operates, according to the newspaper.
Russia has meanwhile been modifying its weapons in an effort to overcome Ukrainian electronic countermeasures. According to WSJ, Night Watch discovered in late 2024 that Russian missiles and drones were being equipped with Chinese-made antennas capable of identifying sources of interference and rapidly adjusting to avoid them.
Night Watch and Lima developer Cascade subsequently spent about three months developing an updated version of the system known as Lima Quant.
Earlier, Ukraine reported that the Lima electronic warfare system had neutralized 26 Russian Kh-47M2 Kinzhal missiles in the first three months of 2026, bringing the total to 58 since the system entered service. Lima uses a combination of jamming, spoofing, and cyber interference to disrupt the navigation of incoming missiles and drones.

Leaked Emails Expose Rosatom’s Hidden Delays and Corruption at Hungary Nuclear Plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:39:13 UTC
20:39:13 KST

- Category
- World
Leaked Emails Expose Rosatom’s Hidden Delays and Corruption at Hungary Nuclear Plant
Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom privately prepared to terminate contracts with a major subcontractor at Hungary’s Paks II nuclear power plant while publicly maintaining that work was proceeding as planned, Politico reported on October 5.
Internal Rosatom documents reviewed by Politico show the company had made about $66 million in advance payments to Moscow-based Orgenergostroy for work that had not yet been completed. The documents also recorded roughly $12 million in unpaid debts owed by Orgenergostroy to Hungarian subcontractors.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Orgenergostroy was at the time caught up in a corruption scandal in Russia involving an official accused of bribing a Rosatom executive who was later convicted and sentenced to 12 years in prison.
After Orgenergostroy began laying off workers at the Paks II construction site in late 2024, Rosatom publicly maintained that the contractor would continue working without disruption, Politico noted.
Behind closed doors, however, Rosatom was preparing for the opposite.
“Following the review, Rosatom [CEO] Alexei Likhachev approved the start of preparations to terminate contracts between Rosatom entities and [Orgenergostroy] and issued corresponding directives,” minutes from a December 2025 Rosatom meeting stated.
“An analysis was carried out of the risks associated with various scenarios for the future relationship with OES on each project,” the document continued.
Politico reported that replacing Orgenergostroy with local contractors was expected to delay construction by three to four months and increase the cost of its remaining work by nearly 20%.
Rosatom told Politico that the documents were “outdated” and stated that the problems involving Orgenergostroy had “been resolved, and work on the Paks II nuclear power plant project is proceeding as planned.”
The company did not answer whether Orgenergostroy had completed the work covered by the advance payments, repaid Hungarian subcontractors, or why Rosatom had considered terminating its contracts with the company.
The documents emerge as Hungary’s government reviews the Paks II project, which is being built by Rosatom and has faced repeated delays and scrutiny over its links to Russia.
Politico also obtained an email in which a Rosatom manager openly criticized claims by the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, that Russia was meeting all of its commitments on overseas nuclear construction.
“Putin stated — and emphasized several times — that ‘Russia is 100% fulfilling ALL contractual obligations regarding the construction of nuclear power plants abroad’????” the manager wrote. “Yet they blew it with Turkey, Egypt, and Bangladesh… Deadlines have slipped everywhere.”
The manager then directly blamed Putin for problems inside the company.
“This just goes to show once again that he’s a BULLSHITTER,” the manager wrote. “And the worst part […] is that the entire chain of command below him is doing the exact same thing, believe me… We can really feel it here.”
Hungary had previously launched a review of the Rosatom-led Paks II project, examining its financing and technical design after years of delays. Prime Minister Péter Magyar noted that the plant had originally been expected to operate by 2024, while construction had advanced far more slowly than planned.

EU ambassadors on Wednesday, Oct. 7, approved proposed sanctions against approximately 1,650 individuals and entities, primarily targeting Russia’s military-industrial complex and those involved in elections held in occupied Ukrainian territories.
Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty Europe Editor Rikard Jozwiak said the ambassadors had given the “green light” to sanctions against 743 individuals and 826 entities connected to Russia’s defense industry.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The ambassadors also approved listings against 77 people purportedly elected to Russia’s State Duma from Ukrainian territories occupied by Moscow.
The measures are not yet legally final. They are expected to be submitted to EU foreign ministers for formal adoption on Monday, Oct. 12, Reuters reported.
Largest wave of listings since 2022
The package would represent the EU’s largest single set of sanctions designations since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
According to Reuters, approximately 1,570 of the proposed listings cover individuals and organizations involved in Russia’s military-industrial complex. More than half are associated with missile production.
The sanctions are intended to restrict Russia’s ability to manufacture weapons and obtain the equipment, financing, and technology needed to continue its war.
People added to the EU sanctions list generally face asset freezes and travel bans throughout the bloc. EU citizens and companies are also prohibited from making funds or economic resources available to listed individuals and organizations.
Russia's September Jet Drones Use Spike to Nearly 3,500, Air Force Says
The EU already has sanctions in place against nearly 3,000 individuals and entities associated with Russia’s invasion, occupation of Ukrainian territory, and efforts to circumvent international restrictions.
Sanctions target occupation elections
The proposed list also includes 77 people who were purportedly elected to the Russian State Duma from occupied regions of Ukraine.
Russia held State Duma voting on Sept. 18-20, including in Ukrainian territories under Moscow’s control. Ukraine and the EU do not recognize the vote conducted in those regions as legitimate.
The European External Action Service had proposed sanctions against the 77 candidates before the election results were finalized.
Their inclusion would target individuals involved in extending Russia’s political system into occupied Ukrainian territory and attempting to legitimize Moscow’s control over the regions.
Chemical weapons sanctions extended
EU ambassadors also agreed to extend a separate sanctions framework targeting the use and proliferation of chemical weapons.
That regime currently applies to 31 individuals and six entities. It includes Russian officials, scientists, and institutions accused of involvement in prohibited chemical weapons programs.
In July, the EU added six Russian individuals allegedly connected to the poisoning and death of opposition leader Alexei Navalny. The bloc said the listings included researchers and officials associated with Russia’s chemical weapons infrastructure.
The restrictions include asset freezes, bans on providing funds to listed parties, and travel prohibitions for sanctioned individuals.
The latest move follows the EU’s 21st package of sanctions against Russia, adopted in July after weeks of internal disagreements. That package targeted Russian banks, oil revenues, military suppliers, and companies helping Moscow evade existing restrictions.

There was no information about any danger facing him, special status, or possible admission into the European Union, and he does not fall into the category of vulnerable persons. The decision was made not to let this person in.

The US tech giant announced in September a _€_13 billion investment in digital infrastructure in Finland over the next two years to power its artificial intelligence ambitions. It had called it its single biggest investment in Europe.
The Finnish Supervisory Agency (LVV) said on Tuesday it had demanded that Tuike Finland, a company representing Google, "immediately suspend, and no later than 23 October 2026, all preparatory measures that would significantly alter the environment in connection with the planned data centre projects in Muhos and Kajaani".
The agency has been investigating whether Tuike Finland cleared hundreds of hectares of forest in Muhos and Kajaani without a mandatory environmental impact assessment.
The chair of the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation, Hanna Halmeenpaa, told AFP last week that "nature sites which should be preserved" had been logged in a deforested area of more than 300 hectares (741 acres).
Tuike Finland must provide an explanation and detail how it intends to proceed by October 14. If it does not comply with the demand, the agency said it may initiate "enforcement proceedings."
According to the head of LVV's environment department, Tommi Muilu, trees have been removed, topsoil stripped, site roads and storage areas constructed and ditches altered.
Google spokesman Sondre Ronander acknowledged the company's shortcomings.
"We understand the concerns and have fallen short of our own high standards in this instance," he said in a statement sent to AFP. "We will study the LVV's findings and follow their guidance."
He added the company had "acted in good faith" and implemented environmental surveys and measures.
"As we continue our long-term work in the region, we are advancing our landscaping and biodiversity plans, which include tree planting across 130 hectares at Muhos," Ronander said.
Finland's Minister of the Environment and Climate, Sari Multala, said Google's projects will likely be delayed due to the problems with the environmental assessments.
Multala told newspaper Helsingin Sanomat on Tuesday that "this is a serious matter: all companies operating in Finland must comply with the law. In this case, that has not happened."

AI hijab removal fuels 'gendered harassment' of Muslim women
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:31:26 UTC
20:31:26 KST

Breadcrumb
AI tools removing hijabs fuel 'gendered harassment' of Muslim women
AI tools that digitally remove Muslim women's hijabs are enabling a new form of "gendered harassment and humiliation", a leading UK anti-Muslim hate monitoring group has warned, amid growing concerns over the use of generative AI to target Muslims online.
Speaking to The New Arab, Tell MAMA director Iman Atta OBE warned that manipulating images to remove women's religious clothing could cause significant distress and expose Muslim women to further abuse both online and offline.
"Such acts are another form of gendered harassment and humiliation that seek to cause Muslim women hurt and distress," Atta said. "Because the headscarf is worn for religious reasons, these actions fundamentally target their religious beliefs in a deeply personal way, risking the targeting of Muslim women both in and out of public life."
The warning follows an investigation by The Guardian, which found that several leading AI chatbots would remove hijabs from images of Muslim women when prompted.
The newspaper tested ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini and Claude using an AI-generated image of a hijab-wearing woman. ChatGPT and Grok complied with requests to remove the headscarf, while Gemini initially refused but subsequently generated an image without the hijab after being asked to make the woman appear more "western". Claude said it would not carry out such an edit.
The tests came after Julien Odoul, an MP for France's far-right National Rally, posted a digitally altered image of a real Muslim woman in which her hijab and long-sleeved clothing had been removed. The politician posted the manipulated picture on X alongside the words "LIBERTÉ FRANÇAISE", or "French Liberty".
'AI slop' targeting Muslims
Atta said the issue extended far beyond the removal of hijabs, with Tell MAMA receiving reports of generative AI content portraying Muslim men and women through different racist and anti-Muslim stereotypes.
"In broader terms, the generative AI content reported to Tell MAMA targets Muslim women and Muslim men in distinct, racialised, and harmful ways," she told TNA.
Muslim men, she said, were frequently portrayed as "criminals, terrorists, or a distinctly foreign threat arriving by boat", while other AI-generated material depicted them as cultural threats or dangers to women and girls.
Atta said such content frequently recycled anti-Arab, anti-Black and anti-South Asian stereotypes.
Muslim women, meanwhile, were targeted through both their ethnicity and religious clothing.
Tell MAMA has received reports concerning TikTok accounts using generative AI to depict niqab-wearing Muslim women as cultural threats, Atta said, including images positioning them in opposition to white families carrying English or Union Jack flags.
Other AI-generated content sexualises Muslim women by depicting them wearing headscarves alongside tight clothing, while fake interview-style videos feature AI-generated scripts in which Muslim women purportedly demand "sharia compliance", according to Tell MAMA.
The concerns come amid a wider increase in reported anti-Muslim hate in Britain. Tell MAMA recorded 1,031 reports of anti-Muslim prejudice and hate in London during the first six months of 2026, already exceeding the 1,028 reports recorded during the whole of 2023.
The organisation has separately warned of increasingly aggressive anti-Muslim rhetoric online, including racialised language and threats of physical violence.
'Safeguards completely unsuited'
Atta criticised social media companies' existing safeguards, arguing that automated moderation systems were failing to understand the cultural and religious context behind AI-generated abuse.
"Current platform safeguards are completely unsuited to tackle this wave of synthetic abuse," she said. "Reporting mechanisms rely heavily on automated systems designed to look only for blunt policy violations. This leaves them entirely blind to the cultural dog-whistles, hyper-sexualised imagery, and subtle narratives embedded in AI slop."
The ability to rapidly generate and distribute such material meant malicious users could produce abusive content on a scale that traditional reporting systems were not equipped to handle, Atta added.
"The broader danger is the attempt to go viral with harmful anti-Muslim AI slop, which risks normalising damaging rhetoric and hostile responses toward Muslim communities, including forced removals or calls for violence and abuse."
The issue has not been confined to the UK, as recent research by the US-based Center for the Study of Organized Hate documented the use of generative AI in India to sexualise Muslim women and dehumanise Muslims, while prominent Muslim women in US politics, including Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib, have also been targeted.
Atta called on social media companies to clearly label AI-generated material, make reporting mechanisms easier to navigate and work more closely with specialist organisations to identify forms of anti-Muslim hatred that automated systems can miss.
"This is especially critical because, for many reporting such hate or harmful material online, responses fail to adequately deal with or follow up promptly," she said. "Social media must be a safe place for all; social media companies must remember that and ensure a human eye, not software, reviews such reports."

U.S. Military Imposes Curfew in Okinawa After Marine Arrested for Murder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:30:52 UTC
20:30:52 KST

The U.S. military is imposing a monthlong curfew in Okinawa after the arrest of a marine on suspicion of murdering a local woman, which has sparked public outcry.
The military’s regional coordinator announced on Tuesday that U.S. military personnel in the southern island prefecture would observe a 48-hour pause on operations starting noon on Wednesday. During that period, the military is suspending “off-base liberty, including a complete prohibition of alcohol consumption on or off base,” Lt. Gen. Benjamin T. Watson said. After the pause, the military will impose a curfew on its personnel from midnight to 5 a.m. for 30 days beginning Friday. The Marine Corps said it has yet to determine whether alcohol consumption will be prohibited during the monthlong period, and that a review of “liberty policies and procedures will be conducted” to evaluate if any longer-term changes are needed.
The announcement comes after Japanese police arrested Devin Ballard, a 20-year-old U.S. marine, on suspicion of robbing and murdering Anna Yagi, a 39-year-old Okinawan woman, over the weekend. Yagi was found dead at a hotel in Naha early Saturday, with an autopsy showing she died from suffocation. Police arrested Ballard on Sunday in Okinawa City after obtaining surveillance footage of him entering the hotel with Yagi and leaving alone with what appeared to be her bag. Ballard reportedly denied knowledge of the incident.
“Incidents like this demand we pause for reflection,” Watson said. “Serving on Okinawa comes with responsibility. We live, work, and socialize alongside the people of Okinawa; their home is our home.”
“Every interaction with our neighbors either builds or undermines the trust that is essential to our team. When that trust is damaged, it affects the strength of our alliance and the security of this region,” he continued.
The murder of Yagi has renewed calls to reduce U.S. military presence in Okinawa, where most of the U.S. military installations in Japan are concentrated.
“We never wanted to have the bases,” says Sorane Sakihama, a 24-year-old Okinawan native who organized protests in Tokyo after Sunday’s arrest.
“I want this case to be the last, and I want both governments to take it seriously,” she tells TIME, adding that she feels a sense of responsibility to make the voices of Okinawan women heard. “We have been saying that for 80 years. It’s not our first time saying that, so that’s also our fault, our responsibility that we lost her life.”
The U.S. Embassy in Tokyo and the Marine Corps expressed condolences and said they were cooperating with Japanese authorities.
Diplomatic tension
The incident has placed diplomatic pressure on the alliance between Japan and the U.S. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi registered a protest with the U.S. on Sunday.
“The occurrence of such an extremely brutal and vicious incident is extremely regrettable,” she said in a statement. “The government of Japan has lodged a strong protest with the U.S. side, while firmly demanding maximum cooperation with the investigation, strict discipline among U.S. military personnel, and thorough measures to prevent the recurrence of such incidents and accidents.”
At a press conference on Tuesday, Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi said Japan will discuss with the U.S. “effective measures” to prevent crimes by U.S. military personnel.
“This is an extremely malicious incident that will cause great anxiety among the residents of the prefecture and city. I feel intense anger,” Okinawa Governor Genta Koja said on Monday. Koja, who took office on Sept. 30 after a campaign focused on economic issues, said he and Naha’s mayor filed protests with the Japanese Foreign Ministry’s ambassador in charge of Okinawan affairs and the director of the Okinawa Defense Bureau.
Koja called for a review of the U.S.-Japan Status of Forces Agreement. The legal pact gives Japan the primary right to prosecute off-duty offenses against Japanese civilians by U.S. personnel. But if a suspect is already in U.S. custody, U.S. authorities generally retain custody until Japan files charges.
Critics, including Sakihama who started an organization advocating for a revision of the agreement, argue that it hampers Japan’s ability to investigate and prosecute crimes, and ultimately diminishes accountability when crimes or accidents involve U.S. military personnel.
The Marines said that Ballard, who was based at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, remains in Japanese custody.
Motegi told reporters that the Japanese government will “continuously examine” the agreement.
Historical concerns
The concentration of U.S. bases in Okinawa has long been a key issue in local politics. For years, the prefectural government has pushed to reduce U.S. military presence. In 2012, Okinawa’s prefectural assembly unanimously called for the closure of the Futenma air base and opposed deploying U.S. Osprey aircraft there. It passed a unanimous protest resolution when the aircraft were ultimately deployed.
In 2019, following a prefectural referendum, the assembly called on Japan and the U.S. to stop land reclamation at the coastal area of Henoko, where the national government had begun building a replacement base to replace Futenma. Opponents to the Henoko plan argue that building another airfield on Okinawa would only perpetuate the island’s disproportionate share of bases.
Japan’s national government has sought to address Okinawans’ concerns while maintaining its security alliance with the U.S. Washington and Tokyo see Okinawa as strategically important to deter China in the western Pacific.
Koja’s victory over incumbent Denny Tamaki in September signalled a potential shift in the prefecture’s approach to the U.S. bases. Unlike Tamaki who advocated for the closure of Futenma without building a replacement in Henoko, Koja supported the relocation of Futenma’s airfield operations to Henoko as a way to secure Futenma’s return to Japanese control. Before Ballard’s arrest, Koja asked the Japanese government for a timeline of a separate plan to transfer around 9,000 Marines off Okinawa entirely, including relocating more than 4,000 to Guam.
But the latest case has placed renewed pressure on the Japanese government to reduce U.S. military presence on the southern island.
Protests over U.S. military presence
The alleged murder has triggered protests in Okinawa, with dozens of people rallying outside the prefectural government building.
“As a woman living in Okinawa, I find myself thinking: It could be me next, or my daughter, my niece, or the young girls I care about,” Anri Tomita, a protester, said at a rally on Sunday night. Former House of Councillors member Keiko Itokazu said, “The reason we insist that U.S. military bases in Okinawa must not be increased—and that no new bases should be built—is precisely because incidents like this happen.”
In Tokyo, around 200 people protested outside the U.S. Embassy on Tuesday, holding signs that read, “Okinawa is not your amusement park” and “U.S. military out.”
“With a far higher proportion of bases in Okinawa than in any other part of Japan, locals are exposed to the highest risk of harm at the hands of U.S. soldiers in the country,” Sakihama reportedly said at the rally. “The thought that we must raise our children in such circumstances feels utterly unjust.”
Sakihama first joined a protest against the U.S. military presence in Okinawa at age 13, after the 2016 rape and murder of a 20-year-old Okinawan woman by a civilian U.S. base worker. The case drew a crowd of roughly 65,000 protesters. Months later, the U.S. completed its largest single return of land to Japan since 1972, under an agreement reached in 1996. A Japanese court sentenced the man to life in prison in 2017.
Most U.S. military personnel in Japan are stationed in Okinawa, which the U.S. occupied from the end of WWII to 1972. That includes roughly 30,000 active-duty U.S. military personnel and 25,000 of their family dependents. Despite accounting for around 0.6% of Japan’s land mass, Okinawa makes up around 70% of the land occupied by the U.S. military facilities in the country.
Growing up in Okinawa, Sakihama says she was friendly with the Americans that lived there, some of them being her neighbors. The military’s presence felt like a normal part of life, she says, even when her classes would occasionally be disrupted by noise from the bases. But there was often also a sense of fear or caution, especially when her parents would warn her not to go near the bases at night or when she heard of crimes involving U.S. military personnel.
Several other high-profile crimes involving military personnel have fuelled protests over American military presence in Okinawa. In 1995, three U.S. servicemen were arrested for abducting and raping a 12-year-old Okinawan girl. Around 85,000 people gathered on Oct. 21, 1995, amid weeks of protests demanding stronger military discipline, a revision of the U.S.-Japan legal pact, and a reduction of U.S. bases. The men were convicted in 1996.
In 2024, reports brought several previously unannounced cases of alleged sexual assaults involving U.S. military personnel to public attention, including the indictment of a U.S. airman over an alleged assault of a girl under 16. Okinawa’s prefectural assembly unanimously passed a protest resolution over the cases and called for the revision of the Status of Forces Agreement. Last year, a Japanese court sentenced a Marine to seven years in prison for choking and attempting to sexually assault a woman in 2024.
More than 60% of crimes involving U.S. military personnel in Japan occurred in Okinawa in 2023, according to Japanese newspaper Mainichi. Between 1972 and 2022, there were more than 6,000 criminal cases involving U.S. military personnel, including 134 cases of rape and 27 cases of murder, in the southern island.
Traffic and aircraft accidents have caused anger too. The assembly unanimously protested a fatal crash involving a Marine accused of drunk driving in 2017. The same year, the window of a U.S. helicopter fell on the grounds of Futenma Daini Elementary School, landing around 10 meters from where children were playing sports. In 2025, another Marine was convicted of drunk driving and leaving the scene of a crash that injured four members of a family, including two children.
On social media, Sakihama asked, “Who is the U.S. military protecting, and from what, if it can’t even protect the lives of the residents?”

Earth’s center is moving, and NASA just measured it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:30:51 UTC
20:30:51 KST

Earth’s center is moving, and NASA just measured it
- Date:
- October 7, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- Earth’s center of mass is constantly on the move, shifting by a few millimeters as enormous amounts of water, ice, and even air migrate around the planet with the seasons. NASA scientists have developed a more precise way to track these tiny swings using laser-ranging satellites, GPS data, and measurements of how water and ice deform Earth’s crust.
- Share:
Earth's center of mass does not stay perfectly still. As water, ice, and air move around the planet with the seasons, they redistribute enough weight to push the center of mass back and forth by fractions of an inch relative to Earth's geometric center.
NASA scientists carefully track this subtle motion because Earth's center of mass serves as an essential reference point for satellite navigation and measurements of surface elevation.
Researchers led by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California have now developed a method designed to measure these seasonal shifts with exceptional precision. Their technique and results are described in a new study published in Geophysical Journal International.
The research shows how major seasonal changes, including melting snow, moving ocean water, and dense winter air, redistribute enormous amounts of mass across Earth's surface.
Earth's Center Is Constantly Moving
Scientists have spent decades developing methods to define and locate Earth's center of mass using observations from space. The challenge is that the center does not remain in one fixed location.
If Earth behaved like a completely solid blue marble, its center of mass would line up with its geometric center. Instead, the planet responds to the shifting weight of water, ice, and the atmosphere. As those materials move, Earth's center of mass circles around its geometric center by as much as several millimeters.
Determining the exact size of that movement has proven difficult. The two most recent international estimates, produced in 2017 and 2023, differ by 0.27 inches (7 millimeters), roughly equivalent to the height of three nickels stacked together. That disagreement is nearly as large as the movement scientists are attempting to measure.
To narrow that uncertainty, JPL geoscientist Donald Argus led the development of a new approach that relies on extremely precise satellite tracking.
Gravity causes satellites to orbit around Earth's center of mass. As that center shifts, scientists can detect minute changes in the distances between orbiting satellites and tracking stations on the ground.
Satellites Help Pinpoint Earth's Center
Scientists have long used satellites to determine the location of Earth's center of mass. Two dense metal satellites launched in 1976 and 1992 were built specifically for that purpose.
The Laser Geodynamics Satellites (LAGEOS 1 and 2) resemble 900-pound (408-kilogram) disco balls covered with reflective prisms. Ground stations spread across more than 20 countries fire lasers at the satellites and precisely measure the returning signals.
One challenge with this method is that the laser tracking stations are not evenly distributed around the globe.
The new approach addresses that limitation in two ways. Researchers combine the laser measurements with GPS tracking and orbital information from several satellites in low Earth orbit, giving them a wider range of objects to follow. They also account for how the changing weight of water and ice bends Earth's crust, which means the ground stations themselves move slightly as the surface beneath them shifts.
Argus developed the technique with scientists from JPL's satellite orbit determination team, the University of Nevada, University of Montana, and the Helmholtz Centre for Geosciences in Germany.
"We're now estimating the size of the movement of Earth's mass center back and forth each year to be about half of what we believed it to be eight years ago," said Argus. "Our findings suggest that the mass of Earth's water and air moving between the hemispheres is smaller than previously thought."
Although the distances involved are tiny, their importance extends far beyond the laboratory.
Felix Landerer, one of the study's coauthors at JPL, noted that "while these movements might appear tiny, our modern world relies on extremely accurate positioning measurements. By unraveling and understanding the mechanisms that change reference systems, we can build better reference systems that ultimately benefit mapping and navigation -- from global shipping logistics to precision agriculture."
Snow, Rain, and Oceans Shift Earth's Balance
The researchers followed the seasonal movement of Earth's center of mass and traced it to three major sources: the oceans, the atmosphere, and continental water (made up of land ice, snow, lake and river water, soil moisture, and groundwater).
The effects change throughout the year as water and air accumulate in different parts of the world.
Snow across North America and Eurasia reaches its greatest accumulation in March. That added mass shifts Earth's center of mass about 3 millimeters toward the North Pole.
In April, the Amazon River basin reaches its seasonal maximum for rainwater, holding about 2,400 gigatons. That enormous concentration of water pulls Earth's center of mass 2.2 millimeters toward South America.
Another contribution arrives later in the year. Monsoon water in Southeast Asia peaks at 600 gigatons in November, six months after the Amazon maximum, and adds a smaller amount to the annual movement.
The Pacific Ocean Has an Outsized Influence
Ocean water also plays a major role in the seasonal shift.
From August through October, meltwater and rainfall add mass to the oceans, pushing Earth's center of mass toward the South Pacific Ocean.
Because the Pacific is so vast, changes in its mass can outweigh gains or losses in other ocean basins. Even so, seasonal changes in the Mediterranean, Red, North, Baltic, and Barents seas each make smaller contributions to the movement of Earth's center.
The atmosphere adds another layer to the cycle.
Researchers used a model created by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts to estimate how seasonal atmospheric changes alter Earth's center of mass. Their analysis found that cold and dense winter air shifts the balance toward Arabia, Asia, and northern Africa around Dec. 21 each year. Around June 21, the corresponding effect occurs over South America and South Africa.
GRACE Satellites Confirm the Mass Changes
The mass estimates produced by the new analysis agree with observations from the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment Follow-On (GRACE-FO) mission.
Launched in 2018, GRACE-FO consists of two satellites that measure monthly changes in Earth's gravitational field. Much of that changing gravity is caused by water moving above and below the planet's surface.
The satellites travel together in an extremely precise formation. When the leading spacecraft passes over a region containing extra mass, such as a river basin swollen with water, the stronger gravitational pull changes the distance between the two satellites by a tiny but detectable amount.
GRACE-FO is a partnership between NASA and the German Research Centre for Geosciences (GFZ).
Scientists are already preparing the next generation of these measurements. The GRACE-Continuity (GRACE-C) mission is targeting a launch in late 2028 and is intended to continue the nearly 25 year GRACE series record of tracking how water and mass move around Earth.

Israeli ministers host conference with Europe's far right in Jerusalem
Serving Israeli ministers have joined far-right and national-conservative figures from Europe and the US at a major conference in Jerusalem featuring discussions of "cultural replacement", migration and the future of nationalist politics.
The three-day National Conservatism Conference, which began on Tuesday, has brought together Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar and Diaspora Affairs Minister Amichai Chikli with figures from Europe's nationalist right and the US conservative movement.
The gathering comes as Israel's right-wing government has increasingly cultivated ties with European parties hostile to immigration and Muslims, some of which have historically faced accusations of antisemitism as well as Islamophobia.
Smotrich used his appearance on Tuesday to call for Muslim countries to accept Palestinians who leave Gaza, claiming that encouraging their "voluntary migration" was "not racism".
He also called for Israel to annex the territory it is currently occupying in Gaza and Lebanon.
Who is attending the Jerusalem conference?
The conference programme includes a panel entitled "Immigration and Cultural Replacement", including a talk by former German domestic intelligence chief Hans-Georg Maaßen on "Why Elites Use Migration as a Tool of Cultural, Racial, and Political Transformation".
The language of "replacement" has become closely associated with the far-right "Great Replacement" conspiracy theory, which alleges that political elites are deliberately facilitating mass immigration to transform or replace Europe's white populations.
Other speakers include Harald Vilimsky of Austria's far-right Freedom Party (FPO), former Polish president Andrzej Duda, Heritage Foundation president Kevin Roberts, Christian nationalist William Wolfe and far-right publisher Jonathan Keeperman, better known online as "Lomez".
Wednesday's programme, held on the anniversary of the Hamas-led 7 October attacks, includes sessions entitled "The Meaning of October 7" and "The Middle East After October 7".
Chikli, who has previously called for a nuclear bomb to be dropped on Gaza and played a prominent role in Israel's outreach to the European right, is appearing in the former.
Israel and Europe's anti-Muslim right
The conference comes amid a broader effort by members of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government to strengthen relations with European nationalist and far-right parties, often around a shared hostility towards Muslim communities and Muslim immigration.
Chikli has been particularly outspoken in pursuing such relationships.
His ministry has previously invited representatives of France's National Rally, Spain's Vox and other European fascist parties to Israel, while Chikli personally invited British far-right activist Tommy Robinson to the country, describing him as a "courageous leader on the front line against radical Islam".
Israeli officials have also increasingly connected Europe's changing position on Palestine with the continent's growing Muslim population.
Chikli has argued that European governments are seeking to appease Muslim voters through policies critical of Israel, while Israeli officials have portrayed pro-Palestinian activism, so-called "Islamist movements" and hostility towards Israel as overlapping threats.
This has created common ground with Islamophobic European parties campaigning against Muslim immigration, many of which have positioned support for Israel as part of a broader defence of what they describe as Western civilisation against radical Islam.
Analysts of the international right have also pointed to Israel's growing importance as an ideological reference point for nationalist movements abroad, particularly those advocating tougher borders, restrictions on immigration and a stronger emphasis on national and religious identity.
For some European and US movements, support for Israel has consequently become intertwined with a wider political narrative presenting Islamism, Muslim immigration and multiculturalism as threats to Western societies.
Israel's rapprochement with parts of the European right has nevertheless generated tensions over the histories of some of its new political partners.
The Austrian FPO, represented at the Jerusalem conference by Vilimsky, was founded in the 1950s under the leadership of former SS officers and has long been subject to an Israeli policy of non-engagement.
Sa'ar has recently signalled a possible shift, however, welcoming efforts towards what he called a "substantive, open and sincere dialogue" with the party.
Maaßen, meanwhile, faced an attempt to expel him from Germany's Christian Democratic Union over statements the party said used language associated with antisemites and conspiracy theorists, an accusation he rejects.
The conference's organisers claim to reject racial politics, describing national conservatism as being in "stark opposition to political theories grounded in race".
But the gathering in Jerusalem illustrates the increasingly close relationship between sections of Israel's political right and nationalist movements abroad, with opposition to Muslim immigration, hostility towards pro-Palestinian activism and support for Israel providing important areas of common ground.

Ukraine National Guard Uses Drones to Evacuate Oleshky Kittens in ‘Operation Tiger’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

Ukrainian tactical drone operators delivering supplies to a starving city cut off by the Russian military evacuated cats and kittens to safety after calls for help from human, comment and statements published by the National Guard on Tuesday said.
Pilots and ground crew from Ukraine’s 11th National Guard Brigade used heavy hexadrones to transport six domestic cats more than ten kilometers across a major river, from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky on the left bank of the Dnipro River to a Guard forward operations base on the right bank, said Oleksandr Pivnenko, the National Guard Commander, in published comment.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky, with a reported population of some 2,000 residents is located in no-man’s-land territory. Russian authorities cut the town off from supplies in Spring purportedly to prevent infiltration by Ukrainian forces.
Since then, the humanitarian situation in the city has worsened with people living in the town unable to reach safety on the Russian side of the lines because of military checkpoints and minefields, and on the Ukrainian side because of a natural barrier, the Dnipro River, and 24/7 combat operations on its waters.
Oleshky residents over the summer told Ukrainian forces that domestic animals in the city had been left to fend for themselves by owners that had left, and that starvation was probable because people still remaining in the city had little food for themselves, never mind abandoned cats.
Sweden Sends Patriot to Poland to Guard Ukraine Aid Hub
Ukraine’s 11th National Guard Brigade is an Odesa-based unit normally assigned to combat operations in the southern sector and along the Dnipro River flood plain.
Serhiy Ivanov, commander of 11th Brigade’s Special Operations Bolharychi section, in a Tuesday interview with Ukraine’s Novyny Live news channel, said that artificers in the unit manufactured lightweight drone-transportable cage suitable for air transport of around two medium-sized cats, or more kittens, and pilots dropped the cages at visible locations within the city.
Following heat signatures in one of the cages being spotted by a drone performing a nighttime scout flight, a heavy bomber drone normally used for dropping munitions on foxholes or individual Russian soldiers was dispatched to the pickup site, recovered the cage and flew the cats to the other side of the Dnipro and Ukraine-controlled territory, reports said.
Dynamic video recorded by night vision camera and published by 11th Brigade showed a drop of a pre-fab cat cage and a resident loading a cat and at least four kittens into the container and giving the hand signal “Lift!” to the drone pilot.
Other images showed the cat family clustered together, probably for warmth, as they flew dangling over the Dnipro River at medium altitude. Other video showed Guard ground crew running to stop the cage swaying so that it and its passengers landed gently.
The evacuees – according to reports, one adult cat and five kittens, as of Tuesday – all reached safety “unharmed but understandably frightened” in sorties flown on Oct. 5-6, Ivanov said. Video showed both cat and kittens seemingly in good condition and curious about their surroundings minutes after they landed. Brigade headquarters subsequently named the air evacuation “Operation Tiger.”
Ivanov said that the Russian troops fired on the cats and even launched interceptor drones, but hit neither the cats nor the transport drones. Support to people living in Oleshky was not reduced for the cat evacuation, he said, because the drones used to transport the cats did so on a return trip, after flying supplies to city residents.
“They [Russian forces in the sector] made attempts – shooting down with small arms, interceptors, but we prevented this,” Ivanov said in part. “But this is the fifth year of the war, we already have experience, and we work to stay ahead of the curve [and Russian air defense forces].”
A brigade statement said that homes would be found for all the evacuated cats.
Invading Russian troops overran Oleshky in late February 2022, but Kremlin efforts to establish control there were hindered by Ukrainian partisans and commandos crossing the Dnipro River, and since mid-2025 by Ukrainian drones and artillery that forced Russian troops to quit permanent presence in the city.
By Spring 2026, Ukrainian drone swarms operating around Oleshky had become so dense that Russian forces quit attempts event to patrol into the city or maintain utilities, leaving the city’s residents to fend for themselves.
In late September, in response to the worsening humanitarian situation in Oleshky, the Ukrainian military launched a drone operation called “Help Oleshky” using combat drones to fly food, clean water and medicine into the city.
By early October, between 3.9 and 5.5 tons of emergency deliveries had been landed at more than 100 locations in Oleshky by drone.
By far the most common heavy transport/bomber drone operated by Ukrainian forces is a hexacopter commonly called a “Vampire,” which is manufactured by the local company SkyFall. The Vampire and similar aircraft typically have a useful payload of 10-15 kg (22-35 pounds).
Along with the 11th National Guard Brigade, the Kherson-based 34th National Guard Regiment, the 34th Marine Infantry Brigade, and the 79th Border Guard Detachment are deployed in the lower Dnipro River region and participating in the air logistics operation to supply civilians in Oleshky, the Ukrainian Militarnyi news platform reported on Monday.

WHO seeks clarity on second pneumonia case in Russia amid plague fears
Donald Trump will speak with Vladimir Putin about the situation after the U.S. urged Russia to share more information following the death of a lab worker.
Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus speaks at the opening of the World Health Organization assembly in Geneva, Switzerland on May 18, 2026. | Fabrice Coffrini/AFP via Getty Images
The World Health Organization is looking into reports of a second pneumonia case linked to an anti-plague institute in Irkutsk, Siberia, after the Kremlin said there are no plague cases in the region following the death of a lab worker.
The latest reports suggest Russia is not fully cooperating with international health authorities by rapidly sharing its data on the cause of death of a 28-year-old woman who worked at the anti-plague lab, who died Oct. 2.
“WHO has requested further information to clarify the cause of the severe pneumonia, the pathogen that prompted the public health measures, and media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause,” WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said Wednesday.
Advertisement
"Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks," Tedros said in his social media post.
U.S. President Donald Trump said Tuesday he had a "call scheduled" with Russian President Vladimir Putin "very soon" to discuss the situation.
The WHO is looking into the death of the laboratory worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East. Alexei Tsydenov, head of the neighboring republic of Buryatia, suggested this could be a case of pneumonic plague, as did several initial media reports.
Pneumonic plague is fatal unless patients receive treatment with antibiotics.
Russian authorities have said that “no case of plague had recently been registered in Irkutsk oblast.” Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s national public health agency, said that the employee died from “pneumonia of unknown etiology” and that no microorganisms associated with her work were identified in the patient sample.
The WHO said Tuesday that "no cause of death had officially been confirmed."
Advertisement
More than 200 people had initially been placed under observation following the woman's death. In a statement sent to the WHO Tuesday, Russian health authorities said they conducted an investigation “following the identification of a case of community acquired pneumonia” and that “no pathogens of dangerous infectious diseases were detected among any of the contacts.”
The WHO said they have remained in contact with Russian authorities and "offered technical support."
The EU and the U.S. are both monitoring the situation closely. The European Commission and countries are set to discuss the case at Wednesday’s Health Security Meeting, according to a Commission spokesperson.
But the U.S. is growing increasingly concerned with Russia's transparency over the case. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday urged Russia to share more information, adding that it would be "irresponsible" to speculate until then.
The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that the U.S. sent a formal diplomatic message to Russia requesting more information about the woman's death and reminding the Kremlin that it has obligations under international law to share information about disease outbreaks in a timely manner.
The WHO said Tuesday that the risk is “moderate to low” for the Irkutsk region, “low” for Russia and “very low” for Europe.

Finance ministry proposes retirement age of 70 in debt reform plan
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:29:20 EEST
20:29:20 KST

Finland’s finance ministry has proposed raising the minimum retirement age to 70 and abolishing the home-care allowance as part of a programme aimed at strengthening public finances by €8–11 billion during the next parliamentary term. The proposals have drawn opposition from trade unions, while business representatives have backed parts of the plan.
The ministry published its policy paper on Wednesday, setting out options for the government that will take office after the next parliamentary election.
Officials said spending cuts, tax measures and structural reforms should all remain available as Finland seeks to halt the rise in public debt.
Permanent Secretary Juha Majanen said during the ministry’s presentation that the scale of the adjustment was large but achievable.
“All expenditure and revenue must be on the radar,” Majanen said.
The ministry proposes increasing the minimum old-age pension age by six months for each successive age group until it reaches 70. After that, the threshold would remain linked to changes in life expectancy.
Ministry officials estimate that the change would increase employment by between 50,000 and 120,000 people.
The proposal drew immediate criticism from trade union organisations.
STTK chair Else-Mai Kirvesniemi said Finland’s pension system should remain separate from measures linked to the national debt brake.
“The pension system is well managed and sustainable. It should not be tampered with,” Kirvesniemi said in an STTK statement.
STTK said Finland’s effective retirement age has already risen to 63.2 years. Kirvesniemi also pointed to almost 330,000 unemployed people and argued that extending working lives requires jobs, training and measures addressing workload and employee wellbeing.
She said a higher statutory retirement age would not produce rapid savings for central government finances and would place much of the impact on younger generations.
Akava chair Maria Löfgren also questioned the employment assumptions behind the proposal in an interview with Ilta-Sanomat. Löfgren described the projected increase in employment as a calculation rather than a guarantee that older workers would have jobs or remain fit for work.
The Confederation of Finnish Industries took a different position. Its director Ilkka Oksala described the ministry’s intervention as important and justified.
The finance ministry also proposes abolishing or shortening the home-care allowance for parents of young children. Officials estimate the measure would increase employment by about 10,000 people. Strategy and Research Director Olli Kärkkäinen said the ministry was looking at areas where employment reforms had not been made for some time, including longer working careers and employment among parents of small children.
The policy paper reaches beyond pensions and family benefits. Officials propose reducing the number of Finland’s 21 wellbeing services counties or requiring broader co-operation between them. Another option would transfer responsibility for organising some health services to the state.
The ministry also proposes reducing the number of municipalities, cutting ineffective business subsidies, selling €2–3 billion in state-listed shareholdings and directing funds towards unlisted growth companies.
Officials want greater use of artificial intelligence in taxation, benefit processing and health and social services. They also propose tighter taxation of some fossil fuels, peat and wood used for energy.
The ministry said no major category of expenditure or taxation should be excluded before political negotiations begin. Its officials are due to publish more detailed spending, structural and tax reviews later in October.

Israel declares Oct. 7 massacre roadside shelters national heritage sites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:28:36 UTC
20:28:36 KST

Exactly three years after the Oct. 7 massacre, Heritage Minister Amichai Eliyahu on Wednesday declared the roadside shelters across the Gaza border area that became scenes of both mass killing and extraordinary acts of heroism to be national heritage sites.
Under the precedent-setting decision, the shelters may not be demolished, removed, repainted or otherwise physically altered without professional approval, in an effort to preserve them as what the ministry called “living testimony” to the events of Oct. 7, 2023.
The shelters along Route 232 became known in Israel as the “death shelters.” During the Hamas attack, Nova festivalgoers and people fleeing Zikim Beach sought refuge inside them. Hamas terrorists fired into the shelters, threw grenades inside and abducted several people sheltering there.
Ninety people were murdered in the shelters and five were abducted. Nearly 40 Nova festivalgoers fled into the shelter at Be’eri Junction, where 16 were murdered.
Another shelter near Re’im Junction became closely associated with the heroism of Aner Shapira, who repeatedly threw back grenades hurled inside by Hamas terrorists before he was killed. Other civilians and security personnel also risked their lives in and around the shelters to save others.
Rare use of antiquities law
Eliyahu informed heads of regional councils in the Gaza border area and a senior Israel Antiquities Authority official that the shelters would be formally designated as “antiquities” and national heritage sites.
The decision followed extensive work by the Heritage Ministry and was intended to stop local and bureaucratic initiatives aimed at “clearing the area,” including removing, repainting or covering structures that still bear physical traces of the attack.
Although Israel’s 1978 Antiquities Law was originally designed to protect objects and sites dating from before 1700, Section 1 gives the responsible minister exceptional authority to declare a later object an “antiquity” if it possesses clear national historical value.
Eliyahu used that provision to give the shelters immediate legal protection.
“The events of Oct. 7 seared a deep wound into our flesh, but they also revealed extraordinary strength, heroism and mutual responsibility that will be remembered for generations,” Eliyahu said.
“Amid the inferno, the shelters scattered throughout the Gaza border area became arenas of a struggle for survival, bloodshed and unparalleled heroism,” he added. “Our duty to future generations is to ensure that the stories of heroism and loss are told from the places themselves and are not erased by bureaucratic considerations or by a rush to ‘clear the area.’”
The Heritage Ministry stressed that the declaration does not transfer ownership of the shelters to the state or expropriate them from their current owners.
It does, however, place them under a strict preservation regime. From now on, any physical change will require explicit approval and advance professional coordination with preservation experts from the Israel Antiquities Authority and Heritage Ministry.
The ministry said the directive had been passed to all relevant field and operational authorities to ensure that the structures remain “living testimony” and places of mourning and remembrance for bereaved families and the Israeli public.
‘This is the last place our loved ones were’
Hila, whose brother Avir Lotan was murdered in the shelter at Be’eri Junction, welcomed the decision.
“I’m emotional,” she told ynet. “A long struggle to preserve the commemoration, the narrative, the memory of the massacre, the friendship, mutual responsibility and stories of heroism that took place in these shelters along the route of bloodshed on Oct. 7 is receiving the recognition it deserves.”
“Especially on this day, preserving the shelters manages to calm our hearts a little,” she said.
Ynet reported in June that the Eshkol Regional Council was planning to relocate some of the shelters to the Nova memorial site, a move Hila opposed.
“The shelters are a living reminder of what happened on the morning of Oct. 7, of the disasters and the heroism,” she said at the time. “When every trace of what happened in a place is removed, what is left?”
“The shelters are among the only pieces of evidence that are not inside a kibbutz or city. We have to preserve them where they are. This is the last place where our brothers, our children and the people we loved were. It is important that they not be moved, also for the national memory of the State of Israel.”
She compared moving them to relocating a historic site because nearby residents found it difficult to live beside it.
“This is an attempt to erase the massacre,” she said. “We said from the first day: Leave these shelters as a memorial and put new shelters beside them. The road can also be redesigned to make it safe and provide parking.”

West Bank schools close amid settler violence fears on 7 October
Schools and universities across the occupied West Bank have suspended, rescheduled or moved classes online amid fears of Israeli settler attacks and heightened military tensions on the third anniversary of the 7 October attacks and the start of Israel's genocidal war on Gaza.
The measures come amid an unprecedented surge in Israeli settler violence across the occupied territory, alongside intensified Israeli military raids, movement restrictions, arrests and demolitions since October 2023.
The measures have affected government and private schools as well as universities, with some institutions moving lessons online to protect students, Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
Education directorates in most areas of the West Bank moved Wednesday's classes to Tuesday "in view of the current circumstances" and "to ensure the safety of students".
An-Najah National University in the northern West Bank also said students would attend classes remotely on Wednesday "in light of the prevailing circumstances and out of concern for their safety on the third anniversary of the start of the war on Gaza".
The decision comes as Palestinians face growing violence from Israeli settlers across the West Bank. The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said more than 1,600 settler attacks resulting in casualties, property damage or both had been recorded across 275 Palestinian communities by mid-September this year.
Settler attacks were occurring at an average rate of 6.7 a day, up from five a day in 2025, with the violence spreading across an increasingly wide area of the occupied territory.
The violence has directly affected Palestinian children's ability to attend school. In its latest report, OCHA documented cases in Hebron and Tubas where settler attacks and Israeli access restrictions forced children to relocate, drop out or prevented them from reaching in-person education.
The anniversary also comes a day after armed Israeli settlers attacked AFP photographer Jaafar Ashtiyeh as he covered violence against Palestinian olive farmers near Aqraba in the northern West Bank.
Ashtiyeh was beaten with rifle butts and his equipment was taken during the attack, which took place in the presence of Israeli soldiers who witnesses said did not intervene. Another Palestinian was shot in the foot during the incident.
Government schools in the West Bank are already operating for only three days a week, while Israeli movement restrictions, violence and severe financial pressures on the Palestinian Authority have further disrupted the education system.
The Association for Civil Rights in Israel has reported that more than 813,000 Palestinian students and 50,000 teachers have been affected by disruptions to education.
Violence across the occupied West Bank has intensified dramatically since Israel launched its war on Gaza following the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023.
Over the past three years, Palestinians have faced repeated Israeli military raids, killings, mass arrests, forced displacement, home demolitions and land seizures, alongside the rapid expansion of illegal Israeli settlements and escalating settler attacks.
The UN warned in August that settler violence had reached "unprecedented levels", with thousands of Palestinians displaced this year as a result of settler attacks, demolitions and evictions.
Israeli authorities have also imposed closures and additional restrictions affecting crossings and movement in the occupied West Bank and Gaza.

Lrytas reported that Odintsov was the same man who came to Lithuania via the Nemunas River from Kaliningrad on September 17. Lithuanian border guards returned him back to Russia. The connection was also confirmed by Sigitas Šamborskis, chairman of the Lithuanian community in Kaliningrad.
Further reading
Šamborskis described Lithuania’s decision to return the man to Russia as an “ordinary betrayal”.
Lithuania’s State Border Guard Service, however, said it was unclear whether Odintsov had formally requested asylum because of doubts over whether his statements, which were not clearly or explicitly expressed, could be considered a request for international protection.
According to Lithuania’s Border Guard Service, officers returned the man to Russia on September 17 after he arrived by river from the Kaliningrad region.
Lrytas was the first Lithuanian outlet to report the incident. At the time, Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas told the portal that the man had requested political asylum but was nevertheless sent back to Russia.
The Border Guard Service said there was no information indicating that the man faced threats or had special status that could have led to his admission to the European Union. It also said he was not considered a vulnerable person, leading authorities to decide not to admit him to Lithuania.
The agency said officers also took steps to ensure his well-being before returning him, including providing medical care and dry clothing after his journey on the river.

Ruth Kalda: The value of family doctor lists in the digital age
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:25:00 UTC
20:25:00 KST

Ruth Kalda: The value of family doctor lists in the digital age
A patient's connection to a family doctor or a stable family doctor team creates responsibility so that care is not limited to a single moment. Someone is accountable for the full treatment path, prevention, follow‑up and combining recommendations from different specialists, Ruth Kalda writes.
If a patient's entire medical history is available in the digital record, does he still need his family doctor? A recent opinion piece used an ER example to illustrate this question: doctors there make quick, weighty decisions about people they have never met. But does that mean long‑term care relationships no longer matter?
Yes, ER experience shows that in a well‑organized system it is possible to make quick and very important decisions without a prior relationship with the patient. But that does not prove that long‑term continuity of care is unnecessary. It proves that episodic emergency care can function episodically. But is knowing a person the same as knowing data?
ER and family doctors solve different types of problems
When a patient goes to the ER, the ER doctor's main question is: "Is there anything life‑threatening in this patient's condition right now, and if so, what must be done immediately?"
A family doctor's question is usually very different: "What does this complaint or change in health mean in the context of this person's usual health, past medical history, medications and life situation, and what should be done over the next months and possibly years?" Here, long‑term care and continuity are central.
The digital record allows quick access to documented events, but that is not the same as knowing the patient. The digital record may not show the person's usual condition, which recommendations he can realistically follow, what he fears, what has been discussed before or which small change in health is unusual for him.
That is why a patient's connection to a family doctor or a stable family doctor team creates responsibility so that care is not limited to a single moment. Someone is accountable for the full treatment path, prevention, follow‑up and combining recommendations from different specialists.
What does the evidence show?
The benefits of continuous family doctor care are not based only on professional conviction. In a 2018 systematic review, 15 of 18 studies found that greater continuity of medical care was linked to lower mortality. The connection was found in different countries and different health systems.1
A Norwegian registry study covering almost the entire population found that people who had been on the same family doctor's list for more than fifteen years had about 25 percent fewer deaths, 28 percent fewer acute hospitalizations and 30 percent less use of emergency services compared with patients whose relationship lasted up to one year. The study also found a pattern: the longer the relationship, the better the outcomes.2
A 2022 Danish population‑based cohort study also found a connection between longer ties to a family doctor center and better patient outcomes. Importantly, the study examined not only continuity with one specific doctor but also the value of being connected to one stable practice.3 Estonia's own data show that contact with the family doctor system reduces the risk of hospitalization.4
At least three forms of continuity of care should be distinguished: informational, organizational and continuity based on long‑term relationships.
Informational continuity means necessary information is available to different providers. Organizational continuity ensures that tests, treatment, follow‑up and consultations form a whole. Long‑term continuity means the patient and his background are known over time by the same doctor or a small stable team.
Artificial intelligence in medicine
The digital record and artificial intelligence (AI) can improve informational continuity, but they do not automatically create organizational continuity or long‑term trust.
In the AI era, having your own family doctor becomes more valuable than before. There is a strong substantive reason for this. AI will make medical information, risk scores, personalized treatment suggestions and digital record summaries increasingly accessible to everyone.
But that makes other abilities more scarce: distinguishing what matters from what does not for the patient, interpreting changes in the context of the patient's life course, combining multiple diseases, different doctors' recommendations and the patient's goals into one plan, noticing what was not documented, taking responsibility for follow‑up and outcomes, helping the patient navigate conflicting AI recommendations.
AI may know a great deal about the patient, but it does not understand what that information means for that patient. The value of a long‑term care relationship is not only in having information but in interpreting it over time and taking responsibility for what happens next.
Current AI systems work best with clearly defined tasks. A patient's health, however, is a long‑term journey. No single consultation may be decisive, but its meaning may emerge only through continuous understanding of symptoms, behavior, treatment response and life situation.
In conclusion
The fact that the ER can make quick, good decisions about a patient does not make family doctor continuity unnecessary. The ER handles one critical episode; the family doctor monitors a person's health over time.
The digital record and AI can give doctors more information, but they do not replace knowing how a disease progresses, understanding a patient's values, coordinating treatment or taking responsibility for follow‑up. A strong health system needs excellent episodic emergency decision‑making and excellent long‑term responsibility. Success in one does not prove the other is unnecessary.
--
Editor: Kaupo Meiel, Argo Ideon

Two men sentenced to prison for stealing Nova victim’s sound systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:24:13 UTC
20:24:13 KST

Two days after Hamas’s October 7 attack three years ago, two high-value sound systems were stolen from the Nova music festival massacre site in a scheme involving three men. The systems belonged to a company co-owned by Matan Lior and his business partner, Amitai Rahum.
Lior was murdered at the festival after courageously helping evacuate festivalgoers under fire. On Wednesday, the Beersheba Magistrate’s Court sentenced two of the three men convicted over the scheme to several years in prison, while the third man’s sentencing remains pending.
“Today, exactly three years after Matan was murdered, we are also forced to confront those who stole the equipment that was his life’s work,” Lior’s father, Ofer, said.
“Matan stayed at the scene to save people, and while we were trying to process the disaster, others exploited it to steal. No punishment will bring our son back. This fight is about his dignity, his memory and the demand that those who did this be held accountable for their actions.”
Lior’s mother, Sarah, said returning to court on the anniversary of her son’s murder was particularly difficult.
“For us, Matan is first and foremost our beloved son, and we miss him every day,” she said. “Coming to court precisely on the anniversary of his murder is especially difficult and painful.
“Matan chose to help and save lives in the most difficult moments. It is important to us that people remember who he was and that it be clear that the property he left behind, the product of his work and his dignity also have value. We continue to make his voice heard because he can no longer do so.”
Court orders Hasson to compensate victim's parents, business partner
Judge Amir Doron sentenced Ram Shahin, whom the court described as the driving force behind the scheme and found to have acted fraudulently toward police investigators, to seven years in prison, less time already served in detention in the case.
Shahin was also fined NIS 60,000 and ordered to pay NIS 75,000 in compensation to Lior’s parents and NIS 25,000 to Rahum.
The court also imposed a one-year suspended sentence if Shahin commits a serious property or fraud offense during the three years following his release, and a six-month suspended sentence if he commits a less serious offense of that kind.
The court found that Shahin had arranged for a truck driver to collect the first sound system while falsely claiming that he was retrieving equipment belonging to his missing friend.
After a tracking device on a generator alerted police and officers seized the truck and equipment, Shahin falsely presented himself as Lior’s business partner and persuaded the police investigator to release the truck. Hours later, the second sound system was taken from the festival site.
Shahin argued that he had initially intended to safeguard the equipment and return it to its owners. The court rejected that account, finding that his intention to permanently deprive the owners of the systems had been proven beyond a reasonable doubt through his repeated acts of deception and concealment.
Defendants showed 'complete indifference' where compassion was required
Doron described the offenses as “an extreme moral low,” saying the men had cynically exploited the chaos, grief and helplessness surrounding the massacre to make a profit off abandoned property.
“In a place where basic human compassion and mutual responsibility were required, the defendants displayed complete indifference,” he wrote.
Attorney Michal Hagay Margolin, who represents the Lior family, called the case “despicable and vile.”
“The judgment is of national importance and sends an unequivocal message that there is no room for mercy for those who dishonor the heroes of Israel.”
Daniel Hasson, the second defendant, accepted responsibility and pleaded guilty under an amended indictment after the court had heard some of the witnesses. He was convicted of attempted aggravated theft in connection with the second system.
The court found that his role in the offenses was more limited. Hasson tried to sell the stolen equipment while falsely presenting himself as its owner.
Court ordered defendants to pay compensation to Lior's parents
Hasson told the court that he had not initially gone to the area intending to steal, but admitted that he later tried to sell the equipment for profit.
He was sentenced to three years and four months in prison, with credit for time already served in detention, and fined NIS 30,000. The court also ordered him to pay NIS 40,000 in compensation to Lior’s parents and NIS 15,000 to Rahum.
Hasson also received a one-year suspended sentence if he commits a serious property or fraud offense during the three years following his release, and a six-month suspended sentence if he commits a less serious offense of that kind.
The third defendant, San Lucian Tevel, pleaded guilty under an amended indictment to two counts of aiding aggravated theft. His sentence will be handed down separately.
The Nova Tribe Community Association said it had accompanied the Lior family throughout its effort to make Matan’s voice heard and demand justice.
“Matan worked to save lives, and while his family was contending with its terrible loss, some chose to steal his life’s work,” the association said.
“On the third anniversary of the massacre, that pain takes on especially difficult meaning. We will continue to stand alongside the family after the legal proceedings end and work to preserve the memory and dignity of Matan and all those murdered.”
