US military aid to Israel continues three years into Gaza genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:23:48 UTC
20:23:48 KST

US military aid to Israel continues three years into Gaza genocide
US military aid and arms transfer continue unchanged, as US public sentiment shifts.
Washington, DC – Three years into Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza, little has changed in terms of official US support.
The government in Washington, under former President Joe Biden and current President Donald Trump, has continued near-complete unconditional military aid to Israel since October 7, 2023, even as the region has exploded into wider conflict, including the US-Israeli war with Iran.
The US aid has persisted even through periods when the administrations offered tame criticism of the government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s military offensive in Gaza, repeated violations of a “ceasefire” reached last year, and roadblocks to a more lasting peace in the Palestinian enclave and wider region.
To date, at least 74,243 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel, which killed at least 1,139 people. At least 1,460 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the October 11, 2025 ceasefire went into effect as Israel has continued to expand its area of control.
“The bottom line is that under both the Biden administration and the Trump administration, the US has continued to provide unconditional support for Israel, both in terms of finances, arms transfers and other forms, such as diplomatic support,” according to former Department of State official Josh Paul, who now runs A New Policy lobbying firm.
“That’s before we start adding in the costs of America’s wars in the region, whose causes are greatly attributable to our support for Israel and to Israel’s actions,” he said.
Military aid
The United States has for decades offered Israel outsized military support and preferential access to US weapons, with Washington providing nearly $300bn in aid since its creation in 1948 when adjusted for inflation, more than any other country.
Washington has repeatedly codified support for Israel, most notably through a 2008 law that requires the US government to assure Israel maintains a so-called Qualitative Military Edge (QME) over its neighbours.
Because of that, Israel’s military remains deeply intertwined with the US government and US-made weapons, upon which it relies for its air force, several of its most devastating munitions, tanks and other military vehicles, as well as its Iron Dome, David’s Sling and Iron Beam air defence systems.
Rights groups, including Amnesty International, have repeatedly linked US-made weapons to civilian killings in Gaza and the wider region, although Israel has blocked independent monitors from entering the Palestinian enclave.
“Because Gaza is a genocide, and the US has supplied so much weaponry, there’s really no getting out of the fact that the US has a responsibility,” William Hartung, a defence analyst who has analysed US-Israel aid, told Al Jazeera.
Since October 7, 2023, the US has provided at least $25.5bn in appropriations to Israel, money that comes directly from government coffers funded by US taxpayers.
The most direct form of US military support comes from government appropriations to Israel, which account for $3.8bn a year under a 10-year memorandum of understanding signed by the administration of former President Barack Obama in 2016.
That $3.8bn was appropriated in fiscal years 2024, 2025, and 2026. The total figure also includes a towering supplemental security package of $14.1bn, passed by Congress and signed into law in April 2024.
The funding is predominantly made up of so-called Foreign Military Financing, which provides funds for US-made arms transfers and other services, and to a lesser degree, so-called offshore procurements, which provide funds for Israel to build its domestic arms industry.
Other portions of the funding are specifically allocated to replenish existing weapons stocks and maintain Israel’s air defence systems.
Israel also has access to a so-called War Reserves Stockpile, a programme that keeps a store of certain US weapons in the country, allowing for swift access upon approval from Washington.
Arms sales
Direct US government appropriations overlap with arms sales to Israel. Such sales – which must be approved by the US State Department, which in turn must notify the US Congress – can be paid for with US military aid or from other funding sources.
Nevertheless, Hartung says the vast majority of sales are paid for with US aid.
Sales can take years to deliver, depending on the availability and sophistication of the equipment being bought, entrenching the US and Israeli military in relationships long after the initial agreement.
“It’s a timeline where something approved today will do damage down the road, and the stuff doing damage now was approved some years ago,” he said.
To date, the US has approved at least $33.16bn in arms transfers to Israel since October 7, 2023, according to an Al Jazeera analysis of State Department notices to Congress.
Since the Israel military offensive began, the US State Department under both Biden and Trump has also repeatedly declared an emergency related to US national security interests when it comes to support for Israel, a rarely used legal manoeuvre that allows the administration to bypass some congressional oversight.
State Department-approved sales since October 7, 2023 have included thousands of rounds of 120mm tank munitions greenlit in December 2023 and again in August 2024, F-15 fighter jets and parts valued at $18.82bn approved in August 2024, and a $7.4bn package of bombs, guidance kits and fuses, and Hellfire missiles approved shortly after Trump took office in 2025.
At the time, Trump lifted a Biden-era pause on a pre-approved shipment of 2,000-pound (900kg) bombs to Israel.
Rights groups say the wide radius of the bombs, which can be up to a quarter mile (0.4km), causes widespread civilian devastation. A 2024 study found Israel dropped nearly 600 of 2,000-pound bombs across densely populated Gaza from October 7 to October 23, 2023.
In September, US Representative Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said he had placed a hold on a $2.8bn transfer of 40,000 2,000-pound bombs to Israel, saying he had not received assurances that the “weapons will be used by the Netanyahu government in accordance with US law and with appropriate protections for civilians”.
Diplomatic cover
Beyond weapons, three years into Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, the US has also continued to offer diplomatic cover for Israel.
Before the October 11, 2025 ceasefire, that support showed up most clearly in the UN Security Council, where the US, as one of five permanent members, repeatedly vetoed resolutions calling for an end to the war.
All told, the US vetoed six separate resolutions related to Gaza, most recently in September 2025.
The US approach has since evolved into a pressure campaign against the International Criminal Court (ICC), which has issued an arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant.
Trump initially announced plans to sanction the court and those who work with it in a February 2025 executive order. He charged the ICC had engaged in “illegitimate and baseless actions targeting America and our close ally Israel”.
The US has sanctioned a series of ICC officials, a UN rapporteur, and several Palestinian rights groups, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio promising in July to accelerate an “all of government” approach to dismantle the tribunal.
Joyce Ajlouny, general secretary of the American Friends Service Committee, has called the Trump administration’s approach “an affront to all victims and survivors of war crimes and genocide”.
Washington has taken other efforts to shield Israel from accountability.
The law appropriating the most recent round of military funding further blocks any US funding from supporting an independent commission launched by the UN Human Rights Council in 2021 investigating the occupied Palestinian territory.
It also blocks US funding for the UN agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA).
Growing US opposition
While there has been little divergence from the executive branch in its unconditional support for Israel, the domestic political context in the US has shifted dramatically over the last three years.
A May New York Times/Siena poll found that about 68 percent of Democrats opposed providing additional economic and military support to Israel, climbing from 45 percent three years earlier. A Gallup poll from February found that while 70 percent of Republicans sympathise with Israelis over Palestinians, the share had dropped by 10 percentage points compared with just a year earlier.
Lawmakers in Congress have increasingly reflected that discontent, even if resolutions seeking to block weapons transfers continue to fall short of the two-thirds majority in the House and Senate needed to take effect.
“Years ago, even an amendment to block a sale to Israel would have been unthinkable,” analyst Hartung said. “I think the tide is turning. But I mean, the killing’s happening now, so it’s not a lot of solace unless we really can stop it.”
US Senator Bernie Sanders and lawmakers in the House have introduced legislation to block weapons sales.
A fact sheet compiled by Sanders office in 2024 pointed to the reported use of US munitions, notably 120mm tank rounds, in several high-profile killings of civilians in Gaza, including five-year-old Hind Rajab in Gaza City, as well as the use of Joint Direct Attack Munitions (JDAMS) in several high-casualty Israeli strikes.
A bill to block the sale of military bulldozers received 40 votes in the US Senate in April 2024, in what some advocates hailed as a historic shift.
In September, 47 Senators voted to advance a bill that would require the State Department to conduct an investigation into US citizens killed by Israel in the occupied West Bank, which could eventually lead to restrictions on military aid.
On the opposite side, pro-Israel US lawmakers have sought to formally integrate the US and Israeli military in the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) for fiscal year 2027.
A version of the bill passed by the Republican-controlled House would boost technological cooperation between the US and Israel, potentially funnelling billions of dollars of US funds into Israel’s defence industry and circumventing congressional oversight.
In essence, the provision is an attempt to “transition the defence relationship from the annual appropriations cycle into the deeper machinery of the Defense Department contracting world”, according to A New Policy’s Paul, and in turn, sidestep changing public sentiment.
“[A relationship] that is less transparent, less susceptible to political pressure, and more deeply embedded in the US military-industrial complex,” he said.

- United Aircraft Corporation delivered a second 2026 batch of Su-34 fighter-bombers to the Russian Aerospace Forces, without disclosing how many aircraft were included.

Russia’s United Aircraft Corporation has delivered a new batch of Su-34 fighter-bombers to the Russian Aerospace Forces, the second batch of the jets handed over this year, the company’s parent, state defense conglomerate Rostec, said.
Rostec did not say how many aircraft were in the batch. Photos and video released by UAC show at least two jets and possibly four, defense analyst Guy Plopsky noted, pointing to different weather conditions between the first two and last two images.

“This aircraft combines the capabilities of a fighter and a bomber and can strike ground, surface and air targets, including in difficult weather conditions and under active air defense opposition. Thanks to the large capacity of its internal fuel tanks and economical engines, the Su-34 can perform non-stop flights lasting up to 10 hours without loss of crew performance,” said a Su-34 crew commander with the Russian Aerospace Forces, quoted by Rostec without being named.
Rostec said the jet continues to be upgraded based on its combat use in the war in Ukraine and that new batches of Su-34s are already in production.
The first Su-34 batch of 2026 was delivered on July 9, alongside Su-30SM2 fighters, following a final 2025 handover on December 10. Rostec announced seven Su-34 deliveries in 2025. By the start of 2026, Russia’s air force had received 212 Su-34s, including 18 delivered in 2025, counting seven prototype and pre-production aircraft.
The Su-34, known to NATO as Fullback, is a two-seat, twin-engine strike aircraft developed from the Su-27 that replaced the older Su-24 in Russian service. Russian forces have used it heavily during the full-scale invasion of Ukraine to drop guided glide bombs on Ukrainian positions and cities from standoff range, and it has been among the Russian aircraft lost most often in the war.

Unions and cabinet start budget talks on social security reform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:21:45 UTC
20:21:45 KST

Unions and cabinet start budget talks on social security reform
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Unions and employers say they have had constructive talks with ministers as they try to end the impasse over next year’s budget.
Prime minister Rob Jetten said the “real negotiations still have to start”, but initial discussions had been good-natured and positive.
The government needs to plug a gap of around €6 billion in the public finances after it agreed to abandon plans to reduce the welfare bill by cutting the long-term incapacity benefit WIA and shorten the maximum term for unemployment pay (WW).
The three largest trade unions, FNV, CNV and VCP, last week called off a series of planned strikes that were called to press the government to save the social security “safety net”.
FNV chairman Hans Spekman said the unions were prepared to look at ways to make the benefits system more cost effective and save money, but the cabinet had not set a target figure. “We are not being asked to meet an objective,” he said.
The minority government hopes to secure support from the left-wing opposition parties Pro and Volt in order to get the votes it needs to pass its budget through both houses of parliament.
Capital gains tax
But finance minister Eelco Heinen also wants to make concessions to right-wing parties on issues such as the reform of the “box 3” income tax mechanism, so that it taxes capital gains rather than asset values.
Heinen has already had to revise his original plans after right-wing parties were critical of his proposal to bring around 850,000 small investors and savers below the threshold for wealth taxes in order to make up the budget shortfall.
There was another setback for the cabinet in the senate, where the farmers’ party BBB stepped up its demands for the government to go back to the drawing board on nitrogen pollution.
Agriculture minister Jaimi van Essen unveiled a package of measures before the summer recess to bring down nitrogen compound emissions and protect Natura-2000 conservation areas, including a voluntary buyout scheme.
He warned that there was little room to water down the measures if the government wants to lift the “nitrogen blockade” that has held up construction projects, while the left-wing party Pro has warned it will not accept any weakening of the plans.
BBB block threat
But the BBB says the plans are unacceptable to farms and rural businesses and have warned they will block the budget in the upper house, where they are the second largest party, unless Van Essen withdraws them.
Jetten said during a debate in the Senate that there was little room to renegotiate the package. “It is ultimately up to the BBB in both houses to decide if they want to be work with us on realising the nitrogen measures and whether they want to keep tying it in with the tax plans,” he said.
BBB senator Henk Marquat Scholz told Nieuwsuur his party was “keen to go along with the cabinet, as long as the nitrogen letter is taken off the table.”

Latvia stops armed migrant push from Belarus, then loses border cameras to masked raiders hours later
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07

Armed escorts in masks pushed a group of migrants from Belarus toward Latvia and threatened Latvian soldiers, and hours later masked people crossed into Latvia and stole border surveillance cameras, Latvian Interior Minister Jānis Dombrava said on 6 October. Latvia's military described the incident as part of a continuing hybrid campaign on the border, and Ukraine's foreign minister blamed Moscow.
Russia keeps probing the EU's eastern defenses with migrants pushed from its own soil and through its ally Belarus, alongside drone incursions and sabotage that ISW has linked into one Russian pattern across Europe.
Armed escorts threatened Latvian soldiers
Latvian soldiers stopped at least 20 migrants trying to cross the border illegally from Belarus, the Latvian National Armed Forces said. Masked escorts led the group, and this time they were armed, threatened the soldiers, and urged and drove the migrants toward Latvia, the military said.
"Unlike many previous incidents, this time the provocation was particularly demonstrative and aggressive," Dombrava said.
The incident confirms that deliberate provocations and hybrid threats on the border will continue, the armed forces said. Illegal migration is being used as a tool to pressure Latvia's border and, with it, the external border of the EU and NATO, they added.
Belarus began funneling migrants toward the EU in 2021, a campaign Poland's government called a hybrid attack in which the migrants end up as weapons. In 2023, Finland closed its border crossings with Russia, accusing Moscow of the same tactic, and by mid-July Latvia had logged 111 straight days of migrants pushed across from Belarus.
Masked people stole the cameras
Several hours after the standoff, people in masks entered Latvian territory, damaged a distribution cabinet, and stole surveillance cameras, Dombrava said. They returned to Belarus before the border guard patrol could arrive.
"Belarus should understand that such incidents could lead to more serious consequences for Belarus itself," he said.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Ukraine stands in full solidarity with Latvia. "Make no mistake: Moscow is behind it," he wrote, adding that Russian President Vladimir Putin "deliberately weaponizes migration, with the help of Lukashenka, to destabilise Europe."
Tunnels, tear gas, and damaged cameras on the border
Latvia's border guards stopped 11,384 attempts to cross illegally from Belarus between the start of 2026 and 24 September. In January, Latvia's armed forces and border guard published evidence that Belarusian security agencies were organizing illegal migration across the border. Latvia has also recorded deliberate damage to cables, distribution cabinets, and camera poles on its eastern border, aimed at slowing the rollout of an automated border control system.
Stop arming Ukraine or we shut down your defense firms, pro-Kremlin group tells Latvia, Poland, and Portugal
On 22 July, Latvian soldiers fired warning shots and used tear gas against migrants trying to cross. The next day, Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said Russia and Belarus were stepping up their hybrid war against the Baltic States to distract from Russia's failures in Ukraine. Latvia temporarily halted crossings on the Belarus border on 31 July. In August, Latvian guards found the first tunnel dug from Belarus and turned back 15 migrants who used it.

Rubio In Athens Warns Iran It Will Never Have A Nuclear Weapon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:21:05 UTC
20:21:05 KST

ATHENS -- US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Iran will never be allowed to acquire a nuclear weapon, declaring that preventing Tehran from doing so is a red line for President Donald Trump.
“Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon. Simple, period, end of story,” Rubio said on October 7 in Athens, where he held talks with Greek Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis during the sixth US-Greece Strategic Dialogue.
Asked whether Washington was prepared to accept some Iranian uranium enrichment, Rubio declined to specify what level of enrichment might be acceptable. Instead, he said any agreement would have to ensure that Iran “will never have a nuclear weapon.”
“That is what our position is. That is the reason why this began,” Rubio said.
Rubio also accused Tehran of trying to build such a large conventional military arsenal that it would eventually become difficult for the United States or its allies to act against its nuclear program.
“What Iran was trying to do was build up a conventional capability so massive that they would become untouchable,” Rubio said.
He said US military action had severely weakened Iran, including by destroying or degrading much of its drone and missile capabilities and its navy and air force.
“They are far less powerful militarily today than they were,” Rubio said.
Iran's military capabilities have been significantly degraded during the conflict, although Tehran retains missile and drone capabilities. The current state of its nuclear program remains difficult to assess. with the International Atomic Energy Agency citing limited access for international monitors.
Iran Faces 'Freefall'
Rubio also portrayed Iran as facing a deepening economic crisis, saying its economy was heading toward “complete freefall.”
He pointed to the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the continued flow of oil through the strategic waterway, saying Tehran had lost control of the crucial waterway.
While oil shipments have resumed, traffic through the strait remains disrupted and Iran has continued to insist that its full reopening depends on Washington meeting conditions set by Tehran.
Rubio blamed Iran's leadership for the country's economic problems, accusing the government of spending its resources on Hezbollah, Hamas, Iraqi militias, and the Houthis rather than improving living conditions at home.
“They should have spent their money on their people, and instead they spend the money on terrorism, on weapons,” he said.
Rubio said Tehran had previously had multiple opportunities to reach agreements over its nuclear program but had failed to do so.
Greece A Key Ally
Rubio described Greece as a critical US ally at a time of growing instability in Europe and the Middle East, citing conflicts involving Iran, Russia and Ukraine, and the Red Sea.
He called Greece “a source of stability in an unstable world” and praised Athens for increasing defense spending.
Greece is on track to meet a commitment to spend 5 percent of its gross domestic product on defense this year, Rubio said, with more than 3.5 percent going toward core defense spending.
He also announced that Greece will join the US National Guard's State Partnership Program and be paired with the Florida National Guard, further expanding military cooperation.
The two countries also agreed to strengthen cooperation on counterterrorism and information-sharing between law-enforcement agencies.
Rubio cited Greece's position on major migration and trafficking routes as making it particularly exposed to terrorism, human trafficking, and transnational crime.
Washington and Athens also plan to expand cooperation on US liquefied-natural-gas exports, electricity and gas interconnections, emerging technologies, and regional energy security.
The countries are also working together to combat the trafficking of Greek and other Mediterranean antiquities into the United States.
Rubio To Make Case For The West
Rubio is due to deliver a speech later on October 7 at Athens' Pnyx, overlooking the Acropolis, where he is expected to make a broader argument about democracy, national identity, and the future of the West.
According to excerpts of his prepared remarks released by the State Department ahead of the speech, Rubio will call for what he describes as a “great renewal of the Western spirit.”
He is expected to argue that ancient Athens embodied qualities that came to define the West, including individual ambition, exploration, invention, competition, and a drive to overcome limits.
“Here in Athens, we found the first full realization of all the essential traits that would come to define the West,” Rubio will say, according to the excerpts.
He will contrast the ancient Greek pursuit of excellence with what he portrays as a modern emphasis on safety and comfort at the expense of ambition and achievement.
“The men who made the Parthenon built upwards,” Rubio is expected to say.
'The Next Decade'
Rubio is also expected to portray the West as standing at a historic crossroads.
“The next decade will write the story of the next century,” he will say, according to the prepared remarks.
He is expected to argue that the United States under Trump has chosen “the unapologetic pursuit of national power,” including rebuilding US manufacturing, strengthening defense, securing critical supply chains, and competing for leadership in emerging technologies.
Rubio is also expected to emphasize advanced manufacturing, artificial intelligence, drones, weapons, semiconductors, critical minerals, cybersecurity, energy, and space exploration.
His remarks will also challenge the idea that foreign policy should put the interests of a “global community” ahead of a country's own citizens.
Rubio is expected to argue that loyalty to one's nation and defending its interests are not selfish, invoking ancient Greek examples of duty, sacrifice, and honor.
He will also draw a sharp contrast with Iran's clerical leadership, according to the excerpts, accusing its “radical mullahs” of glorifying death and martyrdom.
“Our heroes may be willing to die for their cause; but they do not worship death,” Rubio will say.
The speech is expected to cast the confrontation with Iran as part of a wider struggle over the values and future direction of the West, taking Rubio's message in Athens beyond security and diplomacy to a broader defense of national power, Western identity, and democratic traditions.

Flávio Bolsonaro’s advance in Brazil’s election is grim jolt for climate campaigners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:20:38 UTC
20:20:38 KST

More fire, more ash, more crime, more death. And a globally important ecosystem driven ever more rapidly towards a point of no return. That is the prospect for the Amazon rainforest for at least the next four years if Flávio Bolsonaro holds on to the lead he established this week in the first round of Brazil’s presidential election.
This appears to be of far more concern to the outside world than to voters in Latin America’s biggest, richest and most biodiverse nation.
The far-right son of the former president and jailed coup-monger Jair Bolsonaro won 47% of the vote, putting him in pole position before the 25 October runoff with the incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who was backed by 44.2%.
The result is an unnerving jolt to climate and nature campaigners. Taken out of context, this appears to be a vote against the forest. The current administration of Lula (as the veteran Brazilian president is best known) has reduced deforestation in the Amazon by almost 50%. But that success secured little noticeable electoral traction for either Lula or pro-forest candidates in other polls held the same day. The former environment minister Marina Silva lost a bid for the Senate and Joenia Wapichana, a former head of Brazil’s Indigenous affairs agency, Funai, failed to win a seat in Congress. Out of 57 Indigenous candidates, only two won.
Flávio Bolsonaro is the heir to the political legacy of his father, Jair Bolsonaro, a former army captain whose four years in power resulted in a 59.5% increase in Amazon deforestation, roughly equivalent to destroying 2bn trees.
If he wins, Bolsonaro has promised to free his father, who was imprisoned for plotting a military coup and attempting to annihilate democracy in Brazil. He has said that his father could have any position he wants in his administration.
Flávio Bolsonaro has shown that he will be just as willing as his father to dismantle protections for climate and nature and allow illegal miners, loggers and land grabbers to invade Indigenous territories. As a lawmaker, he backed a 2019 bill to eliminate requirements for landowners in the Amazon to conserve a proportion of native vegetation. In his manifesto, he completely ignored the climate crisis. And he has courted support from some of the most predatory landowners in the rainforest.
He is also part of a movement – Bolsonarism – that is geared towards maximising profits for extractive industries regardless of the environmental cost. Take its victorious candidate for the Amazonian state of Pará, Daniel Santos, who was fined $275,000 (£208,000) for deforestating 280 hectares (692 acres) of his land without authorisation and is now promising to waive such penalties. As a result of Sunday’s election, Bolsonarists now control seven of the nine states in the Brazilian Amazon, and could win an eighth in the runoffs.
Bolsonarist influence in the legislature, which is dominated by agribusiness interests, is also growing. Jair’s brother, Eduardo, and mother-in-law, Michelle, were elected to the Senate, while an uncle and brother won seats in the lower house of deputies. Even before the election, Congress had been pushing hard to weaken environmental protections. Now it will be almost impossible to stop, particularly given the current chaos in the supreme court, which has been a partial check on untrammelled expansion by miners, ranchers and monoculturalists. Against these forces, Lula would struggle to govern even if he wins the runoff.
As a result, it is not just the Amazon that is in peril, but all of Brazil’s biomes, its traditional peoples and the stability of the global climate. The question now is why voters paid so little heed to these concerns.
That inquest is already under way. Many focus on the influence of social media, which has been used far more effectively by the far right. During the Bolsonaro administration, his sons were part of the “hate cabinet” that spread fear and disinformation via WhatsApp groups and other online channels – Bolsonaro’s second son, Carlos, was indicted by federal police for leading the group. Environmentalists were often the target.
Another factor is the expansion of US-style Pentecostalism, which is steadily supplanting Catholicism across Brazil, particularly in the Amazon. The political and environmental consequences of that religious shift can be seen by comparing the pro-nature treatise of the past two popes with the sermons of many evangelical preachers who encourage followers to seek wealth today as much as, if not more, than following moral creeds to ensure a good afterlife.
Lula, 80, has been slow to adapt. Although he is arguably the most iconic and successful Latin American politician of the 21st century, his messaging seems less attuned to the people than it was in his heyday. The Workers party has struggled in an era of weaker unions and in some ways been the victim of its own success – with education and social policies that raised millions out of poverty and created greater expectations for consumption and entrepreneurism; and huge subsidies to farmers, who now support the right wing because they chaff at environmental limits.
Tied into those explanations are the geopolitics of the climate and nature crisis, which is exacerbating great power rivalry between the US and China and amplifying extreme ideologies as much as extreme weather. In this light, the Brazil election is just the latest in a broader pattern of the far right taking control to expand extractivism despite growing evidence that the capitalist economy is breaking planetary boundaries. In the past two years, Donald Trump has ripped apart environmental regulations in the US and treated the rest of the Americas as his sphere of influence. Argentina was already onboard. Venezuela has been invaded for its resources, while in Colombia, Peru and Chile there has been a sharp shift to the right.
Will Brazil be the next domino to fall to Trumpism and its bonfire approach to nature? The Bolsonaro family certainly hope so. Jair went so far as to salute the US flag. His son Eduardo urged the US to apply tariffs on Brazilian people to “punish” the government for imprisoning his father. The Brazilian intelligence agency has warned that the US was trying to interfere in the election.
That election isn’t over yet. Lula stands a small chance if he can win over the many millions of voters who chose not to mark their ballots for either candidate. But the odds are stacked against him. Most of the eliminated candidates were on the right so their supporters are more likely to switch to Bolsonaro. No first round leader has ever failed to win the runoff of a Brazilian presidential election.
Voters, of course, are allowed to change their minds. Either on 25 October or, constitutionally, in four years’ time. But for how much longer will that be possible? If Bolsonaro wins, it won’t just be Lula that is finished, it could also be the Amazon and democracy itself.

Retired astronaut Ewald says Türkiye taking major steps in space

Tuğba Altun
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Türkiye has taken significant steps in the space sector and emerged as an important actor through its satellite programs and efforts to pursue international cooperation, retired astronaut and professor Reinhold Ewald said.
“Türkiye has undoubtedly taken an important step in the space sector. It has made major efforts to become an important actor, both to meet its own needs through the satellites it launches into space and to seek opportunities for cooperation,” Ewald, a professor of astronautics and space stations at the University of Stuttgart, told Anadolu.
Ewald spoke to Anadolu on the sidelines of the International Astronautical Congress in Antalya, organized by the International Astronautical Federation (IAF), where Anadolu serves as the Global Communication Partner.
He said countries and people around the world benefit from activities conducted in space, pointing not only to human spaceflight but also to navigation and meteorological satellites, Earth observation and communications technologies that support people in their daily lives.
Ewald said awareness of the importance of space has continued to grow, which he said would also benefit further developments in the sector. 
Moon first, then Mars
On the commercialization of space and space stations, Ewald said valuable lessons had been learned from spacecraft such as Soyuz and space stations such as Mir.
Having visited Mir himself, Ewald said the station was considered a “pioneer” because it provided valuable experience that later helped shape the operation of the International Space Station (ISS).
Developments in space do not happen suddenly but are the result of a long chain of progress, he said, noting that experience gained from Mir contributed to the ISS, while further lessons were subsequently learned through the Space Shuttle program.
Ewald said this continuous accumulation of knowledge and experience could now be extended to the Moon, where difficult conditions would pose new challenges in engineering and design.
After the Moon, humanity could eventually, perhaps years from now, explore ways to travel safely to Mars, he added.
Ewald also stressed the importance of mutual trust among crews working together in space, saying astronauts need thorough training and must know how to respond to unexpected situations.
He said it was particularly encouraging to see young people’s enthusiasm for spaceflight at the congress.
“Türkiye has undoubtedly taken an important step in the space sector,” Ewald said. “It has made major efforts to become an important actor, both to meet its own needs through the satellites it launches into space and to seek opportunities for cooperation.”

Vance appears to soften U.S. demands on Iranian nuclear enrichment
Vice President JD Vance appeared to backtrack on U.S. demands on Iranian nuclear enrichment Tuesday, saying Iran needed to make a "meaningful" reduction of its capacity, but not suggesting it should be required to completely give up enrichment, as President Trump has previously.
Iranian nuclear enrichment has been a key issue for the White House, with the president and other top officials stressing that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon as a core objective of the war.
In February, the day before the war began, President Trump said of Iran: "They want to enrich a little bit. You don't have to enrich when you have that much oil … I say, no enrichment. Not 20%, 30%. They always want 20%, 30% … They want it for civil. I think it's uncivil."

In an interview with the Reuters news agency published Tuesday, however, Vance said Tehran should not "build highly enriched fuel," and they should "do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity," in what appeared to be a softening of U.S. demands.
Under the Obama-era nuclear deal, the JCPOA, which President Trump was highly critical of and pulled the U.S. out of unilaterally during his first term, Iran agreed to limit its uranium enrichment to a purity level of 3.75%, with verification by the International Atomic Energy Agency.
After Mr. Trump pulled out of the JCPOA, the Iranian regime steadily ramped up its program and built a stockpile of uranium enriched to at least 60%, which is a short technological step away from weapons-grade material.
"If you don't want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60% enriched fuel? And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don't build highly enriched fuel. That's a very basic threshold issue," Vance told Reuters. "I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity."
"The goal here is to prevent the Iranians from having a nuclear weapon," he added.

US toughens sanctions against sanctions-busting payments operator
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:18:20 UTC
20:18:20 KST

US toughens sanctions against sanctions-busting payments operator
This week the US Treasury designated A7, a major payments system that helps Russia and Iran evade sanctions, a “transnational criminal organization”. The tougher sanctions likely stem from the fact that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard uses the operator.
- А7 is the biggest organization helping Russian businesses evade international sanctions. It was created by state-owned Promsvyazbank, which specializes in financing and serving the Russian defense industry, and Moldovan businessman Ilan Shor, a professional money launderer and one of the architects of a scheme that siphoned $20 billion out of Russia in the 2010s. Promsvyazbank itself estimates that nearly 12% of Russia’s foreign trade flowed through A7 in 2025.
- The Russian core of A7 has been under U.S. sanctions since Aug. 2025, yet payments are specifically routed through foreign firms. According to FinCEN, accounts are held at approximately 435 banks in 83 countries. Since the start of 2025, they have processed more than $17 billion in dollar-denominated payments. FinCEN will not publish a complete list, but it will share it with banks via a secure channel.
- FinCEN has also proposed banning US financial institutions from processing any transfers involving subagents of the network created by A7. This refers to shell companies in the UAE, Hong Kong, Turkey and other countries which A7 uses to transfer funds. Their role is to conceal payments linked to sanctioned sectors and individuals as ordinary commercial activity — for example, the FT reported on a scheme that listed thermal imaging sights as “tempered glass” on invoices — and pay foreign suppliers on behalf of Russian clients.
- At the same time, constant corporate regeneration is part of A7’s DNA. The company has a team dedicated entirely to creating new shell companies when its existing ones are busted.
Why the world should care
The cat-and-mouse game between US financial authorities and Russian sanctions-busting experts will continue. It is impossible to categorically defeat professional money launderers.

Turkey sends drone operators, military support to Saudi Arabia against Houthis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:17:52 UTC
20:17:52 KST

Turkey is sending mainly defensive and technical military support to Saudi Arabia as Riyadh confronts Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis, including drone operators, intelligence assistance and help strengthening Saudi defenses, officials said Wednesday.
The support comes as Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia move to activate the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed in August, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all three.
The countries said Monday they had agreed to begin implementing their collective defense commitments immediately and ensure the “rapid deployment” of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia following a series of Houthi attacks.
Turkey, which has NATO’s second-largest military and a major domestic defense industry, has condemned the attacks on Saudi Arabia and said it is prepared to help meet Riyadh’s technical military needs. Ankara has also agreed to join a Saudi-led coalition aimed at protecting navigation in the Red Sea.
A Turkish official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Ankara’s assistance so far consisted of military equipment, intelligence sharing and weapons systems, adding that no broader Turkish military deployment had taken place under the alliance.
Officials have said some Turkish assistance, including air defense systems, is for now being provided largely through bilateral arrangements because Turkey’s parliament has not yet formally ratified the three-way defense pact. They said the scale and scope of support could expand once ratification is completed.
A U.S. official briefed on the matter said Turkey had so far chosen to provide capabilities that were broadly defensive, including strategic planning and logistical support.
The assistance also included drone operators, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance capabilities, as well as help fine-tuning defensive measures, the official said.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said after an extraordinary meeting of the alliance in Riyadh that the three countries had discussed what assistance could be provided to improve Saudi Arabia’s defensive capabilities.
“We had our Defence Minister and Chief of General Staff with us, and they especially provided very fruitful views on military issues, operational issues, and technical matters,” Fidan told Turkish state media Monday.
Pakistani and regional officials have also said Turkey and Pakistan have supplied military equipment that Saudi Arabia is using in Yemen.
The stepped-up support comes as fighting intensifies around one of the world’s most important maritime routes. This week, Yemeni government forces, backed by Saudi-led coalition air power, launched a counteroffensive aimed at retaking strategic territory near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The narrow waterway links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and serves as a major international shipping route for energy exports and global trade.
Officials said last week that Saudi Arabia was weighing a wider offensive against the Houthis, with options including a push along Yemen’s western coast to secure the Red Sea shipping route or a broader assault on several fronts.
The latest moves mark the first major test of the Saudi-Turkish-Pakistani defense framework, which has rapidly moved from a political agreement toward operational military coordination as the Houthi conflict escalates.

Hungary set to lift veto on Ukraine's EU membership talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:17:26 UTC
20:17:26 KST

Hungary dropped its veto on two clusters of Ukraine's EU accession talks on Wednesday. The next phase depends on Kyiv's parliament passing a minority-rights law.
Hungary has cleared the way for the EU to open two more negotiating clusters with Ukraine, signalling that Budapest is ready to lift its veto if Kyiv passes a minority-rights law next week.
The move removes a major obstacle ahead of next week's European Council summit. It would also allow Moldova's accession talks to advance, as the two candidate countries have been closely linked in the process.
Budapest had blocked further progress until Ukraine adopted legislation strengthening the educational and cultural rights of the ethnic Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia.
Following an agreement at expert level, Ukraine's parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, is expected to adopt the legislation on Monday. That would clear the way for Hungary to approve the opening of clusters two and three at the General Affairs Council in Luxembourg the following day.
At the same meeting, member states are also expected to approve a €4.2 billion cohesion payment to Hungary that had previously been blocked over corruption concerns.
On Wednesday, Hungary allowed technical preparations to proceed for the letters the Council must send asking Ukraine to submit its negotiating positions – a formal step towards opening the clusters.
Budapest had previously blocked even this preparatory work, making Wednesday's move a strong signal that it is prepared to lift its veto once Kyiv adopts the minority-rights legislation.
The clusters could then be formally opened at an Intergovernmental Conference next Tuesday.
The process could still be derailed, however. Ukraine's parliament has yet to approve the minority law, amid difficulties in securing stable majorities in the Rada.
Settling the dispute could also pave the way for the first bilateral meeting between Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The two had previously planned to meet, but Magyar made the talks conditional on progress on minority rights.
The two clusters cover the internal market and competitiveness. Earlier this year, Kyiv opened clusters covering the so-called fundamentals – including the rule of law and judiciary – as well as external relations.
If two clusters are opened next week, Ukraine would then still have two more to open to begin its accession process in full, on the green agenda and EU resources. Brussels aims to open all remaining clusters by the end of the year.
Uneasy relationship
Relations between Hungary and Ukraine soured sharply under Magyar's predecessor, Viktor Orbán, whose government repeatedly clashed with Kyiv and blocked its progress towards EU membership.
Orbán fought a fiercely anti-Ukraine election campaign, portraying Kyiv as a threat to Europe's security.
After a landslide election victory in April, Magyar, who took office in May, promised a more pragmatic approach towards Ukraine. In June, he approved the opening of two negotiating chapters after Kyiv adopted an 11-point action plan on minority rights.
The rights of ethnic Hungarians in Transcarpathia nevertheless remain a source of tension.
After years of hostility towards Ukraine under Orbán, conservative voters remain wary of closer ties with Kyiv. But defending ethnic Hungarians abroad is also popular with conservatives, potentially giving Magyar room to strike a deal.
In September, relations hit another low after Magyar clashed publicly on X with Ukraine's Foreign Minister, Andrii Sybiha, over Hungary's participation in Zelenskyy's Carpathian summit, which aims to boost development in the region.
Magyar criticised Ukraine for listing Hungary as a participant without his approval, while Sybiha accused him of following in Orbán's footsteps. Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán later discussed the dispute with Sybiha at the UN General Assembly in New York.
Last week, the two foreign ministers held intense talks over a Ukrainian website's blacklisting of two Hungarians: footballer Milos Kerkez and opposition MP Balázs Hidvéghi.
The dispute followed a match between the Hungarian and Ukrainian national teams in Budapest, where some Hungarian ultras booed the Ukrainian anthem and several players clashed on the pitch.
Foreign Minister Orbán condemned "the stigmatisation, any form of blacklisting, or potential threats against Hungarian citizens" and said Budapest was in touch with Ukrainian officials to resolve the situation.

French firm develops autonomous 2,000 km strike drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:17:10 UTC
20:17:10 KST

- French startup Harmattan AI unveiled IRIFI, an autonomous strike system designed to hit targets up to 2,000 km away without satellite navigation.
- The company did not disclose IRIFI's payload, speed, price, test status or customers, and said targets are confirmed by human commanders before launch.
French defense startup Harmattan AI has unveiled IRIFI, an autonomous long-range loitering one-way attack drone system that the company says is designed to hit targets up to 2,000 km (1,240 miles) away without relying on satellite navigation or human control during flight.
The company revealed the system on October 6, marking its move into deep strike, the category of weapons used against depots, factories, airfields, command posts and logistics hubs far behind the front line. Harmattan AI did not disclose IRIFI’s speed, payload, unit cost, development status or any customers.
IRIFI fires from a mobile launcher that holds the weapon in a canister, and the company says its architecture is designed for rapid deployment in large numbers. Harmattan AI says the system can carry out a full mission without anyone controlling it after launch, using an onboard navigation system that does not depend on GPS or other satellite signals, plus a camera-based guidance system for the final approach. The company says this lets IRIFI fly low enough to avoid radar detection and strike with meter-level accuracy.
Commanders choose and confirm the targets and set the mission parameters before launch, the company said, and the weapon then flies the mission on its own within those limits. Harmattan AI says a single commander can launch dozens of strikes, supported by an AI system that processes large volumes of satellite imagery.
“The Shahed is cheap and easy to produce at scale, but it is imprecise and easy to shoot down. Tomahawks and Storm Shadows are exquisite pieces of technology with high survivability, but they are expensive and produced in very limited numbers. AI-powered autonomy now makes it possible to combine the best of both worlds, and that is exactly what we did with IRIFI,” said Mouad M’Ghari, chief executive and co-founder of Harmattan AI.
The company pitched the design around jamming and spoofing, which have made satellite navigation and radio control unreliable over long distances in recent wars. Harmattan AI says IRIFI is meant to let forces mount saturation attacks in numbers that traditional missiles cannot match, while keeping costly weapons in reserve for the most critical targets.
Founded in Paris in 2024, Harmattan AI raised $200 million in a Series B round in January 2026 led by Dassault Aviation, the maker of the Rafale fighter, at a valuation of $1.4 billion. The two companies also agreed to work on AI and autonomy for Dassault’s future combat aircraft.
Harmattan AI says it has won several programs of record with the French and British defense ministries. The UK Ministry of Defence ordered 3,000 of its unmanned systems in 2025, and the drone the company supplied to French forces that year was a 1.8 kg (4-pound) quadcopter with 40 minutes of flight time, Defense News reported.
Before IRIFI, the company’s lineup covered short-range air defense, surveillance, tactical strike and training systems, including the Gobi interceptor, the Sahara surveillance system and the Barkhan tactical strike system.

Bulgarian writer Georgi Gospodinov is one of seven authors that German daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung believes deserve this year’s Nobel Prize in Literature. The winner will be announced in Stockholm on October 8.
Gospodinov is Bulgaria’s most widely translated and internationally acclaimed contemporary writer. He became the first Bulgarian to win the International Booker Prize for his novel Time Shelter, translated into English by Angela Rodel.
Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung describes him as one of the most original voices in contemporary international literature. Born in Yambol in 1968 and now living in Sofia, Gospodinov explores Europe in all its moods and states of mind with poetic virtuosity and melancholic irony, the newspaper writes.
It describes his work as perceptive, experimental and diverse, spanning prose and poetry as well as opera librettos and screenplays.

Oil tanker burns off Russia’s Sochi after naval drone attack, sending smoke billowing over the coast. Photos and videos.
An oil tanker caught fire October 6 in the Black Sea off Sochi, in the waters of the Sirius federal territory. Russia’s Transport Ministry said uncrewed boats attacked the vessel. All 23 crew members of the Liberian-flagged tanker were evacuated. Preliminary reports said the tanker Aframax Rio was carrying crude oil from Novorossiysk to India.
A column of smoke from the burning vessel was visible for many kilometers, and the smell of burning reached central Sochi. Sochi and Sirius authorities closed all beaches because of the fire and urged residents to keep their windows and doors shut, wear protective masks when going outside, or, better yet, avoid going outside altogether.
The news outlet Sochi1.ru reported that on the evening of October 6, people continued strolling along the Primorskaya Embankment and cafes remained open, with vacationers only occasionally remarking, “It looks like something’s on fire.” No sirens sounded in Sochi that day, and there was no warning of an attack.
Rospotrebnadzor said on the morning of October 7 that the tanker fire has not polluted the Black Sea near Sochi, though monitoring of the situation continues. Sochi authorities said pollutant levels in the air have not exceeded the maximum permissible concentration. The beaches, however, remained closed as of midday.
Ukrainian naval drones attacked the Sochi embankment on September 9 (which Russia’s Defense Ministry refers to as “uncrewed boats”). The attack injured almost 30 people. A warning about the threat of an attack was issued, but witnesses said many vacationers did not react to it at first and only began to flee after the explosions.

Kagan and Soai have become Nobel laureates in Chemistry: what exactly they discovered, why it matters, and how the discovery will be applied in practice
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:14:39 EEST
20:14:39 KST

Kagan and Soai have become Nobel laureates in Chemistry: what exactly they discovered, why it matters, and how the discovery will be applied in practice
Kyiv • UNN
Henri Kagan and Kensō Soai were recognized for discovering nonlinear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric synthesis. Their work explains the emergence of homochirality.
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to French chemist Henri B. Kagan and Japanese scientist Kenzo Soai. On October 7, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences recognized them for the discovery of nonlinear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis, reports UNN.
Details
Their research helped explain one of chemistry’s longstanding mysteries: how, in a system where molecules can exist in two mirror-image forms, one of them can gain an advantage and eventually almost completely displace the other.
What the Nobel Prize was awarded for
To understand the essence of the discovery, it is enough to imagine the right and left hands. They are similar, but it is impossible to place one over the other so that all their parts coincide. Chiral molecules behave in the same way: they can have two forms, or enantiomers, that are mirror images of each other. In ordinary chemical synthesis, approximately equal amounts of both forms are often produced. In living nature, the situation is different. Proteins, for example, are composed predominantly of amino acids of one “handedness.” This preference for one mirror-image variant is called homochirality. Chemists spent decades trying to understand why nature was able to make this choice and how such a process could be replicated in the laboratory.
In 1986, Henri Kagan showed that in asymmetric reactions, the relationship between the composition of the catalyst and the composition of the product is not necessarily direct. A slight advantage for one mirror-image variant of a catalyst can sometimes produce a disproportionately large advantage for the same variant of the product. This phenomenon became known as the nonlinear effect.
Kenzo Soai went further. In 1995, his team described an asymmetric autocatalytic reaction in which the product itself accelerates the formation of new molecules of the same type. If even a small excess of one enantiomer exists at the outset, the reaction can amplify it. In 2003, Soai demonstrated a system in which an almost complete predominance of one of two mirror-image forms could emerge from an achiral initial environment.
Why this discovery is important
Chirality is directly relevant to pharmaceuticals. Biological molecules are also spatially selective, so two enantiomers of the same substance can interact differently with enzymes and receptors. One variant may produce the desired therapeutic effect, while the other may be less active, inactive, or cause a different effect.
That is why it is important for chemists to control which spatial form they obtain. Asymmetric synthesis helps create the desired compounds more precisely and reduce the proportion of unwanted products.
Kagan’s work became one of the foundations of modern asymmetric catalysis, which is important for synthesizing complex organic molecules, including pharmaceutical compounds. Soai’s reaction is primarily of fundamental importance: it became a model for how a tiny initial asymmetry can amplify itself. This is also important for research into the origin of homochirality and the chemical prerequisites for the emergence of life.
What the Nobel Committee said
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences emphasized that the work of Kagan and Soai provided an answer to a chemical mystery that is more than a century old.
Henri Kagan and Kenzo Soai have given us a solution to a chemical mystery that is more than 100 years old: how homochirality can arise spontaneously. The chemical reactions they developed are impressive
The committee emphasized that the laureates’ discoveries revealed the mechanisms by which a small initial imbalance between two mirror-image forms of molecules can be sharply amplified.
What is known about the laureates
Henri B. Kagan was born in 1930 in Boulogne-Billancourt, France. He earned his doctoral degree in 1960 at the Collège de France. He is an emeritus professor of the former University of Paris-Sud and has studied asymmetric synthesis and catalysis for many decades. In 2001, Kagan, together with Ryoji Noyori and Barry Sharpless, received the Wolf Prize in Chemistry for pioneering work in asymmetric catalysis.
Kenso Soai was born in Hiroshima in 1950. He received his doctoral degree from the University of Tokyo in 1979 and later worked at the Tokyo University of Science, where he is now an emeritus professor. The Soai reaction, one of the best-known examples of asymmetric autocatalysis, is named after him. In 2023, he received the Ryoji Noyori Prize for research into chirality.
How the scientists made their discovery
The 2026 Nobel Prize brought together research that developed over nearly four decades. In 1986, Kagan described nonlinear effects in asymmetric catalysis and showed that a small advantage for one variant of a catalyst could produce a much greater predominance of the corresponding form of the product.
In 1995, Soai and his colleagues published a paper in Nature on asymmetric autocatalysis. They demonstrated that the reaction product could catalyze its own formation while simultaneously amplifying the initial enantiomeric imbalance. Subsequent experiments proved that such a process could drive the system toward the near-total dominance of one mirror-image form.
About 40 years passed between Kagan’s first key paper and the Nobel Prize, while more than 30 years passed since Soai’s landmark publication.
What the laureates will receive
The total prize money for the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry is 12 million Swedish kronor. Kagan and Soai will split the sum equally—6 million kronor each. In addition to the monetary award, each laureate will receive a Nobel medal and a personal diploma. The award ceremony will take place on December 10 in Stockholm—on the anniversary of Alfred Nobel’s death.
Who received the 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry
Last year, the Chemistry Prize was awarded to Susumu Kitagawa, Richard Robson, and Omar M. Yaghi for the development of metal–organic frameworks. These are porous molecular structures with internal cavities that can be used to absorb carbon dioxide, collect water from dry air, store gases, and catalyze chemical reactions.
What is known about the Nobel Prize in Chemistry
The Nobel Prize in Chemistry has been awarded since 1901, in accordance with the will of Swedish inventor and industrialist Alfred Nobel. Laureates are selected by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences on the recommendation of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry.
Before the announcement of the 2026 prize, the Chemistry Prize had been awarded 117 times to 200 laureates. Following this year’s decision, the figures are now 118 prizes and 202 laureate awards. The number of individual people is lower because Frederick Sanger and Barry Sharpless each received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry twice.
It is not possible to nominate oneself for the prize. Candidates are proposed by scientists and institutions that have the relevant authority or receive an invitation from the Nobel Committee. Information about the nominees, those who nominated them, and the materials from the deliberations remains confidential for 50 years.

11:14:24 UTC

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia’s military of deliberately killing civilians and bombing residential buildings as a macabre gift for Vladimir Putin, who celebrates his 74th birthday on Wednesday.
Ukraine’s president described Russia’s overnight drone and missiles strikes, which killed at least 15 people, as “despicable”. “The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively,” he said.
Video showed a ballistic missile slamming into a five-storey apartment block in the town of Pryluky in the northern Chernihiv region. The concrete building collapsed, entombing those inside. Nine people died, including three children, officials said, with 38 people injured.
Rescuers picked through the rubble in an attempt to find survivors. “Today, on Putin’s birthday, the Russian army ‘presented’ him with the destruction of a residential block in Pryluky. It was an ordinary five-storey block of flats,” Zelenskyy wrote on social media.
He acknowledged that Ukraine was struggling to shoot down enemy ballistic missiles, and appealed to allies to provide US-manufactured Patriot interceptors. “Air defence packages for us right now are a vital necessity,” he said.
The bombardment featured 70 ballistic missiles, as well as 46 jet-powered drones, which in recent weeks have been terrorising Ukrainians on a daily basis. Ukraine’s air force said it managed to down just over 80% of the fast-moving drones – an improvement on the previous average of 50% to 60%.
Eleven regions were hit. Two people were killed in Kyiv, with other deadly strikes in the central cities of Kremenchuk and Oleksandriia, where four civilians died. There was also extensive damage in Dnipro.
Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, said Russian generals had given Putin his favourite birthday present: “war crimes”. Moscow’s grim strategy of bombarding the country’s population so it capitulated would not work, he said.
“The Ukrainian people are not going to give up, because it’s about Ukraine’s survival as a nation and as a state,” he said. The “ultimate” present would be a dock in The Hague, home to the international criminal court, where the Russian president would stand trial, Sybiha said.
One resident in Kremenchuk said the attack happened early on Wednesday. The woman told Ukrainian media: “We were making tea in the morning. My husband was getting ready for work. And that was it. I found myself on the floor. What can I say? It was very scary.”
Local people in Dnipro said a blast wave affected 16 buildings, blowing out doors and windows. One woman, Iryna, said her auto parts workshop had been hit for the sixth time. The ceiling collapsed in Wednesday’s strike, she said, with toilets, sinks and equipment damaged.
“The explosion happened around three in the morning. We were sleeping at home. Everyone was scared, probably the whole city heard it. We will restore the shop and continue to work,” she told the Suspline channel.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine had carried out its own long-range strikes on economic and military sites inside Russia. They included two oil complexes and a training ground in the Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions.“These are justified Ukrainian responses to all Russian attacks on our people,” he said.
The president posted dramatic video of a burning oil tanker close to the southern resort city of Sochi. Russian officials said naval drones had hit the Liberian-flagged ship, adding that “crude oil was burning openly on the Black Sea”. Its Indian crew of 23 was rescued, they said.
Both sides have heavily targeted commercial shipping around the Black Sea since Putin’s full-scale invasion in 2022. In recent weeks Russia has picked off vessels carrying Ukrainian grain, paralysing maritime traffic from Ukraine’s southern ports including Odesa.
Earlier this week, a civilian cargo ship sank after a suspected attack by Russian drones in the Black Sea. Its crew is still missing. A second vessel carrying grain was also hit while sailing in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, said the Bulgarian prime minister, Rumen Radev. The search for survivors was called off on Wednesday, according to Vice-Admiral Rumen Nikolov of the Maritime Administration Executive Agency. “There are no traces of the sailors from the first ship, and there will be none,” he said.

MANILA, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- The Philippines' unemployment rate fell to 5.3 percent in August from 6 percent in July, according to the country's statistics authority on Wednesday.
The Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) said about 2.77 million Filipinos were unemployed in August, down from 3.14 million in July.
According to PSA, the decline in unemployment was driven by the labor market absorbing more new entrants, partly reflecting the seasonal influx of graduates.
However, the August unemployment rate remained higher than the 3.9 percent recorded in the same period last year, with about 2.03 million jobless Filipinos, PSA said.
Services remained the largest source of jobs, accounting for 61.7 percent of total employment, followed by agriculture at 20.9 percent and industry at 17.3 percent. ■

Major anti-fraud operation launched in Portugal

20:13:35 KST

LISBON, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- The European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO) launched one of its largest operations in Portugal on Wednesday, with 250 search and seizure actions carried out simultaneously across the country and more than 20 arrest warrants executed.
The operation, targeting suspected fraud involving EU funds including Portugal's Recovery and Resilience Plan, mobilized approximately 700 Judicial Police officers and 300 inspectors, was primarily in the northern region around Porto, with ramifications extending to the Greater Lisbon area.
The suspected losses to the Portuguese state exceed 100 million euros (112 million U.S. dollars), according to local media agencies.
Two separate inquiries are at the center of the operation, both involving VAT carousel fraud schemes in which thousands of mobile phone handsets were traded in simulated cross-border transactions between EU companies, some of them shell companies created solely for the purpose, enabling perpetrators to either avoid paying VAT or fraudulently claim VAT refunds.
Suspects faced charges of criminal association, tax fraud, money laundering, corruption and misappropriation of subsidies. Detainees would be brought before the Porto Criminal Investigation Court, according to the reports.
The operation also involved simultaneous searches and arrests in other EU member states whose public finances were allegedly defrauded. ■

Henri Kagan, Kenso Soai win 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
19:13:03 CST
20:13:03 KST

The 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry is announced in Stockholm, Sweden, Oct. 7, 2026. Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have been awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced Wednesday. (Xinhua/Lyu You)
STOCKHOLM, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have been awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced on Wednesday.
According to the Academy, some molecules, such as amino acids, exist in two variants that are mirror images of each other. However, living organisms only contain one of these mirror-image forms. How such chemical asymmetry, known as homochirality, could emerge had long remained a mystery to chemists.
"This year's prize recognises discoveries that have enabled chemists to drive chemical reactions that lead to homochirality," the Academy said in a statement, noting that the two laureates "made chemistry choose a mirror image."
"Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously. The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular," says Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry.
Kagan, born in France on Dec. 15, 1930, is affiliated with Universite Paris-Sud in Orsay, France. Soai, born in Japan in 1950, is a professor at Tokyo University of Science. ■

INTERVIEW – Three years into Gaza war, ‘genocide is not over,’ UN rapporteur Albanese says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:12:53 UTC
20:12:53 KST

Three years after Israel launched its war in Gaza, UN special rapporteur Francesca Albanese says Palestinians cannot yet simply be described as survivors of genocide because the destruction is continuing.
The “genocide is not over,” Albanese told Anadolu in an interview approaching the anniversary of the war, warning that the devastation in Gaza and worsening conditions in the occupied West Bank demand more than diplomatic condemnation.
“The situation on the ground is catastrophic. It’s really beyond what words can say,” she said.
Albanese, an Italian human rights lawyer who has served as the UN special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territory since 2022, said the continuing destruction raised questions about the international response, including the policies of governments supporting Israel.
Her comments come as Israel’s war enters its fourth year, with more than 74,000 Palestinians killed and over 175,000 injured since October 2023, according to Palestinian figures.
Israeli attacks have continued despite the ceasefire that took effect on Oct. 10, 2025. Palestinian figures put the toll since then at 1,454 killed and 5,090 injured.
Albanese said descriptions of Palestinians as genocide survivors risk suggesting that the danger has passed.
“It gives the sense that the destruction of Gaza is not over; 70% of the strip is under the control of the army, which is leveling as much as it can,” she said.
Asked how Gaza would be remembered alongside past genocides, Albanese drew comparisons with the treatment of Indigenous peoples during colonialism.
“How does history remember the genocide of Native Americans, or the genocide of the Aboriginal people of Australia, or other genocides that have been committed throughout colonialism?”
“It depends on who writes that history. And right now, we don’t know. We don’t know because we are at a crossing point.”
Albanese described Gaza as the site of a wider struggle between two opposing forces: “Those who want to continue the genocide, the exploitation and the erasure of Palestine, and those who want to stop it, all of this.”
She associated the first camp with the US, Israel and their allies, saying it included advocates of “greater militarization, greater surveillance powers in the hand of states.”
“And then, on the other side, there are mostly people with some governments,” she said.
Asked about electoral gains by politicians critical of Israel’s conduct in Gaza, Albanese said the genocide had shaped public perceptions.
“You cannot slaughter kids and cry victim. You cannot. I mean, you can do that, but you are delusional,” she said.
“And this is what Israeli leaders are doing. And some in Europe are following them, but it doesn’t hold water.”
Albanese also warned of deteriorating conditions in the occupied West Bank, citing killings, arbitrary arrests, detention and Israeli restrictions on Palestinian communities.
She welcomed moves by 12 countries to restrict trade with illegal Israeli settlements, while questioning how far the measures would go.
In a joint statement in September, France, the UK, Canada, Denmark, Spain, Finland, Ireland, Iceland, Norway, Poland, Portugal and Sweden announced plans to introduce or support further restrictions, or said they were actively considering them.
Albanese singled out Britain’s announced restrictions on settlement goods and financial support for settlement construction and infrastructure.
“It marks a change of policy in the UK, a very long overdue change of policy that recognizes the illegality of the occupation,” she said.
But she described the approach as “very settlement-focused” and questioned its scope, including what she said was the absence of an explicit reference to East Jerusalem.
She also welcomed efforts to prevent the advertising and sale of Palestinian property from British territory.
“The fact that advertisements and selling Palestinian property from the UK territory won’t be tolerated. This is good.”
Albanese argued that the war had exposed the costs of European dependence on Washington.
“We are not US allies, because if you have allies, you respect them. You talk to them properly. You don’t shout at them.”
She accused the US of using threats against countries it describes as partners.
“You don’t threaten them to invade their territory or to cut ties with them. This is what the US is doing, because we are not allies. We are in a situation of servitude and subalternity.”
Albanese also urged countries in the Middle East to consider what she described as the links between US foreign policy and ambitions for a “Greater Israel.”
“Greater Israel” refers to varying visions of expanded Israeli territory, drawing on biblical or historical claims. Some advocates seek control over the occupied Palestinian territories, while more expansive interpretations include parts of neighboring countries.
Albanese argued that these ambitions were already being pursued.
“Greater Israel is not a future project. It’s happening, and not just in Palestine,” she said. “So it's critical.”
She said some proponents invoke biblical claims extending into Jordan, Syria and as far as Iraq, and urged governments across the region to take the implications seriously.
Albanese’s criticism of Israel has also brought personal consequences.
The US imposed sanctions on Albanese in July 2025, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio accusing her of conducting a “campaign of political and economic warfare” against the US and Israel.
The Trump administration placed her on its Specially Designated Nationals list, which bars US citizens and businesses from dealing with her. Albanese said the effects extended beyond the US, restricting her access to banking and other financial services.
The sanctions followed her UN report investigating the corporate machinery sustaining Israel’s activities in Palestine, alleging that major technology companies like Microsoft, Alphabet, and Amazon were profiting from and facilitating the occupation and conflict.
A federal judge temporarily blocked the sanctions in May, but an appeals court subsequently allowed their enforcement while the legal challenge continued.
Albanese said the restrictions have affected her ability to work, travel and meet everyday expenses. She said she could no longer use her credit cards, had been denied health insurance and remained barred from entering the US.
“The sanctions prevent me from functioning as a UN person, as a UN expert and as a mother. Everything is compromised,” she said.
Unable to carry out financial transactions or receive payments for other work, she said she now depends on relatives.
“I’m totally financially dependent on my family.”
Her UN role is unpaid, but the restrictions also prevent her from being paid for other projects, she said.
“I cannot earn a penny,” she said.

Indian sailors bear growing toll as another ship attacked off Oman
At least 12 Indian seafarers were injured in attacks on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and the Black Sea over the last two days, including 11 aboard an oil tanker struck off Oman on Tuesday.

Twelve of its 19-member crew were injured, including 11 Indians; 17 people on board were Indian nationals. The injured sailors were evacuated with help from the Omani authorities and are receiving treatment in Khasab, India’s Foreign Ministry said. 
“The targeting of commercial shipping, seafarers and civilian infrastructure in the region must end,” the ministry stated, calling for navigation and commerce through international waterways to be restored at the earliest opportunity. 
The International Maritime Organization (IMO) has recorded 93 confirmed attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Middle East as of October 6. 
Indian crews were also caught in similar incidents in the Black Sea. On Tuesday, twenty-three crew members – all Indian nationals – aboard the Liberian-flagged tanker Aframax Rio were rescued after the vessel was set ablaze off Russia’s Black Sea coast following an attack by an unmanned vessel, according to Russia’s Transport Ministry. No injuries were reported.

SINGAPORE, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- Singapore's central bank on Wednesday issued guidelines setting out supervisory expectations for financial institutions to manage risks arising from the use of artificial intelligence (AI), while allowing firms to tailor their approaches according to their risk profiles.
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said in a statement that the guidelines apply to all financial institutions and AI technologies.
