Germany: Did CDU lawmakers support the far-right AfD?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:11:00 UTC
20:11:00 KST

Germany: Did CDU lawmakers support the far-right AfD?
October 7, 2026
Following events in the parliament of the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Tuesday, speculation is rife that lawmakers from the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) helped elect a far-right extremist as parliamentary speaker.
This would not only violate prior internal agreements, but also come despite the insistence of CDU Chairman, Chancellor Friedrich Merz, that his party would not cooperate with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) anywhere.
In the first session of the parliament in Magdeburg, the capital of Saxony-Anhalt, following the AfD's election victory on September 6, Tobias Rausch was elected parliamentary speaker — the first time a representative of a far-right party had held such a position since the end of World War II.
Rausch was backed by his own party and the Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Rationality (BSW), formerly known as the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance, as had been expected. However, he also received four additional votes by secret ballot. Most observers believe these votes could only have come from right-wing CDU lawmakers.
Leading members of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) were quick to take to the streets in protest in Berlin on Tuesday, marching from the Bundestag through the Brandenburg Gate to nearby Bebelplatz — the very spot where, in 1933, the Nazis burned books by authors they deemed unacceptable. The march concluded with SPD Federal Minister of Defense Boris Pistorius leading the crowd in the German national anthem. Many participants displayed copies of the German Basic Law, a symbol of democracy to stand up for the rule of law and the constitution.
Vice Chancellor and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil (SPD) summarized the situation, "Electing far-right extremists to such an office represents a taboo brake. Not only the BSW, but also the CDU must urgently explain how this could have happened." Klingbeil's SPD is, after all, the junior coalition partner in the federal government.
The events in Magdeburg thus also cast a shadow over the governing coalition.
Did the AfD receive votes from the CDU?
It didn't help much that the leader of the CDU parliamentary group, Thorsten Frei, was careful in his wording.
"It's a secret ballot, so of course, in principle, anybody is suspect." he said. He also added, "The fact that this happened is, in my view, extremely troubling and cause for concern."
The result of the first election in the new state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt thus offers only a glimpse of the fierce debates to come on how to deal with the AfD. The far-right party won 44% of the vote after having campaigned on extremely tough immigration policies, climate change denial and calls for the near-total abolition of public broadcasting.
Despite its election victory, the AfD does not have a parliamentary majority on its own. In the small eastern state, the regional branch of the party has been classified by the Office for the Protection of the Constitution as "confirmed right-wing extremist."
Will CDU politicians help elect an AfD state premier into office?
So once again, the debate about the "firewall" returns. The term refers to the stance taken by democratic parties of ruling out any form of cooperation with the AfD.
At the city and municipal levels, this approach has long since stopped working. Many political analysts have pointed out that the "firewall" has not benefited the CDU, but cooperating with the AfD is also seen as a slippery slope.
Georg Maier, the SPD Interior Minister of the state of Thuringia, agrees. "If the CDU continues down this path, it will contribute to its own downfall. The firewall does serve a purpose."
BSW co-leader Fabio De Masi told the Hamburger Abendblatt newspaper, "We have to pull the AfD out from behind the firewall. Until now, it hasn't had to prove anything and has been able to conceal its internal contradictions. I don't want the AfD to continue growing behind the firewall."
The BSW, a party founded by former Left Party politician Sahra Wagenknecht that has retained some left-wing positions while also aligning itself with the AfD on social issues, paved the way for Rausch's election as parliamentary speaker when it announced that it would vote for him.
The BSW barely managed to cross the 5% threshold for representation in the Saxony-Anhalt parliament. How closely its five MPs want to work with the AfD in the future remains to be seen.
AfD caucus leader Oliver Kirchner recently expressed criticism of BSW co-leaders De Masi and Mohamed Ali, who both have an immigrant background.
"Am I now supposed to spend five years in politics with people who are under the leadership of Mohamed Ali and this half-Italian guy who says, 'They're all Nazis'?" Kirchner told the right-wing magazine Compact earlier this month.
Up until now, support from the BSW has been seen as the AfD's only real chance of coming to power in Saxony-Anhalt. The other parties — the CDU, the SPD, the Greens and the Left Party — continue to categorically rule out any cooperation with the AfD. Whether that will remain the case in the coming weeks is now the big question.
This article was originally written in German.

Armed Israeli settlers beat and rob AFP photographer – media

Armed Israeli settlers beat and rob AFP photographer – media
Armed Israeli settlers have beaten and robbed an AFP photographer marked as press in the occupied West Bank, according to media reports. Around a dozen IDF soldiers were present and did not intervene.
Veteran Palestinian photographer Jaafar Ashtiyeh was hospitalized after being repeatedly struck with rifle butts. The assault is the latest in a growing series of attacks on journalists in the West Bank.
The Committee to Protect Journalists documented at least 16 incidents involving 35 Palestinian, Israeli and international journalists in the first eight months of 2026 alone, already exceeding the 13 incidents involving 25 journalists it recorded throughout 2025.
The attack took place near the village of Aqraba on Tuesday as Ashtiyeh, 58, and fellow AFP photographer John Wessels were documenting Palestinians harvesting olives. The journalists saw an Israeli soldier detaining a Palestinian before a man on a quad bike approached and opened fire, according to AFP.
A Palestinian was shot in the foot and hospitalized, the Palestine Red Crescent Society said.
Israeli settlers routinely target theses locals during the annual olive harvest, attacking farmers and seizing or destroying crops and trees that provide a vital source of income.
At least six other armed men then rushed toward the journalists while firing their weapons. As Ashtiyeh tried to enter a vehicle clearly marked “Press,” two men tackled him and repeatedly struck him with rifle butts.
“I could hear his screams,” Wessels said. He was also threatened at gunpoint, while the attackers took Ashtiyeh’s camera equipment.
Ashtiyeh was left with bruises on his head and torso and was hospitalized. Around a dozen fully equipped IDF soldiers were stationed roughly 500 meters away but did not intervene, according to Wessels. AFP said it had contacted the Israeli military for comment.
“We strongly condemn yet another serious attack on journalists trying to report on events in the West Bank and demand a full investigation,” AFP global news director Phil Chetwynd said. He called it “unacceptable” that journalists could be beaten and robbed by armed settlers while Israeli security forces failed to intervene.
The incident comes as settler violence against local residents in the West Bank has intensified, with near-daily attacks, theft and vandalism reported in recent months. Extremist settlers have also reportedly seized Palestinian-owned olive groves.
Journalists documenting the crimes have increasingly been caught up in the violence. In August, settlers attacked a three-person AFP team east of Bethlehem, throwing stones, striking one journalist with a stick and damaging their vehicle.
Days earlier, Haaretz reporter Matan Golan and photographer Itay Rom were attacked near Qusra – showing that even journalists working for Israeli media have not been spared. Settlers surrounded their vehicle, with one kicking and spitting on Golan, while Israeli soldiers nearby did not intervene, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists.
Earlier this year, Palestinian journalists were beaten, threatened or driven from assignments in a string of other incidents, while crews from CNN, Reuters, Al Jazeera and Anadolu were also confronted or attacked by settlers.
The attacks come against an already deadly backdrop for the press. Israel was responsible for 86 of the record 129 journalists and media workers killed worldwide in 2025 – roughly two thirds of the global total – according to CPJ.

U.S. Air Force B-52 pilots learn refueling in VR first
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:09:51 UTC
20:09:51 KST

- U.S. Air Force B-52 student pilots trained on the EARL virtual reality simulator now make contact with a tanker on their first live flight.
- A study of 233 trainees found structured VR training cut an average of 1.7 sorties and 39 flight minutes needed to reach refueling proficiency.
New U.S. Air Force B-52 Stratofortress pilots are now making contact with a refueling tanker on their first live training flight, a skill that once took students several sorties to master, after the bomber’s training unit at Barksdale Air Force Base, Louisiana, built its air refueling instruction around a virtual reality trainer.
A peer-reviewed study of 233 B-52 pilot trainees found that students who learned on the headset under a structured curriculum needed an average of 1.7 fewer sorties and 39 fewer minutes of flight time to reach proficiency than students trained the traditional way. The results were published in the Journal of Aviation/Aerospace Education & Research.
The device is the Experiential Air Refueling Lightweight Simulator, or EARL, built by small business Specular Theory. It pairs a VR headset with custom throttles and a yoke mounted to a chair, letting students practice the final approach to a tanker’s boom on the ground. Lt. Col. Brandon Wolf, an instructor pilot with the 93rd Bomb Squadron, began working with the company on the project in 2020.
“I’m trying to park a half-million-pound aircraft into a twelve-foot box in the sky,” said Wolf. “And every practice run is expensive.”
The B-52 burns roughly 11,400 liters (3,000 gallons) of fuel an hour, Wolf said. Under the old approach, a student might hold position about 15 m (50 feet) behind the tanker’s boom for 20 or 30 minutes without ever making contact or taking on fuel, and training depended on tanker availability, weather and maintenance.
“Air refueling was the long pole in the tent for our training pipeline,” said Wolf. “It was very difficult for students to master in the allotted flights we had. We had to go to heroic efforts to get everyone graduated on time.”
Col. Aaron Bohl, commander of the 307th Operations Group, said the unit lacked a high-fidelity simulator that could reproduce air refueling in the B-52 before EARL arrived.
The study compared three groups of trainees: those taught the traditional way without VR, those who used VR in a semi-structured way, and those trained under a fully structured VR curriculum called I-BUFF, short for Integrated B-52 Unit Flight Familiarization. Wolf developed the model with a team from Louisiana Tech University through an Air Force Global Strike Command fellowship. Early on, simply handing students a headset without a required curriculum produced little engagement, Wolf said.
“It’s like going to the gym: even when you know it’s good for you, it’s easy to put off if nobody’s holding you accountable,” said Wolf.
The command’s Striker STEEL program joined the effort in late 2022 and early 2023, adding cognitive training that raises the mental workload as students improve. Eye-tracking data showed that student pilots’ eyes wander across the instrument panel, while experienced instructors rely on peripheral vision to catch small alignment cues, said Dr. Tucker Readdy, the program’s chief scientist.
“The real difficult cognitive skill is change detection,” said Readdy. “If those three points are aligned, then you should stay connected to the boom, and fuel is good.”
Students must also push 20 to 30 pounds (9 to 14 kg) of force through the yoke while wearing a parachute and breathing through an oxygen mask, which the program says makes ground practice valuable before facing that load in flight.
Wolf said the sorties saved are being redirected to other training, including weapons employment on the range and landings.
“Cutting nearly two sorties saves real money, but more importantly, we’re reinvesting that time in other parts of training,” said Wolf.
Air Force Global Strike Command’s innovation hub, STRIKEWERX, has estimated that EARL could save about $5.8 million a year in real-world training costs. Bohl said the bigger gain for him is safety.
“Students are now working on the fine-tuning of air refueling before their first time behind a live aircraft,” said Bohl.
The program is not yet a formal part of the B-52 training syllabus. The Air Force says the peer-reviewed results open the way for EARL and the I-BUFF model to be written into the curriculum and possibly adopted for other aircraft in Global Strike Command, but it has not announced a timeline.

Turkey sending technical, defensive support to Saudi Arabia to help fight Houthis, officials say
ANKARA/RIYADH, Oct 7 - Turkey is sending mainly defensive and technical support to Saudi Arabia to help it fight Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis, two officials said on Wednesday, after the NATO member and Pakistan pledged to act on the collective defence commitment of their newly formed alliance.
Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member constituted an attack on all. They have been working to set the parameters of the new alliance and have held political and military meetings in response to the Houthi attacks.
On Monday, the countries said they had agreed to move immediately to implement their collective defence commitments and ensure the "rapid deployment" of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.
Turkey, which has NATO's second-largest army and a robust defence industry, has condemned the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, voiced willingness to help meet Riyadh's technical military needs, and agreed to join a Saudi-led coalition to ensure navigational safety in the Red Sea.
A Turkish official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the support expected from Turkey was only in the form of military equipment, intelligence sharing, and weapons systems, adding that no other form of deployment had taken place as part of the alliance so far.
DRONE OPERATORS, FINE-TUNING DEFENSIVE MEASURES
Officials have said that Turkish support for Saudi Arabia — including air defence systems — would largely be in a bilateral capacity for now, as Turkey's parliament has not officially ratified the joint pact. The amount and nature of the support would increase after ratification, they have said.
A US official briefed on the matter said that Turkey had so far decided to send capabilities that were broadly defensive, including strategic planning support and help with logistics. The official said the assistance included drone operators and help with fine-tuning defensive measures, as well as intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, speaking to state media after an extraordinary meeting of the Mecca alliance in Riyadh, said the sides had discussed what support to provide Saudi Arabia to help its defensive capabilities.
"We had our Defence Minister and Chief of General Staff with us, and they especially provided very fruitful views on military issues, operational issues, and technical matters," he said on Monday.
Pakistani and regional officials have said Ankara and Islamabad have provided Saudi Arabia with military equipment that the kingdom is using in Yemen.
This week, Yemeni government forces with Saudi-led coalition air support launched a counter-offensive to recapture strategic territory near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, an international shipping route for energy exports and other trade.
Officials had told Reuters last week that Saudi Arabia was planning an offensive against the Houthis, with options being considered including a coastal push to secure the Red Sea shipping route or an assault on multiple fronts. REUTERS

Russia launched almost 3,500 jet-powered drones against Ukraine throughout September, according to Ukrainian Air Force spokesperson Yuriy Ihnat on Wednesday.
The drones fly faster than propeller-driven drones and are harder to shoot down.

Ihnat announced the figure on television, as reported by state media Ukrinform. September has also seen intensified Russian attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, ranging from passenger trains to gas stations, with data centers and residential buildings in central Kyiv also targeted – a relative rarity in the more than four-year war.
The numbers represent a 10-fold spike from the 350 cited by Ihnat in June, rising to 1,500 a month later before reaching 2,850 in August.
By late September, Ihnat said Russia launched 1,900 jet-powered drones, a week before the month was over – meaning close to 1,600 were likely launched within the last week of the month.
The figure is largely in line with those given by President Volodymyr Zelensky in a recent statement, in which he said on Sunday, Oct. 4, that Russia launched 1,900 strike drones, 1,700 guided aerial bombs, and 25 missiles of various types against Ukraine over the past week.
But Ihnat also noted fewer Russian jet-powered drones launched in October thus far, with around 50 per night and around 30 during the day.
Ukraine’s Military Intelligence (HUR) previously suggested Russia might have trouble obtaining the Chinese jet engines used in the drones, though the agency later said recent models also came with improved navigation and warheads.
British Defence Intelligence Update Ukraine 6 October , 2026
Ihnat also noted the newer jet-powered drones – now capable of reaching 800-900 kilometers per hour (500-560 mph) – are comparable to ordinary cruise missiles and complicate Ukrainian efforts at interception.
Recent reports also suggest that Russia is scaling production of similar weapons by refitting target aircraft with warheads, such as the Dan-Ts, to overwhelm Ukrainian defenses.
F-16s to the rescue?
Ihnat said Kyiv is working with its allies on countermeasures.
“Innovative solutions from our military-industrial complex, our military leadership, and political leadership, in conjunction with our partners, will help us solve this problem,” he said, as reports suggest that US-made F-16s have taken on bigger roles in intercepting the jet-powered drones in recent weeks, with Kyiv seeking additional 20mm autocannon rounds to help down the drones.
As Russia began targeting bridges connecting both sides of the Ukrainian capital across the Dnipro River in October, Kyiv also began deploying automatic machine gun turrets, enhanced by artificial intelligence (AI), along the bridges with some success.
Ihnat said the turrets have already shot down jet-powered drones, leaving him surprised.
Zelensky also vowed to soon scale up production of small air defense missiles to complement layered air defenses around Kyiv, though little is known about the project, including the missiles’ type, performance, and planned production numbers.

AI companies say rivals are ‘distilling’ their models. What does that even mean?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:08:50 UTC
20:08:50 KST

To make grain-based liquor, you heat a fermented mash in a still until alcohol-rich vapor rises and then cool it back into a stronger liquid. Chemists and whiskey makers know this as distillation. Artificial intelligence developers have borrowed the word to describe boiling down a big AI model into a smaller one—and lately the biggest AI companies say that rivals have been distilling like bootleggers.
In September Anthropic and OpenAI each detailed how they caught and killed campaigns to distill their flagship models—that is, to extract enough information from the models to train new models that mimic the originals at a fraction of the size and cost.
Distillation has become a sore spot for American AI companies as they try to justify high valuations and fight off competition from each other and open-source alternatives. If, say, a Chinese model developer can piggyback on all the money and computing power those companies have invested, the incentive to keep making new models starts to evaporate.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
And no one expects distillation to stop any time soon—so we asked the researchers who study it to explain the situation.
What is distillation, anyway?
Just as a still concentrates a large batch of weak liquid into a smaller batch of strong stuff, AI distillation condenses a big model into a smaller one that, ideally, acts like the original. The process starts with the existing large model, called the teacher. Developers prompt the teacher many times over and then feed its responses into the new model, called the student, to train the latter.
In a way, every response contains information about what the teacher learned during training, so that knowledge passes to the student without going through the process of collecting data, finding patterns in those data and getting human feedback. Distillation lets someone reverse engineer an AI model just by using it and watching its responses.
It helps that AI models tend to give away more than just their final answers. “Oftentimes the teacher model doesn’t just give you the label, but it actually gives you more fine-grained information,” says Yevgeniy Vorobeychik, a professor of computer science at Washington University in St. Louis. That could include the odds a model assigns to each possible response or, as in the case OpenAI described, an encrypted record of the step-by-step reasoning its more powerful models work through before they answer.
Why distill in the first place?
Plenty of distillation is aboveboard. Smaller models let developers get more for less. In fact, the concept predates large language models (LLMs); by the 2000s, researchers were studying it as a way to increase efficiency for neural networks. “We cared about making it smaller, easier to use, faster to apply,” says Alexandru Niculescu-Mizil, a machine learning researcher at Qube Research & Technologies, who cowrote an early paper on the idea in 2006.
Distilling someone else’s model is another matter. The term first caught mainstream attention in early 2025, when DeepSeek, then a little-known Chinese start-up, released a reasoning model, called R1, that it said it had trained for less than $300,000—a fraction of what American labs had spent. Allegations quickly emerged that DeepSeek had trained R1 in part on responses extracted from OpenAI’s models.
These days the word is generally associated with accusations of model theft, mostly aimed at Chinese developers such as DeepSeek and Moonshot AI, the maker of Kimi. In their September reports, Anthropic and OpenAI both blamed labs based in China for the recent distillation campaigns they caught, calling the activity “illicit” and “unauthorized.” DeepSeek and Moonshot AI have both fended off these accusations in the past. Of course, Anthropic and OpenAI have themselves been accused of training their models on data obtained without authorization from all over the internet.
Still, though the companies also cast distillation as a security risk, their most obvious interest in stopping it is protecting their competitive advantage. “The text that it produces in response to your prompt is being stolen by some rival companies,” says Alexander Panfilov, a Ph.D. student at the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems in Germany. “But on a conceptual level, what you are stealing [are] capabilities.”
So how does one distill?
In general, distillation is done by collecting thousands and thousands of AI responses to different kinds of queries. Those prompts and responses then become training data for the student, usually through a process called supervised fine-tuning, which treats the teacher’s answers as targets the student should try to emulate. Over many rounds, training nudges the student’s internal settings, called weights, so that its answers more closely match the teacher’s.
The key is getting those data. Anthropic and OpenAI have detailed several creative methods they believe attackers used to do so. According to Anthropic, some labs routed their own customers’ prompts to Claude and then saved Claude’s responses to train their own models. The company also said that distillers try to obscure where they are located. OpenAI, meanwhile, said distillers tried to get at its models’ hidden reasoning by “copying encrypted reasoning from one conversation and asking a model in another conversation to decrypt” it.
Panfilov was co-lead author of a preprint paper detailing that kind of attack, and OpenAI credited him and his colleagues with bringing the attacks to the company’s attention. In this case, the goal was to distill how the models reason, or generate longer responses in order to solve hard problems step-by-step. Panfilov and his colleagues called their project “Stolen Thoughts,” a sign of how tightly the concept has become intertwined with thievery.
How do you catch a distiller?
The AI companies are hesitant to reveal exactly how they caught these latest attempts because doing so would show the next distiller what to avoid. Broadly, though, the firms seem to have watched for accounts prompting their models in suspicious ways, whether by firing off lots of prompts in a short time or by asking telltale kinds of questions. Anthropic, for instance, said that, from May to July, it observed more than 151 million exchanges between Claude and accounts tied to Chinese e-commerce giant Alibaba, which also makes the Qwen family of AI models.
Panfilov says the attack he studied is easy to detect, but he worries that cleverer ones can’t be spotted without trampling everyone’s privacy. “I don’t have a good idea how [AI companies] would do it, especially given that they claim this zero data retention policy,” he says, referring to arrangements under which the companies don’t store some customers’ prompts and responses.
Both OpenAI and Anthropic have warned that the distillers’ methods will only get more sophisticated, given how valuable distillation can be.
Can distillation be stopped?
The trouble is that the very qualities that make AI models informative and useful also make them good to train on. So attempts to make a model harder to distill may also make it worse. Over the summer, Vorobeychik and his colleagues found that a model’s reasoning can be rewritten so that it will make poor training material for a copycat, without making the model’s answers any less accurate. They also found that the rewritten reasoning was harder for people to follow, however. “Just by virtue of the fact that they’re harder to read for the LLM to train, it’s also harder for humans to digest,” Vorobeychik says. That’s an unwelcome trade for a technology whose output already takes flak for being hard to parse.
Panfilov also notes that distillation can be done in pieces in which “each query in itself is benign.” That would make it even harder to distinguish someone prompting a model for ordinary use from someone trying to build a model of their own. AI companies will have to balance protecting their models’ capabilities against actually flexing them for the public, which is, after all, what they’re selling.
All this suggests that stopping illicit distillation will mean finding new attacks before stamping them out. The labs, in effect, are playing revenuers, the liquor-tax agents who once hunted down and dismantled illegal stills. But as fears about distillation intertwine with fears about Chinese AI capabilities more broadly, busting stills one at a time may not be enough to put the American AI industry at ease.

The case involving an offer of $250,000 to arrange for Ukraine's National Security and Defense Council (NSDC) to impose sanctions on a company involves a sitting member of parliament and her accomplices, with an indictment against them sent to court, the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) said Wednesday.
According to the investigation, members of the group offered a representative of the company to arrange for the NSDC to adopt a sanctions decision for $250,000, and planned to transfer the funds received to council officials as payment for securing the decision. To conceal the agreement and guarantee payment, the company representative was offered to formalize the transfer of the money as a loan. After receiving the first part of the amount of $125,000, he was assured that the funds would be handed over to NSDC officials. In reality, however, the money remained with the group members because they failed to find anyone willing to carry out the promised illegal actions.
"In December 2025, NABU and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO), in cooperation with the Main Directorate of Internal Security of the Security Service of Ukraine, notified a sitting member of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine and her accomplices that they were suspected of committing a crime. In June 2026, the investigation in the case was completed. One of the members of the criminal group entered into a cooperation agreement with the prosecution. Under its terms, he provided incriminating testimony against the other accomplices," NABU said.
The High Anti-Corruption Court (HACC) sentenced him to five years in prison, releasing him from serving the sentence on probation. In addition, he transferred UAH 700,000 to support the Armed Forces of Ukraine through the UNITED24 fundraising platform.
As reported, in July the HACC approved a plea agreement concluded between a prosecutor from SAPO and a citizen who, along with others, was exposed for soliciting the provision of $250,000 in an unlawful benefit in exchange for resolving the issue of imposing NSDC sanctions.
The criminal group's activities were organized by a member of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine, who became the "guarantor" of this agreement. The statement did not explicitly name the lawmaker. Based on the details of the case, it appears to be referring to Anna Skorokhod.

The backstory to Mike Evans' 'The Whole World Sings Together'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:07:23 UTC
20:07:23 KST

The Israeli woman who approached Mike Evans in a California restaurant had woken up that morning feeling depressed. Then, he recalled, she turned on the television and heard people from around the world singing. Recognizing the man behind the production, she came over to thank him.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
For Evans, an American Christian evangelist who leads Friends of Zion and has supported Israel and the Jewish people for more than 40 years, the encounter captured what “The Whole World Sings Together” was meant to do: reach people who believed they had been abandoned and let them hear something different. “So, … we believed that the vision was more than a song. It was a movement; it was a global movement,” Evans told The Media Line.
Seventeen singers of different nationalities took part in the production, bringing their own languages, musical traditions, and experiences of belonging and loss. Inspired by the spirit of Michael Jackson and Lionel Richie’s “We Are the World,” the song became part of Evans’ effort to demonstrate international support for Israel and the Jewish people.
That effort includes a 24-hour global prayer broadcast and approximately 2,000 Christians now visiting Israel for Oct. 7 commemorations and solidarity events.
Asked where it all began, Evans recalled the painful experiences of his childhood home. “Well, it started for me at 11, when my father strangled me and left me for dead. He was an antisemite, and he was married to a Jew, my mother, and he hated Jews.” He said that when he regained consciousness, he made a fist to God and asked, “Why was I born?”
He said the answer became his life’s purpose.
“I couldn’t defend one Jew against the Jew-hater. My life’s call was to defend all the Jews, and there’s never been a more important time to show solidarity with the Jewish people globally than right now.”
Producer was flattered, excited when Evans pitched idea
Producer Noam Ben Shalom credits Evans with creating “The Whole World Sings Together” and said that when Evans proposed the production, he was flattered and excited. Then came the almost impossible deadline - a finished video clip to be ready in two weeks.
“I said, well, Mike, with God’s help.”
“He said, you have God’s help.”
Ben Shalom, a freelancer who has worked with Friends of Zion for more than a decade, joined a team that included co-producer Zvi Raviv, musical director Ronit Banit, and Friends of Zion staff. They searched social media and personal connections, requested videos, and conducted screen tests.
“Eventually we managed to gather 17 singers,” he said. “We got into the studio for two very intensive days, and we started working on the clip.”
The frantic search soon gave way to a different feeling once the voices began coming together.
“Once we got into the studio, the atmosphere was electrifying,” Ben Shalom told The Media Line.
“They felt their mission. We felt our mission, Ronit and I. And we really thought and felt that we are doing something great here.”
Banit said she looked beyond talent when choosing the ensemble, weighing the singers’ sensitivity to Oct. 7 and how they treated one another. In the studio, those choices became something she could hear and feel.
“We stopped being just a collection of singers from different places and became a single group, with a real human and musical relationship,” she told The Media Line.
Raviv has known Evans for about 30 years, since running the Jerusalem 3000 project. He describes their friendship as one that has helped bring Christians and Jews together through humanitarian work.
Finding voices for Evans’ latest idea meant drawing on Israel’s diverse population. Raviv cited a description by Israel’s fifth president, Yitzhak Navon, of people arriving from 116 countries. But locating singers from countries such as India and Japan proved harder, and embassies helped.
Even with the performers assembled, the words did not simply fall into place. Music written for English had to accommodate languages with different rhythms and line lengths.
“Now, if I take Hebrew, Hebrew is longer than English. Japanese is shorter than English. How do you fit the music, the words into the music?” Raviv asked.
Another challenge was keeping the song clear of the political arguments surrounding it.
“We wanted to bring … the message of unity, the message of togetherness, the message of just being human without getting into strife and into battles, etc.,” Raviv told The Media Line.
For Ronen Lazarov, Banit, a conductor and pianist with whom he had previously performed, extended the invitation.
“The idea … was not only to sing this song in English, but to sing it in different languages, according to the mother tongue of each one of the singers,” he said. “And my ticket was the Italian.”
A tenor from Milan, Lazarov came to Israel after high school with friends from a Zionist youth movement. His early years included kibbutz life and the army. More than 40 years later, his family connections remain in Italy, but he lives in Israel.
He began developing his operatic voice in his mid-20s, studying privately for years with teachers in Tel Aviv and Jerusalem. He now performs in orchestral and choral projects, gives recitals, and sings with bands.
In the studio, he met unfamiliar faces, including a Chinese participant living in the Upper Galilee and an Iranian singer. Yet the feelings the project stirred were familiar. Each anniversary, he said, changes how Oct. 7 sits in people’s memories; recording brought those emotions back to the surface.
“We felt that we were part of something that can be an ambassador in the world to try to explain in an artistic way what the feelings of our people are about this tragic event and what happened after that,” he told The Media Line.
He called it shlichut - a mission. During the chorus, the singers looked into one another’s eyes and moved with the music. After hours of recording, Lazarov left with a feeling he still struggled to describe. “My feeling was … that I was like seven meters above the ground.”
Cherubin Ngemba had long imagined singing alongside people from different international backgrounds. “I was thinking how one day it can be possible for me to sing with other people from other countries, from other cultures, how we can bring something together for one objective, to be united.”
When Ben Shalom invited him to join Evans’ project, he accepted. “I did it with all my heart.”
Ngemba, 37, said he arrived from the Democratic Republic of Congo in 2016 after threats connected to a youth association led by his father. His father sought somewhere safe to send him, and Israel granted him a visa.
Ngemba’s connection to the project was also personal. A close friend, Bar, was murdered after attending the Nova festival on Oct. 7.
That loss gave Evans’ campaign urgency. He said the protests immediately following Oct. 7 intensified his determination to show another picture. He described demonstrations against Jews and in support of Hamas, including American young people chanting “from the river to the sea.”
“So, we’re showing, no, no, no, it’s not true, that the world is not against the Jewish people. Quite the contrary. The world is with them, and we’re showing that and revealing and exposing the lie.”
Evans said 130 nations would unite in solidarity for the 24-hour prayer event, including thousands participating from Pakistan. He described it as the largest solidarity event in Israel’s history and the largest prayer meeting in the world.
For Evans, its growth is part of a continuing effort rather than a single production.
“Well, it’s a wave. You’re building a wave, and one of the things that I’ve always believed is that the key to happiness is committing your life to a cause greater than yourself, and this is such a cause.”
For many participants, the support he wants Israelis to recognize is rooted in faith. Evans estimates that there are 750 million Bible-believing Zionists and argues that Israel underestimates how many of its supporters are not Jewish.
“Now, they don’t agree on the politics of Israel, but they do agree that this is a Jewish state, and it’s a fulfillment of prophecy,” he said.
“They believe that God will bless them if they bless the Jewish people, and God will curse them if they curse them.”
Pressed on whether Christian leaders sufficiently understand the complexities of Israel, Arab nations, and Iran, he returned to the Bible. “It’s not a problem for them, because they’re moral clarity people, and they based it upon their Bible.”
Evans’ own view of present-day conflict is uncompromising. He describes Israel as a firewall against radical Islam, links hostility toward Jews and Christians, and argues that weakening Israel and American accommodation of the Muslim Brotherhood helped create the circumstances that led to the September 11 attacks.
He draws a sharp distinction, though, between standing with Israel and endorsing its politics. “I’ve never agreed with Israel’s policies. It’s mishigas. It’s crazy stuff.”
Evans criticized the coalition government, the Supreme Court’s structure, and the attorney general’s role, and rejected both right-wing and left-wing labels.
Raviv wants the song to reach beyond those divisions - and beyond Israel. “If you look today into every single country, every single country has a problem of polarization. We need to depolarize the world,” he said.
“And this song hopes to carry the message of depolarization of the world for people to act together for the improvement and betterment of humanity.”
For Evans, young people are a crucial audience. He believes universities, artificial intelligence, and hostile messaging have distorted their understanding, comparing what he sees as their indoctrination to that of Nazi youth.
His response includes social media influencers whose posts, he said, attracted more than a quarter-billion views last year, as well as challenging figures such as Tucker Carlson. “It’s a war of ideas. It’s a media war, also.”
Evans predicts that the event, music, and related social media efforts will generate more than 1 billion views and reach more than 1 billion people within 12 months.
He said the prayer event would stream online and be carried by broadcasters. Ben Shalom expects the music video’s inclusion in the 24-hour broadcast to reach tens of millions, potentially hundreds of millions, of viewers.
Ben Shalom measures its effect in more personal terms.
“You know, feeling the love and support of different nationalities, the message to the world that we are with you, that Israel, you are not alone, is something that is very heartwarming and very rare in these days,” he said.
Evans hopes that support will also challenge perceptions of Israelis as arrogant, aggressive, militaristic, or heartless. He points instead to hospitals treating Muslim patients and employing Muslim doctors. “And it’s just that perception is reality in many people’s eyes, but perception is not truth,” he said.
Raviv, asked what future generations should remember, wants them to hear more than a beautiful performance. “The music is beautiful, but the question is whether people look into the message.”
For him, Jerusalem gives that message religious and historic significance: a city associated with monotheistic faiths, belief in a God overseeing human conduct, and an obligation to do good. He hopes a message emerging from Jerusalem can urge people to end conflict and live in peace.
Lazarov is cautious about the distance between the song’s ambition and the world outside the studio. “We want the whole world to sing together,” he said. “Unfortunately, it’s not what is really happening in the world now. But this can be one drop in the big sea where we can try to influence somehow.”
Evans: Music won't remove 'memories of October 7'
Evans knows the music cannot undo the loss. Asked whether hope might soften or blunt the memories of Oct. 7, he answered directly. “No, hope won’t remove the memories of October 7.”
For Banit, the possibility of something new emerging from grief was there in the studio.
“For me, this song is much more than a musical production. It’s a small proof that even out of great pain, a new encounter can be created. People can come from different countries, speak different languages, and grow up in different cultures, and still find a single, shared voice.”

Sinwar, the Samson of Gaza: Did he bring destruction down on his own people on Oct. 7? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:07:18 UTC
20:07:18 KST

On October 7, Israelis once again return to the morning that changed their country and the region forever.
They remember the communities attacked, the civilians murdered, the families shattered and the hostages taken into Gaza. They remember the fear and the profound sense that the security they had taken for granted had collapsed in a single morning.
The world should remember this too.
There should be no ambiguity about what Hamas did. The deliberate killing of civilians, the taking of hostages, and the attacks on communities were not legitimate political acts. They were brutal and inhumane crimes that deserve unequivocal condemnation.
No political cause, occupation, blockade, or historical grievance can justify deliberately targeting civilians.
But on this October 7, there is another question that deserves to be asked: What did Hamas’s leadership do to the people of Gaza in whose name it claimed to act?
And perhaps an even more uncomfortable question: was Hamas ever synonymous with Gaza?
The answer, for anyone who listened carefully to Gaza before October 7, was no.
Long before the war, there were Palestinians in Gaza who were angry with Hamas, frustrated with its rule and exhausted by the political division between Hamas and Fatah. There were young people who wanted employment, electricity, education and a future. There were families who wanted security and dignity rather than another cycle of confrontation.
There were also Palestinians who simply wanted to live.
The slogan of the “We Want to Live” movement “Bidna Ne’ish” expressed something remarkably simple: Palestinians in Gaza wanted a normal civilian life.
They wanted to work. They wanted their children to study. They wanted functioning institutions. They wanted to be able to criticize those in power without fear.
Most importantly, they wanted their identity to be Palestinian without having to make that identity synonymous with a political faction.
That reality matters when we discuss October 7.
Hamas controlled Gaza, but control is not the same as unanimous consent.
In a society governed by an armed movement, silence cannot automatically be interpreted as political support. A person may remain silent because he agrees, but he may also remain silent because he is afraid. Someone may oppose Hamas but lack the power to challenge it publicly.
This distinction is critical.
The image of Gaza as a single political bloc behind Hamas is not only inaccurate; it also erases the Palestinian civilians who opposed the movement, feared it or simply wanted to live outside the logic of permanent conflict.
This is why one sentence should be repeated clearly on October 7:
Hamas is not Gaza, and Gaza is not Hamas.
A Palestinian who rejects Hamas is not less Palestinian.
A Palestinian who wants civilian government is not less committed to his people.
And a Palestinian who wants peace with Israelis does not automatically abandon Palestinian rights.
These distinctions are essential if the international community genuinely wants to understand Gaza.
Yahya Sinwar was not merely another Hamas commander. He became one of the central figures of the movement’s leadership and one of the defining symbols of its strategy of confrontation with Israel.
His legacy cannot be separated from October 7 and the catastrophe that followed.
This is where the image of Samson comes to mind.
In the biblical story, Samson brings the temple down upon his enemies but the temple collapses upon him as well.
Was Sinwar the Samson of Gaza?
The metaphor may sound harsh, but it captures a political reality that deserves examination.
A strategy that seeks victory through destruction can eventually destroy the society it claims to liberate.
Hamas may have believed that October 7 would fundamentally change the strategic equation with Israel. But for the people of Gaza, the consequences were devastating.
Homes were destroyed. Families were displaced. Children lost parents and parents lost children. Schools, universities, hospitals and civilian infrastructure were devastated. An entire generation saw its future narrowed by war.
None of this erases the suffering of Israelis on October 7.
And none of it excuses Hamas.
It makes the question even more urgent: who had the right to make such a decision on behalf of millions of civilians?
October 7 was a decision made by Hamas’s leadership.
The consequences were borne by an entire population.
This distinction is at the heart of the Palestinian question.
There is also an important Israeli dimension.
The people living in the communities surrounding Gaza are not simply political symbols. They are civilians. They have families, homes, memories and fears. Many experienced October 7 as the destruction of the most basic assumption of modern life: that your home is a place where you are safe.
At the same time, Palestinian civilians in Gaza have lived for years with a different but equally painful reality: the knowledge that whenever the conflict escalates, their homes and lives can be transformed overnight.
Both societies have suffered.
But recognizing Palestinian suffering does not require minimizing Israeli suffering, just as recognizing Israeli suffering does not require ignoring Palestinian civilians.
The principle should be universal.
A civilian is a civilian.
A child is a child.
A hostage is a hostage.
And murder does not become legitimate because it is committed in the name of a political cause.
If October 7 taught Israel that its security assumptions could no longer be taken for granted, the war that followed should also teach Palestinians and the international community that Gaza cannot continue indefinitely under the logic of armed factions deciding the fate of an entire civilian population.
The question therefore cannot only be who will govern Gaza.
The deeper question is what kind of government Gaza needs.
Does Gaza need another armed faction?
Another political monopoly?
Another generation raised to believe that war is inevitable?
Or does Gaza need civilian leadership accountable to its own people?
This is where the voices that existed before October 7 matter.
The people who marched under the slogan “We Want to Live” were not asking for another war. They were asking for dignity.
They were asking for a future.
Their message deserves to be heard again.
Because preventing another October 7 cannot be achieved only through military measures.
Israel needs security, but long-term Israeli security also requires a Palestinian society with a political alternative to Hamas.
Palestinians need freedom and dignity, but those goals cannot be achieved by allowing armed movements to repeatedly turn civilian society into a battlefield.
The two realities are connected.
There are Israeli civilians living near Gaza who want to raise their children without fear of another attack.
There are Palestinian civilians in Gaza who want to raise their children without fear of another war.
These people may have different histories, different memories and different political views.
But they share something fundamental.
They want to live.
For too long, the civilian voices on both sides have been overshadowed by armed organizations, political leaders and international actors speaking on their behalf.
Perhaps the lesson of October 7 is that the civilians themselves must finally become part of the political equation.
Gaza should not be defined exclusively by Hamas.
Israel should not be defined exclusively by its conflict with Hamas.
The future of both societies cannot remain permanently hostage to the logic of October 7.
On this anniversary, Israelis should remember their dead and demand justice for the hostages and their families. That memory should never be erased.
But the world should also listen to Palestinians in Gaza who say that Hamas does not speak for all of them.
There are Palestinians who reject Hamas.
There are Palestinians who reject Fatah.
There are Palestinians who reject the politics of armed factions altogether.
There are Palestinians who want civilian government, economic opportunity, security and a future.
Their voices are not a footnote.
They may be the beginning of a different future.
This is why the question surrounding Sinwar and October 7 is ultimately larger than the man himself.
If Samson brought down the temple upon his enemies and himself, perhaps the real tragedy of Sinwar’s strategy is that the people who paid the greatest price were not necessarily the people who made the decision.
So on October 7, the question should not only be who started the war, who won a battle or who lost.
The question should be:
Who will have the courage to end the cycle?
Gaza may not need another Samson.
It may need civilian leaders who listen to their own people.
And Israel may need to look beyond the immediate question of defeating Hamas toward the longer-term question of what kind of Palestinian society can exist beside Israel without threatening its security.
The future will not be built by pretending that October 7 did not happen.
Nor will it be built by ensuring that October 7 happens again in another form.
It will be built when Israelis and Palestinians can finally say something more powerful than the language of war:
We want to live.
The writer is a Palestinian peace activist from Gaza who advocates for Israeli-Palestinian coexistence and amplifying the voices of Palestinians who reject violence.

Transportation Ministry’s aviation security system under police review following flydubai incident
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:07:08 UTC
20:07:08 KST

Police have opened a preliminary review into revelations involving the Transportation Ministry’s aviation security system, one week after the attempted hijacking of flydubai flight FZ1073.
Maariv has learned that Lahav 433 has begun examining the details of the case, including contracts and conduct within the Transportation Ministry.
Police are examining the conduct of two senior officials in the ministry’s aviation security system: Avri Cohen, head of the Emergency, Security, Information and Cyber Division, and Dvir Rubinstein, director of the Aviation Security Operations Center.
In Rubinstein’s case, police are examining a suspected conflict of interest related to private work he did for foreign airlines, including flydubai, while serving in his government role. In Cohen’s case, authorities are examining his additional work as a “reserve security officer,” after it emerged that he had not received approval from the Civil Service Commission.
At this stage, the matter remains a police review only. No reports indicate that either man has been questioned under caution, and no determination has been made that either committed an offense.
Two different issues under investigation; Cohen’s case may be civil, not criminal
The issues under review also differ in nature. In Rubinstein’s case, the focus is on a possible conflict of interest. In Cohen’s case, the matter could ultimately prove to be disciplinary rather than criminal.
Rubinstein is not a civil servant, but provides services to the Transportation Ministry through an outsourced position. As director of the Aviation Security Operations Center, he oversees and approves security for foreign airlines and flights entering Israel.
According to reports, Rubinstein also privately provided consulting and training services to foreign airlines, including flydubai and Emirates, while working for the ministry. He also received payment from flydubai.
The review is expected to examine whether a conflict of interest existed between Rubinstein’s work for the state and his private activities. The Transportation Ministry said his outside employment was legally approved and carried out outside the hours he worked for the ministry.
One of the key questions is what the approval granted to Rubinstein covered, and whether those who authorized the additional work knew that his clients included airlines with which he had dealings as part of his official role.
In Cohen’s case, the review centers on additional work he carried out for years. According to reports, since 2018 he had also served as a “reserve security officer” in the Ofek aviation security system while working at the ministry, and received additional payment for that work.
The Transportation Ministry initially said ministry management had approved Cohen's additional work when he entered the position. It later emerged that the Civil Service Commission had neither approved the work nor known about it.
The ministry later clarified that the commission, not the ministry, has the authority to approve additional employment at Cohen’s level, and that no such request had been submitted. According to the ministry, when the current management learned of the additional work several months ago, Cohen was instructed to stop it unless and until a permit was granted.
Ministry responsible for certain security aspects involving flights to Israel
Published documents indicated that the Transportation Ministry’s Security Division is responsible for certain aspects of security involving flights entering Israel. The ministry, however, stressed that it is not an intelligence agency and lacks the tools to conduct intelligence background checks on passengers or crew members.
The police review is still in its early stages and is expected to focus on the additional employment, the approvals granted for it, and whether a conflict of interest arose between private activities and roles in the aviation security system.
As of now, there have been no reports that either man has been questioned under caution, and no determination has been made that an offense was committed.
At this stage, the matter remains a preliminary review and not a criminal investigation. No one connected to the affair is currently being questioned under caution by the National Unit for Fraud Investigations, and no criminal investigation under caution is being conducted into anyone involved.
Police are first seeking to collect the relevant details and examine the full scope of the contracts and conduct involved. If suspicions and evidence of criminal offenses emerge during the review, the matter could develop into a criminal investigation.

Ukrainian MP defies Zelensky on NATO

Ukrainian MP defies Zelensky on NATO
A Ukrainian lawmaker has proposed amending the constitution to remove the country’s NATO membership goal and restore its neutral status. One of Russia’s goals in ongoing hostilities with Ukraine is to ensure its return to neutrality.
The proposal submitted on Tuesday by MP Anna Skorokhod is largely symbolic, since the Verkhovna Rada cannot amend the constitution while martial law remains in force. Vladimir Zelensky ordered the emergency after the 2022 escalation of the Ukraine conflict and has since used it to retain presidential powers after his mandate expired in 2024.
Russian officials have described NATO’s growing involvement in Ukraine as one of the principal causes of the conflict.
Skorokhod’s proposal follows a political scandal involving fellow lawmaker Aleksey Goncharenko, who was expelled this week from the opposition European Solidarity faction after calling for peace talks with Russia. Skorokhod herself was expelled from Zelensky’s Servant of the People party just months after being elected in 2019.
When Ukraine became independent in 1991, it declared an intention to remain outside military blocs. Kiev changed course following the Western-backed armed coup in 2014. In 2018, then-President Pyotr Poroshenko proposed enshrining Ukraine’s aspirations to join NATO and the EU in the constitution.
Poroshenko was defeated the following year by political outsider Zelensky. While the incumbent campaigned on Western integration and Ukrainian nationalism, Zelensky presented himself as a candidate who would reconcile Ukrainians of different ethnic backgrounds and improve relations with Moscow.
Goncharenko was a member of Poroshenko’s party before publicly arguing that Kiev needed to make policy concessions to avert what he described as an impending national disaster. European Solidarity subsequently disowned him, and he was added to the Mirotvorets database, a controversial list of people deemed enemies of Ukraine.
Among the concessions advocated by Goncharenko was reversing restrictions affecting Russian culture in Ukraine. Moscow has cited Kiev’s policies toward ethnic Russians as evidence of what it describes as the “Nazi nature” of the Zelensky government.
Zelensky increasingly embraced Ukrainian nationalist policies after early efforts to fulfill his campaign promises faced mass protests and threats from right-wing militias, including groups that had been incorporated into official Ukrainian military and paramilitary structures.
His government continued and expanded many policies introduced under Poroshenko, including the push for NATO membership. Since 2022, Zelensky has repeatedly argued that Ukraine deserves admission to NATO for fighting Russia on behalf of the West.
However, members of the US-led bloc have repeatedly said Ukraine’s supposedly “irreversible” path to membership will take considerable time. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio reiterated on Tuesday that Ukrainian membership is not currently on the table.

Zelensky condemns 'vile' large-scale Russian attacks that killed 20

At least 20 people have died in overnight strikes across central and eastern Ukraine, in what Volodymyr Zelensky has described as one of Russia's "most vile" attacks.
Ukraine's president said a residential building in Pryluky in the Chernihiv region was destroyed as a "birthday 'gift' to Putin", who turns 74 on Wednesday. Strikes also hit Kyiv, Dnipro, Kremenchuk, Zaporizhzhia and Oleksandriya.
Zelensky said Ukraine had struck targets in attacks on Russia's Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions in the past 24 hours, adding there was "also a response in the Black Sea", without providing further details.
Moscow is yet to comment on the latest strikes.
"The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively," Zelensky said, adding that 70 missiles were fired in total.
In the social media post on Wednesday morning, Zelensky said five people had been killed and 26, including five children, injured in a strike on a five-storey apartment building in Pryluky.
He added that people could still be trapped in the rubble.
State Emergency Service of Ukraine later reported that death toll had risen to 14, including the bodies of four children in Pryluky. There have been 50 people injured, including seven children.
Two people were also killed and eight injured after Russian missile strikes damaged five apartment buildings in Dnipro and four high-rise buildings in Kremenchuk, said Zelensky.
Two people were also killed in the capital, Kyiv, and two others in Oleksandriya, he added.
Ukraine's national police posted pictures online showing what it says is an unexploded Russian Iskander missile in the middle of a Kyiv district. BBC Verify has confirmed the images are genuine and the apparent missile fragments came down in an area of open land surrounded by high-rise apartment buildings.
A video posted by the police shows people digging through collapsed remains of a residential building in Pryluky. Another verified video shows damage to cars and what appears to be rubble and a fallen tree in an area surrounded by apartment blocks in Kremenchuk.
Zelensky renewed a call for allies to provide air defence support packages to Ukraine, saying its military only managed to shoot down "some" of the missiles launched by Russia overnight.
According to Zelensky, one of the "key targets" of the attack was the country's energy infrastructure, which Moscow earlier said it would intensify strikes on following Ukraine's strikes on Moscow's energy facilities.
In a separate post on Wednesday, Zelensky said Ukraine had struck four targets in retaliatory attacks in the past 24 hours, including two oil facilities and a training ground in the Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions.
"There is also a response in the Black Sea," the Ukrainian president wrote.
On Tuesday evening, footage emerged showing a huge plume of smoke engulfing an oil tanker off the coast of Sochi, along the Black Sea in southern Russia.
The Russian transport ministry later said unmanned boats had attacked the Liberian-flagged Aframax Rio oil tanker. Authorities claim the crew was rescued.
Separately, Bulgaria has halted a search for the missing crew of a ship that sank after being hit by a drone on Tuesday, Vice-Admiral Rumen Nikolov from the Maritime Administration Executive Agency said, as reported by Bulgaria's BTA news agency. No details of the crew are known, but Nikolov said it was assumed there were Syrians on board.
Tracking data shows the ship was anchored at the southern end of the Bosphorus strait until Monday when it entered the Black Sea heading north. Its last reported position on ship-tracking site MarineTraffic was at 23:43 GMT on Monday in what is known as the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone of the Black Sea.
Bulgarian specialist news outlet Maritime.bg reported the Alfa Watan was attacked by a drone and sank 70nm (130km) east of Byala.
As well as the civilian cargo ship, a second vessel - carrying grain - was also hit within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, its Prime Minister Rumen Radev said on Tuesday. The 18 crew members on the second vessel were rescued.
Bulgaria has not said who it believes was behind the attacks.
It comes as Russia intensifies strikes in the Black Sea, particularly the eastern side, as part of its war against Ukraine.
In an evening address on Tuesday, Zelensky claimed Russia was responsible for the attacks.
Moscow has not commented on the latest incident.
Additional reporting by BBC Verify

A business owner&apos;s reputation under attack: where it may come from and how to defend yourself
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:05:14 EEST
20:05:14 KST

A business owner's reputation under attack: where it may come from and how to defend yourself
Kyiv • UNN
Negative publications can harm a business even without proven wrongdoing. A lawyer explained the sources of reputational damage and the problems with compensation.
In business, protecting honor, dignity, and business reputation is not only about protecting specific individuals — owners or executives. Information published in the media or on social networks directly affects the business itself: the company’s activities, its relationships with partners and clients, and, ultimately, the business’s financial results. The sources of reputational harm and how much a business owner’s reputation actually costs were discussed with UNN by Sviatoslav Bolinskyi, CEO of the Bolinskyi and Partners law firm and an attorney.
The mere publication of negative information about an owner or company does not mean that it is an attack by competitors or ill-wishers. At the same time, this is precisely the method they may use. A single publication, often on a little-known platform, begins to be actively disseminated on other resources, including social networks and messengers. This creates the impression that the information has broad confirmation. It is necessary to establish not only the number of materials, but also their origin and the connections between the resources where the information was published.
It is important to understand that even accurate information may be taken out of context or presented in such a way that the reader or viewer forms a false impression of the situation. For example, a company owner may be summoned for questioning or other investigative actions not as a suspect, but as a witness in criminal proceedings. A summons for questioning may be related to an inspection of counterparties or partners. The mere fact of questioning does not indicate his involvement in an offense.
Depending on the circumstances, information about a person’s participation in investigative actions may be disseminated both by the relevant state authorities and by other participants or interested parties, including competitors. In the first case, this concerns informing the public about the progress of the proceedings. In the other, the information may be used to shape a certain perception of the person or company.
How much does reputation cost?
Protecting honor, dignity, and business reputation is always a matter that requires fairly serious preparation in what may seem to be a simple legal sphere. In each specific case, it is necessary to establish exactly what constitutes the violation infringing upon honor, dignity, and business reputation, and to understand how it occurred. It is important to determine whether the statement is an evaluative judgment or a factual assertion, who disseminated the information, who specifically learned of it, what evidence confirms the published material, and exactly where the information degrading honor, dignity, and business reputation is located.
"There is no universal algorithm for protection—each situation requires separate analysis," notes Sviatoslav Bolinskyi, CEO of Bolinskyi and Partners. "One of the most difficult problems in such disputes is determining the amount of compensation for the moral harm and reputational losses caused. It is not enough to say: ‘I want one million hryvnias.’ Why exactly one million? Today, there are no tools that would allow the cost of the harm caused to honor, dignity, and business reputation to be reasonably determined. Courts may award 20, 30, or 50 thousand hryvnias. However, the question of a methodology that could be used to determine the amount of such compensation remains open. Creativity and a methodical approach to determining the value of harm caused to honor, dignity, and business reputation require flexibility and an understanding that these are philosophical concepts that will be entirely different for each person who has suffered an infringement. For example, a person may experience no moral suffering or distress, while their dignity and business reputation have been harmed, or vice versa. In this regard, if there are methodologies for determining moral harm, there are no methodologies for determining the value of business reputation or honor, which, from our point of view, provides unlimited scope for research and assessment."
The lawyer emphasizes that a combined approach is needed to determine the amount of damage caused to honor, dignity, and business reputation through relevant categories and conceptual frameworks. In particular, such relevant categories may include methods for determining the value of business reputation based on goodwill. Although this category is relevant to legal entities and is defined under the Tax Code of Ukraine as an intangible asset whose value is influenced by high-quality management decisions, market position, and so on, if such a category exists for legal entities, it can also be applied to individuals, since individuals likewise have a position in the market, particularly within a certain business environment. Business and communication skills, experience, and the position held directly influence the effectiveness of certain processes. In other words, it is necessary to answer the question: how much are the "word," "action," and "recommendation" of an individual who has suffered a violation of their honor, dignity, and business reputation worth?
The approach of using something akin to marketing research into the positioning of a product—or, in our case, an injured person —in a particular environment is not without merit. In short, the protection of honor, dignity, and business reputation is not merely a matter of moral damage, given that most courts award only paltry sums in such claims. We need to take into account international practice in considering similar cases, for example, the well-known case of E. Jean Carroll v. Donald Trump (United States), in which information about untrue events and fabricated facts was disseminated through the media. However, unlike Ukrainian courts, the court assessed the costs of restoring the reputation at more than 11 million US dollars. Rush v. Nationwide News (Australia) was a case in which the court found that the publisher had failed to prove the truthfulness of the information disseminated and awarded 2.8 million US dollars in compensation. However, such sums are hardly likely to be encountered in Ukrainian courts, given that the supposed discretion in presenting evidence has effectively been reduced to the need to prove specific data in philosophical categories—morality, honor, and dignity
Sources of reputational damage
Any situation in which information about a person or company becomes known to third parties can become a source of reputational damage: publication in the media, a blog, or a social network; a statement by competitors; a public speech; a client’s comment; or an account by former employees or counterparties.
Sviatoslav Bolinskyi:
In each case, it is necessary to determine what the negative impact of the information consists of and whether it truly demeans a person’s honor, dignity, or business reputation. It is important not only to assess the accuracy of an individual fact, but also how it was presented and precisely what conclusion the audience may draw. Freedom of speech should not mean the absence of responsibility for disseminating inaccurate and manipulative information. It is particularly dangerous when a person is called a criminal in a headline even though their guilt has not been established by a court, while we clearly understand that the case may not even reach court. Not everyone reads beyond the headline or delves into the substance of the material. Therefore, particular attention must be paid to information sources, wording, and context. In our view, today it is necessary to create sufficiently strong legal positions and court precedents so that informing the public is objective and does not cause harm to the subject, and so that the information itself is civilized.
Publications containing negative information or an organized reputational campaign?
First of all, the situation needs to be broken down into parts and the following verified: what specific claims are contained in the publication; whether they constitute facts or opinions; whether the information corresponds to reality; in the case of truthful information, whether it has been taken out of context; who said or wrote it and why, and whether the claims can be verified by documents. It is also necessary to assess whether the information damages the reputation and whether the rules governing its dissemination were violated, and to distinguish criticism from a factual assertion.
It is by no means worth responding from a legal standpoint to every negative review and defending one's honor and dignity. Comments about service are common practice. In the case of clearly commissioned publications in little-known media outlets, it is also not always worth resorting to a legal response. Such a publication may not have sufficient reach to cause actual reputational damage. The response itself may draw more attention to it.
There are several possible ways the situation may develop. In one case, it is best not to respond—the information will already be irrelevant tomorrow. In another, a response may lead to even greater publicity. In a third situation, it is necessary to immediately collect evidence, conduct expert examinations of the publications if needed, assess the damage caused, and file a lawsuit. At the same time, courts analyze specific statements, as well as the content and context of the publication.
Why launch a discrediting campaign?
Launching a discrediting campaign is not merely an act of revenge. It may arise from a corporate conflict, when one owner pressures another. The reason may be a desire to retaliate for a lost case, an unsuccessful tender, or revenge by a dissatisfied former employee. A legal dispute may also be taking place at that moment, and it may be necessary to shift the other party's position by creating reputational risks. In most cases, it is enough to raise doubts about whether it is worth cooperating with this company.
What can be demanded and what should be done?
It is worth having an action plan in case of a possible reputational crisis. When negative publications bearing signs of a commissioned campaign appear, it is necessary to record the date, time, author, source of the publication, link to it, comments, number of views, and so on. The next step is to analyze the consequences for the person about whom the publication was written and for the business, as well as to prepare a legal defense.
The problem is that negative information spreads quickly. A rebuttal, meanwhile, does not receive the same level of publicity. This is particularly telling when the messages are based on assumptions, an unfinished court proceeding, or criminal proceedings. Often, a court may later establish completely different circumstances. This raises the question: will the media return to this story and inform its audience that the original information turned out to be incorrect? In practice, this happens far from always. Nevertheless, monitoring media publications is in the MUST HAVE category, since pretrial (criminal) investigations are conducted on the basis of publications, with consequences; certain actions are blocked; and even contracts may be terminated precisely because of the dissemination of inaccurate information that damages business reputation
Today, we quite often encounter publications in the information space that may demean honor, dignity, and business reputation. At the same time, a subsequent rebuttal of the disseminated information is practically never seen. However, the process of rebutting information and obtaining fair compensation for disseminating inaccurate information requires the development of effective judicial practice that takes a critical view of the fact that, through the dissemination of inaccurate information, a business may be subjected to persecution by regulatory and law-enforcement authorities, while actions to restore business reputation cannot always be measured using specific tools and expert examinations. The highest social value enshrined in Article 3 of the Constitution of Ukraine—honor and dignity—must receive protection in the form of fair compensation, a rebuttal of the information, and restoration of business reputation.

Ukraine's new EV market share plunges 3.6-fold in Sept – Ukrautoprom
