Hungary agrees to opening of negotiating clusters 2 and 3 for Ukraine
Hungary has agreed to allow Ukraine to move forward in its EU accession negotiations, clearing the way for the opening of Clusters 2 (Internal Market) and 3 (Competitiveness and Inclusive Growth).
Source: European Pravda, citing an EU source familiar with the negotiations
Details: Budapest has lifted the block that until now had prevented Ukraine from moving to the next stage in the procedure for opening negotiating clusters 2 and 3.
"COELA [the Working Party on Enlargement and Countries Negotiating Accession to the EU] has approved the screening results for Clusters 2 and 3 for Ukraine, and today at Coreper, the EU member states' ambassadors agreed to send letters to the governments of Ukraine and Moldova inviting them to present their negotiating positions," the European Pravda source said.
The source said the next procedural steps could be completed very quickly.
The EU's draft negotiating position on both clusters is due to be drawn up at a COELA meeting in the coming days.
EU member states are expected to be able to agree on the negotiating position for opening the clusters as early as Monday 12 October, after the Verkhovna Rada (Ukrainian parliament) adopts legislative amendments on education in national minority languages.
Once the EU negotiating position has been approved, a Ukraine-EU intergovernmental conference could be held the following day, 13 October, and Clusters 2 and 3 could be formally opened.
Hungary had blocked approval of the screening results for these clusters for several months, preventing Ukraine from moving on to the next procedural stages required for them to be opened.
Background:
- A bill on education in national minority languages was registered in the Verkhovna Rada on 1 October. Its adoption was expected to help lift Hungary's veto, which had blocked progress on the two negotiating clusters.
- On 6 October, the European Commission adopted a package of proposals on pre-enlargement policy reviews, which are intended to enable the EU to admit new members, including Ukraine.
- European Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos outlined five groups of measures proposed by the European Commission for future EU enlargement: greater use of qualified-majority voting and limits on vetoes in certain areas; closer integration of candidate countries into parts of the EU before membership; safeguards to prevent new members from backsliding on the rule of law, democracy and fundamental rights; adjustments to EU policies to accommodate enlargement, including targeted measures for sensitive Ukrainian agricultural products; and roadmaps for the four most advanced candidate countries.

"The robbery-murder this time hugely shocked local residents," he said, requesting a committee be convened swiftly to discuss the issue.
Earlier Benjamin T. Watson, Okinawa area coordinator and commanding general of III Marine Expeditionary Force, announced a "complete prohibition of alcohol consumption on or off base" starting Wednesday.
Watson said that the 48-hour period – described as "an operational pause" – would give commanders the time to lead training with all service members on "standards, discipline, and our responsibilities as members of the Okinawan community."
Operations will cease during this period and "we will not allow off-base liberty," said Watson in a statement posted on X late Tuesday.
The lieutenant general, the most senior U.S. military figure on Okinawa, also announced a 30-day "period of reflection" beginning Friday.
"During this period, we will implement a curfew in which liberty will expire at 2400 for all hands, meaning you must be back on base in your assigned quarters or at your off-base domicile from midnight to 0500."
Police said Sunday that a US Marine stationed on Okinawa was arrested on suspicion of killing a 39-year-old woman at a hotel in the city of Naha and stealing her wallet.
Local media reported she was choked to death and that the Marine is denying the allegations.
The United States has around 54,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, mostly on Okinawa.
Crimes committed by U.S. personnel have been a thorn in relations between the close security allies.
Koja, who won the gubernatorial election last month, is the first Okinawa leader in 12 years who approved of a contentious U.S. military base relocation plan.
The central government plan is to keep the U.S. Marine Corps' Futenma air base on Okinawa's main island, but move it to a less populated location.
On Wednesday, Koja also met Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi in Tokyo where he said the murder case had "caused deep anxiety" among Okinawa residents.
"The prefectural government has repeatedly demanded that the U.S. military take measures to prevent a recurrence every time an incident occurs, but the fact that such an incident has happened again forces us to conclude that discipline within the U.S. forces and their human rights education are not functioning at all," he told Koizumi.
Koizumi said that he would "advance discussions with the United States on how to implement effective measures" to prevent such incidents occurring.
Last year, a Japanese court sentenced a U.S. Marine accused of choking and attempting to rape a woman in her 20s to seven years in prison.
In 2017, a former U.S. Marine and civilian military base worker was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa.
The same year, U.S. Forces Japan banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated U.S. Marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing its 61-year-old local driver.

Bill for new election law passes confidence tests before final vote
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:28:25 CEST
19:28:25 KST

A bill presented by the parties of
Premier Giorgia Meloni's ruling coalition to bring in a new
election law passed the last of three important confidence votes
in the Lower House on Wednesday, clearing the way for the final
vote, which will be a secret ballot, on Thursday.
                                    
After articles 1 and 2 of the bill got the green light with ease
in confidence votes on Tuesday, article 3 was approved in
similar fashion with 228 votes in favour and 144 against.
                                    
This show of unity from the ruling alliance suggests the bill
should have no problem passing the final vote, even though the
secret nature of the ballot makes it easier for lawmakers to
buck the line of their parties without facing consequences.
                                    
The opposition has cried foul about the drive to overhaul the
electoral system, saying the ruling alliance is changing it
because it fears losing the general election set to take place
next year and wants to minimize the chances of this happening.
                                    
The bill will see the current system, a mix of
first-past-the-post and proportional representation, replaced
with a proportional-representation system with bonus seats for
the coalition that obtains the most votes, as long as it reaches
a threshold of 42%, to ensure it has a working majority in
parliament.
                                    
If no coalition reaches the threshold, or the votes for the
Lower House and the Senate produce different results, a purely
proportional system is used.
                                    
The opposition have said that, among other things, the
envisioned system of bonus seats is unconstitutional.
                                    
Coalitions will have to say who their candidate to be premier is
before the election.
                                    
The bill will also give voters the option to express preferences
for up to three candidates out of six on a party list in which
candidates names must alternate according to gender.
                                    
The opposition says that in reality this gives "fake
preferences" as the head of the ticket would always be
"blocked", arguing this was also be a step back for equality,
as, in theory, it would be possible for all the ticket heads to
be men.
                                    
The current system does not give voters any option to express
preferences about which of the candidates on a party list they
want to represent them.

NATO Military Committee delegation in Kyiv: Russia will not succeed in undermining support for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:28:00 UTC
19:28:00 KST

NATO Military Committee delegation in Kyiv: Russia will not succeed in undermining support for Ukraine
Cavo Dragone made this statement in a video address from Kyiv, according to a Ukrinform correspondent.
“After an eight-year hiatus, the NATO Military Committee comes back to Kyiv on an official visit. But while we were not physically here, Ukraine is in our thoughts, discussions, decisions, and following action every single day. This visit fulfills the promise I made to the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, Mykhailo Drapaty, my good friend, during our last conversation in August of this year,” he emphasized.
The admiral noted that the Military Committee arrived in Kyiv following the North Atlantic Council’s visit to the Ukrainian capital in June.
“We are here in full strength with a a clear message: the bond between NATO and Ukraine is stronger and stronger. In facing Russia continued aggression against Ukraine and its reckless hybrid activities in NATO countries. We stand unwavering with Ukraine in the heroic defense of its sovereignty, territorial integrity, and the future of its people,” Kavo Dragone emphasized.
The delegation included military representatives from 32 Alliance member states. They arrived to hear the latest assessment of the situation on the front lines from the Commander-in-Chief and the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine and to learn how they could further support Ukraine.
The Chairman of the Military Committee added that the delegation members paid tribute to all Ukrainian soldiers, especially those who gave their lives or were wounded.
“To those who think that by perpetrating act of sabotage, cyberattacks, and violations of the airspace in national NATO territory, they will undermine this support and our resolve, I will respond. You are failing. NATO support for Ukraine continues to grow and our unity is stronger than ever. Russia bears full responsibility for this dangers and unacceptable behavior,” Kavo Dragone emphasized.
As reported by Ukrinform, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte stated that the allies must be prepared for further hostile actions by Russia against the Alliance, and the response to them must be increased support for Ukraine.

Documents
Details
Timetables for operational low flying (OLF) training by RAF fast jets and Hercules aircraft. These timetables cover 3 tactical training areas (TTA) only. These are:
- LFA 7(T): central Wales
- LFA 14(T): northern Scotland
- LFA 20(T): the borders of southern Scotland and northern England
When the TTA is not in use, there may be other flying activity in the area. The MOD is unable to provide a timetable for all low flying activity as the information can very quickly become outdated due to weather conditions and training requirements.

UK Detains Seventh Suspect Over Possible Attack on Fairford Air Base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:27:33 UTC
19:27:33 KST

UK police have detained a seventh suspect in connection with an alleged plot to carry out a terrorist attack near Fairford Air Base in Gloucestershire.
Reuters reported that the 22-year-old British man was detained in Westminster, London, on Tuesday. He is suspected of preparing terrorist attacks.
Law enforcement officers also searched a property in the area but provided no details about what they may have found. The man remains in custody.
“This investigation remains ongoing, and our specialist teams continue to carry out extensive inquiries into the circumstances surrounding the events near RAF Fairford,” said Vicki Evans, the senior national counter-terrorism coordinator.
Earlier in the investigation, six men aged between 23 and 25 were detained, including a man who holds both British and Iranian citizenship.
All six were later released on bail. However, they remain under investigation and must comply with restrictions on their movements and contacts.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there are signs that Iran may have been involved in an alleged plot to carry out a terrorist attack near Fairford Air Base.
On September 27, British police were alerted to three suspicious vehicles traveling toward the airfield. Bomb disposal officers were sent to the scene, and around 85 households in the area were evacuated as a precaution.
After examining the three vans, police said they had found no improvised explosive devices. However, they did find a quantity of petrol.
UK counter-terrorism police reported that they were investigating several possibilities, including whether the suspects may have been acting on behalf of a foreign state. At the time, officials did not publicly name any specific country.
The Iranian Embassy in the UK rejected claims of possible Iranian involvement, calling them baseless. Following Burnham’s remarks, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also denied the allegations.
Fairford is one of the UK’s key air bases and is also used by US military aircraft, including aircraft involved in strikes on Iranian territory. Amid the investigation into the alleged terror plot, the US withdrew all of its B-1B bombers from the air base on October 4.

Paramount wraps up mega Warner Bros merger to create Hollywood powerhouse Skydance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:26:27 UTC
19:26:27 KST

Paramount Skydance completed its blockbuster $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros Discovery on Tuesday, creating a Hollywood heavyweight that hands CEO David Ellison control of one of the world's largest entertainment and news businesses. The deal brings together the studios behind "Mission: Impossible," "Harry Potter" and DC Studios alongside major television and streaming networks such as CBS, CNN and HBO Max. The Ellison family has notably held a long relationship with Republican President Donald Trump, who said that Skydance is “going to be a great company.”

Italian Army orders armored INEOS Grenadier 4x4s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:26:13 UTC
19:26:13 KST

- The Italian Army has selected the armored INEOS Grenadier Enhanced Protection Vehicle, with deliveries expected to begin in 2027.
- Italy is the first NATO country to place a large-scale military order for the Grenadier, which will serve mainly in secondary and logistics roles.
The Italian Army has selected an armored version of the INEOS Grenadier 4×4, making Italy the first NATO country to place a large-scale military order for the British-designed off-roader. Deliveries are expected to begin in 2027.
The army chose the Grenadier Enhanced Protection Vehicle, or EPV, in its armored configuration. The vehicles will mainly serve in secondary roles, including internal logistics. INEOS and the Italian Defense Ministry did not disclose the number of vehicles ordered or the value of the contract.
INEOS has also signed a supply agreement with the Austrian government, Italian motoring magazine Quattroruote reported, making the two deals the company’s first military contracts. Details of the Austrian agreement were not released.
The EPV is built around a purpose-built armored steel cabin instead of armor panels added to a standard body. INEOS says the cabin meets Level 2 of NATO’s STANAG 4569 protection standard, which covers assault rifle fire and blasts from small mines. Its developers originally pitched the variant for client and VIP protection.
The armored model came out of Team Grenadier, the industrial group INEOS Automotive formed with SMT Defence and NMS UK and later expanded with Hobson Industries and TVS Supply Chain Solutions. The consortium is competing in the British Army’s Light Mobility Vehicle program, which is meant to replace the service’s Land Rover and Pinzgauer fleets, and has adapted the civilian Grenadier into nine military configurations for the bid. The EPV was shown alongside other variants at the DVD 2026 defense vehicle exhibition at UTAC Millbrook on September 16 and 17, and Quattroruote reported that the Grenadier has passed the first selection stage of the British program.
The Grenadier is assembled at the INEOS plant in Hambach, France, and uses BMW six-cylinder gasoline and diesel engines paired with a ZF eight-speed automatic transmission. Several key components come from Italy: the solid axles are made by Carraro in the Padua area, the brakes by Brembo, and suspension and steering parts by Turin-based Frap.
Civilian versions of the Grenadier already serve with police and border units in Germany, France, Spain, Hungary, Poland, the Czech Republic, Serbia and Slovakia, where they are used for border patrols and emergency services. Spain’s National Police is among the users. INEOS has opened talks with other European Union countries about military versions, Quattroruote reported.

France's Henri Kagan, Japan's Kenso Soai win 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:25:11 UTC
19:25:11 KST

Necva Taştan Sevinç
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
French scientist Henri B. Kagan and Japanese scientist Kenso Soai won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry on Wednesday for discoveries that helped explain how the molecular asymmetry essential to life can emerge.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the prize “for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis.”
Their research addressed a longstanding question about homochirality, a feature of living systems in which molecules favor one of two possible mirror-image forms, according to a statement.
Some molecules can exist in two forms that mirror each other, much like left and right hands. In proteins, however, living organisms use only one mirror-image form of amino acids.
Understanding how this asymmetry emerges has also been crucial to pharmaceutical development, as different mirror-image forms of a molecule can have different effects in the body.
“Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously. The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular,” said Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry.
Kagan made a decisive breakthrough in 1986, discovering a way to manipulate chemical reactions to produce a greater excess of one mirror-image form than previously thought possible.
Soai advanced the work in 1995 by designing a reaction with the potential to produce only one mirror-image form. In 2003, he succeeded in demonstrating such a reaction, according to the academy.
Their discoveries have been decisive for chemists designing reactions to manufacture pharmaceuticals, it said.

Font size
Bulgarian-Australian trade has grown steadily over the past decade, with Bulgarian exports to Australia rising by more than 141%, from $25 million in 2015 to $60 million in 2025. The figures were presented by Bulgarian Deputy Foreign Minister Hristo Polendakov at the EU–Australia FTA: What It Means for Bulgarian Business forum in Sofia, BTA reported. Polendakov said the growth was encouraging, but there was still considerable scope to expand bilateral trade.
Bulgarian companies already export pharmaceuticals, machinery, dairy and agricultural products to Australia. Polendakov said there was potential to increase exports of medicines, engines and electrical appliances, medical instruments, machinery, essential oils, sunflower seeds, food products and chemicals.
He said relations between Bulgaria and Australia had never been stronger or more important.
Australia’s Ambassador to Greece, Bulgaria and Romania, Alison Duncan, told the forum that the EU-Australia free trade agreement was expected to add around €4 billion to the EU’s GDP by 2030, increase EU exports to Australia by about 30% and save European businesses around €1 billion a year in customs duties.
Duncan noted that Australia is the world’s 12th-largest economy, worth around $2.7 trillion, and has one of the highest levels of GDP per capita in the world.

‘Ensuring dignified life’: how an app keeps advanced cancer patients out of hospital
HKU’s SUPPORT+ mobile app, offering weekly symptom tracking and nurse follow-up, has attracted 76,000 registered users since 2022
Advanced-stage cancer patients could spend half as long in hospital and avoid more than a third of unplanned admissions if a symptom-tracking mobile app is added to their routine care, according to new research from the University of Hong Kong.
The SUPPORT+ mobile app, developed by HKU’s clinical oncology department, provides symptom-management information and a direct line of communication with healthcare staff.
Launched in 2022 with private backing, the app has attracted 76,000 registered users, including 2,800 families with cancer patients.
“Advanced-stage cancer patients often experience severe, worsening symptoms such as pain, shortness of breath, fatigue and loss of appetite … if those problems were not handled early, it could increase the risk of hospitalisation and emergency department visits,” said Clinical Associate Professor of Practice Wendy Chan Wing-lok, who developed the app.

Putin’s Focus is Now French Elections

Reviewing the Ukraine war watchers I think there had been a general assumption, or fear, that after the State Duma elections in Russia, last month, that Putin would launch a new mobilization campaign as a prelude to yet another big offensive in Donbas. The consensus was also that this would be pretty futile – just providing more bodies to the Russian meat grinder, which has been running at tens of thousands of Russian casualties per month for much of 2026.
Actually Putin appears to have held back from the mobilization track – perhaps fearful of the domestic political consequences of the war being brought home to the elites of Moscow and St Petersburg, finally losing their sons, brothers, uncles and fathers to this futile war to massage Putin’s ego.
Instead, Russia appears to have been pushed back along the front lines: September was the first month since Ukraine’s ill-fated counteroffensive in autumn 2023 that Russia suffered a net loss of territory in Ukraine.
Putin seems to have changed strategy to one of being content to maintain the frontlines in Donbas, while moving to an all-out campaign against the Ukrainian economy.
Herein we have seen a step up in Russian drone and ballistic missile attacks on Ukrainian industrial assets, energy infrastructure, transport, retail and logical hubs and supply chains.
We have seen attacks on Ukraine’s steel industry - with five blast furnaces taken out of service and rendering its once export leading steel industry dormant.
Triumph of Common Sense: Dissecting the Carlson-Rees-Mogg Interview
There have been attacks on key bridges across the Dnipro in Kyiv – again to sap moral but also to undermine the functioning of the capital’s economy.
And in the Black Sea, Russia has spurned efforts by Turkiye, the US, et al to agree a ceasefire covering grains, and Ukrainian grain exports have slowed to a trickle.
A similar ceasefire effort to cover energy assets has also been rejected by Russia. The aim seems to be to wear down Ukraine’s economy, erode its military industrial capability and sap the moral of Ukrainians.
I think the aim is also to push the economy into recession, create large budget and balance of payments shortfalls which will impose larger funding asks on Europe at a time when public finances are already under strain across the continent and playing out in market worries about the sustainability of public finances in France, the UK, et al.
I think there have been opportunities for a serious peace process, and a peace under the Trump presidency. But Trump has so mismanaged this process, that he has given heart to Putin that under Trump’s leadership the NATO alliance will fracture, and with that its willingness to support Ukraine.
And in Trump’s backing for far-right parties in Europe - the AfD in Germany, FN in France, and Reform in the UK, I think he has presented light at the end of the tunnel for Putin, that elections will inevitably usher in new governments in Europe which will pull the plug on European funding for Ukraine.
Key I think in this respect are French elections in May where I think Putin thinks a victory by Le Pen will see not only French support to Ukraine ended but a spanner put in the works of EU funding and support for Ukraine.
So I think Putin now sees advantage in fighting on and through the winter to get to next May and the prospect then of a collapse in European support for Ukraine. And thru the winter the strategy is to maximize destruction on Ukraine to increase the bill on Europe for supporting Ukraine.
All this just seems obvious to seasoned Ukraine watchers like me (40-year track record there) – it is possible to read Putin, and unfortunately Trump, like a book.
Putin is not difficult to read. He is a bully, a Russian style mafia like character forged from his KGB background. He respects strength and power and pushes on when he sees weakness. In Europe and in Trump he sees weakness and a lack of leadership.
Trump has imposed few costs on Putin, or Russia, for the war in Ukraine. Rather Trump seems to suggest he wants to reward Putin for his land grab in Ukraine, by his show of strength by trying to get US – Russia business back to normal.
Putin sees no penalty or sanction in continuing to test NATO borders in Europe through cyberattacks, attacks on NATO munition dumps, assassination attempts on European industrialists, drone forays against targets in Europe, and lately by attacks on shipping in NATO members waters.
Each effort that Putin gets away with just reveals the weakness of NATO, its lack of a response, and the lack of assurance on the US backstop. So he will continue.
And by heightening fears of Russia in Europe, he will hope to gift his far-right allies in Europe electoral ammunition as they will offer their electorates the offer of appeasement with Russia to secure a peace. Or that’s what they think they will achieve. But knowing Putin he will take whatever gifts are offered by the AfD, RN, and Reform and ask, and take more.
Leadership is needed in Europe but is in short supply.
On the Ukraine financing piste, the war is costing Ukraine more, and the war looks set to extend longer into 2028. This means that the €90 billion EU USL agreed at the EU Council meeting in December 2025 is not enough.
Ukraine has spoken about a $27 billion military financing gap in 2026, and a $32 billion financing gap in 2027, and that’s even without thinking of the tens of billions of extra funds needed if the war extends to 2028.
The right approach for Europe is to get ahead of the game, and the risks from French elections. To insulate Ukraine’s financing from those elections with potentially new facilities, and even finally tapping the $300 billion in immobilized CBR assets in Western jurisdictions.
But when leadership and vision is required from European leaders, we are seeing dithering and penny, or Euro cent pinching.
And the argument to our taxpayers should be that a $100 billion investment in Ukraine’s defense, to stop Russia, could save 1-2% per year in European defense spending over the longer term, that’s potentially a €250-500 billion saving per year.
It all looks a no brainier. But Europe so often has no brains, and invariably only acts when actually hit by crisis – in this case it would be a Russian victory in Ukraine.
Imagine that, it would mean tens of millions of Ukrainians moving West, straining the social, economic and political fabric of Europe and Russia moving further up on NATO’s borders but augmented by the capture of Ukraine’s substantive military capability. Europe would be facing the combined military capabilities of Russia, and subsumed Ukraine, and without a US backstop.
That would be a simply disastrous scenario for Europe – hence the cheapest option is to fund Ukraine NOW.

Christa Pike is awake after surviving execution: What happens now?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:22:11 UTC
19:22:11 KST

Christa Pike is awake after surviving execution: What happens now?
Tennessee death row inmate survives execution attempt, sparking legal and medical concerns.
Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike, who survived a failed execution by lethal injection in a US prison last week, is conscious and speaking at a hospital, her lawyers have said.
Fifty-year-old Pike was convicted of murdering her classmate in 1995.
The Death Penalty Information Center, which publishes data and analysis on capital punishment in the United States, said Pike was the first inmate ever to survive “after being injected with lethal doses of execution drugs”.
Pike’s “unprecedented” survival raises questions about her medical and legal future.
Here’s what we know.
What is Christa Pike’s condition now?
Pike is under guard, recovering at a hospital in Nashville where she was rushed after surviving the lethal injection administered by the Tennessee Department of Correction. Her arms were swollen, burned and blistered when she arrived at the hospital on September 30.
“Against all odds”, Pike is now “conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care”, her lawyers said, adding that “she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed”.
They called her recovery “medically unprecedented”.
Pike’s prognosis remained “unclear”, they said, adding that, at a minimum, she faced a lengthy recovery.
Why was Pike on death row?
Fifty-year-old Pike was sentenced to death after being convicted of a murder as a teenager.
The case sparked debate over the death penalty for young offenders, as Pike was 18 when she and her boyfriend beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old classmate Colleen Slemmer at a job training camp in 1995.
Pike’s lawyers sought clemency, citing her age, childhood sexual abuse and mental health problems, including post-traumatic stress disorder.
The case had already attracted attention in the run-up to the execution date, as Pike would have been the first woman put to death by the state of Tennessee in more than 200 years.
What went wrong in the death chamber?
7:30pm – The attempt to execute Pike got under way on September 30 in the death chamber at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. Pike was given a chance to make a final statement before two doses of the chemical pentobarbital were administered as executioners attempted to put her to death.
7:35pm – Pike raised her head and said her arm was hurting.
8:53pm – Media were escorted out of the witness room.
9:14pm – An ambulance arrived at the prison to take Pike to hospital.
Journalists who witnessed the execution said a black curtain was drawn from inside the death chamber during the process to insert the intravenous lines into Pike, in line with state regulations. This is done to conceal the identities of the workers who perform the procedure.
Tennessee’s execution protocol calls for a secondary set of pentobarbital-filled syringes in case the condemned person does not die after the first set. But there are no instructions for how to proceed if the person does not die after a second lethal injection dose.
How will Pike’s lawyers proceed?
Pike’s lawyers are due in court on Wednesday, where they will be seeking more information from the Tennessee Department of Correction about the botched execution attempt.
They are seeking a court order to require the prison system to preserve information from the attempted execution, including drug lot numbers, needles, execution logs and other information.
Medical and lethal injection experts said it is possible there was a problem with the way the IV line was inserted, causing the drug to collect in her tissue rather than enter her bloodstream.
“Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realise that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown,” Pike’s lawyers said in a court filing.
Prior to the execution attempt, Pike’s lawyers had requested her death penalty to be carried out by firing squad or hanging, because she had small veins and a blood-clotting condition called thrombocytosis. They feared the condition could make the insertion of intravenous needles difficult and increase the risk of a failed procedure.
Pike’s lawyers have called for her death sentence to be commuted to life in prison without the possibility of parole after the failed execution attempt.
What do Tennessee government officials say?
Republican Governor Bill Lee called what happened “deeply disturbing” and ordered a “comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred”.
The governor postponed the state’s only other execution scheduled for this year.
Frank Strada, the former commissioner of the Tennessee Department of Correction, who was the prison chief at the time of Pike’s failed execution, agreed to step down later this month.
US Senator Marsha Blackburn, the state’s Republican candidate to replace Bill Lee, called on Tennessee to explore other methods of execution to ensure it can continue carrying out capital punishment.
It is unclear whether or when Tennessee could attempt to execute Pike again. Lawyers have argued it would be cruel and unusual punishment and that a new attempt could violate the prohibition on double jeopardy, trying or punishing someone twice for the same offence.

What the OpenAI-Hugging Face hack reveals about AI accountability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:21:10 UTC
19:21:10 KST

Rachel Feltman: For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman.
Have you heard about the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident? (Sidenote: Does that string of words also make you think of something Timothy Olyphant’s character might get up to on the show Alien: Earth? You know ‘cause he is AI, the aliens hug faces. Anyway.)
The incident in question went down a few months ago, when OpenAI agents messed with an artificial intelligence platform called Hugging Face. This definitely wasn’t supposed to happen, and it freaked a lot of people out. But what actually happened? According to many headlines and lots of online chatter, more than a thousand “rogue” AI agents collaborated to conduct an unsanctioned attack. While all of that could technically be considered true, some of the words I just used imply a sort of intentionality and dare I say impishness that simply wasn’t involved. The truth is a lot less science-fiction-y: The human beings who designed these models and gave them their prompts made some missteps. But while that might sound less apocalyptic than the headlines did, it doesn’t mean we shouldn’t find this incident deeply troubling.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
My guest today is an artist and AI researcher who’s thought a lot about the way we talk about this and other AI mishaps. His name is Eryk Salvaggio, and he’s a Gates scholar at the University of Cambridge working at Cambridge Digital Humanities.
Thank you so much for coming on to chat with us today.
Eryk Salvaggio: Thank you for having me.
Feltman: So I brought you on because I read a piece of yours about AI and how we are talking about it, and I’m really excited to get into that with you. But to give a little context for our listeners, could you tell us a little bit about the work you do and your professional relationship with AI?
Salvaggio: Yeah, certainly. So I’ve been working with technology and thinking about technology and ethics since I was a teenager. Basically, I’ve worked in and around policy spaces around technology, and I came to it through a kind of cultural background. I worked as an artist, and I was working with this technology to make work, and that exposed me over time to some of the ethical questions, some of the questions around technology and power and the way that technology is changing our social lives, our political lives and culture in general.
So I come at it from that lens, trying to think differently about the stories that technology is telling us about itself, in a way, and trying to think about how I can look at that from a different angle, a different perspective.
Feltman: Well, so the piece I referenced earlier was about the [Hugging Face] incident. Could you just briefly summarize, for our listeners, what happened there and, sort of, what the prevailing narrative around it was? And then we can get into, a little bit, the ways in which you disagree with that narrative.
Salvaggio: Yeah, sure. So the prevailing narrative of what happened comes from OpenAI. They released [an] alert. Basically, this company Hugging Face announced that they had been hacked by an agent of some sort of large language model or AI system had hacked them. And then OpenAI said, “Oh, sorry, that was us. Looks like we did that, and we understand kind of what happened, and we’re gonna do a full report.”
A couple weeks after that, we get this report, and there was, kind of, pandemonium, right? A lot of the way that people understood what happened was filtered through this lens of going rogue. The artificial intelligence had kind of learned to coordinate with other instances of itself and had identified a target and had gone after Hugging Face in order to basically do this kind of weird exam for AI models called ExploitGym. And so it “broke containments”—this is another phrase that we heard in some of the headlines—and got online and went to the Hugging Face website and did what it did there.
And so this created a lot of concern about these AI agents and what they were becoming capable of doing and their coordination and their persistence, right, their perseverance. They weren’t giving up until they got in and this kind of stuff. And so you really had a lot of, I think, fear, a lot of mystery, and a lot of, kind of, talking about the agents and the AI system as if it was its own thing that acted on its own volition.
And sometimes I refer to this as, like, a system from nowhere. Like, no one built this thing. No one knows how it works. It just happens to everybody. And I take some umbrage to that frame. I think there is something to look at and say that there’s some real accountability that we can see when we look closer at this incident.
Feltman: Yeah. Well, and I think for a lot of people, this idea that the agents were communicating with each other on a message board, and it really evoked the idea of these distinct individuals, you know, collaborating—which, correct me if I’m wrong, but that’s not really what we’re talking about with an AI model, right?
Salvaggio: Right. What we’re talking about these days is something called an agentic system, which really is multiple versions of the same model, for the most part, being spun up and run with a kind of subroutine, you could call it, or a side task of some kind. And so ultimately—and it’s interesting, Anthropic had this interesting diagram where they showed Claude pointing an arrow at another box that said Claude, and that had an arrow pointing to another box that said Claude, and then both of those converged, right? And it was just Claude all the way down. And this is pretty much how they’re running.
And so, when we talk about these agents, what we’re really talking about is a kind of narrow slice of a bigger model, but it’s all optimized toward the same goals. It is trained on the same training data. It is basically the same model being run multiple times. Now, with the Hugging Face incident, OpenAI had two models, and they were kind of collaborating, but most of the stuff that we’re talking about actually happened within the single model, which is their internal model that only they have access to right now.
Feltman: Well, and one thing I really appreciated about the way you wrote about this is that you weren’t denying that there is reason for concern here but rather that we might be missing the actual areas of concern by, you know, focusing on this sort of like, Skynet scenario. Could you tell us a little bit more about, you know, what you think we should actually be learning from this incident?
Salvaggio: So a lot of the way this has been talked about has been using intentional language, right? This is this idea that the model wanted something, the model believed something, the model was trying to do something. And this can be a really, kind of, straightforward way of getting the basics down of what exactly happened.
But if you stop there, you basically kind of say that the model did all of this on its own, and you stop looking at the human decisions about how this model was designed and how it was deployed, how the testing environment was built and deployed, right? So we know, for example, OpenAI says this is a persistent model. It didn’t give up. It kept trying. And what that, kind of, moves you away from is asking the question, “Well, why?” And there’s a real answer to that, and it’s a human decision about how we train these models. And what it turns out: they trained it not to stop. Most of the time, these language models have something called a stop token. It comes up, and it looks like it’s the end of something that someone would say, and so it finishes. This didn’t really have that. It was designed to keep trying. If it failed, it would just, kind of, step back and repivot and try and try and try again. So there’s one aspect of this that, I think, is that we lose sight of when we look at just the model’s behavior and instead start saying, “Well, how was it designed?” and we’re constantly optimizing models, training models. We’re involved in making decisions about pre-training, what we do to the data, in other words, what we do to the models once they’re trained, and what we kinda ask them to do.
All of this stuff is human decisions happening inside the organizations, and we can ask for accountability by looking at those decisions. Whereas if we look only at what the model did and attribute all of this to its desires, or wants, we kind of lose sight of exactly how those desires and wants came to be.
Feltman: Yeah, and it seems like a company that’s creating this kind of AI product would have a lot of incentive to make people believe that it’s becoming super smart and autonomous and not a lot of incentive to admit that they need better guardrails internally.
Salvaggio: Yeah. A lot of this language is doing that work of saying, “We actually don’t understand this, and we don’t have control over it.” And when you are a company that is building models, and you’re saying that we’re not in control of what we’re building, there’s something going on there, and I think we can ask some real questions about what purpose that serves.
And they’re constantly trying to share this story of competency and almost overwhelming competency, right? And of course they are, because they’re asking people to use these models in situations that really we want to be able to trust them. We want to be able to ask it for information and get information back that we trust. And so they’re constantly trying to say, “Well, these models are intelligent.” And I actually think that’s the wrong frame. I think intelligence is, kind of, this idea, this kind of name that we gave to this category of computing. And really what we’re looking at is: We have no idea what’s going on when we say that something is intelligent or not. This is a well-known kind of philosophical problem. But what we do know is that they produce language, and these models are really interesting because even if it’s opening up your e-mail application, even if it’s running a piece of code, it’s doing all of this through language.
And so the way I approach it is: What exactly is this language doing? And how can we look through the language that the model’s producing, how it generates that language? And all of that is human optimization, it’s someone’s decision about the type of language these models are gonna produce, how it gets there, what it’s rewarded for producing and saying and doing. So I would like to look at more—less at thinking about these as artificial intelligence and try to focus it at more on artificial language, the idea that this language is doing something to us to influence us but also to act in the world. So how do we understand that, and how do we understand the—how these are being steered through this language?
Feltman: Could you tell us a little bit more about that, you know, in terms of what you would like to see from these technology companies in the future to steward good AI?
Salvaggio: I would say probably the most important thing for thinking about the way this particular technology is developed is really to think through where accountability can be found. When we are talking about models as if they are happening to the companies that are building them, and we hear this a lot in the rhetoric, we hear that they are grown, not built, which really kind of only refers to, sort of, the scaling of the training data. Getting more and more training data makes them bigger. But there is a building side of this, too, which is to say that they are making decisions about what exactly these things are doing. Whether they stop was a classic example of OpenAI and this incident, right? Whether they coordinate, that’s a human decision.
When you have so much that is unpredictable—and so, as you say, I’m not dismissing that there are real concerns about the unpredictability here. But when you know that something is unpredictable, I think we have, still, a responsibility to manage the kind of scope and the boundaries of where that unpredictability might lead.
And so what I wanna see is more accountability, saying, “Well, if you design a model that does something that you should’ve anticipated that it could be unpredictable,” and I know from my experience that these models are unpredictable. I work with very tiny versions of them, all the time, and they’re doing weird stuff, and I know that, so clearly these companies know that, and they can build better safeguards, guardrails, whatever you wanna call them, to make sure that unpredictability doesn’t have real-world consequences.
Feltman: Absolutely. Well, thank you so much for coming on to chat about this. It’s been super interesting.
Salvaggio: My pleasure.
Feltman: That’s all for today’s episode. We’ll be back on Friday to talk to a doctor who’s developed and tested a new pain-relief method for an infamously uncomfy procedure: IUD insertion.

2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry awarded to pioneers in 'mirror' chemistry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:20:40 UTC
19:20:40 KST

The 2026 Nobel Prize for Chemistry has been awarded to Henri Kagan of the Universite Paris-Sud, in France, and Kenso Soai of the Tokyo University of Science, in Japan, for their work exploring the fundamental geometry of molecules.
The pair are known for pioneering research into autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis. Molecules that are chiral are those whose mirror images cannot be superimposed on one another. Kagan and Soai figured out, for the first time, a way to create just one of those mirror images.
Soai on Wednesday after finding out he had won the prize, told the Nobel Committee that he had been out shopping when he was notified he had won, saying it's "one of the most exciting days of my life. I'm very glad to share the prize with Professor Henri Kagan."
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
He noted that chirality in amino acids is essential to the formation of DNA, and therefore to life as we know it, and many mysteries remain as to how it first emerged. "This is not the final answer," Soai said. "This field should be (moved) forward more and more to understand life."
Chirality is fundamental to understanding organic chemistry. Amino acids and sugars are chiral, for example, in that these molecules all share the same 3D spatial orientation, a property also known as handedness. Imagine your right and left hands—they are mirror images of one another, and you cannot superimpose one on the other. Most people favor one or the other hand—homochirality is similar. Amino acids are all left-handed; sugars are right-handed.
One of the most famous ways humans interact with chirality every day has to do with the senses: reversing the chirality of the molecule lemonene from right handed to left-handed can change our perception from smelling an orange to smelling a lemon.
Rigoberto Hernandez, president of the American Chemical Society, compared the chirality of molecules to a human couple dancing.
"You need to have just the right fit and relative orientation," he says. "It turns out that molecules, when they have one orientation, keep that orientation for a long time. That matters in how they pair up and align," and lead to complex chemical reactions.
Peter Somfai, a member of the Nobel Committee, said after the announcement that "taken together, the groundbreaking discoveries by Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have reshaped our understanding of molecular chirality, how it is created, amplified and transmitted."
Kagan and Soai showed that it is possible to increase the ratio of one mirror image compared to the other. They also showed that it is possible to create one of the mirror images “from nothing,” as Somfai said, using autocatalysis, which is a chemical process where one product of the reaction acts as its catalyst, speeding up the reaction.
The discovery could be the key to understanding how life first arose on Earth, Somfai said.
While producing molecules is relatively easy, problems arise when trying to produce molecules with specific chirality, says Hernandez. Statistically, half the molecules would be of one handedness, and the remainder would be the other handedness. Kagan was able to demonstrate that using specific catalysts could lead to producing one form of handedness more than the other, while Soai advanced the field by using chirals as their own catalyst to produce more of itself.
"Once you have done the mathematics, you understand the theory, and once you've demonstrated it's possible, then you can start to replicate it in many more systems, and then you can do that with intentionality, so that you have a product, a medicine, a material that is intentionally more than the other," says Hernandez.
The work has also been integral to the pharmaceutical industry and the development of novel molecules. Somfai noted that it is "difficult to say that this drug or that drug was developed using this. I would say all of them, because we use this as a tool."
That this year's award was given to such fundamental research should serve as a reminder about how essential that kind of work is for paving the way for advances that are felt in every day life, says Hernandez.
"This this is a reminder that the world is better today because of fundamental and basic science advances that were made 10, 20, 50, years ago," he says. "It means that we need to make investments today in science to ensure that we have those solutions tomorrow, whether it's 10 or 20 or 30 years from now."
The Nobel Prize for Chemistry has been awarded 117 times, to 198 laureates in total, since its inception in 1901. That year, the winner was Dutch physical chemist Jacobus Henricus van’t Hoff for his work uncovering how chemicals interact with each other in solutions.
Among the prize’s most famous laureates is Marie Curie, who was the first woman to receive the award and the first person to receive two Nobel Prizes. Curie's initial Nobel was for physics, but the second, for chemistry in 1911, recognized her work on polonium and the isolation of pure radium.
Another notable dual winner was Frederick Sanger, who won in 1958 for sequencing the amino acids that make up insulin, and again in 1980 for developing a method to sequence strands DNA.
Other awards have recognized research into nanoparticles that can produce a stunning array of colors called quantum dots, the developers of CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing technology, and a way to make molecular sponges that may be used in everything from cancer treatments to cleaning wastewater.

General Dynamics puts U.S. Army drone defense on a pickup
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:18:08 UTC
19:18:08 KST

- General Dynamics Land Systems will display an M-SHORAD Increment 4 air defense system mounted on a Ford Ranger pickup at AUSA 2026.
- The SLED-based system comes in light, medium and heavy variants and is designed for counter-drone defense of the U.S. Army's Mobile Brigade Combat Team.
General Dynamics Land Systems will show a version of its M-SHORAD Increment 4 air defense system mounted on a Ford Ranger pickup truck at the Association of the U.S. Army annual meeting in Washington, D.C., which runs October 12 to 14.
The display puts a short-range air defense and counter-drone package on a commercial pickup, a far lighter carrier than the Stryker armored vehicle used for the U.S. Army’s current M-SHORAD system. General Dynamics did not say which weapons or sensors will be fitted to the Ranger, or whether the company has submitted the design to the U.S. Army’s Increment 4 effort.
The company describes the system as built around a Self-Loading Equipment Dock, or SLED, a self-contained pallet that can be loaded onto different vehicles. It comes in light, medium and heavy variants that carry weapons and sensors on several types of remote weapon stations, which let crews aim and fire from inside or away from the vehicle.
General Dynamics said the system is meant to provide air defense for the U.S. Army’s Mobile Brigade Combat Team, works with the service’s command-and-control systems and can fight drones either on its own or as part of a wider network.
The design follows the path the U.S. Army set for Increment 4. The service first asked industry for ideas in May 2024, seeking air defense for dismounted troops that could fly on a C-130 transport, be dropped by parachute and be carried under a helicopter. In 2025, Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George approved the requirements document for the program.
At last year’s AUSA meeting, the Army’s air and missile defense requirements officer, Col. Marc Pelini, described the sled approach as a move away from a fully integrated vehicle toward a pallet that could go in the back of an Infantry Squad Vehicle, a Humvee, a Joint Light Tactical Vehicle or even a civilian-style pickup.
A follow-up U.S. Army request for information in March 2026 set out the requirements in more detail. The SLED must keep working when removed from its vehicle, and the vehicle must return to full use once the SLED comes off. The system is to counter small and medium drones, along with fixed-wing aircraft and helicopters supporting enemy ground troops.
The U.S. Army plans to reach initial operational capability with Increment 4 by late fiscal 2029 and requested $108.1 million in fiscal 2027 research and development funding for the effort, according to the Congressional Research Service.
General Dynamics Land Systems is the prime contractor and integrator for M-SHORAD Increment 1, known as the SGT Stout, which mounts Stinger missiles, Hellfire missiles and a 30 mm cannon on a Stryker. Increment 2, a laser-armed Stryker, was canceled, and Increment 3 is set to upgrade the Stryker system with the Next Generation Short Range Interceptor, a Stinger replacement, and the XM1223 30 mm cannon.

Denmark proposes up to four years in prison for mediation councils that seek to prevent prosecution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:17:41 UTC
19:17:41 KST

The Danish government has introduced a bill that would make it a criminal offense to participate in a mediation council with the aim of preventing public prosecution of a crime.
The proposed penalty is a fine or up to four years in prison. The bill targets councils that attempt to settle criminal matters outside the Danish justice system.
Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen, a Social Democrat, introduced the proposal on Wednesday, arguing that such councils undermine the rule of law.
“It must come to an end that, for example, imams or prominent criminal families can exploit their position to act as judges of law and order and attempt to override the Danish rule of law,” he said.
The proposal revives a bill from the previous government that was not passed before a general election was called in February.
Police have encountered councils in Aarhus
Wammen said several police districts were aware of mediation councils, although he could not give a figure for how many exist.
In 2024, Jyllands-Posten reported that East Jutland Police had encountered such councils in western Aarhus for several years. The newspaper described them as widespread among groups with other ethnic backgrounds.
One anonymized police interview report described a case from 2020 in which a group of “important men” visited the parents of a man who had reported a violent assault.
The visitors wanted to avoid police involvement and suggested compensation for the assault, according to Jyllands-Posten.
Under current rules, a victim and perpetrator can agree to settle a conflict without police involvement, provided there is no criminal conduct such as coercion or witness intimidation. This has made it difficult for police to act against the councils.
The proposed law would also criminalize participation in a council when the purpose is to evade prosecution.
“What we are doing with this bill is that we are taking targeted action against those who sit at the head of the table,” Wammen said.
He cited wiretapping as a tool police could use to establish whether an illegal council was taking place.
“That is because this is something that takes place behind closed curtains and in environments that do not want to talk to the police. That is why we need better tools to combat it,” he said.
The government still needs a majority in the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, to pass the bill. It is intended to take effect on January 1, 2027.
Serum Institute expects high flu levels this winter
Influenza infections are expected to reach a high level in Denmark this winter, according to Statens Serum Institut (SSI).
“We expect a winter where influenza will once again be prominent, while COVID-19 appears to remain at a lower level,” Bolette Søborg, chief physician and head of section at SSI, said in an update published by the institute.
SSI expects both influenza A and B to circulate during the coming season.
“Both the number of influenza cases and influenza-related hospitalizations are assessed to potentially reach a high level,” the institute said.
Influenza A has dominated recent seasons, while influenza B has circulated at relatively low levels. SSI said this may mean that the population has less naturally acquired immunity to influenza B, which could make it account for a larger share of infections this season.
COVID-19-related hospitalizations, meanwhile, are expected to remain at a low to medium level.
People aged 65 and over are being offered free vaccinations against both influenza and COVID-19. SSI said the vaccines are expected to provide good protection against the two respiratory infections.
The institute also expects vaccination against respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, to reduce serious illness among infants.
Since October last year, the Danish Health Authority has offered RSV vaccination to pregnant women. SSI said hospitalizations among infants fell by about 70% during the latest transmission season compared with previous years.
“We therefore also expect that the vaccination will significantly reduce the burden of disease among the youngest infants this winter,” Søborg said.
RSV is still expected to circulate among older children and adults, although for most people the infection causes symptoms similar to a common cold, including coughing.
False alarm prompts heavy police response at school
Police evacuated HF & VUC on Ejlskovsgade in Odense on Wednesday afternoon after a panic alarm was triggered by mistake.
Fyn Police initially said officers had responded with “many patrols” after an assault alarm was activated at the school.
Students were evacuated from the building, while members of the public, including parents, were asked to stay away from the area and respect police cordons.
At 15:42, police said the incident had turned out to be a false alarm.
“It turned out that it was a false alarm. The alarm was triggered by accident,” police said on Politi Update.
“There is no danger, but we are investigating the area just to be safe and will be present with a reassurance effort over the coming hours,” police added.
Police said they expected to lift the cordons “within the foreseeable future.”
Earlier, a student told Fyens Stiftstidende that his class was watching a documentary when a “Red alert” suddenly came over the school loudspeakers.
“Our teacher barricaded the door with a stopper, and then we waited for the police to arrive. I am okay, but it was an intense way to be kicked out,” he said.
No injuries were reported.
Danish prison service to review training after two Kosovar officers charged with assault
Danmarks Fængsler, Denmark’s prison service, will review its training of Kosovar prison officers after two were charged with assaulting an inmate at Vestre Prison in Copenhagen.
“It is clear that when something like this happens, we are going to look at whether our training of them is good enough. Is our practical training with them good enough?” said the service’s director, Ina Eliasen.
The officers are training in Denmark ahead of the opening of Danish prison places in Kosovo, now expected in late 2027 or early 2028.
Eliasen said the service had otherwise had good experiences with the Kosovar officers.
“We expect that this is an isolated incident, because it is so different from what we have otherwise seen,” she said.
According to the police charge, the two officers jointly punched an inmate several times while on duty in Vestre Prison’s South Department on Monday. Both pleaded not guilty during a preliminary hearing on Wednesday.
The officers had completed their practical training, but Eliasen said Kosovar officers must still be accompanied by Danish colleagues.
“They are always with Danish officers. And when they are in training, they are in on-the-job training. They do not walk alone,” she said.
She declined to comment on specific details of the case. The two officers were arrested on Tuesday and appeared before Copenhagen City Court at Vestre Prison on Wednesday.
Denmark signed the agreement to rent prison places in Kosovo in 2021. The plan is for foreign nationals sentenced to deportation from Denmark to serve their prison sentences there.
The opening has been delayed repeatedly, with another delay announced in mid-September. The prison places are now expected to be ready in late 2027 or early 2028.
A leak involving nearly nine million people’s CPR numbers could increase administrative costs for Danish businesses if it leads to restrictions on access to the register, according to the Confederation of Danish Industry, known as DI.
The CPR register is Denmark’s civil registration system. Banks, insurance companies and unemployment insurance funds use it to identify customers, employees and members.
“If companies’ access were closed or severely limited, a lot of information would instead have to be collected and checked manually,” Jeppe Engell, a cybersecurity expert at DI, said in a press release.
“That would both increase companies’ administrative costs and the risk of errors, outdated customer data, and mistaken identity.”
On Monday, the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization announced on its website that unauthorized people had unlawfully accessed the CPR numbers of nearly nine million people in Denmark.

Danish cinemas pause screenings of “Naza” on anniversary of Hamas attack

“Naza” premiered in Denmark on October 1.

Drivers should expect heavier traffic and possible delays on Denmark’s motorways at the start and end of the autumn holiday, the Danish Road Directorate has warned.

Danish companies and organizations should use other methods to verify people’s identities after unauthorized parties accessed information on 8.8 million people in the CPR register, authorities said Tuesday.
“One must expect that one can no longer identify oneself with CPR,” said Laila Reenberg, director of Samsik, the Agency for Public Security.
“You can no longer count on that if you receive a CPR number, you have identified a specific citizen. That is the consequence of this leak.”
Unauthorized parties collected information over 10 days in September through a small Danish company that had access to the CPR system. Authorities discovered the activity when the company was invoiced for the large number of searches.
The CPR system contains information on people living in Denmark as well as people who have died or moved abroad.
CPR numbers are sometimes used to identify people when they call their doctor or collect prescription medicine from a pharmacy.
Samsik recommends using other forms of identification, including MitID, two-factor authentication or one-time codes sent by text message or email.
“You cannot use it to authorize buying something or receiving sensitive personal data,” Reenberg said about CPR numbers.
Mikkel Leihardt, a department head at the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization, said an overall security review of the CPR system is being launched.
“It is important to emphasize that the information accessed is name and address. There is also other information that has not been accessed,” Leihardt said.
“As a system, CPR is intact.”
Reenberg said authorities have also introduced measures covering critical state IT systems.

Additional checks may also apply when collecting medicine for another person. The association said bringing that person’s health card or other identification would be the easiest option. Otherwise, pharmacies may ask verification questions.

Unauthorized people collected information on 8.8 million living, deceased and emigrated people over 10 days in September by abusing a private Danish company’s legal access to the CPR system.

Around 687,000 people in Denmark currently owe money to the public sector, down from more than 1.1 million in 2023, according to the Danish Debt Collection Agency.
That represents a decline of 454,000 people. The debt can include money owed to the police, municipalities or tax authorities.
Søren Bork Hansen, deputy director at the agency, said several factors have contributed to the decline.
“It is due to a combination of people being able to log in to ‘Mit gældsoverblik’ and pay the debt, but also that we can write off the debt if we have attempted to get the debt paid, and it is for a low amount,” he told Ritzau.
The agency can also recover debt through tax refunds or deductions from a person’s salary.
Debts can be written off when the amount is small, generally below a few thousand DKK, and collection has been attempted for at least a year. In such cases, the cost of collecting the money can be too high.
People living in Denmark owed the public sector around 108 billion DKK in total as of June 2025. Including businesses, deceased and missing people and people living abroad, the figure was 164 billion DKK in June 2026.
Since 2023, around 690,000 people have become debt-free, while others have accumulated new public-sector debt, resulting in the net decline of 454,000.
In the second quarter of 2026 alone, 110,000 people became debt-free while 62,000 took on public-sector debt, the agency said.

Denmark’s government wants to build a prison unit at Kærshovedgård for departure center residents who receive prison sentences.

The unit could hold residents convicted of repeatedly violating requirements to report to authorities.
“Those residents who are sentenced to prison must be able to serve their sentence behind lock and key in a prison unit located in connection with Kærshovedgård,” Frederiksen of the Social Democrats said.
Kærshovedgård houses foreign nationals who have been ordered to leave Denmark or whose asylum applications were rejected but who cannot or will not return to their countries of origin.
Some say they would face persecution or torture. In other cases, their home countries will not cooperate with Danish authorities on returns.
Frederiksen said residents had caused problems for people living near the center, including theft, drug dealing and dangerous driving.
Authorities have previously introduced stricter reporting duties, removed some residents’ driving licenses and established electronic ankle monitoring.
The Danish People’s Party and others have called for all residents to be confined at the center.
The government rejected that proposal because residents who are not serving criminal sentences cannot legally be detained under international agreements.
The planned locked unit would apply only to residents convicted of crimes and sentenced to prison.

More than seven in 10 Danish cancer patients survive at least five years
Just over seven in 10 cancer patients in Denmark are alive five years after diagnosis, according to the Danish Health Data Authority.
The latest figures cover patients diagnosed from 2023 through 2025 and five-year survival was slightly above six in 10 during 2011 to 2013.
“Survival is still increasing, even though it is not happening at the same pace as previously,” authority deputy director Jesper Juel-Helwig said.
Lung cancer showed the largest improvement for both sexes.
Among women, five-year lung cancer survival increased from 21 percent in 2011 to 2013 to 39 percent in the latest period. For men, it rose from 14 percent to 29 percent.
Survival also improved for some of the deadliest cancers. Five-year survival among men with liver cancer doubled from 10 percent to 20 percent.
Among women with pancreatic cancer, it increased from nine percent to 16 percent.
Kræftens Bekæmpelse, the Danish Cancer Society and the country’s main cancer organization, welcomed the progress but said further improvement was needed.
“We have gone from being at the bottom in Europe to being up near the top,” managing director Jesper Fisker said.
Fisker linked the improvement to national cancer care programs introduced almost 20 years ago and a stronger focus on research and coordinated patient treatment.
Dementia patients wait five times longer than legal limit for assessment
Nearly 25,000 people have waited more than the statutory 30 days for a dementia assessment over the past four years, according to a new report from Denmark’s National Audit Office.
The Public Accounts Committee has now issued sharp criticism of the country’s regions over the delays, using the second-highest level of criticism on its scale.
Under Danish law, patients should be assessed within 30 days. In practice, however, the average waiting time nationwide was 165 days last year, more than five times the legal limit.
“The Public Accounts Committee sharply criticizes that 84 percent of patients are not assessed for dementia within the 30 days prescribed by law,” the committee said.
The criticism follows a report by the National Audit Office, which found significant differences in both waiting times and the quality of assessments across Denmark.
In the Region of Southern Denmark, the average waiting time was 133 days. In Region Zealand, it was 244 days.
“The report shows that we are very far from the target of patients being assessed for dementia within 30 days, and that waiting times are growing,” the Public Accounts Committee said.
“There are far too large differences between our regions and between citizens with a strong and a weak social background when it comes to the quality of the specialized assessment and access to necessary examinations. We sharply criticize this.”
The report also found that social background can influence how quickly patients receive an assessment.
On average, the assessment process was 24 days shorter for patients with what the National Audit Office defines as a strong social background.
This includes people with greater wealth and medium- or long-cycle higher education, as well as those who have a partner and adult children with a similar level of education.
Patients with a weak social background are defined as people with debt, no vocational qualifications and no partner or adult children.
The Public Accounts Committee said the reasons behind these differences should be investigated.
“The Public Accounts Committee agrees with the National Audit Office’s recommendation that the causes of differences in the quality of assessment and the differences in assessment waiting times and quality for patients depending on their social background should be investigated,” it said.
Mads Duedahl of the Liberal Party, chairman of Danish Regions, which represents Denmark’s five regional authorities, said the criticism was justified.
“Waiting time is often very burdensome for both patients and relatives, and therefore the regions will make every effort to get more people assessed,” he told Danish Regions’ website.
Duedahl said the system needs to be “rethought” to increase assessment capacity. One option under consideration is to allow general practitioners to carry out more dementia assessments.

Stolen CPR data could make phishing attacks more convincing, cybersecurity expert warns
Personal information obtained through unauthorized access to Denmark’s CPR register could help criminals create more convincing phishing attacks, a cybersecurity expert said.
Names, addresses, identification numbers and birth dates can be used to make fraudulent emails and text messages appear to come from authorities, Aarhus University professor Jens Myrup Pedersen said.
“The more data you have about people, the more realistic attacks you can also create,” he said.
Phishing is digital fraud in which criminals pretend to represent a company, public authority or police force to obtain sensitive information.
Denmark’s Digitalization Ministry said Monday that unauthorized people had accessed names, addresses and CPR numbers belonging to about 8.8 million people.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers. The register includes living and deceased people, as well as former residents.
Pedersen said the information should not be sufficient by itself to obtain loans in another person’s name. Service providers cannot assume that someone knows a person’s identity simply because they possess a CPR number, he said.
However, the information could support other forms of identity misuse and might be sold or combined with publicly available data and photographs.
Pedersen described the breach as unusually extensive.
Unlike a 2015 incident in which records on more than five million Danes were mistakenly delivered to a visa company, the new unauthorized access appears deliberate, he said.
Danish minister says security was inadequate after access to 8.8 million personal records
Security surrounding a private company’s access to Denmark’s national personal information register was inadequate, Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund said Monday.
Unauthorized parties used the small Danish company’s legal access to obtain records on 8.8 million people over about 10 days in September.
“It is clear to me that the security measures surrounding this company’s access to CPR have not been good enough,” Egelund of the Moderates told the Danish news agency Ritzau.
The accessed information includes names, addresses and CPR numbers, Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The total exceeds Denmark’s population of about six million because the records also cover deceased people, emigrants and others registered in the system.
An employee in the CPR administration detected unusual activity Friday, October 2. Authorities had established by Saturday that a security incident had occurred.
The company had permission to search the CPR register, but unauthorized people abused its access. That access has since been closed.
Egelund acknowledged that warnings should have been triggered sooner because the activity continued for several days.
“It is a serious incident. It should not be able to happen,” she said.
The minister declined to identify the company or say whether authorities believe those responsible had criminal intentions, citing the ongoing investigation.
Authorities have not disclosed who accessed the records or how the company’s credentials were compromised.
