Man sentenced to 7 years for looting Nova victim’s equipment on Oct. 7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:16:43 UTC
19:16:43 KST

Exactly three years after the Oct. 7 massacre, the Be'er Sheva Magistrate’s Court on Wednesday sentenced Ram Shahin, 34, to seven years in prison for stealing sound equipment belonging to Matan Lior Mordechai, who was murdered at the Nova music festival after remaining at the scene to help save others.
Shahin was also fined 60,000 shekels and ordered to pay 75,000 shekels in compensation to Mordechai’s parents. Daniel Hasson, 30, who was also involved in the theft, was sentenced to 40 months in prison, while sentencing for a third defendant, San Lucian Tevel, 35, was postponed because of medical circumstances.
Shahin was convicted of aggravated theft and obtaining property by deception under aggravated circumstances after contesting the charges. The court found that he lied and behaved manipulatively during the proceedings. Hasson and Tevel were convicted under plea agreements, each according to his role, of aiding aggravated theft and attempted obtaining of property by deception under aggravated circumstances. The three were arrested in November 2023.
Mordechai was later awarded a civilian heroism medal by the president for his actions during the massacre, after taking responsibility for the area around him and helping save numerous lives before he was killed.
Judge Amir Doron wrote in the sentencing decision that “Shahin cynically exploited the chaos that prevailed at the Nova site. He knew the chances that anyone would suspect his intentions were slim.”
The court rejected Shahin’s claim that he had acted out of “generosity and altruism” and intended to return the equipment to Mordechai’s family.
“The defendant chose to take only the victim’s expensive sound systems, worth hundreds of thousands of shekels,” Doron wrote. “His audacity and insistence on continuing to steal the second system led to the conclusion that this was premeditated conduct under horrifying circumstances. He chose deceitful methods to break down resistance.”
Doron added: “The morning of Oct. 7, 2023, was etched into the history of the State of Israel as a day of darkness, when young people were murdered, among them Matan, who remained behind to save others until he fell.”
“At a time when the victims’ blood was soaking into the killing fields, while the entire nation was in mourning, the defendants chose to exploit the public’s suffering and take abandoned property for financial gain,” he wrote. “This is an extreme moral low without parallel. Where human compassion was required, the defendants displayed complete indifference. Their actions amount to an abomination at the country’s most difficult hour.”
The judge also said their crimes diverted valuable public resources toward investigating the thefts.
Hasson later attempted to trade Mordechai’s property, conduct the court said demonstrated “callousness.” He was ordered to pay Mordechai’s parents 40,000 shekels in compensation.
“The defendants sought to profit from the disaster, and the court must send a message that anyone who desecrates the dignity of the dead will face the full force of the justice system,” the court said.
Before the hearing, Mordechai’s mother, Sara, said: “These are despicable people. As far as I’m concerned, they are not human beings. They came after the massacre, with the smell of bodies and burned cars, and they did not care.”
According to the indictment, the three falsely claimed that they had come to collect equipment belonging to a missing friend, then loaded the sound system and generator. One of them later allegedly told police that he was Mordechai’s business partner, leading authorities to release the truck carrying the equipment.

Scientists urge local approach to enhance seawater alkalinity for CO2 removal
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
18:16:02 CST
19:16:02 KST

MELBOURNE, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- Scientists urge that the focus of ocean alkalinity enhancement (OAE) be shifted from a science fiction-flavored geoengineering intervention to a practical, flexible tool for local CO2 management.
Scientists initially saw increasing the ocean's natural alkalinity as a potential geoengineering solution capable of removing gigatonnes of CO2 annually, but the reality is far more complex, according to a statement released Wednesday by Australia's University of Tasmania (UTAS).
OAE increases seawater's natural alkalinity, reducing acidity and converting CO2 into mainly inert bicarbonate ions that can remain stored in the ocean for millennia, according to the study published in Nature Reviews Earth & Environment.
"Integrating small-scale OAE into diverse local contexts could deliver the achievable carbon mitigation goals defined by individual governments and communities," said lead author UTAS Associate Professor Lennart Bach, a biogeochemical oceanographer.
For example, wastewater emissions could potentially be mitigated through alkalinity from silicates, while excess electricity from a regional wind farm could be used to increase seawater alkalinity electrochemically, Bach said.
The researchers said small-scale projects should be environmentally responsible, demonstrably carbon negative and trusted by the public. ■

Office for Future reveals plans to transform school into housing for displaced Ukrainians

Unknown Publisher

Office for Future reveals plans to transform school into housing for displaced Ukrainians
Architecture studio Office for Future has unveiled plans to remodel a former school in Stavyshche into temporary housing, wrapped around a courtyard, for families affected by the war in Ukraine.
Located around 140 kilometres south of Kyiv, Dvir will provide shelter for 42 families displaced due to Russia's invasion of the country, which has been ongoing since 2022.
Office for Future will create 42 apartments of various sizes in the former school building, including one, two and three-bedroom flats along with several accessible apartments.
Supported by the charity Housing for IDP, Dvir will also include shared spaces designed to build a sense of social connection between the residents.
"Our goal was twofold: to guarantee high-quality private living spaces for the new residents and, at the same time, to offer the city meeting places where the two communities can get to know each other and experience shared moments, transforming the architectural project into a true social project," said Office for Future founder Paolo Russo.
"Through this intervention, architecture becomes a tool for social reconstruction, demonstrating how the recovery of a historic building can contribute to the regeneration of a community affected by conflict."
Common areas, children's play areas and meeting spaces will provide space for people to gather and host cultural activities for the community.
A courtyard at the centre of the building will be transformed into a planted green space with portions of the existing asphalt surface retained as walkways.
Office for Future will top the existing building with a timber roof covered with photovoltaic panels, and connect apartments with freestanding wooden walkways.
The studio hopes that adapting an existing, familiar building in Stavyshche will better help settle the residents in the rural town.
"We asked ourselves how this place could best welcome people who have experienced the trauma of losing their homes," said Russo.
"We worked on a building that is already a landmark for the citizens, a former school that is part of their memory," he continued. "We wanted a new community to be born here, capable of integrating into the broader community of Stavyshche."
A number of significant buildings in Ukraine have been damaged by Russian strikes this year, including the UNESCO-listed Dormition Cathedral and Bernardine Monastery.
Dezeen's Jennifer Hahn investigated the unexpected trend of striking interiors popping up in the country, despite four years of war and the constant threat of Russian bombardment.
The images are by Office for Future.

Poland has launched new combat uniforms for its army. It is the first time that the designs have been updated in 33 years, and also the first time that they include a version specially created for women, who now make up around 16% of soldiers.
“A soldier’s safety and comfort during service are paramount,” said defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, announcing the new uniforms, which have been undergoing testing by various branches of the military,
“[They are] adapted to the needs of women and men serving in the Polish army, because both deserve not only respect and gratitude, but also the creation of conditions that will encourage service as much as possible,” he added.
The new tactical uniform features new camouflage patterns that are intended to better reflect the colours and shadows found in natural environments, “allowing the soldier to remain invisible for as long as possible”. According to the armed forces, testing shows it provides 30% better camouflage effectiveness.
The defence ministry says that the outfits, which will be produced completely in Poland, are created from “lighter, more flexible and durable materials” than before.
The women’s version features a more “closely fitted shape” with a “choice of tops and bottoms to suit women’s figures”, allowing “greater freedom of movement”.

“For the first time in the history of the Polish military, female soldiers will no longer have to choose the size that fits them from men’s uniforms,” said deputy defence minister Magdalena Sobkowiak.
She noted that women now make up 16% of soldiers in the army, and as much as 20% of those serving in the Territorial Defence Force (WOT), a volunteer reserve formation.
Kosiniak-Kamysz says that the new uniforms, which cost around 1,000 zloty (€228) each, will be rolled out gradually, with 7,500 delivered this year. The defence ministry recently signed an agreement with logistics giant InPost to use its parcel lockers to deliver uniforms to soldiers.
Poland has dramatically increased the size of its armed forces in recent years. NATO figures show that the number of Polish military personnel has risen from 101,600 in 2016 to an estimated 263,600 this year.
That means Poland now has the alliance’s largest armed forces in continental Europe, ahead of France (202,000), Italy (191,600) and Germany (183,200). In NATO as a whole, only the United States (1.3 million) and Turkey (395,800) have more military personnel.
Meanwhile, both the number and proportion of women serving in the armed forces have increased dramatically. In 2015, there were only 4,000 professional female soldiers in Poland, a number that has now risen to almost 37,000.

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un wished President Vladimir Putin “victory and glory” on his 74th birthday Wednesday, pledging to deepen ties as Pyongyang continues to support Russia’s war in Ukraine.
“My dearest friend, Comrade Vladimir Putin, please accept my most heartfelt and warm congratulations and best wishes on the occasion of your birthday,” Kim wrote in a telegram published by North Korea’s state-run Korean Central News Agency.
Kim praised Putin’s “outstanding and skillful leadership,” saying Russia had strengthened its standing as a world power over the past two decades. He also claimed that Putin enjoyed the Russian people’s “great trust and support.”
Russia would “certainly achieve victory in its just and sacred war” and defend its sovereignty, security interests and territorial integrity, Kim said.
The North Korean leader pledged to keep expanding the countries’ comprehensive strategic partnership, describing Russia as a “brotherly” nation.
Moscow has deepened cooperation with Pyongyang since launching its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
According to South Korean military intelligence, North Korea has supplied Russia with more than 12 million artillery rounds and ballistic missiles. It has also sent around 13,000 troops to Russia’s Kursk region, of whom about 2,300 have been killed, the intelligence service estimates.
Bloomberg Economics estimates that North Korea has earned over $14 billion from military support for Russia since 2022, including $849 million from sending troops.
Ukrainian officials have warned that Pyongyang plans to expand its military presence in Russia.

The head of the International Monetary Fund has called on governments across big economies to tighten their belts as soaring bond yields hit budgets.
Speaking in Singapore, the IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, said global debt-to-GDP ratios were at their highest level since the second world war and on course to hit 100% in the coming years.
She said governments could not rely on rapid economic growth to lift the burden of debt – and instead would have to make “very tough political choices”.
Georgieva was speaking before the IMF and World Bank annual meetings, which are to be held in Bangkok next week. “My message to the world’s economic policymakers will be this: we cannot keep delaying necessary policy action – you have the tools, now have the wisdom to use them.
“And yet we don’t see decisive action in the high-debt advanced economies where the need of the hour is for credible medium-term fiscal consolidation plans, supported in some cases by upfront fiscal measures,” she said.
Bond yields – effectively the interest rate on the debt – have jumped in recent weeks, raising the cost of borrowing for many governments to multi-decade highs as markets adjust to the prospect of higher inflation as a result of the war in the Middle East.
“Elevated yields are inflating the interest bill at a time of tight budget constraints and competing spending priorities, including defence,” Georgieva said, calling for “an urgent and comprehensive set of policy responses”.
The Bulgarian economist suggested central banks should be prepared to raise interest rates to see off resurgent inflation.
The ECB, US Federal Reserve and Bank of Japan have already tightened policy in the face of rising inflation – moves Georgieva said were “highly appropriate” – but the Bank of England has so far left rates on hold at 3.75%.
“Now may be a good time for a prudently hawkish bias in many countries’ monetary policy,” Georgieva said, suggesting central banks might want to err on the side of caution.
She also stressed the importance of tackling some of the risks of AI, which has buoyed the US stock market but raised fears of mass layoffs.
She highlighted IMF research predicting that the adoption of AI could add half a percentage point to global economic growth if carried out effectively. However, she urged policymakers to “help manage AI’s substantial perils, including large-scale labour market fallout, serious cyber and stability risks and frontier models threatening to escape human control and run amok”.
The Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, who is also chair of the Financial Stability Forum that brings together the world’s central banks, recently warned of the “real and significant” risks posed by frontier AI models and called for the “right to intervene”.
In the UK the chancellor, John Healey, has said he will stick with his predecessor Rachel Reeves’s plans to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenues – borrowing only to invest – and bring the debt-to-GDP ratio down over time.

Ukraine built a $9K drone to hunt a $10M Russian jammer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:14:16 UTC
19:14:16 KST

- Ukraine's Brave1 Market has listed the SHOT-L1, a strike drone that automatically homes in on radio emissions from Russian electronic warfare systems.
- The drone has a range of up to 80 km, carries a 4 kg payload and costs UAH 416,000 (about $9,300).
A Ukrainian fixed-wing strike drone built to find Russian electronic warfare systems by their own radio signals and dive onto them has been listed on Brave1 Market, the government-run online store where Ukrainian military units order weapons, Ukrainian outlet Defender Media reported.
The drone, called SHOT-L1, can strike targets up to 80 km (50 miles) away and is priced at UAH 416,000 (about $9,300) per unit on the platform. The manufacturer has not been named, and there is no information yet on whether the drone has been codified, the formal approval that admits a product into service with the Ukrainian military.
An operator sends the SHOT-L1 toward the area where a target is believed to be, and once the drone reaches the assigned zone, an onboard system scans it for radio emissions, works out the direction of a detected source and steers the drone onto it automatically. If it picks up several emitters at once, the drone goes for the strongest one, the manufacturer says.
If no active signal turns up within a set time, the drone switches to a backup mission and attacks a fixed ground target chosen before launch.
The SHOT-L1 carries a 4 kg (8.8-pound) payload and cruises at 100 km/h (62 mph) with up to 60 minutes of flight time. It has a thermal camera, an analog video link and a terminal guidance system for the final approach.
The manufacturer lists three Russian jamming systems as typical targets: the R-340RP Pole-21, the R-330Zh Zhitel and the Mgla. Pole-21 is designed to jam satellite navigation signals such as GPS, while the truck-mounted Zhitel is built to jam satellite phones, cellular networks and navigation signals. Ukrainian estimates put the cost of a single Zhitel at around $10 million. Russian forces have used both systems widely in the war in Ukraine, where jamming is a constant problem for Ukrainian drone units that depend on radio control links and satellite navigation.
Brave1 Market launched in 2025 and lets Ukrainian units buy drones, ground robots and electronic warfare equipment with their own budgets or with points earned for confirmed combat results. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said troops ordered more than 590,000 drones through the platform in the first nine months of 2026, with interceptor drones the most popular category.

Nobel prize in chemistry awarded for work on mirror-image molecules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:14:02 UTC
19:14:02 KST

The Nobel prize in chemistry 2026 has been awarded to two scientists for discoveries that showed how chemical reactions can produce an overwhelming excess of one of two mirror image forms of a molecule.
Henri B Kagan at Paris-Sud University in France and Kensō Soai at Tokyo University of Science in Japan have been awarded the prize “for the discovery of nonlinear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis”.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winners in Stockholm, Sweden, on Wednesday. They will each receive an equal share of a prize of 12m Swedish kronor (about £900,000).
Many molecules, including amino acids that form the building blocks of proteins, can exist in two forms that contain the same atoms, but are mirror images of one another, much like a person’s left and right hands. This property is known as chirality.
However, the chemistry underpinning life is surprisingly “homochiral”, or same-handed. Proteins are built almost exclusively from L-amino acids, while the sugars that form the backbone of DNA and RNA have the opposite D- configuration.
How this homochirality could have emerged when chemical reactions in the laboratory typically produce equal quantities of both forms had long puzzled scientists. The question also had practical consequences: “Although these molecules look very similar, they can behave very differently when they interact with other molecules,” said Prof Andre Cobb, an organic chemist at King’s College London.
“This matters enormously for medicines because many of the molecules in our bodies, including proteins that drugs target, are themselves chiral. So the ‘left-handed’ and ‘right-handed’ versions of a drug can interact with the body in different ways which can lead to different or weakened drug effects.”
The drug thalidomide provides a potent example. During the early 1960s, thousands of children were affected by birth defects after their mothers were prescribed it to combat morning sickness during pregnancy. Researchers subsequently found differences in the biological effects of the drug’s two mirror image forms.
Manufacturers wanted a way of steering reactions towards particular forms of the molecules that they produced, and Kagan and Soai eventually provided a solution.
It began in 1986, when Kagan discovered that a relatively small imbalance between left- and right-handed forms of a catalyst could create a greater excess of one of the mirror image products than the other.
Soai took the idea further, developing a reaction in which the molecules produced themselves acted as catalysts for making more of themselves, a process known as autocatalysis. “You have to be aware, this is probably the coolest experiment in organic chemistry ever,” said Prof Peter Somfai, an organic chemist at Lund University and a member of the Nobel committee for chemistry.
In 2003, Soai demonstrated a reaction that produced almost exclusively one mirror-image form, reproducing the kind of molecular one-handedness found in living organisms for the first time.
Speaking by telephone at Wednesday’s announcement, Soai, 76, said he was “very proud” of the experiment as it offered a potential explanation for how the molecular one-handedness of life could have arisen. He described hearing the news about the prize as “one of the most exciting days of my life”.
Taken together, Kagan and Soai’s discoveries had “reshaped our understanding of molecular chirality, how it is created, amplified and transmitted”, Somfai said.
These insights have since become embedded in the development of catalysts that steer chemical reactions towards producing a particular mirror image form across different industries. “It is in the backsides of our heads all the time,” said Somfai.
“It might be difficult to say that this drug or that drug was developed using this. I would say all of them because we use this as a tool. We use this as an understanding of how to develop catalysts and how they function.”

Unknown

France's President Emmanuel Macron and Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrive for an EU summit in Brussels, on March 19, 2026. | John Thys/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — France and Germany said Wednesday that they will release diesel stocks that were already committed in March as part of the G7 pledge to tap stockpiles of oil products, leaving it uncertain as to whether any new barrels will be released in addition, two diplomats familiar with the matter told POLITICO.
The comments suggest Europe's promise to U.S. President Donald Trump last week to release millions of barrels of the transport fuel was less generous than it sounded.
The G7 club of rich countries committed Friday to release a "substantial" amount of diesel in the next 20 days to bring down global prices after senior Trump administration officials threatened to impose an export ban on the fuel if European countries didn't unlock their reserves.
Advertisement
But in a closed-door meeting of EU energy officials Wednesday, the countries acknowledged that the release wouldn't include new barrels of diesel but rather barrels already pledged under a wider European commitment to release 100 million barrels, two-thirds of which were refined products, the diplomats said. That deal was brokered by the International Energy Agency in March weeks after the outbreak of the war in Iran.
The exact quantities Germany and France will release remains unclear, but they will represent a portion of the remainder of the stocks committed in March, the diplomats and a German government spokesperson said.
Of the 2.65 million tons of oil, diesel and jet fuel promised, Germany has so far released only 600,000 tons onto the market. It remains unclear how much France has contributed of its own commitment to release 14.6 million barrels of oil products. However, Paris has indicated privately that it still has 8 million barrels left under the March commitment, which it will contribute under the latest push, two other diplomats told POLITICO.
The countries, which boast some of the largest reserves of refined oil products in Europe, have been criticized by the Trump administration for not contributing the full share committed in March. Germany attributes that to weak demand for the barrels, according to a document seen by POLITICO.
It's not clear whether countries will ultimately decide to commit additional barrels, with one European official telling POLITICO Monday that the fresh commitment "necessarily implied" a fresh release. France on Wednesday signaled it could release 2 million barrels of diesel on top of the quantities agreed in March — as part of the G7 vow to prioritize releases of the motor fuel over the next 20 days — but stopped short of offering a clear commitment, two diplomats said. An extraordinary meeting of the IEA will take place today, two other people familiar with the matter said.
The move came amid confusion from other member countries over who was committing how much and when, with some Eastern European countries like Bulgaria also expressing concern that blowing through reserves to combat prices would leave them exposed in the event of a supply crisis, the people said.
Advertisement
A spokeswoman for Germany's economy and energy ministry confirmed on Tuesday that Berlin would be releasing no new barrels.
"The G7 has asked the IEA to monitor a swift and complete implementation of the commitments made for March 2026," the spokeswoman told POLITICO. "Against this background, and taking into account commitments already fulfilled, the obligations are to be implemented through a coordinated release of 100 million barrels via the IEA."
She added "as of now, no additional quantities" would be released.

Cemil Tugay, who won İzmir for the CHP with a 314,000-vote margin in 2024, received his AK Party badge from Erdoğan in Ankara on Wednesday, ending 27 years of centre-left rule in Turkey's third-largest city.
İzmir Mayor Cemil Tugay joined President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan's AK Party on Wednesday, shocking the Turkish left and handing the ruling party a symbolic prize it has failed to win in elections three times in a row.
Erdoğan presented Tugay — who ran for mayor as centre-left CHP party candidate two years ago — with an AK Party badge at the party's Ankara headquarters on Wednesday morning and welcomed him in a speech to MPs at the opening of the legislative year.
"İzmir is different today. Very enthusiastic," Erdoğan said. "Good things await İzmir," Tugay told reporters.
Tugay reversed a series of public pledges that he would never join the ruling party, which he previously described as "not even a one-in-a-million chance."
The switch makes Tugay the first right-wing mayor of Turkey's third-largest city in 27 years. İzmir has been governed by centre-left or left-wing mayors since 1999.
In the March 2024 local elections, Tugay won 48.97% of the vote against AK Party candidate Hamza Dağ's 37.06%, a 314,000-vote margin.
In August 2025, Tugay told a television programme "there is not even a one-in-a-million chance" of him joining the AK Party, adding that a mayor elected from the CHP had no right to switch parties.
"I find that very shameful. I am not that kind of person," he said. In January, he told the outlet T24 that his mother said she'd disown him and his wife would divorce him if he were to join the AK Party.
Tugay left the CHP in June following a court ruling that reinstated Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu as party leader, and served as an independent for three months.
He was expected by many observers to join the YENİ or New Party founded by former CHP leader Özgür Özel, but did not.
In August, Tugay said joining any party was "out of the question". "I will remain independent, I have said many times that I will stay independent, but in truth I am upset that this keeps being talked about every day," he explained.
"Of course I will also map out a path for myself," Tugay said.
Yet on 30 September he met Erdoğan at the presidential complex and two days later he resigned from both the Atatürkist Thought Association and the Social Democracy Association.
The day before the announcement, the AK Party posted a video showing a rubbish-strewn street being covered with flowers as a patriotic Turkish song about İzmir from the 1920s played, with the date "7 October 2026" appearing at the end without specifically naming Tugay.
New Party leader Özgür Özel said on Tuesday that Tugay had faced "threats, blackmail and pressure" and that the AK Party had "never won İzmir at the polls and never will."
"This is not something you can achieve with grab-and-run tactics," Özel said, addressing Erdoğan.
New Party spokesman Zeynel Emre said party switches could not be assessed independently of judicial proceedings against opposition mayors.
Despite Tugay's defection, the AK Party does not control İzmir's city council. New Party remains the largest group with 91 members, while the AK Party now has 39 seats and independents 11.
Tugay joined the CHP in 2010, was elected mayor of the Karşıyaka district in 2019, and became İzmir metropolitan mayor in 2024.

She moved to Israel under a program for Jewish youth at the end of 2020. After the program ended, due to quarantine restrictions and closed airports, Natalia faced a choice: obtain a work visa or acquire citizenship under the Law of Return. She chose the latter—and with it, she also became obligated to perform military service.
In May 2022, Natalia joined the Israeli military and chose a combat unit.
“When the war started in Israel itself, I still had six months of mandatory service left. I was discharged and immediately transferred to reserve service. Once I managed to resolve all the bureaucratic issues so that this would not be considered desertion, I returned to Ukraine,” the young woman says.
Natalia returned to Ukraine in March 2025, and in August signed a contract with the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
“The army—both Israeli and Ukrainian—gives you a deeper understanding of what society is made of”
Among the advantages of the Ukrainian army, she highlights its ability to quickly adapt to circumstances. In particular, she mentions the use of drones, OSINT, and solving complex technological tasks with minimal resources.
“The West could learn from this situational agility. They often spend huge budgets on developments that should be cheap and mass-produced,” the veteran says.
However, such Ukrainian ingenuity is largely a consequence of a lack of funding, Natalia notes.
In the Israeli military, Natalia highlights society’s readiness for the constant threat of war and more systematic planning of military service.
“There, preparation for and perception of the army begin at school: by the age of 14–15, teenagers already understand where they want to go, what skills they need, and undergo selection for special or intelligence units,” the young woman says.
She then gives the opposite example of the situation in Ukraine.
This Ukrainian female soldier flies one of war’s heaviest drones. She turns down promotion twice to keep doing it
“In Ukraine, with very rare exceptions, people hide until they are mobilized, and suddenly face the reality of conscription without having any understanding of the system,” the veteran says.
Asked how adapted the Ukrainian army is to women, she answered: “In no way,” adding that the Israeli army is “also largely not fully adapted.”
In Ukraine, this is reflected, in particular, in the provision of clothing and equipment that often does not correspond to women’s sizes and physiology. She says she had to purchase her own anatomically fitted body armor. She cited the example of veteran Natalia Lishchyshyna, who had her breasts amputated due to prolonged wearing of body armor that was not adapted to the female anatomy.
In Israel, by contrast, there is a practice of reimbursing expenses for equipment that service members purchase at their own expense.
Serving in the military in both countries provides an opportunity to better understand what society is actually made of, the young woman says.
“The army—both Israeli and Ukrainian—gives you a deeper understanding of what society is made of. You encounter people you would never have crossed paths with in your civilian bubble because of differences in views or socioeconomic circumstances,” Natalia says.
She believes this makes it easier to accept mistakes, difficulties, and new challenges.
The Ukrainian army is not adapted to women in any way, Natalia says
In Natalia’s view, the problem is not only the living and working conditions but, above all, the lack of mechanisms necessary for the systematic mandatory mobilization of women. At the same time, she believes voluntary recruitment should be encouraged and expanded.
One of the problems is the lack of a legal procedure for temporary childcare in cases when both parents are simultaneously carrying out combat missions, Natalia says, stressing that she means the period of their service, rather than situations involving the death of one of the parents.
Another shortcoming is insufficient protection against sexual violence and harassment in the Ukrainian military.
“Here, any complaint goes through the direct chain of command. If the commander is not interested in resolving the problem or is involved in it themselves, the woman is left defenseless,” the veteran says.
In Israel, by contrast, there is a separate hotline and mechanisms for documenting such cases without directly approaching a commander.
Women in combat positions can also still be taken insufficiently seriously, denied participation in combat missions, or transferred to staff positions without their consent.
Natalia also emphasizes the lack of systematic military training for civilian women “at any level” and gives school education as an example.
“Even with the weak level of the school curriculum for the subject ‘Defense of Ukraine,’ boys had at least some basic knowledge. Girls were not involved in it at all,” the veteran says.
For now, Natalia believes that women’s military service should remain voluntary, as society as a whole is still not ready to fully accept women in the military.

2026-10-07
10:09:54 UTC

PRYLUKY, UKRAINE -- Russian missile and drone strikes pounded Ukraine on Russian leader Vladimir Putin's birthday, leaving dozens of people dead or injured in one of "the most vile" attacks in recent times, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
"The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively," Zelenskyy wrote on X, adding that the October 7 attack included "70 missiles in total, many of them ballistic, as well as Shahed-drones" launched on 12 Ukrainian regions.
The death toll across the country rose to 19, including two in the capital, Kyiv, and 14 in a strike that also injured 50 people, including seven children, in Pryluky in Ukraine's northern Chernihiv region, which borders Russia.
There, Zelenskyy said, Russian forces "destroyed" a residential building "as a birthday 'gift' to Putin," while at least 10 other such buildings were damaged elsewhere, along with Ukraine's energy infrastructure, one of Moscow's other "key targets."
Reporting from the aftermath in Pryluky, RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service showed a five-story apartment building torn apart by the Russian strike with its roof destroyed, windows blown out, and debris scattered around the site.
"The fire was right in front of my eyes. There were explosions. I was screaming in my apartment. Extremely scary. I can't describe it," local resident Lidiya told Current Time, saying the doors and windows in her apartment had been shattered and her balcony had been "smashed up."
"So many people have died. I knew everyone here," she added, holding back tears.
Ukrainian police said search operations were still under way as emergency workers were seen recovering bodies from beneath the rubble.
With a fifth wartime winter approaching, Russian strikes on Ukraine have become a daily occurrence. Moscow has previously sought to pressure Kyiv into accepting its hard-line demands by attacking the country's energy infrastructure and leaving thousands without heat or electricity amid freezing temperatures.
Since this year, however, Kyiv has increasingly responded to Russian attacks with a campaign of long-range strikes targeting military and energy sites inside Russia and middle-range strikes targeting its key logistics in Ukraine's occupied eastern and southern regions.
Tanker Hit In Black Sea
Following the latest Russian attacks, Zelenskyy later reported on what he called Kyiv's "just responses." He said Ukrainian forces had targeted two of Russia's oil facilities and a military training ground overnight on October 7, adding, "There was also a response in the Black Sea."
Hours earlier, Russia's Transport Ministry said a Liberian-flagged tanker had been attacked by "naval drones" near the country's major southern city of Sochi, known for its luxury resorts.
The ministry reported an intense fire following the attack, saying that "crude oil is burning openly" on the surface of the Black Sea. It later added that the crew of 23, all Indian citizens, had been rescued and the fire had been extinguished.
According to the Ukrainian monitoring site BlackSeaNews, the vessel was used by Russia as part of its so-called shadow fleet, a network of vessels used to transport Russian fuel and evade sanctions.
Sochi's local authorities said access to the city's coast and beaches was being restricted. Previous Ukrainian strikes on energy targets in southern Russia have caused oil slicks, prompted beach closures, and led to toxic black rainfall.
The developments came amid renewed US interest in negotiating a diplomatic settlement to the long-running war. While US President Donald Trump has long said it is one of the key goals of his presidency, Kyiv and Moscow remain far apart in their negotiating positions.
Since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion almost five years ago, the Kremlin has shown no willingness to compromise on its key demands, including full control over Ukraine's key eastern Donetsk region, a stronghold Russian forces have not yet been able to capture.

European leaders marked three years since the Oct. 7 massacre on Wednesday with tributes to those murdered by Hamas terrorists, renewed warnings over rising antisemitism and declarations of solidarity with Jewish communities across the continent.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain remembered those “senselessly killed by Hamas terrorists,” noting that the impact of the attacks continued to be felt by Jewish communities worldwide and pointing to what he called a disturbing rise in antisemitic behavior in Britain. Referring to subsequent attacks against Jews and Jewish institutions, he told the country’s Jewish community: “We stand with you. Abuse and violence against you, in any form, will not be tolerated.”
Burnham said Britain was funding security for synagogues, schools and community buildings and would act forcefully against antisemitism in schools, universities and neighborhoods. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz wrote that “the Hamas attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, marks a profound turning point.” Germany, he said, mourned with the victims and their families and must fight antisemitism with even greater determination. “Jews must be able to live here without fear,” he added. Merz also reaffirmed Germany’s support for Israel, saying the country’s Israeli friends could count on Berlin to work to ensure such a crime was never repeated.
French minister visits Israel as Paris honors Bibas family
French President Emmanuel Macron also commemorated the massacre, writing: “Three years since Hamas’s barbaric terrorist attacks claimed the lives of over 1,200 people, including 51 of our compatriots.” He said France continued to share the grief of Israel and the bereaved families and had forgotten neither the names nor the faces of the victims. Macron reaffirmed France’s commitment to fighting antisemitism and terrorism while working for peace and security for all.

She compared the scenes to pogroms once thought confined to humanity’s tragic past and condemned those who supported, excused or sought to relativize the atrocities.
Paris, meanwhile, inaugurated a path in Parc Monceau in memory of Shiri Bibas and her sons Ariel and Kfir. The French Embassy in Israel described the family as a mother and two redheaded boys whose story shook the world, saying their faces had come to symbolize shattered innocence and that placing their names in the public space would ensure their story continued to be remembered.
Dutch anniversary message sparks political clash
Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten’s anniversary message remembered the nearly 1,200 people killed in the Hamas attack and the more than 250 taken hostage, while also referring to the Palestinians killed during the subsequent war in Gaza. He said Israeli and Palestinian bereaved families continued to live with fear and insecurity and expressed hope for peace.
Geert Wilders, the right-wing Dutch leader known for his strong support for Israel, responded by accusing Jetten of betraying Israel and the Jewish people through measures including boycotts, condemnations, support for the International Criminal Court and sanctions. He also accused the government of leaving the Netherlands vulnerable to the type of violence Israel experienced on Oct. 7. The wording of both Dutch statements is rendered here in indirect speech because the original posts could not be independently accessed in full.
Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Janša wrote that Palestinian terrorists had unleashed “unspeakable barbarism” on Israel three years earlier, killing around 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages. He said Slovenia remembered the victims and stood with their families, Israel and Jewish communities worldwide, while urging continued opposition to attempts to justify or minimize the massacre. “‘Never Again’ is not merely a promise. It is a duty,” he wrote.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, who has frequently criticized Israeli policy, also marked the anniversary. “The Oct. 7 attacks were a barbaric act of terror,” she wrote, saying Europe must firmly reject antisemitism and that Jewish communities must be able to live openly and without fear. Kallas said Hamas had brought immense suffering to Israelis and insisted that Hamas must disarm for the Gaza peace plan to move forward.

Russia says plague institute worker's death does not risk an epidemic
MOSCOW/LONDON, Oct 7 - Russia's health regulator said on Wednesday there were no risks of an epidemic breaking out in Siberia after a plague institute worker there died, as the World Health Organization pressed Moscow for more information about her cause of death.
Russian authorities say the 28-year-old laboratory worker died on Friday from pneumonia of an as-yet unestablished origin, in a case that has prompted international concern, including from US President Donald Trump, and which saw around 200 people initially placed in quarantine.
Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's health watchdog, said in a statement it was winding down precautionary measures it had put in place after concluding there was no risk of an epidemic and that it had shared its latest information with the WHO.
No cases of plague had been detected among anyone who had come into contact with the deceased worker, Darya Shipilova, it said, and 90% of those placed in quarantine had been released after nearly 5,000 lab tests had failed to detect any dangerous pathogens.
It said Shipilova had been vaccinated and had therefore been "immune to the dangerous infections with which she worked". It did not say though what had caused the pneumonia which killed her or how she fell ill.
WHO CALLS FOR MORE INFORMATION
Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the director general of the WHO in Geneva, said in a statement on X earlier on Wednesday that his organisation needed more information from Russia to understand what had happened.
"WHO has requested further information to clarify the cause of the severe pneumonia, the pathogen that prompted the public health measures, and media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause," he said.
"Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks."
KREMLIN BLASTS 'FALSE INFORMATION' IN MEDIA
The Kremlin said Russia had properly informed the WHO about the incident in line with established procedures.
When asked about the WHO's request to respond to reports about a second person in Siberia allegedly falling ill, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged caution when it came to using media reports as a reference for what was happening.
"There is a great deal of media coverage, and the vast majority of what the media are reporting about this situation is false information," said Peskov.
He advised the media and others to rely on information provided by the health regulator. It did not immediately respond to a Reuters comment request on Wednesday about the WHO's questions.
EXACT CAUSE OF DEATH REMAINS UNKNOWN
Some Western media outlets have reported — citing unnamed "Russian media" — that a second person in Siberia had died, saying they had died of plague.
Reuters was unable to find any such stories in Russian media or any evidence that a second person in Siberia had died although some bloggers on social media were making — without evidence — such assertions.
Contacted by Reuters, the WHO said it had nothing further to add on the matter beyond what Tedros — who was due to give a press conference later on Wednesday — had already posted on X.
Tedros' call for more information echoed that of US Secretary of State Marco Rubio who has also said Moscow needs to share more information about the incident.
Pneumonia, a lung infection, can have a variety of causes including plague as well as other bacterial infections or viral respiratory diseases, such as flu or COVID-19. REUTERS

EU wants to impose a tax on U.S. big tech - media
Kyiv • UNN
Brussels is considering expanding the CORE levy to large companies, including Apple, Meta and Google. In this way, the EU seeks to increase revenue and avoid conflict with the United States.
Brussels is considering taxing large American technology groups (Big Tech) by expanding the levy on large corporations in an effort to increase EU revenues while avoiding a backlash from the Trump administration. Financial Times reports, writes UNN.
Details
The European Commission is reportedly working on new ways to generate more revenue from technology groups such as Apple, Meta and Google without singling them out, Reuters writes.
The report says that Brussels has been considering changes to its "Corporate Resource for Europe" (CORE) proposal, which would require all companies operating in the EU with annual revenue exceeding €100 million ($112.32 million) to pay a one-off annual tax contribution.
In its current form, CORE requires these companies to pay a fixed annual levy of between €100,000 and €750,000, covering only a small portion of a multinational company's profits.
"Some (EU) capitals are opposed to a purely digital tax because they do not want to upset the Americans, while many others are opposed to CORE," an EU official told the FT. "The solution is to expand (the tax) so that it covers virtually all large companies."
"The European Commission remains ready to support the Council (of the EU) and the European Parliament in reaching an agreement on a new own-resources package... as these are essential to ensuring adequate funding for our shared priorities over the next decade," a spokesperson for the EU executive told Reuters.
Apple, Google, Meta and the Computer & Communications Industry Association (CCIA), which represents several U.S. technology companies, did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment outside normal working hours.
U.S. President Donald Trump threatened in June to impose a 100% tariff on all goods from any country that levies a digital services tax on American companies.
The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, which has long threatened European countries with retaliatory tariffs if they impose such taxes, claims that these levies discriminate against American companies, which dominate the sector worldwide.

Lithuania gets its first Switchblade 600 attack drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:07:57 UTC
19:07:57 KST

- Lithuania has received its first batch of AeroVironment Switchblade 600 anti-armor loitering munitions, the country's defense ministry said.
- The drones come from a December 2022 deal worth about €45 million (about $50.4 million) signed with the U.S. government.
Lithuania has received its first batch of Switchblade 600 loitering munitions, U.S.-made attack drones built to hunt tanks and other armored vehicles, the Lithuanian Ministry of National Defence said on X.
The ministry did not disclose how many drones arrived, which units will operate them, or when the remaining deliveries are due. Lithuania signed the purchase with the U.S. government in December 2022 in a deal worth about €45 million (about $50.4 million) that also covers launch and control equipment, a maintenance package and a training simulator.
“The system gives the Lithuanian Armed Forces a new long-range precision strike capability against armored targets,” the Lithuanian Ministry of National Defence wrote.
AeroVironment, based in Arlington, Virginia, builds the Switchblade 600. Soldiers launch it from a tube and guide it with a tablet-based control unit, letting the drone circle over an area until they pick a target and send it diving in. The company lists more than 40 minutes of flight time and a demonstrated standoff range of more than 40 km (25 miles) for the original version, which carries the same type of anti-armor warhead used on the Javelin missile.
When the contract was signed, then-Defence Minister Arvydas Anušauskas said the drones would let Lithuanian forces destroy enemy tanks and other armored equipment up to 40 km away, a capability the military had not had before. The ministry said Lithuania was the first country after the United States to buy the system, and a ministry spokesperson declined at the time to say how many Switchblade 600s had been ordered. Deliveries were scheduled for 2025 and 2026.
The 2022 announcement also said the United States would supply the smaller Switchblade 300, paid for with U.S. military assistance funds. The ministry’s latest post did not mention the Switchblade 300.
AeroVironment unveiled an upgraded Switchblade 600 Block 2 in October 2025, with about 20 percent more endurance, more than 50 minutes of flight time and a reach of more than 100 km (62 miles) when control is handed off between operators. The company said it had raised Switchblade 600 production from 40 to 240 systems a month over the previous year. The ministry did not say which version Lithuania received.
Ukraine has used the Switchblade 600 in combat against Russian armor after the United States began sending the drones following Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022.
The Switchblade order is one of several major U.S. purchases Lithuania has made in recent years, alongside HIMARS rocket launchers, Joint Light Tactical Vehicles and UH-60 Black Hawk helicopters.

   The evening brought together Italian and Mozambican musicians and singers, along with the young members of the Xiqitsi orchestra and choir, conducted by the renowned Mozambican oboist Kika Materula.

So that we don’t have to start over from scratch every time,” he emphasized.

Most Republicans in tight midterm distance themselves from Trump, Reuters review finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:04:43 UTC
19:04:43 KST

Most Republicans in tight midterm races distance themselves from Trump, Reuters review finds
Oct 7 - Two-thirds of Republican candidates in competitive US House and Senate races have broken with President Donald Trump on policy or played down ties to him, a Reuters review found, revealing a widespread effort to distance themselves from the president as his unpopularity threatens the party's hold on Congress.
The review of voting records, public statements and campaign materials found candidates in 41 of 62 competitive congressional races seeking some distance from Trump ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
The candidates have largely criticized or diverged from Trump on individual issues rather than repudiated his broader agenda. The findings suggest an effort to attract independent voters while avoiding a direct break with their party leader.
Policy differences were the most common point of divergence, appearing in 23 of the 62 races.
In 12 contests, the split centered on the Iran conflict, with vulnerable Republicans either voting to curb Trump's war powers or calling publicly for an end to the fighting that has raised gas prices and squeezed household budgets.
Data centers are among the issues dividing Trump and some Republican candidates. Reuters identified three candidates in competitive races who have criticized or sought to slow such projects despite the president's support for faster development.
The shift is notable because Trump has spent the past decade remaking the Republican Party in his own image and has been swift to punish lawmakers and candidates who defied him through primary challenges, personal attacks or public pressure to fall into line.
In response to questions about the Reuters findings, White House spokesman Davis Ingle pointed to the administration's accomplishments and said Trump was "the unequivocal leader, best messenger and unmatched motivator" for the party.
While news organizations have highlighted individual cases of distancing, the Reuters review is the first to systematically measure the trend across competitive races that will decide whether Republicans retain control of either or both chambers of Congress.
A new Reuters/Ipsos poll underscored the challenge facing Republicans: Trump's approval rating remained stuck at a career-low 32%, while registered voters favored Democrats over Republicans 44% to 37% ahead of the midterms. Among independents, Democrats led 37% to 21%.
CREATING DISTANCE FROM TRUMP
Reuters also found a broad effort to play down ties: A dozen candidates removed his name, image or endorsements from campaign websites, most after securing their party's nomination.
Others acted in subtler ways, skipping his events or declining to say whether he should campaign on their behalf.
Direct criticism was relatively rare, underscoring Trump's dominance of the Republican Party and the risks candidates face in openly challenging a president who still commands the loyalty of many ardent supporters.
Candidates distancing themselves from an unpopular president before an election is not unusual. Democrats employed similar tactics in the 2014 and 2022 elections.
While Reuters did not conduct a comparable review of competitive races in the 2018 midterms during Trump's first term, analysts said Trump has rarely faced such widespread pushback by vulnerable Republican candidates.
"(Candidates) are reflecting voter attitudes in these races," said Republican strategist Ron Bonjean. "If (voters) are not with Trump, then they need to show a break."
Privately, campaign advisers told Reuters that candidates needed to dial back ties to Trump to attract independent voters. Publicly, they dismissed criticism of the repositioning.
BALANCING ACT
Republican Senator Pete Ricketts, who faces a tough challenge from independent Dan Osborn in Nebraska, exemplifies the 11 candidates identified by Reuters who broke with Trump on one policy issue while backing him on everything else.
The balancing act was on display this week when Ricketts, who criticized Trump's plan to expand beef imports, joined the president at a Nebraska rally.
"President Trump, I have been fighting for you in Washington," Ricketts told the crowd.
Mariannette Miller-Meeks, a Republican in one of the country's most competitive House races in Iowa, has also shown a growing willingness to break with the administration. She was among 12 candidates identified by Reuters who split with Trump on multiple issues, criticizing his beef-import policy and later voting to limit his war powers in Iran after previously opposing similar measures.
Yet, less than two weeks after her war-powers vote, Miller-Meeks joined Trump at the White House to announce a major steel plant investment in Iowa.
"It is a balancing act," said Republican consultant Jeanette Hoffman, adding that candidates are trying to capitalize on the administration’s successes while creating some distance from Trump because of “how toxic the Trump brand is at the moment.”
SCRUBBING TRUMP REFERENCES
As Republicans in competitive races seek to expand their appeal beyond Trump's core supporters, some candidates have begun dialing back public displays of loyalty to the president.
Mike Beltran, a former Florida state representative running against Democratic US Representative Kathy Castor, is among candidates who have scrubbed prominent references to Trump from their campaign websites.
In August, his homepage featured a photo of Trump and said he stood with the president, according to the Wayback Machine, an internet archive website. Now Beltran's homepage shows only him and his family and makes no mention of Trump.
Beltran's campaign had no immediate response to a Reuters request for comment.
Representative Mike Lawler of New York, facing one of the most competitive US House races, embodies the balancing act confronting many Republicans in battleground districts: staying close to Trump while demonstrating independence from him.
Lawler has highlighted breaks with Trump on issues including temporary legal protections for Haitian immigrants and a Trump-backed proposal to restore Turkey's access to F-35 fighter jets.
His campaign manager Ciro Riccardi said Lawler acts on behalf of his constituency regardless of a president's stance.
Lawler acknowledged the disagreements in a speech to Trump supporters at the Republican midterm convention in September, saying, "The truth is that the president and I don't always agree. And that's OK." REUTERS

Trump makes third Texas trip in a month as Republicans defend longtime stronghold

Trump makes third Texas trip in a month as Republicans defend longtime stronghold
Oct 7 - US President Donald Trump heads to Texas on Wednesday for the third time in a month, placing unusual focus on a state he won easily in 2024 but where Republicans now face unexpectedly tight midterm election battles as they seek to retain control of Congress.
Trump is due to speak in San Antonio alongside Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, who is locked in a close race with Democrat James Talarico. A loss on November 3 would complicate the party's path to retaining its slim Senate majority and mark a major setback in a Republican stronghold.
The rally is Trump's latest effort to mobilize his supporters for Paxton after staging an unusual midterm conventionin Dallas, in part to boost him. But Trump has also publicly criticized his longtime ally, calling Paxton "a pain in the ass sometimes" last week before adding that Republicans "need Ken so badly."
Trump's repeated trips to Texas are part of a broader push in Republican-leaning states, which were expected to be safely in hand but have instead become midterm battlegrounds. His 32-day campaign blitz has taken him through Texas, Oklahoma, Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska, while Vice President JD Vance has campaigned in Alaska. Trump and Vance carried all six states in the 2024 presidential election.
Republicans are struggling as voters focus on high costs and the war with Iran, giving Trump record-low approval ratings. A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed Monday put his approval at 32%, with Democrats leading Republicans 44% to 37% among registered voters.
Trump surprised some Republicans in May by backing Paxton in a party runoff over longtime Senator John Cornyn, whom party leaders saw as a safer bet. Republicans are now spending heavily to defend territory they once expected to win comfortably.
Trump won the state by 14 points in 2024, but recent polls have shown Talarico ahead of Paxton. Republicans are also defending competitive House of Representatives seats in South Texas.
For Trump, the stakes are also personal. James Henson, director of the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas at Austin, said losing the Senate race would be "devastating for Republicans and devastating for Donald Trump" given his support for Paxton. "I think the president clearly will do a lot to try to avoid that outcome," Henson said.
Trump's political operation has also poured millions into competitive House races. In San Antonio, Republican Carlos De La Cruz, an Air Force veteran, is running in a newly redrawn district, part of a Republican-led remapping that Democrats have called a partisan gerrymander. De La Cruz is expected to speak at Wednesday's rally.
AN UNEASY ALLIANCE
Trump and Paxton's relationship has appeared awkward at times. Paxton was recorded telling donors that Republican candidates' numbers fell after the Trump-centered convention in Dallas, according to The New York Times, while Trump has publicly mocked Paxton's clothes, speaking style and appearance.
"So to be honest with you, the numbers, when we did that convention, it dropped our numbers. Everybody's numbers dropped," Paxton said in the recording. His campaign has disputed suggestions that the remarks amounted to criticism of Trump. A spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.
A Siena College poll released October 3 showed Talarico leading Paxton 51% to 45% among likely voters. Brandon Rottinghaus, a political science professor at the University of Houston, said rallying Trump's base was "necessary but not sufficient" for Paxton.
"Trump's visits are a Catch-22," Rottinghaus said. "The president can inspire as much as he can repel."
Texas Republican Governor Greg Abbott, a close Trump ally who is also in a closer-than-expected re-election race, plans to skip Wednesday's rally, citing other campaign events.
"My rallies are saving the Republican Party, again," Trump said in an all-caps post on Truth Social on Tuesday.
Republicans are betting Trump can still turn out the voters who powered his 2024 victory even as his broader standing has weakened.
The latest Reuters/Ipsos poll showed that just 24% of Hispanic voters approved of his performance. They were an important part of Trump's success in 2024, when he won nearly half the Hispanic vote, and are a bigger demographic in Texas than most states.
Wednesday's rally is scheduled for the Freeman Coliseum in San Antonio, with Trump expected to speak at 6 p.m. Central Time (2300 GMT). REUTERS

Three years of Gaza genocide: How Israel devastated water and power lifelines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:03:56 UTC
19:03:56 KST

In Gaza, getting enough water is no longer a routine part of daily life.
Instead, families must carry buckets, wait for water trucks and decide how much they can spare for drinking, cooking, bathing or washing clothes.
For children, it means spending hours helping their families collect water instead of going to school.
“Before the war, we did not have this struggle,” Hanadi Al Aff told the International Committee of the Red Cross in June.
Al Aff, one of the many displaced Palestinians, lives with her five children opposite a rehabilitated desalination plant in Gaza City.
“We now carry water in buckets. It has become a burden on our children. Instead of going to school and studying, they carry water,” she said. 
Al Aff said her family did not have enough water for all their needs.  
“We save water and keep it for the most important thing, which is drinking, cooking and bathing the children. If there is extra, we use it for washing the dishes and doing the laundry.”
Three years after Israel began its genocidal war on Gaza in Oct 2023, the territory's water, sanitation and electricity systems remain severely damaged, leaving millions of Palestinians dependent on emergency measures and infrastructure operating far below its former capacity.
According to a survey cited by the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) in September, 91% of households experienced moderate-to-high water insecurity.
Nearly one-third, 31% of households, had total water access below minimum humanitarian standards, while 57% fell below minimum standards specifically for drinking water.
Meanwhile, 88% households reported difficulties accessing safe and clean sanitation facilities.
The shortages are compounded by damage to the infrastructure on which Gaza's water supply depends.
Another report cited by the UN in September, showed that 88% of above-ground Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) assets and 76% of underground networks had been damaged.
Red Cross also said in June that water production in Gaza had fallen to around 40% of pre-October 2023 levels, while independent production from wells was less than a third of what it had been before the war.
Gaza's remaining water supply also remains vulnerable to disruptions.
According to a UN humanitarian situation report issued in late September, the three Mekorot water lines from Israel supplied about 40% below contracted quantities during the reporting period because marine algae affected desalination plants in Israel.
In Deir al-Balah, the Al Basa Desalination Plant was operating below capacity because of a brine-pumping failure and overuse of generators.
Humanitarian partners were working to increase groundwater production through wells to partially offset the shortfall.
In August, a UNICEF-supported water well and desalination facility in Deir al-Balah was also severely damaged by a strike, disrupting access to safe drinking water for more than 4,000 people, including about 2,000 children.
The water crisis cannot be separated from Gaza's electricity shortage.
Wells, desalination plants and sewage pumping stations all require electricity to operate.
Yet September UN figures indicate that 90% of energy infrastructure, including the electricity distribution network and associated assets, has been destroyed.
With the electricity system largely unavailable, generators have become essential for keeping remaining water and sanitation infrastructure operating.
But generators themselves depend on fuel.
The Red Cross reported that Gaza has gone for more than two-and-a-half years without a regular electricity supply, leaving people dependent on generators.
Officials cited by the Alliance for Water Justice in Palestine in June estimated that rebuilding the electricity system could take three to five years, even if reconstruction materials were allowed to enter immediately.
The work would require thousands of utility poles, hundreds of kilometers of power cables, transformers, heavy equipment and specialized machinery simply to restore basic services.
The question is not only how much water Palestinians can obtain, but whether it is safe to drink.
In August, health partners collected 938 water samples across Gaza and tested them at the seven water-quality monitoring laboratories that remain functional despite severe operational constraints.
More than 73% of the samples did not meet WHO-recommended free residual chlorine levels, while 18% showed microbiological contamination.
Reinhilde Van De Weerdt, the WHO representative in Palestine, said at a September press briefing that over 6,700 water samples had been tested between January and August.
Microbiological contamination nearly tripled during that period, rising from below 6% in January to more than 18% in August.
She said cases of acute watery diarrhea nearly doubled over the same period.
The deterioration of sanitation is closely linked to the water crisis.
Thirty-nine percent of assessed households reported solid waste accumulating around their shelters, while 36% observed sewage or sludge near where they were living.
The situation is particularly difficult in displacement sites, where families live in overcrowded and makeshift shelters.
Site safety audits covering about 230 displacement sites hosting at least 187,400 people reportedly found unsafe latrines, open pits, wastewater hazards and poor drainage in low-lying areas, alongside inadequate lighting and overcrowding.
The approaching rainy season adds another layer of danger.
Humanitarian agencies warn that damaged sewage and stormwater drainage systems will increase the risk of flooding and disease.
According to a Doctors Without Borders (MSF) survey, almost one in four people interviewed between May and August 2025 had experienced diarrhoea in the previous month.
Skin diseases accounted for nearly 18% of MSF primary healthcare consultations in 2025, while poor water and sanitation conditions have also contributed to the spread of scabies and lice.
The effects extend beyond physical health.
MSF said its mental health professionals observed high levels of distress linked to the struggle to obtain sufficient water and hygiene supplies, with children carrying heavy responsibilities.
“The inability to maintain hygiene has become a source of distress and undermined people’s sense of dignity,” it wrote.
“Israeli authorities have used access to water as a weapon against Palestinians, systematically depriving people in Gaza, Palestine, of water in a campaign of collective punishment,” MSF said in April.
It noted that the “deliberate denial” of water from Palestinians was an integral part of Israel’s genocide and was part of a “recurrent, systematic and cumulative pattern” rather than being isolated acts.
The organization stressed that the destruction and attacks on infrastructure, obstruction of humanitarian access through forced displacement and denial of movement, and the blocking or delay of essential supplies were the main mechanisms Israel’s weaponization of WASH access.
MSF said it had documented several incidents involving the shooting at or destruction of its clearly identified water trucks and boreholes.
“Since 1 January 2026, all MSF requests for the entry of any supplies through the dedicated system, where approval is determined by the Israeli authorities, were denied,” MSF said.
Some water infrastructure has been repaired and humanitarian partners continue to use alternative sources.
Yet restrictions on equipment, generators, spare parts, chlorine and other essential supplies, alongside fuel shortages, continue to threaten the operation of remaining systems.
UNICEF says 19.4% of its $746.8 million humanitarian funding requirement for the occupied Palestinian territory is allocated to water, sanitation and hygiene.
For Palestinians living through the crisis, recovery starts with what should never have become a struggle.
A tap that works. Water that is safe to drink. Functioning sanitation and reliable electricity.
And for children like those in Aff's family, it is the possibility of putting down the water bucket and picking up a schoolbook instead.

EU-Parlament verschärft vor Šefčovič-Reise Haltung zur China-Politik
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Maroš Šefčovič speaks with reporters during the second day of the G20 Trade Ministerial in Wisconsin, U.S. on Oct. 1, 2026. | Kamil Krzaczynski/AFP via Getty Images
STRASSBURG – Im Europäischen Parlament versammeln sich Politiker aller Lager zunehmend hinter einem härteren Kurs in der China-Politik der EU - auch über Handelsfragen hinaus.
Ein neuer Bericht des Ausschusses für Auswärtige Angelegenheiten über die Beziehungen zwischen der EU und China stellt das asiatische Land nicht nur als wirtschaftlichen, sondern auch als geopolitischen Gegner dar, der die Sicherheit Europas untergräbt.
Das EU-Parlament wird an diesem Mittwoch über den Bericht abstimmen – kurz vor der Reise von Handelskommissar Maroš Šefčovič nach Peking am Donnerstag. Er trifft sich dort mit dem chinesischen Handelsminister Wang Wentao zu entscheidenden Gesprächen über den eskalierenden Handelskonflikt.
Advertisement
„Ich möchte, dass er mit einem möglichst starken Mandat dieses Hauses dorthin reist“, sagte Hilde Vautmans, die Verfasserin des Berichts, am Dienstagabend in einer Debatte. „Europa verfügt über wirtschaftliche Macht. Es ist an der Zeit, diese einzusetzen.“
Die Äußerung deckt sich mit Positionen, die Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz und Frankreichs Präsident Emmanuel Macron Anfang der Woche in einem gemeinsamen Papier vereinbart haben. Sie sprechen sich dafür aus, der EU-Kommission mehr Befugnisse zu geben, um Importe aus Ländern, die „schwerwiegende und systematische Verzerrungen“ in der EU verursachen, zu beschränken oder sogar zu unterbinden.
Mehrere Europaabgeordnete lobten die gemeinsame Haltung der beiden größten Volkswirtschaften der EU. Der polnische Europaabgeordnete Mariusz Kamiński von den Europäischen Konservativen und Reformisten ging weiter. Er nannte „pragmatische wirtschaftliche Beziehungen“ zu China unverantwortlich oder schlichtweg dumm. China sei eine „kommunistische Diktatur, die eine Bedrohung für die freie Welt darstellt“, sagte er.
Damit steht er nicht allein. Vielen Abgeordneten genügt es nicht, lediglich gegen Chinas aggressive Exporte aus subventionierten Überkapazitäten vorzugehen. Die EU-Kommission müsse sich auch mit Menschenrechtsverletzungen in China, der Aggression gegen Taiwan und Chinas Rolle bei Russlands Krieg gegen die Ukraine befassen.
„Wir müssen anerkennen, dass China sich in einer Weise verhält, die unsere Interessen gefährdet. Nicht nur im Handel, sondern auch in den Bereichen Sicherheit und Verteidigung“, sagte der spanische Europaabgeordnete Nicolás Pascual de la Parte von der Europäischen Volkspartei. „Die Menschenrechtslage hat sich nicht verbessert, ist aber in den letzten Jahren von unserer Agenda verschwunden.“
Vautmans wertete die Debatte als Beleg dafür, dass die EU dabei sei, eine einheitliche Haltung gegenüber China einzunehmen. „Das ist nicht mehr nur die Position des Europäischen Parlaments oder einer einzelnen Fraktion“, sagte Vautmans nach der Debatte. „Es setzt sich zunehmend die Erkenntnis durch, dass Europa eine kohärentere China-Politik braucht: offen für Dialog und Zusammenarbeit, aber viel entschlossener, seine Interessen zu verteidigen, wenn es nötig ist.“
Der Artikel ist zuerst auf Englisch bei POLITICO erschienen.

Disinflation expected to accelerate: Karahan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:03:47 UTC
19:03:47 KST

Disinflation is expected to accelerate in the coming period if supply-side pressures continue to fade, said Fatih Karahan, the Central Bank Governor.
Speaking at an event in Istanbul on Oct. 7, Karahan said the underlying inflation trend rose during the March-June period when the effects of the war became more pronounced but resumed its decline from July onward.
“On an annualized basis, the underlying trend, which climbed to around 30 percent during the war period, stood at 23.7 percent as of September. This level is approximately 6 percentage points below the current annual inflation rate,” he said.
Karahan said the fact that the underlying trend remains below annual inflation provides an important signal for the period ahead, adding that disinflation would continue at an accelerating pace if supply-side pressures ease.
He said the development reflects the impact of tight monetary policy on demand conditions and pricing behavior, adding that the disinflation process is expected to regain momentum as the effects of shocks diminish, supported by the central bank’s tight policy stance.
Karahan said the slowdown in domestic demand has become more evident thanks to tight monetary policy and noted that disinflation has been more pronounced in components directly affected by monetary policy.
“Inflation expectations and pricing behavior will remain important for the course of disinflation. In this framework, we will continue to use all our tools decisively in line with our objective of achieving price stability,” Karahan said.
