Trump to speak to Putin about plague lab worker's death in Russia
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:59:13 BST
18:59:13 KST

Trump to speak to Putin about plague lab worker's death in Russia
- Published
US President Donald Trump has said he will speak with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin soon about the death of a lab worker at a plague research centre in Siberia.
"So far we are in very deep discussions," Trump said, adding that he would be able to report on his talks with Putin "probably" on Thursday. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said no phone call had been scheduled.
Russian officials say they are investigating the cause of the 28-year-old's death and have not confirmed that the suspected disease is pneumonic plague - a serious lung infection, often described as the most virulent form of plague.
They insist "there are no epidemic risks for the population".
The US, however, has issued a formal diplomatic message to Russia requesting additional information. Peskov told reporters he was not aware of such a request.
The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) has called for transparency from Russia.
"Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks," Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said.
Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, President Vladimir Putin's spokesman said Russia's reporting of the death to the WHO was in line with standard practice. He accused the media of reporting "false information".
Reports first emerged on Friday of almost 200 people being placed under observation in Siberia's Irkutsk region following the death.
The lab worker, named in Russian media as Darya Shipilova, had reportedly fallen ill a couple of days earlier.
Unconfirmed reports suggested that she had become ill after breaking a test tube containing the pathogen at the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East where she worked - or following a field trip to a region where plague occurs naturally among wild rodents.
As the US and the WHO sought more information, the country's health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, issued a statement saying "there are no epidemic risks for the population of Irkutsk and the Irkutsk region".
It said more than 90% of the people who had been in contact with the victim had "completed medical observation" and "no health disorders associated with infectious pathology were detected".
In the immediate wake of the laboratory worker's death, Rospotrebnadzor had issued a statement saying the woman had died of "pneumonia of an undetermined etiology" and that testing found "no microorganisms related to her professional activities".
However, after this announcement, a pro-government federal news outlet deleted five posts mentioning a possible plague case, and authorities in the town of Baikalsk deleted a message advising against travel to Shelekhov because of a possible plague infection.
Ongoing speculation into the lab worker's death has sparked a back and forth between Russia and the US, with questions about a possible spread outside of Russia.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US had "measures" available to help Russia if the situation turned out to be more serious than claimed.
According to the WHO, pneumonic plague has a very short incubation period - sometimes just 24 hours - and can be fatal, if not diagnosed and treated early.
People can be infected through:
- infected flea bites
- contact with bodily fluids or contaminated materials
- the inhalation of respiratory particles
Symptoms include shortness of breath and coughing, often with blood-tainted phlegm.
The bacterium that causes the plague, Yersinia pestis, found among rodents such as marmots in the area.
It killed up to half the population of Europe in the 14th Century when it was known as the Black Death.
It was in response to an outbreak in the 1920s that the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, was founded just over 100 years ago.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The first batch of US-made Harpoon anti-ship missiles is expected to arrive by the end of the year.
Taiwan has purchased 100 sets of the land-based Harpoon Coastal Defense System, including 400 missiles, four training missiles, 100 launcher transporter units, and 25 radar trucks, per Liberty Times. The first shipment is reportedly expected to include 128 missiles.
The Navy’s Littoral Combat Command has already formed mobile missile vehicle units for launchers and radar vehicles that were delivered earlier. The Navy has also completed integrating the US Harpoon system with its existing surveillance, communications, and command systems using command-and-control equipment developed by National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology.
The Littoral Combat Command was formed on July 1 and has three coastal combat groups, as well as a maritime tactical reconnaissance group operating Albatross drones, Liberty Times reported. Forming a fourth coastal combat group next year would mean five operational groups.
The Navy has disbanded its former Maritime Surveillance and Reconnaissance Command, integrating fixed surveillance sites and mobile coastal defense radars into the coastal combat groups. This gives each group both radar surveillance and anti-ship strike capabilities, allowing it to conduct missions independently.
The coastal combat groups are also being reorganized around mobile, vehicle-based operations, with vertical-takeoff-and-landing drone units expected to be assigned directly to the groups, according to Liberty Times. The drones would serve as the missile units’ eyes at sea, providing long-range surveillance.
Once the new group is established next year, Harpoon systems are expected to operate alongside domestically developed Hsiung Feng II and Hsiung Feng III anti-ship missiles, as well as extended-range Hsiung Feng III variants. The systems will be integrated into a unified command-and-control network, with a Marine Corps security battalion protecting the mobile missile vehicles.

Experts urge toxin testing for Taiwan’s potato imports

18:56:38 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Food safety experts in Taiwan have called for imported potatoes to undergo toxin testing even when they show no signs of sprouting.
Visual checks can miss sprouts obscured by a potato’s shape, National Taiwan University food safety professor Wu Kuen-yuh (吳焜裕) said, per UDN. Some sprouts may have yet to fully grow.
The Food and Drug Administration said Tuesday that a US shipment contained 248 milligrams per kilogram of total glycoalkaloids, above the limit of 200 milligrams per kilogram, per CNA. The shipment showed no sprouts.
All 339,580 kilograms were returned before reaching the domestic market. The importer’s subsequent shipments now face a 20%–50% inspection rate, and further violations could lead to checks of every shipment. This was the first imported-potato violation involving total glycoalkaloids in the past six months.
Prolonged heat without refrigeration during shipping and longer exposure to sunlight can increase the likelihood of solanine emerging, said Taipei Veterans General Hospital toxicologist Yang Chen-chang (楊振昌). He described solanine as part of potatoes’ defense against insects and called for testing even when no sprouts are visible.
Sprouting does not affect whether potatoes must meet the limit, which has been in force since Jan. 1, 2019. The FDA said food safety requirements remained unchanged following the introduction of new quarantine rules for US-processed potatoes in February.

Taiwan study finds shingles vaccine associated with lower risk of kidney failure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:56:35 UTC
18:56:35 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwanese doctors have found that the shingles vaccine may help patients with chronic kidney disease lower their risks of kidney failure, heart problems, and death.
At least 2 million people in Taiwan have chronic kidney disease, and recent statistics from the Taiwan Society of Nephrology showed that about 100,000 are receiving dialysis treatment.
A study published in late August in the journal Hypertension Research found that patients with chronic kidney disease who had received at least one dose of the zoster vaccine had a 37% lower risk of kidney failure, a 26% lower risk of cardiovascular events, and a 49% lower risk of all-cause mortality.
To examine the effects of the recombinant zoster vaccine, researchers compared 13,218 vaccine recipients with 13,218 unvaccinated patients. For patients with chronic kidney disease, getting the zoster vaccine is not only about lowering the risk of complications from shingles but also about preventing the effects of viral infections on the whole body, the researchers said.
The researchers said these patients are a high-risk group for infections and cardiovascular diseases, and the immune and inflammatory responses to a viral infection can place a burden on their already fragile cardiovascular and renal systems.
Wang Wei-jie (王偉傑), a co-author of the study and director of Lo-Sheng Hospital in New Taipei, said the findings are based on an association, and further research is needed to confirm the underlying mechanisms and any causation.
The zoster vaccine is intended to prevent shingles and related complications, he said. Vaccination is not a replacement for medical treatment and should not be considered a medication for cardiovascular or kidney diseases.
The Centers for Disease Control recommends the recombinant zoster vaccine for adults aged 50 and older and adults aged 18 and older who are immunodeficient or immunocompromised. The vaccine is given in two doses, with the second dose administered two to six months after the first dose.

Gaza's lost medical records after three years of genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:56:06 UTC
18:56:06 KST

Breadcrumb
In Israel's genocide in Gaza, patients are losing more than hospitals — they are losing their medical histories
Hassan Shobir was not afraid of cancer alone. He feared something else he had never imagined would become part of his treatment journey: having to reconstruct his medical history from scratch.
The 54-year-old has colon cancer. Before Israel's genocide, he received treatment at Al-Shifa Medical Complex and the Turkish Hospital for Oncology. His medical file contained his biopsy results, CT scans, tumour marker tests and details of the chemotherapy regimen he had already begun.
However, those records no longer exist.
Hassan lost his biopsy report, CT scan results, tumour marker tests and treatment protocol. With oncology services disrupted and cancer treatments in increasingly short supply across Gaza, continuing his care has also come to depend on piecing together what had happened inside his body before his medical history disappeared.
So far, some of his assessments have been repeated, including an abdominal ultrasound and an MRI scan, and an urgent referral has also been issued for treatment outside Gaza.
But Hassan has been waiting for months for permission to travel and restart treatment.
"The delays in treatment have become part of my daily life," Hassan tells The New Arab. "Every time I go to ask about the referral, they tell me to wait and be patient. They say I am not the only one, that there are thousands of patients waiting just as I am."
The last contact with Hassan was on 30 September 2026. For a man living with cancer, losing a medical file is not simply a matter of losing documents. It means losing part of the clinical story a doctor needs in order to decide what treatment should come next.
Hassan’s story comes at a time when the World Health Organisation says the destruction of Gaza’s healthcare infrastructure has also damaged health information systems and medical records, including paper files and electronic servers.
The absence of effective centralised databases has made it increasingly difficult to follow patients over time and transfer their information between healthcare facilities.
When the patient becomes his own medical record
Under normal circumstances, doctors do not have to start from the beginning every time they see a patient.
A biopsy result, an imaging report, a list of medications, a documented drug allergy, a record of previous surgery, or even a brief note written by another doctor can all influence a clinical decision.
But Israel's war in Gaza has damaged far more than the places where healthcare is delivered.
Hospitals and health facilities have been destroyed or damaged; some have stopped functioning altogether, and essential infrastructure the health system depends on has been disrupted.
In January 2026, the World Health Organisation said that damage to infrastructure, including major data centres within health facilities, had weakened Gaza’s health information system, affecting both medical records and clinicians’ ability to make timely decisions.
For patients, this can mean their medical histories are scattered across facilities that no longer operate, paper files lost during displacement, or electronic systems they can no longer access.
Patients arrive at new doctors carrying only fragments of their medical history.
The rest may remain in a hospital that no longer exists, in a file lost during displacement, or on an electronic system that has become inaccessible.
What appears at first to be an administrative problem can quickly become a clinical one: what does a doctor do when a patient’s medical history is unknown?
'Everything about my pregnancy was in the file'
Walaa Abu al-Omrain, 28, is currently displaced in Al-Zawayda, in central Gaza.
She fled the Al-Rimal neighbourhood after her home was destroyed and now lives in a tent on land being used to shelter displaced families.
When she contacted me seeking a free medical consultation, she was 30 weeks pregnant.
During her current pregnancy, she had been diagnosed with placenta previa and pregnancy-related hypertension, and was receiving follow-up care at a medical tent providing free services in the displacement area.
But for Walaa, the problem went beyond losing the place where she had previously received care.
She once had medical records documenting her previous deliveries and pregnancy complications. During her most recent delivery, she suffered severe postpartum haemorrhage and had to return to the operating theatre. She then spent around two weeks in intensive care.
She also had a medical file at Al-Huda Centre in western Gaza, where her condition had been monitored before the Centre was bombed.
"Every detail of my pregnancies and previous deliveries was in that file," Walaa shares with The New Arab. "The doctor looking after me knew what had happened during my last delivery. He knew that I had suffered severe bleeding, that I had gone back into surgery and that I had spent time in intensive care. Now, when I see a new doctor, I cannot give him the same level of information that was in my file."
She adds: "The doctor I see now does not know exactly what happened during my previous delivery. He tells me that the position of the placenta and my history of severe bleeding are important, and that we have to prepare for the possibility of a Caesarean section, haemorrhage and a blood transfusion. But he needs to know all of my risk factors in order to decide where and how I should give birth."
Some of that information, Walaa says, was contained in her previous medical records.
Today, she has to try to reconstruct that history herself.
In a high-risk pregnancy, knowing a woman’s previous obstetric history — including deliveries, haemorrhage, surgery and test results — can be an important part of assessing risk and preparing safely for childbirth.
In a damaged health system marked by repeated displacement, transferring such information between healthcare providers has become considerably more difficult.
Children who lost their vaccination records
For Ghada Masoud, 32, the problem may appear smaller in scale, but it is not necessarily less important.
Ghada lost her three-year-old son’s vaccination card while fleeing Jabalia in northern Gaza.
Her son had previously received his vaccinations at a clinic in Jabalia. When Ghada later went to another health facility to continue his immunisations, the nurse needed to know how many doses of the DTaP vaccine — which protects against diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis — the child had already received.
But Ghada no longer had his vaccination record.
"The nurse asked me how many doses of the DTaP vaccine my son had received, but I did not have the vaccination card with me," she says. "I told him I could not remember exactly. He said he could not give him another dose without knowing what he had received before. Since then, I have stopped following up on his vaccinations, and he has not received any new ones."
Under normal circumstances, a vaccination card contains a simple but crucial history: the names of vaccines, the doses administered, and the dates they were given.
Once that record is lost, however, a straightforward process becomes far more complicated: Which vaccines has the child received? When were they given? And which doses are still outstanding?
The World Health Organisation has said that vaccination services in Gaza have been severely disrupted by the deterioration of the health system and shortages of medical supplies, making continuity of children’s health information all the more important.
'I don’t even know the name of the medicine I’m allergic to'
Tawfiq al-Maghribi, 67, from Sheikh Radwan, lives with several chronic illnesses, including diabetes, high blood pressure and heart disease.
He knows that he is allergic to certain painkillers and antibiotics, but he does not know their names.
"I don’t know the name of the medicine I’m allergic to because I cannot read or write," Tawfiq tells The New Arab. "I used to rely on the doctor and on my medical file."
As patients move between facilities and see doctors who have never treated them, clinicians increasingly have to rely on patients’ own memories of their medical histories.
For someone living with several chronic conditions and taking multiple medications, an accurate record of previous treatments and drug allergies can help doctors avoid dangerous interactions or inappropriate treatment choices.
When that information disappears, patients lose more than a record of their past. They lose information doctors need to make safer care decisions.
'We are practising medicine blindfolded'
For doctors, the consequences are no less severe.
Dr Mahmoud Hamouda, a general surgery specialist, previously worked at Al-Shifa Medical Complex and is now based at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital. He says that in emergency situations, doctors may be forced to make rapid, potentially life-changing decisions without access to a patient’s full medical history.
"It is like asking a surgeon to perform a complicated operation in complete darkness," Dr Mahmoud tells The New Arab.
A patient may arrive in the emergency department unconscious or in shock, while there is no reliable way to quickly determine their medical history.
"Have they had surgery before? Are they allergic to a medication or anaesthetic? Are they taking any regular medications? Do they have a chronic condition that could affect decisions about surgery or anaesthesia?" Dr Mahmoud asks.
"We are forced to make critical decisions based on guesswork, or on the memory of a patient who may themselves be traumatised. Medical records are not simply pieces of paper or electronic data. They are an important line of defence for a patient’s life. Without them, providing safe emergency care becomes far more difficult," he explains.
A war on hospitals — and on medical memory too
A destroyed hospital is easy to see. So is an operating theatre that has stopped functioning, or a scanner taken out of service.
But the loss of medical records is far less visible. There is no building to photograph when a biopsy result disappears. No visible ruin remains when a woman loses her pregnancy records during displacement. And the consequences of a child losing a vaccination record are not easily captured in an image.
It is an invisible loss, but one whose effects may continue long after the war ends.
A patient who has lost a test result may have to repeat the assessment. A woman who has lost her obstetric history may begin treatment with a new doctor working from incomplete information. A child who has lost a vaccination record may struggle to establish which doses have already been given.
And for people living with chronic illnesses, obtaining an accurate list of previous medications, allergies and surgical procedures may remain an ongoing challenge.
Rebuilding Gaza’s health system will mean more than reconstructing walls and replacing equipment. It will also mean trying to recover medical histories lost by thousands of patients during years of war and displacement
Some information may eventually be retrieved from servers or databases. But files that burned, test results that disappeared and vaccination cards lost during displacement may have no surviving copy.
One of the challenges facing Gaza’s health system after Israel's genocide ends will be determining which records can still be recovered, what can be reconstructed from patients’ memories, and how a future system can protect such information so that a person’s treatment no longer depends on a piece of paper that can be lost or on a hospital that can be destroyed.
Dr Haya Hijazi is a gynaecologist and obstetrician from Gaza

IKEA launches UK and Ireland marketplace to buy and sell second-hand furniture
Swedish brand IKEA has created an online marketplace for pre-owned furniture and products, which retail at around 60 per cent less than comparable items bought new.
Launched today, the UK and Ireland marketplace allows people to list and sell their IKEA products online, with the exception of mattresses, appliances and food.
Eligible items can be scanned by a seller to create a listing.
Recommended pricing, professional product photography and accurate measurements are then offered by the platform, as well as assembly instructions and care information for the furniture and products.
Once an item is purchased, the seller can choose to be paid directly or receive their funds as an IKEA voucher with 15 per cent additional credit.
Originally trialled in Madrid and Oslo in 2024, the marketplace was designed to significantly reduce waste and provide cheaper alternatives to new IKEA products amidst a global cost of living crisis, with the brand reporting average prices on the platform to be 60 per cent lower than comparable shop-bought products.
The marketplace also allows buyers to access discontinued IKEA designs, prompted by recent IKEA-conducted consumer research that revealed that 87 per cent of UK adults are now shopping for second-hand goods.
"The way people furnish their homes has changed," said IKEA UK and Ireland sustainability manager Greg Lucas.
"Our research found that more than one in four people said a personal history or story would make pre-owned furniture more desirable to them," he added.
"IKEA products are designed to be used, maintained and enjoyed over time, and the second-hand marketplace, as well as our in-store buyback service, gives people a straightforward way to pass on items as their needs change, with the practical information they need to buy and sell with confidence."
The brand's Buy Back and Resell service was introduced in 2021, which allows customers to sell eligible items back to IKEA in exchange for in-store credit.
Both the online marketplace and the buyback service are part of a wider push from the brand to make its products more sustainable and affordable.
In August, IKEA also launched the limited-edition Konstrunda collectible design collection, which brings together 22 pieces by seven designers all retailed at under £200.
The photography is courtesy of IKEA.

In Pictures
Photos: Three years of Israel’s war on Gaza as tent cities spread amid ruin
Tent cities in Gaza grow as families mourn the dead, care for the injured, and endure relentless displacement.
More than one in 10 people from Gaza’s pre-war population has been killed or wounded by Israeli fire since Israel launched its genocidal war against Palestinians in the territory in October 2023.

With almost the entire population left homeless, the coastal territory has effectively become one of the world’s largest tent cities. Ramshackle canvas and nylon shelters blanket beaches, cover former agricultural lands and fill vacant lots.

The “ceasefire” agreement’s plan for large-scale reconstruction has stalled, as Israel and Hamas have yet to reach an agreement on disarming the group and the withdrawal of Israeli forces.

"Find Me, Okay?": Three years after October 7, Eden Yerushalmi's family lets the cameras in — one last time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:55:00 UTC
18:55:00 KST

- i24NEWS
- Israel-Hamas war
- "Find Me, Okay?": Three years after October 7, Eden Yerushalmi's family lets the cameras in — one last time
"Find Me, Okay?": Three years after October 7, Eden Yerushalmi's family lets the cameras in — one last time
A new documentary follows the family of the Nova festival hostage murdered in Hamas captivity, from the fight to bring her home to the struggle to keep living without her
"Find me, okay?"
Those were Eden Yerushalmi's last words to an emergency dispatcher on the morning of October 7. She was 24, hiding behind a bush near the Nova music festival, whispering into her phone while Hamas terrorists closed in.
"They're shooting at me," she told the dispatcher. "I can't believe this is happening to me."
Hours earlier, she had been dancing with her friends. By the end of the call, she was gone, kidnapped into Gaza.
Three years later, those three words are the title of a new documentary. Her younger sister May is showing me around the family home, and almost nothing in it looks the way Eden left it.
"The house is not the same without her"
There's new furniture. New walls. A new layout. On the way in, a memorial to Eden's beloved motorcycle. The patio is full of the flowers that she so loved.
"A lot of things have changed," May says. "The house is not the same without her, so we couldn't live in a house that she isn't part of. Eden didn't see it like this."
After Eden was murdered, the family completely renovated the house. May says their old home belongs to the past, to a period when the home was always full of people coming and going while the family fought to bring Eden back.
"At some point we just wanted some kind of new starting point," she says. "Even though the ending wasn't a good one, we wanted a new beginning."
The house used to be a happy place. Eden was always dancing in it.
"Eden is always here, in the heart," May says. "But this house is not the same home. A lot of things I had in common with Eden, I don't have anymore, because I don't have someone to do these things with. Like dancing in the house. So everything is changed. My identity is changed."
"You stay with me!"
On October 7, Eden was working as a bartender at Nova. When the attack began, she and her friends tried to flee by car. Terrorists opened fire on the vehicle and killed her friends Dorin Atias and Lior Maimon.
Eden hid among their bodies, and later in the forest. For hours, she was on the phone with her sisters and with emergency services, begging for someone to find her.
"I'm alone, and I'm in the bushes," she told the dispatcher. "I really need you to help me."
Then her sisters heard gunshots on the line. Eden cried out that they had caught her. The phone went dead.
Her childhood best friend, Arbel, who was at the festival with her, managed to escape. She has spent the past three years living with that.
"These days I wake up in the morning, and it's like, why you? Why you and not her, and not the others?" Arbel says.
She describes strangers stopping her on the street, people who follow her on Instagram, telling her how strong she is. "And I'm like, you don't see the panic attack and the nervous breakdown I had an hour ago, that almost tore my house apart."
Ask them who Eden was, and they light up for a moment.
"Eden was the funny one, the lazy one, but the stronger one," Arbel says. "It's a cliché, but she really was everything."
"She was a free spirit, the life of the party," May adds. "She was always dancing – at home, outside, everywhere. She had friends of all ages. And she was kind. She had a really, really good heart."
Eden was a newly certified pilates instructor. She loved animals, fashion and sewing, played matkot on the beach, and rode her motorcycle all over Tel Aviv. She had a trip to Greece planned for right after the festival.
A film meant to end in a reunion.
About a month after October 7, filmmakers began documenting the Yerushalmi family. Everyone thought they knew how the story would end.
"It was meant to be a triumphant story," says producer Yaniv Hoffman. "It was meant to be a story about hope, about reunion."
May remembers that optimism. "It was all about when Eden's coming, when she's coming back. This fantasy of meeting her for the first time after she was kidnapped."
Arbel remembers it too. In the middle of the war, she and May would sit in her room and picture the moment. "We imagined how we'd go to the hospital," she says. "How we'd buy her a crown."
Then, in late August 2024, almost a year after she was taken, Eden was shot dead by her captors along with five other hostages: Hersh Goldberg-Polin, Carmel Gat, Alex Lobanov, Almog Sarusi and Ori Danino. The IDF recovered their bodies two days later from a Hamas tunnel deep beneath Rafah in southern Gaza. The army said they had been murdered shortly before troops reached them.
Eden was shot in the head at close range. There were marks on her hands from trying to defend herself.
May chose to see her sister's body. She gave her one last hug goodbye and could feel her bones. When Eden died, she weighed just 36 kilos, about 79 pounds.
"And I thought the movie was over," Hoffman says. "We said, that's it, we're done."
But it wasn't. The family decided there was more to tell. The film became something else: not the story of bringing Eden home, but a record of a family trying to figure out how to live once she wasn't coming back.
Arbel never wanted to make it in the first place.
"It's not normal to film this in our situation. Cameras, people asking questions. No way," she says. "But Eden hadn't come home. It was like, okay, if it can help bring Eden home, let's do it."
"This is what post-trauma is"
Now the film is out, and watching it means reopening everything.
"It's very scary to let people into our life – not our life, our trauma," May says. "These are moments I don't really want to remember."
"This is the most exposed thing I've done in my life," Arbel says.
What they both want people to understand is that October 7 never ended for them.
"I'm 23. I'm a kid," May says. "This happened to me when I was 20. And I feel like I'm not myself. I don't enjoy the simple pleasures in life. The passion I had is gone. The faith I had is gone."
For a while after the murder, she says she stopped believing altogether. "After all your prayers, you're just left with nothing.
"Some days you don't want to get out of bed. Some days you're afraid to leave the house," she says. "This is what post-trauma is."
"I hope you're waiting for me at home"
The documentary also reveals something few people knew. For months, the family had almost no idea what Eden went through in captivity. Then the army found hours of footage Hamas had filmed of her in Gaza.
"We knew nothing about Eden in captivity. We wanted to see something of her," May says. "When they told us there was a lot of footage, it was amazing."
In one clip, Eden speaks to her family directly. "She said, 'I hope you're waiting for me at home.'"
Over three years, the family pieced together what that waiting really looked like. Three times, they received proof that Eden was alive, the last just three weeks before she was killed. After her body came home, the army told them more. For her final weeks, Eden was held in a narrow tunnel where the hostages could barely stand. They had to sleep in a single line. There were no windows, no light, and almost no air. There was hardly any food, and a bucket served as a toilet.
"I don't know if I could be in there a day," her older sister Shani said in a past interview.
May puts it differently. "She was a hero," she says. "She survived 11 months in those tunnels."
May has the footage on her phone. She doesn't watch it.
"I'm happy it was filmed, because this is mine forever," she says. "But she's not there. It's not something you can watch and smile."
One of the film's most powerful moments, Hoffman says, was caught by accident on the family's street, on the day the last hostages came home from Gaza. A neighbor walked past the camera and asked who they were filming for. When the cameraman said the Yerushalmi family, the neighbor told him this was the saddest day since October 7.
"This day was supposed to be happy, because the last of them came back," May says.
"We were happy," Arbel adds. "But we have our sadness."
"Eden's Complex"
Part of the family home has now been transformed into a memorial. May calls it Eden's Complex, and her father built it. Every Tuesday, a Torah lesson is held there in Eden's memory.
The walls are covered with photos and news clips. Arbel stops at one article and shows me her arm. "This one gives me chills," she says. She remembers how, whenever the family went to relatives for a meal, they packed an extra change of clothes, just in case word came that Eden was on her way back.
May points out a photo of Eden as a newborn, wrapped in a yellow blanket. Yellow, the color of the hostage campaign.
"There are all these little things," she says. "We call them signs."
Suggested articles
Choosing to live
For three years, the Yerushalmis have fought to keep Eden's name alive. Making this film has also helped them see that remembering Eden can't mean disappearing themselves.
"We want people to still remember her and keep her name here," May says. "But we're not doing interviews anymore. It's very hard to put all this energy into it all the time, always putting Eden first. Right now we need to put ourselves first."
"This is life," Arbel says.
"This is life," May agrees. "We need to heal ourselves, be together as a family, and live."
"To be happy," Arbel adds.
"Yes," May says. "To go on."
"Find Me, Okay?" is directed and edited by Yula Gidron and produced by Jeff Hoffman, Hilla Medalia, Maria Ionova, Yaniv Hoffman and Omer Hazan, for Above the Clouds Productions and Medalia Productions. It is now being screened in select theaters across the globe.

Russia Keeps Producing 1963-Era SVD Sniper Rifles Despite Newer Replacement

Russia Keeps Producing 1963-Era SVD Sniper Rifles Despite Newer Replacement
Russia’s Kalashnikov Concern has completed its 2026 contract to supply Russian security agencies with the original 7.62mm Dragunov sniper rifle, or SVD, a weapon that has remained in serial production since 1963.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi on October 6, Kalashnikov announced that it had fulfilled the annual order but did not disclose how many rifles were delivered or which Russian security agency received them.
The contract covers the standard SVD rather than later versions such as the folding-stock SVDS or modernized SVDM.
Designed under Yevgeny Dragunov between 1958 and 1963, the SVD entered serial production in 1963 and remains in production more than six decades later. The semi-automatic rifle is chambered for the 7.62×54R cartridge and uses a 10-round magazine.
According to manufacturer specifications cited by Militarnyi, the SVD is designed to engage personnel and unarmored targets at ranges of up to 800 meters.
The rifle remains in use across Russian military and security units. Kalashnikov announced increased SVD production in 2024 and planned to expand output several times over in 2025, Militarnyi reported.
Russia also operates several SVD derivatives. The SVDS features a folding stock and more compact configuration, while the modernized SVDM adds a heavier barrel, adjustable folding stock, bipod, and Picatinny rail for modern optics. The less common SVDK uses the larger 9.3×64mm cartridge.
Meanwhile, Russia is serially producing the Chukavin sniper rifle, or SVCh, developed as a modern successor to the SVD. Production began in 2023, and the rifle has since been delivered to Russian forces.
Despite the introduction of the SVCh, Kalashnikov continues to manufacture the original SVD alongside its successor, keeping the Soviet-designed rifle in serial production more than 60 years after its introduction.
Russian troops have also been documented using Canadian-made Cadex precision rifles despite Western sanctions and export bans. An investigation by Global News and The Insider found that the weapons may have reached Russia through intermediaries in the US and Kazakhstan.

🔴Nobel Prize in chemistry awarded to France's Henri Kagan, Japan's Kenso Soai
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:54:25 UTC
18:54:25 KST

Nobel Prize in Chemistry awarded to France's Henri Kagan, Japan's Kenso Soai
Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai were jointly awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for solving a 100-year-old chemical mystery, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said on Wednesday. Nobel Prize recipients receive a prize of 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million).
France's Henri Kagan and Japan's Kenso Soai on Wednesday won the Nobel chemistry prize for solving the mystery of why only one version of some molecules' mirror-image forms appears in nature, a discovery decisive for the development of pharmaceuticals.
The pair were honoured "for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis", the jury said.
Like hands, all amino acids exist as two mirrored variants, but only one of them is found in the proteins in the body's cells.
The other is rarely found in nature, a phenomenon known as "homochirality", the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences explained.
Chemists have long wondered how that process occurs, and the two Nobel laureates' discoveries have "enabled chemists to drive chemical reactions that lead to homochirality", the jury said.
"Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously. The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular," said Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry.
"Their discoveries have been decisive for chemists who design reactions for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals," the jury said.
Nobel Prize in Medicine jointly awarded to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel
Last year, the chemistry prize went to Japan's Susumu Kitagawa, UK-born Richard Robson and American-Jordanian Omar Yaghi for developing a method of designing molecular structures.
The chemistry prize follows the physics prize, which on Tuesday honoured Belgian physicist Francis Halzen for groundbreaking work using Antarctic ice to capture particles originating in the distant cosmos.
On Monday, the medicine prize was awarded to US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and German scientists Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel.
The literature laureate will be revealed on Thursday, with some pundits suggesting that the Swedish Academy could follow up last year's award to Hungary's Laszlo Krasznahorkai with a prize for a woman writer, possibly from Latin America.
The most keenly anticipated award – the peace prize – is due on Friday.
The economics prize wraps up the Nobel season on October 12.
The Nobel consists of a diploma, a gold medal and a 12-million-kronor ($1.2-million) prize sum, which is shared if there is more than one winner in a discipline.
The laureates will receive their prizes at a formal ceremony on December 10, the anniversary of the death in 1896 of scientist Alfred Nobel, who created the prizes in his will.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Russia unleashed a massive overnight missile-and-drone barrage across Ukraine, killing at least 13 people and injuring 59—including three children—as a residential building was hit in Pryluky and an unexploded ballistic missile landed among homes in Kyiv.
Russia launched a large-scale combined missile and drone strike across Ukraine overnight into October 7, killing at least 13 people, damaging homes and industrial facilities, and leaving an unexploded ballistic missile embedded among residential buildings in Kyiv.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported damage across several districts of the capital. In the Darnytskyi district, a fire broke out at a garage complex following the strike.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Elsewhere in Darnytskyi, Kyiv police and emergency specialists began a complex operation to neutralize an unexploded ballistic missile discovered among residential buildings. Explosives experts were working to remove its warhead before transporting it to a testing range for final disposal.
The wider Kyiv region was also targeted by both drones and ballistic missiles. In the Obukhiv district, three production and warehouse facilities were damaged and fires broke out, according to Kyiv regional administration head Tymur Tkachenko. A truck and trailer were also damaged, though no casualties were reported there.
“Overnight, the region came under a combined attack by enemy drones and ballistic missiles. In the Obukhiv district, three production and warehouse facilities were damaged. Fires broke out—they have now been contained,” Tkachenko said.

Russia also launched 130 Shahed-type, Gerbera and Parodiya drones from several directions, including Russian territory, occupied Donetsk, and occupied Crimea. Of those, 46 were jet-powered UAVs.
Ukraine’s Air Force reported neutralizing five ballistic missiles, 39 cruise missiles and 117 drones during the overnight strike.
The main targets were the Kyiv, Kharkiv, Poltava and Dnipropetrovsk regions.
One of the deadliest strikes was recorded in Kremenchuk, Poltava region, where preliminary reports indicated that two people were killed and seven others wounded.
“According to preliminary information, two people were killed. My condolences to their families and loved ones. Seven more people were injured,” Poltava regional administration head Volodymyr Diakyvnych said.
The heaviest confirmed toll was reported in Pryluky, Chernihiv region, where a Russian missile struck a multi-story residential building.
UPD. The death toll in Pryluky rose as rescuers continued searching the ruins of the five-story apartment building. Emergency crews recovered the bodies of three children from beneath the rubble, bringing the number of people killed at the site to nine.
At least 50 people were injured in the strike. Twenty-three are being treated on an outpatient basis, while 27 were hospitalized, including three in serious condition. Rescuers have pulled 12 people alive from the damaged building.
Chernihiv regional administration head said five people were confirmed killed and at least 25 injured, warning that the number of victims could still rise as emergency crews continued clearing the rubble.
“At present, it is known that the missile strike on the multi-story building claimed the lives of five people. At least 25 people were injured. Unfortunately, the number of victims may be higher. The relevant services are working—clearing the rubble,” he said.
Three people were rescued from the damaged building, including a child.

The Dubai-based airline has touched down in Finland’s capital Helsinki for the first time as it reports operating at around 93% of its pre-disruption capacity.
Emirates says it is operating at around 93% of its pre-disruption capacity, as winter bookings strengthen following a turbulent year for airlines flying through the Middle East.
The Dubai-based airline carried more than 8.6 million passengers in July and August. It said summer demand “exceeded expectations”, with momentum “continuing to build” as the winter travel period approaches.
Bookings for the winter season, which begins in late October, are “tracking positively”, Emirates said, despite passengers “making travel decisions closer to departure”. Demand from markets including South Africa, Brazil, India, Portugal and Saudi Arabia is currently ahead of last year, according to the airline.
Emirates is responding by expanding its network and adding capacity. Alongside a new daily route to Helsinki, which launched last week, it plans second daily services to Accra, Tokyo Narita, Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi. It will also deploy the Airbus A350 to Larnaca, Malta, Nairobi and Hamburg from late October, followed by Mauritius in November.
On 1 November, the A350 will make its debut on scheduled US services, replacing the Boeing 777 on Emirates’ existing daily Orlando route.
Daily flights launched to Helsinki
Emirates touched down in Helsinki for the first time on 2 October, establishing a daily, year-round connection between Dubai and the Finnish capital. It joins Copenhagen, Oslo and Stockholm on the airline’s Nordic network.
Operated using an A350, the daily EK167 flight departs Dubai at 8:15 am local time and arrives in Helsinki at 2:30 pm. The return flight, EK168, leaves Helsinki at 4:20 pm and lands in Dubai at 12:20 am the following day.
The launch also maintains a direct Dubai-Helsinki option during the coming winter. Finnair has cancelled its flights between the cities from 25 October 2026 to 27 March 2027, citing the unstable situation in the Middle East. Emirates announced its Helsinki service in January, before Finnair confirmed the suspension in August.
“Helsinki is an exciting addition to our global network, connecting Finland with Dubai and our extensive network beyond, year-round,” said Adnan Kazim, Emirates’ Deputy President and Chief Commercial Officer, following the inaugural flight.
"As a gateway to Finland, Helsinki offers travellers a unique blend of vibrant culture, beautiful nature and an abundance of opportunities for business and trade, while also serving as a key connector for travellers to explore more of Finland."
Demand grows for winter travel
The new Dubai-Helsinki route gives passengers another way to visit the Finnish capital and travel onwards to Lapland. It also comes amid growing interest among UAE travellers in winter holidays, according to dnata, which is part of the Emirates Group.
Speaking to Euronews Travel at Arabian Travel Market in September, dnata Group CEO Nabil Sultan Al Murr said demand for winter travel was growing.
“People going out for skiing, which was never the trend almost four to five years ago, is becoming such a huge trend,” he said.
Responding to that interest, dnata recently launched a winter programme featuring around 10 ski destinations. The company is also looking beyond conventional ski holidays towards other winter experiences such as seeing the Northern Lights.
“These are all new kinds of features and experiences that we're trying to bring to the traveller and actually meet their emerging demand that we continue to see,” he said.

Nobel Prize in Chemistry goes to Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Nobel Prize in Chemistry goes to Henri B. Kagan, Kenso Soai
October 7, 2026
The Nobel Prize in Chemistry on Wednesday was awarded to Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai "for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis."
Kagan, who is 95 years old and was born in France, is affiliated with France’s Université Paris-Sud, and Soai, who is 76 years old and was born in Japan, is based at the Tokyo University of Science.
The scientists share the Nobel Prize for answering longstanding questions in chemistry about life's origins.
Specifically, the duo solved an age-old mystery that has long puzzled chemists: some molecules, like amino acids, exist as two variants that are mirror images of one another, but just one of the variants out of the two is found in living organisms.
The two answered questions about why life chooses one variant over another.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winner in Stockholm.
Nobel chemistry prize goes to scientists who answered questions about homochirality
In chemistry, life's building blocks are what scientists call homochiral, after the Greek words for "same" and "hand."
The Nobel Committee said the chemistry prize recognizes discoveries that have enabled chemists to drive chemical reactions that lead to homochirality.
"Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously," Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, said in a news release. "The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular."
The duo's discoveries, the news release said, "have been decisive for chemists who design reactions for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals."
Who won the Nobel chemistry prize last year?
- Last year, Susumu Kitagawa, Richard Robson and Omar Yaghi won the Nobel Prize in chemistry for the development of new molecular structures that can trap vast quantities of gas inside. Their discoveries can help tackle some of the world's most pressing problems, like climate change.
What do laureates receive?
- Laureates receive a tailored diploma, a medal and a document detailing the cash award that is set this year to 12 million Swedish kronor, which is equivalent to just over €1 million or $1.2 million.
Who else has received a Nobel Prize so far?
- The Nobel Prize in medicine was awarded Monday to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their pioneering work on optogenetics, a method of controlling nerve cells with light, which makes it possible to study how the brain works.
- The Nobel Prize in physics was awarded Tuesday to Francis Halzen, a Belgian-born astrophysicist whose efforts helped demistify a rare group of neutrinos that launched a new era of astronomy.
Nobel prizes in literature and peace also this week
- The Nobel Prize in literature is set to be awarded Thursday and the Nobel peace prize will be announced on Friday.
- After that, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced on Monday.
- All prize announcements are streamed live by the Nobel Prize organization.

NSC loses last seat in parliament as MEP Dirk Gotink quits party
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:50:59 UTC
18:50:59 KST

NSC loses last seat in parliament as MEP Dirk Gotink quits party
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The last elected politician representing Nieuw Sociaal Contract (NSC), the party formed three years ago by former CDA MP Pieter Omtzigt, has resigned in a row over whether to work with a new hardline Eurosceptic group.
Dirk Gotink, NSC’s only member in the European Parliament, quit the party over the decision to explore a possible collaboration with Mona Keijzer’s Project 2029, a right-wing conservative movement that sees the European Union as a federal superstate in the making.
Gotink, 45, said in a post on LinkedIn that seeking closer ties with Keijzer, another former Christian Democrat (CDA) MP, was “incomprehensible”.
“When it comes to Europe, we take a very different stance,” he said. “For me the EU is a precondition for our freedom and prosperity … Sowing doubt about the importance of the EU is not just irresponsible but also goes against the interests of the Netherlands.”
The party’s board said it had invited Keijzer to be a guest speaker at this weekend’s conference in Breda without any promise of entering into a formal partnership. But Gotink said the appearance of the former farmers’ party (BBB) housing minister was a “clear choice of political direction”.
NSC leaderless
Gotink has been the only NSC member in any parliament since the general election last October, when the party lost all 20 seats in the Dutch parliament that it won two years earlier, three months after its foundation. It has had no leader since Omtzigt’s successor, Eddy van Hijum, quit in January.
Gotink said he was grateful for the opportunity given him by Omtzigt, but he would be continuing as an independent MEP within the conservative EPP group.
“He redefined Christian Democrat thinking and tied it to tangible ideas such as basic living standards and the rule of law,” he told AD.nl. “He gave me the chance to contribute as an MEP. I am very grateful to him for that.”
Omtzigt founded NSC in August 2023 with a promise to make government in the Netherlands more accountable through constitutional reform and improve people’s basic standard of living (bestaanszekerheid).
Coalition with PVV
But after the party entered a coalition with the far-right PVV, the right-wing liberal VVD and the farmers’ party BBB, NSC fell apart under pressure from PVV leader Geert Wilders, who accused it of obstructing his asylum policies.
Omtzigt resigned as party leader and stepped down as an MP last year on health grounds, having taken several months off work with burnout symptoms. In a parting press conference he said the “poisonous” political climate in the Netherlands was preventing politicians from tackling the country’s real problems.
Omtzigt had quit the CDA in 2021 following a dispute with the party leadership, which wanted the campaigning backbench MP to be offered a “position elsewhere”.
His efforts to seek justice for families who were wrongly accused of benefit fraud in what became known as the toeslagenaffaire triggered the downfall of Mark Rutte’s third coalition government, which included the CDA, in 2021.
He stood for the leadership of the CDA in 2020 but lost narrowly to Hugo de Jonge, the health minister during the coronavirus pandemic. The third-placed candidate in that race was Mona Keijzer.

Royal Mail to cut up to 2,500 jobs amid restructure and fall in letter deliveries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:50:45 UTC
18:50:45 KST

Royal Mail is to cut up to 2,500 jobs as the embattled company seeks to restructure its business amid intense competition and the continuing decline in letter deliveries.
The postal service, which has been fined a total of £37m since 2023 for missing delivery targets set by the regulator Ofcom, said the job cuts would focus on head office and “support function roles” with the restructure to be completed by the end of next year.
Pointing out that the volume of letter deliveries had declined more than 70% since their peak in the mid-00s, Royal Mail said the cuts would be achieved through “natural attrition” and a voluntary exit programme with no compulsory redundancies.
The company said there would be no reduction in operational frontline roles in delivery and processing, including the number of postal workers and drivers it employs. The cuts amount to less than 2% of Royal Mail’s workforce of more than 131,000.
However, the Communications Workers Union (CWU), which represents frontline staff, said about 200 members with jobs in administration and revenue protection would be affected.
“We will be meeting management to discuss this announcement, which is further evidence of a company that is demoralising staff and failing to deliver for customers and the wider community,” said Martin Walsh, a deputy general secretary of the CWU. “We urge the government to confront the reality of a collapsing Royal Mail and intervene to save this national institution.”
The cuts are the first to be made since the completion of the £3.6bn takeover of Royal Mail’s parent company, International Distribution Services, by the Czech billionaire Daniel Křetínský’s EP Group last year.
Royal Mail last made a big round of cuts in 2022 when it said it was looking to eliminate up to 10,000 roles, including 6,000 full-time frontline jobs.
“We have been working hard to reduce costs and simplify processes across all areas of the business as we transform to win in a very competitive market,” said Alistair Cochrane, the chief executive of Royal Mail. “These proposed changes remove duplication and allow us to invest further in the service we deliver for our customers.
“The proposed changes will not be easy, but they are an important part of building a stronger, simpler and future-ready Royal Mail for our customers and colleagues.”
The union Unite said further job cuts were likely unless the government and the regulator Ofcom addressed a number of issues facing Royal Mail, most notably high competition from rivals that operated “gig economy postal services”.
“These devastating job losses have been directly caused by years of inaction, without urgent action, this will happen again,” said Sharon Graham, Unite’s general secretary. “More jobs will be lost, employment standards will continue to fall and customers will continue to be let down.
“The answer cannot simply be another round of job cuts. Unite is now supporting our affected members at Royal Mail during this very difficult time and is committed to fighting this decision every step of the way.”
Last week the company announced it was to hire 22,000 temporary workers – in roles including sorting, delivery and collection and HGV and MGV drivers – to cover the seasonal jump in mail volumes, including online purchases over Black Friday and Cyber Monday in November, and Christmas deliveries.
In June, the postal regulator launched an investigation into Royal Mail for once again missing its annual delivery targets, with almost a quarter of first-class mail arriving late. Royal Mail has not hit its Ofcom-mandated delivery target for first-class post since 2017, or for second-class mail since 2020.
In April, Royal Mail faced criticism for raising the price of a first-class stamp by 10p, or 6%, to £1.80. The cost of a first-class stamp has more than doubled since 2020.
The cost of the second-class service rose by 4p, or 5%, to 91p. Royal Mail blamed the need for price increases on the “continued rise in the cost of delivery for every letter”.
Last July, Ofcom gave IDS permission to loosen Royal Mail’s universal service obligation, ending second-class post on Saturdays and reducing the service to alternate weekdays from Monday to Friday.
A decade ago Royal Mail was delivering 20bn letters a year, but that has shrunk to 6.7bn and could drop to 4bn within four years. Over the same timeframe the number of addresses it serves has risen by 4m.

Hybrid Kub and Buk SAM Launchers Used to Shoot Down Jet-Shaheds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:50:35 UTC
18:50:35 KST

To shoot down Russian jet-powered Shaheds, Ukrainian air defense forces used a hybrid of a Kub system launcher and a Buk firing unit.
The 156th Maksym Kryvonis Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment demonstrated how such a pairing operates in combat.
The joint use of a Kub launcher and a Buk self-propelled firing unit within an integrated air defense network is based on the similar architecture of these systems.
This partially addresses one of the Kub system’s main limitations— the lack of an autonomous target illumination and guidance radar. For the Buk SAM system, it addresses missile availability.
The Buk SAM system’s self-propelled firing unit features an integrated radar that detects and tracks targets, including aerial objects, at significantly greater ranges and transmits their coordinates.
How the Kub and Buk SAM launchers hybrid works:
“This hybrid has performed very well in destroying aerial targets. The Kub and Buk pairing alone has accounted for around 20 aerial targets,” the military personnel said.
Most of them were Russian Shahed jet-drones.
Although this pairing is not typical, the technical capability to use missiles from one system with another was incorporated during the transition of air defense forces from the Kub SAM system to the Buk in the 1970s and 1980s. Thus, the 9A38 self-propelled firing unit was developed for the Kub-M4 SAM system.
Its launcher was designed with interchangeable rails (or adjustable mounts), allowing it to carry either three 9M38 missiles (Buk) or three 3M9M3 missiles (Kub). However, the video features a hybrid of a Kub SAM launcher and a Buk self-propelled firing unit.
Another solution to the missile shortage for Buk SAM systems is adapting its self-propelled firing units to use American RIM-7 missiles, creating a system known as FrankenSAM. The 156th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment also operates it.
According to the commander of one of the crews, some vehicles equipped with these missiles have 34 or more confirmed aerial targets destroyed. It is also reported that one launcher has carried out 131 RIM-7 missile launches.
“We operate a modified Buk SAM system, popularly known as ‘Frankenstein,’ equipped to fire RIM-7 surface-to-air missiles. It has already proven its effectiveness in one area. One vehicle has 34 confirmed kills. Other vehicles have more, while some have fewer.”
Last year, it was reported that Ukraine had received technical documentation for FrankenSAM systems and could now produce them independently.

Why are Melania Trump staffers gloating about ‘Digger’ and its box office woes?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:49:18 UTC
18:49:18 KST

A senior advisor to Melania Trump posted a comparison online that doesn't make much sense...
What is it they say about one person’s misfortune...? Well, Melania Trump’s staff seem to be embracing that opportunistic sentiment with regards to Digger ’s woes at the box office.
As reported earlier this week, Oscar-winning director Alejandro González Iñárritu’s Digger, starring Tom Cruise as a powerful oil tycoon who has triggered an environmental disaster, made just $8 million in the US and $20 million in total globally in its opening weekend.
Considering Digger had a production budget of up to $180m (plus hefty marketing), this means the divisive film is on track to become one of 2026’s biggest flops with estimated losses projected at between $150-200 million.
As if that wasn’t bad news enough, some are indulging in schadenfreude and getting their gloat on...
Marc Beckman, a senior advisor to Melania Trump, posted a comparison online, stating that the Cruise-led satire had been outperformed by the biographical film Melania released earlier this year.
“On a per-theater basis, MELANIA outperformed Tom Cruise’s DIGGER by approximately 67%, despite opening in roughly half as many theaters,” wrote Beckman on X.
Granted, Melania was a hit in US cinemas for a non-fiction movie, eventually grossing $16.7 million. However, given that Amzon spent $40 million to acquire the documentary and a reported $35 million to market it, that still makes it a sizeable loss.
Following Beckman’s post, many were quick to point out that the comparison between Melania and Digger was not appropriate. Check out some of the reactions below:
Regardless of Digger ’s misfortunes, you have to hand it to Iñárritu and Cruise for delivering an ambitious piece of cinema.
In Euronews Culture’s review of Digger, we said that the director had made “both the boldest film of 2026 and this year’s wildest misfire.”
“It’s hard to write more about Digger without spoiling Iñárritu’s brave but misguided gambit, but safe to say that once he does pull the rug from under the audience, he leaves viewers with a boated folly that’s both hollow and heavy-handed.”
We also noted how “high concepts are always to be applauded”, even if they end up feeling like "empty theatrics". Read the full review here.
Conversely, when reviewing Melania at the start of the year, we wrote that it was a “self-congratulatory portrait of privilege, one singularly uninterested in mining anything beyond the surface” and that it was both a “despicable” and “soul-crushingly bleak”. Read the full review here.
Put simply, compared to Melania, Digger is Citizen Kane. Back-handed compliment though that may be, that comparison feels apt.
Euronews Culture interviewed documentary filmmaker Raoul Peck for his 2026 film Orwell: 2+2=5, in which the filmmaker said about the Melania film: “First of all, I wouldn't call that a film. It’s not even propaganda, because propaganda can be more intelligent. This is basically a publicity stunt. It’s a bribe."
"This film happened because a network could spend $40 million to make it. I know many other filmmakers who would have loved to have that kind of money to make a more convincing film.”
He added: “Ethically speaking, no documentarian would accept to make a film where the subject is the executive producer of the film and basically calling the shots. That's ethically unacceptable. That's why I cannot call it a film.”

MOSCOW, October 7. /TASS/. New batches of Su-34 fighter-bombers are already being manufactured, according to Rostec.

France suspends stun grenade use at protests ahead of PM’s speech after student loses hand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:48:00 UTC
18:48:00 KST

France suspends stun grenade use at protests ahead of PM’s speech after student loses hand
- France has suspended police stun grenades at student protests after a 15-year-old lost a hand, as Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said the move is temporary until facts are clear.
- The protests began over poor school conditions and teacher shortages, and spread nationwide. More than 500 schools stayed partly closed, while 488 people were arrested on Oct 6.
- Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu will address the crisis and budget concerns, but unions say talks are not enough. Police have opened 18 internal probes, and injuries and arrests keep rising.
AI generated
PARIS – France has suspended the use of stun grenades by police at student-led demonstrations, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said on Oct 7, as allegations of police brutality mounted after days of sometimes violent demonstrations across the country.
Tens of thousands of people took to the streets across France on Oct 6, demanding better conditions in high schools. That same evening, President Emmanuel Macron held an emergency meeting with Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu and other key ministers to find a way out of the crisis.
Lecornu will speak later on Oct 7 on the school protests as well as the national finances, his office said, against the backdrop of heated debates over the country’s 2027 budget.
Nunez told radio broadcaster RTL early on Oct 7 that he had suspended the police use of stun grenades at the protests.
A 15-year-old lost a hand on Oct 5 after police fired a stun grenade.
“I am suspending their use in the high school student protests until the facts of the incident have been clarified,” said Nunez.
He stressed that this suspension was “only for the high school student protests” and for “just long enough to understand what happened”.
Last week, a 14-year-old student in north-west Paris was hit in the face with a tear gas grenade at such close range that he lost several teeth. A policeman was charged on Oct 6 over that incident.
Police have opened 18 internal investigations into allegations of misconduct since the protests began, Nunez said.
“It took several children being maimed for life for Nunez to give up using grenades against high school students,” said Manuel Bompard, national coordinator of the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI).
The government has blamed the LFI for stoking tensions around the protests.
‘Need something more’
The protests started in late September with students blocking entrances to hundreds of high schools for 15- to 17-year-olds over complaints of dilapidated facilities and teacher shortages.
While most schools reopened on Oct 7, more than 500 remained at least partially closed with students blocking doors with mounds of rubbish bins.
Parents, teachers and union workers joined the demonstrations in the capital and other cities for a national day of mobilisation on Oct 6.
At least 488 people were arrested and 43 members of the security forces wounded in the protests, which saw a quarter of a million people mass across France, the Interior Ministry said.
Most of the Oct 6 demonstrations were peaceful but there were sporadic clashes across the country with protesters throwing projectiles and security forces using tear gas, AFP correspondents said.
Lecornu announced a half-day of class time would be set aside in schools on Oct 7 to allow for “internal democratic” dialogue, intended to give students and staff the opportunity to voice their issues.
However, student union leader Ryad Rani told local press that the effort was “yet another attempt to muzzle the debate” and to gain time.
And the union representative for school principals, Nicolas Bonnet, told broadcaster franceinfo that “to get out of this crisis, we will need something more than simple consultation periods”.
Lecornu on Oct 6 condemned the violence and told lawmakers the violence would not be tolerated, while also rejecting accusations that the government had ordered “police repression” against protesters.
More than 6,500 people, mostly minors, have been arrested.
The government has reported that at least 215 students and 715 police officers have been injured since the start of the movement.
The prime minister’s office said 85 teaching staff have also been injured. AFP

Over a third of Ukrainians expect more military aid from EU – poll
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:47:00 EEST
18:47:00 KST

Over a third of Ukrainians expect more military aid from EU – poll
A poll has found that over 34% of Ukrainians see the EU's security and defence role primarily in increasing military assistance to Ukraine. In comparison, around 19% expect stronger financial support, and about 11% want the EU to help facilitate peace talks.
Source: European Pravda, citing an Info Sapiens poll conducted for the New Europe Centre from 11 to 22 September
Details: In an open-ended question about Ukrainians' views of the EU's security and defence role, 34.9% of respondents named increased military assistance.
The five most common responses also included stronger financial support for Ukraine, mentioned by 19.1% of respondents; assistance in ending the war or facilitating peace talks (11.2%); stronger sanctions and pressure on Russia (9.7%); and an overall increase in EU assistance and engagement (8.3%).
A total of 7.7% of respondents said the EU should monitor the use of funds in Ukraine and support efforts to combat corruption. Meanwhile, 3.5% said helping Ukraine join the EU is important.
Background: The same poll also found that over 60% of Ukrainians see the EU as a reliable, long-term partner for Ukraine in the field of security and defence.

US Vice President Vance ties ending war to Iran cutting enrichment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:47:00 UTC
18:47:00 KST

Vice President JD Vance has said that Iran must "meaningfully" reduce its nuclear enrichment capacity to end the seven-month war, though he noted Washington remains uncertain how Tehran reaches negotiating decisions.
Vance, a longtime skeptic of U.S. involvement in foreign wars, has taken a leading role in negotiating a settlement to the conflict and brokered a provisional peace agreement in June that quickly fell apart.
The war has jolted global energy markets and become a political liability for President Donald Trump and fellow Republicans ahead of November midterm elections.
Speaking to Reuters after a campaign trip in Alaska Monday, Vance said any agreement would require Iran to reduce its nuclear enrichment capacity, rather than offer assurances of future nuclear drawdowns.
"If you don't want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60% enriched fuel? And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don't build highly enriched fuel. That's a very basic threshold issue," Vance said.
"I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity."
Iran and the U.S. have exchanged proposals in recent weeks aimed at ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy shipping route. Trump rejected Tehran's latest offer and has warned that military operations could intensify after the midterms.
Vance said the U.S. remained open to an agreement but would require concrete Iranian nuclear concessions.
"We're not going to trade words for actions," Vance said.
Complicating matters, Vance said Washington is uncertain who makes decisions in Tehran.
Vance said the U.S. was in talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. But it was unclear how much authority they wield within Iran's power structure, he said, after joint U.S.-Israeli strikes at the start of the war killed then Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
"One of the things we picked up on is it's not totally clear how their country makes decisions," Vance said. Separately, Trump said on Tuesday his "biggest problem" is no one knows who is running Iran.
Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson said Sunday that U.S. officials are well aware of who their Iranian counterparts are and how Iran's decision-making system works.
"The problem is actually the opposite: it lies in the contradictory positions and mixed messaging from U.S. officials," Esmaeil Baghaei told a weekly press conference.
Vance told Reuters he has held personal conversations with field commanders to gauge battlefield conditions. He dismissed concerns over critical munitions shortages and added that while Iranian troops are periodically able to strike commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, they are largely unable to prevent energy exports through the waterway.
Vance declined to say if he was leading peace talks, though he is frequently cited as the White House's top negotiator.
"We're certainly involved," he said. "Ultimately, the president of the United States is driving things."
The war – and its $3 billion monthly price tag – has become a key issue on the campaign trail. Higher energy prices have put Trump and Republicans on the defensive in competitive states that will decide control of Congress.
Vance has sought to temper criticism of Trump’s handling of the conflict, telling voters they should not let that issue keep them from backing Republicans in next month's elections.
In Alaska, Vance rallied for Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, who is locked in a tight reelection battle with Democratic challenger Mary Peltola. Trump carried Alaska by 13 percentage points in 2024, but rising everyday costs have put the state in play.
Before speaking with Reuters, Vance focused much of his speech on affordability concerns, especially around energy. Alaska's remote locale makes consumer goods more expensive, and energy production is a key industry.
Rally attendees roared when Sullivan nearly introduced Vance as the president of the U.S., rather than the vice president. Vance is seen as a leading Republican contender to succeed Trump in the White House.
Vance told Reuters afterward that he had not decided whether to seek the presidency in 2028.
"I'm inherently a procrastinator," he said. "I really haven't thought about it much."

The European Commission proposes new rules for future EU members
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:46:17 EEST
18:46:17 KST

The European Commission proposes new rules for future EU members
Kyiv • UNN
Candidates are to be granted broader access to EU programs in key areas. At the same time, it is proposed that their rights be restricted for failing to fulfill their obligations.
The European Commission proposes granting EU candidate countries more benefits as part of their gradual integration, as well as introducing new safeguards that would limit their rights if, after joining the EU, these states halted reforms or refused to fulfill their obligations. EU Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos announced the preparation of a package of relevant changes in Strasbourg on Tuesday, October 6. DW reports, UNN writes.
Details
According to her, a preliminary assessment of how the accession of new countries could affect the European Union showed that "the EU is already ready for enlargement, but there are areas that will require adjustments." In particular, to make the European Union "more flexible and effective," the Commission proposes applying the so-called passerelle clauses of the EU treaties and replacing unanimity with qualified majority voting.
This would allow the European Union to narrow the range of issues on which one country can use its veto to block a decision. This concerns, in particular, interim decisions in the EU accession negotiation process, such as opening negotiating clusters, which currently require unanimity.
Gradual integration before joining the EU
As for gradual integration, under which a candidate country that successfully implements certain reforms gains access to individual EU programs or funds, this approach is not new to the enlargement methodology. Some countries, including Ukraine, already have such benefits.
At the same time, Kos asserts that the document proposed by the European Commission envisages "more ambitious involvement of candidate countries in certain areas of EU activity," particularly in the fields of energy, transport, artificial intelligence, security, and defense.
At the same time, the European commissioner emphasized that gradual integration is not a substitute for full membership, but rather "a tool that accelerates the enlargement process."
