Mali reclaims rebel stronghold with Russian support (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:27:03 UTC
18:27:03 KST

Mali reclaims rebel stronghold with Russian support (VIDEO)
Malian troops backed by Russian forces have retaken the northern separatist stronghold of Kidal, the government has announced, reversing the loss of the strategic town during a coordinated rebel and jihadist offensive in April.
The transitional authorities said troops consolidated their positions in the regional capital on Tuesday following intensive air and ground operations. Their return would enable the gradual restoration of public administration and basic services, according to the government statement.
The Tuareg-led Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) acknowledged leaving Kidal and claimed there had been “disproportionate” airstrikes by Mali’s military and the Russian Defense Ministry-run Africa Corps. Its spokesperson, Mohamed Elmaouloud Ramadane, described the move as a “controlled withdrawal” to preserve personnel and equipment, saying its forces had pulled out without direct combat and that the retreat was temporary.
Kidal has long been a center of separatist demands for an independent state in northern Mali. Malian troops and fighters from the Russian private military company Wagner recaptured it in November 2023, before losing control following a nationwide offensive in April by the FLA and the Al-Qaeda-linked Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) that also killed Defense Minister Sadio Camara.
The West African nation has been gripped since 2012 by a jihadist insurgency that has spread to neighboring Burkina Faso and Niger despite years of French military intervention. Nearly 49,000 people have been killed in violence linked to militant Islamist groups across the Sahel since 2022, the Africa Center for Strategic Studies said in August.
Bamako and its Sahel allies have accused foreign powers of supporting the armed groups. Addressing the UN General Assembly on September 28, Malian Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Diop accused Ukraine of aiding jihadists and separatists, citing coordinated attacks in April and July. Mali severed diplomatic ties with Kiev in August 2024 after Ukrainian military intelligence spokesman Andrey Yusov said rebels received information enabling an ambush on Malian and Wagner forces.
Last month, CNN reported that about 15 Ukrainian specialists were assisting the FLA with drone training and operations, citing Ukrainian personnel. Kiev has rejected allegations that it supports terrorist groups in the Sahel.
Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger have also accused France of supporting terrorist groups in the Sahel. All three former French colonies have ended defense cooperation with Paris and strengthened security ties with Moscow. Personnel from the Africa Corps, which replaced Wagner in Mali by 2025, have since supported Malian troops in operations against jihadists and separatist armed groups.
Since 2020, a wave of military coups has reshaped politics across the Sahel region in Africa, toppling civilian governments in Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger.
France, once the region’s dominant external power, has steadily lost influence amid rising anti-French sentiment and deep frustration over insecurity, economic stagnation, and foreign interference. The former colonial power was forced to withdraw troops from Mali in 2022, Burkina Faso in 2023, Niger later that year, and Chad in early 2025.
About 4,500 soldiers had been deployed under Operation Barkhane, France’s largest overseas mission, across Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger, and Chad – a campaign that the military governments in Bamako, Niamey, and Ouagadougou have said only permitted Islamist insurgents to expand their activities.
The three West African states have established the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) and withdrawn from the International Organization of Francophone Nations (OIF) operating in Francophone countries, many of them former French colonies. The AES has forged new alliances, including with Russia, which its leaders hail as a more reliable economic and security partner.
In July, the joint forces recaptured Anefis, a strategic town about 100 km south of Kidal, after more than a week of fighting. Mali’s military said operations there and in two nearby localities killed nearly 100 militants and destroyed 12 combat vehicles.

South Korea’s astronaut urges girls: ‘Don’t limit your dreams or abilities’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:25:52 UTC
18:25:52 KST

Sümeyye Dilara Dinçer
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
South Korea’s first astronaut, Yi So-yeon, has urged young people, particularly girls confronting prejudice or perceived barriers, not to place limits on their ambitions.
“Don’t limit your dreams or your abilities,” Yi told Anadolu during the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC) in Türkiye’s Mediterranean resort city of Antalya.
“If you do your best, you can achieve anything you want,” she said.
Yi, who became the first South Korean to travel into space in 2008, said she had never imagined becoming an astronaut while growing up because her country had neither a space agency nor a human spaceflight program at the time.
“It never even occurred to me to think about becoming an astronaut,” she said. “I hardly knew what the word ‘astronaut’ meant.”
That changed while she was completing her doctorate, when the South Korean government launched a program to select the country’s first astronaut.
“I thought, ‘What if I conducted experiments in space instead of on the ground?’ That would be amazing, because in space you are constantly floating and experiencing so many different things,” she said.
With no previous astronaut in South Korean history, Yi said she became curious about how someone could qualify for the role.
“That pure curiosity led me to apply for the astronaut program,” she said.
Yi did not expect to be chosen from nearly 36,000 applicants. After a selection process lasting around 10 months, however, she was selected for the mission.
She traveled aboard a Russian Soyuz spacecraft to the International Space Station in April 2008, spending approximately 10 days in space and conducting scientific experiments. 
‘You can turn your dreams into reality’
Reflecting on her journey 18 years later, Yi said technological advances were creating opportunities that earlier generations could not have imagined.
“I especially want to tell children growing up today, and girls who feel they face certain limits or prejudices, not to restrict their dreams and abilities,” she said.
“We now have so much technology, and artificial intelligence is one of those technologies.”
Yi said young people hoping to become astronauts should preserve their passion, curiosity, love of learning and energy while also caring for their physical and mental health.
“You can turn your dreams into reality,” she said.
Yi has attended several editions of the International Astronautical Congress, which brings together space agencies, companies, researchers and students from around the world.
She described the gathering as an important opportunity to learn about emerging technologies and meet prospective research and commercial partners.
“It is also a wonderful environment for learning about space,” she said. “That is why I greatly enjoy being here and participating in the event.”
Making her first visit to Antalya for the congress, Yi said she was enjoying the city and its warm weather.

Ex-Buddhist monk who founded Thai Aids hospice convicted of embezzlement
Alongkot Poonmook, who was forced to leave the monkhood last year after he was arrested, has been sentenced to 50 years in prison
A former Buddhist monk in Thailand was convicted on Wednesday of misusing donations to a highly praised hospice he established for people with HIV/Aids and given the maximum term of 50 years in prison.
Alongkot Poonmook, formerly known as Phra Ratcha Wisutthiprachanat, was forced to leave the monkhood after he was arrested last year along with an associate, Seksan Sapsubbsakul, who served as a fundraiser for the project.
The Central Criminal Court for Corruption and Misconduct Cases found both men guilty on multiple counts of embezzlement and money laundering.
Some Buddhist temples in Thailand are extremely wealthy because worshippers donate large amounts as a way of making religious merit, and the country has seen cases of senior monks being accused of misappropriating temple funds. The case has drawn widespread attention since questions about the handling of funds for the hospice emerged online and prompted an investigation.

Swiss pharma giant Roche sends lab equipment to DRC to tackle Ebola outbreak
Roche is supporting efforts to contain the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) by providing laboratory equipment.
The Basel-based pharmaceutical company is supplying the National Institute of Public Health (INSP) with two molecular testing devices, Roche said on Wednesday.
More
Ebola vaccine: ‘In an outbreak situation we’re racing against time’
Once the equipment has been prepared and local laboratory staff have been trained, the devices will be deployed in Bunia. Roche’s PCR test for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola will also be trialled there. The test can detect the virus’s genetic material in samples. It is currently intended for research use only and has not yet been approved for diagnostic use.
Following successful testing, Roche plans to supply additional tests and provide further equipment if needed. The aim is to help expand the country’s limited testing capacity.
More
Inside Geneva Summer profile: tackling Ebola in DRC
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), the Ebola outbreak that began in May is the largest ever recorded in the DRC. By the end of September, nearly 8,000 cases and about 3,800 deaths had been confirmed and 63 health zones across seven provinces had been affected, with Ituri among the hardest-hit areas. The WHO has classified the risk level in the DRC as very high.

Messi ends 21-year Argentina career with goal in farewell win
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:23:37 CST
18:23:37 KST

BUENOS AIRES, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- Lionel Messi bid farewell to international football on Tuesday with an emotional final appearance for Argentina in its 3-0 friendly win over Benin.
Messi scored a late penalty, his 126th international goal, and provided assists for second-half goals from Nicolas Otamendi and Nico Paz.
But the result was secondary at the Monumental Stadium, where more than 80,000 fans turned out to say goodbye to the player who helped Argentina win a World Cup and two Copa America titles.
The tone was set early as Messi walked onto the pitch for his 208th and final Argentina appearance, flanked by his three children, while his wife, Antonela Roccuzzo, and mother, Celia Cuccittini, watched from the stands.
The match was stopped in the 10th minute for a standing ovation for Argentina's most-capped player and all-time leading scorer.
In the second half, Messi repeatedly looked around the stadium as chants of "Messi, don't leave, we're not ready to say goodbye" rang out around the ground.
After the game, a drone show lit up the Buenos Aires sky with images of the 39-year-old and messages of gratitude for his 21-year international career.
Argentina coach Lionel Scaloni and midfielder Enzo Fernandez wept as Messi delivered an emotional post-match speech.
"The truth is I don't want to leave," Messi said. "I just want to tell you that I love you, I'm going to miss you and I am grateful. I'm proud to have fulfilled the dream with all of you."
Messi announced his retirement plans in August following the death of his father, Jorge, and just weeks after Argentina's 1-0 loss to Spain in the World Cup final.
"In the last World Cup, we were very ... very close," he said during the 10-minute address. "We gave everything. The [semifinal] match against England was a very big physical drain for us and the reality is that we barely made it [to the final]. We fought for it like we always did ... but unfortunately we couldn't be champions. But have no doubt that all the teammates I had by my side always gave everything for this jersey."
Messi will continue playing for Inter Miami, where his contract runs through December 2028.
He vowed to continue supporting Argentina "from the other side" and urged fans to unite behind a new era for the national team.
"I gave it my all; I have nothing left to give, and besides, there are great young players coming up who deserve their chance," he added. ■

Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade unveils medals, torch
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:23:34 CST
18:23:34 KST

Staff members display uniforms and equipment at the 100-day countdown event for the Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade in Changchun, northeast China's Jilin Province, Oct. 7, 2026. The medals, torch, uniforms and equipment for the Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade were unveiled on Wednesday at a 100-day countdown event held at the Changchun International Aviation Expo City. (Xinhua/Xu Chang)
CHANGCHUN, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- Medals, the torch, uniforms and equipment for the Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade were unveiled Wednesday at a 100-day countdown event at Changchun International Aviation Expo City.
The torch, named "Ji Xiang," or "Auspicious Flight," is inspired by the clivia, Changchun's city flower. Its upper section features a filmstrip motif and 12 winter sports icons representing the Games' disciplines, a reference to Changchun's film industry.
Snowflake and ginseng flower motifs appear near the top, while ski-inspired lines run down the sides and a wheel-hub pattern decorates the base.
The torch stands 711 millimeters tall, a reference to the highest elevation in Changchun's urban area, 711 meters.
The medals, named "Ji Meng," or "Auspicious Dream," combine traditional Chinese cultural elements, winter sports imagery and features associated with Changchun.
The front features patterns inspired by skate blades and ski tracks, while the reverse depicts the "First Jade Bird of Ancient China," an artifact unearthed at the Wutaishan historic site in Nong'an, Changchun. Part of the bird design is inlaid with Songhua stone from Jilin.
A filmstrip pattern along the medal's edge also references Changchun's film heritage. An embedded NFC chip allows athletes to access images of their medal ceremonies and seasonal scenery from Changchun by tapping the medal with a smartphone.
Uniforms for torchbearers, torch escorts, volunteers, staff, technical delegates and ceremony personnel were also unveiled.
The Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade will be held from January 15 to 25, with competitions in Changchun and nearby Jilin City. ■

JERUSALEM, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- The Israeli military said Wednesday that it has struck about 100,000 targets across the Middle East since October 2023 and expanded its reserve forces by 36 percent, outlining the scale of its operations on the conflict's third anniversary.
The military said combat reserve units were serving an average of 80-100 days in 2026, compared with a planned average of about 55 days, attributing the increase to "evolving operational needs."
It said about 22,000 reservists previously released from service have been called back to duty following an August 2024 call-up order.
The target tally included about 65,000 in Gaza, 28,000 in Lebanon and Syria combined, 4,500 in Iran and 80 in Yemen. The military did not specify whether repeated strikes on the same site were counted.
In the occupied West Bank, the military said it has detained about 45,000 people for questioning over three years, including people accused of throwing stones or possessing weapons and those suspected of planning attacks.
It said it has confiscated more than 3,800 weapons since the war began.
Over the three years, about 10,200 projectiles have been launched toward Israel from Gaza, 20,000 from Lebanon, 1,200 from Iran, 50 from Syria and 90 from Yemen, according to the military. The figures could not be independently verified.
It said 970 Israeli soldiers have died during operations and more than 70 percent of soldiers wounded during the war have returned to service.
The Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, killed about 1,200 people and triggered a massive Israeli military campaign across Gaza that has killed, according to Gaza-based health authorities, more than 74,200 people. It subsequently expanded into fighting across the region. ■

====================================================================================================

China Focus: Culture-infused tourism gains traction during National Day holiday
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:22:48 CST
18:22:48 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- On the morning of Oct. 1, the first day of China's National Day holiday, the Confucius cruise ship slowly pulled away from a port in Jining, east China's Shandong Province, setting off for Nanyang ancient town on the city's southern outskirts.
Named after the famous ancient Chinese philosopher Confucius, the ship was bound for a 2-hour-plus journey, passing stretches of the Grand Canal, the world's oldest artificial waterway system, which connects rivers in northern and eastern China and was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2014.
"We chose the cruise after seeing online that it offered a rich cultural experience," said Zhao Xiaojie from the provincial capital Jinan, as she and her 11-year-old son read the ancient texts on the cabin's decorations inspired by the Six Arts -- the six foundational disciplines of ancient Confucian education.
Her choice reflects a broader trend during this year's National Day holiday, as cultural content is weighing more and more heavily in China's tourism products.
NATIONAL DAY EXTRAVAGANZA
"Cruises have operated on the same route before, but the Confucius incorporates many cultural elements and intangible cultural heritage experiences, turning it into a moving showcase of Confucianism on the Grand Canal," said Zhang Feng, head of the cruise route.
The round-trip ticket includes shuttle services to scenic spots and admission to the Kangqian Bieyuan and Huji Qianzhuang attractions. Visitors can also watch a traditional fishermen's wedding ceremony and cormorant fishing performances in Nanyang ancient town, Zhang said.
Such packages bring together Confucianism and the culture of the Grand Canal, he added.
The unusual holiday calendar this year, with the Mid-Autumn Festival falling just three working days before the National Day holiday, has given fresh momentum to the integration of culture and tourism.
Data from Chinese online travel platform Ctrip showed that one in 10 travelers chose to combine the two holidays by taking three days off to create a 13-day break. Nearly half of those taking an extended break traveled for more than eight days.
The longer holidays have expanded the travel radius of Chinese tourists, bringing cultural and tourism products in more remote and lesser-known destinations into the spotlight.
In Cangyuan Wa Autonomous County, southwest China's Yunnan Province, for example, tourists gathered at a square to pound freshly harvested rice and prepare new rice, filling the air with its aroma.
"New rice festival activities and service facilities have been upgraded this year, allowing visitors to experience the authentic culture of the Wa ethnic group," said Li Lei, deputy general manager of the Cangyuan County Tourism Investment Company.
Traditional culture is not the only draw. A growing number of travelers are also visiting landmarks associated with China's revolutionary history, driven in part by the patriotic sentiment associated with the National Day holiday.
This year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March, which lasted from 1934 to 1936. The arduous journey helped lay the foundation for the eventual victory of the Chinese revolution.
In Yudu County, east China's Jiangxi Province, the Memorial Park of the Starting Point of the Central Red Army's Long March has attracted large numbers of study-tour groups and is expected to receive nearly 300,000 visits during the seven-day holiday.
Dai Bin, president of the China Tourism Academy, said the flow of visitors to revolutionary landmarks reflects people's emotional identification with the revolutionary traditions.
When they travel, they don't just want to see history; they also want to draw deeper inspiration from the revolutionary legacy for their lives today, according to him.
INNOVATION REMAINS KEY
The trend has also fallen in line with a series of development plans China released recently.
The 15th Five-Year Plan for culture and tourism development, released by the Ministry of Culture and Tourism in September, calls for deeper integration between culture and tourism and their mutually reinforcing development with other areas of the economy and society. It stresses supporting the development of distinctive cultural industries and tourism in former revolutionary base areas.
Moreover, it calls for expanding the space for cultural and tourism development, with deeper integration moving from resource consolidation and product integration toward new business models and broader applications.
Hong'an Township in Xiushan Tujia and Miao Autonomous County, southwest China's Chongqing Municipality, has put such innovation into practice, drawing 190,000 tourist visits in the first two days of the holiday.
Leveraging the cultural appeal of Border Town, a novel by renowned Chinese writer Shen Congwen, as well as its unique location where three provincial-level regions meet, the township has developed immersive, scenario-based tourism offerings that combine folk experiences, local cuisine and the nighttime economy.
In Shandong, seven cities have joined forces to combine seven popular online-literature IPs with the region's landscapes and historical sites, encouraging fans to turn fictional worlds into real-life travel destinations.
The model uses storytelling familiar to Generation Z to breathe new life into traditional cultural and tourism resources, converting online popularity into real-world tourism consumption.
"The route runs from west to east, so fans can take a high-speed train and visit a different 'chapter' every day, which is very convenient," said Liu Wei, a fan of online literature born in the 2000s.
For industry insiders, such efforts to generate more immersive cultural tourist activities are also necessary.
Wu Liyun, a professor at Beijing International Studies University, said scenic spots once relied mainly on ticket sales, which is often unsustainable today.
"The core of the industry transformation lies in adding more experiential offerings and opportunities for secondary consumption, with the focus on everyday settings, local culture and lifestyle-oriented services," she said.
GLOBAL DRAW
The shift has appealed to inbound travelers as well.
With China offering unilateral visa-free entry to citizens of 50 countries and full mutual visa exemptions with 29 countries, its tourism industry has also been working to offer overseas tourists a wider range of immersive trips centered on cultural experiences.
In Jingdezhen, east China's Jiangxi Province, where the Jingdezhen Handicraft Porcelain Industry Sites were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in July, growing numbers of overseas visitors are exploring historic sites, taking part in art workshops and browsing handicraft markets, while enjoying distinctive cafes and homestays.
The city, known as the "Porcelain Capital," now offers a range of experiences for visitors seeking to explore its centuries-old ceramic traditions, according to Zhang Chen, a local tourism industry insider. Options include a one-day program combining an introduction to local ceramic culture with hands-on pottery making, or a three-day workshop led by inheritors of intangible cultural heritage.
"Many overseas visitors now seek a deeper cultural connection, rather than simply sightseeing," Zhang said.
In Beijing, veteran tourist guide Dou Junjie feels a similar trend. He provides guided bicycle tours along the Beijing Central Axis, a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2024 that covers former imperial palaces and sacrificial structures.
"More overseas visitors to Beijing would like to experience local life and learn about local culture," Dou said.
According to Gao Zhengyang, a guest researcher with Jiangsu Su Merchants Bank, immersive travel across destinations is replacing sightseeing and photo stops, a wider range of trendy Chinese products is making its way onto tourists' shopping lists, and the mix of visitors is becoming more diverse. Gao said all of these trends point to improvements in the quality of "China Travel."
Data from Ctrip shows that bookings for one-day tours by inbound tourists during this year's National Day holiday and the Mid-Autumn Festival holiday surged by over 400 percent year on year, with scenic spot ticket sales up more than 220 percent and train tickets more than 170 percent.
Li Xinjian, a professor at the Beijing International Studies University, said the growth in inbound tourism during what is traditionally a peak season for domestic travel reflects the increasingly diverse experiences on offer.
"Overseas tourists are finding that China offers not only beautiful scenery but also engaging cultural experiences," he said.
For Wu Liyun, value-added services such as the cultural experiences in Jingdezhen and Beijing are particularly important, as they are far more appealing than standardized products and usually leave a much deeper impression on travelers.
Wu believes Jingdezhen's model can be replicated in terms of how cultural content is presented. She cited her hometown of Linyi in Shandong Province, where willow weaving products are widely exported, and tourists can try their hand at the traditional craft and take their own creations home.
"Every city has its own ways of life passed down through generations," she said. "What you are accustomed to in the place where you live can be incredibly fresh and novel to outsiders." ■

Raid Regiment Strikes Snizhne Machine-Building Plant Supplying Russia’s Aviation Industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:20:44 UTC
18:20:44 KST

The Raid Regiment, in coordination with other components of Ukraine’s Defense Forces, struck the Snizhne Machine-Building Plant in the temporarily occupied territory of the Donetsk region.
The regiment reported the strike on social media and published footage of the attack.
The strike took place in September 2026. Operators of the 4th Battalion’s UAVs carried out the operation.
The video footage suggests the strike used “middle-strike” drones manufactured by Ukrainian company Fire Point.
The Raid Regiment said the Snizhne Machine-Building Plant plays an important role in Russia’s military industry.
Russia uses the plant’s facilities to manufacture components for military aircraft and helicopter engines.
The plant specializes in producing parts for gas-turbine engines, including compressor and turbine disks and blades.
On September 11, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported that the plant had been successfully struck in the temporarily occupied territory.
The Snizhne Machine-Building Plant was a separate division of the Ukrainian company Motor Sich JSC. It was located in the city of Snizhne in Donetsk region, which came under Russian occupation after 2014.
In December 2017, Motor Sich JSC announced that it had lost control of the assets of the Snizhne Machine-Building Plant. In January 2018, Vyacheslav Boguslaev told Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty that the company had transferred the Snizhne plant to a foreign company.
“Ownership remained with us. This is management, not ownership. We transferred the plant to another company for management. We cannot operate there under Ukrainian law. We hired a company to manage our plant. But the plant remains fully subordinate to and under the full control of Motor Sich,” he said.
He also noted that Motor Sich would continue purchasing products from the plant, but in “another country,” without specifying which country at the time.
In 2023, Boguslaev was formally notified that he was suspected of paying “taxes” and “fees” to the budget of the self-proclaimed “Donetsk People’s Republic” after Russia’s full-scale invasion began. This was linked to his continued cooperation with the Snizhne Machine-Building Plant, which is located in occupied territory.

Lithuanian company, ESA complete space medicine experiment for ISS launch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:20:00 UTC
18:20:00 KST

Lithuanian biotechnology company Delta Biosciences and the European Space Agency (ESA) have completed final integration of an experiment designed to determine how space radiation affects medicines, clearing the payload for a planned December launch to the International Space Station.
According to the company’s press release, the Compound Degradation experiment has passed safety and verification reviews and was transferred to NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida ahead of its planned launch aboard Northrop Grumman’s NG-25 commercial resupply mission.
The experiment is the first ISS mission designed to isolate the effects of space radiation on medicines. It will examine 134 medicines and molecules, including newly developed formulations designed to resist radiation damage.
Samples will be returned to Earth in three batches over three years, allowing researchers to track changes over time. The experiment is intended to provide data that could help develop medicines with longer shelf lives and greater stability, both for astronauts traveling to the Moon and Mars and for people on Earth who live far from medical supply hubs and depend on medicines surviving cold-chain transportation.
“We are flying formulations we first developed in our labs on Earth – but now, using space radiation as a stress test to learn how to rebuild medicines that are safer, more effective and last longer,” Delta Biosciences co-founder Dominykas Milašius said.
The experiment includes emergency medicines, radioprotectors, vitamins and nutraceuticals. Samples will be placed at two locations on the space station with different radiation levels, while matched control samples remain on Earth.
Additional samples will be exposed to heavy ions and simulated galactic cosmic radiation at the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research in Darmstadt, Germany. Radioprotectors and specially designed formulations will be tested alongside the medicines they are intended to protect.
Each compound will be measured at three time points in two radiation environments and compared with ground controls, producing more than 1,500 data points for analysis and predictive algorithms.
ESA said earlier ISS studies showed that some medicines lose potency more quickly in space but could not establish the cause.
“By pairing samples in orbit with heavy-ion irradiation on the ground, this experiment is designed to identify the role of radiation, and to test whether protective formulations can counter it,” said Christiane Hahn, ESA’s science lead for biology.
Delta Biosciences and ESA designed, built and integrated the payload in less than two years. The compact, modular system uses two levels of containment to isolate samples from the station environment.
The German Aerospace Centre also contributed to the mission and payload design. The teams will now focus on launch, orbital operations and the first sample return.

Jaguar unveils $130,000 electric vehicle two years after controversial rebrand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:18:30 UTC
18:18:30 KST

Luxury carmaker Jaguar has launched its new all-electric vehicle, two years after the famed British company's controversial rebrand prompted a social media backlash.
The automotive manufacturer, which is owned by India's Tata Motors, unveiled the Type 01 model on Tuesday at an event in New York City, describing it as the "most technically advanced" and "most powerful and aerodynamic" Jaguar ever.
It marks a radical new direction for the company, which was criticized in November 2024 when it revealed a series of changes ahead of becoming a fully electric brand.
Jaguar posted a 30-second clip on X at the time which featured several models in brightly colored clothing and marketing slogans such as "live vivid", "delete ordinary" and "copy nothing."
Notably, the ad did not feature a car or the company's traditional cat logo. Among those to criticize the ad was Elon Musk, with the owner of the X social media platform asking: "Do you sell cars?"
Jaguar sought to defend the ad campaign, telling Sky News at the time that the company wanted "to be bold and disruptive."
Italy's Ferrari and Britain's Bentley have also launched their first EV models this year, seeking to test wealthy buyers' appetite for going electric as luxury carmakers seek to compete with cheaper Chinese car brands.
Jaguar's Type 01 has a starting price of £130,000 (roughly $172,000) in the U.K. and around $130,500 in the U.S., according to multiple media reports, which is significantly higher than previous comparable models.
Jaguar later confirmed to CNBC on Wednesday morning that the Type 01 model has a minimum price tag of $130,000 in North America.
The four-door "Grand Tourer" has an ultra-long bonnet, low roofline, frameless doors and a camera instead of a rear window. It has a range of up to 450 miles and can accelerate from 0-62 miles per hour in 3.2 seconds.
The launch of the model comes as Jaguar Land Rover continues its recovery from a cyberattack that forced the company to halt production last year, and one month after JLR announced it would cut 4,000 jobs as part of a major cost-cutting drive.
JLR CEO PB Balaji described the unveiling of Type 01 as the start of "an exciting new era" for Jaguar.
"Combining British heritage, bold creativity, advanced technology and groundbreaking engineering, it reflects our ambition to create objects of desire that will help us invite a new generation of clients into Jaguar's loyal and passionate customer base," Balaji said in a statement.

2026-10-07

18:17:43 KST

The Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) warns that Russia has intensified preparations for a series of information and psychological operations (PSYOP) concerning the situation in the temporarily occupied town of Oleshky in Kherson region.
The SBU reported in its Telegram channel on Wednesday that such data was uncovered during counter-intelligence activities.
"Thus, according to operational information, servicemen of one of the occupiers' units received an order to prepare a series of 'compromising' interviews featuring residents of the temporarily captured town," the report states.
The Ukrainian intelligence agency emphasizes that in these videos, according to the enemy's design, "local residents are required to: blame Ukraine's Defense Forces for constant shelling and the blockade of the town; discredit the decisions of the military-political leadership of our state; express a positive attitude and gratitude toward the aggressor country's military."

Nasa releases striking image of dawn on Mars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:17:37 UTC
18:17:37 KST

Nasa releases striking image of dawn on Mars
Curiosity rover captures scene an hour after sunrise while climbing Mount Sharp in Gale Crater
Nasa has released a striking image of dawn on the Martian surface taken by its Curiosity rover, showing sunlight bathing jagged crags formed billions of years ago as the car-sized vehicle continues to explore Earth’s planetary neighbour.
Curiosity landed in 2012 in Gale Crater near the Martian equator, and since 2014 has been climbing Mount Sharp, a 5km-tall (3-mile-tall) mountain rising from the crater floor. The image was taken by the six-wheeled rover’s Mastcam camera about an hour after the sun rose above a landscape featuring wind-carved cliffs in the distance.
“The bright craggy peaks in the distance are a rock layer that is quite different in appearance from all the layers the rover has driven through so far. We think it once was windblown sediment, maybe sand or maybe even ash that blew into the crater from nearby volcanic activity. After the sediment hardened into rock, aeons of wind carved up the rock layer into ridges called yardangs,” said planetary scientist Ashwin Vasavada of Nasa’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California, the Curiosity project scientist.
The yardang layer most likely formed about 3 billion years ago, around the same time as the rest of the mountain, according to Vasavada. This layer spans about 16km across the northwestern reaches of Mount Sharp.

An ominous syntactic ambiguity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07

An ominous syntactic ambiguity
« previous post |
Beth Simone Noveck, "How AI can be good for democracy", NYT 10/6/2026:
Governments can also use their enormous purchasing power to demand more from A.I. companies and to build more A.I. with them. In return for providing government funding, South Korea is securing contracts with multiple tech and telecom companies to give A.I. access to all of its 51 million citizens.
Giving AI access to everyone! That sounds like a good idea, right?
But wait a minute, what's the syntax here? Is access to AI being given to all of the citizens? Or is AI being given access to all of the citizens?
Why not both? For the details, see Jiyoung Sohn, "South Korea’s ‘AI for All’ Push Gives Free Access to Every Citizen", WSJ 8/28/2026:
South Korea plans to give its entire population free access to generative AI services, the first major state-led offering treating the technology akin to a public utility.
The program seeks to connect more South Koreans to homegrown AI chatbots with the goal of advancing the country’s push for AI sovereignty. By giving premium-level AI services free to its citizens, South Korean officials hope to avoid an overreliance on models from the U.S. and China.
The AI tools will be linked directly to government systems and allow South Koreans to book doctor’s appointments, receive help with apartment hunting or get tax advice. Small businesses will be able to tabulate their taxes and check their eligibility for government-support programs, and parents will receive suggested educational content for their children.

Lauri Laats: Talk of tidy state finances unfounded as both taxes and deficit soar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:14:00 UTC
18:14:00 KST

Lauri Laats: Talk of tidy state finances unfounded as both taxes and deficit soar
With the new state budget, the government is acknowledging that its policies have reached a dead end. Taxes have been raised, yet public finances are still not in order. Spending cuts have been promised, yet the need to borrow remains, Lauri Laats writes.
In recent years, the people of Estonia have had to listen to the same justification over and over again: Taxes must be raised and spending cut because the country's finances need to be put in order. To that end, we have paid higher value-added tax, gotten used to the motor vehicle tax and watched as everyday purchases eat up an ever-larger share of our incomes.
Now we are looking at the 2027 state budget and the deficit still amounts to 4 percent of GDP. So where are the promised results?
Prime Minister Kristen Michal calls the new budget prudent and responsible. I would ask a much simpler question: How will this budget make life better for people in Estonia? Will groceries become more affordable? Will the fuel people need to get to work become cheaper? Will businesses have greater confidence to hire people and expand production? These are precisely the questions I expect the government to answer.
Borrowing to cover current spending
Before passing judgment, it is worth looking at how we got to where we are today. According to recently revised data from Statistics Estonia, the general government deficit was 2.5 percent of GDP in 2021, 1 percent in 2022, 2.7 percent in 2023, 1.4 percent in 2024 and 2.2 percent in 2025. Those are the actual figures. This year's deficit is forecast at 4.2 to 4.5 percent, while a 4 percent deficit is planned for next year.
The deficit, then, has not risen steadily every year; the situation has improved at times as well. Yet after tax hikes and promises of spending cuts, this year's projected deficit is nearly twice as large as last year's. The government can compare the new budget with an earlier, even worse forecast and talk about progress. People nevertheless have every right to ask why they must keep making greater sacrifices when the country's finances are still not being put on a sustainable footing.
The increase in the deficit is primarily being attributed to defense spending. Money must indeed be found to defend Estonia, but the country's security needs cannot explain away every decision the government has made. At the same time as the government's funding needs increased, it decided to significantly reduce its own revenue. Abolishing the so-called tax hump is one important reason a larger hole has emerged in the budget, a connection the Fiscal Council has also emphasized.
The tax hump (Estonia's gradual basic exemption reduction scheme — ed.) was abolished on January 1, 2026, so it cannot be used to explain deficits in previous years. It can, however, help explain the deterioration this year and the funding shortfalls in the years ahead.
Annely Akkermann, a representative of the Reform Party itself, estimated that this change would have an impact of approximately €500 million on the 2026 budget. Together with the decision to scrap the planned income tax increase, officials spoke of leaving about €780 million in the economy. These were two separate decisions, but both reduced government revenue compared with previous plans.
The most important point about this decision tends to get lost: The tax cut was not backed by sufficient permanent funding and the deficit is being financed through borrowing. In effect, the hole in the budget created by abolishing the tax hump is being filled with borrowed money. The government does not, of course, take out a separate loan for each tax decision, but lower tax revenue increases its financing needs, all else being equal. The bill for the tax relief, including interest, is therefore being left to future taxpayers. That is a deliberate choice by the government and one it must take responsibility for.
Spending deferred
Of course, I too want people to keep more of their money, but who benefits and by how much? As a rule, a lower-paid worker who previously made full use of the tax exemption gains €10 a month from the change to the universal tax-free allowance. For someone whose tax-free allowance was previously zero, the same change can mean an extra €154 a month. The calculation is based on a 22 percent income tax rate and full use of the tax exemption. Both, however, will share the burden of the additional debt and interest payments.
People earning the average wage need relief as well, but how do you explain to a lower-income family that it will get an extra €10 while continuing to pay high value-added tax at the grocery store? Tax policy must be based on people's actual ability to make ends meet. When money is tight, it is especially important to choose carefully how to use it to help the greatest number of people.
What concerns me greatly about the new budget is that the fundamental issues remain unresolved. Revenue is projected at €19.4 billion, spending at approximately €20.2 billion and investment at approximately €1.2 billion. The budget includes necessary spending and measures to support businesses, but taken as a whole, I see fine-tuning at a time when Estonia needs a clear shift in its economic and tax policies.
This assessment is not based solely on dissatisfaction from the opposition. According to the Fiscal Council, next year's budget position will improve by approximately €220 million compared with the summer forecast, mainly through adjustments involving investments, foreign funds and accounting. This does not produce a lasting improvement in the balance between revenue and spending.
Under current plans, the deficit will remain at 4 percent in both 2028 and 2029. Moving an expense into the following year may make the current figures look better, but someone will still have to pay the bill eventually.
Banking tax
We need to ease the tax burden on everyday expenses by lowering value-added tax on staple foods, cutting fuel excise duties and supporting jobs in the food service sector through a temporary VAT reduction. People's purchasing power and the fortunes of businesses are interconnected. If families cannot afford to spend, local businesses lose revenue as well.
These decisions require sources of funding. That is why the Center Party has advocated higher taxes on bank profits and proposed a conventional 24 percent corporate income tax for banks. The exact additional revenue would have to be calculated in light of changes to the existing tax regime. The government's administrative costs, overlapping functions and the effectiveness of subsidies must also be reviewed. Cost-cutting must be evident in the way the government itself operates.
Borrowing can be justified for necessary investments or exceptional defense needs. But permanent obligations cannot be financed indefinitely with new debt. According to the Fiscal Council, Estonia will spend nearly €2 billion on interest on government debt over the next four years. Every euro spent on interest reduces the resources available to improve healthcare, education and people's sense of security.
With this budget, the government is acknowledging that its policies have reached a dead end. Taxes have been raised, yet public finances are still not in order. Spending cuts have been promised, yet the need to borrow remains. Now expenditures are being shifted from one year to another and presented as an improvement. A government whose solution amounts to postponing problems is leaving the substantive decisions to its successors.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

Ex-Google boss warns Ukraine over Russia’s ‘Starlink rival’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:13:43 UTC
18:13:43 KST

Ex-Google boss warns Ukraine over Russia’s ‘Starlink rival’
Russia’s emerging Rassvet satellite network – often described as a “Starlink rival” – could provide Moscow’s military with sustainable communications and data to attack any target in Ukraine at will, former Google CEO Eric Schmidt has warned.
Speaking to The Economist last week, Schmidt noted that while Ukraine was initially seen as the main innovator in the conflict, Russia had largely closed that gap while pressing its advantage with far greater resources.
Schmidt noted that one of these domains is Russia’s Rassvet satellite project, which he suggested was about a year from maturity. “Once that network is in place, it is more or less unblockable,” he warned, adding that this could let Russian forces “hunt anywhere” inside Ukraine.
The ex-Google CEO also weighed in on the idea of granting Ukraine access to Starlink over Russia, which could allow Kiev to rely on Elon Musk’s satellites to target oil refineries and civilian infrastructure, calling it “really a political decision.”
“It’s really a government decision. And the US government needs to grapple with this question,” he said.
Developed by private Russian aerospace firm Bureau 1440, part of the IKS Holding conglomerate, Rassvet debuted in 2023 with the launch of three experimental satellites. The network is designed to offer speeds of up to 1Gbps with latency below 70 milliseconds and to operate at an orbit of around 800 km – higher than that of Starlink to balance the number of satellites against an increased coverage area.
This year, the company launched a total of 32 satellites, after six experimental spacecraft sent up in 2023 and 2024, with plans to have 292 satellites by some time in 2027.
On Tuesday, the company also unveiled a line of user terminals, some of which claimed speeds of up to 700 Mbps. The Ukrainian outlet Militarny suggested that some of the showcased terminals could eventually be fitted to strike drones.
Russia’s deployment of Rassvet has sparked major concern in Ukraine across the spectrum. In July, satellite communications expert Vladimir Stepanets told Militarny that the first satellite group provided at least two stable “communication windows” over the country daily, each lasting more than an hour.
Ukraine’s military intelligence separately told Janes it had recorded Russian forces using Rassvet communications over Ukraine for “several hours” by late July and warned the system could support real-time reconnaissance and strike-drone operations.
Vladimir Zelensky’s technology adviser, Sergey Beskrestnov, also warned that a fully deployed Rassvet could become a “small catastrophe” for Kiev as it would provide Russia with online control of strike drones and missiles.
Zelensky himself told the Financial Times last week that he had repeatedly asked US President Donald Trump to sanction companies involved in Rassvet development and production while warning that the network could become operational “by the end of this year or early next year.” Trump has not publicly responded to the request.
Former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev, who now serves as deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council, said that attempts to “block” Rassvet would amount to destroying it and could trigger “full-scale space warfare.”

NASA rover takes striking image of dawn's early light on Mars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:09:22 UTC
18:09:22 KST

NASA rover takes striking image of dawn's early light on Mars
WASHINGTON, Oct 7 - NASA has released a striking image of dawn on the Martian surface taken by its Curiosity rover, showing sunlight bathing jagged crags formed billions of years ago as the car-sized vehicle continues to explore Earth's planetary neighbor.
Curiosity landed in 2012 in Gale Crater near the Martian equator, and since 2014 has been climbing Mount Sharp, a 3-mile-tall (5-km-tall) mountain rising from the crater floor. The image was taken by the six-wheeled rover's Mastcam camera about an hour after the sun rose above a landscape featuring wind-carved cliffs in the distance.
"The bright craggy peaks in the distance are a rock layer that is quite different in appearance from all the layers the rover has driven through so far. We think it once was wind-blown sediment, maybe sand or maybe even ash that blew into the crater from nearby volcanic activity. After the sediment hardened into rock, eons of wind carved up the rock layer into ridges called yardangs," said planetary scientist Ashwin Vasavada of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California, the Curiosity project scientist.
The yardang layer most likely formed about 3 billion years ago, around the same time as the rest of the mountain, according to Vasavada. This layer spans about 10 miles (16 kilometers) across the northwestern reaches of Mount Sharp.
"However, the yardang layer doesn't appear to be part of the continuous stack of layers that make up the layer-cake of Mount Sharp. It was added on a little later. It's above what geologists call an unconformity: a gap in time where previous layers eroded down before new layers were deposited on top," Vasavada said.
The rover on its gradual ascent up the mountain has gained upwards of 0.6 miles (1 km) in elevation, the most ever climbed on Mars, according to NASA.
Mount Sharp is built of layers, each recording a period of the planet's geological past. In studying these layers, scientists have learned more about bodies of water — lakes and streams — that long ago covered this region, at a time when Mars was wetter and warmer than the cold and desolate place it is today.
Vasavada said NASA hopes Curiosity will reach the yardang layer in 2027 or 2028, at which time it will use its instruments to scrutinize the geology there.
Curiosity has been studying the geology and climate of Mars and examining whether it once bore conditions conducive to harboring microbial life. It is one of two NASA rovers operating on Mars. The Perseverance rover is currently traversing the margins of Jezero Crater in the northern hemisphere.
Curiosity's new image of Martian dawn is certainly otherworldly.
"This scene has a wildness that reminds me of a road trip through Monument Valley, Arizona. You can almost feel the silence and the endless open space under the sky. But as familiar as that sounds, the sky is orange and the sunrise has shades of blue. It's like Earth, but it's definitely Mars," Vasavada said. REUTERS

French police suspend use of stun grenades after high school protester loses hand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:09:07 UTC
18:09:07 KST

France is suspending the use of stun grenades by police at high school demonstrations, the interior minister has said, amid mounting accusations of police brutality during a fortnight of protests marred by often violent clashes that have injured hundreds.
Laurent Nuñez told RTL radio on Wednesday that he had ordered a temporary halt to the use of the grenades “in the context of the high school students’ movement” after a 15-year-old lost a hand during a protest in Lens, northern France, on Monday.
Authorities have not confirmed the exact circumstances – in particular, whether the boy had picked up the grenade or been struck by it – but said up to 200 protesters had been hurling projectiles at police when the riot squad intervened.
Nuñez said he was suspending use of the grenades “until we know exactly what happened”.
The boy’s mother said on Wednesday that her son’s hand had been amputated. She told BFMTV: “His life has been stolen. He’s a 15-year-old kid, how can children be treated like that?” She said her son had not tried to pick up the grenade.
The education ministry said classes had been wholly or partially suspended in 429 of the country’s 3,700 lycées – high schools attended by pupils aged between 15 and 18 – on Wednesday, a significantly lower number than on Tuesday.
However, 80 university campuses, including the prestigious Sciences Po in Paris, were being blockaded by students on Wednesday, student unions said, and teachers’ and other unions said they would back further strike action on Thursday.
At least 215 teenagers and 85 school staff have been injured since the start of the protests over chronic teacher shortages, crowded classes, dilapidated buildings and long school days. About 750 police offers have also been injured.
Nuñez said 18 internal police investigations had been launched over allegations of brutality during the demonstrations, including one incident in which a young protester lost multiple teeth and another in which a student lost the use of an eye.
He said inquiries were always opened over accusations of “non-proportional” policing, but he insisted officers were there to protect the students. Rights groups and trades unions have repeatedly accused the police of using unnecessary force.
On Tuesday at least 250,000 pupils, parents, teachers and unionists took to the streets in cities across France on the biggest day yet of the campaign, prompting the president, Emmanuel Macron, to hold an emergency cabinet meeting.
Most marches passed off without serious incident but some, including in Paris, ended in sporadic vandalism and running skirmishes with riot police, with officers firing teargas and carrying out baton charges to disperse protesters.
The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, is due to make a speech on Wednesday on the demonstrations as well as the dire state of the country’s finances, which is severely constraining the government’s capacity to act on the protesters’ demands.
Lecornu on Tuesday condemned the violence and told parliament it could not be tolerated, while also rejecting accusations that the government had ordered “police repression” against the protesters.
Over the past fortnight, demonstrators have set dustbins on fire outside their schools, destroyed bus shelters and hurled projectiles at riot police, who have responded using batons, teargas and riot-control rounds.
Twenty-four schools have been burned or ransacked, while more than 6,500 people have been arrested, almost all of them minors. More than 1,800 are being prosecuted, nearly 1,500 of them under 18, the justice ministry has said.
Anne Savinel-Barras, the president of Amnesty France, said earlier this week that images and testimony from the protests “raise alarming concerns about the dangerous use of teargas, batons and policing techniques”.
The protests, months before key presidential elections to choose Macron’s successor, have rattled a government trying to reduce a ballooning budget deficit amid mounting investor concern over France’s sky-high debt and weak economic growth.
They have also sparked a heated political row, with the government accusing the radical-left La France Insoumise party of encouraging and even orchestrating the movement after numerous LFI MPs attended school blockades.
The party’s veteran leader and presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, has strongly supported the protests while urging non-violence.

Victoria Roshchyna, Tortured to Death by Russia, and Imprisoned Ukrainian Journalists Receive Human Rights Award
The international human rights organization Reach All Women in War (RAW in War) has named several journalists held in Russian captivity and occupied territories as recipients of the 2026 Anna Politkovskaya Award , as reported by Detector media on October 6.
The announcement honors media workers reporting on Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and human rights abuses while detained by Russian authorities.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Prominently recognized among the recipients is Victoria Roshchyna, a Ukrainian journalist who documented war crimes during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and died in Russian custody in September 2024 following torture and mistreatment.
Other Ukrainian media professionals awarded include Melitopol journalist Iryna Levchenko, who was sentenced by Russia to 15 years in a penal colony on espionage charges.
The honors also recognized RIA Melitopol reporter Anastasiya Hlukhovska, held in Russian captivity since August 2023, and Yana Suvorova, a local Telegram channel administrator sentenced to 14 years on terrorism and espionage charges.
Crimean journalist Iryna Danylovych, who was detained in April 2022, was also recognized. She received a 7-year sentence from an occupation court and has suffered severe health deterioration due to poor conditions and torture during her imprisonment, Detector media reported.
The nomination committee cited the courage of these Ukrainian media workers who risked their lives and freedom to report on Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and protest human rights violations. RAW in War called for the immediate release of all detained journalists and stated that those responsible for abuses and torture in custody must face justice.
The award marks 20 years since the assassination of Russian investigative journalist Anna Politkovskaya on October 7. Founded in 2006 by Bulgarian journalist and human rights defender Mariana Katzarova, RAW in War presents the annual prize to honor women working in active regions who protect human rights at great personal risk.
Anna Politkovskaya was a prominent Russian investigative journalist, author, and human rights activist known for her reporting on Russia’s full-scale invasion of Chechnya and exposure of state corruption and human rights abuses by Russian forces.
She was assassinated on October 7, 2006, after being shot dead in the elevator of her Moscow apartment building in a targeted contract killing linked to her reporting.
The persecution and illegal sentencing of Ukrainian media workers coincides with broader violations of international law by Russian forces against Ukrainian captives. Previously, it was reported that Russian forces have established a specialized combat brigade made up of Ukrainian prisoners of war and Ukrainians coerced into defecting.
Forcing prisoners of war into military service would violate international law governing the treatment of captives. The reported use of POWs for military purposes also follows broader patterns of coercion and abuse documented in Russian detention facilities, where Ukrainian captives have reported systematic torture, deliberate deprivation of food, and other forms of physical and psychological abuse.

Ayhan Şimşek
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Chancellor Friedrich Merz reaffirmed Germany’s support for Israel while also calling for a Palestinian state alongside Israel as the best path to peace and security in the region.
Merz, a conservative politician who has long backed Israel, renewed that stance in a written statement Wednesday. He said Germany stands firmly by Israel and that Israeli friends can count on Berlin’s commitment.
Blaming Hamas for the conflict, Merz said Germany’s thoughts were with the victims of the October 2023 attacks, the survivors and former hostages. The country, he said, stands in solidarity with the victims’ families and mourns the dead. 
Security and Palestinian state
“We stand for the security and existence of Israel. That is a lesson from the Shoah and part of German identity,” Merz said.
The Shoah, the Hebrew term for the Holocaust, was the systematic murder of about 6 million Jews by Nazi Germany during World War II.
Merz renewed his call for a political solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, saying the task now is to lay the foundation for a new order in which Israelis, Palestinians and their neighbors can live in peace and security.
“The German government is committed to this,” he said. “In our conviction, this goal is best achieved through the establishment of a Palestinian state alongside Israel.” 
Antisemitism in Germany
Merz also warned of growing antisemitism in Germany that, he said, too often goes unchallenged. He pledged that the government would do everything in its power to fight antisemitism in all its new and old forms.
“Jews must be able to live without fear throughout Germany. Jewish life must be able to continue to flourish in our society,” he said. “That is why we are acting with all determination against antisemitic incidents and attacks.”
He said the government would oppose those who relativize or question Israel’s right to exist, not only on this anniversary, but every day.

EU Considers Limits on Market Access and Funding for Sensitive Ukrainian Agricultural Products
The European Commission is proposing targeted arrangements that would significantly limit financial support and market access for certain sensitive Ukrainian agricultural products after Ukraine joins the EU, according to Hromadske.
The measures are part of a broader document package adopted on October 6, aimed at updating policies in preparation for future expansion of the European Union.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
European officials highlighted the substantial scale, structure, and high efficiency of Ukraine's farming sector as key reasons behind the proposal.
To manage the impact on the bloc, targeted mechanisms would substantially cap both funding and market access for specific sensitive items.
While Brussels did not specify which goods would face constraints, the policy document stressed the importance of helping Ukraine re-establish trade access to its historical export markets outside the European Union.
Ukrainian authorities expressed strong opposition to long-term trade caps during membership talks. Ukrainian Minister of Agrarian Policy and Food Taras Vysotskyi stated in an interview with Politico that Ukraine cannot agree to an accession framework that permanently restricts sales within the bloc.
Vysotskyi noted that temporary transitional periods are acceptable, but permanent restrictions contradict the core logic of full European Union membership.
He urged European partners not to view Ukraine solely as a competitive threat to local producers, pointing out that Ukrainian agriculture can help lower Europe's reliance on third-country imports of fertilizers, soy, and lysine, while expanding access to Black Sea shipping routes, according to Politico.
He added that the goal is to enter the single market not just as a supplier of raw grain, but as a producer of animal feed, food ingredients, processed products, and biofuels.
Previously, Ukraine’s Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food requested €220 million ($254 million) in non-repayable aid from the European Commission to support small and medium agricultural producers following Russian attacks on Black Sea ports.
The requested funding was intended to subsidize loan interest rates under the state "Accessible Loans 5-7-9%" program, helping farmers secure financing for the autumn sowing campaign amid sharp drops in crop prices and severely restricted export routes.

Morocco’s First F-16 Block 72 Fighter Takes Flight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:04:26 UTC
18:04:26 KST

Lockheed Martin conducted the first flight of an F-16 Block 72 fighter intended for the Royal Moroccan Air Force.
The company said the aircraft is moving into the flight-testing phase before being transferred to the customer.
The Block 72 is the latest and most advanced F-16 version, featuring upgraded avionics, cutting-edge sensors, enhanced combat mission systems, and improved safety and reliability features.
“The F‑16 remains a vital component of today’s and future air defense, and we’re proud of the role it will continue to play in supporting Morocco’s sovereignty and contributing to regional stability for decades to come,” the company stated.
In 2019, the U.S. Department of State approved the sale of 25 F-16V Block 72 fighters to Morocco, valued at an estimated $3.8 billion.
The package also includes 29 Pratt & Whitney F100-PW-229 engines and 26 AN/APG-83 radars.
The AN/APG-83 radar is a key component of the Block 72’s combat capabilities.
The AESA radar provides improved target detection and tracking, greater reliability, and better resistance to electronic warfare compared with older F-16 systems.
Combined with modern onboard computing systems, a helmet-mounted cueing system, and precision-guided munitions, this creates a fighter designed to detect and engage threats more quickly.
The contract also deepens Morocco’s integration into the U.S. defense ecosystem.
In 2004, Washington designated Morocco a major non-NATO ally of the United States. Since then, U.S.-Moroccan security cooperation has expanded to include combat aviation, ground forces, and long-range systems. Procurement has included F-16 fighter jets, M1 Abrams main battle tanks, AH-64E Apache attack helicopters, and HIMARS multiple rocket launchers. Last year, the Royal Moroccan Air Force received the first six of the 24 AH-64E Apache attack helicopters ordered.

Taiwan aims to halt birth rate decline next year

Unknown Publisher

09:03:55 UTC
18:03:55 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan aims to stop its birth rate from falling further next year, Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) said Tuesday.
The country has continued to expand childcare subsidies in response to its low birth rate. More than NT$210 billion (US$6.6 billion) is earmarked for related measures in next year’s central government budget, according to CTEE.
Cho said the package draws on the experiences of neighboring countries and covers several areas, including expanding education support, strengthening childcare services, promoting family-friendly workplaces, and reducing housing costs. He acknowledged that the policies would not produce immediate results, saying it could take one to two years for their effects to become apparent.
The initial goal is therefore to stop the birth rate from falling further before gradually raising it in subsequent years, Cho said. Taiwan recorded 107,812 births last year, marking the 10th consecutive year of decline and a new low, according to CNA.
The National Development Council projects that Taiwan’s population will continue to shrink as low fertility and an aging population reshape the country’s demographics. The number of newborns is projected to fall below 100,000 this year, according to CNA.
The package includes about NT$185 billion (US$5.82 billion) for a monthly NT$5,000 (US$157) child development allowance. Under the plan, children aged 0 to 18 would receive NT$5,000 per month, according to InsFeel.
For children aged 0 to 6, the allowance would be paid directly to their families. For those aged 6 and above, half of the monthly amount would instead be placed in a child savings account and could be withdrawn after the child reaches adulthood.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Ministry of Transportation and Communications held a bridge-joining ceremony to celebrate the halfway completion of the new Mataian Bridge, CNA reported.
Heavy rain from Typhoon Wipha caused landslides near the river and formed a barrier lake in July 2025. Two months later, heavy rain from Typhoon Ragasa caused the lake to overflow and fail, flooding central Guangfu Township, per UDN.
The original bridge, which ran along Provincial Highway 9, was destroyed by the barrier lake on Sept. 23. The transportation ministry's Highway Bureau set up a passage on the creek bed 18 days after the event, followed by a temporary bridge in October 2025 before the reconstruction, which began on Dec. 31, 2025.
Minister of Transportation and Communications Chen Shih-kai (陳世凱) said that the northbound section is now open and the southbound route is expected to be completed in July 2027. He added that the new bridge's piers will be broadened to strengthen durability.
The finished bridge will be 14 meters wide and 1,128 meters long, with a span of 85 meters. Its upper part uses steel beams protected by concrete panels, while the lower part uses full-casing piles. The piers are lined with steel plates for reinforced protection.
The bureau said that it has completed 282 beams and two piers. It added that southbound construction is currently at 66.51%, about 5.71% ahead of schedule.
Highway Bureau Director Lin Fu-shan (林福山) said joining the northbound section marks the final construction phase. Chen noted that builders Kseco and Cheng Shine Machinery also built New Taipei's Danjiang Bridge.

Chinese diplomats have also organized events to gain support from overseas Chinese communities for these goals, Hope said. During an event in France, Ambassador Deng Li said that overseas Chinese in France will “always firmly support the path of national development and consciously safeguard the core interests of the country.”
Attendees committed to “upholding their patriotic aspirations … and joining hands with their motherland to embark on a new journey of national rejuvenation”
During a similar event in the UK, the host Wu Lili declared in a speech that “all overseas Chinese in the (UK) have always upheld the original aspiration of ‘living in Britain but with hearts connected to China,’” according to Hope. UK Ambassador Zheng Zeguang said that overseas Chinese cultivate a strong patriotic spirit and become “promoters of the great cause of China’s unification.”
Hope said these statements are essentially loyalty oaths to the CCP, adding that “such statements are likely to become increasingly standard.”
He cited a China United Front magazine article as saying, “in the long run, the importance of overseas Chinese affairs related to Taiwan within the overall framework of overseas Chinese affairs work will undoubtedly become increasingly prominent.”
Hope said that while it is clear that overseas Chinese are an integral part of Beijing’s plan to annex Taiwan, “too little is known about the pledges and agreements made by overseas individuals and organizations with ties to the Party, and how they are working to provide practical support for an agenda that contravenes the interests.”

Taipei mayor inspects methadone treatment clinic as drug policy becomes issue

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) on Wednesday visited a methadone clinic to observe the city's opioid addiction treatment program as drug policy becomes an issue in the upcoming Taipei mayoral election.
Chiang visited the Taipei City Hospital Kunming Branch to learn about treatment practices. Staff explained that patients first consult a doctor and receive a prescription, and at the dispensing counter, their identity and prescribed dosage are verified before a nurse measures the medication.
Patients must drink the full dose and open their mouths so staff can confirm it has been swallowed. Throughout the process, patients must receive methadone under medical supervision and consume the medication at the clinic, per Upmedia.
Methadone is an opioid medication used to treat dependence on illicit drugs such as heroin. In Taiwan, it is classified as a Schedule II controlled drug and requires medical supervision for treatment and to reduce intravenous drug use health risks.
Taipei has provided such treatment since 2005, and is offered at four medical institutions: Taipei City Hospital's Kunming, Yangming, and Songde branches and the Beitou branch of Tri-Service General Hospital. Wang Chien-chun (王建淳), director of the Kunming Branch, said approximately 600 people receive methadone treatment in Taipei each year, per TVBS.
The mayor's visit comes amid a dispute with DPP Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) over drug prevention and harm-reduction policies. On Wednesday, Shen said methadone treatment and other harm-reduction efforts by health care workers had been unfairly politicized during the election campaign.
He welcomed Chiang's visit to the clinic and said he hoped it would help ease concerns among frontline medical workers. The Kunming center also operates a clean-needle program. Taipei has 19 automated clean-needle vending and collection machines, according to a Taipei City Hospital press release.
