Dutch government told to rule on 140,000 Ukrainian asylum claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:21:04 UTC
17:21:04 KST

Dutch government told to rule on 140,000 Ukrainian asylum claims
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The European Court of Justice has ordered the Dutch government to process the asylum applications of 140,000 Ukrainian refugees, adding to the pressure on an overstretched system.
Ukrainians who fled the country in the wake of the full-scale Russian invasion in February 2022 are covered by the European Union’s temporary protection rules, which give them the right to live, work and receive medical care in the Netherlands.
Under Dutch rules they are also required to apply for asylum, but until now the immigration service IND has shelved their applications because the European regulations give them more rights.
The European Court of Justice (ECJ) in Luxembourg said in a judgment last week that the rules requiring the Netherlands to process all asylum claims within 21 months also applied to people who fled Ukraine.
The case was brought by a man from the Chinese Uighur minority who was married to a Ukrainian woman and lived in Ukraine with his wife and child before the invasion.
He won a ruling at the district court in The Hague forcing the asylum minister to rule on his claim by January 2024. The court also imposed a conditional penalty on the government of €100 foe every day that a decision is overdue, up to a maximum of €7,500.
Extra pressure
The government appealed, and the case was referred to the ECJ, which said the man had the right to claim asylum as a third country national through the regular procedure even though he was already protected by the EU rules for Ukrainians.
Asylum minister Bart van den Brink admitted that the decision would put “extra pressure” on the system, but the court also recognised that the Netherlands needed time to process all 140,000 claims.
“For a long time we chose not to process claims from Ukrainians because of the fact that they were already protected,” he told NOS. “It’s also because it was a very large number. Now the court has clearly said we have to do it.”
The Netherlands is one of the few countries in the EU that require Ukrainian refugees to apply for asylum through the regular channels in addition to the EU’s temporary protection rules, which are currently valid until March 2028 but are reviewed every year.
“In hindsight it wasn’t such a good idea to link temporary protection to the submission of a claim for asylum,” asylum lawyer Wil Eikelboom said.
Waiting list
Vluchtelingenwerk, the Dutch refugee council, said the need to have asylum claims processed would cause “more worry and uncertainty” for Ukrainians. “Returning to Ukraine is not a realistic option at the moment,” a spokesman said.
Van den Brink said the government planned to deal with the Ukrainian applications in reverse order, beginning with people who have just arrived in the Netherlands and then working through the 5,000 who are currently on the waiting list for a first response from the government.
Ricky van Oers, lecturer in migration law at Radboud University in Nijmegen, said European rules allowed the government to take more time to process applications when there was a large number from a single country at once.
“They can also decide to prioritise certain groups, such as families,” he said.

‘We saw devastation’: IDF fighters return to haunting Kfar Aza photo that became an Oct. 7 symbol
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:20:36 UTC
17:20:36 KST

In uniform, standing beside the ruined holiday table in Rachel Cohen’s home in Kfar Aza, Yair rests his head against Netanel and bursts into tears. “We are human beings before we put on uniforms. We saw devastation,” the two said as they looked again at the photograph taken just two days after the Oct. 7 massacre.
Now, three years later, they have returned to the same house, the same table and the same memory.
A day before the war broke out, Lt. Col. Netanel Makayes, then head of Lotar, the IDF Counterterrorism School, landed in Israel after returning from a military delegation to the United States. On the morning of Saturday, Oct. 7, he woke to a phone call from a friend who lived near the unit’s base.
“Bro, I need you to help me with a force,” the friend told him. “Something crazy is happening in the south.”
After speaking with a team commander in the unit and receiving information through his wife, Adi, a Magen David Adom paramedic, Makayes decided to leave his home in Zikhron Ya’akov, saying goodbye to her and their daughter Tamar.
Sgt. 1st Class (res.) Yair Ansbacher also immediately understood what was happening. He said goodbye to his wife, Naama, and their five children and headed south, where he joined a force from the Counterterrorism School.
“We knew war was coming,” Ansbacher, who had worked in security research, said. “The moment I woke to the sirens in Jerusalem and saw the image of the pickup truck in Sderot, I knew a full-scale war had begun. It’s in our DNA to get up and move, going from zero to 100 in an instant.”
At the entrance to the Urim base, Makayes assembled a team from fighters already in the area. During the fighting, Ansbacher and another soldier joined him. The battle continued until Makayes received an order over the radio to head to Kibbutz Nir Yitzhak, where troops had gathered residents and were defending them.
That night, the two learned that the unit’s former commander, Lt. Col. Eli Ginsberg, had been killed. “To this day, I still can’t believe Eli was killed,” Makayes said. “He was an incredible fighter, someone you felt could not be hurt.”
On Oct. 7, the Lotar unit lost four of its fighters and commanders: Staff Sgt. Ben Rubinshtain, Master Sgt. (res.) Omri Belkin, Maj. (res.) Roee Negri and Maj. (res.) Sagi Golan.
The photograph taken on Oct. 9, 2023, came during a mission led by Lotar and marked the first time photographer Ziv Koren joined them. “No one was dealing with the media at the time, but the unit understood how important it was,” Ansbacher said of the decision to bring a photojournalist along. “They cleared the destruction very quickly. People did not see what we saw.”
With Koren accompanying them, the troops entered Kfar Aza. “It was still a combat zone. There were encounters, bodies scattered around, everything destroyed,” Ansbacher recalled. “You could clearly see where the fire had burned everything, where everything was scorched and riddled with holes, and where ordinary life had been.”
While documenting the devastation, they entered Rachel Cohen’s home. “At the entrance, there was still a sukkah with family photographs inside,” Makayes recalled. “There were two challahs on the table, and all around them were shrapnel, blood and destruction.”
It was there that Koren’s camera captured an unguarded moment between the two fighters. Standing beside the holiday table, Ansbacher could no longer hold back his tears. “That moment shook me to my core. Netanel was beside me and supported me. I didn’t even know Ziv had taken the picture,” Ansbacher said.
“Yair is like my brother,” Makayes added. “The melting pot of the military and the intensity of combat connect and unite people.” 
“We all cried there. It was a breaking point. There wasn’t a dry eye left,” Koren said. He said the image became a symbol in Israel and abroad because of the powerful emotion it conveys. “That moment, fighters standing in front of a holiday table with challah and wine on it, breaking down after days of fighting,” he said. “All the elements came together in that photograph. Someone looking at it can undergo a profound emotional experience and identify with that sense of rupture.”
Three years later, the three men returned to the entrance of the same home. “Each of us remembers a different detail,” Koren said. “The home blessing hanging by the entrance, the cabinet with the dishes, the bullet holes in the walls.”
“Since Oct. 7, I’ve been back to the kibbutzim dozens of times. I know every house here and the story of every person who was wounded, kidnapped or murdered,” Koren said. “Now I’m here with them, as they return for the first time since then. It’s deeply moving to come back together to the place where that moment, which became a symbol, was captured.”

US forces in Japan's Okinawa face alcohol ban, curfew after murder arrest

US forces in Japan’s Okinawa were on Wednesday barred from drinking alcohol for 48 hours and also face a 30-day curfew after the murder of a woman allegedly committed by an American Marine.
The case has triggered outrage in Japan, where any crimes involving US forces have long inflamed criticism of the troops' presence.
The governor of Okinawa, where the bulk on the 54,000 US military personnel are based in Japan, is due to meet the Japanese premier on Wednesday to voice his concerns.
Benjamin T. Watson, Okinawa area coordinator and commanding general of III Marine Expeditionary Force, announced a "complete prohibition of alcohol consumption on or off base" starting on Wednesday.
Watson said that the 48-hour period, described as "an operational pause", would give commanders the time to lead training with all service members on "standards, discipline, and our responsibilities as members of the Okinawan community".
During this period, operations will cease and "we will not allow off-base liberty", said Watson in a statement posted on X late on Tuesday.
The lieutenant general, the most senior US military figure on Okinawa, also announced a 30-day "period of reflection" beginning on Friday.
"During this period, we will implement a curfew in which liberty will expire at 2400 for all hands, meaning you must be back on base in your assigned quarters or at your off-base domicile from midnight to 0500".
Police said on Sunday that a US Marine stationed on Okinawa was arrested on suspicion of killing a 39-year-old woman at a hotel in the city of Naha and stealing her wallet.
Local media reported she was choked to death and that the Marine is denying the allegations.
The United States has around 54,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, mostly on Okinawa.
Crimes committed by US personnel have been a thorn in relations between the close security allies.
On Wednesday, Okinawa governor Genta Koja met Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi in Tokyo where he said the case had "caused deep anxiety" among Okinawa residents. He is due to meet Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi later on Wednesday.
"The prefectural government has repeatedly demanded that the US military take measures to prevent a recurrence every time an incident occurs, but the fact that such an incident has happened again forces us to conclude that discipline within the US forces and their human rights education are not functioning at all," he told Koizumi.
Koizumi said that he would "advance discussions with the United States on how to implement effective measures" to prevent such insidents occuring.
Last year, a Japanese court sentenced a US Marine accused of choking and attempting to rape a woman in her 20s to seven years in prison.
In 2017, a former US Marine and civilian military base worker was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa.
The same year, US Forces Japan temporarily banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated US Marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing its 61-year-old local driver.

Palestine: The Lost Team
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:17:02 UTC
17:17:02 KST

Al Jazeera World
Palestine: The Lost Team
A forgotten battle over football, identity and recognition – how a Jewish team competed as Palestine in the 1930s and beyond.
In 1934, a team called Palestine entered the qualifying rounds of the football World Cup in Mussolini’s fascist Italy. But it did not include any Palestinian players. It was drawn largely from the Jewish sporting movement under the British Mandate, at a time when football reflected the changing face of Palestine.
This documentary uncovers the forgotten history of Mandate-era football – how British rule, Zionist organisation and Palestinian exclusion shaped the makeup of the first team to compete internationally as Palestine. Through archives, interviews with specialist historians and the story of the 1934 qualifiers against Egypt, the film traces how the established football association became Israel’s, while Palestinian football was plagued by revolt, war and the 1948 Nakba. Decades later, Palestinians fought to reclaim their place in world football, finally securing FIFA recognition in 1998.

More
Why more Jewish people in Switzerland are considering a move to Israel
Three years on from the October 7 attacks, concern remains high among Switzerland’s Jewish community. “Violence against Jews has become commonplace,” Johanne Gurfinkiel, secretary general of CICAD, told the Keystone-SDA news agency.

More
Anti-Semitism in Switzerland
Some Jewish people choose to conceal their identity for fear of being stigmatised. Jewish children are being targeted at school, while Jewish institutions remain under heightened security. “There is no excuse for anti-Semitism,” said Gurfinkiel, stressing that criticism of Israeli government policy must not turn into collective blame against Jews.

Experts warn of ‘social contagion’ risk after school attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:16:21 UTC
17:16:21 KST

This photo shows Şeyh Şamil Imam Hatip Middle School, where the Oct. 6 school attack happened.
A series of school attacks in Türkiye has raised concerns over a potential “social contagion” effect, with experts warning that extensive media coverage and social media exposure could encourage copycat violence, particularly among vulnerable young people.
The latest incident occurred on Oct. 6 at Şeyh Şamil Imam Hatip Middle School in Istanbul’s Başakşehir district, where a 15-year-old student from another school stabbed students. Eight students were injured, one of whom later died. The incident followed attacks or shootings reported in Şanlıurfa, Kahramanmaraş, Manisa and Osmaniye in recent months.
Ayhan Erbay, founding director of Istanbul Kültür University’s Justice and Crime Lab, said research based on U.S. data suggests that a school attack remains “contagious” for about 13 days and is associated with an average of at least 0.22 subsequent incidents.
Another study found that intensive news coverage of school attacks increased the likelihood of subsequent attacks, with the effect lasting between four and 10 days, Erbay said.
Erbay also cited research from Finland showing that people interested in school attacks can form global online subcultures. While some seek to imitate attackers, others contribute to glorifying perpetrators or circulating their motives. “Heroization works in two directions,” Erbay said. “It is a reward given to the attacker afterward, but also a promise to the next person: Becoming someone everyone talks about instead of remaining invisible can be attractive.”
Barış Erdoğan, head of the Sociology Department at Üsküdar University, said violence that once remained largely within schools can now continue online, where images of incidents are recorded and widely circulated. “This can turn violence, for some young people, from an expression of anger into a display of power, visibility and status,” he said, while cautioning against attributing the problem solely to social media. Peer bullying, family problems, exclusion, anxiety about the future, lack of belonging and access to weapons or knives can also contribute.
Erbay urged media outlets to avoid making perpetrators identifiable, particularly when they are minors, and to refrain from publishing details that could facilitate imitation. He also advised against rankings or comparisons such as “deadliest attack,” which could create a perceived benchmark for future attackers. Instead, coverage should focus on victims, those who intervened and what families and institutions can do to prevent further violence, he said.
Parents described shock and fear following the Oct. 6 attack. One parent whose daughter attends the school called for stronger security measures, including controlled entry systems. “The children are not psychologically well. They saw very disturbing things,” the parent said. “This cannot continue like this.”
The Education Ministry said classes at the school were suspended on Oct. 6 and 7 and that psychosocial support had been launched for affected students, teachers and parents. It also said judicial and administrative investigations were underway and assigned two education inspectors to the case. The Radio and Television Supreme Council (RTÜK) said a court had imposed a broadcasting ban covering reports, interviews and commentary on the incident until the investigation is completed.

IMF chief signals austerity is back as global public debt heads for 100% of GDP
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:14:53 UTC
17:14:53 KST

IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva has urged heavily indebted governments to tighten their belts and central banks to take a hawkish stance, signalling a return to austerity as the energy shock from the Iran war, record public debt and a credit-fuelled AI investment boom weigh on the global economy.
The days when governments could lean on cheap money and fast growth to keep their debts in check are over, according to the head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), who called for spending discipline and tighter monetary policy around the world.
Speaking in Singapore on Wednesday, ahead of the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok next week, Kristalina Georgieva said policymakers "can no longer rely on higher growth rates alone to solve fiscal problems".
Worldwide public debt is close to levels last seen after World War II and could top 100% of GDP before 2030, the IMF chief warned, singling out developed economies as the "worst offenders".
"Yet, we don't see decisive action in the high-debt advanced economies where the need of the hour is for credible medium-term fiscal consolidation plans," Georgieva said, adding that "fiscal space is crying out for replenishment".
Borrowing costs are already climbing, she noted, with 10-year government bond yields in the US, Germany and Japan at their highest levels since 2007, 2009 and 1996 respectively.
On monetary policy, Georgieva described recent rate hikes by the US Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan as "highly appropriate".
"Now may be a good time for a prudently hawkish bias in many countries' monetary policy," she said.
The IMF chief also warned that the global economy is being pulled in opposite directions by a negative energy supply shock from the Iran war and a positive demand shock from artificial intelligence, adding that "the combined impact of these two forces is highly uneven across the world".
Oil prices remain at about $100 a barrel, she said, well above the $89 the IMF assumed for this year in its July forecasts, which put global growth at 3% in 2026 and 3.4% in 2027.
"Even if the war in the Gulf were to end soon, the problem of high energy prices will likely persist for some time," Georgieva said.
An AI boom with risks attached
"Love it, hate it, or fear it, AI is here," the IMF chief said, describing the technology as "rapidly becoming a key driver of countries' relative fortunes in the world economy".
If done right, AI could lift global growth by as much as half a percentage point a year, according to IMF estimates.
Over a decade, that would be like adding "an economy the size of ASEAN to the world economy", Georgieva said, referring to the Southeast Asian bloc.
But she cautioned that "the AI building boom is inflationary", with spending on the technology, relative to the size of the economy, likely to outstrip past investment waves in railways, power grids and telecoms.
A letdown for investors could become "a far-reaching shock," she warned.
Georgieva also flagged dangers ranging from job losses and cyberattacks to cutting-edge models that could "escape human control and run amok".
The IMF is due to publish updated global growth forecasts during next week's meetings in Bangkok.

Bulgaria halts rescue operation for crew of sunken ship
SOFIA, Oct 7 - Bulgaria has halted its search for the missing crew of a ship that sank after being hit by a drone on Tuesday about 70 nautical miles (130 km) off its coast, Vice-Admiral Rumen Nikolov of the Maritime Administration Executive Agency told Nova TV on Wednesday.
Early on Tuesday, two ships were hit in a drone attack in Bulgaria's Black Sea exclusive economic zone. One sank and the other was damaged. The crew of the damaged ship were rescued, but the crew of the sunken one remain missing.
Nikolov said the rescue operation for the crew of the sunken ship would not resume on Wednesday.
"There are no traces of the sailors from the first ship, and there will be none. There is also no information about drone remains," he said on a Nova TV morning show.
"A boat, three life rafts and parts of the ship's equipment have been found."
It was not immediately clear who carried out the attack involving air and sea drones in waters off the coastal town of Byala in eastern Bulgaria, but there are growing concerns about hybrid attacks by Russia as it wages war in Ukraine.
In an emailed statement to Reuters, the Russian embassy in Sofia said the merchant ship was not among the targets hit by Russian drones on Tuesday.
Nikolov said the incident occurred in a so-called "responsible search and rescue zone" and not in the country's territorial waters, which extend to 12 nautical miles off the coast.
In a separate incident, Romanian authorities said on Monday that two people had died in a fire on a ship in the Black Sea outside the country's territorial waters.
Bulgaria does not border either country, but as a NATO member it holds a strategic position on the Black Sea, where both Ukraine and Russia have major ports.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, speaking in a nightly video address, said an investigation jointly with Bulgaria's navy had shown that Russia was behind the attack.
Radev said on Wednesday that following the attack his government would approve the purchase of five more surface-to-air missile systems. REUTERS

Unknown Publisher

07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Moscow and Kyiv on Wednesday traded accusations concerning overnight airstrikes that killed at least 11 people in Ukraine. 
The Kyiv City Military Administration said in a statement on Telegram that the Ukrainian capital was attacked by Russia with ballistic missiles overnight, with damage from the strikes recorded in two districts of the city. 
“Tragically, two men were killed in the enemy shelling. … In the Podilskyi district, a missile struck a non-residential building, causing a fire,” the statement said. 
It further said that a missile strike ignited a fire at a garage cooperative in Kyiv’s Darnytskyi district, noting that the blaze had been extinguished, though damage occurred. 
“Debris also fell in an open area at a separate location,” it added. 
In the Dnipropetrovsk region, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said two people were injured in strikes that damaged an industrial enterprise, apartment buildings, and a sports club in the regional capital. 
Chernihiv Governor Vyacheslav Chaus said at least five people were killed and 25 others injured after a missile strike on an apartment building in the city of Pryluky, while Poltava Governor Vitaliy Dyakivnych said two people were killed and seven others injured in his region. 
“One of the key targets was our energy infrastructure. The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively. This was one of the most vile strikes: 70 missiles in total, many of them ballistic, as well as ‘shaheds.’ Unfortunately, only some of them were shot down,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on US social media company X.
Describing the overnight strikes as a “birthday gift” to Russian President Vladimir Putin, Zelenskyy said ballistic missiles remain the greatest challenge for Ukraine and that air defense packages for Kyiv are a “vital necessity.” He added that two more people were killed in the city of Oleksandriya in the Kirovohrad region. 
The Russian Defense Ministry claimed it launched a “massive strike” against Ukrainian military-industrial complex facilities in Kyiv and the Kyiv region, as well as in the Chernihiv, Kirovohrad, Dnipropetrovsk, Poltava, Kharkiv, and Odesa regions. 
The ministry also claimed that Russian air defenses downed 311 Ukrainian drones over 16 regions, as well as over the Black Sea, the Sea of Azov and Crimea, which Russia annexed in 2014. 
In Russia’s border region of Belgorod, Governor Alexander Shuvaev said seven people were injured over the past 24 hours in three districts due to Ukrainian strikes. 
In the Russian-controlled part of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region, Russian-installed Horlivka Mayor Ivan Prikhodko said three people were injured in a Ukrainian drone attack. 
Voronezh Governor Aleksandr Gusev said a power line was damaged in the southern part of his region due to falling debris, adding that several villages were temporarily without electricity and emergency services were working at the site. 
Ukraine’s Air Force claimed that its air defenses shot down 117 of 130 strike drones, as well as 44 ballistic and cruise missiles launched by Russia overnight. 
Separately, Zelenskyy claimed that Ukraine struck four targets that help Moscow "finance and wage its brutal war" over the past day, including two oil facilities and a training ground in Russia's Perm, Samara, and Astrakhan regions. 
Independent verification of the claims is difficult due to the ongoing war. 
Moscow and Kyiv have ramped up strikes in recent months, targeting each other’s logistics centers, ports, and energy infrastructure. 
They deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining that the strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities.

The Song of Stork and Dromedary: Nobel worthy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:12:07 UTC
17:12:07 KST

The Song of Stork and Dromedary: Nobel worthy
Molly Quell
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Novelist Anjet Daanje has been tipped as a serious contender for the Nobel prize in literature and, from her 2022 work The Song of Stork and Dromedary, for very good reason.
Published in Dutch as Het lied van ooievaar en dromedaris, the book is loosely based on the life of Emily Brontë, the author of Wuthering Heights. The work opens in 1847, with a villager laying out the body of Eliza May Drayden, who, like Brontë, has written a book widely derided at the time it was published but would go on to become a classic.
The opening scene is tinged with the Gothic horror of Wuthering Heights, Drayden’s eyes refuse to close for her burial.
The next 650 pages follow 11 interconnect stories that orbit around Drayden, and her sister Millicent, the fictionalised Charlotte Brontë who authored of Jane Eyre. Similar again to Wuthering Heights, all are largely set on the moors in England, though the final story takes the reader to the Daanje’s hometown of Groningen.
Rather than a traditional narrative, the book is written like an expansive biography, incorporating news articles, excerpts from diaries, letters, citations from fictional biographies and even parts of Drayden’s novel.
Each of the tales could be novellas in their own right, vivid and sometimes nail-biting, sending the reader off on tangents such as the mistreatment of two half-German sisters during the Second World War, or a pair of French half-sisters whose shared father creates a wedge between them.
The nature of sisterhood and the relationship between various female characters is one of the central themes of The Song of Stork and Dromedary. The work also reflects on the status of women at different times across the novel’s 200-year span.
Death is another important theme. Drayden’s death, with which the book opens, is an event that brings characters together but also tears them apart.
Anjet Daanje published eight novels before The Remembered Soldier (De herinnerde soldaat) became a hit in 2019. It was longlisted for the Libris Literature Prize, took home the F. Bordewijk Prize and the English-translation, which was published in 2025, was longlisted for International Booker Prize and included on The New York Times Book Review’s 100 Notable Books of 2025.
The Song of Stork and Dromedary took home both the Boekenbon Literature Prize and the Libris Literature Prize, the first book to ever net both awards. It was named the Best Book of the Century by the NRC newspaper. The English translation was published this year.
In 2023, Daanje was awarded the Constantijn Huygens Prize for her oeuvre.
The book was translated by David McKay, who also translated War and Turpentine by Stefan Hertmans and Multatuli’s Max Havelaar. He renders the complicated work thoughtfully, retaining Daanje’s character.
The Song of Stork and Dromedary is compelling and brilliant, and the author is worthy of the highest honour in literature.
The Nobel prize for literature winner will be announced on Thursday by the 18 members of the Swedish Academy.
You can get your copy at the American Book Center.

Israel continues demolishing buildings in Gaza a year after ceasefire
With almost the entire population homeless, displaced Palestinians face an unrecognisable landscape
It’s perhaps the most dramatic wound inflicted on the Gaza Strip by Israel’s military campaign over the past three years: the city of Rafah, once home to a quarter million people, has been erased.
Satellite imagery shows the Israeli military has systematically razed the southern city and other towns and districts to the ground and in some places ploughed away the rubble. Demolition, using bulldozers and explosives, has continued unabated since the Israel-Hamas ceasefire deal reached a year ago, as the military solidifies its hold over the around 60 per cent of the territory that it still controls.
Gaza’s mangled landscape is just one of the wounds on top of wounds that the enclave’s 2 million Palestinians have endured since Israel launched its campaign to destroy Hamas after the militants’ October 7, 2023, attack on southern Israel.
More than one out of every 10 people from Gaza’s pre-war population has been killed or wounded by Israeli fire. While nearly every family mourns dead or cares for wounded, most also had to move multiple times to escape fighting and Israeli evacuation orders.

Antwerp police to arrest known troublemakers even when they are not committing any offence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:10:23 UTC
17:10:23 KST

Antwerp local police are to arrest known troublemakers more quickly, even if they are not doing anything wrong at the time. Those arrested will also immediately be detained for up to 12 hours, the maximum allowed. The new approach is set out in an internal memo seen by daily Gazet van Antwerpen. The police have also confirmed the switch to VRT NEWS. In this way, the police and the city aim to protect quality of life and encourage people to accept help. According to the Human Rights League, this approach is not lawful.
Antwerp police to arrest known troublemakers even when they are not committing any offence
Antwerp police are compiling a list of troublemakers, whom they also refer to as ‘claimers, a word used to refer to a known repeat offender or structural nuisance maker.’. “You aren’t simply registered as a claimer. These individuals are known for systematically causing a nuisance,” say the police.
Under the new guidelines, these claimers must be immediately placed under administrative detention for up to 12 hours if they are found anywhere, for example during a check. It is no longer necessary for them to be committing a criminal offence or actually causing a disturbance at that moment.
“This approach aims to protect the quality of life in Antwerp, to report people without lawful residence to the Immigration Service, and to refer people with addiction problems to support services.”
The police have discussed the approach with the office of Mayor Els van Doesburg (Flemish nationalist N-VA). According to the mayor’s office, there are as yet no administrative means to compel people to seek help.
“As long as we cannot compel these individuals to seek support services, we will, in the meantime, use this approach to strongly encourage them to accept help,” says spokesperson David Cleiren.
The measure applies throughout the city of Antwerp, but in practice is mainly enforced in Antwerp’s North District. This is a neighbourhood that the city itself has designated as a ‘neighbourhood requiring special attention’. Systematic identity checks had already been introduced there previously. Regular checks are also carried out to tackle public nuisance behaviour.
“Unlawful”
According to the Human Rights League, the approach is unlawful. “Making someone feel unsafe is not sufficient grounds for administrative detention,” says chair Kati Verstrepen.
“The Police Act permits administrative detention, but only if someone is actually disturbing the peace. You cannot simply detain people preventively just because you think they are going to disturb public order.”

China has called bilateral trade ties with the 27-member EU “highly integrated and mutually dependent,” stressing a need for dialogue over trade “concerns.”

The EU imported €559.4 billion ($634 billion) in goods from China in 2025 while exporting €199.6 billion, leaving a goods trade deficit of €359.8 billion.

Defense industry leader says firms getting Ukraine funds should be disclosed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:08:00 UTC
17:08:00 KST

Minister warns revealing defense companies supplying Ukraine would expose them to Russian threats
Estonian defense companies receiving state funding to support Ukraine should be publicly named, says Taavi Veskimägi, the head of the defense industry council, while Minister of Defense Martin Herem argues that disclosing the firms would endanger them.
All companies receiving state money have signed non‑disclosure agreements with the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK), Veskimägi said on an ERR webcast.
"But I definitely think this should be public. I don't see any reason why it shouldn't or couldn't be public," he said.
"There is a clear effect here: Estonian products go to Ukraine using Estonian taxpayers' money. By sending these products to Ukraine, we actually finish them there, because every defense industry product is ultimately completed on the battlefield. And if one day we need them here in Estonia, we won't be dealing with prototypes. We will get products from Estonian companies that have been tested in Ukraine and have earned their combat credentials there," Veskimägi said.
"And when our own boys and girls have to use them, we know it's something reliable, something we can trust. So the more Estonian companies benefit from this measure, the more Estonia benefits, the more our defense capability benefits, and the more Estonian companies benefit," he added.
In September, the Ministry of Defense said it would not disclose which Estonian companies received financial support to help Ukraine, citing security concerns. In 2025 and 2026, Estonia purchased €200 million worth of Estonian defense industry products for Ukraine.
Veskimägi said all interested parties, including Russia, will find out who these companies are anyway.
"The only ones who don't know today are the general public, and because of that we lack an understanding of what capabilities we have sent to Ukraine for €100 million. Are these capabilities and technologies also needed for Estonia's defense? Does one company receive most of the funding, or is it distributed among many companies, which would be in the interest of Estonia's defense industry sector? Then we could have a public discussion about it, as well as a professional discussion between the Estonian Defense Industry Association and the Ministry of Defense about what kind of defense industry we actually want to develop in Estonia and whether this Ukraine measure supports that development," Veskimägi said.
Veskimägi said dozens of Estonian defense industry products have proven themselves on the battlefield in Ukraine.
The state should help ensure the security of defense companies
Veskimägi said Estonia has 260 defense companies. "Estonian defense industry companies today offer many technologies for many capabilities," he said.
Speaking about the arson attack on Milrem's production building, Veskimägi said defense companies have been aware of such risks for years and have made their own risk plans. "But the Milrem incident once again highlighted that this is something that cannot be ignored, must be addressed and must be invested in," he said.
"As a result, we agreed with security agencies to increase security briefings for companies and make them more frequent. I believe companies themselves will invest even more in their security systems, especially perimeter security. It was bad, but in some ways a necessary wake‑up call for our companies that this is something that must be dealt with," Veskimägi said.
Since most defense companies cannot ensure high‑level security on their own, Veskimägi said the state should step in.
"If the state sees — and the current coalition has said that defense industry and its development are priorities, which is a prominent part of the coalition agreement — then the state must provide support and guidance. Security agencies must support these companies by giving them a clear picture of the threats around us, because companies are simply not capable of doing this themselves in most cases, and they also lack the money to do it," Veskimägi said.
Defense minister: Naming firms funded for Ukraine would put them at risk
Defense Minister Martin Herem says he would not disclose which Estonian defense companies receive government funding to support Ukraine, arguing that doing so would endanger those firms. He added that disclosure could be considered if the companies themselves request it.
"In my view, there is no need to make them public, because they could become targets for the Russian Federation's special services, just as Foreign Minister [Sergei] Lavrov has threatened and as has already happened in Estonia and elsewhere," Herem told ERR.
Herem said disclosure could be reconsidered if the companies agree to it.
"Right now, my understanding is that we have an agreement with them not to disclose. If the contract says we do not disclose, then we will not. If the companies say they want it or agree to it, then of course we can do it. It's somewhat a matter of agreement, and the Defense and Aerospace Industry Association has been involved in the process. If they have proposals, they should come to the Ministry of Defense and we will review them," Herem said.
He added that he does not shape his positions based on media commentary.
"In the media we can say all sorts of things. I have no intention of making any changes because of this. There is a commission that deals with reviewing Ukraine aid — the principles on which we provide it and how. This topic will likely come up in that work. But if you ask whether opinions expressed in the press influence me much, honestly, I cannot even keep track of them," Herem said.
This article has been updated on 7 October with a comment from Defense Minister Martin Herem.

jaguar type 01 launches electric era with four-door grand tourer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:07:39 UTC
17:07:39 KST

jaguar type 01 launches electric era with four-door grand tourer
the first production model on jaguar’s dedicated electric architecture combines a low-slung gt profile with more than 1,000ps, 400 miles of EPA range, and an explicitly british design lineage.
Jaguar Type 01 brings its electric design language to production
After revealing the Type 01’s interior back in August, including its distinctive full-length central ‘spine,’ Jaguar now unveils the finished electric GT in New York, marking the first production model in a new generation for the British marque. Designed, engineered, and built in the UK, the Type 01 is an all-electric four-door grand tourer developed on Jaguar’s dedicated Electric Architecture (JEA). Its arrival introduces a new approach to the proportions, performance, and occupant experience of Jaguar’s next generation of electric vehicles.
The Type 01 is defined by a long bonnet, low roofline, and stretched silhouette, with proportions that recall the E-type and XJS while establishing a new visual language for the electric era. Jaguar says the design began with a single line and a blank sheet of paper, allowing its aerodynamic requirements to shape the clean, elongated surfaces of the car.
Turning heritage into a new identity
Underneath the bodywork is JEA, an 850-volt electrical architecture developed specifically for Jaguar’s next generation of electric vehicles. The Type 01 produces more than 1,000PS and is claimed to offer a 400-mile EPA range. The British vehicle brand says the vehicle can add 200 miles of range in 13 minutes when connected to a 350kW charger. The technical specifications position the Type 01 as a vehicle around which Jaguar is rebuilding its approach to performance and design.
The Type 01’s name also establishes the logic for the new generation. ‘Type’ refers to Jaguar’s history of naming significant vehicles, ‘0’ refers to zero tailpipe emissions, and ‘1’ identifies it as the first model in the new product series.
From E-type references to a new identity
Jaguar’s challenge is to use recognizable elements of its past without allowing heritage to become the entire design language. The Type 01’s long bonnet, low proportions, and emphasis on a dramatic silhouette make that connection explicit, while its electric platform allows the company to reconsider the relationship between exterior form and mechanical architecture.
Its New York launch occupied parts of Times Square, DUMBO, and the Lower East Side before moving to STORIED in West Chelsea, where visitors encountered objects representing different stages of the Type 01’s development. One of these was an aluminum version of the original line drawn by Jaguar’s designers at the beginning of the program. Another, described as the ‘Impossible Panel,’ represented the engineering effort required to translate the vehicle’s complex body shape into a production form. Jaguar also presented tire marks taken from its test track, pointing to the hundreds of thousands of kilometers of development and validation behind the car’s stated combination of composed and dynamic driving characteristics.

Taming the Curse of Dimensionality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:04:09 UTC
17:04:09 KST

Many problems in computing boil down to a deceptively simple question: given one thing, how do you find the thing most similar to it? Imagine, for example, that you want to find the person who is physically closest to you. The answer seems obvious when there are only a few people around. But what happens when we have to search through increasingly complex spaces?
When you're standing in a straight line and want to find the person closest to you, the job is simple: you look left and then right, comparing your distance to the people around you. If you're in a room, however, you need to find the closest person in two-dimensional space. Again, it's not much of a problem since you can turn around and check the distances in different directions.
What if people could float in 3D space? In this case, things become complicated because you have to search in height, depth, and width. By adding a temporal dimension, things start to get frustrating. As the number of dimensions keeps growing, the task quickly becomes impractical.
Here's the shocking truth: much real-world data is represented in far higher dimensions, sometimes 100 dimensions or even more! Hence, the apt adjective “cursed” is used to describe this data.
An innovative solution for quick search among similar data in large datasets was proposed by Dr. Vahab Mirrokni, an Iranian researcher and graduate of Sharif University of Technology and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). His "Locality-Sensitive Hashing" (LSH) algorithm is now considered one of the popular hashing techniques in big data processing and artificial intelligence. Mirrokni, who is now a senior researcher at Google, was awarded the Mustafa(pbuh) Prize in 2025 in recognition of this achievement.
For a better grasp of this technique, we must first address one of the fundamental challenges of the age of data, a challenge which has made finding a piece of valuable information among a vast amount of data like searching for a needle in an ever-growing haystack.
Cursed Data
With the advancement of technology and the emergence of diverse forms of data into the world of computing and processing, we have encountered cursed data with remarkably high dimensionality. A color image of 1000 x 1000 pixels (where each pixel is one dimension) is considered a three-million-dimensional data on a computer! This is because each pixel is represented by the triple combination of red, green, and blue values, which is one of the standard methods of storing color images. Even after applying dimensionality reduction methods, we still deal with hundreds or thousands of dimensions in image processing.
When processing text files, we enter the realm of natural language processing, where words are converted into numerical vectors using certain methods. Each word is assigned an n-dimensional numerical vector (100-300 dimensions) so that similar words have similar vectors. Then, to process a text, key words are identified, extracted, and examined. With these methods, a text, which consists of several words, becomes highly dimensional. Thus, a paragraph can have tens of thousands of dimensions!
Another class of data that has received a lot of attention in the last decade is genetic data. Each cell of every living being contains a molecule called DNA, which is made up of four types of simpler molecules called bases. Given that the length of DNA in humans reaches about 3 billion base pairs, when represented and analyzed computationally, this enormous sequence can give rise to extremely high-dimensional data. Parts of DNA, called genes, are largely conserved over generations, determining the function of an organism's body. The preservation of each human's DNA information can be done in two ways: either the entire molecular sequence is preserved, or only parts of the gene, of which there are approximately 25,000 parts with different lengths, are preserved. In either case, we face a vast amount of information.
Close, Yet So Far Away: The Challenge of Searching in High-Dimensional Data
In such a high-dimensional space, the “curse of dimensionality” occurs. The data is uncommonly sparse, so that almost everything is equally spaced apart. In other words, the concept of “similarity” disappears as all data looks almost identical, and searching for the nearest neighbor becomes an impossible mission and computation becomes impractical.
Searching for the closest neighbor is one of the central issues in data science, machine learning, and information retrieval. The main objective of this process is to find the nearest point (or points) to a given point, which can be determined based on a similarity criterion. There are various metrics for measuring data distance, two of the simplest of which are Euclidean distance and Manhattan distance. In the former, the length of the line segment that directly connects two points in space is measured, while in the latter, the distance is calculated as if moving from one point to another step by step, that is, the sum of the differences in the data across different dimensions.
On the surface, it seems a straightforward job to find the image that most closely resembles our target image from an image database, or to find the most genetically similar organisms to create an evolutionary family tree, but these tasks present highly complex challenges. Sometimes there may be requirements for detecting textual similarity and plagiarism, or analyzing the emotions expressed in the texts. The advertising market and recommendation systems are not exempt from these challenges if they want to recommend a product based on individuals’ tastes and those of similar users. In fact, in all these cases, we are only looking for the most similar data to a specific data point. If the data were low-dimensional, the answer would be ready within a fairly reasonable time using traditional methods and fast algorithms. However, what makes it difficult to meet the demands is their high dimensionality.

Israel pauses in moment of silence to remember those killed on 7 October
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:00:41 UTC
17:00:41 KST

A group representing the bereaved families organised tributes, including a silence at 6:29am - the minute the attack began - and a ceremony that will follow tonight in Tel Aviv.
Israelis gathered in a moment of silence on Wednesday to mark three years since the Hamas-led attack of 7 October 2023, which a UN inquiry confirmed killed 1,200 people and saw 252 taken hostage.
In southern Israel, families mourned at road junctions, bomb shelters and the site of the Nova music festival, all places overrun by militants in the deadliest attack against Israel.
It is the first anniversary on which all the hostages that survived have returned home, bringing a new phase of mourning.
Among those marking the day was Elkana Bohbot, 37, who was abducted from the Nova festival and is spending the anniversary in Israel for the first time. He was freed last year after 738 days in captivity, most of it in a tunnel 50 metres underground. He said his daughter's birth in August this year was a message to his captors that "we [Israelis] were here, and we will always be here forever".
At the site of the Nova music festival, where Hamas militants in trucks and paragliders opened fire around dawn on October 7, family members bowed their heads in silence, although AFP reported at least one put on techno music in tribute to the fallen.
European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen paid her respects to the victims and their families in a post on X.
"The unspeakable savagery and terror of 7 October must never happen again," she wrote.
"The EU remains ready to help turn today's fragile ceasefire into a durable peace, based on a two-state solution."
The ceasefire von der Leyen referred to took effect last October, two years into the war Israel launched against Hamas in response to the attack.
Up to 75,000 Palestinians have been killed in the retaliatory campaign, according to the UN.
The UN said this summer that about 1.7 million Palestinians, roughly 80% of the population, were living in tents and temporary accommodation while Israeli maps show more than half of the Gaza strip is now controlled by its troops.
On Wednesday, AFP reporters in Israel heard loud bangs from across the border in Gaza during the commemorations as Israel carried out new strikes, despite the ceasefire agreement.
Gaza officials said at least two people were killed in overnight strikes in the region, most of which has been reduced to rubble.
Wednesday's gatherings were separate from the government's official memorial services, held on 5 October to fall closer to the anniversary in the Hebrew calendar.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed there would be "no forgiveness for the murderers" and promised never to allow Hamas to rule in Gaza.
More than 200 former hostages and relatives wrote to Netanyahu last year demanding an inquiry into the 7 October attacks or his resignation but Israel's leader opted to publish redacted government documents instead of launching an investigation and described the attacks as "a serious intelligence failure".
An election follows at the end of the month.

Police routinely failing to investigate ‘revenge porn’, research reveals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:00:38 UTC
17:00:38 KST

Police forces are routinely failing to investigate complaints about the circulation of image-based abuse, previously known as “revenge pornography”, according to research that has triggered a super-complaint over the way such crimes are handled.
Lawyers have gathered evidence from 100 people who reported intimate images being shared online without their consent. Their research suggests that image-based abuse is still frequently dismissed or not recognised as criminal offending, despite being described by the former prime minister Keir Starmer as a national emergency.
Referrals to the Revenge Porn helpline, the charity that helps victims get non-consensual images removed from the internet, increased by more than 4,000% between 2015 and 2025, but data from 39 police forces in England and Wales shows that charges were lodged against perpetrators in an average of just 4.5% of cases last year. In some forces the figure was lower than 1%.
Some police officers responded inappropriately when women tried to register complaints, researchers found. One reported that the officer “almost giggled on the phone to me”, while another said the officer responded: “Boys will be boys.” Another said: “I bet you’ve learned your lesson.”
Image-based abuse overwhelmingly affects women and girls, who make up 98.9% of reported images.
Lawyers from Leigh Day and the charity the Centre for Women’s Justice are working with the charity #NotYourPorn to highlight systemic police failings in responding to image-based abuse, defined as “the taking, sharing or creating of intimate content without the survivor’s consent, or threatening to do so”.
They note that rapid innovations in AI are helping abusers find new ways to create and disseminate synthetic explicit material, sometimes known as deepfake content.
Their research classifies the policing response as “fragmented, inconsistent and incapable of meeting the scale of the threat posed by image-based abuse”. “Despite the increased public awareness, and the creation of new criminal offences designed to address this conduct, there has been no corresponding increase in charging rates, prosecutions or convictions,” the complaint says.
“The unavoidable conclusion is that the overwhelming majority of this offending goes unaddressed.”
Home Office data shows that there were only 569 charges issued for image-based abuse in 2025/2026. The Revenge Porn Helpline received almost 25,000 reports in 2025.
Researchers found that the vast majority of survivors of image-based abuse did not report it to the police, noting that “embarrassment, shame and fear” contributed to their reluctance. Police outsourced the evidence-gathering process to survivors in many cases, the report notes, leaving them to work out how to collate proof that the images were being disseminated widely and how to get the content removed from the internet.
“It felt like to them it wasn’t a priority, it wasn’t even a crime,” one woman told researchers. Another said: “Police involvement has not alleviated the harm caused by this offence. Instead, it has intensified my distress and left me feeling powerless and completely unsupported as a victim.”
A police super-complaint is a mechanism introduced in 2018 to allow concerns to be raised about ways in which the police operate that may significantly harm the interests of the public generally, rather than focusing on an individual force of officer.
The complaint will be jointly considered by the College of Policing and the Independent Office for Police Conduct, which will decide whether to respond by opening a wider investigation.
Harriet Bland, a lawyer with the Centre for Women’s Justice, said: “Without an urgent overhaul of police guidance and training on image-based abuse – which must be regularly updated – and a clear national strategy rolled out across forces, survivors will continue to be let down.”

‘The nurse used the torch on her phone to do the op’: hospitals stripped of resources in Ukraine’s occupied territories
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:00:38 UTC
17:00:38 KST

Earlier this summer, the once bustling corridors of the district hospital in Hola Prystan, a city in the Russian-occupied Kherson region of Ukraine, were ominously quiet. At times, it was plunged into darkness during power cuts lasting hours.
Much of the hospital’s medical equipment and supplies had been stolen and redirected to the military, and many experienced staff had gone.
“They [the Russian forces] even took some of the furniture,” says Natalia Sergeevna, who spent more than two decades working as a nurse in the hospital before escaping to Ukrainian-held territory in July.
In some ways, her hospital had been lucky, she says, with others in Russian-occupied territories repurposed for military use – as has been happening in regions bordering Ukraine – or simply closed down.
Despite its bare-bones infrastructure and dark corridors, people still came to the hospital, says Sergeevna, often making difficult journeys across the mine-infested landscape of occupied Kherson.
“They came with injuries and wounds; they came looking for oncologists or endocrinologists or palliative care. Women still came with pregnancies,” she says, “but every day it was getting harder to help them.”
In recent months, the situation has deteriorated further, with blockades and supply shortages leaving some Russian-occupied territories with limited medical support.
In June, the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine said conditions in Oleshky and Hola Prystan, where Sergeevna worked, were becoming desperate, with thousands of people left without food, water and medicines.
It said ambulances had stopped coming to people’s homes, with medical assistance only available for the most urgent cases and patients dying during attempted evacuations.
Sergeevna says she had stayed in the hope of liberation, but by the summer things had become unbearable. “There is almost no available support to do any kind of surgeries; even basic procedures like removing polyps aren’t possible.
“In one case this year, we were performing a C-section, and the woman developed uterine bleeding, but there was no blood available for transfusion, because all of the supplies had been sent to the [Russian] soldiers,” she says.
Another obstacle is the forced “passportisation” of the population in occupied territories, with medical services refused to people who do not have a Russian compulsory health insurance policy, which can only be obtained through a Russian passport.
“They treat you very badly if you are Ukrainian. We have no rights, they tell us to our face, ‘you’re a nobody’,” says Marina*, who lives in a town occupied by Russian forces. She says she had to be taken to hospital in 2023 after she developed complications during her pregnancy and went into early labour.
“The baby was coming with the backside down, and I needed an emergency C-section. I was in a lot of pain,” she says. “But it was 11.30pm, and the curfew was in place. We tried getting out, but they shot at us.”
Marina says she spent an excruciating night cared for by her husband and a neighbour, before rushing to the clinic as soon as the curfew lifted. “When we got there, there was no obstetrician, no qualified staff for pregnancy, no one to help. I eventually had a C-section with the help of my neighbour, who was a nurse, and thankfully my baby and I survived.
“In a normal circumstance, we would have known about this complication, but because there were no tests or medical professionals left in our town, not even an ultrasound machine, I had no way of diagnosing this,” she says.
In another case, from earlier this year, Sergeevna says her colleagues were forced to treat a patient with endometriosis without anaesthesia.
“She was bleeding when she came to the hospital. So there was no anaesthesia, not even power. And the nurse at the time used the torch on her phone to do the procedure because there was no other option.”
Accurate figures are not available; but organisations monitoring the situation in the region detect an anecdotal rise in maternal and child mortalities, as well as long-term health problems. There are also reports of difficulties in accessing contraceptives and abortion.
Sergeevna says the situation is particularly acute for women, and that she had been dealing with women facing a range of mental health issues because of the lack of medical care and trauma they had suffered, including rape and sex slavery.
She says one 18-year-old had come with the letter “Z” cut into her torso with a blade. While inspecting her wound, Sergeevna discovered the girl had been raped. “But that was not why she came to us; she was too ashamed to admit that. She came only because she couldn’t tolerate the wound any more because of swelling and inflammation.”
With few doctors left in her district and depleting resources, Sergeevna and her team did their best to stitch her up. “But there was nothing else we could do for her. There were no resources to check her for STDs or provide her with contraceptives. We did not even have any way to provide psychological support.”
* Name has been changed

Wearable drone detector unveiled for individual soldiers
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:00:22 BST
17:00:22 KST

A drone detector light enough to be worn by a single soldier, and able to analyse the radio spectrum for threats that are not yet in any threat library, has been launched by the Swindon-based company MyDefence, the firm stated.
The device, called Wingman Edge, weighs under a kilogram, which the company puts at 17 per cent lighter than the generation it replaces. It combines signature-based detection, meaning it recognises signals already catalogued, with continuous artificial intelligence analysis of the spectrum running on the device at the same time.
That second capability is the part of the device the company is selling hardest. Rather than only matching against a stored library, the system is designed to identify and classify a wider range of activity including drone signals, controllers, communications links, Wi-Fi, analogue video and signals it has never seen before.
Dan Hermansen, chief executive of MyDefence, said: “The evolving drone threat does not wait for a database to be updated. For more than a decade, we have put wearable drone detection into the hands of soldiers. Wingman Edge builds on that foundation by giving the individual soldier a much deeper understanding of what is happening in the spectrum around them, including activity that does not match an existing signature.”
Processing on the device rather than in a remote system matters in the places this equipment is meant to work, since a soldier in a jammed or disconnected environment cannot wait for a server somewhere else to tell him what he is listening to. The system is passive, monitoring the electromagnetic environment without radiating anything itself, which keeps the wearer from becoming a target for the sort of equipment that homes on emissions.
Individual units can share detections with other soldiers, vehicles and connected systems, so that what one man picks up feeds a wider picture. Underlying all of it is what the company calls MyDefence Spectrum Intelligence, its software layer combining radio frequency data, threat knowledge and machine learning.
MyDefence says the United States Army has bought its wearable drone detection systems to a cumulative value of 77 million dollars over the past eighteen months, which is a considerable sum for equipment carried on a soldier’s body armour.
Wingman Edge is the first of what the company is calling its Edge Generation, a family of products intended to push sensing and processing out to deployed platforms rather than back to headquarters. The direction of travel matches what has been learned in Ukraine, where small drones have made the ability to detect an approaching threat in the last few seconds a matter of individual survival rather than a staff function.

====================================================================================================

Loyalty vs. Competence: Pete Hegseth’s policies have become the Pentagon&#039;s greatest threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:00:18 UTC
17:00:18 KST

Despite the “strange war” Donald Trump is waging against Iran, the purges at the Pentagon have continued unabated in recent months. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has fired some generals without warning and blocked others from promotion, all while using the Pentagon’s civilian leadership to impose Donald Trump’s political and cultural agenda on the military. Meanwhile, the world’s most powerful fighting force is running short of ammunition, its personnel are exhausted, and its staffing levels have been depleted. Experts say Hegseth has created (or, at the very least, exacerbated) many of these problems himself — focusing more on political issues and the loyalty of his generals than on supplying the military and ensuring the competence of his subordinates.
The blitzkrieg drags on
Criticism of Pete Hegseth had been building for months before some Republicans in Congress finally began challenging the Trump administration’s agenda when it comes to military affairs. Finally, it was Republican Congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky who, on Sept. 15, introduced eight articles of impeachment against the defense secretary in the House of Representatives. Three accuse Hegseth of launching the war ing Iran without congressional authorization, while the others concern alleged abuses against civilians, the legality of military operations against drug traffickers and Yemeni Houthis, and the reprisals against Senator Mark Kelly after the Arizona Democrat called on service members to refuse to obey unlawful orders.
Other Republicans, however, secured enough votes to postpone consideration of Massie’s motion until November — after the midterm elections. Congress is likely to take the matter up in the future provided that Democrats gain control of the chamber (as polls currently suggest that they will).
There are ample grounds for criticism of Hegseth. The war launched by the United States and Israel in February was initially intended to swiftly decapitate the leadership in Tehran, resulting in a pro-Western shift. The allies achieved the first objective but not the second: after the old leadership was eliminated, power in Iran consolidated in the hands of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which has not been afraid to escalate the conflict.
In September, the war shifted toward oil exports and maritime routes, with the U.S. beginning to strike Iranian oil tankers and Tehran responding with attacks on commercial vessels. Iranian missiles also began striking ever closer to American ships, and shortly after Saudi Arabia asked the United States for military assistance, Iranian attacks damaged a critical overland pipeline that had become an alternative to the waterborne route. Iran-backed Houthis also recently seized footholds in another part of the region’s maritime corridor, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The U.S. administration is now being forced to plan for a long war. Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly even warned Trump that Iran could continue resisting until the end of his term — meaning early 2029 — a message that is consistent with what Hegseth is hearing from his own generals. According to the Washington Post, as early as August the military’s top commanders told the Pentagon chief that the war could not continue indefinitely at its current pace given that U.S. Central Command, which oversees the Middle East, has kept more than 50,000 troops on heightened combat readiness for months.
As early as August, the military’s top commanders told Hegseth that the war in Iran could not continue indefinitely at its current pace
Generals are concerned that the operational tempo is increasing, service members are growing exhausted without relief, and rotations may not come until early 2027 (or even later). Meanwhile, stocks of precision-guided weapons are not being replenished.
When the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln recently pulled into port in Thailand after a 286-day deployment – one of the longest in the U.S. Navy's modern history – sailors complained about poor living conditions, a lack of variety in their food, and their deteriorating psychological state. Trump, however, responded that the carrier had been at sea for “not long enough.”
Chief of Naval Operations Daryl Caudle said outright that the Navy could not sustain the current level of operations against Iran with no end date in sight and sailors already stretched to their limits. Even U.S. convoys helping tankers pass through the Strait of Hormuz are now operating on a limited schedule and no longer providing 24-hour air-defense coverage. The United States is, of course, still capable of waging war against Iran, but its problems are mounting — and not only in the Middle East. As forces have been pulled in from other regions, deterrence of other potential U.S. adversaries, above all China and Russia, has weakened, generals warn.
Generals vs. the secretary
The resource shortage is compounded by strained relations between the secretary and the military leadership. For the past year and a half, Hegseth has systematically purged the top brass, removing officers he considers disloyal to his political agenda.
Although the U.S. military is subordinate to civilian political leaders, the armed forces have traditionally enjoyed considerable professional autonomy. The assessments of the Joint Chiefs of Staff have often differed from what politicians wanted to hear, and military leaders themselves handled operational planning and execution, assessed military risks, developed doctrine and standards, and made promotion recommendations.
Trump and Hegseth began “purging” the military leadership almost immediately after the current administration came into office. The president fired Joint Chiefs Chairman Charles Brown, while Hegseth ousted then-Chief of Naval Operations Lisa Franchetti and several other senior commanders — without making any allegations of misconduct against them. Brown later indirectly criticized the administration for politicizing military appointments.
More recently, Hegseth has shifted from firing officers to controlling who gets promoted. He has personally intervened in promotion lists drawn up by the military, removing many officers he considers unacceptable. According to media reports, participation in programs connecting with Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) was among the reasons some officers fell out of favor. In one instance, Hegseth removed all three women and two African American officers from a list of candidates for rear admiral. During the war with Iran, Hegseth also forced Army Chief of Staff Randy George to retire.
For the officers who remain, this inevitably raises the question of where the line now lies between professional assessments of their service and political loyalty. The upheaval in the Army continued when Army Secretary Dan Driscoll left his post in late August. The civilian head of the Army and one of its leading advocates for accelerated modernization, Driscoll was also Hegseth’s biggest rival for influence — and a potential successor as SecDef.
However, the personnel shakeups have not eliminated professional disagreements within the military leadership. As reported by U.S. media, in August the commanders of European Command, Indo-Pacific Command, and Southern Command, along with the Chief of Naval Operations, formally objected to extending the deployments of some forces stationed in their regions.
This was not a refusal to follow orders — which the generals and admirals were still required to carry them out. However, they still made clear that they considered the decision risky. Hegseth has yet to respond, and the dissenting commanders remain in their posts for now.
Where are the weapons, Hegseth?!
Personnel conflicts are only part of the problem. Even setting aside Hegseth’s relationship with the generals and its impact on military readiness, the armed forces simply lack sufficient ammunition and equipment. The U.S. is burning through its expensive weapons far faster than the American defense industry can replenish them. Meanwhile, cheap Iranian drones are creating a stark cost imbalance between offense and defense: Tehran can force the United States and its allies to spend many times more to intercept a drone than it costs to launch one.
According to The Washington Post, the U.S. has already expended 850 Tomahawk cruise missiles used against fortified targets, along with more than 1,000 missiles for Patriot air-defense systems and THAAD interceptors. In addition, CNN has reported that by August the United States had used about half of its prewar stockpile of Patriot missiles and roughly 80% of its THAAD interceptors. The U.S. also lost at least 45 MQ-9 Reaper heavy drones – about a quarter of its prewar fleet — as the slow, expensive UAVs proved relatively easy targets for Iran and its allies.
The United States has not only reduced its ability to strike, but also left its regional allies without adequate air defenses. They were willing to spend their oil revenues on American systems, but there are no longer enough of the systems to go around. It is hardly surprising that the Gulf monarchies are now turning to Ukraine for technology and expertise in countering cheap drones – the very experience Kyiv has gained through years of war with Russia.
The United States is learning the same lesson. The global drone market was already valued at $20 billion in 2025 and is expected to exceed $50 billion by 2034. The U.S. intends to take a leading position, albeit belatedly, with the Pentagon investing about $1 billion in the Drone Dominance initiative to produce up to 200,000 attack drones by 2027. Young people who until recently competed in drone racing are now winning half-billion-dollar Pentagon contracts to produce “killer drones” costing $5,000 apiece, and a whole new crop of companies is vying for billions of dollars being distributed by the Pentagon.
By 2034, the global drone market is expected to exceed $50 billion, and the United States wants to take a leading position
But once again, the key issue is Hegseth's arbitrary personnel shakeups, which could undermine combat readiness. After Randy George was forced out, the Army’s new leadership disbanded a 600-member experimental battalion that had spent nearly a year specializing in drone warfare — in part by absorbing lessons from Ukraine.
The Pentagon says a dedicated unit is no longer necessary and that drone skills should be spread throughout the Army. But lawmakers from both parties are demanding an explanation for why the experiment is being ended now, during a war in which cheap Iranian drones have become one of the main threats to U.S. forces.
Hegseth did not create the shortage, but he did arrive in the Pentagon promising to revive the defense industry, overhaul the procurement system, and speed up the adoption of new technologies. Instead, innovation is moving slowly — with any actual progress occurring almost in spite of a leadership that is disbanding specialized units. The military’s inability to replenish its losses is increasingly becoming a problem for which Hegseth bears primary responsibility.
Preparing for the last war
It is still too early to say that the personnel policies implemented by Hegseth and Trump have significantly weakened the U.S. armed forces. But warning signs are coming from all directions. The missile shortage, slow production, and strain on the Navy did not begin under Hegseth. As the old saying goes, U.S. generals prepared for the last war.
They were unprepared for a war of attrition against a major adversary like Iran. Hegseth, however, came to the Pentagon promising to “restore combat readiness” but is making the situation worse through personnel that appears to prioritize ideology over effectiveness. The U.S. military, for which Trump has requested a staggering $1.5 trillion defense budget for 2027, is working to address these shortcomings, with the Pentagon drawing up emergency plans to replenish its arsenal. Nevertheless, the political agenda pushed by Hegseth has already cost the military substantial resources and effort, and possibly lives as well.
The Secretary's politics are likely to remain the main obstacle to modernization programs and decisions. In other words, the Pentagon chief himself could become the U.S. military's biggest problem.
