Didea creates steel-clad streetwear store inside ZHA's Mercury Tower
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:00:16 UTC
17:00:16 KST

Didea creates steel-clad streetwear store inside ZHA's Mercury Tower
Architecture studio Didea designed the interior of the Super F streetwear store in St Julian's, Malta, as a flexible, modular grid to avoid invasive architectural alterations inside the Mercury Tower by ZHA.
The store exterior has a glazed, curved facade that welcomes visitors from the outside and is partly echoed inside the store with a central curved clothing display and rounded steel fitting rooms.
However, Didea mostly worked with gridded and angular geometric shapes, which were designed not to impact the building's architecture.
"We avoided invasive architectural alterations and masonry work, choosing a bespoke dry-assembled system designed with millimetre precision," Didea creative director Nicola Andò said.
The shop is located in the commercial podium of Mercury Tower, which was completed in 2024, and Didea wanted the store design to respond to the building.
"Mercury Tower inspired us to explore movement and how the space gradually reveals itself, from the square into the store," Andò told Dezeen.
"The layout, materials and lighting respond to the building's energy, while giving Super F a distinct identity."
The studio imagined the interior as a modular grid and used display systems, panels and furniture to define the different functions.
A black steel ceiling hides the building services, distributing electrical systems, fire protection, lighting and air conditioning, while brushed, polished and mirrored steel clads the interior.
"Steel reflects Super F's urban character and provides a backdrop for the colours of the products and the changing light," Andò said.
"We were interested in the contrast between its industrial origins and the care put into each detail. Precise detailing gives an everyday material a tailored feel."
As well as the curved steel fitting rooms, the Super F store also has steel-block plinths and garment rails, designed to be flexible and interchangeable.
"We developed a comb-like system that keeps the heavy plinths in place while allowing the garment rails to be moved easily from the window display into the store," Didea co-founder Giuseppe De Lisi said.
"They slot into purpose-made circular sockets, without screws or other fixings."
Didea wanted the 600-square-metre store to be a space not just to buy clothes in, but also for cultural experiences.
"Super F draws inspiration from global metropolises and streetwear culture," Andò said.
"It brings fashion, beauty, art and music together in one place. We designed the store to change character through sound and lighting, transforming into a club where people can come together for events and performances."
Other recent store designs include a wood-filled shop selling Danish design in Seoul and a sculptural jewellery boutique in New York.

Trump’s Lithuania base remark sparks excitement – and questions – in Vilnius
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

A few words from US President Donald Trump were enough to set off a wave of excitement in Lithuania: The United States, he said, would consider establishing a permanent military base in the Baltic country.
Asked by LRT correspondent Augustinas Šemelis whether he would consider Lithuania’s invitation to establish a permanent American base, Trump offered an enthusiastic, if noncommittal, response.
“They’re friends of mine. They are wonderful people. So we will certainly look at it,” Trump said. “I know so many people in Lithuania. They are great people”
In Vilnius, the remarks were quickly welcomed as a sign that Lithuania’s push for a permanent US military presence could be gaining traction.
President Gitanas Nausėda called Trump’s statement “very good news” and said it showed that the United States trusted Lithuania.
“The most important thing now is to act consistently and wait for the rotation of US troops,” Nausėda said.
But even among those welcoming Trump’s words, there was caution about what they actually mean.
Conservative MPLaurynas Kasčiūnas, deputy chairman of the Seimas Committee on National Security and Defence, called the US president’s statement “wonderful news” but said it was too early to speak of a concrete plan.
“It’s wonderful news when the US president says such words, but, on the other hand, whether there is a real plan to establish a permanent military presence or permanent military base here, it is probably too early to talk about,” Kasčiūnas said.
Lithuania’s defence minister, Robertas Kaunas, said the idea had already been formally put to Washington. He submitted the proposal to the Pentagon about two weeks ago.
“There have been no decisions as of today. Discussions are underway. As you can see, the signals are positive,” Kaunas said.
Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said Lithuania had also raised the issue with John Coale, the US special envoy for Belarus, about a month ago.
For Lithuania, the timing is particularly significant. After a six-month pause, about 1,000 US troops are expected to return to the country beginning in late October, but only for a rotational deployment.
“The fact is that only a couple of weeks ago it was announced that, after a six-month break, the US rotation is returning, 1,000 troops,” Sinkevičius said. “They will begin deploying at the end of October, but for now only for nine months.”
A permanent base, Lithuanian officials argue, could provide greater continuity.
“Even if a permanent base is not established, those rotations would run more smoothly and there would not be such large gaps,” said Remigijus Motuzas, chairman of the Seimas Foreign Affairs Committee.
Kaunas said Lithuania was ready to contribute financially.
“Lithuania already covers the costs of the presence of US troops. We have good infrastructure in Pabradė, which we can continue to expand,” he said. “We are not far from being able to have a permanent presence.”
The defence minister said the Pabradė area could accommodate about 1,500 troops.
But experts warned that Lithuania’s existing infrastructure would not by itself amount to a permanent American base.
“This is not infrastructure where Americans could settle with all their families and civilian personnel,” said Tomas Jermalavičius, research director at the International Centre for Defence and Security in Tallinn.
There is another missing piece: an actual US decision.
Former US Ambassador to Russia Michael McFaul has noted that Trump’s formulation – “we will look at it” – can often mean that the president has not previously considered the issue in detail.
Jermalavičius said that makes diplomacy particularly important now.
“This is an impulsive reaction that now simply needs to be taken advantage of – strike while the iron is hot,” he said.
That effort could be especially important in persuading sceptics inside the Pentagon, where the discussion has increasingly focused on reducing US troop levels in Europe rather than establishing new permanent bases.
And Lithuania is not the only country seeking a deeper US military commitment.
Trump has also signalled support for Poland’s long-running campaign for a permanent American base. Warsaw has pursued such a base for nearly a decade and at one point proposed naming it “Fort Trump”.
“They want it. And I like their president,” Trump said when asked about Poland.
That raises a question for Lithuania: Would Washington establish two permanent bases so close to each other on NATO’s eastern flank?
“It’s very close to Poland, and it is unlikely that such a decision would be made,” Motuzas said.
Jermalavičius said Washington had historically been reluctant to commit large permanent forces to the Suwałki corridor, the strategically sensitive area linking Poland and Lithuania.
“Enthusiasm for keeping large forces on this side of Suwałki has been very limited. They always wanted to maintain as much flexibility as possible,” he said.
He also pointed to another potential complication: the Trump administration could seek to link its security commitments to other issues in the region, including the transit of Belarusian fertilisers.
Lithuanian politicians have repeatedly denied that Washington is linking the two issues.
But Jermalavičius said the possibility should not be dismissed.
“This administration is very businesslike in its international relations. It is obvious that it will use such promises as a pressure tool or compensation for reopening transit,” he said.

Second death reported in Siberia as Russia denies plague outbreak
Unknown

2026-10-07
07:58:36 UTC
16:58:36 KST

A second person has reportedly died in Russia’s Irkutsk region amid growing concern over a possible pneumonic plague incident, Russian media reported, as international health authorities pressed Moscow for more information about the unexplained death of a researcher at a Siberian anti-plague institute.
The reported second death has not been independently confirmed, and Russian authorities have not acknowledged that plague caused either death.
The alarm began after Darya Shipilova, 28, an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, was hospitalized on Sept. 29 with severe pneumonia and died on Oct. 2.
Russian and independent media reported that Shipilova may have been exposed to Yersinia pestis, the bacterium that causes plague, while working at the institute. Some reports claimed she had accidentally broken a test tube containing live bacteria, though Russian authorities have not confirmed that account.
Russia’s health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said Shipilova died from pneumonia of an unspecified origin and insisted that no plague cases had been detected in the region. Authorities said people who had been in contact with her were placed under medical observation and tested.
Russian media later reported that a second unidentified person had died at a hospital in the Irkutsk region after allegedly contracting plague. No laboratory results or other official evidence have been released linking the reported death to the disease.
The uncertainty has drawn scrutiny from international health authorities. The World Health Organization has sought additional information from Russia about Shipilova’s death, the pathogen suspected by authorities, the public health measures imposed in the region and reports that another employee developed pneumonia of unknown origin.
Nearly 200 people who had contact with Shipilova were reportedly placed under monitoring, while dozens of employees at the institute were isolated. Hospitals in the Irkutsk area also imposed restrictions, and residents reported seeing health workers wearing protective equipment.
Several Russian media reports concerning the suspected outbreak have meanwhile disappeared from news websites. Independent Russian outlets said reports from major broadcasters and newspapers were deleted, while a local government warning urging residents to avoid travel to the Shelekhov area was also removed shortly after publication.
Russian authorities continue to deny that a plague outbreak is underway. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged the public to rely on official information from Rospotrebnadzor rather than “rumors and speculation.”
The United States has also said it is monitoring developments. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the situation was not considered a cause for alarm but warranted close attention, while President Donald Trump said Washington was prepared to assist Russia if necessary.
Pneumonic plague is the most severe form of plague and can spread between people through respiratory droplets during close contact. It can progress rapidly if untreated, but antibiotics are effective when administered early.

WHO releases first global guidelines on child obesity as cases surge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:56:51 UTC
16:56:51 KST

WHO releases first global guidelines on child obesity as cases surge
Child and adolescent obesity has quadrupled since 1990, rising from two per cent to around eight per cent of youngsters in the five-to-19 age group, according to the UN World Health Organization (WHO).
In 2024, there were around 170 million children and adolescents living with obesity – including 70 million children aged five to nine and some 100 million adolescents up to 19.
The UN health agency defines obesity as a “chronic, relapsing disease” triggered by excessive fat deposits which can nonetheless be managed through effective care.
What’s at stake
Children and adolescents with the disease can face both medical and social repercussions from very early on in life, WHO warns.
Obesity increases the risk of noncommunicable diseases, including type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.
It also increases their likelihood of experiencing stigma, discrimination and bullying, which can strongly negatively affect mental health.
In its new set of guidelines, WHO strongly recommends dietary changes, physical activity and other behaviour-changing interventions.
Weight loss drugs: a last resort
It does not recommend pharmacological treatment, bariatric surgery (surgery that changes the digestive system to induce weight loss) or weight-loss devices for children aged 0-9 years.
For adolescents aged 10-19 years, treatment with approved medicines – such as GLP-1 therapies – should only be considered when a supervised lifestyle programme has failed to make improvements.
Similarly, bariatric surgery may be considered under strict conditions for those with severe obesity.
“The foundation of obesity care for children and adolescents is not medicine or surgery, but access to comprehensive support that enables healthy eating, physical activity and sustainable behaviour change,” said Dr. Luz María De Regil, Director of the Department of Nutrition and Food Safety at WHO.
Keeping spirits up
The new recommendations also emphasise the importance of addressing mental health alongside obesity, because it is both a cause and a consequence of the disease.
Anxiety, depression, low self-esteem and emotional dysregulation can contribute to unhealthy eating behaviours, physical inactivity and social withdrawal, while children and adolescents living with obesity may also experience stigma and bullying that harm their emotional well-being.
The guidelines stress that obesity care should go beyond weight loss and aim to improve health, functioning and well-being, notably by being tailored to the specific needs of each child and by ensuring long-term follow-up.
Political action
At the same time, WHO acknowledged that treatment cannot reverse the rise in obesity by itself: systemic changes are needed.
The agency called for policies and measures that make healthy diets and physical activity more accessible and affordable, including regulatory and fiscal measures and action across education, urban planning, transport and social protection.
“Our priority must be to ensure that every child and adolescent can access quality care and supportive environments from an early age, helping them achieve and maintain a healthy weight and laying the foundation for lifelong health and well-being,” said Dr. De Regil.

The General Staff added Ukraine would continue fighting Russian forces to secure a just and lasting peace.
Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha also used Putin’s birthday to highlight Russia’s military losses and call for greater international pressure on Moscow.
“On Putin’s birthday, Russian generals brought him his favorite present: war crimes,” Sybiha wrote on X, referring to Russia’s latest massive missile and drone attack on Ukraine.
Sybiha said the attack hit residential buildings and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Dnipro, Zaporizhzhia, Kremenchuk, and Pryluky, killing over 10 people across the country.
“What Russian generals fail to tell Putin is that he is not winning this war and never will,” Sybiha wrote, adding that Russia had lost 1.6 million troops killed and injured without achieving a single strategic goal of its invasion.
He also argued that Russia’s advances had stalled and that Ukraine had begun liberating more territory than Russian forces were managing to occupy.
According to Sybiha, Russia’s economy is declining and its global influence is waning because Putin “refuses to end this war.”
Acknowledging the heavy cost of the war for Ukraine, Sybiha said Ukrainians would continue fighting because the conflict concerns “Ukraine’s survival as a nation and as a state.”
“Russia’s terror must not go unanswered,” he added, urging Ukraine’s international partners to give Putin “real presents” that could push him toward diplomacy.
Sybiha called for stronger sanctions against Russia’s military-industrial complex, including facilities producing ballistic missiles and the Rassvet satellite system. He also urged partners to increase support for Ukraine, particularly air-defense systems and energy assistance ahead of winter.
He said the “ultimate present” for Putin would be a dock in The Hague, referring to Ukraine’s plans to establish the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression Against Ukraine.
“We are preparing the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression Against Ukraine for practical launch already next year,” Sybiha wrote. “Putin and his friends should know that accountability is inevitable.”
Meanwhile, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un congratulated Putin on his birthday, pledging Pyongyang’s “invariable support” for Russia and calling Moscow’s war against Ukraine a “sacred war of justice.”
The message comes as North Korea has evolved from a political supporter of Russia’s invasion into a direct military partner.
Pyongyang has supplied Moscow with weapons and deployed thousands of troops to Russia, including forces that fought alongside Russian units in the Kursk region.
The two countries significantly deepened their military ties after Putin’s June 2024 visit to Pyongyang, when they signed a comprehensive strategic partnership agreement containing a mutual defense clause. Western and South Korean officials have said Russia has provided North Korea with economic assistance, military technology, and battlefield experience in return for its support.

UK house prices flatline as rising mortgage costs weigh on market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:56:02 UTC
16:56:02 KST

UK house prices flatlined in September, according to a leading index, as rising mortgage costs started to weigh on the market.
The average cost of a home was £298,441, roughly the same as it was a year earlier and in the previous month, according to the tracker from Lloyds previously known as the Halifax HPI.
Economists polled by Reuters had predicted a 0.1% monthly rise in prices, according to the median forecast, as well as a 0.2% annual increase.
It came after house prices fell by 0.3% in August, the first decline in three years, as prospective buyers were hit by geopolitical uncertainty, combined with higher mortgage rates and stretched affordability.
In recent weeks most big banks and building societies have put prices up as a result of turmoil in the global bond markets, even though there has not been a change in the Bank of England base rate since December last year.
Andrew Asaam, the mortgages director at Lloyds, said: “While the market overall has been fairly subdued, property prices have so far proved resilient during a period of higher mortgage rates, which has been driven by changing expectations around the future path of base rate.”
On Monday the average cost of a five-year fixed-rate mortgage reached 6% for the first time in three years. Rising mortgage rates are bad news for borrowers whose fixed-rate deals are ending, as well as prospective buyers who are hoping to take out a mortgage to buy a home and the sellers who want the best price from them.
It also adds to the squeeze facing consumers as a result of higher energy bills, linked to the Iran war, while rising prices elsewhere are raising concerns of a new cost of living crisis.
Asaam said: “While higher mortgage rates and wider economic uncertainty are encouraging some people to take a more measured approach, new inquiries from prospective buyers are now at their highest since February.”
He added that any movement in house prices was likely to remain modest.
Tom Bill, the head of UK residential research at the estate agent Knight Frank, said: “This year has been a story of rising energy prices and stalling house prices, as the unpredictable Middle East conflict unfolds and drives borrowing costs higher. This month’s budget adds to the uncertainty as buyers and sellers wonder which of the recurring tax rumours proves to be true.”
The number of people applying for a mortgage to buy a property fell between July and September, as higher borrowing costs continued to affect prospective housebuyers’ budgets, according to quarterly figures from Stonebridge, one of the UK’s largest independent mortgage and protection networks.
Mortgage applications for home purchases fell by 18.2% in the third quarter compared with a year earlier, Stonebridge found, while applications from first-time buyers slumped 18.6% over the same period.
However, rising numbers of applications for remortgaging helped to slow the decline in overall mortgage activity.

Yemen's Houthi rebels targeted Aden International Airport with ballistic missiles and explosive drones early Wednesday, the Transport Ministry said, amid intensifying combat between the Iran-aligned group and Saudi-backed forces.

Yemen's government said that forced the Houthis out of areas they had captured last month, reviving a complex 12-year war, which led to one of the world's worst humanitarian crises and fragmented the Arab world's most impoverished country.

Authorities cancelled the landing and diverted the aircraft to Jeddah, while two planes on the runway were moved away from the area over fears of further strikes, it added. There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.
Aden International Airport is the main international gateway for parts of Yemen outside of Houthi control.
The Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognized government said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile north of Riyadh.
It said it was tracking the launch platform over Houthi-controlled Sanaa and would destroy it, but gave no details of casualties or damage.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a statement that the group had targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with several drones. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of an attack on the airport.

A U.N.-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted heavy fighting, but it did not lead to a lasting settlement, with a spillover from the Iran conflict triggering the latest fighting.
The Saudi-led coalition accuses Iran of arming, training and funding the Houthis. The group, mountain fighters who have emerged as a force of tens of thousands with missiles and drones that threatens the region, denies being part of Iran's Middle East proxy network and says it develops its own weapons. Tehran also rejects the allegations.
Earlier Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile launched towards the southwestern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait, Saudi state television reported.
In a separate statement, Saree said the Houthis had attacked Abha International Airport and an airbase in Khamis Mushait with ballistic missiles and drones. It was not immediately clear whether this was linked to the missile the coalition said it had intercepted near Khamis Mushait. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm an attack on Abha airport.

The event focused on opportunities for cooperation between Türkiye and Czechia in recycling and sustainable waste management.
Participants included Istanbul Deputy Governor Cengiz Karabulut, Czech Consul General in Istanbul Olga Hajflerova, the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality's Head of Foreign Relations, Barbaros Buyuksagnak, and its Head of Environmental Protection and Control, Aysen Erdincler.
Representatives of Türkiye's Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Ministry and the Turkish Environment Agency also attended.
Alongside public institutions and local authorities from both countries, the forum brought together representatives of companies, industry organizations and civil society groups operating in recycling, plastics, waste management and environmental technologies.
Discussions covered sustainable waste management, recycling technologies and industry cooperation and investment opportunities as well as potential commercial and technological partnerships between Turkish and Czech companies.
Our World Foundation President Kahraman Haliscelik delivered the first opening address.
Haliscelik said the forum brought together representatives of public institutions, local authorities, industry and the private sector from Türkiye and Czechia on a common platform.
Its main objective, he said, was to move beyond exchanging views and pave the way for concrete cooperation.
He said relations between the two countries could be further strengthened through new partnerships in recycling and sustainable waste management.
"Our aim is to turn dialogue into cooperation, and cooperation into concrete projects and commercial partnerships," he said.
Haliscelik stressed that recycling and sustainable waste management could no longer be viewed solely as environmental issues, saying they were becoming increasingly strategic in terms of technology, investment, competitiveness and economic opportunities.
Strong cooperation among public institutions, local authorities and the private sector would play an important role in implementing sustainable solutions, he said, expressing hope that contacts established during the forum would mark the beginning of new projects and long-term partnerships.
Haliscelik thanked Hajflerova for her support in organizing the forum as well as ISBAV, TUDAM and the Turkish and Czech institutions, organizations and companies that contributed to the program.
Speaking after Haliscelik, Hajflerova highlighted the importance of developing cooperation between Türkiye and Czechia in sustainability and recycling.
She said bringing public and private sector representatives from both countries together on the same platform was important for establishing new business connections.
Hajflerova said the forum provided an important platform both for sharing knowledge and experience and for establishing concrete, long-term partnerships between Turkish and Czech institutions and companies.
She said the two countries had significant potential to complement each other in this field.
She added that bringing together different stakeholders from Türkiye and Czechia would strengthen the exchange of experience.
Contacts in sustainability, recycling and waste management could also create new opportunities for the two countries' economic and commercial relations, she said.
Following the opening remarks, representatives of Czech public institutions and businesses delivered presentations.
Vlastislav Kotrc from Czechia's Environment Ministry, Jan Trnobransky from the Czech Environmental Information Agency (CENIA), Matyas Kousek from Czechia's Industry and Trade Ministry and Eva Langerova from the Czech Chamber of Commerce's International Relations Department discussed their institutions' work and opportunities for cooperation between Türkiye and Czechia.
Their presentations covered Czechia's activities in recycling, environmental protection and waste management, environmental information and data management, industrial policies, and potential cooperation between the private sectors of the two countries.
Representatives of Czech companies attending the forum also gave short presentations outlining their areas of activity and the solutions they had developed.
The presentations highlighted potential partnerships that Czech companies could establish with institutions and businesses in Türkiye.
The forum also featured a panel titled "The Future of Recycling in Türkiye: Sustainable Waste Management, Industry Cooperation and New Opportunities."
Speakers included Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality's Head of Environmental Protection and Control, Aysen Erdincler, TUDAM board member Kayhan Ural, and Salih Kanbak, representing the Turkish Plastics Industry Foundation (PAGEV).
Panelists discussed the current state and future of Türkiye's recycling industry, addressing sustainable waste management, the role of local authorities, industrial transformation and cooperation across sectors.
Alongside recycling's environmental benefits, the panel examined its potential to create economic value.
Participants exchanged views on improving coordination among public institutions, local authorities and the private sector, adopting new technologies, and expanding sustainable recycling models.
The panel also addressed challenges facing the recycling industry, more efficient use of resources, improvements to recovery processes, and new investment and cooperation opportunities that could emerge in the coming period.
During the afternoon session, company representatives from Türkiye and Czechia held business-to-business meetings.
Participants exchanged information about their activities, technologies and projects while discussing potential commercial partnerships, technology cooperation and investment opportunities in recycling and sustainable waste management.
The B2B meetings aimed to ensure that the forum would serve as more than a platform for public institutions and industry representatives to share knowledge and experience.
They also sought to establish direct connections between Turkish and Czech companies and lay the groundwork for developing concrete projects.
On the second day of the two-day program, the Czech delegation is scheduled to make technical visits to facilities operating in recycling and waste management in Kocaeli.
The visits are expected to allow delegates to examine practices and facilities in Türkiye firsthand, establish direct contact with industry representatives, and continue discussions initiated in Istanbul through on-site meetings.
They aim to help turn opportunities for cooperation between Türkiye and Czechia in recycling and sustainable waste management into concrete projects while developing contacts among public institutions, industry organizations and companies into long-term partnerships.

Operation “VILKATIS” in Latvia’s Eastern Border Area to Continue until 31 December
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:52:05 UTC
16:52:05 KST

On Tuesday, 6 October, the Cabinet of Ministers decided to extend Operation “VILKATIS” – an operation to combat illegal migration being carried out in Latvia’s eastern border area, until the end of this year – 31 December.
Given the ongoing work to restore border infrastructure damaged by the storms of 22–23 August and efforts to strengthen the capacity of the State Border Guard, including by expanding the use of unmanned aerial vehicles, the government decided to extend the security operation. Accordingly, security along the Latvia–Belarus border will continue to be subject to enhanced monitoring in order to prevent illegal migration.
The instrumentalization of migration by Belarus constitutes a hybrid threat that has contributed to a disproportionately high number of illegal border crossing incidents in Latvia. During Operation “VILKATIS”, several people transporting illegal border crossers have so far been detained in Latvia, while more than 1,400 people have been prevented from crossing the border illegally. Two tunnels used to organise illegal border crossings from Belarus have also been discovered and dismantled.
More than 11,000 people have been deterred from crossing the state border illegally so far this year. Transporting and accommodating illegal border crossers constitute criminal offences. A total of 155 criminal proceedings have been initiated for the illegal movement of people across the state border and the organisation of such activities. Amendments to the Criminal Law proposed by the Ministry of Justice are currently before the Saeima; the amendments propose tougher penalties for organising illegal border crossings – up to 12 years’ imprisonment.
Operation “VILKATIS” is coordinated by the Crisis Management Centre of the State Chancellery, while its implementation primarily involves the services of the Ministry of the Interior – the State Border Guard and the State Police, and the National Armed Forces. Soldiers of the National Armed Forces and members of the National Guard carry out border surveillance and patrols, provide logistical and transport support, and perform engineering works necessary to strengthen the security of the country’s external border.
To ensure the security of Latvia’s eastern border, Operation “VILKATIS” was launched on 11 August. It is Latvia’s targeted and coordinated response to a hybrid threat – the instrumentalization of illegal migration by Belarus. The Operation aims to significantly reduce the number of illegal border crossings in eastern Latvia and to prevent such incidents in the future.

Kumu exhibit explores how Finno‑Ugric heritage shaped Estonian identity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:50:00 UTC
16:50:00 KST

Kumu exhibit explores how Finno‑Ugric heritage shaped Estonian identity
Kumu's new exhibition "Expedition" explores how Finno‑Ugric heritage and linguistic kinship became an important part of Estonian identity. Interest in Finno‑Ugric heritage grew especially in the 1970s and 1980s, supported by creators across cultural fields as well as scholars, says curator Linda Kaljundi.
"With this exhibition, we want to invite viewers to reflect on why being 'Finno‑Ugric' has become so central to Estonians' identity and self‑image, when this happened, and how it took shape," Kaljundi said.
The exhibition examines, among other things, how Finno‑Ugric heritage entered different cultural spheres. In the 1970s and 1980s, filmmakers, artists, writers, and musicians began to take interest in it. At the same time, they collaborated with researchers and the Estonian National Museum. "We see cooperation between different cultural fields, as well as collaboration between art and science."
According to Kaljundi, turning toward Indigenous peoples was not unique to Estonia. Similar interest emerged elsewhere in the world, but in Estonia's case, linguistic kinship added a distinct dimension.
"What makes the Estonian case different is certainly the aspect of linguistic kinship, which allows people to identify with and relate to Indigenous groups living very, very far from Estonia," Kaljundi explained.
Interest in Finno‑Ugric heritage was also fueled by the crisis of the Soviet Union and broader disillusionment with industrial modernity. Other Soviet peoples likewise turned toward folklore and traditional culture.
In Estonia, this coincided with an active interest in national identity. Kaljundi pointed to cultural works created in the 1970s and 1980s and to the treatment of history and cultural heritage. She mentioned, among others, Lennart Meri's films and Jaan Kross's historical novels.
A central part of the exhibition is the Estonian National Museum's Finno‑Ugric collections. In addition to the collections themselves, the museum has studied their formation history, revealing contradictions tied to the expeditions.
"On one hand, there was a strong desire to help and support these small Finno‑Ugric peoples; on the other hand, there existed the entire Soviet research system and infrastructure that made such extensive field expeditions possible," Kaljundi said.
The exhibition includes materials from Finno‑Ugric expeditions organized in the 1970s and 1980s under the leadership of Kaljo Põllu. Art students participated in these trips, producing ethnographic drawings and photographs. The exhibition also features works by other artists, including graphics by Anu Kalm and Evi Tihemets.
"We want to show once again that the Finno‑Ugric turn did not emerge solely through the contributions of three major figures — Meri, Põllu, and Veljo Tormis — but that many other people played a role. We wanted to highlight this cultural diversity," Kaljundi said.
The exhibition also addresses environmental issues faced by small Finno‑Ugric peoples. According to Kaljundi, the exhibition begins with the theme of oil, because the rise of Finno‑Ugric interest in Estonia coincided with the expansion of the Soviet Union's oil and gas industry into the homelands of these peoples.
Kaljundi believes the topic of Finno‑Ugric heritage is again relevant today, as identity‑seeking often intensifies during periods of crisis. Current interest is influenced, among other factors, by Russia's full‑scale war in Ukraine.
In an international context, Kaljundi sees the exhibition's theme as part of a broader movement in which Indigenous peoples seek a voice in how their heritage is represented. She pointed to examples such as the Sámi, Native Americans, and Indigenous Australians. She believes Estonia's experience could be of international interest, as the relationship between Estonians and small Finno‑Ugric peoples differs from the classic Western colonial context.
"Estonia's story could contribute a great deal internationally, especially in its complexity — how Estonians, themselves occupied by the Soviet Union, went to study small Finno‑Ugric peoples," she said.
At the same time, she added that Western colonial research frameworks cannot be applied one‑to‑one to Estonian expeditions. Still, ethnographic fieldwork inevitably involves historical power relations and knowledge infrastructures.
The new exhibition was developed over several years. The long preparation period allowed time both for studying the collections and for artists' research. The exhibition also emerged in dialogue with the Sámi contemporary art exhibition "No Beginning, No End" shown at Kumu at the same time.
"We repeatedly visited various museum collections in Estonia, especially the Estonian National Museum, and also traveled to neighboring countries to study Sámi and Finno‑Ugric collections," Kaljundi said.
The exhibition features investigative artists Jaanus Samma and Karl‑Joonas Alamaa. For Kaljundi, it was important to give them time to explore the collections, ask their own questions, and design installations that intervene in the exhibition.
"It has been time‑consuming but very exciting. This certainly does not mean that I have exhausted the topic — rather, it is part of a longer journey with much more research ahead."
The Finno‑Ugric exhibition will remain open at Kumu until February next year.
--
Editor: Karmen Rebane, Argo Ideon

Russian attack damages Dovzhenko Film Studio for third time
The National Oleksandr Dovzhenko Film Studio has been damaged for the third time as a result of a Russian attack on Kyiv on the night of 6-7 October.
Source: Ukraine's Ministry of Culture
Details: The ministry said that debris from a Russian missile had fallen on the film studio, piercing the roofs of the sixth and seventh sound stages. A fire broke out at the site, which has since been extinguished.
There are no casualties at the studio. A commission is currently inspecting the damaged buildings and assessing the damage caused.
This is not the first time the film studio has suffered from Russian strikes. In early summer, on 2 and 15 June, two missile hits damaged 18 buildings, utility networks and cultural heritage sites on its territory.
That attack damaged the Main Sound Stage, built in 1927-1928, office and laboratory buildings, the Shchors Building (the Film Factory Museum), service buildings, special-effects workshops, a canteen, an electrical substation, a film library, student accommodation and other structures. Some of these are designated nationally or locally as significant monuments of the history of science and technology.
The greatest losses were caused by a direct hit on the costume department, which housed one of Ukraine's largest collections of stage and film costumes.
This included a collection of footwear and hats from various periods, as well as a significant number of military uniforms from the First and Second World Wars, the studio's director general said.
Some unique items were saved because they had been held in museums and at exhibitions.
In July, emergency repair work began at the film studio.

Myanmar’s Min Aung Hlaing visits Malaysia amid concerns over repatriations
Myanmar leader Min Aung Hlaing arrives in Malaysia for his first visit since the 2021 coup, as deportations of Myanmar nationals draw concerns from the UN and rights groups.
Myanmar’s military leader-turned-president has arrived in Malaysia for talks with Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, as Kuala Lumpur seeks his cooperation to send back thousands of Myanmar nationals.
Min Aung Hlaing touched down at Kuala Lumpur international airport at 04:30 GMT on Wednesday, state media images showed.
The two-day visit comes as Malaysia pushes ahead with a controversial move to repatriate thousands of Myanmar nationals, despite warnings from the United Nations and rights groups that returnees could face serious danger amid a raging civil war.
“The visit provides the prime minister with an opportunity to sustain his direct engagement with Myanmar,” the Malaysian government said in a statement on Tuesday.
Key bilateral issues include the “voluntary, dignified and safe repatriation of Myanmar nationals of all ethnic groups who have been in Malaysia illegally”, it added.
A spokeswoman for Min Aung Hlaing said “the agenda will include discussions on the voluntary, dignified and safe repatriation of Myanmar nationals currently in Malaysia”.
Myanmar has been in turmoil since Min Aung Hlaing led a military coup in 2021, triggering a civil war that has killed an estimated 100,000 people and displaced more than 3.5 million.
The military engineered a widely criticised election that allowed the retired general, who is subject to Western sanctions, to take up a civilian role — a transition that has led to some moves towards re-engagement with Myanmar.
Since formally becoming president in April, Min Aung Hlaing has visited ASEAN member countries Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam, and also made trips to China, India, Russia and Belarus.
Repatriation of Rohingya
In Malaysia, following a wave of online hate speech and misinformation earlier this year, pressure on undocumented migrants and refugees has grown, particularly against Rohingya, many of whom fled a brutal 2017 military crackdown in Myanmar’s Rakhine state.
Last month, Anwar said in a podcast that he would invite Min Aung Hlaing for an official visit if Myanmar accepted the return of thousands of Rohingya refugees.
Malaysia has deported about 10,000 Myanmar nationals since January, according to Anwar, who said Myanmar authorities had given assurances those returning would not be harmed.
Malaysia is home to about 215,600 refugees and asylum seekers registered with the UNHCR, including about 126,000 Rohingya who make up one of Southeast Asia’s largest refugee communities.
Despite hosting them, Malaysia is not a party to the UN Refugee Convention and treats refugees as undocumented migrants.

U.S. troops on Okinawa facing curfew, alcohol ban after Marine charged with murder
U.S. forces on Okinawa were barred from drinking alcohol for 48 hours on Wednesday and were put under a 30-day curfew in the wake of the murder of a local woman allegedly committed by an American Marine.
The case has triggered outrage on the Japanese island, where any crimes involving U.S. forces have long inflamed criticism of the troops' presence. Locals also object to noise and pollution caused by the U.S. military, though many residents recognize the strategic value of having U.S. bases there due to what's widely viewed as a growing threat from China.
Genta Koja, the governor of Okinawa — where the bulk of the 54,000 U.S. military personnel in Japan are based —told Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi during a meeting in Tokyo on Wednesday that there was an "urgent need to reduce base-related burdens" on the island, without providing specifics.
"The robbery-murder this time hugely shocked local residents," he said, requesting a committee be convened swiftly to discuss the issue.
Earlier, Lt. Gen. Benjamin Watson, commander of III Marine Expeditionary Force, announced a "complete prohibition of alcohol consumption on or off base" starting on Wednesday.
Watson said the 48-hour period — described as "an operational pause" — would give commanders the time to lead training of all service members on "standards, discipline, and our responsibilities as members of the Okinawan community."
During this period, military operations will cease and "we will not allow off-base liberty," said Watson in a statement posted on X late Tuesday.
The lieutenant general, the most senior U.S. military figure on Okinawa, also announced a 30-day "period of reflection" beginning Friday.
"During this period, we will implement a curfew in which liberty will expire at 2400 (midnight) for all hands, meaning you must be back on base in your assigned quarters or at your off-base domicile from midnight to 0500 (5 a.m.)."
Police said Sunday that Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, a 20-year-old U.S. Marine stationed at Futenma Air Station in Okinawa, was arrested on suspicion of killing 39-year-old Anna Yagi at a hotel in the island's capital city of Naha early Saturday and stealing her wallet and backpack. He has denied the allegations, according to Japanese media.
Prior to his meeting with Japan's premier, Koja, the Okinawa governor, met Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi in Tokyo, where he said the case had "caused deep anxiety" among Okinawa residents.
"The prefectural government has repeatedly demanded that the U.S. military take measures to prevent a recurrence every time an incident occurs, but the fact that such an incident has happened again forces us to conclude that discipline within the U.S. forces and their human rights education are not functioning at all," he told Koizumi.
Koizumi said he would "advance discussions with the United States on how to implement effective measures" to prevent such incidents from occurring.

Libya's eastern lawmakers elect new parliament speaker amid discontent
Libya's eastern-based House of Representatives elected Al-Salhin Abdulnabi as speaker on Tuesday, replacing Aguila Saleh after nearly 12 years in the post amid growing discontent among lawmakers over his leadership.
The vote came a day after 98 members of the House approved a new term system limiting the speaker and deputy speakers to a single 12-month term, ending an arrangement that had remained in place since the chamber's first leadership was elected in 2014.
"There was significant discontent among MPs with the previous leadership over numerous errors. We tried to engage with the leadership to address these issues, but to no avail. Among these errors were decisions made without consulting MPs," lawmaker Jebreel Oheida told Reuters.
The House also elected Tarek al-Ashtar and Mesbah Douma as first and second deputy speakers, respectively.
Abdulnabi, who comes from the same tribe as Saleh, represents the eastern city of Tobruk and has chaired parliament's Libyan-Turkish friendship committee. He holds a master's degree in civil engineering.
Libya, a major oil and gas producer, has been split since 2014 between rival administrations in the east and west, with the internationally recognised Government of National Unity based in the western capital Tripoli.
Saleh, an ally of eastern military commander Khalifa Haftar, has long played a central role in diplomacy aimed at resolving Libya's conflict.
Libya has two legislative chambers. The House of Representatives was elected in 2014, while the High State Council was established under a 2015 political agreement and drawn from a parliament elected in 2012.
The House is based in the east, while the High State Council is in Tripoli alongside the Government of National Unity.

The solar boom is rapidly transforming emerging economies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:48:00 UTC
16:48:00 KST

The solar boom is rapidly transforming emerging economies
October 7, 2026
As emerging economies and global living standards rise, is the world in for another fossil fuel boom? The data says not. Countries from Southeast Asia to Sub-Saharan Africa aren't investing in fossil fuels as the West did; they're investing in electricity powered by renewables.
When the US and Europe industrialized in the 19th and 20th centuries, they did so using fossil energy. From coal ovens, gas heating and combustion-engine cars to electricity produced in coal and gas power plants, entire societies relied on polluting fuels.
Yet while burning fossil fuels allowed industrialized countries to boom, it also caused the climate crisis that is linked to extreme weather events around the world today.
Renewable electricity is rapidly becoming the cheapest option
Many of the same countries that became economically powerful off the back of fossil fuels are now trying to transition to renewables, but centuries of legacy infrastructure hold them back.
Because a gas boiler won't run on wind power and a diesel truck cannot be solar-powered, societies looking to shift to green energy need to use more electricity and increase their share of renewables.
That is where many middle- and lower-income countries have an advantage. With less existing energy infrastructure built around fossil fuels, they are better placed for a faster rollout of renewable electricity sources.
In many instances, solar power in particular is now cheaper to produce than fossil electricity. And unlike large coal or gas plants, which take years to construct and millions in investments, solar and wind farms can be built quickly and with much less upfront cost.
At the same time, according to an analysis by renewables think tank Ember, electronic devices like refrigerators, electric stoves or air conditioners have all become much cheaper in the last decades, making electricity a more affordable option as an energy source for cooking, heating and more.
While electric cars are still a luxury item in most places, their prices are coming down too. And a UN study found that in India, Indonesia and Vietnam electric scooters and motorbikes already cost the same as petrol models. Yet a lot less to fuel.
All this means that renewable electricity is quickly becoming the best choice for the wallet — not just for the climate. And countries are taking note.
"We're seeing a leapfrog take place right across the emerging markets,” said Kingsmill Bond, energy strategist at Ember. "The whole of Asia is electrifying quickly, and the whole of Europe and the United States is stagnant."
Lower-income countries are electrifying faster
In 2023, only around a quarter of global electricity was generated by renewables. But that figure is rising fast, and almost all new capacity added these days is based on solar or wind power.
Lower-income countries already use less fossil fuels and more renewables than higher-income ones.
And large middle-income economies are outpacing richer ones as well. In 2023, solar power alone made up at least six percent and ten percent of electricity in India and Vietnam, respectively. The global average was five percent.
Lower-income countries are electrifying without the fossil detour
This boom has meant middle- and lower-income countries are electrifying fast, consuming less energy directly from fossil fuels than richer countries. Vietnam, for instance, is already using more electricity than the US, Europe and even China, and India is following the same path.
But the potential for energy leapfrogging might be particularly high in low-income countries, especially across Sub-Saharan Africa.
Countries such as Kenya, Ethiopia and Namibia are rapidly expanding their energy infrastructure to meet the demands of a growing, young population. But rural areas in many countries are not connected to electricity grids.
Joel Nana, project manager at South African NGO Sustainable Energy Africa says that "even when there is access to power, it's often not reliable."
Until a few years ago, he says, people defaulted to diesel generators to meet their energy needs. That came at a cost because importing fuel is particularly expensive in many African countries, meaning energy crises and oil price fluctuations hit much harder.
Renewables for energy access and independence
These factors make solar power a solution for both energy access and independence. And it has become so cheap that Nana says it's a "no-brainer."
"Some businesses can make back their investment in just two years, so why would you want to deploy anything else?” he said. "Solar has rapidly become the de facto default technology that everyone falls back on.”
And once it is set up, it is very effective. Sub-Saharan Africa is extremely well-suited to solar power. It gets more sun than almost anywhere in the world, and has enough space for solar farms to cover electricity demand hundreds of times over.
"If you add solar plus batteries, you can get cheap electricity about 90 percent of the time from the sun alone”, said Kingsmill Bond.
Countries like Namibia, South Africa, Kenya and Senegal have expanded their solar capacity massively in the past few years.
In a 2026 report for African Tech Futures Lab and Ember, Nana analyzed import data from China and estimated that around 100,000 solar panels were installed across Africa every day in 2026, up 45 percent from just the previous year.
Similar trends are emerging all across the world. In Pakistan, for example, people have been buying solar panels from China en masse in the past few years to avoid steep electricity grid prices and frequent power outages.
Cheap energy boosts economies
Aleksi Lumijärvi, director for knowledge, policy and finance at the International Renewable Energy Association says these decisions can have a major impact on the global economy in the coming decades.
"Industrial companies will find that it will be cheaper to move production to, for example, somewhere in Sub-Saharan Africa, because they have this cheap, clean solar power plus batteries available.”
Kingsmill Bond says where electricity is cheap and abundant, wealth will follow.
"You're going to have faster growth in the emerging markets, you will have fewer financial crises. It will make a material difference to people's quality of lives.”
Nana says the next step for African countries is to establish policies that ensure everyone benefits from the solar boom.
"We are heading towards the most decentralized grid in the whole world within the next five years,” he told DW. His mantra for governments, he says, is: "This is happening, whether you like it or not.” He expects a wave of new energy regulations, many of which are now in the final stages of negotiation, to come into effect across Africa in the coming months and years.
"Countries are realizing it's in their interest to integrate this technology into national strategies, to share the benefits and to make use of this competitive advantage."
Edited by: Tamsin Walker and Gianna Grün

Switzerland hosts major European disaster response exercise

Switzerland hosts major European disaster response exercise
Switzerland and European countries are stepping up their cooperation in civil protection. This is the first time that Switzerland has organised and hosted such an exercise. Some 500 people are taking part in the simulated earthquake disaster in the cantons of Vaud and Geneva.
From Tuesday to Friday, exercises are taking place in Epeisses (in canton Geneva), Geneva and Payerne (in canton Vaud) under the European Union’s UPCM civil protection mechanism. The aim is to practise international cooperation in the aftermath of a major earthquake.
+ Zurich research could help predict earthquake patterns
More than 250 emergency responders from EU countries and Armenia are expected to take part. Swiss participants include civilians, members of the armed forces and volunteer role-players.
More
Swiss AI model ‘listens’ to the mountain to detect avalanches
Under the scenario for the EU MODEX Switzerland 2026 civil protection exercise, the damage in the cantons of Vaud, Geneva and Fribourg is so severe that Switzerland has to request assistance through the UPCM civil protection mechanism.
The mechanism came into play at Crans-Montana
If national resources are overwhelmed, Switzerland, like any other UPCM-associated country, can request assistance from its European partners. In January, Switzerland activated the mechanism following the devastating fire in Crans-Montana, in canton Valais, which killed 41 people and injured 115 others. This support enabled patients to receive treatment in several countries.
More
Crans-Montana tragedy highlights limits of Swiss federal system
From Tuesday afternoon, additional teams were deployed to deal with the scale of the simulated earthquake. Under the exercise scenario, volunteers playing the role of casualties were trapped beneath two piles of rubble in Epeisses.
“It is particularly important to test how well teams from different countries can work together,” Philippe Boeglin, spokesperson for the Federal Office for Civil Protection, told the Keystone-SDA news agency. “We need to speak the same technical language to avoid losing valuable time,” said François Fleuti, commander of Vaud Civil Defence.
Planned improvements
At the site, his team and their counterparts from Geneva spent the morning searching for, locating and rescuing people trapped beneath the rubble. Once the area had been assessed using specialist equipment and search dogs, rescue operations began. The rubble first had to be ventilated to prevent a build-up of gas or other hazardous substances. The site also had to be stabilised to ensure it was safe for rescue teams to work, the Vaud commander explained.
More
Truth or tale: Is it true Switzerland has enough bunkers for its population in case of a war?
The exercise was carried out under realistic conditions. The aim is to deal with the disaster using national resources in the first instance, with international assistance requested only if they prove insufficient, according to the spokesperson for the Federal Office for Civil Protection. “In Switzerland, we’re only at the start of the process. We’ll need to draw a lot of lessons from this and make further improvements,” the Vaud official said.
During the exercise, Switzerland is coordinating the entire operation, from the arrival of international teams at the border to their deployment in the affected areas and their eventual return home. Several federal agencies, cantonal authorities, civil protection units and the army have been mobilised.
For this exercise only, members of the Swiss Civil Protection service are wearing uniforms displaying the EU flag as part of EU MODEX Switzerland 2026.

Our screening teams observed that he had normal temperature at the time of departure from Entebbe (airport)," Olaro said.
"The public is encouraged to remain calm, rely on official information and continue observing recommended public health measures," he added.
The ministry said it is working closely with relevant authorities and partners to intensify cross-border surveillance, enhance information sharing and ensure the timely detection and management of potential public health threats.
Kenya on Tuesday confirmed its first imported case of Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease, one day after a man died in a Nairobi hospital, the country's health authorities said. ■

====================================================================================================

Letter from Mideast: My three years in limbo as a Gaza journalist
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:45:07 CST
16:45:07 KST

by Sanaa Kamal
GAZA, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- The day before the war began, I sat by the window in my office, sipping coffee and feeling secure in the future I had worked so hard to build.
After years in journalism, I had bought a car and, just weeks earlier, an apartment in the Tel al-Hawa neighborhood of western Gaza City.
I thought I had finally built a decent life for myself. I did not know I was looking at its final day.
The next morning was Oct. 7, 2023.
Within a week, my family and I had fled our home. In the turmoil that followed, I learned how quickly a future can disappear -- and how deeply the life you leave behind can remain within you.
I stayed in Gaza for another seven months. During that time, even getting food and water became a daily struggle.
After my brothers lost their jobs, I became the main provider for our extended family of about 25 people, most of them children.
I had no time to dwell on the home or car I had lost in the strikes, or the life I had planned. Each day, we had to find food and water and keep the children safe.
I began to realize that the place I had always called home could no longer sustain the life I had known. In April 2024, I left Gaza by bus for Cairo. The journey took 18 hours.
I left Gaza, but only physically.
From Cairo, I continued working as a journalist, following what was happening in Gaza every day. I wrote about bombings, displacement, and death, and then stepped away from my computer to call my brothers and make sure they were still alive.
Working from outside Gaza felt surreal. In Gaza, I had reported on the war while living through it. In Cairo, I watched it unfold on a screen while my family was still there.
Once, a strike hit near my brothers' shelter. I called them again and again for hours, but no one answered. I was no longer thinking like a journalist. I was simply a sister, terrified that something had happened to them.
Moments like this repeated themselves. The fear became so overwhelming that I went to therapy for about six months simply to keep functioning.
I was not the only one carrying that burden.
I spoke with my colleagues in Gaza every day. We discussed not only work but also strikes nearby, homes destroyed in neighboring areas, and people we knew who had been killed.
Across Gaza, the suffering was measured in numbers. The Gaza-based health authorities said in late September that over 1,400 people had been killed in Israeli strikes since a ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hamas was announced in October 2025, bringing the total toll since Oct. 7, 2023, to more than 74,000.
Some 90 percent of Gaza's infrastructure had been damaged or destroyed, leaving homes, schools, hospitals, roads, water networks, and other essential facilities in ruins, said the Hamas-run government media office in late 2025.
For me, these are not just numbers. I see my own family in them.
My brother Radi, 42, lives with his wife and their six children -- five daughters and one son -- in a camp in Al-Zawaida in the central Gaza Strip.
For them, getting through each day is a challenge. "We don't live the way people did before the war," Radi told me. "Every day has its own challenges. We think about water first, then food, then where we'll sleep, and after that, we ask ourselves what we'll do tomorrow."
What worries him most is his children.
"The hardest thing for me is watching my children grow up in the camp," he said. "The girls have grown, and the boy has grown, yet they haven't lived a normal childhood. I try to laugh with them, but deep down, I'm always wondering: For how long?"
When I left Gaza, the children were very young, some barely able to speak. Now, some of them go to makeshift schools in tents.
They have learned to recognize the sounds of war. Some can distinguish missiles from shelling. Some can even judge from the force of an explosion whether it may have caused heavy casualties.
Over the past three years, they have grown older, but they have not had the chance to grow up like children elsewhere in the world.
What they have endured has made me reflect on what the war has changed in my own life.
Before the war, life seemed fairly simple. I would work, build a career, buy a home, and then plan for the future. I believed one stage of life would naturally lead to the next.
Three years have passed, and life no longer feels that simple.
The war has changed my role in the family. I am no longer just the breadwinner. I have become the person everyone turns to for decisions, advice, and help.
I lost my home and car, but I lost more than possessions. I lost the belief that what I worked for would still be there tomorrow.
Now I do not know what comes next.
I do not know when Radi and his children will leave the camp.
I do not know when my colleagues in Gaza will be able to work without fearing for themselves and their families.
I do not know when I will be able to picture a future without wondering whether I will lose it again.
All I know is that going back to the life we once had is becoming harder to imagine.
On Oct. 6, 2023, I thought the future was mine to build.
Today, I am still learning how to believe in one. ■

====================================================================================================

Oct 7: Trauma, tragedy and the normalisation of Palestinian suffering
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:44:14 UTC
16:44:14 KST

Three years is long enough for a child to learn to speak, to walk and to begin discovering the world.
In Gaza, three years have instead been measured in children killed before they could grow, families erased from the civil registry and neighbourhoods reduced to landscapes of dust.
On October 7, the world marks three years since the Hamas-led blitz on Israel and the beginning of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
For Palestinians, however, this date does not mark the beginning of their suffering. It marks the moment when decades of occupation, siege and dispossession erupted into a campaign to make Gaza unliveable—and when much of the world chose to watch it happen.
For three years, Palestinians in Gaza have been subjected not merely to bombardment but to the systematic destruction of the conditions required for collective life.
Homes, hospitals, universities, schools, bakeries, water networks, farmland and places of worship have been reduced to rubble. Entire families have been killed together.
An overwhelmingly displaced population has been repeatedly ordered from one supposedly safe area to another, only for those places to be attacked too.
By rough estimates, over 74,000 Palestinians have been reported killed. More than 21,000 of them are children.
The true toll will be higher: bodies remain buried under collapsed buildings, while deaths caused by hunger, disease and the destruction of healthcare are harder to count.
Around 1.9 million people have been displaced, many repeatedly.
More than 371,000 housing units have been damaged or destroyed, nearly every school has been struck, and more than half of Gaza’s hospitals are no longer functioning.
A joint UN, EU and World Bank assessment says Gaza’s human development has been set back by 77 years.
The violence has not been confined to Gaza.
Since October 2023, Israel has sharply intensified its attacks across the occupied West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem.
More than 1,100 Palestinians, including over 240 children, have been killed by Israeli forces and illegal settlers.
Military raids, home demolitions, illegal settler attacks, illegal settlement expansion and land seizures have all accelerated, forcing thousands of Palestinians from their homes and communities.
While the world’s attention remained fixed on Gaza, Israel used the moment to tighten its control over the occupied West Bank and push forward its illegal annexation.
Gaza and the occupied West Bank face different forms of Israeli violence, but the objective is the same: to erase Palestinians from their land.
Names behind numbers
Numbers of this magnitude can make horror feel abstract. But every statistic was a person with a name, habits, arguments, ambitions and people who loved them.
The dead must not be reduced to evidence of a catastrophe the world already understood and repeatedly chose not to stop.
Nor did the announcement of a ceasefire deal in October 2025 bring safety. More than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed since then.
Israeli occupation forces still control about two-thirds of Gaza, while Palestinians are confined to an overcrowded fraction of their own land.
Reconstruction has barely begun. Restrictions continue to obstruct building materials, medical supplies, clean water and the machinery needed to clear the mountains of rubble.
A ceasefire agreement under which Palestinians continue to be killed, displaced and denied the ability to rebuild is not peace. It is violence managed at a tempo the international community finds easier to ignore.
Throughout these three years, Palestinians have repeatedly been praised for their “resilience”.
It is usually intended as admiration. But the word has become increasingly uncomfortable.
Too often, celebrating Palestinian resilience allows the world to marvel at how much a people can endure without asking why they are still being forced to endure it.
The language of resilience can also depoliticise what is happening. It recasts a people confronting military occupation, apartheid and genocide as recipients of humanitarian sympathy.
It turns rights into needs, political responsibility into tragedy, and crimes with identifiable perpetrators and enablers into an unfortunate disaster without an author.
The focus shifts from the machinery producing Palestinian suffering to the ingenuity with which Palestinians survive it.
That framing is convenient for governments that issue statements of concern while continuing to arm, trade with and diplomatically protect Israel.
Images of Palestinians cooking beside ruined homes or holding lessons in tents are offered as uplifting proof that life continues.
Yet the celebration of their resourcefulness can obscure the central fact: those homes should never have been destroyed, and those children should be learning in schools, not beneath sheets of plastic surrounded by rubble.
Resilience is a mother packing what remains of her life and fleeing for the seventh time.
It is a father searching through rubble for a photograph, a birth certificate or the body of his child.
It is doctors operating without anaesthetic, teachers gathering children inside tents, and families making meals from almost nothing.
These acts are extraordinary, but Palestinians should never have needed such extraordinary strength merely to remain alive.
Beyond October 7
Palestinian steadfastness—sumud—is not a picturesque quality for outsiders to praise. It is a political refusal to disappear.
Palestinians rebuild because Israel destroys. They teach because Israel has damaged or destroyed almost every school. They plant because land is being seized. They tell the names and stories of the dead because erasure is part of the crime.
But resilience must never be used as a substitute for justice.
Survival does not absolve those who armed Israel, protected it diplomatically or continued trading with it while Gaza was being starved and destroyed.
Nor can expressions of sympathy erase three years of deliberate political choices.
In September 2025, a UN Commission of Inquiry concluded that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.
The international community can no longer claim that the nature of the crime is unclear. Yet accountability remains absent, and impunity has allowed the destruction to continue even under the language of a ceasefire.
The appropriate response is not another speech honouring Palestinian courage. It is an arms embargo, sanctions and prosecutions for those responsible.
It is unrestricted humanitarian access and Palestinian-led reconstruction.
It is ending the occupation and apartheid, protecting the right of Palestinian refugees to return, and allowing Palestinians to determine their own future rather than having another political arrangement imposed upon them.
Three years on, Palestinians are still alive, still speaking and still refusing to surrender their claim to their land and their humanity. That endurance is powerful. But it should not comfort the world.
Palestinian survival is not the conclusion of this story. It is an accusation against everyone who made such resilience necessary.

WHO endorses lifestyle changes over GLP-1 drugs in child obesity fight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:44:09 UTC
16:44:09 KST

WHO endorses lifestyle changes over GLP-1 drugs in child obesity fight
Oct 7 - The World Health Organization on Wednesday recommended diet, exercise and counseling over popular weight-loss drugs in its first global guidelines addressing rising obesity among younger children.
According to UNICEF data, obesity has surpassed being underweight as the most common form of malnutrition in school children and adolescents worldwide.
The health agency said weight-loss drugs may be considered for adolescents aged 10 to 19 with obesity but only after supervised interventions have failed. Bariatric surgery could be considered for physically and mentally mature adolescents with severe obesity after six months of unsuccessful treatment, it said.
For children under 10, WHO endorsed diet, physical activity and combined behavioral support instead of obesity medication, surgery or devices because of doubts over their safety and long-term effectiveness.
Luz María De Regil, director of the Department of Nutrition and Food Safety, said there is currently insufficient evidence on GLP-1 drugs, though researchers are monitoring efficacy and safety trials and may revise that assessment as more data emerges.
"The foundation of obesity care for children and adolescents is not medicine or surgery, but access to comprehensive support that enables healthy eating, physical activity and sustainable behaviour change," De Regil said.
Some GLP-1 medicines are already approved for weight-loss in younger patients. Novo Nordisk's Wegovy and Saxenda can be used by certain adolescents 12 and older in the United States and the European Union. The EU also allows Saxenda for some children aged six to 11.
For children and adolescents with obesity, WHO strongly suggested tailored diets, physical activity and behavioral programs involving caregivers, with supervised digital support cited as optional.
Healthy diets and physical activity must also be accessible and affordable because treatment alone cannot halt rising obesity, WHO said.
About 400 million people aged 5 to 19 were overweight in 2024, including 170 million living with obesity, WHO said. Obesity prevalence in the group has quadrupled since 1990. REUTERS

Cashpoint operator concedes “there are problems with ATM deposits and withdrawal”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:42:45 UTC
16:42:45 KST

For some time now VRT’s consumer programme WinWin has been receiving complaints from people experiencing problems with the ATMs at Belgian CASH points. Sometimes people have deposited cash without the amount appearing on their account. Sometimes no money, or too little, comes out of the ATM, yet the full amount is still debited from their account.
Cashpoint operator concedes “there are problems with ATM deposits and withdrawal”
Last summer, Delfien Verhelst wanted to deposit 4,500 euros in cash – the takings from her veterinary practice in Drongen (East Flanders). After she had inserted the banknotes into the machine, it suddenly jammed.
“A slip of paper came out saying there was a technical problem, but that my money was safe. Everything would be credited to my account within 10 working days at the latest.” Except… that didn’t happen, and she was kept waiting by cashpoint operator, Batopin, and by her bank. Until Delfien called in the police.
What is Batopin?
Batopin is a company founded by four major banks operating in Belgium: ING, Belfius, BNP Paribas Fortis and KBC. Under the name CASH, it installs cash machines throughout Belgium. The federal government has reached agreements on this matter with the banking sector and Batopin, to ensure that there remain sufficient locations where people can withdraw cash. By the end of 2027, there should be around 1,065 CASH points available in the country, and 95 per cent of all Belgians should be able to find an ATM within a 5-kilometre radius of their home.
‘We contacted Batopin and our own bank on several occasions. We never heard anything back from Batopin itself, apart from the fact that they couldn’t help us. We did hear from the bank, but the money still hadn’t been paid into our account,’ explains Delfien. "A few weeks after the problem with the cash machine, we finally went to the police. Shortly afterwards, part of our money – around 2,300 euros – suddenly appeared in our account.”
Delfien eventually received the other half of the amount from her own bank. According to Delfien, this was “a goodwill gesture”. So, the money has been returned, but Delfien is still left with many questions. “They claim they never found the money I put into the cash machine. So where did all those notes go?”
Batopin admits that there are problems with transactions where money is not deposited or withdrawn correctly. Commercial Director Maria Janart is keen to emphasise, however, that these problems are exceptional.
What should you do?
Various accounts from victims suggest that Batopin often refers people who are duped back to their bank – and vice versa – when they ask for help. Once and for all: who should you turn to for help if something goes wrong at an ATM? “It is always your own bank that is your point of contact in the event of problems, whether it concerns withdrawing or depositing money. We cannot access users’ details. Only the banks can do that. People are customers of their bank, not of us.”
According to Janart, there has indeed been some confusion about this in the past. “We’ve reviewed this internally and made clear agreements with the banks.”
Batopin does, however, state that it cooperates with the investigation launched by the bank whenever something goes wrong. According to Janart, the company can, amongst other things, retrieve timestamps and transaction details from the ATMs and provide this information to the banks. CCTV footage can also be supplied.
More cashpoints needed
As well as the problems with how the cashpoints operate, there is also the issue of accessibility. In the space of three years, more than 2,000 ATMs disappeared in Belgium – around 35 per cent of the total number of cash machines in 2022.
Batopin must now help to make up for that shortfall. By 2027, there should be 1,065 CASH locations across Belgium. “We already have 945 active locations,” says Janart. “98 locations are currently under construction, and we are still looking for a suitable site for 22 others. So, we will certainly achieve that target.”

TOKYO, October 7. /TASS/. Disappointment over the profitability of major tech companies developing artificial intelligence (AI) technologies could trigger a massive market shock, International Monetary Fund (IMF) Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned.
