Estonia and Albania established diplomatic relations on 17 January 1992, and in 2027 the countries will mark the 35th anniversary of diplomatic relations. Estonia’s embassy accredited to Albania is based in Athens.
Piret Urb has extensive diplomatic experience, having worked in Estonia’s foreign service for more than 20 years. She has represented Estonia on the UN Human Rights Council and led the Freedom Online Coalition during Estonia’s first chairmanship in 2013–2014, which culminated in the adoption of the Tallinn Agenda. For five years, Piret Urb served as Head of International Relations at the Estonian Information System Authority (RIA), which manages the core infrastructure of Estonia’s digital state and is responsible for the country’s cyber security. As Special Envoy for Connectivity in 2023–2024, she was responsible, among other things, for the substantive preparations for the high-level international Tallinn Digital Summit hosted by the Prime Minister. In 2025, Piret Urb worked in Geneva, coordinating the work of the Central and Eastern European Group at the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO). Ambassador Piret Urb has undertaken further studies and professional training in the United States and France.

Paysera removes bank transfer fee for merchants in the Baltic States
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:39:31 UTC
16:39:31 KST

Payments company Paysera has stopped charging a fee for bank transfers collected through the payment initiation service (PIS) in the Baltic States. The change takes effect with the launch of the new Checkout Modern payment platform, which is now open to all of the company’s merchants in Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia.
More than 10,000 merchants in the Baltic States use the Paysera Checkout payment gateway. In total, the service operates in 42 countries and covers more than 13,000 active payment projects, though free bank transfers are currently offered only in the three Baltic States.
Until now, two pricing models have dominated online retail payments: a percentage fee on the card transaction, or a fee per bank transfer. On the new platform, Paysera is dropping the second.
The platform’s own data shows the logic behind the decision: two out of three payments made through it (66%) are bank transfers rather than card transactions. At the same time, the market price of the payment initiation service has fallen so far that the fee brings the company little revenue, while the merchant still pays for it as a separate line.
A single bank transfer costs 5–20 cents on the market. At those rates, a shop collecting a thousand bank transfers a month would save between 600 and 2,400 EUR a year.
“In the Baltic States, buyers choose a bank transfer more often than a card â€“ on our platform, two purchases out of three are paid for that way. Once the market price of the service fell to a few cents, charging for it separately stopped making sense for us or for the merchant, so we are dropping the fee. Cards remain important, but they should not be the only method a business can afford,” says Justina Šidlauskienė, CEO of Paysera.
What Checkout Modern is
The platform replaces the Checkout system used until now. In a single payment window it brings together bank transfers made through open banking, card payments (Visa, Mastercard), and the Apple Pay and Google Pay digital wallets. A buy now, pay later solution with Inbank is offered alongside them. Bank transfers work in Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia â€“ the main banks in these countries are connected directly to the platform.
The new version introduces a payment splitting (Split) function, which automatically divides a single payment from a buyer among several recipients. The solution is intended for marketplaces, where money has to reach several sellers. Activation of card payments has also been simplified, and project management in the merchant module has been updated.
Integration and expansion
Merchants can connect through ready-made plugins for the WooCommerce (WordPress), PrestaShop, OpenCart, and Shopify platforms – with Magento to follow shortly – or through the API.
In the self-service area, merchants manage projects and payment methods themselves, monitor transactions in real-time and issue full or partial refunds. Payment links can also be created, making it possible to collect payments even without a website. The platform complies with the PCI DSS standard for card payments.
The old Checkout version will continue to operate and will be supported until banks in every country the service currently covers are connected to the new platform. The PIS fee remains in force there. To move to the new Checkout, a merchant only needs to install the new Paysera plugin on their e-shop platform and create a new payment project in self-service. Once the plugin is installed and the project activated, the new system starts working immediately.
Bulgaria’s UBB bank is already connected to the new platform, and integrations with eight more banks in Romania and Bulgaria are being built â€“ the company plans to expand into these markets.
Source: paysera.lt

AI expansion could boost annual global growth by 0.5 percentage points — IMF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:39:28 UTC
16:39:28 KST

TOKYO, October 7. /TASS/. The development of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies could add up to 0.5 percentage points to annual global GDP growth, International Monetary Fund (IMF) Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said.
"IMF research suggests that AI, if done right, could over time deliver up to half a percentage point of extra world growth annually. Just think of it: going from 3 percent to 3Ѕ percent - it will add an economy the size of ASEAN to the world economy over a decade," Georgieva said. She was speaking in Singapore ahead of the IMF and World Bank Autumn Meetings, scheduled for next week in Thailand.
"Global investment-to-GDP in AI will reach and likely exceed the amounts that went into building the railroads, the electricity grid, or the telecommunication network. We estimate AI hardware and related tech products now account for more than one-tenth of world goods trade and rising," the IMF chief said.
According to Georgieva, the surge in AI-related trade reflects an investment boom among nations embedded in its supply chain. The biggest beneficiaries are India, China, and the US, alongside Asian suppliers of microprocessors, memory, chip-making equipment, and robotics.
However, the rest of the world is largely being left out of this boom, which increases "the risk of widening economic inequality across the globe.".

INTERVIEW – Israeli lawmaker vows to oust Netanyahu’s ‘fascist government’ in Oct. 27 election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:36:24 UTC
16:36:24 KST

Israeli lawmaker Ofer Cassif said the Joint List will do everything in its power to remove Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government in Israel’s Oct. 27 general elections.
“We will do everything we can to get rid of this fascist government,” Cassif, a candidate representing Hadash, the Democratic Front for Peace and Equality, an Arab-Jewish political party and a constituent party of the Joint List, an alliance of Arab-led parties in Israel, told Anadolu in an interview.
Election itself ‘at risk’
Cassif said his first concern was whether the election would take place as scheduled, warning that Netanyahu and his coalition partners could seek to provoke a wider confrontation to postpone or even cancel the vote.
“We have to hope, first of all, that the elections actually take place,” he said.
Cassif said the government could attempt to ignite a major conflict in the occupied West Bank or elsewhere in the region, including Lebanon, Syria, Iraq or Iran.
“They will do everything they can to ignite a fire,” he said, arguing that an escalation could be used as a pretext to postpone the election or boost the coalition’s electoral prospects.
He called the possibility deeply concerning and urged efforts to prevent any further escalation.
Court ruling ‘a right, not a privilege’
Cassif also addressed the Israeli Supreme Court’s decision allowing him and the Joint List to contest the election after attempts to bar Arab lists and candidates.
He said the ruling should not be treated as a favor.
“The right to vote and to be elected is a right, not a privilege,” he said.
The Supreme Court overturned a decision by the Central Elections Committee barring the Joint List and the United Arab List, or Ra’am, and cleared Cassif to run.
Cassif, however, condemned the exclusion of Balad party leader Sami Abu Shehadeh, calling it “outrageous” and warning that similar attempts to exclude Palestinian political representatives could follow.
Arab turnout could shape race
Cassif said efforts to disqualify Arab candidates could ultimately mobilize Palestinian citizens of Israel ahead of the election.
“I believe the attempt to disqualify Sami and to disqualify all of us has mobilized people,” he said.
He predicted a strong showing for the Joint List and said an increased turnout could also attract Jewish voters opposed to the government.
Arab citizens make up around 20% of Israel’s population, while polls project Arab parties to win around 12 to 14 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
Recent surveys show neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the main opposition camp reaching the 61 seats needed to form a government on its own, potentially giving Arab parties a significant role after the vote.
No automatic support for opposition
Asked whether the Joint List could support opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot in forming a government, Cassif said the question first rested with opposition parties, many of whose leaders have ruled out relying on Arab parties.
“The ball is in their court, not ours,” he said.
Cassif said the Joint List was determined to remove Netanyahu, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir from power.
But he ruled out automatically backing any government that replaced them.
“We cannot support a government that would simply be a carbon copy of the previous one,” he said.
Cassif said policies involving annexation of occupied Palestinian territory or a continuation of the current government’s approach would make such support impossible.
Concern over younger Israeli voters
Cassif also voiced concern over support for extremist political movements among younger Israelis, particularly those serving in the military.
He attributed the trend to sustained incitement against Palestinians, the Israeli left and Jewish opponents of the government’s policies.
Cassif said reversing that trend would require profound political and social change.
“I have to be optimistic,” he said. “But optimism is not just an assumption. It is something we fight for.”
‘Open your eyes and your hearts’
Cassif ended the interview by calling for greater international attention to developments in the occupied West Bank and Gaza.
He accused Israeli occupiers, often accompanied by soldiers, of attacking Palestinians during the olive harvest and called for international action.
“Open your eyes and your hearts, and stop these crimes,” he said.
“Stop the ongoing genocide in Gaza, stop the ongoing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, and stop the fascism that dominates Israel.”

Overnight Russian drone, missile strikes kill 8 across Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:34:00 UTC
16:34:00 KST

Massive Russian drone and missile barrage killed at least 20 people across Ukraine overnight into Wednesday, damaging residential buildings, industrial facilities and infrastructure, officials said.
Emergency services picked through the rubble of the flattened five-story building in Pryluky, in the Chernigiv region, in a frantic search for survivors.
But hopes faded as the toll jumped by early afternoon.
"The death toll ... has risen to 14, including four children," the state emergency services said. "Fifty people were wounded, including seven children."
Fifteen people, including a child, were rescued, they wrote on Telegram.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had warned the public Tuesday night that Russia was planning "massive" strikes, particularly against the country's energy infrastructure.
"The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively," he said Wednesday, calling it "one of the most vile strikes" in the nearly five-year conflict.
Two people were killed when missiles slammed into high-rise buildings in Dnipro and Kremenchuk in central Ukraine, while two others lost their lives in Oleksandriya, he added.
In the capital, Kyiv, strikes killed two people.
Kyiv has come under increased attack in recent weeks as winter approaches, with air raid sirens wailing nearly constantly to warn of incoming Russian strikes.
Residents hunkered down in subway stations overnight, hauling duffel bags, sleeping mats and blankets, after air alerts sounded warning of attacks.
"We grabbed our things and came here, we live right next door," Iryna Rybalchenko, who works in a bank, told AFP, sitting on the platform wrapped in a dark hoodie and surrounded by bags.
"The whole of Kyiv is in a state of fear. We were stuck at work today and everyone – our group chats, our bosses – were messaging us to be careful."
Russia launched at least 50 missiles and 130 drones overnight against several regions including Dnipropetrovsk, Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Poltava, Ukraine's air force said.
Zelenskyy said that although some were shot down, ballistic missiles were "the greatest challenge," and new air defenses were "a vital necessity" to help Ukraine defend itself.
The two victims in Kyiv died in a fire in the densely populated Darnytskyi neighborhood as a result of Wednesday's attack, Mayor Vitaly Klitschko said.
He had warned last week the capital should now be on a war footing as the enemy was "tearing Kyiv apart" with strikes on bridges and energy infrastructure.
The renewed attacks had triggered scheduled power cuts Tuesday, which plunged parts of Kyiv into darkness to ease the pressure on the battered grid.
A familiar rumbling sound of the generators, used to get through power cuts, filled the streets again, bringing back memories of the previous winter, when systematic Russian attacks regularly cut power and heating.
In the evening, Zelenskyy warned residents to monitor for air raid sirens, saying in his nightly address that "there is updated intelligence information regarding the preparation by the Russians of a massive strike."
Military monitoring channels also said they expected a large-scale Russian attack, combining cruise and ballistic missiles with fast-moving jet-powered drones.
Zelenskyy said the military was "ready to respond, to the extent that our defense systems allow."
The air force said in the morning that it intercepted five ballistic missiles, as well as 39 cruise missiles and over 100 drones.
Ukraine has been struggling to down the new and fast-moving jet-powered drones, as well as the ballistic missiles that are harder to intercept.
"The children were absolutely terrified. Whenever there's heavy shelling, we try to head underground," Daria Medvedeva, 36, told AFP.
Concern has mounted about rising civilian casualties on both sides, as Ukraine also steps up its long-range attacks on Russian targets that it says are vital to its war effort.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine's "just responses" to Russian strikes saw it hit two oil facilities and a training ground in the Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions, as well as the Black Sea.

====================================================================================================

INTERVIEW - Europe has no weapons in space, but watching developments ‘very carefully’: European space chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:33:57 UTC
16:33:57 KST

Europe has no weapons deployed in space, but such capabilities must be watched "very carefully," the head of the European Space Agency (ESA) said, weeks after the US confirmed that it has weapons in orbit for the first time.
"Of course, having weapons in space is concerning if they are deployed. That means if they are damaging other satellites or other space infrastructure," ESA Director General Josef Aschbacher told Anadolu on the sidelines of the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC 2026) in Antalya.
"It's one thing to have the weapon. It's another thing to use it," he said.
On Sept. 14, US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink told a defense conference in Maryland that the US Space Force has “on-orbit space control weapons” capable of defending American forces against hostile action.
It was the first time a Pentagon official had publicly acknowledged that the US operates weapons in space. Meink did not say what the weapons are, how they work or when they were placed in orbit.
US officials have long said such capabilities are needed to counter Russian and Chinese programs designed to attack or disrupt American satellites. In 2024, Washington accused Moscow of developing a new anti-satellite weapon that could be launched from space.
The disclosure drew swift criticism from Beijing and Moscow the following day.
China's Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said Beijing opposes the weaponization of outer space and turning it into a war zone. "We urge the US to stop expanding military build-up in outer space," he told a routine press briefing.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia believes "space must be free of any weapon." He called for broad international efforts toward the complete demilitarization of space.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova accused Washington of ignoring the "catastrophic consequences for humanity of any armed conflict in orbit" in pursuit of its own interests.
She also dismissed US accusations that Moscow is developing anti-satellite weapons as an attempt to divert attention.
Zakharova said Russia would present resolutions to the UN General Assembly on barring weapons from space.
The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, to which the US, Russia and China are all parties, bans nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction in orbit. It does not explicitly prohibit conventional weapons.
‘Think twice’
Aschbacher said any use of weapons in space would carry huge risks.
"It is very clear that if there would be the use of weapons in space, that would destroy all the orbits or the satellites in those orbits, and therefore it's a very high threshold to overcome," he said.
"Of course, you need to protect your own satellites, but I think it is really something that we have to watch very carefully. Europe does not deploy weapons in space, certainly not from the European Space Agency."
Asked whether this was Europe's stance on a possible war in space, Aschbacher said he considered such a conflict unlikely.
"I'm not assuming a war in space. This would be very far-fetched for many reasons. First of all, it is a very complex environment," he said.
When a satellite is destroyed in orbit, it breaks into fragments that can stay in space for years and hit other spacecraft.
"If there would be a war in space and satellites would be destroyed, the aggressor would also destroy his own satellites because the debris would destroy his own satellites. So, I think people would think really twice before they do that," he said.
"I think it's really a message to say, 'Look, we have strength in space,' but I do not believe today that these weapons will be utilized in space."
‘Europe is moving just as fast’
Last year, at a ministerial meeting in Bremen, ESA member states approved €22.3 billion in contributions. It was the largest funding package in the agency's history. Ministers hold these meetings roughly every three years to decide the space agency's main programs and budgets.
Asked where Europe most urgently needs to catch up with the US and China, he disagreed with the premise.
"Europe is moving just as fast. We have a smaller budget compared to the United States, but I'm very proud to say that we have some world-leading programs," he said.
He described Copernicus, the EU's Earth observation program that ESA helps develop, as "the best Earth observation program in the world." He said Europe's satellite navigation system Galileo, its alternative to the US-run GPS, is "more precise than any other system in the world."
Decision on post-ISS access expected in December
The International Space Station (ISS), where European astronauts have worked for more than two decades, is scheduled to be retired around 2030. Europe does not yet have its own vehicle to send astronauts into orbit.
Asked whether Europe will have guaranteed access to low Earth orbit after 2030, he said member states had given him a mandate to develop plans on guaranteed European access to space, "not only for satellites, but also for astronauts."
ESA has said the interim ministerial meeting will take place in Rome in December.
Earlier this year, member states endorsed a plan to buy a dedicated SpaceX Crew Dragon flight to the ISS in early 2028. The aim is to give more European astronauts the chance to fly before the station is retired.
AI in orbit
Aschbacher also discussed the growing interest in putting computing power and artificial intelligence directly in orbit, including proposals for large data centers in space. He said the concept "is in development."
The ESA chief added that Europe was examining several approaches but believes processing information directly on satellites could offer the greatest practical benefit.
“The European Space Agency was the very first one using an AI chip on an Earth observation satellite and do processing in space of that information,” he said, referring to Φ-sat-1, a small experimental satellite launched from French Guiana in September 2020.
ESA has described it as Europe's first Earth observation mission to carry an AI chip. The chip filtered out cloud-covered images on board so that only usable data was sent back to Earth.
Asked about concerns over giving AI more autonomy in space, Aschbacher said the technology is already widely used.
Partnerships with Türkiye
International Astronautical Congress runs Oct. 5-9 and is the first edition of the world's largest annual space conference to be held in Türkiye. The Turkish Space Agency (TUA) is hosting it, with defense and tech firm SAHA Istanbul as co-host.
Türkiye and ESA signed a framework cooperation agreement in 2004. It was valid for five years and covered areas such as space science, Earth observation and satellite navigation.
"If there are new activities to come, we would need to negotiate a new agreement," Aschbacher said.
He pointed instead to direct cooperation between Turkish and European companies. He cited Turksat, Türkiye's satellite operator, whose 5A and 5B communications satellites were built by European manufacturer Airbus Defence and Space.
"This is happening since many years already, that our industry is working very closely with Turkish industries or institutions to provide hardware, satellites, infrastructure on a daily basis," he said.
“I see this increasing in the future,” he added.
Aschbacher, an Austrian, has led ESA since March 2021. His mandate was renewed in 2023 for a second four-year term that runs until 2029.

After years of Israel genocide, Gazans trapped in forced exile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:32:30 UTC
16:32:30 KST

Breadcrumb
After three years of Israel's genocide, Gazans are trapped between forced exile and the dream of return
Three years after Israel's genocidal war forced tens of thousands of Palestinians out of Gaza, many of those who left remain caught between two lives: one they were forced to abandon and another they never chose.
In Egypt, Turkey and elsewhere, Palestinians from Gaza have rented homes, found work and sent their children to school, slowly building a life in exile.
Gaza remains ever-present in their daily lives, manifesting through memories of homes destroyed, family members killed, and ordinary moments gone for good.
The dream of return to Gaza has never faded for some Palestinians. But they are left with painful questions: when can they return and what will they return to?
Into exile
When Ahlam Abu Marq hears an aircraft overhead in Egypt, she knows it is not an Israeli warplane. Her body does not—her pulse quickens, fear returns, and echoes of strikes and death rush back.
"I know it's an Egyptian plane, and I know I'm in Egypt, but I'm afraid [...] The sound takes me back to the bombing. I feel as though I'm still there, as if something is about to happen at any moment," she remarked to The New Arab.
Ahlam left Gaza about two and a half years ago with her only surviving child, Mohammed, now six, after losing her husband and five other children.
She rents a home in Egypt and tries to provide her son with a stable life amid rising rents and living costs. But financial hardship is not her deepest struggle.
"Life here is hard; rent consumes a large part of my money, and there are so many responsibilities," she said. "But the hardest part isn't the money. The hardest part is trying to go on living after losing all of them."
Before Israel's genocidal war, Ahlam said she had lived a simple life that she did not realise was precious.
"I lived an ordinary life without realizing it was a blessing. I used to complain about little things. Today, I wish those days would return, exhaustion and all," she added.
Despite the time that has passed, she does not feel that she has escaped the war. An aircraft, a picture of Gaza or news of another attack can bring back the fear and grief.
She misses Gaza, but fears returning. "I don't know how I could go back to the places where my children died. How could I walk past there as if nothing had happened?" she said.
Mohammed has become her reason to continue.
"When I see him, I tell myself I must live and protect him. He didn't choose this life, and the least I can do is provide him with a safe one," she explained.
Life with uncertainty
Mohammed Abu Hasira, 55, left Gaza in April 2024 after losing his parents and siblings.
He arrived in Egypt and opened a seafood restaurant to support himself and his three children. Despite establishing a new livelihood, he remains unable to make long-term plans.
"I live day by day […] I open the restaurant, work, and try to get through the day. I don't think much about the future because I don't know what will happen," he told TNA.
Prior to 2023, Mohammed thought about his children's education and imagined what their lives might look like years later. Now, even the following year feels uncertain.
"Before the war, I thought about my children, their education and what our lives would look like years down the line. Now, I don't know what will happen a year from today," he said.
Abu Hasira finds himself remembering simple moments he once overlooked: sitting with his father, talking to his siblings and even the disagreements that once seemed insignificant.
"Today, I wish I could live just one of those days again […] I did not leave Gaza to seek a better life," he added. "I didn't choose to start a new life; the war chose for me. There is a vast difference between someone who travels because they want to change their life and someone who leaves because they want to survive."
He does not know whether Egypt will remain his home. "The restaurant is here today, but I don't know what tomorrow holds. I might stay, or I might go back," he explained.
But Gaza remains home regardless of its physical destruction.
"Gaza isn't just the place where I lived; it is my family and my memories. Even if the house is gone, Gaza remains my home," Abu Hasira remarked.
Homeland remembered, transformed
For 42-year-old Amal Hijazi, the consequences of the war are physical and emotional.
She was living with her five children in Gaza when her home was bombed in December 2023. She was wounded, suffering severe burns to her feet and losing one of her hands.
She currently lives in Turkey, relying on aid while trying to keep her children in school and give them a semblance of normality.
"The hardest part is knowing you used to do everything for your children, only to find yourself needing help with the simplest things," she described to TNA.
Hijazi refuses to let her injuries determine her children's future. "The war took our home, took my hand, and injured my feet, but it will not take my children's future. I want them to learn and to move forward with their lives," she said.
She remembers her home in Gaza in intimate detail. "Our home was an ordinary place. I knew where every child slept, and where we sat and ate. I didn't know that a home could turn into a memory in an instant," she recalled.
Hijazi wants to return one day, but not simply to the ruins of what once existed.
"I want my children to return to Gaza, but I want there to be a life there. I want a home, a school, a hospital, and a safe place for them," she said.
The Israeli war on Gaza began on 7 October 2023 following the Hamas-led attack on Israeli military bases and civilian settlements within and around the Gaza envelope. Around 1,200 Israelis died and about 250 people being taken captive, according to Israeli authorities.
Israel's subsequent genocidal war has killed at least 74,000 Palestinians, mainly women and children, and injured around 175,000, according to the Palestinian health ministry, while thousands remain missing.
Across Gaza, homes and neighbourhoods have been destroyed, along with hospitals, schools, water and electricity networks and other essential infrastructure. Most of the population has also been displaced, often repeatedly.
The scale of destruction means that returning cannot simply mean crossing a border and reopening a door.
Fundamental questions about Gaza's future remain unanswered: Who will govern the Strip? How security and border crossings will be managed? When reconstruction will begin and under what conditions displaced Palestinians will be allowed to return?
To more than 100,000 Palestinians, the number according to conservative Palestinian figures, who left Gaza during Israel's genocide and remain outside the besieged coastal enclave, those questions are deeply personal.

Obesity among children, adolescents has quadrupled since 1990, affecting 170M: WHO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:32:29 UTC
16:32:29 KST

Beyza Binnur Dönmez
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Obesity among children and adolescents aged 5-19 has quadrupled globally since 1990, with 170 million living with the chronic disease in 2024, the World Health Organization (WHO) said Wednesday.
According to the WHO, prevalence among the age group rose from 2% in 1990 to 8% in 2024. Of those affected, 70 million were children aged 5-9 and 100 million were adolescents aged 10-19.
The figures came as the WHO released its first guidelines on obesity care for children and adolescents, recommending structured interventions focused on diet, physical activity and behavioral change.
The agency said weight-loss medicines, bariatric surgery and weight-loss devices should not be used to treat children aged 0-9.
For adolescents aged 10-19, approved medicines "may be considered" only when a supervised multimodal lifestyle program has failed to achieve the desired results, while bariatric surgery may be considered under strict conditions for severe obesity.
The WHO warned that obesity can increase the risk of diseases including type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease from an early age.
It also highlighted the mental health consequences associated with obesity, including stigma, bullying, anxiety, depression and low self-esteem, calling for physical and mental health conditions to be addressed together.
“The foundation of obesity care for children and adolescents is not medicine or surgery, but access to comprehensive support that enables healthy eating, physical activity and sustainable behaviour change,” said Dr. Luz Maria De Regil, the director of the department of nutrition and food Safety at the WHO.
She stressed that the priority must be to ensure that every child and adolescent can access "quality care and supportive environments from an early age, helping them achieve and maintain a healthy weight and laying the foundation for lifelong health and well-being.”
The WHO stressed that obesity care should go beyond weight loss, focusing on overall health, functioning and well-being, with long-term, age-appropriate care tailored to children and their families.
It also warned that treatment alone cannot reverse rising obesity rates, calling for measures to make healthy diets and physical activity more accessible and affordable.

US Justice Department directs staff to use 'super intelligence' in communications: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:30:22 UTC
16:30:22 KST

Yasin Güngör
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
The US Justice Department instructed its personnel to substitute the term artificial intelligence with "super intelligence" across all official communications and court documents, Bloomberg Law reported Tuesday.
"Terminology used by the Federal Government should reflect the transformative capabilities of extraordinary technologies being pioneered by American innovators," Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter wrote in an internal memorandum sent to department staff.
The guidance implements a Sept. 29 executive order issued by US President Donald Trump titled "Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence," which mandates that federal departments apply the nomenclature "to the maximum extent permitted by law" in their official functions.
According to the policy, which also covers attorney filings, staff must adopt the phrasing "super intelligence" or the abbreviation "SI" in legal filings when appropriate.
The directive represents an internal US government terminology change rather than a global redefinition of artificial intelligence.
Trump previously ordered the shift across federal websites, policy reports, and communications, arguing that the word "artificial" makes technological systems sound fake.

Defence show opens in London with focus on near-term kit

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:30:01 BST
16:30:01 KST

A new defence technology event built around operational problems opens at The Magazine in London on Wednesday, the first time the Apex series has been staged in Britain, according to the organisers.
Apex Europe runs on 7 and 8 October and is organised by Clarion Defence and Security, the company behind DSEI in Britain, Germany and Japan. It runs as a counterpart to Apex Defense, held each January in Washington, and the organisers describe the London edition as operator-driven, aimed squarely at European and NATO operational priorities and at solutions that could be deployed in the near term rather than in a decade.
The format puts operational leaders, acquisition staff, startups, scale-ups, investors and established industry in the same room to work through what the organisers call pacing threats facing European and allied commands.
Seven operational problems have been set as the agenda for the two days. They cover the interoperability and integration of autonomous systems across European and NATO forces; winning autonomous warfare at scale and mass; generating combat power through long-range strike and precision effects; countering undersea threats and protecting critical infrastructure; countering low-cost and rapidly proliferating uncrewed systems; enhancing layered and integrated air and missile defence across domains; and fighting in a denied, degraded and contested battlespace.
Read as a list, those seven amount to a fairly blunt statement of what has gone wrong with European defence over the past four years. Three of them concern drones in one form or another, two concern defending infrastructure and airspace that was previously assumed safe, and one concerns operating when the electromagnetic spectrum is being taken away.
Several exhibitors have timed announcements to coincide with the show. Cody Aerospace and Defence, which describes itself as building a new British sovereign prime for complex weapons, will announce its first products during the event. Labrys Technologies unveils the latest version of its Axiom secure communications platform, and Voyant Innovations arrives having just demonstrated satellite-free navigation to the Ministry of Defence aboard an uncrewed vessel in the Solent.
The exhibitor list leans towards smaller companies, with British entrants including Helix Geospace on anti-jamming antennas, Drone Evolution on first-person-view drones and training, Q5D on automated wire harness manufacture and Talos Technology on electric motors for drones. Granta Autonomy arrives from Lithuania with equipment already in Ukrainian service, and BlueShadow, founded last year and operating from Copenhagen and Kyiv, shows maritime security software.

Source: European Pravda, citing Reuters

The main EU regulation on sanctions against Russia currently contains just over 3,000 entities subject to EU travel bans, transaction restrictions and asset freezes.

Designing the In-Between: From Tactical Interventions to Urban Policy in Barcelona

2026-10-07

In Europe, cities are confronting the challenge of adapting existing urban conditions to a changing climate and warming summers while improving access to nature, quality public spaces, and the resources of everyday routines. ReGreeneration, a Horizon Europe initiative working across nine European cities, approaches this challenge through urban renaturing at the neighborhood scale. Combining strategies for complete neighborhoods, communal spaces, and nature-based solutions for cities, the Barcelona project examines how climate adaptation is embedded within residual, peripheral spaces of daily life. As part of a series following ReGreeneration across the participating cities, this article turns to Barcelona, where the project is working in the Trinitat Nova neighborhood to explore how small, often overlooked, urban spaces contribute to broader models of regeneration.
Barcelona offers a unique, particularly significant context for this ambition because of the city's urban and architectural legacy, which has become internationally associated with the reclamation of streets and public spaces. From the transformation of its public realm following Spain's democratic transition to the well-known Superblocks project and ongoing traffic reduction measures, there is a storied, layered history of tactical urbanism and temporary urban changes in Barcelona. Across various scales, the city demonstrates how streets and undervalued spaces can be designed as places for walking, activity, community, playfulness, and urban nature. Tactical urbanism is an essential component of this process, allowing new programs to be introduced and tested at higher speeds than traditional urban development can accommodate. The celebration of tactical urbanism in cities around the world energizes designers and planners alike, but this project dives into a deeper, more difficult question about the process. How can the flexibility and responsiveness of temporary urban interventions translate into long-term planning and policy in cities?

====================================================================================================

Three years after October 7: How crisis rewired Israel’s defense tech ecosystem - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:28:20 UTC
16:28:20 KST

It’s been three years since October 7.
Three years since Hamas rampaged through southern Israel, destroying the long-held belief that the Gaza-based terrorist group was held back by advanced technology and “diplomatic measures” such as millions of dollars in cash transferred to them in briefcases.
It has been three years since the face of the Middle East changed forever. It wasn’t just terrorist groups like Hamas or Hezbollah warring against Israel; The event also led to the first true state-vs-state war in the region in years, when the wars with Iran broke out.
But three years after the deadly Hamas attack, Israel’s defense tech ecosystem looks fundamentally different from what it was before the war. It’s larger, faster, more integrated with the military, and, most importantly, more mission‑driven than at any point in the country’s history.
The deadly Hamas massacre exposed painful gaps in Israel’s technological defenses. But it also triggered a transformation in the country’s defense tech ecosystem, bringing start-ups, investors, the IDF, government research bodies, and established defense companies into a far tighter relationship.
Before the war, Israel was already a global center for defense innovation. Yet much of the start-up ecosystem remained oriented toward civilian markets, particularly cybersecurity. Defense was often viewed by investors as a difficult market with long procurement cycles, demanding government customers, and a path from prototype to revenue that could take years.
October 7 changed that calculation.
Within weeks and months, reservists returning from Gaza and engineers working in tech companies began identifying problems they had encountered firsthand behind enemy lines. The result was a new generation of companies building counter-drone systems, autonomous platforms, artificial intelligence, battlefield communications, electronic warfare, robotics, intelligence, and logistics.
The Israeli defense tech ecosystem has grown from roughly 160 companies before October 7 to over 300 today. The Defense Ministry says hundreds of start-ups are now working with its Directorate of Defense, Research and Development (MAFAT).
Israel's defense tech workforce also underwent a cultural shift. Every aspect had become mission-driven.
A model of hi-tech security … until it wasn’t
The October 7 attack was not only a major human catastrophe and a failure by the security establishment, but also a systemic shock.
Israel’s border with Gaza had been promoted as a global model of hi‑tech security. While the IDF was still shackled to legacy systems, using fax machines, outdated servers, and siloed intelligence, the southern border with Gaza featured a multilayered smart fence with subterranean barriers, AI‑enhanced surveillance, remote‑operated weapons systems, and a doctrine built on the assumption that technology could contain threats at a manageable cost.
In 2021, the Defense Ministry reported that over 1,200 workers from various countries contributed to the project, which involved multiple points along the border and the establishment of six concrete plants.
Some 330,000 trucks poured some 3 million cubic meters of concrete for the project, “enough to pave a road from Israel to Bulgaria,” said then-Fence Administration Director Brig.-Gen. Eran Ofir.
Another 140,000 tons of iron and steel were used in the construction of the barrier, “equivalent to the length of a steel wall from Israel to Australia,” he added.
The fence included an underground barrier running along the entire border with Gaza, as well as a maritime border wall. It featured a system of advanced sensors and monitoring devices to detect tunnels. It was combined with a six-meter-high above-ground fence, similar to the one that runs along the Israeli-Egyptian border.
But the AI‑based intelligence system and advanced technologies the IDF gloated about five years ago failed to perform as expected on October 7. Low‑tech tools such as explosives, bulldozers, motorcycles, and commercial paragliders and drones neutralized those billion‑dollar systems in mere minutes.
The failure was not simply technological; it was doctrinal.
Israel had come to treat technology as a shield rather than as one layer within a resilient, human‑centered defense architecture. Despite warnings from junior officers about the looming threat across the border, they were ignored.
And no one - and no technology - was able to grasp the enormity of the danger before thousands of Hamas terrorists broke through Israel’s walls and massacred over 1,200 people and kidnapped another 251, living and dead.
Catalyst for transformation
That collapse of confidence became the catalyst for a profound transformation in the shattered country.
In the months that followed, the defense tech ecosystem entered a period of hyper‑acceleration driven by a sense of national urgency.
Capital followed, with private investment surging from around $1 billion in 2025 to an estimated $3b. in 2026. Specialized funds also emerged to bridge the gap between early‑stage innovation and military procurement, accelerating the path from prototype to deployment.
The domains of innovation reflected the lessons of October 7. AI and machine learning became central tools for anomaly detection, drone swarm prediction, real‑time battlefield analytics, and automated threat classification. Counter‑drone technologies exploded in importance, driven by the recognition that cheap aerial platforms had become one of the deadliest tools in Hezbollah’s arsenal.
Autonomous ground vehicles, robotic logistics, and battlefield medical systems advanced rapidly, shaped by the realities of urban combat and mass‑casualty response. Cyber defense also intensified, as Israel confronted simultaneous threats from Iran, Hezbollah, and Hamas targeting critical infrastructure.
Yet the most significant shift may actually be the relationship between the Defense Ministry and the start-up ecosystem.
Bureaucratic barriers fell, procurement processes were streamlined, and the military began inviting small, agile companies into what had traditionally been a closed clique. Wartime urgency shortened development cycles dramatically. Technologies that once took years to test and certify were piloted and deployed within months, sometimes weeks. Upgrades took place in the mud, behind the front lines.
The change has also forced the government to rethink its approach to technology procurement.
Traditional defense procurement around the globe has been built around large contractors, lengthy development programs, and major platforms. But with the modern battlefield increasingly defined by systems that can be developed and upgraded quickly, a start-up does not need to build the next fighter jet to become strategically important. It could provide the software, sensor, autonomous system or electronic-warfare capability that makes dozens, if not hundreds, of existing legacy platforms more effective.
The Defense Ministry has introduced initiatives to make it easier for start-ups to enter the defense market and to shorten the gap between development and procurement.
Its growing focus on artificial intelligence and autonomy reflects another important lesson from the war: the future battlefield will depend less on individual platforms and more on the ability to integrate sensors, weapons, communications, intelligence and autonomous systems into a single operational picture.
All this has made Israel’s defense tech ecosystem more diversified, more adaptive, and more deeply integrated with operational needs. The country now fields a more layered defense posture by combining AI, drones, cyber capabilities, autonomous systems, and human intelligence.
Despite all the public political disputes, the global defense industry has taken notice, and foreign militaries and companies are actively seeking partnerships, technologies, and lessons from Israel’s accelerated innovation model.
Because they want what works, and Israeli defense technology works. Israel has paid with lives to ensure it works.
Will it survive?
The question, though, is whether Israel can sustain this pace of innovation.
The trauma of October 7 created urgency, but urgency is not a strategy. Israel has always been exceptionally good at developing technology quickly. The harder question is whether it can produce that technology at scale. A start-up may develop a working system in months, but getting thousands of systems into soldiers' hands remains a much more complicated process.
The last three years of war in Israel and the past five years of war in Ukraine and overall global tensions have highlighted dependence on global supply chains, the importance of domestic production capacity, and the limitations of procurement systems designed for a different era.
As militaries and governments study the lessons of Ukraine and the wars in the Middle East, European and Asian countries are dramatically increasing defense spending. That has helped Israeli defense exports reach a record $14.8b. in 2024, followed by $19.2b. in 2025.
For Israeli defense tech companies, the opportunity is much larger than the domestic market. The real test, however, will come when wartime urgency eventually recedes.
Can a start-up survive long defense procurement cycles? Can investors remain patient? Can Israel manufacture at the speed and scale that match the pace of its entrepreneurs' innovation? And can the defense establishment keep absorbing new technologies once the immediate pressure of war diminishes?
Three years later, we are still witnessing the legacy of October 7 unfold. It is reshaping Israel’s defense tech ecosystem not only by accelerating innovation but also by forcing a reckoning with the limits of technological confidence.
The challenge now is to ensure that the tools built in crisis can serve a future defined not only by security but also by stability.

US defense funding paths for Israeli tech: Navigating the Pentagon’s innovation gateways - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:28:19 UTC
16:28:19 KST

Theodore von Kármán, one of the greatest minds of the 20th century, said, “Scientists discover the world that exists; engineers create the world that never was." Von Kármán was the pioneer of modern aerospace science, and a lifelong champion of turning laboratory breakthroughs into military advantage.
Nowadays, a new generation of innovative Israeli defense tech startups is doing exactly that, and the Pentagon has a set of programs designed to provide the runway.
In mid-October, Washington, DC will host AUSA, the flagship expo of the US Army, which, with an annual budget north of $200 billion, is the single largest buyer of land-warfare technology on Earth. As Israeli defense tech companies with battle-tested technologies and deep domain expertise prepare to participate in the largest defense conference and expo in the US, it would be prudent to become familiar with some of the Pentagon’s programs that could help launch their products in the United States.
Most of the programs are designed to support the growth of the US defense base. However, Israeli defense tech companies planning to establish a US manufacturing or assembly presence may want to make an effort to connect with the relevant program managers while at the expo. Subject to eligibility and regulatory compliance, such programs can provide validation, funding, and access to the right branches for follow-on procurement opportunities.
Army PIT & FUZE
The Army's Pathway for Innovation and Technology (PIT) is a relatively new initiative designed to streamline and centralize the Army's approach to engaging with innovative technology companies. PIT brings together innovation organizations, acquisition leaders, and industry partners tasked with accelerating the delivery of advanced capabilities.
FUZE, operating within PIT, applies approximately $750 million annually through a venture capital-inspired model to Army technology investments, scouting, evaluating, and backing promising technologies with the goal of rapid integration into Army programs of record.
FUZE brings together a suite of innovation programs under a unified portfolio: Small Business Innovation Research and Small Business Technology Transfer (SBIR/STTR), Expeditionary Technology Search (xTech), Technology Maturation Initiative (TMI), and Manufacturing Technology (ManTech).
SBIR and STTR programs provide government funding to small businesses and research partners.
The Army, Navy, and Air Force each run their own SBIR/STTR programs with tailored critical priorities, and similar programs are also run by several defense agencies and commands including, for example, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA), Missile Defense Agency (MDA), and US Special Operations Command (SOCOM).
Eligibility requires, among other things, that the company be more than 50% owned by US citizens or permanent resident aliens. Army’s SBIR/STTR currently focuses on areas including AI, Contested Logistics and Sustainment, Immersive and Wearables, and sensors.
xTech is the Army’s entry point for announcing and spurring competition within the industry by allocating prizes to companies that can solve known operational and technological gaps. It serves as a key “on-ramp” for innovative companies to enter the Global Tactical Edge Acquisition Directorate (G-TEAD) Marketplace, a platform designed to accelerate delivery of equipment and software to the Army. xTech competitions are generally open to US-based small businesses. Some competitions have allowed international participation at early stages, though eligibility rules varied across different competition types.
TMI and ManTech serve to provide funding for de-risking and operationalizing the successful prototypes from SBIR/STTR and xTech. And JIOP, the Joint Innovation Outpost at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, is PIT's operational arm. It is a collaborative space where companies work directly alongside soldiers to prototype and test solutions.
DEFENSEWERX
DEFENSEWERX is the parent organization that manages a network of regional innovation hubs serving different Pentagon components. The network provides localized engagement points between the defense community and commercial innovators. These hubs, located across the US, include ERDCWERX (Army Corps of Engineers), SOFWERX (US Special Operations Command, SOCOM), CFIC (Army Cyber Command-aligned), Nautilus/NavalX (naval innovation), and Doolittle Institute (Air Force Research Laboratory), among others.
Each hub facilitates connections to its respective Pentagon component's funding mechanisms, including SBIR/STTR, Other Transaction Authorities (OTAs, flexible contracting agreements that bypass the standard Federal Acquisition Regulation), Cooperative Research and Development Agreements (CRADAs), and prize challenges. Specific funding eligibility will depend on the mechanism being used.
ATEC
The Army Test and Evaluation Command (ATEC) manages the Army's premier test ranges and evaluation facilities. In a significant shift announced in August 2026, ATEC has opened these world-class testing facilities to private industry, allowing companies to test and validate their technologies in realistic military environments. This addresses a critical gap for startups that lack access to the testing infrastructure needed to demonstrate military relevance.
Through the new industry scheduling portal, companies can submit a request to pay for range time and testing services directly, and in some cases, testing may be funded by an associated Army program or through cooperative agreements. Programs are open to both domestic and international companies, subject to approval. The focus is on technologies that align with Army testing needs and modernization priorities. For companies with mature defense products, demonstrating performance on US ranges can be a powerful differentiator.
FCT
The Foreign Comparative Testing Program (FCT) is specifically designed to identify and evaluate allied and partner nation military technologies for potential adoption by the US military. The program funds the testing and evaluation of foreign defense items in US military operational environments.
This is one of the few Pentagon programs explicitly designed to bring foreign technologies into the US defense ecosystem. FCT provides funding for testing and evaluation of high Technology Readiness Level (TRL). A US military sponsor, a service or combatant command, must nominate the technology for FCT evaluation. Typical project funding ranges from several hundred thousand dollars to several million dollars for comprehensive testing.
Other funding opportunities
The Pentagon has a robust funding mechanism designed to support the US industrial base development and production of solutions in line with its critical technologies’ priorities. For munition technologies, for example, there is a slew of funding programs from early research through production and industrial base expansion. The Joint Enhanced Munition Technology Program (JEMPT), Joint Hypersonics Transition Office (JHTO) and Joint Energetics Transition Office (JETO) each run award programs with substantial funding opportunities for research and prototyping. For production scaling, there are a number of other programs that can award, on average, up to $50m.
The Pentagon also provides, via The Accelerate the Procurement and Fielding of Innovative Technologies (APFIT) procurement funding for innovative projects that have completed development and are ready to transition into operational use.
The Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital (OSC) provides debt financing with direct loans to primarily finance projects in the US, as well as investment fund financing. OSC targets companies that have demonstrated technology viability and need capital for scaling. In fiscal year 2026, OSC committed more than $5b. in debt financing for industrial and defense-related projects, helping mobilize over $11b. in combined public and private capital.
DARPA and DIU
The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA), with an annual budget of approximately $4.3b., focuses on high-risk, high-reward projects to maintain a technological advantage for the US. Funding usually involves a team of industry and academic partners and “hands-on” involvement by the program manager. The Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) is another funding mechanism soliciting proposals through its Commercial Solutions Opening process, which awards prototype agreements and is, in many cases, open to international entities as well. Vendors that successfully complete a prototype project are awarded a Success Memo, enabling any federal agency to procure the solution without recompeting.
One more interesting resource is some of the long-standing well-established consortiums across the defense industry verticals, such as for example on munition. Those provide an excellent platform to connect with both the Pentagon, industry and academia. Among the newly formed consortiums of interest for those wishing to connect with SOCOM and meeting the eligibility requirements, is the Special Operations Forces Rapid Acquisition Consortium for Emerging Requirements (SOF RACER). It is designed to bring innovative commercial technology into the special operations community quickly.
Critical and emerging technologies
In August 2026, the White House National Security Science & Technology Strategy (NSSTS) explicitly directed agencies to "invite, facilitate, and expedite foreign investment from allied and partner sources, especially in advanced technology." NSSTS identified three top priorities for US battlefield dominance: undersea superiority, space, and AI & autonomy, all supported by 12 high-priority enabling technology areas. Among those are Advanced Manufacturing and Materials, AI & Autonomy, Directed Energy, Hypersonics and Advanced Missile technologies, to name a few. These are all areas that Israeli Defense Tech excels in.
The opportunities for Israeli Defense Tech are real and timely. However, those visiting the Pentagon would surely agree that navigating it, literally and figuratively, is not an easy task. Unless seeking funding or a procurement opportunity that is specifically open to Israeli-based entities, a careful review of eligibility would be required.
Both US regulatory compliance and corporate structure would have to be well planned in advance, as well as a strategy determination on whether establishing a US presence is feasible and truly serves the company’s goals. To support a full understanding of the pathway of doing business in the US defense industry, companies may want to consider working with both legal advisors, as well as government affairs advisors, to raise their profile among the key decision makers.
The author is a Partner and Co-Chair of the Israel Practice of Holland & Knight, a leading US-based law firm, and the president of the Women in Defense South Florida Chapter.

India hikes interest rates for first time in over three years as Iran war fuels inflation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:27:44 UTC
16:27:44 KST

The Reserve Bank of India raised borrowing costs for the first time in over three years on Wednesday, as the Middle East war pushes up prices in Asia's third-biggest economy and weighs on an already fragile rupee.
India's central bank has switched to tightening, delivering a quarter-percentage-point increase as the fallout from the Iran war lifts prices and drags on the national currency.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) lifted its benchmark repo rate, the rate it charges commercial banks for loans, by 25 basis points to 5.50%, with all six members of its monetary policy committee voting in favour.
The move puts India alongside several other central banks that have tightened policy to rein in inflation or prop up their currencies.
The RBI had kept rates on hold since the war erupted in February, as it gauged how swings in oil prices would affect the fastest-growing of the world's biggest economies.
Robust economic growth in the last quarter gave policymakers room to turn their attention to rising prices in a country that relies on imports for the bulk of its energy, and where a poor monsoon threatens to push up food costs.
Consumer price inflation climbed to 4.82% in August, exceeding the central bank's medium-term target of 4% for a third month in a row, and the data suggested price pressures were no longer confined to food and transport.
The RBI is also contending with a sliding rupee, which has hovered close to all-time lows in recent days.
To support the currency, it has introduced a series of measures to attract US dollars, among them a deposit scheme aimed at Indians living abroad that drew in about $127 billion (€113bn).
Those efforts halted the rupee's slide for a time, but it has come under renewed strain as overseas investors keep selling Indian shares and oil prices hover near $100 per barrel.
As the world's third-biggest oil importer, India usually gets around half of its crude via the Strait of Hormuz, a route that has been all but shut since the conflict began.
That leaves India among the economies most exposed to a worldwide energy shock, analysts say, with costlier crude and fertiliser inflating its import bill.

Eva Marie Saint, ‘North By Northwest’ star and 'On the Waterfront' Oscar winner, dies aged 102
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:26:08 UTC
16:26:08 KST

The Oscar-winning actress was one of the last stars of the Golden Age of Hollywood and was the oldest living Oscar winner.
Hollywood legend and acting royalty Eva Marie Saint has died aged 102.
Saint, whose acting work lasted well into her 90s, died of natural causes at her home in Los Angeles on Tuesday, confirmed a family representative.
Seen as one of the last stars of the Golden Age of Hollywood, Saint was best known for winning an Oscar for her feature film debut On The Waterfront and for her work on one of Alfred Hitchcock’s greatest films, North By Northwest.
Born in Newark, New Jersey, on 4 July 1924, Saint studied acting at Bowling Green State University in Ohio. She started her career in television, making appearances in game shows and advertising segments.
Her film career began in 1954, when she was cast opposite Marlon Brando in Elia Kazan’s celebrated drama On The Waterfront, playing Edie Doyle - whose brother's death sets the film's drama in motion. The film was nominated for 12 Academy Awards and ended up winning eight, including Best Picture, Best Actor for Brando, and Best Supporting Actress for Saint.
A star was born and following her impressive debut, she starred in a musical adaptation of Thornton Wilder’s Our Town (1955) co-starring Paul Newman and Frank Sinatra; Bob Hope’s That Certain Feeling (1956); opposite Elizabeth Taylor and Montgomery Clift in Raintree County (1957); and in A Hatful of Rain, a pioneering drug-addiction drama which earned Saint further recognition and nominations at the Golden Globes and BAFTA.
Then came the role that would go on to define her career: North By Northwest. Alfred Hitchcock’s 1959 masterpiece spy thriller saw her play Eve Kendall, the femme fatale, agent undercover opposite James Mason and love interest of Cary Grant.
Even though North By Northwest was a huge hit and propelled her to stardom, Saint decided to limit her film work and spend time with her family. She had married director Jeffrey Hayden in 1951 and had two children.
Still, her film career continued with memorable roles opposite Paul Newman in 1960’s Exodus and with Warren Beatty and Angela Lansbury in 1962’s All Fall Down. Other notable acting credits include John Frankenheimer’s hit racing drama Grand Prix, The Sandpiper, 36 Hours, and the comic satire The Russians Are Coming, The Russians Are Coming.
In the 70s and 80s, Saint returned to television and recieved Emmy nominations for the 1977 miniseries How The West Was Won and 1978’s Taxi!!!. She also played the mother of Cybill Shepherd’s character in Moonlighting and the mother of Peri Gilpin’s Roz Doyle in Frasier.
Later in her career, she played Superman’s mother Martha Kent in Superman Returns (2006) and made her final film appearance in 2014’s Winter’s Tale, starring Colin Farrell, Russell Crowe and Will Smith. In 2021, she played Marisa Tomei's aunt in the brief audio play “The Bus Ride”, part of The Pack Podcast.
Saint’s husband Jeffrey Hayden died in 2016. She is survived by her two children, Darrell and Laurette, four grandchildren, Eli, Tyler, Molly, and Stella and two great grandchildren, Arlo and Finley.
RIP Eva Marie Saint 1924 - 2026

Sweden to Send Patriot Air Defense System to Poland to Guard Ukraine Aid Hub
The Swedish Armed Forces will deploy a Patriot air defense system along with approximately 100 personnel to Rzeszów, Poland, to strengthen NATO’s eastern flank and protect a vital logistics hub supplying military and civilian aid to Ukraine.
This mission will mark the first time Sweden deploys its Patriot surface-to-air missile system on an official NATO task, according to a press release by the Swedish Armed Forces on October 6.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The unit is scheduled to operate under NATO command from early December through the end of the year, with plans to extend the mission through the first half of 2027.
The Patriot air defense system is a ground-based air and missile defense platform built to shield forces and critical areas from airborne threats. Operating under NATO Security Assistance and Training for Ukraine (NSATU), the deployment will contribute to NATO’s Integrated Air and Missile Defense.
The mission will be carried out by personnel from the Air Defense Regiment (Lv 6) alongside support teams from the Blekinge Air Wing (F 17).
Chief of the Swedish Army Johan Pekkari emphasized the dual commitment of the deployment, stating, “As Allies, we share responsibility for protecting and defending NATO territory. At the same time, supporting Ukraine remains a priority for Sweden. By deploying advanced capabilities from the Air Defense Regiment and Blekinge Air Wing, Sweden will strengthen NATO’s eastern flank in Poland while helping to protect the vital support effort for Ukraine.”
Addressing the demands of the mission, Sofia Westermark, Commander of the Air Defense Regiment, noted, “The security environment and the complexity of the mission place significant demands on the unit. We are well trained, well prepared and have the right composition to accomplish the mission.”
This deployment comes as NATO's eastern flank faces heightened security threats, underlined by recent incidents along the border. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk stated that Russian drone strikes had occurred near the Ukrainian-Polish border in the Volyn region, targeting a gas station near the Yahodyn checkpoint.
In response, Poland deployed military aircraft and temporarily suspended operations at the Lublin and Rzeszów airports. Although an unmanned aerial vehicle crashed roughly four kilometers from the border, military officials confirmed that no violation of Polish airspace took place and no direct impacts occurred at the border crossing facility.

IEA, EU discuss proposed oil, diesel stocks release, sources say
BRUSSELS, Oct 7 - The International Energy Agency and European Union on Wednesday were discussing an oil and diesel stocks proposed last week with diplomats and analysts expecting it to include volumes pledged in March.
War with Iran and Ukraine has damaged refineries and disrupted tanker traffic, helping send diesel prices to record highs and impacting inflation and sectors including trucking and agriculture.
Group of Seven countries agreed on Friday to release 100 million barrels after President Donald Trump warned he might ban US diesel exports if they did not put more of the fuel into the market.
It remains unclear how much diesel and how much crude oil will be released.
On Wednesday, IEA countries met to discuss the plan, as did the EU's oil co-ordination group, diplomats said.
The EU's energy task force was scheduled to hold a call at 1600 local time (1400 GMT), a European Commission spokesperson said.
The G7 includes EU members France, Germany and Italy along with the US, UK, Japan and Canada.
EXTENT OF NEW VOLUME NOT CLEAR
The IEA advises industrialised countries and coordinates their emergency oil stocks for use during major supply disruptions.
Polish Energy Minister Milosz Motyka said on Wednesday that Poland was ready to release oil and diesel stocks if a consensus is reached, but he did not expect an IEA decision on this on Wednesday.
In March, the IEA announced a record release of 400 million barrels of oil from strategic stockpiles to combat a spike in crude prices and supply losses.
Of this, about 325 million barrels have so far been released, the IEA said on Friday.
EU countries expect the remaining 75 million barrels to count towards the new 100-million-barrel plan, two EU diplomats said.
JP Morgan analysts also said much of the release in Friday's announcement would represent the completion of the March release.
"Our interpretation of the press release is that the headline 100 million barrels does not represent 100 million barrels of new intervention," the bank said in a report.
Germany's economy ministry said it was working on the approval of the release of energy reserves without mentioning any new amount.
"Germany will participate in the further release of the volume already determined by the IEA in March," the ministry said in a statement. REUTERS

Russia has lost around 1,545,950 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 7.
The number includes 1,690 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,396 tanks, 25,498 armored combat vehicles, 159,128 vehicles and fuel tanks, 50,836 artillery systems, 2,192 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,690 air defense systems, 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,878 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

07:21:06 UTC
16:21:06 KST

Following the attempted hijacking of a Flydubai aircraft and revelations about failures in the security screening of foreign flights to Israel, the Israel Police Investigations and Intelligence Division has opened a probe into two senior Transport Ministry officials suspected of conflicts of interest while serving in the ministry’s aviation security apparatus.
At the center of the case is Avri Cohen, head of the ministry’s security division, who according to the report also worked for the past eight years as a reserve security officer responsible for protecting Israeli airlines at foreign airports.
The Civil Service Commission said Cohen had not received authorization to hold an additional job. According to a report in Haaretz, Cohen served as a security representative for Israeli airlines at airports abroad and received separate payment for that work while simultaneously heading the Transport Ministry division responsible for overseeing security arrangements for foreign flights.
Police are also examining allegations involving Dvir Rubinstein, director of the Transport Ministry’s aviation security operations center.
Rubinstein owns a private company that allegedly provided paid training and consulting services to foreign airlines, including Flydubai and Emirates. Those were among the carriers he was required to oversee as part of his Transport Ministry role.
Calcalist reported this week that the Transport Ministry acknowledged Cohen had worked in an additional position without approval and would be required to end that employment.
“The authority to grant permission to an employee at his rank rests with the Civil Service Commission, and the ministry’s management did not submit such a request on his behalf. Therefore, no permit was granted,” the Transport Ministry said.
The ministry added that it operates according to Civil Service Commission rules and stressed that “the obligation to request and receive permission before carrying out additional work rests with the employee.”
The police probe comes amid intense scrutiny of Israel’s aviation security procedures following the Flydubai incident, which raised broader questions over the vetting of foreign pilots and the officials responsible for supervising airlines flying into Israel.

Prosecutors requested a prison sentence of 18 months for Cheng as he was uncooperative during the investigation. They asked for suitable punishment for three other suspects who had admitted to the facts.

Businesses are increasingly focused on bolstering resilience, reliability, and trust, she said.
The vice president said the priority is to deepen cooperation in shaping the future of technology and industry. Through agreements like the Economic Prosperity Partnership Dialogue and the Taiwan-US investment memorandum, there is expanding collaboration in areas including AI, digital infrastructure, critical minerals, supply chain security, and developing high-tech talent, she said.

The two countries also need to build a stable and predictable business environment, she said. She added the two countries would continue to address practical concerns facing businesses and investors, such as avoiding double taxation.
Finally, Taiwan and the US must strengthen the foundations of domestic development, Hsiao said. “That means reliable energy supplies, sufficient water resources, skilled talent, strong cybersecurity capabilities, resilient infrastructure and regulations that can keep pace with innovation.”
The vice president said Taiwan will continue bolstering national defense and whole-of-society resilience, as well as deepening partnerships with the US and other global democracies.
“In an increasingly uncertain world, the importance of trusted partnerships will only grow, not diminish,” she said.
