Miaoli County announces start of Chinese mitten crab season
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:15:34 UTC
16:15:34 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Miaoli County Government on Wednesday promoted Chinese mitten crabs raised in the county, inviting the public to visit and taste the crabs at their source.
At a city hall press conference, Miaoli County Magistrate Chung Tung-chin (鍾東錦), Agriculture Department Director Chen Shu-i (陳樹義), crab farmers, and county councilors announced the start of the county’s Chinese mitten crab sales season, per CNA. Chen said the county government conducts rigorous origin tracing and drug-residue testing to ensure the safety of locally raised crabs.
Commenting on Miaoli’s mitten crab farming industry, Chen noted the local climate is well-suited to crab farming and highlighted the county government’s efforts to support the industry and promote green aquaculture. He said that there are around 29 crab farms in the county, raising about 415,250 crabs across 21 hectares, per Liberty Times.
Chung encouraged food lovers from across Taiwan to visit Miaoli to experience both its local cuisine and culture, noting that the crabs could sell out within a month.
Galaxy Macau Assistant Vice President of Food and Beverage Sammy Wu wrote in 2017 that Chinese mitten crabs from China’s Yangcheng Lake are often considered to be among the highest quality because the lake has clean, nutrient-rich, and shallow water, in addition to strong currents. He said September is generally considered the best season for female crabs, while male crabs are at their best in October.
Taiwan’s Chinese mitten crab farming industry emerged this year after customs officials detected residues of banned drugs in imported Chinese crabs, per AgriHarvest. However, the industry did not become commercialized until Miaoli County Government signed a cooperation agreement with Shanghai Ocean University in 2011.
Former Fisheries Agency Deputy Director Chen Chien-yu (陳建佑) said in 2018 that allowing Chinese mitten crab imports in 2012 contributed to the decline of the domestic industry. Fisheries Agency data showed about 39 registered mitten crab farms in 2025, with Miaoli County accounting for 34 of them.
The figure represents a steep decline from the more than 100 farms operating at the industry’s peak. However, conditions in Miaoli appear to be more stable, with the county losing four farms between 2018 and 2025, compared with 24 elsewhere in the country.
Farmers said the industry’s decline has been driven by structural challenges, including difficulties in obtaining high-quality crab larvae and low yields, as well as the ease of traveling to China, per Liberty Times.
Taichung Dajia District crab farmer Hsu I-ching (許一清) expressed confidence in Taiwan’s mitten crabs, saying their lack of drug residues and good flavor could give them an advantage over imported Chinese crabs, per Liberty Times. However, he acknowledged that the income from crab farming is insufficient to support a family, objecting to his son taking over the business.
In addition to the industry’s structural problems, National Taiwan Ocean University professor Liu Ping-chung (劉秉忠) said Taiwan’s warmer climate has delayed mitten crab maturation by about one month, giving Chinese crabs an advantage in reaching the market earlier. Still, award-winning crab farmer Chiu Chun-i (邱俊義) said the remaining farmers produce high-quality crabs that attract buyers through word of mouth alone.
Crab farmer Fan Hsien-ta (范賢達) said that as consumers place greater emphasis on healthy food, high-quality Chinese mitten crabs continue to have a place in the domestic market, per TVBS. He also noted that the cultivation area in Miaoli County Touwu Township has expanded by one hectare.
In related news, China’s Yangcheng Lake mitten crab industry faces challenges from climate change, with longer and hotter summers affecting production, per PTS. Farmers have reported declines in both the quality and quantity of crabs, expressing concern about the industry’s future.

Kosovo’s parliament elected a new president, avoiding snap elections
Kyiv • UNN
Vjosa Osmani-Sadriu received 81 votes in Kosovo’s parliament. Her election prevented new snap elections in the country.
Kosovo’s parliament elected economist Justina Shiroka Pula as the country’s president, a position that is largely ceremonial. This took place shortly before the constitutional deadline, helping to avoid yet another early election in one of Europe’s poorest countries. Reuters reports, UNN writes.
Details
On Wednesday morning, Shiroka Pula received 81 votes in the 120-seat parliament—one more than required for election. Had lawmakers failed to elect a new president, the country would have had to hold early parliamentary elections, as it did in June.
This mandate does not belong to one person alone. It belongs to our citizens... I will be the president of all citizens
Shiroka Pula’s election resulted from an agreement between Prime Minister Albin Kurti’s ruling Vetëvendosje party and the opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo to limit the powers of the war crimes court for Kosovo, which operates in The Hague.
On Monday, police used tear gas and water cannons to disperse demonstrators who were demanding approval of the relevant changes. Critics say the sentences handed down by the Hague court are too harsh.
The office of president in Kosovo is largely ceremonial, but it often becomes a source of political instability because electing a president requires two-thirds of parliament’s votes, and parties find it difficult to agree on a candidate.
Shiroka Pula, who was born in 1953, is president of the Kosovo Academy of Sciences and Arts and a professor of economics. From 2008 to 2011, she served as minister of economy.

Cancer diagnoses set to rise by almost a quarter by 2045
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:14:04 UTC
16:14:04 KST

Cancer diagnoses set to rise by almost a quarter by 2045
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The number of new cancer diagnoses in the Netherlands is expected to rise by almost a quarter to nearly 170,000 a year by 2045, mainly because the population is growing and ageing, the national cancer centre IKNL said on Wednesday.
The number of people dying of cancer each year is also set to rise, from just over 46,000 in 2024 to just over 57,000. Some 136,000 people were diagnosed with cancer in 2024.
IKNL said in its new 20-year projections that the age-adjusted risk of getting cancer will stay mostly the same, while the risk of dying from the disease will continue falling.
The increase is driven by the growing number of older people. Five-year survival rates have improved for decades, reaching 72% for women and 69% for men, up from 55% and 42% in the early 1990s.
Skin cancer is set to become the most common form of cancer among both men and women, overtaking breast and prostate cancer. Besides ageing, the rise is mainly down to sun exposure and sunburn earlier in life, IKNL researcher Jaike Schilte-Praagman told NU.nl. People are also getting suspicious spots checked sooner, she said.
The projections do not account for new treatments, and there may be breakthroughs in the coming years. “We don’t know what treatments are still to come, so we can’t include them in our calculations,” Schilte-Praagman added.
“Without targeted measures, demand for cancer care threatens to grow faster than capacity,” IKNL board chair Ernst Kuipers told the website.
At least a third of all cancer diagnoses could be prevented through healthier lifestyles and living environments, according to cancer charity KWF.
IKNL calculated in 2024 that if no young people smoked by 2032 and the adult smoking rate fell to 5%, some 120,000 cases of lung, bladder and oesophageal cancer would be avoided by 2045.
“You can’t just tell people to live more healthily,” Schilte-Praagman said. “The government has a role to play too. It has to create an environment that makes healthy choices easier.”

Estonian folktronica band: Nightclubs are the modern village swing
For Viljandi folktronica band Oopus, it's clear that nightclubs today fill the same social role the village swing once did, bringing people together through music and dance.
Last weekend, Viljandi hosted the Etnokulp folk music awards, where hometown heroes Oopus swept Album of the Year, Artist of the Year and New Folk Artist of the Year.
The band blends rave culture with traditional Estonian music, and musician Mari Meentalo said electronic dance music and Estonian folk have more in common than may first appear, from repeating melodic lines to the shared aim of keeping people moving.
"Once the music starts, there's no telling when the party will end!" said bandmate Johannes Ahun, adding that Oopus deliberately brings the two worlds together.
Meentalo believes modern-day nightclubs aren't actually that modern of a concept at all.
"Back in the day, people used to gather by the village swing to socialize," she said. "Nowadays, it's nightclubs where people come together and celebrate."
Vinyl, cassette and reel-to-reel tape
Oopus' latest album, "Reivlender," was released not only on digital platforms but also on reel-to-reel tape, cassette, vinyl and CD. Ahun said the band is interested in exploring older physical formats as they make new music, especially given the renewed interest in those formats.
"As we make music, we're learning how people actually used to make it on these older formats," Ahun said, crediting friends and collaborators who helped make the physical releases possible.
"And there are fans in Estonia, young people like us, who still dream of having music on tape," he added.

Exporter VAT refunds in Ukraine halted since Sept 5 – MHP rep
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:13:22 EEST
16:13:22 KST

A reduction in the amount of budget reimbursement of value-added tax (VAT) to exporters halted on September 5 is creating a shortage of working capital for Ukrainian companies amid the full-scale war and logistical problems, Pavlo Moroz, director of the Corporate Social Responsibility Department at PrJSC MHP, said.
"As of September 5, VAT is not being refunded to exporters... Export-oriented businesses are not receiving the working capital needed to continue operations. Therefore, there must be government support," he said during a discussion of economic support and recovery issues at the EFBM Forum 4.0 in Kyiv held at the premises of the Faculty of Economics of Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv on Tuesday.
According to him, export-oriented businesses are not receiving the financial resources they need to operate steadily and maintain their operations.
Former MP Vadym Denysenko also stated on Facebook on Tuesday that the government has "practically halted VAT refunds."
He claims that, as a cost-saving measure, the government made an unofficial decision to suspend VAT refunds to exporters, while the business community is currently discussing the matter only "behind closed doors," hoping the situation will change.
Moroz said that, despite the importance of various grant programs and initiatives for small and medium-sized enterprises, the state should take a comprehensive approach to addressing urgent issues facing the large business sector, which generates the bulk of the country's foreign-exchange earnings.
"We can create thousands of grant programs to support small and medium-sized businesses, but if we do not take a comprehensive approach to solving the problems and pressing issues of large businesses, it will not produce results," the MHP representative said.
He also drew attention to the need to support NGOs working on issues related to internally displaced persons and to create incentives for young people to remain in Ukraine.
According to operational data from the Ministry of Finance, budget VAT reimbursements fell to UAH 9.9 billion in September 2026, compared with UAH 15 billion in September last year and UAH 21.4 billion in July. At the same time, total VAT reimbursements amounted to UAH 170.9 billion in January-September, compared with UAH 131.2 billion in the same period last year, while VAT receipts from goods produced in Ukraine reached UAH 255.2 billion.
The Interfax-Ukraine agency has not yet been able to obtain comments from the Ministry of Finance and the State Tax Service (STS).

Swiss to vote on loosening arms-export restrictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:12:25 UTC
16:12:25 KST

Swiss to vote on loosening arms-export restrictions
On November 29, the Swiss will vote on a controversial proposal: easing the export rules for war materiel. Backed by parties on the right, the reform aims to support Switzerland’s arms industry. But its opponents, who initiated the referendum, fear it will undermine the country’s neutrality and humanitarian tradition.
Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Swiss arms-export rules have been the subject of intense debate. So far, the Swiss government has refused to allow several European countries to re-export Swiss war materiel to Ukraine. A number of these countries – close partners of Switzerland – have found this decision incomprehensible. On November 29, voters will decide whether to loosen these rules.
What does current law stipulate?
The existing federal act on war materiel prohibits exports to countries involved in armed conflict or committing serious and systematic human-rights violations. In 2021, parliament tightened export restrictions by passing an indirect counter-proposal to the popular initiative “No arms exports to countries in civil war”. These stricter rules went into effect in 2022, and since then the government has no longer been able to grant exemptions.
Current law also requires purchasing countries to sign a declaration prohibiting re-exportation. This specifies that they cannot transfer Swiss war materiel to a third-party state without prior authorisation from the Swiss government. Since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, the rule has created frictions between Switzerland and some of its close partners. Countries such as Germany, Spain, the Netherlands, and Denmark have wanted to transfer Swiss-made materiel to Kyiv, but the Swiss government has refused permission to do so.
How does the law relate to Switzerland’s neutrality?
Switzerland’s neutrality does not prohibit it from exporting arms. The existing restrictions originate primarily from policy choices that led to the current federal act on war materiel, which goes beyond the requirements of international law on neutrality.
What rules does the reform change?
The reform proposes special treatment for states that Switzerland considers to be close partners with similar export rules. Exports to these countries would be authorised, except in exceptional circumstances, even if the states are involved in armed conflict. Nineteen European countries as well as the United States, Canada, Australia, Japan, New Zealand, and Argentina are on the list.
In addition, the amended law abolishes the declarations banning re-exportation. The Swiss government would nonetheless be able to require them on a case-by-case basis.
Why is a popular vote necessary?
In 2024, the Swiss government asked parliament for permission to grant exceptions to the rules governing exports. Parliament went beyond the government’s initial request and approved the reform in December 2025.
A cross-party alliance subsequently submitted 75,000 valid signatures in opposition to the reform – enough to trigger a referendum. The authorities were therefore obliged to organise a vote on the matter.
Who are the supporters and opponents?
The law’s amendment is supported by the government and by parliament. In parliament, it was approved by the majority on the right, specifically the right-wing Swiss People’s Party, the centre-right Radical-Liberal Party, and the centre-right party The Centre. The arms industry also supports the reform.
The alliance that launched the referendum comprises the left-wing Social Democratic Party, the left-wing Green Party, the centre-left Protestant Party, the Group for a Switzerland without an Army, and several civil-society organisations.
Arguments for the reform
Supporters of the reform feel that existing policies are too restrictive compared to those of other countries. In their view, current law penalises the Swiss arms industry at a time when many European countries are investing heavily in defence. The strict re-export rules have already led Germany, the Netherlands, and Denmark not to place certain orders in Switzerland.
The supporters also emphasise that a robust defence industry is essential for supplying the Swiss army. They fear a weakening of the sector, which would then erode the country’s ability to ensure its own security.
Why did the opponents launch a referendum?
The opponents of the reform worry that loosening restrictions will increase the risk of Swiss weapons ending up in conflict zones. They also deplore the reform’s failure to increase support for Ukraine, which Russia attacked in violation of international law. Ukraine is not on the list of countries receiving special treatment under the amended law.
According to the opponents, the reform serves the economic interests of the weapons industry to the detriment of human rights. They also dispute the idea that the arms sector is facing an existential crisis.
The opponents feel the loosened restrictions undermine Switzerland’s neutrality and weaken its humanitarian tradition. Furthermore, they criticise the policy U-turn only a few years after the stricter rules entered into force.
Lastly, the opponents believe the reform gives the government too much leeway in granting exceptions to the export criteria.
How is the Swiss arms industry doing?
In the last few years, export figures for Swiss war materiel have fluctuated significantly. After declining in 2023 and 2024, exports rebounded sharply in 2025, reaching nearly CHF950 million ($1.15 billion), an increase of 43% over the previous year. Germany has remained by far Switzerland’s largest customer.

‘The Happiest Soul on the Wing’: Remembering a Fallen Ukrainian Pilot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:10:00 UTC
16:10:00 KST

“He was the happiest soul on the wing.”
That is how a fellow aviator and friend of Captain Marat Mambetov described to me the heroic MiG-29 pilot who lost his life on Oct. 1 while flying a combat mission in defense of Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
At just 25, Marat was a flight commander in Ukraine’s 40th “Ghost of Kyiv” Tactical Aviation Brigade. According to the Ukrainian Air Force, he was carrying out missile and bomb strikes against Russian occupation forces along a sector of the front when an enemy missile struck his aircraft. He ejected but did not survive.
Those facts explain how Ukraine lost him. His friends’ recollections begin to explain whom Ukraine lost.
“It did not matter how bad the day was or potentially dangerous the circumstances, he would say ‘I’m not f***ing worried. Let’s do that.’”
Others described how he could be cheerful and full of life one moment, then serious and responsible the next when the situation required it.
Marat’s death strikes a personal chord. Over the past year and a half, I have lost two close friends, Pavlo “Pasha” Ivanov and Maksym Ustymenko, both extraordinary pilots and defenders of their nation. Both were posthumously awarded the title Hero of Ukraine and the Order of the Gold Star. I did not know Marat, but I have come to understand what the loss of a fallen aviator means to his fellow pilots, family and friends.
Russia’s Jet Drones Could Reach 900 Km/h, Air Force Warns
The death of a pilot brings deep, quiet grief to the aviation community. Security requires silence.
There is little time to process the loss of a comrade. Work does not stop.
One hour, a close friend goes down in the line of duty. The next, his fellow aviators are airborne, protecting children as they sleep.
To those who know them, the psychological and emotional stamina this demands can seem superhuman. But they cannot fail. Too much is at stake. So they mount their birds, take to the skies and fight another day.
Yes, Marat’s friends will “burn the piano” in his memory – a tradition adopted by Ukrainian pilots and associated with the RAF of World War II. It is a ceremonial reminder that this extraordinary cadre of men who defend the skies includes poet-warriors, steeped in tradition and willing to die for the innocent.
Originally from the Zaporizhzhia Region, Marat studied at the Kharkiv National Air Force University. Friends credit his intense focus, hard work and devotion to his nation with helping him accomplish so much at such a young age.
“Even though he was often the younger pilot, he would often take the lead on a mission,” a colleague of Marat’s explained to me.
Every Ukrainian defender is special. Every one has a story. Every loss reaches a circle of family and friends, and the nation is diminished by every death.
But the ranks of Ukraine’s elite fighter pilots are small. In this war, fighter jets are precious, but they can be replaced with the help of international friends.
An elite Ukrainian fighter pilot cannot easily be replaced. Nor can we ever fully know how many lives a single pilot has protected through repeated missions to clear the skies of enemy threats.
Marat’s friend explained it to me this way: “Pilots never die. They fly higher to protect their family and the children below.”
The name Marat is sometimes translated as “one whose coming is hoped for.” It is a fitting name for the man who arrived just in time for Ukraine’s darkest hour and who left this world with an unblemished record of courage when it mattered most.

Russia hits Ukraine with drones and missiles, killing at least eight
KYIV, Oct 7 - Russia launched a barrage of drones and missiles at Ukraine on Wednesday, killing at least eight people and damaging residential buildings, industrial facilities and infrastructure, Ukrainian officials said.
Two people were killed in the capital Kyiv, four in the northern city of Pryluki and two in the central Poltava region, authorities said.
"Ukraine has once again been hit by Russian missiles throughout the night," Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's parliamentary commissioner for human rights, said on the Telegram app.
'ANOTHER SLEEPLESS NIGHT'
"Another sleepless night, another act of terror, after which people still have to plan their working day despite everything," he added.
Russia launched 130 drones, 48 cruise missiles and also ballistic missiles to attack Ukraine, the Ukrainian air force said. Air defence units downed 161 targets, it said on Telegram.
Kyiv and Poltava in central Ukraine, the southeastern region of Dnipropetrovsk and Kharkiv in the northeast were the focus of the Russian attacks, the Ukrainian air force said.
Russia's defence ministry said its forces had carried out a "massive strike" on military-industrial facilities in Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions, using high-precision land-, sea- and air-launched weapons, as well as drones.
It said the targets included sites where Ukrainian defence company Fire Point manufactures and stores its Flamingo cruise missiles and medium- and long-range drones in Kyiv as well as regions of Kyiv, Chernihiv, Kirovohrad, Dnipropetrovsk, Poltava and Kharkiv.
Last week, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said Ukraine had fired its first domestically made ballistic missile in combat, produced by Fire Point.
In an interview with Reuters last week, Zelenskiy said he expected the company to have a longer-range FP-9 missile ready by the autumn, which the company has said will be capable of reaching Moscow.
MISSILE HITS APARTMENT BLOCK
In Pryluki in the northern Chernihiv region, a Russian missile slammed into a five-storey residential building, regional authorities said. At least four people were killed on the spot and 20 more were wounded, while more residents could be buried under the rubble, local authorities said.
Video images showed rescuers pulling people from beneath the wreckage.
Many Kyiv residents took shelter in the city's deep underground metro stations as warnings of the upcoming attacks were shared by Ukrainian officials and military intelligence.
Several loud explosions reverberated through the capital during the night, Reuters witnesses said.
"The metro is better, because we live on the 9th floor of a high-rise, and it's really scary when you're on the 9th floor and missiles are flying at you," Lesia, a 49-year-old Kyiv resident, told Reuters.
Ukrainian officials said Russian ballistic missiles targeted Kyiv in addition to the drones.
For months, Ukraine suffered from a critical lack of air defences, prompting Zelenskiy and other officials to repeatedly plead for help and more supplies.
Overnight air strikes on the southeastern city of Dnipro damaged an industrial facility, transport infrastructure in Zaporizhzhia and apartment buildings in Kremenchuk, regional officials said on the Telegram messaging app. REUTERS

World Bank keeps its forecast for Bulgaria's economic growth unchanged

World Bank keeps its forecast for Bulgaria's economic growth unchanged
Wednesday 7 October 2026 09:38
Wednesday, 7 October 2026, 09:38
PHOTO EPA/BGNES
Font size
Following growth of 3.1% in 2025, the World Bank expects Bulgaria’s GDP to increase by 2.6% in both 2026 and 2027, with growth accelerating slightly to 2.7% in 2028.
Compared with its spring forecast, the estimate for 2026 remains unchanged, while the projection for 2027 has been revised down from 2.9% to 2.6%.
Strong domestic demand, supported by rising real wages, expanding credit and a loosening of fiscal policy, has sustained economic activity in Bulgaria, but at the same time has accelerated inflation and significantly widened the budget deficit, the report says.
The World Bank forecasts that the deficit will rise to 5.3% of GDP in 2026, up from 3% in 2025. The main factors cited are the rapid increase in social spending, higher municipal investment and increased energy subsidies.
Expected fiscal tightening and slower growth in real wages will limit economic growth to around 2.6% annually in 2027-2028, the institution forecasts, as cited by BTA.

Royal Mail to cut 2,500 head office and support jobs by end 2027
Royal Mail plans to cut up to 2,500 jobs by the end of next year, as it struggles with a slump in letters being sent and seeks to compete in the cutthroat parcel delivery market.
To simplify its processes and save money, Royal has carried out a review of its head office and support functions, and will reduce them by “up to 2,500” – less than 2% of its workforce of more than 131,000 people, it said.
The company, owned since April 2025 by the Czech billionaire Daniel Křetínský, hopes to achieve the reductions through “natural attrition” (people leaving anyway) and voluntary redundancies, without the need for compulsory redundancies.
It stressed that its frontline roles in delivery and processing, including posties and drivers, will not be affected.
Royal Mail said it needs to adapt to a rapidly-changing market: Letter volumes have declined by more than 70% since their peak, whilst customer demand for faster and more convenient parcel delivery services continues to grow.
Royal Mail has briefed its unions, the Communication Workers Union (CWU) and Unite CMA, on the proposals and formal consultation with both unions is now underway.
Alistair Cochrane, the chief executive, said:
We have been working hard to reduce costs and simplify processes across all areas of the business as we transform to win in a very competitive market. These proposed changes remove duplication and allow us to invest further in the service we deliver for our customers.
We are committed to treating everyone fairly and respectfully throughout this process, working closely with our trade unions. The proposed changes will not be easy, but they are an important part of building a stronger, simpler and future-ready Royal Mail for our customers and colleagues.
Back to Royal Mail’s planned 2,500 job losses. Cat Hobbs, director of the campaign group We Own It, said:
This is absolutely disgraceful. The very last thing Royal Mail needs is massive staff cuts. It’s already failing to deliver letters - with reports of people picking up their own mail and the government saying statutory targets are not being met. This is despite increasing our stamp prices by a shocking 107% since privatisation in 2013. It’s truly shameful that this is the state of our once proud 500 year old Royal Mail.
Andy Burnham must make good on his promise to reverse Thatcher’s legacy by taking it back. He can either buy it back directly for around £3.6 billion - although he could easily negotiate a price cut after the damage done by its Czech billionaire owner - or he can squeeze it with regulation until Kretinsky hands our asset back over. Shareholders have pocketed £2 billion since privatisation while households now wonder if the postie is ever coming. Enough is enough.
Burnham must step in directly. Stop these absurd staff cuts, reduce stamp prices, reinstate proper deliveries and force the company to deliver. If it goes bust, take it back and run it properly so we can rely on it. People still need letters and people would send more post if prices weren’t so outrageous and the Royal Mail could be trusted. It used to be ours, Burnham must give it back to the public.
Boots acquired by Canadian branch of billionaire Weston family for $8.9bn
Boots has been acquired by the investment company of the Canadian branch of the billionaire Weston family, for $8.9bn including debt.
Wittington Investments said it had entered into a “definitive agreement” to buy Boots, which is majority owned by the US private equity firm Sycamore Partners, in partnership with Stefano Pessina and his family.
Boots, which dates back to 1849 when it was founded in Nottingham by John Boot, has 1,800 stores in the UK and employs 51,000 people.
Under the terms of the deal, Wittington will acquire Boots’ retail operations in the UK and Ireland; Boots Opticians; and the No7 Beauty Company; and its Thailand and franchised businesses.
Wittington said it plans to invest in the chain, upgrading stores, improving the website and expanding healthcare services.
Sycamore, in partnership with Pessina and his family, will retain ownership of the Boots group’s other interests in Farmacias Benavides and Alliance Healthcare Deutschland. Sycamore bought the wider Walgreens Boots Alliance business for $23.7bn in 2025.
The Boots chief executive Alex Baldock said:
Boots matters. Every day, our colleagues give millions of people longer, healthier and happier lives.
For all of our social impact and commercial success to-date, the opportunity ahead is even greater. I look forward to making the most of that opportunity and building a world class Boots for our colleagues, customers, patients, and communities.
The deal marks the return of the Canadian branch of the Weston family to the UK high street, after it previously owned Selfridges. The family later sold the department store chain for £4bn in 2022. The Westons are widely known throughout Canada for owning the grocery store Loblaws and the pharmacy chain Shoppers Drug Mart.
The UK branch of the family, which operates its businesses through a separate investment vehicle, is known for holding a majority stake in Primark through the parent company Associated British Foods.
News of the prospective Weston deal comes months after Sycamore tried and failed to sell Boots to the Australian pharmaceutical group Sigma Healthcare in a deal that would have valued the business at $10bn this summer.
Galen Weston, who chairs Wittington, will become chairman of Boots. He said
Boots is one of Britain’s most enduring businesses, with a rich heritage, a trusted name and a vital role in everyday life across the UK and Ireland. We have great respect for Boots’ legacy and leading market position. We see a meaningful opportunity to make a great business even better through stable long-term ownership, further capital investment, and the renewed operating focus required to serve customers with excellence for generations to come.
Pessina described Boots as “an iconic brand and a British institution”.
It has been one of the privileges of my and Ornella’s life to have been so closely associated with Boots over the last 20 years. We are delighted to be passing on a thriving Boots to strong and reliable owners who understand the value of its great heritage.

Unite has slammed Royal Mail’s plans to cut up to 2,500 jobs by the end of next year as the result of “years of inaction” and said it would fight this decision “every step of the way”.

Unite CMA [Communications Managers’ Association within the union] has been warning for some considerable time that unless the government and Ofcom address the serious challenges facing Royal Mail, further jobs will be put at risk.

These devastating job losses have been directly caused by years of inaction. Unite will not stand for our members being penalised for a situation that is not of their making.

Five ex-Barclays traders clear their names over Libor rigging
Five former Barclays traders, jailed in the UK for plotting to rig global benchmark interest rates used to set mortgages, loans and other financial products, won an appeal to clear their names today.
London’s Court of Appeal quashed the convictions of Philippe Moryoussef, from France, Calcutta-born Jay Merchant, Britons Colin Bermingham and Jonathan Mathew and Alex Pabon, an American. Judges will lay out their reasons later today.
This unravels some of the UK Serious Fraud Office’s most high-profile prosecutions.
Prosecutors portrayed the traders as a symbol of banker greed at a time of taxpayer fury at staggering bank bailouts during the 2007-2009 financial crisis, which sent stock markets plummeting and economies into recession.
Last year the Supreme Court overturned the convictions of Tom Hayes— a former star trader at UBS and Citigroup — and ex-Barclays trader Carlo Palombo for rigging the now-defunct interbank interest rate Libor and its euro equivalent, Euribor.
The Supreme Court ruled that the trial judges had misdirected juries and that legal errors undermined the fairness of the trials, laying the groundwork for today’s Court of Appeal decision.
Merchant, Pabon, Moryoussef, Bermingham and Mathew were sentenced to between 33 months and eight years in jail between 2016 and 2019 after a series of landmark SFO trials.
Designed to estimate the costs at which banks would lend to each other, Libor and Euribor were once a benchmark for interest rates underpinning around $450 trillion of financial contracts, from derivatives to student loans.
“It’s hard to take in,” said a tearful Bermingham, 70, outside the courtroom, according to Reuters. “You don’t believe it until you hear it.“
Moryoussef, now 58, gained notoriety for jumping bail and fleeing to his native France. He was tried in London in his absence, sentenced to eight years in jail and has remained a fugitive since.
“Today, I am regaining my soul, and for the first time, I can envision my next chapter in peace,” he said in a statement.
Mathew, 45, said that having his conviction quashed was about “finally having validation that this is an injustice that never should have happened.“
The SFO, which did not contest the appeals, reiterated in a statement that the Supreme Court had found “ample evidence” on which a properly directed jury could have convicted Hayes and Palombo.
But it added:
After carefully considering this judgment and the full circumstances, we do not oppose the appeals of five individuals convicted by juries in relation to Libor and Euribor.
A further appeal by Christian Bittar, a French former star Deutsche Bank trader sentenced to jail in 2018, is expected to be heard on Friday.
Bittar, once described as one of the world’s most skilled traders, is the only case being contested by the SFO following his guilty plea more than eight years ago.
US startup reports positive results for Parkinson's drug
A US startup has reported positive results for an experimental new Parkinson’s treatment from a late-stage clinical study, and plans to meet with the regulator.
Boston-based Cerevance,a company part-funded by the UK’s SV Health Investors Dementia Discovery Fund, carried out a phase 3 trial with 341 volunteers to test its Parkinson’s medication solengepras, which met its main goal with statistical significance.
When given the drug as an add-on treatment once a day, patients reported improvements in daily function, daytime alertness, and quality of life. The company says the medication restores balance by regulating just one side of brain circuit, and doesn’t act directly on dopamine unlike other therapies, which means there are fewer side effects.
Parkinson’s affects around 166,000 people in the UK and nearly 12 million worldwide, with the global number projected to more than double by 2050.
Cerevance plans to meet with the the US regulator, the FDA, to discuss the path to a potential application for approval.
Other Parkinson’s therapies target the molecule dopamine, which acts as a brain messenger that helps muscles to move smoothly. Daytime sleepiness, a known side effect of today’s dopamine-based drugs, improved, Cerevance said.
Cerevance was founded in late 2016 as a joint venture between Californian venture fund Lightstone Ventures and Japanese drugmaker Takeda Pharmaceuticals.
South West Water owner taps investors to fund infrastructure investment
Joanna Partridge
The owner of embattled South West Water, Exeter-based Pennon Group, has launched a £550m investor cash call and cut the water company’s shareholder dividend to help it fund infrastructure investment, just days after it was hit by a record £7.9m fine for hundreds of sewage spills.
The London-listed company, which supplies water to some 3.5m customers across the south west of England, as well as 380,000 business customers around the UK, said the rights issue would help to support a £1bn investment “to drive improved outcomes for customers and communities”.
Pennon’s new boss, Keith Haslett, who was appointed chief executive in April, said he had conducted a comprehensive review of the business and had identified areas for improvement, including customer service and the firm’s environmental performance.
South West Water was fined nearly £8m in September by a judge, who issued the largest fine for environmental offences in the region and said the company’s conduct amounted to reckless failures in management systems and response to known risks.
The company was fined after hundreds of sewage spills during a six year period at popular bathing spots including the coastal village of Harlyn in north Cornwall and in sensitive habitats, like the River Camel, which is home to otter and Atlantic salmon and popular with birdwatchers and sailors.
Pennon said it would also slash its shareholder dividend by about 30%, including the impact of the equity raise, as part of its “operational reset”.
Shares in Pennon, which also owns Bristol Water and SES Water, tumbled as much as 22% during morning trading following the company’s announcement, named “project Proteus”, after a sea god in Greek mythology. The shares are still the biggest loser on the FTSE 250 index, down 21.1%
Haslett told reporters the reaction to the company’s plans had been “mixed”, saying:
Investment is needed to achieve improvements – we’re funding the plans in the right way.
He added this would not be funded by further increases to customers’ bills and said he was also bringing some critical roles back in-house, including leakage teams which were previously outsourced.
O2 signs record £200m deal to keep London venue’s naming rights
O2 has struck a record deal thought to be in the region of £200m to retain the naming rights to the London venue the O2 in the largest renewal of its kind in UK history.
The 10-year agreement will extend O2’s relationship until at least 2038. It cements the sponsorship as the second longest-running UK stadium naming rights deal after Arsenal’s partnership for the football club’s London ground,
Under the deal with Anschutz Entertainment Group (AEG), which bought the site of the ill-fated Millennium Dome five years after it was shut following the millennium celebrations, O2 is thought to be paying about £20m a year in the wide-ranging partnership.
This is an almost 50% increase on the annual amount under the existing deal which was due to expire at the end of next year. It is more than triple the £6m a year O2 paid in its initial 10-year deal when the future success of the O2 and surrounding site was far from certain.

Poland’s ‘solidarity’ push for EU energy resilience in face of Russian aggression
Also on the energy front, our economics correspondent Richard Partington travelled to Gdansk, to look at Poland’s ‘solidarity’ push for EU energy resilience in face of Russian aggression.
Two miles off the coast of Gdańsk, the white steel piles of Poland’s first offshore gas terminal rise from the slate-grey Baltic. Installed at a height eight metres above the waves, the floating cranes and construction vessels here are on the frontline of Europe’s push for energy security.
Since the taps were turned off on Russian gas after Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine four years ago, Poland has turned to the global energy market for supplies. But while conditions are far from ideal as the Middle East war drives oil and gas prices to stratospheric levels, strengthening the diversity of the country’s energy mix remains a top priority for Poland, its Baltic neighbours, and the EU at large.
Looking out to sea from the windswept beach backed by pine forest, Maciej Wawrzkowicz, the offshore project manager at the national gas company Gaz-System, and the construction manager Krzysztof Polatynski say the Baltic is not an easy place to build.
Before work could start, Polish navy minesweepers were called in to torpedo unexploded mines and bombs from the second world war. Construction is halted by storms, while the sea froze over last winter. But speed is important in this project of international significance.
Shell expects refineries to almost double the profit from every barrel of fuel made
Shell’s refineries are expected to make almost double the profit from every barrel of fuel produced owing to record prices caused by shortages around the world.
In a market trading update, the energy supermajor forecast profit margins of $42 a barrel in the July to September period, far above the $24 a barrel of the second quarter and the previous high of about $28 in mid-2022.
The margins reflect the steep increase in the price of refined fuels, including diesel, relative to the cost of crude oil, as the shutdown of war-damaged refineries in the Middle East and Russia squeezes supplies.
The Middle East crisis helped Europe’s biggest oil and gas company to a profit of almost $10bn (£7.5bn) for the second quarter of 2026, more than double the figure for the same period last year and its second highest quarterly earnings on record.
Today, Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, has risen $1.27 or 1.3% to $101.84 a barrel.
Royal Mail to cut 2,500 head office and support jobs by end 2027
Royal Mail plans to cut up to 2,500 jobs by the end of next year, as it struggles with a slump in letters being sent and seeks to compete in the cutthroat parcel delivery market.
To simplify its processes and save money, Royal has carried out a review of its head office and support functions, and will reduce them by “up to 2,500” – less than 2% of its workforce of more than 131,000 people, it said.
The company, owned since April 2025 by the Czech billionaire Daniel Křetínský, hopes to achieve the reductions through “natural attrition” (people leaving anyway) and voluntary redundancies, without the need for compulsory redundancies.
It stressed that its frontline roles in delivery and processing, including posties and drivers, will not be affected.
Royal Mail said it needs to adapt to a rapidly-changing market: Letter volumes have declined by more than 70% since their peak, whilst customer demand for faster and more convenient parcel delivery services continues to grow.
Royal Mail has briefed its unions, the Communication Workers Union (CWU) and Unite CMA, on the proposals and formal consultation with both unions is now underway.
Alistair Cochrane, the chief executive, said:
We have been working hard to reduce costs and simplify processes across all areas of the business as we transform to win in a very competitive market. These proposed changes remove duplication and allow us to invest further in the service we deliver for our customers.
We are committed to treating everyone fairly and respectfully throughout this process, working closely with our trade unions. The proposed changes will not be easy, but they are an important part of building a stronger, simpler and future-ready Royal Mail for our customers and colleagues.

Apparent exodus of super-rich suggests UK is no longer billionaires’ playground
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:00:37 UTC
16:00:37 KST

London was once globally renowned as the “billionaires’ playground”, where the world’s super-rich could relax in the Georgian townhouses of Mayfair undisturbed by the grasping hand of the state.
But if recent complaints by fleeing ultra-high net worth individuals are to be believed, the city is no longer as welcoming for those who consider themselves to be Britain’s most-persecuted minority.
They complain of Labour’s stricter tax regime and the antipathy of others towards those with extreme wealth. One even suggested that he was leaving the country because of London’s low-traffic neighbourhoods.
“If I want to organise a gathering now, I have to take into account a lot of my friends are not here any more,” said the financier Ben Goldsmith. “How the hell are we supposed to pay for health services and everything if we are driving out the highest rate taxpayers?”
This weekend, one of the UK’s richest people, David Reuben, was revealed to have left the UK for the tax haven of Monaco. The 88-year-old is a property tycoon and Newcastle United shareholder who, along with his younger brother, Simon Reuben, has a combined estimated net worth of nearly £28bn. A spokesperson did not expand on why he left, but tax is thought to be a factor.
Sir Peter Lampl, the millionaire founder of the Sutton Trust charity, said he had absconded to the US because of Sadiq Khan’s traffic policies, complaining that motorists are “pariahs” in London.
Another billionaire, Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who owns the chemicals company Ineos, has said he can see why rich people are leaving the UK, describing the country as “on the slide”. Ratcliffe, who fled Britain for Monaco in 2018, complained that “the UK has got a bit of a green eye towards wealth at the moment”.
Others, meanwhile, are unimpressed by the ultra-wealthy’s complaints and the warnings of economic doom for the nation that each new announced exit tends to bring.
Arun Advani, director of CenTax, who is influential in Labour circles and helped design a hiked inheritance tax, said he was unconcerned about billionaire flight.
“Mobility among billionaires is high,” he said. “Many wealthy people leave every year, it just isn’t always reported as loudly as at the moment. So a couple of highly reported examples don’t in themselves indicate anything has changed.”
Multimillionaire Dale Vince said ultra-wealthy individuals need to “stop whingeing”. He confirmed he will be staying in the UK, and added: “The tax system is already skewed in favour of rich people. We have so many allowances, loopholes and exemptions.”
For better or worse, the data shows a clear trend; an analysis of Bloomberg’s Billionaires Index has found that super-rich UK residents worth a combined £121bn have either left or loosened ties with UK since the Labour government came to power in 2024. This represents more than half of all billionaire wealth. Among those who have left are Lakshmi Mittal, Aston Villa co-owner Nassef Sawiris and shipping magnate John Fredriksen.
Rachel Reeves’ removal of the “non-dom” system, which allowed individuals to only pay tax on income generated in the UK, is blamed for many of the exits. Others say they fear new taxes on property as well as hiked inheritance taxes.
Sir James Dyson, worth £12bn, faced criticism for absconding to Singapore in 2019, after telling the country to vote Brexit. He returned in 2021, and has been investing in businesses in the UK ever since.
Denise Coates, founder of gambling company bet365, is worth £8bn and appears to have no plans to leave the country. Billionaire John Caudwell, who founded phones4U, confirmed he was remaining resident in the UK.
There are even some super-rich folk coming to the UK – albeit not universally popular ones. Crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne, who gave Reform UK leader Nigel Farage a controversial £5m undeclared gift before he was elected as an MP in 2024, recently registered himself as a UK resident. So did Ben Delo, another crypto billionaire, who has given tens of millions to the party.
Paddy Renouf, who runs luxury concierge service Serendipity, says his ultra-rich clients are still in the UK and spending money.
“I am puzzled as much as anybody else about the rumours of the exodus. England is incomparable to the super-rich. There is no culture as rich with art, restaurants or history; Monaco and Dubai cannot compete on that level.”
He did concede there was some “nervousness” among his clients, adding: “Very wealthy people don’t mind paying taxes if they can anticipate them. But there is a lot of uncertainty at the moment. It is bad if we do lose them.”
Philip Munro, partner at law firm Withers, said more entrepreneurs are asking about leaving the UK, and a steady stream of reports that their peers are also leaving has “concentrated their minds”.
He blames capital gains tax and removal of business property relief on inheritance tax and said inquiries are coming in about moving residency to Dubai, Greece, Italy, Monaco and Switzerland.
Goldsmith agreed that there is “herd behaviour” caused by “social media hype” around the UK’s supposed hostility to the rich.
He added: “People overestimate crime and tax, they underestimate the downsides of living elsewhere.
“London was a hub for foreign billionaires. They pay a lot of tax, they hire a lot of people, they spend a lot of money, they are the most mobile people around, so getting money out of them is an art form.
“There’s nothing to force them to stay here; you have to attract them, and we were once good at that.”
Vince has less sympathy. Pointing at Ratcliffe’s exit as an example, he said: “He got rich here and then made off to Monaco to save himself money.
“He avoided giving back to the economy that made him a billionaire and now he bangs on that it is a bad place to do business when he became a billionaire here!
“It’s pathetic. He and anyone else who leaves here to not pay tax should be stripped of their honours.”

Three years on from the 7 October attacks, antisemitism has taken hold in Britain: Jews aren’t safe | Dave Rich
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:00:37 UTC
16:00:37 KST

On another anniversary of the 7 October attacks, the lasting impact on Britain’s Jews is found in the essential daily decisions we now have to make. Beyond the simple fear that you or your children might get killed the next time you go to synagogue or visit your local kosher shop, Jews are hiding the fact they are Jewish.
This has gone beyond the choice of whether to wear your Star of David necklace inside or outside your shirt. It is found in the job applicants who remove their Jewish community volunteering from their CV; the people who use false names when ordering an Uber; the parents who move their children from mainstream schools to Jewish ones.
The danger for Britain runs deep, for if Jews cannot live an open Jewish life here, then modern Britain as a cohesive, diverse liberal democracy will have failed.
This didn’t begin with Jews. The murder of Terence Carney, a 70-year-old man from Hartlepool, County Durham, may not seem an obvious starting point when trying to understand the impact the Hamas attack and what followed has had on Britain, but it has proved to be a chilling portent of much of what has followed since.
Carney had gone for his regular morning walk in October 2023 when he was fatally stabbed by Ahmed Alid, an Islamist extremist who had arrived in the UK illegally three years earlier. Alid had already tried to kill his Iranian housemate Javed Nouri, who had converted to Christianity and whom he regarded to be an “apostate”. Nouri managed to fight him off, but Carney was not so lucky.
When police asked Alid why he had committed these appalling acts, he said he wanted “Palestine to be free from the Zionists” and that he had murdered Carney, a random passerby with no connection to the Middle East, “because Israel was killing children”. This was just eight days after the 7 October attack on southern Israel – the day on which about 1,200 people, mostly civilians, were killed by Hamas – but already the ripple of that attack had washed on to British shores.
People rarely speak about Terence Carney now, but he was the first victim of terrorism on British soil related to 7 October and the subsequent tragedy in Gaza.
As I describe in my new book, From Be’eri to Bondi: Global Antisemitism After October 7, the Hamas attack and the wars in Gaza and the wider Middle East that followed unleashed a lethal combination of terrorist violence and extremist incitement, street protests and viral campaigns, rising hate crimes and falling social cohesion, with hostile states such as Iran stoking the fire. All of this was both predictable and predicted: it was no surprise that after the atrocities by Hamas in the Be’eri kibbutz and elsewhere in southern Israel in 2023 came the massacre of Jews on Bondi Beach two years later.
At first, Britain largely avoided the wave of anti-Jewish violence that swept world after 7 October. In the past 12 months that has changed. Since the terror attack at Heaton Park synagogue in Manchester last year that killed Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby, injured others and left a community traumatised, Britain has witnessed the stabbing of Jewish men in Golders Green, arson attacks on synagogues “almost certainly directed” from Iran, and the conviction of two Islamic extremists for a terrorist plot against Manchester’s Jewish community that could have killed hundreds. Just this week, two Iranians have been charged with an alleged plot, also to target Jewish people in the Manchester area. This has gone well beyond a problem for Britain’s Jewish community. In its scale and impact, it’s a threat to our national security.
Why these attacks are occurring is where things get complicated. It has become impossible not to notice that the justifications anti-Jewish terrorists offer for their crimes echo the language and ideas that motivate large numbers of people to march peacefully against Israel. Alid’s desire to expel Zionists from Palestine and avenge Palestinian children’s deaths in Gaza, for example, is more widely held than ought to be comfortable, given how he acted as a result. You can even hear an echo of that desire in the recent Green party vote condemning Zionism to be racism. I am sure most protesters who march for Palestine would never endorse Alid’s bloody methods, but the similarity of slogans is troubling nonetheless.
We think of democratic protest and terrorism as two opposing categories of behaviour, but the world is not so neat. Political violence always draws sustenance from a hinterland of ideas and rhetoric shared by many more people who would never pick up a knife or a gun, but who articulate the same grievances.
The belief that Israel is engaged in a “war on children” is common across the pro-Palestine movement, promoted by major NGOs and found in a thousand Instagram reels about genocidal Zionist baby-killers. Without doubt, it is deeply upsetting that thousands of Palestinian children have been killed in Gaza, and many feel that Israel could have done more to minimise civilian casualties. But to describe this not as the result of a tragic and unbearable conflict, but as a “war on children”, is to imply that killing children is the whole point: a charge that echoes the medieval blood libel. From that assumption to Jihad al-Shamie yelling: “This is what you get for killing our children” as he tried to batter down the doors of Heaton Park synagogue last Yom Kippur is not as big a leap as some might wish.
I know this reality is uncomfortable for some. It would be far more convenient if the people attacking Jews always wore swastikas rather than, as has happened, keffiyehs. The riposte that British Jews should take more care not to conflate themselves with Israel misses the point entirely. Nobody tells Russians in London not to conflate themselves with Russia, just as nobody threatens to protest outside their local Chinese takeaway about the Chinese government’s treatment of the Uyghurs, as some have protested at Israeli-owned restaurants in Britain. It wouldn’t even occur to people to do so. The double standard, the unique demand, is the first stage of discrimination.
We are in an extraordinary period. That the Home Office has had to commit £250m to increase policing in Jewish communities across England and Wales, while also raising the national terrorist threat level, recognising the scale of anti-Jewish terrorism and far-right extremism, shows the staggering cost of failing to tackle antisemitism at its source. The government now has plenty of reviews and recommendations to implement regarding how to reduce the extremism that drives anti-Jewish hatred. Civil society, too, needs to step up: it can’t all be left to Whitehall.
The history of antisemitism is marked by moments in time and place when it has been politically weaponised by dangerous actors who are able to lure millions to its toxic scent. The blending of vengeful anti-Israel sentiment with older antisemitic tropes over the past three years, all while Jews are being murdered on multiple continents, makes me fear we have entered such a phase. Antisemitism matters once more, and we all have a role to play in addressing it.
- Dave Rich is director of policy at the Community Security Trust. His new book, From Be’eri to Bondi: Global Antisemitism After October 7, is published by Routledge

Five Marmomac highlights that explore natural stone and new technology
From experimental stone forms that defy gravity to a showcase of Lessinia's vernacular building traditions, this video, produced for Marmomac, highlights the top exhibits at this year's event in Verona, Italy.
International trade show Marmomac returned to Verona for its 60th edition in September, showcasing new approaches for working with natural stone, such as marble and granite.

View this post on Instagram
Dezeen's highlights from the international trade show in Verona
Italian architect Giuseppe Fallacia brought together researchers and universities to experiment with new ways of working with natural stone. Titled C'era Una Volta Il Cielo Dell'Architettura, the exhibit explored how stone could be made to rise against gravity through new forms, lighter structures, engineered materials and new construction methods.
Elsewhere, industrial designer Raffaello Galiotto curated Carisma Materico, a small exhibition exploring how computer-aided design and numerical technologies can be applied to stone production and architecture in the digital age.
At the centre of the exhibition, a large tactile architectural sculpture demonstrated how the natural qualities of stone could be expressed through digitally driven forms.
Another highlight was On Stone – Learning from Lessinia by British architect Joseph Grima and researcher Space Caviar, which explored the region's vernacular stone-building traditions.
Located between Verona and Trentino, Lessinia has a centuries-old tradition of constructing dwellings from locally sourced stone. The exhibition considered how these approaches could offer lessons for contemporary construction and the challenges facing the industry today.
Designer Davide Fabio Colaci presented 10 projects created between 1953 and 2022 to demonstrate the use of natural marble in interior design.
Visitors could walk across an inlaid surface made from reclaimed marble offcuts from each project. Colaci described marble as more than a finishing material, suggesting it can be used "as active elements in the construction of space."
Marmomac also presented 18 works by Italian and international artists located across the city of Verona and its most notable landmarks. The artists used natural stone to carve contemporary sculptures, as well as benches and seating for public spaces.
Marmomac took place in Verona, Italy, from 22 to 25 September 2026, marking the fair's 60 anniversary of bringing together natural stone, technology and design.

Leonardo DRS to build tactical radars in Britain
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:00:21 BST
16:00:21 KST

The American arm of Leonardo has set up a British subsidiary and opened a purpose-built plant to manufacture tactical radars in the United Kingdom, according to Leonardo DRS.
The new company, DRS UK, is intended to give the business a local presence serving British defence customers, industry partners and system integrators, with the parent describing the investment as strengthening long-term support for UK programmes and giving it more flexibility as requirements change.
The radars in question detect, track and classify airborne and ground threats, among them uncrewed aircraft and incoming rockets, artillery and mortars. They are used in counter-drone work, air defence, force protection and active protection systems fitted to armoured vehicles, and the company says more than 10,000 of its radar panels are deployed worldwide in service with the United States armed forces, NATO allies and other customers.
John Baylouny, president and chief executive of Leonardo DRS, said: “Establishing DRS UK and launching a full local tactical radar capability, strengthens our ability to support customers and partners with the proximity, responsiveness and manufacturing capacity needed to meet evolving operational requirements.”
Max Cohen, the senior vice president running the tactical radar portfolio, said: “Our investment in UK-based manufacturing for advanced sensing technologies reinforces the industrial capability, supply chain resilience and skilled workforce needed to support critical defence priorities.”
The site is intended to serve as a hub for the tactical radar business across the United Kingdom and Europe rather than solely for the British market.

CANBERRA, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- The Australian Defense Force has suspended the use of a troop carrier that was involved in a fatal rollover during a training exercise in the Northern Territory (NT) on Monday, Chief of Army Susan Coyle said on Wednesday.
Australian Army Corporal Brendan Hannam, aged 28, died and five other soldiers were injured when a vehicle rolled at the Mount Bundey Training Area in the NT on Monday.
Coyle confirmed that the vehicle was a Supacat High Mobility Transporter and that Hannam was not driving at the time of the incident.

The five soldiers who were injured in the rollover were all airlifted to hospital on Monday night, including two in critical condition. Two of the five remained in hospital on Wednesday.
Defense Minister Richard Marles said on Wednesday that there would be a series of investigations into the rollover. ■

S. Korea's appellate court acquits ex-President Yoon in free polling case
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:56:58 CST
15:56:58 KST

SEOUL, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- A South Korean appellate court on Wednesday acquitted former President Yoon Suk-yeol of charges that he received free opinion polls from a political broker in violation of the Political Funds Act.
The Seoul High Court overturned a lower court's partial guilty ruling, clearing both Yoon and self-proclaimed political broker Myung Tae-kyun of charges that Yoon illegally accepted free public opinion polls from Myung in exchange for political favors.
The team of Min Joong-ki, an independent counsel who led an investigation into corruption allegations involving Yoon and his wife, Kim Keon-hee, sought a four-year prison sentence for Yoon and a three-year sentence for Myung.
The appellate bench stated that there was no evidence of an agreement between the Yoons and Myung about the conduct or free provision of public opinion polls, saying that it was difficult to establish criminal intent to donate illegal political funds.
It directly contradicted the lower court's finding, which ruled that there was a tacit agreement between the former first couple and Myung.
Yoon was accused of conspiring with his wife to receive customized opinion polls free of charge from the political broker on 58 occasions from June 2021 to March 2022, ahead of the 2022 presidential election, in exchange for the illegal nomination of a former People Power Party lawmaker in a parliamentary by-election later that year.
In the initial trial, the lower court found Yoon guilty of receiving 14 of the polls, where Myung directly delivered the results to the couple, sentencing Yoon to two years in prison and Myung to 18 months.
The lower court acquitted them of the remaining 44 polls due to the lack of definitive proof of a mutual agreement, given that Myung's direct delivery could not be established.
The appellate court's verdict on Yoon aligned with the previous rulings for his wife, who was acquitted of the same charges in both her first and second trials.
Kim's case was currently pending a final decision by the Supreme Court.
Yoon was sentenced to life in prison in February for the insurrection stemming from his martial law declaration and 30 years in prison in June for the general treason relevant to the infiltration of drones into the Democratic People's Republic of Korea.
The emergency martial law was declared by Yoon on the night of Dec. 3, 2024, but it was revoked hours later by the National Assembly.
The constitutional court upheld a motion to impeach Yoon in April 2025, officially removing him from office.
He was indicted under detention in January 2025 as a suspected ringleader of the insurrection, becoming the first sitting president to be arrested and indicted. ■

TOKYO, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- Japan's Fair Trade Commission on Wednesday searched the offices of the country's four major brewers on suspicion of violating the antimonopoly law by forming a cartel to raise the prices of beer and beer-like drinks, local media reported.
All the four beer makers -- Asahi Breweries Ltd., Kirin Brewery Co., Sapporo Breweries Ltd., and Suntory Spirits Ltd. -- separately confirmed the raids and said they intend to cooperate with the probe, Kyodo News reported.
The companies, which hold large shares of the market, are suspected of coordinating on the timing and size of price increases for beer and beer-like drinks over several years by having sales representatives meet to exchange information, the report said.
Those companies' representatives are believed to have held secret meetings to discuss price increases after they attended regular gatherings held about once a month by the Brewers Association of Japan, it added.
The antitrust watchdog is expected to continue its investigation and may consider filing a criminal complaint with prosecutors.
The four brewers consecutively raised prices of beer and beer-like drinks in October 2022, October 2023, and April 2025, citing rising costs for raw materials and energy. ■

S. Korea's Nuri rocket deploys 14 out of 15 satellites
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:56:53 CST
15:56:53 KST

SEOUL, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's homegrown space rocket, Nuri, successfully blasted off on Wednesday but failed to deploy one of its 15 onboard satellites into orbit, the aerospace authorities confirmed, correcting an earlier announcement that all payloads were delivered.
The three-stage liquid-fueled rocket, officially known as Korea Space Launch Vehicle (KSLV)-II, lifted off at 12:25 p.m. local time (0325 GMT) from the Naro Space Center in Goheung, about 400 km southwest of the capital Seoul.
While the first stage, payload fairing, and second stage separated flawlessly, the subsequent tracking data revealed a minor anomaly during the final satellite ejection phase.
Around 12 minutes and 30 seconds after liftoff, Nuri's third-stage engine shut down to initiate a highly sophisticated sequential satellite deployment at its target altitude of 575 km.
The main mission of Nuri's fifth launch was to safely deliver five New-space Earth Observation Satellite Constellation for National Safety (NEONSAT) microsatellites, which were successfully released one by one at intervals of 35 to 40 seconds.
It represented a major advancement in complexity from the fourth launch, which carried a single primary payload.
To prevent mid-space collisions, the rocket's upper stage was rotated by 30 and 60 degrees between each release.
However, a glitch occurred during the subsequent release of 10 smaller academic and commercial CubeSats, which were scheduled to be ejected in pairs at 10-second intervals.
The Korea AeroSpace Administration (KASA) corrected its initial statement, saying nine out of the 10 CubeSats were confirmed to have separated.
Nuri will perform a series of post-mission maneuvers to prevent collisions before re-entering the Earth's atmosphere and burning up. ■

1 dead in Narva care home blaze, cause likely careless smoking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
06:54:00 UTC
15:54:00 KST

1 dead in Narva care home blaze, cause likely careless smoking
One person perished in a fire at a care home in Narva on Tuesday evening, with the cause believed to be smoking without due care and attention, the Rescue Board said.
The fire was confined to a smoking corner and, with the facility's fire doors and compartments in order, did not spread, meaning no evacuation was needed.
The alarm was called in at 8:51 p.m. on Tuesday to the care home on Rahu põik, on the northern outskirts of Narva.
The first Narva rescuers to arrive identified smoke on the second floor of the facility, began ventilating the rooms and discovered the body of a deceased woman in the smoking corner.
Care home staff had extinguished the localized blaze themselves with fire extinguishers, meaning the fire was no longer active by the time firefighters arrived.
Rescue Board (Päästeamet) personnel then checked the entire building with measuring devices. No carbon monoxide was detected, and ambulance crews examined all residents.
Rescue teams from the Narva and Narva-Jõesuu stations and a field manager from Jõhvi took part in the response.
The fire may have started from careless smoking, and the exact circumstances will be established in further proceedings.
A total of 23 fire fatalities have been reported in Estonia so far this year.

Israel marks third anniversary of October 7 Hamas terror attacks with memorials

Israel marks third anniversary of October 7 terror attacks
October 7, 2026
Israel is marking the third anniversary of the October 7, 2023, Hamas terrorist attack on Wednesday with memorials across the country.
At the site of the Nova music festival, where more than 300 people were killed, families gathered at dawn for a moment of silence and paid tribute in front of portraits both of festival-goers and security forces who died on October 7.
At the Kfar Aza kibbutz, another attack site, mourners watched the raising of an Israeli flag in silence.
Others gathered at intersections and bomb shelters to mark the deadliest terrorist attack on Israeli soil in the history of the modern state, which killed more than 1,200 people and saw 251 others taken hostage.
The last living hostages were released a year ago under a US-brokered ceasefire deal.
How did Netanyahu, Hamas and others mark the anniversary?
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu attended official ceremonies in Jerusalem, saying there would be "no forgiveness for the murderers" and that Israel would never again tolerate Hamas rule of Gaza.
Hamas, meanwhile, issued a statement calling October 7 "a glorious day in our people's history." It called the attack a "natural response to, and culmination of" decades of suffering in Gaza.
The anniversary of the attacks also comes ahead of the October 27 elections in Israel.
Naftali Bennett, a former Israeli prime minister seeking to challenge Netanyahu in those elections, attended the ceremony at the Nova festival site.
"This was a colossal failure of the state of Israel, which was established to defend Jews in our land," he said.
The center-left Democrats party leader, Yair Golan, also took aim at the Israeli government, saying, "A government that for three years has not destroyed Hamas' rule in a government dangerous to Israel."
Germany stands firmly by Israel's side, says Merz
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Wednesday reaffirmed Germany's support for Israel on the anniversary, saying the country stood firmly by Israel's side and was committed to preventing a repeat of the October 7 attack.
"We stand for the security and existence of Israel," the German chancellor said.
Merz also called for a political settlement, saying peace and security in the region "can best be achieved through the establishment of a Palestinian state alongside Israel."

Haiti has postponed its long-planned general elections indefinitely, as widespread gang violence, territorial blockades, and administrative hurdles continue to prevent the vote, authorities confirmed.
"Following consultations with political actors and in view of the adoption, in the Council of Ministers, on October 5, 2026, of the amendments made to the Electoral Decree of June 2, 2026, certain deadlines of the electoral process are being rescheduled," the Provisional Electoral Council said in a statement released Monday.
The council explained that the campaign period has been suspended and that new dates will be announced once it finalizes an updated framework with authorized political bodies. General elections were scheduled to take place on Dec. 13 to select a president alongside all members of the Senate, the Chamber of Deputies, departmental assemblies, and municipal administrations.
The country remains without any nationally elected officials, having held no general vote since 2016. Haiti was plunged into a deeper political vacuum following the July 2021 assassination of President Jovenel Moise, while legislative terms progressively expired.
A transitional arrangement established in 2024 currently governs the Caribbean nation. The Transitional Presidential Council, formed after former Prime Minister Ariel Henry resigned under gang pressure, leads the executive alongside appointed Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aime, who governs largely by decree.
The Transitional Presidential Council's mandate ended in February, leaving Fils-Aime and his Cabinet in charge of the interim period.
Heavily armed criminal groups control extensive sections of Port-au-Prince and outlying regions, displacing approximately 1.5 million people and severing transit corridors required to distribute voting materials.

Gokhan Ergocun
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
The global economy faces dual pressures from a negative energy supply shock and a positive artificial intelligence (AI) demand shock, the head of the International Monetary Fund said Wednesday.
Kristalina Georgieva delivered a speech in Singapore ahead of the upcoming annual meetings in Thailand; highlighting that the global economy must navigate three major crosscurrents, which are the rapid arrival of AI, persistently high energy prices and record levels of public debt.
She noted that global public debt tracks to soon exceed 100% of the gross domestic product, reaching its highest levels since the end of World War II.
Advanced economies stand out as the worst offenders with some of the highest gross debt loads, Georgieva said.
The managing director pointed out that opposite forces pull the global economy in two different directions.
Georgieva warned that oil prices remain around $100 per barrel due to transport costs and other risks.
She emphasized that natural gas supply from the Gulf remains severely impaired because shipping through the Strait of Hormuz faces threats.
On the technology front, Georgieva stated that AI hardware and related products now account for more than 10% of world goods trade.
She added that AI could eventually deliver up to 0.5% of extra world growth annually if countries manage it correctly.
Georgieva urged economic policymakers to stop delaying necessary actions and implement credible fiscal consolidation plans.
She also advised central banks in various countries to maintain a prudently hawkish bias in their monetary policies because the AI building boom, energy shocks and high public debt fuel inflation.

Conservative lawmaker Agnė Bilotaitė has decided to give up her seat in Lithuania’s parliament and withdraw from active politics, her party said Wednesday.
Bilotaitė submitted a written request Monday to the Central Electoral Commission asking it to terminate her parliamentary mandate before the end of the current term.
She said personal circumstances had prompted her decision to leave the Seimas.
“This is not an easy decision, and it has been developing for some time. I realised that I could no longer delay and needed to take care of my health and my family’s needs. The intensive work in parliament did not allow me to do that properly,” Bilotaitė said in a statement.
She also said she was stepping away from active political life but would remain a member of the Homeland Union-Lithuanian Christian Democrats.
“I want to apologise to those who may be disappointed by my decision,” she said. “I feel responsible for the work I cannot continue and am handing over to others. But it would be unfair and unacceptable to me to continue without putting in all the effort and time possible.”
Bilotaitė said the withdrawal was necessary so that she could take on new projects in the future. She thanked her party colleagues, fellow lawmakers and her team for their work and cooperation.
During her current term, Bilotaitė served on the Seimas Committee on Legal Affairs and the Parliamentary Commission for the Control of Criminal Intelligence. She also chaired the temporary parliamentary group for women and headed a working group established by the Seimas board to improve legal regulations on preventing and combating sexual harassment and violence.
She served as Lithuania’s interior minister between 2020–2024.
Bilotaitė has served in parliament since 2008. She was re-elected in 2024 on the Homeland Union-Lithuanian Christian Democrats’ party list.
Her seat is expected to go to Kęstutis Masiulis, the next candidate on the party’s list.

Christa Pike is awake after failed execution - attorneys
Ukraine
