Christa Pike is awake after failed execution - attorneys
Kyiv • UNN
Christa Pike survived an execution attempt in Tennessee and is in the hospital. Her attorneys are demanding that evidence be preserved and the causes of the failure be determined.
In the United States, death-row inmate Christa Pike regained consciousness after Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute her by lethal injection last week. Her lawyers intend to go to court on Wednesday, October 7, to obtain more information about what went wrong. UNN reports this, citing AP.
Details
Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital when executioners attempted to execute her on September 30 for beating and murdering her classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in 1995. Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived the administration of lethal injections.
Pike’s lawyers are due to appear in court on Wednesday to obtain more information from the Tennessee Department of Correction. Chancellor’s Court Judge I’Ashea Myles scheduled a preliminary hearing in the case for Wednesday in Nashville.
"Against all expectations, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care," Pike’s lawyers said in a statement. Pike’s prognosis remains unclear, and at a minimum, she faces a lengthy recovery, the lawyers said. They said Pike’s arms were burned and covered in blisters after the lethal-injection attempt, and that she is shackled to a hospital bed.
Pike’s lawyers are seeking a court order requiring the prison system to preserve information about the execution attempt, including drug lot numbers, needles, execution protocols, and other information.
Lawyers from the Tennessee attorney general’s office wrote in a court filing on Tuesday that a court order was unnecessary because the prison system "is obligated to preserve this evidence in other cases and should ensure its preservation." They said state officials had taken "the necessary steps to provide medical care for Pike and determine what happened."
Republican Governor Bill Lee called what happened "deeply troubling" and ordered a "comprehensive third-party review to determine exactly what happened." The governor postponed the state’s only other execution scheduled for this year.
Experts in medicine and lethal injections have focused on the possibility that a problem with the intravenous catheter caused the drug to accumulate in her tissue rather than enter the bloodstream. Pike’s lawyers wrote in their court filings that "apparently, no member of the execution team realized that the intravenous catheters had been improperly placed or that the veins had ruptured."
The execution attempt began at around 7:30 p.m. local time on September 30, when Pike was given an opportunity to make a final statement. Approximately five minutes later, Pike raised her head and said that her arm hurt. At some point, she appeared to lose consciousness, but her breathing could be heard until members of the media were escorted out of the witness room at 8:53 p.m. At 9:14 p.m., an ambulance arrived at the prison to take Pike to the hospital.

South Korea launched 15 satellites into orbit during the fifth launch of the &quot;Nuri&quot; rocket
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:40:18 EEST
15:40:18 KST

South Korea launched 15 satellites into orbit during the fifth launch of the "Nuri" rocket
Kyiv • UNN
The "Nuri" rocket launched five NEONSAT satellites and 10 CubeSats into orbit. The NEONSAT satellites will be used to monitor the Korean Peninsula and surrounding areas.
The South Korean domestically developed Nuri launch vehicle placed 15 satellites into orbit during its fifth launch, including five that will become part of the country’s first domestically launched micro-satellite constellation, the country’s space agency said. Yonhap reports, UNN writes.
Details
The 200-ton Nuri rocket lifted off from the Naro Space Center in Goheung, about 400 kilometers south of Seoul, at 12:25 and completed its flight 20 minutes later.
The payload consists of five New-space Earth Observation Satellite Constellation for National Safety (NEONSAT) microsatellites and 10 CubeSats.
Nuri successfully separated its first and second stages, after which it released the satellites at an altitude of approximately 575 kilometers.
The five NEONSAT satellites — Nos. 2–6, each weighing less than 100 kilograms — separated at intervals of 35 to 40 seconds. Meanwhile, Nuri’s upper stage rotated approximately 45 degrees between each separation to prevent collisions. The 10 CubeSats were launched in pairs at 10-second intervals.
"The Nuri rocket reached its planned orbit according to schedule," said Oh Tae-seok, administrator of the Korea AeroSpace Administration (KASA), adding that the launch team is conducting a detailed analysis to confirm the successful deployment of the satellites.
After deploying all 15 satellites, Nuri performed a collision-avoidance maneuver and released its remaining fuel, completing its flight. The rocket will remain in orbit before eventually entering Earth’s atmosphere and burning up.
The Korea Aerospace Research Institute will track the flight from ground facilities in South Korea and Palau in the western Pacific Ocean.
The fifth flight marked Nuri’s first attempt to sequentially place several primary satellites into orbit intended to carry out the same mission.
Each NEONSAT weighs less than 100 kilograms and is equipped with an electro-optical camera capable of distinguishing objects measuring at least 1 meter in black-and-white images and at least 4 meters in color images.
The satellites will monitor the Korean Peninsula and surrounding areas for national security and natural disaster response purposes.
The NEONSAT constellation will eventually consist of 10 satellites. Five more will be launched on Nuri’s sixth flight, scheduled for next year, allowing the constellation to be completed.
Once fully operational, the constellation will be able to obtain images of the Korean Peninsula more than three times a day and reimage the same area within 24 hours.

Russian forces destroy central warehouse of the ATL auto service network in Kyiv
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:38:00 EEST
15:38:00 KST

Russian forces destroy car parts retailer ATL's main warehouse in Kyiv
A Russian attack on Kyiv has completely destroyed the central warehouse of the ATL car parts retailer and servicing chain. As a result, its shops and service stations will have to rely on existing stock in the coming days, limiting the range of products available.
Source: ATL on Facebook
Details: Most of the engine oils, batteries and other automotive products supplied by the company were stored and distributed through the warehouse. No employees were injured.
Their car parts retail outlets and service centres are continuing to operate as usual. ATL said it had prepared for such a disruption by distributing supplies across its facilities and building up stocks in advance.
Meanwhile, the loss of the central warehouse will disrupt logistics. In the coming days, customers will only have access to products already in stock at the network's shops and service centres.
The company says it is continuing to meet its commitments to partners and suppliers. The extent of the damage is still being assessed, and no figure has been given for the losses.
Background:
- On the night of 6-7 October, Russian forces conducted a large-scale combined attack on Ukraine, using ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and attack drones simultaneously.
- The Russians launched the massive attack using various air attack weapons. According to the Air Force, air defence brought down 161 aerial assets.

Terror attack, hostages, assassinations: Key events that defined October 7 and the resulting war

- The outbreak, the hostages, the assassinations: Key events that defined October 7 and the resulting war
The outbreak, the hostages, the assassinations: Key events that defined October 7 and the resulting war
The complete timeline of the war that changed Israel: the surprise attack, the ground offensive, the hostage release deals, the additional fronts, and the defining moments along the way
Three years ago today, the State of Israel awoke to a horrible reality, as the Hamas terrorist organization launched an unprecedented terror attack, the scale of which had never been seen before. Since then, Israel has been in one of the most complex and tumultuous periods in its history, with a war that has expanded from a single focal point to multiple regional arenas.
From the first sirens, through the ground offensives, the direct confrontation with Iran, and the hostage release deals, these are the events that have shaped the war from its beginning until today, changing Israel and the entire Middle East.
October 7, 2023 | 06:29 - The surprise attack begins
At 6:29 a.m., on Simchat Torah, Hamas launches a large-scale attack on Israel. Alongside heavy rocket barrages targeting communities in southern and central Israel, thousands of terrorists breach the border fence and infiltrate Israel by land, sea, and air.
The terrorists raid communities near the Gaza border, military posts and bases, including Be’eri, Kfar Aza, Nahal Oz, Netiv HaAsara, Nir Oz and Sderot. At the same time, they reached the Nova music festival near Re’im.
According to the Ministry of Defense, about 6,000 terrorists managed to infiltrate Israeli territory. A total of 251 people were kidnapped and brought into the Gaza Strip.
October 7 | 07:00–09:00 - The attack spreads
Simultaneously with the fighting in dozens of communities, the terrorists arrive at the Nova party. Hundreds of partygoers try to escape the scene, and many are murdered or kidnapped.
At Re'im, about 35 people fleeing the festival arrive at the kibbutz between 7:00 and 7:30 a.m. At 7:51 a.m., the first terrorists infiltrate the kibbutz; at 08:01, dozens more enter. By 9:00 a.m., about 80 terrorists are already in Re'im.
October 7 | 06:29–09:55 - The political leadership’s timeline
According to the timeline published by the Prime Minister’s Office, Netanyahu receives his first update about the attack at 6:29 a.m. At 6:44 a.m., he speaks with his military secretary and raises the issue of mobilizing reservists. At 7:30 a.m., he departs for the Kirya military headquarters, arriving sometime between approximately 8:00 and 8:22 a.m.
October 7 | Throughout the day – Battles in the Gaza border communities
The fighting continues in the communities and outposts for hours. In Be'eri, Kfar Aza, Nahal Oz, Sderot, Ofakim, Re'im, and elsewhere, residents and local security teams fight terrorists alongside police and IDF forces.
The IDF later determined that full control over all southern communities was not restored until October 10, although large-scale fighting inside most communities had already ended by October 9.
October 7 | Evening hours – Israel goes to war
As fighting continues inside Israeli territory, the air force begins extensive strikes in Gaza. At 9:23 p.m., according to IDF updates from that day, the air force strikes infrastructure used by senior Hamas figures and units. Fighting inside some communities continues beyond 10:00 p.m.
October 8, 2023 | The second front opens
A day after the Hamas attack and the raids on Gaza border communities, Hezbollah begins firing at an IDF force on the Lebanese border. Israel responds with strikes. This marks the opening of the northern front, which will remain active throughout almost the entire war and develop into a broad campaign against Hezbollah in 2024.
October 19, 2023 | The Houthis Join the Campaign
The Houthis in Yemen also enter the conflict, launching missiles and drones toward Israel. The attacks from Yemen will later develop into another front in the war, with Israeli strikes in Yemen and American operations against the Houthis.
October 27, 2023 | Israel begins the ground maneuver
After three weeks of airstrikes, the IDF significantly expands its ground operations in Gaza. Troops enter northern Gaza, and the war moves into a phase of extensive ground combat.
October 30, 2023 | The first hostage is rescued
The IDF and Shin Bet rescued in a special operation the observer Ori Megidish, who had been abducted from the Nahal Oz base. This is the first rescue of a live hostage from the Gaza Strip during the war. Later, the IDF will define the return of the hostages as one of the main objectives of the campaign.
November 24, 2023 | The first hostage deal
After weeks of fighting, a temporary ceasefire is signed as part of a deal between Israel and Hamas. During the days of the truce, 105 hostages are released, including women, children, and foreign civilians, in exchange for the release of Palestinian prisoners.
The fighting resumes on December 1. The deal transforms the hostage issue from a purely humanitarian concern into a central factor in the conduct of the war.
December 2023–January 2024 | The war expands to southern Gaza
After taking control of large parts of the northern Gaza Strip, the IDF is expanding its ground operations to Khan Yunis. The war is now also focused on the southern part of the Strip, to which hundreds of thousands of Palestinians have fled.
December 15, 2023 | "The Shuja'iyya Incident" - Three hostages killed by IDF fire
An IDF force operating in the Shuja'iyya neighborhood of Gaza City spots three figures approaching them, shirtless, unarmed, and waving a white flag. Despite this, the force decides to open fire at them.
It was later revealed that the three were the abductees Yotam Haim, Alon Shamriz, and Samar Talalka, who had managed to escape from their captors. An IDF investigation determined that the shooting was carried out in violation of the rules of engagement.
February 12, 2024 | "Golden Hand" - Two hostages rescued in Rafah
In a special operation by the IDF, Shin Bet, and Yamam, two Israeli hostages are rescued from Rafah: Fernando Simon Marman and Louis Har. The operation lasts less than an hour and a half and is carried out under fire, as the forces break into the apartment where the two were held.
April 13, 2024 | Iran directly attacks Israel
After months of operating through proxies, Iran is directly attacking Israel in response to the assassination of a senior Revolutionary Guards official in Syria and Lebanon, Mohammad Reza Zahedi, in a strike attributed to Israel near the Iranian embassy in Damascus.
Iran is launching hundreds of UAVs, cruise missiles, and ballistic missiles toward Israel. Most of the threats were intercepted in a joint operation by Israel and its allies. This is a dramatic shift: for the first time during the war, Israel and Iran are confronting each other directly.
May 2024 | The campaign moves to Rafah
The IDF is beginning ground operations in Rafah, in the southern part of the Gaza Strip, after months in which the city became a concentration point for hundreds of thousands of displaced persons.
The operation in Rafah is becoming one of the most controversial moves on the international stage, but from Israel's perspective, it is presented as part of the effort to dismantle the remaining Hamas battalions in the area.
June 8, 2024 | "Operation Arnon" - Four hostages return alive
One of the most dramatic actions of the war: Shin Bet and Yamam forces, backed by the IDF, raid two buildings in the Nuseirat refugee camp and rescue Noa Argamani, Almog Meir Jan, Andrey Kozlov, and Shlomi Ziv.
Yamam commander and fighter, Chief Inspector Arnon Zamora, was critically wounded during the operation and died of his injuries. The operation was named after him.
July 13, 2024 | Israel eliminates Mohammed Deif
The IDF is striking a compound in Khan Yunis where, according to Israeli intelligence, Mohammed Deif — the head of Hamas's military wing, who has been at the top of Israel’s most-wanted list for years — was staying. Subsequently, Israel announced that Deif has been eliminated.
27 July 2024 | 12 children killed by a Hezbollah rocket strike in Majdal Shams
On Saturday evening, Hezbollah launched a rocket that hit a soccer field in Majdal Shams while children were present. Hezbollah denied involvement in the incident, but intelligence sources in Israel and the United States stated that there is no doubt Hezbollah was responsible for the attack.
July 31, 2024 | Assassination of the Hezbollah Chief of Staff
The IDF kills Fuad Shukr in Beirut. Hezbollah’s most senior military official, Shukr effectively served as its chief of staff. The strike follows the escalation along the northern border and the attack on Majdal Shams.
On October 3, 2024, Khader al-Shahabiya, the commander of the Har Dov sector in Hezbollah, who commanded the rocket fire on Majdal Shams, was eliminated.
July 31, 2024 | The assassination of Ismail Haniyeh
Ismail Haniyeh, the head of Hamas's political bureau, was eliminated in a guest apartment of the Revolutionary Guards in Tehran after attending the inauguration ceremony of the Iranian president. In addition to Haniyeh, his bodyguard was also eliminated; the bodyguard was one of the perpetrators of the infiltration attack near Kibbutz Nahal Oz during Operation Protective Edge, in which five Israeli soldiers were killed.
The assassination of Haniyeh is attributed to Israel, even though at the time Israel did not officially claim responsibility.
August 20, 2024 | Recovery of the bodies of six hostages
The IDF and Shin Bet recover from a tunnel in Khan Yunis the bodies of: Chaim Peri, Yoram Metzger, Alex Dancyg, Avraham Munder, Yagev Buchshtab, and Nadav Popplewell.
An IDF investigation published several months later determined that the six were murdered by Hamas terrorists on February 14. The operation highlights the shift in the campaign: alongside efforts to secure the release of hostages alive, Israel is also working to locate and recover the bodies of the fallen.
August 31, 2024 | Six hostages are murdered in a tunnel in Rafah
Hamas lookouts notice IDF forces approaching the tunnel where six hostages were held: Hersh Goldberg-Polin, Eden Yerushalmi, Ori Danino, Alex Lobanov, Almog Sarusi, and Carmel Gat. Once the information is received, the terrorists holding the six hostages are ordered to execute them, and they shoot them at close range.
On August 31, several days after the murder, an IDF force located the tunnel, inside which were the six bodies of the fallen. After their bodies were returned to Israel, they showed signs of extreme neglect and being underweight, as well as severe signs of violence and gunshot wounds.
Hamas initially claims that the casualties were killed as a result of an IDF attack, but later releases a statement saying that following Operation Arnon, new instructions were issued to the terrorists in charge of guarding the hostages: to murder them if the IDF approaches their location.
September 17–18, 2024 | The Northern Front Erupts: The Pager Operation in Lebanon
Thousands of walkie-talkies and beepers used by Hezbollah operatives explode across Lebanon and Syria in two waves. 59 people are killed in the operation, and about 4,500 are injured, 450 of them in critical or serious condition. Approximately 1,500 terrorists have been rendered unfit for action, among other things due to blindness or loss of limbs.
The operation is attributed to Israel, although Israel does not claim responsibility at the time. Two months later, Prime Minister Netanyahu acknowledges that Israel carried out the attack.
This marks a turning point in the campaign against Hezbollah. The security cabinet adds returning northern residents to their homes to the list of war objectives. Several days later, the IDF strikes approximately 1,000 Hezbollah launchers aimed at Israel, preventing a broad retaliatory attack in response to the pager operation. Hezbollah subsequently fires hundreds of rockets a day at northern Israel, expanding its range to the Jezreel Valley and Haifa Bay.
September 27, 2024 | "New Order": The Elimination of Hassan Nasrallah
The air force carries out a heavy bombardment of Hezbollah’s headquarters in Beirut’s Dahieh district, targeting the organization’s leader, Hassan Nasrallah. A day later, the IDF officially confirms that Hezbollah Secretary-General Hassan Nasrallah has been killed.
Other senior figures are killed alongside Nasrallah, including Ali Karaki, Hezbollah’s southern front commander, and the commander of the Revolutionary Guards’ Quds Force in Lebanon. It is one of the war’s most significant assassinations, coming after more than three decades in which Nasrallah led the organization.
October 1, 2024 | Israel launches a ground incursion into southern Lebanon
The IDF is beginning ground operations in southern Lebanon as part of Operation "Northern Arrows," to target Hezbollah infrastructure and push the threat away from northern communities. At the same time, tens of thousands of Israelis are being evacuated from their homes in the north, and Hezbollah is starting to launch missiles at the central region as well.
October 1, 2024 | Iran launches hundreds of missiles at Israel
In response to Israeli actions against Hezbollah and assassinations of the organization's senior members, Iran carries out a direct ballistic missile attack on Israel for the second time. Israel intercepts a significant portion of the missiles, and in the following months plans its response.
October 17, 2024 | Yahya Sinwar is killed
The IDF spots a group of Hamas fighters in Rafah and opens fire. It later emerges that one of the terrorists was Yahya Sinwar, killing the man regarded as the principal architect of the October 7 attack and Hamas’s leader in Gaza.
November 27, 2024 | Ceasefire with Lebanon
After months of fighting in the north and a ground incursion into southern Lebanon, Israel and Lebanon agree to a ceasefire. The agreement is supposed to bring an end to the fighting and to distance Hezbollah forces from the border area.
December 2024 | The fall of the Assad regime in Syria – Israel enters an additional front
The fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime in Syria transforms the regional landscape. Israel takes advantage of the change to target Syrian military infrastructure and prevent weapons from reaching hostile actors.
The IDF entered the buffer zone along the Syrian border and took control of several strategic points, including the summit of the Syrian Hermon.
January 19, 2025 | The second hostages deal
After months of negotiations, a ceasefire agreement in the Gaza Strip has come into effect, which includes the release of 30 live hostages, 8 deceased hostages, the release of hundreds of terrorists and Palestinian detainees, and the expansion of humanitarian aid entry into the Strip.
The first phase begins with the gradual release of Israeli hostages. On January 19, the first three hostages released under the deal, Romi Gonen, Emily Damari and Doron Steinbrecher, return to Israel.
Dozens more hostages are subsequently released, including the five military lookouts abducted from the Nahal Oz post: Liri Albag, Karina Ariev, Daniella Gilboa, Naama Levy and Agam Berger, as well as Yarden Bibas.
On February 8, Israeli hostages Eli Sharabi, Or Levy and Ohad Ben Ami are released in a state of severe malnutrition. Images of them spark outrage in Israel and around the world.
February 20-22, 2025 | The return of the bodies of the Bibas family
On February 20, under the ceasefire agreement, Hamas returns four bodies to Israel. Three are identified as Oded Lifshitz and brothers Ariel and Kfir Bibas, who were abducted from Nir Oz and murdered in captivity.
Hamas claimed that the fourth body was that of Shiri Bibas, but the body did not match her or any other hostage. It was eventually determined that the body belonged to a Palestinian resident of the Gaza Strip. Shiri Bibas's body was finally returned to Israel on February 22.
The Institute of Forensic Medicine determined that Shiri, Ariel, and Kfir Bibas were murdered by Hamas terrorists in November 2023. The IDF spokesperson also said that Ariel and Kfir were brutally murdered by hand, with an attempt to cover up the evidence.
March 18, 2025 | “Might and Sword” — Fighting resumes in Gaza
After nearly two months of ceasefire, Israel resumes extensive strikes in Gaza. The operation is named “Might and Sword.” Hundreds of Palestinians, including senior Hamas figures, are killed in the opening strikes, and fighting later expands into Rafah. The war in Gaza enters a new phase that lasts for months.
June 13-24, 2025 | “Rising Lion” — Israel attacks Iran
At 3:30 a.m., Israel launches a broad operation against Iran. The operation targets Iran’s nuclear program, ballistic missile capabilities, and security and command structures. It includes the killing of senior Iranian officials and significant damage to air defense and missile systems.
The campaign lasts 12 days, during which Iran launches numerous missiles toward Israel. Thirty-three civilians are killed by Iranian missile strikes, and thousands of buildings in Israel are damaged, including the Haifa oil refineries, Soroka Hospital and the Weizmann Institute.
After 12 days of fighting, Israel and Iran reach a ceasefire, following, among other developments, the American attack on the Fordow nuclear facility.
The direct confrontation marks another shift in the war: from a conflict fought primarily through proxies to a sustained direct campaign between Israel and Tehran.
Summer 2025 | "Gideon's Chariots" – The war in Gaza continues
Fighting continues in Gaza alongside repeated efforts to reach a deal. Operations to locate and recover the bodies of hostages also continue. In August 2025, for example, the IDF and Shin Bet recover the body of Ilan Weiss, who was murdered in Be’eri and whose body was taken to Gaza.
September 9, 2025 | The Israeli strike in Doha
Israel attacks a Hamas target in Doha, Qatar, in an attempt to harm the organization's leadership, which fails. The event becomes one of the most dramatic moments in the diplomatic campaign, as the attack takes place in a country that mediates between Israel and Hamas.
The attack on Qatar was sharply condemned by the United States, which subsequently provided Qatar with security guarantees. Three weeks after the strike, Prime Minister Netanyahu called the Emir of Qatar at the request of the United States to apologize.
October 2025 | The deal that brings the living hostages home
After about two years of war, a new agreement was signed between Israel and Hamas. As part of the first stage of the agreement, all the living hostages remaining in the Gaza Strip will return to Israel.
On October 13, Israel held a day marking the return of the living hostages to their families after 738 days in captivity. At the same time, a new ceasefire began in the Gaza Strip.
In the weeks that follow, the remaining bodies of the abducted fallen who remained in the Gaza Strip are returned to Israel, including the body of Hadar Goldin, who was abducted during Operation "Protective Edge."
January 26, 2026 | The last hostage returns
More than two years and three months after October 7, Israel announces, following a military operation, the recovery of the remains of Ran Gvili, the last hostage still in Gaza. Gvili, a member of the police’s Yasam special patrol unit, was killed on October 7, and his body was taken into Gaza.
The IDF announces that after identification, the return of all the hostages, both the living and the deceased, from the Gaza Strip has been completed. The event marks the closure of one of the main chapters of the war.
February 28, 2026 | Operation “Lion’s Roar”
On Saturday morning, Israel and the United States launch a massive surprise attack on Iran, aiming to strike its nuclear program, ballistic missile array, and military and governmental targets.
In the opening strike, the air force drops dozens of heavy bombs on the compound of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. Israel subsequently announces that Iran’s supreme leader has been killed. Iran responds by launching missile attacks on Israel.
March 2, 2026 | Hezbollah re-enters the campaign
Two days after the initial strike in Iran, Hezbollah officially announces the end of the ceasefire with Israel and joins the fighting, beginning to launch rockets and UAVs toward Israeli communities and IDF bases in the north.
At the same time, the IDF, which has not fully withdrawn from Lebanon, begins a broad ground invasion of the south of the country. On March 11, Hezbollah launches a massive barrage of about 200 rockets towards Israel, in an operation that was pre-planned with Iran.
April 7, 2026 | Temporary ceasefire with Iran
The United States and Iran sign a memorandum of understanding brokered by Pakistan, which leads to a temporary two-week ceasefire between the two countries, as well as between Israel and Hezbollah.
June 19, 2026 | As part of direct negotiations taking place between Israel and Lebanon under American mediation, another ceasefire agreement was signed between Israel and Hezbollah. Despite the agreement, the IDF still controls large areas in southern Lebanon and continues operations to destroy Hezbollah infrastructure in the area.
October 7, 2026 | The campaign is not over yet
The return of Ran Gvili in January 2026 completed the recovery of all hostages from Gaza, but it did not bring a complete end to the fighting.
The IDF continues to carry out strikes in Gaza and holds a substantial portion of its territory. Meanwhile, Hamas is not cooperating with the Board of Peace and is trying to maintain its position in Gaza while rebuilding its military capabilities.

SpaceX plans to raise $40B to buy Nvidia chips, FT reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
06:35:14 UTC
15:35:14 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
US aerospace company SpaceX seeks to raise $40 billion in a financing effort led by Apollo Global Management to purchase Nvidia chips.
The company looked to raise about $10 billion in bank loans and $30 billion in investment-grade debt to fund the massive chip order, the Financial Times reported on Wednesday.
Private capital group Apollo expected to lead the deal and help sell the debt to a broad base of investors.
Bond group Pimco participated in talks among a small group of lenders to fund the transaction, which companies plan to close in 2027.
The financing plans underscored the massive sums that tech firms raised to pay for data centers, chips and other infrastructure underpinning artificial intelligence (AI).
Insurance and pension funds gained the opportunity to buy the debt of SpaceX due to its BBB credit rating, which marks the second-lowest investment-grade ranking.
Apollo and Pimco declined to comment on the matter, while SpaceX and Nvidia did not immediately respond to media inquiries.
The deal strengthened ties between SpaceX and Nvidia after SpaceX Chief Executive Officer Elon Musk vowed to double down on the technology of the group for his AI initiatives.
Musk said during the earnings call of SpaceX in August that his company decided to build exclusively on Nvidia because they considered the Vera Rubin architecture as the best architecture.

Agency says specialized care shortage critical as 2,000 waiting for service
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
06:34:00 UTC
15:34:00 KST

Agency says specialized care shortage critical as 2,000 waiting for service
Just over 2,000 people are on the waiting list for specialized care services, with the number remaining at roughly the same level month after month. The Social Insurance Board considers the situation critical.
In April this year, the Supreme Court ruled that if a person needs a place in a specialized care home, the state must provide one and that the state may not budget less money for specialized care than is needed to meet its statutory obligations. Despite this, as of early October, just over 2,000 people are on the waiting list for specialized care services, with the number remaining at roughly the same level month after month.
Lagle Kalberg, head of the specialized care and rehabilitation unit at the Social Insurance Board (SKA), told ERR that the situation in the sector is currently critical.
"We have a very large number of people on the waiting list who need services right now. We have 2,000 people on the waiting list and based on an analysis of their information and feedback, just over 700 have said they are ready to start receiving services immediately if we can offer them a suitable place. In other words, that is one-third of the people currently waiting for services," Kalberg said.
However, SKA cannot help them because, for example, an applicant may want a place close to home but none is available or funding for the service may be lacking.
"So the situation is critical for us," Kalberg said.
In October, 2,049 people are on the waiting list, while there are more than 2,200 service places for which applications have been submitted. Kalberg explained that the difference between the figures is because one person may receive several specialized care services at the same time or be on the waiting list for several such services, as a person is entitled to use up to three services simultaneously.
Compared with the beginning of the year, the waiting list is about 200 people shorter, while the number of service places is roughly unchanged. According to Kalberg, this means more people have been referred to services and more service places have been filled. The change may also be related to adjustments made to working procedures in the spring, which resulted in intensive efforts to call people on the waiting list.
"We contacted them to understand their current situation while they were on the waiting list and, given the vacancies we were able to offer, whether they were ready to start receiving services," the SKA representative said. "The change in our working procedures has resulted in more people moving from the waiting list into services."
Some people choose to leave the waiting list after SKA contacts them and assesses their ability to cope independently, the support available from their family and other services they may be able to receive.
As of early October, 54 service places were vacant. SKA is waiting for people offered those places to respond within 10 days on whether they will accept them.
Tight state finances cannot justify leaving people without services
Under the Supreme Court's ruling this spring, a lack of state funding does not justify leaving a person without assistance if the Social Insurance Board (SKA) has determined that they meet the eligibility requirements for assistance established by law. The state must actively work to ensure that a sufficient number of places are available and, if necessary, cooperate with the private sector and local governments to do so.
During state budget talks, the Ministry of Social Affairs sought an additional €200 million over the next four years to create new specialized care places and raise the salaries of people working in specialized care homes. Secretary General Maarjo Mändmaa, speaking about the plan in early June, also cited the Supreme Court ruling, expressing hope that it would prompt the government to take the ministry's proposal more seriously.
However, the draft state budget submitted to the Riigikogu last week does not provide for such an allocation. The government decided to add up to €37 million to the sector over the next four years and that amount is intended not only for specialized care but for the entire social affairs and health sector.
As the coalition no longer has a majority in the Riigikogu, it needs additional votes to pass the state budget. Media reports have previously speculated that the coalition hopes to secure those votes from the Social Democrats, who, for example, would like to be able to point to additional funding for specialized care as a political achievement. Social Democratic Party (SDE) Chair Lauri Läänemets told ERR last week that his party was not engaging in horse-trading.
The Estonian Chamber of Disabled People has previously advised people left without assistance and their loved ones to seek help through the courts. However, after the draft state budget was unveiled, the chamber's head, Maarja Krais-Leosk, said that although the amount planned for specialized care was not what had been hoped for, the allocation of up to €37 million was still something to welcome.
In mid-September, specialized care service providers held a protest outside the Riigikogu on Toompea to draw attention to the sector's worsening underfunding.
Specialized care services are intended for people diagnosed with mental disorders who, because of their mental health condition, need guidance, counseling, assistance and supervision from a specialized care support worker in their daily lives and whose needs cannot be met through other social welfare support measures.
The aim of specialized care is to develop people's abilities and increase their capacity to live independently.

Has Russia’s fuel crisis given Iranian oil an opening in Central Asia?

Has Russia’s fuel crisis given Iranian oil an opening in Central Asia?
Iran’s oil exports have struggled amid a US blockade. A Russian energy crisis because of Ukrainian attacks could help.
Countries in Central Asia have begun buying oil from Iran as the Russian fuel supplies they have long depended on run dry amid Ukraine’s mounting attacks on Russian energy infrastructure to degrade Moscow’s war effort.
In August, Tajikistan announced it was receiving oil and petroleum products from Iran as Dushanbe faces uncertainty over its fuel supply from Russia. Tehran also agreed to establish a joint refinery in Kyrgyzstan in August, and supply the country with crude oil.
Moscow has been facing fuel shortages due to Ukrainian drone strikes on its refineries as Russia’s war on its neighbour continues to rage.
Can the Russian fuel crisis give Iran a new oil opening in Central Asia?
Here’s what we know:
Which Central Asian countries have been affected by Russia’s fuel crisis?
Ukraine’s offensive against Russian energy infrastructure has caused panic across Central Asian countries like Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan, which are dependent on Moscow for oil and petroleum products.
Tajikistan has traditionally sourced up to 80 percent of its petroleum products from Russia. Kyrgyzstan also relies on petroleum product imports, sourcing more than 90 percent of its petrol from Russia.
“They’ve been hurt the most,” Galiya Ibragimova, a Moldova-based expert on Central Asia with Carnegie Politika, which has its headquarters in Berlin, told Al Jazeera in an interview in August.
Kyrgyzstan is a member of the Eurasian Economic Union, the free trade bloc of five former Soviet nations dominated by Russia and the Kremlin’s political decisions.
Tajikistan is not a member of the group, but it bought discounted Russian fuel as “payment for political loyalty, not because [Russian President Vladimir] Putin is so kind”, Ibragimova added.
Kazakhstan, meanwhile, boasts three giant, Soviet-era oil refineries. Still, fuel prices in the country have increased by 15.6 percent this year, the UlusMedia website reported on July 10.
Uzbekistan, on the other hand, is less dependent on Russian energy, with domestic production capable of reaching 100,000 tonnes of petroleum products per month, satisfying most of the country’s needs. But due to the increase in oil demand from its regional neighbours, Uzbekistan has also been forced to diversify its imports and has begun striking deals with countries like Georgia and Iraq.
Why is there a fuel crisis in Russia?
Russia has been facing a severe fuel deficit as Kyiv’s drone strikes – launched in an effort to degrade Moscow’s ability to maintain its ongoing invasion of Ukraine – have knocked out an estimated quarter to half of its total oil refining capacity.
To tackle the problem, Russia has imposed fuel rationing. Sales are often limited to about 20-30 litres (about 5-8 US gallons) per vehicle, and drivers must pump fuel strictly into vehicle tanks. Filling jerry cans is largely prohibited.
Earlier, the government banned petrol and jet fuel exports. Officials are now weighing a ban on diesel exports, too. Authorities have loosened fuel-quality regulations, temporarily allowing lower-grade fuel for the domestic market.
A state of emergency has also been declared in Russian-occupied Crimea, which Moscow annexed from Ukraine in 2014. A Russian-owned oil firm in India, Nayara Energy, has reportedly sold petroleum to Russia.
While Russian President Putin acknowledges the crisis, he appears reluctant to end the war on Ukraine and insists the situation is under control.
“These attacks on our facilities certainly create problems – that is obvious. We are currently seeing a certain shortage, though I would say it is not critical,” he said earlier this year.
“First and foremost, we have to rapidly and significantly increase production of air defence systems that are most in demand. We must also continue to improve them… Repairs at refineries must be completed more quickly.”
So, how is Iran helping Central Asia?
Amid Russian fuel shortages, Central Asian countries like Tajikistan have begun striking deals with Iran.
In August, Tajikistan’s Energy and Water Resources Ministry told the Asia-Plus news agency that the country is receiving oil and petroleum products from Iran. The ministry has not disclosed the route used to transport the products, but Tajikistan expects to receive 2.55 million tonnes of oil and petroleum products from Iran.
Besides Tajikistan, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian welcomed a proposal from Kyrgyzstan in August to establish a joint refinery in the Central Asian country, according to a report by Iran’s Tasnim news agency,
Under the agreement, Pezeshkian said, “The crude oil needed by the refinery can be supplied by Iran, and the products can be divided between the two sides.”
Will exporting oil to Central Asian countries help Iran?
The United States and Israel’s war on Iran has affected Tehran’s oil revenues. Data released by the government-administered Statistical Center of Iran in September showed that gross domestic product (GDP) shrank by 10.1 percent year-on-year between March 21 and June 20, the first quarter of the Persian calendar.
Tehran’s ability to sell crude has also been dramatically curtailed by the US naval blockade of Iran’s ports, imposed for most of the war, which began in late February.
Iranian crude and condensate loadings collapsed from about two million barrels per day (bpd) in March to roughly 740,000bpd in July and just 220,000-255,000bpd in August, according to estimates from Kpler and Vortexa.
TankerTrackers.com told the Reuters news agency in September that 29 tankers, carrying 36.11 million barrels of crude, were trapped in the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, Vortexa estimated that total Iranian crude afloat had fallen from 135 million barrels at the end of July to 107 million barrels by late August.
Amid these challenges, Iran has been scrambling to find new countries to trade oil with. Russian fuel shortages have opened up new opportunities for Iran in Central Asia, at least in the short term, according to analysts.
How does Iranian oil reach Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan?
Iran does not share a border with either country.
To get to Tajikistan, Iranian “oil and refined products have to cross Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan by rail”, said Frederic Schneider, a nonresident senior fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs.
To get to Kyrgyzstan, Iranian oil would also need to pass through Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.
Is trading oil with Iran logistically sustainable for Central Asia?
It is unlikely, Schneider said.
“This opportunity [for Iran] depends on Ukraine continuing to hit Russian refineries, which seems unlikely, both given the waning of Ukraine’s strike capability and the US government’s demand to stop the attacks as they put too much strain on global oil markets,” he told Al Jazeera.
He noted that US President Donald Trump has pressed his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, repeatedly in September for an “energy truce” with Russia, since diesel prices have become a political problem for Trump ahead of the November midterm elections in the US.
“Those truces have so far collapsed within hours, but the direction is clear. Once the strikes stop, or once Russia repairs its plants, Russian fuel will come back to Central Asia duty-free under Eurasian Economic Union arrangements, and Iran will struggle to compete on price,” he said.
Logistics also favour Russia with respect to importing oil to countries like Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan, he said.
Unlike Iran, Russia shares a border with both.
“Tajikistan’s own request [for oil] would need around 51,000 rail tank cars, and its main refinery at Dangara has never operated commercially at scale. Russia, by contrast, has decades’ worth of logistics infrastructure, pipelines, rail links, and supply contracts into the region,” Schneider said.
Is Central Asia a big enough market to compensate for Iran’s Hormuz losses?
No, according to Schneider.
Tajikistan’s total demand, Schneider said, was about 50,000bpd.
That is a drop in the ocean compared with the 1.7 million bpd Iran exported by sea a year ago. China reported $9.96bn in two-way trade with Iran in 2025, a figure that does not include some $31.2bn in Iranian oil shipments, according to the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission.
“This suggests that Central Asia can be a useful outlet for Iranian diesel and gasoline, but it cannot replace the Chinese market,” Schneider said.
For Tehran, Central Asia’s importance depends on how the US-Israel war on Iran develops, he said, adding that Tehran also needs to stay on good terms with Russia, with which it has a deep strategic partnership.
“Iran cannot afford to be seen as poaching Russian customers too aggressively, so it will present itself as a stopgap supplier, which, again, limits how much it can earn there,” he said.
What other risks does Central Asia face in buying Iranian oil?
Schneider warned that Central Asian nations could be hit with Washington’s secondary sanctions on Iran.
“Legally, US secondary sanctions apply to any foreign company or bank that conducts a significant transaction in Iranian petroleum, wherever it is based, and the Treasury expanded the list of sanctionable conduct in August. A Treasury official has already warned publicly that anyone in this trade ‘incurs that risk themselves’,” he noted.
But Schneider said that, politically, the US sanctioning Central Asian governments is unlikely.
“Central Asia is the arena of a new ‘Great Game’ between Russia, China and the United States, and Washington is courting the region harder than at any point since the 1990s, chiefly for its critical minerals. Kazakhstan alone holds about half of the minerals the US classifies as critical, including uranium and tungsten,” he said.
“Sanctioning a Central Asian government for buying fuel from Iran would push them straight back into closer ties to Russia and China,” he noted.
“What I would expect instead are targeted designations of individual traders, rail and logistics operators and smaller banks, combined with quiet pressure on the region’s correspondent banks. That alone is enough to raise the cost and slow the trade, but will come at the price of these countries redoubling their efforts to decouple economically and financially from the US.”

15:30:13 KST

A Ukrainian uncrewed surface vessel armed with a mounted gun destroyed a Russian one-way attack boat in the Black Sea last month, in what is assessed as the first direct engagement between drone boats from the two sides, according to British Defence Intelligence.
In its daily update on Tuesday, Defence Intelligence said: “On 12 September 2026 Ukraine successfully interdicted a Russian one-way attack uncrewed surface vehicle (USV) in the Black Sea. Ukrainian forces employed a Sargan-3000 USV with a mounted gun to destroy the Russian craft before it could pose a threat to Ukrainian sea lines of communication. It is highly unlikely the Russian USV was armed with any counter-drone capability. This event almost certainly marks the first time a Russian and Ukrainian USV have engaged each other directly.”
The update went on: “Ukraine has innovatively combined weaponry in its USV fleet. In early 2024, Ukraine began to equip some of its Magura USV’s with air to air missiles, which it used to successfully shoot down a Su-30 Russian fighter and a Russian military helicopter in 2025. Ukraine’s latest iteration, displayed on Ukrainian Independence Day in Kyiv on 24 August 2026 is a Magura MV11 designed to intercept Russian uncrewed aerial systems.”
Those qualifiers are not loose language, and carry defined meanings in British intelligence reporting. Under the probability yardstick Defence Intelligence publishes alongside its updates, highly unlikely means a five to twenty per cent chance, while almost certainly, the term applied to this being the first such engagement, means ninety-five per cent or more.
The Magura began as a means of attacking Russian warships at Sevastopol and Novorossiysk, and did so effectively enough to push much of the Black Sea Fleet out of Crimea. It then became a launcher for air-to-air missiles, achieving shootdowns that had no precedent anywhere. It is now being built to intercept drones, which is three roles in under three years.
Russia has meanwhile been fielding one-way attack boats of its own, and the September engagement is where the two developments met. A drone boat that can find and destroy another drone boat is a different proposition from one built to ram a frigate, and it means the Black Sea now has an uncrewed fight going on inside the crewed one.

Marlon Blackwell Architects’ U.S. Pavilion for the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale to Be Reconstructed at Crystal Bridges, Arkansas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

The timber-framed structure designed by Marlon Blackwell Architects for the U.S. Pavilion at the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale will be reconstructed at Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas, in late 2027. Originally installed in the Giardini as part of PORCH: An Architecture of Generosity, the structure will return in a new setting as a freestanding pavilion on the museum's 134-acre campus. Following the close of the Biennale in November 2025, it was dismantled and transported from Venice to Arkansas, where it has remained in storage ahead of its planned reconstruction.
PORCH explored the porch as an architectural space for gathering, exchange, and civic life, considering its continued relevance across different social and cultural contexts in the United States. The exhibition was commissioned by the Fay Jones School of Architecture and Design at the University of Arkansas, DesignConnects, and Crystal Bridges, with Peter MacKeith, Susan Chin, and Rod Bigelow serving as co-commissioners. Alongside the structure, the U.S. Pavilion presented approximately 50 projects selected through an open call, while performances, workshops, readings, and discussions expanded the program beyond the exhibition itself.
The pavilion structure was developed by Marlon Blackwell Architects in collaboration with designers Stephen Burks, Julie Bargmann, and Maura Rockcastle, bringing together architectural, design, and landscape perspectives around the exhibition's central theme. Rather than functioning solely as an architectural object, the porch provided an outdoor setting for the Biennale's public program and was used for gatherings throughout the exhibition. Its reconstruction in Arkansas will allow the structure to continue serving a public function beyond its original presentation in Venice.
At Crystal Bridges, the pavilion will be installed within a 134-acre campus that combines museum buildings with native Ozark forest, streams, ponds, and more than five miles of walking trails. The museum has described its grounds as an integral part of the visitor experience, with architecture and landscape connected through paths, outdoor spaces, and works of art.
The reconstruction comes as Crystal Bridges continues to expand and adapt its campus. Earlier this year, the museum completed a 114,000-square-foot addition designed by Safdie Architects, extending the original 2011 building with new galleries, educational facilities, public gathering spaces, and connections to the surrounding landscape. Coen+Partners led the landscape design, incorporating native planting, limestone, restored stream edges, and new outdoor areas. The planned reconstruction of PORCH will add another freestanding structure to this evolving architectural and landscape setting.
In other recent news, several national pavilions have begun announcing their curators and exhibition proposals for the 2027 Venice Architecture Biennale. Luxembourg will present Excess! On the Overconsumption of Living Space, curated by Céline Zimmer, Bùi Quý Sơn, and Paul-Antoine Lucas of Exutoire, exploring the unequal distribution and overconsumption of living space. Germany will present CONVIVERE — A Repertoire of Living Together, curated by Kawahara Krause Architects, Andres Lepik, and Olga Cobuscean, focusing on shared spaces within housing as sites of everyday coexistence. Türkiye will present Spolia Futures, curated by ba-be commons, which examines spolia, the reuse of architectural elements, as an evolving architectural practice.

Netanyahu faces another fine over election propaganda filmed at military base

Israel’s Central Elections Committee has ordered Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, for a second time, to remove a video from his personal social media accounts and pay legal costs after ruling it amounted to election propaganda.
Israel’s Channel 7 reported on Tuesday that committee chairman Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg ordered Netanyahu to delete footage filmed at Tel Nof Air Base and pay 2,500 shekels (about $821) in costs.
Sohlberg ruled that publishing the video on Netanyahu’s personal accounts violated election law by using public resources, including a military base and an Israeli Air Force aircraft.
Netanyahu posted the footage on September 29, with an Israeli Air Force aircraft visible in the background.
He warned that Israel could face attacks before the election, saying there were “indications that our enemies will try to attack us before the elections”, according to Israeli Channel 15.
The latest decision followed Sohlberg’s ruling on Sunday on five petitions concerning Netanyahu’s use of official speeches and the military for election propaganda on his personal accounts.
The petitions included a video showing Netanyahu during a visit to an Israeli military position in southern Lebanon.
Sohlberg ruled that the edited clip focused on the achievements of the government and prime minister, while parts relating to boosting soldiers’ morale and honouring them had been removed.
“This is, of course, election propaganda,” Sohlberg said. He ordered Netanyahu to remove the posts and pay 29,000 shekels (about $9,000) in costs.
Israel is scheduled to hold a Knesset election on October 27. Parties in Netanyahu’s governing coalition, led by his Likud party, are competing against opposition parties.
Recent polls suggest neither bloc would independently secure the 61 seats needed to form a government. A poll by public broadcaster KAN on Sunday projected 52 seats for opposition parties and 51 for Netanyahu’s coalition.
Netanyahu has led the government since late December 2022. He is standing trial on corruption charges, which he denies, and the International Criminal Court has issued an arrest warrant for him over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.

Estonia hold on for 0-0 Nations League home draw against Iceland
Estonia played out a hard-fought 0-0 draw at home against Iceland in the Nations League on Tuesday, leaving them second in Group C4 after four games.
The same teams opened the cycle on September 26 in Reykjavik, drawing 1-1, with Andri Guðjohnsen (Blackburn Rovers), son of former Chelsea legend Eiður Guðjohnsen, scoring in the 45th minute and defender Maksim Paskotši (KAA Ghent) later equalizing.
Estonia came into the game knowing a win would put them top of the group with two rounds left, and having beaten Luxembourg at the weekend.
Estonia sat second on five points before the match, two behind Iceland, and were without captain Karol Mets (VfL Bochum) through suspension — Paskotši wore the armband in his absence.
Elron put its last train to Keila 25 minutes back in the timetable Tuesday night to accommodate fans, and President Alar Karis, who leaves office on Monday, was present at the match, as was Estonian FA (EJK) President Aivar Pohlak.
On the night, Iceland created two dangerous situations from set pieces early on, with both requiring referee decisions on penalty appeals. The most threatening came in the 12th minute, when a corner struck Levadia midfielder Rasmus Peetson at the near post and Estonian goalkeeper Matvei Igonen (Degerfors) cleared the ball off the goal line.
Peetson has so far emerged as Estonia's most dangerous attacking player in this Nations League window, and he proved it in the first half: early on, Iceland's 'keeper Hákon Valdimarsson (Brentford) dealt with his effort toward the far corner, and in the closing minutes of the half Peetson sent a strong shot into Valdimarsson's body after a good pass from Patrik Kristal.
An hour in, striker Patrik Kristal turned brilliantly on the right and delivered an accurate cross for Estonia into the Icelandic box, but substitute Mattias Käit and Kristal's teammate at FC Thun failed to connect with his head, and the ball fell to forward Robi Saarma (K Pardubice), who was completely unmarked but not ready in time.
Estonia had 13 shots over the match and continued searching for a winner, with manager Jürgen Henn handing a debut to young Levadia midfielder Maksimilian Skvortsov. Iceland were more dangerous in the final quarter-hour, however, but Paskotši, Erko Jonne Tõugjas (Halmstads BK) and Märten Kuusk (Polonia Warsaw) all defended well.
"Very positive result, although we came to win," captain-for-a-night Paskotši told ERR post-match. "Against this team, two draws is quite a good result. Hard fight, lots of running and duels. It maybe wasn't the most beautiful game, but for me as a defender: I really enjoyed it!"
"I knew what group we're actually in. Maybe our previous results haven't been the best, but in this window we showed that these are the games we have to do properly," he said. "I want to really praise all the players. Both those who started and those who came on: they did so much and I hope our fans see that too," he went on.
The UEFA Nations League is a biennial competition in which Europe's national teams are divided into four tiers, with promotion and relegation between them and a path to the European Championship playoffs.
After Tuesday, Iceland lead Group C4 on eight points, Estonia are second with six, while Bulgaria have four points and Luxembourg three.
The next and final fixtures are on November 13 (away to Luxembourg) and November 16 (at home against Bulgaria).

Ukraine's Defense Forces neutralized 161 Russian air targets overnight Wednesday, including 44 missiles, five of which were ballistic, while missile and strike UAV hits were recorded at 18 locations, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
"According to preliminary data, as of 09:00, air defense shot down/suppressed 161 targets: 5 Iskander-M/KN-23/S-400/Zircon/Onyx ballistic missiles; 39 Kh-101, Iskander-K, and Kalibr cruise missiles (information regarding another 6 cruise missiles is being clarified); 117 Russian Shahed-type UAVs (38 of them jet-powered), Gerbera, and other types of drones," the report says.
Overall, on the night of October 7 (from 18:00 on October 6), Russia attacked with: Zircon/Onyx anti-ship missiles from Russia's Rostov region; Iskander-M/S-400/KN-23 ballistic missiles from Russia's Bryansk and Voronezh regions; 48 air-, ground-, and sea-launched Kh-101, Iskander-K, and Kalibr cruise missiles from the Vologda and Kursk regions and the Caspian Sea, respectively; and 130 Shahed-type strike UAVs (46 of them jet-powered), Gerbera, and Parodiya-type decoy drones from the directions of Oryol and Primorsko-Akhtarsk in Russia, and temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in the Autonomous Republic of Crimea.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile troops, electronic warfare (EW) and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine's Defense Forces.
Meanwhile, Russian missile and strike UAV hits were recorded at 18 locations, and the fall of intercepted debris was recorded at 5 locations.
The Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine informed that the main directions of the attack were Kyiv region, Kharkiv region, Poltava region, and Dnipropetrovsk region.

Here are some of the tributes by world leaders for the third anniversary of the 7 October attack (we reported earlier on Andy Burnham’s message here):
German chancellor Friedrich Merz has vowed to fight antisemitism in Germany and continue to advocate for a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine. In his message, Merz said his country was witnessing rising antisemitism “that far too often goes unchallenged” and that his government “will do everything in its power” to combat it. “Germany stands firmly by Israel’s side. Our Israeli friends can count on our commitment to ensuring that such a crime never happens again,” he added.
French president Emmanuel Macron said his country shares the grief of Israel and the bereaved families. “We do not forget the names or the faces: those of Maya, Ohad, Valentin, and so many others,” he said. “Combating antisemitism and terrorism, everywhere and always, working for peace and the security of all: that is France’s commitment.”
Australian prime minister Anthony Albanese said his country stands with the Jewish community both at home and abroad as he reflected on the Bondi beach attack in December that killed 10 people. “For so many, no day since has been easy, but anniversaries fall with their own terrible weight,” he said in a statement. “And for many others, what compounds the pain is the approach of the first anniversary of the antisemitic terror attack at Bondi Beach. These few years have been hard beyond measure.”
European Commission presidentUrsula von der Leyen said the EU “stands with all those whose lives were forever changed by that day”. She added that the bloc “remains ready to help turn today’s fragile ceasefire into a durable peace, based on a two-state solution”.
'The suffering did not begin nor end that day,' says Mamdani on 7 October attack anniversary
New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani has issued a statement marking the 7 October attack, saying “the suffering did not begin nor end that day” as he criticised the Israeli government for continuing attacks in Gaza despite a so-called ceasefire.
Mamdani said the anniversary was a “profoundly painful” day for New Yorkers and condemned the “horrific war crimes” committed by Hamas.
A staunch and vocal supporter of Palestinian rights, the bulk of Mamdani’s statement focused on Israel’s conduct in Gaza, where he denounced the war crimes committed “with impunity” by the Israeli government while he also criticising the US’s “complicity” in shipping arms to the country.
His statement on X said:
This day is profoundly painful for so many New Yorkers. It marks three years since the horrific war crimes of October 7. On that day, Hamas killed more than 1,100 Israelis and abducted 251 others. We grieve alongside our many friends and neighbors who still carry that unthinkable loss.
The suffering did not begin nor end that day. It instead continued through the Israeli government’s devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza, in which it has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians-including more than 21,000 children. Even since the so-called ceasefire, more than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed. That suffering has intensified with every Israeli bomb dropped on ambulances waiting outside hospitals, every drone strike targeting a residential building or journalist, and every shipment of food aid turned away at a border crossing. Many New Yorkers are reckoning with this unbearable grief, and we mourn alongside them – all while knowing that our tax dollars fund these war crimes.
Three years later, we must refuse to accept a world in which occupation and apartheid continue, where war crimes are met with impunity, and our federal government continues its complicity with every arms shipment.
To honor the dead, we must fight for a world in which every person can live with freedom, safety, and dignity.”
Rubio: 'We will never forget this act of barbarism'
US secretary of state Marco Rubio said his country “will never forget this act of barbarism against an ally” in his message to mark the anniversary of the 7 October attack in Israel.
In a post on X, he said:
Three years ago today, Hamas terrorists tortured, mutilated, and murdered 1,200 innocent civilians in Israel.
Among those slain were men, women, and children – including dozens of Americans.
We will never forget this act of barbarism against an ally and recommit ourselves to the defense of civilization.”
British Jewish organisations will gather in central London for a vigil honouring victims of the 7 October attacks in Israel on Wednesday, after a day of tributes from politicians and community leaders.

Meanwhile, the Jewish Leadership Council said 7 October had been “the deadliest day for our people since the Holocaust.”
Commenting on the pro-Palestine march in London, the Board of Deputies of British Jews said it “would not be threatened or intimidated” after the protest reached the organisation’s headquarters in the city.

Protesters arrested at pro-Palestine march in London
In London, police have arrested five people at a student pro-Palestine demonstration on the anniversary of the 7 October attacks.
Despite calls for a ban or for the protest to be moved to a different date, about 100 people marched and chanted “free free Palestine” and “free the people, free the land” in central London, with a group holding a banner reading: “Holocaust survivor descendants against Gaza genocide”, the PA news agency reported.
Students from the University of London Coalition umbrella group demonstrated against what they said was complicity by the UK government, universities and businesses in Israel’s genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

The Board of Deputies of British Jews is expected to hold a vigil in Richmond Terrace, just off Whitehall, later today.
AFP is carrying some words from Naftali Bennett, the Israeli former prime minister who will be competing in Israel’s elections later this month. At the Nova music festival site he told reporters “This was a colossal failure of the state of Israel, which was established to defend Jews in our land.”
The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, had warned yesterday that Hamas could carry out an attack on Israel before the general election on 27 October.
Speaking at a government meeting, he said Israel was prepared to respond to any attack with “overwhelming force”.
“Precisely because Hamas is so weak, it will try to challenge us with the remainder of its forces ahead of the elections to try to influence them,” Netanyahu said, according to Israeli media.
“We are prepared for this.”
He added: “Israel is the strongest country in the Middle East, and our enemies are weaker than ever.”
The cemetery at Nir Oz contains two lines of fresh headstones, marking lives that all ended on 7 October 2023. A shared plot for a family of five – a mother, father and their three young children – has been made into a garden with space left for their still-living grandparents.
Caretaker Shlomo Margalit, who will soon turn 89, points to the graves of three of his oldest friends, founding members of the kibbutz who came to Nir Oz from Haifa with him in the 1950s.
“This is my life project, as well as my home,” Margalit said, explaining why he has come back to a place of such loss. He is waiting for a new house but, for now, staying in the former home of Gadi Moses, 82, who survived 482 days as a hostage.
The graves he tends are a silent testament to the brutality of the attacks and the scale of the state’s failure, which in Nir Oz was staggering, even on a day of terrible failures.
A five-person volunteer defence force held Hamas at bay for at least two hours, Margalit said. When they had all been shot, the kibbutz was taken over and sacked, homes burned, families slaughtered and kidnapped.
Then, before the first Israeli soldier arrived, the Hamas forces, other Palestinian gunmen and civilian looters all left. Nir Oz had been forgotten by the army and ripped apart without the military firing a single shot to defend it.
In total, 47 people were killed and 76 taken to Gaza, including Shiri Bibas, her 10-month-old baby Kfir and four-year-old Ariel, who were killed in Gaza. The dead and hostages represented more than a quarter of the small community.
Revisiting that terrible day, and the trauma that followed, is painful and exhausting for Margalit, but he still accepts interviews for a simple reason. “I want people to know what really happened here,” the 89-year-old said.

Palestinians recall life before war that 'destroyed everything we loved'
In Gaza, Palestinians recalled life before Israel launched a devastating war that transformed the Strip beyond recognition and displaced nearly its entire population.
Hamas’s 7 October attack on southern Israel ignited a war that would kill more than 74,000 Palestinians in Gaza and reduce the territory to rubble. A ceasefire declared last October has brought little relief for Palestinians, who continue to face humanitarian and economic challenges as they struggle to rebuild their lives.
The ceasefire deal has left the Israeli military in control of about two-thirds of Gaza, where it has carried out sporadic strikes and razed large areas to the ground. In its latest assault, the Israeli military carried out airstrikes in Beit Lahia in northern Gaza and in Khan Younis in the south, killing at least two Palestinians and wounding others, the Gaza health ministry said. The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) claimed it had struck a militant target in Beit Lahia, without providing details. It did not immediately comment on the strike in Khan Younis.
Umm Mohammad, a mother of five displaced from Gaza City in the north, lives with her husband and children in a makeshift camp in the central city of Deir Al-Balah. She said they were “one happy family” before the war had ripped them apart.
“The war displaced us. My son left Gaza, the other went to a separate tent, my daughters left with their husbands to other parts of the Strip and we rarely meet,” she told Reuters.
On this day, she said, “we recall how happy, despite all problems, we were before the war broke out, destroying everything we loved”.
Israel held state events on Monday, the national memorial day for the attacks. The date for official remembrance is set according to the lunisolar Hebrew calendar, one of two official calendars of the State of Israel, rather than the Gregorian calendar.
The attack was launched on the Jewish holiday of Simchat Torah. Memorial day was set for two days later, because memorial events can’t be held on the holiday.
Flags were lowered at government buildings, military bases, police stations and the communities attacked by Hamas, and Israel’s leaders gathered at Mount Herzl cemetery in Jerusalem for two events. One remembered security forces killed on 7 October, and the other the civilian victims.
A bereaved father interrupted the speech by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the second event to accuse him of negligence. “You did not protect my son on 7 October, you did not protect 1,200 people murdered in one day, Shame!” Yaakov Godo shouted, before being ushered away.
Many survivors and bereaved families accuse Netanyahu of putting his political survival ahead of the lives of Israeli citizens. Top US and Israeli officials have said the prime minister rejected ceasefire deals that could have halted the war in Gaza and brought hostages home sooner.

Lithuania could restrict transit from Russia if plague threat confirmed – minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
06:23:00 UTC
15:23:00 KST

Lithuania could restrict the transit of Russian citizens through the country if reports of pneumonic plague in Russia are confirmed and the disease poses a threat to Lithuania, Health Minister Linas Kukuraitis said Wednesday.
Kukuraitis told LRT RADIO that any such measures would be coordinated with the European Union, which has established procedures for restricting movement during public health emergencies since the Covid-19 pandemic.
“If we saw even the slightest threat, this issue would be raised by us, and decisions would then be made jointly,” Kukuraitis said.
He said he met Tuesday with the country’s main institutions responsible for managing such an outbreak. Lithuania has established response procedures and sufficient reserves of medication, he said.
Kukuraitis stressed that reports of a pneumonic plague case in Russia have not been independently confirmed.
“It is both a worrying situation, and we would like to reassure the public,” he said, adding that information coming from Russia is being treated cautiously because it is a “warring, hostile country”.
Lithuania, other European countries and the United States are closely monitoring the situation, he said.
Lithuania’s National Public Health Centre said there is currently no increased risk of plague infection for people in Lithuania. It said available information is limited and there is no way to independently confirm that the reported case involved pneumonic plague.
Reports emerged Friday that 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, who worked at a plague research institute in Russia’s Irkutsk region, had died of pneumonic plague. Some reports said special restrictions had subsequently been imposed.
The Russian news outlet Lyudi Baikala, citing unnamed sources close to regional security services, reported that Shipilova may have contracted the disease after a test tube broke. Other media reports linked her death to a possible laboratory incident. Lyudi Baikala also reported that about 200 people who may have had contact with her were under quarantine.
Russian officials, however, have said tests conducted after her death did not detect the disease. US President Donald Trump said Monday that his administration was closely monitoring the situation.
Pneumonic plague is a rare infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. It can spread through respiratory droplets, generally requiring close and prolonged contact with a person showing symptoms. The incubation period is one to four days.
The disease can cause fever, headache, weakness, cough, chest pain and rapidly worsening breathing difficulties. When diagnosed promptly, it can be successfully treated with antibiotics, which are readily available in Europe and Lithuania.

Miran and Miran-Lavi recounted the morning of October 7, his abduction and captivity in Gaza, and her nearly two-year campaign for his return. They also spoke about life since his release and the challenges facing former hostages and their families.

Addressing Miran directly, Herzog added: “Seeing all of you here today, and seeing you here with us, Omri, is an important part of our recovery as a nation.”
First Lady Michal Herzog said the anniversary underscored the need to preserve testimony from those who experienced the attack.
“Today marks three years since October 7. The pain does not ease with time, and we carry it with us every day,” she said. “Gatherings like ‘Salon Otef,’ which bring people together to share their stories and experiences, are incredibly important for Israeli society.”

Taipei 101’s A Joy debuts autumn menu

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Perched on the 86th floor of Taipei 101, Taiwan’s highest and most expensive buffet, A Joy, is redefining luxury dining with a newly unveiled autumn menu created in partnership with celebrity chef Andre Chiang (江振誠).
The seasonal lineup, running through Nov. 30, marks the autumn chapter of the restaurant’s yearlong "Four Seasons Symphony" series. Built around the concept of "0rigin," the menu shifts the buffet narrative from abundance to culinary precision and nostalgic storytelling.
"Diners visiting a high-altitude buffet are no longer looking for endless variety," Chiang said. "It is about the quality and refinement of every single dish."
Chiang has introduced a "limited dining" philosophy, prioritizing small-batch craftsmanship over mass production. He has also created "flavor pathways," encouraging guests to pair distinct culinary components to unlock personalized flavor profiles instead of eating standalone items.
At the center of the autumn lineup is a focus on restorative, soul-warming fare suited for cooler weather. Chiang’s flagship dish is a green Sichuan pepper and peeled chili black-feathered chicken soup, blending 30 years of French culinary technique with memories of his mother’s cooking.
The dish features a slow-simmered hen broth infused with tender chicken thigh, sweet peeled chilis, and green peppercorns that impart a mild numbing warmth believed in traditional food culture to promote circulation.
Presented inside a vessel styled like the ancient medical text “Compendium of Materia Medica,” the menu opens with the word "welcome" — a gesture intended to feel like a comforting home-cooked meal served high above the clouds.
The autumn offerings also highlight what Chiang calls “Taiwanese flavors after seeing the world.” Notable dishes include a elevated take on a Shilin Night Market street snack: crispy kuruma prawn wrapped in Hong Kong-style shrimp roe noodles, encased in a seared Mexican tortilla, and seasoned with Japanese sweet sauce and truffle mayonnaise.
Another creation pairs classic French bouillabaisse with Japanese wheat gluten wafers, wild sea bass, king crab, and kelp-infused sushi rice, bridging Eastern and Western traditions in a single bowl.
