====================================================================================================

Invasive plant spreads across Portugal and lengthens allergy season
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
06:03:55 UTC
15:03:55 KST

Known for its showy plumes and used as an ornamental for decades, pampas grass, also known as Cortaderia selloana, is spreading, threatening biodiversity and raising vegetation management costs. Experts call for urgent action to halt its advance and reduce pollen exposure.
For decades, pampas grass, also known as Cortaderia selloana, was seen mainly as an ornamental plant. Its large feathery plumes made it a familiar sight in gardens and, more recently, in decorative arrangements indoors. But what many still regard as a showy plant is, in Portugal, an invasive alien species that can spread rapidly and has potential consequences for health.
This invasive plant has already been identified in at least 208 municipalities in mainland Portugal, according to a study published in 2025 (source in Portuguese). The real number may, however, be higher, as existing maps depend on records submitted by people on the ground.
The species’ spread is particularly visible along the coast. Areas where there used to be isolated specimens have been turning into zones densely occupied by the species, according to biologist Hélia Marchante, a lecturer at the School of Agriculture of the Polytechnic University of Coimbra and a specialist in invasive plants.
"It is a very, very fast-spreading species", she told Euronews. Unlike other invasive plants that can benefit from specific triggers such as wildfires, the plant also known as cortaderia has an especially effective advantage for spreading: "It only needs the wind."
A plant that has learnt to escape the garden
The history of the invasion helps explain how serious the problem has now become. Native to South America, cortaderia was introduced in different parts of the world as an ornamental plant. For decades, the fact that only female plants were present in gardens is thought to have limited its ability to reproduce.
According to Marchante, that changed at the end of the last century, when hermaphrodite plants were introduced, 'almost certainly by accident', as "pollen donors". Fertilisation of the female plants then allowed the production of large quantities of seed.
"From then on it only needs the wind," the researcher said.
The process repeats itself every year. During flowering, the plants that produce pollen release it into the atmosphere. In female plants, once fertilisation has taken place, each flower can give rise to a seed. The plumes end up acting as a kind of transport system: thousands of tiny seeds can be carried by the wind and colonise new sites.
Spread does not depend solely on natural phenomena, however. People who move the plumes to use them as decoration, as well as vehicles, clothing or equipment, can also inadvertently help to carry seeds to other places.
"It is the movement of the plant itself that has the potential to spread it", warns Marchante, also pointing to cases where plumes are taken indoors.
Pampas grass is no longer just an ornamental feature of the landscape. It is also an invasive species capable of altering the ecosystems where it becomes established. Once the species moves from isolated specimens to large stands, it becomes dense enough to exclude other plants, which can no longer survive in those areas.
The impact extends to fauna as well, since the plant’s sharp leaves and the high density of the stands can make it harder for animals to move through.
There are also less visible effects. According to Marchante, some studies show that the species can also alter nutrient cycles and modify the soil and the microorganisms that live in it.
The problem goes beyond the environment
The environmental dimension of the invasion is only part of the story. Cortaderia also has consequences for human health.
Mário Morais de Almeida, an immunoallergology specialist and president of the World Allergy Organisation, explains that pampas grass belongs to the grass family and therefore releases pollen that can trigger symptoms in sensitised people.
"As this is a grass species, it will indeed release its pollen into the atmosphere, again carried by the wind, and it can cause significant allergic symptoms."
The problem is particularly serious because of the time of year when cortaderia flowers. The grasses most familiar to Portuguese people are prominent in spring and early summer. Cortaderia can extend that exposure into late summer and autumn.
For people with allergic rhinitis or conjunctivitis, exposure can lead to sneezing, itching, runny nose, congestion, red and watery eyes. In those with asthma, exposure can contribute to respiratory symptoms and more severe attacks.
"This grass, which can indeed release very, very large amounts of pollen, manages to do so throughout the summer, and even into autumn," says Morais de Almeida.
However, the doctor stresses that there is currently no specific epidemiological evidence that would allow a given number of allergy cases in Portugal to be attributed to pampas grass. What exists is knowledge about grass allergies, clinical experience and evidence of the allergenic capacity of this species’ pollen.
"At the moment we do not have evidence that is directly linked to pampas grass," he notes, adding that there is nonetheless a perception that allergic complaints are lasting longer. According to the specialist, the combination of climate change, different types of pollen and other agents present in the atmosphere makes the picture more complex.
Because the seeds are carried by the wind, the impact is not necessarily confined to the immediate vicinity of the plant. Marchante explains that the seeds can travel several kilometres, especially in conditions of strong wind, while the pollen can also be transported over long distances.
There is another issue: people can unwittingly help to move the pollen around.
"People pick the plumes because they are very beautiful, they paint them, they take them home," the biologist explains. In addition to contributing to the spread of seeds, that behaviour can bring potentially allergenic material into homes.
Morais de Almeida therefore offers an important piece of advice: do not take the plumes home and avoid handling the plant. On top of its allergenic potential, the leaves themselves are sharp enough to cause injuries.
"The pleasant appearance the plant may have" should not make people forget the risks associated with exposure to it, the doctor warns.
The danger of letting another year pass
For Marchante, one of the main challenges is precisely time. The more a plant grows and produces seed, the greater the likelihood that new individuals will emerge nearby and that the invaded area will expand.
"Each one that is left on its own in a more isolated area is another that will produce thousands of seeds, which will germinate and give rise to new plants next year," she explains, stressing that "if we fail to act now, next year it will be much, much more difficult, much more expensive and much worse to intervene".
The strategy does not necessarily have to focus on trying to eliminate all the large stands that are already established in one go. The biologist argues for the identification and priority removal of isolated specimens and small clusters on the edges of the areas currently occupied. The aim is to prevent these hotspots from acting as new starting points for invasion of fresh territory.
In some of the areas where the species has been established for longer, complete eradication will be much more difficult, if not practically impossible, the specialist believes. The alternative is control and ongoing intervention.
"What I think is that we still have a huge amount of work we can do, because there are so many places with small nuclei of individual plants," she says.
The timing of intervention is equally important. Removing only the plumes after the seeds have already been shed can mean working without preventing the spread that has already occurred.
"To be sure of eliminating this plant, there has to be a window of time before May; it is during that period that it should be pulled out," she explains.
And she has a clear message: "In fact, I say pull it up, pull it up by the roots, pull everything up, always pull it up; that is what we want."
However, during the period when the seeds are being released, any intervention must be carried out in such a way as to avoid the control measures themselves contributing to their dispersal.
Prohibited species still widespread
Cortaderia has been on the Portuguese national list of invasive species (source in Portuguese) since 2019. The legislation bans, among other actions, its possession, planting, sale and introduction into the wild.
In practice, however, it can still be found in private gardens, municipal spaces, industrial areas, roadsides and other locations.
Marchante points to a lack of awareness of the law and a lack of enforcement as some of the obstacles to controlling the species.
There is also a coordination problem. A municipality may remove plants from a garden under its management, only to find specimens in private plots or in infrastructure managed by other bodies.
The invasion also has a socioeconomic dimension, as the presence of large cortaderia plants makes vegetation management more difficult and more expensive, particularly in areas where vegetation has to be cleared for wildfire prevention.
There are already projects such as LIFE COOP Cortaderia (source in Portuguese), which brings together institutions in Portugal, Spain and France to fight this invasive species, and municipalities involved in control measures, but the researcher calls for a coordinated strategy.
The Institute for Nature Conservation and Forests (ICNF) has drawn up a proposal for a National Action Plan for the Control of Cortaderia under Decree-Law No. 92/2019 (source in Portuguese), although its official publication and implementation have been delayed.
The biologist hopes that the forthcoming National Action Plan against invasive alien species will set out priorities, responsibilities and ways of intervening.
To make those measures effective, she argues that the plan should be accompanied by funding mechanisms enabling municipalities, non-governmental organisations, parish councils, road management bodies and even private citizens to cover the costs of removal.
"To remove one of the big cortaderia plants, you often need a mini excavator," she notes, stressing that the size of some specimens makes control operations costly, and not everyone can afford them.
What can you do if you come across cortaderia?
For citizens, the first recommendation is not to plant or move the species. Anyone who has cortaderia in their garden should seek to remove it, ideally with technical support if it is a large specimen.
People who spot specimens in public spaces can also help to build knowledge about the species’ distribution. Hélia Marchante recommends using the iNaturalist (source in Portuguese) platform, where it is possible to photograph a plant and record its location. These data help build maps that can then be used to set priorities for action.
"That is very important when strategies are being drawn up to eliminate it," she stresses.
While the plant has not yet been removed, cutting the plumes before the seeds are released can help to curb dispersal. But that is only a temporary measure. "Removing the plumes does not solve the problem," the biologist stresses. "The aim must always be to remove the whole plant."
For people with respiratory allergies, Morais de Almeida also advises reducing exposure during periods of higher pollen concentration. In certain circumstances, wearing a mask and eye protection may be useful, along with sticking to medication prescribed for diagnosed allergic disease.
"We know that early in the morning and later in the afternoon are the times when pollen levels are highest, so at those times we should avoid airing or ventilating our homes; otherwise we may be contaminating the indoor environment. If we are travelling by car, we should probably keep the windows closed; if we are on a motorbike, we should opt for a full-face helmet and wear goggles," the immunoallergology specialist recommends.
The doctor also draws attention to specific weather conditions. During storms, humidity can contribute to the fragmentation of pollen grains, making them easier to inhale, which can worsen respiratory symptoms in sensitised individuals.

Cambodia subsidizes nearly 500 mln USD to curb rising fuel, power costs: PM
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:03:44 CST
15:03:44 KST

PHNOM PENH, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet said on Wednesday that the government has injected nearly 500 million U.S. dollars in subsidies to cushion the domestic impact of soaring global fuel prices driven by ongoing conflicts in the Middle East.
"To date, we have subsidized almost 500 million dollars to curb rising fuel costs and stabilize electricity prices for our citizens," he said during a ceremony celebrating the 80th anniversary of the University of Health Sciences in Phnom Penh.
The prime minister emphasized that these subsidy programs will continue as long as global fuel markets remain elevated.
He said the financial relief has been delivered through direct subsidies on electricity tariffs alongside targeted tax relief. This includes lowering import duties and taxes on oil and gas, as well as reducing tariffs on electric vehicles (EVs), plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs), electric stoves, and solar-powered devices.
According to the Ministry of Commerce, the retail price of regular gasoline in Cambodia stood at 5,150 riels (about 1.27 dollars) per liter on Wednesday, a 33.7 percent surge compared to pre-conflict levels. Meanwhile, diesel prices reached 5,650 riels per liter, marking a 46.7 percent spike.
Thong Mengdavid, deputy director of the China-ASEAN Studies Center at the Cambodia University of Technology and Science, said that surging energy costs directly inflate local transportation and production expenses.
"This trend drives domestic inflation and erodes consumer purchasing power, particularly impacting food and agricultural products," he told Xinhua.
He added that these government subsidies act as a crucial fiscal cushion, ensuring long-term economic resilience and national growth.
The Southeast Asian nation relies entirely on imported petroleum and diesel, as its offshore oil reserves remain unexploited. ■

Economic Watch: Russian tourism industry eyes attracting more Chinese visitors
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:03:35 CST
15:03:35 KST

MOSCOW, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- During China's week-long National Day holiday this year, Chinese tourists are frequently seen on the streets of Moscow. "Russia is a unique country and a must-visit," said Wang Xinzuo, who visited several Russian cities and described his trip as smooth and enjoyable.
In the first half of 2026, Chinese tourists accounted for over 50 percent of all inbound tourist trips to Russia.
"We are witnessing a substantial rise in travel volumes. In 2025, the number of mutual tourist visits exceeded 3 million. According to our data, 154,200 Chinese tourists visited Russia in the first quarter alone this year, marking a 44 percent increase year on year," Chinese Ambassador to Russia Zhang Hanhui said before the holiday.
Russia is preparing for further growth. In early September, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Chernyshenko said the country aims to accommodate more than 5.5 million Chinese tourists by 2030.
Behind the figures lies an industry adapting to a new generation of Chinese travelers.
MOSCOW: FROM GROUP TO INDEPENDENT TRAVEL
Moscow remains the main gateway for Chinese tourists. According to the Border Service of the Russian Federation, 240,000 Chinese tourists visited Moscow in the first half of 2026, up 7 percent year on year.
But the profile of visitors is changing. Guided group tours are becoming less dominant as younger and more independent Chinese travelers arrive.
More than 80 percent of travelers from China come to Moscow independently, including for business, according to Bulat Nurmukhanov, deputy chairman of the Moscow Tourism Committee.
In response, a China Friendly certification program is expanding in Moscow, covering services such as Chinese-language information, adapted menus and trained staff.
The Cosmos Hotel Group told Xinhua that two of its four- and five-star hotels in Moscow have received the certification, with more properties planned to join the program.
Moscow has also strengthened its promotion in China through Chinese-language tourism services, social media and cooperation with Chinese travel platforms, while highlighting its cultural heritage and modern attractions.
REGIONS SEEK NEW OPPORTUNITIES
Beyond Moscow, Russian regions are increasingly competing for Chinese tourists.
In St. Petersburg, the number of Chinese tourists has risen by nearly 60 percent since 2021, according to Nana Gvichiya, deputy chair of the city's Tourism Development Committee. Chinese visitors are showing a growing interest not only in historical sites but also in local cuisine and creative spaces.
In the Altai region, the number of Chinese tourists increased 1.5 times in 2025 from the previous year, exceeding 6,000 for the first time, said Alexander Baryshnikov, head of the regional Department for Tourism and Resort Development.
Although the region receives fewer Chinese visitors than Moscow and St. Petersburg partly because of a lack of direct flights, local businesses are improving services and developing China-friendly tourism products. Several hotels and resorts have received China Friendly certification, while tour operators have developed specialized routes and promoted them through international exhibitions and Chinese social media.
In Russia's Far East, the Amur region has recorded a 60 percent increase in Chinese tourists since the introduction of the visa-free policy between China and Russia in 2025, Governor Vasily Orlov said. The region plans more than 200 joint events with China in 2026.
A planned cross-border cable car linking Blagoveshchensk and Heihe is also expected to boost tourism. Once completed, the journey between the two countries will take just over two minutes, with an annual capacity of 2.5 million passengers.
ADAPTING SERVICES
The rapid growth has also exposed gaps in Russia's tourism infrastructure. Experts and tourists cite language barriers, difficulties with digital payments and a shortage of qualified staff, particularly outside major tourist destinations.
"Special attention should be paid to the training of professional guides for Chinese groups in Russia," said Anastasia Pavlova, an expert on cultural and tourism cooperation at the Russian State University for the Humanities.
Ilya Umansky, president of the Russian Union of Tourism Industry, stressed the need for closer cooperation between the two sides in the tourism sector.
"Today we find ourselves in a unique state of revival of our mutual tourist exchanges," Umansky said. "I am confident that we have a great future." ■

How Verifactu will affect Spanish SMEs and self-employed after its delay
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
06:03:25 UTC
15:03:25 KST

The Government's delay in bringing the Verifactu e-invoicing system into force gives firms and the self-employed more time, but fuels uncertainty over its rollout.
The Spanish government has postponed until 2027 (source in Spanish), and later to 2028, the entry into force of Verifactu, the electronic invoicing system designed to strengthen tax control over companies and self-employed workers. The move pushes back by one year the original timetable, which had set its implementation for 2026 (source in Spanish).
Under the new calendar, companies subject to Corporation Tax will have to adapt from 2028, while the self-employed and SMEs will have until 1 July of that same year.
The system requires invoices to be issued using certified software that guarantees the authenticity, integrity and traceability of records, as part of the fight against tax fraud.
More time, but also uncertainty
The postponement gives more time to adapt IT programmes and internal processes, reducing the immediate pressure on millions of small businesses.
However, different voices in the sector point out that the delay has also created confusion because of the lack of clarity about technical requirements and the final implementation deadlines.
These doubts are compounded by warnings from organisations representing the self-employed and from the business community itself. The National Federation of Associations of Self-Employed Workers (ATA) had for weeks been calling for an extension (source in Spanish), citing adaptation difficulties and a lack of clear information.
Even so, the union representing technicians at the Ministry of Finance, Gestha (source in Spanish), believes the extension is a "key tool" that could be "useful" for millions of taxpayers.
A structural change still to come
Despite the extension, Verifactu remains a structural change in Spain's tax system that will affect most of the business sector. The rules, promoted by the Tax Agency, form part of measures to digitise the economy and strengthen fiscal transparency, with possible sanctions for non-compliance once they come into force.
According to Eurostat data, only 58% of small and medium-sized enterprises in the EU have reached a basic level of digital services, well below the 90% target set for 2030. The gap is even wider compared with large companies, where the level of digitalisation reaches 91%, highlighting the specific difficulties SMEs face in adapting to technological and regulatory change.
In the case of Spain, the figures show progress but also limits to business digitalisation. According to a survey (source in Spanish) by the National Statistics Institute (INE), 44.3% of companies use cloud computing services and 21.1% use artificial intelligence, while 84.5% have a website.
However, the level of adoption of more advanced technologies remains uneven, especially among small companies.
Moreover, various official indicators place Spanish SMEs in an intermediate position within the EU: around 60% reach a basic level of digitalisation, in line with the European average, but still far from the goals set by Brussels for this decade.

Europe out to support chemicals industry, but at a price
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
06:02:06 UTC
15:02:06 KST

This photo shows an environmental protest held in front of the BASF pesticide factory in Saint-Aubin-lès-Elbeuf, France, Nov. 17, 2025. (AFP Photo)
Europe, spurred on by France, wants to provide support for its crucial chemical industry, which is struggling with high energy costs and global competition.
Yet a slew of stakeholders fear that bolstering the sector will harm the environment, public health and even consumers.
France Chimie, the sector lobby in France, along with its Dutch, Hungarian, Italian and Spanish counterparts, said in a joint press release at the start of the month that the European chemicals industry, which produces fertilisers, plastics, medicine and industrial gases, is facing a "systemic crisis."
The European Commission, the European Union's executive arm, has set up a "Critical Chemicals Alliance" (CCA) with industry groups, and holds its general assembly on Oct. 8 in France's eastern Moselle region.
"Over the past two years we have witnessed the announcement of closures of more than 20 major production sites in the EU, with associated job losses and the erosion of our market position," Siobhan McGarry, an EU spokesperson for industrial policy, told AFP.
"The Alliance is focused on maintaining our chemicals industry during its clean transition," McGarry said.
Between 2008 and 2024, Europe's share of the global chemicals market slid from 23 percent to 13 percent, while China's share rose from 19 percent to 46 percent, according to European industry association Cefic.
Over the same period, the global market expanded in value from $2 trillion to $5 trillion.
The European chemical sector, which is a major consumer of gas and processes petroleum-based products, is also grappling with rising fossil fuel prices owing to the war in the Middle East, which comes on top of 2022's price surge following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
Cefic told AFP that "competitive pressures, declining investment and production challenges in certain value chains" were now so high that it "currently acts as a disincentive to large-scale investments."
The association, which brings together industry giants such as Arkema, TotalEnergies, BASF, Dow, Syensqo and Ineos — as well as public bodies and several NGOs — is hoping to reach a consensus on what chemical production is most critical to Europe's economy.
The group calls for a "level playing field" with China, arguing that it subsidises its companies, enabling them to undercut prices.
Some others fear rising customer prices if the right balance on protectionism is not struck.
France plays a key role in pushing the EU to support the chemical industry.
In mid-September, the French Minister Delegate for Industry, Sebastien Martin, urged Europe to "take concrete and swift measures" to "protect and strengthen our chemical production."
But the push has sparked concern among environmental protection groups.
On Oct. 1, the European Environmental Bureau (EEB) announced it was walking away from the alliance, which it believed would "preserve current chemical production — including hazardous substances, high emitters, and those reliant on fossil fuels — rather than initiating the transformation Europe needs."
The EEB's Tatiana Santos said the alliance comprises "around 300 industrial groups and four or five NGOs. So we know the outcome and we just don't want to be linked to any of these proposals that are so threatening for protecting human health, the environment and climate."
In July, the EEB published a report with another NGO, Corporate Europe Observatory, expressing concern that "several problematic and hazardous substances," specifically PFAS, or "forever chemicals", might be classified as "critical."
Vicky Cann of Corporate Europe Observatory says she fears that the alliance's conclusions will serve "established players in the chemical industry," making the "transition to a cleaner, safer, and more sustainable industry even more difficult."

Israel Police clarified Wednesday that two women detained in Namibia were not Israeli mother and daughter Mali and Liel Yahalomi, as initially reported, but Iranian nationals who were allegedly posing as Israelis.
The clarification came hours after an earlier report said Mali and Liel, who left Israel and drew national attention after disappearing in Europe in August, had been arrested in the southwestern African country on suspicion of possessing forged passports.
According to the police, the women detained in Namibia were Iranian and had falsely identified themselves as Israelis. The source said they presented a forged passport while claiming Israeli identities.
Chabad Rabbi Yosef Rahimi, who is active in Africa, said: “We received a report from the police. I went to see them at breakfast, and it wasn’t them. They are Iranian, a mother and daughter. During questioning, they claimed they were from Israel.”
The development overturns the initial identification of the detainees as Mali and Liel, whose disappearance earlier this year prompted fears in Israel that they may have been caught up in a serious security incident.
The mother and daughter made headlines in August after disappearing while traveling in Europe. About a week later, they were located on a bus in Buenos Aires, Argentina, after concern in Israel had grown over their safety. They were questioned by an Israeli police representative in South America, who ruled out suspicion of criminal wrongdoing, and were allowed to continue on their way.
Authorities later assessed that financial distress may have been behind their disappearance.
Their journey had not begun in Vienna, as first believed, but in the Czech Republic, where mobile phones can be purchased without presenting a passport. Investigators believed the two then traveled to Vienna and recorded videos intended for relatives, but sent them only after they had already moved on to another country, apparently Germany.
A senior police official said at the time that the delayed transmission of the videos appeared intended to create the impression that they were still in Vienna.
From Germany, Mali and Liel traveled to Argentina, where they were eventually located and questioned. Authorities believed at the time that Buenos Aires was not intended to be their final destination and that they planned to continue to another location, which officials did not disclose.
Namibia, where the two Iranian women were detained, is located in southwestern Africa along the Atlantic coast. It borders Angola and Zambia to the north, Botswana to the east and South Africa to the south.
Namibia gained independence in 1990 and has maintained diplomatic relations with Israel since 2013, although the two countries do not maintain embassies in each other’s territory. Relations have also faced tensions in recent years over the war in Gaza.

HMS Queen Elizabeth trials all-day dining at sea

Sailors aboard HMS Queen Elizabeth are being fed around the clock rather than at fixed meal times, under a trial the Royal Navy has chosen the carrier to run on behalf of the whole fleet, according to the service.
The ship, currently training around the United Kingdom, is the testbed for what the Navy calls its Generational Change to Feeding programme. Fleet Caterer Warrant Officer 1 Wes Cain and Chief Petty Officer Chris Roberts of the Flag Officer Sea Training organisation have been working with nutritionists and scientists from the Institute of Naval Medicine on how the service feeds people at sea, and on what today’s sailors actually want to eat.
The carrier has two main galleys, and the forward one has been turned into what the ship’s company have taken to calling the grazing galley, serving food without a break from nine in the morning until six in the evening. Salmon bagels, fruit salad and toasted paninis are among the options, batch cooked to keep up with demand, while the aft galley carries on providing three traditional meals a day.
Warrant Officer 2 Barney Barnes, the ship’s catering warrant officer, said: “Everyone onboard is busy, so giving people a chance to eat at a time that suits them and their working pattern should be a big help to a lot of people.
“For example, we were finding many of our watchkeepers would skip breakfast to prioritise rest after a busy watch. This new way of feeding allows them to still be able to have something to eat, which in turn increases both their morale and operational effectiveness.”
He added: “Our golden rule is that we’re not taking anything away. There will still be meals served at set times; all-day feeding gives our sailors options to eat something else instead.”
Part of the purpose is easing the load on the catering department itself, which numbers 50 and faces a punishing schedule when the carrier has her squadrons embarked and around 1,600 people aboard. Spreading demand across the day rather than concentrating it into three rushes is intended to even out the shifts.
The ship’s logistics officer, Adam Cook, said: “A huge part of why we introduced this was to balance our caterers’ workload against the demands they’re facing.
“Our goal is to make catering easier in the long run. Spreading demand throughout the day will ease some of the pressure on those working regular galley shifts.”

France: government slams Marine Le Pen's alternative budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
05:55:45 UTC
14:55:45 KST

"You're dreaming in colour", "a Potemkin budget, flimsy as cardboard", "purely incantatory, utterly unenforceable": the government torpedoes the counter-budget put forward by National Rally leader Marine Le Pen.
The ministers for the economy and public accounts have launched a blistering attack on the budget proposal put forward by Marine Le Pen, leader of the National Rally (RN) and favourite in the polls for the 2027 presidential election.
"You’re dreaming in colour"
"You’re dreaming in colour," blasts Economy Minister Roland Lescure. "It’s a Potemkin budget, made of cardboard," says Public Accounts Minister David Amiel.
"140 billion in savings by 2032"
Marine Le Pen is putting forward a programme of "€140 billion in savings by 2032", bringing the public deficit down below 3% by 2030 (compared with around 5.4% expected in 2026), and cutting France’s debt to 112% of GDP, from 119% today, all while reducing taxes by €30 billion.
The RN calculates the amount of savings it is promising on the basis of immigration reforms, a cut in France’s contribution to the EU and lower spending by local authorities.
Pensions
Marine Le Pen nonetheless wants to lower the retirement age back to 62, or even 60, compared with 64 at present. According to the RN leader, a return to 60 would be possible thanks to "a major reform of individual and collective capital-funded schemes."
Yes, 'we do dream in colour'
Yes, "we do dream in colour, it is France’s rebirth with Marine Le Pen," claims RN MP Jean-Philippe Tanguy.
The government notes that the RN is building its budget plans on a forecast growth rate of 1.8%. "That is well above what all serious French and international economists are projecting," Roland Lescure fires back.
'Golden rule'
The RN wants to enshrine a constitutional "golden rule" forcing governments to reduce public debt every year.
For Roland Lescure, it is not enough "to write a text into the Constitution for the savings to follow."
The minister points to the €9 billion in savings the RN says it would make by cutting France’s contribution to the EU. "That would need to be approved by our 26 partners," he notes, and "that is far from certain." And even if it were, Roland Lescure says, those hit first would be "French farmers, the main beneficiaries of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), French companies that receive subsidies, and French research laboratories funded by European research programmes."
Moreover, according to Roland Lescure, the €15 billion in savings the RN claims it can make on immigration would come from "measures that are for the most part unconstitutional (…), slapdash measures cobbled together on the hoof."
'Major structural reform' of environmental policy
Marine Le Pen also wants to "end loss-making subsidies for intermittent energy sources" and promises "a major structural reform" of "environmental and energy policy". Her ambition is to reach "carbon neutrality before 2050."
'A Potemkin budget'
For Public Accounts Minister David Amiel, the RN’s proposal is "a Potemkin budget, all cardboard and paint."

Argentine footballer Lionel Messi called leaving international football "the saddest day of my career." He said this on Tuesday, October 6, after his final match for Argentina, which ended in a 3–0 victory over Benin, UNN writes, citing AFP.
Details
Messi, who scored a goal and provided two assists in the victorious match at the Monumental Stadium, took to the field after the win to thank the fans and his teammates, reflecting on his 21-year career with the Argentina national team.
"It was an enormous source of pride for me to wear this shirt for more than 20 years," Messi told the stadium.
"Even in the worst moments that we and I experienced, I never stopped fighting, I never stopped being here," he added.
"Not coming here anymore will be very painful. I swear, I would like to play my whole life, because playing for the Argentina national team is the most wonderful thing that can happen to you," he said.
Messi said that returning to the Monumental, where Argentina played its first match after winning the 2022 World Cup, was bittersweet.
"Now I am here on the saddest day of my career, the day when I have to say goodbye to the national team, say goodbye to all of you. But now I will be on the other side (with the fans), supporting all the boys, everyone who comes along. Always united," he said.
Messi, however, said that despite the sadness, he has no regrets about the time he is leaving the national team, referring to the difficulties of Argentina’s campaign at this year’s World Cup, where the South Americans reached the final but lost to Spain.
Messi said that the emotional roller coaster of that tournament, which included a 2–1 defeat to fierce rivals England in the semifinal, had taken its toll.
"Although I want to be here my whole life, I feel that this is the right moment. The last World Cup was too difficult, everything I had to go through," Messi said.
"We had a dream of fulfilling my dream and the dream of the whole country—to become world champions again. At the last World Cup, we came very close, and the reality is that nothing extraordinary happened, as people say. The match against England affected us greatly physically, and emotionally—very much. We arrived with enough strength, we fought, as always, for this shirt, with all the teammates I had to be with and with whom I could share moments, not only with them but also with those who were around at the time when we managed to win. We came very close," he said.

Estonia's inflation accelerates to 3.5% in September due to fuel costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
05:51:00 UTC
14:51:00 KST

Estonia's inflation accelerates to 3.5% in September due to fuel costs
Estonia's consumer price index (CPI) rose 3.5 percent on year to September, faster than in recent months, driven by higher fuel and housing costs, Statistics Estonia reported.
The price of gasoline went up 33.8 percent during that time, and that of diesel, subject to an excise duty, by 58 percent year on year.
The price of food and non-alcoholic beverages fell by 1.2 percent on year to September, exerting a downward pressure on the overall rise.
Goods were 3.6 percent and services 3.5 percent more expensive than a year earlier.
Statistics Estonia says the on-month CPI figure between August and September this year was for a 0.9 percent rise.
Commenting on the results, Lauri Veski, Consumer Price Statistics Service Manager at Statistics Estonia, said the rate of price increases had been slower for several months but picked up again in September.
"Year on year, the index rise was influenced the most by the higher costs of housing and transport," Veski said. "The index rise was slowed down by the prices of food and non-alcoholic beverages which have fallen year on year."
The rise in fuel prices resulted from the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. Housing costs were primarily influenced by electricity (which went up by 6.1 percent), natural gas through networks (up by 44.5 percent), refuse collection (up 56.6 percent) and wood fuel (10.6 percent).
"Food and non-alcoholic beverages is the commodity group with the biggest weight in the consumer price index. Prices in this group fell by 1.2 percent year on year, which limited the overall index rise," Veski noted.
Compared with August 2026, gasoline prices were up 9.5 percent and diesel 9.3 percent in September. Clothing and footwear rose 5.9 percent month on month but remained 1.5 percent lower than a year earlier. Electricity cost 4 percent more and natural gas through networks 22.2 percent more.
Rental payments fell by 3.2 percent month on month, and childcare services were 30 percent cheaper — mainly due to changes in Tallinn municipal kindergarten fees, with most families in the capital now exempt. Hotel accommodation was 10.1 percent cheaper and international flights 13.8 percent less.
Food products were 0.5 percent costlier in September than in August, driven by vegetables (1.8 percent), fruits and nuts (1.9 percent) and milk, dairy products and eggs (0.4 percent).
More detailed information is available from Statistics Estonia's website here and here.

Türkiye’s growth expected to ease in 2026, says World Bank

05:50:59 UTC
14:50:59 KST

Tighter economic policies and higher prices for imported energy are projected to slow growth in Türkiye to 2.8 percent in 2026 from 3.7 percent in 2025, said the World Bank.
The growth will pick up to 3.8 percent in 2027 and 4.5 percent in 2028, according to the bank’s latest Europe and Central Asia Economic Update.
Restrictive policies have weakened domestic demand and helped contain inflationary pressures, while tight credit, weaker real wage growth, and sharply higher diesel prices have weighed on consumer spending, said the bank.
“Export growth remained volatile amid geopolitical uncertainty, weak EU demand, and stronger competition. However, trade diversion for certain products toward Türkiye, partly reflecting higher logistics costs and disruptions elsewhere, provided some support,”
Economic growth in Europe and Central Asia is expected to slow to 2.2 percent this year as higher energy prices, increased global uncertainty and weaker growth among trading partners weigh on activity, according to the bank. The forecast compares with growth of 2.6 percent in 2025.

On the Kostiantynivka front, 14 Russian attacks were recorded. The Russians conducted assaults near the settlements of Kostiantynivka, Novoselivka, Mykolaipillia and Osykove.
On the Pokrovsk front, Ukrainian defenders stopped 27 Russian attacks. The Russians concentrated their main efforts near the settlements of Serhiivka and Molodetske and also conducted assaults towards Kucheriv Yar, Vilne, Bilytske, Vodianske, Dobropillia and Novohryshyne.
On the Huliaipole front, Ukrainian forces repelled 13 Russian attacks near the settlements of Hirke, Rybne, Vozdvyzhivka, Dolynka, Rivne, Kopani, Yehorivka, Novoselivka and Charivne.
On the Orikhiv front, Ukrainian defenders repelled two Russian attacks near the settlements of Stepnohirsk and Plavni.
On the Sloviansk, Oleksandrivka and Prydniprovske fronts, the Russians did not conduct any active operations.

UBS only European bank in top 10 of AI adoption as JPMorgan Chase leads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
05:45:47 UTC
14:45:47 KST

UBS is now the only European lender among the top 10 banks judged most advanced in adopting artificial intelligence, after HSBC dropped out of the top tier of the Evident AI Index, while JPMorgan Chase widened its lead and North American banks tightened their grip.
Switzerland's UBS stands alone for Europe in the top ten of an annual league table measuring how far major banks have gone in putting AI to work, as North American lenders led by JPMorgan Chase pull further ahead.
The ranking, published on Tuesday by Evident, a firm that tracks AI adoption in financial services, rates 50 large lenders in North America, Europe and Asia-Pacific using only public data.
Banks are deploying the technology to catch fraud, write software, vet loans and help advisers serve clients, and the 50 lenders have made public over 1,100 distinct uses of AI since 2021.
They are scored on AI talent, which carries the most weight, as well as innovation such as research and patents, leadership focus and transparency on responsible use.
UBS climbed one place to sixth this year, while London-headquartered HSBC, eighth in 2025, slipped to 11th.
European banks dominate the next ten places, including British lenders Lloyds Banking Group, unchanged in 15th, NatWest in 17th and Barclays, which rose four places to 19th.
JPMorgan Chase, which ranked in the top two in all four categories, widened its lead over second-placed US lender Capital One. Royal Bank of Canada was third and Australia's CommBank fourth, with six US and two Canadian banks in the top ten.
Evident found that the banks' AI capabilities improved almost three times as fast over the past year as in the three preceding years on average, the quickest progress since it began measuring in 2023.
"This was the year AI in banking went industrial," said Alexandra Mousavizadeh, Evident's co-founder and co-CEO.
Hiring, not firing
Evident also challenged the idea that AI will gut bank workforces, finding that the leaders are still recruiting AI specialists and prioritising growth over job cuts.
That contrasts with London-based Standard Chartered, which said in May it would cut around 7,800 back-office jobs by 2030 as it leans on AI and automation.
Software implementation roles grew 4.3% across the 50 banks over the past year.
US bank Morgan Stanley is reinvesting more than one million developer hours freed up by its DevGen.AI platform rather than trimming IT teams, while UBS's STAAT Insights tool saves its advisers roughly 1,200 hours a week.
"Roles are changing, and some are not being backfilled, but the banks at the top of our Index are growing, and growing headcount," Mousavizadeh stated.
Twelve banks now report a realised or projected return on AI, up from eight, including newcomer Lloyds, which said in January that generative AI delivered around £50 million (€58.8mn) in value in 2025 and should add more than £100 million (€117.6mn) this year.
"With AI budgets at record levels, the banks that can prove their returns will keep the money flowing to the right places," said Daniel Shackleford Capel, managing director of banking at Evident.
Amid growing concern over keeping ever more capable AI under control, 80% of the leading banks have advanced safeguards, such as checks on the data that models use and the answers they give, against 40% of the remaining banks in the index.
In the EU, AI used to assess people's creditworthiness is classed as high-risk under the AI Act, though the rules for such systems were pushed back in July to December 2027.
Evident plans to add a fifth pillar to the index in 2027, measuring the outcomes banks actually achieve from AI.

Nobel Peace Prize haunted by the ‘spectre’ of Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
05:45:00 UTC
14:45:00 KST

Nobel Peace Prize haunted by the ‘spectre’ of Trump
- Donald Trump is unlikely to win the Nobel Peace Prize, but his pressure and criticism will hang over Friday’s Oslo announcement.
- The committee may choose a broad-consensus winner, such as child protection or humanitarian groups, or a choice that could anger Trump.
- Experts say the world faces record conflict, with 65 armed conflicts in 2025, so the prize may matter more than ever.
AI generated
OSLO – US President Donald Trump’s chances of winning the Nobel Peace Prize are seen as minimal, but his “spectre” will cast its shadow over the announcement of the winner in Oslo on Oct 9, experts say.
The Norwegian Nobel Committee knows it will be under close scrutiny: since his return to the White House in January 2025, the billionaire Republican has campaigned intensively for the prize and has not hidden his disappointment at not winning it yet.
The chances of him getting the nod are, however, undermined by his war against Iran, his territorial ambitions – sometimes at the expense of allies, as in Greenland – and his attacks on international cooperation institutions and the media.
Even though he has not been lobbying as openly for the Nobel in recent weeks, Trump remains on everyone’s minds, with strong chances that the committee’s pick will, regardless of who they choose, be interpreted as direct or indirect criticism of the US president.
Trump is “the spectre in the room”, said the head of the Peace Research Institute in Oslo (PRIO), Haakon Gjerlow.
Given the reactions that could emerge from the White House, Gjerlow said the Nobel committee must be asking itself: “Is there any potential for this prize to create harm rather than good in awarding it?”
The Nobel Institute says it is unfazed.
The secretary of the committee, Kristian Berg Harpviken, told AFP news agency: “There’s always a lot of lobbying, and ultimately perhaps also attempts to exert pressure on the committee. So, in one sense, we’re very used to that.
“It’s not something we don’t discuss. Of course we have to discuss it, but it’s not like that influences the discussions in the room and decisions that come out.”
‘Age of predators’
In 2025, the prestigious prize went to Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, a choice generally considered palatable to Trump.
Machado even gave him her Nobel gold medal, judging he deserved it after the capture of President Nicolas Maduro – though she failed to obtain his political backing in exchange.
Those events could prompt the committee to choose in 2026 a laureate who enjoys broad consensus, such as an individual or organisation working to protect children or humanitarian efforts.
That could include the Save the Children charity and Mykola Kuleba, a Ukrainian children’s rights activist campaigning for the return of children illegally taken to Russia from occupied territories – a cause close to the heart of Trump’s wife Melania.
Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms, a vast network of volunteers risking their lives to help people facing the double threat of war and hunger, could also be a potential laureate.
But the committee may also choose a laureate that could rub Trump the wrong way.
That could include the UN special rapporteur for the occupied Palestinian territories Francesca Albanese, Pope Leo XIV, the Committee to Protect Journalists, or international justice bodies such as the International Criminal Court (ICC) and the International Court of Justice.
“We live in an age of predators. We have Trump, Putin, Netanyahu,” said Nobel historian Asle Sveen.
“They don’t want to have an international order. They want to have big powers with spheres of influence. And this court stands in the way,” he said, referring to the ICC.
A total of 287 individuals and organisations have been nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize, though the names on the list are kept secret for 50 years.
But peace remains elusive in many parts of the world: 65 armed conflicts involving at least one state actor were registered in 2025, the highest number since 1946, according to PRIO.
“At an overall level, it is clear that the world is not developing in the right direction,” said Harpviken.
“At the same time... there is no lack of good initiatives. There is no lack of organisations or individuals who do good work,” he said.
“A peace prize may make more sense than ever.” AFP

How three years of Israel’s genocidal war have changed Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
05:41:54 UTC
14:41:54 KST

How three years of Israel’s genocidal war have changed Gaza
War has devastated Gaza’s economy, education, healthcare, infrastructure and public services, transforming how Palestinians live, work, learn and survive.
Gaza City, Gaza Strip – Three years after Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza following the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, the Palestinian enclave has been transformed beyond recognition.
Israel’s sustained aerial and ground assault has devastated vast parts of the Gaza Strip, destroying homes and neighbourhoods and severely damaging its infrastructure and essential services.
The war has shattered the lives of a population of around two million people. Repeated displacement and evacuation orders have uprooted families and communities, while more than 74,245 Palestinians have been killed, according to Gaza’s Ministry of Health.
Although a “ceasefire” was announced in October 2025, it has not brought an end to the suffering. The Ministry of Health says 1,462 Palestinians have been killed since the “ceasefire” took effect, while Israeli attacks and other military activity have continued across the Strip.
Years of war have brought the collapse of education, healthcare and the economy, while access to food, water, shelter and other basic necessities has become a daily struggle.
Surviving daily life
For people in Gaza, the war has changed not only where they live, but how they carry out the most ordinary parts of daily life.
A home, running water, electricity and a mode of transport – the basic infrastructure of everyday life – no longer exist for many Palestinians in Gaza.
In September, according to the UN, 94 percent of Gaza’s population remained in urgent need of shelter and basic household assistance, while 65 percent of households were living in tents or makeshift shelters offering little protection from the elements, having been forced from their homes by Israeli attacks or forced evacuation orders.
Many families also lacked adequate bedding, lighting, kitchen equipment and sanitation facilities, according to the United Nations.
Water has become another daily challenge. Ninety-one percent of assessed households experienced moderate-to-high water insecurity in early August, up from 84 percent in June, according to the UN.
Electricity is similarly unreliable. Gaza has remained without a functioning electricity grid, leaving essential services and households dependent on generators and increasingly scarce fuel, engine oil and spare parts.
Damaged roads and communications networks have also made transport, phone and internet access and access to basic services more difficult.
The result is a daily life reorganised around survival: collecting water, charging a phone, cooking, washing and moving between services all require resources and planning that were once unnecessary.
Economic grief
Gaza’s economy has been devastated by the war, with the destruction of businesses and local industries leaving families with little income and sharply reduced purchasing power.
In September, the UN Conference on Trade and Development estimated that 92 percent of Gaza’s economic establishments had been damaged or destroyed since October 2023, while unemployment had reached 78 percent.
GDP per capita stood at just $212 in 2025, around 17 percent of its 2022 level. Agriculture and industry were each operating at just 6 percent of their 2022 output, while construction had fallen to 1 percent.
The economic collapse has also made basic goods increasingly unaffordable. Restrictions on the movement of goods have deepened the damage to Gaza’s economy, where most goods traded with the outside world have historically passed through Israeli-controlled crossings.
The impact has been felt directly by consumers. In September, prices remained around 200 percent above pre-October 2023 levels, according to the UN.
As jobs and incomes have disappeared, economic activity has increasingly centred on aid, debt and small-scale informal work. Economic researcher Rami al-Zaygh told Al Jazeera that the war had “pushed society back decades”, reviving old professions and creating new types of work using basic tools and whatever resources are available.
Many families in Gaza now rely on cash assistance from humanitarian groups. Physical cash itself has become increasingly scarce, with people using digital payments and e-wallets instead.
Struggle to study
The war has drastically changed education in Gaza. For nearly three years, hundreds of thousands of children had no regular access to in-person schooling as schools were damaged or destroyed, while many of those still standing are used as shelters.
Nearly 98 percent of schools have been damaged or destroyed, according to UNICEF. As of April 2026, around 700,000 children aged 4 to 17 had missed almost three consecutive years of in-person education.
Instead of returning to classrooms, many children have been learning in tents and temporary learning spaces. Around 200,000 children have no access to education.
The disruption has also widened the gap in children’s learning. The Palestinian Ministry of Education has warned of a serious loss of basic skills and a growing academic gap, with nearly three years of interrupted education threatening the long-term educational prospects of an entire generation.
Healthcare decimated
Gaza’s health system has been pushed close to collapse.
All 36 of Gaza’s hospitals have been damaged, and only 19 are currently functioning, according to the World Health Organization. None is operating at full capacity.
The few facilities still operating are struggling with severe shortages of essential medicines, medical equipment, diagnostic supplies and fuel. These shortages have disrupted cancer treatment, dialysis and care for people with chronic diseases.
Access to treatment outside Gaza has also remained limited. Since October 2023, about 12,400 patients have been medically evacuated, but the WHO says tens of thousands more still require specialised care unavailable inside the Strip.
The collapse of the health system, combined with deteriorating living conditions, has also created increasingly dangerous public health conditions.
The WHO warned in September that overcrowding, inadequate shelter, water and sanitation were increasing the risk of disease outbreaks.
It said the health system was not equipped to cope with these growing risks and called for sustained humanitarian access, essential medicines and equipment, rehabilitation of health facilities and expanded medical evacuations.
A shrinking space
Gaza’s geography has been transformed by the war. Israeli military control and access restrictions have divided the territory, pushing Palestinians into an increasingly smaller area while cutting them off from homes, farmland and vital facilities.
The so-called Yellow Line is a military demarcation inside Gaza marking areas of Israeli military deployment and restricted access. Since it was established under the October 2025 “ceasefire”, Israel has moved it deeper into populated areas, forcing families to leave.
In September, Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor said Israeli military control and access restrictions covered around 70 percent of Gaza, leaving more than two million Palestinians concentrated in less than 30 percent of the Strip.
Rafah is one of the clearest examples of this transformation. Located in southern Gaza along the border with Egypt, the city became a refuge for more than one million Palestinians displaced from across the Strip during the war.
In May 2024, Israel’s military operation in Rafah displaced more than 800,000 people, according to the UN. Today, almost all of Rafah, except for the western area, Mawasi Rafah, is under Israeli control, leaving Palestinians displaced from the city unable to return to their homes.
Euro-Med warned on September 29 that the expansion of Israeli-controlled areas was entrenching forced displacement, denying Palestinians access to their homes and land and leaving them without guarantees of return.
Security and governance
Before the war, Hamas had governed Gaza since 2007, running its civilian administration and security services. The war has disrupted that system, leaving Gaza with a severely degraded civilian administration.
In July, Hamas announced that it would hand administrative powers to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), a Palestinian technocratic body established under the post-war plan. But the transition has yet to take place.
The war has also weakened the systems responsible for maintaining public order.
Israeli forces have repeatedly attacked police officers and security posts. The UN Human Rights Office recorded at least 12 attacks on police between January and May 2026, killing 53 people, including 35 police officers. The targeting of public governance institutions had contributed to chaos and undermined civilian protection, the UN said.
The Palestinian Centre for Human Rights has similarly warned that attacks on police and security personnel have weakened Gaza’s civilian protection system, contributing to a security vacuum, kidnappings, attacks on property and looting of humanitarian aid.
For people in Gaza, three years of war have left behind a sense of uncertainty with no clear path forward.

Anatolian masterpieces go on display on world stage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
05:39:15 UTC
14:39:15 KST

The exhibition displays large-scale marble sculptures depicting members of the imperial family, Roman elites and people from different parts of the empire.
Eighteen works from the Burdur Museum collection are being exhibited at the Glyptotek Museum in the Danish capital Copenhagen.
“We are bringing Anatolia’s cultural heritage together with art lovers around the world,” Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy announced in a social media post, noting that the artifacts are part of the exhibition “The Power of Fashion in the Roman Empire.”
The exhibition explores how clothing, jewelry and hairstyles reflected identity, social status and power during the Roman period. Works from Anatolia are displayed alongside pieces selected from major museum collections around the world.
“The exhibition tells how clothing, jewelry and hairstyles reflected identity, social status and power in the Roman period. Our artifacts are displayed alongside works selected from important museums around the world,” Ersoy said.
“We are pleased to bring Anatolia’s rich history to international visitors through this exhibition, which will remain open until March 29, 2027. I thank everyone who contributed to its preparation,” he added.
The exhibition centers on large-scale marble sculptures depicting members of the imperial family, Roman elites and people from different parts of the empire. Archaeological textiles, jewelry and footwear also offer visitors an insight into clothing culture in the Roman world and how people represented themselves within society.
Anatolian heritage meets international collections
The 18 artifacts loaned by the Burdur Museum are displayed alongside works from the Glyptotek’s Roman collections and pieces selected from the British Museum, the National Museum of Denmark and the Thorvaldsens Museum.
The combination provides an opportunity to examine Anatolia’s Roman-period cultural heritage alongside artifacts from different regions and to explore the relationship between clothing, identity and social status in a broader scholarly context.
The exhibition also connects ancient clothing practices with contemporary discussions about fashion, identity and visual representation, highlighting the historical roots of the relationship between fashion and power.
Scholarly publication and events to accompany exhibition
A comprehensive peer-reviewed publication in Danish and English is being prepared as part of the exhibition under the editorship of curator Cecilie Brøns and museum editor Anna Manly. The publication consists of 12 chapters contributed by international scholars and examines clothing and identity in Roman sculpture from different perspectives.
Educational programs, guided tours, lectures, interdisciplinary events and audio guides are also planned during the exhibition, along with collaborations with fashion designers and publishing organizations.
The return of cultural artifacts illegally removed from Türkiye to their places of origin not only helps address past injustices but also creates opportunities for a new period of trust-based cooperation between institutions. The process that developed following the return of a head of Septimius Severus is cited as an example of how restitution can lead to lasting mutual cooperation through scholarly research, exhibitions, artifact loans and cultural exchanges.
Opened on Oct. 1, “The Power of Fashion in the Roman Empire” explores the role of clothing and personal appearance in the formation and expression of social identity in antiquity.
The exhibition uses different groups of artifacts to show how clothing, jewelry, hairstyles and personal adornment served as visual indicators of status and power in the Roman world.
The exhibition at the Glyptotek Museum will be open to visitors until March 29, 2027.

Tourists drawn to Midyat’s 3,000-year-old filigree tradition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
05:38:23 UTC
14:38:23 KST

Tourists admire geographically indicated telkari silver jewelry at a workshop in Midyat, one of Mardin’s most popular cultural tourism hubs.
A nearly 3,000-year-old silver filigree tradition in the southeastern province of Mardin is attracting growing interest from domestic and international tourists, with handcrafted jewelry among the most popular souvenirs sought by visitors.
Known locally as telkari, the art involves shaping silver into extremely thin wires and intricately weaving and soldering them into decorative designs. The craft, closely associated with Midyat district and passed down through generations through a traditional master-apprentice system, was granted geographical indication status in 2021 under the name “Midyat Telkarisi” by the Turkish Patent and Trademark Office.
Local artisans continue to produce rings, necklaces, earrings, bracelets and brooches using traditional techniques, preserving a craft that has become an important part of the district’s cultural identity.
The popularity of the area has also been boosted by Uzak Şehir (Far Away), a hit television series filmed in the district, which has contributed to increased cultural tourism and demand for local handicrafts.
Shopkeeper Elif Kılıç said tourists particularly favor handmade silver pieces as gifts.
Filigree master Mahmut Aykat said the craft has a history of around 3,000 years in Mardin and Midyat and remains distinctive because of its handmade character. “Visitors are very curious about it. They buy it for themselves, their spouses, friends and relatives as gifts. We are proud because it is not found elsewhere in the same way,” he said.
Tourist Merve Şalk said she had long wanted to visit Midyat and was impressed by both its historic architecture and the craftsmanship of its filigree jewelry.
Tour guide Aydeniz Kamer said visitors should experience the craft as part of Midyat’s broader cultural heritage rather than visiting the district solely because of television productions.
“Filigree is one of the most important traditional arts here,” Kamer said, calling for greater recognition of the craft and encouraging visitors to learn about its history while exploring the district.

The ranking asks residents to assess whether brands are socially responsible and contribute to positive change in society. LIAA’s inclusion reflects public trust in the agency’s work and recognition of its contribution to business development, export promotion and investment attraction in Latvia.
This year’s study assessed 368 brands across 40 categories, surveying 1,004 economically active Latvian residents aged 15–74. Alongside businesses, the ranking of the most human brands also includes public sector organisations and media outlets.
“The moments that give me the greatest satisfaction are when an entrepreneur returns from their first trade mission with their first overseas client, or when a technology developed in Latvia attracts the interest of a world-class company. This also changes the entrepreneur’s own belief in how much they can achieve. We want more Latvian businesses to experience this kind of success and grow internationally — so they can expand production here, create greater added value and provide well-paid jobs. It starts with our colleagues’ commitment and willingness to get involved, even when an entrepreneur is still finding their way. That is why I am truly delighted by this recognition. Thank you to our team and to the entrepreneurs who place their trust in us,” says LIAA Director Ieva Jāgere.
LIAA helps businesses prepare for exporting, find partners and reach potential customers at international exhibitions and trade missions. Its network of overseas representatives provides local market knowledge and helps establish business contacts. Turning these opportunities into deals requires close cooperation with entrepreneurs and an understanding of their businesses’ needs.
“Recently, we organised a seminar and a meeting with SAF Tehnika’s partners and customers in France. We involved LIAA’s representative in Paris in the preparations, and the event took place at the Latvian Embassy. The meeting went extremely well — LIAA’s representative helped with organisational matters, while more partners and customers attended than we would have expected had we organised the event ourselves at a hotel. Latvia’s positive image also played an important role,” says Jānis Bergs, Co-President of the Latvian American Chamber of Commerce (LACC).

'The picture of manpower': IDF reports defense accomplishments three years into war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
05:37:33 UTC
14:37:33 KST

The IDF has attacked nearly 100,000 targets since the October 7 massacre, the military showed in a Wednesday report detailing defense accomplishments over the past three years.
Around 65,000 of the targets were in Gaza, 28,000 in Lebanon and Syria, 4,500 were located in Iran, and 80 were in Yemen.
The report also showed the total number of ballistic missiles launched from each country, with 50 having come from Syria, 1,200 from Iran, 20,000 from Lebanon, 10,200 from Gaza, and 90 from Yemen.
A graphic depicting high-ranking officials who had been killed by the IDF was also included in the report.
Among the officials in the image are high-ranking officials from Hezbollah, Hamas, and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
Hezbollah’s former Secretary General Hassan Nasrallah and former head of Hezbollah's Executive Council Hashem Safieddine were among those killed, as well as fourth chairman of Hamas’ political bureau Yahya Sinwar, sixth commander of Hamas’s Izz al-Din al-Qassam Brigades Mohammed Deif, IRGC Aerospace Force Commander Ali Hajizadeh, and IRGC Commander-in-Chief Hossein Salami, among many others.
IDF recounts accomplishments across commands
The report also described lessons learned and accomplishments achieved by different defense divisions during three years of war.
The IDF's Southern Command, for example, established about 40 new outposts, while the Intelligence Division established a unique data division for preserving and extracting intelligence information within the division.
The Air Force learned to formulate dedicated commands and decentralize authorities on the ground in readiness for sudden scenarios.
Central Command saw the establishment of the 96th “Gilead” Division on the eastern border and the Dead Sea Air Command for regional defense.
Home Front Command, on the other hand, worked on developing warning and defense capabilities, including extending defense times and adapting them to the threat and location.
The IDF’s Technology and Logistics Division created an “acceleration” program to rapidly restore weapons and infrastructure to operational capability.
The report also included a section with data on the military's troops, noting that 970 soldiers have been killed since the start of the war and highlighting soldiers' willingness to participate in defense efforts.
More than 70% of wounded soldiers returned to service, according to the report, and reserves increased by about 36%.
Finally, the report listed the nine new divisions that have been established in the military over the last three years, including the Hashomer Brigade, the David Brigades, and Division 38.

Cigarettes in Türkiye release more fine particles than German counterparts: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
05:37:30 UTC
14:37:30 KST

A study comparing identical cigarette brands sold in Türkiye and Germany found that products purchased in Türkiye emitted up to 51 percent more fine particulate matter.
Researchers from Goethe University Frankfurt tested 402 cigarettes, including 11 products bought in Türkiye, four from Germany and a U.S. reference cigarette. The cigarettes were burned in an enclosed 2.88-cubic-meter chamber, measuring both mainstream smoke inhaled by smokers and sidestream smoke released directly into the air.
The study measured PM10, PM2.5 and PM1 particles, with smaller particles more likely to penetrate deeper into the respiratory system.
Among four matching brands, German versions had 3.6 percent to 51 percent lower PM10 emissions and 3.6 percent to 50 percent lower PM2.5 emissions than their Turkish counterparts.
Researchers said differences in tobacco blends, additives, paper or filter design could explain the findings.
The study, published in Tobacco Use Insights on Sept. 8, also noted that PM1, representing the smallest and most dangerous category of particulate matter, accounted for 92.3 percent to 95.3 percent of PM10 across the tested products. Türkiye and Germany regulate tar, nicotine and carbon monoxide emissions but have no specific limits for PM1, PM2.5 or PM10.

The AKP’s parliamentary group established a working group under the coordination of Group Chairman Abdullah Güler to address issues related to fund transactions in capital markets. Based on assessments by a team, a legislative proposal concerning transactions in capital markets was prepared.
Under the temporary bill, assets worth up to 1 million Turkish Liras held by 455,578 investors would be liquidated. The proposal is expected to consist of 10 articles.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of National Defense tracked 14 Chinese military aircraft, seven naval vessels, and one official ship around Taiwan between 6 a.m. on Tuesday and 6 a.m. on Wednesday.
Nine of the 14 People’s Liberation Army aircraft entered the country’s northern, central, and southwestern air defense identification zone, according to the MND.
In response, Taiwan deployed aircraft, naval ships, and coastal-based missile systems to monitor PLA activity.
So far this month, Taiwan has tracked Chinese aircraft 25 times and ships 84 times. Since September 2020, China has increased its use of gray zone tactics by incrementally increasing the number of military aircraft and naval vessels operating around the country.
Gray zone tactics are defined as “an effort or series of efforts beyond steady-state deterrence and assurance that attempts to achieve one’s security objectives without resort to direct and sizable use of force.”

FBI says alleged Chinese spy tracked Taiwanese 'anti-CCP' official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
05:34:47 UTC
14:34:47 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — A Chinese American real estate agent accused of surveilling the son of President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) in the US was also allegedly tasked with obtaining the address of an elected Taiwanese official.
Zhang “Heather” Wanying, 34, was arrested at Los Angeles International Airport on Sunday and charged with acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government, according to an affidavit by FBI Special Agent Kevin Holt. Law enforcement sources told CBS the alleged surveillance target was Lai’s son, Lai Ting-yu (賴廷與).
According to the affidavit, Zhang appeared to film the victim and sent photographs, videos, and vehicle license plate information to a person believed to be a Chinese government official. FBI investigators also found that Zhang maintained contact with at least two people believed to be Chinese government officials.
Zhang lives in Irvine, California, and previously studied at the University of International Relations in Beijing, which Holt said has ties to China’s intelligence apparatus, including the Ministry of State Security. She was classmates with one of the suspected Chinese officials, identified in court documents as “PRC Official 1,” and remained in contact with him after they graduated around 2014.
In a 2022 WeChat exchange, Zhang asked the official what bureau he was in at the ministry, according to the affidavit. Holt said the exchange indicated Zhang appeared to know that he worked for the Chinese government.
On March 3, 2025, Zhang contacted PRC Official 1 about an address, saying she remembered the street number but had forgotten the street name, according to the complaint. She suggested possible street names and asked him to confirm whether one was correct.
The official replied that they had already figured out the matter and that there was no need to trouble her, according to the affidavit. The two then arranged to meet when Zhang returned to Beijing.
Holt concluded that PRC Official 1 likely tasked Zhang during an earlier trip to China with obtaining information about the address. The investigator said Chinese intelligence agencies frequently assign tasks to people while they are in China to reduce the risk of detection by US authorities.
An FBI footnote states that, based on discussions with other investigators, the address Zhang referenced was in Irvine and had previously been associated with “a Taiwanese elected official, with vocal anti-CCP views.”
Holt said that Beijing has engaged in coercive activities intended “to erode Taiwan’s will to fight a war against China.” He said information about the homes, vehicles, and locations of close relatives of senior Taiwanese officials could give China leverage over those officials.
Zhang made her first appearance in Los Angeles federal court Monday, where she confirmed her name and that she understood the charge, according to CBS News. Judge Steve Kim scheduled a detention hearing for Wednesday, and Zhang faces a maximum sentence of 10 years in federal prison if convicted, according to the Justice Department.
