Former German foreign intelligence chief August Hanning arrested on suspicion of espionge, attempted treason
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
04:23:25 UTC
13:23:25 KST

August Hanning is accused of illegally receiving classified information during his time in office and after vacating his post, which were improperly used for his personal consultancy work.
A former head of Germany 's foreign intelligence service was arrested on Tuesday on suspicion that he had passed state secrets to a foreign intelligence service, the federal prosecutor's office said.
August Hanning, who led the Federal Intelligence Service, known by its German acronym BND, from 1998 to 2005, is “strongly suspected of treasonous espionage, spying out state secrets, attempted treason, and espionage,” the federal prosecutor’s office said in a statement.
Hanning, 80, was arrested in Bad Toelz-Wolfratshausen in southern Germany. A former aide, identified as Manfred D, was also arrested on Tuesday in Steinfurt in western Germany and has been charged with aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage.
“In one instance, there is suspicion that Mr. Hanning used classified information to prepare an analysis for an employee of a foreign intelligence service,” Ines Peterson, a spokesperson for the federal prosecutor’s office, told German media outlets.
“In another instance, he is alleged to have passed on information following an extensive exchange — also with an employee of another intelligence service.”
Neither Peterson nor the earlier statement by the prosecutor's office revealed who exactly the two men were suspected of spying for or which foreign intelligence services they provided with classified information. Premises belonging to both men were searched late on Tuesday.
The prosecutor's office said Manfred D. worked as Hanning's chief of staff and later served as chief of staff for several subsequent BND presidents from 2012 until 2026. “In his role, he had access to confidential information,” the prosecutor's office said.
Both suspects are believed to have agreed in 2010 to have Manfred D. continuously transmit valuable intelligence from the BND to Hanning in exchange for payment, the statement said.
“The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D. provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the federal intelligence service for internal purposes, particularly for executive intelligence briefings,” the statement said.
Hanning used the information in private consulting work and Manfred D., who in line with German privacy rules cannot be identified by his full name, provided Hanning with classified information until June 2022, Peterson said.
Hanning came under scrutiny in a separate investigation into the abduction of Hamburg businesswoman Christina Block’s children from her ex-husband in Denmark in January 2024 in a lengthy custody battle. The investigation into that case led to Tuesday's arrests.
The current proceedings stem from evidence found during a search of Hanning’s residence in connection with that case, the federal prosecutor’s office stated.
Hanning and a retired official from the Hamburg State Criminal Police Office are suspected of having accepted a contract from the businesswoman in 2022 to abduct her children while serving as executives of a security firm, the public prosecutor’s office announced in the fall of 2025, according to German news agency dpa.
The Blocks are a prominent Hamburg family best known for their popular national steakhouse chain ‘Block House’. The custody trial has received a lot of attention in the country, with German tabloids offering heavy coverage from the court.
German opposition lawmaker Konstantin von Notz expressed shock about the allegations against Hanning and called for a quick investigation.
“This is a hard-hitting and deeply troubling story,” said von Notz, a member of the Greens party and also the German parliament committee overseeing the intelligence services.
“We expect a swift and thorough investigation into the egregious allegations levelled against former BND chief Hanning,” he said.
Van Notz also called on the German state to bar former top executives and those with top level security clearances from engaging in private consultancy work after vacating office, a matter he classified of national security interest.

South Korea launches homegrown Nuri rocket carrying 15 satellites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
04:19:09 UTC
13:19:09 KST

Faisal Mahmud
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
South Korea launched its homegrown Nuri space rocket Wednesday on its fifth flight, carrying 15 satellites into orbit, including five intended for the country's first domestically launched microsatellite constellation.
The 200-ton rocket blasted off from the Naro Space Center in Goheung, about 400 kilometers (248 miles) southwest of Seoul, at 12.25 pm local time, Yonhap News Agency reported.
The payload comprises five New-space Earth Observation Satellite Constellation for National Safety (NEONSAT) microsatellites and 10 CubeSats.
The five NEONSATs, numbered 2 through 6, were scheduled to be deployed at intervals of 35 to 40 seconds at an altitude of around 575 kilometers (357 miles), followed by the CubeSats.
Each NEONSAT weighs less than 100 kilograms (220 pounds) and carries an electro-optical camera capable of distinguishing objects as small as 1 meter (3.3 feet) in black-and-white imagery.
The satellites are designed to monitor the Korean Peninsula and surrounding areas for national security and disaster response.
Another five NEONSATs are due to be launched on Nuri's sixth flight next year, completing the 10-satellite constellation.
In November 2025, Nuri successfully placed 13 satellites into orbit during its fourth flight, including the CAS500-3 and 12 CubeSats. That mission marked the rocket's first nighttime launch and its first led by private company Hanwha Aerospace.

Coffee prices at some cafes rise by 10pc after RBA card surcharge ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
04:18:08 UTC
13:18:08 KST

Coffee prices at some cafes rise 10pc after Reserve Bank imposes card surcharge ban
In short:
Cafes and restaurants have begun lifting prices in response to the RBA's surcharge ban.
The ban was intended to lower prices, but the price hikes appear to be an unintended consequence.
What's next?
Former RBA official Luci Ellis says the ban is unlikely to have a significant impact on inflation.
A ban on card surcharges has resulted in some cafe owners raising the price of their coffee.
About 17 per cent of cafes are now charging more for a flat white, compared with prices prior to October 1, when the Reserve Bank's ban took effect.
That is according to Small Flat White, an online platform that tracks coffee prices across more than 1,500 cafes.
Typically, the increase was 50 cents, or almost 10 per cent of the coffee's price, which is much higher than the typical 0.5 to 1.5 per cent surcharge consumers used to pay on their credit or debit card transactions.
Not every hospitality business has raised its prices in the immediate aftermath of the ban.
Avtar Singh, owner of a Thai restaurant in Hobart, said he was currently absorbing the cost of the surcharges but eventually would have to raise prices.
"The government needs to understand small businesses are already at a very thin margin," he told the ABC.
"If you squeeze it any further, it'll come to a point where doing business is very, very difficult."
RBA kicks 'own goal'
Most cafes or restaurants have raised prices in some way, either by raising menu prices or increasing weekend or public holiday surcharges, said Wes Lambert, chief executive of the Australian Restaurant and Cafe Association.
"Increasing prices can always affect demand, so that certainly is an unintended consequence that the RBA could not have predicted, because they believed that prices would only go up 0.1 per cent," he said.
Mr Lambert said some businesses had started taking cash-only payments or accepting bank transfers.
"Ultimately, we think that the RBA kicked an own goal in this,"
he added.
"They should have known better that inflation was going to remain pesky and that this ban would come online during a cost of living crisis and potentially should have delayed the ban during this high inflationary and high interest environment."
The RBA has said the previous system was no longer working as intended, with surcharges increasingly difficult for consumers to avoid.
The central bank has also said only about 16 per cent of businesses were surcharging and the ban was designed to reduce card acceptance costs, particularly for small businesses.
Reforms unlikely to affect interest rates
If the surcharge ban results in higher inflation, that effect would likely be temporary and have no effect on interest rates, according to Westpac chief economist Luci Ellis.
"Previously surcharges were imposed to reflect the cost of accepting certain types of payment; that's now been bundled into the price, so some business have increased their prices, but that's a one-off, not inherently inflationary," she said.
"Most of the reports we've seen of prices increasing … more than what the surcharge had been were in hospitality.
"There are plenty of other inflationary forces going round, including the pass-through of high energy costs onto other prices that the Reserve Bank's going to be much more focused on."
AMP chief economist Shane Oliver agreed.
"The overall macroeconomic impact from higher prices flowing from the ban on surcharges may not be that significant," he said.
Mr Oliver said many large businesses were already not charging surcharges.
"It's really just an issue for small businesses, but there still may be some upwards boost to inflation, albeit minor," he said.
"In theory, the RBA may just look through it as it's a one-off impact, but it may be hard to disentangle a general rise in prices from the impact of the surcharge versus other factors."
The Reserve Bank declined to comment.

====================================================================================================

Putin Reaches 74 as the CIS Hits 35 – or What Little Is Left of It
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
04:14:47 UTC
13:14:47 KST

As Vladimir Putin marks his 74th birthday on Oct. 7, Moscow is preparing for another gathering of the Commonwealth of Independent States – a bloc once meant to preserve Russia’s political gravity across the former Soviet Union, but which now offers a much clearer measure of how far that influence has receded.
The CIS Council of Heads of State is due to meet in Awaza, Turkmenistan, on Oct. 9, two days after a meeting of the bloc’s foreign ministers. The summit comes as the organization marks its 35th anniversary.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
From 12 states to a shrinking post-Soviet club
The CIS was created on Dec. 8, 1991, by Russia, Ukraine and Belarus to manage the Soviet collapse while preserving ties among the former republics. It eventually encompassed 12 former Soviet states after Georgia joined in 1993.
But that structure has steadily hollowed out.
Georgia withdrew from the CIS in 2009, following Russia’s 2008 war against the country.
Ukraine was one of the organization’s founders, but after Russia’s aggression began in 2014, Kyiv progressively dismantled its participation.
Moldova became the latest state to make the break. Its parliament completed the process of leaving the CIS in April 2026, formally ending participation in the Moscow-led organization after years of gradual disengagement.
What remains is a far smaller political space centered on Russia, Belarus and the Central Asian republics, alongside Armenia and Azerbaijan. And even within that remaining circle, membership no longer means automatic alignment with Moscow.
Russian Shadow Fleet Tanker Burns off Sochi After Black Sea Attack
Armenia provides perhaps the clearest example. The country remains formally tied to several Russia-led structures but has frozen its participation in the Collective Security Treaty Organization and increasingly developed relations with the EU and the US.
Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan may well congratulate Putin on his 74th birthday, but Putin notably did not congratulate Pashinyan on his victory in Armenia’s June parliamentary election.
Pashinyan later joked about the omission after speaking with Putin by phone. “He didn’t want to, so he didn’t congratulate me.” But then the question arises: Who was he speaking to?
Central Asia presents a different challenge to Putin.
Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and other states have not broken with Russia. Instead, they have increasingly pursued multi-vector foreign policies, expanding relations with China, the EU, Turkey and the US while maintaining pragmatic ties with Moscow.
For Moscow, that is another sign of how much the old model has changed. Membership in a Russia-centered institution no longer guarantees political loyalty to the Kremlin.
That is why the symbolism of the Awaza summit may matter almost as much as its final communique, allowing the Kremlin to present the CIS as evidence that Russia still retains regional influence despite its confrontation with Ukraine and the West.
The smaller Russia’s circle becomes, the more politically useful the remaining circle is.
When the CIS was created 35 years ago, it encompassed nearly the entire former Soviet space.
Today, Georgia is gone. Ukraine is gone. Moldova has left. Armenia has distanced itself from Moscow’s security architecture. Central Asian states increasingly diversify their alliances.
Thirty-five years later, the remaining capitals of the post-Soviet space are marking a different milestone. As Vladimir Putin prepares to toast the longevity of the CIS, many of Russia’s neighbors are also celebrating 35 years of their own independence – and that means independence from Moscow.
Ukraine changed the geopolitical calculus. By surviving Russia’s full-scale invasion and denying Moscow the quick victory it expected, Kyiv shattered the myth of Russian military invincibility.
As the wartime joke goes, Russia entered the war boasting of having the “second strongest army in the world” – only to end up fighting to avoid becoming the second strongest army in Russia itself.

Sánchez announces 21 urgent housing measures after nationwide protests ahead of snap election

Sánchez has come under fire domestically after an 87-year-old woman was evicted from her residence in Madrid, sparking national controversy. Pressure have piled on Sanchez’s administration to step down as protesters accused the government of not doing enough to tackle a rampant housing crisis.
Spain’s government approved urgent measures to tackle the housing crisis on Tuesday after violence erupted in Barcelona and tens of thousands took to the streets demanding a quick resolution.
The angry protests followed nationwide demonstrations over the weekend. All were triggered by the eviction of 87-year-old María del Carmen Abascal from her Madrid home last month.
The approved steps were similar to those Parliament rejected last week.
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's coalition government lacked a majority and suffered a bruising legislative defeat when right-wing opposition parties voted down emergency decrees to address the housing crisis. He has called an early election for 29 November in response to the pressure.
The 21 approved measures include facilitating renting or buying a new home, extending eviction protections for vulnerable residents, regulating room rentals, imposing a new tax on seasonal rentals, prohibiting speculative real estate purchases, and granting tax breaks to property owners and tenants who pay on time.
“We will not allow any more evictions like the one Maricarmen suffered or like those that have occurred since the decrees were repealed,” Sánchez told reporters at the Presidential Palace, referring to Abascal by her nickname.
The government will also set up a €10 billion fund to provide loans of up to €50,000 to buy a first home, as well as construction subsidies, added the Spanish premier.
The steps will need to be ratified by an interim legislature instead of the Parliament, which was dissolved after a call for a snap election. It consists of 69 members rather than the 350 that sit in the regular Parliament. Sánchez's coalition will need just 35 votes to pass the measures.
The prime minister still asked for opponents' votes, saying: “We are not talking about an ideological issue, but about common sense.”
“Many Spaniards are waiting for solutions, not just those gathering in town squares, nor the thousands of protesters in the streets. I’m referring to millions of citizens who are waiting for their representatives to show the courage to stand up to the powerful, rather than submit to them,” he said.
Protests turn violent in Barcelona
In Barcelona, Spain’s second-largest city, a severe weather alert over the weekend had forced organisers to reschedule the protest for Monday.
What began as a massive peaceful march turned violent when groups of hundreds of hardcore activists clashed with police, throwing stones and setting fire to trash containers.
Alejandro Quiroga, professor of political science at Madrid’s Complutense University argued that having decrees approved by the interim legislature was constitutional but also a necessary political move by Sánchez.
“I don’t think Sánchez had an alternative,” said Quiroga. “If you are calling early elections so you can keep the public’s focus on housing, you can’t just sit back and do nothing about it. That wouldn’t have been smart."
Rising costs and a housing shortage are pricing many Spaniards out of the housing market, despite strong economic growth in Europe’s fourth-largest economy.
The protesters have been demanding stronger tenant protections, measures to combat fraud, and a ban on evictions when alternative housing is unavailable.

NASA’s preliminary Artemis II lunar science and data release, artificial intelligence for Mars missions and a new agreement between the International Astronautical Federation (IAF) and Japan will be among the highlights Wednesday as the 77th International Astronautical Congress enters its third day in Antalya.
NASA is set to release the first comprehensive collection of preliminary lunar science findings from Artemis II including data, images, audio and related resources during an afternoon session.
Earlier in the day, NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson and Maj. Gen. Roberto Melgar Sheen, director of Peru’s space agency, will brief reporters following the fifth annual Artemis Accords Principals’ Meeting. The US and Peru are co-hosting the meeting, which will focus on recent developments and commitments to safe, transparent and sustainable space exploration.
AI will also feature prominently, with NASA researcher Steve Chien scheduled to discuss the use of trusted artificial intelligence on Mars.
The program will also turn to Europe’s plans for future exploration, while a session will examine the next generation of orbital infrastructure and how the space sector is evolving beyond the International Space Station era.
Türkiye’s first lunar mission will take center stage in the afternoon, with TUBITAK UZAY presenting plans for the world’s first Lunar Water Lifecycle Observatory. The mission is planned to launch in early 2027 and aims to study processes related to water on the Moon.
Space governance will return to the agenda later in the day, with a session on Hong Kong’s role in the evolving space sector examining governance, research, talent development and commercialization, as well as the city’s potential contribution to the growing space economy.
Later, the IAF and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) are due to sign an agreement formally announcing Japan as the host of the 2028 Global Space Exploration Conference scheduled for May 16-18, 2028.
Other Wednesday sessions will explore nuclear propulsion for future space missions, planetary defense through a space-crisis simulation and the role of satellite resources in disaster response.
The five-day IAC, described as the world’s largest annual gathering dedicated to space, is bringing together space agency chiefs, astronauts, scientists, researchers and industry leaders from more than 100 countries in Antalya. The event is organized by the IAF and hosted by the Turkish Space Agency, with SAHA Istanbul as co-host.

Israel remembers the third anniversary of the October 7 onslaught by Hamas | LIVE BLOG
Three years ago, the terrorist group Hamas together with other terror groups in Gaza invaded Israel's borders with roughly 6,000 men, killing 1,200 Israelis and foreign nationals then held 251 hostage
On the morning of October 7, 2023, in what became the deadliest attack against Jewish people since the Holocaust, about 6,000 Hamas terrorists and members of other groups invaded Israel from Gaza. They brutally attacked the Nova music festival, numerous IDF bases and posts, and dozens of Israeli civilian communities, which included multiple Kibbutzim like Be’eri, Kfar Aza, and Nir Oz, near the Gaza border, burning them down. The invading terrorists massacred at least 1,200 people, mostly civilians, who were shot, mutilated, burned, tortured, raped, and decapitated or dismembered, among them babies and children, the elderly, the disabled, men and women. The terrorists further kidnapped 251 people, including internationals and non-Jewish people. Among those kidnapped were the Bibas Shiri Bibas and her two baby children, Ariel and Kfir, who were strangled to death after being taken hostage.
Following a detailed report by Israel's Health Ministry, it was discovered that under Hamas captivity, Israeli hostages detailed sexual violence and torture at the hands of the terrorist group. The treatment by captors included severe beatings, branding, sexual violence, food and water deprivation, hair-pulling, humiliation, and isolation. According to the report, half of those who returned were starved, according to the medical data. Two of the children who returned reported being tied together, and two others had signs of branding that witnesses who returned said were intentionally inflicted. Upon their retrieval, some also displayed signs of overfeeding, evidence that the terrorists attempted to improve the hostages' appearance and weight before being shown to the public. There will be numerous ceremonies and remembrances throughout Israel today; its leaders warn to be on heightened alert against possible terror attacks.

Yemen civil war: what sparked latest escalation and who is involved?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
04:00:34 UTC
13:00:34 KST

Armed forces of the UN-recognised Yemeni government in clashes with Houthis near the Bab al-Mandab strait. Photograph: Yemen Giants Brigades Media Centre/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Armed forces of the UN-recognised Yemeni government in clashes with Houthis near the Bab al-Mandab strait. Photograph: Yemen Giants Brigades Media Centre/AFP/Getty Images Explainer Yemen civil war: what sparked latest escalation and who is involved? Conflict between UN-recognised government and Iran-backed Houthis has impacts far beyond country’s borders Yemen has been plunged into a civil war that has extended to one of the world’s most vital maritime choke points and to Saudi Arabian oil sites. What was the spark? The semi-dormant conflict over Yemen’s future reawakened in the summer, when Saudi Arabia bombed the runway of the airport in the Houthi-controlled capital, Sana’a, in an attempt to prevent an Iranian plane carrying Yemenis who had attended the funeral of Iran’s supreme leader from landing. Saudi Arabia said a charter plane could land, but not an Iranian-owned one. The plane eventually flew to the port of Hodeidah on the Red Sea coast. The Houthis described the bombing as part of a Saudi siege of Houthi-controlled Yemen, and vowed “a siege for a siege”. The Houthis announced a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia and sent missiles towards the country’s oil facilities. The Saudi-Houthi ceasefire in place since 2022 was over. After months of failing to help their ally Iran in its war with the US, the Houthis had opened a new front. What did the Houthis do next? The Houthis have sporadically used their strategic position on the coast of the Red Sea to disrupt commercial traffic, mainly linked to Israel. But its leadership decided in mid-September to escalate and to try to tighten its grip on the waterways by pushing south down the coast to the narrowest part of the waterway, the Bab al-Mandab strait. It succeeded within days. By 16 September, they had captured the coastal town of Mocha and small islands in the strait, as well as an airport. The battle then moved into the al-Waz’yah district and the high mountain chains overlooking the strait and towards Taiz governorate, including Taiz itself, Yemen’s third city and the home town of the president of the UN-recognised government, Rashad al-Alimi. A map of Yemen Why did the Houthi advance succeed? Some have blamed betrayal by Tareq Saleh, the nephew of Yemen’s former president and leader of the National Resistance Forces in the region, but others say the forces of the UN-recognised government are divided, suffer from poor command and control networks, and lack the military intelligence the Houthis possess. The Houthis also had Iranian support; by saying they would block Saudi oil from the port of Yanbu, they were aligning themselves with the Iranian war effort. But the Houthis are not pure proxies of Tehran. Their hostility to the Saudi presence in Yemen is self-standing and has religious as well as political roots. How did the Saudis respond to the shock of the Houthi advance? It took three weeks, but over the weekend Alimi announced a broad counteroffensive called Operation Yemen Dawn, designed to end the “Houthi coup”. It saw 100 Saudi jets fly in support of Yemen ground forces driving towards Bab al-Mandab. Fighting is happening across at least three fronts, including in the mountains west of Taiz, in Marib and in Sana’a. The Houthis have sent missiles towards at least five Saudi cities. The scale of the Houthi reverse has probably been exaggerated. What is the relationship between the legitimate UN-recognised government and Riyadh? The two countries share a 1,200km-long contested border, secured only after the 1934 Saudi-Yemen war. Since the British departure in 1967, Yemen has come to rely heavily on Saudi Arabia to remain an economically viable state. There are officially 2 million Yemenis working as migrants in Saudi Arabia. Many send money home and are just now being given legal status. Riyadh regularly provides grants to the Yemeni government to prevent its collapse (up to $12.6bn in the last 14 years). This heavily shapes its choice of leaders. Indeed so much of Yemen’s leadership resides in Riyadh’s hotels, instead of Aden, that critics call the administration the hotel legitimacy. Are the anti-Houthi forces inside Yemen aligned? No. Yemen is a maze of tribes, governorates and religious beliefs, which is reflected in its politics and militia armies. A dispute over which force can take credit for leading the counteroffensive also reflects political rivalries, but the southern forces are prominent, even though they are fighting to dislodge the Houthis from land that would not form part of a separate southern state. The separatist political wing, the Southern Transitional Council, will test its latent support with a popular mobilisation on 23 October and this may determine whether its leader, Aidarous al-Zubeidi, can risk returning from exile. He has been charged by the legitimate government with high treason for trying to set up a secessionist state in January. Fearing arrest by the Saudis, he fled to the UAE. His aides fear his one-time military ally Abu Zara has aligned himself with Riyadh. What is the role of the United Arab Emirates? The UAE joined the 2015 Gulf coalition to dislodge the Houthis from Sana’a but, as Saudi methods became ever more unpopular, the UAE distanced itself. It had its own anti-Muslim Brotherhood agenda and regarded the Islah party – strong in the Yemeni government – as an offshoot of the Brotherhood. It slowly aligned itself with the southern separatists, largely as a way of gaining leverage inside Yemen, just as Saudi Arabia ironically did during the 1994 Yemen civil war. They trained the STC and National Resistance Forces. The UAE left Yemen in January 2026. It remains wary of Saudi intentions. Why is the US so reluctant to intervene? It has its hands full and its munitions stocks are empty due to the war in Iran. Ahead of the midterms, Donald Trump does not want to launch another forever war. After bombing the Houthis for 50 days in spring 2025, he struck a bilateral ceasefire with the Houthis – a deal that excluded Israel. He has twice rejected Saudi pleas that the fate of the strait is a matter for the world. Is anyone else involved? Yes. European countries, including the UK, are providing some air refuelling for Saudi jets. More importantly, rumours swirl around the new Mecca joint defence agreement, signed on 7 August 2026, by Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan. Its purpose is clear: filling the Gulf security vacuum exposed by the US-Israeli war on Iran, but its relevance to Yemen is sketchy. There are reports Pakistan is sending weaponry to Aden. Who will win? Many doubt Saudi Arabia has the staying power to reach Sana’a. Saudi energy infrastructure is vulnerable. The attack on the Saudi east-west pipeline on 11 September from Iraqi territory showed how a broader regional confrontation could open multiple fronts for Riyadh. Over nearly two decades the Houthis have shown themselves to be the masters of ground combat. But Yemen is now part of an international conflict and so many assumptions are up for review. Zack Polanski had the chance to show real leadership. He blew it | Rafael Behr
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
04:00:34 UTC
13:00:34 KST

When Donald Trump calls someone a socialist he is not using the word in the same way that, say, Zohran Mamdani does. The mayor of New York espouses democratic socialism as a mission of equitable distribution of wealth and opportunity. The US president says socialism only pretends to be democratic “because it sounds so nice”; that “it’s really communism you’re talking about” and that people such as Mamdani pose “the biggest threat to our nation … since its founding”.
People who despise an idea, seeing it as the manifestation of everything wicked, cannot be expected to define it accurately. As with the radical right and socialism, so it is with the left and Zionism.
There are interwoven historical, biblical and intellectual strands to the belief that Jews have an ancestral homeland on the eastern border of the Mediterranean. It is a belief that has evolved across centuries. It was expressed as liturgical yearning before being crystallised in the modern era as a political ambition to be safe from persecution, given urgency by mass slaughter before achieving realisation in 1948 with the foundation of the state now called Israel. Since then it has been refracted through different lenses of war and contemporary Israeli politics.
That process defies capture by a single word. Zionism can be left and right; moderate and extreme. It contains multitudes. Unless you want to join the Green party of England and Wales, in which case, there is only one permitted definition. Last weekend, the party voted for a motion that declares Zionism “fundamentally incompatible with anti-racist principles, equality and justice” because it is based on “European settler-colonial systems of domination and oppression”. The Greens are now an “anti-Zionist” party to their constitutional core.
Any objection on the basis that such a policy vilifies Jews who recognise other definitions of Zionism is dealt with in a pre-emptive clause. The only target is Zionism “as defined” in the motion and not the “religious or ethnic background of those who may identify as Zionists”.
By this Orwellian formula, Jews who call themselves Zionists are still tolerable to the Greens, but only if their personal understanding of Zionism is something the party considers to be the wrong one. If they want to be loyal members, they should adopt the doctrinally correct definition. But then they would have to stop being Zionists. Jews are welcome as long as they repress undesirable features of their cultural identity and religious practice to satisfy the party line.
Naturally, the drafters of the motion do not think this is antisemitism. Here is another word whose meaning is defined not with reference to the experience of Jews but to the grievance of those who don’t like to be accused of targeting them. In the radical-left lexicon, antisemitism is addressed most commonly as the charge that cannot fairly be levelled against an “anti-Zionist” – the tool that Zionists use to deflect criticism of their nefarious ways.
In practice, the Greens have made themselves hostile to the vast majority of British Jews, given the density of kinship connections and emotional sympathies, past or present, that most have to the idea of Israel as a place of sanctuary.
Many hate the government of Benjamin Netanyahu, are repulsed by the racist pronouncements of his far-right ministers, horrified by the atrocious conduct of the war in Gaza and prepared to condemn it without equivocation. They despair at the ultra-nationalist trend in Israeli politics but hold that feeling alongside a belief that the country itself should be allowed to exist.
The Greens disagree. They reject a two-state solution in the Middle East on the basis that Israel – not just occupied Palestinian territories, but the whole country – is illegitimate in its conception. It is an aberration whose erasure from the map is a non-negotiable demand in the global struggle against racism.
That position is more extreme than the one held by the Palestinian Authority. It has brought censure from the European Green group, to which the Green party of England and Wales is affiliated. It has issued a statement observing that fewer than 1% of members voted for the anti-Zionism motion and that Green MPs and other senior figures in the party opposed it. In light of that contradiction, they seek “clarity from the leadership”.
They won’t get it from Zack Polanski. If the Green leader had wanted to make his position clear he could have stayed in Brighton for the debate, spoken his mind and cast his vote. But he slipped away to campaign ahead of this week’s byelection in Holborn and St Pancras, the north London seat vacated by Keir Starmer.
Polanski is Jewish. His stated attitude to Zionism is convoluted. He recognises that it means different things to different people. He endorsed a homeopathic “safeguarding” amendment to reassure Jewish Greens that attendance at synagogues, most of which hold to some idea of Zionism, would not lead to sanction by the party. The amendment was rejected.
Polanski’s influence over the process was limited by the Green party’s rulebook, which gives the membership control over policy. It is unclear whether he could have swayed opinion by deploying the charisma that won him the leadership last year and, by viral contagion on social media, massively boosted party membership. He didn’t appear to try. Maybe he doesn’t know what he believes. Perhaps he feels more like a hostage of the movement that carried him to the top than its leader. Probably both.
That is the suspicion of some Green veterans. They feel their party has been captured by a well-organised, itinerant caucus of militant left activists who have been looking for a new host since Jeremy Corbyn and his acolytes lost control of Labour. Obsession with Israel, crowding out the party’s environmental message, is a tell.
There is an ideological chain of association in the view that climate justice can only be realised by the defeat of oppressive capitalist systems of which Zionism is the ne plus ultra. That approach can be effective for animating the passionate ideals of a young crowd that sees the horrors of Gaza as the defining moral cause of their generation. But it also alienates a wider audience of people who want a Green party that campaigns effectively on the climate and who don’t see why the road to a low-carbon future has to be paved with rows about antisemitism of the kind that poisoned Labour under Corbyn.
Polanski is not going to resolve that tension. He is a talented communicator as long as his audience is predisposed to like the message. His authority is solar-powered, activated only when the light of an enthusiastic crowd shines directly on him. If there is a risk of no applause, he powers down. He had the opportunity at the Brighton conference to demonstrate a different kind of authority, generated from within, expressing conviction derived from a stable core of belief, made compelling by courage. It is the stuff of which leadership is made. Polanski doesn’t have it. If those are also qualities the voters of Holborn and St Pancras care for in a local MP, they will have to seek them elsewhere.
- Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

EU negotiators head to China hoping to curb cheap imports of hybrid electric cars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
04:00:34 UTC
13:00:34 KST

EU trade negotiators are heading to China for two days of crunch talks aimed at sealing a breakthrough deal tackling Beijing’s record £1bn-a-day trade surplus by curbing its exports of cheap hybrid electric cars into Europe.
Trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and his team fly out on Wednesday and will be negotiating up to the wire in talks scheduled to start the following day and continue late into Friday.
Sources say they hope to achieve “tangible, meaningful and measurable” results before the meeting of EU leaders in Brussels on Thursday next week, where China is high on the agenda.
The main focus is on what has been described as a “proof of concept” pilot agreement involving one sector, which is expected to be cars, which could be scaled up for other sectors in the coming months.
Diplomatic efforts to avert a full-scale trade war started at the end of June, albeit with little hope that China could curb exports to the EU given its historic ability to pivot quickly any time trade barriers are put in its path. For example, after the EU imposed tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles in October 2024 there was a boom in exports of hybrid cars, which were not subject to tariffs.
Last month, the EU asked China to voluntarily restrict hybrid exports to address soaring sales, warning that if they did not restrict them, safeguards – which could include quotas – could be enacted.
It is not known what China’s response was. But sources say the mood in talks has changed as EU member states have hardened demands for protection against Chinese imports that threaten their own industries.
On Monday, Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, agreed a “historic U-turn” on its policy on China by siding with the French president, Emmanuel Macron, in authorising effective permission for EU leaders to approve a new instrument to allow them to defend trade by cutting access to the single market at short notice.
In a joint paper with Emmanuel Macron, the two countries spoke of “a massive industrial shock … affecting sectors at the heart of the European industrial model and of systemic relevance [pharmaceuticals, aerospace, automotive, machine tools, chemicals, etc.]”.
The paper called for the use of all existing trade defence tools, but also for a new diversification instrument and “possible additional” new measures to allow the bloc to react when “third countries seek to undermine the restoration of a level playing field”.
Andrew Small, a former EU adviser on China, said Šefčovič’s talks will test the resolve of both Beijing and Brussels and will “determine whether China is willing to put sufficiently serious offers on the table”.
Small, who is the Asia director at the European Council on Foreign Relations in Berlin, warned: “China’s most effective tactic may be to draw Europe into a ‘process trap’ offering just enough to delay action, without addressing the forces driving European deindustrialisation.”
Sources say the Franco-German proposals for a new instrument, dubbed a “kill switch”, were born out of frustration, particularly in Paris, that a so-called “trade bazooka” available to Brussels, officially known as the anti-coercion instrument, has never been used.
Paris pushed for the use of the ACI following Trump’s threat of tariffs last year but it never gained traction from others as it could take up to a year to implement.
Handlesblatt, the Germany business newspaper, described Monday’s change in policy as “nothing less than an economic turning point”, with chief political reporter Martin Greive concluding in a hard-hitting column that Merz was “putting an end to years of naiveté towards Beijing”.
“Merz has recognised in recent months that Germany is the epicentre of the China shock 2.0; that there might not be much left of German industry if Germany continues to stand by and watch as China gains enormous export advantages through trillions in subsidies, the unilateral siphoning off of knowhow, and a – to put it mildly – questionable monetary policy,” he wrote.

Poland’s ‘solidarity’ push for EU energy resilience in face of Russian aggression
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
04:00:33 UTC
13:00:33 KST

Two miles off the coast of Gdańsk, the white steel piles of Poland’s first offshore gas terminal rise from the slate-grey Baltic. Installed at a height eight metres above the waves, the floating cranes and construction vessels here are on the frontline of Europe’s push for energy security.
Since the taps were turned off on Russian gas after Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine four years ago, Poland has turned to the global energy market for supplies. But while conditions are far from ideal as the Middle East war drives oil and gas prices to stratospheric levels, strengthening the diversity of the country’s energy mix remains a top priority for Poland, its Baltic neighbours, and the EU at large.
Looking out to sea from the windswept beach backed by pine forest, Maciej Wawrzkowicz, the offshore project manager at the national gas company Gaz-System, and the construction manager Krzysztof Polatynski say the Baltic is not an easy place to build.
Before work could start, Polish navy minesweepers were called in to torpedo unexploded mines and bombs from the second world war. Construction is halted by storms, while the sea froze over last winter. But speed is important in this project of international significance.
“Every quay that’s available right now in the area that has some prefabrication workshop space, a contractor is occupying them. And you are seeking for more. Gdańsk harbour is a significant construction place right now.”
Poland used to import more than half of its gas from Russia but refused to pay in rubles in 2022 as the Kremlin became a pariah in the west over Putin’s war on Ukraine. A Norwegian pipeline under the Baltic and liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal at Świnoujście, close to the border with Germany, helped to keep most homes warm and the fires of industry burning.
At Gdańsk the construction of the floating storage and regasification unit (FSRU) – a specialised marine vessel used to store and convert LNG – is planned to further bolster Poland’s booming economy. But it will also increase the country’s capacity beyond domestic needs – turning it into a hub for eastern Europe and its Baltic neighbours.
Poland has LNG regasification capacity of 8.3bn cubic metres a year. Once the FRSU is operational in early 2028, that will add 6.1bn cubic metres a year of additional capacity. A second vessel at the Gdańsk FRSU is also planned for 2030 to lift total capacity to more than 20bn cubic metres a year.
In an age of geopolitical challenges, the FSRU vessel also has a symbolic name: “Solidarity”, in a nod to its home port’s history, and Poland’s drive to strengthen EU ties in the face of Russian aggression.
In the 1980s, as the Soviet Union crumbled, strikes at Lenin shipyard in Gdańsk over communist rule launched Poland’s Solidarność (Solidarity) movement. Led by Lech Wałęsa, it paved the way for independence and the transition to a free-market economy. Living standards have shot up since, from 40% of the EU average in the mid-1990s to 81% last year.
Agnieszka Ozga, the director of the energy transition division, and her deputy, Paweł Sęk, say Poland has been working to diversify energy supplies for decades, with the 2014 annexation of Crimea by Russia accelerating the process. But 2022 was a “gamechanger,” says Sęk.
“After the war started, we knew what was going on and we knew many countries in our region would end up with no gas flows coming from Russia”.
Since then the Gdańsk FSRU has grown in importance, says Ozga. “Not only for Poland. But also Slovakia; central and eastern Europe countries; the Baltic states. It is also very, very important for the European Commission: to end the isolation of the Baltic states, because they were fully dependent on inflows of gas from Russia.”
However, there is also plenty of evidence in Gdańsk highlighting the energy challenges Poland must still confront.
On the edges of the old town’s narrow cobbled streets, the red and white-banded chimney stacks of a Soviet-era coal-fired power plant belch out thick plumes of smoke. Tourist boats ferrying visitors to the Westerplatte peninsula – where the first shots of the second world war were fired – must also pass through the jet-black mountains of a coal dock.
Coal accounts for more than half of electricity generation in Poland, significantly above the EU average. The legacy of Soviet fossil-fuel infrastructure and centuries of domestic production in this resource-rich country mean it remains key for the economy.
More than 80,000 people still work in coalmines, mainly in the south around the industrial city of Katowice – once called Stalinogród – as one of the few remaining coalmining regions still digging among EU countries fully committed to decarbonisation.
However, cutting out coal in favour of LNG, renewables and nuclear power is seen as critical for Poland’s future sovereignty and prosperity.
Relying on heavily polluting and costly fossil fuels, the country’s average wholesale electricity prices are the ninth highest in the EU – holding back growth in a country accustomed to powering ahead.
As wages and living standards catch up to western European levels, Polish manufacturing is beginning to lose its competitive edge from cheap labour – a factor that had long attracted multinationals such as Volkswagen and Toyota to locate factories in the country. As a result, keeping down other production costs – such as energy – is growing in importance.
Rafał Brzoska, the billionaire founder of InPost, the pan-European parcel locker company started in Krakow, is among Poland’s concerned entrepreneurs.
“The competitive cost of energy is not our big advantage. So we need to somehow change and reshape and focus on those elements of our economy that we can compete against, let’s say, France, that has the cheapest cost of energy. We cannot compete on the most cost-driven industries.”
Warsaw has pushed in recent years to decarbonise with a strategy up to 2040. However, critics warn that it still puts the country on a path to being the last EU economy to be producing the most of its power from fossil fuels by 2030, endangering economic security and prosperity.
It will also require vast levels of public investment, at a time when the national debt is piling up and borrowing costs are rising. There are also political challenges in the run-up to a general election next year, with rightwing opponents of Donald Tusk’s liberal government pushing to rally Eurosceptic voters by weaponising the green transition.
The government is also investing in nuclear, building a plant on the Baltic coast. However, critics highlight an eye-watering price tag of more than €42bn (£35.6bn), for a facility that will not come online until the late 2030s.
Poland’s deputy foreign minister Marcin Bosacki says EU membership is, however, aiding a transition that will strengthen the economy. “We inherited from communist times the worst electricity or power mix of all EU members. It is changing – maybe not fast enough – but it is changing quite fast.”
Poland has secured €54.7bn in funding through the EU’s post-Covid recovery and resilience facility, with 40% going primarily to energy-related objectives. It is also the largest beneficiary of a Brussels fund intended to support the introduction of the EU’s emissions trading system carbon-pricing scheme.
“Poles are the world champions in getting EU funds,” Bosacki says. Since joining the bloc in 2004 he estimates more than €300bn has flowed to Warsaw, supporting road building, railways and other critical infrastructure to power its economic boom.
“We calculate the growth of Polish GDP would be half of what actually happened in the last 20 years if Poland was not a member of the EU. Almost a half.”
After annual output surpassed $1tn (£756bn) last year – ranking Poland as the sixth largest economy in the EU, ahead of countries including Belgium, Sweden and Austria – the flow of catchup funds from Brussels is, however, likely to dwindle.
Mateusz Urban, a Warsaw-based economist at Oxford Economics, says changing the energy system by 2040 will be tough. But ditching its status as a laggard in the green transition is vital – for the climate, for energy independence, and economic security.
In the past, Poland has come under pressure from the Kremlin using its gas supplies for political ends, including attempts in 2010 to extract punishing terms from Warsaw that would have stitched up the Polish gas market in Russia’s favour.
“If you have one big supplier through a pipeline you have no power,” Urban says.
With the closure of the strait of Hormuz and as Donald Trump rattles the global energy market by threatening to limit diesel exports, risks remain. Large volumes of the LNG imported by sea to Poland are from the US and Qatar. But Polish energy officials are sanguine, suggesting that other markets could still be utilised, and argue widening horizons beyond Russian imports remains critical.
Urban agrees that diversifying energy supplies, while renewable power generation takes time to develop, could help strengthen Poland’s hand.
“We need it for geopolitical security. Moving away from Russian gas, and coal, is a huge step forward. If you have a diverse supply, then you’re more insulated from trouble in each region.”

After the Cornell Case, Should Colleges Ban Fraternities?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
04:00:03 UTC
13:00:03 KST

A lawsuit alleging the drugging and gang rape of a student by seven members of Cornell University's Chi Phi fraternity in 2024 has led to calls for greater scrutiny of fraternities on campus, and even banning them.
The case has drawn national attention in recent weeks after it was revealed that only two of the seven men alleged to have been involved were expelled. Both the university and local authorities have come under criticism for their handling of the case.
Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff said in a video message to the university community on Saturday that the school would take “a serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life” among other steps aimed at creating a safer campus environment. At a protest on the university campus on Monday, people chanted “Ban the frats!”
TIME spoke to Nick Syrett, author of The Company He Keeps: A History of White College Fraternities and chair and professor of gender and women’s studies at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, about the case, what makes fraternities different, and why they have proved so hard to rein in.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
TIME: You've written a book about white college fraternities. What about this case shocked or surprised you, if anything?
There's a long history of events like this happening in fraternities. Since at least the 1970s and 1980s, there have been incidents of gang rape of intoxicated, incapacitated women in fraternity houses. So it is not surprising that it has happened once again.
TIME: Is there something unique about fraternities that encourages this kind of behavior?
I do think there is something particular about fraternities. One of the things is the single-sex nature of the organization. Aside from sports teams on college campuses, these are the only single-sex organizations, and the men who join them have decided that they want to be in a single-sex organization that allows them to live out their masculinity in particular kinds of ways. They know that these organizations already have a reputation for partying, for drinking, for sometimes hazing, for being places where you can meet women, and so some men join them and other men don't. But when they get in the organizations, the pressure ratchets up because there is an emphasis upon sex and dating and hooking up. That is some fraternities' mandate that like people report who they've hooked up with, who they've had sex with, they talk about these things. It's a way to enhance masculinity.
The other thing is fraternities just have lots of power on campus. Most of them own their own houses, which means they don't have lots of oversight from university officials.
TIME: In the wake of the Cornell case, there have been calls for greater regulation and even bans on fraternities. What do you think those regulations would look like, or should look like?
It's hard to say. I think one of the things to know is that all fraternities and sororities are regulated at least to a certain degree. That is, they're recognized student organizations. They have to abide by certain rules that often have to do with things like rushing and pledging—that is how people become members of the organizations in the first place. Social events where fraternities and sororities mix with one another and with unaffiliated members are usually at least registered with university officials.
The difficulty here is that when a university does the ultimate thing, which is to ban an organization from campus altogether, it loses any ability to regulate because now they're not an official organization. But by and large, the fraternities own their own houses, and so young men who are students at any university can still choose to become members of that fraternity and live in that house if they want to, if that chapter remains recognized by its national organization. So we see that happen with some regularity. There's a fraternity right here at my school, the University of Wisconsin, that two weeks ago the police busted for illegal hazing. That fraternity hasn't been recognized by the university for 10 years, but it's still admitting members, having them pledge, hazing them, and breaking the law.
TIME: How widespread are these issues that you’re talking about among fraternities? Is it limited to a few bad fraternities, or is this kind of just a part of the life?
It's a hard question to answer, in part because we don't always know how people are behaving behind closed doors. There are a few things we know. One, we know that men in fraternities are more likely to sexually assault and participate in hazing than men who choose not to join fraternities. Of course, not all men who are in fraternities do either of those things. It's just that they are more likely to do so than non-affiliated men. So, to my mind, those are the major problems: that is, sexual assault, hazing, and also binge drinking. And most evidence suggests that people in fraternities do drink more than those who are unaffiliated, but it also gets to this question, sort of a chicken and egg question: like, are people who are more interested in those activities more likely to join fraternities in the first place? I think the answer is probably yes, but then those behaviors are simply reinforced in fraternities by older members as well, who make environments that are conducive to those behaviors.
There are, in fact, chapters that have gone to great lengths to limit binge drinking. Some have eliminated hazing altogether. Hazing is in fact illegal in most states, and all the national fraternities forbid it. But some people do it anyway.
TIME: Why do fraternity members so rarely report on each other when these things happen? Where does that loyalty come from?
Part of it is historical in that when fraternities were first founded, they were secret organizations and they were illegal on college campuses for about the first 25 years of their existence, from 1825 through the 1850s. So joining at all was breaking the rules and keeping a secret. And now there are secrets that are imparted during the rituals, like the secret of what the meaning of the motto is, and that sort of thing. They're not unique or interesting in any way, but definitely fraternity pledges learn loyalty during the period of pledging because they're often asked to do things that are demeaning. If it's hazing, it's illegal in most states, and they're bonded to one another through the process of pledging and having to be humiliated and sometimes physically harmed in some way. So that creates a bond between the members of that pledge class and then the fraternity to which they are demonstrating their loyalty by being hazed and pledged in the first place, so all of it is pretty classic anthropological ritual, and it does in the end create loyalty.
TIME: If all fraternities went away tomorrow, these issues probably wouldn't disappear entirely, right? Is it the case that they exacerbate these issues rather than create them?
I think that's right. I don't think sexual assault would go away, but I think that fraternities are organizations that exacerbate and encourage both sexual assault and binge drinking and hazing. I also think, importantly, we would see less organized versions of sexual assault and binge drinking, especially, fewer occasions when a group of men together planned out a sexual assault, which in some sense is what happened at Cornell. I think we would see less of it because there would be less pressure placed upon the men in these organizations to carry out these sorts of things. And granted, it's pressure from within, but it's generally pressure from older brothers upon younger ones.
TIME: Fraternity membership has proved remarkably resilient despite decades of scandal. Why?
When universities have attempted to regulate and/or ban fraternities, they get big pushback. There's evidence to show that alumni who were in fraternities are more active in their schools and give more, and so that is a base of alumni that universities don't want to upset because they're generous and they're powerful.
There is a subset of incoming college first year students, men and women, who find these organizations really appealing, and some of it is entirely understandable. That is, at a big school, what fraternities and sororities promise you is an instant group of friends, which is very comforting on a college campus where you know no one. Especially if you're going to a school that's farther away from home, when others from your high school are not going there, so you don't know anyone at all. So fraternities promise that kind of friendship and loyalty, and also for young people, 18-year-olds, many of whom are unsure of themselves, fraternities and sororities say this is the way to be popular. This is the way to make friends, have a good time, and you'll get to go to the good parties and you'll be part of an in-group.

In the face of the climate crisis and within the framework of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, the reuse of materials has become prominent in the fields of construction and architecture in recent years. A new way to fight gum disease without wiping out good bacteria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
03:55:00 UTC
12:55:00 KST

A new way to fight gum disease without wiping out good bacteria
- Date:
- October 6, 2026
- Source:
- University of Minnesota, Twin Cities
- Summary:
- Scientists discovered that disrupting the chemical messages bacteria use to communicate can push dental plaque toward a healthier microbial balance. The approach could lead to new treatments for gum disease that control harmful bacteria without destroying beneficial species.
- Share:
Bacteria are remarkably good at adapting. That ability helps them survive changing conditions, but it can also create problems when harmful species become resistant to antibiotics and disinfectants.
At the same time, bacteria are not simply enemies to eliminate. Many species play important roles in human health, including the hundreds of different microbes that live in the mouth. That raises an intriguing possibility: instead of trying to kill bacteria, could scientists influence how they behave and encourage healthier microbial communities?
Research published in 2025 in npj Biofilms and Microbiomes suggests that may be possible. Scientists studying dental plaque found that interfering with the chemical signals bacteria use to communicate can change which species thrive, potentially shifting the community toward bacteria associated with better oral health.
How Bacteria Communicate in the Mouth
The human mouth is home to roughly 700 species of bacteria. These microbes do not simply grow alongside one another. Many exchange chemical signals through a process called quorum sensing.
Quorum sensing allows bacteria to detect how many neighboring cells are present and coordinate group behaviors. Some oral bacteria communicate using molecules known as N-acyl homoserine lactones (AHLs).
Researchers from the College of Biological Sciences and the School of Dentistry examined how these signals shape dental plaque. Their goal was to determine whether bacterial communication could be manipulated to help maintain a healthier oral microbiome.
The oral microbiome refers to the community of microorganisms living in the mouth. When that community becomes unbalanced, potentially harmful bacteria can become more dominant and contribute to conditions such as periodontal disease.
Chemical Signals Can Cross the Gumline
The researchers found that bacteria within dental plaque produced AHL signals in aerobic environments (such as above the gumline), where oxygen is available.
Those chemical messages could also be detected by bacteria living in anaerobic environments (beneath the gumline), where oxygen levels are much lower.
This connection was important because conditions below the gumline can favor bacteria associated with periodontal disease.
The team also used specialized enzymes called lactonases to remove AHL signals. Lactonases break down these communication molecules, effectively interfering with the bacterial conversation.
When researchers disrupted AHL signaling, the dental plaque community shifted toward species more strongly associated with oral health.
Their findings suggest that carefully chosen enzymes might someday be used to alter the makeup of dental plaque and help maintain a healthier balance of microorganisms.
Dental Plaque Behaves Like an Ecosystem
"Dental plaque develops in a sequence, much like a forest ecosystem," said Mikael Elias, associate professor in the College of Biological Sciences and senior author of the study. "Pioneer species like Streptococcus and Actinomyces are the initial settlers in simple communities -- they're generally harmless and associated with good oral health. Increasingly diverse late colonizers include the 'red complex' bacteria like Porphyromonas gingivalis, which are strongly linked to periodontal disease. By disrupting the chemical signals bacteria use to communicate, one could manipulate the plaque community to remain or return to its health-associated stage."
In other words, dental plaque changes over time rather than appearing all at once. Early communities may contain relatively harmless bacteria, while more complex communities can eventually include species strongly associated with gum disease.
The researchers hope that interfering with bacterial communication could make it possible to guide plaque toward an earlier, healthier state rather than attempting to eliminate the entire microbial population.
Oxygen Changes How Bacterial Signals Behave
One of the most important findings was that the effects of bacterial communication depended heavily on oxygen levels.
"What's particularly striking is how oxygen availability changes everything," said lead author Rakesh Sikdar. "When we blocked AHL signaling in aerobic conditions, we saw more health-associated bacteria. But when we added AHLs under anaerobic conditions, we promoted the growth of disease-associated late colonizers. Quorum sensing may play very different roles above and below the gumline, which has major implications for how we approach treatment of periodontal diseases."
That difference suggests that the same chemical signals can influence microbial communities in very different ways depending on where they occur in the mouth.
Above the gumline, where oxygen is more plentiful, disrupting AHL signaling favored bacteria linked with better oral health. Beneath the gumline, adding those signals encouraged later colonizing species associated with disease.
A Different Strategy for Preventing Gum Disease
The researchers now want to investigate how bacterial communication varies throughout the mouth and among people at different stages of periodontal disease.
Rather than broadly attacking oral bacteria with antimicrobial treatments, the long term goal is to find ways to influence the balance of the microbial community itself.
"Understanding how bacterial communities communicate and organize themselves may ultimately give us new tools to prevent periodontal disease -- not by waging war on all oral bacteria, but by strategically maintaining a healthy microbial balance," said Elias.
The approach could eventually have implications beyond dentistry. Similar microbial imbalances, often called microbiome dysbiosis, occur elsewhere in the body and have been associated with a range of health problems, including certain types of cancer.
Researchers hope that learning how to manipulate bacterial communication could eventually provide a foundation for therapies designed to steer microbial communities toward healthier states rather than simply destroying them.
The research was funded by the National Institutes of Health.

The Oct. 7 battle for Sderot still rages in the minds of its survivors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
03:52:07 UTC
12:52:07 KST

Shalom Aida was at home when the first air raid siren sounded at 6:29 a.m. on October 7, 2023, but he wasn’t initially fazed.
Rocket sirens were a common occurrence in his city of Sderot, which is less than a mile from Gaza at its closest point.
It wasn’t until he heard gunshots that Aida, a retired police officer, realized that dozens of heavily armed Hamas terrorists had infiltrated Sderot and were gunning down any civilian, soldier, or police officer they came across.
By the time he arrived at the police station, “it was a battlefield,” he said. The sight almost paralyzed him.
“The entire street in front of the station was full of bloodied people. Police, civilians, dead or dying. Hamas kept firing.”
One of the police officers killed that day was Aida’s cousin. Many others were his friends.
Three years later, he is still haunted by the memories.
“Sderot seems quiet now, but it’s not quiet or peaceful inside our heads,” he said as he watched groups of visitors walk around the Sderot Memorial and Heroes Park. It sits on the site of the police station, which was destroyed that day and rebuilt elsewhere.
Wouldn't dream of moving elsewhere, Aida says
Despite the ongoing trauma of Oct. 7 and its aftermath, Aida said he wouldn’t dream of moving elsewhere.
“I never once thought about leaving,” he said, shocked by the question. “The best people in the world live in Sderot.”
Not all residents of the “Gaza Envelope” who experienced the horrors of Oct. 7 returned home when the government gave the all-clear, after ordering them to evacuate for their own safety. But the vast majority of Sderot’s residents — set at over 37,000 by the Central Bureau of Statistics in 2024 — who had already lived through two decades of rocket barrages from Gaza, returned to the city within months.
Once it was a struggling development town where successive governments sent immigrants who had just arrived from the Middle East and the former Soviet Union.
It generated domestic and international headlines over the last two decades, as it became the first city hit by Hamas rockets as early as 2001, and remained one of the places the Gaza-based terror group has most frequently targeted.
International dignitaries, including UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon in 2009 and then Sen. Barack Obama during his 2008 presidential campaign, visited Sderot.
Initially a city without adequate protective shelter for its residents, it became the only place in Israel where every single apartment and bus stop has its own bomb shelter.
City has prospered despite challenges
Despite it all, the city has prospered: gleaming new apartment buildings, parks and a sprawling mall greet visitors as they enter.
“If you were to input all the data about Sderot into OpenAI, the 25 years of rockets and Oct. 7 and the bomb shelters, it would say this must be a ghost town. But that’s not the reality here,” said Ilan Abecassis, a retired educator and now tour guide who has lived in the city all his life.
Rather than shrinking, he said, the city’s population has grown by about 5,000 people since the Oct. 7 attack.
“I know it’s counterintuitive, but the more they try to destroy us, the stronger we become,” Abecassis said. “In the Torah, a new pharaoh sees the Israelite population growing and enslaves them. But the Torah tells us ‘the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and grew.’ We are like those Israelites.”
Arie Yagudaev, 30, from Sderot, and his cousin Eitan Izayev, 28, who lives in nearby Kibbutz Nir Am, said they are also committed to staying, even after they encountered terrorists in the street on Oct. 7.
Drinking strong coffee outside his family’s grocery store in Sderot, Izayev recounted how he had begged his cousin to pick him up from the kibbutz, which terrorists were trying to infiltrate, so he could help defend loved ones in Sderot. Along the way, they picked up two teenage girls, survivors of the Nova music festival.
“As we approached the roundabout into Sderot, we saw some pickup trucks ahead of us,” Izayev recalled. “We thought the men in the bed of the truck were IDF soldiers. But when the terrorists saw us, they shot at us nonstop.”
“One of the bullets shattered my car’s back window. It’s a miracle we survived,” Yagudaev said. Even though he suffered from PTSD every night as an evacuee in an Eilat hotel room, he said, “I wanted to go home.”
“It wasn’t just because the hotel room was cramped,” he said. “Leaving Sderot and Israel is exactly what the terrorists want. We’re not going anywhere.”
One Sderot restaurant owner, who was born and raised in Sderot but moved to Kibbutz Nir Am several years ago, feels the same way.
“Not to return would be rewarding Hamas for its terrorism,” said the restaurant owner who requested anonymity because of his ongoing stints in the IDF reserves.
As it was, he and his wife and baby spent almost a year in a small Tel Aviv hotel room before returning to their kibbutz two years ago. It wasn’t an easy homecoming, he said. For one thing, IDF soldiers had lived in their empty house, and it needed major repairs. Returning to the area also triggered traumatic memories from the Hamas attack.
“For 22 hours I stood outside our house to protect my wife and newborn baby,” he recalled, sitting at a table in his restaurant. “Eventually we decided to flee in our car with just the clothes we could throw into a trash bag. We placed the baby under the seat of the car, hoping to protect him.”
Once the owner of three restaurants, he now owns only one. He needed to sell the two popular restaurants he owned at another kibbutz because he couldn’t operate them from Tel Aviv, and, back then, the Gaza border was an active war zone.
Although the Gaza border is much more secure due to the buffer zone the IDF maintains in Gaza, “it’s not quiet on the border,” he said. “We live one kilometer from Gaza. Every day we hear the choppers and the shooting.”
Still, he and his wife have no plans to leave.
“My parents live here, my grandparents live here,” he said. “On Oct. 7 I saw an apocalypse, bodies on the ground. I knew 100 people who were killed or kidnapped. The ground beneath us is soaked with their blood. I can’t leave.”

Viral trapped shark in South Korea brings tourism, retail windfall to Busan
‘Bukangi’ has attracted over a million visitors, boosting the local economy, as vendors capitalise on the stranded shark’s fame
The shark, nicknamed “Bukangi” in reference to the park where it has become trapped, has become an internet darling and tourist sensation after non-stop local media coverage about multiple failed efforts to encourage it back into the open ocean.
Busan authorities have moved to capitalise on the frenzy. The city has appointed the shark – which experts believe is a dusky shark – an honorary ambassador, giving it a starring role in local promotional campaigns. Some 1,062,800 people have visited the park to see the shark since September 19, the Busan Infrastructure Corporation said.
Bukangi is the latest example of how wildlife straying into urban environments can become tourist sensations supercharged by the internet, boosting the local economy.

Where New Yorkers will commemorate the anniversary of Oct. 7 and its aftermath

Jewish institutions in New York are gearing up to mark the third anniversary on Wednesday of Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attacks on Israel, as some anti-Zionist groups prepare to hold demonstrations against Israel.
About 1,200 people were killed in Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel that day three years ago, most of them civilians, with another 251 taken hostage, according to Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Another 452 soldiers have been killed in the fighting since then, according to the Israel Defense Forces. In the ensuing war in Gaza, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed, according to Gaza’s Ministry of Health, which doesn’t distinguish between civilians and combatants. The war has reshaped the region and reverberated around the world.
Here is a list of events around New York City to commemorate the attacks and their aftermath.
Manhattan’s Marlene Meyerson Jewish Community Center is holding “a day of remembrance, music, and community” in its lobby, from noon until 7 p.m. “Strokes of Hope,” an exhibition of drawings by Israeli artist Zeev Engelmayer, will be on display.
UJA-Federation of New York is launching “Rooted,” a public art installation at the Museum of Jewish Heritage, which will be on display until Oct. 25, made up of thousands of hostage solidarity tags and pins. At 92NY on the Upper East Side, Claire Shipman – the former acting president of Columbia University – is moderating a conversation between an Israeli father, Jonathan Dekel-Chen, and a Palestinian father, Jaser AbuMoussa.
Omer Shem Tov, an Israeli former hostage, will speak at Yeshiva University’s memorial at 8 p.m.
In Brooklyn, the Park Slope Jewish Center will host an event at 7 p.m. including personal testimony from Atir Vinnikov, a survivor of the Nova music festival massacre.
At 7 p.m. in Union Square, the group Israelis for Peace is set to meet for an evening of “quiet reflection and mourning” of the people killed on Oct. 7 and in “its bloody aftermath.”
Anti-Zionist student groups planning walkouts
A number of anti-Zionist student groups are planning walkouts on campuses across the city, including City University of New York campuses, Columbia and NYU.
The walkouts will culminate in a rally held outside City Hall at 4 p.m., organized by Pal-Awda and endorsed by a number of groups, calling on Mayor Zohran Mamdani, himself a strident critic of Israel, to stop “[capitulating] to Zionist pressure.”

Report finds over 70% eSIMs connect to networks in countries outside advertised destinations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
03:49:49 UTC
12:49:49 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — More than 70% of eSIMs tested by Taiwan’s Consumers’ Foundation used internet networks outside countries where the services were advertised to work, according to a recent report by the foundation.
The foundation tested 172 eSIMs sold to travelers traveling to popular destinations and found only 27.9% used networks registered to operators in the countries listed on the products. Most connected through roaming services in third countries or regions, or through networks registered elsewhere.
The top travel destinations for Taiwanese travelers include Japan, China, South Korea, Hong Kong, Vietnam, and Thailand, according to the National Immigration Agency.
The foundation found 40% of the tested eSIMs used networks operated by Chinese state-owned telecom groups, including China Mobile, and 70% of the networks were located in Hong Kong.
The foundation said it is often difficult for consumers to tell what network an eSIM will use until they arrive at their destination and activate the service. Only then can they find out whether the eSIM connects directly to a local telecom operator or routes their traffic through a roaming service in a third region.
The Ministry of Digital Affairs said in July that eSIMs may route users’ internet traffic to servers in third countries before forwarding it to local networks.
The foundation advised travelers using eSIMs to avoid logging into online banking, entering credit card information, or handling other sensitive data unless they have confirmed the security of the network. It also recommended using HTTPS-encrypted websites or a VPN when possible.
The foundation called on authorities to consider requiring eSIM providers to clearly disclose the telecom operator providing the service, the data transmission architecture, and if traffic is routed through a roaming service in a third region.
