'Looking at Australia': Sidney Nolan in six definitive paintings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
03:00:00 UTC
12:00:00 KST

Six Sidney Nolan artworks to see at Nolan: Origins at the Art Gallery of New South Wales
Australian artist Sidney Nolan was interested in the stories and myths we tell about ourselves, from the life of bushranger Ned Kelly to the trials of saints.
"Sidney Nolan has to be one of our most creative and inventive painters that emerged out of the period of war and the decades following," says Denise Mimmocchi, senior curator of Australian art at the Art Gallery of New South Wales (AGNSW).
"He posed questions about place, our identity, and our individual search for meaning within the continent and landscapes of Australia."
Born in 1917, the modernist artist would prove to be one of Australia's most influential and prolific, initially as part of the infamous Heide Circle alongside Albert Tucker, Arthur Boyd and Joy Hester. He would go on to be acquired by the likes of the Museum of Modern Art in New York and the Tate Modern in London.
Curated by Mimmocchi, AGNSW's new exhibition Nolan: Origins charts the artist's career from 1939 until he moved to London in 1953. It features places like St Kilda and central Australia — environments that would continue to spark his imagination throughout his life.
"I wanted to look at what inspired him," Mimmocchi says. "And what we're looking at really is Australia."
Kiata
In 1943, during WWII, Nolan — who had been conscripted in 1942 — was stationed at Nhill, guarding Australia's food reserves.
The job left him with a lot of time to paint. One work he made during this period is this landscape of the nearby town Kiata, in western Victoria.
"Kiata is really a breakthrough moment," Mimmocchi says. "This is when the abstract artist also becomes a landscape painter."
As he figured out how to capture the vastness he encountered, Nolan came to appreciate an earlier generation of Australian artists, the Impressionists, like Arthur Streeton, Tom Roberts and Charles Conder, who would often paint outdoors.
"He looks to and echoes in his own way the idea of painting the Australian light and landscape, but he does it through his own modern sensibility," Mimmocchi says.
A year later, in 1944, when he found out he was going to be sent to fight in Papua New Guinea, Nolan deserted the army.
In 1948, he received an amnesty for deserters and was formally discharged.
Fire, Palais de Danse, St Kilda
When Nolan was nine and growing up in Melbourne's St Kilda, the Palais de Danse burned down. It was an event that became etched in the artist's memory.
He painted the scene 20 years later, in 1945, while living between his studio in Parkville, Melbourne, and Heide on the city's outskirts, in the home of philanthropists Sunday and John Reed.
There, Nolan had an affair with Sunday, before marrying John's sister, Cynthia, a writer, in 1948.
"When he's living in hiding, he starts to paint with greater intensity these memories of his childhood in St Kilda," Mimmocchi says.
"He goes up in scale as well. In that expansion comes this incredible impact of the energy contained within them."
She describes that energy as "frenetic", with the human figures in the painting appearing almost like ants.
"You get this sense of palpitating movement," Mimmocchi explains. "It's wonderful and vibrant but at the same time, for me, a little tense. There's something deeply anxious about them."
Mimmocchi boils that anxiety down to Nolan viewing these moments from his childhood through the lens of the "wartime present".
Ned Kelly
While living at Heide, Nolan spent a year, starting in 1946, creating a series of 27 paintings of bushranger Ned Kelly.
One inspiration for the series came from the stories Nolan's grandfather told him when he was a child, of being part of the search for the Kelly gang. But it also stemmed from his own desertion from the army.
"He's a bit of an outlaw in his mind himself," Mimmocchi says.
"He saw the Kelly figure as a rebel poet. He saw him and his family as the victims of great injustice.
"At the same time, coming out of that experience of war, where he was trained to use the 'utmost violence', the idea of brutality was at the forefront of his mind."
To create the series, Nolan pored over newspaper clippings and the 1881 Royal Commission report into the Victorian police, and visited Glenrowan, the site of Kelly's final shoot-out with police in 1880.
"He's interested in painting the landscape and the stories within it; how history becomes legend becomes mythology," Mimmocchi says.
That's perhaps exemplified by the view through the letterbox-style slit in Kelly's helmet.
"We view the landscape through the Kelly helmet," Mimmocchi says. "It's almost as if Nolan is saying our experiences of place are shaped or framed by these stories, by these figures."
The Ned Kelly series and the now-iconic blocky shape of Kelly's helmet also marked a turning point in Nolan's practice.
"He said he was an abstract painter and then he became a painter of the landscape, and this brought the two together," Mimmocchi says.
Quilting the armour
This 1947 painting from the Ned Kelly series depicts a moment of tenderness between the bushranger and his sister Margaret, where she stitched padding into his helmet.
"It's quite a beautiful and powerful image of this woman creating padding for Kelly in this foreboding landscape, perhaps in anticipation of the violence which is to come," Mimmocchi says.
"It sits so distinctly from a lot of the other paintings, which are about the guns, the violence, the bloodshed.
"It says something about a female notion of creativity or the importance of women in the Ned Kelly story."
Also hidden in the painting is a reference to Nolan's desertion from the army, living under the alias Robin Murray. On a fencepost sits a red robin.
The Ned Kelly series fell flat when it was first exhibited in Melbourne in 1948, but the Reeds were determined the paintings would find an audience, sending them to Paris and Rome.
In Paris in 1949, museum director Jean Cassou described them as "the work of a true poet and true painter".
"It wasn't until they'd had this life overseas that they came back to Australia and started to gain the recognition they deserve," Mimmocchi says.
Central Australia
In 1949, Nolan spent months travelling through central Australia, Arnhem Land and the Kimberley in Western Australia, with his wife, Cynthia, and adopted daughter Jinx.
The artist would join aviator Eddie Connellan as he delivered mail to remote communities. The view from these flights inspired this 1950 painting.
"He was deeply inspired by this vision of a country, which was so vast, so seemingly infinite, but had this vital energy in the movement and passages of the landscape," Mimmocchi says.
"It was painted at a time when city Australians commonly referred to the centre of Australia as its dead heart. Nolan encounters and paints a country that couldn't be more different to that."
The vivid red of the work comes from Nolan's use of Ripolin, a quick-drying enamel paint he first used in the early 40s.
"That gave him a saturated colour and the ability to paint the intense, clarified light of the desert," Mimmocchi says.
In 1950, in a letter to fellow artist Albert Tucker, Nolan wrote that Indigenous peoples "show you that the country is a gentle, dreaming one; the barrenness and harshness is all in our European eyes".
Mimmocchi explains: "First Nations connection to Country shaped his vision."
Temptation of St Anthony
In 1950, Nolan travelled to Europe for the first time, to Italy, Spain, Greece and the UK, where he was inspired by Christian paintings.
When he returned to Sydney, he started taking biblical scenes and imposing them onto the unforgiving Australian landscape.
In Temptation of St Anthony, from 1952, he depicted the story of early Christian monk Anthony the Great's pilgrimage through the Egyptian desert, where he was tormented by demons and faced a series of temptations.
In Nolan's telling, those demons and temptations included a goanna, a giant dragonfly and an angel with horns.
"He was deeply interested in the stories that shape us," Mimmocchi says. "It was the idea of myth. He saw the stories of the Bible as another myth that could be painted in relation to the landscape.
"In these biblical works, he's marrying this sense of the ancientness of the stories of Europe with the ancientness and the vital presence of the Australian landscape."
For the curator, Temptation of St Anthony is "pure Nolan".
"He's able to bring the action of this biblical story into the Australian desert so evocatively," she says.
Nolan: Origins is at Art Gallery of New South Wales, Sydney, until February 7.

New tool aims to find terrorist material on devices
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:00:31 BST
23:00:31 KST

Police officers are to be given a way of checking a seized phone or computer against a library of more than a million files produced by recognised terrorist organisations, returning an answer in minutes rather than weeks, according to Cyacomb, the Edinburgh firm behind it.
The company has developed the capability with Human Cognition, using that firm’s Terrorist Authored Material Contraband Filter. The filter draws on a curated dataset of modern and historical terrorist material which has been checked by people rather than only by machines, and verified as having been produced by recognised terrorist groups.
Behind it sits an archive of more than 3.3 million files that have circulated in terrorist online ecosystems over the past three decades, of which more than a million have been identified as terrorist-authored. A suspect device is checked against that material using secure matching technology, with the stated aim of supporting faster action against people moving towards violence.
Chris Johnson, chief executive of Cyacomb, said: “Technology has completely changed the environment in which radicalisation can take place. Traditionally becoming involved with an extremist organisation would require physical contact, but today an individual can access huge volumes of extremist material without leaving their bedroom.”
Dr Ali Fisher, co-founder at Human Cognition, said: “The speed, agility and resilience of the terrorist networks that share content online, and the mobility of potential terrorists in the physical world, requires tools that enable law enforcement to rapidly identify content on digital devices.”
The companies say the process does not expose unrelated personal information held on the device, since it matches only against material already in the dataset rather than reading everything stored. That distinction is the one that usually decides whether a tool of this kind survives contact with the courts, and it is the same approach Cyacomb has taken in its existing work on child abuse imagery, where the firm built its reputation.
A full forensic examination of a modern phone can take weeks, and a backlog of devices waiting for examination has been a recurring theme in inspectorate reports on counter-terrorism and serious crime investigation. A triage tool that tells an officer within minutes whether a device holds known material lets investigators decide where to put the specialist effort. Language is the other claimed advantage, with the companies saying the matching works whatever the nature or language of the content, because it compares files rather than reading them.

EU toughens China stance ahead of Šefčovič’s Beijing visit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
02:51:22 UTC
11:51:22 KST

Maroš Šefčovič speaks with reporters during the second day of the G20 Trade Ministerial in Wisconsin, U.S. on Oct. 1, 2026. | Kamil Krzaczynski/AFP via Getty Images
STRASBOURG — Policymakers across the political spectrum are coalescing around a stronger approach to the European Union's relationship with China — one that goes beyond trade measures.
A report from the Committee on Foreign Affairs on the EU-China political relationship paints China not just as an economic foe but also a geopolitical one that is undercutting European security.
The European Parliament will vote on the report on Wednesday, just in time for Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič's trip to Beijing on Thursday, where he will meet with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao.
Advertisement
"I want him to go there with the strongest possible mandate from this house," Hilde Vautmans, the report's author, said in a debate on Tuesday evening. "Europe has economic power. It’s time to use it."
The remarks echo those made by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron in a joint letter earlier this week, advocating that the European Commission be handed more powers to restrict or even cut off imports from countries that create "severe and systematic distortions" in the EU.
While some MEPs hailed the French-German joint approach as proof of a unified position, Polish MEP Mariusz Kamiński from the European Conservatives and Reformists said creating "pragmatic economic ties is not only cynical, but irresponsible or outright stupid."
China is a "communist dictatorship that poses a threat to the free world," he continued.
He's not alone in that sentiment, as for many lawmakers, simply tackling Chinese overcapacity isn't enough. The Commission needs to address China's growing human rights abuses, escalations in the Taiwan Strait, and its role in the war in Ukraine, they said.
"We have to recognize that China is behaving in a way that is endangering our interests. Not just on trade but on security and defense," said Spanish MEP Nicolás Pascual de la Parte from the center-right European People's Party. "The human rights situation has not improved, but it has disappeared from our agenda in recent years."
Advertisement
The lawmakers called out Beijing's treatment of the Uyghur minority group in Xinjiang, which China has systemically placed in camps and prisons and persecuted. The Parliament stopped just short of calling the action a genocide in a 2024 resolution, saying it amounts "to crimes against humanity."
Others like the EPP's Michael Gahler called out Beijing's encroachment on the island of Taiwan, which China claims as its own territory. China's role in propping up the Russian economy while it fights Ukraine also received plenty of airtime.
The issues diverged, but the MEPs used Tuesday's debate to call out the EU's unequal relationship with China — a sign that Vautmans says is proof the bloc is coming to a unified stance toward the country.
"This is no longer just the position of the European Parliament or of one political group," Vautmans said after the debate. "There is a growing recognition that Europe needs a more coherent China policy: open to dialogue and cooperation, but much more willing to defend its interests when necessary."

WASHINGTON, October 7. /TASS/. Iranian authorities should significantly reduce their uranium enrichment capacity in order to end the war with the United States, US Vice President JD Vance said in an interview with Reuters.
"If you don’t want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60% enriched fuel? And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don’t build highly enriched fuel. That’s a very basic threshold issue [when ending the conflict]," Vance said. "I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity."
He said the United States remained open to reaching an agreement but would demand concrete concessions from Iran in the nuclear sphere. "We’re not going to trade words for actions," the vice president said. In his view, the situation is complicated by the fact that Washington is unsure who makes decisions in Tehran. Vance said the United States was holding talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. However, he claimed, it was unclear how much influence they wield within Iran’s power structure. "One of the things we picked up on is it’s not totally clear how their country makes decisions," Vance said.
The United States and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding envisaging an immediate ceasefire on all fronts, including in Lebanon. However, the United States resumed large-scale attacks on Iran overnight to July 8, having accused it of breaching the existing agreements in what concerned the Strait of Hormuz, a global chokepoint for approximately 25% of oil and some 20% of LNG supplies.
The Donald Trump administration recently signaled an end to any large-scale use of force against Iran and a transition to putting economic pressure on the Islamic Republic through sanctions instead.

Mali: Junta forces retake strategic town of Kidal
October 7, 2026
Mali's army, supported by Russian paramilitary forces, has re-entered the northern town of Kidal, forcing the Tuareg separatists to withdraw from the strategic hold, in a symbolic boost for the country's military government and its Russian allies.
The Tuareg separatist Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) said in a statement it had "decided to carry out a strategic and controlled withdrawal of its forces from the town of Kidal." It said the withdrawal took place without direct fighting.
This followed the "disproportionate use of aerial assets by Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps," according to an FLA spokesperson.
How did Kidal fall earlier this year?
The FLA and al-Qaeda-linked Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) seized Kidal during a series of attacks earlier this year in April that also killed Mali's defense minister.
Tuareg separatists from the Azawad Liberation Front have been fighting for years to create an independent state in northern Mali.
Mali's junta, which came to power in back-to-back coups in 2020 and 2021, has increasingly relied on Russian paramilitary support against fighters linked to al-Qaeda and the Islamic State.
What does Kidal's recapture mean for Mali's junta?
Analysts say the latest advance is largely a symbolic victory for Mali's junta.
"A successful recapture... affirms the military-led government's authority and boosts the army's morale, particularly after several high-profile setbacks both in the north and the central regions in recent weeks," Beverly Ochieng, associate director of Control Risks, told Reuters.
Ochieng, however, added the retaking of Kidal is largely "symbolic" and not "decisive" in Mali's campaign against jihadist and separatist groups.
Human rights organizations have often accused the Malian army and Russian paramilitaries of killing civilians during military operations, with all sides also accused of committing war crimes.

U.S. Pennsylvania measles cases surpass 1,000

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- More than 1,000 confirmed measles cases have been reported in the U.S. state of Pennsylvania in 2026, with five deaths and 198 hospitalizations, making it the largest state measles outbreak in more than three decades, according to state health officials.
The Pennsylvania Department of Health said Monday that 1,004 measles cases had been confirmed across 39 counties. A total of 27 new cases had been reported since Oct. 2.
Only four of the confirmed cases were among people who had received the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, accounting for less than 1 percent of the total. The outbreak began in late April.
Health care providers have also seen a surge in MMR vaccinations. In a typical month, Pennsylvania health care providers administer approximately 25,000 doses of the MMR vaccine. More than 49,000 doses were administered in August and more than 53,000 in September, according to the state health department.
Full vaccination offers the best protection against measles. Two doses of the MMR vaccine provide 97 percent lifetime protection, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health.
In response to the growing outbreak, New York State Governor Kathy Hochul on Monday declared a state disaster emergency. As of Oct. 3, New York had reported 108 measles cases this year, including 92 cases reported since July 15 in 18 rural counties with under-immunized communities, according to the state government.
The New York state government said measles cases reported this year had increased markedly beyond the typical number in the state, particularly since July 15, constituting a significant public health concern.
As of Oct. 1, the United States had reported 3,887 confirmed measles cases in 2026, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, making 2026 the worst year for measles in the country since 1991. ■

The scam warning Australians have heard for years is now out of date
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
02:35:03 UTC
11:35:03 KST

IN BRIEF
- ANZ has warned businesses about sophisticated scams in upcoming busy commerce periods.
- Cybersecurity experts say AI improves every stage of a scam.
Australians are being warned that some of the most common advice for spotting scams is becoming less effective, as criminals use artificial intelligence to create convincing emails, phone calls and video deepfakes.
Banks and cybersecurity experts say artificial intelligence (AI) is helping fraudsters impersonate trusted colleagues, businesses and even family members with a level of sophistication that can be almost impossible to detect.
The warning comes ahead of the Black Friday sales period and summer holidays, when scammers typically exploit heightened spending and pressure to target victims.
More than 84,000 cybercrime reports were made in 2025, while the average self-reported cost of cybercrime to businesses rose sharply, according to the Australian Signals Directorate.
How AI is changing the scam landscape
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
AI is transforming every stage of a scam, from impersonation to execution, according to Sanjay Jha, a professor at UNSW's School of Computer Science and Engineering.
"What’s genuinely new is three things: the impersonation of real, trusted people, real-time deepfakes, and the scale and personalisation that the technology brings to financial crime," he said.
AI technology allows criminals to produce deepfake videos of trusted people, including doctors, celebrities and business leaders, to promote fake products or investments. It can clone voices of family members, colleagues or executives asking for money.
The volume and quality of scam techniques are a concern, as large language models can write fluent, personalised messages in any language, with fewer spelling mistakes, and can run thousands of conversations at once.
"We used to tell people to look for spelling mistakes," Jha said, adding that advances in AI mean scammers can produce fluent, convincing messages with few obvious errors.
Scammers can appear on a live call impersonating someone else, Jha said, pointing to a 2024 case in Hong Kong, when United Kingdom engineering firm Arup transferred about HK$200m ($36.5 million) to criminals after a deepfaked multi-person conference.
"AI has turned scamming from a craft into a factory. A few seconds of your voice is now enough for a criminal to become you," he said.
Professor in CyberCrime and Cyberwar at UNSW, Richard Buckland, said any information available on the internet is accessible to criminals using AI, and that experts were "just scratching the surface" of its abilities.
"If I wanted to scam you, you might have published all sorts of stuff in your youth, your dad might have said things, your friends may have, but it's in a thousand locations, and before AI, no one would ever find it," he said
"But that's actually all inside the AI now. So AIs can access a vast amount of information about us and know about us."
AI lets criminals enact existing scams faster, at scale and more convincingly, he said, and the technology was easily accessible.
"It's really a world of outsourcing now; you could pay someone to do it, you could buy a model that does it."
The most common scams targeting businesses
The most common scams affecting businesses include the impersonation of legitimate business email accounts, known as Business Email Compromise (BEC), payment redirection scams, impersonation scams, mule accounts, identity fraud, investment scams and goods and services scams.
BEC and payment redirection scams involve criminals gaining access to or impersonating legitimate business email accounts. Victims often believe they are paying a genuine supplier or business partner, when the funds are being transferred to a fraudulent account.
Jha said scammers use AI to study a company’s public information, past emails where accounts have been compromised, and the writing style of its executives and suppliers. They then send a "perfectly worded email, in the right tone, at the right moment in a real transaction", asking to update banking details.
AI can also generate realistic fake invoices and receipts that match a supplier’s branding. "Instead of just an email, the 'CEO' now follows up with a phone call in their cloned voice, or joins a video call."
Similarly, scammers can pretend to be trusted organisations or individuals, including banks, suppliers or government agencies.
Impersonation scams generally rely on urgency and social conditioning to pressure victims to share information, click malicious links or approve payments or transfer funds.
One of the most significant emerging threats identified by ANZ is the use of stolen or falsified identities to open accounts that can receive scam proceeds. Known as "mule" accounts, these are used to facilitate financial crime, including money laundering.
Identity fraud was the most common scam reported in 2025, and ANZ said it has identified a "growing misuse" of mule accounts across the financial system.
Investment scams trick individuals and businesses into investing in fake or non-existent opportunities by promising attractive returns or exclusive offers. They rank consistently among the highest-loss scam categories reported to ANZ.
"AI easily produces deepfake videos of well-known business figures, journalists or politicians endorsing a trading platform, fake news articles, fake dashboards showing ‘profits’, and chatbots that keep victims engaged for weeks," Jha said.
"In short, AI removes the tell-tale signs we taught people to look for: bad grammar, a stranger’s voice, a generic greeting. The scam now looks and sounds like business as usual."
Individuals and businesses are also urged to look out for goods and services scams — advertised goods and services that are fake, misrepresented or never delivered after payment is made, commonly occurring through online marketplaces, social media platforms and fraudulent websites. While often lower in value, goods and services scams remain among the highest-volume scam types reported by ANZ.
ANZ general manager specialist sales, Cosi De Angelis, said that as AI evolved, financial crime was becoming harder to detect because it is "often hidden within legitimate businesses, trusted relationships, and everyday transactions".
"In many cases, criminals are exploiting trust as effectively as they are technology," De Angelis said.
How to defend against 'routine' scams
Jha said that scams would only become more sophisticated.
"We'll see real-time deepfake video calls become routine, AI agents that run entire scam conversations end to end, and scams that combine stolen data, cloned voices and fake documents in one coordinated attack," he said.
"It is an arms race, and criminals adapt quickly to every new defence."
Between October 2025 and June 2026, ANZ customer scam losses fell by 24 per cent compared with the same period the previous year. During that time, the bank said it also prevented and recovered more than $100 million in scam and fraud-related funds.
ANZ said it is encouraging businesses to review their cyber security practices and ensure staff understand the warning signs of cyber-enabled scams and fraud.
"Technology will continue to evolve, but human judgement remains one of the strongest defences," De Angelis said.
Jha said there was real progress being made by banks, telcos and digital platforms using AI to detect and prevent cybercrime.
"Reported losses have come down from their peak in recent years. Banks are also intercepting and recovering more stolen money than before. That shows coordinated action works," he said.
But Buckland said in the meantime, large financial institutions needed to stop contacting customers by phone and email.
"If you get an email, there's actually no way you can absolutely be sure it's the right email. And if we get a call, there's no way we can be sure we're speaking to who we think we are, even if the correct number shows on the screen.
"So companies have to stop doing it," he said.
While banks were "lucky" to have physical branches, Buxton anticipated acting against these threats would be a problem for many organisations, in a future where the only trustworthy communications would be "in-person".
"If you can only contact your customers electronically, you can no longer be distinguished from a scammer," he said.
"So how's it going to work?"

Football: Lionel Messi plays final game for Argentina
October 7, 2026
Lionel Messi made his 208th and final appearance for Argentina on Tuesday night, scoring his 126th and final international goal as the Albiceleste beat Benin 3-0 in a friendly in Buenos Aires.
In emotional scenes at a packed El Monumental stadium, Messi stepped up to convert a penalty in the 71st minute, prompting wild celebrations from teammates and fans alike.
Earlier, the 39-year-old superstar had already set up goals for teammates Nicolas Otamendi – who was also making his final appearance for the national team – and Nico Paz – the youngster who is widely tipped to inherit Messi's iconic number 10 jersey.
"It was a source of great pride for me to wear this jersey," Messi told fans in an address after the final whistle. "I can only express my gratitude... not coming back anymore will be deeply painful."
"Gracias, Leo!" read an intricate drone show in the sky above the stadium at full-time, which concluded with the drones forming a profile of Messi's face.
Messi: 'Proud to be Argentinian'
Widely considered the best player of all time, Messi announced his retirement from international football on August 31 – barely a month after Argentina lost 1-0 to Spain in the World Cup final.
"It was a decision which hurts and still hurts but I know it's the right time," he wrote in a statement composed just two days after the defeat in East Rutherford, USA.
"I swear that I have always given everything and that I have always fought for this shirt to make you happy and make you proud to be Argentinian through football," he said.
"Thank you, God for making me Argentinian."
Messi: following in the footsteps of Maradona
Argentina may have lost the 2026 World Cup final, but Messi's crowning moment came four years earlier when he led his nation to glory in Qatar, beating France on penalties after a spectacular final had ended 3-3.
The triumph crowned an international career which hadn't always been easy as Messi, so prolific in club football for Barcelona, struggled to live up to expectations in his home country, where fans worshipped him as the successor to the great Diego Maradona.
He announced his international retirement once before in 2016 after losing three consecutive finals with Argentina – the 2014 World Cup final vs. Germany in Brazil and the 2015 and 2016 Copa America finals, both to Chile.
But he reversed his decision and led his country to the Copa America title in 2021, ending Argentina's 28-year wait for a trophy, before finally winning the World Cup in 2022.
Messi may have retired from international football, but he still has a contract with his current club, Major League Soccer (MLS) side Inter Miami, until 2028.

"Gryphon": Ukrainian forces combine robots with drones to strike Russians deep in the rear. Interview with the commander of "NC13"
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
05:30:00 EEST
11:30:00 KST

"Gryphon": Ukrainian forces combine robots with drones to strike Russians deep in the rear. Interview with the commander of "NC13"
In January of this year, the "NC13" strike UGV unit of the 3rd Separate Assault Brigade tested a new tactic deep behind Russian lines. Since then, the unit has successfully carried out more than 100 similar operations, turning what began as an experiment into a proven combat system.
The new tactic was named "Gryphon" in honor of a service member from the unit who went missing in action in 2023 while carrying out a combat mission near Andriivka in the Donetsk region. It was in this area, near Bakhmut, that Oscar-winning Ukrainian director Mstyslav Chernov filmed the documentary "2000 Meters to Andriivka" during a different Ukrainian counteroffensive.
The concept behind the new tactic involves deploying kamikaze UGVs, essentially ground robots, deep behind enemy lines using heavy bomber drones. After landing, the robotic systems continue moving toward their targets and can be used to strike key positions, logistics, and personnel while also creating disruption in the enemy rear.
The "NC13" unit was also behind an operation that drew significant international attention about a year ago, when Ukrainian forces captured Russian positions without deploying infantry, using only UGVs and drones.
As a result, two Russian service members surrendered to the robotic systems, after which the machines escorted them to Ukrainian positions as prisoners of war.
Today, the new tactic is part of the Third Army Corps' large-scale operation known as "Vivaldi." Since the start of the offensive, Ukrainian forces have liberated 176 square kilometers of territory (68 square miles).
According to the Office of the President of Ukraine, Russian forces suffered more than 5,000 casualties, including those killed, wounded, and captured, during the first three stages of the operation. It is currently known that Ukrainian forces have taken 250 Russian service members as prisoners of war (POWs). The Third Army Corps separately reported 2,000 Russian personnel casualties during the latest stage alone.
Approximately 80% of logistics and 90% of wounded evacuation for Ukrainian troops during all three stages of the operation were carried out by unmanned ground vehicles, or UGVs.
"NC13" commander Mykola Zinkevych, call sign "Makar," explains how the new "Gryphon" tactic works, how the idea of air-dropping ground robots emerged, what happened during the first operations, how Russian forces are reacting to the technology, and why he believes Ukraine is shaping the future of technological warfare.
He also discusses how Western partners are becoming less able to understand Ukrainian military technologies and, more broadly, the needs of modern warfare.
Can you please explain, in general, what this new tactic involves?
In general, this is a sabotage-operation tactic that was fully planned, developed, and implemented by the "NC13" strike unmanned ground systems unit of the 3rd Separate Assault Brigade.
The tactic is genuinely new and has no equivalent anywhere in the world because no one had previously deployed unmanned ground vehicles from unmanned aerial vehicles.
The concept itself is that, using heavy bombers, we drop small ground-based kamikaze systems deep into enemy territory, at a distance of 5 to 15 kilometers (3 to 9.3 miles). From there, we carry out different sabotage operations: eliminating enemy personnel, destroying logistics, and so on.
When did you begin using this tactic? Any first operation is essentially a test. How confident were you that it would work?
We carried out the first operation about eight months ago (in January 2026- UP).
We spent quite a long time developing the tactic itself and modifying the equipment because standard ground-based kamikaze systems are not designed for this kind of use.
The engineers spent a great deal of time making it work. The pilots also had to learn how to operate with these systems and deploy them correctly. The planning department, accordingly, spent a lot of time preparing the operation.
But when it worked for the first time, the excitement was incredible. Our first operation went 15 kilometers (9.3 miles) deep behind enemy lines. We deployed two ground-based kamikaze systems near the target, and from there, the systems themselves moved into the shelter.
It was an enemy staging point where personnel were brought in. They would stop there to rest before moving on to carry out their missions. We eliminated that staging point using two ground-based kamikaze systems.
What was the enemy's reaction? What did it look like from their side?
In fact, the enemy did not understand what had happened, what system had been used, what had struck them, or what tactic we were employing.
Even now, it remains a major surprise for them because we operate in different sectors within the Third Army Corps' area of responsibility.
We combine different technologies in order to change the rules on the battlefield.
We have been able to strike the enemy from the air at significant depth for quite some time. We have also been using unmanned ground vehicles to strike enemy forces for a while.
But this combination (UGV + UAV) allows us to operate at greater depth, in areas where the enemy does not expect to be reached and where they feel relatively safe. So we are going to take that freedom away from them.
How many such operations have been carried out so far?
More than one hundred. We always work systematically. If something works once, twice, or three times, we still do not consider it a fully established capability because it could be accidental.
But when something is carried out more than ten times, it becomes a systematic approach. We have SOPs, standard operating procedures, in place for this tactic: how to use it, where it can be implemented, and what its capabilities are.
It can be used for reconnaissance, mining deep behind enemy lines, striking targets, hunting moving enemy personnel, disrupting logistics, and more. We have fully developed this tactic, identified all of its capabilities, and now use it as a full-fledged tool on the battlefield.
War in general, and especially Russia's war against Ukraine, is a war of speed. Everything depends on who can come up with something new and adapt faster. Are the Russians already trying to do something similar?
I am confident that we are far ahead of the enemy. Even when it comes to the systematic use of strike unmanned ground vehicles on the battlefield, which we have been doing for about a year, the enemy is still far behind.
So when it comes to tactics like "Gryphon," which we are discussing today, there is still a very large gap between us and them.
But I would not rule out the possibility that, over time, the enemy will begin copying this approach and using similar methods.
In fact, during more than 100 successful missions, there have been many almost meme-like moments when the enemy had no idea what they were looking at and would actually approach the robots to inspect them.
There was one occasion when we managed to completely disrupt a Russian mechanized assault that had been planned for foggy weather conditions. At the time, we were actively targeting one of the enemy's logistics routes. We eliminated several personnel over the course of the day.
They started to panic because they did not understand what was happening. They thought a sabotage and reconnaissance group, or SRG, had broken through into their rear. As a result, they canceled the mechanized assault they had planned for that day.
So these small robots can create very significant disruption.
In general, there was serious panic among enemy forces at the depth where we were operating. And panic is actually very important because if we create panic within enemy ranks, they begin to have problems controlling their personnel. Soldiers start refusing to carry out missions, which then creates panic at the command level because commanders do not understand what is happening in their rear, and so on.
That creates destabilization, and all of that works in our favor.
Why exactly do they panic?
Even when you know what it is, you can become even more afraid. You do not know where it might be waiting for you, where it might drive, where it might catch up with you, and so on. So in some ways, it is even better when they know.
You know, now you have to watch not only the sky, but also the ground beneath your feet. Not just for mines, but because something might come after you.
There was one interesting intercepted communication where an enemy soldier reported to his commander that a "Baba Yaga" (russian military slang for heavy bomber drones - UP) had flown in, landed, then started driving and chasing them.
It was pretty funny to listen to.
But it did catch them in the end.
This tactic seems to have many advantages. Which one do you consider the most important?
- The absolute advantage of using any technology is that, first and foremost, we do not have to put people at risk. We preserve human lives.
For me, as the commander of a strike UGV unit and as a former infantryman, it is actually more important to preserve our own personnel, to protect Ukrainian infantrymen, assault troops, and soldiers, than it is to destroy the enemy. Destroying the enemy comes second.
And in fact, by destroying the enemy, we prevent them from advancing toward our forces and make life easier for our infantry. So above all, any technology helps us protect human life. Robots do not bleed, and human life is priceless. That is essentially our guiding principle throughout everything we do.
The next advantage, of course, is depth. The depth at which we can operate with these systems.
Yes, 10 to 15 kilometers (6.2 to 9.3 miles) is not the maximum range. Unfortunately, I cannot disclose the exact figures. But we are deployed and then continue moving very, very deep into enemy territory. The deeper we go, the more valuable, so to speak, the resources and targets we can destroy.
You touched a little on the future. Is there already a vision for how this technology could develop? I will not ask exactly how, but should we expect it to be scaled up further?
Yes. By the end of 2026, there will be many large-scale, exciting, and interesting stories, announcements, and new tactics from our unit.
We already have a number of newly implemented applications and tactics involving unmanned ground vehicles, (including the use of UGVs equipped with grenade launchers, which is also a new and unique tactic -UP).
It is simply not yet the right time to talk about them. And we have many more things planned. So we just need to wait a little longer.
Western countries have traditionally been considered leaders in military technology. You speak with foreign military officials. How well do they understand the technological breakthrough currently taking place in Ukraine?
I attended the Munich Security Conference in February and had the opportunity to speak with many foreign military officials, various partners, and government representatives.
In reality, they are very far behind. Absolutely.
They understand what we are talking about, what we are deploying, what we are using, and how it works. But they do not fully understand its importance and value on the battlefield, or just how much the battlefield itself has changed.
And I am more than certain that the rest of the world is lagging very, very far behind.
Even the technologies I see being introduced into militaries around the world are still quite far removed from what is actually being used on the battlefield between Ukraine and Russia.
Looking specifically at unmanned ground vehicles, I have seen their entire evolution on the front line, from 2024 until today.
We work, interact, and collaborate with many manufacturers. A great deal of equipment has been developed because we provided our expertise and doctrine.
I also have a certain number of systems produced by foreign manufacturers, and there is a very significant difference between them (Ukrainian and Western UGVs - UP).
We are not even talking about price, although the prices are extremely high. But in terms of actual battlefield use, Western systems still fall far short of the needs of the modern battlefield.
Are foreign partners reaching out to Ukrainian military personnel often enough for this kind of expertise? Is there interest in contributing to the development of these innovations?
I would say they do reach out, but not nearly as actively as they should. In my opinion, this is the kind of expertise people should be actively pursuing, not just occasionally asking, "So, what are you working on?"
No one knows what will happen in the world tomorrow. We live in a time when you never know what to expect.
If Ukraine can offer something to its partners, what can it receive from them in return?
Ukraine is the sword and shield of Europe. It is defending not only itself and its own future, but the future of the entire continent.
So every time other countries help us, they should understand that they are not only helping Ukrainians. They are also helping themselves.
Right now, Ukraine especially needs effective and timely weapons deliveries from its partners. First and foremost, this means air defense systems capable of protecting Ukrainian cities from attacks, as well as heavy weapons, including artillery and armored vehicles, that can help Ukraine regain the initiative on the battlefield.
Of course, this support must always be justified. Because Ukraine is doing everything possible to defend its territory, - liberate occupied land, and protect the future of the country and the nation, - that is why all of these processes and technologies have emerged.
The battlefield has effectively become a testing ground for innovation. On the one hand, that is a positive thing.
But on the other hand, it is deeply tragic, because every such achievement comes at a price. And that price is not paid in money. It is paid with the lives of Ukrainian service members and people who should have been the future of the Ukrainian nation.
History has seen many cases where a promising technology or a major breakthrough emerged, but it was overlooked, underfunded, or never scaled up...
This is not something that appeared only today. It is something that has been developed and planned over a period of time, has already been implemented for quite a while, and is constantly being modernized.
It will continue to evolve and eventually grow into something new.
Because there are technologies that work today. There are technologies that will work tomorrow. And there are technologies that worked yesterday but no longer work today.
But each of them becomes a driving force behind the next one.
Kateryna Lisunova, Ukrainska Pravda

Animals may have evolved 200 million years earlier than we thought
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
02:29:56 UTC
11:29:56 KST

Animals may have evolved 200 million years earlier than we thought
- Date:
- October 6, 2026
- Source:
- University of Oxford
- Summary:
- New research suggests animals could have evolved as early as 800 to 700 million years ago, roughly 200 million years earlier than some previous estimates. If so, the first animals may have lived before or during Snowball Earth, leaving behind little trace because their soft bodies were rarely preserved.
- Share:
New research suggests animals may have evolved up to 200 million years before they first appear clearly in the fossil record, challenging a key assumption scientists have used to estimate when animal life began.
A study led by the University of Oxford suggests the earliest animals may have existed hundreds of millions of years before the first unmistakable animal fossils appear. The findings, published Oct. 2 in Science Advances, indicate that animals could have originated deep in the Neoproterozoic Era, possibly before some of the most severe ice ages in Earth's history.
The research could reshape scientists' understanding of a major evolutionary puzzle. Animals seem to appear relatively abruptly in the fossil record shortly before the Cambrian Period (539 to 487 million years ago), even though other lines of evidence have long suggested their evolutionary story began much earlier.
At the center of the new study is a question about how researchers have used ancient fossil deposits to place a maximum age on the origin of animals.
Rethinking a key fossil assumption
One important site is the Weng'an Biota in China, a roughly 590 million year old fossil deposit preserved in rocks of Ediacaran age. The site contains microscopic organisms preserved in exceptional detail, but none can be definitively identified as animals.
Because of this absence, scientists have previously argued that animals likely evolved after the Weng'an Biota formed. The reasoning was that if animals had already existed at the time, such an unusually well-preserved fossil deposit should have captured evidence of them.
The new research calls that assumption into question.
Mongolia fossils offer a crucial test
The international team, which included scientists from the University of California Berkeley, ETH Zürich, and Yale University, conducted an extensive study of exceptionally preserved microfossils from the Kheseen Biota in Mongolia.
The Kheseen Biota is more than 40 million years younger than Weng'an, although the two fossil assemblages share some species. Importantly, animals are already known from other locations around the world by the time the Kheseen Biota formed, including sites in Namibia and South China.
Researchers examined more than 140 samples, including material collected from previously undocumented locations, using scanning electron microscopy. Their analysis revealed exquisitely preserved new microfossil species, including acritarchs (tiny spherical organisms with spines and branching projections), along with embryo-like fossils containing internal cells.
Despite the remarkable preservation, none of the fossils can confidently be identified as an animal.
Senior author Associate Professor Ross Anderson (Museum of Natural History, Oxford University) said: "The Kheseen Biota breaks the argument that the exceptional microfossils of Weng'an mean we would have seen animal fossils in the assemblage had they existed at the time. The Kheseen microfossils are just as well-preserved, yet animals continue to be absent - despite the fact we know at that point they existed."
This suggests animals may have occupied environments different from those represented in the Kheseen deposits, or that the chemical conditions responsible for fossilization there were not suitable for preserving animal remains.
A potentially hidden history of animal life
Because animals were already present when the Kheseen Biota formed but still do not appear in its fossil record, the researchers argue that the absence of animals from Weng'an cannot automatically be taken as proof that animals had not yet evolved 590 million years ago.
Instead, the team examined much older fossil deposits dating from about 850 to 730 million years ago. These included the Svanbergfjellet Formation (Norway), Bitter Springs Group (Australia) and Chuar Group (Arizona, USA) -- all fossil rich deposits considered capable of preserving animals, although no confirmed animal fossils have yet been found in them.
These sites have previously been used to define maximum possible ages for the origin of animal life.
Using those older geological constraints, the researchers carried out molecular clock analysis. This technique compares genetic differences among living species and combines them with fossil dates and estimated rates of evolutionary change to calculate when common ancestors may have lived.
When the researchers used these older deposits rather than the younger Ediacaran Weng'an site as constraints, the estimated origin of animals moved backward by about 200 million years. The new range places the possible emergence of animals between 800 and 700 million years ago.
Clues from ancient chemical fossils
Other evidence already hints that animals could have a much deeper evolutionary history than their body fossils indicate.
Chemical fossils, also known as biomarkers, preserved in ancient rocks contain evidence consistent with sponges living at least 650 million years ago. That would place them tens of millions of years before the oldest definitive macroscopic animal fossils.
The earliest animals would likely have been small and soft-bodied. Without shells, bones or other hard structures, they would have been far less likely to survive the fossilization process than many later animals.
Their chances of being preserved would also have depended heavily on where they lived and on a rare combination of chemical conditions after death.
Did animals exist before Snowball Earth?
If animals originated between 800 and 700 million years ago, the timing raises an extraordinary possibility. Animal life may already have existed before Earth entered some of the most extreme ice ages in its history, or animals may even have emerged during that harsh period.
The Cryogenian Period began around 720 million years ago, when massive glaciers expanded across the planet during episodes commonly called Snowball Earth.
The new findings reopen questions about whether the environmental conditions associated with Snowball Earth influenced the origin and early evolution of animal life.
First author, PhD student Orin Lole Durbin (University of Oxford undergraduate at the time of the study, now at Virginia Tech) said: "Pre-Ediacaran animal body fossils still elude us, and this analysis does not prove that animals existed 800 million years ago. However, our new fossil evidence from Mongolia undermines one of the main arguments for restricting animal origins to the Ediacaran interval. Meanwhile, our molecular-clock analyses show how much further back their evolutionary history could extend."
Searching for the earliest animals
The researchers say future studies should examine fossil deposits from a wider range of locations, environments, and preservation conditions in the search for evidence of early animals.
That search should also combine every available line of evidence, including animal body fossils, traces of animal activity, and chemical biomarkers.
Professor Anderson added: "Until that evidence becomes available, the precise birth date of the animal kingdom remains uncertain."
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Oxford. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Orin M. Lole Durbin, Eliel S.C. Anttila, Derek E.G. Briggs, Francis A. Macdonald, Ross P. Anderson. Re-evaluating molecular clock maximum age calibrations revives pre-Ediacaran divergence estimates for animals. Science Advances, 2026; 12 (40) DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeg6289

Brazil to stay in BRICS after elections — Russian Federation Council speaker

TURKMENBASY, Turkmenistan, October 7. /TASS/. Brazil will not leave BRICS after the elections as the association benefits all its members, and its leadership should understand this, Russian Federation Council Speaker Valentina Matviyenko said.
She called BRICS an "established, globally recognized association" that is gaining strength and momentum, "enjoys authority in the world and plays a very important role."
"And more and more countries are recognizing this and want to become members of BRICS. Whoever comes to power in Brazil cannot fail to understand that participation in BRICS is a great benefit for Brazil because they have gained tremendous opportunities for mutually beneficial international cooperation and for developing their economy, where no one imposes someone else's will, where there is no dictate. This association is built on mutual respect and mutually beneficial cooperation. And it seems to me that whoever comes to power - it would be a big mistake if they were to somehow reconsider their participation in BRICS. I am sure that this will not happen because any elected head of state should be guided above all by national interests and the well-being of their people, and BRICS is precisely a benefit for all its members, including Brazil," she said.
Russia, Matviyenko stressed, "never interferes in the internal affairs of any country," proceeding from the premise that the decision regarding the future head of state is up to the people of Brazil. "Of course, we would like to believe that this is exactly what will happen, that foreign manipulators will not interfere in the elections and attempt to change the will of the Brazilian people," she said.
The runoff between incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro is scheduled for October 25.

Are Test cricket batters getting worse? The stats say yes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
02:22:30 UTC
11:22:30 KST

Australia's men's head cricket selector, George Bailey, pointed out some home truths recently when questioned on the woes of Test number three Marnus Labuschagne.
"Our batting group in its entirety, not just Marn, probably hasn't been functioning as successfully as we would like," Bailey said, and he's not wrong.
With the first of three Tests against South Africa beginning on Friday ahead of a mammoth run of matches against New Zealand, India and England, Australia's batting line-up will be scrutinised like never before.
Since the beginning of the Border–Gavaskar Trophy at home in 2024, Australia has played 18 Tests with only three batters averaging more than 40: Steve Smith (49.4), Travis Head (46.25), and Alex Carey (40.3).
Beau Webster (33.5) and Cameron Green (30.16) are the only other batters averaging over 30 during the period.
Australia's bowlers have repeatedly dug the batters out of a hole, with the team winning 13 of those 18 matches.
But Australia's batters aren't alone: Across all 12 Test-playing nations, the game has undergone a huge transition with batters fading and bowlers dominating.
The rise of T20 cricket, better balls and seaming wickets have all played a part.
ABC Sport has done an analysis of all Test batters over the past 40 years with the help of ABC radio cricket statistician, Ric Finlay.
We've looked at batters from one to seven and found the same patterns across all positions.
We could list a table of 40 years but to make things easy, we've broken it down to five-year periods that include every test played from the beginning of 1987 to the most recent Test between England and Pakistan.
To see the patterns, we're narrowing the numbers down to batting averages, run rates and average balls per wicket.
Looking at these figures, you can see that the average of all batters in positions one to seven peaked in the period between 2002 and 2016 before dropping back to the low 30s.
It's easier to visualise with a chart that shows the year-by-year average as well as a rolling five-year average to even out the yearly variations.
The period between roughly 2003 and 2014 is when averages were highest.
This coincides with a golden period for world-class test batsmen when the likes of Sri Lanka's Kumar Sangakkara, Australia's Ricky Ponting, South Africa's Jacques Kallis, England's Kevin Pietersen, India's Virender Sehwag and the West Indies' Shivnarine Chanderpaul, to name just a few, were at their peak.
The rolling five-year average is now at a 40-year low, but that only tells part of the story.
To understand more about the decline of Test cricket batting, two other charts fill in the picture.
The first is strike rate: how many runs batters score per 100 balls.
Batters' strike rates have increased across the board from 41.34 to 58.13: that's almost 17 runs per 100 balls, which is the equivalent of an extra run per over.
But while batters are scoring much faster, they're also getting far out more quickly.
Bowlers are now taking wickets faster than at any time in the past 40 years.
In 1989, top-order batters were lasting more than 85 balls between wickets in the rolling five-year average, while as of this year, wickets are falling every 58 balls — an all-time low.
From the peak to the current trough that's a fall of more than 32 per cent.
It's no accident that we're seeing so many shortened Test matches, like the two-day match in McKay against Bangladesh in August.
The overall figures are mirrored in virtually every individual batting position with averages on the whole going down.
In other words, we have seen a fundamental shift in the battle between the bat and ball playing out over the past four decades and right now, while batters are scoring more quickly, the bowlers are on top.
The same is true for Australia's one to seven batters.
Again we see the early 2000s peak in averages when Ricky Ponting, Matthew Hayden, Justin Langer, Damien Martyn and Adam Gilchrist were in their pomp.
The combined batting rolling average for positions one to seven is now at a 40-year low.
The strike rate rolling average is at an all-time high, although only marginally ahead of that early 2000s era.
But the balls per wicket figure rolling five-year average has dropped alarmingly from its starting high of 98.33 to its current all-time low of 54.26
That's a fall of almost 45 per cent.
To put it another way, opposition bowlers are taking Australian wickets almost twice as quickly as they were 40 years ago.
So, why is this happening?
Former Australia coach and batter, Darren Lehmann, who's currently coaching English country side Northamptonshire, highlights four major changes in cricket that are all linked.
The first is the rise and rise of T20 cricket.
"Now they [batters] just don't leave balls," he told ABC sport.
"They have to score off more, so they play more shots to more risky balls in Test cricket,"
"Hence they go at balls they shouldn't go at, which they normally wouldn't have 20 years ago."
The second reason, Lehmann said, was the state of Test wickets around the globe, which he said were spinning and seaming more and earlier.
"They've got more in them and that is a by-product of making sure you get results," he said.
Lehmann said the balls used in Test Cricket, the Kookaburra and Duke, had added an extra layer of lacquer, which meant they stayed harder and the seam stayed prouder for longer, creating more movement.
"Blokes are playing shots to balls they shouldn't because they're trying to score before they get one that gets them out," Lehmann said.
The fourth reason bowlers are on top of batters is the one that ties it all together: data analytics.
"You're honing in on the weakness of players better than you did in the past and you're relentless with that.
"So, if a bloke can't cover drive or doesn't play well off the front foot, you now target that area with more balls, and you don't go away from that."
"If a bloke gets out to a left-armer all the time, well you get Mitchell Starc straight on."
Sooner or later, the batter's lack of patience, the moving ball and seaming wicket combined with the bowler's knowledge of their opponent's weakness will result in a wicket.
Cricket's delicate balance between bat and ball has fundamentally shifted and the cost is two-day test matches like the Boxing Day Ashes test, which cost Cricket Australia millions.
Lehmann said wickets needed to get flatter or lacquer taken off balls in order to shift the balance back towards batters.
"There are consequences: two-day games in Test cricket can cost people their jobs."
Failing Test batters can also lose one of the most coveted jobs in Australian sport.
The ABC of SPORT

Australia top court rules against coal mine expansion, citing climate harm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
02:17:07 UTC
11:17:07 KST

Australia top court rules against coal mine expansion, citing climate harm
Campaigners say ruling sets a ‘binding national precedent’ requiring climate damage be weighed when fossil fuel projects are considered.
Australia’s highest court has ruled against the expansion of a major coal mine, finding that planning authorities had failed to ensure that emissions of planet-warming greenhouse gases would be “minimised to the greatest extent practicable”.
Environmental campaigners called Wednesday’s court decision the first ruling on climate change. They said it set a “binding national precedent” requiring climate damage be weighed when fossil fuel projects are considered.
In the ruling, three of the High Court’s five judges found that the expansion of the Mount Pleasant mine in New South Wales must be halted. Planning authorities, they said, were obliged to consider granting consent only with conditions ensuring that all greenhouse gas emissions were minimised, and had not done so in this case.
The case was brought by retired science teachers Wendy Wales and Tony Lonergan, who had fought for years to halt the planned mine expansion in Australia’s rural coal-digging heartland.
“Today the High Court has said what we have always known,” Wales said in a statement. “We cannot dig up coal, ship it overseas, watch it drive climate change, and then pretend the consequences have nothing to do with us and won’t be felt by us.”
The mine’s operator, Mach Energy, had sought to extend the life of the open-cut mine in the Hunter Valley by more than 20 years, to 2048, and to nearly double its annual output. Mach is owned by Droxford International, a subsidiary of Indonesia’s Salim Group.
Mach argued that coal exported and burned overseas could not be clearly linked to environmental effects felt near the mine.
The company’s proposal was initially approved by the New South Wales Independent Planning Commission. But environmental campaigners disagreed, saying every ounce of greenhouse gas released into the atmosphere made bushfires, floods and drought more likely.
“Today, the highest court in the country agreed that those decisions have to account for the damage they cause,” said Lonergan. “This isn’t the end of coal overnight. But it is the end of coal mine approvals that look the other way on climate.”
Australia is one of the world’s largest fossil fuel exporters, ranking among the top sellers of both coal and liquefied natural gas.
Anita O’Hart, a lawyer for Wales and Lonergan’s community group, said the “historic” ruling was expected to affect how future fossil fuel projects are handled.
“The High Court has confirmed that planning authorities cannot ignore the chain of causation from a project’s emissions through to real, local climate harm,” she said.
“This ruling will be applied by courts and planning authorities across Australia, and it will be studied internationally as one of the most significant domestic climate law decisions in the world.”
Mach Energy said it was “disappointed with the outcome” but accepted the court’s decision.
“We will continue to actively pursue all available options to ensure the long-term continuity of the Mount Pleasant operation,” the company said in a statement.

Empty nets in Latin America as fish flee El Nino
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
02:15:00 UTC
11:15:00 KST

Empty nets in Latin America as fish flee El Nino
ECUADOR – Fishermen along Latin America’s Pacific Coast are reeling in half-empty nets as ocean warming aggravated by El Nino causes tuna, anchovies and other top catches to migrate to cooler waters.
From Ecuador and Peru in South America, to Panama and Guatemala in Central America, some skippers have stopped going out all together as fish stocks dwindle close to shore in seas running at up to 6 deg C above normal.
“The water is warm,” Juan Ollague, 56, told AFP in the south-western Ecuadoran port of Santa Rosa, where hundreds of idle fishing boats are crammed into a small port.
After a night on the water, Ollague returned with just six small tuna.
“We came away empty-handed,” he lamented.
“Fishing used to be good, now it’s terrible,” fellow skipper Darwin Zambrano, 53, complained as he untangled a net that has not scooped up big tuna like albacore or bonito in weeks.
El Nino is the warming phase of a natural cycle in the tropical Pacific that causes hotter and drier conditions in some places, and cooler and wetter in others.
The 2026 “super” El Nino, which is expected to peak later in 2026, is already wreaking havoc in Central America, where drought is endangering animals and stunting crops.
The average sea surface temperature, excluding polar regions, reached 21.07 deg C in August, tying with March 2024 as the hottest on record, according to the European Union’s Copernicus climate change observatory.
The average sea temperatures off Ecuador’s coast rose by 2.5 deg C to 3 deg C at the surface and up to 6 deg C at a depth of 40m in the past 10 weeks, said oceanographer Jonathan Cedeno, who led a mission from Guayaquil’s Polytechnic University to measure the temperatures.
‘Losing money’
On Panama’s Pacific coast, Rigoberto Gonzalez said he has to sail farther and farther from shore to earn a living.
This means spending more on fuel, food and ice to preserve the fish on the small boat he uses to catch snapper, kingfish and barracuda.
“We go out with US$100 (S$128) worth of petrol, and when we come back, we earn US$150 from selling the fish, which has to be divided among four workers”, Gonzalez, 59, told AFP, on Veracruz beach.
In nearby Panama City, some fishermen have thrown in the towel and decided to remain in port.
“We can’t keep losing money,” Jesus Morales, leader of the artisanal fishermen’s union of Panama, said.
Farther north, in Iztapa, Guatemala, 50-year-old Eliseo Ovando said it now takes three days to catch what he used to pull from the water in a day, and complains that only commercial fisheries receive government assistance to ride out the shortages.
“The big fish eat the little ones,” he said, referring to the struggles of small-scale operators like himself.
In Peru, the world’s biggest catcher of anchovies, fishermen are turning to construction to feed their families as their tiny prey slips out of reach.
Economic ripple effect
In Panama City, the poor catches are visible at a wholesale fish market next to the dock that supplies the city’s supermarkets.
“Less is arriving” off the boats, said Carlos Nieto, a 46-year-old vendor. And sometimes the catch is “damaged by the heat”, he said.
Nieto now spends about US$600 a month on ice, “practically a whole salary”.
For now, vendors in Panama have not passed on their higher costs and reduced income to consumers in the form of significantly higher prices.
But in Ecuador, the world’s second-largest tuna producer after Thailand, the prices of mahi-mahi (also known as dorado) and swordfish have doubled due to the shortage, according to the industry.
In Santa Rosa, the sea’s dwindling bounty has a knock-on effect, leading to the temporary closure of food stalls along the port.
Francisco Orlando, who earns a living filleting fish, is worried that he could soon be out of a job.
“We’re hoping they (fishermen) catch fish,” the 37-year-old said as he sharpened his filleting knives.
“If they do, we work. If they don’t, we don’t.” AFP

concrete mini skatepark brings XPOME’s graffiti into Gabrovo
SKATEABLE is a project by Bulgarian graffiti artist XPOME, created for an ongoing exhibition on the history of skateboarding in Bulgaria at the Christo and Jeanne-Claude Center in Gabrovo.
