‘Nobody wants a new Greece’: Calls grow for crisis election in Romania
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

‘Nobody wants a new Greece’: Calls grow for crisis election in Romania
Far-right leader George Simion tells POLITICO Romanian president Nicușor Dan will face a campaign to oust him if he keeps refusing a snap poll to end months of deadlock in Bucharest.
Romanian President Nicușor Dan faces demands from allies and adversaries alike to call a snap election, the first in the country’s modern history, if his latest attempt to end five months of political paralysis fails.
The key NATO and EU member has lacked a fully functioning government since the coalition collapsed in May, and lawmakers have rejected a succession of Dan’s prime ministerial nominees.
Political parties are now weighing up whether to support Dan’s latest prime ministerial candidate, the diplomat Luca Niculescu, who must win a confidence vote in parliament within the next nine days to be confirmed in the role.
Advertisement
In an interview, Dan’s arch-rival on Romania’s hard right, George Simion, warned that no stable government can form without an election and accused the president of mounting a “blockade” against democracy because he is “afraid of us coming to power.”
Speaking separately to POLITICO, Dan’s most recently defeated candidate for prime minister, Member of the European Parliament Siegfried Mureșan, warned the country was already paying an economic price, with investment decisions being delayed. “Postponing early elections and staying in this stalemate situation would, at some point, also have economic negative consequences,” he said.
Bordering Ukraine, Romania has the sixth-largest population in the EU and plays a critical role in NATO’s defense of the region as home to a major military base and a U.S. missile shield site. The country has been plagued by political instability, corruption and a ballooning budget deficit in recent years, conditions that have fueled a surge in support for hard-right nationalist politics.
Since the coalition fell apart amid infighting over budget cuts in the spring, Romania’s deadlocked parliament has been unable to agree on a new government.
Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR) leader Simion, a staunch euroskeptic who has called for a halt to aid for Ukraine, told POLITICO the president must face his duty and give voters a chance to end the stalemate with a fresh election, or face being ousted. His party has been leading Romania’s opinion polls for almost two years.
Simion has been building support in parliament to censure the president, which he believes will gain momentum if Niculescu fails and Dan again refuses to call fresh elections.
Advertisement
“Everybody says, ‘OK, if this won’t pass, we will go to snap elections,’ but they do not know Nicușor Dan as I do,” Simion said. The president is “very stubborn” and could defy calls for elections even if all parties want them, he said. “In that case we will have the numbers of signatures and votes to suspend him at least, if not sack him.”
Dan has refused to contemplate handing AUR a role in government. He defeated Simion for the presidency last year and regards his rival’s politics as a threat to Romania’s pro-Western, pro-European direction. The president says he opposes a snap election because the campaign period would delay budget reforms and healthcare funding.
‘A new Greece’
The Romanian leu has weakened against the euro in the months since the crisis blew up. Simion urged international investors to remain patient and sought to reassure them that AUR would be fiscally responsible if it won power. “Nobody wants a new Greece,” he said. “We will do everything it takes to respect our commitments to our international partners and for them to recover the debts.”
The call for an early election is gaining traction in Bucharest.
So far, the leader of Dan’s former party, the Save Romania Union, has joined politicians from the National Liberal Party, and the leader of the Social Democratic Party and AUR, in suggesting an unprecedented emergency election could be required.
George Simion has been building support in parliament to censure the president. | Robert Ghement/EPA
Dan’s latest plan still has time to work, but political feuding between parties remains a problem. The Liberals say they could support Niculescu as prime minister if the Social Democrats do not get too much influence, while the Social Democrats say they want the PM-designate to take the country in a new direction — away from the austerity policies of the outgoing Liberal premier, Ilie Bolojan.
Advertisement
Mureșan, a pro-EU Liberal and European People’s Party vice-president, said the economic risks of prolonging the crisis were real. He told POLITICO a snap election could be inevitable, though this is not his “preferred” option. “The political uncertainty which exists now in the country can easily transform into economic uncertainty,” Mureșan warned. “We are already now seeing investors holding back on their investments, waiting with major investment decisions before they have more certainty.”
While Mureșan said he wants Dan to succeed, he criticized the delays in resolving the longest-running crisis since the fall of communism in 1989. “Had the president moved fast in appointing a prime minister in May and not delayed the nominations, we might even have had early elections [by] now, and we would be in a situation with a new parliament, and with a stable government with the four-year agenda,” he said.
“So, clearly, the options are narrowing down and are not getting better, following the prolongation of the political crisis.”

====================================================================================================

Can ‘Berlin’s Mamdani’ convince Jewish Berliners to trust the Left?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Getting into Gideon Joffe’s office takes some doing. Above the historic building in the heart of Berlin rises the golden dome of the New Synagogue, built in the 19th century. Out front, police officers ask who you are and where you’re headed. Past the first security door, your bag goes through a scanner. Then come more doors, all of them extra thick.
It’s not paranoia. Since the Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel by Hamas and the outbreak of the war in Gaza, antisemitism has surged across the Western world, according to a study by Tel Aviv University. Berlin — where senior Nazi officials gathered at a lakeside villa in 1942 to coordinate the murder of Europe’s Jews — is no exception.
Joffe, 54, who chairs the Jewish Community of Berlin, one of Germany’s largest, has grown used to a life under protection. For decades, such security has been a fact of Jewish life across Europe, with synagogues and schools fortified and, in many cities, guarded by armed police. But the situation has rarely been as bad as it is now, he tells me.
Advertisement
The Tel Aviv-born former businessman does not come across as a timid man: a firm handshake, a shirt straining at every seam and a deep and penetrating voice. Yet the mood at his conference table, where the community’s secretary general and its spokesperson also sit, is one of great concern.
The subject of that concern: The result of the recent Berlin election, in which the Left Party — a successor to the communist party that ruled East Germany until 1989 — came in first with 26% of the vote. It’s a record for the party in the capital, and more than double its previous result. Germany has been arguing about the consequences ever since.
Among the trio sitting at the table, the Left Party’s Berlin branch is seen as not just radically left-wing but also a hotbed of antisemitism. The party made opposition to Israel’s war in Gaza a central plank of its election campaign. While some Jews have declared their support for the Left, leading Jewish institutions have criticized it.
Elif Eralp takes a selfie while campaigning in the Marzahn district ahead of Berlin state elections on Sept. 15, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
At the center of the debate is Elif Eralp, the Left’s lead candidate in the Berlin election who has become the face of the party’s transformation. Under Eralp and a younger generation of activists, many with immigrant backgrounds in the Muslim world, the party has expanded well beyond its East German roots and built a new urban coalition around housing, inequality and opposition to the war in Gaza.
Eralp and other prominent Left officials concede there have been troubling incidents among their supporters, and have condemned them. At a party conference shortly after the election, Eralp pledged to “strengthen the diverse Jewish life in Berlin and combat antisemitism.”
It was an acknowledgment of an issue that has been central to her effort to become mayor. In Germany, a single party is rarely strong enough to rule alone; forming a government means weeks of haggling among parties that dislike each other to varying degrees. If Eralp is to govern, she will need to form a coalition with the center-left Social Democrats and the Greens. Among their demands: “combating antisemitism and protecting Jewish life,” according to a joint statement by the two parties.
Advertisement
“There needs to be a binding agreement that not only condemns antisemitism and affirms Israel’s right to exist, but also stipulates clear consequences for antisemitic incidents,” SPD state chair Steffen Krach told the German press agency dpa.
The Left’s new face
“Elif! Elif! Elif!” As the petite woman in the black bomber jacket enters the hall, her comrades rise from their chairs and chant her name in rhythm. “Elif for Berlin,” read the banners in big, bright red letters. Her first major appearance since the Sept. 20 election is in a small hall at the headquarters of Neues Deutschland, a newspaper that once served as the official mouthpiece of East Germany’s communist dictatorship.
Eralp — a 45-year-old lawyer, mother of two and the daughter of Turkish socialists who fled to Germany in 1980, the year of a military coup in Turkey — is the new star of Germany’s hard left. She has thrilled young women and Muslim voters in droves. Her plea for economic justice, especially on Berlin’s crowded housing market, is what won the election, say her supporters. Critics say her success mainly depended on mobilizing pro-Palestinian activists, including some sharply hostile to Israel.
Eralp speaks to the media in Berlin on Sept. 21, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
Eralp has been dubbed “Berlin’s Mamdani” by the press, and the comparison is more than cosmetic. Berlin’s Left borrowed from New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s playbook, right down to the political strategist who helped engineer his success: Morris Katz, a 27-year-old consultant who helped steer Mamdani to victory and flew to Berlin to coach Eralp this spring.
“If a leftist can win in New York, then one can just as well win in Berlin,” Eralp said after Mamdani’s 2025 election.
Where Mamdani, New York’s first Muslim mayor, promised city-owned grocery stores, Eralp promises neighborhood canteens with meals from €3. She wants a rent cap for the Berlin’s publicly owned housing and the “socialization” of big corporate landlords, taking public control of more than 200,000 apartments — which a majority of Berliners backed in a 2021 referendum. Mamdani had his potholes; Eralp has Berlin’s “garbage chaos.” Both have proven that rent bills and trash cans can win big-city elections. And both have had to rebut the same accusation of antisemitism, either personally or within their ranks.
Advertisement
Mamdani — a fierce critic of Israel who has called for the country’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to be arrested — spent his campaign declining to condemn the slogan “globalize the intifada,” while saying he doesn’t use it himself and that it pains him to be called an antisemite. He eventually said he would discourage use of the phrase.
Since taking office, Mamdani has also sought to address the concerns of Jewish New Yorkers. In late September, he announced his city’s first municipal strategy to combat antisemitism, vowing that Jews in the city would be “safe and celebrated.”
Eralp, who like Mamdani calls herself a “democratic socialist,” faces similar skepticism from much of her city’s Jewish community. While international debate about antisemitism in the country has focused on the rise of the far-right Alternative for Germany party, since the election in Berlin, the controversy has centered on the Left.
Zohran Mamdani waves onstage in New York City on Oct. 3, 2026. | John Nacion/Getty Images
The party’s Berlin platform explicitly opposes antisemitism, but Eralp’s critics are not interested in what’s on paper. Instead, they point to an unofficial picture assembled from numerous examples: a campaign poster demanding “Freedom for Palestine”; the Berlin youth wing of the party that attributes a “colonial and racist character” to the “Israeli state project”; a rapper who shouted “Yalla yalla intifada” and “Death, death to the IDF” — Israel’s army — at a campaign event; and the appearance of a leading supporter of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, an EU- and U.S.-designated terrorist organization, at a Left victory party in Berlin.
Opposition to Israel’s policies in Gaza is not the same as antisemitism, and Eralp has condemned the appearances of the rapper and the PFLP supporter, blaming local party officials. But that hasn’t convinced her critics. Josef Schuster, president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, has dismissed her expressions of concern about antisemitism as “lip service.”
Balancing act
Nowhere in Berlin has the Left changed more than in Friedrichshain-Kreuzberg, a borough of about 267,000 people. For decades, it was a stronghold of the Green Party. This time the Left won 44% there, more than double its previous result. The local party used to be run by old-school socialists, many of them veterans of the Socialist Unity Party, or SED, which ruled East Germany as a one-party dictatorship until the Berlin Wall fell in 1989.
Advertisement
Today, it is driven by young activists who have expanded the party’s base into immigrant communities, above all among young Muslims. For many of them, the principles that have guided German politics since the Holocaust — the duty to protect Jewish life and solidarity with Israel — carry little weight, and some reject them outright.
That leaves Eralp with a delicate balancing act: reassuring Jewish Berliners concerned about elements of her party while holding together the coalition that helped propel it to victory. In her first major speech after the election, she tried to do both.
The Left’s vision of an affordable and good life, she said to applause, had been stronger “than all attacks and stronger than the hatred.” She would not be showered with insults by the “most unpopular chancellor of all time” — a swipe at Merz — and other politicians in the federal government.
Israel supporters hold flags as people march to commemorate the anniversary of the Nakba, in Berlin on May 16, 2026. | Michele Tantussi/Getty Images
These centrist politicians, Eralp continued, were dividing the country, cutting labor rights and pensions and adopting the anti-migrant positions of the Alternative for Germany (AfD), the far-right party on track to secure its first state government after a breakthrough election last month. “While a fascist party in Saxony-Anhalt is on its way to power, these people seriously think they can stop a democratic party that stands for social justice, diversity and democracy with this smear campaign,” she said.
Next, Eralp presented an offer of reconciliation: The point was to “build bridges and bring people back together.” Then she offered a kind of self-criticism, but without getting specific. The Left, too, she said, must be clear “that there must never be calls for violence, and that statements that frighten Jewish people can never come from our platforms.”
Here, too, there was applause. But quite a few listeners had their arms folded. Some wore Palestinian scarves, known as keffiyehs, around their necks.
Advertisement
Eralp was not available after the party meeting, and her party’s co-chair, Ines Schwerdtner, declined an interview.
“Leave this country”
Michael Wolffsohn has grim advice for Jewish Berliners. The prominent historian and conservative commentator was born in Tel Aviv to a family of Jewish merchants from Berlin, who fled the Nazis for Palestine in 1939. As a boy, he came back with his parents to West Berlin.
In the magazine Cicero, Wolffsohn, 79, said what he would tell a young Jewish Berliner who asks whether to stay: with a heavy heart, “Leave this city and this country.” He himself, he added, was too old to uproot. Were he younger, he, too, would leave.
It is not hard to see why Berlin’s estimated 20,000 to 40,000 Jews are on edge. In the five years before the 2023 Hamas attack in Israel and the resulting war in Gaza, RIAS Berlin, a watchdog that tracks antisemitic incidents in the city whether or not they are crimes, logged just under 1,000 a year. Last year it counted 2,197. The police recorded an even steeper increase in crimes classified as antisemitic: from 381 in 2022 to 2,268 in 2025.
RIAS follows the definition of antisemitism laid out by the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance, counting conduct ranging from insults and graffiti to statements at demonstrations. It says it did not simply count criticism of Israel’s conduct in Gaza or of the Israeli military as antisemitic, but did so when the situation in Gaza was used to disparage Jews collectively, justify violence against them or trivialize the Holocaust.
Some incidents were violent. RIAS recorded 39 physical attacks in Berlin last year, 16 of them in Friedrichshain-Kreuzberg. RIAS says multiple people who reported antisemitic incidents described becoming more cautious in daily life, including no longer openly wearing Jewish symbols after repeated harassment.
Advertisement
Speaking to POLITICO on the phone, Wolffsohn details his concerns: “Elif Eralp is the party’s star. But there is a broad base, and that’s what matters.”
Is the Left fit to govern the capital? His answer is categorical: “Is such a party capable of fulfilling the elementary task of a state — protecting its citizens, and not only the Jewish ones, at home and abroad? My answer is: No, absolutely not. The Left does not disqualify itself through opinions but through its demonstrable activities.”
A volunteer attaches portraits of Israelis killed since the Oct. 7, 2023 attack by Hamas at a commemorative installation in front of the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin on October 7, 2025. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
Wolffsohn says he wouldn’t take a coalition contract at its word. Or a potential agreement that would commit all partners to fight antisemitism. “Paper is patient,” he says, using a German proverb: Paper will accept anything written on it.
At the moment, there isn’t even paper. Berlin’s leaders of the Left, the Social Democrats and the Greens have been meeting over the past week in “constructive” preliminary talks. They are gathering for a third round Wednesday, but have not yet agreed on a common line on antisemitism.
The trust test
Joffe, the chair of Berlin’s Jewish Community, extends the blame for rising antisemitism to Germany’s mainstream parties, which he says failed to tackle the problem. “I don’t know a single Jewish community member who is sure that his children or grandchildren will still be living in Germany.” A 2024 survey of more than 2,500 Jews across Germany found that more than half considered it unsafe to live visibly as a Jew in their city, while three-quarters said they felt less safe since Oct. 7, 2023.
In his heavily secured office, Joffe says he understands why many people find Eralp likeable. “She’s nobody’s fool, and she knows how to express herself,” he tells me. “But the antisemitic spirits in her party — she probably won’t be able to get them back into the bottle.”
Advertisement
Joffe often pauses to choose his words carefully. “There have been many statements from the Left Party that have unsettled the Jewish community,” he says. “But I don’t want the issue of antisemitism alone to decide whether a coalition comes together in Berlin or not. Then conspiracy theories will just resurface that we Jews are so powerful we can even help decide who governs this city.”
His test for Eralp’s party is less about what the Left promises than about what happens in the capital in the coming years, especially in schools and kindergartens.
The Left’s Berlin platform promises to fight antisemitism “effectively,” but also warns against the “instrumentalization” of antisemitism allegations. Joffe worries that its broader law-and-order agenda — including proposals to reduce police staffing, curb police resources and loosen restrictions on masked protesters — would make it harder to contain antisemitic intimidation and violence.
RIAS recorded antisemitic incidents at a record 239 rallies and marches last year. That’s four or five a week. On Sept. 27, 2025, the Left was among the groups that called for a Gaza march that drew up to 100,000 people. RIAS documented antisemitic incidents at the march and rally that followed, including placards equating Israel’s war with the Holocaust and chants of “child murderers” — language the watchdog says either trivializes the Nazis’ industrial-scale murder of six million Jews or draws on the centuries-old antisemitic blood-libel trope.
To leave Joffe’s office, you walk back through the three security doors and past the police officers at the entrance.
“Our Jewish institutions are physically protected, but not defended against antisemitism,” he told me at the end of our conversation. “What do I mean by that? A cocoon was built around our kindergartens, schools and synagogues. But socially, nothing was defended.”
Advertisement
Eralp has promised to make Jewish life safer. Whether she can persuade people like Joffe that she means it — and can deliver — is another question.

EU quietly braces for nightmare scenario of multiple-casualty hybrid attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

EU capitals are quietly preparing for how the bloc should respond to a major hybrid attack that leaves several citizens dead — an outcome that looks increasingly likely, according to five EU diplomats and officials.
But the efforts to prepare are exposing splits on how much of a role the EU should play on security matters, and whether the bloc’s efforts are redundant with NATO.
The talks about a nightmare attack scenario have taken place in recent weeks among EU ambassadors from all 27 countries gathering in “restricted format,” meaning without phones or assistants. Discussions have ramped up since the discovery of an explosives-laden drone at Leipzig airport in August, said the diplomats and officials, who were granted anonymity to discuss the confidential exchanges.
While the EU has discussed such scenarios for years — unveiling a “hybrid toolbox” geared at coordinating responses to cyberattacks, election interference, and sabotage — the latest talks zeroed in on the risk of more serious attacks that cause large-scale casualties. Two diplomats said a meeting among EU ambassadors last Wednesday focused specifically on such examples.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the EU says Moscow has intensified a campaign of cyberattacks, sabotage and other covert operations across the bloc.
“Europe’s democracies are facing a growing number of threats,” European justice Commissioner Michael McGrath told POLITICO. “We are strengthening our capacity to anticipate and detect threats, improve early warning and ensure that Europe can respond quickly and collectively when our democratic resilience is tested.”
The talks among EU diplomats and ministers have focused on deploying emergency response teams, freeing up pockets of EU money to help the affected state, and how EU institution leaders should communicate, one EU official said.
“We have to be prepared for something serious,” a senior EU diplomat said. “Unfortunately, Leipzig showed us that a very serious incident, something that causes multiple casualties, is not out of the question.”
A second EU official added: “Given the scope and scale of Russia’s action there are bound to be casualties sooner than later. It’s sheer luck there haven’t been any yet.”
‘Very confusing’
The bloc is reeling from near-daily reports of so-called hybrid attacks — a label used by the EU and NATO to describe subversive activity that falls below the threshold of a direct act of war. On Tuesday, several sailors were declared missing after their ship was sunk by drones in the Black Sea, according to Bulgarian officials.
This followed the Leipzig airport incident, a suspicious fire at a Polish ground-link station handling Starlink communications, and a plot to plant incendiary devices in commercial transport hubs around the EU and U.K., alongside regular airspace violations.
“It is quite obvious that when Russia is using more and more lethal tools to test our preparedness and willingness to take counter measures, at some point there will be casualties,” said Teija Tiilikainen, director of the European Centre of Excellence for Countering Hybrid Threats. “At some point, intentionally or unintentionally, this is what happens.”
If several EU or NATO-member citizens are killed in what appears to be an attack, the pressure to act will be overwhelming on both institutions. “We’re very afraid that at some point an allied life” will be taken, said one NATO diplomat, which will make the “pressure very high” to act.
Yet EU-level discussions are prompting criticism from some capitals that the EU is overstepping its security role and potentially duplicating NATO’s core functions, the transatlantic alliance that has underpinned European security for 80 years.
“It risks being very confusing for decision-makers at all levels,” said Oana Lungescu, a distinguished fellow at RUSI and former spokesperson for NATO. “If there is confusion or duplication, that risks slowing down the decision-making, which has implications because time is always of the essence.”
Another problem is the EU’s lack of secure communications and suspicion that sensitive information shared during ambassador gatherings can be leaked, several diplomats said. Reports that Hungary’s ex-foreign minister shared the contents of leader-level talks with his Russian counterpart only deepened these concerns, leading capitals to restrict truly sensitive information to NATO formats.
“My government is very suspicious of sharing sensitive intelligence in Coreper or even in the leaders’ room,” said a diplomat from an eastern flank state. “It either shows up in the media or goes straight to Moscow.”
Overlapping protocols
The pushback coincides with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s efforts to bolster the bloc’s security credentials.
In her latest State of the European Union speech in Strasbourg, the former German defense minister pitched an “emergency security protocol” to help EU states coordinate in exactly the kind of scenario being discussed. The protocol, along with von der Leyen’s pitch to create a “European Security Council,” is expected to feature in a landmark “European Security Strategy” due out in early November, according to two diplomats.
But several diplomats pushed back, arguing these efforts would take months to set up and potentially duplicate functions that already exist inside the EU.
Instead of creating new formats that add complexity, one senior national diplomat said the EU should double down on the crisis-response tools it already has.
“We’re very uncomfortable about [the] emergency security protocol,” the diplomat said. “We already have mechanisms in place. If there is a crisis, we have the Integrated Political Response (IPCR) that worked very well during the pandemic and other crises.”
Putin doesn’t care
Established under the scope of the Lisbon Treaty, the IPCR allows the holder of the EU’s rotating presidency, at the request of an affected country, to call emergency meetings involving experts from NATO, the U.N., or other international bodies.
In the event of a major hybrid attack, the onus remains on the affected country to decide on the best way forward. France triggered the EU’s Article 42.7 following the 2015 Bataclan attacks, marking the only time the mutual assistance clause has been invoked. However, Lungescu noted this was a “political decision” by Paris that did not lead to major displays of mutual assistance beyond coordinating terror investigations between France and Belgium.
To avoid confusion over who does what during a mass-casualty event, Lungescu said both parties should divide labor: NATO handling intelligence-sharing and military deterrence, and the EU focusing on civilian response.
For Tiilikainen, EU efforts to coordinate responses to hybrid attacks are useful — within limits. However, she noted they are “not comparable with resilience measures at a national level,” such as Finland’s “comprehensive security” approach.
Lungescu also stressed that Moscow makes no distinction between the two organizations. “Frankly, [Russian President Vladimir] Putin doesn’t care whether decisions are taken by Coreper 2 or the NAC,” she added, referring to the meetings of EU ambassadors or NATO’s decision-making body. “This is not how Moscow thinks.”
Victor Jack contributed reporting.

What is celebrated on October 7 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
04:49:12 EEST
10:49:12 KST

What is celebrated on October 7 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
October 7 marks the International Days of Cotton, Decent Work, Safe Way to School, and Trigeminal Neuralgia Awareness. Religious commemorative dates are also observed.
On October 7, the world marks International Walk and Bike to School Day and Trigeminal Neuralgia Awareness Day. What other holidays and commemorative days are observed on October 7 — read in the UNN article.
World Cotton Day
An official international UN observance proclaimed by the General Assembly in 2021 at the initiative of the “Cotton Four” countries and with the support of the FAO and the World Trade Organization.
The event highlights the importance of cotton as a critically important agricultural crop and global commodity that provides income for more than 100 million families in over 75 countries worldwide, stimulates the development of the textile industry, and contributes to poverty reduction in developing countries.
World Day for Decent Work
Established in 2008 by the International Trade Union Confederation. The event unites labor organizations around the world to protect workers’ fundamental rights, ensure fair wages, safe working conditions, social protection, the elimination of discrimination and forced labor, and the development of quality jobs.
International Walk and Bike to School Day
A global initiative launched in 1997 that brings together millions of schoolchildren, parents, and educators in more than 40 countries worldwide.
The event aims to promote an active and healthy lifestyle among children, reduce traffic congestion and harmful emissions around educational institutions, and draw attention to the creation of safe pedestrian and cycling infrastructure, the development of safe school routes, and the reduction of the risk of child injuries on the roads.
Trigeminal Neuralgia Awareness Day
A worldwide medical observance dedicated to a rare and extremely severe chronic neurological disease — trigeminal neuralgia, which, due to the intensity of its painful attacks, is often called the “suicide disease.”
The purpose of the day is to disseminate information about the symptoms and diagnostic methods for this condition, support patients and their families, encourage scientific research in neurosurgery and pharmacology to find effective treatment, and increase physicians’ awareness to ensure timely diagnosis.
Feast of Our Lady of the Rosary
A Catholic liturgical feast established by Pope Pius V in 1571 to commemorate the Holy League’s victory over the fleet of the Ottoman Empire in the naval Battle of Lepanto on October 7, 1571, which averted the threat of an Ottoman invasion of Europe.
The feast is dedicated to the prayer of the Rosary as a symbol of spiritual protection and the unity of the faithful.
Day of Remembrance of the Holy Martyrs Sergius and Bacchus
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic faithful commemorate the Holy Martyrs Sergius and Bacchus — prominent Roman military commanders of the 3rd century during the reign of Emperor Maximian.
As secret Christians holding high positions at the imperial court, they refused to participate in pagan sacrifices, for which they were stripped of their military insignia, subjected to humiliating torture in Syria, and suffered martyrdom for their faith.
According to the old calendar, the faithful commemorate Saint Thecla of Iconium, the First Martyr and Equal-to-the-Apostles — a disciple of the Apostle Paul in the 1st century. Inspired by his preaching, she took a vow of virginity and refused to marry a wealthy pagan, enduring severe trials and torture for her faith.

India detains opposition leader Rahul Gandhi during massive election protest

Indian police have detained opposition leader Rahul Gandhi during a protest march demanding the resignation of the country's election chief over the large-scale deletion of millions of names from national voter lists.
Police intercepted Gandhi, a senior leader of the main opposition Congress Party, along with fellow lawmakers as they marched from parliament to the Election Commission of India headquarters.
Officers took Gandhi into custody after he climbed atop a police barricade waving the national flag, releasing him shortly afterwards.
Gandhi and his lawmaker sister, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, then barricaded themselves inside the adjacent offices of the state broadcaster.
"The country has been hijacked by Narendra Modi through vote theft," Gandhi told reporters from behind the building's iron gates.

The street demonstrations follow explosive revelations published last month by The Indian Express, which reported that two of the election commission's three panel members formally objected at least 14 times to key decisions regarding the roll revision.
The report disclosed that authorities have struck roughly 130 million citizens off electoral registries since the purge began in 2025.
Opposition figures argue the exercise disproportionately disenfranchises marginalised and minority communities, particularly Muslims, accusing the commission of doing the bidding of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
The Election Commission maintains the revision seeks solely to remove fraudulent registrations and eliminate "foreign illegal immigrants", though commission chief Gyanesh Kumar has declined to comment publicly.
Meanwhile, youth movements and left-wing student groups have called for mass mobilisations on Saturday, as India's Supreme Court ordered the government and the election authority to formally justify the revision decisions ahead of hearings next week.

MADRID, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- Mikel Merino scored twice in the second half as world champion Spain fought back from a goal down to beat Croatia 2-1 in Split on Tuesday.
The win extended Spain's unbeaten run to 42 matches and secured its place in the UEFA Nations League quarterfinals with four wins from four group games.
Merino provided the goals, while goalkeeper Unai Simon made several crucial saves to keep Spain in the contest.
Croatia coach Slaven Bilic, responding to his team's humiliating 7-0 defeat to England on Saturday, said he wanted a "game for men" and got the physical response he sought in a robust first half.

Simon made an acrobatic stop to deny Josip Stanisic and later blocked Igor Matanovic after a counterattack, only for Ivan Perisic to follow up and score from the rebound in the 20th minute.
Simon made another point-blank save to deny Matanovic shortly afterward before getting down quickly to smother an effort from Josko Gvardiol.
Mikel Oyarzabal wasted Spain's best first-half opportunity with a tame header from Aymeric Laporte's cross, while Yamal dragged a shot into the side netting.
Spain coach Luis de la Fuente replaced Alex Baena with Merino at halftime, and the substitution paid off. Merino equalized in the 60th minute after a clever pass from Dani Olmo, with Dominik Livakovic having earlier denied Yamal.
Simon produced another fine stop in the 78th minute after an error by Martin Zubimendi, who had replaced Rodri, presented Perisic with a chance. Perisic was sent off a minute later after receiving a second yellow card for a reckless challenge from behind on Marc Cucurella.

====================================================================================================

Eva Marie Saint, last star of Hollywood's Golden Age, has died at 102
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
01:42:46 UTC
10:42:46 KST

Eva Marie Saint, the last star of Hollywood's Golden Age, dies at 102
Eva Marie Saint, who has died aged 102, was showered in awards across her long career. Her performances spanned from her first stage appearances in 1942 to her final film appearance in 2019.
But while she was the last star of Hollywood's Golden Age, it was television's Golden Age where she began her long career. And it was television and then even newer formats like podcasting that sustained it.
Saint was celebrated as a film star, particularly for her landmark performances working with Hollywood's best directors, including Elia Kazan, Alfred Hitchcock, Otto Preminger and John Frankenheimer.
While her film acting led to awards and nominations from the BAFTAs to the Oscars, films are only one part of a diverse career.
She received an Oscar in 1955 for On the Waterfront and an Emmy in 1990 for the miniseries People Like Us. There was a Drama Critics Award in 1953 for The Trip to Bountiful on Broadway. In 2012, she received a Behind the Voice Actors Voice Acting Award for her work on the animated series The Legend of Korra (2012–14).
Her many awards, and even more nominations, reveal her astonishing capacity to reinvent herself not just in the roles she played but the media she appeared on.
Saint showed rare versatility by changing image and style and medium and format across eight decades.
The golden age of television
Born in 1924, before the development of television and even the talkies, Saint made her television debut in 1947 in Charles Dickens's A Christmas Carol.
Saint was fortunate to be in the right place at the right time for the first Golden Age of American television.
This Golden Age gave Saint and other actors not just employment but a national audience for serious drama.
Commercial sponsorship also meant actors like Saint were infamously obliged to advertise products as well as act.
Saint had an ongoing role in the successful TV drama Martin Kane Private Eye (1949–54). But sponsorship from the United States Tobacco Company meant the cast had to, not too subtly, advertise pipes and cigarettes by talking about smoking in each episode.
Television kept her fully occupied until her big screen debut in 1954's On the Waterfront.
A move to the big screen
Today, Saint's fame rests on two entirely different films: the intense black-and-white drama about dockside corruption in On the Waterfront (1954), and spy thriller film North by Northwest (1959).
From director Elia Kazan, On the Waterfront was Saint's breakout film role in a heavy hitting movie set among men who worked on the docks. Also starring Marlon Brando, the film received eight Oscars, including Best Supporting Actress for Saint.
At least one person wasn't a fan — Alfred Hitchcock wanted to use Saint in a more glamorous role and setting.
"It's drab in that tenement house. Women go to the movies, and they've just left the sink at home. They don't want to see you at the sink," Hitchcock told her.
Normally, one break out role would be enough for any actor. But Saint had two. Showing the cycles of invention and reinvention that propelled her career, Saint moved from black-and-white intensity to colour adventure.
The "Hitchcock Blonde" is a fixture of the director's films — Grace Kelly, Tippi Hedron and Kim Novak are among them — and in North by Northwest Hitchcock added Saint to their ranks.
Playing a femme fatale (or is she?) pitched against good guy Cary Grant, Saint stepped far away from the drabness of On the Waterfront in an adventure sweeping across the United States to the final exciting chase across Mount Rushmore.
North by Northwest remade Saint's image as a glamorous blonde but her film career afterwards lacked consistency: Exodus (1960) was a hit; All Fall Down (1962) lost money at the box office.
Back to television — and to podcasts
Saint began on television, and it was television that sustained her career.
After her big screen career declined in the 1970s, Saint returned to television with award-winning success.
She received Emmy nominations for How the West Was Won (1976–79) and Taxi!!! (1978), and appeared on TV in works as diverse as Frasier (1992–2004) and Moonlighting (1985–89).
Other changes involved a shift to the superhero film in 2006's Superman Returns, and children's animation in Nickelodeon's The Legend of Korra (2012–14). Finally, she was podcasting in scripted comedy The Pack Podcast, aged 98.
Other golden age legends like Olivia de Havilland lived long lives, but few remained so active across so many mediums as Eva Marie Saint.
Fewer still showed the same ability to change in ways that found new audiences and new media over a career of 80 years.
Marcus Harmes is a professor in pathways education at the University of Southern Queensland. This piece first appeared on The Conversation.

All suffering is a kind of loss. I want to escape from suffering, so I try to control my attention…
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
01:35:35 UTC
10:35:35 KST

All suffering is a kind of loss. I want to escape from suffering, so I try to control my attention and actions towards that goal. But in doing so, I lose the opportunity to reach the more joyful life that I could be living. That this loss occurs only because I’m attached to my own intentions is a tragedy.
I don’t need to suffer, but I do because I’m not well-accustomed to existing as the kind of being that I am. I reflect on my experiences and I automatically judge them to be good or bad, which means I form intentions about the world around me. This entirely ordinary human capability causes me to be sucked into attachment. And the result of attachment is always suffering and the loss of joy. This loss is not valuable. I do not gain anything by suffering more. I’ve already suffered enough to understand suffering, provided I’m willing to examine it.

Dr Zhisheng (Edward) Wen is an associate division head and senior lecturer in the College of Professional and Continuing Education at Hong Kong Polytechnic University, where he researches and teaches second language acquisition, translanguaging and cognitive science. 
Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s vision of an “AI city brain” is bold and timely. An integrated system linking data across transport, public works, environmental monitoring and emergency response could help Hong Kong manage risks more proactively and coordinate services more effectively.

IN BRIEF
- Richard Morecroft has died aged 70, after sharing his cancer diagnosis in July 2026.
- Morecroft spent almost twenty years leading the ABC's 7pm NSW news bulletin.
Former ABC News presenter and SBS host Richard Morecroft has been remembered as a generational talent.
Morecroft died "at a time of his choosing" on NSW's south coast on Tuesday, aged 70, following his cancer diagnosis earlier in 2026, his family said.
"We are devastated to lose such a warm, generous and caring human and hope that all those who knew him, if only through their TV screens, will remember him fondly," they wrote in a statement shared via Morecroft's Instagram page.
Morecroft moved from England to Australia aged 10, studying at the University of Adelaide before taking a post at the ABC via the university's radio station.
He presented ABC's South Australian news bulletin before moving to Sydney, where he went on to host the network's 7pm NSW news bulletin from 1983 to 2002.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Morecroft also hosted the quiz show Letters and Numbers on SBS and ABC's popular children's current affairs program Behind the News.
'A beloved part of Australian life'
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese described the former presenter as a consummate professional with heart.
"I was very sorry to hear of the passing of Richard Morecroft," he said on Wednesday.
"As the face and the voice of the news of the ABC, Richard became a beloved part of Australian life."
He reflected on revelations Morecroft, a passionate environmentalist, sometimes kept a baby flying fox under his desk while presenting the news.
"Richard was a great Australian and we were lucky to have him as part of our lives," Albanese said.
SBS Managing Director Jane Palfreyman said the broadcaster was "deeply saddened" by the passing of "one of Australia's most respected and familiar broadcasters".
"We extend our heartfelt condolences to Richard's family, friends and former colleagues, and pay tribute to his wide and varied contribution to Australian television," she said.
Morecroft hosted the SBS quiz show Letters and Numbers from 2010 to 2012, alongside Lily Serna.
"Richard brought warmth, intelligence and a dry wit to SBS's Letters and Numbers," Palfreyman said.
He introduced a "generation of viewers to the joy of words and numbers across a remarkable 450 episodes".
"These episodes continue to be repeated today, reflecting Richard's enduring appeal."
'Universally admired and respected'
Fellow ABC veteran and Australian Story presenter Leigh Sales said Morecroft took pains to welcome her to the Sydney newsroom as a junior reporter.
"Richard Morecroft was not only a consummate presenter, he was a true gentleman — generous and courteous to a fault," she said.
"He was universally admired and respected."
Hugh Marks, ABC's managing director, said Morecroft was among the "great broadcasters of his generation".
Morecroft shared an update about his cancer diagnosis to social media in July after returning home to the south coast from a long stint in hospital.
"Soaking up the last rays of the winter sun on a chilly Jervis Bay afternoon," he wrote alongside a beachside selfie.
"It's heaven to come home after nearly six weeks in hospital at the Chris O'Brien Lifehouse in Sydney."

US Vice President JD Vance has said that Iran must make a “meaningful” reduction in its nuclear enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the country’s seven-month war, even as Washington was unsure how Tehran makes decisions in negotiations.
Vance, a longtime sceptic of US involvement in foreign wars, has taken a leading role in negotiating a settlement to the conflict and brokered a provisional peace agreement in September that quickly fell apart.
In an exclusive interview with Reuters, Vance said any agreement would require Iran to reduce its nuclear enrichment capacity, rather than offer assurances of future nuclear drawdowns.
"If you don't want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60% enriched fuel? And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don't build highly enriched fuel.
That's a very basic threshold issue," Vance said.
"I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity."
Vance said the US remained open to an agreement but would require concrete Iranian nuclear concessions.
"We're not going to trade words for actions," Vance said.
Unclear how Tehran makes decisions
Vance said Washington is uncertain who makes decisions in Tehran.
The US vice president said that White House was in talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi. But it was unclear how much authority they wield within Iran's power structure, he said, after joint US-Israeli strikes at the start of the war killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei.
"One of the things we picked up on is it's not totally clear how their country makes decisions," Vance said. Separately, Trump said on Tuesday his "biggest problem" is no one knows who is running Iran.
Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Sunday that US officials are well aware of who their Iranian counterparts are and how Iran's decision-making system works.
Vance told Reuters he has held personal conversations with field commanders to gauge battlefield conditions.
He dismissed concerns over critical munitions shortages and added that while Iranian troops are periodically able to strike commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, they are largely unable to prevent energy exports through the waterway.
The war — and its $3 billion monthly price tag — has become a key issue on the campaign trail. Higher energy prices have put Trump and Republicans on the defensive in competitive states that will decide control of Congress.
Vance is seen as a leading Republican contender to succeed Trump in the White House.
Vance told Reuters afterwards that he had not decided whether to seek the presidency in 2028.
"I'm inherently a procrastinator," he said. "I really haven't thought about it much."

What happens in the brain when cannabis makes you anxious?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
01:26:07 UTC
10:26:07 KST

What happens in the brain when cannabis makes you anxious?
Scientists have pinpointed brain cells that may explain why cannabis can suddenly turn a calm experience into intense anxiety.
- Date:
- October 6, 2026
- Source:
- Northwestern University
- Summary:
- Cannabinoids may intensify anxiety by removing a natural brake on specific neurons in the brain’s fear center, particularly during stressful situations. In mice, shutting down those neurons sharply reduced cannabinoid-related anxious behavior.
- Share:
Northwestern scientists have identified, for the first time, a specific group of neurons -- cells in the brain -- that appear to contribute to anxiety caused by cannabinoid drugs, particularly when those drugs are combined with stressful conditions. Cannabinoids are a category of substances that includes THC, the main psychoactive ingredient in cannabis.
To investigate how cannabinoids influence fear and anxiety, researchers exposed mice to a threatening smell derived from fox urine. Before encountering the odor, the animals were given either a placebo or a synthetic cannabinoid drug.
Mice that received the cannabinoid froze more frequently and spent less time exploring the predator scent. Researchers traced these anxiety related behaviors to increased activity in a small population of brain cells known as somatostatin neurons. These neurons are located in the central amygdala, an area of the brain involved in processing fear and stress.
When the researchers genetically silenced the somatostatin neurons, the mice that received the cannabinoid became less likely to avoid the predator odor. The result suggested that these cells play an important role in producing the anxious response.
"The results of this study could explain why a good trip can turn bad pretty quickly if people consume too much cannabis or the situation they are in turns stressful or scary," said study senior author Dr. Sachin Patel, chair of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine.
The study was published on Oct. 2 in Nature Communications.
Tracking the Brain During a Threat
Patel and his colleagues gave mice several different doses of the synthetic cannabinoid and measured their reactions to the predator odor. The researchers recorded how much time the animals spent near the scent and whether they responded by freezing or fleeing.
At the same time, the team monitored activity inside the brain by implanting a small microscope into the mice's brain.
Researchers also studied brain tissue to determine how cannabinoids changed communication between neurons. Their experiments showed that the drug weakened a natural brain mechanism that normally acts as a "brake" on somatostatin neurons. With that restraint reduced, the neurons became more active.
"Higher doses of cannabinoids and environmental stress worked together to synergistically release the 'brake' on the central amygdala, which in turn drove excessive anxiety," Patel explained.
Why Cannabis and Anxiety Matter
Cannabis use in the U.S. has steadily increased in recent years. At the same time, emergency department visits involving adverse effects from the drug have also risen.
Previous studies have found an association between cannabis use and a higher long term risk of anxiety. Anxiety and mood disorders are also on the rise globally.
"Understanding how cannabis affects brain function to generate its psychoactive effects could ultimately reveal new ways to counteract negative consequences should they arise in some people," Patel said.
The researchers believe the findings may also have relevance beyond cannabis related side effects. Patel said the same neurons could potentially represent a broader target for understanding or reducing anxiety.
"Suppressing the activity of somatostatin neurons in the central amygdala could represent a final pathway for reducing anxiety symptoms, not just in the context of cannabis side effects," he explained.
Other Northwestern co-authors are Farhana Yasmin, Saptarnab Naskar, Danyal Zaidi, Isaac Kandil, Michelle Kwon and Dr. Luis Rosas-Vidal.
The study is titled, "Cannabinoid Modulation of Central Amygdala Population Dynamics During Threat Investigation." It was supported by the National Institutes of Health (grants MH100785 and K08 MH126166) and the Brain & Behavior Research Foundation's Young Investigator Awards.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Northwestern University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Farhana Yasmin, Saptarnab Naskar, Danyal Zaidi, Isaac Kandil, Michelle Kwon, Luis E. Rosas-Vidal, Sachin Patel. Cannabinoid modulation of central amygdala population dynamics during threat investigation. Nature Communications, 2026; 17 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-77957-4

Houthis launch missiles at Yemen's Aden airport as fighting intensifies
Unknown

Houthis attack Aden airport as fighting intensifies in Yemen
SANAA – Yemen’s Houthis attacked Aden’s international airport with ballistic missiles and explosive-laden drones on Oct 7, said the country’s Transport Ministry, as fighting between the Iran-aligned group and Saudi-backed government forces intensified.
Fighting has been focused in recent days on areas around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a shipping route that has become more crucial for energy exports since the conflict between the US and Iran restricted trade through the Strait of Hormuz.
This week, Yemeni government forces with Saudi-led coalition air support launched a counter-offensive to recapture strategic territory near the strait and around the town of Mokha that the Houthis had captured in September, but it is unclear if their advance will hold.
The fighting, a spillover from the wider US-Iran conflict, has revived a complex 12-year war in Yemen that led to one of the worst humanitarian crises globally and fragmented the Arab world’s most impoverished country.
The Houthis have repeatedly targeted infrastructure including airports, oil refineries and pipelines in Saudi Arabia, an American ally.
On Oct 7, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile north of the Saudi capital Riyadh. It said it was tracking the launch platform over the Yemeni capital Sanaa and would destroy it, but gave no details of casualties or damage.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said in a statement that the group had targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with several drones. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of an attack on the airport.
Battles over the strait
Fighting on the western front remains concentrated in the Dhubab district overlooking Bab el-Mandeb, with pro-government forces attempting an advance in the strategic hills to the east of that coastal plain, Yemeni military and government sources said.
Fierce clashes have taken place, with the Houthis claiming they have repelled attacks.
On Oct 5, the Yemeni government said it had reached Mokha, which sits at a junction with a supply route to the critical battleground of Taiz, but the claim was premature, according to Yemeni military officials and analysts.
Hussam Radman, a researcher at the Sanaa Center, a Yemen-focused think-tank, said pro-government forces including the Giants Brigade, a conservative Sunni Salafi group that has led the counter-offensive, are trying to take control of Dhubab and to advance in the mountains to its east.
Control of those highlands would allow government forces to more easily advance up the rest of the coast, he said.
Airport struck
Along Yemen’s coast to the east, one missile landed near the runway at Aden International Airport minutes before a flight from Cairo was due to land, the Transport Ministry said.
The authorities cancelled the landing and diverted the aircraft to Jeddah, while two planes on the runway were moved away from the area over fears of further strikes, it added. There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.
Aden International Airport is the main international gateway for parts of Yemen outside Houthi control.
The Houthis, who control much of Yemen’s north, seized Sanaa in 2014, prompting a military coalition led by Saudi Arabia, fearful of rival Iran’s influence in Yemen and chaos on its borders, to intervene.
A UN-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted heavy fighting, but it did not lead to a lasting settlement.
The Saudi-led coalition accuses Iran of arming, training and funding the Houthis.
The group, mountain fighters who have emerged as a force of tens of thousands with missiles and drones that threatens the region, denies being part of Iran’s Middle East proxy network, and says it develops its own weapons.
Tehran also rejects the allegations.
Earlier on Oct 7, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile launched towards the south-western Saudi city of Khamis Mushait, Saudi state television reported.
In a separate statement, Saree said the Houthis had attacked Saudi Arabia’s Abha International Airport and an airbase in Khamis Mushait with ballistic missiles and drones.
The Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm an attack on Abha airport. REUTERS

Awad Rjoob and Rania Abushamala
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Israel has refused to allow representatives of the Palestinian Central Elections Commission to enter Gaza and occupied East Jerusalem ahead of legislative elections scheduled for late November, a Palestinian source said Tuesday.
The Palestinian news agency Wafa quoted an unnamed official source as saying the Israeli government had denied the commission entry to oversee the electoral process. No further details were provided.
On July 9, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas issued a decree setting Nov. 28 as the date for legislative elections in East Jerusalem, the occupied West Bank and Gaza. If held, they would be the first such elections since 2006.
The commission began accepting applications to register electoral lists on Sept. 26, receiving eight applications during the first four days. Registration remains open until Oct. 13.
Palestinian Vice President Hussein al-Sheikh told journalists on Aug. 2 that an alternative arrangement would be pursued if elections could not take place because they were prevented or obstructed in Gaza or any other part of the Palestinian territories.
“The alternative plan is to form the Palestinian National Council by consensus, as the Palestine Liberation Organization is the sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people,” he said.
About 2.97 million Palestinians are eligible to vote, including approximately 1.59 million in the West Bank, 1.24 million in Gaza and 140,000 holders of Jerusalem identity cards.
The last Palestinian legislative elections were held in 2006, when Hamas won a majority of seats.
A political split followed between Hamas and Fatah. Hamas took control of Gaza about a year later, while the Fatah-led Palestinian Authority remained in the West Bank.
The Palestinian Legislative Council has been inactive since 2007. The Supreme Constitutional Court ordered its dissolution in 2018.

Italian Sports Day in Mexico City
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
03:12:12 CEST
10:12:12 KST

The “Italian Sports Day Around the World” was held at the Italian Cultural Institute in Mexico City, an initiative promoted by the Ministries of Foreign Affairs and Sports together with CONI. This year’s edition in the North American country’s capital focused on motorcycle racing, which was also celebrated through an exhibition of motorcycles in the building’s cloister.
                                    
Representing Ambassador Alessandro Modiano, Valentina Valente, head of the Economic and Commercial Office at the Italian Embassy, highlighted the formative role of competitive sports. “Sport teaches us to triumph through sacrifice, and without dedication and commitment, it is impossible to achieve anything significant,” she stated. The Institute’s director, Gianni Vinciguerra, then clarified the connection between motorsports and the humanities, emphasizing that “culture isn’t just found in books, museums, movies, or works of art.” Culture, he added, also involves sharing passions and a common memory, concluding that “yes, sports are culture.”
Italian technology was showcased by Ducati Mexico’s Country Manager, Daniel Konrad, who traced the company’s 100-year history. Finally, a roundtable discussion featured two professional riders, the Italian-Mexican Nicole Zanco and Abraham García, who shared the personal challenges and rigorous mental preparation required to manage the risks of high speeds.

Awad Rjoob and Tarek Chouiref
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Israeli occupiers injured four Palestinians in separate attacks across the occupied West Bank on Tuesday, including a couple whose home was besieged south of Hebron.
Dozens of Israeli occupiers surrounded the home of Yousef Shnaran in Wadi al-Rakhim in the Masafer Yatta area before assaulting him and his wife, leaving both injured, relative Ayman Shnaran told Anadolu.
He said the occupiers had earlier erected a tent just meters from the house before gathering there in large numbers.
Israeli soldiers later arrived but did not lift the siege, while ambulances were unable to reach the injured couple, he said.
Seven children remained inside the home.
Elsewhere in the Hebron area, Israeli occupiers attacked Palestinian homes and opened fire in Beit Ummar, according to the official Palestinian news agency Wafa.
Israeli forces also raided several homes in the town. No injuries or arrests were reported.
In the northern West Bank, two Palestinian farmers who are brothers were injured after Israeli occupiers attacked olive harvesters from Marda and nearby Jamma’in north of Salfit.
Both were taken to a hospital in stable condition, Wafa said.
The occupiers also stole olives collected by the farmers.
Israeli occupiers have carried out more than 14,742 attacks across the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since October 2023, killing 66 Palestinians, according to the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission.

UN should clarify criteria for neutral state status — Russian Federation Council speaker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
01:09:41 UTC
10:09:41 KST

TURKMENBASY, Turkmenistan, October 7. /TASS/. The United Nations should clarify the criteria for the status of a neutral state and update the concept in line with modern realities so that it is not "blurred," Russian Federation Council Speaker Valentina Matviyenko told reporters.
According to Matviyenko, Switzerland, which has traditionally been considered a neutral state, is moving away from this status because it follows the European Union’s directives and supports what she described as illegal sanctions, resulting in the "erosion" of the concept. Switzerland is not the only country behaving this way in today’s turbulent world, Matviyenko noted.
"I think the time has come for the United Nations to once again analyze its documents and provisions and ensure that if a state has permanent neutrality status, it strictly complies with all international rules established by the UN Charter and adheres to them. Perhaps the status of a neutral state should be clarified, perhaps updated in light of what is happening, so that the concept is not blurred and does not become merely decorative," she said.
At the same time, Turkmenistan, as the Federation Council speaker noted, is a genuinely sovereign state pursuing an independent and balanced foreign policy in the interests of its country and people. It is a state that does not succumb to any pressure, is not beholden to anyone and does not support illegal sanctions, she said. "This is exactly how countries with neutral state status should behave. And I want to say that Russia highly values Turkmenistan’s consistent position in maintaining permanent neutrality," she said.

Politicians slam Trump’s suggestion that Iran ‘take’ San Diego, Los Angeles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
01:07:21 UTC
10:07:21 KST

Trump says Iran could ‘take’ San Diego, Los Angeles; draws cross-party ire
Both Democrats and Republicans have expressed outrage at Trump’s remarks, as the White House disputed their interpretation.
Members of the Republican Party have joined Democrats in questioning remarks made by United States President Donald Trump about the California cities of Los Angeles and San Diego.
Much of the backlash came on Tuesday, a day after Trump told a midterm rally in Nebraska that Americans should be willing to make sacrifices to deny Iran a nuclear weapon — even though Tehran has long rejected accusations that it is seeking atomic bombs.
“It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe,” Trump said, seemingly in reference to the knock-on effects of the war, including rising fuel and fertiliser prices.
Then, he said: “They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego. This is a very small price to pay, and it’s going to be over with very soon.”
The White House said Trump was arguing that if Iran were allowed to secure a nuclear weapon, it could strike US cities.
But Democrats and some Republicans accused the president of suggesting that some of the country’s cities were expendable.
Gavin Newsom, the Democratic governor of California and outspoken critic of Trump, said the president was “deranged”.
“This is not only madness. This is dangerous,” Newsom said in a video on the social media platform X, in which he called for Congress to rein in Trump’s behaviour.
Trump has downplayed the impact of the US-Israel war on Iran – now in its eighth month – despite polling that shows the conflict is widely unpopular in the country. He has also repeatedly promised the war would end soon, though no lasting ceasefire has been reached so far.
Newsom, a possible contender in the 2028 presidential race, has clashed repeatedly with Trump.
Last year, the two faced off over Trump’s decision to deploy federal troops to California, as part of an effort to support a crackdown on undocumented immigration in the Los Angeles area.
In December, a federal judge ruled that the deployment had been illegal and ordered its end. Newsom, who opposed the deployment, cited that conflict in his remarks about Trump’s Nebraska rally.
“The president of the United States – the same one who sent in the National Guard into Los Angeles, sent 700 active duty Marines to the second-largest city in the United States of America – just invited Iran to take out Los Angeles and San Diego,” Newsom said.
He added that Trump’s remarks should convince those who “didn’t think the November election mattered” to vote in the upcoming midterms.
Some from Trump’s party have also expressed shock at his remarks.
Jim Desmond, a Republican running for California’s 48th congressional district, was among those who distanced themselves from Trump’s statement.
“I vehemently disagree with President Trump’s comments. America must stand up to Iran and defend our interests, but the first responsibility of our Commander in Chief is to protect the American people and our homeland,” Desmond wrote on X.
“No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage.”
US Representative Kevin Kiley, an independent who caucuses with Republicans and is running for re-election in northern California, also called Trump’s comments “unhelpful”.
But the White House has dismissed criticism of the remarks, calling it part of a “media freakout” that “is not rooted in reality”.
“He was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped,” Steven Cheung, White House director of communications, wrote on social media.
“America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money.”
California has the largest population and economy of any state in the US. Because of its population, it also has the most seats in the House – 52.
All 435 seats in the House are up for grabs in November’s midterms, along with a third of the Senate. Also on the ballot are key state and local races.
With Republicans’ control of Congress on the line, the results of the midterms are expected to weigh heavily on the final two years of Trump’s second term.

MPs want 130,000 trained civilians ready for national crises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
01:06:29 UTC
10:06:29 KST

MPs want 130,000 trained civilians ready for national crises
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
MPs want 130,000 civilians trained to support the police, army and emergency services during major crises, and have asked the cabinet to open up defence ministry facilities to help make it happen.
A majority in parliament backed a motion by the centrist Christian Democrat CDA on Tuesday calling for that number of so-called civilian reservists within 4 years, public broadcaster NOS reported.
The volunteers would not join the armed forces, but would be a support force around them. Their specific role would be to stop chaos breaking out in the first three days of a disaster, when the emergency and security services are not expected to cope alone.
According to NOS, they would be trained in 3 areas – technical, logistics and security – drawing on people such as mechanics, drivers and security guards.
MPs want the cabinet to help in kind rather than with money, by making defence ministry training grounds and classrooms available free of charge. The cabinet has said it shares the aim.
From 1,000 to 130,000
The 130,000 figure matches the long-term target of De BurgerReserve, a privately run organisation that began training volunteers last year. Its two-day course at the national training centre in Vught ends with a simulated disaster and is paid for by employers and private individuals.
The organisation has trained around 1,000 people so far this year, NOS said. Reaching 130,000 within 4 years would mean training more than 30,000 people a year, while the courses listed on its website take up to 64 people each.
Fears over cyberattacks and strikes on infrastructure through AI have spread rapidly this year, with intelligence service AIVD warning the Netherlands has not been at such a high level of risk since the second world war.
Catching up
The vote follows a government campaign urging households to prepare for the first 72 hours of a crisis. Every home received an emergency booklet over the winter, and in February half of households said they now stock emergency provisions accordingly.
Karen van Oudenhoven-van der Zee, director of the social and cultural planning bureau SCP, told current affairs programme Nieuwsuur that investment in the armed forces was out of proportion to the attention paid to people and society.
She said the 2027 budget sets aside €40 million for neighbourhoods and communities, falling to €20 million in the two years after that.
“When it comes to resilience, we have catching up to do,” she said.

Haiti postpones elections indefinitely amid gang violence

Haiti postpones elections indefinitely amid gang violence
Haiti has indefinitely postponed elections scheduled for December and February, the electoral council said Tuesday, citing technical and operational requirements as gang violence continues to disrupt preparations. The delay leaves Haitians without a democratic process as authorities struggle to register voters and secure areas needed for the poll.
Haiti, which has been engulfed by years of gang violence and political chaos, has indefinitely postponed elections due to be held later this year, officials said Tuesday.
Haiti has not held elections since 2016, and its last president, assassinated in 2021, has not been replaced.
The first round of presidential and legislative elections was set for December 13, and the second round for February 21, 2027.
"The period originally scheduled for the electoral campaign has been postponed," the Provisional Electoral Council's statement said, omitting any mention of a new election date and adding that the timetable "will be made public as soon as possible".
The council says the schedule will be updated to take into account the "technical and operational requirements of the process, as well as the conditions necessary for the proper conduct of the various stages".

It adds, however, that voter registration is continuing.
A member of the electoral council, speaking to AFP on the condition of anonymity, confirmed that "the December 13 date no longer stands", adding that "we are working on a new timetable".
As of Tuesday, only 769,000 voters had been registered since the process began on July 20.
Holding elections has been seen as a crucial step to stabilising the Haitian government and tackling rampant gang crime.
"I didn't have high hopes about going to vote this year," Davidson Jean Baptiste, a taxi driver in the capital Port-au-Prince, told AFP.
"Who can claim to hold elections in a country where the citizens are more concerned about insecurity and the abuses by armed groups?"
Some Haitians hope their country can get back on the path to democracy as soon as possible.
"The people have been long kept out of the political debate," said Claudette Piard at a voter registration centre in Delmas.
"We finally want to vote for a government that will bring solutions to the masses," she added.

Engulfed by violence
The Caribbean country, the poorest in the Americas, has long faced a political, economic and security crisis, but the situation has deteriorated in recent years as gangs step up killings, kidnappings, rape and child recruitment.
Of its approximately 11 million inhabitants, nearly 1.5 million are internally displaced by violence, according to the International Organization for Migration, which stressed that attacks were not confined to the capital.
Watch moreHaiti trapped by violence: Humanitarian aid deliveries struggle to reach local population
The security crisis has also presented challenges to organisers hoping to coordinate a vote across the country.
Several municipalities under gang control did not have registration centres, and the closure of roads from gang threats have prevented the delivery of electoral materials to several parts of the island nation.
The country's gang violence crisis has left at least 5,700 people dead or wounded this year while more than 1,000 women and girls have been raped, UN human rights chief Volker Turk said last week.

The figures, compiled by the UN mission in Haiti up to September 11, also include 230 kidnappings, though Turk said "the real figures are likely much higher".
A UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) is being slowly deployed to assist overwhelmed local police. The mission is intended to reach 5,500 personnel but currently only has about 1,500 so far.
The GSF replaced the Kenya-led Multinational Security Support mission, which was seen as under-equipped and underfunded.
The UN Security Council late last month approved a six-month extension of the mandate for the GSF with the resolution authorizing it, emphasising "the importance of ensuring security conditions conducive to holding free and fair elections".
