OpenAI came to Australia to apologise. It will leave without answering these key questions | Toby Walsh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
01:00:37 UTC
10:00:37 KST

OpenAI’s CEO Sam Altman was asked to appear before the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence in Australia and explain how and why their agents have been hacking into multiple government websites. Altman didn’t turn up but sent Jason Kwon, his chief strategy officer, instead to answer the committee’s many tricky questions on its first day of public hearings on Tuesday.
The committee is conducting a comprehensive inquiry into the economic, societal, regulatory, and national security implications of AI for Australia. It will report back to parliament at the end of November. This is an unusually fast pace, but then it’s an unusually fast paced technology.
Kwon spent much of the inquiry apologising for the company’s failings. A chief strategy officer would know there really was no other strategy than to eat a lot of humble pie and promise none of this would happen again.
Humanity was lucky that it was just the incompetence of OpenAI’s employees that resulted in these hacking incidents, rather than the competence of their AI agents. The hacks were relatively modest. For instance, as far as we know, no personal data was compromised.
But we now get a chance to prepare for much worse. Because you can expect AI agents to become much more competent, and AI hacks to be much more harmful. It won’t just be human hackers that understand cybersecurity that will be trying to hack into your website. And those AI hackers will be coming at you at machine speed.
Given OpenAI’s carelessness, it was disappointing that the committee didn’t lob a few harder questions at Kwon.
Someone should have asked him why OpenAI had no oversight for months over the swarm of agents hacking websites around the world? How many millions of dollars were spent on these experiments with no insight on what the agents were doing?
Someone should have asked him why OpenAI thinks it is safe to release Dots, their latest agent framework which puts similar technology into the hands of the public? OpenAI failed completely to monitor and prevent their agents doing harm. How do they expect random members of the public to do better?
Someone should have asked him why we should accept “bad things” in return for the benefits of AI (as Altman said in an interview on Monday)? We don’t accept drugs killing a few patients because they cure most patients. Or a few planes crashing because most land safely.
And someone should have asked him whether OpenAI is burning money so fast it’s cutting corners to get its products into the hands of paying customers quicker? For every dollar of income OpenAI currently takes, it spends about three dollars.
None of this needed to have happened. The problem is that companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are rushing to IPO to raise billions of dollars for their founders.
At the start of the aviation industry, planes regularly fell out of the skies. But we quickly realised that we needed to move more slowly, with strong regulatory oversight, to realise the potential of air travel. And flying now is the safest form of transport and the aviation industry is worth more than $1tn annually.
We could roll out AI in a similar, slower and more responsible way.

Gaza journalists pay heavy price after 3 years of Israeli war, with 263 killed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
01:00:04 UTC
10:00:04 KST

Three years of Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza have exacted a devastating toll on Palestinian journalists, with 263 media workers killed and hundreds more wounded, detained or displaced, according to Palestinian authorities and journalism organizations.
Journalists have lost homes, workplaces and family members, with many moving between bombing sites, displacement camps and hospitals to continue reporting.
They remain the main source of on-the-ground coverage as Israel continues to bar foreign journalists from entering the territory.
263 media workers killed
Ismail al-Thawabta, director of the Gaza Government Media Office, told Anadolu that Israel had killed 263 journalists and media workers during the war.
He said 50 journalists had been detained in Israeli prisons, with 23 still in custody.
“Three journalists remain missing: Nidal Suheil al-Wahidi, Haitham Jamal Abdul Wahid and Ahmad Issam al-Agha,” he added.
Israeli attacks have damaged or destroyed 16 satellite television offices, 11 radio institutions, 12 newspaper and magazine offices, 23 digital media organizations, 27 printing houses and five union and rights organizations involved in media work, he said.
Al-Thawabta estimated losses to the media sector at about $1 billion, including premises, equipment, broadcast vehicles and technical devices.
On Sept. 7, the International Federation of Journalists said the journalist death toll in Gaza was the highest in modern journalism history, noting that it reviews and updates its lists as new information emerges.
More than a fifth of journalists killed
The Palestinian Journalists Syndicate said in earlier statements that 27 women journalists were among those killed, while nearly 500 journalists had been wounded.
The syndicate estimates that Gaza had about 1,200 journalists, meaning more than a fifth have been killed during the genocide.
It said between 60% and 75% of surviving journalists had lost their homes or been forcibly displaced, estimating the number affected at between 700 and 900.
More than 80% of media offices and institutions have been completely or partially destroyed, according to the syndicate.
The destruction has forced journalists to report from tents, displacement sites and areas surrounding hospitals amid shortages of electricity, internet access, protective equipment and cameras.
Deadly attacks in 2023
Anadolu’s monitoring documented a series of killings of journalists while they were working or present at reporting and displacement sites.
Bilal Jadallah, director general of Press House-Palestine, a nonprofit that supports the development of independent Palestinian media, was killed in November 2023 when an Israeli strike hit his vehicle in Gaza City.
Jadallah also helped establish the Sawa news agency and worked to train journalists and provide them with safety equipment.
In early December, Anadolu freelance cameraman Montaser al-Sawwaf was killed alongside his brother Marwan in Israeli airstrikes in the Gaza Strip.
Montaser, who had worked with Anadolu since 2014, had survived an attack on his family home two weeks earlier that killed his parents and several siblings. Despite injuries to his eye and nose, he continued reporting.
Born in 1990, he was married with two children and had studied journalism and media at Al-Aqsa University. His brother worked in documentary production.
Al Jazeera cameraman Samer Abu Daqqa died after a Dec. 15, 2023 drone strike at the Farhana school in Khan Younis, Gaza because emergency rescue crews were blocked from reaching him for over five hours
Although his family lived in Belgium, Abu Daqqa had chosen to remain in Gaza to continue his journalism.
Losses continued in 2024
Journalists Hamza al-Dahdouh and Mustafa Thuraya were killed in January 2024 when an Israeli strike hit their vehicle west of Khan Younis.
Hamza, the son of Al Jazeera’s Gaza bureau chief Wael al-Dahdouh, had lost his mother and siblings in an Israeli strike on a house sheltering the family in the Nuseirat refugee camp in October 2023.
Photojournalist Hassan Hamad, who worked with several media outlets, was killed in an Israeli strike in northern Gaza in October 2024.
His remains were taken to Kamal Adwan Hospital, where his brother identified him by his hair and press vest.
Journalists killed in tents and hospitals in 2025
Anadolu freelance journalist Saed Abu Nabhan was killed by an Israeli sniper on Jan. 10, 2025 while carrying out journalistic and humanitarian work in the Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza.
In June that year, an Israeli attack killed Palestine Today correspondent Suleiman Hajjaj, the channel’s cameraman Ismail Badah and Shams News editor Samir al-Rifai.
Journalist Youssef al-Nakhala of Al-Watania Media Agency died of wounds sustained in an Israeli strike on May 31.
On Aug. 10, an Israeli airstrike on a tent near Al-Shifa Hospital in western Gaza City killed six journalists, including Al Jazeera correspondents Anas al-Sharif and Mohammed Qreiqeh.
Al-Sharif became widely known for reporting on bombardment, starvation and displacement in northern Gaza, which faced intensive Israeli air and ground attacks early in the war.
Qreiqeh worked with local media before joining Al Jazeera. His mother was killed during the Israeli military’s assault on Al-Shifa Hospital in March 2024.
On Aug. 25, an Israeli strike on Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis killed five journalists while they were working: Mariam Abu Daqqa, Hossam al-Masri, Mohammed Salama, Moaz Abu Taha and Ahmad Abu Aziz.
Deaths after ceasefire
Government Media Office figures show that the death toll among Palestinian journalists rose from 254 to 263 after the ceasefire announced on Oct. 10, 2025.
On Oct. 12, the office documented the first journalist killing during the truce: Saleh al-Jaafarawi, who it said was shot by armed gangs linked to Israel while reporting in the Sabra neighborhood of southern Gaza City.
Journalists killed by the Israeli military in 2026 included Al Jazeera correspondent Mohammed Wishah in April and his brother Ahmad, a cameraman for the channel, on June 20.
Others included Amal al-Shamali, Anas Ghoneim, Abdul Raouf Shaat and Mohammed Qishta.
‘Journalism without walls’
Beyond the human toll, the genocide has fundamentally reshaped journalism in Gaza.
With homes, offices and equipment destroyed, many reporters and photographers have worked from displacement tents and hospital courtyards, moving with their families while carrying whatever equipment they could salvage.
The Palestinian Journalists’ Syndicate has described this reality as “journalism without walls,” reflecting the loss of hundreds of journalists’ homes and offices as they continue reporting from displacement sites.
Since October 2023, Israeli attacks have killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and wounded over 175,000 in Gaza. About 90% of the territory’s infrastructure has been destroyed.
Despite an October 2025 ceasefire agreement between Israel and the Palestinian group Hamas, Israeli attacks have since killed 1,454 Palestinians and wounded another 5,090, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.

‘I’m getting fed up’: Early US midterm voters line up before dawn in Ohio
- - Early voting began in Ohio before dawn, and Democrats outnumbered Republicans on day one in Medina County, suggesting stronger motivation ahead of the 2026 midterms.
- - Voters voiced anger over high prices, political ads, and the US war with Iran, with many blaming Donald Trump for worsening economy and endless conflict.
- - Ohio’s Senate and two House races are tight toss-ups, and independents may decide control of Congress as both parties fight for votes.
AI generated
MEDINA, Ohio – Voters started lining up while it was still dark on the morning of Oct 6 at the Medina County Board of Elections as early voting began in Ohio, a state that looms large in the nationwide campaigns between Republicans and Democrats battling for control of the US Congress.
By the time polling in the north-east Ohio county closed for the day, the Democrats’ turnout eclipsed that of Republicans in a possible early sign that they are more motivated to vote in 2026.
Though turnout is typically higher in presidential elections, which are run every four years, the 2026 midterm voters in Ohio have a say in one key US Senate race and two for the US House of Representatives that are seen as “toss-ups”, according to the Cook Political Report.
Registered Republicans, Democrats and independents interviewed by Reuters all shared similar frustrations: They are exhausted by political ads they see as deceptive and mean, they hate the US war with Iran, and they really hate the inflation that they believe has become chronic.
Nobody said they expected things to improve any time soon.
The third person in line waiting for polling to open at 8am local time was Eddie St John, 83, a retiree from the town of Wadsworth. Asked what he most wanted to see fixed as a result of the election, which ends on Nov 3, St John said: “Mostly it’s our economy. It sucks.”
“You can’t afford nothing any more. Everything’s so high. Gas is getting worse all the time,” he said, adding, “This guy in office now, he promises this, he promises that... (but) nothing’s coming down.”
“This guy,” St John said, is US President Donald Trump, who is not on the ballot but whom St John blames more than political parties.
Inflation, war on ballot
The party in power usually suffers in midterm elections. With Republicans holding the White House and both chambers of Congress at a time when Trump’s approval rating is at a record low of 32%, Democrats are feeling increasingly competitive.
Political analysts will be watching closely what unfolds in Ohio, as Trump has been a dominant force, especially among blue-collar workers who used to align with the Democratic Party.
But with inflation running at around 3.4%, there is deep discontent over rising food, energy and housing costs. The US war with Iran, launched by Trump on Feb 28 for reasons that critics say he has not clearly articulated, also has voters worried that it will become yet another “forever war”.
Troy Flohr, 59, a retired policeman with the Medina County Sheriff, complained about the array of campaign ads that he said were riddled with “half-truths”.
Standing just feet away from a voting booth, Flohr said he usually backs Republicans but was still undecided whether to vote to re-elect Republican Representative Max Miller for a third term. “I tend to like the rest of them” running as Republicans on the 2026 ballot, Flohr added.
He said his nephew is serving in the US Army and stationed in the Middle East.
Without mentioning Trump by name, he said: “I’m tired of him saying the war’s going to end in two weeks, the war’s going to end next month... I’m getting fed up with that.”
Yet, Flohr said he would “probably” vote for Trump again, given the chance. “I don’t like where the Democrat Party has gone. I’m going to leave the rest of that comment alone,” he said when asked to elaborate.
Independents
Trump won Ohio and the state’s 17 electoral votes handily in 2016, 2020 and 2024 despite losing the 2020 presidential race to Democrat Joe Biden.
This election could depend on whether disaffected Democrats return to their party and whether many independents turn their backs on Trump’s Republicans.
Medina County, seen as a swing district, has 132,345 registered voters, of whom 29,466 are Republicans and 15,872 are Democrats. Election officials say there are 86,762 independents who could determine whether Republicans continue their success there.
Despite Republicans’ advantage in registered voters in the county, 499 Democrats cast ballots on Oct 6, compared with 374 Republicans, along with 291 independents.
That is a significant reversal from the first day of voting in 2024, when 369 Democrats voted, compared with 702 Republicans and 433 independents, according to county data.
Even more telling is data from the 2022 midterm election, when 198 Republicans cast a vote on the first day of early voting, compared with 139 Democrats and 68 independents.
Senate seat in play
Former senator Sherrod Brown, a Democrat from Ohio, is trying to return to the Senate, where he served for 18 years before being defeated two years ago by Republican Senator Bernie Moreno.
This time around, Brown, a populist Democrat who has long railed against US trade deals with foreign competitors, is attempting to unseat Republican Jon Husted in a special election, with the winner holding the seat through 2028.
Political analysts see the race between Husted and Brown as a toss-up.
With Republicans currently holding a 53-47 majority in the Senate, Democrats are hoping for a net gain of at least four seats, including in Ohio, in order to control the Chamber.
Close House races
Meanwhile, two neck-and-neck US House races could help determine the 2026 majority in that Chamber, which Republicans currently hold with a 218-214 margin. One independent is aligned with Republicans and there are two vacancies that will be filled in the midterm elections.
In the seventh congressional district, which includes Medina, just south of Cleveland, incumbent Miller is seen facing a tough challenge from Democrat Brian Poindexter.
While Miller has raised far more funds than his Democratic opponent and has Trump’s endorsement in a Republican-leaning district, his campaign has been hit by allegations of domestic violence, which he denies.
Poindexter is a labour union ironworker and member of a suburban city council.
Meanwhile, in Ohio’s ninth congressional district that covers most of north-west Ohio and hugs the shores of Lake Erie, Democratic Representative Marcy Kaptur, a moderate who was first elected in 1982, is battling in another toss-up race against Republican challenger Derek Merrin, who nearly defeated her in 2024.
Annie Wild, 64, a retired public schoolteacher, said she will vote for all Democrats on the ballot.
She also said that since the early days of Trump’s second term, she has begun to see some of the President’s supporters saying they are abandoning him. But that is not coming from the voters she calls “MAGA (Make America Great Again)”.
“I’ve lost friends that I’ve had for 50 years,” she said of some Trump supporters, because of the gulf between them. REUTERS

October 7: Hamas’s profit-and-loss statement - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
01:00:00 UTC
10:00:00 KST

On August 3, Ghazi Hamad, a member of Hamas’s political bureau, sat across from Piers Morgan for a half-hour interview. Most viewers remember the denial. Hamad said he was “100%” confident that Hamas never committed crimes against civilians, and that whatever happened at the Nova music festival, in the kibbutzim, and in the homes set on fire was, at most, a “mistake” by individuals.
The denial was shocking, and rightly so. It was also the predictable part of the interview. The important part came some 15 minutes later, when Morgan asked whether October 7 had been a strategic failure, given what it brought down on Gaza.
Hamad conceded that “we paid a big price” and moved straight to the profit column. Israel is isolated. Its prime minister is wanted by the International Criminal Court. And, in his words, “All the world now, they put the Palestinian cause on the table.”
Before October 7, he said, there were only Security Council meetings and Arab statements that changed nothing on the ground. Now there are “strategic achievements.” He closed the answer by saying Hamas had not changed.
This was a profit-and-loss statement, delivered by one of the people who signed off on the investment.
The massacre dividend
For Hamas, the massacre was an investment. The killing, the rape, and the abductions were meant to provoke a harsh Israeli response, the images from Gaza that followed, and the international pressure those images would generate. Call it the massacre dividend: the political return a terrorist organization extracts from its own atrocity once the world translates it into urgency to “solve the issue.”
Gazans paid the price. Hamad himself left the Gaza Strip before October 7 and never went back, as he acknowledged in the same interview. The dividend is being collected in European capitals, and Washington may be next.
Whoever rewards a massacre with statehood is inviting the next one, and not only in Israel. Paris and London are within range as well.
The Israeli wall
On the Israeli side, the picture is the reverse. The Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs has measured public opinion seven consecutive times over 30 months. Opposition to a Palestinian state has held steady at 64% to 68% of the public, and at 75% among Jewish respondents in the latest wave. Total support, including conditional support tied to recognition and demilitarization, has not exceeded 25% in any survey.
One figure is rising sharply. Concern about an October 7-style attack from Judea and Samaria climbed from 62% in February 2025 to 77% in September 2026. Even among left-wing respondents, a majority now shares that concern.
A poll captures attitudes at a given moment and cannot predict how the public will respond to sustained pressure. But three years on, this is no longer post-traumatic shock. Israelis understood Hamad’s sentence better than most of the West: a state established now would be credited to the massacre.
Pressure from outside
Europe reads the same map and draws the opposite conclusion. In September 2025, the European Commission proposed suspending part of Israel’s trade preferences under the EU-Israel Association Agreement. The proposal stalled, and Spain’s attempt to revive it in spring 2026 ran into broad opposition. Yet the economic lever is now legitimate in Brussels, and it has advanced alongside a wave of European recognitions of a Palestinian state. All this on a continent where the Islamist voice, in the street and at the ballot box, grows louder every year.
In Washington, the process is slower, but it cuts across party lines. If Democrats retake Congress in November’s midterms, the wing that wants to condition aid to Israel and impose sanctions will gain committees, budgets, and a platform.
And on the same Morgan episode, Joe Kent, former director of the National Counterterrorism Center, called for ending American funding of Israel and spoke of a new political movement on the Right. By 2028, the issue will be on every candidate’s desk.
Hamad was right about one thing: the issue is back on the table. The question is who will pay for it, the slaughtered or the slaughterers.
What is required
For anyone who still believes a Palestinian state would end the conflict, Hamad supplied the answer in the same interview. When Morgan told him he supports a two-state solution and a full Palestinian state, Hamad shot back: “So why should Israel exist?”
At the end of the interview, when asked three times for a yes or no on whether he still believes Israel should be annihilated, he would not say no. Instead, he called Israel “a big burden on the shoulder of the world” and said the world “should reconsider the existence of Israel.”
For Hamas, a Palestinian state is a stage. The destination has not moved.
Jerusalem must stop treating recognitions of a Palestinian state as symbolic gestures, and should put Hamad’s words before every international forum: Hamas itself is declaring that recognition is a reward for October 7. European capitals must understand that every economic measure against Israel tied to the demand for statehood is recorded in Gaza as a return on the investment.
In Washington, in both camps, anyone who talks about sanctions should answer one question: How much is he willing to pay an organization that has openly admitted the massacre was worth it?
The writer is the communication director of the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs (JCFA) and a former senior editor in Israeli and international media.

When Acoustic Control Needs to Move
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
01:00:00 UTC
10:00:00 KST

Acoustic design is often associated with permanent building elements, such as walls, roofs, ceilings, and insulation systems, which help control how sound travels through a space. However, not all noise sources or environments are permanent. A construction site changes as work progresses; machinery is replaced or relocated from one area to another; an industrial space may incorporate new equipment; and a temporary work area may emerge in a space that was never designed to accommodate it. Acoustic conditions are not static—they change over time and require solutions that can respond to these transformations. So, what happens when acoustic control becomes a flexible strategy?
Controlling sound does not always mean eliminating it. In many cases, the goal is to reduce sound transmission, contain it within a specific area, or minimize its impact on people working or living in the surrounding spaces. The challenge, however, arises when the source of the noise also moves. For example, introducing new machinery or modifying production lines in industrial environments can alter existing acoustic conditions without making it feasible to reconstruct the space each time a change occurs.
In these situations, portable solutions introduce a different approach by bringing acoustic control to where the sound is produced rather than permanently modifying the building envelope. Temporary barriers, acoustic blankets, curtains, and portable enclosures, such as those offered by Acoustical Surfaces, can act as a second layer that is installed, repositioned, or removed according to the needs of each space. These solutions can complement permanent acoustic strategies, transforming sound control into an adaptable element that can respond to changing conditions.
How to Design Spaces Intended to Change
When designing mobile acoustic systems, it is possible to recognize that certain needs are temporary. An intervention lasting only a few weeks does not necessarily require a permanent modification to the building. Similarly, a factory that regularly reorganizes its operations can work with elements that accommodate these changes without becoming obstacles to future configurations.
Acoustical Surfaces offers a range of solutions—including barriers, blankets, curtains, and enclosure systems—that can be used to create acoustic control zones around specific noise sources or temporarily separate areas within larger spaces. Beyond their acoustic properties, dimensions, or material composition, these systems make it possible to introduce layers of sound control according to the specific conditions of each situation. An acoustic curtain can establish a temporary separation; a barrier can define a work area; a blanket can help contain or reduce sound transmission around a specific source; and a portable enclosure can transform the conditions of a particular area without altering the space that contains it. Understood as temporary envelopes, these elements can act as lightweight infrastructure, modifying the acoustic performance of a space without architecturally redefining it.
For example, Acoustical Surfaces' Indoor Soundproof Quilted Acoustic Curtains combine sound absorption and sound blocking through flexible, modular designs. Custom-made to suit specific applications, they feature a dense mass-loaded vinyl core, available in 1- or 2-pound-per-square-foot densities, enclosed on both sides by a durable, quilted, sound-absorbing material. Suitable for industrial, commercial, and even residential applications, the curtains are often used to isolate machinery, separate noisy work areas, or create movable acoustic barriers. Designed for demanding environments, they are resistant to water and chemicals and can be easily installed, removed, and reconfigured as needs change.
How to Design Acoustics Without Compromising Flexibility
From acting studios to workplaces, portable solutions can transform not only the experience of a space but also the routines of its users. At Open Shop Studio, Acoustical Surfaces' STOP-25 fiberglass quilted curtain panels were installed to provide acoustic separation. The panels had a Sound Transmission Coefficient (STC) rating of 26 and absorbed sound on both sides. A track system was combined with interconnected panels joined by vertical Velcro seams, allowing the room to be transformed into a larger open space, divided into several smaller rooms, or configured to combine both conditions.
But this is not the only example of how design flexibility can intersect with acoustic design. In office environments, creating acoustic barriers between workers can sometimes be necessary to optimize workflows while achieving the desired levels of comfort and well-being. At Zamboni's office, however, the acoustic barrier could not be a permanent addition; it needed to be easily removable. The use of BSC-25 quilted acoustic curtains, featuring a 1-inch (2.5-centimeter) black steel tube frame that rests on the floor and a 1/8-inch (3-millimeter) thick high-density vinyl core, provided sound blocking comparable to that of a conventional 2-by-4-inch wood-stud wall with drywall panels on both sides. The screens were fabricated with the curtain material extending beyond the frame, allowing one panel to overlap and connect with the next.
Expanding the way acoustic design is understood means recognizing that not every challenge in contemporary spaces is permanent. While walls, ceilings, and insulation materials remain fundamental to establishing a building's overall acoustic conditions, mobile solutions such as those offered by Acoustical Surfaces can also address situations that cannot be fully anticipated during the design process. In response to this reality, architecture can rely not only on elements that remain in place, but also on systems that know when to arrive, where to be positioned, and when to be removed. Acoustic control thus becomes more than simply constructing barriers against sound; it becomes a strategy that can accompany the movement, transformation, and temporality of spaces.

Cornell names former acting US attorney-general to lead review on rape allegations

Cornell names former acting US attorney-general to lead review on rape allegations
Debra Kamin
- Cornell University has appointed Sally Yates to lead an independent review of a former student’s rape claim and the school’s sexual assault policies.
- The case has caused anger after Jane Doe sued Cornell, saying it mishandled her report and failed to investigate properly after an alleged 2024 fraternity assault.
- Yates will review support and investigation rules, while state and campus probes continue; the case has renewed national debate on campus sexual assault.
AI generated
Cornell University named Sally Yates, the former acting US attorney-general, on Oct 6 to lead an independent internal review of a former student’s rape claim amid growing outrage about how it was first handled.
Yates, 62, will also examine the school’s policies related to sexual assault allegations, including how they are investigated and what support is given to students, the university said in a statement.
Anne Smalling, the head of the committee that hired Yates, told The New York Times that the university was obligated to the woman who had filed the rape complaint.
“We owe it to her and to our community to take a hard look at what happened so that we can determine what we can do better around both prevention and response,” she said.
Yates and the white-collar law firm King and Spalding, where she is a partner, will “have independence in conducting the review”, Cornell said in a statement on Oct 6.
Students and politicians have demanded answers from Cornell after the former student sued the university, seven men, a fraternity and her sorority in September, claiming she was sexually assaulted in October 2024 at a fraternity party. She claimed the university allowed a culture to flourish that led to the assault, and then did not conduct a thorough and proper investigation after she alerted campus police.
Her claims have set off a wave of shock and anger across the country and renewed national conversations over sexual assault on college campuses.
Three weeks after the incident in 2024, the woman, identified as Jane Doe in court papers, filed a report with campus police, which was then passed to the Tompkins County district attorney, who declined to file charges.
All of the men have denied any wrongdoing. None of the men have been charged with a crime. Their fraternity, Chi Phi, has been banned from campus.
The university, though, conducted its own months-long investigation, which includes more than 1,000 pages of transcripts, text messages, hours of interviews with a dozen people and the woman’s statement to police, which she signed.
A three-member panel at the school met on Zoom over 12 days in May 2025 and expelled two men, barred one who had graduated from campus, suspended two and gave lighter punishments to the rest, according to the documents.
The panel did not conclude that Jane Doe was sexually assaulted by all the men she had accused, according to discipline summaries reviewed by the Times.
The district attorney, Matthew Van Houten, has said that the Cornell University Police Department only forwarded a six-page summary to him. But, according to the records, the police did offer Van Houten more evidence to review, but he declined to do so.
Governor Kathy Hochul rebuked Van Houten on Oct 1 and appointed the state’s attorney-general, Letitia James, to review the evidence and determine whether criminal charges should be filed.
It is a common practice for universities to turn to outside law firms when faced with a significant public scandal, and the reactions to those inquires have typically been mixed.
In 2011, Penn State hired former Federal Bureau of Investigation director Louis Freeh of the firm Freeh, Sporkin & Sullivan to identify what the university might have known about the allegations of child abuse against Jerry Sandusky, a former assistant football coach.
Freeh delivered a damning indictment that declared several leaders had known about the abuse and concealed it from law enforcement. Critics said he had overstepped his mandate.
Columbia University also commissioned Joan Loughnane, a partner at Sidley Austin, to conduct an external investigation into the school’s handling of sexual abuse allegations made against former Columbia gynaecologist Robert Hadden in 2012. In her findings, released in 2026, Loughnane documented systematic failures by administrators to address his abuse, but the university was criticised for the slow process of the report.
Yates is a high-profile choice for a role that will inevitably be deeply scrutinised. She previously led the US Soccer Federation’s investigation into allegations of abuse and misconduct in women’s professional soccer, and currently leads King and Spalding’s crisis management practice.
She has spent nearly four decades with the Department of Justice. She became assistant US attorney for the northern district of Georgia, her home state, in 1989 and rose through the ranks to become the first woman to lead that office in 2010.
She became deputy US attorney-general in 2015 under then President Barack Obama.
In that role, she wrote a policy memo, known as the Yates memo, redefining how the country prosecutes white-collar criminals.
In 2017, just days after accepting the role of acting attorney-general under then President Donald Trump, she was fired for refusing to enforce the president’s immigration ban. NYTIMES
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

09:36:41 KST

Two days after the state memorial day, Israel marks on Wednesday three years since the October 7 massacre. Most of the memorial and protest events will be led by the October Council, protest organizations and the Kumu movement, with events planned at some 400 locations across the country.
The day of remembrance will begin at 6:29 a.m., the time the massacre began, with a series of ceremonies, installations and events across the country. Events will be held, among other places, at the site of the Nova music festival in the Re’im forest and at Sha'ar HaNegev arches junction, where the flag will be lowered to half-staff. Demonstrations are expected at additional locations, while October Council member families will take part in displays and other protest activities in Caesarea and Jerusalem.
At 7 a.m., several organizations will hold memorial ceremonies outside the homes of ministers who were serving in the government on the day of the massacre. Ten minutes later, a vehicle convoy will leave Caesarea for Tel Aviv along what organizers are calling the “Route of Abandonment.” At 8:30 a.m., the women’s protest movement will hold an event at Tel Aviv’s Trumpeldor Beach under the banner “From Abandonment to Responsibility,” centered on an installation intended to symbolize the events of October 7.
At noon, the October Council plans to hold a nationwide minute of silence at hundreds of locations. At the same time, the exhibition “The Space Left Behind” will open to the public at the Peres Center for Peace and Innovation in Jaffa, displaying personal belongings of dozens of people murdered on October 7. A brief ceremony will also be held there with representatives of October Council families.
Throughout the afternoon and evening, a series of demonstrations will be held across the country. Demonstrations involving protest groups and October Council members are planned in Haifa, Afula, Tzemach Junction, Rosh Pina Junction and Sde Boker, among other locations. At 6:29 p.m., a ceremony will be held at the Nova site in the Re’im forest with bereaved families and members of the Nova Tribe association. At 7:30 p.m., a stage for testimony will open at the Arches Junction in Sha’ar HaNegev.
The day’s events will culminate at 9:15 p.m., when the Kumu movement and October 
7 families hold their national memorial ceremony at Yarkon Park in Tel Aviv. The ceremony will also be screened at locations across the country. It will be hosted by former hostage Eli Sharabi and actress Shani Cohen.
Kibbutz Nir Yitzhak began events marking the October 7 anniversary on Tuesday with community memorial gatherings, which will continue Wednesday in memory of kibbutz members who lost their lives. Artists from the Israeli Opera accompanied the families Tuesday, with performances in memory of those who fell and those who were murdered. Another gathering will be held at the cemetery at 9:30 a.m. Wednesday in memory of deceased kibbutz members.
The Eshkol Regional Council also gathered Tuesday evening to commemorate the 259 residents murdered in the massacre. Council head Michal Uziyahu said: “We will continue this journey together, demanding accountability and the establishment of a commission of inquiry, and ensuring that we create a different reality with meaningful security, not merely a sense of security.”
Southern Command chief Maj. Gen. Yaniv Asor said at the Eshkol ceremony: “The work is not finished, the journey of recovery is not complete. We are determined not to rest until we break their strength and their spirit. I would like to use this sacred platform to issue an unequivocal warning to Hamas: Any attempt to attack IDF soldiers or residents of the Negev will be met with a sharp and powerful response from us.”
In Hadera, a walking trail was inaugurated in the Beit Eliezer neighborhood in memory of Master Sgt. Boris “Buka” Danilov, in a ceremony attended by Mayor Nir Ben Haim and Israel Police Commissioner Daniel Levy.
The government, it should be recalled, faced fierce criticism over the fact that the state memorial day was effectively set by the same elected officials who were in office when the October 7 massacre occurred, none of whom resigned or acknowledged any responsibility for the failures. Bereaved families, hostage families and survivors of the massacre accused the coalition of trying to shape the memory of October 7 while obscuring its own failures, including by designating the war the “War of Revival,” rather than the commonly used “Swords of Iron War” or “October 7 War.”
On the other side of the debate, bereaved families from the Din V’Tzedek and Gvura forums gathered Tuesday evening at a protest tent in Jerusalem to demand the establishment of a “national” commission of inquiry.
Orly Cohen, whose son Amit was murdered in a roadside shelter near Re’im, said in a statement on behalf of the families: “We will not allow the establishment of a ‘state’ commission of inquiry whose members are appointed by a Supreme Court justice who stands at the heart of the social dispute and has lost the trust of broad sections of the public. The role of the court, which for years gave our enemies a tailwind, must be investigated. We represent hundreds of families affected by Octber 7 who do not trust a state commission of inquiry led by Supreme Court justices who will serve as the bulletproof vest for those who abandoned our security.”
Timeline of the war
Three years have passed since the surprise attack that shook the country. During that period, Israel has experienced a long series of dramatic events: from the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, through the ground offensive in the Gaza Strip, the campaign against Hezbollah and direct confrontations with Iran, to operations that expanded far beyond Israel’s borders and hostage-release deals.
This is a timeline of the major events that have shaped Israel since that morning plunged the country into the longest war in its history.
From the surprise attack to a dramatic rescue
October 7, 2023 — Surprise attack and declaration of war: The Hamas terrorist organization launches a massive surprise attack involving thousands of rockets and the infiltration of thousands of terrorists into Gaza border communities, IDF bases and the music festival near Re’im. About 1,200 people are murdered and 251 Israelis and foreign nationals are abducted to the Gaza Strip. Israel declares a state of war, launching Operation Swords of Iron.
October 8, 2023 — Hezbollah joins the fighting: The Shiite terrorist organization begins firing rockets and anti-tank missiles from Lebanon at IDF positions and northern Israeli communities.
October 8-15, 2023 — Evacuation of residents: Large-scale evacuations begin from Gaza border communities and communities along the northern confrontation line. About 60,000 northern residents are evacuated from their homes.
October 12, 2023 — National emergency government formed: The National Unity party, headed by Benny Gantz, joins the government and a smaller war cabinet is established to oversee the campaign alongside Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Yoav Gallant.
October 20-23, 2023 — First hostages released on humanitarian grounds: In the early stages of the war, before the ground offensive begins, Hamas releases four female hostages in two separate rounds following international mediation. On October 20, Judith Raanan and her daughter Natalie Raanan, abducted from Nahal Oz, are released. On October 23, elderly hostages Yocheved Lifshitz and Nurit Cooper, abducted from Nir Oz, are released.
October 27, 2023 — Ground offensive in Gaza begins: IDF forces enter the northern Gaza Strip on the ground with the goal of dismantling Hamas infrastructure and bringing back the hostages.
October 30, 2023 — Ori Magidish rescued: In a joint nighttime operation by the IDF and Shin Bet, abducted surveillance soldier Pvt. Ori Magidish is rescued alive from the Gaza Strip, days after the ground offensive begins.
November 24-30, 2023 — First hostage deal: A weeklong pause in the fighting results in the release of 105 hostages, Israelis and foreign nationals, in exchange for the release of Palestinian security prisoners and the entry of humanitarian aid. Fighting resumes December 1.
From the daring Rafah rescue to the pager attack
January 2, 2024 — Saleh al-Arouri eliminated: Hamas deputy leader Saleh al-Arouri is killed in a targeted strike in Beirut.
February 12, 2024 — Operation Golden Hand: Special forces from the Israel Police’s Yamam counterterrorism unit, Shin Bet and IDF rescue hostages Fernando Marman and Louis Har alive from an apartment in the heart of Rafah in a complex operation under fire.
April 13-14, 2024 — First Iranian attack: Iran directly launches hundreds of drones and missiles at Israeli territory for the first time. The vast majority are intercepted by the IDF and an international coalition.
May 6, 2024 — Rafah operation begins: The IDF begins operating in eastern Rafah after issuing evacuation orders to the population in the area. On May 7, forces take control of the Palestinian side of the Rafah crossing and later that month establish operational control over the Philadelphi Corridor.
June 8, 2024 — Operation Arnon: Security forces rescue four hostages — Noa Argamani, Almog Meir Jan, Shlomi Ziv and Andrey Kozlov — from the heart of Nuseirat in a daring operation.
June 9, 2024 — National Unity leaves the government: Benny Gantz and his party announce their withdrawal from the emergency government, and the smaller war cabinet is formally dissolved.
July 13, 2024 — Mohammed Deif killed: A major strike in the al-Mawasi area kills the head of Hamas’ military wing.
July 30-31, 2024 — Senior figures killed in Beirut and Tehran: Hezbollah military commander Fuad Shukr is killed in Beirut and Hamas leader Ismail Haniyeh is killed in the heart of Tehran.
August 27, 2024 — Farhan al-Qadi rescued: IDF and Shin Bet forces, led by the Israeli Navy’s Shayetet 13 commando unit, rescue hostage Farhan al-Qadi alive from a tunnel in the southern Gaza Strip.
September 1, 2024 — Murder of six hostages in Rafah tunnel cleared for publication: Hersh Goldberg-Polin, Ori Danino, Eden Yerushalmi, Alex Lobanov, Almog Sarusi and Carmel Gat, later collectively known as the "Beautiful Six," are executed by Hamas terrorists in an underground tunnel in Rafah. Their bodies were located and recovered by IDF forces on August 31.
September 17-18, 2024 — Pager operation: Thousands of communications devices used by Hezbollah operatives in Lebanon explode simultaneously, severely damaging the organization’s command and control structure.
September 27, 2024 — Hassan Nasrallah eliminated: In Operation New Order, Israeli Air Force jets drop dozens of tons of munitions on Hezbollah’s central headquarters in Beirut’s Dahieh district, killing the terrorist organization’s longtime leader.
October 1, 2024 — Second Iranian attack and Lebanon ground offensive: The IDF begins a limited ground operation in southern Lebanon. At the same time, Iran launches about 180 ballistic missiles at Israel.
October 16, 2024 — Yahya Sinwar eliminated: The Hamas leader and architect of the October 7 massacre is killed by IDF troops in Rafah.
October 26, 2024 — Operation Days of Repentance: Israel carries out an overt, direct retaliatory attack in Iran, striking military targets, air defense systems and missile production facilities.
November 5, 2024 — Defense Minister Yoav Gallant fired: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announces Gallant’s dismissal as defense minister over disagreements about the conduct of the war and appoints Israel Katz in his place.
November 27, 2024 — Lebanon ceasefire agreement: A ceasefire on the northern front with Lebanon takes effect.
December 8, 2024 — Assad regime falls in Syria: Syrian rebel forces unexpectedly capture Damascus, bringing about the collapse of Bashar Assad’s regime. Assad flees to Russia. The IDF redeploys in the buffer zone and on the Syrian side of Mount Hermon to prevent weapons from reaching hostile forces.
Hostages released — and war with Iran
January 19, 2025 — Second hostage deal: Another agreement with Hamas takes effect. Over the course of about two months, 33 living hostages are released, including elderly civilians, wounded hostages, female surveillance soldiers and civilians Avera Mengistu and Hisham al-Sayed, along with the return of eight bodies. In exchange, Israel agrees to an extended ceasefire, the release of hundreds of Palestinian security prisoners and the withdrawal of IDF forces from key routes in the Gaza Strip.
March 18, 2025 — Operation Might and Sword: Following the collapse of the ceasefire under the second hostage deal, the IDF launches a large-scale surprise operation across the Gaza Strip. A series of senior figures in Hamas’ civilian and military leadership are killed in the opening airstrikes.
May 18, 2025 — Operation Gideon’s Chariots: The IDF expands its ground offensive in the central and southern Gaza Strip, including Deir al-Balah, Nuseirat and Rafah, to seize strategically important territory, destroy underground infrastructure and dismantle remaining Hamas battalions in central Gaza.
June 13-24, 2025 — Operation Rising Lion: Israel and the United States launch a large-scale, coordinated surprise attack against Iran’s nuclear program and missile array. More than 1,200 strike sorties are carried out during the operation, including against nuclear facilities in Natanz and Isfahan, and Iranian scientists and senior officials are killed. Iran responds with barrages of ballistic missiles at Israel until a ceasefire is announced June 24.
July 16, 2025 — Syrian General Staff headquarters struck in Damascus: Following massacres of the Druze population in southern Syria by sectarian and government forces, the Israeli Air Force strikes the Syrian military’s General Staff building in Damascus.
September 9, 2025 — Assassination attempt in Qatar: Israeli Air Force jets strike a secure compound in Doha where Hamas’ overseas leadership is meeting. Senior Hamas officials Khalil al-Hayya and Zaher Jabarin survive, but several of their associates and al-Hayya’s son are killed.
October 9-13, 2025 — Third hostage deal and agreement ending the war: Following sustained military pressure and an internationally mediated framework, an agreement is signed leading to the release of the final 20 living hostages held in captivity in a single round on the eve of Simchat Torah 5786, along with the return of the bodies of deceased hostages. In exchange, fighting in the Gaza Strip ends, about 2,000 Palestinian prisoners are released and IDF forces withdraw to agreed lines.
The last hostage recovered and Khamenei killed
January 26, 2026 — Last hostage returned: In a military operation, the body of Israel Police special patrol officer Master Sgt. Ran Gvili, the last hostage held in the Gaza Strip, is located and returned to Israel, bringing a painful chapter to a definitive close.
February 28, 2026 — Operation Roaring Lion: Israel and the United States launch a large-scale preemptive attack against Iran aimed at its nuclear program, missile array and military and government targets. The IDF announces that Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei has been killed and strikes targets across Iran, while Iran launches missiles at Israel. On March 2, Hezbollah joins the fighting, launching missiles, rockets and drones from Lebanon at Israel.
March 11, 2026 — Hezbollah launches more than 200 missiles at Israel.
April 7, 2026 — Temporary ceasefire in campaign against Iran: After weeks of fighting between Iran and the United States and Israel, a two-week temporary ceasefire agreement is reached with Pakistani mediation.
April 17, 2026 — Israel-Lebanon ceasefire during Operation Roaring Lion: A ceasefire between Israel and Hezbollah is declared, although the fighting does not end entirely.
June 19, 2026 — Israel-Hezbollah ceasefire: Israel and Hezbollah agree to another ceasefire under U.S. mediation. The IDF remains in parts of southern Lebanon.
July 17, 2026 — Knesset dissolved: The 25th Knesset ends its term and enters an election recess ahead of elections for the 26th Knesset.

Anthropic CEO Amodei made US$18 million in 2025, putting him in middle ranks of tech executives

Anthropic CEO Amodei made US$18 million in 2025, putting him in middle ranks of tech executives
- Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei made US$18 million in 2025, placing him in the middle of major tech bosses as the firm prepares for a possible IPO.
- Most of his pay came from stock and equity, while sister Daniela Amodei earned US$16.4 million and other co-founders also received large awards.
- The filing says the Amodei siblings and other founders will give 80% of their Anthropic equity to charity, as AI wealth and pay face growing scrutiny.
AI generated
NEW YORK/BOSTON – Dario Amodei made US$18 million (S$23 million) in 2025 as chief executive officer of Claude AI developer Anthropic, the company’s initial public offering (IPO) filing shows, putting him in the middle ranks of top executives at major technology firms in terms of compensation.
Anthropic is preparing for an IPO as early as this autumn that could value it at more than US$2 trillion, according to its IPO prospectus seen by Reuters. Amodei’s pay in 2025 puts him above CEOs at Alphabet and Amazon, but behind those at Oracle and Nvidia.
Amodei’s pay leans heavily towards stock and other sorts of compensation, suggesting that like many other tech founders, his yearly salary will account for just a fraction of his wealth.
Dario Amodei and his sister, Anthropic president Daniela Amodei, each had their annual salaries doubled this past July to US$1.4 million. Stock and options awards made up the bulk of their packages in 2025, with Daniela Amodei receiving a total of US$16.4 million in 2025.
Anthropic’s board in 2026 granted the pair the promise of further equity in the form of restricted stock units, which promise a future payout if certain conditions are met. Some of that is tied to their remaining at the company, and some of it is tied to the IPO.
Chief financial officer Krishna Rao earned US$720,250 in 2025. He was granted options to buy 1.4 million shares when he was hired in 2024, and exercised options worth US$385,285 in 2025.
An Anthropic spokesperson declined to comment on the figures.
Middle of the pack
The rise in US CEO pay in recent years has far outpaced the gains for the average worker, a dynamic critics worry could be exacerbated by AI’s widespread adoption.
S&P 500 CEO average annual compensation rose 21% to US$22.8 million in 2025, and that does not include the extraordinary case of Tesla’s Elon Musk and his US$158 billion restricted stock plan, according to the AFL-CIO trade union group.
Courtney Yu, director of research for executive compensation data firm Equilar, said Amodei’s haul “seems on the lower end for a company valued at US$2 trillion, but it will be interesting to see how that changes once the company goes public” and his full ownership stake is shown.
With six other co-founders, Amodei may wind up getting a lesser share of the wealth created by the IPO compared with other major tech CEOs, Yu added.
Top executives at AI-focused tech firms earned amounts that varied widely in 2025, based on US Securities and Exchange Commission filings. At the high end, Oracle co-CEO Clayton Magouyrk earned US$627.5 million, while the lowest was the US$54,080 paid to Musk as CEO of SpaceX, before it went public. SpaceX has also promised super-voting restricted shares to Musk, already the world’s richest person, if its market value grows to US$7.5 trillion and the firm puts one million people on Mars.
Other giant companies pay less on a year-by-year basis, with executives benefiting from enormous stock ownership while having only salary and security costs reflected in annual filings.
For instance, Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai made US$10.9 million in 2025, including US$8.8 million for personal security “due to Sundar’s significant public profile”. By “compensation actually paid”, Pichai earned $213.9 million in 2025, which among other things reflects the change in value of his unvested shares.
Amazon CEO Andrew Jassy made US$2.1 million in 2025, a disclosure said, mainly reflecting travel and security. On an “actually paid” basis, Jassy received US$13.2 million.
Living off the stock
Yu said the disclosures show how these executives do not need to worry about year-by-year pay.
“Founder CEOs typically own enough equity that when the company does well and the stock prices increases, they can just live off the wealth of the equity they already own, and typically don’t take in a lot in annual compensation,” Yu said.
Anthropic said in the filing it offered a mix of salary, equity awards and other benefits. The S-1 statement seen by Reuters does not describe the founders’ share of ownership in the company, which could be worth billions of dollars, depending on the final terms and valuation of the IPO.
The Amodei siblings and their fellow co-founders pledged in the IPO filing to dedicate 80% of their personal Anthropic equity to charitable causes.
Asked about the 80% figure on Oct 5, an Anthropic spokesperson noted an essay Dario Amodei posted earlier in 2026, where he wrote that wealthy individuals have an obligation to help address problems stemming from AI adoption, and decried that many wealthy people, particularly in the tech industry, “have recently adopted a cynical and nihilistic attitude that philanthropy is inevitably fraudulent or useless”. Yemeni forces launch offensive to retake Houthi-held al-Waziiya in Taiz
The mountainous district is key to control of Mocha, the Red Sea port the Houthis seized last month.
Houthis, Saudi-led forces claim victories as Yemen fighting rages on
Forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government have launched an operation to capture a strategic mountainous district from the Houthis as part of a wider push to retake the Red Sea coast and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
The offensive on the district of al-Waziiya in Taiz governorate on Tuesday came as Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen’s government, intercepted a Houthi ballistic missile targeting the city of Khamis Mushait.
The operation is part of the “Dawn of Yemen” offensive that was announced on Sunday by Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, to retake all remaining Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, which the Iran-backed group has controlled since 2014.
The media centre of Yemen’s army said in a post on X that the Homeland Shield Forces, a pro-government military faction, have begun “a large-scale operation” to retake al-Waziiya.
“The armed forces have secured strategic hills overlooking the al-Mansoura area, amidst a mass retreat by the Houthi militia,” it said, citing a military source.
The Houthis, however, denied the claim, saying they had successfully repelled the Yemeni government advance in al-Waziiya.
The mountainous district is located west of Taiz, east of the Red Sea port of Mocha. The Houthis had seized Mocha and areas around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait – a strategic maritime corridor – in a lightning offensive last month.
“These are the mountains that the Houthis took control of prior to the takeover of the city of Mocha,” Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry said, reporting from Sanaa.
“If the Yemeni government is serious about taking over the city of Mocha, they cannot do so unless they take over the region in the district of al-Waziiya,” he added.
Saudi interception
The fighting came as the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said it intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis towards the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait.
Major-General Turki al-Maliki, the spokesperson for the coalition, said the Houthi missile threats originated from Houthi-held Sanaa and the governorates of Saada and Amran.
“The coalition continues to neutralise the threat posed by ballistic and surface-to-surface missiles and to destroy their launch sources,” he added.
Earlier on Tuesday, Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement that King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz airport in Jazan and Najran airport, near the Yemen border, were hit in attacks that wounded three people.
The attacks caused injuries of “varying severity” and material damage, and the injured have been taken to hospital, the authority said.
The Houthis said late on Monday that their forces targeted sites across southern Saudi Arabia, including airports and military sites.
The Saudi-led coalition, meanwhile, has confirmed its participation in the Yemeni government offensive to retake all Houthi-held territory, saying 100 of its fighter jets are providing air support.
Pakistan and Turkiye have also agreed to activate “deterrence measures” under their mutual defence pact with Saudi Arabia and rapidly deploy forces to the Gulf kingdom to counter attacks by the Houthis.

US arrests person in connection to Canada school shooting, officials say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
00:34:26 UTC
09:34:26 KST

US authorities arrested a person in Washington state on Tuesday whom they accuse of providing advice and offering to live-stream a deadly mass shooting carried out earlier this year in Canada.
James Cody Bryant, 30, was detained on a charge of conspiracy to murder people in a foreign country in connection with the shooting at Tumbler Ridge, according to the US Justice Department. The charge carries a penalty of up to life in prison.
Bryant was in repeated contact with the shooter, Jesse Van Rootselaar, offering technical advice, sending money, including for the shoes to be used during the attack, and agreeing to live stream the event, law enforcement officials said.
"James Cody Bryant had the information and ability to alert law enforcement and even discussed that possibility with the shooter, but he chose not to, and he encouraged and offered assistance to a murderer," Acting US Attorney for the Western District of Washington Neil Floyd told reporters.
Court records did not immediately list an attorney for Bryant.
Nine people, primarily children, were killed in the school shooting in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia, in one of Canada's worst mass shootings.
Van Rootselaar, 18, who had suffered a series of mental health problems, killed her mother and stepbrother at home before shooting dead a teacher and five young students at her former school in Tumbler Ridge, a settlement of around 2,400 in the Canadian Rockies, according to police. Van Rootselaar, who police said was born a male but began identifying as a woman, then died by suicide.
Bryant, who officials said they understood was also born a man but identified as female, agreed to live stream a feed of the attack and broadcast it "in a way that would maximize notoriety for the shooter," Mike Herrington, FBI Seattle special agent in charge, said.
The live stream on Twitch was shut down after about 20 seconds, officials said.
Shooter was dependent on Bryant's help, Herrington alleges
"Without Bryant's misplaced loyalty and willingness to operate the live stream, we don't ultimately know if the shooter would have gone through with the crime," Herrington said.
"We certainly know the shooter was concerned that not enough people would see the live stream without Bryant broadcasting it, and was depending on Bryant to amplify the live stream because the shooter did not have many followers on social media."

“I found some real camaraderie and some really cool music crew here, and it's ironically just been easier to create here because Israel's arts scene is really mature,” Banks stated. “This is the most creatively enabled I've felt in years."

Banks has also repeatedly praised Itamar Ben Gvir, at one point writing that he was "right about everything. Quite possibly the most important politician in the Middle East."
Banks shifts stance on Israel over years
The rapper has had an erratic relationship with Israel, at times condemning the country and at other times staunchly defending it.
In 2018, Banks stood up to the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions (BDS) movement ahead of an early Tel Aviv show.
At the time, she slammed cancellation demands as “totally antisemitic,” arguing that giving in would mean unfairly targeting Jewish fans. However, shortly after the trip, she temporarily vowed never to return, citing alleged encounters with racism.
In mid-2025, Banks re-emerged as an outspoken supporter, publicly identifying as a Zionist.
After European promoters canceled her UK and EU tour bookings because she refused to chant pro-Palestinian slogans on stage, she traveled to Israel for a multi-week solidarity tour.
Banks participates in Oct 7 anniversary show

During that trip, she toured Yad Vashem and the site of the Nova music festival.
In March, Banks abruptly turned on Israel via social media amid heightening geopolitical tensions between the US, Israel, and Iran. In a series of profane, viral posts, she rescinded her support, wrote “F*** ISRAEL,” and heavily criticized Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
However, later in the year, she booked her third performance in Israel to take place at the Tel Aviv Amphitheater on October 8 and is reportedly using Tel Aviv as a creative refuge to work on new music with prominent local producer Yinon Yahel.

Iran must cut enrichment to end war, US uncertain who makes decisions in Tehran, Vance says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
00:34:13 UTC
09:34:13 KST

US Vice President JD Vance said in an exclusive interview with Reuters that Iran must make a “meaningful” reduction in its nuclear enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the country’s seven-month war, even as Washington was unsure how Tehran makes decisions in negotiations.
Vance, a longtime skeptic of US involvement in foreign wars, has taken a leading role in negotiating a settlement to the conflict and brokered a provisional peace agreement in June that quickly fell apart. The war has jolted global energy markets and become a political liability for US President Donald Trump and fellow Republicans ahead of November midterm elections.
Speaking on Monday after a campaign trip in Alaska, Vance said any agreement would require Iran to reduce its nuclear enrichment capacity, rather than offer assurances of future nuclear drawdowns.
"If you don't want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60% enriched fuel? And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don't build highly enriched fuel. That's a very basic threshold issue," Vance said.
"I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity."
Iran and the US have exchanged proposals in recent weeks aimed at ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy shipping route. Trump rejected Tehran's latest offer and has warned that military operations could intensify after the midterms.
Vance said the US remained open to an agreement but would require concrete Iranian nuclear concessions.
"We're not going to trade words for actions," Vance said.
Unclear how Iran makes decisions, says Vance
Complicating matters, Vance said Washington is uncertain who makes decisions in Tehran.
Vance said the US was in talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi. But it was unclear how much authority they wield within Iran's power structure, he said, after joint US-Israeli strikes at the start of the war killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
"One of the things we picked up on is it's not totally clear how their country makes decisions," Vance said. Separately, Trump said on Tuesday his "biggest problem" is no one knows who is running Iran.
Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson said on Sunday that US officials are well aware of who their Iranian counterparts are and how Iran's decision-making system works.
"The problem is actually the opposite: it lies in the contradictory positions and mixed messaging from US officials," Esmaeil Baghaei told a weekly press conference.
Vance rallies for Alaskan candidate says he's unsure if he will run for president
Vance told Reuters he has held personal conversations with field commanders to gauge battlefield conditions. He dismissed concerns over critical munitions shortages and added that while Iranian troops are periodically able to strike commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, they are largely unable to prevent energy exports through the waterway.
The war — and its $3 billion monthly price tag — has become a key issue on the campaign trail. Higher energy prices have put Trump and Republicans on the defensive in competitive states that will decide control of Congress.
Vance has sought to temper criticism of Trump’s handling of the conflict, telling voters they should not let that issue keep them from backing Republicans in next month's elections.
In Alaska, Vance rallied for Republican Senator Dan Sullivan, who is locked in a tight reelection battle with Democratic challenger Mary Peltola. Trump carried Alaska by 13 percentage points in 2024, but rising everyday costs have put the state in play.
Before speaking with Reuters, Vance focused much of his speech on affordability concerns, especially around energy. Alaska's remote locale makes consumer goods more expensive, and energy production is a key industry.
Rally attendees roared when Sullivan nearly introduced Vance as the president of the US, rather than the vice president. Vance is seen as a leading Republican contender to succeed Trump in the White House.
Vance told Reuters afterward that he had not decided whether to seek the presidency in 2028.
"I'm inherently a procrastinator," he said. "I really haven't thought about it much."
Washington's aims at odds with Tehran's demands
Washington's "requests and ideas" about Iran's nuclear program are at odds with Tehran's demands, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Wednesday when asked about Vance's comment that Tehran must cut enrichment to end the war with Washington.
"Vance's comments are Washington's ideas and requests... Americans are free to make requests and have ideas, but they are at odds with Iran's demands," the senior Iranian official, who is directly involved in indirect negotiations with the United States, said.
The official added that no negotiations had taken place with the US about Iran's nuclear program and that Washington must first meet Tehran's conditions before nuclear talks can start.
The official said US recognition of Iran's right to nuclear enrichment is Tehran's red line, which "it will not show flexibility on in any way. However, he added that details of enrichment can be discussed later. ”

Head of the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) David Zini warned during a Political-Security Cabinet meeting on Monday of unprecedented terrorist organization efforts in Bedouin communities in the Negev.
In his remarks to cabinet members, the head of the service detailed that the defense establishment often identifies attempts to create infrastructure of a military nature inside Israeli territory. "There are places in the Bedouin diaspora with military infrastructure that we are constantly thwarting, attempts to establish quasi-military battalions; this is a very concerning phenomenon," he said.
The warning comes against the backdrop of increasing involvement of Israeli citizens from Bedouin communities in terrorist incidents, in arms smuggling along the Egyptian border, and in ties with terrorist elements in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip.
Shin Bet and Police officials have identified that the spillover of illegal weapons on a massive scale into the Negev, alongside processes of nationalist and religious radicalization, has created fertile ground for the rise of local armed organizations.
Officials from the defense establishment pointed to several key trends fueling the phenomenon: Weapons smuggling has turned the Negev into a procurement hub for standard-issue weaponry, including assault rifles, standard explosive devices, and night-vision gear.
In addition, the line between criminal and nationalist activity is blurring: infrastructures that began as criminal organizations and protection-racket operations are undergoing radicalization processes and turning their weapons toward attempted terror attacks.
'Right under your noses, armed militias capable of slaughtering Israeli citizens'
Hamas and ISIS propaganda on social media has led youth from the Bedouin communities to establish local cells and attempt to emulate operational patterns of terrorist organizations in the West Bank.
Targeted counterterrorism efforts by the Shin Bet, Police, and the IDF in Bedouin communities continue, including nighttime arrests, weapons seizures, and the use of advanced intelligence tools to cut short attempts to establish these "battalions" while still in their initial organizational phases.
On Monday, during a conference held in Rahat with the participation of retired Major General Yoav Segalovitz, former Deputy Minister of Public Security and second on the Ra'am list, bursts of gunfire were heard nearby as part of an intra-clan conflict in the city.
"During the meeting, bursts of gunfire were heard right next to us, in the early evening hours. The inconceivable thing is that here in the city, this has almost become routine. Just yesterday, bursts of gunfire were heard for eight consecutive hours," Segalovitz said, adding: "Such a thing must not become routine. This is a severe failure of the government, which has abandoned the personal safety of its citizens."
The Amcha Yisrael party, led by Ofer Winter, responded to Zini's warning that "the report regarding the Shin Bet chief's warning about attempts to establish military battalions in the Bedouin diaspora is supposed to serve as a flashing red flag for the Government of Israel and the defense establishment." Winter further added, "Where is the Prime Minister? Where is the Minister of Police?"
Winter continued his attack, stating, "Right under your noses, armed militias capable of slaughtering Israeli citizens are being formed. What are you doing about it? The stinging failure to confiscate weapons in the Arab sector will blow up in our faces. No misconceptions and no excuses. The time for decisive resolution has come. The time for Winter has come," he urged.
Bedouin leaders respond to Zini's comments
The head of the Hura Local Council, Habes Al-Atawna, responded to Zini's comments, telling Walla that "there is no such thing among us. Even the timing, twenty days before the elections, is very strange. This is a democratic election campaign, and the timing of making such statements is because of the elections. Most Bedouins are law-abiding people to the law, and contribute to the state. There is criminality among a small minority, but this is under no circumstances terrorism. That small percentage has been neglected for decades."
Ahmad, a resident of Rahat, expressed outrage over the Shin Bet chief's statement.
"Unfortunately, the heads of the defense establishments are also not helping to calm tensions or halt the incitement against the Bedouins. We have always pleaded for the phenomenon of illegal weapons in Arab society in general, and among the Bedouins in particular, to be combated, with no response. The Bedouins in the Negev are waiting to receive recognition for their villages and treatment of their problems so they can live in dignity like human beings. If it turns out that there is any criminal or nationalist organizing, we all condemn and oppose it."
The Regional Council of Unrecognized Villages also reacted to the Shin Bet chief's words, claiming they stem from political considerations.
"The entire country already knows that Zini has turned the Shin Bet into a branch of Likud, with all the accompanying lies. These headlines were not drafted in the Shin Bet offices, but in the office of Yonatan Urich, and they are completely fabricated from A to Z. A total spin whose sole purpose is to add a few votes of Arab-haters to the coalition of disasters. We view this unprecedented incitement with utmost severity."
Ra'ed Al-Qian, a resident of Hura and a social activist, said they have been sounding alarms for years regarding illegal weapons, gunfire, and violence in Bedouin society. "We have repeatedly pointed out the scale of the phenomenon and the heavy price in human lives, but the governmental response was inadequate. Over the past decade, many Bedouin citizens have paid with their lives, so this cannot be viewed merely as an issue of policing and enforcement," he said.
"The fight against violence requires deep, cross-systemic intervention. Alongside resolute enforcement, what is needed is education, employment and vocational training, urban planning and housing, infrastructure and public services, leisure and sports frameworks, and opportunities for youth," Al-Qian said.
He added that "when planning and housing solutions have been lacking for years, and instead families are primarily met with enforcement against unpermitted construction, one must also examine the link between planning policy and social reality.
"The question is not just how many weapons were seized and how many suspects were arrested, but what is being done today so that in five years there will be fewer weapons and less violence, and more education, employment, personal safety, and hope," he concluded.

Conflicting accounts

Sudan’s al-Burhan rejects talks, vows to retake all territory from RSF
At least 10 civilians were killed in West Kordofan and 5,500 displaced in Blue Nile as clashes widened on Tuesday.
Sudan’s military chief, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, has promised to seize “every inch” of territory under the control of the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), rejecting negotiations to end three and a half years of war.
Al-Burhan made the comments on Tuesday while addressing a gathering in Village 5, located in the northern Sudanese locality of Merowe, according to the Sudan News Agency.
He said the “military option” would continue until the RSF was removed from Sudan.
The Sudanese army and the RSF have been fighting since April 2023 after leaders of the groups fell out over plans to integrate the paramilitary force into Sudan’s army. The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.
Al-Burhan’s pledge to continue fighting came as 10 civilians were killed and several others were wounded in an attack by the RSF in Sudan’s West Kordofan state, according to a local charity group.
In a statement, the Dar Hamar Emergency Committee accused the RSF of multiple violations against civilians in Abu Ajal village in the southeastern countryside of En Nahud.
The RSF has been massing in West Kordofan as Sudan’s army advances towards the cities of En Nahud and Al Khuway after gains in neighbouring North Kordofan.
In Sudan’s Blue Nile state, more than 5,500 people were displaced from villages over three days amid deteriorating security, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said on Tuesday.
Meanwhile, an envoy of US President Donald Trump said Sudanese parties must take the lead in talks to end the war.
In a post on X on Monday, Massad Boulos, the US senior adviser for Arab and African affairs, said peace could be achieved “through an inclusive Sudanese-owned and Sudanese-led national dialogue, transition toward a civilian-led government”.
The US State Department said last month that neither the Sudanese Armed Forces, the RSF, nor their respective leaders “represent legitimate, constitutional governance for Sudan”.

Russia slams Kyiv in mass missile, drone attack on Putin's 74th birthday
