Russia slams Ukraine with missiles, drones on Putin's 74th birthday, at least 22 dead
Locals and rescuers carry an injured man from a residential building destroyed in a Russian missile strike in Pryluky, Chernihiv Oblast, Ukraine, on Oct. 7, 2026. (Evgeniy Maloletka / AP)
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
At least 22 people have been killed in yet another Russian overnight mass missile and drone attack on Ukrainian cities on Oct. 7, coinciding with Russian President Vladimir Putin's 74th birthday.
In the city of Pryluky, in Chernihiv Oblast, a Russian cruise missile hit a residential building, killing at least 18, including four children, and wounding at least 55, including seven children.
"Today, as a 'birthday gift' to Putin, the Russian army destroyed a residential building in Pryluky, in the Chernihiv region," President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a post on social media.
"It was an ordinary five-story apartment block. There may still be people under the rubble. First responders are working nonstop at the site – doing everything possible to find every person," he added.
The Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, was also heavily targeted, as were the cities of Dnipro, Oleksandriya, Zaporizhzhia, and Kremenchuk in Poltava Oblast.
In Kyiv, city authorities reported that two people were killed in the Darnytskyi district of the capital.
Multiple explosions were first heard in Kyiv at around 3:15 a.m. local time, according to Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground. Ukraine's Air Force previously warned of several Russian Tu-95 bombers approaching the border.
"The missiles are falling one after another. At least 10-12 explosions from what I can count. It's pretty loud in the city center," the Kyiv Independent's Tim Zadorozhnyy reported.
Other Kyiv Independent journalists described strikes around Kyiv's Podil district with flames and smoke seen in the capital.
Explosions were again heard two hours later at 5:15 a.m. amid a second wave of missile attacks.
read also
According to the Ukrainian Air Force, Russian forces used a variety of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, anti-ship missiles, and drones in the overnight attack.
Out of an unspecified number of ballistic missiles launched at Ukraine, five were shot down or suppressed by electronic warfare, according to the Air Force.
Thirty-nine of 48 cruise missiles were confirmed shot down or suppressed as of 10 a.m. Kyiv time, while 117 Russian attack drones were shot down or suppressed out of 130 launched.
Hits by enemy missiles and drones were recorded at 18 locations, according to the Air Force.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said a strike was reported at an unspecified "non-residential area" in the Obolon District, while warehouse facilities were hit in the Podil district.
The full extent of the damage caused was not immediately clear.
Earlier, drones headed toward Ukraine's capital at 9 p.m. local time, Ukraine's Air Force reported, and an air raid alert was announced in the city shortly after, lasting from 9:09 p.m. until 9:58 p.m.
Russian missile strikes also damaged five apartment buildings in Dnipro and four high-rise buildings in Kremenchuk, Zelensky confirmed in a statement, reporting a further two people killed and eight more injured in these strikes.
While in the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia, transport infrastructure was damaged amid the large-scale attack, officials reported.
President Volodymyr Zelensky earlier in the day urged citizens to take air raid alerts seriously and warned that Russia is preparing a large-scale attack on Ukraine, citing recent intelligence.
"Please, please, take care of yourself. Please respond to signals of missile danger," he said.
The latest large-scale attack comes as Putin turns 74 years old on Oct. 7. The average male life expectancy in Russia is 68 years as of 2024, according to the World Bank Group.
Russia attacked Kyiv the previous night, damaging cars, and has targeted the city's key bridges in recent days.

US forces in Okinawa, Japan have imposed a 48-hour operational pause, a complete alcohol ban, restrictions on off-base liberty and a midnight-to-5 am curfew for one month following the arrest of a US Marine on suspicion of murder.
Lt. Gen. Benjamin T. Watson, Okinawa Area Coordinator and commanding general of the III Marine Expeditionary Force, said Tuesday that service members' conduct affects trust with Okinawa's residents and ultimately the strength of the alliance and regional security.
The announcement came after Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, assigned to Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, was suspected of killing Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in Naha’s Wakasa district early Saturday.
Police said Yagi died of asphyxiation after Ballard allegedly pressed on her neck. Ballard has denied the allegations, and the case was forwarded to prosecutors Monday.
Residents held an emergency protest rally in Okinawa City on Sunday evening, where participants observed a moment of silence for Yagi and criticized the US military's repeated pledges to enforce discipline.
Japan summoned the US envoy over the incident.
During the 48-hour period, commanders and senior enlisted leaders will lead training with all service members on standards, discipline and their responsibilities as members of the Okinawan community, he said.
"Every member of this force must understand that individual conduct has consequences," he said.
During the 30-day curfew beginning Friday, all personnel will be required to return to base by midnight and remain there until 5 am, with increased gate supervision at all Okinawa installations.
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said Tuesday that some aircraft training at the US Air Force’s Kadena Air Base will be transferred to the Japan Air Self-Defense Force’s Tsuiki Air Base from Oct. 19-29 to reduce the burden on Okinawa while emphasizing that Tokyo takes seriously the significant burden borne by Okinawa’s residents.
Okinawa hosts the majority of US military facilities in Japan.
Approximately 50,000 to 55,000 US military personnel are currently stationed in Japan under the US-Japan Security Treaty, which was originally signed in 1951 and revised in 1960.

Libyan parliament elects new speaker after lawmakers amend internal rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
00:18:51 UTC
09:18:51 KST

Muetaz Wannes and Rania Abushamala
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Libya’s House of Representatives in the country’s east elected lawmaker Al-Salihin Abdul Nabi al-Obeidi as speaker, replacing Aguila Saleh, parliament spokesman Abdullah Blihaq announced Tuesday.
The election took place during a session at parliament’s official headquarters in Benghazi, chaired by Second Deputy Speaker Misbah Doma and devoted to electing the presidency, according to Blihaq’s statement.
Al-Obeidi represents the first electoral district in Tobruk, in Libya’s far east, and serves on parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee.
Before his election, he chaired the Libyan-Turkish Parliamentary Friendship Committee, established by the House of Representatives in April 2024.
He has worked to develop ties with Türkiye through parliamentary diplomacy and economic and cultural cooperation.
His election came a day after 98 lawmakers voted to amend parliament’s internal rules and form a new presidency, ending the tenure of the existing presidency led by Saleh.
Lawmaker Mohammed Tamer previously told Anadolu that 102 members attended Monday’s session in Benghazi, which Doma chaired.
He said 98 lawmakers approved an amendment introducing a parliamentary term.
Saleh rejected Monday’s session, describing it in a statement as “unofficial” and saying it had “no legal effect.”
He said its decisions lacked a legal basis because the procedures stipulated in the law governing parliament and its internal rules had not been followed, particularly those concerning the amendment and adoption of laws.
Two weeks earlier, 86 lawmakers accused Saleh in a joint statement of preventing them from entering parliament’s headquarters and holding a session with the required quorum to discuss parliamentary reform and amendments to its internal rules.
Their demands focused particularly on Law No. 4 of 2014, which adopted the House of Representatives’ internal regulations.
The law does not set a fixed term for the speaker or require a new election after a specified period. Some lawmakers oppose that arrangement and have called for annual internal elections to renew parliament’s leadership.
Libya remains divided between two rival governments: the Government of National Unity, headed by Abdul Hamid Dbeibeh and based in Tripoli, which governs western Libya, and the government of Osama Hammad, which was appointed by the House of Representatives in early 2022 and based in Benghazi, governing the east and most southern cities.
The UN mission in Libya has been pursuing efforts to lead the country toward elections that could resolve the crisis.

South Sudan’s aid crisis deepens as food stocks run low
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07

South Sudan’s aid crisis deepens as food stocks run low
More than one million people could lose life-saving aid by October as funding shrinks and arrivals from Sudan continue.
Renk, South Sudan – The arrivals begin before dawn. Women carry children and plastic bags; men walk with almost nothing. Every week, about 3,000 refugees and returnees cross into South Sudan from Sudan.
Many arrive hungry, exhausted and with little or no money. But the food assistance they depend on is also running out.
More than one million vulnerable people could lose access to life-saving food and nutrition assistance by October unless additional resources are secured, according to the World Food Programme (WFP).
In Malakal, one of the agency’s key logistics hubs in the Upper Nile state, food stocks have fallen from 10,000 metric tonnes at this time last year to less than 300 tonnes now. The drop comes as humanitarian agencies face shrinking resources while needs continue to rise, WFP says.
WFP assistant executive director Matthew Hollingworth visited Renk and Malakal in Upper Nile and Pigi county in Jonglei state this month, where he witnessed firsthand the pressures facing communities already struggling with conflict, displacement, hunger and climate shocks.
Hollingworth told Al Jazeera that the war in Sudan had driven up prices and put additional pressure on a country already stretched by the influx of refugees.
“The war in Sudan has been catastrophic for the north of this country. Prices have gone so much higher due to the complexity of importing goods from Sudan,” he said. “Moreover, the influx of refugees [comes] to a country that is really stretched when it comes to helping them.”
In Renk, Hollingworth saw the effects of drought alongside areas still affected by flooding.
“It all comes at the time when the international community has a lot less to give, and we don’t have the same resources we used to have,” he told Al Jazeera.
“On the other side, the government of South Sudan has to consider the issue of illegal checkpoints that prevent us from being able to get everywhere. We need to reach vulnerable people across the country.”
Peter Maker, a displaced person in Pigi, said insecurity and the arrival of people displaced from other areas had made it difficult to farm or find work.
“We face major challenges due to national insecurity and an influx of people from other areas. Our main issues are insecurity and lack of access to farmland,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Although I am able-bodied and qualified to work, insecurity prevents me from travelling for opportunities or farming safely outside, leaving us heavily reliant on the UN and aid.”
Maker said longer-term solutions were needed and warned that further cuts or blockages to assistance would be devastating. He attributed much of the local suffering to political leadership and divisions between communities, while saying people currently survive by sharing resources, relying on God and receiving occasional aid.
A border under pressure
Renk, in Upper Nile state near the border with Sudan, has become a major entry point for people fleeing the war that erupted there in April 2023.
More than 1.4 million refugees and returnees have crossed into South Sudan since the war erupted in Sudan in 2023, according to the World Food Programme. Many arrive after journeys marked by checkpoints, extortion and violence, with little idea of what comes next.
Zainab Musa, a mother of six staying at a transit centre in Renk, recently crossed from Sudan. She said conditions were difficult and there was little food.
“The humanitarian situation is hard and there is nothing to eat, just hunger,” she told Al Jazeera. “I thought of moving from the border at Jodha to the transit centre to look for help.”
Musa said she planned to travel to her grandfather in Bunj, in Maban county, in Upper Nile.
The transit centres in Renk were not designed for the scale of arrivals they are now receiving. Families wait for onward transport to Malakal or other parts of South Sudan, while some remain for months.
The WFP has been forced to reduce rations and cut support as funding has dried up.
In August, the WFP and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) warned that more than 650,000 refugees and asylum seekers were at risk of losing food assistance. They said food and nutrition assistance for the most vulnerable 240,000 refugees was expected to run out in September without additional funding.
Nura Mohammed Ahmed, a Sudanese refugee, said hunger and a lack of adequate nutrition were already taking a heavy toll at the transit centre.
Malakal’s fragile refuge
Malakal has hosted families displaced by conflict and disaster for years.
The former Protection of Civilians site, redesignated as an internally displaced people’s settlement earlier this year, hosts nearly 40,000 displaced people across more than 6,000 households. Many have been displaced for years.
But basic services are also coming under pressure.
The International Organization for Migration (IOM) has warned that water, sanitation and hygiene services in Bentiu and Malakal are at risk because of funding shortfalls. Without drainage pumping and dyke maintenance, Malakal also faces a heightened risk of flooding during the rainy season.
Najah al-Tayieb al-Fadhul, a Sudanese refugee and mother of four, arrived at a transit centre in December 2023 after her husband was killed.
“My husband was killed by the Sudan armed forces in front of me, and I could not stay with my kids there because the situation was traumatising,” she told Al Jazeera.
“I entered South Sudan, and I have tried my best to hustle and earn some small job with the humanitarian organisations based in Renk.”
Al-Fadhul said hunger, sickness and malnutrition were part of daily life.
“There are massive cases of hunger, sickness and malnutrition among the children,” she said. “Even my child has a heart disease, and I cannot afford to treat him.”
She said she sometimes earned about $2.50 a day from work in the market, but struggled to find stable employment despite having a college degree.
“The humanitarian situation is worsening despite securing a job with one of the organisations,” she said. “WFP only helped us here with the small ration for the children in particular. Elders and most individuals lack energy to work due to hunger.”
The funding gap
The WFP says it faces an immediate $86m funding gap and a $416m shortfall over the next six months, threatening its ability to assist refugees, displaced people and vulnerable host communities.
For the wider population, the hunger crisis is already severe. The WFP says 7.8 million people, more than half of South Sudan’s population, face high levels of acute food shortage, while 2.2 million children are acutely malnourished.
The WFP’s current South Sudan emergency response also lists a $258m funding shortfall for the remainder of 2026.
For people arriving from Sudan, the crisis continues after they cross the border.
Nura Mohammed Ahmed put the choice facing some refugees in stark terms: “Many people died here because of hunger and lack of nutrition. There’s nothing, or food that can give us strength. The only solution is to return to war-torn Sudan despite the risks, or die here from hunger.”

Former German spy chief suspected of spying for Azerbaijan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
00:09:36 UTC
09:09:36 KST

German magazine Der Spiegel reported Tuesday evening that former German Federal Intelligence Service (BND) chief August Hanning is suspected of gathering information for Azerbaijann. The report came hours after German prosecutors disclosed that Hanning, who headed Germany’s foreign intelligence service had been arrested on suspicion of espionage and treason. Authorities had said earlier that he was suspected of seeking to pass classified information to a foreign country’s intelligence service, prompting hours of speculation around the world over which country was involved.
Der Spiegel reported Tuesday evening that, according to information obtained by the magazine, the person who commissioned the classified information from Hanning was an Azerbaijani intelligence operative. Investigators are now examining whether a security analysis Hanning prepared for the Azerbaijani operative, using classified information obtained from a senior BND official, ultimately reached him.
The magazine noted that Hanning’s ties with Azerbaijani representatives are well documented. Among other things, he was a board member of the German-Azerbaijani Forum, as documented in an organization statement published in July 2025.
Hanning, 80, served as head of the BND from 1998 to 2005. According to reports, he was arrested Tuesday morning at his home in Nordwalde, near the western German city of Münster. His former aide, identified only as Manfred D., was also arrested in Bavaria.
Prosecutors did not say at the time of Hanning’s arrest which country he was suspected of spying for. They said, however, that his alleged accomplice, D., who served as Hanning’s chief of staff and remained a senior BND official until March 2026, supplied him with thousands of classified documents in exchange for money over a period of more than a decade. Searches were conducted at the homes of Hanning and his alleged accomplice as part of the investigation.
D., who served as Hanning’s chief of staff while Hanning headed the BND and then as chief of staff to subsequent BND chiefs from 2012 to 2026, had access through his position to the classified information he allegedly passed to Hanning.
Prosecutors said the two are suspected of reaching an agreement as early as spring 2010 under which D. would regularly provide Hanning with valuable BND intelligence in exchange for payment.
“Current findings indicate that over the years Manfred D. passed around 2,000 documents to Hanning, many of which contained classified information intended solely for internal use by the Federal Intelligence Service, particularly for intelligence briefings of senior agency officials,” prosecutors said Tuesday morning.
Prosecutors also said Hanning used the classified information in his work as a security consultant for companies.
German newspaper Bild reported earlier Tuesday that Hanning worked as a consultant for businesses around the world and was also known to have ties to Russia and China, including government agencies in those countries. The newspaper said this meant he also allegedly had links to the Kremlin.
Around the same time as his arrest, several German media outlets, including public broadcaster WDR, published a joint investigation reporting that the arrested aide had passed classified information to Hanning at least through 2022.
Investigators are examining suspicions that, in at least one case, Hanning used the information to conduct a “security analysis” for a foreign intelligence service. The analysis was unrelated to Russia and Der Spiegel’s latest report indicates that it was prepared for the Azerbaijani agent.
In another case, according to the joint media investigation published earlier Tuesday, Hanning is suspected of using internal BND documents in dealings with a foreign agent.
According to reports, the espionage suspicions emerged during a separate investigation into Hanning’s alleged role in the kidnapping of the children of steakhouse empire heiress Christina Block. Israelis have also been implicated in the case and are suspected of being part of a group Block allegedly hired to abduct her children, Klara and Theodor, while they were staying with her former husband in Denmark on New Year’s Eve 2024.
Block is currently on trial in a case that has gripped Germany. Hanning was allegedly involved in an earlier attempt to abduct the children, a claim he denies.
The latest investigation reported that while examining equipment seized from Hanning’s home and office in September 2025 as part of the kidnapping investigation, investigators discovered an electronic storage device containing the classified BND information.
The material immediately raised suspicions because Hanning, who had left his position as BND chief in November 2005, should not have had access to it.
Overall, D. allegedly passed around 2,000 documents to Hanning. According to the media investigation, many were briefings prepared for weekly “situation meetings” at the German Chancellery, where the heads of Germany’s security agencies exchange intelligence.
The investigation said the documents concerned highly sensitive matters, including Iran’s nuclear program and the Russian military.
“Security officials note that the documents also included information received from foreign intelligence agencies that are partners of Germany. A leak of such material is considered an extremely serious failure within intelligence services. Intelligence agencies of allied countries could lose confidence in the BND and stop providing it with vital information,” WDR reported.
If Hanning is convicted of the most serious charge against him, espionage constituting treason, he could face between six months and 10 years in prison.

Kosovo parliament elects new president, avoiding snap election

Kosovo parliament elects new president, avoiding snap election
PRISTINA, Oct 7 - Kosovo's parliament elected economist Justina Shiroka Pula as the country's largely ceremonial president just before a constitutional deadline, avoiding another snap election in one of the poorest countries in Europe.
She received 81 votes, one more than she needed, in the 120-seat parliament in the early minutes of Wednesday. Failure to elect a new president would have triggered snap parliamentary elections in the Balkan country, as it did in June.
"This mandate does not belong to just one person. It belongs to our citizens... I will be the president of all citizens," Shiroka Pula said after the vote.
Shiroka Pula's election followed a deal between the ruling Vetevendosje party of Prime Minister Albin Kurti and opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo to limit the powers of a Kosovo war crimes court in The Hague.
Police fired tear gas and used water cannon on Monday to disperse demonstrators demanding the changes be approved. Critics have asserted the Hague court's punishments are too harsh.
The court on September 16 sentenced former President Hashim Thaci and three others to a combined 81 years in prison for war crimes during the territory's violent break from Serbia in 1998-1999.
The presidency is mainly ceremonial in Kosovo but has often been a source of political instability because a two-thirds parliamentary majority is needed to elect a president and parties have struggled to agree on a candidate.
Shiroka Pula, born in 1953, is the president of Kosovo's Academy of Sciences and Arts and an economics professor who served as minister of the economy between 2008 and 2011. REUTERS

Jaguar "inaugurates a new era" with Type 01 electric car
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
00:00:46 UTC
09:00:46 KST

Jaguar "inaugurates a new era" with Type 01 electric car
British car brand Jaguar has unveiled it electric Type 01, which has thin headlights, a long bonnet and rear-leaning stance designed to set it apart from "homogenous" EVs as the first car in a "complete reset" for the brand.
Revealed today at an exclusive launch event in New York, the Type 01 is the first car in a new era for the brand, which was kicked off with a highly controversial rebrand two years ago.
The highly distinctive car has a four-door aluminium body with a long bonnet and two sets of thin headlights on its grille. It lacks a rear window and has strong body lines that extend from the so-called Impossible Panel on its rear quarter.
As Jaguar's second fully electronic production vehicle, Type 01 both pays homage to and departs from the Jaguar legacy, inaugurating "a new era" for the manufacturer.
It is a production version of the much-discussed Type 00 concept car, which drew much attention in 2024.
"Jaguar's back," Jaguar managing director Rawdon Glover told Dezeen at the launch event.
Glover said that the vehicle was designed to be a "Jaguar first", with the electric aspect secondary. According to Glover, this approach pushed the car to be distinct from other electric vehicles on the market.
"It's Jaguar first, and it's just enabled by its EV powertrain," Glover said.
"I think the classic EV fell into quite a homogeneous type of design. Having a design and an aesthetic that really connects with people at an emotional level – that's a different sort of thing."
The Type 01 makes this distinct with the Jaguar Electric Architecture (JEA), a shorthand for the combined systems and form of the new look.
Its main distinction from other EVs is its low height. The Type 01 is only 1.4 metres high, placing it firmly in GT territory.
It is also relatively long, especially in its bonnet, with a total length of 5.2 metres and has a rear-leaning stance that evokes heritage Jaguar models.
It has a deep rear overhang and a shallower front overhang, with frameless doors that close directly against the body and no rear window.
The shoulder and cant rails stem from its unique rear-quarter panel with five surfaces intersecting above the rear wheel.
Jaguar called this the "Impossible Panel" because, according to the design team, computer programmes said that cold pressing the aluminium in that configuration was not possible.
According to Jaguar exterior design lead Alexey Andreev, the four-fold headlights are a distinguishing part of this new approach, while its proportions and stance connect it with the legacy.
He said the lamps, hemmed in by the darker tones of the surrounding panels, were made to be recognisable from a distance while appearing clean and modern up close.
"The new face of Jaguar is instantly recognisable even when approaching from a distance," said Andreev.
Type 01 has 23-inch wheels with a distinctive pinwheel-like pattern marking the "patent-pending lightweight wheel inserts" that were engineered for airflow.
Though the brand departs from the classic Jaguar form, the company kept the large luxury gap – the distance between the centre of the front axle and the front door. Jaguar said that this marked the car apart from other EVs.
This gap measures 898 millimetres or 17 per cent of the vehicle and is marked by an anodised brass-effect finishing strip called the Fender Ingot.
Andreev said the team utilised the branding system while staying away from "superfluous ornaments". Jaguar's classic leaper logo is laser-etched on the finisher, while the strikethrough detail appears on the bonnet and rear.
The brand's monogram, redesigned in 2024, was placed in the centre of the wheel, while the new wordmark features on the grille and on the trunk.
Behind the rear door is the Impossible Panel. This rear quarter panel was pressed in six ways, allowing the glass seals to be hidden. The curve of the Impossible Panel continues underneath the bottom of the windows on both doors, flattening out into the hood.
Foregoing the full glass roof seen on many electric vehicles, the Type 01's panoramic glass roof is hemmed in by cant rails that continue the dramatic curve of the rear quarter panels.
The distinctive rear panelling and cant rails play into the performance, and the brand said that the air flowing past the body actually generates accelerative push on the rear. A deployable fender extends from the back.
The car has 1,000 metric horsepower (PS) of power, allowing the driver to reach 62 miles per hour in 3.2 seconds, and a 118 kilowatt-hour (kWh) battery, making it the most powerful Jaguar in production.
An Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) range of 400 miles and a Worldwide Harmonised Light Vehicle Test Procedure (WLTP) range of up to 450 miles.
The length and width of the vehicle allowed for spacious interiors.
It has a single rail that runs down the middle of the cabin, separating the passenger and driver's-side seats in the front and rear.
A screen sits behind the wheel, acting as a dash, with a smaller screen for environmental controls above the centre.
Another screen sits above the dash at the window and replaces the traditional rear-view mirror, with a sound bar extending out from either side.
The upholstery and seating were meant to be furniture-like, and the production vehicle has textiles by Danish brand Kvadrat as well as brass detailing.
Jaguar chief materiality designer Mary Crisp noted the lightweight luxury nature of the textiles, adding that Kvadrat is on "the top of their game".
"I wanted to add that warmth you get in your home," said Crisp, noting the multi-toned nature of the wool blends.
On show at the New York event was a silver vehicle with satin finishes.
The release follows a slate of other luxury electric vehicles, including Ferrari's first electric vehicle and Bentley's, both released in the past year.
The photography is courtesy of Jaguar Land Rover.

As bear attacks rise in Japan, fearful residents change daily routines
A foreign resident who has been attacked multiple times says he now carries bear spray and a baseball bat when he visits his lodge in Gunma
Jeff Kingston used to take long walks with his dogs across the hills of Gunma in central Japan. But not this year.
He has good reason. Kingston says he has encountered bears in those mountains more than 100 times over the years and been charged by aggressive bears around a dozen times. In 2014, a black bear knocked him down and attacked him across the skull with its claws, leaving a gash that required nine stitches.
“This year, I have actively refrained from going into the hills precisely because I want to avoid encounters,” said Kingston, an American academic who lives in Tokyo but has a lodge in Gunma. “And when I do go, I always carry bear spray and a baseball bat just in case.”
His caution reflects a wider concern in Japan, where bear encounters have surged in recent years, including in residential areas and farmland, prompting authorities to warn people to take extra care as the animals prepare for winter.

Jaguar targets young Americans with Type 01 EV – but it’s too long for UK parking spaces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
00:00:28 UTC
09:00:28 KST

It has no rear window, will not fit into a UK parking space and – starting at £130,000 – ($172,000) is aimed squarely at rich tech industry buyers driving the wide open roads of America.
Jaguar’s electric car, the Type 01, was launched in New York on Tuesday night and marks the culmination of a two-year rebrand that has been one of the most scrutinised in automotive history.
Bosses hope the vehicle will appeal to a younger, richer audience than the manufacturer’s previous “shrinking and ageing” customer base of “men in their 50s”, said Rawdon Glover, 58, Jaguar’s managing director.
With an ultra-long bonnet, low roof and muscular design, the Type 01 is a sharp departure from its predecessor, the F-Type. It is also double the F-Type’s starting price of about £62,000.
Buyers are likely to be rich, “urban” and “very design literate, very technology literate”, Glover said. “The person making this purchase will be choosing the car because it’s a bold choice.”
A senior JLR executive close to the Type 01 project put it more bluntly: “It’s the type of car that you park up and everybody stops and says: ‘Fucking hell, what have you just turned up in?’”
The launch comes at a critical juncture for parent company Jaguar Land Rover (JLR), which has grappled with falling sales as cheaper Chinese rivals eat into its UK market share. It is still recovering from a massive cyber-attack last year that cost the economy an estimated £1.9bn.
JLR recently announced 4,000 job cuts in an attempt to save £1.7bn over two years, citing “intense competition and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty”. The Guardian understands Jaguar employees working on the Type 01 programme were offered voluntary redundancy along with the rest of JLR’s non-manufacturing workforce.
The car will go on sale in early 2027, with the first deliveries anticipated in the second half of the year.
“It’s really important that we put Jaguar back on a more solid financial footing,” Glover said. Asked if doubling prices would be effective, he said it was better than “to toil away as we have done for the last two decades in the volume premium space”.
Range Rover also unveiled its first fully electric model in September with a starting price of £154,070 compared with £107,530 for its combustion engine predecessor.
Waning demand in China, a key market for luxury cars, has also hit Jaguar hard. Glover revealed that the Type 01 will not launch in the country for “a couple of years. We’ve decided just to hold off on that.”
However, he added that China would eventually be “an important part of the equation … it’s very difficult for any car manufacturer to exclude the single largest car market in the world”.
PB Balaji, the JLR chief executive, has said the parent company will pivot towards North America and target more sales to millionaires and billionaires to turn its fortunes around.
Glover admitted that while the Type 01’s launch was in New York, it “absolutely” could have been in Silicon Valley instead, reflecting the type of buyer Jaguar is targeting. He recently took a prototype to the offices of Nvidia, the California-based AI company, whose boss, Jensen Huang, had a ride and “loved it”.
The car has no rear window, instead using a rear-facing camera feeding a screen where a traditional mirror would be. The car produces more than 1,000 horsepower and Jaguar says it will travel up to 400 miles on a single charge.
It follows a controversial rebrand that started with an ad in late 2024 featuring stern-faced models without a car in sight. The ad prompted a backlash online and was followed by the Type 00 concept car that was unveiled in “Miami pink”, which Donald Trump described it as “woke” while Nigel Farage said Jaguar deserved to go bust.
Glover admitted the backlash “wasn’t always easy” but added: “The reality is we will need to attract a new audience.”
It is just as well: at 2 metres (6ft 5in) wide the Type 01 will hog the British country lanes frequented by Jaguar’s old customer base, while at more than 5.2 metres in length it will not fit in a standard 4.8 metre UK parking space.
“There are long cars out there on the market,” Glover argued, adding that a Land Rover Defender with a wheel on the back is longer than the Type 01, which he claimed had the “turning circle of a Fiat 500” with its all-wheel steering. “It is incredibly manoeuvrable.”
The business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said: “Jaguar’s new EV is a crucial step in JLR’s plans to invest over £15bn in the UK, and another big vote of confidence in our world-class automotive industry.
“This cutting-edge new model being designed, engineered and built in Britain will support thousands of jobs across the West Midlands and North West, and builds on over £1bn of UK automotive investment secured just last month – marking another step forward in our mission to reindustrialise Britain.”

Jaguar Finally Reveals Its Biggest Gamble: the Type 01
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
00:00:00 UTC
09:00:00 KST

The day has finally arrived. Jaguar began its long road to electric reinvention in November 2024 with a firestorm of a rebrand featuring no cars. Just a month later, it revealed a prototype: the Type 00—a car so polarizing it practically broke the internet’s automotive enclave. Some loved it; others hated it so much that Jaguar’s own staff were targeted for supposedly betraying the company’s 90-year history.
Since this chaotic but undoubtedly viral launch, major departures have followed, including Jaguar Land Rover’s (JLR) chief creative officer Gerry McGovern, the notable car designer who signed off on Jaguar’s divisive all-electric design and the no-car ad campaign.
Jaguar’s managing director, Rawdon Glover, is a brave man. Through this shitstorm, and a frighteningly long period of selling no new cars whatsoever, he’s remained unflappable; utterly confident that, when people see the final car—the finished version of the luxury four-door GT that is “like no other”—everything will make sense. That moment is here. The company finally revealed the Jaguar Type 01 at an event in New York City on Tuesday—the finished version of the Type 00. (Jaguar Land Rover paid a portion of WIRED's travel expenses so we could attend the launch.)
“A bold grand tourer that never arrives unnoticed, like all the best Jaguars of the past,” Jaguar’s press material says. This is most certainly true: you will see this thing coming. The low roofline, short front and extended rear overhangs, long hood, and huge 23-inch wheels all remain from the prototype, just as promised. The cab-rear design hides a 50–50 weight distribution, and the huge surfaces make it hard to square the fact that this is the most aerodynamic Jag ever, with active vanes, a deployable spoiler, and airflow trickery delivering a drag coefficient of 0.23 Cd.
Crucially, the production model’s extra doors make more sense of the design, shifting the Type 01’s look away from Thunderbirds territory to more familiar ground. The front has been softened ever so slightly as well, which again is preferable to the prototype’s exceedingly bluff nose. The rear, however, is where the exterior design really shines with hidden-until-lit, full-width lights embedded in horizontal strikethroughs.
Let’s get the specs out of the way: the Type 01 is the most powerful Jaguar road car, with up to 1,030 Pferdestärke (PS) and 1,365 Newton-meters. It goes from standstill to 62 mph in 3.2 seconds. Justifying the tagline of “power in reserve,” the car can rocket from 62 to 112 mph in a further 4 seconds. I’ve been driven in it, and it feels like the acceleration never ends thanks to the tri-motor setup of a 260-kilowatt (kW) front motor paired with twin 310-kW rear motors.
It stands 5,235 mm long and 1,403 mm tall, but all-wheel steering makes it feel much smaller on the road. The 850-volt bespoke Jaguar architecture and 118-kilowatt-hour usable battery supposedly deliver an EPA range of up to 400 miles (450 miles on WLTP), with a “sustained highway speed” range of up to 320 miles. Drivers can add up to 200 miles of range in 13 minutes using 350 kW rapid DC charging. So the TL;DR? It’s huge, fast, aerodynamic, powerful, and, most definitely, unique.
Inside, a dramatic central spine runs the full length of the cabin, creating a zone for each occupant. Lots of “brass-inspired” finishes are intended to underline the luxury message. A panoramic glass roof with adjustable virtual blinds brings in the light, but there’s no rear windscreen. Instead, a digital “ClearSight” rearview display is embedded centrally in the full-width panoramic soundbar at the base of the windscreen to show what’s behind. Cleverly, the feed from this rear-facing camera is positioned at the same height as the door mirrors, supposedly reducing the annoying focal adjustment these systems usually demand.
Ahead of the driver is a 24-inch OLED screen that extends toward the center of the car. A central 7-inch smartphone-style display sits between the driver and front passenger for common controls such as climate and audio, operated entirely by touchscreen with (sadly) no physical switchgear in sight. “Hot stone massage effect” seats, whatever those are, are also electrically adjustable in 12 different ways. Cabin air purification removes allergens, toxins, and particulates, and a fragrance diffuser offers a choice of scents—which seems to be the pinnacle of what Western auto companies think a luxury car interior needs these days.
As a grand tourer, luggage space is important. The Type 01 offers 450 liters of load space, expanding to 1,000 liters with rear seats folded. And then there are the production stories: Jaguar built more than 150 prototypes, drove 700,000 miles, and filed more than 360 patents while developing the car.
Jaguar is most proud, and rightly so, of its “impossible panel.” It's a single, unbroken panel that runs more than 3 meters from the A-pillar to the rear of the Type 01. Pressing this huge piece with five different acute angles in it was deemed not possible by Jaguar's modeling system. After roughly 22 weeks and 1,500 hours of development (supposedly requiring someone to come out of retirement), Jaguar realized this “impossible” panel.
Pricing of the Type 01 is possibly the most important thing Jaguar has to nail. Starting at around $170,000 (or £130,000—no confirmed pricing yet), this puts the Jag well below Ferrari Luces, electric Merc G-Wagens and Lamborghinis, and even the new Bentley Torcal, exactly where Glover wants to sit. Jaguar thinks it has a sweet spot in luxury EVs, a Goldilocks zone where buyers are eager to part with cash for electric cars that aren’t astronomical but priced high enough above the premium sector to be legitimately highfalutin.
No one has really succeeded with the luxury EV market. Porsche has tried. So has Lamborghini. Mercedes has had a very tough time. Now Bentley is having a crack at it. Glover thinks that the Type 01 has a shot.
“One of us is going to break through the glass ceiling and make a success of EVs at elevated price points,” Glover tells me. “The best way to do that is not to play into the tropes of EVs. You’re not going to get there because it’s an electric car. You’re going to get there because the car itself looks a certain way, feels a certain way, drives a certain way. If you can do all of those things, [it doesn’t matter] whether it’s combustion or electric. Just being an electric car was enough for such a short period. Cars have got to earn their right in somebody’s garage.”
Glover has openly said the Type 01 will have to earn its place with “almost an entirely new client base,” one that is supposedly younger, more affluent, urban, independently minded, creative, and wishing to “carve their own path.” We shall see very soon exactly what kind of person signs on the dotted line to reserve a Type 01. Will they look like the youthful, vibrant characters in Jaguar’s initial launch campaign, or like traditional Jaguar, Lotus, and Aston owners with gray hair, flannel shirts, and bad shorts?
“We’ve got to make sure that new audience comes along," Glover says. “But I don’t want to alienate anybody.” The Chinese do well with that youthful audience. “I’ve driven some of the Li Autos. I’ve driven some of the XPeng cars. They’re impressive in terms of the amount of technology in them. The quality of fit and finish is increasing at a pace.”
But Glover still thinks a big gap exists between Chinese cars and established Western autos; though with Xiaomi’s achievements after only a few years of making cars, it’s hard to see this view staying true for long. “They’re playing in a commodity space," he says. "It’s about how many features, how much tech, how much range, and how can I do it at the lowest price. I’m not saying we’re immune to all of that, but it certainly validates us getting out of the volume premium market.”
Like Bentley, Jaguar is leaning into its heritage to look for things the Chinese will find harder to emulate. But it could be argued that the Type 01 lacks any obvious heritage. The pioneering spirit is there, for sure, but this is an EV very much looking forward, not back. With that in mind, what does, say, two years of success look like to Glover for this electrified rebirth of the brand?
“Success will be we’ve established ourselves at the [new] price point,” he says. “People are saying, ‘Yep, Jaguar is worth paying more for.’ I know what volumes we need to achieve. I’m not going to articulate those, but just under that we need to generate a certain level of volume to create that critical mass.”
For Glover, this level of volume requires customers to see Jaguar as a more current, culturally relevant brand, and to be genuinely interested in what the company will do next.
“Is it just the man in the bad shirts and bad shorts, or have we actually been successful in attracting a new audience?” Glover says. “We start seeing that in the first two years.”

Three years since October 7: Why Zionism is more relevant than ever - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
00:00:00 UTC
09:00:00 KST

The events of the Hamas-led invasion and massacres on October 7, 2023, and the war that followed, brought fundamental questions back to the center of Israeli discourse – questions that for years had seemed to have already been settled.
What is the role of the State of Israel in the life of the Jewish people? To what extent can the Jewish people rely on the international community when it comes to matters concerning their security? And what remains of Zionism in an era in which Israel is a strong, prosperous state integrated into the international system?
Three years after that morning, it has become clear that Zionism, which has sometimes been portrayed as an idea belonging primarily to the era of state-building and pioneering, is not merely a chapter in the history of the State of Israel. It continues to provide an answer to fundamental questions concerning the condition of the Jewish people in the 21st century as well.
The revival of Zionism
Political Zionism was not born merely out of an aspiration to establish a Jewish state. It emerged from a historical diagnosis of the condition of the Jews as a people. Emancipation in Europe granted Jews civil rights; opened to them the gates of universities, the liberal professions, and high society; and gave rise to the hope that full integration into the broader society would gradually resolve the “Jewish Question.”
Yet Zionist thinkers understood that legal equality, economic success, and social acceptance do not necessarily eliminate the political vulnerability of a minority that ultimately depends on the protection of others.
As the years passed, it was precisely the success of the State of Israel that, to some extent, diminished the sense of urgency surrounding the idea that had led to its establishment. Israel became a regional military, economic, and technological power, while Jewish communities in the West integrated into society, academia, the economy, and politics to an unprecedented degree.
After World War II, an international system also emerged that placed, at least rhetorically, human rights, the protection of minorities, and the prevention of genocide at its center.
Under these conditions, it was easy to assume that Jewish history had entered a new era, and that at least some of the warnings on which Zionism had been founded had lost their relevance.
October 7 challenged that assumption
The images of families hiding for hours in their homes, civilians fleeing for their lives, and Jewish communities being attacked by terrorists brought back into Israeli consciousness scenes that seemed to belong to other chapters of our history.
However, the conclusion is not that Zionism failed. On the contrary. The events demonstrated precisely the profound difference between the condition of the Jewish people today and their condition throughout most of history.
ZIONISM DID not promise that Jews would not be attacked. It sought to ensure that when they were attacked, they would not be helpless.
This is perhaps the deepest expression of the meaning of Jewish sovereignty. When communities in Israel were attacked, there was no need to wait for the mercy of a foreign ruler, hope that another government would send forces to defend the Jews, or rely on the willingness of the international community to intervene.
The State of Israel, despite the terrible failure of that morning, was able to mobilize hundreds of thousands of soldiers and reservists, fight back, and defend its citizens. For centuries, that possibility was simply unavailable to the Jewish people.
Yet October 7 and the period that followed also raised another question concerning the status of Jews in the Western world. Many Jews, both in Israel and in the Diaspora, were shocked not only by the scale of the attack but also by the responses to it.
At some of the most prestigious universities in the West, the massacre was quickly translated into familiar ideological frameworks of “oppressors” and “oppressed,” “colonialists” and “indigenous peoples.” Instead of beginning with the facts and the moral responsibility of those who carried out the massacre, some rushed to interpret the events through theoretical frameworks in which the identities of victim and aggressor are almost predetermined.
The US congressional hearing in which the presidents of Harvard, the University of Pennsylvania, and MIT were required to answer questions concerning calls for the genocide of Jews on their campuses became, for many, a symbol of a deeper crisis. Institutions accustomed to speaking with great confidence about justice, equality, and the protection of minorities suddenly appeared hesitant precisely when Jews were the targets of threats.
For many Diaspora Jews, this was a deeply unsettling experience. Those who believed that their full integration into Western societies had made their Jewishness a secondary component of their identity discovered that, in the eyes of parts of the societies around them, Jewish identity still carries profound political and social significance.
Not because their American, British, or French identities are not genuine, but because Jewish history teaches that Jewish identity is not always something the individual alone can determine the significance of, in the eyes of those around them.
The international arena also exposed the limitations of relying on external institutions. Shortly after the massacres, resolutions were adopted at the United Nations calling for a ceasefire without including an explicit condemnation of Hamas. UN Secretary-General António Guterres stated that the Hamas attack “did not happen in a vacuum.”
Proceedings in international courts placed Israel at the center of some of the most serious accusations in international law, while organizations responsible for defending women’s rights struggled for a considerable period to give adequate expression to the evidence of sexual violence committed during the Hamas-led attacks.
THE CUMULATIVE picture recalls a truth that Zionism understood more than a century ago: the international community can be a partner, a friend, and an ally, but Israel cannot entrust its existential security to it. This was one of the fundamental principles of political Zionism, and since October 7 it has taken on renewed significance.
For generations, the Jewish people witnessed the rise and fall of kingdoms and empires, often without having any meaningful ability to influence the forces that determined their fate. They survived, and at times even prospered, but time and again it became clear how fragile their achievements could be when their security depended on the goodwill of others.
The State of Israel changed that equation. It does not guarantee that the Jewish people will not be attacked, that antisemitism will disappear, or that the world will always stand by their side. It gives them something more fundamental: the ability to act, defend themselves, and take responsibility for their future.
Three years after October 7, this is perhaps the most important Zionist lesson: the principle that the Jewish people are no longer mere spectators in their own history. Responsibility for our fate rests, first and foremost, in our own hands.
The writer is the deputy chairman of the Institute for Security Policy of the Israel Defense and Security Forum.

open fields and concrete paths create shared sports landscape in tijuana
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
23:55:42 UTC
08:55:42 KST

open fields and concrete paths create shared sports landscape in tijuana
centro deportivo abejas’ continuous layout by border arquitectos creates connections between sports, recreation, and public space.
Sports and community spaces connect across public landscape
Centro Deportivo Abejas by Border Arquitectos is a 60,000-sqm public sports complex in Tijuana, Baja California, designed for a rapidly growing neighborhood with limited access to recreational facilities. The project brings sports, recreation, and community activities together through a continuous public landscape.
Instead of organizing the complex as a series of separate buildings and sports fields, the design uses open space as its main organizing element. Soccer fields, basketball courts, running tracks, training areas, and support facilities are connected by pedestrian paths, plazas, and shared gathering spaces.
Paths, plazas, and edges create an everyday public environment
The design team treats spaces between the sports facilities as active parts of the complex, creating areas for movement, informal gathering, observation, and interaction. Landscape, circulation, sports infrastructure, and architectural elements are conceived as parts of one urban framework, allowing the site to accommodate both organized sporting events and everyday public use.
A restrained palette of concrete and durable hardscape surfaces defines circulation and gathering areas, while sports surfaces and landscape elements distinguish different zones across the site. The architectural components remain integrated with the landscape, reinforcing the continuity of the public space.
By combining sports facilities with open space and pedestrian connections, Centro Deportivo Abejas extends the role of public sports infrastructure into a broader civic setting, creating a place for movement, recreation, gathering, and everyday use within Tijuana’s expanding urban fabric.
project info:
name: Centro Deportivo y Recreativo Abejas
architect: Border Arquitectos | @border_arquitectos
location: Tijuana, Baja California, Mexico

Christa Pike awake after failed Tennessee execution: lawyers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
23:49:00 UTC
08:49:00 KST

Christa Pike awake after failed Tennessee execution: lawyers
October 7, 2026
A prisoner who survived an attempt to carry out the death penalty in Tennessee, the United States, last week is conscious and speaking as she continues to receive treatment in hospital.
"Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care," the inmate's attorneys said in a statement on Tuesday.
"Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed. Her recovery is medically unprecedented."
Pike, who was sentenced to death for the beating, stabbing and murder of a classmate in 1995, survived two doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital – which her lawyers said left her arms burned and blistered.
Christa Pike not 'free of further serious risk'
"She's still in the ICU," said Dr. Joel Zivot, a professor of anesthesiology and surgery in Atlanta in neighboring Georgia, who consulted as an expert for Pike's legal team.
"She has recovered to a certain degree that she's able to be off a ventilator and able to speak, but in no way would I announce her free of further serious risk. There's still a lot of bad things that can happen here, even when everyone is doing their job well."
Tuesday's updates were the first indication that Pike's condition has improved since the failed execution attempt at a Nashville prison last Wednesday.
Her attorneys thanked first responders and medical staff who they said have "treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her" – as they prepare to go to court on Wednesday seeking to learn more about what went wrong with the lethal injection.
Pike's attorneys seeking to commute sentence
The lawyers are seeking a court order requiring the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve evidence, including drug lot numbers, records and other information from the attempted execution.
Ultimately, they are looking to have Pike's sentence commuted to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
While Dr. Zivot said Pike's current state "bodes well for a good recovery," her attorneys warned that her prognosis is still "unclear" and said she faces "a long recovery."
"Christa is a survivor and will take recovery one day at a time," they said.
According to the Death Penalty Information Center, which publishes data and analysis on capital punishment in the United States, Pike is the first prisoner ever to survive "after being injected with lethal doses of execution drugs."

LA and San Diego residents ‘horrified’ by Trump suggesting Iran bomb them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
23:45:02 UTC
08:45:02 KST

Donald Trump’s extraordinary implication that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego have sparked condemnation across the political spectrum. As residents of the two major west coast cities awoke on Tuesday to another sweltering day in a record-breaking heatwave, the president’s comments sent blood boiling even higher.
Jessica, a 28-year-old Los Angeles hair stylist, was scrolling through social media early on Tuesday morning and was shocked to see that Trump had just suggested Iran should decimate her home town.
For Jessica, who declined to be identified by her full name because she fears for the safety of her Mexican-born parents, the comments marked a new low for a president who had already spent years attacking immigrant families like hers.
“I was just thinking what the fuck is wrong with him?” she said while waiting for a Waymo outside grocery store in LA’s Koreatown neighborhood. “He hates us. He hates LA. He hates any Democratic state ... It’s just a really sad situation.”
In southern California, Trump’s unprecedented musing before a cheering crowd at a Nebraska rally on Monday night – that perhaps a foreign power should decimate two of the country’s best-known cities – has been met with reactions ranging from deep hostility to dismissive incredulity. Gavin Newsom, the state’s governor, called the remarks “dangerous – if not treasonous – putting a target on two of our biggest cities and one of America’s largest naval hubs”.
Perhaps most of all, California residents see it as a sign of the president’s fixation on tearing down west coast progressivism and diversity, most visibly through the deployment of national guard troops in Los Angeles during a series of brutal ICE raids in 2025.
During a bustling lunch service at Grand Central Market, a food hall in downtown LA, tourists and residents milled between taco stands and dumpling stalls. Many had yet to hear of the president’s threats, until asked by a reporter. One of those who had was Jens Midthun, a downtown resident who often stops at the market for coffee.
“Trump has tried to paint Los Angeles as a dystopia despite it being a wonderful place,” said Midthun, sipping an iced coffee under a shaded outdoor table as the temperature approached the triple digits. (Midthun serves as the president of the downtown LA neighborhood council, but was speaking in a personal capacity.)
“It reminded me that the president is obsessed with us – obsessed with California, obsessed with Los Angeles,” Midthun said. “We try not to think about him and yet, here he is with Los Angeles’s name right there in his mouth.”
Trump’s remarks have sparked a particularly strong reaction in San Diego, which is home to roughly a quarter-million veterans and has one of the largest concentrations of military personnel in the US.
“His statement was so irrational, it’s hard to explain exactly what he was saying, but it sounded like he was willing to give us up,” said Gil Field, communications director for San Diego Veterans for Peace, a group that opposes the war. “It’s horrible and we’re horrified.”
The military supports nearly 357,000 local jobs in the region, representing $61.3bn of San Diego county’s economy, according to a report released last year. Defense spending accounts for 22% of San Diego’s gross regional product and the area is home to multiple naval bases and Marine Corps stations, with one out of four active-duty marines based in San Diego.
“This is a military town, so you’ve got bipartisan objections to his comments,” said Field, who noted that there were always concerns that San Diego could be targeted in war due to the heavy military presence. “So for him to say this about San Diego is particularly galling. He did San Diego a disservice.”
Jim Desmond, a Republican naval veteran running for a congressional seat in San Diego, also offered a pointed rebuke.
“I served to protect Americans, not write off American cities as an acceptable price of war. Our job is to keep Americans safe, stand up to our enemies, and make sure a threat like that never becomes reality,” Desmond said on X. “No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage.”
Back in Los Angeles, far from the negative fantasies that Trump spins in his speeches, Midthun sees an economic powerhouse and vibrant cultural center sandwiched between the beach and the mountains, and enriched by some of the largest diaspora communities from across the world – South Korea, Mexico, El Salvador, Armenia and even Iran.
“The president keeps talking about us, and talking about us,” Midthun said. “He’s got a lot of issues to solve. He should work on those issues instead of obsessing over the beautiful, great people of Los Angeles.”

Russia says no risk of epidemic following plague institute worker’s death
Russia’s health watchdog says it is winding down precautionary measures it put in place and has shared its latest information with the WHO
Russia’s health regulator said on Wednesday there were no risks of an epidemic breaking out in Siberia after a plague institute worker there died, as the World Health Organization pressed Moscow for more information about her cause of death.
Russian authorities say the 28-year-old laboratory worker died on Friday from pneumonia of an as-yet unestablished origin, in a case that has prompted international concern, including from US President Donald Trump, and which saw about 200 people initially placed in quarantine.
Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s health watchdog, said in a statement it was winding down precautionary measures it had put in place after concluding there was no risk of an epidemic and that it had shared its latest information with the WHO.
No cases of plague had been detected among anyone who had come into contact with the deceased worker, Darya Shipilova, it said, and 90 per cent of those placed in quarantine had been released after nearly 5,000 lab tests had failed to detect any dangerous pathogens.

Apple’s smart home push includes doorbell, lock, thermostat co-developed with LG
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
23:42:00 UTC
08:42:00 KST

Apple’s smart home push includes doorbell, lock, thermostat co-developed with LG
CUPERTINO, California – Apple’s upcoming push into smart home devices will include a doorbell, thermostat and other accessories developed through an unusual partnership with LG Electronics.
The products will be part of an ecosystem of devices that work with Apple’s new smart home hub, as well as an upgraded HomePod mini and fresh TV set-top box, according to people with knowledge of the matter.
The new Apple devices are set to be introduced on Oct 13.
The products developed with South Korea’s LG will also include a smart deadbolt lock, indoor security camera, outdoor security camera and floodlight camera, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the undertaking is private.
Though the two companies worked together to develop the accessories, the products will carry the LG brand. The South Korean firm is handling manufacturing and product support.
Apple has used this strategy before: It has discreetly worked with companies like Foxconn Technology Group’s Belkin and Logitech International SA to develop products that sell under other brands.
This arrangement with so-called second-party suppliers gives Apple a way to quickly expand its ecosystem without shouldering the full cost and complexity of producing and supporting a wide range of accessories.
Apple can also help shape the products’ design, tailor their features and oversee engineering while keeping the work largely under wraps.
Development of the LG accessories has lagged behind Apple’s own devices, and the products are not expected to reach consumers for at least a few more months.
Spokespeople for Apple and LG declined to comment.
In recent weeks, LG has sought regulatory approval for the devices, including with the US Federal Communications Commission and UL Solutions, a product certification company.
In many cases, the databases for both organisations include filings that reveal product names, specifications, features and drawings of the accessories.
That includes products labelled as the LG Video Doorbell Wired, LG Floodlight Cam, LG Outdoor Cam Plug-In, LG Indoor Cam Plug-In, LG Smart Deadbolt Lock, LG Smart Thermostat and LG Temperature Sensor.
LG requested that photos and more precise details on the products remain confidential until early 2027. The filings do not mention Apple’s involvement.
Many of the devices include support for Wi-Fi and Bluetooth networks, as well as Thread and Matter, two smart home protocols embraced by Apple and its rivals in recent years.
The door lock also supports UWB, or ultra-wideband capability, a feature that allows for auto-unlocking when users approach their door.
For Apple, the new home ecosystem and devices will mark a formal reboot of HomeKit, a platform it launched in 2014 that has gained little traction compared with offerings from Amazon.com and Alphabet’s Google.
Apple aims to use its smart home devices and Siri AI assistant to breathe new life into the category.
The company is also planning its own additional offerings in the future, including a privacy-centric home-monitoring device, a version of its smart home hub that attaches the screen to a robotic arm, and an in-home security monitoring service, Bloomberg News has reported.
For LG, a company better known for TVs and washing machines, the devices will mark its own smart home expansion.
The line-up represents its first indoor camera in nearly a decade, as well as its first outdoor camera, thermostat, floodlight camera and doorbell in recent history. The company also is selling its first smart lock outside of South Korea.
This would put Apple and LG in closer competition with Amazon’s Ring and Google’s Nest, which are firmly entrenched in the smart home.
Each already offers similar devices that let customers keep tabs on every corner of their house and surrounding property.
Apple and LG have a long history. Once rivals in the smartphone space, Apple and some of LG Electronics’ sister companies are critical partners.
LG Display supplies displays for many Apple products, including screens for devices.
Apple has also worked with LG Electronics on integrating its services into LG TV sets.
Nearly a decade ago, when Apple temporarily exited the external computer monitor market, it co-developed monitors with LG to work with the iPhone maker’s laptops. BLOOMBERG

Don’t forget the women saving lives in Gaza: Wounded IDF paramedic fights to be seen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
23:41:27 UTC
08:41:27 KST

Gaya Tzuberi, 22, from Ramat Gan, was seriously wounded by gunfire in both legs while trying to rescue wounded soldiers under fire in Shijaiyah.
Role at time of injury: Paramedic with the IDF Armored Corps’ 53rd Battalion
On the final Saturday of the IDF’s prestigious paramedic course, just before the trainees were due to scatter to different units after a year and three months together, the young paramedics decided to spend the weekend together at Kibbutz Sufa near the Gaza border.
It was October 7.
“There were several girls from the course who had previously attended a pre-military academy at Kibbutz Sufa,” Tzuberi recalls. “They said the academy was away for the holiday and that we could sleep in their rooms. We had Friday night dinner together, everyone dressed in white, we made Kiddush. It was a great evening.”
“The next morning at 6:30, we woke up to the sound of Red Alert sirens. Most of us didn’t know what that was. There was huge panic. There were six to eight of us in each room. We went into safe rooms that had no locks and pushed beds against the doors and windows.”
“Think about it. There were more than 20 paramedics near the end of their training in the Gaza border area, and we couldn’t do anything because we had no weapons and no medical equipment.”
“It was a feeling of helplessness. We started tearing up clothes and breaking hangers to make improvised tourniquets, but they couldn’t bring wounded people to us. After 32 hours, a bus arrived, took us to Tze’elim and from there we went home.”
Immediately after being evacuated from Sufa, Tzuberi was assigned as a paramedic to the Armored Corps’ 53rd Battalion. On the morning of December 7, she joined a military force heading into an offensive operation in Shijaiyah. “We were a convoy of armored vehicles, tanks, D9 bulldozers and Namer armored personnel carriers,” she recalls.
“I was in a Namer with about 10 other people when suddenly a terrorist came out of one of the alleys with an RPG and hit the first tank, which started burning.”
“We wanted to run over and help them, but there was no way to reach them with the Namer. We stopped about 100 meters away. The doctor and I ran toward the tank, and they brought out the first wounded soldier. We put him on a stretcher and ran back toward the Namer, where another paramedic and a medic were waiting for us, and then we ran back toward the tank.”
“We treated another wounded soldier there who was in serious condition, unconscious and barely breathing. Then my medic called me back. I ran toward the tank for the third time, and then a burst of gunfire started coming toward me. I fell onto my stomach and stopped feeling my legs.”
“I was hit in my thighs, close to the pelvis. The medic tried to lift me, was hit by gunfire and ran for cover. I tried to put tourniquets on my own legs and couldn’t.”
“Out of the corner of my eye, I saw a reservist named Avi Baldasar in front of me. I shouted to him that he had to put a tourniquet on me. Even though he has four children at home, he decided to rescue me, an act that goes against every human instinct. He managed to get me to the doctor’s Namer.”
“I was in terrible pain, bleeding nonstop, and I was already looking up at the sky and asking God what this situation had to do with me. Then they evacuated me by helicopter to Soroka.”
How long were you there?
“Five months hospitalized, and then I moved to rehabilitation at Sheba and learned how to walk from scratch. All the movements you take completely for granted became so difficult and complicated. I’m still receiving treatment, and I’ll never be what I was before.”
Who was there to support you through all of that?
“My mother never left me for a moment, my sister and brother took care of me, and so did the whole extended family. I got tremendous support from the friends I met in rehabilitation. In the end, they were my anchor because we went through everything together, and we are the only ones who can really understand one another.”
What is the damage?
“I have a complex nerve injury. I danced for many years, and I can’t dance the way I used to. I’m also receiving psychological treatment. In the end, every physical injury is also emotional, but slowly you learn to live with it.”
“Today I have a brace on my leg that is hard to miss, and I have scars. If I wear a swimsuit, that alone draws strange looks.”
What is the biggest difficulty?
“That things don’t come easily anymore like they used to. Mainly accepting the physical damage.”
What do you miss most about your old life?
“Going back to being a normal person whose life isn’t only about rehabilitation, but other things too. I was a dancer, as I said. It’s what I love most and what I’m best at.”
What gives you strength?
“Mostly sports. A few months after the injury, I joined the PosSEAble nonprofit and started surfing. It was something I had never done before.”
“I didn’t choose to be injured, but I feel the injury taught me a lot about my own strength. I learned not to take anything for granted. And in the end, I also managed to change something. I changed the minds of some people who say, ‘Oh, you were wounded in Gaza? What? There are women there?’”
Do you feel wounded men and wounded women are treated differently?
“If I’m walking with a male friend and both of us are on crutches, they’ll tell him, ‘Hero of Israel,’ and they’ll ask me, ‘What happened? An accident?’”
“There are so many female combat paramedics in Gaza who have saved lives. People need to appreciate that and say thank you to the women who choose to do this.”
