Pressure Mounts on Cornell to Explain Its Handling of Sexual Assault Allegations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
23:39:47 UTC
08:39:47 KST

Students and faculty at Cornell University are demonstrating mounting displeasure with the school’s administration over its handling of the alleged gang rape by fraternity members that occurred in 2024, calling for greater accountability and an overhaul of investigatory procedure.
Hundreds of students, faculty members, and other supporters gathered Monday in front of the school’s student center under the banner of “Justice for Survivors.” Attendees wore purple ribbons and held signs that asked questions such as “Cornell, can you hear us now?” and “When will we start protecting survivors?”
The peaceful protest was led by dozens of student organizations, including Students for a Democratic Cornell (SDC).
“We found it incredible,” Soham Bera, the vice-chair of SDC, tells TIME. “This was a moment where you had hundreds, if not thousands, of students coming together—despite the fact this administration has been known for cracking down on protesting and still deciding this is our moment.”
Read More: The System That Failed Cornell’s Jane Doe
The groups also presented Cornell’s leadership with demands for disciplinary action and changes to how the university handles sexual assault complaints.
Among the chants from demonstrators were calls for Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff to resign and chants of “Ban the frats!”
Athena Holloway, the former president of Cornell’s Black Students United and president of Cornell NAACP, was one of the speakers at the student-led event. She noted the long history of students using their voices to demand change on campus, including the Afro-American Society Willard Straight Hall Takeover of 1969.
“Cornell has changed before, and we can change it again,” she said.
Why the Cornell sexual assault case is drawing new outrage
Recent demonstrations come as a response to the civil lawsuit filed Sept. 14 by a former Cornell student, who is identified in the complaint as Jane Doe. Doe not only alleges in the lawsuit that she was sexually assaulted by seven members of the school’s Chi Phi fraternity but also claims that Cornell was negligent in its response and violated New York law.
Cornell’s response to the incident—and its broader approach to handling sexual assault reports on campus—came under scrutiny after Doe’s lawsuit alleged negligence, breach of contract, and violations of New York law.
“We need to speak up. This miscarriage of justice cannot continue to go on,” Bera says.
Bera and other protesters point to what they consider insufficient punishments from Cornell University after it conducted its Title IX investigation, which began in January 2025. Doe’s attorney, Thomas Giuffra, has said that Cornell expelled two of the seven accused students and that it required some of the other fraternity members to write essays.
Cornell has confirmed that its disciplinary process resulted in expulsions and suspensions, but it has not disclosed individual outcomes. It also clarified last week that “none of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement.”
Giuffra also claims that Doe was denied her request for a tuition refund when she sought to leave Cornell. He says that she eventually withdrew from the university, citing a lack of institutional support.
Cornell subsequently gave a response to Inside Higher Ed saying that it regularly works with students seeking leave and has in the past refunded payments, but it did not respond directly to the accusation related to Doe.
As more information comes to light, tensions continue to mount.
Over the weekend, the school’s newspaper, the Cornell Daily Sun, reported that campus police made a drug-related arrest at the Chi Phi fraternity house less than 24 hours before the alleged assault and referred an individual to Cornell’s student conduct office. Doe alleges in her lawsuit that she was coerced into using drugs before the assault. Cornell declined to tell the Sun when the student conduct office learned of the referral.
On Sunday, Giuffra told CNN’s State of the Union that the consequences against Doe have persisted, saying that she has been receiving threats since filing her lawsuit against her alleged attackers and against Cornell.
“There are people out there trying to track her down,” he shared in the interview. “They said, ‘We’re gonna shut you up.’”
As the students continue to assert their frustration with the university, so too does the faculty.
Faculty Senate member Paul Ortiz, a professor of labor history, sponsored a no-confidence resolution—which is an official statement demonstrating that the faculty no longer trusts or approves of the school’s leadership. It was introduced Monday for review by the University Faculty Committee.
“The faculty Senate has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University,” the resolution states, according to The New York Times.
The resolution is not legally binding, and faculty governing boards are not required to replace administrators because of a no-confidence resolution. The measure is expected to be put to a vote when the faculty Senate meets Oct. 14.
TIME has reached out to Ortiz for further comment from the Senate.
Dissatisfaction was also expressed anonymously early Monday when the school's main administration building was splashed with graffiti and had its doors damaged.
In a statement, school spokesperson Kyle Kimball said, “We understand the frustration and strong emotions being expressed across our community. Those concerns deserve to be heard, but damaging property is not the answer. We are investigating the vandalism at Day Hall and will address it in accordance with University policy and applicable law.”
Anger is also mounting beyond Cornell, as the case has drawn an outpouring of solidarity on social media. An “I am Jane Doe” online support campaign has gained traction by inviting others to share similar incidents that they experienced, with one TikTok video garnering over 4 million views.
Alumni has taken a stand, as well. Sami Sage, who graduated from Cornell in 2011, launched an online petition that has collected over 61,000 signatures pledging to withhold financial and other means of support until the university demonstrates accountability, transparency, remedy, and prevention. TIME cannot independently confirm that all of the signees were formerly enrolled at Cornell.
What Cornell students and faculty want to see changed
Ahead of Monday’s protest, the organizing groups called on Cornell to expel or revoke the degrees of students they say were involved in the alleged assault; establish independent hearings and minimum sanctions for sexual assault; require prevention training for students and trauma-informed training for campus police; and commission an external review of Cornell’s handling of the case.
Bera says the groups also want to restore a university judicial system independent of the administration.
"What Cornell needs is a judicial system that is independent of an administration that uses it to protect the university's image and the opinions of donors and trustees at the expense of the student body,” Bera says.
She points to 2020, when the school approved a new Student Code of Conduct, placing disciplinary authority in the administration's hands. SDC and its collaborators believe that this independent judicial system needs to be re-implemented “as soon as possible,” Bera says.
Kate Manne, a Cornell philosophy professor, also urged accountability in a Substack post. She advocated banning fraternities across campus, describing them as “a hotbed of misogyny” with “no valid role in the modern university.” Cornell says the Chi Phi chapter closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus.
What happens next for Cornell?
The pressure on Cornell is now moving on several fronts: an independent review, a state investigation, a faculty vote and further protests.
Over the weekend, Kotlikoff recorded a video for students promising more transparency and accountability—pledging, without specificity, to “do better.”
“What happened to Jane Doe in 2024 is deeply disturbing and will weigh heavily on our community for years to come,” he said.
On Tuesday, Cornell University's Board of Trustees named Sally Yates, a former acting U.S. attorney general and career federal prosecutor, to lead an independent review of the university’s handling of the case.
“The review will examine Cornell’s policies, practices and resources across the full range of prevention and response, including how reports are received and investigated; how students are supported; how hearings, disciplinary decisions and appeals are handled … and policies and oversight involving fraternities, sororities, and other student organizations,” according to the accompanying statement.
It also said that Yates will investigate the Cornell Board of Trustees’ oversight on the issues.
TIME has reached out to Cornell for comment.
Outside of the school’s contested internal investigation, parallel lines of inquiry are continuing through a criminal investigation overseen by the state.
The criminal investigation was reopened Sept. 28 by Tompkins District Attorney Matthew Van Houten.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, however, has criticized Van Houten’s handling of the case. The DA had reviewed the original complaint filed by Jane Doe in 2024 and declined to prosecute at the time. She appointed State Attorney General Letitia James on Oct. 1 as the special prosecutor on the case.
“Think about that—in what world would the police learn from a victim that she'd been literally gang raped while intoxicated by five men in a fraternity house and not elevate those allegations to the District Attorney?” Hochul said in a press conference on Oct. 2. “In what world does the District Attorney not even interview her or anyone else involved—or even request the full transcript?”
Bera says that the independent review by Cornell is a good first step—but SDC and other organizations plan to continue holding protests until the rest of their demands have been met.
Next is a sit-in protest “in solidarity with Jane Doe and all survivors of sexual assault and sexual violence,” she says. That takes place Wednesday.
External advocates are also rallying around Jane Doe, with an independent protest organized by groups unaffiliated with Cornell scheduled for Oct. 13.
“Cornell Administration supports known rapists,” the organizers’ post said. “We demand answers.”

Access to coastline restricted in Odesa region
According to Ukrinform, the Odesa Regional Military Administration announced this on Facebook.
The administration said that in the Odesa region, the start and end of the recreational season are determined by joint orders of the "Odesa" Operational-Tactical Grouping and the Odesa Regional Military Administration.
"These orders determine the sections of the Black Sea coast that have undergone safety inspections and are permitted for visitors. After the season ends, the relevant order expires, and access to the designated beach areas is restricted," the administration said.
The administration explained that the measures are related to safety. After the season ends, the relevant services no longer continuously monitor water safety, inspect the seabed, check the territory for explosive objects, or operate lifeguard stations.
"In this regard, we ask residents and visitors to refrain from visiting beach areas," the administration said.
As Ukrinform reported, 48 beach areas were officially opened in Odesa region during the summer of 2026. Of these, 47 were located in Odesa and one in Chornomorsk.

US death row inmate Christa Pike conscious, speaking after botched execution: Attorneys
Unknown

Diyar Guldogan
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike is conscious and speaking nearly a week after a botched execution left her critically injured and temporarily dependent on a ventilator, her attorneys said Tuesday.
Pike, 50, remains hospitalized and is receiving medical treatment after surviving two doses of pentobarbital during a failed execution attempt on Sept. 30 in Nashville, they said in a statement.
“Her recovery is medically unprecedented,” they said. “Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery.”
The attorneys said Pike has suffered “severe damage” to her arms and remains handcuffed to her hospital bed.
Pike was taken to a hospital after the failed execution, where she was treated after being removed from the execution chamber. Her attorneys said she was placed on a ventilator but is now conscious and able to speak.
“We are incredibly grateful to the first responders and the medical team at the hospital who treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her,” they said.
They said her recovery remains ongoing and that her long-term prognosis is not yet known.
Pike, the only woman on Tennessee's death row, was sentenced to death for the 1995 killing of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.

NEW YORK, October 7. /TASS/. Christa Pike, who survived a botched execution attempt in the US state of Tennessee, faces a lengthy recovery, her lawyers said after their client regained consciousness.
"Her prognosis remains unclear, <…> she faces a long recovery," Pike’s lawyers said in a statement cited by Associated Press.
They described what happened to Pike as "medically unprecedented" and noted that "despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed."
On September 30, Pike was scheduled to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in over 200 years on Wednesday. However, she was rushed to a hospital following two failed attempts to administer the drugs.
Christa Pike was 18 years old at the time of the crime in 1995. She and her accomplice were convicted of the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, who attended the same educational institution as Pike. According to the prosecution, Pike feared Slemmer was pursuing her boyfriend, lured her to a secluded area, where she and her accomplice tortured and killed her. The case drew widespread attention due to the brutality of the murder, the age of the participants, and the fact that a satanic symbol was carved into the victim’s body.

FBI spied on Trump’s family – declassified docs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
23:32:38 UTC
08:32:38 KST

FBI spied on Trump’s family – declassified docs
The FBI tracked the movements of Donald Trump’s wife and teenage son and monitored the phone contacts of one of his closest aides during its investigation of him prior to his return to the White House, newly declassified documents have revealed.
The disclosures are fueling accusations from the White House that the administration of then-US President Joe Biden weaponized federal law enforcement against its main political rival. The files shed new light on an FBI probe codenamed Plasmic Echo, which examined Trump’s handling of classified documents and ultimately led to the 2022 raid on his Mar-a-Lago residence.
Internal planning records show that agents sought detailed information on the travel of Trump, Melania and their son Barron while preparing to search the Florida estate.
One FBI task list instructed investigators to “finalize FBI understanding of FPOTUS/FLOTUS/minor son’s travel,” including the type of aircraft being used and a “specific timeline.” Another internal message indicated that any search warrant would be executed only after Trump had left Mar-a-Lago.
The surveillance dragnet later extended to Susie Wiles, then one of Trump’s closest advisers and now his White House chief of staff.
Between February and May 2023, investigators used a pen register and trap-and-trace system to monitor metadata associated with Wiles’ phone. It allowed agents to track numbers, timing and duration of calls involving lawyers, campaign advisers, journalists and others in Trump’s orbit.
In one instance, investigators reviewed Wiles’ phone activity shortly after interviewing her, apparently seeking to determine whom she contacted following the meeting. Agents also sent preservation requests to Google, Microsoft, MSN and Yahoo for information associated with her email accounts and examined political endorsements and social-media activity by Trump allies.
The newly released White House materials also say agents scrutinized political endorsements, social-media activity and other constitutionally protected conduct while trying to determine whether Trump had broken the law by taking classified documents to Mar-a-Lago after leaving office.
“Jack Smith’s surveillance operation was a disgraceful abuse of government power,” White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News. “Spying on political opponents is weaponization of law enforcement, plain and simple.”
The investigation was conducted under Biden and overseen by senior Justice Department and FBI officials. Trump and his allies have repeatedly accused the former president of turning federal agencies into political weapons, an allegation the previous administration denied.
Trump was ultimately charged with illegally retaining classified material and obstructing efforts to recover it, but denied wrongdoing. A federal judge dismissed the case in July 2024 after ruling that special counsel Jack Smith had been unlawfully appointed. Smith later abandoned the prosecution following Trump’s election victory.

Top US senator presses for answers on Greece envoy amid lobbying scrutiny

United States Senator Jeanne Shaheen has demanded an urgent investigation into the conduct of US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Ann Guilfoyle, blowing the lid off a toxic web of corporate lobbying, backroom pressure, and political work connected to Athens.

According to the Mexican Constitution, state governments are prohibited from signing security agreements with foreign governments, as such matters fall exclusively under federal authority and require approval from the Security Cabinet.
“The problem is not the presence of an ambassador at an activity like this, but rather the nature of the activity and the permits they must have to develop the academy they announced at the event,” Sheinbaum said at the press conference.
According to the president, the Mexican government had approved nine cooperation projects between the state of Queretaro and US security agencies. However, the academy inaugurated by Ambassador Johnson and the governor is not among the authorized projects.
“We have a good relationship with the US government on security matters and on other issues. What we ask the state governors, the ambassador and the US government is that Mexican laws be followed in everything related to international cooperation,” the president added.
This is the second time during Sheinbaum’s administration that a state government has gone over the authority of the federal government and established security agreements with the United States.
In April of this year, it was revealed that the two US agents who died in Chihuahua in a car accident were Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) agents deployed in Mexico at the invitation of the state government to support security operations, which led to a federal investigation into the government of Maru Campos.
The International Police Training Academy in Queretaro would conduct training for state police officers to detect and intercept drugs, weapons, large amounts of illicit cash and contraband.
Sheinbaum reiterated the need for the Kuri government to submit the academy for authorization by the federal government.
“This is a warning to the government of Queretaro,” Sheinbaum concluded.

Christa Pike regains consciousness after botched Tennessee execution attempt
Convicted murderer Christa Pike regained consciousness and began speaking Tuesday after surviving a botched execution by lethal injection. Pike, the first woman the state of Tennessee has attempted to put to death in 200 years, remains hospitalised with severe injuries to both arms.
Convicted killer Christa Pike, who survived Tennessee's effort to execute her by lethal injection last week, foiling the state's first attempt to put a woman to death in two centuries, has regained consciousness and is speaking, her lawyers said in a statement on Tuesday.
Despite severe injuries to her arms from the insertion of intravenous lines during the attempted execution last Wednesday, Pike, 50, is "still handcuffed and shackled" to her hospital bed while she remains under medical care, her team of public defence attorneys wrote.
"Her prognosis remains unclear, but at a minimum we expect a long recovery," the lawyers' statement said, adding that a court hearing on Pike's case was scheduled for Wednesday in Davidson County Chancery Court.
Pike, sentenced to death for her role as a teenager in the torture-murder of a 19-year-old schoolmate Colleen Slemmer three decades ago, survived the botched execution attempt on the night of September 30 at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, the state capital. She has been hospitalised since then.
Her lawyers said on Friday that their client remained unconscious, critically ill and hooked to a ventilator to breathe, as doctors laboured to clear the drug pentobarbital from her system.
"Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking and continues to receive critical medical care," they wrote on Tuesday.
Read moreTennessee prison chief who oversaw botched Christa Pike execution resigns
Pike's petition for clemency, denied last week by Governor Bill Lee, argued that her death sentence had failed to properly account for Pike's own childhood trauma as the victim of sexual abuse, neglect and untreated mental illness.
Pike went from being the first woman Tennessee had tried to put to death since the early 19th century to becoming the first person in the United States known to have survived after execution drugs were administered.
Death penalty opponents said the incident exposed the inherent barbarity of executions. It also highlighted the difficulties of carrying out lethal injections while respecting constitutional prohibitions on cruel and unusual punishment.
'None of it was normal'
Pike's attorneys and journalists who witnessed the execution attempt described it as roughly 2-1/2 hours of disarray and prolonged distress for her as Department of Correction personnel struggled to administer two doses of pentobarbital intravenously.
"None of it was normal," Catherine Sweeney, a reporter for Nashville public broadcaster WPLN, recounted. "It went really poorly."
Pike was heard gasping, crying, whimpering and breathing loudly through much of the procedure, at one point saying, "my arm feels like it's about to burst open".
The bungled attempt to establish intravenous lines left both of Pike's arms "swollen, burned and blistered", the apparent result of the pentobarbital, a highly alkaline and caustic substance, seeping into the tissues under her skin, her lawyers said in court filings.

The lawyers accused state officials of having shrugged off prior warnings from Pike's doctors that her small veins and a blood disorder called thrombocytosis would make placing IV lines especially difficult.
In the midst of the procedure, Pike's lawyers filed an emergency court motion seeking to halt the procedure. By then, prison officials had ceased their execution efforts and called an ambulance, according to court records.
The night of the execution attempt, the Department of Correction defended its handling of the situation, saying it had "followed every step of the state's lawful, established execution protocol". But agency commissioner Frank Strada has resigned and will leave his post this month, the governor announced on Saturday.
Lee had previously ordered a suspension of any scheduled executions for the rest of the year and a third-party review of what happened in Pike's case.
Two days before Pike was due to meet her fate, Lee rejected a petition seeking to commute her death penalty to a life prison term without the possibility of parole.

Pike was 18 in January 1995 when she, her 17-year-old boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, and a third companion lured Slemmer into a wooded area on the University of Tennessee campus in Knoxville and killed her.
The gruesome nature of the slaying, which involved Shipp carving the shape of a pentagram in the victim's chest and Pike bashing Slemmer in the head with a chunk of asphalt, then taking a piece of her skull as a souvenir, drew intense media coverage at the time. Trial testimony indicated that Pike viewed Slemmer as a rival for her boyfriend's affections.

Their co-defendant, Shadolla Peterson, who was 18 at the time of the murder and had acted as a lookout for the other two, testified for the prosecution and received probation.

You Probably Aren’t Going to Get the Plague
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
23:09:20 UTC
08:09:20 KST

A mysterious death of a woman in Russia following a lab accident has stoked fears about plague spreading. But the odds of that actually happening remain very low, with the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention saying on X Tuesday afternoon that the circumstances of the case remain unconfirmed and that there is “no indication of a broader threat to the United States” at this time.
“We are working across the US government to assess developments as additional information becomes available,” the agency said. “CDC and our interagency partners are prepared and will continue to monitor the situation closely.”
Last week, a young researcher died from severe pneumonia of “unknown” origin after reportedly breaking a test tube at her workplace, the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute in Siberia. The hospital that treated her before her death was placed under quarantine, and her coworkers at the lab were isolated, according to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty.
Christian Lindmeier, a spokesperson for the World Health Organization, told reporters in Geneva on Tuesday that the group has been in touch with Russian authorities. Based on currently available information, WHO says the public health risk to the general population is very low.
“I think that’s the correct assessment,” says Gigi Gronvall, an immunologist and senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security. “We don’t know anything about anything right now.”
Russian authorities have said contact tracing hasn’t yielded any signs of dangerous pathogens spreading, according to the Associated Press. Infamous for causing millions of deaths in Europe during the Middle Ages, plague is rare today. It is caused by the bacteria Yersinia pestis, which is found in wild rodents and their fleas in many parts of the world. It’s spread to humans through the bite of an infected flea and occasionally through direct contact with an infected animal. Antibiotics can cure plague, but they must be started as soon as an infection is suspected.
Pneumonic plague occurs when a person inhales infectious droplets that contain the bacteria. In July 2025, an Arizona man died from pneumonic plague after exposure to infected cats. It can also spread from person to person through respiratory droplets during close contact. But human-to-human transmission is rare, with the last reported occurrence happening in 1924 in Los Angeles. The possibility, though, is why the CDC says it’s important to rapidly identify cases and treat them.
“Once you know that somebody has been exposed to it, and even if you have a doubt that somebody has been exposed to it, you can immediately start antibiotics to prevent the person getting afflicted with the disease and to avoid the continuous spread of the disease,” says Rutul Dalal, an infectious disease physician at Penn State Health St. Joseph Medical Center.
Dalal says if the Russian lab worker did die from plague, he is confident that the disease could easily be contained. “With Covid, that was a virus we had not dealt with in the past,” he says. That required novel interventions, while “here, we do have antibiotics to deal with this.”
The incident also occurred in a remote part of Russia, which could naturally limit its spread. “Siberia is not exactly Paris,” Gronvall says. “There’s not a lot of travel going back and forth.”
Whether plague is the culprit or not remains an open question. Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s federal public health and consumer protection agency, said “extensive” testing found “no microorganisms associated with the patient’s professional activities.” But the US has urged the country to share as much information as possible, while other nations that share borders or are near Russia, including Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan, have set up quarantine protocols.

OpenAI unleashes hundreds more math results upon a field already in shock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
23:08:24 UTC
08:08:24 KST

The floodgates are open. Right on the heels of OpenAI’s new large language model producing the biggest math breakthrough in two decades, the company just released no less than 372 results from the same model. Each resolves or makes substantial progress on a major open question in mathematics or theoretical computer science, the company says.
OpenAI revealed the results in a GitHub repository at 6 P.M. EDT. The deluge will take mathematicians months to parse through and understand—including to determine whether the proofs contain novel and important ideas or are mostly mash-ups of existing techniques. But many of the results have already been verified in Lean—a programming language that validates a proof’s logic—and are therefore all but certain to be correct.
Among the results claimed are a solution to the four-dimensional Kakeya conjecture, improvements on some of the world’s most important computer algorithms, and actual progress toward math’s scariest problem, the Riemann hypothesis.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
A spokesperson for OpenAI told Scientific American that the new model—which the company has not released to the public—produced almost every one of the results in response to a single prompt handed to a single AI agent. This would be a striking difference from OpenAI’s earlier blockbuster solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, which was produced through the collective efforts of a 10,000-strong agentic swarm that cost millions of dollars in computing power. If true, it would mean that unprecedented mathematical power could soon be accessible to anyone. But OpenAI’s reputation, among mathematicians, for bold claims and little transparency is causing considerable skepticism.
“Until and unless they release the model and people can replicate their results, I think you should treat any claims about one-shotting problems with a single agent as unverified,” says Andrew Sutherland, a mathematician at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. “We should ask for receipts.” (The OpenAI spokesperson also told Scientific American that some results might have taken multiple attempts.)
OpenAI’s handling of the Navier-Stokes solution’s release has proved so controversial that, on September 21, the company announced it was assembling an independent advisory group of mathematicians to provide recommendations on responsibly publishing AI-generated results. The recommendations that the group developed call for a company that releases such results to make public the model, exact prompt and compute time behind each one. In spite of the group’s recommendations, though, OpenAI is choosing only to reveal the average compute time for a problem, with some additional statistics—and no prompts.
The OpenAI spokesperson told Scientific American that the team is taking the advisory group’s guidelines seriously and doing its best to comply but added that the company is not bound by these recommendations.
The recommendations are particularly critical of AI companies using “proprietary internal models” that aren’t broadly accessible to mathematicians. OpenAI told Scientific American that the company is working to release the model as quickly and responsibly as possible.
As the Navier-Stokes dispute unfolded, comments from OpenAI personnel led some mathematicians to believe the company’s model had produced additional results but that it was hesitating to publicize them. This raises a vital question: Is it more harmful to unload heaps of unexplained proofs on the community or withhold them entirely?
“If we want to know the answers to these math questions, I see no reason why we should ask the company to keep them secret from us,” says Daniel Litt, a mathematician at the University of Toronto. “To me, it’s going to be a good thing for mathematics.”
On the other hand, the famed mathematician Terence Tao has vocally criticized OpenAI and other “frontier” AI labs for the “insane” pace of their AI-generated results.
Such results may even be coming too fast for the labs themselves—the OpenAI spokesperson told Scientific American that many of the company’s newly released results are not yet understood by its own mathematicians. Still, they don’t plan on slowing down. The company wants to put as powerful a tool as possible in mathematicians’ hands.
Moreover, OpenAI maintains that it can’t slow down because these math problems are an indispensable test to show that their AI really is getting smarter.
But for the practitioners who see mathematical truth as an end rather than a means, the consequences of this race are becoming harder and harder to predict.

‘We are desperate’: Venezuela’s power cuts fuel growing public anger
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
23:05:38 UTC
08:05:38 KST

The hum of the kidney dialysis machine that Onasis Munoz is connected to suddenly stops. The fluorescent lights overhead flicker out, and his room at a clinic in Valencia, Venezuela, is plunged into darkness.
It is not the first time a power cut has interrupted one of the three weekly sessions Munoz needs to do the work his failing kidneys can no longer do, filtering waste and excess fluid from his blood.
For years, electricity would go out every couple of days across parts of Venezuela's Carabobo state.
But in recent months, Munoz said, the outages have grown to be daily, lasting around seven hours. The clinic's emergency batteries have since been depleted, and its backup generator no longer works.
He explained that the frequent power failures have disrupted his treatment. His health has slumped as a result.
"I arrive home, exhausted, as if I had run a marathon," the 34-year-old said.
But often there is no electricity there either, and recent weeks have been sweltering. "I can't switch on the air conditioning. I cannot rest because of the heat and the mosquitoes. There's no relief," Munoz said.
Across Venezuela, the prolonged outages are riling locals, as the electricity supply to homes, businesses and essential services becomes unstable.
Some of the cuts are deliberate, as the government of interim President Delcy Rodriguez rations electricity.
The resulting frustration has spilled onto the streets, where demonstrators hold "cacerolazos" – a traditional form of protest that involves banging pots and pans.
Some have gone as far as blocking roadways and setting tyres on fire. The electricity crisis has also raised concerns about how the government is managing the country's vast oil supply, a key source of income for the country.
"We are desperate. We cannot understand how a country so rich in resources can be practically left in the dark," said Patricia Cueva, a lawyer from Maracaibo, the capital of oil-rich Zulia state.
"We cannot rest. We cannot work. Our children cry."
A recent study by ANOVA Policy Research, a consultancy firm, found that 62.8 percent of Venezuelan households – or nearly two out of every three families – experienced daily electricity cuts in 2026, compared with 37.1 percent in 2024.
Only 6.9 percent reported a continuous supply of electricity.
The energy crisis has its roots in multiple causes. Previous governments have blamed foreign sanctions for weakening Venezuela's economy.
The Rodriguez administration, meanwhile, has cited the climate phenomenon El Niño for the crisis. Some 90 percent of Venezuela's electricity is generated by hydropower, making the system vulnerable to extreme heat and drought.
But energy specialist Nelson Hernandez is among the Venezuelans pointing a finger at the government for this year's surge in outages.
Hernandez acknowledges that climate conditions can have an impact on electricity production. But he underscored that Venezuela's electricity crisis is not a "random event".
"Practically the entire crisis stems from the systematic neglect of the infrastructure," he told Al Jazeera, pointing to what he called "profound failures" in management, lack of strategic planning and ageing technology.
He also signalled that shifting government policies towards oil extraction plays a key role.
Venezuela sits on the largest proven oil reserves in the world.
Much of the oil industry was nationalised, but that started to change in January, after the US conducted a military operation to abduct and imprison Venezuela's then-President Nicolas Maduro.
Since then, relations between Washington and Caracas have shifted. Under pressure from US President Donald Trump, Rodriguez – Maduro's former vice president – has implemented reforms to allow greater foreign investment in the country's oil sector.
Trump, meanwhile, has eased restrictions on the oil's export and expanded the US role in the industry.
The result has been an uptick in output. Oil production in Venezuela has risen by almost 30 percent this year, from 924,000 barrels per day in January to 1.201 million in August, according to the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC).
As Venezuela revives its dilapidated oil industry, Hernandez says increased production is putting pressure on an already strained electricity system.
"Because electricity supplies to oil fields cannot be rationed without jeopardising oil production, the burden of adjustment and the power cuts fall directly on the residential and commercial sectors," he said.
Hernandez estimates the oil industry requires around 1,600 megawatts or more for extraction, pumping, transportation and refining.
The Rodriguez government says it is working to stabilise the system, with plans to add 1,300 megawatts of generation in the final quarter of the year.
It has also put in place legal measures that compel energy companies to invest in their own electrical infrastructure, to lessen the strain on the public power grid.
But industry experts say lasting solutions require major investments to repair ageing power plants, while building more locally generated and renewable power.
For families and businesses who can afford them, backup generators provide some respite during outages. But many cannot afford them and are forced to find other ways to cope.
"My family owns a bakery, and with the constant power cuts, it is impossible to maintain consistent production," said Manuel Reyes of Naguanagua, in Venezuela's Carabobo state.
"There are days when we stay open until after midnight to make the most of the hours when there is electricity and produce something to sell."
Residents across several states who spoke to Al Jazeera said the prolonged power cuts were taking a toll on their mental health.
Mileidy Blanco, who lives in Maracay in the state of Aragua, gets up before dawn at 4am to prepare the day's food for her family before the electricity goes out.
But she said she is increasingly worried about her six-year-old daughter, who is showing signs of stress.
Recently, the electricity went out at her daughter's school, then at home and again at her dance class.
"She broke down; she couldn't take it anymore. She started crying, asking how long the lights were going to be out and how long this would last," Blanco told Al Jazeera.
Blanco took her daughter to a psychologist, who advised her to keep the child occupied during outages with board games and trips to the park.
"Her only concern should be getting good grades, studying, doing her homework, cleaning her room," Blanco said.
Instead, when the power goes out, she has noticed that her six-year-old reaches for pots and pans. She bangs along with the cacerolazo demonstrations outside in the streets – protests that show no sign of stopping.

An extinct crocodilian was found among rocks that built the Great Sphinx

Unknown Publisher

08:05:00 KST

An extinct crocodilian was found among rocks that built the Great Sphinx
Much like the huge statue that was born from the same rocks, Herugavialis is missing its nose
The Great Sphinx of Giza isn’t the only ancient, stony visage in the area missing its nose.
A fossil crocodilian discovered in the same 45-million-year-old limestone that ancient Egyptians used to build the Sphinx is also missing the tip of its snout. But the broken specimen is intact enough to be reclassified as a new branch of the gavial family tree, which may help uncover these mysterious animals’ evolutionary history, researchers report October 7 in Royal Society Open Science.
Most living crocodilians are in either the crocodile or alligator families. But there are also two species of gavial living in tropical Asia. These are huge, critically endangered, fish-eating crocodilians with long, slender snouts full of needlelike teeth. Fossils of extinct gavials have been found around the world. In 1927, German researchers reported a gavial skull fossil collected from hills near Cairo. The fossil was identified as an extinct species of Tomistoma, a genus found today only as a single species in Southeast Asia.
But more recent evolutionary studies including this fossil suggested this classification didn’t fit. In 2023, while working on a doctoral degree at University College London, paleontologist Paul Burke went to Germany to study the fossil in detail. Burke and his colleagues made careful measurements of the skull, using 3-D X-ray methods to measure the insides of the brain and nasal cavities.
“As we’ve advanced in the last 100 years, we’ve got so many new methodologies we could implement to figure out what kind of species this fossil is,” says Burke, currently at the Sweden Museum of Natural History in Stockholm.
The team compared the measurements to those taken of living and fossil gavials and found that this purported Egyptian Tomistoma was actually an undescribed gavial genus. The researchers named it Herugavialis cairensis, referencing the Egyptian god Heru (or Horus), who has been associated with the Great Sphinx. Coincidentally, the Herugavialis skull is missing the end of its snout — something it shares with the noseless statue.
“So many species are found from the same [geologic] formation,” Burke says, including fish, sharks and mammals. “But this is the first one with the name associated with the Sphinx.”
Today, gavials are only found in freshwater environments. But tens of millions of years ago, the reptiles also inhabited nearshore saltwater environments. Herugavialis appears to have been a coastal predator back when the ancient Tethys Ocean covered northern Egypt.
Khalafallah Salih, a paleontologist at Al Neelain University in Khartoum, Sudan, says the finding supports the idea that the evolution of gavials and their relatives in Africa was much more complex than researchers thought. Herugavialis doesn’t appear closely related to other known gavial-type crocodilians in Africa or the Mediterranean, he says. It appears to have branched off from the lineage early in its evolution.
Burke notes that gavials barely breach the public consciousness compared to alligators and crocodiles.
“They’re still alive today and they’re endangered,” he says. “So, we should know about them and their long history.”

Ikea to pilot online buyback service for secondhand furniture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
23:01:26 UTC
08:01:26 KST

Ikea is to test an online version of its buy-back service where the retailer offers vouchers for unwanted secondhand furniture.
The service will be tested in Spain and Portugal before the end of December and will be launched in the UK if it proves successful. Ikea already offers buy-back in stores, including in the UK. The online version will extend it to a much wider audience, with Ikea predicting pre-owned goods are likely to grab 16% of the UK homewares market by next year
The new plan emerged as the world’s largest furniture retailer takes on Vinted and eBay with its own secondhand online marketplace which launches in the UK this week.
The platform, which is already online in other countries including Spain and Portugal with bestsellers including the Kallax shelving system and Malm chest of drawers, will enable shoppers signed up to the Swedish company’s membership scheme to connect directly to one another to buy and sell pre-owned Ikea items locally.
The UK service will be free initially, but a “buyer protection fee” of about 5% of an item’s price will be introduced in time. At launch, buyers and sellers will arrange collection or delivery directly with one another through the marketplace. Ikea said it is exploring ways to make delivery easier in future.
“The secondhand market is growing and growing. It is now really significant,” said Greg Lucas, sustainability manager at Ikea’s UK & Irish division. “Secondhand browsing and shopping is now mainstream.
“The way people furnish their homes has changed. Whether they are moving, redecorating or looking for a particular piece, more customers are considering pre-owned furniture alongside new and are actively searching for items that can help create a home that feels personal to them.”
The secondhand home products market is now worth more than £4.5bn in the UK and is growing at about 6.5% annually. Ikea said its products accounted for about 9% of furniture sold on secondhand marketplaces in the UK.
Ikea said it was making the sale of used versions of its products easier by providing pre-filled product descriptions and price suggestions. The company also offers sellers 15% extra on the price of the item sold if they agree to be paid in the form of an Ikea gift card.
The change is part of a revolution in retail, where shoppers of all ages are now prepared to consider secondhand items.
In 2025, 63% of UK consumers bought products through reselling platforms, up from 51% in 2024.
The trend has boosted sales at Vinted, which began as a clothing resale site but is now expanding into homewares and electronics, as well as at Facebook Marketplace, Gumtree and smaller, more upmarket sites such as Vinterior.
The US secondhand site eBay recently bought UK fashion seller Depop for $1.2bn (£900m). Preloved items now make up about a 10th of global fashion sales.
There is heavy competition for the secondhand market, with the electrical goods retailers Currys and AO, for example, both selling pre-owned items.
AO expanded its secondhand position after acquiring MusicMagpie, which sells refurbished electronics and secondhand video games, in 2024. It recently also bought camera specialist Jessops, which controls the Camera Jungle secondhand site.

Christa Pike lawyers say she is speaking one week after failed execution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Christa Pike lawyers say she is speaking one week after failed execution
The 50-year-old has regained consciousness and is receiving care nearly one week after being sent to the hospital following a botched lethal injection.
Lawyers for Christa Pike say she is awake and able to speak after her botched execution attempt by the state of Tennessee on September 30.
Tuesday’s statement marks the first public indication that Pike’s condition has improved after she was transported to a Nashville hospital after receiving two doses of pentobarbitol, lethal injections intended to end her life.
Her failed execution has sparked debate about the use of the death penalty in the United States. Pike is thought to be the first person to have survived such an injection in the country.
“Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care,” Pike’s lawyers said in a statement.
“Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed. Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery.”
The statement also expresses gratitude to medical workers who the lawyers say have “treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her”.
Pike’s lawyers had previously stated that she was unconscious and on a ventilator. They described her arms as “swollen, burned and blistered” by the failed execution.
Pike was convicted and sentenced to die in 1996 for her participation in the murder of a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, when she was 18 years old. Two co-defendants received lesser sentences.
Pike’s defence lawyers had pointed to her mental health struggles in their attempts to commute her sentence. But the Slemmer family had advocated for the death penalty, pointing to the violent nature of the 19-year-old’s murder.
Accounts of Pike’s failed execution describe her kicking off the sheet covering her body and, at one point, appearing to snore. She reportedly expressed feeling pain as the lethal injections were administered.
The incident has brought attention to the prevalence of botched executions in the US criminal justice system.
Critics have argued that botched executions — defined as those that deviate from established procedures through unforeseen issues, delays or administrative incompetence — can cause unnecessary pain and suffering for those being put to death.
Citing the researcher Austin Sarat, the Death Penalty Information Center, a nonprofit, estimates that 3 percent of executions in the US from 1890 to 2010 were botched.

“A toaster is a wedding gift. A private-island party paid for by a Putin-connected oligarch is something else,” Curtis said last month.

On flydubai, Israelis took responsibility. Regarding October 7, leaders must do the same - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

Everyone was surprised when airplane hijackings returned to our lives. No one was surprised to learn that the people who foiled the hijacking were Israelis who lunged at once to confront the first officer in the cockpit.
That absence of surprise is rooted in the Israeli DNA, which carries within it a readiness to fight. Not out of a thirst for blood, but as a deep expression of responsibility toward the people around you and a willingness to risk your own life against anyone who threatens you and your community.
This incident takes place precisely in the middle of a barren and futile controversy over a single question: was Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu informed before the war?
On the Left, they are certain: “Of course, he knew, and he did not lift a finger.”
On the Right, they cry out: “If only they had woken him, everything would have looked different.”
The argument is empty. It is meaningless because it tries to force a narrow legal logic onto reality, hanging everything on a direct causal chain running from protocols, hours of sleep, and intelligence reports to the terrible outcome. It is the product of an ancient and basic logic that we lost somewhere along the way.
To understand how warped and destructive this pedantic sifting of details is, this effort to prove guilt or to wash it away, picture the following: You left the children with a babysitter and went out to a movie. When you came home, you found the children slaughtered in the house.
It may well be that this babysitter could not have prevented a thing. It may be that no other person in their place would have managed to avert the decree. And still, that particular babysitter will carry the full weight of it, the fact that the horror took place on their watch, until their last day.
If they trade that paralyzing responsibility, that unbearable weight, for technical questions, for hairsplitting about procedures and calculations of circumstance, they will be seen, and rightly so, as a monstrous human being, someone without humanity.
The babysitter example is not quite precise. Netanyahu did not happen to be minding the children at the wrong time and the wrong place. He is a leader who, on the strength of his talent and his charisma, was handed the roles of building manager, architect, and engineer all at once.
In the updated image, the children were killed when part of the structure collapsed. This building manager, architect, and engineer can complain from here to eternity that the residents’ committee (in Israeli apartment buildings, an elected committee of tenants that controls the building’s budget and maintenance decisions) tied his hands, but he still owes answers: how does 20 years of having his hands tied release him from responsibility, and why is the fact that he was unaware of the severe water damage in the infrastructure supposed to lift that responsibility from his shoulders?
But long before any of that, there has to be crushing guilt. Because the children died, on his watch.
THIS IS exactly the logic that the philosopher Bernard Williams uses in his book Shame and Necessity. Williams shows how the modern conception shrank the idea of responsibility down to pure legal guilt: for someone to bear responsibility, we now demand a proven causal link, full control, and clear intent. And if the right boxes were checked, or the hour was simply too late, the responsibility evaporates.
Among the ancient Greeks, by contrast, the view was far more realistic and clear-eyed. Oedipus had no capacity whatsoever to resist his fate, which was sealed before he was born. He did not know the facts, yet it never occurred to him to claim that no one had woken him in time, and so to disown the catastrophe that happened on his watch. He paid the full price for what he had done, because in a chaotic world the sheer rush of events is not a writ of exemption from responsibility but an uncompromising demand to take it on.
Using today’s endless stream of information to maneuver, to hurl blame or to dodge it, dismantles the most basic idea of leadership. But it also threatens something more important: the Israeli DNA.
Taking responsibility is in Israel's DNA
This readiness to fight, to sacrifice, and to take responsibility for another person is a kind of miracle, but it is also a distinct psychosocial phenomenon that has been studied and decoded in depth.
In their paper “Transcultural pathways to the will to fight,” social psychologist Ángel Gómez and his colleagues show how the great powers failed again and again – in Vietnam, in Iraq, in Afghanistan, and nearly in Ukraine, when they focused on overwhelming material superiority and ignored the will to fight, that intangible factor mistakenly treated as impossible to measure.
Drawing on 31 studies among thousands of fighters and civilians, Gómez demonstrated that the willingness to sacrifice one’s life rests on a clear scientific chain: identity fusion, the sense of being at one with the collective, which produces a perception of spiritual strength that outweighs the physical balance of forces, and which is translated into action through unshakable trust in one’s own people.
The survival of the Zionist enterprise is not magic. It is the fruit of those three components existing here at a level unmatched anywhere in the Western world. The present tragedy is that in the name of political survival, flight from responsibility, and a technical, alienating legal discourse, we work our own hands to shatter those very components.
We erode identity fusion through internal incitement; we hollow out the spiritual strength through discrimination and cynicism toward the value of service, and we collapse the basic trust that allows a person to risk his life for the collective. No nation can survive over time when that foundation is coming apart from within.
Political discourse is supposed to be about advancing policy. But in the coming years, anyone prepared to push aside, to bracket, or to walk right over the communities that serve in Israel, simply because advancing their own policy is the most critical thing of all, has to take one thing into account: we have reached a watershed.
We have reached a tangible danger to the very existence of the most basic core that allows the Zionist enterprise to exist. It may be a decision that makes sense in short-term political terms, but its meaning is clear: to seize the wheel on deck, they are willing to wreck the engine and breach the hull.
What is at stake in the coming years is not only the physical survival of the State of Israel against enormous challenges, but the preservation of our most basic DNA: responsibility, service, and loyalty. These must be fought for and guarded with everything we have, before we find ourselves with a generation that does not prevent planes from crashing, because that, after all, is not their responsibility.
The writer is the CEO of the Ribo Center.

Episode 130: Radioactive Russian Drones - A Conversation with Vitaly Shevchenko

Episode 130: Radioactive Russian Drones - A Conversation with Vitaly Shevchenko
Vitaly Shevchenko of BBC Monitoring joins Natia Seskuria to explore the implications of a radiation warning found on a downed Russian drone.
In April 2026, Ukrainian air defences shot down a modified Russian Geran-2 strike drone near Chernihiv, and investigators found a radiation warning label on the warhead, recording gamma readings far above natural background levels. Within hours the story spread internationally, often described as Russia deploying radioactive weapons or a dirty bomb, but neither description is accurate. Ukrainian investigators say the drone was carrying an R-60 air-to-air missile fitted with a depleted uranium fragmentation element, a modification Russia appears to be using to threaten Ukrainian aircraft intercepting the drones. The SBU has since documented further cases and opened a war crimes investigation.
This episode looks at the weapon itself, how claims like this are verified, and what the incident reveals about information warfare and media monitoring in a fast-moving conflict.
It also explores:
- What Ukrainian investigators found in the drone wreckage, and what the modification reveals about Russian production and stockpiles.
- How BBC Monitoring verifies claims of this kind, and what separates an established finding from an allegation.
- How radiation has featured in Russia-Ukraine information warfare since the 2022 ‘dirty bomb’ claims.
- The social and cultural resonance of radiation stories in Ukraine and Russia.
- What responsible media monitoring looks like in an environment of overload and disinformation.
Vitaly Shevchenko is Russia Editor at BBC Monitoring, where he has spent more than a decade analysing Russian and Ukrainian media.
BBC Monitoring is a specialist service within the BBC World Service, delivering trusted analysis of open-source media around the world

The Putin Tax and the Cost of Russian Hostility to Britain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

The Putin Tax and the Cost of Russian Hostility to Britain
Britain repeatedly uses sanctions to impose costs on Russia. But what does Russian hostility cost Britain? A new report asks a question government must answer.
On 1 October, the UK government announced its latest round of sanctions against Russia in response to the Kremlin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Alongside providing financial and military support, issuing sanctions in response to Moscow’s illegal war of aggression has been central to the response of Ukraine’s allies since 2022 as they seek to restrict the funding and resourcing of the Russian military.
But Russia’s hostility is not restricted to its military action in Ukraine. Sabotage and cyberattacks also target European countries. While these attacks cannot be compared with those suffered on a daily, and hourly, basis by Ukrainians, they do inflict costs on the UK, costs that the government has yet to assess and articulate systematically.
An Unmeasured Burden
A parliamentary answer to Graeme Downie MP on 9 September illustrates the gap. Asked about Russia-originating cyberattacks and their economic cost, the government supplied incident statistics but no cost estimate. Its figures concerned hostile states collectively, leaving Russia’s share unresolved. While the government can describe the threat, it must also explain the economic consequences.
Collecting evidence of the cost of Russian hostility will help the government justify its spending choices, strengthen the case for effective public and private sector resilience and identify where investment would make the greatest economic difference
This gap matters and deserves attention. In an era where governments link economic and national security at every opportunity, protecting businesses from disruption and minimising the diversion of already stretched public resources into recovery and protection should be a priority. Understanding the cost inflicted by Kremlin hostility should inform how the government determines – and prioritises – its response.
Estimating the Putin Tax
A new report, The Putin Tax, makes a welcome attempt to fill this gap. Drawing on parliamentary questions, public reporting and industry evidence, it proposes a working estimate of an annual £2–2.5 billion burden. The analysis begins with identified costs from individual incidents including the Royal Mail cyberattack, the Leyton arson attack and the Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) cyber incident. Public reporting puts the combined costs of these incidents at approximately £1.6–2.1 billion, dominated by JLR.
The report also considers industry data identifying more than 300 Russia-linked cyber incidents since 2022, alongside government research on the average cost of significant cyberattacks and the wider annual burden of cybercrime. It separately examines potential losses from disruption to subsea infrastructure.
The analysis is necessarily approximate. These figures cover different periods, and Russia-linked criminal activity must be distinguished from operations directed by the Russian state. There is also an ambiguity of language of attacks that originate from Russia. An ambiguity that Vladimir Putin and those like him use to their advantage and which the UK has fed by the use of terms such as ‘sub-threshold’ activity.
Potential future losses are also distinct from damage already incurred. The annual estimate is therefore a starting point for further investigation. Government should build on this work with the resources and evidence available to it.
Costs Beyond the Immediate Target
The cases show why the burden extends beyond the immediate target. The Russian-ordered arson attack in Leyton in March 2024 caused approximately £1 million in physical damage, according to Counter Terrorism Policing. A fuller account would consider business interruption and the public resources required for investigation and response.
Figures were largely unavailable for drone-related airport disruption, but the research finds that the cost of the police investigation alone following the 2024 drone activity at RAF Lakenheath was in excess of £600,000.
JLR illustrates how cyber disruption can spread through an interconnected economy. The Cyber Monitoring Centre estimated the economic cost from the incident to the UK economy of £1.9 billion. Its scale demonstrates the importance of considering suppliers and customers alongside the directly affected company.
Why Measurement Matters
Assessing and quantifying this tax is important. With public finances under pressure, the government must constantly make spending decisions, and understanding this burden matters for the effective allocation of resources. Collecting evidence of the cost of Russian hostility will help the government justify its spending choices, strengthen the case for effective public and private sector resilience and identify where investment would make the greatest economic difference.
Spending on protection is visible, while the losses this investment prevents are harder to evidence. Better evidence would allow proposed investment to be weighed against the harm it could avert. It would also clarify who bears the costs: business losses and public expenditure both matter but have different implications for government.
Three Steps for Government
So, what should the government do?
First, to coin a phrase, ‘what gets measured, gets done’. Government needs a coordinated effort to quantify the Putin Tax, with a named department responsible and Treasury involvement in developing the methodology. The necessary data will be held across businesses, public bodies, insurance companies and infrastructure providers. Gathering it should capture recovery costs and wider disruption while protecting commercially sensitive information.
Second, the government should distinguish between measured losses, resilience spending and future exposure, and publish an annual assessment. This should explain attribution and uncertainty, avoid double counting and identify gaps in the evidence. Perfect information is unlikely; a transparent baseline that improves over time would already be valuable.
Third, this assessment must inform action. It should be accompanied by operational and investment commitments, identifying where stronger protection, faster recovery or disruption of hostile networks would reduce harm. Progress should be judged against those outcomes. Publishing a total is useful only if it changes decisions and helps explain them to the public.
The public also deserves a clearer explanation of this burden. Hostile activity can seem remote until its consequences emerge as interrupted services, lost business income or scarce public resources diverted into recovery. Explaining those effects would give substance to warnings about Russia and help make the case for preparedness, without suggesting that every economic loss represents money the Exchequer could otherwise spend.
‘Economic security is national security’ has become a familiar government refrain. Taking it seriously requires an understanding of how hostile activity damages the economy and what can be done to reduce that harm. Britain rightly devotes attention to imposing costs on Moscow – comparable attention should be applied to the costs Moscow imposes here. Understanding the price Britain is paying is essential to protecting its future.

Investigative outlet ProPublica reported in September that Kremlev paid hundreds of thousands of dollars toward Trump Jr’s three-day wedding celebrations with Bettina Anderson in the Bahamas, including the rental of a private island.
Trump Jr and his wife later acknowledged Kremlev’s involvement, describing him as a friend who “very generously hosted” two nights of festivities after their wedding ceremony.
The president defended the arrangement and had previously told reporters that his son had repaid the money.
“It’s totally allowed,” Trump said. “That’s very common.”
Trump has not addressed why the gift – from a national of an adversarial nation that has sought to meddle in US elections – was accepted in the first place, or the relationship that prompted it.
Republican Senator John Curtis of Utah has asked the Senate Judiciary Committee to investigate and subpoena Trump Jr, arguing that presidential families should face the same scrutiny regardless of party.
“A toaster is a wedding gift. A private-island party paid for by a Putin-connected oligarch is something else,” Curtis said last month.
Kremlev, who has received Russia’s Order of Friendship from Putin, dismissed suggestions that the gift carried political significance.
“Why can’t we be friends... We are simply friends and what unites us is love for sports,” said Kremlev, who was speaking through an interpreter. AFP

Modi's 25 years in office: A study in seva and action
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
22:57:55 UTC
07:57:55 KST

In a democracy, when someone completes 25 consecutive years as the head of a govt, it is indeed special. I heartily congratulate Shri Narendra Modi ji on 25 glorious years of service as head of govt. He is someone I am very fond of and someone I have interacted with closely over the years.Who is Modiji? What makes him successful? What drives him? These are very common questions and are worth pondering over.
For me, Prime Minister Modi is a blend of both leadership and spirituality.When I reflect upon the life of Narendrabhai, one quality that draws my attention is this sense of an underlying purpose running through very different phases of his life. I have often spoken of the divided heart - a heart pulled in many directions by competing desires. There is an inherent tension between freedom and desire, between what is pleasant and what is good. Aspirants on the spiritual path encounter this tension and have to work at resolving it before real progress is possible.In Narendrabhai's life, we can see that this work happened quite early on. I recently learned that at seventeen, he left home, travelled across India and spent time in the Himalayas; influenced by Swami Vivekananda and his encounters with different communities and traditions, his life began to orient itself towards service.
Thereafter, the outer form kept changing - from pracharak to organiser, from CM to PM, but the idea of service remained a recurring thread. When the heart becomes united in purpose, positions cease to be destinations in themselves. They become different instruments through which that purpose can find expression.The devastating flood at Morbi in 1979, following failure of the Machchhu dam, gave this commitment a demanding field of action. Narendrabhai worked there as a volunteer in the aftermath of disaster. Years later, while visiting landslide-affected Wayanad in 2024, he recalled that experience as helping him understand suffering of families who'd lost so much. When we serve people in their hour of distress, their difficulties cease to be concerns. They become responsibilities we feel within ourselves.A sense of purpose finds expression in the way we respond to the person before us. When Seva takes root in the heart, even an ordinary encounter becomes an opportunity to care. An incident from Narendrabhai's earlier life brings this quality to mind.In her account "A train journey and two names to remember," published in The Hindu in 2014, Leena Sarma recalled her journey from Delhi to Ahmedabad in 1990 with Utpalparna Hazarika. Both women were Railway Traffic Service probationers, travelling for the next phase of training without confirmed berths. The ticket examiner found them space in a first-class compartment occupied by Narendra Modi and Shankersinh Vaghela. That evening, Narendrabhai paid for all four vegetarian meals. Later, when the ticket examiner explained that no berths could be arranged for the women, both men surrendered theirs, spread a cloth on the floor and slept there, leaving the berths to the two probationers.What touches me is the ease with which they gave up their comfort. In Sarma's recollection, the kindness came without ceremony. This was long before Narendrabhai became chief minister or Prime Minister, and the need before him was simple and immediate. Such moments invite us to reflect on how we behave when no one is watching as an example of leadership. Can we notice another person's difficulty and respond without seeking recognition? To me, this is generosity of heart. It gives a human warmth to purpose and allows seva to become part of everyday life.Doubt will visit every sincere seeker, just as uncertainty accompanies every person who accepts a great responsibility. If one listens to its whisperings, faith is progressively fractured; the will loses its ability to drive action and real spiritual progress becomes difficult. The question is not whether doubt arises, but whether we allow it to become the driver of our lives. This is where shraddha becomes so important.Shraddha is more than belief; it contains trust, self-confidence, sincerity, determination and inner conviction. I am reminded here of Narendrabhai becoming CM of Gujarat in 2001. At fifty-one, he had never contested an election and had never held an administrative position. He was asked to govern a state still recovering from a devastating earthquake and there were understandable questions about whether an experienced organiser could become an effective administrator. Yet he accepted the responsibility and learnt while carrying it. His early tenure as chief minister was fraught with many challenges that he had to overcome, challenges that could have tested the faith of many.Conviction does not mean that we know beforehand that we will succeed. It means that uncertainty does not prevent us from taking the next step. We may hear the voice of doubt, we may learn from it, but we need not hand over to it the direction of our lives. Narendrabhai's life is one where doubt has never been allowed into the driver's seat; in fact, courage and conviction have been given that place.Fear asks, "What if?" while faith responds, "Even if." Fearlessness does not mean that a human being never experiences fear. What matters is whether fear is permitted to determine our direction. Narendrabhai's life offers examples of accepting responsibility in very different circumstances of uncertainty. In his mid-sixties, when Narendrabhai accepted the mantle of being Prime Minister of India, the scale of uncertainty was enormous: he moved from leading one state to assuming responsibility for India's national security, diplomacy and relationships with the world, at a time when questions were being asked about how a state leader would make that transition.Later came a spell of challenges that may constitute one of the most turbulent periods in recent history. The Covid pandemic, trade wars, the geopolitical upheaval following the war in Ukraine and the recent West Asia crisis, along with domestic challenges, feature among circumstances that would have tested the fortitude of any leader, let alone one who holds the hopes of 1.4 billion. To navigate this with poise is exemplary. Perhaps this is one way of understanding courage spiritually. It is not to say, "Nothing can happen to me." It is to say, "Whatever may happen, I will not allow fear alone to decide what I must do."And so, for any student of leadership, there is a clear lesson from his life. Cultivating a heart free from division, allowing generosity to guide our actions, anchoring mind in conviction and developing a spirit that does not act from fear are spiritual principles that have helped shape Narendrabhai's path as a karmayogi. These principles are universal and when we see them manifest in someone's life, we can use them as inspiration.
I take this occasion to wish Narendrabhai all the very best; may the divine grant him a long life to carry forward this era with leadership and guidance, and may he continue to take India to greater and greater heights.(The writer is the president, Shri Ram Chandra Mission, Global Guide of Heartfulness Meditation)
