ATO convenes snap meeting over credit card ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
22:57:42 UTC
07:57:42 KST

ATO will not budge after snap meeting over credit card ban
In short:
Business groups have accused the ATO of having "double standards" for refusing to accept credit card payments from November 30.
The tax office said it was not appropriate for it to absorb the surcharge fees itself because that would effectively transfer the cost to the taxpayer.
What's next?
The ATO has stood firm on its decision, despite calling a special forum for frustrated small business groups to discuss the changes.
The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) will not budge on its decision to stop accepting credit card payments from December 1, after holding a snap crisis meeting with business groups angered by the move.
Australia's tax chief convened a meeting with business groups this morning to the discuss the changes in the wake of widespread backlash.
But the ATO has indicated it is not going to reverse the credit card ban, according to a spokesperson from the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI), which attended the meeting.
"We will continue to seek to have the ban overturned," the ACCI spokesperson said.
The ABC has approached the ATO for comment.
Last week the tax office announced it would stop accepting credit card payments at the end of next month.
That step came in response to the Reserve Bank of Australia's reforms to scrap card surcharges from October 1, which the bank said was "in the public interest" and would save customers about $1.6 billion a year.
The ATO said it would continue accepting credit cards until November 30 to allow for a transition period, saying it was untenable beyond that point.
Small business owners say they have been expected to absorb the fees of card transactions themselves, and have lost the option of using credit card payments to the ATO as a cash flow method.
Some feared the sudden change would mean they needed to source cash quickly to begin paying by debit instead, or they would be forced to go into arrears with the ATO, and that could result in enforcement against their businesses, including possible closure.
Earlier Andrew McKellar, chief executive of the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI), had called for the ATO's credit card ban to be reversed.
"There is a clear double standard here. Government is telling small business to absorb the hit from the surcharge ban and its cost, while the tax office is saying a different set of rules applies to it," he said.
"Small business is the backbone of the economy. They are doing it tough, with rising costs and a fourth interest rate increase last week."
The Council of Small Business Organisations Australia (COSBOA) said it raised issues for businesses that used credit cards as a cash flow tool and said the decision "warrants a rethink".
"However, the broader issue remains the card surcharge ban itself," it said in a statement, adding it was concerned about the capacity of small businesses to take on the cost.
"The ATO's own response highlights that concern," it said.
"If absorbing the cost of accepting credit card payments is not sustainable for a government agency, it is difficult to expect small businesses already operating on tight margins to simply absorb those costs themselves."
Master Builders CEO Denita Wawn said the surcharge card ban and other regulatory decisions were made "without consultation" and showed a "lack of practical understanding of the impact of decisions being made by this government".
"It's quite incredulous," she told News 24 yesterday afternoon.
"Who would want to be a small business operator in this country at the moment?"
The ABC understands business groups were frustrated by the meeting, and it was unclear who had made the decision to end credit card payments, and when.
ATO says absorbing costs 'not tenable'
In a statement on October 2, taxation commissioner Rob Heferen said the ATO "would have preferred to continue accepting credit cards" but credit card companies declined to offer a rate that was low enough.
"The costs associated with accepting credit card payments are significant, with merchant fees estimated to be almost $200 million annually and expected to continue increasing over time," he said in the statement.
"It is not tenable for the ATO to absorb the costs associated with accepting credit cards on an ongoing basis.
"This would result in less revenue being collected by the ATO and, ultimately, less funding being available for all government services."
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor called for the government to "instruct" the ATO to reverse its decision.
"This is a government that says to small businesses, 'You've got to absorb the surcharges,' and then the Australian Tax Office says, 'We're not going to accept credit card payments because we can't accept the surcharges,'" Mr Taylor said.
"The hypocrisy of this government knows no bounds."
Chris Rodwell, CEO of the Australian Retail Council, also called on the tax office to rethink the decision.
"Removing credit card payments will disrupt how some small businesses manage their cash flow at an already difficult time," he said.
"Small businesses deserve a fair go. If they are expected to wear these costs, so should the tax office."
Other entities have also signalled they will stop accepting credit card payments, including StrataPay, some private schools, local councils, and rental payment platforms.
The ATO has said credit card payments make up only 2.3 per cent of payments to the tax office.
It said "more than 60 per cent of credit card payments by value were made by privately owned and wealthy groups, and public and multinational businesses", while about 5 per cent of all small businesses used credit cards to pay their taxes.

‘Nobody seems to care’: Russian city shrugs off plague reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
22:55:00 UTC
07:55:00 KST

‘Nobody seems to care’: Russian city shrugs off plague reports
Irkutsk, Russia – Reports of a plague laboratory worker’s death in Siberia have caused waves of speculation outside Russia, but in the city where she worked, many appeared unfazed.
The laboratory worker’s death was first reported on Oct 2. Several Russian media outlets reported she had died from pneumonic plague, a highly contagious form of the deadly disease, and that dozens of people had been quarantined.
But Russian officials played down the reports this week, saying that post-mortem tests did not detect the disease in her body and that no special measures were in place.
“If it were really serious, I think they would have shut everything down by now,” one man, who did not provide his name, told AFP in the remote Siberian city of Irkutsk.
“As it stands, nobody really seems to care,” he added.
Another man in Irkutsk said he had asked his parents to take precautions like washing their hands, but that he did not view it as a “serious threat”.
Russian news outlet People of Baikal reported on Oct 2 that the laboratory technician, whom it named as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, may have contracted plague from a broken test tube.
Other media reported a possible link between her death and a lab accident at the facility.
US President Donald Trump has offered to help Russia, if necessary, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio has called for Russia to be “transparent”.
On Oct 6, Trump said he was due to speak shortly with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the reports.
‘We can handle it’
Some residents in Irkutsk questioned whether the laboratory worker had died of plague at all.
“I don’t think it was actually plague,” one man in the city said, without giving his name.
Plague is a bacterial disease that can occur in several forms, including pneumonic plague, which is the most contagious type and can be transmitted by respiratory means.
Pneumonic plague can be fatal if not treated early, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
In a press briefing earlier on Oct 6, a WHO spokesman said the risk from the incident appeared to be “moderate to low”.
The governor of the Irkutsk region said that the health authorities found no evidence that the woman had died of plague.
Moscow appeared to counter Washington’s offer to help on Oct 6, saying it was ready to help the US with its own infectious diseases.
“Today I read that Trump wants to help the city of Irkutsk,” said another local resident.
“We can handle it ourselves,” the man added.
The US national public health agency, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, said in a post on X that it was “closely monitoring reports” of a suspected plague case in Russia, adding that there was “no indication of a broader threat to the US”. AFP

Transcript of US Vice President Vance interview in Alaska
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
22:54:20 UTC
07:54:20 KST

Transcript of US Vice President Vance interview in Alaska
FAIRBANKS, Alaska, Oct 6 - US Vice President JD Vance gave an exclusive interview to Reuters on Monday while campaigning in Alaska, a state that has emerged as a key battleground in the November elections that will determine control of Congress.
This transcript of the interview, which took place after a rally at Fairbanks International Airport for Republican US Senator Dan Sullivan, has been edited lightly for length and clarity.
Jacob Bogage, Reuters:
Mr. Vice President, let's start here. Can you tell me about where things stand with Iran right now?
Vice President JD Vance:
Well, you know, we're at a place where the Iranians are trying to terrorize the world economy by shooting at commercial shipping. They're largely failing. They're hitting some ships, but not enough to stop the flow of oil and gas. So what that means is, their response to us destroying the nuclear program was to try to terrorize commercial shipping and exercise leverage over the United States of America.
And where we are is, as the president said, the nuclear program's been destroyed, but every time they try to squeeze the world economy, we actually squeeze them harder. And so I think what the president has said is, look, you guys fundamentally are not in a game that's going to work out for you. Every time they try to cause damage to the world economy, they end up causing much greater damage to themselves, and eventually they're going to have to decide either to make smarter decisions or to suffer the consequences.
Bogage:
You've played a pivotal role in terms of American foreign policy writ large, turning how the US engages on the world's stage from conflicts without direct American interests, like Ukraine, to conflicts with direct American interests, like Iran. Tell me a little bit about what does it take for the US to resume kinetic attacks? What do you need to hear? Or, rather, what do you need to not hear?
Vance:
That's obviously a decision the president of the United States will make. But you know, we have to start with a fundamental goal here. The goal here is to prevent the Iranians from having a nuclear weapon, and really to prevent regional nuclear proliferation. Because, as the president's reminded people, it's if the Iranians get a nuclear weapon, then other countries will get a nuclear weapon.
Bogage:
Is that a larger focus than where this conflict began?
Vance:
To finish that question, what that means is their nuclear facilities, their enrichment facilities, have been destroyed, and we're going to ensure that they can't rebuild those facilities and rebuild their nuclear capacity.
That's fundamentally the goal here, and everything else that's happening, from them terrorizing shipping to our response to that, is really a subplot of the much bigger goal of keeping them from having a nuclear weapon.
Bogage:
You talk about preventing regional proliferation. Is that a goal that has expanded from the original goal of this operation?
Vance:
No, no. I mean, I think that's one of the reasons why the president didn't want Iran to get a nuclear weapon, because he realized that if they did, then a lot of other countries would then sprint for a nuclear weapon.
So, you know, you don't want the world's largest state sponsor of terrorism to have a nuclear weapon. You also don't want to radically increase the number of nuclear weapons in the world. The president hears a lot about that.
It's interesting. It's something that came up in the conversation with (Chinese President) Xi (Jinping) that the president has said multiple times publicly. He doesn't like mass proliferation of nuclear weapons. It's one of the core parts of his foreign policy, and frankly, something that both Democrats and Republicans should have been a little more focused on over the last 40 years.
Bogage:
Who is the US negotiating with right now?
Vance:
Well, that's a good question.
You know we're negotiating with the political leadership of the country, specifically, you know, the foreign minister has led the negotiations, the president of the country, a number of people work for them. But one of the things we picked up on is it's not totally clear how their country makes decisions.
If you go back to the original agreement that we struck, it was very simple. It was not a complicated document. It basically said we're going to open up the Strait of Hormuz, the United States is going to lift our blockade, and we're going to talk about the nuclear program. That's really all it said.
And they couldn't even keep the end of the bargain where they didn't shoot at commercial shipping. And our assessment of why that is, is because, yeah, you have people in the country who want to make a deal, and we're willing to talk to them. You also have people in the country who are trying to sabotage a deal, which I think is very stupid for their country. But you know, it's ultimately their decision to make.
Bogage:
Iran has said for 47 years, and I'm not going to weigh in on whether it's believable or not, that they don't want a nuclear weapon. How do they communicate that any differently, in a way that helps the United States wind down its operation?
Vance:
Well, I guess I would say, if you don't want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60% enriched fuel? And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don't build highly enriched fuel. That's a very basic threshold issue.
Sixty percent enriched uranium, you know, I'm hardly a nuclear scientist, but I've learned this: you don't need that for any energy production. You don't need it for anything except to have threshold weapons-grade uranium.
So I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity. So far, we haven't seen a long-term commitment to do that.
Bogage:
There's been reporting that you are leading these talks. Are you leading these talks?
Vance:
We're certainly involved. I mean, ultimately, the president of the United States is driving things and is issuing direction. And then, you know, we're trying to get the president's mission accomplished as best we can.
You know, what the president has said is, you know, look, from the very beginning, we're willing to strike an agreement where the Iranians commit to not rebuilding their nuclear program and take real steps in order to do that, but it takes two to tango, and we're not going to trade words for actions.
In other words, the United States is not going to do things for mere promise of actions on the Iranian side. We need to trade actions for actions here, and we'll see what the Iranians do.
Bogage:
Since we spoke earlier this morning, the New York Times reported there was an Iranian operation in motion in the UK at RAF Fairford, similar to perhaps what the Ukrainians had done in getting drones deep into the country. Do you have any intelligence on that that you're in a position to share?
Vance:
I'm not going to speak to classified intelligence. Nothing has happened yet. We're very aware that the Iranians are trying to conduct strikes against American assets all over the world. You know, we also have incredibly capable guys on the military side and the intelligence side. So far, nothing has happened. We'll keep praying and working to ensure that it doesn't.
Bogage:
On munitions stocks, we hear one thing from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. We hear other things from commanders in the field, but I know you speak to them personally. Have they conveyed concern about munition stocks to you?
Vance:
I'd be surprised if the commanders in the field were saying something different than what Secretary Hegseth is saying, because obviously they're communicating to him and they're communicating to all of us.
I think what is undoubtedly true is that warfare has changed. I mean, you mentioned this Ukrainian attack on a Russian airfield, and you know whatever the reality is, people are using drones and asymmetric capabilities in a totally new way, and that does require a totally new kind of defensive and offensive capability.
Do I think that we're far ahead of anybody else in the world? Yeah. Do I think that we always need to be thinking about how to build more? The president, I wouldn't even say laser-focused. I would say he is obsessed with this question of how we stay ahead in terms of military-grade technology.
I think that sometimes this munitions conversation gets reinterpreted through a lens of American weakness, when in reality, what the president is just trying to say is, we need to build the weapons of the future, and we need to build enough so that we can properly defend ourselves.
Bogage:
It would be malpractice, Mr. Vice President, if I didn't ask this.
Vance:
Go ahead.
Bogage:
These good people at the rally seem like they want you to run for president. Are you going to run for president, sir?
Vance:
Man, I've been asked that question a lot. I'm inherently a procrastinator, and I really haven't thought that much about it. We're going to try to win the midterms, get Dan Sullivan elected, which I'm very confident we're going to do, and then, you know, we'll figure it out after that. REUTERS

In interview, US Vice-President Vance says Iran must cut enrichment to end war

AI generated
FAIRBANKS, Alaska – US Vice-President J.D. Vance said in an exclusive interview with Reuters that Iran must make a “meaningful” reduction in its nuclear enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the countries’ seven-month war, even as Washington was unsure how Tehran makes decisions in negotiations.
Vance, a long-time sceptic of American involvement in foreign wars, has taken a leading role in negotiating a settlement to the conflict and brokered a provisional peace agreement in June that quickly fell apart.
The war has jolted global energy markets and become a political liability for US President Donald Trump and fellow Republicans ahead of the November midterm elections.
Speaking on Oct 5 after a campaign trip in Alaska, Vance said any agreement would require Iran to reduce its nuclear enrichment capacity, rather than offer assurances of future nuclear drawdowns.
“If you don’t want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60% enriched fuel? And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don’t build highly enriched fuel. That’s a very basic threshold issue,” Vance said.
“I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity.”
Iran and the US have in recent weeks exchanged proposals aimed at ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy shipping route. Trump rejected Tehran’s latest offer and has warned that military operations could intensify after the midterms.
Vance said the US remained open to an agreement but would require concrete Iranian nuclear concessions. “We’re not going to trade words for actions,” he added.
Unclear how Iran makes decisions: Vance
Complicating matters, Vance said Washington is uncertain who makes decisions in Tehran.
Vance said the US was in talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. But it was unclear how much authority they wield within Iran’s power structure, he said, after joint US-Israeli strikes at the start of the war killed Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
“One of the things we picked up on is it’s not totally clear how their country makes decisions,” Vance said. Separately, Trump said on Oct 6 that his “biggest problem” is no one knows who is running Iran.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson said on Oct 4 that US officials are well aware of who their Iranian counterparts are and how Iran’s decision-making system works.
“The problem is actually the opposite. It lies in the contradictory positions and mixed messaging from US officials,” Esmaeil Baghaei told a weekly press conference.
Vance told Reuters he has had personal conversations with field commanders to gauge battlefield conditions. He dismissed concerns over critical munitions shortages and added that while Iranian troops are periodically able to strike commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, they are largely unable to prevent energy exports through the waterway.
Vance declined to say if he was leading peace talks, though he is frequently cited as the White House’s top negotiator.
“We’re certainly involved,” he said. “Ultimately, the President of the United States is driving things.”
The war – and its US$3 billion (S$3.8 billion) monthly price tag – has become a key issue on the campaign trail. Higher energy prices have put Trump and Republicans on the defensive in competitive states that will decide control of Congress.
Vance has sought to temper criticism of Trump’s handling of the conflict, telling voters they should not let that issue keep them from backing Republicans in the November elections.
In Alaska, Vance rallied for Republican Senator Dan Sullivan, who is locked in a tight re-election battle with Democratic challenger Mary Peltola. Trump carried Alaska by 13 percentage points in 2024, but rising everyday costs have put the state in play.
Before speaking with Reuters, Vance focused much of his speech on affordability concerns, especially around energy. Alaska’s remote locale makes consumer goods more expensive, and energy production is a key industry.
Rally attendees roared when Sullivan nearly introduced Vance as the president of the US, rather than the vice-president. Vance is seen as a leading Republican contender to succeed Trump in the White House.
Vance told Reuters afterwards that he had not decided whether to seek the presidency in 2028.
“I’m inherently a procrastinator,” he said. “I really haven’t thought about it much.” REUTERS

WASHINGTON, October 7. /TASS/. The United States does not need Iranian oil, US President Donald Trump said.
Speaking in Baltimore, Maryland, he claimed that the Strait of Hormuz is currently fully controlled by the US Navy. "In other words, the Hormuz Strait belongs to the United States Navy and the United States of America: that’s where it belongs, and that’s where it is right now," Trump asserted. "With all of that being said, we don’t need their oil, others need their oil, and they need it badly," the US leader said. "But we’re getting it out, and we’re getting it out at record levels," he added.
In addition, the US president stressed that Washington intends to prevent Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons. Trump believes this objective has already effectively been achieved. "That will never happen. That will never happen. That’s already fait accompli," the president declared.
Tehran has repeatedly stressed that it is not seeking to develop nuclear arms. Moreover, Western intelligence agencies have found no evidence of Iran developing nuclear weapons. The New York Times also confirmed this at the end of January. Additionally, a fatwa (religious edict) issued by the former supreme leader of the Islamic Republic, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, has been in effect in Iran since 2003, prohibiting the production of nuclear weapons.

US President Donald Trump said Tuesday he would speak “very soon” with Russian President Vladimir Putin over the reported death from plague of a laboratory technician, as Washington and the World Health Organization pressed Moscow for greater transparency and clarity over conflicting accounts of the incident in Siberia.
US President Donald Trump said Tuesday he would speak very soon with Russian President Vladimir Putin over the reported plague death of a laboratory technician, as Washington pressured Moscow for transparency.
Russian authorities denied that they were imposing anti-plague measures and played down the reports of an incident at an anti-plague institute in Siberia's Irkutsk region last week.
But Washington is showing growing concern, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio calling on Russia to be open about the situation.

"We encourage Russia to be transparent and share more information with the world so that all of us could react accordingly and appropriately," Rubio said during a trip to Iceland.
"Depending on what we learn about it, we would learn how to respond."
Trump later said he would be speaking to Putin about what happened.
"I have a call scheduled, yes," Trump told reporters at the White House when asked if he had spoken to Putin on the issue yet, adding that it would happen "very soon."
The Wall Street Journal reported that the US State Department had sent Russia a confidential diplomatic communication known as a demarche warning Moscow that failure to disclose details runs counter to its international health obligations.
Cause of death 'undetermined'
Russian news outlet People of Baikal reported Friday that the dead woman – named as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova – may have contracted pneumonic plague from a broken test tube.
Other media reported a possible link between her death and a lab accident at the facility.
The People of Baikal outlet also said up to 200 people with whom she may have had contact were under quarantine.
But Russian authorities say the cause of death is not confirmed and health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor has denied claims circulating in a document online that special measures had been put in place.
"We wish to clarify that the document and information in question do not originate from official sources and are untrue," it said on Telegram.
Russian officials said postmortem tests had not detected the disease.
Irkutsk Regional Governor Igor Kobzev said Monday that a Rospotrebnadzor inspection had found the woman died of pneumonia and the cause was "undetermined".
"No microorganisms linked to the young woman's professional work were found in her biological samples," he said, adding that no other staff at the institute had sought medical attention since her death.

The World Health Organization said that an update received Tuesday from Russia stressed that "no case of this dangerous disease has been recorded in the city of Irkutsk."
"Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks," WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus wrote on X.

'Moderate to low' risk

Plague is a bacterial disease that can occur in several forms, including pneumonic plague, which is the most contagious type and can be transmitted by respiratory means. Bubonic plague is transmitted by infected fleas.
Pneumonic plague, which causes lung failure, can be fatal if not treated early, according to WHO.

From Gujarat CM to India's PM: Modi's 25 years in office
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
22:51:25 UTC
07:51:25 KST

A push for manufacturing semiconductors as well as for startups and self-reliance, continues to be Modi’s focus in his third term as PM
Narendra Modi was thrust into the thick of governance in 2001 as the party suffered a setback in local polls in Gujarat and the response of the state government headed by CM Keshubhai Patel to the massive Kutch earthquake was found wanting.Within months of his swearing-in as CM, riots swept the state in the wake of the Godhra train-burning incident. BJP's win in the 2002 assembly polls cemented his position and dissidents in the party were marginalised as he set about implementing his governance agenda.
Kutch rebuilt. In 2003, Gujarat passed India's first state disaster management law.
Vibrant Gujarat Summit launched in 2003 to showcase its strength & attract investors.
Jyotigram Yojana, launched in 2006, prioritised reliable power supply over subsidised but erratic electricity to villages. Soon, all 18,000 villages had access to reliable three-phase power as non-farm economic activity expanded and subsidies were nearly halved.
Sagarkhedu Sarvangi Vikas Yojana launched in 2007 adopted an outcome-oriented mission for coastal communities, combining infrastructure, livelihoods, irrigation, salinity control, coastal security and fisheries development.
Launched in 2009, Garib Kalyan Mela took welfare delivery to citizens.
Check dams, farm ponds, recharge wells, canals and inter-basin transfers were planned as surplus floodwater was carried through 332km of canals and Narmada water reached reservoirs across Saurashtra, opening over 10 lakh acres of irrigation potential. A CAG report in 2017 recorded groundwater recharge roughly 50% above 2002 levels.
His government linked ports with power, roads, rail and industrial estates. Mundra, Hazira and Pipavav grew into major private ports.
Nudged by RSS, the BJP brass named Modi in June 2013 as its campaign committee head for the 2014 polls and soon elevated him as its PM candidate. When results were announced on May 16, BJP more than doubled its tally to 282, its first majority in the then 545-member Lok Sabha. It was the first majority government since 1984.
2014-2019: First term as PM
His government launched Jan Dhan Yojana, and 59 crore accounts were opened with over Rs 3.1 lakh crore in deposits. Women owned 33 crore of these accounts. This helped in ushering in direct benefit transfer, changing welfare delivery. By Aug 2026, DBT had transferred Rs 53.2 lakh crore across 320 schemes and 56 ministries.
In his Aug 15 speech at Red Fort, Modi spoke of the indignities women suffer due to lack of toilets and announced a sanitation campaign. Swachh Bharat Mission was launched. PM Ujjwala Yojana, launched in 2016, gave 10.5 crore free LPG connections to women from poor households by May 2026.
His government expanded the social security net, including free treatment for the poor under Ayushman Bharat. By 2025, official estimates say 94.3 crore Indians were covered by some form of social protection, up from 19% in 2015 to 64%.
GST was rolled out in July 2017 in what the PM lauded as economic unification of India as tax borders came down and the market became one.
2019-24: Second term as PM
Few people outside the top echelons of government were aware when it took probably its most significant political calls: revoking the special constitutional status enjoyed by J&K under Article 370, downgrading the state to the status of UT and hiving off Ladakh as a UT.
A verdict from SC paved the way for construction of Ram Mandir in Ayodhya. The idol was consecrated in Jan 2024.
CAA was passed in 2019, providing a path to citizenship for persecuted non-Muslim communities from Pakistan, Bangladesh and Afghanistan.
The Covid pandemic and lockdowns tested government as India suffered a large human toll. Scaling up of indigenous vaccines and the world's largest vaccination campaign helped. Government launched the Atmanirbhar Bharat programme. It was also a period when UPI use began zooming and has become a definitive success.
2024: Wins a third term
BJP went into the 2024 elections with supreme confidence and was humbled as a section of voters balked at its "abki baar 400 paar" slogan. However, it won a majority with its allies even as it lost its own majority after a decade.
A manufacturing push in semiconductors, startups and self-reliance continues to be the focus. Govt cited India's high growth rate to emphasise handling of global headwinds.
Security forces' success in virtually eliminating Naxalism, cited by predecessor Manmohan Singh as the biggest internal threat to India, has been a boost to BJP's national security agenda.Operation Sindoor targeted terrorist hideouts in Pakistan in May 2025 after the Pahalgam attack.

Türkiye’s investment fund market remains sound despite investigations, fund liquidations: Central Bank governor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
22:50:14 UTC
07:50:14 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Türkiye's investment fund market continues to function soundly despite current investigations and the liquidation of some funds, with no problem affecting the broader financial system, the nation’s Central Bank governor said Tuesday.
Speaking to lawmakers at parliament's Planning and Budget Committee, Fatih Karahan said the volatility had been concentrated in individual funds within a limited segment of financial markets.
“We assess that the fund market overall continues to function soundly and that there is no problem affecting the financial system as a whole,” he said.
The Central Bank increased repo auction amounts, raised banks' borrowing limits tenfold, eased collateral requirements, and accelerated bond purchases to contain spillovers.
“We will continue to take the necessary steps depending on market conditions,” he said.
Fund outflows slow
Karahan said substantial fund withdrawals since Aug. 28 had partly shifted into bank deposits, with commercial and savings deposits rising by more than 800 billion Turkish liras ($16.3 billion).
Including investment funds, the Turkish lira's share remained stable at around 61%-61.4%, while fund withdrawals recently slowed.
Three investment banks whose shareholder rights were transferred to the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund represented just 0.2% of the banking sector, he said, adding that no systemic risk is currently expected.
Supply shocks prolong tight policy
Karahan said inflation's decline from 75% to the 30% range shows progress, although the targeted level has yet to be reached.
Persistent rent and education inflation, slower monetary policy transmission, and food and energy supply shocks required interest rates to remain high for longer, he said.
Acknowledging costs for workers, businesses, and public finances, he said low and predictable inflation is essential.
“Disinflation is being pursued not to impose costs on Türkiye, but because it is the only lasting solution to the problems being experienced today,” he said.

Tennessee execution survivor Christa Pike is conscious and speaking, lawyers say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
22:44:47 UTC
07:44:47 KST

Convicted killer Christa Pike, who survived Tennessee's effort to execute her by lethal injection last week, foiling the state's first attempt to put a woman to death in two centuries, has regained consciousness and is speaking, her lawyers said in a statement on Tuesday.
Despite severe injuries to her arms from the insertion of intravenous lines during the attempted execution last Wednesday, Pike, 50, is "still handcuffed and shackled" to her hospital bed while she remains under medical care, her team of public defense attorneys wrote.
"Her prognosis remains unclear, but at a minimum we expect a long recovery," the lawyers' statement said, adding that a court hearing on Pike's case was scheduled for Wednesday in Davidson County Chancery Court.
Pike, sentenced to death for her role as a teenager in the torture-murder of a 19-year-old schoolmate Colleen Slemmer three decades ago, survived the botched execution attempt on the night of September 30 at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, the state capital. She has been hospitalized since then.
Her lawyers said on Friday that their client remained unconscious, critically ill, and hooked to a ventilator to breathe, as doctors labored to clear the drug pentobarbital from her system.
Pike first person in the US known to survive execution drugs
"Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking and continues to receive critical medical care," they wrote on Tuesday.
Pike's petition for clemency, denied last week by Governor Bill Lee, argued that her death sentence had failed to properly account for Pike's own childhood trauma as the victim of sexual abuse, neglect, and untreated mental illness.
Pike went from being the first woman Tennessee had tried to put to death since the early 19th century to becoming the first person in the United States known to have survived after execution drugs were administered.
Death penalty opponents said the incident exposed the inherent barbarity of executions. It also highlighted the difficulties of carrying out lethal injections while respecting constitutional prohibitions on cruel and unusual punishment.
'None of it was normal'
Pike's attorneys and journalists who witnessed the execution attempt described it as roughly 2-1/2 hours of disarray and prolonged distress for her as Department of Correction personnel struggled to administer two doses of pentobarbital intravenously.
"None of it was normal," Catherine Sweeney, a reporter for Nashville public broadcaster WPLN, recounted. "It went really poorly."
Pike was heard gasping, crying, whimpering and breathing loudly through much of the procedure, at one point saying, "my arm feels like it's about to burst open."
The bungled attempt to establish intravenous lines left both of Pike's arms "swollen, burned and blistered," the apparent result of the pentobarbital, a highly alkaline and caustic substance, seeping into the tissues under her skin, her lawyers said in court filings.
The lawyers accused state officials of having shrugged off prior warnings from Pike's doctors that her small veins and a blood disorder called thrombocytosis would make placing IV lines especially difficult.
In the midst of the procedure, Pike's lawyers filed an emergency court motion seeking to halt the procedure. By then, prison officials had ceased their execution efforts and called an ambulance, according to court records.
The night of the execution attempt, the Department of Correction defended its handling of the situation, saying it had "followed every step of the state's lawful, established execution protocol." But the governor said agency commissioner Frank Strada has resigned and will leave his post this month.
Lee had previously ordered a suspension of any scheduled executions for the rest of the year and a third-party review of what happened in Pike's case.
Two days before Pike was due to meet her fate, Lee rejected a petition seeking to commute her death penalty to a life prison term without the possibility of parole.
Pike was 18 in January 1995 when she, her 17-year-old boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, and a third companion lured Slemmer into a wooded area on the University of Tennessee campus in Knoxville and killed her.
The gruesome nature of the slaying, which involved Shipp carving the shape of a pentagram in the victim's chest and Pike bashing Slemmer in the head with a chunk of asphalt, then taking a piece of her skull as a souvenir, drew intense media coverage at the time. Trial testimony indicated that Pike viewed Slemmer as a rival for her boyfriend's affections.
Pike and Shipp confessed to the killing, and both were convicted of first-degree murder. Pike was sentenced to death, while Shipp received a life sentence with the possibility of parole.
Their co-defendant, Shadolla Peterson, who was 18 at the time of the murder and had acted as a lookout for the other two, testified for the prosecution and received probation.

Kosovo Elects President After Opposition Agrees To Last-Minute Deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
22:39:30 UTC
07:39:30 KST

PRISTINA — Parliament elected Justina Shiroka Pula as Kosovo's new president early on October 7 following a last-minute political deal that secured lawmakers' approval of legal changes restricting the powers of a Hague-based war crimes court.
The secret ballot began just six minutes before a midnight deadline, with lawmakers racing to complete the presidential election -- which averted parliament’s automatic dissolution and another early election -- in time.
Shiroka Pula secured 81 votes to clinch the post in the first round. She needed at least 80 in the 120-seat legislature.
"This mandate does not belong to one person alone. It belongs to our citizens, our institutions, and the state for which so many generations sacrificed," Shiroka Pula said in an address to parliament after being sworn in.
While the election appeared to avoid a political crisis, some experts noted that the process didn't end until 12 minutes after midnight, creating the potential for a legal challenge, though none was immediately announced.
The vote followed a day of deadlock between Prime Minister Albin Kurti’s ruling Vetevendosje party and the opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo (PDK).
Shiroka Pula, an economist and the first woman to lead Kosovo’s Academy of Sciences and Arts, was proposed by Kurti late in the evening. PDK leader Bedri Hamza accepted her candidacy and nominated Eliza Hoxha as the opposing candidate.
Shiroka Pula previously served as energy and mining minister from 2008 to 2011 and as a PDK lawmaker from 2011 to 2014.
Immediately before the presidential election, parliament approved amendments to the law governing the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in a second and final reading, with 88 votes in favor.
Protesters gathered outside parliament applauded as lawmakers approved the amendments.
The PDK had insisted that lawmakers complete passage of the amendments before electing a president. Kurti initially demanded the reverse.
The two leaders exchanged proposals and responses through press conferences after Hamza refused further face-to-face talks until the court amendments were passed.
A breakthrough came with Kurti’s third offer: proposing Shiroka Pula, a former member of Hamza’s party, and agreeing to hold the court-law vote first.
The amendments sharply narrow the jurisdiction of the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, cap prison sentences at 15 years, require sentences to be served in Kosovo and make people convicted by final judgments eligible for presidential pardons.
The legislation also narrows the period covered by the court to July 1, 1999–December 31, 2000, excluding the wartime period, and restricts its jurisdiction to offenses directly linked to alleged organ-trafficking operations at detention sites identified in a 2011 Council of Europe report.
Parliamentary approval does not by itself establish whether the changes can take effect. Legal experts have warned that Kosovo must respect its international commitments and that the amendments could face constitutional review.
The PDK submitted the proposal following the September 16 war crimes convictions of four former Kosovo Liberation Army leaders.
Former President Hashim Thaçi and Jakup Krasniqi received 25-year prison sentences, Kadri Veseli 18 years and Rexhep Selimi 13 years.
All four, however, were acquitted of other crimes against humanity charges. Their defense teams have announced plans to appeal.
The dispute unfolded amid protests demanding passage of the court legislation. On October 5, some demonstrators threw glass bottles and pyrotechnics, while police used tear gas and water cannons to disperse crowds near parliament.
Police said six officers were injured, 11 civilians sought medical attention and three protesters were taken to a police station. Kosovo’s Police Inspectorate opened a preliminary investigation into police conduct during the protest.
Demonstrators gathered again on October 6. Police reported that one person was injured by pyrotechnics thrown by protesters.
Kosovo’s president serves a five-year term, beginning upon taking the oath before parliament.

Oil tanker ablaze after sea-drone attack off Russian Black Sea coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
22:39:16 UTC
07:39:16 KST

Oil tanker ablaze after sea-drone attack off Russian Black Sea coast
An oil tanker caught fire off Russia’s Black Sea coast after being attacked by unmanned boats near Sochi, the Russian Transport Ministry has said. Its 23-member crew of Indian nationals were all rescued and no injuries have been reported.
The Liberian-flagged Aframax Rio, which was carrying crude, was struck by sea drones on Tuesday, according to the ministry. The attack triggered an oil fire in the Black Sea, with emergency crews initially unable to approach the tanker because of the intensity of the blaze.
Russian Transport Minister Andrey Nikitin convened an emergency response headquarters, while the ministry said sufficient personnel and equipment had been deployed to deal with the consequences.
Authorities temporarily closed beaches in the nearby federal territory of Sirius, adjacent to Sochi, as a precaution. Local officials said subsequent monitoring found pollutant concentrations below permitted limits and that there was no immediate danger to public health.
In a separate incident on Tuesday, two merchant vessels were struck by unidentified naval and aerial drones in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, some 128 km off its coast. The Togo-flagged Alfa Watan suffered critical damage and sank, while the Palau-flagged Able caught fire.
Eighteen crew members were rescued from the latter vessel, two of whom had severe injuries. One indicated that the Able was carrying Ukrainian cargo.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev condemned the attacks as a “blatant violation of international law and maritime law” and warned that repeated strikes were disrupting Black Sea shipping and driving insurance costs higher.
No-one has claimed responsibility for the strikes. Moscow has already been targeting vessels it says are carrying military or dual-use cargo to Ukrainian Black Sea ports, while the Russian Defense Ministry said Zelensky would bear “full personal and political responsibility” for any further escalation.
Ukraine has sharply expanded attacks on Russian oil infrastructure and commercial shipping in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov in recent months, using combinations of naval and aerial drones to strike vessels linked to Russian ports.
Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky vowed over the weekend to intensify attacks on Russian oil refineries, prompting Moscow to announce that it would expand strikes on Ukrainian military-industrial facilities and related infrastructure.
The strikes have also become a factor in the global fuel market. US President Donald Trump said on Monday that rising American gasoline prices were now being driven less by disruption around the Strait of Hormuz and more by Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries.
“What’s driving up gasoline is no longer the Strait of Hormuz,” Trump wrote, arguing instead that Russian refineries “are being blown up by Ukraine.”
Trump had previously urged Zelensky to “stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” saying the campaign was “hurting the world.” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has similarly said Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy assets and refined products are contributing to a broader “energy shock.”

Trump says nobody knows who is running Iran
WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump said on Oct 6 that nobody knew who was running Iran during the US-Israeli war with Iran, now in its eighth month.
“Their leaders are gone, their second group of leaders are gone, and the biggest problem I have is nobody knows who the hell is running the country,” Trump said.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman said on Oct 4 that Washington knows very well who their counterpart is in Iran and how the decision-making system in Iran works.
“The problem is actually the opposite: it lies in the contradictory positions and mixed messaging from US officials,” Esmaeil Baghaei said in a news conference.

His son, Mojtaba Khamenei, succeeded him but has not been seen in public since he was injured in the same strike that killed his father.
Iran responded with its own strikes on Israel and Gulf states that host US bases.
US-Israeli strikes on Iran and Israeli attacks on Lebanon have killed thousands and displaced millions.
Fuel prices that have risen in response to the war are also a risk to Trump’s Republican Party ahead of the November US midterm elections in which control of Congress is at stake.
Trump, whose approval rating has held at a record low amid concerns of high cost of living spurred by soaring petrol and diesel prices, has offered shifting timelines and goals for the war. REUTERS

Dimensions: An Ephemeral Manifesto on Creativity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
22:33:31 UTC
07:33:31 KST

Dimensions: An Ephemeral Manifesto on Creativity
by Taylor Borgelt, Rebecca-Eli Long, Rebecca Martinez, Hanna Newell, Olivia Palepoi, Jayvaughn Peter, David Tortolini, Juan Manuel Arévalo Viveros (Purdue University)
We are a student collective brought together through a graduate-level visual anthropology course taught by Professor Dada Docot. In this document, which we’ve framed as a manifesto, we’ve outlined the values that we centered while cultivating our creative projects for this course. Writing a manifesto emerges out of our interest in documenting and recording our experiences as researchers in a creative, expressive space and from a desire to valorize artistic work in a limiting academic environment. We wrote this because we believe in and value challenging larger institutions and systems that have historically devalued the work we find conducive, generative, and beautiful. As both a record and an expression, this manifesto was an opportunity for us to maintain the community we built in class and to engage with larger discourse around the use of creative artistic work in social science spaces.
At the end of this manifesto, we’ve included images of our creative pieces that we showcased during the course’s public-facing exhibit in The ALab in the Department of Anthropology at Purdue University. At the conclusion of the course, we, the students, were tasked with creating and presenting individual visual anthropology projects that worked through the intersections of the major course themes, our own research, and creative expression. Each piece was developed throughout the semester, through drafting and feedback stages, and speaks to the very personal connections that we have towards our larger programs of work. Writing this manifesto was something that came out of reflections on this process of consideration, creation, and presentation, so we wanted to also share what we were all able to create during this time. The commitments and values that we describe throughout this piece are attached to and embodied through our creative work, so putting our writing and our visuals in tandem is meant to affirm our argument. Artist statements for each piece are linked to the titles in the captions.
In writing this collective manifesto, we've attempted to navigate through the confines and tensions of our own respective contexts, backgrounds, histories, identities, and goals. Thus, this piece reflects the relational ventures we took to understand the kaleidoscope of our unique identities and commitments. The significance of this piece is not cohesion or agreement, but respect and care. Acknowledging these existing tensions is also meant to highlight the ways in which this text is itself limiting in how we can (and cannot) adequately express our journeys through our work. Nonetheless, these are pieces and parts that have been collaboratively contributed and edited, but not prescriptively or boundedly provided. Aiming at being a framework for practice (praxis), this manifesto is meant to explore and expand upon how creative works and research can be done in a space like a university classroom, relative to anthropological interests and aims. We’ve offered values that we hold now for work we are doing in the now. This written piece, in furthering a non-prescriptive want/aim, is representative of who we are and how we’re working, with full understanding of and appreciation for how we will continue to change and grow as people and as scholars.
Collective work and livingness are not without conflict, and the scope of this work aims to be demonstrative of the tensions and challenges inherent to existing within an intellectual/practical community at any point in time. Thus, at the core of this piece, our class, and our exhibit, relationality exists not as a means to an end, but as an end in and of itself.
Our Dimensions
This is a non-exhaustive list of some of the values - which we call “dimensions” - we’ve used to foreground our creative work and research practices. In choosing the term “dimensions,” we recognize that our projects are situated in different spaces –geographically, topically, disciplinarily, and beyond – and different contexts. Because our work goes off in various directions, some of our projects may engage more closely with some dimensions than others; however, this does not mean that the other dimensions are unimportant. Our work(s) can never be situated within a single dimension. Instead, dimensions are layered and intersectional. Rather than articulating a set of prescriptive keywords, we give ourselves and each other permission to let some values surface and other values move into the background. In recognizing that there is no perfect or complete list of values that will apply equally to every project, we move away from perfectionism and open spaces of experimentation and improvisation.
Each dimension was written by an individual student and then collectively edited. We each picked the value that felt most significant in our work and our writing. The processes of making our pieces for the course exhibit were personal trials in reflection and critical consideration.
Some of these dimensions build on each other, while others sit more on their own. There is also no significant order to these dimensions – there is no applied sense of hierarchy or prioritization because we’ve aimed to work more horizontally and collectively.
We’ve included images of our creative pieces from the course exhibit, along with a list of their corresponding titles, in the appendices at the end of this paper.
Context (Taylor)
We, as people, do not and cannot live outside of the bounds of culture. Life and meaning are so deeply informed by categorical, indexical, symbolic, and embodied relationality – who we are, how we live, how we value each other, and the cultural systems that surround/involve us all work to provide context for how we make sense of ourselves, each other, and the world (Crenshaw, 1991; Nash, 2008). Because of this intersecting, netted relationality (Osorio, 2021) and the dynamic reality(s) of existence, context is both inevitable and highly significant. In this vein, being able to conceptualize and appreciate the context of people, and their work, is important in prioritizing relativity and working to not hierarchically value people along lines of imposed, enforced, or qualified ‘difference’. In our own work (creative, research, or otherwise), it is important to recognize the ways in which it sits within context(s) and how this creates and exists in relational responsibility, to highlight the ways in which there are always the impacts of people and culture in everything we do. Particularly highlighting creative work – but not exclusively bounding this dimension/ principle to creative work – nothing is devoid of ourselves and we (ourselves) are made up of the people, places, and things around us; the separation of people from others or the environment works to perpetuate systems and conceptualizations of harm, so ethical creative work should attend to this inherent relationality and contextualization.
Expertise (Rebecca-Eli)
For research, creative, and other work to be ethical, it must sincerely believe that interlocutors have expertise, including expertise about what work should or shouldn’t be done, and how. This expertise may not look like standard “Knowledge” and can encompass felt or embodied ways of knowing. Recognizing expertise necessitates the belief that it is possible for people to take part in research, that potential interlocutors are able to decide if they want to participate in a project (or not), including allowing the dignity of risk, as part of a research relationship. This relationship does not assume commensurability between researcher, artists, scholars, and interlocutors or erase power differentials. Rather, it seeks to strategically leverage resources to meet aims of those involved in the research relationship with an awareness of historic power imbalances and harms.
Voices (David)
The era of translating and paraphrasing communities is over. Individuals and organizations who perform research and scholarly work cannot claim to be in collaboration or working in the spaces/places with marginalized and oppressed people(s) if they are not listening to and including their voices within their work(s). As we position these voices at the forefront of our work, a process that incorporates de-centralization and recognition can begin. Collaborative dimensions of voice involve listening, but not everything needs to be written or transcribed. This is self-censorship, where the marginalized and oppressed are given the power and agency to share and distribute their knowledge on their terms. This appreciation and respect challenges academics (researchers, creatives, scholars) to confront the violent, normalized practices in which knowledge is created and shared. Breaking the chains of tradition and listening, we must include all forms of knowledge- making and consider them as academically rigorous. The written word is still important and will never depart, but we should also incorporate other forms of meaning making/ knowledge production. These alternative forms of knowledge production should be recognized as ways of showing people’s voices using the same standards, ethical guidelines, and considerations as the tradition of creating written works. These alternative forms are expressed in various formats, such as art, dance, music, and cooking. An appreciation for and valuation of non-dominant forms of knowledge production allows for an ability to showcase voices as multi-dimensional and significant. As a marginalized person whose voices of my ancestors and communities I carry with me every day; all I can demand is to listen and carefully manifest how we use and share our voices with y’all.
Embracing Tensions (Rebecca)
I embrace the tensions that come with generating creative work and research (or any work), as a scholar expected to “produce”, and the need to “rest” in order to move through this liminal space; to find a subject and be a subject of inquiry to some; to want to be legible and to not know what that means or to make the choice to not be legible. Through continuous reflexive practice, keen observation of my surroundings, and a critical yet generative stance, I prioritize and hold an ethic of engaging with power, in all spaces, and to consciously explore my relationship with it. Are there opportunities for change? Perhaps. Is now the time? Or is tomorrow the stage? The tension of time (needing more, not having enough, not wanting any) is also relevant to learning, crafting, and generating in a way that is considerate and critical. Regardless we all have an opportunity to say something and do something, at least for/within ourselves, to make our worlds more beautiful, weird, bold, kind, compassionate, interesting, poetic, and more.
Re-connection (Liv)
“Va is the space between, the betweenness, not empty space, not space that separates but space that relates, that holds separate entities and things together in the Unity-that-is-All, the space that is context, giving meaning to things. The meanings change as the relationships/the contexts change” - Albert Wendt (1996, 18-19).
“A well-known Samoan expression is ‘Ia Teu Le Va.’ Cherish/nurse/care for the va, the relationships” (Wendt 1996, 19). This creative work focuses on re-centering the essence of the vā in the Samoan diaspora amidst actions of assimilation, acculturation, and erasure as someone born and raised in the state of Utah. As our context in the diaspora fluctuate, so should our responses to nurturing, cherishing, and respecting the relationships we hold. It’s important to remember that vā does not just exist on its own. Rather, it must be the betweenness located within the relationships. As such, I cannot exist without my relationship to those around me and the vā is that which holds me accountable.
Using the frame of “in-betweenness” I write about my experiences navigating spiritual and/or metaphysical connections (disparate from denominational affiliations). I use various mixed mediums to portray the processes of reclaiming, mending, repairing, and rebuilding relationships to spiritual groundings (which is still in processing, as spiritual is definitely open to critique as a term). Overall, this all coalesces to inform the tensions of diasporic experiences as an “in-betweenness” or a processual relational ethic that is built through day-to-day, minute-to-minute, second-to-second practice.
Centering Care (Hanna)
Care needs to be foundational to research and creative work. Care is a prerequisite to the conduct of ethical work. Centering care involves genuine commitment to fostering trust, respect, reciprocity, and meaningful collaboration between people, researchers, and interlocutors. Ethical research means centering care in the pursuit of understanding, while also recognizing that care does not exempt me from my role and position in violent institutions. With care as a cornerstone of ethical research and creative work, prioritizing the voices and perspectives of marginalized and Indigenous communities calls for me to consider the impact of my work, and at times will require the refusal to do work when necessary. This refusal is important for ethical research that centers care, recognizing instances where research may perpetuate harm, like through the use of extractive practices, or reinforce colonial power dynamics and legacies.
Attending to Violence(s) (Taylor)
It is perhaps overly reductive to place knowingness as a significant rebellious action, because knowledge and action are important, connected tenants of praxis, but it is important to see and acknowledge the worlds around us, in all of its complexity. In recognizing that, consciousness and awareness (as activities, not passivities), are meaningful and generative political acts because non-critical complacency is a well manipulated (manipulatable) tool of power. In understanding and appreciating context – specifically acknowledging our context(s) within a university, as graduate students – it is important to first acknowledge how adjacency to and positions within systems/ structures of power afford privilege and how they are built upon violence and harm. Honest personal contention with how we (I) fit into and benefit from a structure predicated on genocide and forced displacement, slavery, racism, sexism, classicism, ableism, and other forms of violence is an early step in developing and enacting (more) ethical creative and intellectual work.
Strategic Concealment (Jayvaughn)
Drawing from the Pohnpeian way of being, known as kanengamah, strategic concealment can refer to restraint through withholding knowledge, emotions, and intentions (Petersen, 1993). Bringing this to academic research spaces, wherein the pursuit of knowledge is inherently central – or the uncovering of truth, can allow us to exercise a power that is necessary for the work we do with communities we owe responsibility to with topics that are complexly in tension with the general missions of academic institutions we are entangled with. What makes this concept strategic is the critical understanding that research institutions are often places of normalized reproductions of harm and that every choice made here is political. Practicing strategic concealment can manifest as a self-imposed filter dependent on audiences, to ensure preservation of self, communities, and ideas from encroaching powers. Allowing our intuitions and understanding of our settings to guide us on what to share in any moment. It can be outright refusal to share or a deferment, acknowledging that the right time is not now. This practice is especially helpful for the complex relations of early researchers in academia that may feel disadvantageous. The result is a state of mindfulness for each of our decisions and the impacts they might have – one that is wary of our individual positioning and can aid in navigating uncertain situations.
Ethical Decolonial Endeavors (Juan Manuel Arévalo)
Modernity hinges on a double historical version: on the one hand, it is deemed as a European-western invention (ad-intra version), based on the scientific cognizance, whose main aim (so far incomplete) has been yielding far-reaching material and symbolic shifts in order to pull ‘global enfranchisement’ off. On the other hand, and parallelly, this ontological project has historically involved irrational and interworked processes of extractivism, imbalance, displacements, subjugation, and coloniality in multifarious loci world over (ad-extra version). The latter is the obverse side of the coin--the dark side of modernity. Now, it is known and well documented that research and art have supported this damaging Western civilizational project. Thus, the fields of research and art do not revolve around objectivity and neutrality, and as researchers and artists today, we can ground ourselves in political roots that may affect the world positively. Consequently, binding social research and creativity to ethics could be critically productive. In attempting to do so, scholars and artists must constantly, in ad infinitum, carry out a two-fold reflection on: their ties with colonial projects and their material commitment to decolonial possibilities towards fairer worlds. As the Zapatista Movement has warned, the hegemonic/colonial system is a hydra (the mythological image) with several heads, and adding to this, ethical de-colonial endeavors must constantly explore how to deal with them through this two-fold act, researchers and creative people might raise awareness about the hegemonic system, its injustices and victims, as well as enact alternatives.
Conclusion
While not fundamentally cohesive, these dimensions express some of our values and commitments that we’ve shared with one another. Many of these speak to larger concerns and attentions in our own lives. We pulled these specific values from a broader reflection on personal values and so, while not encompassing, these represent some of the things we’ve come to actionably prioritize and live out through our creative pieces. At the end of the day, we came together, learned, and tried some things out. Through writing this collective manifesto, we actualized and worked through the tensions inherent to and inevitable in doing collective, relational work that offers and prioritizes space for individual contribution towards a larger, collaborative goal. Like all media, text offers one way, perhaps a limiting way, to convey these ideas, these values, and this experience. This exercise had us think about how to write together with an active abandoning of hierarchy. We’ve had to sit in and exist through the mess, the tension, the chaos, and the limitations of academic writing. The act of writing this piece exemplified why our creative pursuits during this semester-long course were both so generative and so vulnerable.

Russia prepares key bridges for potential Ukrainian ballistic strikes — ATESH
According to Ukrinform, the ATESH partisan movement reported this on Telegram.
Agents of the movement among employees of the Road Administration of Rostov Region report that civilian and military authorities received an order from the headquarters of Russia’s Southern Military District to urgently prepare logistics hubs for attacks by the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
Instructions from the Russian General Staff and district headquarters were reportedly received by Rosavtodor, Russian Railways, and regional administrations. The measures concern key crossings used to supply Russian military groupings.
In particular, in the Rostov Region, work is underway to reinforce road and railway bridges across the Don River, as well as to prepare alternative routes. Similar measures are reportedly being implemented in the Taganrog direction.
In the Crimean direction, Russian forces are reportedly anticipating renewed strikes in the area of Syvash and Armyansk.
In the Belgorod Region, bridges near Shelyayevo and Urazovo are being placed on heightened alert. It is expected that targeted strikes against local crossings could significantly slow the delivery of ammunition and force military equipment onto detour routes.
The planned protective measures at these sites include round-the-clock posts staffed by Rosgvardiya and military commandant offices, the installation of anti-drone nets and electronic warfare equipment, as well as the creation of pontoon crossings and engineering teams.
“Bridges remain the main supply arteries of the Russian army. Their damage blocks the delivery of fuel, ammunition, and personnel,” ATESH stated.
As Ukrinform reported, President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Ukraine had responded proportionally and would continue to respond to Russian terror, including attacks on bridges.

How a 1965 Moscow protest demanding that the Soviet government obey its own laws helped launch the USSR’s dissident movement
