Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
22:26:29 UTC
07:26:29 KST

How a 1965 Moscow protest demanding that the Soviet government obey its own laws helped launch the USSR’s dissident movement
Sixty years ago, a protest in Moscow received almost no coverage in Soviet newspapers but helped launch the human rights movement. Several dozen people gathered in Pushkin Square to demand that the state abide by its own Constitution. They sought neither a change of government nor political reforms. The organizer, mathematician and poet Alexander Volpin, decided to remind the authorities publicly, for the first time, of citizens’ right to an open trial. The rally lasted only a few minutes before the authorities dispersed it, but its consequences reached far beyond the square. Meduza looks back at how this first attempt at open protest came about in a country where public demonstrations had been suppressed for decades — and why it marked the start of the Soviet dissident movement.
This article was originally published in Russian in December 2025.
Anti-Soviet demonstrations: How the Bolsheviks suppressed protest
From their first years in power, the Bolsheviks made clear that they would not tolerate independent political demonstrations. On January 5, 1918, a peaceful demonstration took place in Petrograd in support of the Constituent Assembly. Students, office workers, and factory workers carrying red banners demanded that the elected representative body remain in place. The authorities responded by banning the march and shutting down newspapers that supported it. Red Guard units and machine guns were stationed along the marchers’ routes to block their passage. When the unarmed crowd moved forward, the guards opened fire. Dozens died, and many were wounded. What followed became a familiar pattern: The press accused the demonstrators of a “provocation,” and an investigation confirmed that the rally had been peaceful, but no one responsible for ordering the shooting was punished.
The same approach prevailed within the party itself: The leadership saw any independent demonstration as a threat to its control. On November 7, 1927, supporters of Trotsky and Zinoviev’s “United Opposition” in Moscow and Leningrad tried to march in separate groups during the anniversary demonstrations. They carried banners calling for “workers’ democracy” and criticizing the party’s policies. The authorities quickly stopped them: They broke up the opposition groups, tore down banners, beat some participants in Moscow, and instructed the security agencies to stamp out all factional activity. This was the last public demonstration within the party. By the end of the 1920s, all unauthorized protests had disappeared from political life, and street parades had become tightly controlled ceremonies.
After Stalin’s death, the political atmosphere began to change noticeably. The Thaw brought a cautious easing of restrictions and a sense that public life could revive after years of silence. Young people who sensed this change began looking for their own ways to participate in city life. One gathering place was an improvised “island of freedom” by the Mayakovsky monument in Moscow. People read poetry, discussed the news, argued, and got to know one another — a small but important space where they could speak openly after decades of silence.
But this freedom had strict limits. The Novocherkassk massacre in June 1962 was a harsh reminder that the Thaw did not mean people were free to stage mass protests. Workers took to the streets over rising prices and cuts to wage rates. It was an ordinary protest over living conditions, with no political demands. People expected a dialogue with the leadership, not a confrontation. Yet the authorities responded with force: They opened fire on the demonstrators, killing and wounding dozens. Closed trials followed, courts swiftly handed down sentences, and the authorities classified information about the tragedy. Novocherkassk showed that even in this new era, any mass demonstration could bring a harsh crackdown if it strayed even slightly beyond the rules imposed from above.
When Khrushchev was removed from office in October 1964, the country’s direction was unclear. Some expected a return to stricter rule; others hoped the policies of the Thaw would continue. New forms of cultural life began to emerge in cities. One was the literary group SMOG, whose name stood for the Russian words for “Courage, Thought, Imagery, and Depth.” Founded in January 1965, it brought together young poets who wanted to write without regard for official standards. They held readings by the Mayakovsky monument, published samizdat, and discussed subjects that Soviet censors would not allow. This was more freedom than the authorities would tolerate, and they soon intervened: Some members were expelled from universities, while others were forced out of Moscow. Despite the pressure, SMOG showed that young city dwellers wanted an independent space to socialize and create. The Sinyavsky–Daniel case emerged at a time when hopes for continued change clashed with the state’s determination to maintain control.
The Sinyavsky–Daniel case: How the authorities underestimated the response to repression
The Sinyavsky–Daniel case was the first major public trial of writers in the post-Stalin Soviet Union. Andrei Sinyavsky and Yuli Daniel could not publish their writing in the USSR: It went beyond the bounds of “socialist realism” and would not have passed censorship. After Boris Pasternak was hounded over his novel “Doctor Zhivago” and prevented from accepting the Nobel Prize, it was clear how an attempt to publish “unwelcome” fiction at home might end. So Sinyavsky wrote under the pseudonym Abram Tertz and Daniel under the name Nikolai Arzhak, sending their work abroad. Their novellas and short stories used grotesque and fantastical elements to deliver sharp critiques of Soviet life: fear, lies, bureaucratic cruelty, questions of guilt and responsibility for repression, and the danger of a renewed cult of personality.
After the campaign against Pasternak, it became clear that “unwelcome” fiction would not be published in the USSR, and some authors began looking for ways to publish abroad. In 1956, the publishing house Posev, which was associated with NTS, used the journal Grani to call on writers and scholars in the Soviet Union to send work banned by the censors. A network for tamizdat — the publication of Soviet authors’ work in the West — gradually developed. Sinyavsky and Daniel took this route, sending their work to the West, where the American publisher Inter-Language Literary Associates published it under the pseudonyms Tertz and Arzhak.
Despite their precautions and use of pseudonyms, the KGB identified the writers and moved against them. Sinyavsky was arrested on September 8, 1965, and Daniel on September 12. For many in the USSR, the arrests came as a complete surprise: Both writers were known within a small literary circle but were not considered outspoken “opposition figures.” The authorities, however, decided otherwise. Daniel and Sinyavsky were charged with “anti-Soviet agitation and propaganda” — effectively for publishing fiction abroad that would not pass Soviet censorship.
The response within the Soviet Union was far more visible than the authorities had expected. The case alarmed Moscow’s intelligentsia. In editorial offices and research institutes, and among young writers, people began saying that it was a step backward, an attempt to restore fear and ideological discipline. People began drafting letters defending the arrested writers, first personal letters, then open letters. These included the “letter of the 62,” signed by many prominent authors, including Bulat Okudzhava, Vladimir Voinovich, Lydia Chukovskaya, Varlam Shalamov, Konstantin Paustovsky, and Ilya Ehrenburg. For Soviet cultural circles, this was an almost unprecedented step: Publicly opposing a prosecution meant risking one’s career — and sometimes even one’s safety.
The international response was louder still. PEN, Arthur Miller, Heinrich Böll, Alberto Moravia, Graham Greene, and dozens of other leading writers from Europe and the United States came to Daniel and Sinyavsky’s defense. The Western press characterized the trial as ideological and incompatible with the Thaw. It became the first major political case of the post-Khrushchev era and brought people together in a new social movement — from the first letters of protest to the rally for an open trial in Pushkin Square.
The rally for an open trial: From an idea to a demonstration
Alexander Volpin, the son of Sergei Yesenin and translator Nadezhda Volpin, was a mathematician and poet known in Moscow for insisting, with a persistence rare for the time, that the state follow its own laws to the letter. Volpin had already faced court proceedings and understood how easily legal provisions in the USSR could become mere formalities. He later recalled that in the fall of 1965, after Sinyavsky and Daniel’s arrests, he spent a long time walking through a grove in Golitsyno, trying to work out what could be done: “Those devils are bound to hold the trial behind closed doors. So now’s the time to demand an open trial!” Volpin’s reasoning was simple: The more often the authorities were forced to hold trials publicly, the harder it would be for them to conceal arbitrary decisions. This led him to propose a public rally on December 5 with a strictly legal demand rather than political slogans: Hold an open trial, as the Constitution required.
Volpin’s legal approach caused serious disagreements even among his closest allies. Many dissidents believed that invoking the Constitution and the law was pointless in a country where the authorities themselves ignored them. Others feared that attempts to “teach” the state its own rules in public could only make things worse for the arrested writers. Volpin, however, insisted that upholding human rights enshrined in law should be the central aim of resistance. He told friends that even the harshest regimes had to create laws that at least partly matched society’s ideas of justice; otherwise, the state simply could not function.
The problem was that the authorities had no intention of following these rules and did not expect citizens to demand that they do so. Volpin argued that this was precisely where resistance was possible: Citizens could “use the authorities’ own laws to trap them” and force them to act openly. Many found this approach unfamiliar. Lyudmila Alexeyeva, who would become a prominent human rights advocate, recalled: “We didn’t know what would happen to those demonstrators, but we thought it would end badly — they’d grab people. And what they’d do to them after that, I couldn’t even imagine. Maybe things would turn out all right, maybe they wouldn’t. They might just arrest everyone. The last thing we needed, on top of Sinyavsky and Daniel, was another dozen people under arrest. What was the point?”
Nevertheless, Volpin’s approach became the basis for the first human rights initiatives, including preparations for the December 5 rally. Leaflets distributed at universities and passed around small circles of acquaintances reflected this approach. They explained in detail that a closed trial of Sinyavsky and Daniel would violate the provision requiring public court proceedings and that any hearing “behind closed doors” left room for arbitrary decisions. They therefore proposed a “rally for an open trial,” with a single slogan: “We demand an open trial.” The authors said participants must act strictly within the law: They were not to shout political slogans or allow themselves to be provoked, and if the authorities ordered them to disperse, they were to comply after stating the purpose of the gathering. The emphasis on legality was fundamental: The rally was intended to show that citizens were demanding compliance with the rules the authorities had enshrined in their own laws, rather than a change of political system. They decided to hold it on December 5 — the anniversary of the adoption of the first Soviet constitution in 1936.
The dispersal of the rally: A few minutes that changed how people saw the struggle for human rights in the USSR
The rally on December 5, 1965, lasted only a few minutes. Among those gathered were people who had decided to raise banners and many who had come simply to watch — some out of curiosity, others out of sympathy. Viktoria Volpina, the chief organizer’s wife, recalled that everything happened almost instantly: “The banners shot up, then I saw hands reaching for them… the roar of cars, hands reaching, banners falling.” She recalled a tightly packed crowd of several dozen people that quickly broke into small groups when officers rushed in from the outer ring of onlookers. Volpina estimated that there were about 60 demonstrators; far more people stood around watching, not daring to join openly.
Lyudmila Alexeyeva also recalled how quickly and harshly it all ended. She estimated that no more than 50 people actually participated: “Volpin, [the artist Yuri] Titov, and someone else raised signs. They’d barely had time to raise them before they were grabbed.” Camera flashes went off throughout — both Western journalists and KGB officers were taking photographs.
Although the police acted quickly, they used little physical violence. Participants later attributed this to the lingering influence of the Thaw in 1965 and the authorities’ fear of excessive brutality amid the already considerable international outcry over the Sinyavsky–Daniel trial. Those detained, including Volpin, were questioned for several hours, but all were released that evening.
For most onlookers, the rally was a brief, tense moment when, for the first time after years of silence, several dozen people openly gathered in a square to demand that the state uphold the law. For the authorities, it was a warning sign. But for those who stood in Pushkin Square that day, even “behind the bushes,” as Viktoria Volpina put it, the rally also made the possibility of civic action in the USSR publicly visible for the first time.
The rally’s consequences: How the Soviet dissident movement emerged and developed
The next day, Soviet KGB Chairman Vladimir Semichastny told the Politburo that “some participants in the gathering began shouting demagogic slogans under the banner of upholding civil liberties.” His report also said “that among the most active participants in the gathering were seven people known to be mentally ill: Four of them (Volpin (Yesenin), [the poet Yuri] Galanskov, Titov, and [the worker Viktor] Khaustov) had previously participated in various antisocial acts.”
To combat future protests, a new Article 190-3 was added to the Criminal Code of the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic in September 1966. It made it a criminal offense to engage in the “organization of or active participation in group actions that grossly violate public order” or that involve disobedience to the authorities’ demands. The maximum penalty was three years in prison. The wording was broad enough to cover political demonstrations, strikes, student protests, and any gathering the authorities deemed “dangerous.”
Despite the authorities’ opposition, the rally had taken place. One participant, Dmitry Zubarev, later said: “For me, as for everyone I knew, December 5 marks a kind of historical turning point: the emergence of a new, open, nonviolent mass movement in the Soviet Union.”
A year later, the rally was held again, this time as a quiet reminder of the right to a public trial. At the appointed hour, people gathered in Pushkin Square, silently removed their hats, and stood looking at the Pushkin monument. Among them was Andrei Sakharov, a member of the Academy of Sciences who was not yet an outspoken opponent of the authorities. Steps like these set him on the path to becoming one of the leading moral authorities of the future human rights movement.
The rally’s long-term effect was greater still. People who had previously acted separately — scientists, students, young writers, and engineers — began coming together to demand open trials and compliance with the law. The rally showed that there were people in the country willing to speak publicly and nonviolently about rights. From these small groups and the onlookers who had stood “behind the bushes” that day, the dissident movement gradually grew.

Teaching a Decolonial Visual Anthropology: An Introduction to a Collective Student Manifesto for Producing Creative Work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
22:19:39 UTC
07:19:39 KST

Teaching a Decolonial Visual Anthropology: An Introduction to a Collective Student Manifesto for Producing Creative Work
by Dada Docot (Purdue University)
I first read poet Tristan Tzara’s 1918 “Dada Manifesto” when I was taking the class of Filipino conceptual artist Roberto Chabet at the College of Fine Arts, University of the Philippines. Chabet spoke about the works of dadaist artists that defied formalism and challenged the sociopolitical conventions of their time. Tzara’s anti-manifesto manifesto was both energizing and confusing as it decried the labor and necessity of writing one, while it also laid out the social conventions that the dadaists were breaking and critiquing. Since reading Tzara’s manifesto, artistic movements’ ideologies expressed through their respective manifestos have always captured my interest. Various artistic movements, including the dadaists, challenge the status quo by bringing into the world change through their art and ideas. What if the classroom could also be a site for producing a manifesto that reflects the spirit and challenges of our era? What ideas might be centered and upheld in a manifesto for producing anthropologically informed creative work?
I decided to take up this challenge in my graduate-level course, “Visual Anthropology,” taught in Spring 2024 at Purdue University, and offer my reflections on my process here to help others who would like to take up the challenge as well. I opened my course with an acknowledgment of the broader discipline’s controversial history as one intimately tied to espionage, betrayal, and extraction. As anthropology embraces multimodality, I have also written about how tools in the anthropological toolkit signal researchers’ access to power and privilege. Of course, anthropology has also changed immensely since then, as many anthropologists have sought to address and correct the harms it has caused in the past. The course takes up some of this work, centering the written and creative works of anthropologists and other creative producers who engage with, and advocate for, marginalized communities. With the intention to avoid re-traumatizing students in my course by (re)exposing them to historical anthropological harm, my course instead begins with a two-week venture into theoretical perspectives that highlight redress and possibilities. Through these texts, my course turns away from the visual anthropological pedagogical canon and instead, orients students towards the ways anthropologists and other researchers decolonize knowledge production. Also in the second week, students in my course watch the comedy documentary, Qallunaat! This film creatively critiques historically extractive practices in anthropology as experienced by the Inuit people. Through introducing these texts and visuals to students, the course invites students to consider how their creative production in the course can address social issues, healing, and repair.
During the third week of the course, we proceeded to discuss Ethics by engaging several powerful manifestos written by Louise Boilevin et al., Patricia Alvarez Astacio et al. and The Combahee River Collective. Boilevin et al.’s Research 101: A Manifesto for Ethical Research in the Downtown Eastside, for example, presents illuminating perspectives from the side of the studied/researched on the ways they would like to be treated, addressed, and compensated by researchers. Upon reading the assigned course materials, students drafted a personal manifesto for producing anthropologically informed creative work. After a discussion on these personal manifestos, students worked together in class to create a unified manifesto that would guide their work throughout the course. Beyond merely stitching their manifestos together, students engaged with each other’s individual thoughts, learned from each other about themes that are important to each of them, and distilled the variety of opinions of the collective into a cohesive whole. Pedagogically, the exercise of writing, sharing, and putting the manifesto together opened space for students to express their identities, to learn about each other’s positionalities, and finally, to cultivate empathy and understanding of their differences. Students in the class referred to their individually written and collective manifestos throughout the semester as we examined various topics, highlighting the impact of this creative project in their anthropological thinking and analysis. In these times of polarized worldviews, manifestos could potentially serve as a document through which we can collectively ground our thoughts, actions, and outputs in collaboration.
To read the manifesto by the students in Dada Docot’s visual anthropology course, please visit Dimensions: An Ephemeral Manifesto on Creativity.
Cite As
Docot, Dada. 2026. “Teaching a Decolonial Visual Anthropology: An Introduction to a Collective Student Manifesto for Producing Creative Work.” American Anthropologist website, October 6.

US man arrested as second suspect in Canada mass school shooting planned with ChatGPT

A surprise suspected accomplice has been arrested in connection with a mass school shooting in Canada that was made notorious after an 18-year-old allegedly killed six children after discussing it with the AI chatbot ChatGPT.
The US Department of Justice said on Tuesday it had detained James Codey Bryant, 30, a resident of western Washington state, on a charge of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country.
Bryant offered money and “technical advice” to the suspected shooter for six months leading up to the killings, the justice department alleged.
Canadian police have identified the suspect in this year’s massacre of eight people – including her mother and half-brother, as well as the six children, making it the second-deadliest school shooting in the country’s history – as Jesse Van Rootselaar, who has a history of mental health problems.
It had been known that Van Rootselaar had used ChatGPT to plan the attack, which took place in February. The safety team at OpenAI, the company that owns the chatbot, flagged Van Rootselaar internally after she conducted conversations with it about gun violence, but the company did not alert police. It did reportedly close Van Rootselaar’s account, but she started a second one that was not closed. Victims’ families and the province of British Columbia have sued OpenAI and its CEO, Sam Altman, for failing to report her behaviour.
It was not previously known publicly that Van Rootselaar was also talking to a human about her plans.
In a joint press conference with the justice department and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) on Tuesday, authorities alleged that Bryant and Van Rootselaar met on the now-defunct messaging service Omegle about three years before the shooting and kept in contact.
Neil Floyd, acting US attorney, and W Mike Herrington, the special agent in charge for the FBI’s Seattle bureau, said they believed Bryant sent Van Rootselaar about $100 to buy new shoes and about $15 for a lighter.
Authorities said there is no indication so far that the two suspects ever met in person.
According to an indictment obtained by CBC, Bryant was “knowingly and wilfully” conspiring with Van Rootselaar beginning in or before August 2025.
That August, Bryant told Van Rootselaar the pair should “find a way to delete” their messages, and in mid-December Bryant suggested getting a VPN to avoid detection for “posting a shooting video online”, according to the court document reviewed by CBC.
Police said that on several occasions Bryant tried to talk Van Rootselaar out of committing the attack, but did not contact law enforcement.
They added that after Van Rootselaar shot and killed her mother and brother in their family home, she was unable to start the car. Bryant advised her on how to turn on the engine, thereby allowing the shooter to reach the school and execute the attack, authorities said.
Bryant also allegedly agreed to livestream the mass shooting, which Harrington said police were not sure Van Rootselaar would have committed had Bryant not done so.
It was not clear whether the suspect was represented by a lawyer. Bryant will be prosecuted in the US as a US citizen under an investigation by the FBI, which said it will continue working closely with Canadian authorities.

Two Dover Airmen Sentenced in Multimillion-Dollar Cyber Fraud Scheme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
22:02:52 UTC
07:02:52 KST

A federal judge recently sentenced one Airman and a former Airman to a combined 15 years in prison and ordered them to pay $1.36 million in restitution for a two-year cyber fraud scheme they perpetrated while serving on Active-Duty at Dover Air Force Base, Del.
On Sept. 25, Chijioke Timothy Odimegwu, 25, and Harafat Mogaji, 26, were sentenced to nine years, three months, and six years, six months in federal prison, respectively, for their role in a cyber fraud scheme that targeted at least 15 businesses, towns, and nonprofits while also conducting romance fraud schemes to get victims to act as “money mules” for their more than $2.4 million in stolen funds.
Neither man was involved in cyber career fields in the Air Force.
Odimegwu and Mogaji previously pleaded guilty to charges of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, conspiracy to commit access device fraud, and aggravated identity theft.
The Air Force Office of Special Investigations’ Detachment 306 at Dover assisted the FBI in the investigation. The detachment, a local field unit, helped identify victims, investigated threats made by the defendants, and conducted federal arrests of the two Airmen, according to an AFOSI release.
“This case demonstrates why strong partnerships across law enforcement are critical to protecting the Department of the Air Force and the American people,” said Special Agent Kevin Golden, commander of the detachment.
Mogaji was discharged from the USAF earlier this year; as of his recent sentencing, Odimegwu was still awaiting discharge.
Airman First Class Odimegwu joined the Air Force in February 2023, became a Traffic Management Apprentice, and last served as a household goods specialist, according to an Air Force spokesperson. His awards include the Air Force Training Ribbon, Air Force Outstanding Unit Award, and the Air Force Good Conduct Medal.
Mogaji served from 2022 to July 4, 2026. His terminal rank was Airman First Class; he was a services apprentice and last served as a fitness and sports journeyman. His awards include the Air Force Training Ribbon, the Global War on Terrorism Service Medal, the Air Force Outstanding Unit Award, the Air Force Good Conduct Medal, and the Air Force Longevity Service Award.
According to court documents, the pair spoofed the victims’ email addresses with similar addresses, gained username and password access to the victims’ accounts, and then monitored them for large financial transactions.
“Cyber-enabled crime does not stop at installation boundaries or geographic borders,” Golden said. “Working alongside our federal partners allows us to identify threats, protect our personnel and resources, and hold those responsible accountable.”
In one instance, the pair targeted a victim in Iowa City, Iowa, and were able to gain access to a $1.68 million wire transfer the nonprofit was using for a construction project and divert it to a Chicago bank account.
In another example, the pair phished an official from the City of Athens, Ohio, intercepted a $720,000 wire transfer, and used a romance scam victim as the money mule to take the initial transfer before moving it to their own accounts.
“The city has received $205,000 to date in recovered stolen funds and a $200,000 insurance payout,” Mayor Steve Patterson said at a Sept. 28 city council meeting.In late 2025, the city adopted a state-recommended cybersecurity policy that outlines specific procedures for electronic payments.
“Criminals from all backgrounds attack our digital systems. They strike targets from corporate networks to personal smartphones,” Eugene Kowel, Special Agent in Charge of the FBI Omaha Field Office, said in a Department of Justice release. “No one and no device is immune from the threat. This case demonstrates that we will hold accountable cybercriminals who target our communities. It also serves as a reminder that every organization and every individual should take steps to protect their devices and systems and learn how to recognize and avoid scams.”

====================================================================================================

Newborn circumcision is not linked to autism, large U.S. study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
22:00:33 UTC
07:00:33 KST

A recent study found no evidence that circumcising newborn boys increases their risk of developing autism spectrum disorder. The findings, published in JAMA Pediatrics, may offer reassurance to parents considering the procedure or whose sons have already had it. The researchers also found that acetaminophen was rarely given to the infants, making it unlikely that the pain reliever explains any connection between the procedure and autism.
Autism spectrum disorder is a neurodevelopmental condition that involves differences in how a person interacts socially and communicates with others. It also typically involves repetitive body movements and atypical responses to sensory input. The diagnosis relies on clinical assessments of a child’s behavior and development.
Over the past few decades, the rate of autism diagnoses has grown considerably. For example, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimated that about one in 150 8-year-olds had an autism diagnosis in 2000, compared with one in 31 in 2022. Experts are still working to figure out how much of this increase reflects a true rise in the condition, as opposed to better awareness and changes in how doctors screen for it. Regardless, this trend has prompted scientists to look for environmental factors that might interact with complex genetic predispositions.
One consistent feature of autism is that it is diagnosed much more frequently in boys than in girls. As noted in a 2022 review of sex differences, this disparity may partly reflect differences in how symptoms present and are recognized by doctors. However, the higher prevalence in boys has also motivated experts to investigate early-life exposures that only apply to males. This includes neonatal medical circumcision, a common surgical procedure involving the removal of the foreskin covering the tip of the penis shortly after birth, which is performed on about half of newborn boys in U.S. hospitals, a share that has been declining in recent years.
The research, led by Monica McGrath, a research professor in the Department of Epidemiology at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health and director of the Environmental Influences on Child Health Outcomes Data Analysis Center, examined whether newborn circumcision is linked to autism. In recent years, public speculation has circulated suggesting that the physical stress of the procedure, or the acetaminophen (the active ingredient in Tylenol) provided for pain relief, might contribute to autism.
In October 2025, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said at a Cabinet meeting that two studies showed boys circumcised early had double the rate of autism, and he suggested Tylenol given for pain was the reason. Media coverage of the remarks resurfaced two older observational studies: a 2013 analysis that compared circumcision and autism rates across countries and U.S. states, and a 2015 study of Danish health records that found a 46 percent higher risk of autism among circumcised boys.
“We knew we had the data to help investigate this question,” McGrath said in a news release from Johns Hopkins.
The authors of the new study pointed out that those prior reports suffered from potential biases. For example, in places like Denmark where circumcision is relatively rare, the procedure is mostly performed for religious or cultural reasons. This means that unmeasured factors, such as differences in when and how certain communities seek health care, might have skewed the older data. Because circumcision is routinely performed in hospitals across the United States for a broad range of families, the research team wanted to evaluate the question in a large, diverse American population.
To do this, the research team examined data from the Environmental Influences on Child Health Outcomes project, a national research initiative that tracks children’s health. The analysis included 2,771 male children from 14 different research sites across the United States. All of the children were singleton births, meaning they were not twins or triplets. If a family had multiple children participating in the broader project, the researchers randomly selected one child to ensure that shared family environments did not skew the statistics.
The scientists checked medical records to determine whether each child had been circumcised at a medical facility within 28 days of birth. They then tracked whether the children were later diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder. A diagnosis was recorded if a parent reported that a medical professional had identified the condition, or if there was documentation from standard clinical autism assessments. The average age at which the children received an autism diagnosis was just under four years old.
In addition to formal diagnoses, the team evaluated broader behavioral traits using two standardized questionnaires filled out by parents: the Social Responsiveness Scale, completed for 1,886 children, and the Child Behavior Checklist, completed for 1,880 children. The Social Responsiveness Scale measures the presence and severity of social impairments and traits associated with autism. The Child Behavior Checklist screens for emotional and behavioral problems, including a specific subset of behaviors that align with autism. Because these questionnaires produce scores along a range rather than a yes-or-no diagnosis, they could pick up milder autism-like traits in children who had not been diagnosed.
Out of the 2,771 boys in the study, 1,840 were circumcised before they were discharged from the hospital, making up 66 percent of the group. The remaining 931 boys, or 34 percent, did not undergo the procedure. Overall, 192 children in the sample had an autism diagnosis, which is about 7 percent of the group.
When breaking the numbers down by circumcision status, 6 percent of the circumcised boys had an autism diagnosis, compared to 9 percent of the uncircumcised boys. In other words, circumcised boys were somewhat less likely to be diagnosed. But the two groups also differed in other ways: uncircumcised boys were more often Hispanic, more often born in the West or Puerto Rico, and more often born prematurely or admitted to intensive care. After the researchers accounted for factors that could influence both circumcision and autism diagnosis, such as maternal education, geographic region, family history of autism, and parental age, the gap shrank and was no longer statistically meaningful.
The parent-reported questionnaires told a similar story: after adjustment, circumcision was not linked to higher scores on either measure. The researchers also checked whether the pattern held within subgroups, such as children from different regions, those born prematurely, and those admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit. In most of these checks, circumcised boys had similar or lower autism-related scores. One exception emerged among children born in the West, where circumcised boys were more likely to score in the elevated range on one questionnaire; the researchers suggest this isolated result may be a statistical fluke given the number of comparisons, noting it was driven by a single site.
The team also reviewed pain management records, which were available for fewer than half of the circumcised infants. Among those, only 4 percent received acetaminophen during the procedure, and about 7 percent of all circumcised infants received it within 30 days of birth. Most documented pain care involved a nerve block, an injection that numbs the area (72 percent), or a sugar solution given by mouth (59 percent), and some infants received more than one. Because acetaminophen was so rarely used, the researchers could not test its role directly, but they concluded that a pathway running from the procedure through the medication to autism is unlikely.
“Parents have been concerned about this potential circumcision-autism connection, but hopefully these findings may help allay their fears,” McGrath said.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind regarding this study. The team noted that they had limited information on the participants’ health insurance status. Because insurance coverage can influence both a family’s decision to have a hospital circumcision and their access to developmental evaluations for autism, missing this variable could leave some untracked influences in the data.
The researchers also pointed out that they specifically evaluated medical circumcisions performed in a hospital setting shortly after birth. The findings might not apply to circumcisions performed later in childhood or those conducted outside of a hospital environment. Additionally, the data on acetaminophen use was restricted to what was recorded by the hospital, meaning any doses given by parents at home after discharge were not captured.
Finally, the parent-reported behavioral questionnaires are validated screening tools that help identify children at risk for autism, but they are not formal diagnostic instruments themselves. And though the study included a large number of children from multiple sites across the United States, the sample does not perfectly represent the entire population of American male newborns.
“We observed no association between circumcision and autism in boys, but it remains important to evaluate the safety of common medical procedures,” McGrath said. She and her colleagues are now examining other possible explanations for the increase in autism diagnoses.
The study, “Neonatal Medical Male Circumcision and Child Autism Diagnosis,” was authored by Monica McGrath, Xiuhong Li, Lisa P. Jacobson, Bennett Leventhal, Judy L. Aschner, Brennan Baker, Karla Cardoso Garcia, Aisha S. Dickerson, Amy J. Elliott, Jody Ganiban, Amanda Goodrich, Daniel B. Horton, Melinda Jarnecke, Sarah Keim, Brian K. Lee, Courtney D. Lynch, Mark Klebanoff, Abdul-Manaf Mutaru, Ruby H. N. Nguyen, Rebecca J. Schmidt, Hyeong-Moo Shin, Lauren C. Shuffrey, Jonathan L. Slaughter, Annemarie Stroustrup, Zhaozhong Zhu, Aaron A. R. Tobian, and M. Kate Grabowski.

====================================================================================================

Israel's fourth founding: When the state proved it alone could not keep Israelis safe - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
22:00:00 UTC
07:00:00 KST

This August in Tel Aviv, I joined a panel at CommunityO, a gathering of young Israeli founders. Many had spent hundreds of days on reserve duty since October 7. They were tired but steadfast, aware that the future of their country was in their hands. They came home asking a question I had not heard them ask before: “What kind of state is most worthy of our protection?”
It is a founder’s question. Three years ago, on Simchat Torah, Hamas terrorists murdered more than 1,200 people in Israel and took 251 hostages into Gaza. Rachel Goldberg-Polin, whose son Hersh was murdered in captivity, has said the day split time into a “before” and an “after.” Today, a new generation is asking what “after” should be.
Nations are not founded once. Israel’s purpose, Jewish sovereignty, has not changed since 1948. But the assumptions about how to secure it, and how to build a nation around it, change with each era, and each time an era’s assumptions collapse, Israel is remade.
Israel is now entering its fourth founding, a season in which old assumptions give way to new geopolitical, social, and economic realities, and in which our people decide again who it is and what it is for. Never has so much been at stake in the Diaspora-Israel relationship. That, too, is being reexamined and reinvented.
The foundings of Israel
The first founding came in 1948, when the promise of European emancipation died. For generations, Europe’s Jews had been told that citizenship would make them safe. The Holocaust broke that promise, and the state that rose from it was built from almost nothing: roads, housing, power lines, and hospitals for refugees streaming in from Europe and the Middle East.
The United Jewish Appeal’s 1948 “Year of Destiny” campaign raised more than $150 million from over a million donors, then the largest campaign in the history of private philanthropy.
In 1950, David Ben-Gurion and the American Jewish Committee’s Jacob Blaustein struck a bargain that would define the relationship for decades: Israel would make no political claim on American Jews, and American Jews would not interfere in Israel’s domestic affairs, but the money and political support would keep coming.
The deal rested on an older Zionist conviction, shlilat hagolah, the negation of the Diaspora, which held that Jewish life outside Israel was a lesser form of Jewish life. American Jews were welcomed as donors and advocates, never as partners.
The second founding came in 1967, when Jewish powerlessness died in six days. Israel’s early years had rested on the premise that Jewish survival was fragile and depended on the pity of others. The victory turned that fear into pride and power.
Israel refounded its sense of self: posters of Moshe Dayan adorned the bedrooms of Jewish children, and the Jewish state moved to the center of global Jewish life. But pride is a feeling, not a voice. That year, 94% of Israelis surveyed said Jews abroad must support the state, while only 43% thought they should have an opinion about its internal affairs.
The third founding came in 1985, when the socialist economy died. The pioneers’ utopia had begun to crack after 1967, but it took inflation of roughly 445% to bury it. A painful stabilization plan, with deep budget cuts, wage and price controls and a sharp devaluation, cleared the ground for the Start-Up Nation: inflation fell below 20%, and per capita output was growing about 4% a year by the early 1990s.
Seventy-eight years after the British Mandate ended, the Jewish state held $235 billion in foreign reserves, more than the empire that once governed it. A country that had survived on the generosity of others could now stand on its own, and the negation of the Diaspora seemed nearly complete.
Yet the old bargain, money without a voice, outlived the need for the money. In 2016, after years of negotiation, the government approved a pluralistic prayer space at the Western Wall, with a council that would have given Reform and Conservative leaders a role in running it. In 2017, under pressure from its ultra-Orthodox coalition partners, it froze the deal, and many American Jews felt insulted and abandoned. A voice granted could be withdrawn. It would take a catastrophe to change the terms.
THE FOURTH founding begins with what died on October 7: the idea that the state alone could keep Israelis safe. The onslaught did more than murder and kidnap; it forced a Jewish reckoning.
Israelis, shocked by the establishment’s failure to detect the threat and to protect them, lost trust in their government and felt that the state had broken its covenantal promise to prevent the mass murder of Jews.
Civilians rushed in where the government could not, caring for devastated communities in the Gaza border region and the North. New kinds of philanthropy emerged because Israelis would not wait for the government to act.
In the first weeks of the war, they raised hundreds of millions of shekels, much of it in small gifts, and roughly half of all Israeli adults volunteered. Last year alone, Israeli donors put $140m. into Israel’s first donor-advised fund.
When I met with Tali Nir, CEO of 121, a nonprofit shaping social policy in Israel, she acknowledged a sea change happening in Israeli society. The generations before hers built the essential infrastructure of the state: its roads, its army, its politics. Her generation’s job is to build the society. Social change, she said, is the next wave of Zionism.
The Israelis of October 8 are the new “New Jew”: resourceful and resilient, and they take care of their own. They have also learned that their bond with American Jews is indelible and invaluable for both of our futures.
The grand bargain of the past is being renegotiated. Israelis no longer negate the Diaspora; they embrace it. And North American Jews must adjust to a new power dynamic in the relationship: Israel no longer needs patrons. It needs partners.
Some will say talk of partnership is premature, with the North and South still rebuilding, an economy strained by war, and a military that leans on American support. But Israel’s survival no longer depends on American Jewish charity, and what kind of society it becomes may depend on whether Israelis and American Jews build it together.
More than a century ago, Ahad Ha’am hoped that a renewed Jewish culture in Palestine would one day produce a state that was “not merely a state of the Jews, but a really Jewish state.” That is our work now: the civic infrastructure of a society that is democratic, pluralistic, and compassionate.
Israelis know they cannot build it alone. Many I met see something to learn from more than three and a half centuries of Jewish life in America: our institutions, our philanthropy, our pluralistic Judaism. We have at least as much to learn from them about resilience, courage and service.
Partnership will make uncomfortable demands and require concessions from both parties. American Jews must invest alongside Israelis rather than on their behalf, and let Israelis set the priorities.
Both parties will have to exercise humility; we are each other’s teachers, and each other’s students. We both have hard things to say to one another about what we think is best for the Jewish future. In this, we are joint stakeholders, neither silent donors nor distant critics.
“Hatikvah” sings of “the hope of two thousand years.” The first founding gave the Jewish people a state. The second gave us pride, and the third gave Israel prosperity. The fourth can give us a society worthy of that state, and a bond across oceans built on choice rather than need. After so much shared grief, the future most worth building is the one Israelis and Diaspora Jews build together.
The writer is the president and CEO of the Jewish Federation Los Angeles.

Read the charter for the White House’s ‘Super Intelligence Force’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
21:51:30 UTC
06:51:30 KST

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, who will lead the new force, is seen during his confirmation hearing on Capitol Hill in Washington on July 15, 2026. | Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images
The Trump administration has given its newly created “Super Intelligence Force” broad authority to determine how the tech industry and the federal government should address threats to national security and civil liberties posed by fast-evolving artificial intelligence technology, according to a charter obtained by POLITICO.
Three people familiar with discussions about the task force confirmed the document’s authenticity. The people were granted anonymity to share details that are not yet public.
The task force will identify “measures to improve the preparedness and response capability of both the government and the private sector to threats to the homeland and the American people,” the charter states. It will also produce a report on the risks of AI, focusing on “potential threats to civil liberties,” cybersecurity, standards for advanced models, and the impacts of possible overregulation.
Both Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill were caught off guard by President Donald Trump’s announcement of the task force’s creation, with four tech-sector representatives telling POLITICO the industry was not widely informed beforeTrump’s social media post. Super intelligence is Trump’s preferred term for artificial intelligence.
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton will lead the task force in his newly minted role as the administration’s AI czar, with Under Secretary of Defense Emil Michael, Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor, and Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson serving as vice chairs.
Its members include administration officials across the federal government, including at the National Security Agency and the Health and Human Services Department. Senior White House officials, including Vice President JD Vance and chief of staff Susie Wiles, will also be closely involved. Former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice and venture capitalist David Sacks, who served as the administration’s AI czar until March, will also provide “advice” to the group on national security and technology, respectively.
The task force will stand for 120 days, but its work can be extended – or functions transferred to another government agency – at Wiles’ direction, per the charter.
Advertisement
The task force will undertake work spanning financial services, energy infrastructure, transportation, agriculture and emergency services, per the charter, and will work with the Pentagon, the Justice Department, the Homeland Security Department and the Federal Trade Commission to outline its recommendations.
The document also calls out two risk areas that have come under increased scrutiny in recent months: biosecurity and threats to the water supply. OpenAI recently threw its weight behind a slate of bills aimed at preventing AI models from exacerbating the threat of biological weapons, and rival lab Anthropic disclosed several incidents in which scientists in foreign countries used their models to research dangerous pathogens.
The Trump administration also rolled out a program in August to protect vulnerable U.S. water facilities from cybersecurity threats, following a series of cyberattacks on local water systems across the country.
The task force will also be responsible for reviewing “the current protocols and mechanisms in place” for AI labs to notify the government of breaches, hacks and jailbreaks, in addition to developing recommendations for improvements to the government’s response to such incidents.
The document refers to the technology “as both an amplifier and accelerant of both risks and opportunities” but ultimately places responsibility for any risks associated with AI on the labs developing advanced models.
“Though the labs are ultimately responsible for the risks and opportunities that their models amplify and accelerate, it is the role of the federal government to recognize and understand this era of change and to enforce our nation’s laws so that the fundamental principles of our Republic are safeguarded and advanced,” the document reads.

Ronaldo wants Portugal 'punishment' but not retiring from international football

Ronaldo wants Portugal 'punishment' but not retiring
- Published
Cristiano Ronaldo says he is not retiring from international football but deserves to be punished for walking out on Portugal after head coach Jorge Jesus twice "broke his word".
The 41-year-old captain left his country's Nations League camp last week after being an unused substitute against Norway and then finding out he would not start against Denmark.
Al-Nassr forward Ronaldo has scored 146 goals in 234 Portugal appearances - both world records - helping them win Euro 2016 and the Nations League twice.
In a lengthy statement, external, which ran to nearly 2,000 words, the former Real Madrid and Manchester United player said he should be held accountable for his actions.
But he accused Jesus of an "absolute breach of trust" for firstly not playing him against Norway after saying he would, before going back on a decision to present an agreed version of events to the media.
"The Portuguese Football Federation must assess the consequences of my actions and punish me for them. I believe the punishment should not be reduced," Ronaldo said.
"I have already apologised, but I know that actions have consequences."
Ronaldo's statement comes after Portugal head coach Jesus said there was no rift with the captain, following claims the five-time Ballon d'Or winner had refused to train.
Jesus said on Sunday that the door was still open for Ronaldo to play for the country's national team.
Ronaldo said that, provided he was "physically fit, playing with my team, and hopefully scoring goals", he would like to continue to play international football.
"After my suspension period ends, I will be available, as I always have been, to compete and win with our national team," he added.
BBC Sport has approached the Portuguese Football Federation (FPF) for comment.
What does Ronaldo say happened?
Ronaldo's statement struck a conciliatory tone in places, but he was also critical of Portugal coach Jesus as he provided his version of the dispute which prompted him to walk out on the squad last week.
He said Jesus had agreed a plan under which the forward would miss the Norway and Denmark matches to manage his fitness.
However, on the day of the Norway game, the 72-year-old coach told him he would play for 30 minutes.
"Everyone knows the rest. I warmed up from half-time onwards, watched the minutes tick by and wasn't called on," Ronaldo said.
"The manager had broken his word to me."
A later meeting with Jesus produced an agreement for the coach to clarify matters at his next news conference.
Ronaldo said an eight-point document was prepared saying he had never demanded playing time, had respected Jesus' decisions and that the coach asking "someone of the stature of Pele or Maradona" to warm up without bringing him on had been a mistake.
Portugal's record appearance holder said the agreed notes did not require Jesus to apologise to him but said the coach's public remarks did not reflect their private discussion.
"The conference was what is known: the attitude had nothing to do with our meeting," Ronaldo explained.
"I heard expressions and an aggressiveness I believe I did not deserve, a "High and mighty" attitude that he never showed me, not even remotely, in private the day before."
Ronaldo said it was the "second time" Jesus had "broken his word to me" and he decided to leave the training camp "without waiting for any further broken promises".
Prior to his appointment as head coach, Ronaldo said he had described Jesus - who had previously managed him at Al Nassr - as the "right choice".
Ronaldo had considered retiring from international football after this summer's World Cup - at which Portugal exited at the last-16 stage - and said he had written a letter to fans containing the words he wanted to tell them when he announced it, but he was urged to reconsider by the FPF's president, Pedro Proenca, on the flight home from the United States.
Ronaldo's behaviour drew contrasting opinions in his homeland with Jesus getting some support in the media and among fans at odds with those loyal to legendary player.
Ronaldo said that, despite the "absolute breakdown of trust" in Jesus' word, he should not have left and the "responsibility is mine alone", as he said sorry to his fellow players and Portugal's supporters.
He added: "I owe an apology to my national team teammates for having left the camp... I apologise to the Portuguese people once again, but a broken word has, for me, a defining impact."
Ronaldo's search for a record 1,000 career goals continues and he has returned to training in Saudi Arabia with Al-Nassr.
He has scored 979 times for Portugal, Sporting, Manchester United, Real Madrid, Juventus and Al-Nassr.
Portugal won the matches against Norway and Denmark without Ronaldo in the side, and are back in action in November in their final Nations League group games against the Danes and Wales.

How a Soviet physicist’s 1960 idea led to the birth of neutrino astronomy and this year’s Nobel Prize in physics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
21:48:06 UTC
06:48:06 KST

How a Soviet physicist’s 1960 idea led to the birth of neutrino astronomy and this year’s Nobel Prize in physics
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Belgian physicist Francis Halzen for his “decisive contribution to the IceCube neutrino observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin.” Neutrinos were long considered almost impossible to detect, especially those arriving from deep space. Tracing them to their cosmic sources is even harder here on Earth because the vast majority come from the Sun or are produced in the planet’s magnetic field. Yet scientists managed to detect them with a project of astonishing scale, first proposed by Soviet physicist Moisey Markov in the 1960s and built through Halzen’s efforts in recent decades: IceCube, an observatory buried deep in the Antarctic ice. What should we know about the project’s history? How does a cosmic neutrino detector work? And what can studying these particles tell us?
The Soviet roots of the 2026 Nobel: How Moisey Markov’s idea won over the physics world
Russian-language popular science writing about physics, like the field itself, is in much better shape than its counterparts in the other Nobel science disciplines, biology and chemistry. Experts have already written many in-depth articles about neutrinos and the IceCube neutrino observatory, the brainchild of this year’s laureate, Francis Halzen. It’s hard to add anything new to these accounts, so they’re a sensible place to start.
Readers are especially fortunate that Mark Bowen’s book “The Telescope in the Ice: Inventing a New Astronomy at the South Pole” was translated into Russian a few years ago. It tells the story of this remarkable project, conceived and built through Halzen’s efforts. Written in 2017, the book is now quite dated, but only in its account of neutrino “discoveries” (modern physics moves fast). Its central story — that of Halzen and his creation — remains accurate and fascinating.
In 2021, physicists Dmitry Naumov and Igor Ivanov of the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research’s Laboratory of Nuclear Problems gave our readers a detailed explanation of what neutrinos are and how scientists search for cosmic neutrinos in the depths of Russia’s Lake Baikal. That article focused on IceCube’s counterpart, the Baikal-GVD neutrino observatory. This is one of the rare fields in which Russian science contributes research that complements work elsewhere in the world, rather than trying to catch up.
Baikal-GVD is in the opposite hemisphere from IceCube and operates in water rather than ice. This is a major advantage, rather than a compromise dictated by circumstances (though working at Lake Baikal is certainly easier than working in Antarctica). Data from the two facilities complement each other: Their positions on opposite sides of the Earth help pinpoint the sources of incoming particles, while detectors in water offer greater precision than those in ice, where light scatters more readily.
The Russian — or, more accurately, Soviet — connection to this year’s prize is clear. The USSR began building a similar neutrino telescope back in the early 1980s. More significantly, Soviet physicist and Academy of Sciences member Moisey Markov proposed searching for traces of neutrinos in large natural bodies of water or ice, such as lakes or seas, as opposed to building purely laboratory-based detectors, which also exist.
Markov proposed the idea at a conference in Rochester in 1960. This wasn’t a case of an idea that occurred to a lone Soviet scientist, appeared in an obscure journal, and was rediscovered in the West many years later. Markov presented it in Rochester himself, and many Western physicists immediately recognized its potential and embraced it. Francis Halzen was among those who embraced it. The laureate himself recalled that moment:
How is such a detector built? That has also been known since 1960. I like to recall a photograph […] of Markov, who had the idea, together with Pontecorvo, because Pontecorvo had basically every idea in neutrino physics – except this one. This one was Markov’s idea. What you do is build a Cherenkov detector. You go deep in the ocean, or in the case of Russia, you go deep into Lake Baikal. It is dark. You install light sensors, filling a kilometer cube of water with them.
You take your imaginary kilometer, and you detect particles coming through the Earth. If a particle comes through the earth, it is a neutrino. No other particle comes through the Earth. What does this neutrino do? It goes through the detector, and you do not see anything. However, about one time in a million, in the region we are interested in, and where IceCube operates, the neutrino will crash into a proton. Then you get a nuclear reaction, and the water turns blue, precisely as it does in a nuclear reactor […]
These two paragraphs essentially explain everything you need to know about how IceCube works and the idea that earned the Nobel Prize. To unpack this concise description, we’ll start with neutrinos.
What is a neutrino, and why look for it?
“The neutrino joined the ranks of elementary particles tentatively and timidly,” Moisey Markov wrote in his 1964 monograph. “For several years, it was unclear whether the neutrino was a real particle or a theoretical concept that successfully described, in quantitative terms, the disappearance of energy and angular momentum in various reactions.”
In plainer, modern language, this means that physicists initially just made neutrinos up. They invented them to save the law of conservation of energy in certain radioactive decay processes that produced electrons. Under the conservation laws, these electrons should have had specific, fixed energies — but for some reason, they didn’t: Their energies formed a continuous spectrum rather than a set of discrete values. That was when, as the story is now understood, Austrian-German physicist Wolfgang Pauli proposed that these decays also produced a hypothetical particle that carried away some of the energy and angular momentum.
This saved the law of conservation of energy, but at a considerable cost: The “invented” particle had to have no charge, no mass, and almost no interactions with anything at all. Proving that it even existed was virtually impossible at the time, which naturally troubled physicists, who dislike such intangible things.
The neutrino’s defining property — both its strength and its weakness as a tool for studying the world — is that it participates only in what is called the weak interaction. Gravity also affects it, but so slightly that this effect can often be ignored. The weak interaction is one of the four fundamental interactions, alongside the strong interaction, electromagnetism, and gravity. It acts over an extremely short distance, smaller even than an atomic nucleus.
Neutrinos are often described as light, almost ethereal particles that pass through matter like incorporeal angels. But that description isn’t quite right. Nearly 65 billion neutrinos do pass through every square centimeter of our bodies every second without us even noticing. But that isn’t because these particles are so light.
Although the neutrino’s exact rest mass is still unknown (another remarkable property of these particles), its tremendous speed can give it as much energy as a tennis ball delivers on impact. If a neutrino like that somehow decides to interact with you, you’ll certainly notice. The probability is vanishingly small, however: It has to hit a suitable atomic nucleus with precision down to fractions of a femtometer. Only then does the neutrino have a chance to interact and release its energy at the end of its journey. The fact that this never happens to people tells us less about how light and insubstantial neutrinos are than about how people, like all visible matter, consist mostly of empty space.
So how did scientists prove that neutrinos exist, and even build detectors for them? As you might guess, even very rare events can be detected if they have enough opportunities to happen. For neutrinos, this means entering a medium where they can interact to produce other, more tangible particles that scientists can detect. Even in a detector, the neutrino itself remains invisible. What scientists can detect is the electron, or another, heavier charged particle called a muon, produced by the interaction.
From here, the physics becomes somewhat more familiar: Charged electrons and muons moving at tremendous speeds through a medium such as water begin to emit what is called Cherenkov radiation. It resembles the shock wave produced by a supersonic aircraft in air and occurs when a particle moves faster than light travels in that particular medium — water, for example. (Don’t worry: The speed of light in a vacuum is still unattainable!)
Cherenkov radiation is what makes the water tanks in nuclear reactors glow pale blue. Essentially, all that neutrino detectors such as IceCube and Baikal-GVD do is record flashes of this radiation.
Of course, this makes everything sound too simple. In practice, neutrino physicists’ main challenge is contending with constant noise from an endless stream of other particles. These particles also produce Cherenkov radiation that the detectors pick up, but they aren’t neutrinos. Or they are neutrinos but come from other sources: those same nuclear reactors, the center of the Earth, where radioactive decay occurs, the center of the Sun (the main source of noise), or space.
But cosmic neutrinos come in different kinds. Some — the overwhelming majority by number — are produced near Earth through the decay of protons that have entered the region of the planet’s magnetic field. These are neutrinos too, of course, but they aren’t the ones most physicists and astronomers are interested in.
Much more interesting are particles produced outside our solar system, or, better still, outside our galaxy altogether. They are far, far less numerous than neutrinos from other sources, but only these can have extremely high energies, in the hundreds of teraelectronvolts. No processes on Earth can produce particles with such energies, but supernova remnants and the centers of quasars can. Detections of these particles are fairly rare, and some remain unique, such as the recent detection of a neutrino with an energy of 120 petaelectronvolts by KM3NeT, a deep-sea telescope in the Mediterranean.
Exactly which processes produce these extraordinarily energetic particles remains a mystery. IceCube, Baikal-GVD, KM3NeT, and other similar detectors are being built to investigate that question. This means creating a new kind of astronomy in which neutrinos take the place of light or radio waves. Gravitational waves recently opened a second “window” onto the sky; detectors such as IceCube have opened a third, a neutrino window. The Nobel Committee recognized the opening of that window this year.

Could Texas Elect a Democratic Governor for the First Time in More Than 30 Years? Polls Show a Tight Race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
21:46:19 UTC
06:46:19 KST

A Republican has occupied Texas’ governor’s seat for more than three decades. But recent polls show that Gov. Greg Abbott, who has led the state since 2015, is facing a tight race against his Democratic challenger.
Abbott last won re-election by a more than 10-point margin four years ago. Most polls, though, indicate that the governor holds a small, single-digit lead as the November election approaches. In one Fox News survey conducted between Sept. 24-28 by the Beacon Research/Shaw & Company Research, the Republican incumbent led Gina Hinojosa, a Democratic state Representative, by roughly five percentage points.
Some other polls, meanwhile, show Hinojosa ahead of the governor by a narrow margin. A poll conducted by the New York Times/Siena University between Sept. 21-30, for instance, found that 49% of likely Texas voters said they would back Hinojosa for governor, while 46% said they would re-elect Abbott.
“This is an unusual situation in Texas politics,” says Joshua Blank, the research director of the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas at Austin. “It’s rather uncommon to see any Democratic candidate leading in anything other than a single outlying poll leading up to the election.”
And the governorship isn’t the only race threatening to upend the political scene in the state this fall: the Texas Republican Party is also grappling with a close-fought Senate contest, in which Democratic state representative James Talarico is leading the GOP’s nominee, state Attorney General Ken Paxton, in most polls by a razor-thin margin.
Here’s what experts think could be behind the apparent shift in voters’ sentiments—and how real the chance of the governorship flipping really is.
How Trump is affecting the Texas elections
Experts largely attribute the unusual competitiveness of the gubernatorial race to voters’ dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump and the national Republican Party.
“The polls are indicating that this is a very difficult year for Republicans nationwide, but especially in red states like Texas where the unpopularity of the Donald Trump presidency is dragging candidates down below the normal benchmark and cushion that they have enjoyed, in the case of Texas, for close to 30 years,” says Mark Jones, a professor of political science at Rice University.
Nationwide, Trump’s approval rating has hit a new low; according to the latest Associated Press/NORC polls, roughly 31% of adults in the country approve of the President, far below the approval rating he had when he was sworn in for a second term in January 2025. When it comes to how Trump has handled the economy in particular, his approval rating is even lower, at 26%, according to AP/NORC polling.
Support for Trump is higher in Texas—around 42% of respondents in the state for polling conducted by the Texas Politics Project said they had a “favorable” opinion of him in August. But the portion of respondents in that Texas survey who said they had an unfavorable view of the President—51% in August—exceeds those who said they held a positive opinion of him. And the number of people who hold a positive view of Trump has fallen since December 2024, when 54% of respondents said they had a favorable opinion of Trump, according to the Texas Politics Project.
Blank points out that Trump’s approval rating in Texas is higher on certain issues, such as immigration and border security.
But Texas voters are concerned about the cost of living, Blank says, and have expressed disapproval of how Trump is handling the economy. Texas is a large state that is geographically sprawling, so voters are particularly affected by the soaring gas prices sparked by the war in Iran, according to Blank.
“The challenge for Republicans is that the issues that voters consistently tell us are the most important to them are the ones that Trump is finding his ratings at their lowest,” Blank says. “While Texas is less negatively disposed towards the President as some other states, and certainly as the country as a whole, Texas is still part of the broader political conversation, and Texans are expressing less positive evaluations of the President than we’ve seen in the past.”
Jones posits that another possible explanation for the unusually tight gubernatorial race could be that Abbott has been in office for so long that the polls are showing “voter fatigue.”
Texans last elected a Democratic governor in 1990
If Hinojosa were to win the governorship, it would mark the first time since 1990 that Texas voters have elected a Democrat to be their governor—a remarkable shift in partisan politics in a staunchly Republican state. If that were to happen, experts predict that Hinojosa would use her veto power to stall much of the state legislature’s conservative agenda. Hinojosa has said that, if elected, she would use her veto power to block partisan congressional redistricting efforts.
“It would be a major seat change in the direction of Texas government,” Blank says. “It’s not that a victory by Hinojosa would lead to a significant or drastic change in policy, but it would lead to a significant stoppage in the advancement of conservative legislation in the state. It’s not that she could control what the legislature could do, but she could exercise her veto in a way that would fundamentally change the focus of the legislative output.”
He notes, though, that even if Hinojosa were to win the governorship, it doesn’t mean that Texas is “turning blue;” it would just be "a reflection of the increased competitiveness in a ... diverse, huge state like Texas."
How likely is the governorship to flip?
Jones says he believes that Hinojosa has a “relatively low probability” of defeating Abbott for the governorship, in part because Hinojosa has a strong liberal voting and policy record that is “well to the left of where the average Texas voter is.” Jones says that if Abbott can convince Republican voters to vote “based on partisanship and policy, not based on other factors,” he has a strong advantage.
Abbott also has far more campaign resources than Hinojosa, and can outspend his Democratic challenger on TV, radio, and digital media “by a dramatic margin,” Jones says.
“I think we’re still in a situation where Abbott, at the end of the day, should be able to pull this one out, but it’s going to be the smallest margin that he has had in any of his gubernatorial elections,” Jones says.
Blank, meanwhile, says that “right now, this election is really going to hinge on turnout.”
Republicans are expending a lot of effort to mobilize their base to show up at the polls next month. “One of the things to watch is whether or not all of the money that’s being spent now is effective in re-engaging Republicans who would never vote for Democrats, but if enough of them stay home, a Democrat might get elected,” Blank says. “If Republicans are able to turn out their voters, they are almost guaranteed of winning the election.”
He says it’s hard to predict at this point what will happen in November.
“For those who are waiting to see whether or not a Democrat can win Texas, 2026 provides the best opportunity in the last two decades,” he says, “but that doesn’t mean it’s a sure thing.”
