Türkiye, Italy explore closer space cooperation at International Astronautical Congress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
21:07:20 UTC
06:07:20 KST

Tugba Altun, Sumeyye Dilara Dincer, and Mucahithan Avcioglu
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Türkiye and Italy discussed expanding their space partnership at the 77th International Astronautical Congress in Antalya, southern Türkiye, with officials highlighting opportunities for joint missions and cooperation under a decade-long framework agreement.
The session brought together astronauts, diplomats, and space agency representatives to discuss cooperation between the two countries, building on their shared participation in the Axiom Mission 3 to the International Space Station in 2024.
Organized by the International Astronautical Federation, the congress is being held at Antalya’s NEST Congress Center under the coordination of Türkiye's Industry and Technology Ministry, with the Turkish Space Agency (TUA) and SAHA Istanbul as hosts. Anadolu is the event's global communications partner.
Italy's Ambassador to Ankara Giuseppe Manzo said President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni discussed space cooperation during their meeting at the NATO summit in the Turkish capital Ankara this July.
He described the field as a priority for both countries and said their longstanding ties provided a foundation for partnerships extending beyond national borders and into space.
Mario Cospito, special commissioner of the Italian Space Agency, said the countries are moving from dialogue toward structured cooperation.
He pointed to a 2025 memorandum of understanding between the two space agencies providing a 10-year framework for cooperation across a broad range of space activities.
Cospito said work is underway to turn that framework into a concrete joint mission, with projects under negotiation involving shared technological objectives, responsibilities, and capabilities.
Türkiye targets lunar mission early next year
Turkish Space Agency board member Arif Karabeyoglu said Türkiye plans to send a domestically developed and manufactured spacecraft to the Moon in the first months of 2027.
The spacecraft is ready, he said, describing the mission as one of the challenging objectives within the country's 10-point space roadmap.
Other goals include establishing a Turkish spaceport, Karabeyoglu said, highlighting plans involving the African nation of Somalia and the potential for cooperation with Italy, which has launch infrastructure off the coast of Kenya, bordering Somalia.
Türkiye's first astronaut, Brig. Gen. Alper Gezeravci, said the decision to send a Turkish citizen into space changed what younger generations could imagine for their future.
“This was not the realization of one person's dream, but the realization of a nation's dream. Our children are now much more confident about stepping into the future,” he said.
Gezeravci also praised Italy's support in aviation.
“From the very beginning, we felt Italy's support very strongly and deeply,” he said.
Italian astronaut Walter Villadei, who served alongside Gezeravci on Axiom Mission 3, emphasized the importance of trust among crew members, citing their 11 months of joint training.
He said spaceflight was a collective effort and offered numerous opportunities for Italy and Türkiye to become strong partners in the future.
Following the session, Massimo Comparini, the managing director of aerospace/defense company Leonardo's space division, highlighted the rapid transformation of the space industry and the importance of space technologies and Earth observation capabilities for sustainability.

Christa Pike is conscious and speaking after botched execution attempt, lawyers say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
21:05:41 UTC
06:05:41 KST

Christa Pike, a Tennessee prisoner who survived the state’s attempt to execute her, is awake and speaking as she receives treatment at a hospital, her attorneys said, as they head to court on Wednesday seeking a court order requiring preservation of all evidence relating to the botched exercise by the state.
Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital, a sedative, as Tennessee officials attempted to put her to death last Wednesday in a case that shocked many in America and created headlines around the world. She was set to be the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
“Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking and continues to receive critical medical care. Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed. Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery,” attorneys for Pike said in a statement on Tuesday.
Her legal team will ask a court on at a hearing on Wednesday to require the Tennessee department of correction to preserve all “relevant physical, written and electronic evidence” related to the failed execution, court documents said. A press conference is also scheduled.
Her attorneys said they were grateful for the first responders and the medical team at the hospital “who treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her”.
“She is the only person known to have survived a complete execution attempt in the US. Christa is a survivor and will take recovery one day at a time. We continue to ask the Governor of Tennessee to commute Christa Pike’s sentence to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole,” Pike’s attorneys added.
The statement was the first indication that Pike has improved since an ambulance carried her away from a Nashville prison on the night of 30 September.
Witnesses to the attempt to execute Pike described how they heard she was choking and struggling for an hour after receiving the first injection. She was then hospitalized after a second dose failed to kill her. In hospital, she was put on a ventilator and had been in critical condition.
Following the botched execution attempt, one of Pike’s lawyers, Randy Spivey, called the process “cruel and torturous”, adding that he had counted seven needles in Pike’s left arm, “one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her”. Her lawyers had warned before the execution that officials might struggle to locate veins and cause her suffering in the process, but the state had pushed to proceed and the US supreme court allowed the prison to move forward.
The disastrous attempt sparked widespread condemnation across the political spectrum and among advocates for banning the death penalty. Tennessee’s prison chief, Frank Strada, also resigned in the aftermath. Strada was facing intensifying scrutiny, with lawyers saying Pike’s case was the fifth “botched” execution under his leadership across two states.
Pike and her boyfriend, who was 17 at the time, killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, one of their classmates at Knoxville Job Corps, in 1995.
According to prosecutors, Pike was worried Slemmer was trying to take her then boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, away from her. Together, they lured Slemmer into a wooded area behind the agriculture campus steam plant at the University of Tennessee on 12 January 1995, tortured and killed her.
Shipp was convicted of first-degree murder in 1997 and was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole.
Pike has never denied her involvement in Slemmer’s killing. She was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder.
As a child, Pike had been subject to various abuse, including multiple rapes by different men, as well as beatings by her relatives.
Pike later underwent nearly 30 years of solitary confinement while on death row.
In the wake of the botched execution attempt Helen Prejean, a Catholic nun who is perhaps the best-known advocate for abolition of the death penalty in America, told the Guardian: “This is the essence of cruelty. Take a conscious, imaginative human being, give her a date for her death, have her anticipate it over and over again, and then take her out and try and kill her.
“She was rendered defenceless as they deliberately attempted to kill her – what greater mental torture for a human being is there?”
Sam Levin and the Associated Press contributed to this report

Bokov was convicted of undergoing training for terrorist activities (Article 205.3 of Russia’s Criminal Code), preparing to join a terrorist organization (Article 205.5), weapons offenses (Article 222), and preparing a terrorist attack (Article 205).
Bokov was detained in October 2025. He was accused of attempting to join the far-right movement “White Power,” which is banned in Russia. He was later charged with preparing a terrorist attack on a mosque and illegally possessing ammunition. According to Ostorozhno, Novosti, investigators treated his attendance at a classroom session on how weapons work at Patriot Park, self-defense lessons run by the patriotic initiative Chistota, and several driving lessons at a Moscow college as terrorist training.
Bokov’s relatives said the charges were based on a smartphone that did not belong to him, seized during a search. His father told Msk1 that his son refused to give the officers the passcode to his own phone. “He didn’t want to give them [the iPhone passcode], and they shocked him in the leg several times with a stun gun. He still didn’t tell them. Then they cuffed him again, this time with his hands behind his back, took out a field telephone cable, and wrapped the wires around his hands and fingers,” he said.
Bokov’s relatives also said the officers asked him not to mention the torture in court, promising he would be placed under house arrest. Instead, he spent the entire period before his trial in a pretrial detention center.

Three years of Israel's genocide in Gaza. Has US forgotten the besieged Palestinians?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
21:00:44 UTC
06:00:44 KST

Three years since Hamas blitz on Israel and the latter's genocide in Gaza, ordinary Palestinians in the blockaded enclave say they feel abandoned by the United States. While Washington helped broker a multilateral deal that resulted in an initial ceasefire and captive releases, its longer-term objectives remain stalled.
"Gaza means nothing to America. We were just a card used to help charm in the election, nothing more," a Palestinian man told TRT World in Gaza.
Another Palestinian in the enclave argued when US President Donald Trump came to power again, the war stopped but “America is in the region to protect Israel, nothing more,” he added .
US President Trump's year-old plan to end the Gaza genocide has stalled, with Israel mounting near daily attacks and occupying around two-thirds of the shattered enclave where Palestinians face dire conditions.
An initial phase secured a temporary ceasefire on October 10, 2025 and facilitated the release of captives held in Gaza, alongside approximately 2,000 Palestinian hostages held by Israel.
However, subsequent benchmarks — including the withdrawal of Israeli forces from roughly 60 percent of Gaza and the commencement of reconstruction — remain unrealised.
Palestinian health authorities report that Israeli attacks have killed more than 1,400 Palestinians since the October ceasefire, predominantly women and children.
"It (US) forgot about us and look at the situation of the people in Gaza," a Palestinian woman told TRT World. "Everyone is living in tents and we are heading into winter while the war is still ongoing. Israel is carrying out strikes. They say there is a ceasefire, but I don't see any ceasefire."
On October 7, 2023, Hamas fighters launched a blitz targeting Israeli military installations and surrounding settlements.
The blitz followed recurring Israeli incursions into the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound and escalating violence by illegal settlers across the Occupied West Bank.
The Israeli genocidal war — including reports referencing the controversial Hannibal Directive — resulted in the deaths of hundreds of Israelis, including soldiers and civilians.
Subsequent disclosures indicated that hawkish Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and military officials had received intelligence warnings regarding an impending blitz.
Nevertheless, Israel initiated a genocidal war against the besieged population, killing more than 74,000 Palestinians, wounding hundreds of thousands, displacing nearly the entire 2.3 million population, and destroying roughly 90 percent of civilian infrastructure.
Independent researchers and public health experts estimate that the indirect and unrecorded death toll could exceed 200,000.
Iran and Yemen wars
Analysts say the escalating US-Israel war with Iran and now fighting in Yemen have diverted the US and larger global attention away from the ongoing humanitarian crisis in Gaza.
"Remember, (President) Donald Trump said he was going to solve the war in Gaza on day one. So, here we are, these many years, you know, almost two years after his presidency started, doesn't seem like a real solution is at hand whatsoever," Richard Goodstein, a former adviser to Bill and Hillary Clinton, told TRT World.
"On the other hand, within Democratic politics for sure, and I think increasingly more in Republican politics, this notion of where do you stand, what's the solution, I think those are actually going to be fairly front burner as the 2028 presidential election starts. So, I think it's not really off. It's off the front burner now. It will be a front burner issue I would say six months from now."
Peter Roff, a contributing editor and columnist at Newsweek, told TRT World that the US may not have forgotten Gaza, but shifting geopolitical priorities have overshadowed the crisis.
"Just because (Gaza) it's off the front page doesn't mean it's forgotten, but in America, we have a tendency to confuse the urgent with the important, and right now, Iran, Strait of Hormuz, Red Sea exits for Saudi oil, and the elections all seem more urgent and worthy of coverage than Gaza," Roff argued.
Trump announced the establishment of the "Board of Peace" on January 15 as part of his broader plan meant to oversee governance and reconstruction in postwar Gaza, after a ceasefire agreement was reached on October 10, 2025.
The board was authorised by UN Security Council Resolution 2803 in November 2025.
After what has been a one-sided truce, the transition to the second phase — involving Hamas's disarmament and a gradual withdrawal of the Israeli army, which still occupies more than 60 percent of Gaza — has been stalled, while international attention has been focused on Iran.
Robert Malley, a Middle East expert who served under Presidents Bill Clinton, Barack Obama, and Joe Biden, told TRT World that the Trump administration did one thing which the Biden administration had been unable to do, which is to reach a ceasefire.
"And even though people would question what kind of ceasefire it is when Palestinian are being killed every day, it was better than at the height of the onslaught that Israel was waging. So, you gotta give that much credit at all, if anything, to the Trump administration for having achieved it and for having put some pressure on Israel to agree to that," he said.
Malley, who is also the co-author of "Tomorrow Is Yesterday", a book about the pursuit of peace between Israel and Palestine, however conceded that since the ceasefire "there has been an attempt to reduce the Palestinian question to a humanitarian question."
"Can we make their lives a little bit better? Can we get a little more humanitarian goods in? But the political question of Palestine is… the attempt is to bury it, right? And there's no recognition that it's a political problem, what's happening in Gaza is a political decision, what's happening in the West Bank is a political decision, and that there are political aspirations that are being completely trampled, as we speak," he added.
Will the US ever stop arming Israel?
Even as Gaza reels under the genocide, Israeli authorities and illegal settler movements are advancing land grabs, settlement expansions, and outposts in the occupied West Bank and occupied East Jerusalem, leveraging regional distractions.
Zionist groups have engaged in violent aggression, entering Palestinian villages, setting fire to structures, vehicles, and mosques, clashing with local residents and even killing them with state-supplied weapons.
According to the Palestinians and UN reports, Israeli military and illegal settlers have killed more than 1,100 Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem, since October 7, 2023.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) has determined that Israel's occupation of the West Bank and East Jerusalem violates international law and must end.
Furthermore, the International Criminal Court has issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant over war crimes and crimes against humanity, while Israel faces genocide proceedings before the ICJ.
Despite these legal rulings and international appeals, Washington maintains its annual $3.8 billion baseline military support to Israel, having provided tens of billions in supplementary security grants since late 2023 without attaching binding human rights conditions to arms transfers.
Since 1946, the US has provided over $310 billion in military and economic aid to Israel, adjusted for inflation, according to the American think tank, Council on Foreign Relations
Democratic strategist Goodstein argued that the US is committed to Israel remaining a Jewish state and being able to defend itself, "and that commitment looks fairly unshakable."
"Will we stop giving them as opposed to selling them weapons? I don't think we're going to see a day where that stops. However, they're gonna get help. Israel's gonna get help from the United States. "
Public opinion in US
Malley, who has followed the politics of the region for four decades, said American public opinion has changed in ways he has not previously seen. He pointed to a pronounced shift among younger Americans and described the polling data as incontrovertible.
"If you wanna look for one change that should bring hope to those who are still longing for a peaceful settlement, self-determination for the Palestinian people. The shift in public opinion here, which is yet to fully manifest itself at the political echelons, but you're already seeing," Malley added.
Candidates are now being pressed on whether they will accept money from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), a pro-Israel lobbying group, and conditioning US aid—or military sales—to Israel has become a litmus test, he said.
Malley argued that questions once confined to the political fringe in the US, including whether Israel’s actions constitute genocide or whether Israel is an apartheid state, are now subjects that every serious US political candidate must address.
He said the effect is likely to intensify as the 2028 Democratic primaries approach, with candidates forced to calibrate their positions against what he called "a political earthquake in public opinion."

Israeli settlers beat press photographer as soldiers watch in West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
21:00:28 UTC
06:00:28 KST

Armed Israeli settlers beat a photographer in the presence of Israeli soldiers, hospitalising him, as he covered worsening settler violence against olive farmers in the occupied West Bank.
Jaafar Ashtiyeh, a 58-year-old veteran photographer for Agence France-Presse in Palestine, was assaulted by a group of settlers, who beat him with the butts of their rifles, despite him being marked as press. He was assaulted in view of about a dozen armed Israeli soldiers.
Ashtiyeh suffered bruises to his head and torso and was taken to hospital, according to witnesses, his family and fellow journalists.
His assault came amid a worsening wave of Israeli settler violence in the West Bank. Every year, settlers attack Palestinian farmers trying to harvest their olives – an economic lifeline for the beleaguered Palestinian economy – with few legal consequences.
This harvest season has been particularly violent as the Israeli elections approach at the end of the month.
Ashtiyeh and another AFP photographer, John Wessels, were near the northern village of Aqraba when they noticed an Israeli soldier detaining a man as local Palestinians picked olives.
A quad bike suddenly raced towards the AFP journalists on top of a hill and a man on it opened live fire, with one Palestinian dropping to the ground. He was also hospitalised, with a gunshot to the foot, according to the Palestine Red Crescent Society.
At least six other people then rushed towards the AFP journalists firing guns. As Ashtiyeh attempted to enter a car, which was clearly marked “Press”, two men jumped on him and beat him repeatedly with the butts of their rifles.
A group of at least a dozen Israeli soldiers were about 500 metres away at the time of the attack, according to Wessels.
“I could hear his screams,” said Wessels, who was also threatened at gunpoint. The assailants also took Ashtiyeh’s camera equipment.
Ashtiyeh, who is Palestinian, was conscious in a hospital in Nablus. He underwent X-rays which did not detect broken bones but he will remain in hospital for round-the-clock observation, his son, Zain Jaafar, said.
The man who initially fired the gun was wearing a long white shirt as well as military fatigue trousers and boots, which are commonly worn by soldiers, Wessels said.
AFP has asked the Israeli military for comment. Settlers are rarely arrested or charged for their attacks against Palestinians.
“We strongly condemn yet another serious attack on journalists trying to report on events in the West Bank and demand a full investigation. It is unacceptable that journalists can be beaten and robbed by armed settlers in front of Israeli security forces who made no attempt to intervene,” said Phil Chetwynd, AFP’s global news director.
The Foreign Press Association, which represents international media in Israel and the Palestinian territories, said it was “deeply alarmed”.
“Israeli authorities must investigate why soldiers present in the area did not intervene in this attack against clearly identified journalists,” it said.
“This attack is a blatant attempt to intimidate the press and obstruct accurate reporting from the West Bank. International media have a responsibility to tell all sides of the story and will not be deterred by physical assaults or threats.”
Israel was the world’s leading killer of journalists in 2025, and has killed at least 225 journalists in Lebanon and Gaza, according to the UN Human Rights Office.
Violence has flared in recent months in the West Bank with near-daily attacks, thefts or vandalism by Israeli settlers against Palestinians.
There have also been attacks against Israelis, with a Palestinian shooting dead a settler last month.
Extremist Israeli settlers have been seizing olive groves owned by Palestinians, who consider the trees a cultural symbol.
About 500,000 Israeli settlers live in the West Bank – which Israel captured in 1967 – among 3 million Palestinians. Settlements in occupied territory are illegal under international law.
Media rights groups say Israeli settlers have increasingly targeted journalists and that authorities have imposed growing impediments to coverage.
Israeli authorities have detained 19 journalists in the West Bank, including one AFP contributor, in the three years since the 7 October, 2023 Hamas-led attack on Israel, according to Paris-based Reporters Without Borders.
Agence France-Presse contributed reporting

Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1686: Sanctioned tankers carried fuel from South Korea to Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Exclusives
Military
Ukrainian units hit record number of Russian air defense systems and radars in September, one of them 552 kilometers away. Every result is recorded on video in the Delta battlefield system.
At ruined Donetsk’s airport, three Russians snap selfies and ready jet-powered Geran-4. Ukrainian drone slips in unseen and rams their launcher. The pickup truck was converted to launch Russian drones.
Ukraine’s drone pilots hit 76.5% more Russian infantry than two months ago: 2,699 in first five days of October. Commander Robert Brovdi says the pilots count only losses verified in the military's Delta system, so the real toll is higher.
Ukraine’s battlefield gains may be pushing Putin to shift focus to early winter strikes, ISW says. Russia is likely starting its recurring winter campaign earlier than usual while Ukraine is still developing defenses against the ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones being used in increasingly large strike packages.
The tanks that fuel Moscow’s airliners are reported burning after Ukraine’s latest drone raid on the capital region. Footage geolocated by OSINT analysts placed the blaze at the Volodarskaya station, part of Russia's state pipeline network.
Intelligence and technology
Ukraine’s war leadership sets new electronic warfare tasks as Russia’s jet-powered drones slip past nearly half of its air defenses. Zelenskyy said the main criterion is that Ukraine must be able to respond in kind to Russian strikes.
Ukraine is third in world for cyberattacks after US and Israel, and first in Europe. Machine-speed assaults run continuously and without fatigue. Malware accounts for 33% of incidents in the first half of 2026, and system compromises for 4.5%.
Ukraine’s Defense Ministry says some suppliers cannot build weapons ordered, and drops contracts to free $346 million for front. Technology and tactics change quickly, the ministry says, and some weapons no longer match combat tasks.
Proven on Ukraine’s front line, now made in Germany. National Guard signs for the Linza and Zoom drones. The German-Ukrainian venture Quantum Frontline Industries will build both systems and is scaling up as its first production year wraps up.
Türkiye’s Korkut guns now shoot down Russian drones over Ukraine. Almost half of the jet-powered Shaheds still get through. Russia launched about as many of the fast ones as slow ones in September, by one analyst's count, and its winter assault on the power grid is still ahead.
International
Seoul backs Ukraine, but sanctioned tankers carried fuel from South Korea to Russia. The trade could cast Seoul as a gap in the West's effort to squeeze Moscow, the Guardian said.
Russia is out to break Ukraine’s economy this winter, Jetten says—and the Netherlands will help keep Ukraine’s drone-hunting F-16s in the air. Ukraine is finding ammunition for its F-16s “virtually all over the world,” Zelenskyy said on 5 October.
Humanitarian and social impact
Three ambulances hit, a woman killed at home: 25 minutes of Russian drone attacks on Kramatorsk. The strikes on medical vehicles and a high-rise are now under investigation as war crimes.
Ukraine’s civilian casualties 55% higher in first eight months than in the same period in 2025, UN says. Strikes on energy facilities and businesses have surged, while damage to power plants is causing outages as winter approaches.
Political and legal developments
Ukraine cuts more than 4,000 vacant government posts and trims deputy ministers by about 20% in the first stage of civil service reform. Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi says the number of deputies will be tied to how much work each office carries.
New developments
Germany accuses Russia of a drone bomb attempt at Leipzig. Now its eight biggest airports get drone detection. The air traffic controller's system spots drones in approach and departure paths and alerts the police, who remain responsible for stopping them.
Two ships sunk and a third set ablaze off NATO coasts in two days, and neither Bucharest nor Sofia will say “Russia”. Romania and Bulgaria have described the attacks only as drone strikes, without saying where the drones came from.

Qatar says Washington, Tehran exchanging messages as mediation continues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
20:57:39 UTC
05:57:39 KST

Hussien Elkabany and Mohammad Sio
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Qatar said Tuesday that Washington and Tehran are exchanging messages as mediation efforts and diplomatic contacts continue in an attempt to achieve progress amid months of stalled negotiations about ending the war.
Ibrahim al-Hashimi, director of media and communications at the Foreign Ministry, made the remarks at a news conference in response to a question about Iranian Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni’s visit to Doha.
“Contacts and visits are continuing with the aim of reaching progress that can be built upon between Washington and Tehran,” al-Hashimi said.
He stressed that mediation efforts between the two sides “are continuing and have not stopped.”
The efforts are aimed at achieving progress “that can be built upon and that includes all issues of concern to both parties,” according to a Foreign Ministry statement.
“Talks are continuing, there is an exchange of messages between Washington and Tehran, and Qatar is a mediator between the parties,” said al-Hashimi.
He added that a resolution requires the “best efforts” through negotiated solutions that take into consideration the concerns of all parties.
Qatar, alongside Pakistan, has been mediating between Washington and Tehran to end the war that began in late February. An initial agreement in June failed to halt the fighting.
 
Iranian pilots
Asked about the case of Iranian pilots who were shot down, al-Hashimi said Qatar had “been clear from the beginning that this issue has been dealt with” and that Iran had been informed of the latest developments.
He said Doha is open to a visit by Iran to review measures taken in the case.
Iran’s official IRNA news agency reported Tuesday that Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni is visiting Doha for talks.
Momeni said discussions were held about the pilots and another technical delegation will be sent to continue work on the issue.
He said regional developments were also discussed and described the meeting as “productive and constructive,” saying it offered promising prospects for future cooperation, according to IRNA.
Iran’s General Staff said Aug. 15 that Qatar is holding three of four Iranian pilots who had been aboard two fighter jets that went down during the war with the US and Israel, and had been held in Qatar for six months. Doha denied the claim.
Qatar said March 2 that it had shot down two Iranian Su-24 aircraft approaching from Iran. Tehran said its fighter jets had been targeted during attacks on a US base in Qatar.
Iran later said the body of Majid Kazemi had been returned and buried, while the fate of the other three pilots remained unclear, according to Iranian officials.
 
Mecca Alliance
On regional developments, al-Hashimi said Qatar supports initiatives taken by countries in the region to safeguard their security, sovereignty and territorial integrity, including the Mecca Defense Alliance between Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.
He said the alliance strengthens regional cooperation aimed at preserving countries’ capabilities and stability.
Qatar supports any initiative that contributes to regional security and stability, he said, adding that it is “too early to talk about Qatar joining the Mecca Alliance.”
Al-Hashimi reiterated Doha’s support for Saudi Arabia in measures it takes to safeguard its security and territorial integrity.
“We condemn the irresponsible approach adopted by the Houthi group in targeting the Kingdom, Islamic holy sites and civilian objects, and we support the Kingdom in all measures it takes to preserve its security and territorial integrity,” he said.
He added that additional details regarding the Iranian minister’s visit will be announced by the Interior Ministry.

US CDC says it’s ‘aware of and closely monitoring’ Russian plague case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
20:54:07 UTC
05:54:07 KST

US CDC says it’s ‘aware of and closely monitoring’ Russian plague case
The top US public health agency’s remarks come as the Trump administration said it’s ‘closely’ watching the incident.
The United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has said it’s “aware of and closely monitoring” a suspected pneumonic plague outbreak in Russia.
The top US public health agency released a statement on social media Tuesday, attempting to ease rising global concerns after the unexplained death of Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old woman who worked at an anti-plague laboratory in Siberia.
“While the circumstances of this reported case remain unconfirmed, plague is a serious bacterial disease that is treatable with antibiotics, particularly when recognized and treated early,” the CDC said.
Russian authorities, who have released few details on the events surrounding Shipilova’s death, have quarantined a hospital in the country’s Irkutsk region and are tracing the laboratory technician’s contacts.
Russian media reports also say authorities have placed nearly 200 people under medical observation.
The CDC emphasised the need for “rapid identification and treatment of infected individuals”, but said the incident posed little risk to the US.
“CDC and our interagency partners are prepared and continue to monitor the situation closely,” the agency said.
The remarks from the US health agency come as the Trump administration said it’s “closely” watching the incident, which Russia has said is under control.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday pushed Moscow for more information on Shipilova’s death.
“I think it’s incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world,” Rubio told reporters in Iceland.
Rubio added that the US has “measures” available to help Russia if the situation becomes more serious, but needed to know more before it could step in.
President Trump also said that he had a call scheduled with Russian President Vladimir Putin to discuss the reported outbreak “very soon”. Trump added that US intelligence agencies were “closely monitoring” the issue and they would report on it “probably tomorrow”.
Dr Ashish Jha, who coordinated former US President Joe Biden’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic, said on Tuesday that it is unlikely Shipilova was the only person who contracted a case of pneumonic plague.
“That would be great,” Jha wrote on X. “But given the context and history, to assume it is that would be unwise.”
“We need to understand exactly what has happened. And we have to assume we may not know the full truth,” he added in a separate post as he echoed the Trump administration’s calls for more transparency from Russia.
Pneumonic plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which is usually found in small mammals and their fleas. According to the World Health Organization, the plague is highly infectious and can be transmitted through respiratory particles. It can be fatal if not treated early.

Libya parliament speaker ousted after 12 years amid power shift
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
20:54:00 UTC
05:54:00 KST

Libya’s parliament removed its longtime speaker on Tuesday after 12 years in office, ousting a key ally of east-based Khalifa Haftar in a move analysts said could signal a shift in the country’s political balance.
MPs voted to replace Aguila Saleh with Al-Salhin Abdelnabi al-Obeidi, the parliament's spokesman announced on X.
Libya has been beset by violence and instability since the overthrow of Moammar Gadhafi in 2011.
It remains divided between the U.N.-recognized government in Tripoli led by Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah, and a rival administration in the east backed by military commander Haftar.
Haftar's camp relies in particular on the parliament, which sits in the eastern city of Benghazi under their control.
Saleh, 82, has long been considered a staunch ally of the Haftar clan, but he appeared to be weakened as Haftar's sons, in particular Saddam Haftar, consolidated their positions.
Emadeddin Badi, an analyst at the London-based Chatham House, said: "Aguila Saleh appears to be the latest casualty of Saddam Haftar's drive to centralize decision-making in eastern Libya and bulldoze his way into a political role."
His removal comes as a U.S. initiative aimed at reviving the political process and unifying Libya's institutions is under discussion.

Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike is awake and speaking at a hospital after surviving the state’s attempt to execute her, her attorneys said Tuesday.
"Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care. Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed. Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery," attorneys for Pike said in a statement.
Her attorneys said they are grateful for the first responders and the medical team at the hospital "who treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her."
The statement was the first indication that Pike has improved since an ambulance carried her away from a Nashville prison last Wednesday.
A spokeswoman for the Tennessee Department of Correction said she could provide no information other than that Pike remained hospitalized Tuesday.
Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital as they attempted to put her to death for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. The lethal injection drug didn't kill her, but her lawyers said her arms were left burned and blistered.
Dr. Joel Zivot, a professor of anesthesiology and surgery in Atlanta who consulted as an expert for Pike's legal team, said the development "bodes well for a good recovery." But, he added, it could be weeks or months before anyone knows exactly what her recovery might look like, and whether her competency could be restored to a level that might enable the state to try again to execute her.
"She's still in the ICU," he said. "She has recovered to a certain degree that she's able to be off a ventilator and able to speak, but in no way would I announce her free of further serious risk. There's still a lot of bad things that can happen here, even when everyone is doing their job well."
Pike's attorneys are set to go to court Wednesday as they seek to learn more about what happened in the failed lethal injection.
The attorneys are seeking a court order requiring the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve evidence, including drug lot numbers, records and other information from the Sept. 30 attempted execution. Chancery Court Judge I'Ashea Myles scheduled a Wednesday morning status conference in the case.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia carried out a combined attack with sea and aerial drones against civilian vessels in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, while Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said it was still impossible to establish whether the drones were Ukrainian or Russian.
In his evening address on October 6, Zelensky said two civilian ships had been attacked in Bulgarian waters the previous night, with one sinking and the other suffering significant damage. He stressed that Ukrainian forces had not conducted operations in the area.
"Ukrainian defense forces have not carried out any operations in this area of the sea," Zelensky said.
Zelensky said Ukrainian authorities had contacted their Bulgarian counterparts and that the information had been verified between the two sides. He said the Ukrainian Navy had communicated with Bulgaria’s naval authorities and that the attack had been identified as a Russian operation involving both sea and aerial drones.
"Our Navy contacted their counterparts in Bulgaria, and it was determined that this was a Russian combined attack using sea and aerial drones," the Ukrainian president said.
Zelensky said the attack was part of what he described as Russia’s effort to make the western Black Sea dangerous for shipping. He also said the incident was another escalation in Moscow’s actions against civilian shipping.
"This latest tragedy involving civilian ships continues Russia's attempts to render the western part of the Black Sea completely unsuitable for navigation," Zelensky said.
He ordered Ukraine’s Armed Forces, Defense Ministry, intelligence agencies and other services to coordinate with the country’s partners in response to the attack.
"I have instructed our Armed Forces, the Ministry of Defence of Ukraine, our intelligence agencies, and all our services to cooperate as fully as possible with our partners so that both we and they have greater defensive capabilities," Zelensky stated.
The Ukrainian president also referred to the recent attack on a ship in Romanian waters.
"Just recently, a ship was hit in Romanian waters. Now - Bulgaria," he said.
Zelensky described Russia’s actions as a continuing escalation and also cited cases of Russian drones entering Moldova, as well as earlier attacks on ships and Ukrainian ports.
"That is exactly what the Russians are planning - to constantly ramp up the escalation," Zelensky declared.
He said Russian drones were repeatedly entering Moldova and that attacks on ships in the waters of Ukraine’s partners and on Ukrainian ports were continuing.
"Their drones are now constantly entering Moldova, and this is not the first attack on ships in the Black Sea within our partners' waters; attacks on our ports are continuing ceaselessly," he said.
Zelensky called for a direct response to what he described as Russian aggression.
"There must be a clear reaction to this Russian aggression. Absolutely clear countermeasures are needed," the Ukrainian president added.
Earlier, however, Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov told bTV that Bulgaria could not yet establish whether the drones that struck the two vessels were Ukrainian or Russian.
Stoyanov said investigators would need to recover drone wreckage or receive a claim of responsibility from one of the sides, neither of which had occurred. He assessed that maritime drones had been used in the attack.
"We need to find the drone wreckage or have one of the sides claim responsibility, but neither has happened; therefore, we cannot confirm whether they are Ukrainian or Russian. Our assessment is that the attack was carried out using maritime drones," the minister said.
Stoyanov said the incident was a deliberate attack rather than an accident and noted that there had been fatalities. He described Bulgaria as evidently being part of the hybrid war between Ukraine and Russia, regardless of which side was responsible.
"This is not an accident but a deliberate attack; there have been fatalities. We are evidently part of the hybrid war between Ukraine and Russia - whether on one side or the other. This is part of the war being waged close to us. There is nothing surprising here," the defense minister emphasized.
Stoyanov also said there was no information at that point about the cargo carried by the two ships. He explained that the information available had come from crew members and that a Bulgarian reconnaissance aircraft had not landed on the vessel to verify its cargo because the ship was still on fire.
"There is currently no information regarding the cargo of the struck ships. The information comes from the crew; one of our reconnaissance aircraft has not landed on the ship to verify the cargo. No such aircraft of ours will land there because there is currently a fire on the ship," Stoyanov said.
Zelensky later reiterated in his nightly video address that the attack had been carried out by Russia, saying Ukrainian authorities had confirmed the details with the Bulgarian side and that the two countries’ naval forces had been in contact.
He again said Ukrainian forces had not conducted operations in the area where the ships were attacked and described the incident as a Russian assault involving naval and aerial drones. He repeated his call for Ukraine’s armed forces, Defense Ministry, intelligence services and other agencies to work closely with partners to strengthen their self-defense capabilities.
The Ukrainian president also interpreted the attack in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone as part of Russia’s effort to make the western Black Sea dangerous and unsuitable for navigation. The incident involved two ships struck by drones in Bulgarian waters, one of which sank.
Zelensky also warned in his evening address that Moscow was preparing a large-scale attack against Ukraine.
"Ukrainian defense forces did not conduct operations in this area of the sea. This latest tragedy involving civilian ships continues Russia's attempts to make the western part of the Black Sea completely dangerous for navigation. We have clarified all information with the Bulgarian side: our Navy contacted their Bulgarian counterparts, and it was established that this was a combined Russian attack involving naval and aerial drones. I have instructed our Armed Forces, the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, our intelligence services, and all our agencies to cooperate as fully as possible with our partners so that both they and we have greater self-defense capabilities." Trump loves to bash California to rally the base. 'Let 'em take out' L.A. is just the latest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
20:53:09 UTC
05:53:09 KST

Trump loves to bash California to rally the base. ‘Let ’em take out’ L.A. is just the latest
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
WASHINGTON — As President Trump zigzags across the country in the final weeks before the midterm elections, he has made California his favorite foil as he tries to fire up his base.
On Monday, he blamed the Golden State for the rising cost of gas prices, claimed without evidence that its elections are rigged, and at a Nebraska rally suggested Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego.
“It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe,” Trump said. “They can take out a city, let them take out Los Angeles, let them take out San Diego. This is a very small price to pay.”
The president’s team on Tuesday said his remarks were misunderstood, arguing the president “clearly” stated that U.S. cities would have been threatened “if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped.” Trump declined to clarify what he meant by his statements when asked by a reporter Tuesday.
But by then, Trump’s remarks had already drawn fierce condemnation from California leaders, including Republican Jim Desmond, a Navy veteran running in a highly competitive race that is key to helping Republicans retain control of the House.
“I vehemently disagree with President Trump’s comments,” Desmond wrote on social media. “America must stand up to Iran and defend our interests, but the first responsibility of our Commander in Chief is to protect the American people and our homeland.”
The backlash exposed the risk of Trump’s closing midterm strategy. Bashing California is a reliable applause line in red states like Nebraska, Alabama, Texas and Oklahoma, where the president has been holding rallies trying to ensure his supporters get out to vote. But in this modern era, an incendiary comment can travel fast online and leave Republicans running in competitive districts in awkward spots, trying to distance themselves from Trump.
Trump made the remarks during a rambling speech in which he said gas prices would be lower soon, touted his ouster of Venezuela’s dictator, and made attacks on news outlets.
Overall, political observers see the episode as an example of how the president’s political strategy can be unpredictable at a time when Republicans are trying to control the message the most.
“Whether you like Trump or not, he is good at getting his message out and coming up with a message that can resonate and catch fire,” said Mindy Romero, founder and director of the nonpartisan Center for Inclusive Democracy. “I think the question now is: Is he starting to fail himself when it comes to his messaging?”
California Democrats were quick to use Trump’s remarks as a line of attack against him. Gov. Gavin Newsom called him “deranged and dangerous” and opened the state emergency operations center to assess potential threats. San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria told Trump to “keep our city out of your reckless war talk.” And Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said his comments could “potentially compromise our safety.”
Trump’s remarks about the California cities on Monday were the most striking example yet of the president using California as a foil to rally a base in GOP strongholds.
In Nebraska and other red states in recent days, Trump has repeatedly cast California as a political boogeyman as a means to motivate voters to cast their ballots for the GOP candidates.
At an Oklahoma rally last week, Trump told the crowd that Republicans need to keep the party in control of Congress so that his administration can continue the work of combating fraud in blue states, like California. The administration’s efforts, led by Vice President JD Vance, have sometimes been overestimated or nebulous.
But Trump tells supporters that in places like California, the administration is seeing “billions and billions of dollars of fraud.”
In a social media post Monday, Trump began blaming the cost of fuel — a defining issue for voters this election cycle — on states like California.
“What’s driving up Gasoline is no longer the Strait of Hormuz,” Trump wrote. The issue, he said, is refineries being “closed up in Blue States, like California, by the Dumocrats.”
Hours later, while rallying in Nebraska, Trump seemed to contradict himself as he promised the crowd that fuel costs would go down once the war in Iran was over.
“That will end very quickly, one way or the other, very soon, maybe a little after the election, maybe a little before, but it is going to end very soon,” Trump said. “When that happens, the oil will come tumbling down.”
Trump’s messaging underscores how the war with Iran, which has gas prices topping $6 a gallon, has emerged as a potential liability for Republicans that the president is trying to address in subtle ways.
Polling on Trump’s handling of the economy has remained low, even among Republicans. A University of Massachusetts Amherst poll last month found that only 22% of Americans perceive the economy in a good or fair state.
In California, a poll by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies, co-sponsored by The Times, found that 70% of California voters disapprove of Trump’s decision to go to war in Iran, including 1 in 5 Republicans.
The softening of Trump’s approval even among those who still support his performance could translate into lower GOP turnout in the state’s few competitive races, the poll’s director, Mark DiCamillo, said.
Trump’s strategy in the final stretch before the midterms has largely focused on rallying the base in hopes that they will turn out to vote. Part of that strategy includes using California as a punching bag.
One particular line of attack has been disparaging the state’s voting systems. He suggested Monday that Democrat-led cities are trying to cheat in November as he touted the fast count of ballots in foreign countries.
“In Detroit, Philadelphia, California and numerous other U.S. Cities and States, the results, with much smaller numbers, will often take weeks to Rig, I mean, calculate,” Trump wrote on Monday. “Voting in America is CORRUPT!!!”
In another social media post, he said: “California: Took 38 days with 16.1 million ballots in 2024.”’
Trump using California as a foil for any given issue could be a risky strategy, Romero said.
“He’s expanding the types of things that he’s blaming California for, like the gas crisis,” she said, arguing that such statements could “start to lose credibility with those people that he has credibility with.”
For Republican voters in California, the ploy may be even riskier, especially when Trump suggests Iran could “take out” their cities.
“I don’t think that message necessarily plays well here because Californians are Californians,” DiCamillo said. “There is a certain pride in being a Californian, certainly not held by everybody ... but I would think that the mainstream would be defending the state.”

India's central bank raises rates by 25bps for first time in nearly four years
As per Reuters:
The Indian central bank raised its benchmark repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.5% on Wednesday, marking the first rise in nearly four years amid mounting inflation and strong economic growth.
The central bank also signalled further rate hikes by changing its stance from "neutral" to "calibrated tightening", but Governor Sanjay Malhotra said the extent and timing of any more increases would be contingent on actual inflation and growth outcomes.
India has joined major central banks in raising rates as higher oil prices triggered by the Iran war fuel inflation, squeeze purchasing power and weigh on currencies.
Weak monsoon rains linked to El Niño have compounded price pressures in Asia's third-largest economy.
The six-member rate panel voted unanimously in favour of the rate hike. Nearly 60% of economists in a Reuters poll had expected a 25 bps increase in the repo rate.

How do you build more homes without the resources available?
Just following on from the Housing Industry Association's (HIA) press release today about the shortfall in Australia's housing target and the billions of dollars of economic activity that could have occurred if the housing target was being met.
Back in July the HIA's own quarterly Trades Report, which provides a quarterly assessment of skilled labour availability in residential construction, said Australia simply doesn't have enough builders to meet demand.
It estimated that Australia needed an additional 83,000 skilled tradespeople if it was to build enough homes to meet the nation's housing needs.
"While conditions improved slightly over the quarter, trade shortages remain substantially worse than a year ago and continue to constrain the industry's capacity to build the homes Australia needs," it said.
"Skilled trades are still in high demand because builders are still working through a substantial pipeline of homes that were sold many months ago and are awaiting commencement.
"Even if new work entering the pipeline slows in the short term, Australia's underlying housing shortage has not disappeared.
"Australia continues to face strong population growth, historically low unemployment, tight rental markets and growing demand for construction workers from renovations, transport infrastructure, energy projects, data centres and preparations for the Brisbane Olympics.
“These competing demands are expected to place ongoing pressure on the residential construction workforce once current market uncertainty passes."
So, when you frame the conversation in terms of the resources available to build things, rather than the financing, it puts things in a different perspective.
To build the homes we need to meet the national housing target what other construction projects should be deprioritised to free up the resources?

Housing target shortfall an $11 billion black hole for states and territories
The Housing Industry Association (HIA) says today's ABS data on dwelling commencements has provided an opportunity to see how Australia is tracking in its National Housing Accord and its 1.2 million homes target.
It says after the first two full years of the accord, data shows that we're currently 94,980 dwellings behind target.
It says that shortfall translates into billions of dollars of economic activity that could have occurred, but didn't.
HIA managing director Jocelyn Martin says:
“Not only does this equate to a significant shortfall in meeting the new homes target, but it also represents $45 billion in economic activity that the building shortfall would have generated had it occurred.
"The shortfall of homes could have housed potentially 242,160 Australians based on average household sizes.
“In addition, what can’t be undersold is the economic activity that is generated by residential construction, creating jobs and benefits that flow throughout the economy.
“On top of this, governments generate significant revenue from taxation on housing. Where housing construction does not occur, the capacity of governments to generate revenue and deliver services to the community is diminished."
It says using the shortfall against housing targets and reflecting state and territory taxation regimes, it estimates that nationally $2.8 billion of stamp duty and $8.2 billion of GST was not generated and collected during this two-year period.
It says that extra revenue could have funded the equivalent of 43,455 essential workers Australia-wide over the last two years.
“New housing is revenue positive to government, whereas additional taxation as we saw in this year’s federal budget will only serve to reduce supply," Ms Martin says.
“While the building activity results for the June 2026 quarter showed improvement, this is more an indication of approvals and sales from 2025 and does not reflect the budget changes with respect to housing taxation or interest rate rises this year – the effects of which we expect to become evident on the ground in 2027.
“With headwinds of potentially further interest rate rises and uncertainty caused by international events, this reinforces the need for governments and other policymakers to reduce the costs of land and housing if Australia is to meet its long-term housing needs."
Now, what the HIA didn't mention in that press release is inflation.
It also didn't mention the current shortage of workers in the building industry, nor the high construction costs that the industry has struggled with in recent years.
One can appreciate the argument the HIA is making, but when thinking of the economy's available resources at this moment, in the context of the fiery political debate about inflation, would their counter-factual world have been possible? We'll never know.

But host David Taylor followed up by asking: "Surely there's a simple logic here ... if you cut migration that much, it hurts productivity".

He also said "it depends on how the program is made up" and "what it consists of".
"Do we get the skills where we need to get them? Are they in really specific areas?" he said.
"We're short of engineers. We're 42,000 engineers short before the data centre boom occurred.
"Will it get people in construction to build the houses we need?
"Will it provide the cyber security specialists that we need?
"Will it provide the abattoir workers that we need?
"That's where the rubber will hit the road around how this impacts not just productivity, but our economy more broadly."

Cornell names Sally Yates to review university’s response to rape case
Yates will examine Cornell’s sexual assault investigations, disciplinary process and campus police response.
Cornell University trustees have named former United States Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates to conduct an independent internal review of how the university handles allegations of sexual assault and harassment, following widespread criticism over its response to a former student’s rape allegations.
The trustees announced on Tuesday that Yates will examine how Cornell investigates reports of sexual misconduct and assault, its disciplinary procedures, campus police responses and the university’s oversight of fraternities.
Yates served as deputy attorney general during the administration of former President Barack Obama and as acting attorney general at the start of Donald Trump’s first presidency. Trump fired her in 2017 after she directed Justice Department lawyers not to defend his initial travel ban that targeted Muslim-majority countries.
“It is imperative that Cornell be willing to examine itself with the same rigor we expect of others,” Cornell Board of Trustees Chair Anne Meinig Smalling said in a statement.
The appointment comes after renewed criticism of Cornell’s handling of allegations made by a woman, identified in court filings as Jane Doe, who said she was sexually assaulted by multiple members of the Chi Phi fraternity in October 2024.
The case resurfaced after Doe filed a civil lawsuit against the university, the fraternity and seven former students in September.
No criminal charges have been filed in the case. Cornell has said it expelled some students and suspended others who were accused following its own investigation, while the Chi Phi chapter was shut down.
“We don’t have all the answers, but we are committed to investigating and finding the answers our community deserves,” Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff said in a video message on Saturday.
Yates, now a partner at the law firm King & Spalding, conducts independent investigations and previously led a 2022 investigation into sexual abuse and misconduct in the National Women’s Soccer League that found systemic failures.
New York Attorney General Letitia James is separately conducting a criminal investigation into the allegations after Governor Kathy Hochul appointed her special prosecutor last week.
Hochul had called for an independent review of Cornell’s handling of the case amid criticism from students, faculty and others.

Till 4 pm, no political party had sought an appointment, EC said
NEW DELHI: Election Commission on Tuesday, while willing to meet the 240 opposition party MPs at their request conveyed through Delhi Police, declined to do so at their suggested venue of Parliament House annexe, saying the poll panel's protocol required such meetings to be held only on EC premises and based on a request from the parties' authorised representative."EC considered this request as unusual and therefore, it could not be accepted," the panel said in a statement.As an alternative, EC proposed that its most senior officer on duty could be sent to the meeting venue to receive a memorandum, "which in itself would have been an unprecedented step", said an EC spokesperson. However, this offer was declined by the MPs.While emphasising that any political party may request for a meeting with EC, which would then schedule a date and time, the commission said it must balance its respect for parliamentary and democratic processes with that for its own protocols and conventions, "which are of utmost importance".EC said during the march by certain political parties towards Nirvachan Sadan, "it was learnt through the media that some MPs wished to meet the commission along with their delegation"."It is clarified that, till 4pm, no political party, through its representatives, had sought an appointment for a meeting with EC," the commission said. EC said around 4pm, information was received from police that a delegation of MPs led by Rahul Gandhi wished to meet and submit a memorandum.
Referring to the procedure laid down in 2025 for meetings with political parties, EC said if a delegation wishes to meet, it seeks an appointment through its authorised representative. The meeting is thereafter held at a time mutually agreed upon by both sides. "This is a regular practice," EC said.When the panel was considering the proposal, it was informed by the Delhi Police DCP that the meeting was sought to be held with 240 MPs and the proposed venue was the Parliament House annexe, it said. "EC, considering its protocol to meet political parties only on its own premises and its procedure to only schedule such meetings in consultation with the parties' authorised representative, declined the offer," it said.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Drone operators tracked down and destroyed the military vehicle while it was transporting anti-aircraft guided missiles intended to reload the Buk-M3 missile system.
This marks the only confirmed loss of this specific equipment modification.
This precision strike builds on a series of coordinated operations by Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces aimed at systematically degrading Russian air defense and radar infrastructure.
In a broader operation coordinated through their Deep Strike Center, Ukrainian drone units struck a Russian uncrewed surface vessel base in temporarily occupied Crimea while simultaneously targeting radar stations and air defenses across occupied regions and inside Russia.

Ukraine cuts more than 4,000 vacant government posts and trims deputy ministers by about 20% in the first stage of civil service reform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
20:47:23 UTC
05:47:23 KST

Ukraine is thinning its state bureaucracy. Central government bodies will cut more than 4,000 vacant positions in the first stage of a civil service reform, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi says, with the number of deputy ministers to fall by about 20% and deputy heads of other central bodies by nearly 18%.
The reform aims to build a professional state apparatus that can carry out tasks quickly and effectively, Koretskyi said. It comes as Ukraine faces an economic crunch, and about $20 billion in EU aid is on hold, blocked by reforms Kyiv has not completed.
The cuts are only the visible first step, and the final headcount is not set yet. The number of deputies will be tied to the volume of tasks each office carries, Koretskyi states.
"The most important thing is that we are running a functional diagnostic of the state apparatus," he continues.
The Ukrainian government will assess which functions the bodies have and whether they align with the state's realities and priorities, and only then will it define the structure and final headcount.
Training is tied to the job
Another track reshapes how officials learn. Training will be linked to the tasks of each specific post, with outreach and internships for young people and a separate program for veterans, Koretskyi says.
The Public Administration Council, which brings together officials, members of parliament, and experts, has resumed work, presenting a detailed plan on the task and assigning responsibility for each area.
The squeeze that forces the cuts
The reform lands in a tight budget. The war is costing Ukraine about $155 billion a year, and with Western aid running late, Kyiv has frozen almost everything except the army, pensions, and public wages.
On 1 October, the state suspended a veterans' gym subsidy that had cost about $13 million and drawn more than 800,000 users, for lack of funds.

In Germany, the number of conscientious objectors to military service tripled in a year - DW
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
23:46:04 EEST
05:46:04 KST

In Germany, the number of conscientious objectors to military service tripled in a year - DW
Kyiv • UNN
By the end of August, more than 12,000 applications for conscientious objection to military service had been submitted in Germany. The reasons cited include the security situation and the law on the new military service system.
The number of conscientious objectors to military service in Germany is steadily increasing. By the end of August, more than 12,000 applications had already been submitted. This is three times more than during the entire previous year. DW reports this, according to UNN.
Details
It is noted that the strength of this trend is illustrated by a comparison with the figures from the middle of the year: by the end of June 2026, the Federal Office had reported receiving 5,862 applications. Thus, their number doubled in just two months.
The tense security situation and the law on new military service, which came into force on January 1, are likely the reasons for this increase. The measure is based on mandatory military service registration for young men born in 2008 or later. It is intended to attract volunteers to expand the armed forces. All German citizens will receive questionnaires in the year they turn 18 to assess their fitness for military service
It is indicated that completing the questionnaire is mandatory for men, while it is voluntary for women and people with other gender identities. At the same time, there is still no general obligation to perform military service after this. Men who could potentially be subject to conscription have the right to refuse armed military service on grounds of conscience pursuant to Article 4, paragraph 3, of the German Constitution.
At the same time, the military reports serious problems with many applications. There is currently a "large number of improperly submitted applications that contain insufficient information and therefore have to be returned without consideration".
We remind you
In September, school students in Germany held around 100 protest rallies against compulsory military service.

Why Flavio Bolsonaro outperformed the polls in Brazil’s election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
20:44:12 UTC
05:44:12 KST

Why Flavio Bolsonaro outperformed the polls in Brazil’s election
A late right-wing shift, a banking scandal and economic frustration may be behind Bolsonaro’s last-minute gains, experts say.
With three weeks to go until Brazil’s presidential runoff, President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva finds himself in a weaker position than he — or most pollsters — had expected.
A second round of voting was widely predicted. But most recent polls had Lula entering a runoff from first place, putting him about three percentage points ahead of rival Senator Flavio Bolsonaro.
Instead, Bolsonaro took about 47 percent of the vote on Sunday to Lula’s 45 percent, a reversal that surprised analysts and raised questions about what happened in the final days of the campaign, and what the polls may have missed.
What changed in the final days
Carlos Pereira, a political scientist at the Getulio Vargas Foundation think-tank in Brazil, believes part of the answer lies in a late shift among voters who had planned to support smaller right-wing candidates.
Bolsonaro himself had said he was banking on exactly that, telling reporters on election day that he expected a “protest vote” from people who might have otherwise backed another candidate but were united in their opposition to Lula.
“Usually, voters, they vote [sincerely] in the first round, and they vote strategically in the second round,” Pereira told Al Jazeera.
This time, he said, some voters who were planning to cast their ballot for candidates like the former governor of the central state of Goias, Ronaldo Caiado, and businessman and founder of the right-wing Free Brazil Movement, Renan Santos, appear to have made the strategic choice earlier.
“They thought, ‘Let’s try to resolve this election right now,’” Pereira said. “If you’re gonna vote for Flavio anyway in the second round, why not vote for him right now?”
That early consolidation could also matter in the runoff. Political analyst Rafael Favetti told Reuters news agency that some of the support Bolsonaro would have usually picked up only in a second round had already been “front-loaded,” potentially leaving him less room to expand his coalition.
Another factor, Pereira said, was the Banco Master scandal, a sprawling alleged banking fraud that rattled both campaigns in the final weeks, touching figures across the political spectrum.
Among them was Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who oversaw the case that sent Bolsonaro’s father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, to prison. De Moraes was accused of improper ties to Banco Master owner Daniel Vorcaro after documents emerged appearing to show the banker seeking legal advice from him. De Moraes has denied the allegations.
Pereira believes that connection may have acted as a late “trigger” for some voters. Bolsonaro’s supporters have seen Moraes as a political ally of Lula, with Flavio making a direct link between the two on the campaign trail earlier this year, saying, “Anyone voting for Lula is voting for Alexandre de Moraes.”
A September Datafolha poll found 34 percent of Brazilians associated the Banco Master scandal more with the left, compared with 27 percent who associated it more with the right.
Andre Pagliarini, a professor of history and international studies at Louisiana State University and author of Lula: A People’s President and the Fight for Brazil’s Future, agreed the scandal may have hurt the president. A campaign dominated by “spectacular, unceasing scandal involving seemingly the entire political class”, he said, played to Bolsonaro’s strengths as an “anti-institutional insurgent”.
“The irony, of course, is that Flavio himself was directly implicated in the Banco Master scandal in a way that Lula is not,” he said in an email.
The younger Bolsonaro is under investigation over allegations that he sought money from Vorcaro to finance a film about his father. He denies wrongdoing.
A broader shift to the right
Neither analyst saw the result as a wholesale failure of the polls.
For Pagliarini, the bigger surprise was the scale of support for the right, which extended well beyond the presidential race.
Bolsonaro won nearly four percentage points more than his father did in the first round in 2022, while his Liberal Party emerged with the largest bloc in Brazil’s Senate. The right also came out strong in gubernatorial races and made significant gains in the southeast of the country.
“There clearly was a powerful information environment around Flavio that allowed his campaign to keep its message in front of voters even as the mainstream press exposed scandal after scandal,” said Pagliarini. “If anything, the polls underestimated the commitment of voters already leaning right.”
But the results also point to a deeper challenge for Lula and the Brazilian left: a sense among many voters that the government is not delivering enough, particularly on the economy and public security.
On paper, Lula can point to a number of positive economic indicators, like record-low unemployment, falling inequality and easing inflation. But that hasn’t necessarily translated into a sense that life is getting easier, as Brazilians have continued to feel squeezed by high food prices and household debt.
A September Quaest poll found nearly half of those surveyed believed the economy had gotten worse over the previous year, compared with just 19 percent who thought it had improved.
“Voters can acknowledge that poverty is down and unemployment is low and still feel overworked, indebted, unsafe and fed up with political conflict,” Pagliarini said. “The right has figured out how to turn those frustrations into a very clear political identity.”
An uphill battle for Lula
Lula now has three weeks to close a gap of about 2.2 million votes. And there are millions potentially up for grabs.
About nine million votes went to other candidates in the first round, while more than 33.4 million Brazilians didn’t vote – 28 percent of registered voters.
“It’s possible, but the arithmetic is tough,” Pagliarini said.
For Lula to turn things around, he’d need to win voters who backed minor candidates, reach some of those who abstained and find more support in the northeast, which is already his strongest region.
His campaign is preparing a new communications team. Pargliarini said he’ll be watching the debates, where Lula could make a case directly against Bolsonaro rather than against his brand.
“The odds are steep, but Lula remains an extremely powerful communicator,” he said. “Going hard at Flavio in this round is his only hope.”

US lawmakers call on Israel to release imprisoned doctor Hussam Abu Safia
Letter from progressive US representatives brings attention to Israeli abuse and detention of Palestinian medical workers.
A group of six progressive Congress members in the United States have released a statement condemning Israel’s abuse of Palestinian healthcare workers, including the Gaza doctor Hussam Abu Safia, who has been held in Israeli detention since 2024.
The Tuesday statement draws attention to Israeli attacks on Palestinian medical workers, who have been targeted and detained during the country’s genocidal war on Gaza.
It was signed by Representatives Rashida Tlaib, Ilhan Omar, Jesus “Chuy” Garcia, Summer Lee, Pramila Jayapal and Delia Ramirez.
“Over the last three years, the Israeli government has systematically destroyed the health system in Palestine, murdering at least 1,700 Palestinian doctors, nurses, paramedics, and other healthcare workers and destroying dozens of hospitals,” the statement reads.
“It has arrested and arbitrarily detained hundreds of Palestinian healthcare workers, including at least 16 physicians who continue to be held in inhumane conditions.”
Among those detained is Abu Safia, who lawyers say was subjected to abuses such as torture, sleep deprivation and beatings during his detention.
Israeli soldiers arrested Abu Safia in December 2024, after he and other medical workers reportedly refused to evacuate from Kamal Adwan Hospital, where they worked.
No charges have been filed against Abu Safia, and he has not had a trial.
Israeli attacks on health infrastructure in Gaza, including the destruction of nearly all of the strip’s hospitals and medical centres, are one component of what rights groups have depicted as an effort to deprive Palestinians of essential services such as food, water and medical treatment.
Tuesday’s statement argues that such efforts are part of an “intentional policy designed to further occupation, apartheid, and genocide against the Palestinian people”.
That assessment is shared by a growing number of rights organisations, scholars and United Nations officials, who have denounced Israeli actions in the Palestinian strip.
Israeli officials have stated that they target hospitals and medical facilities as part of an effort to attack the Palestinian armed groups that allegedly use such facilities to carry out and coordinate operations.
Such claims have often failed to withstand scrutiny. Israel admitted that its soldiers killed a group of 15 emergency workers in southern Gaza in March 2025, after initially stating that the ambulance convoy had approached soldiers “suspiciously” and claiming, without evidence, that several of those killed were linked to Hamas.
A report by the group Forensic Architecture and Earshot found that Israeli soldiers fired more than 900 bullets as they opened fire on a clearly marked ambulance convoy and killed some of the medics “execution-style” before burying their bodies and their vehicles.
