Karaganov: Russia can win a nuclear war in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
20:39:19 UTC
05:39:19 KST

Karaganov: Russia must be prepared to use nuclear weapons
The debate on the use of nuclear weapons has moved into the practical realm, so while NATO is discussing the Russian Foreign Ministry’s warning of a full-spectrum response in the event of an attempt to blockade Kaliningrad Region, Russian experts are discussing nuclear deterrence and President Vladimir Putin’s speech at the Valdai Forum last week.
Russia must be prepared to use nuclear weapons in cases of extreme necessity.
Responding to questions about nuclear weapons, Putin recalled the saying that if a gun is hanging on the wall, it will eventually go off, but the Russian leader called for such a scenario to be avoided.
“At the heart of this escalation lie arrogance and overconfidence. This is a path to the brink of the abyss. All the more so today, when the arsenals of the world’s leading powers contain weapons capable of destroying all life or, at the very least, reducing the Earth to a catastrophic state. We are all familiar with the well-known saying: if a gun is hanging on a wall somewhere on stage at the beginning of a play, it is bound to go off eventually. We must bear this in mind,” said the president.
As Putin emphasized, Russia understands that in the event of a direct attack by NATO countries, “the enemy will be twice as numerous and have far greater economic potential” and Russia’s competitive advantage lies in the fact that no one else in the world possesses such weapons of destruction, he noted.
“How can we stand up to an aggressor? We are not a threat to anyone. We are simply saying that we do not have all that many means of defending ourselves. We will have to use our competitive advantages in this struggle,” concluded Putin.
Why do we need nuclear weapons?
Tensions and conflicts between countries are on the rise worldwide and the West, particularly the EU, having suffered a strategic defeat, is desperate for revenge. Nuclear weapons are necessary to prevent major wars, but this only works if the threat is taken seriously, and at present far too many people have forgotten what a nuclear war entails, so they treat the matter lightly.
Many, particularly Western European politicians, want war; they are actively whipping up military hysteria in their own countries. For the time being, they are acting through the Ukrainians, but they have also begun actively stirring up their own populations.
The Western European elites must be punished for their aggressive policies, meaning Ukraine must be crushed and demilitarized, while the purely Russian regions must be reunited with Russia and an EU that has lost its mind must begin to truly fear.
Without the active use of nuclear deterrence, this can’t be achieved. Now, I hope it will never come to that, but Russia must be prepared, in the event of absolute necessity, to use nuclear weapons effectively and victoriously.
How effective is nuclear deterrence?
Nuclear deterrence has weakened considerably. First, decades have passed not only since the US first used nuclear weapons in combat against Japan, but also since the last known tests. Secondly, the Americans have for a long time deliberately downplayed the role of nuclear weapons in order to emphasize their advantages in other areas of armaments.
Furthermore, people’s mindsets and public sentiment have changed, given that we, the older generation, particularly in Russia, are more acutely aware of the threat of nuclear war, and of war in general, and have therefore been seriously committed to the cause of peace. In the past, it was almost considered improper even to speak of the possible use of nuclear weapons.
Now circumstances have changed significantly and that’s precisely why we need to step up nuclear deterrence and intimidation to the point of being genuinely prepared, God forbid, to use nuclear weapons to prevent a larger-scale war.
Seeking peace through non-nuclear means alone could prove far too costly for Russia and it would be a shame to sacrifice the health and lives of our men simply to quell the aggression of those same Western Europeans.
What would be the consequences of using nuclear weapons?
The reaction of the international community would have to be disregarded because it makes absolutely no difference what the rest of the world thinks or says.
Nevertheless, it would pose a huge moral problem, as the use of nuclear weapons is a grave sin, but, unfortunately, there is very little hope that these Europeans will come to their senses without coming face to face with the threat of nuclear annihilation.
If we refuse to use nuclear weapons, as many are calling for, including here in our own country, we will deprive ourselves and the world of the most effective tool for preventing war and give aggressors free rein, but they can only be restrained by the threat of their use.
If nuclear weapons were used, there would be other negative consequences as even a limited and effective nuclear war would remove the taboo on other countries using nuclear weapons in their own regional conflicts, so I therefore continue to regard such use as a last resort.
Why is the European Union preparing for war with Russia?
There are two reasons for the aggressive anti-Russian sentiment in the EU. First, Western European elites have deteriorated significantly during the period of relative peace in the second half of the 20th century, although we hope that not all of them are complete madmen.
And secondly, they are trying to stir up military hysteria in order to distract their peoples from widespread failures and thereby retain power.
Under these circumstances, it would be sensible and rational for us to strengthen our reliance on nuclear weapons and modernize our arsenal, particularly the part of it aimed at other European countries. At the same time, it is important to continue dialogue with the US in order to avoid a global nuclear conflict.
Nuclear weapons have safeguarded us for 80 years since the end of the Second World War. Nuclear deterrence is the main reason why, throughout these decades, the states of Europe, and subsequently the European Union, have remained relatively peaceful. Throughout their history, they have repeatedly attacked not only Russia but also a vast number of countries across the globe, and they are the primary cause of many of humanity’s misfortunes, such as racism and colonialism.
Western Europe is now returning to its usual state, which is a belligerent one and this means the time has come to remind these Europeans once again who they are and what their belligerence leads to. If the current Ukrainian or German regime, or any other non-nuclear country in Europe, were to acquire nuclear weapons, we would be obliged to launch a preemptive strike because we’d have to stop them. It would be a short war, as a result of which these countries would cease to exist.
Is it possible to win a nuclear war?
It’s possible to win a nuclear war in Europe because the US will never risk its own territory for the sake of the Europeans. If France or the UK continue to stick their necks out, a preemptive, devastating strike could be launched against them. But, I repeat, God forbid.
I hope Western Europe comes to its senses and that this can be avoided. In the meantime, much of Europe should be placed behind a security cordon and a security system should be built within the framework of Greater Eurasia, excluding the Western subcontinent. That said, it will be possible and necessary to cooperate with individual European countries if they shake off the rule of the current madmen in Brussels and Berlin.

your childhood barbie could become gomi’s next marbled speaker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
20:35:05 UTC
05:35:05 KST

your childhood barbie could become gomi’s next marbled speaker
brighton studio gomi melts discarded barbie dolls and accessories into marbled electronics with spiraling colors.
gomi melts old Barbie dolls into marbled consumer tech
A Barbie doll that has spent years in the back of a closet could soon reappear as a Bluetooth speaker. Brighton-based design studio gomi has teamed up with Barbie on the Childhood Memories Collection, a limited series of electronics made partly from dolls and accessories that have reached the end of their time in the toy box. The familiar pinks and candy-colored plastics are melted down, remixed and pressed into gomi’s swirling marbled surfaces, leaving traces of their earlier lives visible in the material itself.
The project starts with the toys themselves. gomi is asking people to send in Barbie and Ken dolls they have stopped using, then processing the recovered plastic at its Brighton workshop. Those materials are blended with discarded plastic bags, a waste stream commonly left out of household recycling, before being shaped into the studio’s housings. Each batch produces its own color distribution and pattern, so every piece comes out differently.
childhood plastic gets a second life
There is something special and quite literal about turning a toy into the casing of another object you might keep around for years. Rather than disguising the recycled material, gomi lets it become the visual character of the collection. Flecks of saturated pink, pale blue and other colors meet in dense swirls across the surfaces, giving the products the irregular appearance that has become part of the studio’s language.
gomi continues the same approach inside. The speakers and power banks use repurposed e-bike batteries, while their housings are assembled with screws in place of glue. Components can therefore be opened up, replaced and repaired as they age. gomi also plans to offer trade-ins and upgrades, allowing parts to move into future products instead of reaching landfill after a single use cycle.
a collection made one object at a time
Handmade production gives the collaboration a scale closer to a small design edition than a conventional electronics launch. The Childhood Memories Collection will arrive through monthly limited releases, with each object shaped by whatever recycled material enters the workshop. Two pieces may share the same silhouette, yet their surfaces retain different mixtures of color and fragments.
That variation is also where the Barbie connection becomes most interesting. The collaboration avoids simply applying the brand’s color palette to an existing product. Barbie itself becomes part of the raw material. A plastic object once designed for imaginative play moves into a speaker or charging accessory, still colorful and recognizable in fragments, though its function has changed completely.
project info:
name: Childhood Memories Collection
brand: gomi | @gomidesign, Barbie | @barbie
launch: September 2026

Satellite images reveal renewed activity at nuclear site Israel struck in Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
20:31:01 UTC
05:31:01 KST

High-resolution satellite images from VANTOR Technologies taken in September and October 2026 showed significant renewed activity at Min-Zadayi, a nuclear weapons development complex in northeast Tehran that was exposed and attacked by Israel during Operation Roaring Lion. Several buildings, and apparently underground structures as well, were destroyed in the strike, according to a report published by the Institute for Science and International Security.
The latest satellite images indicated the return of regular vehicle traffic around the site following an extensive cleanup operation that included removing rubble and debris and repairing damage to the hillside. In one area struck in March 2026, ongoing earthworks can be seen. The work is taking place on a surface designed to resemble a courtyard, where numerous craters were visible after the attacks on the site.
A significant presence of vehicles was observed throughout the site between early September and early October 2026. Cars were parked outside the security fence in a lot, while numerous private vehicles and trucks were seen inside the compound. Given what is known about the site, this activity may indicate an Iranian effort to restore a nuclear weapons development capability and recover what was lost in the attack on the complex.
According to the institute’s report, based on public reporting and statements issued by the IDF, the nuclear weapons work carried out there likely included research and development of nuclear warheads. The IDF originally said that “a group of nuclear scientists operated covertly to develop a key component of the nuclear weapons program,” adding that “the complex was intended to enable the restoration of the required technology and the advancement of capabilities for developing nuclear weapons.”
The X account @IntelliTimes published additional information about the complex. In a post dated Sept. 24, 2026, it claimed that infrastructure related to nuclear weapons had been established in 2022 and “absorbed some of the means from the nuclear warehouse” — a common reference to the Turquzabad site, which was exposed by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in September 2018.
Netanyahu disclosed the site after Iran removed more than a dozen shipping containers from it, which were believed to contain nuclear material and equipment relevant to Iran’s nuclear weapons capabilities.
When the International Atomic Energy Agency visited Turquzabad in March 2019, it found evidence that nuclear material or contaminated equipment had been present at the site. Since then, the IAEA Board of Governors has pressed Iran to answer the agency’s questions about the current location of that material or equipment.
According to @IntelliTimes, Iran did not simply transfer the material or equipment to a new long-term storage site. Instead, it used the Min-Zadayi site in northeast Tehran to establish “an industrial nuclear command center for restoring the research, development and adaptation infrastructure for nuclear warheads,” including the means “to produce cores of enriched uranium and the explosive material required to cast the initiation chain into them.”
During rounds of fighting with Iran, extensive strikes were carried out against nuclear targets in the country. In late June 2025, the United States led a massive strike using B-2 bombers and Tomahawk missiles that hit Iran’s three main nuclear sites — Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan.
Following the attack, Iran formally acknowledged heavy damage to its facilities in July 2025, while the IDF released satellite images and assessed that the operations had succeeded in setting the nuclear program back by years. At the same time, the Israeli Air Force destroyed significant components at the Isfahan facility, though Western intelligence officials cautioned that the bombers’ impact had been limited mainly to external structures and tunnel entrances.
Despite months of prolonged fighting, former senior officials and intelligence agencies warned that the strikes had damaged the program but had not eliminated it entirely. Professional assessments published in August 2026 showed that most of Iran’s stockpile of uranium enriched to 60% remained intact, and that the Iranian regime had moved thousands of advanced centrifuges to protected underground sites deep inside the mountains.
That reality led, as reported in September 2026, to an acceleration in U.S. preparations for additional targeted strikes aimed at preventing Iran from breaking out to a nuclear weapon.

On Wednesday, EU ambassadors will approve the largest package of sanctions against Russia since 2022 - Reuters
Kyiv • UNN
The package will contain around 1,650 sanctions, mainly targeting Russia’s defense industry. More than half of the restrictions will concern missile manufacturers.
European Union ambassadors will approve a new sweeping package of sanctions against Russia on Wednesday, October 7. Reuters reports this, citing European diplomats, UNN informs.
Details
The package will reportedly include around 1,650 new sanctions designations against Russia, most of which concern the Russian defense-industrial complex.
The package, proposed by the EU’s foreign policy body, the European External Action Service, will be the largest since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. After approval by the ambassadors, the lists will be sent to EU foreign ministers next Monday for final approval
It is noted that around 1,570 entries on the new lists are organizations and individuals linked to Russia’s defense-industrial complex. More than half of them are focused on missile production. The sanctions provide for a ban on travel to and transactions with the EU, as well as the freezing of assets.
We remind you
In September, the European Union removed two billionaires from its sanctions list concerning Russia, while extending the sanctions against the remaining 3,000 individuals and legal entities for another three years.

Trump says Republicans will 'do very well' in Nov. 3 midterm elections

Trump is not on the ballot in the US Congress’ midterm elections, but hundreds of members of the House of Representatives and Senate are.
The number of seats Trump's Republican Party wins on Nov. 3 could have a major effect of the remainder of Trump’s term.

Lula campaign scrambles to rebrand before Brazil runoff
- - Lula’s campaign is reworking its message before Brazil’s Oct 25 runoff after he finished about 2.2 million votes behind Flavio Bolsonaro.
- - Allies want to win over millions who did not vote, using a “fear strategy” to warn that a Bolsonaro presidency could threaten social benefits.
- - The Workers’ Party will boost social media, recruit left-wing influencers, and keep key welfare promises, while Lula also plans more radio interviews.
AI generated
BRASILIA - After a bruising first round of Brazil’s presidential election, President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva is rushing to overhaul his campaign communications to engage millions of Brazilians who did not vote, according to people close to the campaign.
Lula finished nearly 2 percentage points – about 2.2 million votes – behind right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in the vote on Oct 4, making the three-term leftist the underdog in an Oct 25 runoff.
As markets cheered Bolsonaro’s odds, Lula’s allies met in Brasilia on Oct 5 to regroup and plan a rebrand.
At the meeting, Lula pushed what is being dubbed internally the “fear strategy” to remind voters of the risks a Bolsonaro presidency he says would pose to popular social benefits.
People close to the campaign say Lula blames the messaging for failing to reach enough young people and women.
Some party figures point to Lula’s social communications minister, Sidonio Palmeira, whose business partner Raul Rebelo runs the campaign’s messaging, for pushing less accessible themes like sovereignty and critical minerals. One TV campaign advert was devoted entirely to rare earths.
Rebelo is staying for now, but Otavio Antunes, a more aggressive strategist, is expected to join the national team, two people with the campaign said.
Lula’s Workers’ Party is courting the 9 million-plus voters who backed minor candidates, but mainly targeting the record 33 million who abstained on Oct 4, which it attributes to apathy rather than opposition to Lula.
A new Workers’ Party social media ad warns that “some losses can’t be undone”, as slips of paper naming government programmes, including one sending doctors to remote areas and above-inflation pension increases, blow from an open hand.
Bolsonaro’s press office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In a recent interview, he pledged to keep Bolsa Familia – Brazil’s flagship cash-transfer programme created by Lula – and let recipients stay on it even after finding formal work or starting a business.
With less than three weeks to go, campaign coordinator Paulo Okamoto said the campaign would build a network of left-leaning influencers to aid the social media push.
Lula himself could prove an obstacle. The 80-year-old does not carry a phone and often criticises screen culture.
While he promised on Oct 5 to make more social videos – which he calls “selfies” – Lula also said he wants to do more radio interviews before the runoff. REUTERS

STRASBOURG — The Greens in the European Parliament chose Terry Reintke and Nicu Ștefănuță as their new leadership team on Tuesday, promising an energetic, campaign-focused push to revive a political group whose influence has diminished since its high-water mark in 2019.
Reintke won another term as co-chair, while Romanian MEP Ștefănuță won the second-place contest over Belgium’s Sara Matthieu and Sweden’s Isabella Lövin.
Reintke cast the result as a mandate for “a very energetic two and a half years,” saying the pair would “do a lot of campaigning” on climate protection, social justice, democracy and the rule of law.
Advertisement
But she also made clear that renewal would not mean a fundamental change of political course.
“Obviously it’s a renewed leadership,” Reintke said. “But we are also going to continue the line on engaging and fighting in this house for everything that we can achieve in the next two and a half years.”
Ștefănuță, meanwhile, presented the new leadership as an attempt to broaden the Greens’ appeal beyond their traditional environmental agenda, pointing to younger voters and bread-and-butter economic concerns.
He said the group had chosen to “invest in dynamism” and a leadership that takes seriously concerns such as “the fact that the cost of living is very high” and problems with energy prices and economic stability.
The pitch is a delicate balancing act: present a sense of renewal ahead of the 2029 European election without abandoning a long-held strategy.
Reintke has led the Greens/EFA group since 2022. Ștefănuță has risen rapidly through its ranks since moving from Renew Europe in March 2023. Nine months later, the group elected him as one of its vice-presidents. He went on to become a vice-president of the European Parliament in July 2024.
Advertisement
The Romanian gives the leadership a different geographical profile, something Reintke herself highlighted after the vote. She said Ștefănuță’s election reflected a desire for greater regional representation and would bring “a broader perspective on the different realities in Europe.”
One of the leadership jobs was opened up by Bas Eickhout’s resignation as co-chair and as an MEP in May. Eickhout said at the time that he had had relationships that were inappropriate for his role and that he took responsibility for them. His departure removed one of the group’s most prominent politicians and triggered an unusually open contest for his replacement.
The two new co-chairs now inherit the task of restoring some of the political weight the Greens enjoyed after the 2019 European election, when the group returned 74 MEPs and became the fourth-largest force in Parliament.
Today, the Greens/EFA have 53 lawmakers and rank sixth.
Reintke suggested that rebuilding those numbers could begin even before voters return to the polls. She said the group has “a strategy of growth” and wants to attract new MEPs, with discussions over possible enlargement expected in the coming months.

Ukraine’s war leadership sets new electronic warfare tasks as Russia’s jet-powered drones slip past nearly half of its air defenses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
20:19:28 UTC
05:19:28 KST

Russia keeps upgrading its jet-powered drones, and Ukraine's electronic warfare is racing to keep up. Kyiv has set extra tasks for its military and manufacturers to scale up the most effective electronic warfare approaches, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said after a meeting of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief's Staff on electronic warfare and infrastructure protection.
Russia keeps modifying its jet-powered Shaheds to beat each new Ukrainian defense, and Ukraine's answers have to keep pace. The race is tight: from 1 to 26 September, air defenses downed only 55 percent of the 2,730 new jet-powered drones, against 90% of the slower ones.
Hidden relays blunt Kyiv's jammers
Jamming has to improve because Russia keeps finding new ways around it. On 3 October, presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said someone had installed Russian MESH radio repeaters in Kyiv, a short control channel that guides Shahed drones onto their targets. As long as they are there, he said, closing the city with electronic warfare will not be effective.
"As long as online control of drones exists, not only the bridges but the air defense assets will be under threat," Flash stressed.
Sanctions aim at the supply chain
Beyond the jamming task, the Staff turned to where Russia gets the parts for those drones. Defense Intelligence reported on Russia's technological priorities for this year and next, and on supplies of critical components and equipment for its weapons production, Zelenskyy said.
New sanctions packages will follow, with Defense Intelligence due to send proposals to the Ukrainian government and the National Security and Defense Council, and Ukraine is working to align its sanctions with partners' jurisdictions.
The Staff also set the main tasks for supplying Ukrainian forces with long-range drones next year.
"The main criterion is that we must be able to respond in kind to Russian strikes," Zelenskyy emphasized.
Those parts, and the drones built from them, keep changing
In August, Intelligence Deputy Chief Vadym Skibitskyi said Russia remained fully dependent on Chinese turbojets for the Geran-4 and Geran-5, each costing about $35,000 to $40,000.
However, two months later, Ukraine reported the Geran-4 had received a locally built engine and a new optical navigation system. Kyiv has to stay attuned to changes to keep pace with the technology race, and so far, it is still trying to catch up rather than get ahead.

Yaakov 'Yaki' Hetz, a hero of the Battle of Ammunition Hill during Six-Day War, dies at 80
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
20:06:06 UTC
05:06:06 KST

Yaakov “Yaki” Hetz, a fighter in the 66th Battalion during the Six-Day War, recipient of the Medal of Courage, winner of the Israel Defense Prize and a torch-lighter at Israel’s 69th Independence Day ceremony, died Tuesday at the age of 80. He was considered one of the heroes of the Battle of Ammunition Hill.
The late Yaki Hetz, born Haymovitz, was 21 during the battle for Ammunition Hill and became one of the symbols of the historic fighting for Jerusalem. During the battle, after his platoon commander Yoram Elyashiv was hit, Hetz took command of the force and continued leading his comrades under heavy fire. He was awarded the Medal of Courage for his bravery and conduct in battle.
Hetz also fought in the Yom Kippur War. Forty years later, he received a special citation for his role in the fighting at the Chinese Farm and for rescuing wounded soldiers in the field while risking his own life.
His story did not end in the trenches of Ammunition Hill. Over the years, Hetz became a figure in defense development and innovation, and as part of his work at Rafael he took part in developing advanced weapons systems.
Among other things, he conceived the idea that led to the development of the “Maoz” system, an advanced attack drone used by IDF troops. The idea grew out of his personal experience as a fighter at Ammunition Hill and from his desire to give future soldiers capabilities that were not available to him and his comrades in 1967.
In 1982, he received the Israel Defense Prize for his defense work, and in 2017 he was chosen to light a torch at the official Independence Day ceremony.
Alongside his military and technological achievements, Hetz devoted himself to heritage, education and remembrance. For decades, he worked to preserve and pass on the story of the fighters for Jerusalem, meeting generations of young people and recounting the battle and the stories of his comrades-in-arms.
In 2023, he published his autobiography, “Baptism by Fire,” in which he described the battle from his personal perspective.
A letter sent by Yaakov Hetz to his family on the second day of the Six-Day War:
Hetz’s story of heroism is commemorated at the Six-Day War Museum at Ammunition Hill, which preserves the story of the war, the battles for Jerusalem and its reunification, and the personal stories of the fighters. His testimony and personal story are part of the legacy passed on to visitors and future generations.
For Ammunition Hill, Hetz was far more than one of the heroes of the battle. He was an integral part of the site’s extended family, one of the generation of fighters who transformed it from a battlefield into a living center of remembrance, heritage and education.
Menachem Landau, chairman of the Ammunition Hill Association, eulogized him: “Yaki Hetz was an inseparable part of Ammunition Hill — not only as one of the heroes of the battle for the liberation and reunification of Jerusalem, but as a man who devoted his life to action, creativity and passing the legacy on to future generations. Yaki was a man of many talents, with vast knowledge, a youthful spirit and endless curiosity. For us, he was far more than a fighter and an Israeli hero — he was family, a partner on the journey and a dear friend.
“His story of heroism is commemorated at the Six-Day War Museum on the hill, but his legacy lives far beyond the museum walls. Today we part from a man whose life story is intertwined with the story of a united Jerusalem, and whose image will continue to accompany us and future generations. Ammunition Hill bows its head at his passing, shares in the family’s grief and painfully bids farewell to an extraordinary man who combined heroism, humility, creativity and a deep commitment to the State of Israel and to future generations.”
Yoav Turgeman, CEO of Rafael, also paid tribute. “The late Yaki Hetz represented the unique Rafael connection between operational experience, engineering thinking and technological vision. He knew how to identify a need on the battlefield, imagine a solution long before the technology made it possible and lead the idea until it became a meaningful operational capability," he said. "His courage and heroism earned him the Medal of Courage, and his innovation and engineering excellence earned him the Israel Defense Prize. The legacy he left behind at Rafael and throughout the defense establishment is one of innovation, determination and, above all, action for the protection of soldiers. We at Rafael will continue to carry his legacy with pride. May his memory be a blessing.”
Dvir Bashan of Yokneam and a member of Mishmar HaEmek also eulogized him.
“Yaki received a citation as a fighter in Brigade 55 in the heroic battle at Ammunition Hill during the Six-Day War, after which he returned to the army and, in the Yom Kippur War, fought as an officer in the terrible battle at the Chinese Farm. For most of his adult life, he worked at Rafael developing weapons systems. As a company commander in the Meitar unit and to this day in the reserves, I was repeatedly exposed to the IDF’s advanced anti-tank array, which for many years was a ‘game changer’ in the army’s preparations for full-scale war, and Yaki was truly at the forefront of its development," according tgo Bashan.
“From many conversations with Yaki, it was clear that he acted out of a personal and national vision, that ‘he who seeks peace must prepare for war,’ and that IDF soldiers should be able to cope better on the battlefield than he and his comrades could with the means available to them. As a son of the moshava, we grew up on his legacy and heroism, but also on the human and family legacy of him, Hani and their eight children — an exemplary family, welcoming and hospitable, always gracious, committed and devoted to ‘Kfar HaHarig’ and its people. Four of his children built their homes here in our regional council.
“Yaki saw passing on the legacy of battle and its lessons — the choice of meaningful service and love of country — as supreme values, and he gave hundreds of lectures at schools, pre-military academies, officers’ courses and elsewhere. Alongside everything he did, everyone will attest that Yaki was, first and foremost, a family man. Yaki was not only part of the landscape of our childhood, our region and our homeland, he was also a man thanks to whom many returned, and continue to return, home safely. May his memory and his life’s work be a blessing.”

Sweden to deploy Patriot air defence systems to Poland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
20:06:03 UTC
05:06:03 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Sweden has announced that it will deploy Patriot air defence systems and around 100 accompanying military personnel to Poland later this year to protect the NATO logistics hub in the city of Rzeszów, which is the main conduit for aid to Ukraine.
The decision follows a number of other recent moves to strengthen defence ties between Stockholm and Warsaw, with Poland’s defence minister today hailing Sweden as an “excellent, proven ally”.
Sweden is deploying the Patriot air defence system to Poland to strengthen the protection of @NATO’s eastern flank. The Swedish forces will protect the logistics hub in south-eastern Poland that plays a key role in providing military and civilian support to Ukraine 🇺🇦. pic.twitter.com/EjGFYFLGnN
— Försvarsmakten (@Forsvarsmakten) October 6, 2026
The Patriot deployment was announced on Tuesday by Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, days after Sweden had also revealed that its Gripen fighter aircraft would patrol Polish airspace from October.
“The task for both the Gripen operation and Patriot [system] is to protect NATO’s logistics hub in Poland at the airport [in Rzeszów],” said Kristersson at a press conference alongside foreign minister Maria Malmer and defence minister Pål Jonson
“[We will] thus ensure that important equipment comes to Ukraine from all the countries that support Ukraine in its defence against Russia,” he added. “This all strengthens NATO, strengthens Europe and strengthens Sweden.”
Jonson added that “repeated violations of allied airspace and Russian attempts to influence support for Ukraine show the importance of protecting the logistics hub in Poland”.
Malmer, meanwhile, made clear that the deployment was intended not only to protect supply lines to Ukraine, but “is also part of our contribution to NATO’s deterrence and defence”.
Sweden will deploy its Patriots to Rzeszów in December and plans for them to remain there until the middle of next year. It will take over the mission from the Netherlands, which has had two of its Patriot batteries in Poland since last December.
Colonel Sofia Westermark, the commander of Sweden’s air defence regiment, told broadcaster SVT that the deployment would be “the most complex operation that Sweden has undertaken as a NATO ally”. The country joined the alliance in 2024.
Sweden will deploy Gripen aircraft to Poland to strengthen NATO’s eastern flank. Poland is a close ally and a vital hub for support to Ukraine. Swedish security is built together with our allies in NATO, and by taking responsibility together. (1/3) pic.twitter.com/4WaSp2UqYD
— Pål Jonson (@PlJonson) September 30, 2026
Poland’s defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, thanked both Sweden and the Netherlands for their role in defending Polish airspace and NATO’s eastern flank.
“The continuity of this mission is an expression of allied solidarity and shared responsibility for the region’s security in the face of the threat from Russia. Together we are stronger,” he wrote on social media.
His deputy minister, Paweł Zalewski, told broadcaster TVN that Patriot systems “are currently the only ones effective against ballistic missiles”, making them vital for protecting Rzeszów. He noted that around 90% of international aid for Ukraine goes through the hub.
Poland has also been taking delivery of its own Patriot systems from the United States. The first were deployed at Warsaw Babice airport in 2023. Last year, Poland announced full operational readiness of its US-supplied Integrated Battle Command System (IBCS), an air-defence network that includes Patriot missile batteries.
Dziękuję rządowi Szwecji za podjęcie decyzji o wysłaniu do Polski systemów Patriot. Szwedzi przejmą ochronę hubu logistycznego NATO w Rzeszowie.
Dziękuję także Holandii 🇳🇱 za dotychczasowe wsparcie Polski i  wschodniej flanki NATO. Ciągłość tej misji to wyraz sojuszniczej…
— Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) October 6, 2026
Earlier this year, Poland’s airspace was violated by a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile, which landed in a field. On one night last year, around 20 Russian drones crossed the country’s eastern borders, and last month a Russian military helicopter briefly entered Polish airspace from Kaliningrad.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk recently warned that, according to intelligence sources, Russia is planning drone and missile strikes on eastern NATO countries, which it would present as accidental.
The growing threat from Russia has pushed Poland to forge closer military ties with other countries around the Baltic Sea, and above all with Sweden. In 2024, the two countries signed a strategic partnership to enhance cooperation on defence and economic development.
Since then, they have held their first bilateral military exercises in the Baltic; Poland has ordered three submarines from Swedish manufacturer Saab; and Sweden bought €274 million worth of Piorun man-portable air-defence systems from Polish firm Mesko.

Tens of thousands of Israelis abroad expected to fly home to vote in 2026 election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
20:05:51 UTC
05:05:51 KST

At least 53,000 Israelis living abroad are expected to travel to Israel to vote in the 2026 election, as the Likud withdrew its petition against organizations helping citizens reach the country for Election Day on Tuesday.
The petition against AID Coalition and its Fly&Vote initiative, which aims to help Israeli citizens living abroad reach Israel to participate in the election, was dismissed by agreement of the parties following a hearing before Central Elections Committee chairman and Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg.
The petition was withdrawn following Sohlberg's recommendation. Likud attorney Ilan Bombach subsequently announced that the party was withdrawing the petition.
Under the agreement, ticket prices for flights already being offered through the initiative will remain those set by the airlines, and no additional flights will be sold through the initiative. The parties also agreed that the judge would rule on legal costs. The respondents were ordered to pay NIS 10,000 in expenses.
Likud had argued in its petition, among other things, that the initiative's activities involved providing a benefit intended to influence voters' choices. The respondents countered that their activities did not include any financial benefit or other benefit with economic value.
Tens of thousands of Israelis abroad expected to return home for Election Day
During the hearing, it emerged that, according to the initiative, it assists no more than approximately 500 to 600 citizens, all of whom pay full price for their airline tickets, without any subsidy from the organization.
Following the dismissal of the petition, Fly&Vote welcomed the decision and said it would continue working intensively with the aim of "turning every Israeli into an Israeli vote" and helping reduce the obstacles preventing citizens from reaching the ballot box.
The decision comes against the backdrop of figures Fly&Vote published in September indicating record involvement among Israelis living abroad. The initiative estimated that at least 53,000 Israelis residing overseas are expected to travel to Israel to exercise their right to vote.
A broad survey conducted by the initiative among approximately 17,500 Israelis outside Israel found that 72% of respondents said they intended to travel to Israel for Election Day in order to vote. Fifty-eight percent had already purchased airline tickets and arranged their travel to Israel.
The figures showed a significant increase and a growing determination to turn intention into action. In a survey conducted in March, only 45% said they would make every effort to travel to Israel to vote. The latest survey found that 58% already held airline tickets.
About half of respondents also said the initiative's activity encouraged them and directly influenced their decision to board a flight to Israel to vote.
The data further showed that airfare prices were the main obstacle for citizens seeking to vote, cited by 58% of respondents, followed by flight availability at 25% and the security situation in Israel.
Initiative to increase open market supply of flights in response to petition
In its response to the petition, the initiative said that following an increase in the supply of flights on the open market, it had shelved most of its planned activity and was now left with only five or six flights.
Under the commitments given to the Central Elections Committee, the organization may provide information about required documents, operate WhatsApp groups, run a search engine for commercial flights and offer a general legal assistance hotline. It may also station volunteers in the arrivals hall at Ben-Gurion Airport, provided that they do not offer services with monetary value or engage in election campaigning.
The organization also committed not to subsidize or discount airline tickets, provide transportation or coordinate accommodation for participants, or operate its planned paid-volunteering program. It may sell full-price tickets only for the six flights already under consideration.
"The data clearly show that Israelis living abroad are still Israelis first and foremost - involved and caring, not only in words but also in actions," AID Coalition President Yonatan Bar-Sadeh said.
"Fly&Vote will continue working to reduce and remove the obstacles on their way to the ballot box, and to enable every Israeli citizen, woman and man, to exercise their basic right to vote."

Los Angeles Rock ’n Roll Fantasy Camp offers October 7 survivors rare respite from trauma
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
20:05:49 UTC
05:05:49 KST

”They tried to kill us. We survived. Let’s eat.”
Alan King’s joke about Jewish holidays gets to the essence of Jewish persistence in the face of horror. He might have added, “Let’s sing.” Music has accompanied the Jewish people for millennia through periods of joy and sorrow. Moses and the Israelites praised God for His salvation from the Egyptians in the “Song of the Sea.” Weddings, the Shabbat table, and kumsitzes all come with joyous soundtracks.
In times of overwhelming devastation, songs have expressed survival, determination, and memory. During the Holocaust, Jews continued to compose and perform them in ghettos and concentration camps, including Theresienstadt. ”The Partisan Hymn,” “Zog nit keyn mol” (“Never Say”), was composed in the Vilna Ghetto.
Three years ago this week, music and tragedy once again intertwined when Hamas-led terrorists attacked the Nova Music Festival as part of the Oct. 7 attacks on Israel. Approximately 1,200 people, including 364 civilians at the Nova festival, were killed that day, and 251 were abducted to Gaza.
Two months later, David Fishof, who founded Rock ’n Roll Fantasy Camp, saw music and trauma bound together at the funeral for Yotam Haim, the red-headed hostage who escaped with two others but was killed by friendly fire.
“Yotam’s brother, Tuval, and father, Raviv, are drummers,” said Fishof, an LA sports agent and entertainment producer. “They performed a 20-minute drum solo in Yotam’s honor, after which Tuval threw the sticks in the grave. At that moment, it hit me: I wanted to bring Tuval and nine other Oct. 7 survivors to Rock Camp in LA”
Ten Oct. 7 survivors flown in to participate in camp
With the help of Sam Grundwerg, former world chairman of Keren Hayesod – United Israel Appeal, the 10 survivors were flown to Los Angeles in March 2024 to participate in the sold-out camp.
Now, their experience is chronicled in The Bridge, a new documentary produced by “Friends” executive producer Kevin Bright that highlights how music can become a pathway from trauma to healing. Its message: “When tragedy strikes the Jewish people, we play louder.” Ahead of a wider theatrical release in November, the film is now playing at select North American venues.
Rock Camp, founded by Fishof in 1997, brings amateur rockers alongside music legends for four days of mentorship, rehearsals, and performances at iconic clubs such as Whisky a Go Go and The Viper Room.
Music, memory and trauma informed Fishof’s upbringing. Music saved the life of his father, Mark, a survivor of Auschwitz and Buchenwald.
“My dad would sing to the Nazis, just to entertain them,” Fishof said. “They would say, ‘Sing this song,’ and he would. Music saved him. It was a way for him to take his mind off of what he was going through.”
His father served as a cantor in Hackensack, New Jersey, for 33 years.
Fishof said his memories of his father’s sufferings made Oct. 7 the worst day of his life.
Camp offered Oct. 7 survivors rare respite from trauma
By contrast, their four days at Rock Camp offered the Oct. 7 survivors a rare respite from their trauma and a chance to reconnect with the joy of making music. The Israelis jammed with rock legends Michael Anthony of Van Halen, Sebastian Bach of Skid Row, Warren DeMartini of Ratt and Tommy Aldridge of Whitesnake, and met Richard Fortus and Slash of Guns N’ Roses.
Among the Israeli rockers was 27-year-old vocalist and guitarist Raz Shifer of Ramat Gan, a Nova Festival survivor who was close friends with two hostages, including Inbar Hayman, who was murdered in captivity.
After that Black Saturday, Shifer says in the film, “I couldn’t sleep. I couldn’t eat. I just sat on my couch, literally in shock, trying to figure out what the f*** had happened. I forgot who I was - the happy, smiley, energetic Raz. Rock Camp was my first time getting back on stage and letting it all out. For me, it was a really big step. I was able to remember myself again. Music is my victory. It’s the reason I get out of bed every day and the power that keeps me alive.”
Also among the group was 28-year-old vocalist and guitarist Bar Rudaeff of Tel Aviv, the son of Kibbutz Nir Yitzhak’s former deputy security coordinator Lior Rudaeff, who was murdered while defending the kibbutz on Oct. 7. His remains were returned to Israel in November 2025.
For Rudaeff, performing with Tommy Aldridge, the legendary hard rock and heavy metal drummer who played with Ozzy Osbourne and Whitesnake, was a way to reach his father through a joy they shared.
“My dad really liked ’80s rock, like Deep Purple, Bon Jovi, Foreigner and Ozzy Osbourne, so when we played with Tommy, it was really meaningful and emotional,” he says in “The Bridge.” “Rock Camp gave me the opportunity to stop thinking, for a little while, about my dad not being here. Music really helped me cope and pulled out a lot of feelings that I was repressing. It was a ray of hope in the middle of one of our darkest periods and gave me the strength to move on.”
At Rock Camp, Fishof said, “Each survivor played on behalf of loved ones - whether family members or friends who had been killed or were still being held in captivity. Every note meant something to them.”
Bright added, “Music enabled them to take a break from Oct. 7 for a week. I think it was a well-deserved respite from everything that was going on in Israel at the time. One of the survivors says in the film, ‘I’m still living Oct. 7. The trauma doesn’t go away.’ At the time that ‘The Bridge’ was made, their trauma was even stronger, and so their ability just to participate was really impressive.”
Three years after that devastating day in October, the survivors are continuing to do what their people have done in the face of adversity for millennia: sing and make music.
Tuval performs regularly and has released two albums, including “Ahim” (“Brothers”), a nod to Yotam. Bar now produces music, including a fellow camper’s upcoming album. And Raz is touring as a full-time vocalist.
“Music is what kept my father alive during the Holocaust,” said Fishof. “It’s what kept him going, and it’s what keeps me and many others going. Because no matter what happens, no one can ever take away our music. If we have that, we have life.”
They tried to kill us. We survived.
Let’s sing.
And eat.
To find local screenings, visit thebridgedoc.com

Israel Police criticize Military Police over handling of Modi'in draft dodger arrest after riot
Unknown

The Israel Police criticized the Military Police over its handling of the arrest of a haredi (ultra-Orthodox) draft evader overnight between Monday and Tuesday in Modi'in's Nofim neighborhood.
According to a police review, the small Military Police force that arrived at the scene did not immediately remove the draft evader after his arrest, despite procedures requiring it to do so. Instead, police gave him an extended period to get organized. Israel Police was only called in after dozens of protesters gathered at the scene, with officers assisting in extracting the force and restoring order.
Police officials stressed that the decision to release the draft evader and issue him an order to regularize his status was made by IDF officials, not the Israel Police. They said police acted at the military's request, dispatched large numbers of officers to the scene, and helped implement the decision while restoring public order.
Also on Tuesday, a senior IDF official said that "the police should assist in arresting deserters," KAN News reported. He claimed that the young members of the Military Police "have no chance" in such a situation, emphasizing that they "must receive police assistance with much larger forces in order to arrest deserters."
Modi'in Mayor Haim Bibas, who also serves as Local Authorities Federation chairman, called on both the police and the military to examine their conduct.
"The police and the military must also provide answers about their conduct and, above all, about their lack of preparation overnight," said Bibas. "How does an operation to arrest a draft evader end without the arrest, while the rioters celebrate? In my view, this result is a serious failure. It sends a dangerous message: Anyone who uses enough force can thwart law enforcement."
Bibas addresses neighborhood unrest amid clashes between protesters, police
He also addressed the unrest in the neighborhood and the clashes between protesters and the forces that arrived at the scene.
"We all woke up this morning to the reports and disgraceful videos of haredi rioters who came in the middle of the night to the Nofim neighborhood to thwart the arrest of a draft evader, disturbed residents and clashed with police officers and municipal policing teams who arrived at the scene to assist," he said.
He said the police and military must ensure that such an incident does not happen again and provide forces on the ground with the backing and resources needed to complete their mission.
"Anyone who comes to Modi'in to riot will encounter a harsh and determined response," Bibas warned. "We will act through every legal means available to us to prevent a recurrence of the incident and protect the city's residents."
He added that the rioters who came to the scene were not residents of the city and did not represent its values.
"Our children serve and fight, residents leave their homes for additional rounds of reserve duty, and families in the city have paid the heaviest price of all," he emphasized.
He then called on the government and haredi leadership to take concrete steps to increase enlistment.
Bibas: Those who cannot enlist should contribute through other means
"Anyone who can enlist must enlist," declared Bibas. "Anyone who cannot serve in the military should contribute through national or civilian service, and anyone who does not contribute should not receive a single thing from the state. Responsibility for the security of the state belongs to all of us."
He concluded by referring to the military service of his children, who completed full combat service and reported for duty on October 7.
"Like many families in the city, my family also knows what service and responsibility to the state mean, including in these days," said Bibas. "We will not accept a situation in which our children are required again and again to report for duty, while others exempt themselves from the same obligation and then come to our city to riot."
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

British Airways plans record 106-seat business class on Airbus A380 jumbo jets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
20:02:00 UTC
05:02:00 KST

British Airways is building what it calls the "world's largest" business-class cabin and ripping out dozens of coach-class seats, the starkest example yet of how airlines are betting their future on high-spending travelers.
The changes are part of a massive overhaul of the British Airways fleet and its ground services, including lounges at its London Heathrow hub.
Here's what's changing:
- British Airways will outfit its Airbus A380, the world's largest passenger plane, with a monster 106-seat business-class cabin, up from the current configuration of 97 business-class seats.
- First class will also be refreshed and will include 12 suites, down from the current A380 configuration of 14.
- Premium economy class will grow to 84 seats from 55.
- Standard economy seats will shrink to just 215 from 303.
British Airways said the 106 business-class suites, with sliding doors, will take up the entirety of the A380's upper deck.
Airlines have been spending years and hundreds of millions of dollars to expand their pricier seats, capitalizing on demand for roomier options and travelers' appetite for more luxurious trips.
British Airways' joint-venture partner, American Airlines, last month debuted a 70-seat business class on its largest Boeing aircraft. Qantas CEO Vanessa Hudson told CNBC in a recent interview that customers are seeking high-end options on long flights, like its Perth-London nonstop.
"There is absolutely a customer who wants this and is prepared to pay a premium for it," she said.
Those more expensive seats command a premium. Even extra legroom on trips across the Atlantic can go for more than $200 per leg, with surcharges of more than $1,000 for premium economy seats after purchase.
The prices can be even higher if they're selected at booking. The top-end seats regularly run $5,000 and even well over $10,000 on lengthier flights.
Deliveries of new aircraft have even been delayed because some of the new seats are so elaborate that carriers have been waiting for parts or federal certification.
British Airways' overhaul of the cabins on its 12 A380s is also a bet on the jumbo jet, which many carriers have retired in recent years, opting for smaller, more fuel-efficient jets. Airbus delivered the last A380 to the plane's largest user, Emirates, in late 2021.

Private health legislation changes appear all but doomed
The federal government's controversial private health insurance changes appear all but doomed, after the Greens sent its strongest signal yet it would not back the legislation in its current form.
It comes as new figures prepared by the Health Department that reveal more than two million Australians affected by the changes live on less than $37,000 a year.
The proposal would wind back the rebate Australians aged 65 and over receive on their private health cover, banking about $3 billion to spend elsewhere in the aged care system.
A parliamentary inquiry examining the impact of the changes on older Australians and the broader health system has now released its report, with the Labor-dominated inquiry recommending the legislation pass parliament.
With the Coalition already vowing to block the legislation in the Senate, the federal government must get the Greens on board for the bill to pass.

Liberals call for action after High Court coal decision

Tripping during a political convention was linked to more support for political violence in a recent psychedelic study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
20:00:34 UTC
05:00:34 KST

People whose most intense psychedelic experience fell on the Fourth of July showed a decrease in support for partisan violence over a two-month period, compared with people who used psychedelics on other dates, according to research published in Psychedelic Medicine. Exploratory analyses found the opposite pattern for psychedelic use during the 2024 party conventions and closer to Election Day. The findings suggest that the broader cultural and political moment may shape what follows a psychedelic experience.
Psychedelics, such as psilocybin and LSD, are substances that alter perception, mood, and cognitive processes by interacting with serotonin receptors in the brain. Over the past several years, experts have expressed concern about support for partisan violence, which refers to the belief that physical harm or force is an acceptable way to advance political goals or defeat political opponents. While a study covered by PsyPost in 2024 found that Americans’ support for political violence declined between 2022 and 2023, it remains a heavily studied topic due to its potential impact on democratic stability.
The psychological effects of psychedelics are thought to depend heavily on context. The authors of a 2018 review argued that a user’s mindset and surroundings strongly shape what a psychedelic experience produces, so the same drug can lead to very different outcomes in different situations.
Extending this idea, the authors of a 2021 paper argued that psychedelics do not automatically make people more peaceful or politically liberal. Instead, they proposed that these substances act as magnifiers of a user’s broader cultural and social environment. This perspective suggests that national events and collective moods could influence a person’s psychedelic experience.
This idea raises the possibility that shared cultural moments might steer the psychological effects of psychedelics in different directions. For example, a 2018 study showed that reminding people of a shared American identity reduces hostility between rival political parties.
“There’s reasonably good evidence that psychedelic outcomes depend on context – what researchers call set and setting,” lead study author Otto Simonsson told PsyPost. Set refers to a person’s mindset and expectations, and setting to the physical and social environment. Simonsson is an assistant professor at the Center for Social Sustainability within the Department of Neurobiology, Care Sciences and Society at the Karolinska Institutet. “Building on this idea, some scholars have suggested that the broader sociocultural context might matter as well, but that idea is difficult to test empirically,” he explained.
Simonsson and his colleagues aimed to test whether taking psychedelics during specific national events is associated with changes in a person’s willingness to endorse partisan violence. “One possible approach is to use dates that carry a shared cultural meaning, and the Fourth of July is a reasonable candidate, since it’s broadly associated with unity and collective celebration,” Simonsson noted. “If the wider cultural context does shape what follows from a psychedelic experience, then using on that date, with that as the backdrop, might be associated with different changes than using on an ordinary date. That was the basic logic.”
To investigate this, the research team used a longitudinal observational design to track changes over time. They recruited a large sample of U.S. adults aged 18 to 50 on Prolific, an age range chosen because earlier research suggested it would include more psychedelic users. The data came from two waves, collected in the summers of 2023 and 2024. The participants did not know the study was specifically about psychedelics when they signed up.
During the initial survey, 21,990 participants answered questions about their demographic background, including age, gender identity, and political affiliation. They also completed a questionnaire designed to measure their baseline support for partisan violence. About two months later, 12,345 of these initial participants returned to complete a follow-up survey.
In this second survey, participants reported whether they had used classic psychedelics during the two-month period. If they had, they provided the exact date and estimated the dose of their most intense psychedelic experience. They also answered the same questions about partisan violence to see if their attitudes had shifted.
The researchers statistically accounted for a range of other factors. They controlled for age, gender identity, political affiliation, prior psychedelic use, survey year, and the use of other substances, including alcohol, cannabis, and stimulants, as well as the participants’ educational attainment and religious beliefs.
Out of the thousands of people who completed the follow-up, 505 participants reported using psychedelics during the two-month window. Within this smaller group, 19 individuals noted that their most intense experience happened on the Fourth of July. The remaining 486 participants had their most intense experience on a different date.
The results indicated that people whose most intense psychedelic experience fell on the Fourth of July showed a larger decrease in support for partisan violence than people whose most intense experience fell on other dates, a difference of about 0.7 standard deviations, though it rests on only 19 people. Participants who did not use psychedelics at all also showed a greater decrease than the other-date psychedelic users.
The scientists also examined other dates with intense political focus using the 2024 data. Exploratory analyses showed that taking psychedelics on the date of the July 2024 assassination attempt on Donald Trump was associated with a decrease in support for partisan violence. This particular decrease was reported almost exclusively by Republican respondents. However, this finding rests on very few Republicans, as about four in five psychedelic users in the sample identified as Democrats.
In contrast, the context of an upcoming election was associated with a different pattern. Using psychedelics during the dates of the Democratic or Republican National Conventions was associated with an increase in support for partisan violence. This increase appeared to be stronger among people who were exposed that day to their own party’s leaders describing the other side as a threat. Similarly, having a most intense psychedelic experience on a date closer to Election Day was linked to increased support for violence.
The authors interpret this pattern as consistent with the idea that psychedelics may amplify the prevailing mood of the moment. A unifying holiday might soften partisan hostility, while a divisive political convention might heighten animosity. An earlier analysis from the same research team’s survey, covered by PsyPost in 2025, similarly found that outcomes varied with context: psychedelic use in illegal settings was linked to increases in psychotic and manic symptoms over two months, while use in legal or decriminalized settings was not.
Simonsson said the main takeaway is “possibly that psychedelics might not push people in any single direction.” “In our data, participants whose most intense psychedelic experience fell on the Fourth of July showed a decrease in support for partisan violence over the study period, while those whose experience fell during the party conventions or closer to Election Day showed an increase,” he added.
However, the researchers note the need for caution when interpreting the results. “That said, this is one study with a small number of relevant participants, so I’d hold the takeaway loosely,” Simonsson cautioned.
As with all research, there are other caveats to consider. The study observed behaviors as they naturally occurred rather than assigning participants to take psychedelics, so the findings cannot confirm that the dates themselves directly caused the changes in political attitudes. Only the Fourth of July test was preregistered. The analyses regarding the assassination attempt, political conventions, and Election Day were exploratory, with no statistical correction for running several tests.
The number of participants who used psychedelics on specific dates was quite small. The researchers also skipped one follow-up analysis for the assassination attempt date because the groups were too small. The high dropout rate between the first and second surveys also introduces the possibility of skewed data. Exposure to the events was not measured directly; participants were asked whether they celebrated the Fourth of July, but not whether they closely followed the conventions, the assassination attempt, or the election.
Because the researchers recruited online and deliberately targeted an age range likely to include psychedelic users, the results might not represent the general public. Participants also reported their own substance use and political views, which can sometimes result in inaccurate answers if people want to present themselves favorably.
The study, “Politically Salient Events May Modulate Effects of Naturalistic Psychedelic Use on Support for Partisan Violence,” was authored by Otto Simonsson, Peter S. Hendricks, Walter Osika, and Simon B. Goldberg.

‘All I want to do is cry’: trauma of 7 October survivors three years after the attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
20:00:23 UTC
05:00:23 KST

Keith Siegel spent many of his long hours in Hamas captivity in Gaza etching everything that happened after 7 October 2023 into his memory. For 484 days, he recited to himself every place he was held, the dates he was moved and every attack or humiliation he endured or witnessed.
He aimed to store intelligence that could help Israeli forces free other hostages if he was released, to keep track of time as the days slid by and be able to tell his family what happened to him. Now his body is free, but he cannot loosen those memories.
“I’m living a kind of dual life,” he said in an interview in Tel Aviv. “I’m here for some of the time, and I’m in Gaza some of time. It’s very challenging to convey in words what it was like.”
Siegel and his wife, Aviva, were among 251 people taken captive to Gaza on the deadliest day in Israel’s history, when Hamas militants broke across the border to launch a wave of attacks on kibbutzim, border towns, military bases and music festivals.
Israel’s security forces were caught by surprise, and by the time they regained control of the area, 1,209 people had been killed, the majority of them civilians, including 36 children, according to records kept by the Israeli newspaper Haaretz.
The cemetery at Nir Oz contains two lines of fresh headstones, marking lives that all ended on that same date. A shared plot for a family of five – a mother, father and their three young children – has been made into a garden with space left for their still-living grandparents.
Caretaker Shlomo Margalit, who will soon turn 89, points to the graves of three of his oldest friends, founding members of the kibbutz who came to Nir Oz from Haifa with him in the 1950s.
“This is my life project, as well as my home,” Margalit said, explaining why he has come back to a place of such loss. He is waiting for a new house but, for now, staying in the former home of Gadi Moses, 82, who survived 482 days as a hostage.
The graves he tends are a silent testament to the brutality of the attacks and the scale of the state’s failure, which in Nir Oz was staggering, even on a day of terrible failures.
A five-person volunteer defence force held Hamas at bay for at least two hours, Margalit said. When they had all been shot, the kibbutz was taken over and sacked, homes burned, families slaughtered and kidnapped.
Then, before the first Israeli soldier arrived, the Hamas forces, other Palestinian gunmen and civilian looters all left. Nir Oz had been forgotten by the army and ripped apart without the military firing a single shot to defend it.
In total, 47 people were killed and 76 taken to Gaza, including Shiri Bibas, her 10-month-old baby Kfir and four-year-old Ariel, who were killed in Gaza. The dead and hostages represented more than a quarter of the small community.
Revisiting that terrible day, and the trauma that followed, is painful and exhausting for Margalit, but he still accepts interviews for a simple reason. “I want people to know what really happened here,” the 89-year-old said.
The third anniversary of the 7 October attacks falls a few weeks before national elections, and much of the country is caught up in a furious debate about responsibility for the deadliest day in Israel’s history and the conduct of the war that followed.
Survivors and bereaved relatives are avoiding the political fray, still grappling with the trauma and the struggle to rebuild something like normality.
In Nir Oz, there is a terrible, almost irreconcilable struggle between re-establishing the kibbutz as a living community, and preserving physical testimony of the attack.
The cemetery echoes with the sound of construction and families have already moved into several rows of new houses near the kibbutz entrance.
But on the other side of the compound, paths still lead between blackened ruins and memorials to the dead. Some bereaved survivors want the homes of loved ones preserved this way as permanent monuments to mark their loss.
“There are families that can’t [bear to] live here, but want a memorial place to come to visit,” Margalit said. “On the other hand, can you build a new kibbutz where children grow up running around between burnt houses?”
He is on the remembrance committee and, two years on, they are struggling to reach a decision on this impossible choice. “Is there right or wrong here? No,” he said. “We are dealing with that, trying to find an answer.”
One compromise might be a memorial garden on the border of the kibbutz. For now, there are plaques with the stories of families attacked on that day and a memorial house to remember the dead and kidnapped.
When the kibbutz took a collective decision to return and rebuild, Margalit and his wife, Hanna, knew they wanted to join. His only concession to the trauma was asking for a new home that did not face Gaza.
“I’ve found myself building this place for the second time,” he said. “I know when I’m gone, I will have done something with my life. I took part in putting this spot on the map.”
The Siegels, who lived in the nearby kibbutz of Kfar Aza, also among the worst hit, have decided not to return as they focus on mental and physical recovery. Aviva was 62 when she was kidnapped. Keith was 64.
“What happened to me in Gaza, what happened with Keith in Gaza, it’s there all the time,” said Aviva.
“I understand that it’s going to be a process of healing. There’s always things that remind me, and if I don’t remember, then he reminds me. If I’m cooking lunch or making a cup of tea and I turn around and see Keith with tears in his eyes, because he just read something or let himself feel.”
The days approaching the anniversary have been particularly difficult, she said. Last year, at this time, she was still campaigning for the release of other hostages, her own emotions held at bay by the urgency of that campaign.
For a time, she tried to deal with the trauma by telling herself, over and over again “I must feel lucky,” simply because she had made it back alive.
Now she has allowed herself to feel again, and as 7 October approached, she has realised how raw the wounds still are. “Getting ready [for the anniversary] has been very very painful,” she said. “The last couple of weeks all I want to do is cry. Now I’m feeling things I didn’t feel before.”
“When I hear my grandson say he is afraid of being kidnapped in the middle of the night, it breaks my heart.”
She has written a book, Survived to Tell, about the ordeal, which she describes as therapy and an act of celebration. She wrote so her grandchildren could read about what she and Keith endured, for other hostages who couldn’t tell their own stories and to inspire a broader audience in Israel and beyond.
After the exhausting campaign to get Keith and other hostages home, she said she had struggled to concentrate on the election. Keith’s political focus is an independent inquiry into 7 October to prevent other families suffering as his has.
He said: “There needs to be an investigation to understand how this happened, in order to do everything possible that it won’t happen again. So many people were killed, injured, traumatised.”
Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister, has fiercely opposed an independent state commission of inquiry. Critics say he is afraid it would expose his own failings.
In the immediate aftermath of the attacks, few people inside or outside Israel expected him to stay in power long, particularly as the country’s coalition governments have rarely served out their full terms.
Netanyahu had for years championed a foreign and security policy based on the premise that Hamas was “contained” in Gaza, behind unbreachable layers of fortifications.
The security officials who were in command that day have all stepped down yet, three years on, Netanyahu is still in power, having deflected all demands for his resignation.
Yaakov Godo, a bereaved father, interrupted Netanyahu’s speech at the official commemoration event this year to accuse him of negligence.
“You did not protect my son on 7 October, you did not protect 1,200 people murdered in one day. Shame!” he shouted, before being ushered away.
Both US and Israeli officials have said Netanyahu rejected ceasefire deals that could have halted the war in Gaza and brought many Israeli hostages home sooner. But criticising the prime minister means venturing into a vicious political debate where age and loss offer little protection.
Yocheved Lifshitz, 88, was taken hostage from Nir Oz with her husband Oded, whose magnificent cactus garden blooms at the heart of the kibbutz. He died in Gaza, she survived and since her return she has been a vocal critic of Netanyahu.
A candidate for Netanyahu’s Likud party, Itzik Bonzel, said last month that he wished he could turn back the clock and return her to Hamas captivity. He later apologised, blaming grief for his son who died fighting in Gaza, but Lifshitz denounced it as a proxy attack driven by the prime minister.
Netanyahu, who is battling a corruption trial and could be more vulnerable legally if he loses power, is pushing to intensify Israeli attacks on Gaza and his coalition partners are calling for ethnic cleansing and annexation of Palestine.
The war Israel launched in response to 7 October has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, the majority of them civilians, including about 20,000 children.
Netanyahu has also waged a years-long campaign to dismantle institutions protecting democracy inside Israel’s 1967 borders. Palestinians under Israeli military rule in the occupied West Bank do not have the rights of Israeli citizens.
Many Israelis opposed to this rightwing vision of perpetual war in a state with diminished institutions consider this election the most critical since Israel was founded in 1948, among them Margalit.
Nir Oz, like many communities targeted by Hamas, had its roots in the leftwing Zionist movement, and although the brutality of 7 October pushed some to the right, others saw their pain as bitter proof that war alone cannot offer long-term security.
“I don’t believe we can ignore the fact that Palestinians live here,” Margalit said. “We have to find a way we can live here with them and be secure. I don’t have an answer, I just know we are here to stay and they are here to stay. Maybe we need someone from the outside.”

Russia Trains Ukrainian Children for War—“Children. How Russia Teaches to Fight” Documents How
The Ukraine War Archive has released a new documentary, Children. How Russia Teaches to Fight, examining how Russian authorities and affiliated organizations seek to shape the identity of Ukrainian children living in temporarily occupied territories and prepare them for service in the Russian military.
The film premiered on the Ukraine War Archive’s YouTube channel and focuses on children who, according to the documentary, are being exposed to Russian propaganda, militarization, and efforts to erase their Ukrainian identity.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to estimates cited in the press release, approximately 1.6 million children under the age of 18 currently live in Russian-occupied territories. Russian authorities have introduced educational programs aimed at integrating these children into Russian language and culture while imposing their own interpretation of history.
The documentary also examines the militarization of education. Schoolchildren are taught shooting, drone operation, and weapons handling, while meetings with Russian military personnel are regularly organized. During compulsory lessons titled “Conversations About Important Things,” children are presented with explanations of the war from Russia’s perspective.
Outside schools, organizations including Yunarmiya, the Movement of the First, and the Eaglets of Russia continue similar activities. The press release states that the Movement of the First involves nearly 595,000 children in occupied territories, while Yunarmiya has approximately 48,000 members.
According to the documentary, participation in the Eaglets of Russia program is effectively mandatory, as refusal can affect children’s academic performance. Children who miss required activities may be registered for monitoring and referred to a psychologist, while their families can face scrutiny from Russian social services. Refusal to participate in “patriotic events” may also be classified as destructive or extremist behavior.
“Everything Russia is trying to do is to turn our fellow citizens, our children, into Russian soldiers who will later fight against their own country,” said Mariia Sulialina, a Ukrainian human rights activist and head of the Almenda Center for Civic Education, who received Sweden’s Civil Rights Defender of the Year award in 2024.
The film also examines the situation of young people who may be mobilized into the Russian military after reaching adulthood. The press release notes that many are unable to leave temporarily occupied territories because they do not have Ukrainian passports.
According to the filmmakers, this raises a broader question about how people who spent years under occupation can later continue their lives in a free Ukraine while preserving ties to the country and a sense of belonging to it.
The issue extends beyond children currently living under occupation. Ukraine has documented more than 20,000 cases of Ukrainian children unlawfully deported or forcibly transferred by Russia, according to figures presented at an international conference in Toronto that opened on September 28.
Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs reported on September 29 that 2,644 children had been returned to Ukraine so far.
