Chancellor plans major intervention to help poorer UK households with rising energy bills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
19:27:59 UTC
04:27:59 KST

John Healey is planning a major intervention to cut energy bills for poorer households in this month’s budget, after ministers became alarmed at forecasts that show bills rising by hundreds of pounds in January.
The chancellor is working on plans to spend more than £1bn to help energy consumers, the bulk of which is likely to go towards increasing the discount given to households on certain benefits.
Sources say final decisions have not been made, but Healey is set to rebuff a call from the energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh to spend billions more on removing levies from bills altogether.
Energy officials are working up more radical changes to bills, however, which could be implemented after the budget and would change how much companies could charge customers, rather than subsidising their bills.
If approved, the energy discount will form a major plank of the budget, which government sources say will be low-key but focused on reducing voters’ cost of living.
The chancellor is facing a cash crunch as he looks for money to fund an additional £4.7bn in defence spending and rebuild his fiscal buffer, which has been eroded by higher borrowing costs.
He is likely to raise taxes to pay for the additional spending, and is rumoured to be looking at higher bank taxes in particular.
Government sources had previously insisted the VAT cut to electricity bills which Andy Burnham announced soon after becoming prime minister would be the last support to be offered this year.
But they have become increasingly concerned by forecasts showing that the Iran war will push the energy price cap up by as much as £442 in January – entirely eroding the impact of the VAT cut.
As a result Healey has been considering submissions from the energy department on how to ease the pressures on households in the coming months.
The most likely solution is understood to be increasing the warm homes discount – a £150 discount to energy bills offered to households on certain benefits.
Healey is understood to be considering increasing this by a further £100, which would be funded by taxpayers, rather than bill-payers as the existing discount is.
Fahnbulleh, meanwhile, has been pushing for more sweeping action to reduce bills for all consumers by as much as £120 by removing all levies.
Under the energy secretary’s proposals, the levies, which fund renewable energy and efficiency schemes, would be paid for through taxation instead.
She told the Guardian last week: “If we want a system that is resilient, if we want a system that can cope, if we want a system that ultimately can deliver the diversity of energy that we want, what is the fairest way in which we pay for it?
“That is both across the exchequer versus our bill-payers, and then within our bill-payers. So we have to ask that question. Every other country is asking that question, and ultimately we’ve got to come to a fair deal.”
Removing levies from bills would reduce inflation, but would cost as much as £3.2bn and would be difficult for the government to unwind should energy costs come down in the future.
Officials in the energy department are working on more radical proposals for after the budget, meanwhile, including proposals to reduce tariffs for poorer households or those that use less energy.
Burnham told the Labour conference last week: “British businesses and bill-payers pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe. Within 10 years, I want those costs to be in line with our neighbours.
“This means reforming a broken energy market so it better serves the public interest.”
A so-called “social tariff” would force energy companies to charge poorer households less for each unit of electricity they consume than richer ones.
Creating such a scheme, however, would involve a large amount of data collection from tax authorities, the Treasury and energy companies – an exercise likely to take far longer than the next few weeks.
An alternative plan, known as a “rising block tariff”, would also vary the tariffs that energy companies can charge, but by consumption levels rather than income.
The idea, which was proposed by the New Economics Foundation (NEF) thinktank when Fahnbulleh ran it, would charge consumers less for a set amount of “essential” use and more once their consumption crossed that level.
Alex Chapman, head of economic and environmental policy at NEF, said: “A serious price spike is coming, and without action, bills will exceed the peak of the last crisis. The government must use the budget to put in place both targeted support for the most vulnerable and, critically, a safety net for all.”
He added: “Repeated crises have exposed the flaws in our privatised energy system – these can only be fixed by fundamental reform. This means capturing the benefits of cheap renewables and offering every household a ‘block’ of essential energy at a truly protected and affordable price.”
Alfie Stirling, economist and director of policy at the Joseph Rowntree Foundation, said: “Energy support for this winter needs to tick three boxes. It needs to support the majority of households; within this, it needs to target the most support towards those in greatest need; and – as far as possible – it needs to actually lower the price, thereby bringing down inflation.
“The UK does not yet have the right toolkit to respond effectively to energy price shocks – building better tools is now a critical priority for our future security and living standards.”
A spokesperson for the Treasury said: “As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”

Italy deported two foreign nationals suspected of attacking Milan Chabad emissary Rabbi Tzemach Mizrahi, Italian Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi announced on Monday.
Piantedosi said the two men had been returned to their countries of origin. The minister said, "There is no place in our country for hatred and violence, and no antisemitic act will be tolerated."
The attack took place on September 16 at a bus stop in Piazzale Bande Nere in western Milan, near an area with a large Jewish population.
The three men surrounded 51-year-old Mizrahi, rabbi of the city's central Chabad synagogue on Via Soderini, as he waited for a bus. They shouted at him in Arabic, grabbed his hat, put it on, and mocked him.
When Mizrahi began filming them on his phone, one of the men kicked him from behind and pushed him off the sidewalk into the road. The three then left the scene.
Mizrahi: Nobody at bus stop intervened in antisemitic attack
Mizrahi said about 20 people were waiting at the bus stop at the time, but none intervened.
According to Milan's Jewish community, footage recorded by Mizrahi helped authorities locate the three suspects shortly afterward.
One of those deported was a Moroccan national whose name was not released. The other was 21-year-old Tunisian national Battar Zahani, who was deported to Tunisia.
The third suspect, Zahani's 20-year-old brother, Ilyes Zahani, remains in Italy under restrictive conditions while awaiting trial.
Walker Meghnagi, head of Milan's Jewish community, welcomed the deportations, calling the move "wonderful news."
In an interview after the attack, Mizrahi said he would not stop wearing his rabbinic clothing or conceal his Jewish identity, but added that he would not allow his children to walk the streets alone.

Progressive Jews embracing ‘craziest’ ideologies are ‘no longer our friends,’ Israeli scholar says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
19:26:59 UTC
04:26:59 KST

Israeli historian and political commentator Gadi Taub sharply criticized progressive Jews abroad on Tuesday, saying those who embrace what he called the “craziest progressive ideologies” are “no longer our friends” and warning that Israel was losing political support on both the Western Left and Right.
Taub made the comments at NatCon Jerusalem, a three-day gathering of conservative politicians, intellectuals, journalists and activists from Israel, the United States and Europe. The National Conservatism movement emphasizes national sovereignty, traditional institutions and the nation-state, and has become increasingly influential within parts of the American and European Right.
Taub, who holds a doctorate in American history from Rutgers University and has written extensively about Zionism, nationalism and liberalism, was speaking during a panel titled “Immigration and Cultural Replacement.” His address was titled “Immigration and the Undermining of Democracy.”
During the discussion, Taub departed briefly from the central subject of his remarks to address the role of progressive Jews outside Israel.
“We, the Jews of Israel, have a great problem with progressive Jews abroad promoting immigration,” he said. “And we should start calling them out before the antisemites do.”
Taub did not identify specific Jewish organizations or individuals, nor did he limit his criticism to a particular Diaspora community.
Taub: Issue connected to Israel's loss of support amongst political Left, Right
He then connected the issue to what he described as Israel’s increasingly difficult political position in the West.
“We have lost the left, not due to Netanyahu or any fault of our own, because the Left has been indoctrinated by Edward Said for 40 years now,” Taub said. “It’s not something new. But we are also losing the Right.”
Edward Said, the Palestinian-American academic and literary theorist who died in 2003, was one of the most influential figures in the development of postcolonial studies. His work, particularly his critique of Western representations of the Middle East, shaped generations of academics and political activists.
Taub argued that parts of the Western Left had adopted an intellectual framework increasingly hostile to Zionism, while warning that Israel and Jews were now facing a separate challenge from elements of the political Right.
His strongest criticism was directed at progressive Jews themselves.
“Progressive Jews who think they will grovel at the feet of anti-Semites by agreeing to the craziest progressive ideologies are no longer our friends,” Taub said. “And we should be clear about it.”
Earlier in the discussion, Taub argued that Western societies had become vulnerable to Islamist movements because of what he described as a loss of confidence in their own civilization.
“There’s a perfect balance between imperialistic Islamic philosophies like the Muslim Brotherhood and the West’s loss of confidence in itself, or I would call it its autoimmune disease,” he said.
He argued that Islamist movements had learned to use Western debates over multiculturalism, racism and minority rights to shield themselves from criticism, saying forces that presented themselves as opposing racism could end up “cooperating in promoting a new form of racism.”
Antisemitism and the American Right
Taub’s warning that Israel was “also losing the Right” comes amid a growing debate within the conservative movement itself over antisemitism, Israel and the direction of the younger American Right.
Yoram Hazony, the Israeli political theorist who founded the National Conservatism movement and chairs the Edmund Burke Foundation, has repeatedly raised concerns about antisemitism gaining influence in parts of the American conservative movement.
Hazony to 'Post': Carlson significantly influenced young conservative political conversation
In a recent interview with The Jerusalem Post ahead of the Jerusalem conference, Hazony singled out Tucker Carlson, arguing that the former Fox News host had significantly influenced the political conversation among younger conservatives.
“In the last two years, his show is the leading clearinghouse for antisemitism on the political Right in America,” Hazony said.
Hazony said polling he had seen suggested Carlson enjoyed a positive image among a large majority of young Republican men, although he did not identify the poll. He stressed that support for Carlson should not itself be taken as evidence that those voters shared antisemitic views.
Earlier this year, Hazony warned more broadly about what could happen to American Jewish life if antisemitic ideas became entrenched across both major political camps. After arguing that antisemitism had become increasingly tolerated in parts of the political Left, he said that if Republicans followed the same course, “it’s not clear what would be left of Jewish life in America.”

'Three years without my Asaf': Mother of soldier killed on Oct. 7 pleads for truth - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
19:26:41 UTC
04:26:41 KST

Three years, my Asaf.
My beloved son.
Three years have passed – yet I wake up this morning as if time had stood still.
I return to that terrible morning, minute by minute.
To the rockets piercing the sky, to the sirens shattering the silence, and to your calming voice – a voice that was also that of a leader, a steady, clear commander’s voice – leading even in moments of truth and in the direst times, taking responsibility, and showing the way.
And above all, to your voice, my beloved son, Col. Asaf Hamami, commander of the Southern Brigade.
I hear you again over the radio: “Scramble the emergency standby squads, tanks, and vehicles. Shift to full combat footing. We are at war.” That was the moment you realized the country was at war. And I am going through it all with you, with Tomer and Kiril, your command team, minute by minute. Hearing your orders.
The attempt to mobilize forces, the speed with which you grasped that this event was far greater than anything we had ever known.
You leave the base with your team, heading into battle. A few against many. A commander and heroic fighters facing down dozens of terrorists.
Right up to the moment you were critically wounded. Up to the moment you fell – alongside Tomer and Kiril – and were abducted to Gaza.
You “returned” home wrapped in the Israeli flag, after 758 days, back to the homeland you loved so dearly.
My beloved, beautiful son, Assaf. In your final moments... I was not there.
I was not by your side like a mother lioness.
I could not cradle you in my arms, hold you tight, rest your head against my heart, and whisper with a mother’s warmth: “Mommy is here, my Asaf. Everything is fine; I’m with you.”
And I cannot stop asking myself: What did you feel in those moments? What were you thinking about?
Who were you thinking of?
Did you see me and Dad? Did you see your younger brother, Eitan, whom you loved so dearly and always worried about?
Did you think of the warm home you built, the woman you loved, and your children, beloved Ella, Alon, and Arbel, of whom you spoke with a face lit up by a wide, happy smile? Alon – who was with you just hours earlier on the holiday eve, and who stayed behind in the room at the base when you went off to fight – did you think of him in those moments?
What images flashed through your mind in those final moments?
And what passed through your heart the moment your beautiful eyes closed forever?
No one can give me the answers to these questions anymore.
But one thing I know: Your smile didn’t stop at that moment. The smile that always lit up your beautiful face lives on within us.
It continues to be with me, with Dad, with your children, with the family, with your friends, and with everyone who had the privilege of knowing you.
I can no longer meet your beautiful, radiant eyes, but the light within them can never be extinguished.
SINCE LAST week, I have been wandering aimlessly.
My stomach churns. My heart knows this day is coming.
Dad and I needed to be close to you. We drove to visit you at your new home, your permanent home at Kiryat Shaul. We bought flowers, washed and cleaned the site, and lit a candle.
A new home, one I never imagined would be the place where we’d be with you. The longing tears at my heart all over again.
I open your WhatsApp messages and read them once more:
“Come visit us at home.”
“Come over for dinner.”
“Love you.”
My heart and mind still refuse to accept this new reality.
How is it possible that your last messages spoke of home, of a visit, of dinner, yet the only visits left for us with you are at Kiryat Shaul?
I stand before you, cradling your beautiful head against the headstone, imagining the tight hugs I used to shower you with whenever we met. For a mother keeps hugging her son even when her hands can no longer touch him.
On Simchat Torah, Ella, Alon, and Arbel, your children and our beloved grandchildren, joined us for dinner, and my heart couldn’t help drifting back exactly three years.
On October 6, 2023, the eve of Simchat Torah, Alon was with you at the base.
I can picture it in my mind.
You, a father overjoyed, and Alon, your son, who so wanted to spend time with you at the base, playing soccer.
Alon is wearing you out, and you are absolutely delighted. Smiling. Beaming with happiness.
The simple happiness of father and son, just the two of you, moments you shared before the rest of the family was set to join you the next day.
And today, I look at your three children and think of how proud you would have been of them.
How much more you would have wanted to see. How many more moments you were meant to share. How much life still lay ahead of you.
There is something unfathomable about this intersection of holidays and joy with pain and bereavement.
How does Simchat Torah, a festival of joy, of Torah, of home, of family, become mingled with the memory of the day that terrible disaster befell us?
How can one process the magnitude of this tragedy, day after day, year after year, without pausing for a moment to ask: What happened to us?
And not just: What happened at the border fence?
Not just: What happened that morning?
What happened to us as a society? What happened to us as a people?
How did we reach a point where the hatred among us became so deep? In the months leading up to October 7, we witnessed a fractured society – arguments turning into battles, words into vitriol, and disagreements into hatred.
And then came that morning.
In an instant, our disputes paled in comparison to an enemy intent on killing, abducting, and destroying.
Thousands of bloodthirsty terrorists breached the border.
Communities were attacked. Civilians were massacred. Soldiers fell.
And you, my Asaf, went out to defend.
You didn’t ask who was Right or Left. You didn’t ask who was for or against. You went out to defend human beings. To defend the residents of the Gaza border area. To defend the country.
Three years later, I believe we owe ourselves one thing above all else: The truth.
Not the truth of the coalition.
Not the truth of the opposition.
The truth of a people.
I hear the debate over which committee will conduct the inquiry, who will appoint it, who will head it, and who its members will be.
AND I SAY: Enough arguing. Just start the investigation.
A state commission of inquiry, a national commission, or any other mechanism – the main thing is that it be established and be independent, professional, and, above all, accepted by everyone – or at least by the broadest possible segments of the public.
It is important to me that there be a commission in which this wounded nation can place its trust. One that bereaved families can trust, knowing it was not set up to shield any particular side. One that investigates everyone; that asks all the questions; that reaches every corner, even those places no one wants to go.
Who knew? Who didn’t know? Who raised the alarm? Who didn’t listen? What failed? Who bore the responsibility?
And above all, what must we, as a society, change so that such a disaster can never happen again?
We do not seek revenge. We seek the truth.
We do not ask for a committee that serves a faction. We ask for one that serves the state.
Because we deserve answers; not for the sake of revenge; not to single out culprits in advance, simply to understand.
And when someone is found responsible, let that responsibility be examined through the proper mechanisms of a well-functioning state, in accordance with the law.
Because without truth, there is no healing.
And without healing, the wound remains open.
I do not want us to remain a country where every disaster immediately turns into yet another war among ourselves.
I want us to finally learn to listen to one another. To argue without hating. To criticize without humiliating. To disagree without tearing each other apart.
To be strong without losing our humanity.
Perhaps this is one of the things you, my Asaf, would have asked of us.
Because you believed in people.
You saw what others did not see.
You listened.
You gave.
You took action.
Throughout your life, you taught – even without grand speeches – that one can be a great person without needing to be greater than others. And today, three years later, perhaps this is our greatest test:
Not only to defeat the enemy from without but to succeed in remaining one people from within.
For in the end – after all the arguments, all the factions, and all the headlines – we are left with one another. And if, after the heavy and terrible price we have paid, we do not understand this: When will we?
MY DEAR Asaf,
Three years.
Three years that you have been so deeply missed, yet so present in our lives.
Today, I no longer ask how one goes on living without you. I know.
We go on with you.
In every child who knows your story. In every value we pass on. In every person we truly see. In every act of giving.
Every time we choose unity over hatred. Every time we take action instead of just talking.
Your path was cut short in battle on that cursed day, but your path did not end.
We will carry it forward.
And I promise you, my beloved son: We will do everything to ensure that life in this country is worthy of the price you – and so many of our sons and daughters – paid for it.
YOU ARE NOT merely a story of October 7.
You are a person. You are a son. You are a father. You are a commander. You are a brother. You are a friend. You are loved.
And above all, you are my Asaf.
Three years. I miss you with every breath. And yet, amid all the pain, I see your smile. That same beautiful, warm, mischievous, radiant smile.
And today, your handsome face and the name Asaf Hamami are with us all across the country – on stickers, flags, walls, signs, classrooms, and in so many places where people have chosen to keep your presence and your path alive.
Your smile continues to be with me, and it is no longer just mine.
It is everywhere in the country.
It accompanies people who never had the chance to know you.
There is something captivating about it, just like your quiet leadership:
Less talking, more action. At eye level.
With a hug full of meaning, and with a goodness that was always directed toward others.
So simple. So genuine. So you.
But home is where we still meet. Your photo is on the fridge; you are waiting for me every morning. We “meet” in the kitchen over the morning coffee you loved so much.
And at the front door, as we leave, we are met by your smiling face and your blessing for the journey ahead.
And when we return, I say – as if you were here: “Asaf, we’re home.”
For even within our home, you are still a part of our lives.
Your eyes have closed forever, but your smile stays with us, and your presence walks beside us.
And I promise you, my beautiful, beloved boy, Mom is here. Just as I always was. And you will always be here with us because there is no love in the world like a mother’s love.
The writer is the mother of Col. Asaf Hamami, the highest-ranked IDF soldier killed on October 7, 2023.

Russia denies imposing anti-plague measures after lab worker death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
19:26:27 UTC
04:26:27 KST

Russia denies imposing anti-plague measures after lab worker death
Russia denies plague cases after laboratory technician’s death; US demands ‘transparency’ as WHO monitors situation.
What we know about Russia’s suspected plague case
Russian authorities have denied that they imposed anti-plague measures after a laboratory technician died of suspected pneumonic plague in a case which has drawn international scrutiny.
Russian media reported that a 28-year-old woman named Darya Shipilova, who had been working at the Irkutsk Anti-plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, died from suspected pneumonic plague on Friday.
Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s health watchdog, said on Tuesday that no cases of plague had been detected among staff who had come into contact with the laboratory worker for the past 10 days.
“This included identifying the widest possible circle of individuals who had been in contact with the patient and arranging for them to be placed under medical observation in hospital with daily laboratory tests,” the watchdog said.
The institute said in a statement that extensive testing during an autopsy on the woman’s body found no microorganisms linked to her work at the anti-plague institute.
It said results had revealed two cases of COVID-19 and two cases of rhinovirus infection, but that no pathogens causing other infectious diseases had been detected.
Elena Sofina, deputy head of the Shelekhov district near Irkutsk, where a local hospital was placed under quarantine, said no “dangerous diagnosis” had been confirmed.
She added that 60 percent of those placed under quarantine as a precaution had already been released.
Local media said about 200 people had previously been quarantined.
‘Transparency’
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday it was incumbent on Moscow to share more information on Friday.
“Anytime you hear there is a disease that infected someone in a lab anywhere in the world, you’re going to be concerned about it, especially given recent events not so long ago in 2020 and 2021 when we saw that happen. That said, it would be irresponsible for me to sit here and speculate,” Rubio said.
The World Health Organization in Geneva said on Tuesday that Russia had told it there were no cases of plague in the city of Irkutsk.
It was unclear if this meant that the laboratory technician’s death was unrelated to plague infection.
Plague is a bacterial disease that can occur in several forms, including pneumonic plague, which is the most contagious type and can be transmitted by respiratory means. Bubonic plague is transmitted by infected fleas.
Pneumonic plague, which causes lung failure, can be fatal if not treated early, according to the WHO.

04:18:09 KST

Israel has refused to allow Palestinian election officials to enter Gaza and occupied East Jerusalem to prepare for upcoming legislative elections, raising fresh fears that the long-delayed vote could once again be postponed, Palestinian officials said on Tuesday.
The Palestinian Central Elections Commission is due to oversee preparations for legislative polls scheduled for November 28. But the reported restrictions threaten to complicate efforts to hold a vote across all Palestinian territories and revive concerns over Israel’s role in obstructing Palestinian political participation.
Wafa, the official Palestinian news agency, reported that Israel had denied the commission access to Gaza and occupied East Jerusalem, citing a Palestinian official.
Israel’s defence ministry and COGAT, the Israeli body responsible for civilian affairs in the occupied Palestinian territories, did not respond to AFP requests for comment.
Palestinian election commission vows to continue
Despite the restrictions, Palestinian election officials say preparations will continue.
Farid Taamallah, spokesperson for the Central Elections Commission, said that the body could still hold the elections, saying its employees in Gaza had already been trained and were present on the ground.
“The Commission is continuing to organise the electoral process despite the Israeli decision,” Taamallah said.
The European Union has also stepped up its support for the vote.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc was “ready to deploy” election observers, stressing that Palestinians have the right to choose their representatives through elections that are “credible, inclusive and transparent.”
Palestinian Vice President Hussein al-Sheikh called for European backing to overcome obstacles to elections and ensure participation by Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, occupied East Jerusalem and Gaza.
A vote two decades overdue
The November election would be the first Palestinian legislative vote since 2006, when Hamas secured victory over Fatah. 
The Palestinian Legislative Council has not met since 2007, when political divisions between the rival factions deepened.
The election was previously scheduled for 2021 but was postponed indefinitely, with President Mahmoud Abbas citing Israel’s refusal to allow voting in occupied East Jerusalem.
Abbas, whose presidential term expired in 2009, won the last Palestinian presidential election in 2005 and has governed largely by decree since then.
Fears of another delay
The prospect of another postponement has already grown.
In September, senior Palestinian official Jibril Rajoub said the legislative election would not take place on schedule and suggested holding presidential elections first.
An August poll by the Jerusalem Media and Communication Center found that only 29 percent of Palestinians expected the November vote to proceed as planned.
With Palestinians having gone nearly two decades without legislative elections, the reported Israeli restrictions add another major obstacle to a process already burdened by occupation and repeated delays.

The EU shelved AI liability rules. Sam Altman has revived the debate.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
19:18:07 UTC
04:18:07 KST

BRUSSELS — EU parliamentarians are digging in on calls to revive an artificial intelligence liability law after receiving support from an unexpected ally: OpenAI’s Sam Altman.
“If something goes wrong with our models during training, there's gonna be some version of that we need to be responsible for,” Altman said in an exclusive interview with Decoded by POLITICO released Monday. “There's gonna need to be a liability framework for companies.”
This spotlight on liability has given influential members of the European Parliament a told-you-so moment after the EU last year scrapped plans to legislate on responsibility and compensation for harms caused by AI makers and agents.
Advertisement
The proposal by the European Commission for an AI liability law was killed amid a deep effort in Brussels to deregulate and reduce the legislative burden on companies — with the Commission arguing at the time that the proposal had little chance of securing sufficient political support.
German conservative lawmaker Axel Voss, who led on the proposal for the European Parliament, wants Brussels to put liability back on the agenda in light of Altman’s comments.
“I welcome this overdue moment of honesty. For years, the tech industry has argued that liability would stifle innovation,” he said. "Now even the CEO of OpenAI admits: Without liability, there is no trust.”
The law, first proposed in 2022, “would have closed exactly the gap Altman is now describing: responsibility before deployment, during training and testing,” Voss said.
One way governments could reduce AI risks is to apply product liability law, assigning responsibility (and penalties) to the makers of the most advanced AI models to nudge their development toward a safety-first approach.
As concerns over the pace of frontier AI development and the harm caused make the question of liability impossible to ignore — and as proposals for AI liability rules gain support around the world — proponents say the EU’s decision to scrap the proposal hasn't aged well.
Advertisement
The Commission has defended its landmark AI Act in response to mounting incidents and fears, while leaving the door open to additional rules addressing liability.
In response to questions by POLITICO last week, the EU’s tech chief Henna Virkkunen said she would look into potential “loopholes” in the current legislation, while reiterating the need to be “very careful” when crafting new rules.
Following the latest comments, the European Commission responded in a statement Wednesday that it "continues monitoring" the existing AI Act and Product Liability Directive. "At this stage," it said, "there is no plan to reintroduce a proposal on AI liability."
Not too late?
Social democrat lawmaker Brando Benifei, who helped write the EU’s AI rulebook, on Tuesday called the withdrawal of the liability proposal “a serious mistake,” saying obligations emerging from the AI Act were originally meant to be complemented by the rules to hold the companies liable.
“Frontier models and high-risk systems need strict liability,” he said.
Together with Irish independent lawmaker Michael McNamara and Greens member Kim van Sparrentak, the senior lawmakers are actively calling on the EU to introduce an AI liability act “to fill the legislative gaps currently existing for these kinds of incidents, so no people or European businesses are left empty-handed against these big providers when they cause harm,” POLITICO previously reported.
Advertisement
"We have an AI Act that regulates use, but we have no clear rules on who pays when a foundation model itself is flawed, biased or causes harm. This is not tenable,” Voss said.
He said it's not too late for Brussels to take another U-turn. “If the builder of a model admits he should be liable, the legislator should not be less ambitious than the industry.”
But one senior Parliament official involved in the liability law proposal said that for the Commission, “it would be admitting they made a big mistake.”
“If there is a major AI accident, creating more and more momentum for [action], they will probably call it differently — maybe an ‘Agentic AI Act,’ or ‘Protecting our Citizens from AI Act’ or whatever in order to hide past mistakes and flawed observations,” the official said.
As Brussels considers how to address new risks, the rest of the world will be watching.
“Altman says there will need to be a liability framework for models like his, but most likely one with many exceptions,” said Artur Bogucki, director of research at the think tank CEPS.
“The EU needs a direct, targeted AI liability instrument, narrow and procedural at its core,” including obligations to log and disclose evidence, he said.
Eliza Gkritsi contributed to this report.This article has been updated.

In September 2026, the Ukrainian Defense Forces intensified their strikes on targets deep within Russian rear areas and set a record for the number of air defense systems and radar stations destroyed since the inception of the e-Points (e-Baly) program.
This was reported by the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine.
By the end of September, 33,087 invaders had been confirmed killed — a figure surpassed only in March and April 2026.
A notable achievement in September was the highest number of Russian air defense systems, particularly radar stations, destroyed since the program’s inception. The destruction of one Russian air defense system at a distance of 552 km was also recorded.
In September, the number of confirmed target strikes at distances exceeding 20 km from the front line exceeded 11,000 for the first time.
The number of strikes at a depth of over 50 km also set a record. A significant portion of these attacks targeted the Mariupol-Crimea logistics route, which Russian troops use to supply their forces in southern Ukraine.
The program’s results indicate a gradual shift in combat operations from the immediate front lines to the enemy’s rear areas.
Every result within the program is recorded on video in the DELTA combat system and verified by the Brave1 defense innovation cluster.
The e-Points system works as follows: confirmed strikes are uploaded to DELTA, after that units receive points that they can spend on equipment on the Brave1 Market. Since March, military personnel have also been allowed to exchange e-Points for equipment components.
The overall trend toward an increase in Ukrainian strikes behind enemy lines is clearly evident in individual operations as well. In September, the Unmanned Systems Forces, in particular, struck dozens of energy facilities in the occupied territories.
To systematize such operations, Militarnyi launched the Deep Strike map in September, which tracks strikes on military, industrial, energy, and other targets in Russia and the occupied territories.
Another notable development in September was the increased effectiveness of Ukrainian air defense against attack drones.
Despite Russia’s increased use of jet-powered UAVs, Ukrainian units shot down 28% more Shahed-type drones in September than in the previous month.
At the same time, specialized interceptor drones are playing an increasingly important role in combating such targets. In May, the share of Shaheds shot down by these drones reached 40%. Since the beginning of September, the Defense Forces have neutralized about 55% of Russian Geran jet-powered drones.

TIMELINE – Messi’s 21-year Argentina journey from difficult debut to final farewell
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
19:15:14 UTC
04:15:14 KST

Lionel Messi will face Benin on Oct. 6 in Buenos Aires in a farewell match arranged after he announced his international retirement following Argentina's defeat by Spain in the 2026 World Cup final.
The 39-year-old will walk onto the Monumental Stadium pitch for the final time in the sky-blue and white jersey, entering his farewell as Argentina's record appearance-maker and leading scorer with 207 caps and 125 goals.
His Argentina career began more than two decades ago with uncertainty and relative anonymity. Before the country embraced him as its captain and World Cup-winning No. 10, Argentina first had to find him.
Messi grew up in Rosario, where he began playing football before joining Newell's Old Boys. At 13, he moved with his family to Spain and entered Barcelona's famed youth system.
In Barcelona, Messi was seen as an extraordinary teenage talent. In Argentina, however, his name was still largely unfamiliar outside Rosario and a relatively small circle of football officials and scouts.
That distance would become one of the defining features of his international career. Messi was developing in Spain while Argentina was only beginning to understand what it had produced.
At the 2003 Under-17 World Cup in Finland, Argentina lost 3-2 to Spain in the semifinals. Messi was not part of the squad, but by then his performances at Barcelona had begun attracting attention from Argentinian football officials.
When Claudio Vivas, assistant to then-Argentina coach Marcelo Bielsa, showed Bielsa footage of Messi, the coach was so impressed by the teenager's speed that he initially thought the video had been accelerated.
The Argentine Football Association began looking for the teenager and his family in Spain, with the Spanish federation also interested in persuading Messi to represent the country where he had developed.
The teenager had spent much of his formative football years in Spain, but when the choice came, he selected Argentina.
Argentina arranged an Under-20 friendly against Paraguay in Buenos Aires that gave Messi his first opportunity to represent his country.
Messi came off the bench and scored twice on his debut for Argentina's Under-20 team.
It was the beginning of a relationship that would eventually make him the country's most-capped player.
Messi's reputation in Argentina exploded at the 2005 Under-20 World Cup in the Netherlands.
He scored six goals, won the Golden Boot, and was named the tournament's best player as Argentina won the title.
The teenager who had been relatively unknown in his homeland was suddenly impossible to ignore.
Messi made his senior Argentina debut against Hungary in Budapest.
The appearance lasted less than a minute. After coming on as a substitute, he was sent off following an altercation with Vilmos Vanczák.
It was a troubled start to what would become one of the most celebrated international careers in football history.
At 18, Messi made his World Cup debut in Germany.
He scored against Serbia and Montenegro and became Argentina's youngest World Cup scorer at the time.
Argentina reached the quarterfinals before losing to Germany on penalties.
For Messi, the tournament marked the beginning of a World Cup journey that would span two decades.
Messi's first major senior international final ended in disappointment when Argentina lost 3-0 to Brazil in the Copa America final in Venezuela.
The defeat was an early sign of a pattern that would define the next decade: Messi's individual brilliance would repeatedly be followed by heartbreak with Argentina.
Messi arrived at the World Cup in South Africa as one of the biggest stars in world football, with Argentina coached by Diego Maradona.
He played in all five of Argentina's matches but failed to score as the team reached the quarterfinals, where Germany handed them a 4-0 defeat.
For Messi, the tournament reinforced an increasingly uncomfortable contrast: his achievements with Barcelona were growing rapidly, while similar success with Argentina remained elusive.
A year later, Argentina hosted the Copa America with Messi at the center of expectations.
The hosts reached the quarterfinals but were eliminated by eventual champions Uruguay on penalties after a 1-1 draw.
Messi again finished the tournament without a goal, and Argentina's early exit added to the scrutiny surrounding his performances for the national team.
Messi captained Argentina to the 2014 World Cup final in Brazil.
Argentina lost 1-0 to Germany after extra time at the Maracana.
Messi won the Golden Ball as the tournament's best player, but the defeat deepened the perception that he could dominate club football with Barcelona without delivering the ultimate prize for his country.
A year later, Argentina reached another major final.
Chile beat Argentina on penalties in the Copa America final in Santiago.
Messi had now lost three major international finals with Argentina, intensifying criticism at home.
Argentina lost another Copa America final to Chile on penalties in 2016.
Messi missed his penalty in the shootout and, overwhelmed by another defeat, announced his retirement from international football.
The decision shocked Argentina.
The country that had spent years questioning whether Messi could reproduce his Barcelona form for the national team suddenly faced the possibility of losing its greatest player.
Messi reversed his decision weeks later after talks with new Argentina coach Edgardo Bauza, citing his love for his country and the national team shirt.
The comeback did not immediately erase the criticism, but it marked the beginning of a gradual change in his relationship with the national team.
He would eventually become the undisputed captain and central figure of a team increasingly built around him.
Argentina defeated Brazil 1-0 at the Maracana to win the Copa America.
For Messi, it was the breakthrough he had waited for throughout his career.
He had finally won a major senior international title with Argentina, easing years of criticism over his lack of success with the national team.
The biggest prize, however, was still ahead.
Argentina defeated France on penalties after a 3-3 draw in the 2022 World Cup final in Qatar.
Messi scored twice in the final and converted his penalty in the shootout.
At 35, he finally became a world champion, claiming the last major prize missing from his Argentina career.
Argentina defeated Colombia 1-0 after extra time in Copa America final in Miami.
Messi lifted the trophy again, giving Argentina back-to-back Copa America titles alongside the 2022 World Cup.
Messi's sixth World Cup ended with Argentina losing 1-0 to Spain after extra time in the final in New Jersey.
The result denied Messi a fairytale ending with a second World Cup title.
Messi announced that he was retiring from international football.
He said the decision hurt but that he had given everything he had to Argentina and believed the time had come for younger players to take their opportunity.
After Messi announced his retirement, the Argentine Football Association invited him back for one final appearance, with President Claudio Tapia saying the captain deserved a farewell in Argentina.
More than two decades after Argentina first discovered the teenage Messi in Barcelona, the 39-year-old will wear the national team shirt for the final time against Benin at the Monumental.
He enters his farewell with a record 207 appearances and 125 goals, alongside a World Cup, two Copa America titles, and a Finalissima.
But his Argentina journey was also about belonging.
Argentina had to discover him, doubt him, lose him, welcome him back — and finally fall in love with him.

IMF warns growing hedge fund footprint could amplify financial market stress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
19:13:02 UTC
04:13:02 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Hedge funds are becoming increasingly important players in global financial markets, but vulnerabilities linked to leverage, fragile funding and crowded positions could amplify market stress, the International Monetary Fund warned Tuesday.
The IMF released the “Hedge Funds and Financial Stability” chapter of its Global Financial Stability Report, ahead of the full report’s Oct. 13.
Hedge funds’ gross assets rose from $4 trillion in 2013 to around $13 trillion by early 2026, according to the report.
Their expanding market presence can support liquidity and efficiency during normal conditions, but can also intensify price disruptions and liquidity pressures during periods of financial stress.
The report identified leverage, fragile funding structures and crowded trades, where multiple funds hold similar positions, as key vulnerabilities behind the risks.
It called for closing data gaps and strengthening risk monitoring, alongside targeted measures to address risks arising from crowded positions and simultaneous reductions in leverage.
IMF officials said in an accompanying blog post that hedge funds’ growing footprint was particularly evident in government bond markets, with funds holding about 9% of US Treasury securities in 2025.
Unlike most other financial intermediaries, hedge funds face relatively few restrictions on investing and borrowing, said officials.
That flexibility allows them to invest in illiquid assets, make extensive use of leverage and adjust positions rapidly.
The characteristics can support liquidity, price discovery and risk sharing in normal conditions. When markets deteriorate, however, they can also transmit and amplify shocks across the financial system, officials warned.

France erupts over schools: Why the violence surrounding surprise movement?
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
It’s a protest movement that a broke, lame-duck French government did not see coming. Civil servants this Tuesday joined high schoolers who are now in their third week of picketing over long-deteriorating classroom conditions. The usual recipe for wearing down movements in France has recently been to match any violence with a heavy hand, with the escalation turning the silent majority against the protesters, as was the case with the pre-Covid Yellow Vests movement.
There has certainly been plenty of violence. But those involved are teenagers, not adults, with many pressing legitimate gripes about growing inequality in education. Some organising on Snapchat and other socials are clearly cynical about their own future prospects and ready to have it out. With France in full pre-election posturing mode ahead of polls next spring, some see pigs where others see hoodlums, with the government borrowing the far right's language and the far left focusing on police brutality.
What President Emmanuel Macron's team doesn't have this time around is what's being called magic money; the funds that French governments usually pull out of a hat to make a crisis go away. With France's highest public debt rate in a quarter of a century spooking the eurozone and beyond, no magic money will this time appear to hire more teachers or build more classrooms. So what's the answer?

Former Obama official will review Cornell’s handling of sexual misconduct complaints

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06

04:11:49 KST

A former high-ranking Department of Justice official will look at how Cornell handles sexual misconduct complaints, university trustees announced on Tuesday as they tried to address an outpouring of anger over allegations of a 2024 gang rape at a fraternity house.
Sally Yates, who was a deputy attorney general in the Obama administration, will spearhead the review, the trustees said. The assessment is to include how the Ivy League university investigates reports of sexual assault and sexual harassment, how the disciplinary process works, the adequacy of campus police responses, and more.
“It is imperative that Cornell be willing to examine itself with the same rigor we expect of others,” the trustee chair, Anne Meinig Smalling, said in a statement.
The announcement comes after days of outrage and a large demonstration over Cornell’s response to a complaint from a woman known publicly only as Jane Doe. She told campus police in November 2024 that she had been sexually assaulted by multiple Chi Phi fraternity brothers the month before after being pressured into drinking and taking drugs.
No criminal charges have been filed. The Chi Phi chapter at Cornell was shut down, and the Ivy League university has said it expelled some students and suspended others.
Yates will look at how the woman’s complaint was handled and at the oversight of fraternities, sororities and other campus groups, Cornell said.
The woman sued the university, seven former students, the fraternity and others last month.
Lawyers for two of the former students denied they participated in a sexual assault. Attempts by the Associated Press to reach the other men or their representatives have been unsuccessful. Court records show that during an investigation that Cornell conducted under the federal Title IX law, some of the accused students contended that the sexual activity was consensual.
The lawsuit put a new, nationwide spotlight on the allegations and how the campus police, university and local prosecutor had reacted.
New York’s attorney general is now conducting a criminal investigation, and the state’s governor called for an independent review of Cornell’s handling of the matter – the review that Yates now will lead.
Cornell students, professors and others thronged a campus plaza on Monday to protest the university’s response to the matter and demand more accountability, greater transparency, an overhaul of the disciplinary process and other changes.
Yates had a decades-long career at the justice department, serving for years as the top federal prosecutor in Atlanta and later as a deputy attorney general.
She achieved particular prominence in January 2017, when, as acting attorney general in the early days of the Trump administration, she directed justice department attorneys not to defend the constitutionality of Donald Trump’s refugee and immigration ban. She was swiftly fired, with Trump accusing her of betrayal and insubordination.
Yates also generated headlines when it emerged that, in a conversation days before her departure, she had expressed alarm to the Trump White House about contacts that Trump’s new national security adviser, Michael Flynn, had had with the Russian ambassador during the presidential transition period. Flynn later was fired.
Yates has been in private practice since her departure from the justice department. Her practice at the King & Spalding law firm includes conducting independent investigations for outside organizations and companies.
She led a high-profile inquiry into alleged abuse and misconduct, including claims of harassment and coercion, at the National Women’s Soccer League. The investigation concluded in 2022 with a finding of systemic abuse.

Russia closely watching NATO over attack warnings: Lavrov
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
19:09:00 UTC
04:09:00 KST

Russia is closely tracking NATO statements about preparations for a potential attack by Moscow and remains vigilant amid heightened tensions with the alliance, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Tuesday.
"So, we hear what is being said, but, as the saying goes, we keep our guard up,” Lavrov told a news conference in Moscow after talks with Bendito Freitas, the foreign minister of Timor-Leste.
Lavrov said Moscow is focused on fulfilling the objectives set by President Vladimir Putin for the war in Ukraine, including preventing threats from its Western neighbors.
He also referred to recent tensions over Kaliningrad, saying Putin made it clear that any attack on the semi-exclave or another part of Russia would receive a response.
"When we issued a very clear statement in response to threats from Baltic and other NATO members-who have gotten out of hand-to attack the Kaliningrad region, we were immediately assured by both NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte and the US Permanent Representative to NATO (Matthew) Whitaker that the bloc has no plans to attack Russia-nor could it-and that NATO is, after all, a defensive alliance,” he said.
On Afghanistan, Lavrov said Russia regretted that participants in the latest Moscow Format consultations failed to adopt a final document because of tensions between Kabul and Afghanistan.
He claimed the dispute was linked partly to the presence of ISIS (Daesh) militants in both countries, and called for an end to interference by countries from outside the region.
"I have no doubt whatsoever that both Afghanistan and Pakistan are interested in normalizing relations. Russia is doing its utmost to facilitate the resolution of both persisting and newly emerging problems," he said.
Lavrov described his talks with Freitas as "highly productive” and said the two sides discussed expanding cooperation in energy, mining, fisheries and tourism.
He said Russia was ready to increase energy supplies to the Southeast Asian country and expressed support for expanding educational and law enforcement cooperation.
The ministers also discussed cooperation through ASEAN and developments in the Asia-Pacific region, with Lavrov criticizing Western efforts to create exclusive bloc-based structures outside the ASEAN-centered framework.
Lavrov said they also discussed Middle East, Iran, and the war in Ukraine. He said Russia and Timor-Leste would prepare for events to mark the 25th anniversary of diplomatic relations in May 2027.
The Russian Foreign Ministry said the ministers held a "substantive” exchange of views on bilateral issues, including deepening political dialogue, expanding trade, economic and humanitarian cooperation and strengthening the legal framework of their relations.
Lavrov said Freitas also discussed key international and regional issues and urged closer coordination between Russia and Timor-Leste within the U.N. system and the Russia-ASEAN dialogue partnership, it said.

Mert Davut
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
The Turkish Space Agency (TUA) has signed two agreements with the space agencies of fellow member countries of the Organization of Turkic States as well as the UK Space Agency to help strengthen international cooperation.
The agreements were signed during the first two days of this week’s 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC 2026) in the Turkish Riviera city of Antalya, which began on Monday.
A new framework agreement builds on existing cooperation under a joint CubeSat project coordinated by the Organization of Turkic States, which Türkiye is a founding member of. It aims to advance joint work and lay the groundwork for future space projects.
The Turkish Space Agency also signed a declaration of intent with the UK Space Agency to develop cooperation and joint projects in space.
Organized by the International Astronautical Federation, IAC 2026 is being held at Antalya’s NEST Congress Center under the coordination of Türkiye’s Industry and Technology Ministry.
The Turkish Space Agency and SAHA Istanbul are co-hosting the event, with Anadolu serving as its Global Communications Partner.

Chinese company to face Australian privacy probe over 'pervert' glasses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
19:00:27 UTC
04:00:27 KST

Australian regulator launches probe into Chinese smart glasses company amid privacy fears
In short:
Chinese software company Shenzhen Qingcheng is being investigated by the Australian privacy commissioner following an ABC investigation.
It revealed last month more than a dozen serious security flaws in the company's app and website used in the glasses for sale in Kmart, Big W Marketplace and Amazon.
What next?
The privacy commissioner is urging retailers to reconsider selling the product for now.
The Australian privacy commissioner has launched a formal investigation into the Chinese software company behind an influx of cheap smart glasses to Australia.
It is the most significant action authorities have taken so far to address mounting community concern over the devices nicknamed "pervert glasses" by their detractors.
In August, Attorney-General Michelle Rowland took the unusual step of asking the regulator to prioritise the issue amid calls for an import ban.
A recent ABC investigation found more than a dozen serious security flaws in the HeyCyan phone app used in smart glasses sold by Kmart, as well as online platforms such as Big W Marketplace and Amazon, among others.
Independent testing of the low-cost glasses found Australians' sensitive data, including email addresses, dates of birth, images and videos, were left exposed to hackers.
It also found the devices could be hijacked by nearby attackers without a password using only a Bluetooth connection, and that data was in some cases being sent to Chinese servers.
"The ABC's reporting … raised the prospect that there haven't been reasonable steps taken to secure [user] information," Privacy Commissioner Carly Kind said.
She said her office had "a range of concerns" about the practices of the company, Shenzhen Qingcheng Future Technology Co (Shenzhen Qingcheng), including about the possible use of facial recognition technology.
"We will certainly bring to bear the full weight of our powers on the matter,"
she said.
Smart glasses, which look like ordinary glasses, allow the wearer to capture images, video and audio with the press of a button or verbal command.
It is not always clear when they are in use.
The regulator also made preliminary inquiries with Meta, Google, Kmart, and an importer called BDI Technology over their supply of similar tech in Australia, but none of the other companies is the subject of a formal investigation.
Shenzhen Qingcheng was the only company which opted to ignore the regulator completely, Ms Kind said.
"The company did not respond at all to our multiple attempts to obtain information … [and] did not even acknowledge receipt of our communications," she said.
"It does suggest that some of the fundamentals may not be in place, for example, compliance teams that are appropriately staffed.
"We would normally expect pretty prompt attention [to] be given to any outreach from the regulator".
A formal investigation means the privacy commissioner will now have the power to compel Shenzhen Qingcheng to provide information about how it is complying with Australian laws.
If the company continues to ignore the regulator, she can seek a court injunction to limit the supply of its products.
Shenzhen Qingcheng could theoretically face fines of hundreds of millions or even billions of dollars if ultimately found to have interfered with the privacy of Australians.
"The Australian Privacy Act provides for really, really considerable monetary penalties in the form of $50 million per contravention … and that can be applied per individual," Ms Kind said.
"That would be what we would be shooting for, should our concerns be borne out".
Retailers urged to pull glasses
In the meantime, the regulator has urged retailers such as Kmart to reconsider selling the product at all.
"We have written to the Australian Retail Council and to other retailers, putting them on notice that this company is under investigation," Ms Kind said.
"Responsible retailers might want to consider whether it is appropriate to continue making these products available."
The federal government has decided not to place an import ban on smart glasses at this stage, but was considering a limited ban within public service workplaces.
Despite ignoring requests from the privacy commissioner, Shenzhen Qingcheng has responded to ABC News twice.
A legal representative for the company said engineers had since fixed security flaws pointed out by the ABC.
But cybersecurity analysts at NSB Cyber and Abstract Shield found that while several improvements had been made, many fixes had not worked or were incomplete as of October 2.

Young anti-war protesters turn a sanctioned Communist Party rally in Moscow into a protest of their own. Police detain more than 60 people.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:59:34 UTC
03:59:34 KST

Young anti-war protesters turn a sanctioned Communist Party rally in Moscow into a protest of their own. Police detain more than 60 people.
On October 4, the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (KPRF) held an authorized rally in central Moscow to mark the anniversary of the shelling of the White House. Besides the Communists themselves, young people unaffiliated with the KPRF unexpectedly turned out, including members of left-wing political groups and Yabloko supporters. Organizers said 65 people were detained at the demonstration, where the young participants chanted sharply critical political slogans. Meduza spoke with Anna (not her real name), a law student at a Moscow university who marched in the youth contingent.
Warning: This article contains profanity. If that’s unacceptable to you, please don’t read it.
— Why did you go to a KPRF rally?
— It’s one of the few authorized rallies these days. As far as I know, the KPRF leadership had a verbal agreement with City Hall to allow a separate group of smaller [left-wing] parties, including the RRP. Yabloko supporters joined us.
The main group was up ahead — maybe they were just walking faster. They had their KPRF banners, and some people carried Soviet flags. We weren’t allowed to carry anything at all: The Communist Party leadership asked us to put away every symbol except those of the KPRF and the USSR.
There was a plant in our group who would walk up to protesters, point someone out, and that person would get detained. Our group had the most people detained. Three police vans followed us.
At first, they weren’t supposed to have a problem with us as long as we didn’t chant slogans [that the KPRF hadn’t approved]. But it didn’t work out that way. We chanted them. So our group got the most attention [from the police].
— Was there some sort of verbal agreement with the KPRF leadership about a separate group for the smaller parties?
— Yes. The KPRF had an agreement with City Hall, and the smaller parties had one with the KPRF.
— And under that agreement, you weren’t supposed to chant slogans?
— The approved slogan was “No to political persecution!” All the slogans allowed at the rally are listed on the KPRF website. But we were chanting about repression.
That was all just a formality, though. They were grabbing people who hadn’t chanted anything — people who were just going to lay flowers [at the Memorial Cross]. They detained someone holding up a copy of Pravda. They were pulling people straight out of the crowd.
— Can you tell us which political party or movement you belong to?
— I’d rather not. The party isn’t registered yet.
— Roughly how old were the people at the rally?
— There were lots of young people in our group. Overall, the rally had young people and old people.
My friends and I got to Ulitsa 1905 Goda metro station by 11 a.m. We were meeting people so we could walk together to the monument. The official part of the rally began there at 11:30, and people stood holding portraits of those who were killed [defending the White House]. People our age and younger came up to us. Mostly college students, though.
— How did the older KPRF supporters react to your group? Were they surprised to see so many young people?
— Yes, they were surprised. One really reactionary guy heard the slogans “Free Morozov” and “Support Bondarenko” and started shouting that “Russia supports Putin.” Another woman did her absolute best to drown out our chants with official KPRF slogans as we marched.
— Tell us how the rally went.
— Zyuganov gave a speech at the monument, followed by Kharitonov. We listened to pompous speeches about how great Russia is and how Ukrainians are “neo-Nazis.” Then Zyuganov said a few words about the elections — that they were rigged because everyone he knows personally voted for the KPRF. Funny.
I agree that the election results don’t reflect the actual vote, but Zyuganov’s speech was the same as always… It’s “Ziganov” [a play on Zyuganov’s name and the Nazi salute “Sieg Heil”] — you know what I mean.
At 1 p.m., the part with the speeches and portraits [of the White House defenders] ended, and we headed toward the [Memorial Cross], where people laid flowers. Unfortunately, not everyone made it there.
— Where did most of the detentions happen?
— They started detaining people on Krasnaya Presnya Street, about half an hour into the march. By then, the main KPRF group had moved ahead — they were standing at the memorial, and nobody was bothering them. For the most part, they left the older people alone.
— How do you feel about the KPRF in general?
— The KPRF is somewhere between being part of the system and being in opposition. The authorities generally have less of a problem with it [than with opposition parties outside the system]. At the same time, Zyuganov is willing to say that the elections were rigged and that blocking the internet is bad.
Obviously, none of these parties except Yabloko is against the war, and on that point, the KPRF can’t offer what young people want. But if you join the KPRF or find yourself among its supporters, you don’t risk getting fired from your job or kicked out of your university or college.
That’s much less likely with the KPRF than it is for Yabloko supporters or people who took part in rallies supporting Navalny — all of that was much more dangerous than turning out on October 4. This rally was officially approved, and at first the police weren’t dispersing anyone. They just watched.
So even though the old guys in the KPRF are shady characters who should’ve retired long ago, it’s still one way to protest. Obviously, just showing up at this rally doesn’t solve anything, but it is what it is.
— Why did you go anyway?
— To show that we exist. There were lots of young people at the rally. I heard chants of “Down with Roskomnadzor [Russia’s internet regulator],” “No to war,” “Down with the gray moth [Putin],” and “Down with the tsar.”
At the memorial, after they started dispersing everyone, people began shouting, “Fuck United Russia.” Basically, people used an approved rally to chant unapproved slogans.
I know lots of people who campaigned for the KPRF, served as the party’s election observers in the parliamentary elections, and go to rallies like this.
— It seems paradoxical to me that someone would go to KPRF rallies while fundamentally disagreeing with the party’s position on the war.
— I think people just want some action. There’s nothing going on, but you want to get involved. You want to get at least something done while you still can.
— Do you know anything about how the KPRF leadership reacted to what your group was doing?
— No. I was busy helping the people who’d been detained.
— When did they start detaining people, and why? There were reports that most of the detentions began after protesters started chanting “Down with the tsar.” Is that true?
— No. They were already detaining people at Ulitsa 1905 Goda metro station. They grabbed someone with a North Korean flag there, and someone else with a white-blue-white flag.
Then, during the march, they took away the person with the copy of Pravda. As we approached Kropotkinskaya, they grabbed someone with anarchist symbols. They were picking people out of the crowd, whoever caught their eye. Then they started detaining people en masse on Druzhinnikovskaya Street — they filled all three police vans right there.
— What set it off?
— Hard to say. It looked more like they were trying to stop something before it started. Because the slogans weren’t all that bloodthirsty yet. We hadn’t started chanting “Down with the tsar.” That was when several people I know got detained. Someone shouted, “Let’s get out of here, they’re taking people away over there,” and I ran with the others toward Krasnaya Presnya Park. There were just over 20 of us.
After that, I went back to the rally — to the people I knew. We tried to find out what was happening to the people who’d been detained and whether they’d be released. But it turned out they didn’t release everyone.
— You said there were more young people at the rally. Does that include the main group?
— I didn’t see it up close. But the youth group was several times bigger than the official one.
— What were people talking about in your group?
— Something happened that says a lot. A girl came up to me at the rally and asked, “How do you feel about Zyuganov?” I told her, “Fuck that Zyuganov guy,” and she shook my hand. Then a bunch of Yabloko supporters came up to me and said, “Listen, do you know if there’s some way we can join your group? So we don’t get detained right away.” And we agreed to let them join us.
— Yabloko itself said its members didn’t take part in the rally.
— There were lots of new Yabloko supporters who hadn’t even joined the party yet. These are really fired-up young people who want regime change and an end to all of this [the war].
— How did the police behave when they were detaining people?
— They didn’t hit anyone. They just intimidated people — surrounded them so they knew that was it, there was no getting out. Then they’d take hold of one shoulder, almost like putting an arm around you, then the other, and press down on your shoulders so you couldn’t break free.
Outside the courthouse, there were some unpleasant characters [officers from the Tagansky police precinct who had arrived in the police vans] who wouldn’t let a lawyer near the van. They wouldn’t even let the lawyer get within two meters [about six feet]. They kept people in the van for four hours, until 6 p.m. As I understand it, they did that deliberately to keep members of the public out of the courtroom [while the judge imposed jail terms for administrative offenses]: The court officially closes after six.
But the ruling in the case of Vladimir Bodyashkin, who’d been detained, came at 1 a.m.
— What do we know about the people who were detained?
— Altogether, more than 60 people were detained. Their cases were heard in three courts. One of the lawyers who went to Krasnoselsky Court told me that many got off with fines. One guy was jailed for 14 days.
At Tagansky Court, two people got fines — their lawyers argued that they hadn’t taken part in the rally at all and were on their way to the zoo. They were released at 11 p.m. Those proven to have taken part in the rally got jail terms of 10 and 15 days.
The judge there was Alexandra Anokhina. As [human rights advocates] told us, she’s one of the main judges handling political cases and cases involving “foreign agents.” So if anyone walks out of her courtroom with just a fine, that’s a godsend.
— Were protesters able to organize help for those who were detained?
— During the rally, people went up [to the police] and asked whether they’d be releasing anyone. Older KPRF supporters also came over and tried to help somehow. One even shoved a police officer so people could get away — and about five did.
After the detentions, friends and family of those who’d been detained went to the police stations.
— Did the KPRF provide legal help to the people who were detained?
— They say it did. But nobody from the party showed up at Tagansky District Court, either on the day of the rally or the next day.
Otherwise, people organized themselves and went to the police stations. Fewer made it to the courts. There were 15 people outside Tagansky Court: friends, fellow activists, parents of those who’d been detained, and a couple of Yabloko supporters who just came to show support.
— You mentioned the rallies in support of Navalny.
— I didn’t take part back then because I didn’t know anyone who shared my political views. I lived in a small town, and my parents asked me to be careful.
— How did you get interested in politics? What set that off?
— A couple of years ago, in high school, I met like-minded people who were interested in politics. Before that, I was pretty apolitical and really worried about my own freedom — being able to walk down the street. Though somewhere deep down, I was unhappy with what was going on.
My friend was among the first sent to fight in the “special military operation” [Russia’s term for the war in Ukraine]. Before it began, he was serving as a contract soldier in the border areas. I lost touch with him then, and when the official announcements started, I put it all together and got really scared for him.
I spent a year worrying like that, until they finally sent him home for treatment. The war was a turning point for me.
— You said you used to be afraid of losing your personal freedom. What about now?
— Much less now. Emotionally, it would be easier for me to end up in the same police van as the others.
— Do you think there’s a way to express opposition to the authorities peacefully in Russia?
— It seems like you can, but you’ll be punished for all of it. They’ll keep track of everything, and at some point that’ll lead to proceedings for administrative offenses — and possibly criminal ones. But going to rallies isn’t the only thing you can do. You can join Yabloko, go to evenings where people write letters to political prisoners.
You can do activism that’s less political, like something to do with the city’s infrastructure. There’s a lot you can do — if you’re prepared to do time for your ideals and sacrifice your personal freedom.
— Are you prepared to do that?
— Up to a point. If we’re talking about an administrative offense, then yes. Anything more than that, I’m afraid I’m not ready. I’m studying law, and I’d like to be able to practice law.
— How dangerous do you think it is to be in opposition now?
— It’s dangerous. But if you do nothing, things will get worse. When you think things can’t get any worse, they do.
— Are young people in Russia politically engaged today?
— Young people are apolitical, but they want to live without websites and apps being blocked. They want more comfortable lives, more personal freedom, and fewer sanctions — that’s about as political as they get.
Though, judging by conversations with my fellow students, people are getting more political. But it’s hard for me to judge, because about 10 years ago I was in school playing “My Little Pony,” sorry.

Russian forces fail to achieve September objectives in Huliaipole and Orikhiv directions — Defense Forces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:59:00 UTC
03:59:00 KST

Russian forces fail to achieve September objectives in Huliaipole and Orikhiv directions — Defense Forces
Anastasiia Shevchenko, spokesperson for the Operational Task Force South, stated this in a comment to Ukrinform.
Shevchenko said that Russian forces had ambitious plans for October in the Huliaipole and Orikhiv directions, but had in fact failed to accomplish the objectives assigned to them in September.
Photo: Spokesperson for the Operational Task Force South Anastasiia Shevchenko
According to her, some enemy units report to Russia's senior military leadership that they have completed their objectives of capturing settlements and advancing, although this has not actually happened. As a result, the Russian command is setting even more ambitious objectives for October.
Shevchenko said that, in particular, by the end of the month, units of the enemy's airborne forces group had been tasked with reaching the barrier line of the Kinska River. At the same time, the objective of capturing designated settlements that had been set for September had not been achieved.
She added that the Huliaipole direction was currently the hottest area, where Ukraine's Defense Forces were facing one of the largest groupings of Russian occupation forces, formed from units of several Russian combined-arms armies. At the same time, the enemy had abandoned large-scale offensive operations along a broad front and was using infiltration tactics.
The spokesperson said that the enemy also periodically attempted to conduct assaults with small assault groups supported by motorcycles and quad bikes, but had achieved no success.
Shevchenko said that in the Orikhiv direction, Russian forces were also continuing their offensive tasks, but no significant advance toward the designated lines had been recorded so far.
She noted that the enemy had not abandoned its intention to capture Orikhiv and Zaporizhzhia, but currently lacked sufficient forces and means to advance directly toward the regional capital.
The spokesperson stressed that Russian forces would likely continue offensive operations and attempt to reach the designated line by the end of October. At the same time, the failure to accomplish some of the objectives planned for September indicated that Ukraine's Defense Forces, including the Operational Task Force South, were effectively containing the enemy.
Shevchenko emphasized that Russian forces continued to suffer significant personnel losses in the operational zone of the Operational Task Force South. In September, units of the group eliminated more than 4,900 Russian troops and destroyed 2,070 pieces of weapons and military equipment.
She concluded that, overall, the operational situation in the area of responsibility of the Operational Task Force South remained largely unchanged.
As Ukrinform reported, on October 5, Russian forces attacked Ukrainian positions five times in the Huliaipole direction, attempting to advance toward Uspishne, Rizdvianka and Yehorivka.
In the Orikhiv direction, Russian forces attempted to attack toward Pavlivka once.
