Ukraine Rejects Permanent EU Limits on Its Farm Exports After Accession
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:45:49 UTC
03:45:49 KST

Ukraine will not accept EU membership terms that permanently cap its sales of sensitive farm products to the bloc, Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi said on Tuesday, Oct. 6, hours after the European Commission backed such restrictions.
Vysotskyi revealed Kyiv’s position to Politico in the form of a written statement. Earlier on Tuesday, the Commission had adopted its pre-enlargement policy review, a package designed to prepare the EU’s institutions, policies and budget for the arrival of new members.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Among the proposals was to curb Ukraine’s access to farm subsidies and the EU market for certain agricultural goods – even after the country joins the bloc.
“For us, there is a fundamental difference between a transitional period and a permanent restriction. Ukraine is prepared for the former,” Vysotskyi told Politico.
“The latter would run counter to the very logic of full EU membership,” he continued.
While Kyiv remains open to temporary arrangements, such as gradually phasing in farm subsidies, temporary quotas and safeguards for sensitive products, it reiterated that every such measure must have a fixed end date.
Leaked draft signaled special terms
The outlines of the plan surfaced a day earlier, on Monday, Oct. 5, when the Financial Times reported on an internal Commission document on reforming the enlargement process which it had reviewed.
According to Ukrainska Pravda citing FT, the draft justified special treatment by pointing to the size, structure and productivity of Ukraine’s farm sector.
Lithuania Moves Closer Toward Scrapping Nuclear Weapons Ban
It also singled out wheat and other grains as products where support and market access could be significantly restricted.
The restrictions were reportedly intended to calm existing members of the bloc that are worried about competition from Ukrainian grain and oilseeds, including Poland, France and Italy.
Instead of full access to the EU market, Brussels proposed helping Ukraine win back traditional export markets disrupted by Russia’s ongoing aggression. According to Politico, the Commission would rather help Ukraine get back into its “historic” export markets, which include primarily the Middle East and Africa.
The draft also proposed tying new members’ access to EU funds to reform progress and it easier to strip a member state of its voting rights for breaking EU rules. It envisaged individual accession roadmaps for Ukraine, Moldova, Montenegro and Albania, none with a fixed membership date.
The EU’s Common Agricultural Policy provides about €55 billion ($62 billion) a year in agricultural funding, including an agricultural reserve of at least €450 million ($507 million) annually to address market disruptions and exceptional events affecting production or distribution.
Vysotskyi pushes back against threat claims
In his statement to Politico, Vysotskyi pushed back against the idea that Ukrainian agriculture is “solely” a threat to EU farmers.
He argued that Ukraine could reduce the bloc’s reliance on imports from third countries for fertilizers, soybeans and lysine used in animal feed.
According to him, Ukraine could also open Black Sea export routes to EU producers and serve as a destination for investment in food processing.
“Our goal is to reach membership with a sector that sells Europe not only grain and other raw materials but also animal feed, ingredients, processed products, and biofuels,” Vystoskyi concluded.
Talks with Kyiv already begun
According to European Pravda, Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said that the scale and productivity of Ukrainian farming called for “targeted arrangements for sensitive agricultural products only.”
She, however, did not provide additional details.
According to Kos, discussions with Kyiv had already begun and the specific terms could be set when the EU opens the agriculture cluster, No. 5 – the last one still closed to Ukraine.
“What we propose now is about protecting European farmers,” she said, insisting that Ukraine could still become a full member despite the special conditions.
Later on Tuesday, the main conditions for another part of the package was outlined; gradual integration, which allows candidates to join selected EU policies before formal accession.
The package, according to Kos, also proposes moving away from unanimity toward majority voting in several policy areas. The change could make it harder for a single member state to stall enlargement.
The EU leaders are set to further discuss the proposals at the European Council summit on Oct. 15-16.

====================================================================================================

‘Artificial’ Roasts AI’s Creators—and Sends a Dark Warning About Its Dangers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:45:39 UTC
03:45:39 KST

Artificial, the new comedy-drama about OpenAI and the artificial intelligence arms race, is a movie of weird walks.
As OpenAI cofounder Ilya Sutskever, Russian actor Yuri Borisov clomps around, like a geeky Frankensteinian monster. As the controversial OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Andrew Garfield bounces and skips boyishly—a gait that Altman himself recently commended for its accuracy. And as Elon Musk, Ike Barinholtz puts on a loping swagger, commanding rooms of computer nerds like some sort of alpha gorilla (a semblance matched by his long, pouting faces, which call to mind those old Bored Ape NFTs).
During the movie’s post-premiere Q&A earlier this week at the New York Film Festival, Barinholtz wryly described his character as “a person who walks normally.” Such are the awkward saunters of the march of history in the making.
Artificial, directed by Luca Guadagnino, waltzed into NYFF with some controversy clinging to it. The film was originally set to be released by AmazonMGM, which conspicuously dropped it this summer after Amazon struck a $50 billion deal with OpenAI. (Indie house Neon swooped in to pick it up.) NYFF artistic director Dennis Lim referenced “the circumstances” around the film in his onstage introduction.
That OpenAI may have brooked issues with Artificial makes sense. The film is almost completely unflattering, depicting Altman and other OpenAI stakeholders—as well as all the major drivers of the AI boom—as vain, reckless, and insufferably boring. Where 2010’s The Social Network succeeded in making Silicon Valley computer savants look like robust titans of industry and architects of the future, Artificial works to opposing ends. It depicts its tech titans as self-regarding dweebs.
Comparisons to David Fincher’s Facebook drama are inevitable. There’s the subject matter, of course. And the fact that both films feature Garfield in a lead role. (It should be said that Artificial is really more of a biopic of Sutskever, here depicted as both the prime mover of the current AI wave and its nagging moral conscience, than it is of Altman.) But Guadagnino and writer-producer Simon Rich’s approach to the material feels diametrically opposed to Fincher’s. The Social Network was a steely, polished, wordy drama. Artificial is pitched as a black comedy that verges on the surreal.
Guadagnino, best known in Hollywood for the coming-of-age drama Call Me by Your Name and the three-way tennis romance Challengers, has mastered a strain of tense eroticism. There are shades of that in Artificial, in Altman’s seductive wooing of Sutskever’s character. But the film is, for the most part, literally and figuratively sexless.
The images are plain, and even a little ugly. You can almost feel Guadagnino’s more rococo style begging to break out. A slo-mo sequence of a room of gawky programmers dousing each other in bottles of Jarritos, celebrating their AI’s latest self-learning benchmark, is stickily unsexy. A climactic scene of Altman and his OpenAI lackeys confronting Sutskever on a sloping San Francisco street recalls the green-screen backdrops of Tommy Wiseau’s cult classic The Room. After the screening, Guadagnino claimed the story captured a different strain of desire—what he described as “the desire to prevail.”
It’s a need many viewers might share, as leaders in the AI industry (including Altman) appear united in tamping down the technology’s acceleration. Artificial intelligence, we are told, is developing so rapidly, and is becoming so sophisticated, that it risks compromising life on Earth as we know it. In a recent interview with WIRED, former Anthropic AI employee Jacob Coxon alleged that his former colleagues have described the next few years as the potential “endgame” for humanity itself. Another Anthropic researcher claimed that there’s a chance that AI could “kill all humans” within a decade. (The odds were set below 10 percent, which still seems extremely high.)
Artificial stages these tensions as a kind of a high moral drama. Borisov’s well-meaning researcher—depicted as being temperamentally incapable of lying—pleads for safeguards, slow-downs, and AI’s “alignment” with humanity’s broader interests. Meanwhile, the case for exponential technological and capital growth is argued by, well, basically everyone else.
Even the idea of safety itself as saleable. In one scene, concerns about OpenAI’s capacity for serious harm is framed as being beneficial only to the company’s bottom line. Sounding alarm bells signals transparency and due diligence. And the harmful capacity itself is seen as proof positive of the technology’s advancement. It’s win-win. And it’s also no-win.
Artificial makes a persuasive, and frustrating, point about the ongoing AI contest. Pick a metaphor: The train has already left the station, the horses have fled the barn, the toothpaste is out of the tube. The technology already exists. And so, as with nukes in the last century, it becomes not a question of the power itself but who is allowed to harness it, and how. (In his post-Anthropic exit interview, Coxon directly compared the company to the Manhattan Project.)
Questions of ethics become academic, or just annoying, when everyone involved is playing by a different rulebook. If it’s not OpenAI that controls computing’s future, it will be Anthropic, or Google, or Elon Musk. Or, worst of all—at least according to the Trump administration—China. (An early scene in Artificial sees Sutskever and his mentor, Nobel laureate computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton, played by Mark Rylance, rebuff the advances of a Chinese investor eager to use their neural network technology for drones and face-recognition systems.)
It may be hard for the average moviegoer, who may only engage with AI for email rewriting or calendar organization, to gauge just how seriously to take Artificial’s alarmist warnings. Not least of all because basically every character in the film is depicted as at least completely self-serving, if not sociopathic. And of course, one may naturally wince a little bit at a star-studded Hollywood movie raising these alarms, with a lavish premiere at a Rolex-sponsored film festival and a glitzy afterparty attended by stars, famous comedians, and notable filmmakers (including octogenarian Taxi Driver screenwriter Paul Schrader, who recently publicly confessed to being dumped by an “AI girlfriend”).
As a message movie, Artificial seems likely only to confirm the worst misgivings of AI doomers, while riling its diehard boosters. It is, however, genuinely funny in places, regarding the bulk of our future’s self-appointed engineers with withering contempt, from their dorky parties to their weird walks.
It was a stance embraced by Barinholtz, who offered the premiere-night audience his own half-hearted, sarcastic reassurance: “The future is bright! We’re all gonna be fine!” Cue a round of very nervous laughter.

Cambridge academics say university’s plans to investigate Jason Arday’s death are inadequate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:44:25 UTC
03:44:25 KST

Senior Cambridge academics have criticised the university’s plans to investigate Prof Jason Arday’s death as inadequate, and said those responsible for “serious failures of leadership” should face consequences.
In a letter to Chris Smith, Cambridge’s chancellor, the academics said “it is not yet clear” how the proposed review will answer difficult questions about the university’s involvement in the events leading up to Arday’s death, including its handling of the criticism Arday suffered after his appointment as professor of sociology of education in 2023.
Arday died at his home in London on 14 August, nine days after he resigned amid allegations of plagiarism and inconsistencies in statements about his career.
An inquest will be held to determine the cause of death.
Arday’s family said he was subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse for more than three years.
Now, a letter signed by more than 40 professors, associate professors and fellows raises concern that Cambridge has backed away from initial promises by Deborah Prentice, the university’s vice-chancellor, to carry out a “thorough and transparent” examination of the circumstances that led to Arday’s appointment and treatment.
Rather than reviewing the “lessons learned”, the group wants the investigation to pinpoint the crucial advice given and decisions made during Arday’s hiring and subsequent career.
“The investigation must establish who authorised and directed the university’s public promotion of Professor Arday; what assessment was made of the risks that accompanied it; who authorised any legal or other communications with journalists investigating the story; what the university knew as racist and ableist abuse and media hounding escalated; and how responsibility for Professor Arday’s protection was allocated and exercised across the university,” the letter says.
The signatories included Cahir O’Kane, a professor of genetics; Caroline Bassett, a professor of digital humanities; Clair Wills, the King Edward VII professor of English literature; and Clément Mouhot, a professor of mathematical sciences.
Cambridge last month announced a two-part review, with part one to be led by Nazir Afzal, a former chief crown prosecutor for north-west England, focusing on the support given to Arday immediately before his death.
The university has not yet named a chair for part two of the review, which it said would be “a broader review of institutional processes and practice” and only consider “the wider context” of Arday’s period at Cambridge, including general appraisals of recruitment and support available to academics facing media scrutiny.
The group behind the letter, which was also sent to Cambridge’s governing council, said the “scope and investigative character” of the second part of the review would be crucial in settling the decisions, structures and processes involved.
They wrote: “To this end, it is vital that the university establishes a clear chain of responsibility for the institutional decisions made in the period following Professor Arday’s appointment, through the events leading to his death and the university’s subsequent responses.
“The university should state clearly how responsibility will be acted upon if the review establishes serious failures of leadership or responsibility … Serious findings must have consequences for the individuals and offices responsible.
“At the same time, individual accountability cannot substitute for the institutional changes required where failures arose from structures of decision-making, scrutiny or governance.”
The University of Cambridge was approached for its response to the letter.
Cambridge publicised Arday’s appointment at the age of 37 as the youngest black person ever appointed to a professorship at the university, saying he would “inspire more people from under-represented backgrounds into higher education, building on the university’s many initiatives in this area”.
Arday denied the accusations of plagiarism but on 5 August Cambridge said it would open an investigation into his academic qualifications. Arday resigned hours later.

California couple charged with child abuse in surrogacy scheme involving at least 21 kids
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:41:13 UTC
03:41:13 KST

A California couple has been arrested on child abuse charges following an investigation into a surrogacy scheme involving at least 21 kids, police said on Tuesday.
Silvia Zhang and her husband, Guojun Xuan are expected to face conspiracy to commit child abuse charges, according to the Los Angeles county sheriff’s department.
Fifteen children were removed from the couple’s opulent home in Arcadia last year after an allegation of abuse, and another six living elsewhere were also located. They ranged in age from two months to 13 years, with most between one and three.
Police believe Zhang gave birth to one or two of the children while the rest were born by surrogate.
Zhang and Xuan were first arrested in May 2025 after a hospital reported that their two-month-old infant had a traumatic head injury, the result of a nanny at the home violently shaking the baby, according to Arcadia police.
Arcadia police did not file charges at the time, in order to finish a full investigation, they said.
The couple told police that they “wanted a large family” and produced what appeared to be legitimate birth certificates, including some from outside California, that list Zhang as the mother of the children. Xuan was listed as the father on at least some of the birth certificates.
Surrogacy is an agreement between parties to have a woman become pregnant, typically through an embryo transfer and deliver a baby for another parent.
The practice has no federal regulation, leaving it up to states to set the rules if they choose to allow it.
California is considered a “surrogacy-friendly state” because it has clear laws governing the process. Both sides are required to have lawyers, and there must be a written, notarized contract before an embryo transfer takes place.

8 arrests out of 80,000: Police blame IDF after hundreds derail draft dodger raid

2026-10-06
18:39:18 UTC
03:39:18 KST

Eight draft dodgers and deserters were arrested during the month of September, out of 15 proactive arrest attempts, according to the IDF. That amounts to just 0.01% of the roughly 80,000 draft dodgers and deserters currently registered, the overwhelming majority of whom are members of the Haredi community.
The IDF Spokesperson's Office released this information on Tuesday afternoon as it sought to clarify the issue of arrests of deserters and draft dodgers after the spokeperson contradicted himself in a response earlier in the day, acknowledging: “We deliberately did not proactively arrest deserters.”
“During the High Holidays, in accordance with the situational assessment, policing teams were reinforced and preparations stepped up for the arrest of draft dodgers and deserters at various border crossings, in addition to routine operations and presence,” the IDF said. “All these operations require planning, preparation and the allocation of appropriate resources. During the High Holidays, more than 200 deserters and draft dodgers were proactively arrested at border crossings.”
In most cases, these were Haredi men seeking to travel to Uman, Ukraine, who were arrested and have since been released.
“At the same time, the Military Police also carried out proactive arrests, all in coordination with the Israel Police,” the military said. “During September, the Military Police Corps made 15 proactive attempts to arrest deserters and draft dodgers, resulting in eight arrests. The IDF will continue to act resolutely to ensure equal enforcement of the law against all offenders.”
Meanwhile, police are blaming the conduct of Military Police officers for the chaos that erupted overnight in Modi’in. Police say the soldiers who arrived to arrest a deserter at his parents’ home in a non-Haredi neighborhood lingered at the scene and did not immediately leave with the detainee. That allowed hundreds of Haredim to arrive, surround them and even break into the building, terrifying its residents.
The deserter ultimately was not taken into custody after the Haredi protesters agreed not to harm the Military Police officers only if they pledged not to arrest him.
The deserter, it should be noted, activated “Black Alert,” a Haredi network aimed at preventing the arrest of yeshiva students. Black Alert has been behind a series of similar riots since the outbreak of the war but, for some reason, has yet to face any action.
Police in the Shfela District reviewed the overnight events and acknowledged that “the rioters understand that they have the upper hand over the police and the law.”
The police review found that, contrary to procedure, the small Military Police force that arrived at the scene did not immediately remove the deserter after he was apprehended, ynet has learned. Instead, the officers gave him time to prepare to leave. As he stalled, rioters began gathering at the scene, and only then were police called in to help extract the military force and restore order.
Police officials also said the decision to release the deserter and issue him an order to resolve his military status was made by the IDF, not the police. Police said they acted at the IDF’s request, dispatching a large number of officers to the scene to help carry out the military’s decision.
'My husband grabbed a gun': Modi’in residents recount night of chaos
Residents of the building experienced the bizarre reality firsthand and struggled to describe what they had endured.
“The Haredim violated my home and the homes of the other residents,” one neighbor said. “This is our private home, the safest place for us and our children, and it was left completely exposed. It took the police a long time to restore order.”
In conversations with ynet, neighbors described the events as a “pogrom.” The rioters entered the building through the main entrance and parking garage, moved between floors, banged on apartment doors and shouted, “We will die rather than enlist.”
According to residents, they began calling police at 12:30 a.m., but a sufficient number of officers did not arrive until around 1:30 a.m.
“It took the police a long time to arrive and it was complete lawlessness,” one neighbor said. “The officers were simply afraid and could not bring the crowd under control until the riot police arrived.”
Another neighbor said: “I felt like they were inside my home, in my living room. I thought they were Arabs disguised as Haredim, so my husband grabbed his gun and we ran with the children to the safe room.”
One neighbor said rioters arrived on buses and gathered below the building.
“We woke up terrified. My daughter thought they were carrying out an October 7 in Modi’in. Everyone in the residents’ WhatsApp group was terrified. No one understood what was happening. We locked the doors and barricaded ourselves inside our homes. Then the fire alarm went off and we were afraid the building was burning until we realized they had activated the smoke detector.”
Neighbors said the rioters struck a policewoman in the head with a flowerpot. She was bleeding from the head and was taken into one of the apartments until a Magen David Adom team arrived and treated her.
A 12-year-old girl who lives in the building and had gone down to the lobby said: “It was scary and I didn’t sleep all night. That’s why I didn’t go to school Tuesday.”
The mother of the deserter, whose last name is Lieberman, sent an apology to her neighbors in the building’s WhatsApp group: “I know you are all very angry, and understandably so, which is why I was afraid to respond until now. I want you to know that I apologize from the bottom of my heart. This is not who I am and, truthfully, it is not who my son is either. Unfortunately, he was taken advantage of, even if he does not realize it right now. I am opposed to any form of violence or vandalism.”
“It is important to me that you know that I did not call them (nor did my son, who only called a rabbi to ask about the deferment they had arranged for him, and apparently everything developed from there). We certainly did not give anyone the code, keys or any other assistance that could encourage the violence.
“In fact, I was also a victim of this violence because they nearly tore my door off its hinges. I am truly sorry for all the distress this caused. My son chose a different path from mine (my son chose a different path from mine, and probably from that of most of the building’s residents). I served as an officer in the IDF, my daughter was also an infantry officer and my other son is a combat soldier in Yahalom [the IDF Combat Engineering Corps’ elite special operations unit].
“My second son chose a different path, but he is still a decent, good young man who helps anyone in need, even if that may not seem so to you right now. He does not live with me but stays here as a guest. None of us anticipated this scenario. In fact, the two of us were already dressed and ready to leave with the officers when everything deteriorated from there.”
Modi’in-Maccabim-Reut Mayor Haim Bibas called the events “disgraceful,” adding: “The city will not tolerate the intrusion and barbaric behavior of draft dodgers. The police and the military must provide answers about their conduct and, above all, their lack of preparedness overnight. How does an operation to arrest a deserter end without an arrest, while the rioters celebrate?
“In my view, this outcome is a serious failure that sends a dangerous message: Anyone who uses enough force can thwart law enforcement.”

Ukraine is third in world for cyberattacks after US and Israel, and first in Europe. Machine-speed assaults run continuously and without fatigue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:35:49 UTC
03:35:49 KST

Only the US and Israel were hit by more cyberattacks than Ukraine this year. Ukraine ranked third in the world and first in Europe among the countries whose organizations and users were most often targeted by cyberattacks in the first half of 2026, accounting for 4.8% of all victims worldwide, up from fifth in the world and third in Europe a year earlier, Microsoft said in its Digital Defense Report 2026.
Microsoft processes more than 165 trillion security signals a day, which lets it show how often attackers go after customers in each country. Russian state hackers aimed 14% of their recorded activity at Ukraine, more than at any country except the US.
The era of machine-speed cyberattacks is here
Government agencies and services were the most targeted sector worldwide at 27%, up from 17% in 2025. Phishing drove 23% of intrusions Microsoft investigated, up from 7% a year earlier, and the median time from finding a vulnerability to weaponizing it has fallen well below 24 hours.
The use of artificial intelligence is pushing cyberspace into an era of “machine-speed” attacks that operate continuously and without fatigue, according to Dev.
“Many AI agents act on behalf of users and with their access rights, so a compromised agent combines user-level access with machine-scale actions,” Natalia Burlakova, Security Sales and Engineering Lead at Microsoft, says.
Deception beats code in attacks on Ukraine
Ukraine's own agency data show a similar pattern. Malware accounted for 33% of cyber incidents in the first half of 2026, and social engineering 31%, the State Service of Special Communications and Information Protection reported on 30 September. System infections made up 15%, and system compromises 4.5%.
Attackers rely less on technical complexity than on trust, according to the report by Ukraine's computer emergency response team, CERT-UA. Hacker groups create fake pages that mimic CERT-UA, Ukraine's Parliament's document management system, and the Brave1 defense technology platform.
Microsoft urges five government steps
Microsoft asks governments to prepare for faster-moving threats by assigning roles and coordinating agencies in advance of a crisis, and to treat AI security as part of national resilience. It also asks them to plan for incidents that spread, noting that 52.2% of intrusions involving valid accounts led to additional credential theft.

After October 7, 'Never Again' isn't enough - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:34:14 UTC
03:34:14 KST

For most of my life, I believed in two words. Like so many of my generation, I grew up on Never Again: a vow built from the ashes of the Holocaust, repeated at every memorial and every Holocaust Remembrance Day. I thought it was a guarantee.
On October 7, 2023, that guarantee broke. Some 1,200 people were murdered in a single morning, and 251 were taken hostage. It was the deadliest day for the Jewish people since the Holocaust. We learned, at a price no one should ever have to pay, that Never Again is a hope. Saying it cannot make it true.
So as we approach the third anniversary, I want to suggest that we say something different. We are not in a position to promise the world what will never happen to us. But we can promise one another what we will do. We will never forget. And no one will be left alone.
'Never Forget' becomes 'Never Alone'
We already know what “alone” costs. Many Holocaust survivors lost entire families and then found no one to help them carry it. There were no support groups and no language for trauma, so they rebuilt their lives and said nothing. Many spoke about whom they had lost only near the end of their lives, and their children grew up in that silence. We can make sure that never again is a bereaved family left to grieve alone.
I say this as someone who has spent 25 years in the company of grief. In August 2001, our daughter Michal was 12 and preparing for her bat mitzvah in Jerusalem when a suicide bomber struck the Sbarro restaurant, killing 15 people.
Michal canceled her celebration and gave the money to the victims’ families. As we got to know those families, we saw their needs went far beyond the first weeks. No one, anywhere in the world, was providing long-term care for victims of terror. That gap became OneFamily.
Here is the most important thing those 25 years have taught me: grief does not get smaller on a schedule. The world imagines that healing moves in a straight line, with each year a little lighter than the last. In fact, trauma comes in waves.
The third year is often among the hardest. The funerals are over, and the meals have stopped arriving. The people who called every week now call on the anniversary, if they call at all. This is when a widow finally faces the paperwork she could not bear to open. It is when a teenager who held himself together for his mother starts to come apart.
Since October 7, more than 1,600 families have joined OneFamily’s circle of bereaved families, along with 316 new widows and widowers and 37 twins who lost their twin brother or twin sister.
In three years, we have taken under our care more bereaved families than we did in the 22years before. We are caring for and supporting more than 5,300 children, teens, and young adults, and more than 3,200 bereaved parents. To meet that need, our annual budget has grown nearly fivefold since 2022.
BEHIND EACH number is a home that has stopped working. A mother who no longer cooks, because setting the table means facing the empty chair. A father who can’t focus at work. Parents so consumed by the son they lost that the children still at home begin to feel invisible. Capable adults who can no longer get through the day.
Bereavement is not only sorrow. It is the slow collapse of ordinary life, and it rarely shows from the outside.
That is why I believe our collective responsibility has grown since October 7, not shrunk. This is not only Israel’s burden. It belongs to the whole Jewish people, in Jerusalem and Johannesburg, in Toronto and Tel Aviv, in New York and Netivot. Recovering from October 7 will take generations of work as a community and as worldwide Jewry: to learn, to remember, to see the pain of others, to lean in and care, and to heal.
The greatest danger now is not that we will forget October 7. It is that we will get used to it.
After three years of sirens, headlines, and funerals, even the kindest heart builds calluses. The days of remembrance ahead are our chance to peel them back and feel again. Learn one name and its story. Call the family you have been meaning to call. Support the unglamorous, long-term work of the therapists and volunteers who stay after the cameras leave.
We have learned what helps. OneFamily’s approach is built on principles drawn from Option B, the book Sheryl Sandberg wrote with psychologist Adam Grant after the sudden death of her husband. They are all important, but three of them matter most: First, people need to know they are not alone. Second, the most helpful support comes from those who have suffered a similar loss. Third, meeting someone farther along the same road gives hope that today’s acute grief will not last forever.
So we bring widows together with widows, parents with parents, orphans with orphans. In a room with people who truly understand each other, the bereaved find words for what they could not say anywhere else.
I have seen what this looks like when it works. Widows who came to us after the Second Intifada now sit with young women widowed in 2024 and say, simply, I know. I’m here. Children who grew up in our programs now mentor children who lost a parent in Gaza or on the Lebanese border. What began as care received has become care given, full circle, again and again. That is the answer I can offer to the broken promise of Never Again: Never alone.
We will come through this stronger. I believe that completely. But strength does not mean the pain is gone. It means we carry it together. We can emerge grieving but strong, missing the people we love but full of love. That is not a slogan. It is work, and it belongs to all of us.
The writer is the chairman and co-founder of OneFamily, Israel’s national organization supporting victims of terror and war and their families. His wife, Chantal Belzberg, received the 2026 Israel Prize in recognition of their 25 years of work healing the nation.

The Guardian view on the Green party and Palestine: rejecting two states is no shortcut to peace | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:34:11 UTC
03:34:11 KST

Last year, the UN general assembly endorsed the New York Declaration supporting two states in the Holy Land by 142 votes to 10. Those voting against included the US and Israel. The wider international diplomatic consensus rests on a 2002 UN security council resolution, which explicitly affirmed a two-state vision for Israel and Palestine. Saudi Arabia’s then crown prince said peace required “two equal parties” and could not survive “oppression and humiliation”. His words remain as relevant now as then.
The Green party has now rejected that two-state framework in favour of a one-state solution. The Guardian strongly disagrees with this move. Peace needs to acknowledge reality: the latest polls in Gaza and the West Bank suggest that a majority support a two-state formula based on the 1967 borders compared with just 10% who back a single democratic state with equal rights. The European Greens also disagree with the new direction of their English and Welsh sister party. The EU-wide representatives argue that the policy is incompatible with previously agreed positions. Europe’s Greens – which include the centrist German party – condemn “the genocide against Palestinians” and call for sanctions against Israel’s government.
Political scientists say that currently, west of the Jordan River, one system under Israeli control enforces unequal laws and relegates Palestinians to a “lower caste”. The international consensus has plainly failed to deliver Palestinian statehood, or indeed prevent the near-total destruction of Gaza by Israel. But a “single democratic” entity in Palestine seems even more remote. There may need to be fresh future thinking about peace, including confederation models being considered as the crisis deepens in the occupied Palestinian territories. The ultimate test of any solution to the Israel-Palestine conflict is whether it ends domination by any one group and provides equal rights so both peoples have a secure political future.
The vote at the Green party conference to adopt a controversial set of policies was decided by about 200 votes – less than one-thousandth of the membership. The Greens’ leader, Zack Polanski, who is himself Jewish, has become embroiled in a row over antisemitism around the third anniversary of the 7 October attacks, at a time when he is fighting a parliamentary byelection in London. The motion defines Zionism as being “to the exclusion and/or domination of the non-Jewish population” in historic Palestine. Most in the Jewish community disagree, seeing it solely in terms of Jewish self-determination. The anger is real and understandable. There could be real-world consequences. The policy declares that an ideology that most Jewish people identify with is racist and raises the question of whether someone who identifies as a Zionist can remain in the Greens.
Green delegates rejected safeguards against disciplining members for affiliation with Jewish institutions identifying as Zionist. Lawyers warn that Zionist beliefs may qualify for protection under equality legislation. On Monday, Mr Polanski ruled out “exclusion, or refusal to engage with anyone” in the Greens because of religious or communal affiliation. The test is whether the party honours this in practice. Whatever the motion’s eventual impact, it is clear that Green party structures urgently need to be reformed for a mass membership base. Mr Polanski, a London assembly member, wants to join the five Green MPs in parliament. He will need to show a surer political touch to get there.

What Israel learned on October 7 and what remains unsolved - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:33:58 UTC
03:33:58 KST

Sadly, Israel knows how to mourn.
It knows how to commemorate the tragedies that have befallen it and the Jewish people. Holocaust Remembrance Day. Remembrance Day for the Fallen of Israel’s Wars.
The country knows the drill: the somber ceremonies, the melancholy music, the radio interviews, the kaddish, and the cloud of sadness that descends over the country.
For decades, two central national days of mourning punctuated the civic calendar, alongside religious days of mourning such as Tisha B’Av. Now, there is a third: October 7.
But with this one, even the calendar is complicated.
The massacre took place on Simchat Torah, the 22nd of Tishrei. The official day of remembrance falls two days later, on the 24th of Tishrei – this year, October 5. Civilian commemorations take place on October 7 itself, including Wednesday’s large ceremony at Ganei Yehoshua.
Disagreements over who should lead the mourning
The different dates have a practical explanation. Commemorating the massacre on Simchat Torah would turn a religious holiday into a national day of mourning. But the separation between the official and civilian ceremonies also reflects something deeper: disagreement over who should lead the mourning, who can speak for the bereaved, and what place a government that presided over the catastrophe should have in commemorating it.
The country experienced a shared catastrophe. Yet, mourning it together has proven difficult.
There are echoes here of the anniversary of Yitzhak Rabin’s assassination – a national tragedy whose commemoration also exposes the country’s divisions.
It would be tempting to conclude that the separate October 7 ceremonies reflect a country that experienced the same disaster but drew entirely different lessons from it.
Tempting, but too simple.
Israel has absorbed more common lessons about security than its fractured public life – a fracture all the more visible during an election campaign – would suggest. The problem is that those shared lessons have not translated into shared obligations.
There is considerable agreement about the dangers facing the country, and substantial agreement about the need to confront them. Take Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu out of the picture, and the differences between Likud, Yashar, B’Yachad, and Yisrael Beytenu – especially on fundamental security questions – become much harder to discern than the heated political rhetoric would suggest.
That does not mean there are no differences. Disagreements remain over priorities, the timing and scope of military operations, and how to best leverage military achievements into diplomatic ones.
But the broad understanding that Israel cannot allow an enemy to build an army on its borders, rely on assurances that the enemy is deterred, and wait for the danger to materialize, is not confined to one political camp.
Israel's post-October 7 mindset
Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir’s call on Monday for an assertive offensive posture and pledge not to rely on deterrence but to prevent Israel’s enemies from building up their strength and capabilities unchecked finds support well beyond the governing coalition. The notion that Israel must act against developing threats, rather than believing they would not dare to act or merely preparing to absorb the next attack, has become part of the country’s post-October 7 mindset.
The same is true of the deep skepticism toward Palestinian statehood.
Much of the international community still presents a Palestinian state as the solution to the problems in the Middle East. For many Israelis, however, October 7 points in the opposite direction: relinquishing control would simply create another territory from which an armed enemy could organize, prepare, and eventually attack.
Many point to Gaza and conclude that there is no reason at this time to believe that an independent Palestinian entity in Judea and Samaria would look any different. The burden of demonstrating that it would is much, much heavier than it was before October 7.
So where do the country’s divisions lie, three years after October 7?
First, there is Netanyahu himself. He remains as much of a fault line after the massacre as he was before it. For some, the subsequent military achievements – the new Middle East emerging from decisions he took – show why he must remain in office. For others, the failure that made those campaigns necessary demonstrates why he must leave.
But the divisions are not only about Netanyahu. They are also about whether agreement on the dangers facing the country carries with it agreement on the obligations those dangers impose.
Two stand out: the obligation to help protect the country, and the obligation to take responsibility when that protection fails.
On the first, October 7 drove home the country’s need for soldiers and reservists. Yet, that lesson has not translated into agreement that the burden must be shared more broadly.
And therein lies the disconnect. If the danger threatens everyone, how can confronting it remain the responsibility of only some? How can one family be expected to send its children to the army and repeatedly to the reserves, with all the risks and disruption that entails, while another family’s sons remain exempt?
On the second question, accountability, the country remains divided over what taking responsibility requires, who must do so, and how the failures should be investigated.
The military achievements since October 7 matter enormously. They have changed Israel’s strategic position. But they do not answer the questions about the decisions, assumptions, and failures that preceded the massacre.
A leader can deserve credit for what happened afterward and still owe an accounting for what happened before. The two are not mutually exclusive.
The overarching issue is reciprocity.
Citizens owe something to the country and to one another. The state and its leaders owe citizens protection, competence, and accountability. October 7 exposed how indispensable those obligations are.
Three years later, it is fair to ask: are these reciprocal obligations being honored?
Are all citizens doing their part, or have extraordinary sacrifices by some become a convenient substitute for participation by others?
Has the state restored its ability to protect its citizens, and have its leaders acted competently and accepted responsibility?
Three years on, the jury is still out. In another three weeks, for the first time since October 7, that jury – the nation – will have its say via the ballot box.

‘We were playing for you’: Hapoel Tel Aviv remembers October 7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:33:53 UTC
03:33:53 KST

Three years after the October 7 massacre, the Shlomo Group Arena was filled with the people who normally come there to celebrate Hapoel Tel Aviv basketball.
On this night, however, the familiar red-and-white stands carried a different weight.
Hapoel held its annual “Together Forever” memorial ceremony, bringing together fans, bereaved families, players, club officials and supporters to remember those who were murdered on October 7, 2023 and those who fell in the battles that followed, while honoring the courage of those whose lives were cut short.
It was an evening of remembrance, grief and reflection, but also of community – a recognition that for Hapoel Tel Aviv, the events of October 7 are not something separate from the club’s story. They are woven into the lives of its fans, its players and its wider family.
Herzog speaks at game, bereaved families heart of the evening
President Isaac Herzog delivered a message of strength to those gathered, while musician Boaz Banai, closely associated with the club, performed several emotional songs.
But the families were at the heart of the evening.
Sharon Kutz spoke about the loss of her brother Aviv, her sister-in-law Livnat and their children Rotem, Yonatan and Yiftach, who had played in Hapoel’s youth academy. All five were murdered in their home in Kibbutz Kfar Aza on October 7.
Shai HarMash spoke about his son Omer, who was murdered in the safe room of his home that day. Amit Halivni shared the story of her husband Yuval, who fell in battle on October 9, while Eyal Eshel spoke about his daughter Roni, an observation soldier who was killed during the battle at the Nahal Oz military base.
Their stories gave a human face to the names and numbers associated with October 7, reminding those in attendance of the individual lives, families and dreams behind every loss.
Hapoel owner Ofer Yanai reflected on how the club responded in the immediate aftermath of the attack and how, for him, the need to tell those stories became personal.
“That Black Saturday was a difficult, bitter and painful event,” Yanai said. “On Sunday, we had to wake up to a world that came after it, and we asked ourselves what we could do. We helped and supported.”
When Hapoel returned to the court soon afterward for a game against the London Lions, Yanai wore a shirt bearing photographs of people who were still believed to be alive and missing.
Over time, the shirt changed as the reality became clearer.
“That shirt ‘evolved’ to include those who had fallen and I would wear it to all of the games,” Yanai said.
Two weeks later, Hapoel traveled to Paris, bringing a group of young fans from the kibbutzim. The children shared their experiences at a press conference, allowing people far from the communities attacked on October 7 to hear directly from those who had lived through it.
“The reason we brought children was because on October 7, I was 30 or 40 kilometers away from the events,” Yanai explained. “I know many people who were affected by what happened and even for me it didn’t feel real. So I wanted people to hear the stories directly from the children.”
For Hapoel’s players, the connection was just as immediate.
Captain Bar Timor spoke about the unique responsibility of representing a club whose supporters themselves had been among those affected by the attacks.
“October 7 touched the homes and families of many Hapoel fans,” forward Tomer Ginat said. “For us as players, knowing that people we see in the stands and who support us wherever we go were hurt so terribly stayed with us. We thought about them then and we think about them today as well.”
Ginat recalled Hapoel’s first game after October 7, in Venice. The players were preparing in the locker room, but basketball hardly seemed relevant.
“Everything felt disconnected,” he said. “We didn’t talk about the team we were facing, not even for a moment. We talked about why we were going out to play, and the reason was very clear: We were playing for you. For the people of Hapoel. For our fans who had been through and were still going through so much.”
That sense of playing for something larger than the scoreboard has remained part of Hapoel’s identity ever since.
Hapoel Tel Aviv owner recalls October 7 experience
Club owner Gili Raanan recalled driving his son to his military base in the south on October 7 before becoming caught in traffic near Kiryat Gat, surrounded by smoke and chaos.
“I told myself one thing: When all of this is over, we will try to do things differently,” Raanan said. “We cannot continue living our lives the way we did before.”
Three years later, the empty seats inside the arena remain a powerful reminder of those who will never return.
“The empty seats in front of me here are not empty seats,” Raanan said. “They represent people who were part of us, part of our community and part of our families. They are part of our hearts, and we miss them every day.”
Nothing, Raanan acknowledged, can truly fill those seats or undo what happened. But he believes the community created around sport can help provide a way forward.
“You can’t truly fix what happened or fill those seats again,” he said. “But out of this terrible tragedy, we have to think about how we build new lives and how we move forward.”
For Raanan, Hapoel Tel Aviv is part of that process.
“Sport, and Hapoel Tel Aviv in particular, are among the strongest ways we have to build and live together as a community,” he said. “To create and build lives, while remembering those who were supposed to be here with us and are not.”
Timor echoed that sentiment, describing October 7 as a day that left behind pain, shattered families and an absence that can never completely be filled.
But he also spoke about the importance of remembering the people behind the loss – their lives, dreams, families and the impact they had on those around them.
“As Hapoel Tel Aviv’s captain, I know how much power there is in our team, our club and our community when we stand together,” Timor said.
“On the court, we play to win, but some things are much bigger than any game or any result.”
And so, three years later, Hapoel’s community gathered once again.
Not simply to look back, but to say that the names and stories of those who were murdered and those who fell remain part of the club’s collective memory.
“We are remembering, honoring, and telling the families who lost those dearest to them that we remember, we will not forget, and we will continue to carry their memory with us,” Timor said.
For one evening, the arena was not about the next game, the next opponent or the next result.
It was about the people who should have been there.
And about a community determined to keep their memory alive.

Israel let over 1,000 aviation crew members from banned countries enter despite restrictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:33:47 UTC
03:33:47 KST

Over 1,200 aviation crew members from countries without diplomatic relations with Israel, including Iran, might have entered the country, according to an N12 News report on Tuesday.
The report cited the Knesset's Intelligence Subcommittee of the Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee, saying the countries also include Syria, Lebanon, and Oman.
The N12 report follows the attempted hijacking of flydubai flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday by its Omani co-pilot, Hamam al-Hammami, who attacked Capt. Smit Machchhar with a cockpit crash axe in an attempt to gain full control of the aircraft.
N12 cited sources present at the committee meeting on the subject, who said that the revelation came as a surprise to the Transportation Ministry representative.
Those involved in the meeting were unaware of how such crew members successfully cleared Israeli border control, or if they just continued onward without entering the country, according to N12.
The report further cited an internal security document stating that the Transportation Ministry is the sole entity responsible for screening foreign aviation crew members.
The document, titled "Security Directive 2026: Security Measures for Foreign Passenger Flights Entering Israel's Aviation Supervision Area," was sent to foreign airline security managers on Thursday following the attempted flydubai hijacking.
Foreign airlines responsible despite ministry not performing checks in practice
According to the document, foreign airlines are responsible for referring to the list of banned nationalities when selecting the crews for their Israel flights, though N12 noted that, in practice, the Transportation Ministry did not enforce such checks.
The ministry further abandoned its practice of screening pilots belonging to foreign companies and also did not require the cross-checking of crew manifests against the list of banned nationalities, N12 reported, nor did it conduct required inspections on the matter.
Amichai Stein and Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

The Road Between Us: The Ultimate Rescue, Barry Avrich’s documentary about retired IDF Maj.-Gen. Noam Tibon’s extraordinary mission to save his son’s family during Hamas’s October 7 massacre is now available for streaming in the US on Paramount+.
The film arrived on the service on September 29, ahead of the third anniversary of the Hamas attack. American viewers can watch it with a Paramount+ subscription through the service’s website or app.
The documentary follows Tibon and his wife, Gali, as they undertake a desperate journey to Kibbutz Nahal Oz. Their son, Haaretz journalist Amir Tibon, his wife, Miri, and their two young daughters were hiding in their home’s safe room as terrorists attacked the kibbutz. Drawing on firsthand testimony and footage from that day, Avrich reconstructs a rescue that unfolds with thriller-like urgency.
The journey involved much more than reaching their own family. Along the way, Noam and Gali helped both survivors fleeing the Nova music festival and wounded soldiers.
Gali drove soldiers to a hospital, while Noam continued toward Nahal Oz, eventually joining troops fighting their way through the kibbutz. After hours of uncertainty, he reached his son’s home and brought the family to safety.
Avrich to 'Post': 'I wanted to make a film about family, not flags'
“I wanted to make a film about family, not flags,” Avrich said in an interview with The Jerusalem Post last year. He explained that seeing Tibon on 60 Minutes prompted him to imagine how he would respond to a message like the one Noam received from Amir, begging for help.
Tibon’s determination to help wounded strangers, even while his family’s fate remained unknown, became a central element of the film.
The documentary won the People’s Choice Award for best documentary at the 2025 Toronto International Film Festival. Its success followed a controversy in which it was initially removed from the festival’s lineup over clearance demands concerning Hamas bodycam footage, then reinstated after widespread protests.
Its arrival on Paramount+ gives American audiences another opportunity to see this account of courage and survival, following its US theatrical release last October. Through one family’s experience, the moving film conveys both the terror of that day and the resolve of those who stepped forward to help.

Karl Bushby completes English Channel swim
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
19:32:50 BST
03:32:50 KST

Karl Bushby completes English Channel swim
- Published
Adventurer Karl Bushby says he has completed a multi-day swim of the English Channel, stepping foot on UK soil after a 28-year journey.
Bushby, 57, left Chile, South America, on 1 November 1998, following two self-imposed rules - not to use transport to advance and not to return home until the journey is complete.
On Tuesday, he announced that he had swum from France to the UK - the final, major hurdle of his journey back to his childhood home in Hull.
Bushby said: "[It] feels good to have UK soil under my feet after all these years. It hasn't been easy, and that's part of the point; proving I'm more capable than I give myself credit for."
He added: "All of us can accomplish more than we will ever imagine."
Bushby said he swam for 20 hours over three days, making landfall at Shakespeare beach, just south of Dover, at 15:30 BST on Monday.
HM Coastguard said it "liaised with French authorities and maritime sector partners to ensure safety protocols were met".
Bushby's team said he was welcomed on the beach by a small gathering of friends and family, including his father, Keith Bushby, a former SAS soldier, and acclaimed filmmaker Werner Herzog, who is directing a feature-length documentary about the journey titled Walk of Life.
For many years, the French have only tolerated cross channel swims departing from the UK - not from France.
However, Bushby's team said permission had been sought from both French and UK authorities, and said they chose not to publicise exactly when it would take place "for safety and security reasons".
To date, Bushby has covered more than 30,000 miles (48,000km), including 29 countries.
He walked the length of South America, crossed the treacherous Darien Gap and continued north to Alaska.
From there he crossed the Bering Strait on foot, swimming where necessary.
Bushby then traversed Siberia and the rest of Asia before swimming across the Caspian Sea, which took 31 days to complete.
He crossed into Europe last year and arrived at the English Channel last month.
The journey has been dogged by problems, with visa restrictions, the 2008 financial crash which cost him sponsors, Covid-19 and geopolitics having all stopped him in his tracks.
In June, Channel Tunnel bosses vetoed his request for access to a service tunnel, which he said left him with no other option than to swim.
In September, when the BBC met Bushby in Belgium, he said how he felt it was "definitely time to call it a day", adding: "I don't want to keep this going for much longer."
He said he had always been fascinated with nature and horizons, which fuelled his thirst for adventure.
It is expected he will reach Hull by early November.

Germany sees sharp rise in requests to refuse military service
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:32:15 UTC
03:32:15 KST

Ayhan Şimşek
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Germany has received more than 12,000 applications from those seeking to refuse military service on grounds of conscience this year, exceeding triple the total in all of 2025, media reported Tuesday. 
The RedaktionsNetzwerk Deutschland (RND) newspaper group reported that the applicants include reservists, active-duty soldiers and young men -- even though military conscription in Germany remains suspended. 
A spokeswoman for the Federal Office for Family Affairs and Civil Society Functions (BAFzA) said the agency registered 12,102 conscientious objector applications in the first eight months of 2026, up from 3,879 in 2025 and 2,249 in 2024.Officials attribute the surge to Germany's new military service law, deteriorating international security conditions and fears of military conflict in Europe. 
Under the new law, which took effect at the start of 2026, all men turning 18 are required to complete a questionnaire assessing their fitness, skills and interest in joining the armed forces. 
While military service remains voluntary, critics say the government aims to reintroduce conscription in stages, beginning with questionnaires.
Medical screening is mandatory for men born in 2008 or later, but limited capacity means it is being phased in. 
Under Article 4 of the Constitution, citizens hold a protected right to refuse armed military service for reasons of conscience. Objectors must submit a written application and a detailed personal statement to the Federal Office for Bundeswehr Personnel Management, which forwards the request to BAFzA for review. 
The Bundeswehr counts roughly 186,400 active troops. To meet NATO commitments and respond to heightened security risks in Europe, the Defense Ministry aims to expand the force to more than 260,000 personnel by 2035. 
Reaching that target will require 20,000 recruits annually -- a goal defense analysts said will be difficult to achieve without mandatory service if voluntary enrollment falters.

US Marines halt Okinawa operations after marine arrested in woman’s killing

03:32:13 KST

The US military in Okinawa is suspending operations for 48 hours and restricting troops from leaving their bases after a Marine was arrested on suspicion of killing a local woman, reigniting long-standing anger over crimes involving American service members on the Japanese island.
Lt. Gen. Benjamin Watson, commander of the III Marine Expeditionary Force, announced the pause in a letter posted on Tuesday, saying incidents such as the latest case “demand we pause for reflection” and stressing that US forces have a responsibility to the Okinawan community.
The stand-down will run from Wednesday through Friday, with troops receiving training on discipline, standards and their responsibilities as members of the local community.
Latest killing revives Okinawa’s long record of military-linked crimes
Okinawa prefectural police arrested Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who is stationed at Futenma Air Station, on suspicion of strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in Naha early Saturday and stealing her wallet and backpack.
Ballard has denied the allegations, according to Japanese media.
Police said security camera footage showed a man entering the hotel with Yagi and later leaving alone. Ballard was arrested later Saturday after a patrolling officer spotted him in an entertainment district in Okinawa City, about 25 kilometers northeast of Naha. Kyodo News reported that his appearance, including a shaved head and tattoos, matched the person seen in the footage.
The arrest has renewed criticism of US military leaders’ repeated use of training and restrictions after serious crimes.
“I must say, discipline and troop education are not working at all,” Kenji Higa, an Okinawa City resident, told the Okinawa Times, referring to previous measures introduced after criminal cases involving US personnel.
The criticism comes against a deeply painful history of sexual violence and other crimes involving US service members.
In 1995, the rape of a 12-year-old girl by three US servicemen triggered huge protests against the American military presence. In 2024, a US service member was accused of raping a teenage girl, with anger also directed at authorities over the delayed disclosure of the case.
Military presence remains deeply divisive
The latest case comes as Japan seeks to strengthen its military capabilities on Okinawa and deepen security cooperation with the US amid concerns about China’s growing military power in the region.
But for many Okinawans, the strategic role of the US military does not erase the burden imposed by its presence.
Okinawa remained under US occupation from the end of World War II until 1972. Today, nearly 80,000 Americans live on the island, including almost 30,000 active-duty US military personnel across all four branches, with Marines making up the largest contingent.
Police data show the number of criminal cases involving US military personnel rose to 101 last year from about 40 in 2020.
Watson acknowledged the damage such incidents can inflict on relations with local residents, saying US troops “live, work, and socialise alongside the people of Okinawa” and that every interaction can either build or undermine trust.
“When that trust is damaged, it affects the strength of our alliance and the security of this region,” he said.
For Okinawans who have repeatedly protested killings, sexual violence and other crimes involving US personnel, however, another two-day pause and round of troop education risks looking less like accountability than another temporary response to a problem that has persisted for decades.

The Guardian view on the French school protests: the political class needs to heed the voice of students | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:31:54 UTC
03:31:54 KST

One of the most famous slogans in France’s May 1968 student protests declared “L’imagination au pouvoir” (Power to the imagination). In a postwar context of steady growth, the ’68ers dreamed of shaping an egalitarian society, freed from the social constraints of their parents’ generation. Nearly five decades on, in a very different economic climate, the goal for most of the tens of thousands of pupils disrupting schools across the country is more modest. As one placard on display had it: “I’d like to be worrying about my maths exam, not my future”.
A huge turnout of hundreds of thousands of protesters on Tuesday – a number that included many parents and teachers – confirmed the depth of resentment at years of budget cuts leading to crumbling school buildings, overcrowded classes and chronic staff shortages. Other complaints point to a lack of resources to deal with the now frequent heatwaves that make classrooms intolerable in May and June, and the unfairness of an opaque, algorithmically driven selection process for universities.
Confronted by the anxieties of a generation facing challenges ranging from the climate emergency to the impact of AI on future job opportunities, the response of Emmanuel Macron’s government has been disastrously heavy-handed. Instead of being instructed to show maximum restraint, given the age of most of those involved, security forces were urged to intervene to break up the school “blockades”. The result has been heightened confrontation and unacceptable violence on both sides. More than 200 students have been injured, as well as over 700 police officers and a number of teachers. One 15-year-old boy had his hand blown off during a protest in Lens, another lost an eye, and more than 4,000 minors were taken into custody, with nearly 1,500 facing prosecution.
At a political level, the eruption of anger over the underfunding of education has underlined the folly of Mr Macron’s ongoing attempt to balance France’s books by taking an axe to social spending. During his chaotic second term as president, five prime ministers have attempted to force through austerity budgets in order to cut the deficit and satisfy increasingly restive bond markets. The latest, Sébastien Lecornu, has belatedly said that the students’ core demands should be addressed. But last month he proposed cuts worth €54bn, including a real-terms reduction in schools funding. A credible approach would require more resources, not less.
Six months out from a presidential election in which Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner, the spectacle of burned-out schools, baton rounds and teargassed protesters feels ominous. As French politics polarises amid a crisis of faith in mainstream leaders, Ms Le Pen has accused the hard left of fomenting the school protests and called for a toughening up of “anti-riot” legislation. Public sector workers were on the streets on Tuesday, demonstrating against wage freezes. The major unions are jointly planning further demonstrations for November. An autumn of discontent now seems possible, as a lame-duck government enters its final months.
Mass protest in the streets is hardly an unknown phenomenon in France. But as calls mount for government spending to be further cut to appease market sentiment, the scale and intensity of the school protests should be heeded by the political class. As the social contract in France comes under increasing strain, the voice of its protesting students needs to be heard.

I have a 'two-strike' friendship rule. I've lost best mates over it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:29:23 UTC
03:29:23 KST

Everyone has a breaking point, but once we decide to take action, how can we be sure it's the right move? From toxic relationships to high-stress jobs and religious beliefs, Insight hears from people who've reached their final straw. Watch our latest episode The Final Straw on SBS On Demand.
I have developed a rule system relating to friendships after noticing I was always organising the next catch-ups.
After a certain amount of time, I make a judgement call: after planning two consecutive catch ups, I don’t reach out for the third.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
I wait for my "friend" to organise it — and if they don’t initiate, that’s my final straw.
I implement my rule and cut them off.
If these so called "friends" are not willing to reciprocate, then they’re not valuing the friendship, let alone respecting my time and effort.
It makes me feel used for a hidden agenda, just like some people feel in romantic relationships.
I decided on this rule as I matured, developed a better judgement of character and started evaluating my friendships.
It was one close friendship from my past who made me shape my current system.
We knew each other from high school and as we moved into our university days, they called me out for not reciprocating, reaching out or organising time together.
It made me think about our different backgrounds and perspectives. When people don’t reach out, sometimes there’s a reason.
We said hurtful things and the friendship ended.
My friendships that end can lead me to reflect on myself as a person; to question whether their lack of initiative may be caused by something I’ve done.
Is there no willingness or initiative from their end because of my tendency to hijack a conversation? Am I seen as a narcissist? Am I high maintenance as a friend? Do I have high standards?
Do I put too much pressure on the friendship?
My family sometimes believe that I go into them too fast, a flame on high from the get-go that can’t be sustained.
However, does that matter? Surely it takes two to tango?
Despite those questions, I would hope and assume there is open communication in my friendships.
I believe there shouldn’t be anything off limits, that they can change the topic if I’m "too much" and feel comfortable to raise any concerns with me.
Making the call
I have one former friend who I cut off after they pushed me to my final straw.
For a time, I called them my best friend. I would have done anything for them.
But I noticed after some time, particularly once we were both at university, that it was always me initiating a catch-up — right down to me picking the place where we’d go and driving to pick them up.
They never seemed to reciprocate.
We caught up twice; I waited for them to initiate another meeting, but there was nothing.
So I made the judgement call.
I no longer contacted them; in my mind, our friendship was over.
The last time we spoke was 2021.
For the first six to eight months, it was difficult. I constantly blamed and doubted myself.
I wondered whether I was to blame and felt angry.
I had tried to communicate. I remember saying to this friend multiple times over messages: "Please let me know if I’m being too much and don’t hesitate to tell me if something is happening with you, even if it’s a petty first-world problem."
I still feel angry that my friend was willing to throw our friendship away.
I even started to regret my rule system.
Putting me first
However, as time goes on, I feel very relieved.
Having less people to catch up with gives me more time to prioritise my nearest and dearest.
I tell myself, if they are not willing to reciprocate, then they don’t respect me as a person.
I could have 1000+ friends on Facebook or 100,000+ followers on Instagram, but who is really going to be there when you’re at your lowest?
But despite my final straw rule, I have ended up reconciling with some friends.
To this day, I regularly meet with friends who I had cut off after implementing my system.
Sometimes, I even think my rule can seem harsh and cutthroat.
My family has mixed feelings around it. Interestingly, the older generation seem to accept my system whereas the generation closer to my age finds it harsh.
However, as I grow older and hopefully maturer, I feel more confident in establishing my boundaries — in line with the famous gen Z meme, "I gotta put me first”.
These days, why when I form new friendships, I try not "have the flame on high" but I always expect respect and reciprocity.
I believe my rule and system will always continue.
In saying that, I accept that this rule will mean that sometimes I may be alone.
But that’s not a bad thing. There is beauty and comfort in doing things alone.

Labour figures rule out working with Greens after ‘Zionism is racism’ vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:26:29 UTC
03:26:29 KST

Senior Labour party figures said it was very unlikely their party would cooperate with the Greens in the future after they adopted a policy treating Zionism as a form of racism.
One Labour minister said they could not foresee how the two parties could work together, while a government official said Labour should formally rule out a future coalition or other arrangement.
There is also pressure within the Liberal Democrats for them to end existing arrangements with Zack Polanski’s party, with some senior Lib Dems calling on the party to end its coalition with the Greens in Southwark, south London.
Green members from England and Wales voted at the party’s conference on Sunday to adopt a binding policy that says Zionism should be treated by the party as racism, and which calls for a single Palestinian state in place of Israel.
After the vote, Bridget Phillipson, the Labour chair, called the move “shameful”, saying it highlighted how vital it had been for her party to tackle antisemitism under the leadership of Jeremy Corbyn.
While Phillipson’s statement was backed by her fellow ministers, there was debate as to whether Labour should go further and formally rule out any ties with the Greens, for example if a future general election delivered a hung parliament.
A source linked to the Jewish labour movement said Labour should “absolutely” rule out governing with the Greens, arguing the policy raised serious questions about whether its treatment of Jewish members could breach equality law.
It follows months of speculation of possible cooperation between the parties. Polanski said earlier this year that the Greens could consider an electoral pact with Labour under Andy Burnham or Angela Rayner, while ruling out one under the former prime minister Keir Starmer.
Labour views the Zionism motion, and the criticism that has followed, as a means to simplify its political argument against the Greens at a time when Polanski’s party has increasingly sought to attract disillusioned Labour voters on the party’s left.
A big test of this will come on Thursday, with voting in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, where Polanski is seeking to win Starmer’s former seat from Labour.
The Greens have poured huge resources into the contest, with Polanski telling the Guardian that it is “really on a knife-edge”. Despite the Greens’ campaigning efforts, helped by their massively increased membership, Labour is considered the favourite to win.
The Lib Dems and Greens already govern together in Southwark after May’s local elections, with the Greens as the senior partner.
Following the Zionism motion, both Southwark parties released a “joint administration statement against antisemitism”. Without mentioning the new Green policy, it said they would “continue to work with Jewish community organisations to make sure they know they have a place in Southwark”.
It brought a scathing response from some senior Lib Dems. Tagging Victor Chamberlain, the Lib Dem deputy leader of Southwark, Sarah Ludford, a peer and former MEP for the party, wrote on X that she did not understand “how you think this greenwash is an adequate response to the Greens’ antisemitic ‘Zionism is racism’ motion, from which I believe you should entirely distance yourselves”.
Another Lib Dem peer, Lynne Featherstone, who was formerly an MP, replied to a post by Chamberlain to say: “I would ditch them. Grow a pair!”
The policy was adopted at the Green party conference in Brighton on Sunday by 1,022 votes to 813, despite being opposed by four of the party’s five MPs.
Polanski, who left the Green conference early on Friday to campaign, stopped short of endorsing or criticising the motion. In a statement on Monday night after the European Greens and German Greens distanced themselves from the policy, Polanski said antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state “are and must always be completely distinct”. Polanski said he remained proud of the party’s stance on Palestinian rights.
