Amid protests, Kosovo’s political deadlock raises prospect of new elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:25:45 UTC
03:25:45 KST

Amid protests, Kosovo’s political deadlock raises prospect of new elections
Kosovo faces mounting tensions as protests against former rebel leaders’ convictions coincide with the prospect of new elections.
Kosovo faces the risk of turmoil as protests against the convictions of former Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) leaders coincide with a midnight deadline to elect a president.
Demonstrators have called for changes to the law governing the Hague-based Kosovo Specialist Chambers, including measures affecting prison terms and where sentences are served. The protests follow the September 16 convictions of former KLA leaders, including former President Hashim Thaci.
The protesters’ demands have become entangled with negotiations over the presidency, raising the prospect of new elections if lawmakers fail to reach an agreement by Wednesday. November 15 has emerged as a likely date for a new vote.
“New elections do not, in themselves, promise anything particularly positive,” political analyst Artan Muhaxhiri told Al Jazeera. “The chances of a radical political change are slim.”
He said that if a president is not elected, a new vote will take place in a tense political climate.
Anger over the verdicts will become a central campaign issue, he said, “overshadowing fundamental questions of socioeconomic development, and deepening the country’s downward spiral of systemic instability”.
How did Kosovo get here?
In 2015, the Specialist Chambers were established under Kosovo law following international investigations into alleged war crimes committed by KLA members during and after the 1998-99 conflict. Although formally part of Kosovo’s judicial system, the court sits in The Hague. But it remains contentious in Kosovo because the KLA is widely revered for having fought against Serbian rule.
In September, protests erupted after the court sentenced Thaci to 25 years in prison.
Later, the opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo (PDK) – formerly led by Thaci – proposed amendments aimed at curbing the tribunal. The plan included capping prison sentences at 15 years, allowing convicts to serve their sentences in Kosovo, enabling appeals before Kosovo’s Supreme Court, granting presidential pardons and narrowing the court’s temporal jurisdiction.
On October 2, 2026, Prime Minister Albin Kurti’s government concluded that there were no legal obstacles to the PDK initiative and forwarded its assessment to the parliament, the Assembly of Kosovo. Days later, Kosovo’s parliament approved the initiative at first reading, although it has not been finally adopted.
Meanwhile, Kosovo has been mired in a political impasse after the expiration of President Vjosa Osmani’s term in April, as the National Assembly has been unable to select a new president.
Now, internal power struggles within the PDK following the September sentencing have left the party fragmented, rendering the largest opposition party incapable of negotiating a cross-party presidential compromise, according to Nexhmedin Spahiu, a Pristina-based professor of political science.
On Monday, as lawmakers failed to secure a quorum to elect a president, police deployed tear gas and water cannon outside the Assembly, following clashes involving fireworks and bottles. The use of force prompted criticism from observers.
Tensions rise
Pristina-based journalist Gezim Baxhaku believes special police units overstepped their legal authority.
“There was an overuse of force,” Baxhaku told Al Jazeera. He said that while protesters threw firecrackers, police “exceeded their legal powers and acted entirely contrary to the situation on the ground”.
Among the hundreds of protesters were KLA veterans.
Pristina had witnessed nearly three weeks of largely peaceful gatherings before Monday’s escalation.
“Citizens were routinely bringing food, water, and coffee to the officers on duty,” Baxhaku said. “There was absolutely no reason for this to happen. For the first time since the late 2000s, police acted in such an uncalled-for manner – reacting upon orders to escalate a situation.”
Spahiu, the political science professor, said the protests should not be understood as a sign that people in Kosovo broadly reject the verdicts.
“A large majority of citizens in Kosovo are satisfied with the decision of the Specialist Chambers in The Hague,” said Spahiu.
He told Al Jazeera that the court’s rejection of Serbian claims of systematic crimes against humanity by the KLA “validated the liberation struggle”.
“Furthermore, people are relieved that individuals are finally being held accountable for crimes committed against political rivals within the Albanian community itself,” he said.
The political deadlock and Kurti’s ‘transactional’ approach
The Assembly remains deadlocked over the election of a head of state, as the PDK and other opposition parties boycott the voting session, denying the legislature its constitutionally required 80-MP quorum.
Muhaxhiri blamed Kurti for the crisis, criticising his decision to link the presidential vote to the Hague court amendments.
“Tensions escalated further when Kurti presented a plan based on a transactional approach to two fundamentally distinct issues: linking the draft law amending the Law on the Specialist Chambers to the election of the new president,” said Muhaxhiri.
“In effect, this amounted to a quid pro quo. By doing so, he appeared to be placing the historical, national, and identity-related significance of the liberation war on the same political bargaining table as the immediate objective of electing a president who would serve his political interests.”

Protests at French schools have led to the highest number of injuries in decades
Kyiv • UNN
Student protests have swept across France: 215 teenagers, 85 school employees, and more than 700 police officers were injured. The government promises to consider the students’ demands.
Today, police used tear gas against protesters near French high schools as students, teachers and parents took to the streets on the day of the largest demonstrations in the protest movement, which Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu called the most severe in the education sector in decades, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
The outlet notes that these protests, during which a teenager lost his hand on Monday, were another manifestation of public discontent in a country where support for both far-right and far-left forces is growing ahead of the presidential election in the spring.
France’s government is under pressure to reduce the national debt amid weak economic growth; in addition, it is struggling to address basic tasks such as passing a budget, ever since allies of President Emmanuel Macron lost their majority in the 2024 parliamentary elections.
Lecornu told lawmakers that at least 215 teenagers and 85 school employees had been injured in the clashes — the "heaviest losses suffered by the school system in decades." His ministry also said that more than 700 police officers had been injured.
BFM TV reported that Macron summoned Lecornu and other senior government officials to an emergency meeting on Tuesday.
In Marseille and Nantes, protesters held signs reading: "The state has killed national education." In Toulouse, parents marched at the front of the city procession, holding hands.
In Strasbourg, Lyon, Rennes and Paris, demonstrations sometimes escalated into violence: police used tear gas, while protesters lit fires in the streets and threw various objects at law enforcement officers.
Paris police said that clashes in the city began when about 300 people attempted to confront law enforcement officers, adding that protests elsewhere were generally peaceful.
By evening, law enforcement officers said they were still holding back a small group of protesters. Storefronts at three shops were damaged.
The protests began in September in the poor suburbs of Paris and later spread across the country.
"There is an enormous gulf between the elites and us," said Hugo Wetzel, who recently graduated from a high school in Strasbourg.
The high school students’ union said that more than half of France’s high schools had been blocked or closed for the day. Some local education authorities attempted to switch classes to an online format.
Human rights organizations, students and parent associations accused the authorities of using disproportionate force against minors. The government claims that the protest movement was hijacked by outsiders and escalated into street violence in some places.
France’s Interior Ministry said that 6,100 people had been detained since the protests began, the vast majority of them minors. According to the Justice Ministry, more than 1,800 people, including 1,483 minors, are facing charges for various offenses.
On Monday in northern France, a teenager’s hand was blown off during clashes between high school students and special police units. The regional newspaper La Voix du Nord reported that the 15-year-old boy lost his hand and part of his forearm after picking up a police grenade considered a non-lethal device.
"They want to divide young people into ‘good’ and ‘bad’ protesters," said Omar Slaouti, a high school teacher in Argenteuil, a northwestern suburb of Paris. "If the trash bins had not been set on fire, the government would not have made concessions or paid attention to the issues on the agenda."
Six months before the election to choose Macron’s successor, the government and the party of far-right leader Marine Le Pen, National Rally, accused lawmakers and mayors from the radical-left party La France Insoumise (LFI) of inciting the riots. LFI rejects these accusations.
"All the young people have taken to the streets. Where there is no police, everything is happening peacefully," said Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the presidential candidate for LFI.
Add to that
Lecornu instructed ministers to work on addressing the students’ main demands. These include ensuring that absent teachers are replaced, reviewing the length of the school day (from 8:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m.), and considering extending lunch breaks.
The government will also consider repairing outdated school buildings, Lecornu said, demanding that ministers submit their initial proposals by the end of October. Émilie Lomm, one of the students’ parents, said during a protest outside the Hélène Boucher school in Paris that the government’s words alone were not enough: "It is all well and good, of course, but it will not change our children’s daily lives," she said.
Finding additional funds to implement the education reforms will not be easy.
The government is under pressure to rein in the rapid growth of the budget deficit, as investors’ concerns about France’s rising public debt, weak economic growth and the authorities’ unwillingness to curb spending are driving up borrowing costs. Last week, the yield on France’s 10-year bonds briefly reached a 24-year high, exceeding 5%.
The increase in France’s borrowing costs has begun to affect the situation across the eurozone, while the fall in the euro’s exchange rate has become another warning signal for policymakers. Finance Minister Roland Lescure said on Tuesday that intervention by the European Central Bank was not currently necessary.
Marine Le Pen — a far-right populist and Eurosceptic who is leading the presidential race ahead of next spring’s election — unveiled plans for sharp cuts in public spending if elected. In this way, she seeks to demonstrate her financial competence against the backdrop of the deepening crisis in the bond market.
Data from the PISA 2025 study indicate that the growth rate of education spending in France is lagging behind inflation, while French students’ performance is lower than that of their peers in other OECD countries.

‘for life is not a spectacle’ barbara kruger wraps tadao ando’s rotunda in monumental texts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:25:03 UTC
03:25:03 KST

‘for life is not a spectacle’ barbara kruger wraps tadao ando’s rotunda in monumental texts
the american artist fills the concrete rotunda at the bourse de commerce in paris with text, covering the curved walls, the floor and twenty four display cases in the passage around it.
The History of Tears at the Bourse de Commerce iN Paris
American artist Barbara Kruger fills Tadao Ando’s rotunda at the Bourse de Commerce in Paris with a monumental work of text and image. Made for the curved concrete walls at the museum’s core, The History of Tears is the opening installation of Remember Me, the Pinault Collection’s exhibition marking two hundred years of photography. Kruger’s words run across the walls, continue under visitors’ feet over the full width of the floor, and carry on into twenty four display cases in the surrounding Passage, which have been turned into lightboxes carrying her own commands.
At the center of the rotunda, in the artist’s signature black, white and red, is a quote from the Martinican poet Aimé Césaire’s Journal of a Homecoming (1947). ‘And above all, my body as well as my soul, beware of assuming the sterile attitude of a spectator, for a life is not a spectacle, a sea of miseries is not a proscenium, a man screaming is not a dancing bear.’ Césaire addressed those words to his own body and soul, and Kruger has left them as they are while changing who is standing in front of them. They now face a museum audience that has paid to come and look.
On view from October 7, 2026, the exhibition around the installation has borrowed its name from Kruger as well. Remember Me, curated by Matthieu Humery with Lola Regard, takes its title from Untitled (Remember me), a 1988 work she rebuilt in 2020 as an LED panel. Some 700 photographs by more than 80 artists follow it through the building.
BARBARA KRUGER’S INTERVENTION INSIDE THE ROTUNDA
Tadao Ando’s intervention at the Bourse de Commerce is a single concrete cylinder, thirty meters across and nine meters high, set inside the old grain exchange without touching its walls. Barbara Kruger has used the inner face as a page, and two enormous white ellipses now sit on it, one in French and one in English, each headed by a single word in red, TOI and YOU, with italic condensed lines bending along the curve.
The French ellipse ends ‘jusqu’à ce que toi, l’observateur, tu disparaisses. plus rien. toi aussi.’, or ‘until you, the observer, disappear, nothing more, you too.’ The English one ends with the instruction ‘come closer.’ Around both, the wall is covered with further text enlarged until the letters break into visible halftone dots. A band of alternating black and white lines runs the full circumference in French, listing what the work is about: love and desire, shame and hatred, who gets what, who owns what, who is remembered and who is forgotten. The word QUI is picked out in red each time, and two red crosses strike through TOI and then MOI.
A second quote covers the floor, from George Orwell’s 1984, spoken by O’Brien while he is torturing Winston Smith: ‘if you want a picture of the future, imagine a boot stamping on a human face, forever.’ Kruger has set it at a size nobody can read from inside the room, so visitors walk over the letters and take them in from the floors above. Power, Pleasure, Desire, Disgust, a two-video work first shown at the Wexner Center for the Arts in Columbus, Ohio, in 1996, has been folded back into the rotunda, and puts face after face in front of the viewer, each one carrying want and threat at the same time.
Kruger describes The History of Tears as ‘an ongoing deluge of the eyes. A fountain of loss and fear. But also of power, pleasure, desire and disgust. This reservoir can accumulate through domination and conquest, both worldly and domestically,’ the artist notes. ‘It spurts in moments of global violence and brutality but also amidst the cruelties of intimacy. It can be both triumphalist in a massive sense but also drizzled like petty melodrama strewn with silly cartoons of seduction and rejection. It’s a bodily production that is both remembered and forgotten.
It’s a crying body lost amidst the wreckage of the battles for money, land, love and other bodies. To map this emotive fountain, to historicise it, can produce a narrative of profound struggle between the powerful and the disempowered, between the loved and the unloved, between winners and losers. It leaks shame, pride, belief and doubt in ways both intensely threatening and tragically comic. It can show and tell us how we were, how we are and how we will be to one another.’
remember me: more than 700 works from The Pinault Collection
Untitled (Remember me), the work the exhibition is named after, sits further on, in an alcove off the Passage: a close-up of an eye shot through with blood on an LED panel, and a stream of pixels issuing instructions that cancel each other out, ‘remember me, dismember me, forget me’, then ‘hug us, replace us, free us’, over an industrial soundtrack.
Surrounding Barbara Kruger’s installation are more than 700 works by over 80 artists displayed across the Bourse de Commerce’s galleries. Curated by Matthieu Humery, with the collaboration of Lola Regard, the exhibition pays tribute to the photographic medium through masterpieces and icons of the Pinault Collection. From Gustave Le Gray to Wolfgang Tillmans and from Dorothea Lange to Cindy Sherman, Humery has arranged the exhibition as a fugue rather than a chronology so the rooms move between genres and periods instead of marching through them. Gallery 2 is entirely dedicated to Irving Penn, bringing together more than 400 photographs, while Raymond Depardon’s series on France is also prominently exhibited in the gallery above.

location: Bourse de Commerce, Paris France | @boursedecommerce
dates: October 7, 2026 – January 18, 2027
curator: Matthieu Humery, Advisor for Photography of the Pinault Collection; with the collaboration of Lola Regard, Projects Officer
artwork name: The History of Tears
artist: Barbara Kruger

A Panamanian-flagged commercial vessel came under attack off Oman’s Musandam Governorate on Tuesday, triggering a fire and forcing the medical evacuation of 10 crew members, according to the Omani Defense Ministry.
The vessel, identified as the ON PEACE, was targeted about nine nautical miles northeast of Lima in Musandam overlooking the Strait of Hormuz, said a ministry statement.
The Royal Oman Air Force, in coordination with the relevant authorities, carried out a medical evacuation operation for 10 members of the ship’s crew following the incident, according to the statement.
The crew members were airlifted to Khasab Hospital in Musandam, where they received necessary medical care.
The ministry did not specify the nature of the attack, the condition of the evacuated crew members, or who was responsible.
The incident occurred near the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic maritime route linking the Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea, with the Omani coast facing Iran.
The strait has been contested in the war between the U.S. and Iran, and the scene of months of maritime attacks.

Russian shadow fleet tanker under Ukrainian sanctions catches fire near Sochi
According to Ukrinform, this was reported by the Astra Telegram channel.
AFRAMAX RIO (IMO: 9273844) is a large crude oil tanker. It is not included on the EU or Ukraine's allies' sanctions lists, but it was added to Ukraine's sanctions list by a decision of the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine dated February 12, 2026, along with 90 other Russian shadow fleet vessels.
According to the National Security and Defense Council, the vessel is owned by a company registered in the Marshall Islands, RIO ENTERPRISES SA. Its operations and chartering were carried out through international operator Navig8 Group of Singapore and Greek management companies, including Hellenic Tankers Co Ltd.
The AFRAMAX RIO tanker is capable of carrying 95,000–100,000 tonnes of oil, or approximately 700,000–750,000 barrels.
According to MarineTraffic, the tanker left the port of Tuzla, Türkiye, on September 11, 2026, and headed for the port of Constanța, Romania.
The vessel made an intermediate anchorage stop in Samsun, Türkiye, departing on September 19 and arriving in Constanța on September 22.
The website does not show any calls at Russian Black Sea ports. The last position was recorded 23 hours ago, when the tanker was approximately 15 kilometers from Sochi.
According to open-source data, between 2024 and 2026, the tanker repeatedly transported oil from Russian ports. Most frequently, it sailed from Ust-Luga, but it also loaded oil in Novorossiysk and Taman. Its listed destinations include India, Singapore and Saudi Arabia.
As Ukrinform reported, Ukraine's Defense Intelligence Directorate identified another 38 vessels flying the flags of Barbados, Russia, Cameroon, Panama, Belize, Liberia, Sri Lanka, Türkiye, Tanzania, São Tomé and Príncipe, Hong Kong and Palau that are used by Russia to circumvent international sanctions.

Russia’s Jet-Powered Drones Now Make Up 40% of Attacks on Ukraine—But Could Rise to 80%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:20:13 UTC
03:20:13 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s Jet-Powered Drones Now Make Up 40% of Attacks on Ukraine—But Could Rise to 80%
Russia is increasingly using jet-powered drones in attacks against Ukraine, RBC-Ukraine reported, citing Deputy Air Force Commander Yurii Cherevashenko. Such systems now account for approximately 40% of all UAVs deployed in strikes, with their share potentially rising to around 80% in the future.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Speaking during a meeting of a temporary investigative commission, Cherevashenko said Russia had stepped up its use of jet-powered drones beginning in July. On some operational directions, such UAVs already account for up to 60% of Russian drone strikes.
“And the figure continues to grow. We predict that around 80% of drones used in strikes will be jet-powered,” Cherevashenko said.
According to the Air Force official, the share of jet-powered drones in Russian attacks is expected to continue rising and could eventually reach approximately 80%.
As Russia expands its use of jet-powered drones, Ukraine is developing new systems to counter them. Several types of small anti-aircraft missiles are being prepared for operational deployment, with the first results expected in the second half of October.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced the development during a joint press conference with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv on October 4. He said the new interceptors had not yet been used operationally but were expected to be deployed later this month.
“There are several types of them. We will obviously see the results this month. Toward the end, in the second half of this month, we expect to see the results. You asked about their use and how widespread it is. So far, there has been no such use. It is yet to happen,” Zelenskyy said in response to a journalist’s question.
Ukraine is also working on five high-speed interceptor drone models intended to counter jet-powered attack UAVs. Zelenskyy said that one of the five models had advanced far enough for production to potentially reach around 400 units by the end of October.
The remaining four interceptor models are still undergoing testing.

Sweden To Send Patriot System to Poland — It Will Defend Ukraine Supply Hub
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:19:29 UTC
03:19:29 KST

Sweden is deploying a Patriot air defense missile system and 100 troops to Poland to reinforce NATO’s eastern flank.
They will defend a logistics hub in Rzeszów in the southeastern part of the country, which plays a key role in supplying military aid to Ukraine, according to the Swedish Armed Forces.
This will be the first time Swedish Patriot systems are deployed as part of an official NATO mission.
The system will be operated by personnel from the 6th Air Defense Regiment, supported by the 17th Blekinge Air Wing.
The Swedish contingent will operate under Alliance command and will be integrated into NATO’s Integrated Air and Missile Defense System.
The mission will begin in early December and last until the end of the year, with a planned extension through the first half of 2027.
The Swedish Armed Forces have four Patriot air defense missile system batteries in service, which are officially designated Luftvärnssystem 103 (LvS103) by the Swedish Army.
In total, under the contract, the country received 12 launchers, AN/MPQ-65 radars, and related equipment.
Sweden uses the modern Patriot Configuration-3+, which is equipped with two types of missiles: the PAC-2 GEM-T (Guidance Enhanced Missile-Tactical) and the PAC-3 MSE (Missile Segment Enhancement) interceptors.
All of these are in service with the 6th Air Defense Regiment, headquartered in Halmstad.
Sweden will deploy its JAS 39 Gripen fighter jets to Poland to reinforce NATO’s eastern flank.
The fighter jets will primarily be based at and operate from airfields in Sweden, while a small forward detachment will be stationed in Poland to provide technical and operational support for the flights.

Naked Trump statue goes on display in Strasbourg
October 6, 2026
A statue of US President Donald Trump was put on exhibit in the European Parliament building in Strasbourg, France.
The 2.5-meter satirical statue, by Danish artist Jens Galschiot, is called "Orange Plague," and it shows the US leader naked, holding a long gold club and sitting on the shoulders of a smaller man.
The artist said it is coated with 23-karat gold. The statue is also known by the name "King of Injustice."
Next to the statue are cards explaining that the "King of Injustice" is "sitting on the back of a man" who is sinking under the burden.
"I would do anything to help him. Except stepping down from his back," the card continues, with the artist blaming Trump for hindering attempts to confront climate change.
No comment from Trump
The statue stands at an intersection connecting two of the parliament's buildings, and is scheduled to remain there until Thursday.
Left-wing Danish European Parliament member Per Clausen, who invited the artist, said he is not worried about a potential reaction by Trump.
"If someone is so thin-skinned that they cannot tolerate this sculpture being exhibited in the European Parliament, then they have no place on the world stage," Clausen said.
The US president has not commented on the statue, which has also been on display in other European cities as well as at the COP30 UN climate conference in Belem, Brazil.

Black Sea drone attacks escalate: Ship hit off Bulgaria sinks, 10 missing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:17:09 UTC
03:17:09 KST

Bulgaria said Tuesday that a cargo ship struck by a drone in its exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea had sunk, leaving 10 crew members missing, in what appeared to mark a further escalation of the threat the Russia-Ukraine war poses to European countries. While it has not yet been determined which side was responsible for the attack, a maritime security official said initial assessments indicated that the drone that struck the vessel, as well as other drones that attacked in the area, were launched by Russia.
The attack reported Tuesday occurred at around 3 a.m., about 112 kilometers (70 miles) from the eastern Bulgarian coastal town of Byala, with drones striking two cargo ships. The Alfa Watan, sailing under the flag of Togo, sustained critical damage and sank, while the ABLE, sailing under the flag of Palau, caught fire following the attack.
All 18 crew members aboard the ABLE — 11 Turkish nationals and seven Indians — were rescued by a ferry. Two of the sailors were found to be seriously wounded and were taken to a hospital in the port city of Varna. Both vessels, which are Turkish-owned, sent distress signals after being hit by the drones.
Tuesday's strikes marked the first time vessels had been attacked in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone and came amid growing concern in Europe over Russian hybrid attacks on countries across the continent as Moscow continues its war against Ukraine.  Although Bulgaria does not border Russia or Ukraine, it occupies a strategic position on the Black Sea, home to major ports of both countries.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev described Tuesday morning's strike as a blatant violation of international law. However, following an emergency government meeting he convened, Radev stressed that it was not yet clear whether the drones had been launched by Russia or Ukraine.
Tuesday's attack came after a separate incident Monday in which the grain-carrying cargo ship Royad Mammadov caught fire and sank off the coast of Romania. One person, believed to be the ship's Azerbaijani captain, was killed and another was reported missing. That ship, also Turkish-owned, was likewise reported to have been struck by drones, which Ukraine said had been launched from Russia.
Drone incidents have become increasingly frequent in recent months across Eastern Europe and the Black Sea. At least 45 merchant vessels have been attacked over the past year in parts of the Black Sea not previously considered high-risk.
Zelensky: Russia preparing 'massive attack' on Ukraine
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Tuesday that the latest intelligence suggested Russia was preparing a "massive attack" on Ukraine.
"There is updated intelligence indicating that Russia is preparing a massive attack," Zelensky said in his nightly video address. "Ukrainian services and our air force are ready to respond to the extent permitted by our available means of defense."
Zelensky said Ukraine's position depended largely on what its allies could provide in terms of weaponry to defend against a new Russian attack. "A great deal depends on our partners, on every leader and every country in the world that has the defensive capabilities we need and can provide them to us," he said.
"It is critically important that there be the political will to do so, particularly in the United States, in Europe and among our other partners."
Kyiv moves to scheduled power outages: 'Use electricity responsibly'
Meanwhile, Russia continues to attack key bridges in the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, as part of a new strategy it has pursued since last Thursday. The attacks have already partially or completely halted traffic on three of the city's six bridges spanning the Dnipro River.
On Tuesday, Russia said it had again attacked Kyiv's Northern Bridge, once more claiming that it did so because the bridge was being used to transport military forces.
Russia has recently begun attacking Ukraine with new, extremely fast jet-powered drones, which Ukraine has so far found much more difficult to intercept than older types of drones. Over the weekend, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy acknowledged that his military was managing to intercept only about 60% of the unmanned aircraft, mainly using fighter jets.
In recent days, the drones have exploded not only on bridges but also at schools, supermarket warehouses and energy facilities. Russia has said the attacks are retaliation for drone strikes Ukraine has recently carried out deep inside Russian territory, which have caused extensive damage to Russia's oil industry and subsequently triggered a fuel crisis in the country. Drone explosions on the bridges have caused massive traffic jams across large parts of Kyiv in recent days.
On Tuesday, journalists and Kyiv residents noticed that authorities had deployed protective nets over the Northern Bridge, one of the city's main crossings, for the first time in an effort to prevent the new drones from hitting it or limit the damage from a strike. It was unclear whether the nets were installed before or after Russia announced Tuesday that the bridge had been hit again.
Protective nets like the one deployed Tuesday in Kyiv had already been widely used by Ukraine in the country's east and south, near the front line, where they are also intended to protect key transportation routes. Elsewhere in Ukraine, such nets stretch across entire streets, particularly in the Donbas region in the country's east.
Ukraine believes Russia's ongoing wave of airstrikes is aimed at plunging the country into an energy crisis ahead of winter. On Tuesday, Ukrainian energy company DTEK announced restrictions and disruptions to electricity supplies in Kyiv following heavy Russian attacks on energy facilities.
"The capital is moving to scheduled power outages to stabilize the grid," the company said on Telegram, adding that the measure was being implemented at the request of national grid operator Ukrenergo.
"Please use electricity responsibly. This will help reduce the load on the grid and prevent emergency power outages."
The company said the outages would begin at 3 p.m. local time and continue through the end of Tuesday.

PARIS - A French policeman was charged on Oct 6 with violence for last week firing a tear gas grenade at close range at a 14-year-old student during high school protests that have shaken the country, a prosecutor said.
The boy, named as Eden, lost most of his teeth and was wounded in the face in the incident on Oct 5 in Saint-Ouen-l’Aumone, north-west of Paris.
The policeman had not been remanded in custody but was placed under judicial control and banned from working until further notice, the local prosecutor said.
In videos of the incident widely shared on social media, three helmeted police officers are seen facing the high school student.
One of them struck the teenager, who kicked him back, before the grenade round fired at his face knocked him to the ground.
Detained for questioning on Oct 5, the officer said he used the weapon in response to the schoolboy’s “resistance”, according to the Pontoise prosecutor, Guirec Le Bras.
But he said, “the conditions for self-defence have not been met” due to “the lack of proportionality” in firing the grenade.
The offence in question can be punishable by up to 15 years in prison, he said.
The teenager lost several teeth and suffered a fractured jaw that required surgery, the prosecutor’s office said.
“His jaw is sealed shut, he can no longer speak and he eats through a straw,” his mother told media on Oct 5, adding all his upper teeth were broken and “his lower teeth torn out”.
Police have used tear gas and other means to try to control what the authorities have described as “urban violence” during the protests.
Unions, rights groups and many of the children have accused the police of using disproportionate force. AFP

1,770 more people displaced in Sudan’s Blue Nile state: UN migration agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:14:08 UTC
03:14:08 KST

Rania R.a. Abushamala
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Another 1,770 people from 354 households were displaced from villages in Sudan’s southern Blue Nile state amid deteriorating security, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said Tuesday.
The UN agency said in a statement that field teams estimated the displacement Monday from several villages in Wad al-Mahi locality.
The affected villages included Amiri, Jabal Nimr, Abu Qaddaf, Bashkarkat, Ab Jankour, Makla, Manqita, Jabal al-Nou, Mezna and Manshilang.
Those displaced headed to Al-Rosaires locality in the Blue Nile state, it added.
The figures bring the number displaced from Wad al-Mahi villages over three days to 5,525 from 1,105 households, according to IOM.
On Monday, the agency reported that 955 people from 191 households fled several villages Sunday. It announced Sunday that 2,800 people from 560 households fled 10 villages Saturday, also because of deteriorating security.
On Sept. 13, IOM reported that 99,277 people from 19,497 households had been displaced in Blue Nile state between Jan. 11 and Aug. 23.
Blue Nile has witnessed a military escalation in recent days as the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the allied Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North launched attacks on several areas.
Sudan’s humanitarian suffering has worsened during the war between the army and the RSF, which began in April 2023 because of a dispute about unifying the military.
The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced 13 million.

Vaping overtakes smoking in UK for 2nd year running
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:11:55 UTC
03:11:55 KST

Aysu Biçer
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Vaping has overtaken cigarette smoking among adults in the United Kingdom for the second year in a row, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
Around 5.4 million adults age 16 and over in Great Britain used e-cigarettes daily or occasionally in 2025, or some 9.9% of the population.
By comparison, 8.7% of adults were current smokers, equivalent to around 4.8 million people. The figures mean e-cigarette use continued to outstrip cigarette smoking, a trend first seen in 2024.
The number of people using e-cigarettes remained broadly unchanged from 2024, when 5.4 million adults, or 10.0%, were recorded as users. However, the proportion has risen substantially over the longer term, from 6.4% in 2020.
E-cigarette use was highest among people age 25 to 34, with 16.4% using vapes daily or occasionally.
At the same time, cigarette smoking continued its long-term decline. Around 4.9 million people age 18 and over in the UK were smokers in 2025, or about 9.8% of the population, down from 10.6% in 2024.
The proportion of current smokers has fallen 10.4 percentage points since the ONS time series began in 2011, when 20.2% of adults smoked.
People age 45 to 54 had the highest smoking prevalence in 2025, at 12.4%.
The sharpest decline since 2011 was among 18- to 24-year-olds. Smoking prevalence in that age group fell from 25.7% in 2011 to 7.2% in 2025, plummeting 18.5 percentage points.
The latest figures point to a continuing shift in patterns of nicotine use, with cigarette smoking declining while e-cigarette use has become increasingly common.
In 2025, the ONS found that 9.9% of adults in the UK were current e-cigarette users, compared with 8.7% who were current smokers.

====================================================================================================

Young voters struggle to afford housing. But they don't expect help from political candidates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:11:51 UTC
03:11:51 KST

ALLENTOWN, Pa. — Mortgage rates are climbing sharply, home prices continue to gain and inflation in the broader economy is hitting consumers, leading housing affordability to weigh heavily on both renters and potential homebuyers.
In Pennsylvania — a swing state where House races could help decide control of the next U.S. Congress — renting or owning a home is cheaper than the national average, but the share of income needed to do either has also risen along with the rest of the country. In 2019, it took 20% of the median income to rent a home and 18% to own. Today it's 22% and 24%, respectively, according to Cotality.
"For that person trying to get an apartment, person moving from an apartment to a starter home, starter home to a larger home, each and every one of those cohorts is reporting that it's a challenge right now, and it's something that is weighing on them in a very important political place," Lehigh University political science professor Christopher Borick said.
Americans, especially renters, feel financially stretched by housing costs, according to a new CNBC and SurveyMonkey Quarterly Money Survey, released Oct. 5. It found one in five Americans who rent or have a mortgage spend at least half of their pre-tax income on housing, while 49% spend between 25% and 49%. Standard guidelines from banks and lenders say consumers should spend 28% to 30% of their income on housing.
The cost of housing is now the top political issue — even higher than the cost of food or protecting democracy — among U.S. voters aged 18 to 34, according to the most recent CNBC All-America Economic survey.
Going into the midterm election, the average rate on the popular 30-year fixed mortgage has jumped well over 7.5%, according to Mortgage News Daily. It hit a low of 5.99% days before the war with Iran started. For buyers of a median-priced home of around $450,000, that means an increase of roughly $300 in the monthly payment since earlier this year.
Home prices, while cooling from their big gains in the first years of the Covid pandemic, were still up 1.8% in August year over year, according to the latest read from Cotality. Home prices are up close to 60% since the start of the pandemic. Combined with sharply higher mortgage rates, potential buyers are increasingly sidelined. Sales of existing homes in August were down from the year before, coming in at an annualized rate below 4 million.
"This figure of 4 million is about as low as we can go. It tells you there is an extreme affordability problem," said Norm Miller, a real estate economist and professor emeritus at the University of San Diego's Knauss School of Business.
The share of median income needed to rent or buy a home has increased nationwide, with homeownership seeing the biggest leap. In 2019, it took a national average of 24% of the median income to rent and 21% to own, according to Cotality. Today, it takes 26% of the median income to rent and 28% to own. For some markets, especially metropolitan areas on both coasts, those numbers are significantly higher.
A separate report from Apartment List finds 52% of the nation's renters are cost-burdened, meaning they spend more than 30% of their income on housing. This spiked dramatically from 2019 to 2022, as rent prices rose sharply in the first years of the pandemic. More than 22 million households in the U.S. are rent-burdened, a new record.
The Lehigh Valley, Pennsylvania's 7th Congressional District, where 19% of residents are young, is one of several toss-up races in the state. It ranks 8th nationally among House races where young voters could most influence the midterm elections, according to Tufts University's CIRCLE Youth Electoral Significance Index.
In that district, a household needs $67,481 per year to afford a typical two-bedroom rental without spending more than 30% of income on housing. The corresponding "housing wage" is $32.44 an hour, according to the most recent National Low Income Housing Coalition's congressional-district profile.
"We've seen a change in the landscape in terms of the cost of housing, access to rental markets, that has really leveraged some of the other broader concerns that we've seen in the area of affordability in a pretty potent way," Borick said. "So when you talk to voters and residents in the area, and you ask them about the things that are driving their concerns right now, housing is always really close to the top of the list."
Jessica Heller, 33, is a newlywed. She and her husband are renting from a friend in Allentown at a reduced rate. Even with a six-figure salary, she said they aren't hopeful homeownership is in their near future.
"Unless I'm putting $50,000 down — but like where do you get that money — your mortgage's still going to be like 2, 3, 4 thousand a month," Heller said. "And in Allentown, some of the most rundown homes are still selling for $400,000. It's like we're not able to get like a starter home and invest into it."
Most renters want to own a home, but few expect to, as nearly three in four Americans say buying a home has become more difficult in the last five years, according to CNBC and SurveyMonkey findings. The results also showed nearly one in four renters don't ever plan to buy a home, with down payments and limited income as the top barriers.
Incumbent Congressman Ryan Mackenzie, a Republican, is up against Democrat Bob Brooks. Mackenzie touts his support for affordable housing tax credits passed in the 2025 budget bill. In January, he co-sponsored the Make American Housing Affordable Act, which would establish a tax credit for homebuyers on their primary home. That bill has yet to see a vote.
"Housing affordability is one of the top concerns of families across the Lehigh Valley and the Poconos. After enduring years of skyrocketing housing costs, first-time homebuyers deserve relief," Mackenzie wrote in a release.
Brooks has also made housing affordability a top priority.
"We need to build more starter homes, crack down on corporate landlords and rent gouging, and expand programs that help first-time homebuyers get their start. And yes, sometimes cut rules and red tape that make it harder and more expensive to get homes built," he said on his website.
In their district, 54% of renters are spending more than 30% of their income on rent, according to the U.S. Census. Home prices in Allentown are up nearly 4% compared with a year ago, according to Zillow. Allentown, in particular, has seen big increases in rent and home prices, as former residents of New York City and Philadelphia have moved there seeking, ironically, more affordable housing.
"If you look at a market like the Allentown metro, it takes almost 60% of the average renter's household income to consider homeownership for the median home in that particular market, and that's a little bit above the national average," Miller said.
Blake Fontaine, 26, is still living at home with his mother in Easton. Fontaine said he makes a six-figure salary at ADP, one of the area's larger employers. He's saved some money and would like to move out, he said, but can't stomach the costs.
"When I started looking at the prices on houses, it completely made me backtrack," said Fontaine, who said he will not vote in the upcoming election. "It's like I'm gonna pay $500,000 for the same thing my mom paid $100,000. Makes no sense."
In another toss-up district, Pennsylvania's 10th, Republican incumbent Scott Perry faces Democrat Janelle Stelson. Perry was the only member of Congress from Pennsylvania to vote against the bipartisan affordable housing bill, the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which was signed into law in July.
"For over 50 years, the federal government has thrown money at housing — which has caused the current housing crisis," Perry wrote in a social media post. "The more money we throw at it, the more expensive it gets."
His rival Stelson has a housing affordability plan that includes expanding small-dollar home loans and cutting home construction regulation.
"I will vote to repeal the tariffs [Pennsylvania] Congressman Scott Perry supports on lumber and drywall that are driving up the cost of every home we build," Stelson said at a campaign event in front of a new apartment complex in Carlisle, Pennsylvania.
Pennsylvania has an outsized number of municipalities, adding to local zoning complaints from builders nationally and, as Lehigh University's Borick calls it, a vast array of municipal rules.
"I don't necessarily know in the short term, or even in the near short term, that you're going to see the changes that would really affect consumer sentiment in terms of this particular area of affordability," he said.

Morrisons is not a must-do deal for Sainsbury’s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:10:08 UTC
03:10:08 KST

Would competition regulators really smile upon a combination of Sainsbury’s and Morrisons? One must assume the two companies believed the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) would give a thumbs up if asked, otherwise they would not have initiated their now-aborted merger talks.
It’s easy to list the arguments the duo could make. First, the combined market share of Sainsbury’s (15.2%, on the latest numbers from Worldpanel analysts) and Morrisons (8.4%) would still be less than that of mighty Tesco (27.8%). It would not be a case of leap-frogging the market leader, which was Sainsbury’s big idea back in 2018 when Asda was in its sights.
Second, Aldi and Lidl are a stronger force in the land. Together, the German discounters represent almost a fifth of the UK market and, since they’re backed by serious international buying muscle, their role as the country’s grocery price police might not be affected one jot.
Third, since Morrisons has already sold its petrol stations, the CMA needn’t worry about the touchy issue of fuel. Fourth, at a push, Sainsbury’s and Morrisons could argue that the UK’s food security (a growing political worry) would improve if the latter’s 18 food-processing factories were housed within a stronger company that could boost local production.
So, yes, one would probably bet that the CMA would ultimately approve some version of a deal. But what version? How many store disposals would be demanded?
The CMA, as in 2018, would presumably conduct a site-by-site analysis of drive-times to judge local competition. The regulatory instinct, one suspects, would be to err on the side of intervention in light of the overall national picture. Never mind Tesco’s size, it would still not be a simple decision for a competition regulator to sanction a supermarket setup in which half the trade, or thereabouts, would be in the hands of just two companies.
Would a deal still make sense after the CMA’s remedies? It’s impossible for Sainsbury’s and Morrisons to know until they go through the process. That’s the distraction factor for Sainsbury’s. Does its chief executive, Simon Roberts, really want to spend a year bogged down in regulatory back-and-forth? In the Asda episode, the effort sucked the life out of his predecessor’s reign.
It’s not as if Sainsbury’s is struggling today. The group is winning market share, profit margins are stable, there’s enough spare cash for share buy-backs and the strategic headaches of its bank and Argos have been solved by selling both. While it would be preferable to square up to Tesco’s buyers on more equal terms, life ain’t bad.
Round at private equity-owned Morrisons, the calculation will be different. Five years after buying the chain for £7bn, owners Clayton, Dubilier & Rice’s thoughts will be turning to how to exit a tricky investment. A disposal will surely look easier than a stock market flotation and the list of potential suitors is short: Sainsbury’s is indeed the obvious candidate.
All of which says Sainsbury’s can afford to do nothing, or wait for the terms of any deal to improve. It was the party that walked away from the talks, reported the FT. That’s not a surprise. If a relative bargain is possible, the hassle of a CMA process might be worthwhile. But this is not a must-do deal for Sainsbury’s.

Sweden will send Patriot air-defences and around 100 troops to protect the Rzeszów-Jasionka logistics hub used to route aid to Ukraine. The mission starts on 1 December and will last seven months.

All in all more than 80% of the military donations sent to Ukraine cross Polish territory.
The country's Deputy Prime Minister and Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz welcomed Sweden’s decision to send Patriot systems to Poland. He also thanked the Netherlands for supporting Poland and NATO’s eastern flank so far.
Sweden steps up its military presence in Poland
The deployment of Patriot systems will be another element in Sweden’s growing commitment to the security of Poland and NATO’s eastern flank. Since the beginning of October, Swedish Gripen fighter jets have been taking part in a NATO mission to protect Polish airspace. Their task also includes helping to safeguard the logistics routes used to transport aid to Ukraine.
Stockholm stresses that increasing its military presence in the region is a response to rising threats to Europe’s security and more frequent violations of NATO countries’ airspace. Sweden, which joined the Alliance in 2024, is gradually stepping up its involvement in NATO operations on the eastern flank.
One of the most important aspects of these efforts is the protection of infrastructure in Rzeszów-Jasionka. At present, its defence includes, among others, Dutch Patriot systems, the Polish Mała Narew short-range air defence system and iLauncher systems armed with CAMM missiles.
The Swedish mission will thus be another example of NATO countries working together to shield strategic infrastructure on the eastern flank.

Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito plans to remain on the court through at least next summer, even if Democrats regain majority control in the Senate from Republicans in November's midterm election, he said in a new report.
Bloomberg reported Tuesday that Alito, 76, has ruled out retiring during the brief lame-duck session of Congress after the election, when Republicans would still hold their Senate majority through early January even if they lose control for the next Congress.
If Democrats are the majority in the next Congress, they may block any Supreme Court nominee of President Donald Trump, a Republican.
"I intend to stick around through this term," Alito told Bloomberg, referring to the court's current term, which began Monday and which will end in late June or early July.
"I made that decision many months ago," said Alito, whose first book, "So Ordered: An Originalist's View of the Constitution, the Court and Our Country," has just been published.
Alito was nominated to the Supreme Court in 2005 by then-President George W. Bush, another Republican. Alito is one of six conservative justices on the nine-member court. Three of the other conservatives — Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett — were nominated by Trump.
Bloomberg reported that Alito, in the interview, acknowledged that the idea of retiring had crossed his mind.
But he also said, "I don't feel mentally or physically decrepit," according to the news outlet.
In a recent interview with CBS News, Alito said he considered retiring this year.
"It's something I think that somebody at my age has to think about every term," he told CBS.
Democrats in the Senate are still stung by then-Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell blocking the Senate from considering the nomination by then-President Barack Obama of Merrick Garland for the Supreme Court in 2016. That block, which McConnell claimed was because there was not enough time to consider the nomination that was made in March, opened the way for Trump to appoint Gorsuch after he became president.
McConnell, R-Ky., after the death of liberal Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg in September 2020 also orchestrated the swift confirmation of Coney Barrett shortly before the presidential election that year, which ended with Trump's defeat and led to President Joe Biden, a Democrat, taking office in early 2021.

====================================================================================================

Kemi Badenoch is the most rightwing leader in Tory history. Isn’t it time she got some actual scrutiny? | Owen Jones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:04:53 UTC
03:04:53 KST

The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, will march on to the conference stage in Birmingham feeling buoyed. “Kemi’s soaring,” coos the Sun, and that sums up the prevailing wisdom. More than four in 10 Britons think she is doing well as Tory leader, compared with a third who think otherwise. As Nigel Farage’s stock has plummeted thanks to scandals over a £5m personal gift and donations from crypto billionaires, the polling suggests that the Conservatives could regain the mantle of Britain’s main rightwing force.
Yet Badenoch has been the beneficiary of circumstance. Her tenure as opposition leader has been defined by Keir Starmer’s project imploding almost as soon as it gained power. When Reform UK enjoyed its seismic polling lead, the Tory plight was double-edged: they were starved of attention, but that inevitably resulted in a lack of scrutiny, too. It has been easy for Badenoch to appear formidable while her opponents have disintegrated.
With the Conservatives now back in the race, the spotlight falls on Badenoch. Let us consider the absurdity of her proposed air defence system. Our would-be prime minister denied comparing it to Israel’s Iron Dome, despite the term appearing in both a press release and a newspaper article under her own name. This amateurishness is one thing, but even on its own terms, her proposal is a mess. It will “protect the whole United Kingdom, our sovereign territories and British bases overseas”, she claims, which would be impossible for the £10bn over 10 years she is proposing to spend on it. The former British general Richard Barrons suggests such a system would cost more than £100bn.
What does this say about Badenoch’s sense of priorities? The actual urgent national security threat Britain faces is not volleys of missile attacks, but the climate emergency. There were estimated to be thousands of excess deaths from heatwaves this summer, while our intelligence services warn of serious disruption to our food supply from 2030. Yet Badenoch has committed to repealing the Climate Change Act and claimed that net zero by 2050 is “impossible” without bankrupting Britain. This not only contradicts the conclusion of the government’s statutory climate scientific advisers, but Badenoch herself. As a Treasury minister in 2021, she told parliament that it would cost less than 2% of GDP, largely from “increased investment in growth markets of the future”. Even three former Tory prime ministers have criticised Badenoch’s shift against net zero – including the former rightwing pin-up Boris Johnson.
Then there’s her economic agenda. A year ago, Badenoch declared that she sought to become Britain’s version of Argentina’s far-right president, Javier Milei. His government has imposed devastating cuts to pensions, universities and public healthcare, while poverty is once more surging. Badenoch proposes welfare cuts worth £23bn, and misleads the public as she does so. In May, she declared: “For the first time ever, the total welfare bill is now higher than total receipts from income tax.” This has been the case since 2011, and as the UK Statistics Authority noted in a letter rebuking her, this was misleading for other reasons: the gap had actually narrowed in recent years, and most of the welfare bill goes to pensioner benefits, including the state pension.
What would £23bn in cuts mean? They would include stripping workers with indefinite leave to remain of social security – people who have lived here for years, worked and paid taxes. That would not only be an injustice to them – consider that there is already a staffing crisis in sectors such as social care that immigration restrictions are worsening. She would reinstate a two-child benefit cap that would drive hundreds of thousands of children into poverty. Most of the rest would fall on the shoulders of sick and disabled people, including those receiving support while they work.
Consider this too: while we still live with the consequences of the 2008 financial crash, Badenoch proposes ending the ringfence for big banks separating retail and investment activities, and reducing their capital requirements.
What of her authoritarianism? Badenoch has declared free speech to be “the birthright of every citizen”, yet has advocated a blanket ban on pro-Palestinian protests. The justification is conflating opposition to genocide with threats to Jewish people, but this is a Tory leader who, when asked about Gaza, said that “Israel is fighting a proxy war on behalf of the UK”. Withdrawal from the European convention on human rights and repealing the Human Rights Act would strip citizens of crucial protections against an overbearing executive and abuses of state power. Badenoch advocates an ICE-style mass deportation apparatus with sweeping powers of surveillance – directly mimicking an institution across the Atlantic that snatches people from the street and kills migrants and US citizens alike.
Her attitude to the rights of minorities, meanwhile, is underlined by her commitment to scrap the public sector equality duty in its entirety. As a minister in 2021, she backed it, saying it helped ensure “that fairness is at the heart of everything we do”.
Yet the average punter knows little about Badenoch. The increasing extremism and scandals of Farageism have allowed her to appear somehow more reasonable and stable in comparison. But Badenoch is easily the most rightwing Tory leader in the party’s history. Her programme is a wishlist of rightwing zealots – one which would be ruinous to our social fabric. Yet few have bothered to look under the bonnet. The danger is that Britain discovers what Badenoch really stands for only when she is close enough to power to put it into practice.
- Owen Jones is a Guardian columnist

Yemeni government fighters recorded driving vehicles over Houthi opponents

Yemeni government fighters recorded driving vehicles over Houthi opponents
Oct 6 - Video posted by government forces in Yemen showed them driving armoured cars over opposing fighters as they recaptured areas around the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait from Iran-backed Houthis on Monday in a deadly new phase of the fragmented country's war.
The videos gave a glimpse into the brutal closing stages of a pitched battle for control of territory near the strait that the Houthis had captured last month. The Houthi advance sent shockwaves through the oil market and pushed up petrol and diesel prices worldwide.
Fighting continued near Bab el-Mandeb on Tuesday as Saudi-backed government forces battled to consolidate Monday's counter-attack, besieging Houthi fighters at a military camp near the strait and pushing into hills to the east, Yemeni military sources said.
The videos, verified by Reuters and filmed from inside the armoured vehicles, showed them striking fighters with their vehicle. Some were armed and some were walking or running. However, others were unarmed and some were sitting, lying or crouching on the sandy shore and made no move to evade the oncoming vehicle as they were run over.
At one point, a vehicle hits a man, running and unarmed, and another crouching on the ground. It then loops back to drive over two men, both with their hands up and unarmed. Shooting can be heard during the video and at one point the vehicle's windscreen is cracked by a gunshot.
A Houthi statement decried the videos as proof of war crimes, saying they showed "the true nature of the Saudi regime and the forces it has mobilised from extremist factions".
The Saudi-led coalition backing the government forces in Yemen did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the videos or the Houthi accusations of war crimes.
A spokesperson for the Giants Brigade — the main Yemeni government force involved in the fighting at Bab el-Mandeb this week — did not immediately comment in response to a Reuters request.
The Homeland Shield Forces, a significant formation in the Yemeni government's military coalition, did not comment directly on the videos but issued a directive on Tuesday urging troops to treat prisoners well and adhere to religious, ethical and legal standards.
Rights groups have previously accused the Houthis of war crimes, including sniper and shelling attacks on civilian targets, seizures of aid, abuse of prisoners and use of child soldiers. The group has denied war crimes.
'TURNING POINT'
Reuters has not been able to independently verify the extent of government gains and the Houthis denied they had lost ground, saying the government claims of advances were baseless.
Intense fighting meanwhile continued around Yemen's third-largest city of Taiz, where Houthi gains in a mountain district have in recent days cut off a main road to Aden, leaving government forces encircled.
Yemen's civil war pits the Houthis against an uneasy coalition of sometimes rival military forces under the internationally recognised government, backed by Saudi Arabia and its allies.
The renewed clashes have added a new front to the Iran-US conflict, with the US rebuffing Saudi requests for military help to reverse Houthi gains on the Red Sea coast near Bab el-Mandeb last month and end the group's missile and drone attacks on their territory.
"The operation itself is significant because it's a turning point in the trajectory of the conflict between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition," said Ahmed Nagi, Yemen analyst at International Crisis Group.
"The biggest test will be when they move towards the mountains," he added.
RELIGIOUS AND REGIONAL FAULTLINES
The Giants Brigade is a southern military formation originally formed by students at ultra-conservative Sunni Muslim religious colleges.
That background gives both a religious and regional edge to their enmity with the Houthis, who originate in north Yemen and belong to the Zaydi school of Shi'ite Islam.
The Giants have themselves fractured this year, splitting between factions backed by Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, illustrating the internal divisions that have long beset the Yemeni government's efforts to fight the Houthis.
As well as further squeezing global trade routes after Iran's disruption of shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, the conflagration in Yemen has poured new fire onto Saudi Arabia, a US ally.
The Houthis have repeatedly targeted Saudi infrastructure, including airports, oil refineries and pipelines. Residents of the Saudi capital Riyadh reported hearing booms overnight and two of the kingdom's southern airports were targeted.
Saudi Arabia's intervention in the latest wave of fighting included intense air strikes on Houthi forces on Monday as the Giants Brigade advanced along the flat coastal strip towards Bab el-Mandeb. REUTERS

Tear gas in Paris and Marseille as school protests grow across France
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
19:03:19 BST
03:03:19 KST

Tear gas in Paris and Marseille as school protests grow across France
- Published
Hundreds of thousands of people have taken to the streets across France, as a wave of protests by high-school pupils spread to their parents, university students and unions.
Crowds of teenagers marched from the Place de la République in Paris, calling for more resources for schools, and what they called less repression from police.
Police clashed with demonstrators in Lyon, used tear gas in Paris and Marseille and water cannon in Rennes, but there was little of the serious trouble that marred previous protests.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu condemned the earlier violence and said since the protests had begun 215 students and 85 staff had been hurt as well as 715 police officers.
The government said there had been disruption in 891 high schools on Tuesday - almost a quarter of all lycées - and said more than 250,000 demonstrators had taken to the streets during the day.
Students' unions put the number at 450,000, and said the number of high schools blockaded was 1,800 on what the protesters dubbed "Act Three" of their movement.
In Marseille, thousands of demonstrators moved around this city, stopping momentarily to chant before moving on as police changed direction.
A group of masked protesters grabbed bollards and bins and tried to barricade themselves off from police. Riot officers fired tear gas, and the protesters dispersed.
"Most of us aren't violent," said Alissa, a student in Marseille. "We're going to the streets because they've closed our schools... schools are falling apart."
Her friend, Sacha, said the ceilings in Marseille's schools were leaking and conditions were generally rather poor, "so we can't really work a lot of time". "We will keep doing this until good measures are taken," he added.
In parliament, the prime minister accused the radical-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of seeking to "sow chaos" ahead of presidential elections in seven months' time.
President Emmanuel Macron is nearing the end of his second and final term in office and LFI leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon is currently runner-up in the opinion polls behind Marine Le Pen of the hard-right National Rally.
Macron was due to chair a meeting with ministers at the Élysée Palace on Tuesday evening to assess the situation.
Education Minister Édouard Geffray said that from the start he had appealed for dialogue rather than school blockades and complained that "ultra-violent elements infiltrated the high-school student movements".
He is now under pressure to respond to the students' demands. What has been offered, including a website for students to express their grievances and an afternoon of internal discussion in schools on Friday, has made little impression so far.
There seems little chance of the protests coming to an end just yet. France's biggest union, the CGT, has said that further protests involving school and university students are being planned for Thursday.
There is widespread concern over allegations of "disproportionate force" by police, and France's IGPN police inspectorate has been investigating a number of cases.
One police officer who fired a tear-gas grenade at a high school student at Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône, north-west of Paris, last week has now been charged by prosecutors with "violence... resulting in mutilation or permanent disability".
Eden, 14, was part of a group blockading the Château d'Épluches lycée for 15-18-year-olds when he was hit in the face. His lawyer said he suffered a fractured jaw, and that his upper teeth were broken and four of his lower teeth were gone.
On Monday, a 15-year-old's hand was torn off after a so-called anti-encirclement grenade was fired in unclear circumstances near a school in the northern city of Lens.
Authorities say he picked up the "sting ball" grenade which then exploded, but students allege he was hit directly after an officer fired.
The grenade is considered a non-lethal weapon and the local prefect has said the incident took place when police were confronted by a group of 200-250 students throwing stones and fireworks.
What began with local anger at overcrowded classrooms, a lack of teaching staff and dilapidated school buildings in the northern Paris suburb of Seine-Saint-Denis in mid-September has since spread across the country, and extended to some universities too.
Late on Tuesday, the French interior ministry said a total of 6,547 had been stopped or arrested by police since 28 September.
Tuesday's protests drew people of all ages. One couple in their 70s, Alain and Michèle, joined the march in central Paris, to show their support for young students, explaining that as former teachers they understood the problems that France's education system was facing.
"We are the grandparents of three students who are all mobilised. They have protested peacefully in front of their respective high schools in Paris in recent days, but they were still tear-gassed," Alain told the BBC, his voice trembling.
Additional reporting by Manon Prat in Paris.

Google told to halt work on datacentres in Finland over environmental concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:02:56 UTC
03:02:56 KST

Google has been ordered to temporarily stop work on two datacentres in Finland after failing to carry out the necessary environmental impact assessments on its construction sites.
The planned datacentres in Muhos and Kajanni are part of a €13bn (£11bn) project across multiple sites in northern Finland by the technology company amid huge demand for space to house online infrastructure.
It comes after it emerged that Tuike Finland Oy, the company representing Google, had felled 330 hectares (815 acres) of forest in Muhos without completing an environmental impact assessment (EIA).
In Kajaani, the company has reportedly been logging across just under 200 hectares (494 acres) of land.
The Finnish Association for Nature Conservation said the sites had been reduced to “sand”, blaming the oversights on the “overheated” market for new datacentres.
On Tuesday, the Finnish Licensing and Supervision Authority (LVV) said it had issued a notice to the company to “immediately suspend” – by 23 October at the latest – “preparatory measures that significantly change the environment” of the two sites until the environmental impact assessment had been completed. Google has until next Wednesday to submit a written explanation.
The EIA is ongoing and expected to be completed later this year. But Google has gone ahead with “extensive preparatory measures”, including removing trees, stripping topsoil and constructing site roads, LVV said.
Tommi Muilu, the head of the environmental department at LVV, said: “In our opinion, the measures in question will change the environment and cause impacts, the identification and assessment of which are among the key objectives of the EIA procedure.”
If Google does not comply, LVV said it would consider enforcement proceedings and a fine.
In response, Google said in a statement “we understand the concerns” and that it had “fallen short of our own high standards”.
The company added: “We will study the LVV’s findings and follow their guidance. We acted in good faith under the Forestry Act, and ran nature surveys and put in place measures to protect high-value areas. As we continue our long-term work in the region, we are advancing our landscaping and biodiversity plans, which include tree planting across 130 hectares (321 acres) at Muhos.”
Tapani Veistola, the chief operating officer at the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation, said the malpractice across two sites appeared to be a “systemic problem”. The site at Muhos, he said, was “not a forest any more. It is a sand area.”
One of the reasons behind it, he said, was the enormous demand to build datacentres in Finland, which is leading companies to work as fast as possible and overwhelming small municipalities.
“The main reason behind everything is the overheated market situation that makes companies speed up processes so much. Also a lack of expertise in municipalities.”

Momeni described Iran-Qatar relations as “brotherly and constructive,” saying bilateral issues are being addressed and resolved through such meetings. He added that the Qatari emir had welcomed the points raised by Pezeshkian and had also conveyed several issues for Momeni to relay to the Iranian president.
The interior minister said the Qatari emir had also shared views and proposals on regional developments, which he would convey to Pezeshkian in Tehran.
Momeni further said he held a separate meeting with Qatar’s interior minister, during which the two sides agreed to establish a joint working group comprising representatives from both ministries to follow up on decisions reached during the talks.
He said there was scope for expanding Iran-Qatar cooperation in both security and trade and that the necessary follow-up would be carried out.
