EU seeks ways to make expansion more palatable to members
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:02:00 UTC
03:02:00 KST

EU seeks ways to make expansion more palatable to members
October 6, 2026
The European Commission on Tuesday published a document called "Preparing for a wider Union," which sought to lay out new proposals on "the policy orientations and actions needed to prepare the [European] Union for future enlargements."
Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that "Europe's future depends on the choices we make today," as she tries to encourage progress at the EU's leaders' summit this month and in other upcoming talks on the matter.
The EU's executive proposed an array of changes — including a gradual integration process for would-be members, new safeguards "to ensure that commitments undertaken during accession negotiations continue to be fulfiled steadily after accession," and changes to voting rules.
They were trying to strike a balance between simplifying the accession process, incentivizing candidate countries to continue to pursue it, and allaying concerns among existing members about potential risks or costs of expansion.
Why is expansion coming back into focus?
In the quarter century after the end of the Cold War, the EU rapidly grew from a union of 12 member states to 28, before dipping back down to 27 when the UK left following 2016's Brexit referendum.
But the process has ground to a halt ever since, with a series of candidate countries stuck in lengthy negotiations and little apparent appetite among members to continue to expand.
In recent years, amid Russia's invasion of Ukraine and signs of the US vying for increased influence in parts of Europe, theoretical interest in expansion has picked up once more. But realizing the idea, with strict rules governing the accession process and the need for unanimous support among existing members for many core steps, has remained challenging.
What did the Commission say about expansion?
Von der Leyen said the Commission was trying to prepare institutions, adapt policies and adjust budgets to reflect shared realities to better facilitate and accommodate expansion.
"Enlargement of our Union is a geopolitical imperative," she said. "Today, we are laying the groundwork to ensure that a larger Union is also a stronger one: more resilient, more effective, and firmly anchored in the values and rules that define us."
She said that as countries progress on their path towards reform, "the EU must be ready to welcome them."
Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said that Brussels' assessment "shows that the EU can accommodate a larger membership." But "there are areas where we see challenges we need to address," she acknowledged.
"One is the rule of law and sincere cooperation, where we are proposing stronger possibilities to prevent backsliding, including reducing funding or restricting voting rights," Kos said.
What changes are the European Commission proposing?
The Commission lays out a number of proposed changes or policies designed to smooth the accession process, including but not limited to:
- Moving from unanimity to qualified majority voting among members in a number of the less significant votes about advancing or progressing membership bids
- It makes no mention of changing the current requirement for a unanimous vote about finalizing membership applications, however
- Gradual and accelerated integration of candidate countries to "bring tangible benefits to citizens and businesses," but which would remain "conditional and reversible"
- "Stronger safeguards against serious backsliding on commitements undertaken during the acession negotiations" in future accession treaties, which could "in the most serious cases" extend to the suspension of voting rights
- Introducing "targeted arrangements" to "significantly limit financial support and market access" for sensitive agricultural products from candidate country Ukraine
- Ukraine's vast agricultural sector had prompted some concerns among EU members looking at how the bloc's budget could handle expansion, given that agriculture is a rare policy area where the bulk of spending and subsidies are orchestrated at the EU level, not by national governments
All these proposals will be subject to further discussion among European leaders and governments, with the next major meeting being next week's EU leaders' summit. Should they gain traction and progress, no doubt after some alterations and amendments along the way, they would ultimately have to face and pass various voting procedures to be implemented.
What's the current situation with EU candidate countries?
A total of eight countries currently have formal candidate status, meaning they are seeking to join the EU and have at least begun the often lengthy process that involves.
Some hope to join the bloc sooner rather than later, not least frontrunner Montenegro, after years of negotiations. Kos told DW last week that Montenegro was currently on track to become the next EU member by 2028.
Others, like Turkey, have nominally been candidates for decades but have made no discernible progress for years.
Ukraine is the newest addition to the list, having only gained full candidate status in 2024, but it is also the one with the most pressing motivation to hurry the process along amid Russia's invasion.
Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Georgia, Moldova, North Macedonia and Serbia are also all seeking membership.
A ninth country, Kosovo, is recognized as a potential candidate but not a formal one — with not all EU members recognizing Kosovo's unilateral declaration of independence from Serbia.

The brain may use a shared code for gender across faces, bodies, and objects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:00:30 UTC
03:00:30 KST

A neuroimaging study suggests that the brain processes cues about gender from faces, bodies, and objects in many overlapping regions at the back and lower sides of the brain. One region, in the right middle temporal gyrus, appeared to represent gender in a similar way whether it was signaled by a face, a body, or an object. The paper, a reviewed preprint, was published in eLife.
Humans are remarkably good at inferring gender from visual information. They make such judgments quickly and with little conscious effort. Faces provide especially powerful cues, but gender can also be inferred from body shape, posture, clothing, and even objects that people associate with men or women.
For faces, this ability remains surprisingly intact even when an image is degraded, partly hidden, or reduced to a silhouette. Such flexibility suggests that the brain may represent gender at a level that goes beyond any single type of visual cue. In other words, the same general concept may be extracted from very different kinds of images.
Scientists have already identified several brain regions involved in judging gender from faces, particularly areas associated with visual and social processing. Much less is known about how the brain handles gender information conveyed by bodies, and gender cues from objects had not been studied in this way before. An important question is whether these different sources ultimately converge on a common neural representation.
Study author Wenjie Liu and colleagues at the Institute of Psychology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which tracks changes in blood flow as an indicator of brain activity, to record participants’ brain activity while they viewed images of faces, bodies, and objects associated with men or women. They aimed to establish whether any brain region encodes gender regardless of what type of image a person is viewing. Identifying such a region could help researchers understand how the brain turns diverse visual signals into abstract social categories, such as gender, that guide everyday perception and interaction.
Study participants were 22 healthy adults between 19 and 28 years of age, with an average age of 22. Eleven of them were men.
In the main experiment, participants viewed six types of images while their brain activity was recorded: male and female faces, male and female bodies, and objects associated with men or with women. Each type included 30 different images. Face images showed Chinese male and female movie actors, and body images showed a body in underwear from below the head to above the knees. The object images, which were strongly associated with one gender or the other, came from a previous study.
Images were shown in 12-second blocks, each containing images from a single condition, such as female faces. Each of the six conditions appeared three times per run in random order, and each run lasted 5 minutes and 30 seconds. Participants completed six runs, except for the first two participants, who completed seven. To make sure they paid attention, participants pressed a button whenever the same image appeared twice in a row, which they did with about 97% accuracy; they were not asked to judge gender.
To analyze the scans, the researchers used a machine-learning approach that tests whether patterns of activity in a given brain area can be used to tell male images from female images. The regions carrying this gender information differed somewhat depending on the type of image. For faces, gender information was found in several visual areas on both sides of the brain (the cuneus, calcarine cortex, lingual gyrus, superior and middle occipital gyri, and middle temporal gyrus), as well as in the right superior parietal lobule and the left fusiform gyrus.
For bodies, gender information was found in a large portion of the occipitotemporal cortex, along with clusters in the superior parietal lobule, inferior parietal lobule, and postcentral gyrus on both sides of the brain. For objects, it was found in the cuneus, calcarine cortex, lingual gyrus, fusiform gyrus, superior, middle, and inferior occipital gyri, and inferior temporal gyrus on both sides of the brain, as well as in the right middle temporal gyrus.
The researchers then tested whether gender information carried over from one type of image to another. For example, they trained the classifier on brain responses to male and female faces and tested whether it could tell the gender of bodies. The only region where this worked for all three pairings of faces, bodies, and objects was a small cluster in the right middle temporal gyrus, and a second type of analysis pointed to the same area.
This region was not dedicated to gender alone. Like most of the gender-related regions the researchers identified, it also carried information about whether a person was viewing a face, a body, or an object.
To probe what kind of visual information this region might be using, the researchers compared its activity with an artificial neural network trained to classify images by gender. Activity in the right middle temporal gyrus most closely resembled the network’s middle layers, suggesting that it relies on mid-level visual features. Mid-level visual features are intermediate representations such as contours, textures, shapes, and spatial arrangements that lie between basic features like color or orientation and the recognition of whole objects or categories.
The researchers also examined how gender-related brain regions communicated with one another. The pattern of these connections was modestly similar when people viewed faces and bodies, but not when they viewed objects.
“Together, these findings identify a category-general neural hub for gender perception and illuminate how mid-level visual features and distributed networks support the abstraction of gender across heterogeneous visual inputs,” the authors concluded.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of the neural basis of social perception. However, eLife’s reviewers rated the evidence as incomplete, citing conceptual concerns, weak statistical methods, and possible confounds from basic differences between the images, such as their size. They suggested the authors temper their claims that the region holds an abstract representation of gender, and the preprint has not yet been revised in response.
The study was also small, with 22 young adults, and participants did not need to attend to gender during the task. Because the faces were of Chinese actors and the gender associations of objects are shaped by culture, the results might differ in other populations.
The paper, “A shared neural code for gender across faces, bodies, and objects in the human brain,” was authored by Wenjie Liu, Xiqian Lu, Yuhui Cheng, Ruidi Wang, Xinquan Lu, Xiangyong Yuan, and Yi Jiang.

Patients hiding use of peptides or weight-loss jabs face 'serious' surgery risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Weight-loss GLP-1 jabs like Ozempic and unapproved peptides pose 'serious' surgery risk
In short:
Anaesthetists are warning patients to disclose the use of GLP-1s or unapproved peptides before surgery.
A new study found there was an 11-fold risk of aspiration or regurgitation under general anaesthetic for GLP-1 users.
National guidelines recommend patients on GLP-1 drugs take clear fluids for 24 hours, followed by a standard six-hour fast before surgery.
Patients who have failed to disclose the use of weight-loss jabs or illegal peptides before surgery could face "serious" consequences, according to doctors, after a new study showed there was an 11-fold risk of regurgitation or aspiration for GLP-1 users.
Pulmonary aspiration, where material like food enters the airways and lungs, can be fatal and experts have described the increased risk for GLP-1 users under general anaesthetic as an "accident waiting to happen".
The Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists (ANZCA) issued a fresh warning to patients, saying some were still failing to declare they were on the medication because they had forgotten, were embarrassed or were trying to conceal the purchase of unapproved peptides.
"That weight stigma can be very strong,"
president Tanya Selak said.
"They do worry that by disclosing these private personal details that they might be judged or they might be treated differently."
The use of GLP-1-based medications such as Ozempic or Mounjaro has been rising rapidly in Australia, with an estimated half a million people using them.
Authorities have also reported people self-injecting unapproved drugs like retatrutide, which is also a GLP-1-based medication.
GLP-1 drugs mimic the activity of a natural hormone, helping people feel full for longer.
But because they slow digestion, standard fasting might not empty a patient's stomach ahead of surgery, posing an increased risk of pulmonary aspiration.
"When you're under anaesthetic, your body's automatic safety reflexes like coughing and swallowing are switched off so food or fluid in there can come back up and then slip into the airway and lungs, and that can cause serious lung injury," Dr Selak said.
"It's quite rare, but it's the reason why we routinely ask patients to fast before surgery."
Doctors have been delaying surgery because of that risk, or using alternative methods to administer anaesthetics.
A new study published in the peer-reviewed Anaesthesia journal last month found patients on GLP-1s were 11 times more likely to regurgitate or aspirate contents under general anaesthetic than those not taking the medications.
The study looked at more than 47,000 patients across the UK and identified almost 1,350 people who had been taking GLP-1 drugs for three months prior to surgery.
Most of the cases only involved regurgitation, and generally patients regurgitated or aspirated as they woke up from anaesthesia, but the authors noted the link was not necessarily causal, as people with obesity or diabetes were already at increased risk of aspiration or regurgitation.
Stopping GLP-1s before surgery 'demonstrably stupid'
The research found around a third of patients were advised to stop taking their medication for a week before surgery.
But Professor Michael Horowitz, who specialises in gastrointestinal function at Adelaide University, says that advice is "demonstrably stupid" as slowed gastric emptying can persist for some time.
Pausing a GLP-1 can also be dangerous for people taking it to manage type 2 diabetes and there could be other possible implications, such as losing associated kidney benefits.
Professor Horowitz said given how "devastating" aspiration could be, there had to be more research to determine how long it took for normal gastric emptying to return after stopping a GLP-1 drug.
"People are getting mixed advice because we don't have a good evidence base to give advice," he said.
"This is an accident waiting to happen."
ANZCA guidelines recommend patients on GLP-1 drugs take clear fluids for 24 hours, followed by a standard six-hour fast before surgery.
They also recommend anaesthetists specifically ask their patients whether they are on GLP-1 medication.
"Some people will come and write that they're not on any medications but by the time I've asked them a number of different things, we've found out … 'oh I'm on a peptide injection someone gave me at the gym'," Dr Selak said.
For Dr Selak, the message to patients is to be honest with their doctor about what medication they are taking.
"There is no judgement, we are partners in your care and that simple conversation can help us make the safest plan."

The RBA isn't trying to stop inflation. So don't expect prices to fall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

analysis
The Reserve Bank isn't trying to stop inflation. So don't expect prices to come down
What is the Reserve Bank trying to achieve by raising interest rates?
In recent days, a video has done the rounds on social media of someone asking for help to understand what the RBA is up to. This is an edited version of what they said:
"If inflation means that prices are higher, does the RBA expect businesses to start reducing prices to make inflation decrease?
"Because I don't see businesses ever reducing prices. I've never seen a company say that they'll permanently reduce their prices.
"So how does inflation actually get fixed?"
It was a great question, but a little confusing. So let's untangle it and answer it.
Inflation is baked into the system
Many people may not know this, but the RBA actually wants consumer prices to rise by 2.5 per cent every year.
Loading...
That's what the RBA's "inflation target" is.
So if prices are rising by more than 2.5 per cent, the RBA tries to slow the pace at which prices are rising.
If prices are rising by less than 2.5 per cent, the RBA tries to get them to rise a bit faster.
The RBA does not want zero inflation. It wants prices to rise by 2.5 per cent every year on average.
What does that mean in reality? It means that once prices rise, they're not coming down.
If prices rise by 2.5 per cent this year, by 2.5 per cent next year, and by 2.5 per cent the following year, prices will clearly be higher after three years, right?
That's the dynamic that slowly pushes prices higher over time. Inflation is built into our system.
It explains why we all feel like we're in a rat race, why we're always chasing wage increases to keep up with constantly rising prices.
Prices rise at different rates over time
The Bureau of Statistics could help people to understand this phenomenon much better if it presented inflation graphically in a more intuitive way.
It should present inflation in a graph like this, because the blue line shows what actually happens to prices over time:
And it reflects how the human brain thinks about inflation.
In Australia, consumer prices are always rising when the economy's growing, but sometimes prices rise at a faster pace, and sometimes they rise at a slower pace.
And the blue line in the graph captures that phenomenon too.
For example, when the blue line steps up sharply, that's a period when prices have risen quickly.
When the steps are smaller, that's a period when prices have risen slowly.
So, the graph makes intuitive sense. It shows how the general price level in Australia's economy is always rising over time, but that it rises in fits and starts.
Is this graph confusing?
But look at how the ABS presents inflation in graphical form on its website:
It requires people to think their way through multiple analytical steps without telling them how to do it.
For example, that ABS graph isn't telling you that prices are rising or falling, as you might assume.
It's telling you that prices have risen constantly in recent years, but sometimes they have risen at a faster rate (when the blue line goes up) and sometimes they have risen at a slower rate (when the line goes down).
If nobody told you that, you'd be forgiven for thinking that the falling line meant falling prices.
It's not very intuitive. One wouldn't be surprised if that graph was contributing to the public's confusion about inflation.
The large increase in prices in recent years
Another reason why the alternative graph is a good way to represent inflation is that it helps us to see how much prices have risen over a specific time period.
For example, when RBA governor Michele Bullock says consumer prices have risen by "20 to 25 per cent over the last few years", this is what she's talking about:
And we can use the graph to tell another intuitive story about inflation by zooming in for a granular look at the blue line.
When we do that, we can see how prices stepped sharply higher in 2022 and 2023 (when inflation got really bad a few years ago).
We can see how prices stepped up more slowly in 2024 (that's when inflation eased considerably, which led to the RBA cutting rates three times in 2025):
And we can see how prices stepped up noticeably again in late 2025 and into 2026 (which explains why the RBA has been lifting rates again this year).
How the RBA is trying to fix inflation
Which brings us back to the question at the top of this article.
The RBA isn't trying to compel businesses to cut their prices to bring inflation down. It's trying to engineer a situation in which businesses stop raising their prices so quickly.
That's it.
The RBA governor has acknowledged that consumer prices have risen more than 20 per cent in recent years and they won't be returning to their old, lower prices.
But she says she wants prices to rise much more slowly for a while.
That's how the RBA plans to "fix" inflation.
The graph below shows how consumer prices would have risen by 8.85 per cent in the last five years if they had kept rising at their 2014–2019 rate, but how they're currently 24 per cent higher.
That's what the RBA is talking about when it says the growth in consumer prices has to slow back down to a less disruptive pace.
Now, it knows it can't do anything to stop inflation hitting Australia from overseas (higher fuel prices due to war in the Middle East) and from climate-related shocks to food prices and insurance premiums.
But it's still lifting interest rates to make financial conditions a little bit tighter in Australia to slow economic activity a bit more and to increase unemployment a little bit more (yes, that's true) so local businesses can't lift prices by more than 2.5 per cent a year in the coming years.
It knows it's flirting with triggering a recession by doing so, but it thinks it's necessary.
And if the ABS published more intuitive graphs that showed how consumer prices were typically always rising when the economy's growing, it would help Australians better understand that inflation was ever-present.
It's the pace of inflation that concerns policymakers, not inflation itself.

Taylor concedes aged care workers would be hit by migration plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Angus Taylor concedes aged care workers would be hit by migration plan
In short:
The Coalition is being warned its migration plan would worsen skills shortages and damage the economy.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has acknowledged some aged care workers would be affected, but flagged "transition" plans for the regions.
What's next?
The Coalition is yet to detail how many aged care workers would be affected and will wait until the election to release costings underpinning its claim its plan is budget neutral.
The Coalition's plan to slash Australia's temporary migration program would damage the economy and push talented workers offshore, education and business groups have warned.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has rejected criticism of the economic impact of his proposal but acknowledged the changes would hit "some" visa holders working in aged care.
"What we need to have is a reset, breathing space, get the economy moving, get the right skills matches for our country," he told 7.30 on Tuesday.
Mr Taylor said he did not have the "exact number" of aged care workers who would be affected, with a "transition" arrangement only flagged for health workers in the regions.
But speaking on Wednesday, Mr Taylor said aged care workers around Australia would not be impacted by the changes due to a "transition" plan.
"There are obviously regional transitional arrangements as well, but, no, this isn't just about the regions; this is across the board," he said.
The Coalition plans to abolish Temporary Graduate Visas but would allow people in the regions, as well as any aged care and healthcare worker, to extend their visa to ease the transition.
Future aged care workers would have to apply for a skilled visa, and even those who obtained their qualification in Australia would be required to leave the country and apply offshore.
The Coalition has anticipated that about a quarter of all migrants on graduate visas would transition into the temporary skilled worker system.
Under the Coalition's plan, graduate, bridging and student visas would be significantly cut to achieve net overseas migration (NOM) of 100,000 people for two years before it returned to about 160,000 in the fourth year.
By comparison, Labor is targeting a NOM of 245,000 this year and 225,000 in 2027-28, while One Nation has pledged a "negative" intake for three years before settling at a target of 130,000 people "long term".
Business groups warned the Coalition's low migration target undermined Australia's capacity to "prosper" while universities argued it would hurt the country's ability to funnel talented students from education into skilled work.
Coalition says skilled migrants will offset cuts
Yesterday Mr Taylor declared he was "confident" the Coalition's migration plan would be "budget neutral" because the deep cuts to temporary visa numbers would be offset by increased taxation income from higher value skilled migrants.
But critics have questioned where the promised extra 100,000 skilled workers would come from, given the program is already demand driven.
There are also concerns that requiring almost all temporary visa holders to leave Australia to lodge an extension or other applications would deter highly skilled workers.
Mr Taylor said the Coalition had worked with the Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO) to determine the policy's impact on the budget but did not release the advice or indicate if modelling on the broader impact to the economy had been conducted.
The PBO's 2026-27 medium-term budget outlook modelled sustained reductions in NOM and found 40,000 fewer migrants each year would worsen the federal budget by $79.1 billion by 2036-27, while 80,000 fewer would cost about $155.5 billion.
This was largely because fewer working-age migrants would mean less income tax revenue.
The Coalition, which has committed to cuts over a four-year period, has argued the budget impact would be neutralised by an increase in the number of skilled workers who generally earned higher wages and paid more tax.
High-skilled migrants generally deliver a stronger return per person due to their younger age, stronger wage and labour-market performance, according to Treasury's 2021 Fiscal Impact of New Australians report.
Migration cuts 'bad deal all around'
Independent economist Saul Eslake said it was "true in general terms" that skilled migrants paid more tax than other temporary migrants, but said without the PBO costings of the Coalition's plan, it was difficult to assess if the policy would be budget neutral.
"They clearly have sought to address concerns about the impact that a big migration cut will have on the economy," he said.
"I'm not sure I buy everything the Coalition has said, but at least it appears they have thought about it."
Mr Eslake said he thought the opposition was "right" to focus on reducing the number of people in the country on temporary bridging visas.
But he said it felt "unnecessary" to halve Australia's humanitarian intake to 10,000 people because it was a "tiny number" in the "grand scheme" of the migration program.
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said the Coalition's policy was a "response" to One Nation's surge in the polls and warned it would negatively impact the economy.
"What does it mean when you get fewer skilled workers? The outcomes are pretty obvious," he said.
"It's bad for businesses, prices go up for consumers — it's a bad deal all around."
Coalition plan will 'end in tears', business groups say
Business Council of Australia (BCA) chief executive Bran Black said the major reduction proposed by the Coalition risked a "significant hit" to the economy and workforce.
"We must avoid a race to the bottom based on an arbitrary migration figure that could hurt Australia's economy while worsening the skills shortage," he said.
"There are many unanswered questions as to how a cut of 650,000 temporary visas will be achieved without creating economic damage."
Property Council chief executive Mike Zorbas said it was "hard to see" how Australia's skills gap would not get "worse" under the Coalition's plan.
"These migration cuts are just too deep for precision outcomes," he said.
Mr Zorbas said he agreed faith in the migration system had "deteriorated", but argued the Coalition's attempt to follow One Nation's policy position would "end in tears".
Master Builders Australia boss Denita Wawn said it seemed "crazy" to require skilled migrants leave the country in order to reapply for a visa in the construction sector.
"We appreciate the concern around visa hopping, but I would have thought where you've got priority issues and priority industries, and you want to get projects and houses built as quickly as possible, you would not delay that," she told News24.
Education sector joins criticism of cuts
Phil Honeywood from the International Education Association described the cuts to student and graduate visas as an "own goal" by the Coalition.
"We're talking about Australia's biggest service industry," he told the ABC.
"We're talking about the number one industry in Victoria and South Australia.
"Here we have 250,000 Australian jobs at risk for people who work in international education-related areas."
Mr Honeywood said international student fees funded Australia's research output and subsidised the study of domestic students.
"Without that income, our universities are really going to be in incredible financial strain," he said.
Universities Australia chief executive Luke Sheehy said the cuts to international student and graduate visas would come with "real consequences" for the economy.
"Restricting post-study work rights … risks making Australia less competitive for talented students and graduates at precisely the time we need more skilled people," he said.
One Nation says renters will save under migration plan
Meanwhile, One Nation has released analysis of the impact of its own migration plan, which includes cutting the temporary program by 750,000 over four years, on rental inflation.
The internal modelling used rental figures from the Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute to assume a substantial reduction in demand for rented properties as a result of the migration cuts.
The party estimated a "middle" case scenario where rental inflation would reduce by 6.5 per cent, which would result in an annual saving of $2,818 on the average rental by the third year of immigration cuts.
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson said her party would deliver "net negative" migration for three years before returning to a long-term "ceiling" of 130,000 NOM.
"A bigger population is not an achievement if Australians cannot afford somewhere to live," she said.

What your favourite book says about you
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Top 100 Australian Books: What your favourite book says about you
ABC Radio National's Top 100 Australian Books asks readers to nominate up to 10 of their favourite literary works produced by Australian writers.
Ten sounds generous — until it comes to the task of choosing them.
Do you vote for the most beautifully written book or the one that kept you awake till dawn under your blanket when you were a teenager?
Maybe you include the one you've re-read so often that its binding is hanging on by a thread.
Or do you choose the one that opened your eyes to a new genre you now can't stop reading, or the one that takes you back to a significant period of your life?
Choosing a favourite book isn't always a judgement based on merit — it can also say a lot about the reader choosing it.
So, what do your favourite books say about you?
Favourite doesn't mean best
A favourite book and a book you consider to be the "best" are not necessarily the same thing.
A favourite book can be attached to a memory, a sense of comfort or nostalgia, a character we identified with, a community we entered, or a specific stage of our life.
In my research into online reading communities, I look at how books become tied up in how readers express themselves and connect with others.
We don't just evaluate books. We form relationships with them, and some of those relationships outlast the first reading. This connection does not end when we close the book.
Taste is also a way of saying 'this is me'
A romance reader might not simply say "I like romance." Online, they might discuss (in detail) slow burn, yearning, spice, particular types of "book boyfriends", and the emotional experience they want from a book.
These preferences tell other readers what kinds of books they enjoy. They can also communicate what kind of reader they understand themselves to be.
Expressing a preference for a trope does not reveal your personality; rather, books give people a vocabulary for presenting their taste.
When you're telling someone "this is one of my [favourite] books", you are also telling them "this is one of my worlds".
Favourite books can help us recognise our people
Books can provide shared reference points: a fellow romance reader gets it when you tell them the book made you giggle and kick your feet, in BookTok parlance. Romantasy readers recognise when you say you can fix the grumpy male main character.
Readers may identify with a genre, such as sci-fi or graphic fiction, an aesthetic such as dark academia, or even a particular way of reading, from immersive fandom and re-reading to seeking books for the feelings they promise.
Rather than simply discerning between what we like or dislike, our taste as readers helps us recognise one another.
This has become more visible with the rise of social media reading communities where our taste, previously more likely to be private, is now expressed publicly in posts, lists, comments and lively conversations.
When loving a book becomes something you display
You may have multiple editions of the same book or arrange your bookshelves according to genre. You may even collect objects associated with characters — who doesn't want a Mr Darcy figurine on their shelf?
We see these visuals displayed on Bookstagram, BookTube and BookTok, the bookish corners of these social media platforms. Readers signal their literary attachment through special editions, themed objects, anniversary rituals or detailed knowledge of the fictional world.
None of these are necessary to enjoy a book, of course, but they show how a favourite book can become something we want to live with rather than something we once read (and maybe forgot).
Much of the discussion around social media reading communities like BookTok focuses on which books become visible, go viral or reach new readers.
But these social media communities make something else visible, too: the reader.
A shelf tour says something about the reader's taste. A trope list says something about the reader's preferred reading experience. A comment defending a character or recommending a book can signal the reader's group membership.
And although these posts are about books, they're also small performances of readership.
Your favourite books
Think again about that final list of your 10 favourite Australian books.
One could be a sentimental favourite that points back to your childhood.
Another might mark the moment you discovered a genre you still love.
Yet another may connect you to a community you found through reading, offline or online.
Or you could choose a book you return to not because it's perfect or flawless, but because it still feels like yours.
Selecting favourites can be a way of tracing your own history as a reader.
Read another way, a list of your favourite books can look a little like a portrait of the person who chose them.
Shakiba Barghi is a PhD candidate in the School of Culture and Communication, University of Melbourne, and is a 2026 ABC Top 5 program recipient.
ABC Radio National will count down the Top 100 Australian Books on air on October 17 and 18.

Ukraine war latest: Russia strikes civilian vessels in Black Sea off Bulgaria's coast
Key developments on Oct. 6:
- Drones strike merchant vessels in Black Sea off Bulgaria and Ukraine, killing at least one
- Russian losses to Ukrainian drones surge in early October, Madyar says
- Despite intensified Russian attacks, 62% of Ukrainians ready to endure war as long as needed, poll finds
- Shadow fleet tanker reportedly ablaze near Russian port city Sochi
- Klitschko's promise of 50 mobile shelters for Kyiv set to fall far short
- Poland to deploy Patriots near Ukrainian border, announces $26 billion civil defense plan
Drones struck several merchant vessels in the Black Sea on Oct. 6, including two ships in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone. A Russian strike on a separate civilian vessel killed at least one crew member and injured several others.
One crew member, a steward, was killed, and seven others were injured when a Russian drone struck a merchant vessel flying the Marshall Islands flag in the Black Sea, according to Odesa Oblast Governor Oleh Kiper. The vessel was carrying rapeseed oil and was damaged in the strike, with a fire breaking out in the superstructure.
"By deliberately targeting civilian shipping and port infrastructure, Russia is grossly violating the norms of international law, thereby posing a threat to global food security," Kiper said.
Separately, two merchant ships, the Togo-flagged Alfa Watan and the Palau-flagged Able, were hit by drones of unknown origin about 112 kilometers (70 miles) off Bulgaria's coast on Oct. 6, according to Bulgarian broadcaster Nova. The incident is believed to be the first reported drone attack on commercial shipping inside Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said in the evening that Ukrainian forces did not conduct operations in this area of the Black Sea. He said that Ukraine verified the details with Bulgaria and concluded it was a Russian attack, calling it a combined attack with sea and air drones.
The Togo-flagged vessel suffered severe structural damage and sank. The fate of its crew remains unknown, with the search for survivors continuing. NOVA reported that life jackets had been spotted near the vessel, but no people had been found.
The second vessel caught fire following the attack. All 18 crew members were rescued by a Bulgarian ferry. Two sailors were seriously injured, one with severe burns, the other with a head injury. The crew members are Indian and Turkish nationals, according to Nova.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev convened an emergency meeting with representatives of state institutions following the attacks. He described the attacks as a "gross violation of international law" and warned that such attacks pose growing risks to Black Sea shipping, increase insurance costs, and further complicate maritime transport.

Russian losses to Ukrainian drones surge in early October, Madyar says
Russian casualties attributed to Ukrainian drone strikes rose sharply during the first five days of October compared with the same period in August and September, Robert Brovdi, commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, known by his callsign "Madyar," said on Oct. 6.
Between Oct. 1 and Oct. 5, Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Forces recorded 2,699 Russian troops killed or wounded, compared with 1,931 during the same period in September, Brovdi said in a Telegram post. The figure represents a 39.7% increase, according to Brovdi.
Compared with the first five days of August, the reported number of Russian casualties was 76.5% higher, rising from 1,529 to 2,699.
The largest increase was recorded in the area of responsibility of the Ukrainian National Guard's 1st "Azov" Corps, covering the Dobropillia-Pokrovsk sector in Donetsk Oblast, according to Brovdi.
krainian drone operators recorded 1,268 Russian troops killed or wounded in that area during the first five days of October, compared with 884 in the same period in September — a 43% increase. The figure was almost twice as high as the 664 casualties recorded during the first five days of August, representing a 91% increase, Brovdi said.
The figures cited by Brovdi cover only casualties attributed to Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces and do not include casualties from other Ukrainian military units.
Ukraine's General Staff said on Oct. 1 that Russian forces suffered an estimated 46,230 personnel losses in September, the highest monthly figure recorded by Ukraine so far in 2026.
Ukraine has increasingly relied on drones to inflict casualties and disrupt Russian operations along the front line.

Despite intensified Russian attacks, 62% of Ukrainians ready to endure war as long as needed, poll finds
Some 62% of Ukrainians are ready to endure Russia's war for as long as necessary, according to a Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS) poll published Oct. 6.
The share has remained largely unchanged since late July and early August, despite the beginning of intensified Russian attacks using jet-powered drones and strikes on civilian infrastructure during the survey period. KIIS said the results show that the attacks had not led to a decline in Ukrainians' willingness to endure the war as of Sept. 21.
Another 4% of respondents said they were ready to endure the war for about a year, while 23% said they could continue for only several months or up to six months.
The remaining 11% were undecided.
"Despite the intensification of Russian terror against the civilian population — and the fact that our Western partners' response has not always been sufficiently decisive or backed by concrete actions — Ukrainians are prepared to continue bearing the burden of war until an acceptable peace is achieved," KIIS Executive Director Anton Grushetskyi said.
The survey was conducted from Sept. 12-21, when Russia had begun a new campaign of attacks involving jet-powered drones and strikes on civilian infrastructure. KIIS noted that the survey was completed before subsequent attacks on bridges across the Dnipro River.
The findings also show that 79% of Ukrainians believe Ukraine will ultimately win the war, including 47% who are certain of victory and 32% who said they rather believe Ukraine will prevail. Only 7% believe Russia will win, while 14% were undecided.
However, confidence in an eventual Ukrainian victory has declined since late July. At that time, 85% said they believed Ukraine would win, including 60% who were certain of it.
The poll was conducted through computer-assisted telephone interviews with 1,002 adults across all regions of Ukraine controlled by the government.

Klitschko's promise of 50 mobile shelters for Kyiv set to fall far short
Kyiv City Mayor Vitali Klitschko's September promise that the capital will receive "40 to 50" mobile shelters "within a month" is set to fall short after it was revealed on Oct. 6 that only 14 will arrive by the end of the year.
"We have already purchased shelters and within a month, the first batch, roughly, as far as I remember, 40 or 50 units, will be set up at transport stops where there are no stationary shelters nearby. And we are continuing this program," Klitschko said on Sept. 12.
But the Kyiv City State Administration (KMDA) told media portal Slidstvo.info on Oct. 6 that far fewer will arrive on a far longer timescale, despite Klitschko saying some had already been purchased.
Currently, only four mobile shelters operate in the city, installed by private organizations, according to Slidstvo.info. Meanwhile, KMDA's press service told the media portal that the city required at least 620 mobile shelters and 7,894 conventional ones.
The municipal transport company Kyivpastrans is supposed to buy the 14 mobile shelters after its new financial plan is approved, Slidstvo.info reports. The new shelters will be placed at Kyivpastrans branches and at the final stops of public transport lines.
The estimated costs are around Hr 54.2 million (about $1.2 million) in total, including VAT, while a single shelter for 50 people costs about Hr 4.8 million (about $107,000), Slidstvo.info said. The city's budget for public safety and civil protection for 2027 to 2029 sits at Hr 300 million.
According to the city administration, the capital's several district administrations did not request funding for mobile shelters when the city budget was drafted, and the city itself did not buy any shelters, Slidstvo.info said.

Poland will station Patriot air defense batteries in its Lublin region, bordering Ukraine, Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz announced on Oct. 5, according to Polish Radio. The money will be spent on shelters, equipment, rescue bases, stockpiles, and securing water and energy supplies during natural disasters and wartime, the prime minister said. Additionally, funding will go toward warning systems and ICT security, Tusk said. Of this money, 30 billion zlotys (about $7.7 billion) will be allocated to the regional authorities, according to him.

Russia drops criminal case against children’s hospice charity founder Lida Moniava
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:57:55 UTC
02:57:55 KST

Russian investigators have dropped a criminal case against Lida Moniava, a prominent advocate for seriously ill children and head of the Dom s Mayakom (lit. “House with a Lighthouse”) charity foundation, her lawyer Mikhail Biryukov told the Interfax news agency earlier today. Moniava had been accused of spreading “false information” about the Russian armed forces — a charge that carries a sentence of five to 10 years in prison.
“According to the investigator, the criminal case has been closed,” Biryukov said, explaining that the case was dropped because investigators found no elements of a crime in Moniava’s actions.
Moniava had been charged under Russia’s wartime censorship law criminalizing the “public dissemination of knowingly false information about the use of the Russian armed forces,” a provision introduced after the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine and which is widely used against individuals who engage in antiwar speech or who share journalistic reporting that contradicts the Kremlin’s official version of events.
The law has been used to imprison scores of Russians for their antiwar statements, including opposition politician Ilya Yashin, artist Sasha Skochilenko, journalist Alsu Kurmasheva, and former Moscow municipal deputy Alexei Gorinov. (Yashin, Skochilenko, and Kurmasheva were released as part of a prisoner exchange between Moscow and the West in August 2024, while Gorinov remains in prison.)
Moniava was detained on Sept. 2 after law enforcement officials searched her home. Investigators alleged that she had posted in her public Telegram channel what they described as “knowingly false information” about Russian military actions against Ukrainian civilians. In February, Moniava had already been fined 45,000 rubles ($530) for “discrediting” the Russian military in three Telegram posts.
In 2020, the “Dom s Mayakom” children’s hospice was inspected by the Interior Ministry’s drug control division. The institution was found to have violated rules governing the handling of narcotic drugs under Article 6.16 of Russia’s Administrative Code and was fined 200,000 rubles (around $2,800 at the time). The Moscow City Court later overturned the penalty, ruling that the violation was minor.
Moniava has worked in the nonprofit sector since 2008. She co-founded the “Dom s Mayakom” hospice with prominent Russian palliative care advocate Nyuta Federmesser, becoming head of the foundation in 2018.

Netanyahu ordered to remove Air Force base video from personal social media
The Central Eelctions Committee also ordered Netanyahu and the Likud Party to pay NIS 2500 to the petitioner as well as remove the video
The Central Elections Committee (CEC) ordered Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday to remove a video filmed in an Air Force base from his personal social media accounts, but not from official accounts.
The ruling refers to a video Netanyahu posted to his social media from Tel NofAir Force base, warning that a security threat before the election was likely.
The video triggered a serious reaction from the opposition, which demanded that Opposition Leader Yair Lapid be briefed on the security situation to prove that his claims were not part of an election campaign.
Lapid said following the briefing that he did not think that the security briefing warranted Netanyahu's announcement, saying, "There is no reason to cause public panic."
The CEC ruled that because Netanyahu did not dispute that he used military assets (an IDF base and IDF fighter jet), there was justification for posting the video on the Prime Minister's official accounts, but not on Netanyahu's personal social media accounts.
The CEC also ordered Netanyahu and the Likud Party to pay NIS 2500 to the petitioner.

Missing the Forest for the Trees in Taiwan’s Defense Preparations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:52:00 UTC
02:52:00 KST

In recent years, Taiwan’s military issues have received considerable discussion, from changes in Taiwan’s annual large-scale Han Kuang exercises to recommendations on equipment procurement. These are all quite important areas of change, but the most core issue seems to have received much less discussion: how exactly the Taiwan military may fight. The aforementioned changes in exercises and equipment procurement, in the end, are all meant to serve the kind of war Taiwan is prepared to fight. Taiwan has had some developments in this area that have received limited attention and discussion, but their importance is definitely no less than the developments in exercises and equipment.
The key is to comprehensively understand Taiwan’s efforts and preparations from the strategic level, using what the Taiwan military most often says about what kind of war to fight, what equipment to have, what kind of force structure is needed, and what training to conduct. Taiwan has moved from its past concepts of defeating the enemy on the opposite shore or seeking a decisive battle in the littoral area to actually carrying out an erosion strategy and sustained operations in recent years. To that end, Taiwan has continued to strengthen the army’s active-duty combat power in the northern region to build a layered defensive network and regional force superiority. Meanwhile, the cumulative duration of large-scale exercises in 2026 has already accumulated to nearly one month. There is also something that many people might have noticed but not realized: the significant expansion of Taiwan’s navy in recent years.
At the same time, these developments also bring out the current difficulties Taiwan faces in joint operations across the services. This is one of the most critical areas to watch in Taiwan’s future defense development. In recent years, experts have paid considerable attention to the Taiwan military’s efforts toward decentralization, but in practice, joint command and control is the key to whether Taiwan’s combat capability can be improved.
Further Concentration of Forces in Northern Taiwan
The key to an erosion strategy and sustained operations is to delay and strike enemy forces through layered forces. Although Taiwan emphasizes decentralized command and control, this means emphasizing that a single operational unit can continue to carry out assigned actions based on higher-level operational objectives when command and control is disrupted. In terms of military operations, strategically concentrating forces to make it difficult for the enemy to break through and advance is quite important. And this is also what Taiwan is doing.
Northern Taiwan is where the political center is located, and it also concentrates important operational command organizations and transportation hubs. More than one-third of Taiwan’s population lives there. More than about half of the Taiwan active-duty brigade-level forces of the Republic of China (ROC) Army and Marine Corps are normally stationed in the northern region (north of Miaoli and Yilan), including the main combat forces, combined arms brigades, Army Aviation units, and Marine Corps forces.
In particular, in recent years Taiwan has continued during exercises to additionally move units from other regions into the northern region to conduct reinforcement missions. This makes the forces concentrated in the northern region possibly reach nearly two-thirds of Taiwan’s active-duty ground forces. During the 2025 Han Kuang Exercise, the main reinforcement was carried out by units from the Marine Corps 99th Brigade moving north from southern Taiwan to reinforce Taoyuan and the greater Taipei area. The 2026 Han Kuang Exercise further expanded the reinforcement forces, including forces under the Marine Corps 99th Brigade and Army 564th Combined Arms Brigade from southern Taiwan, and the Army 586th Combined Arms Brigade from central Taiwan, which moved and deployed to the northern region.
This kind of deployment and training concentrates forces in northern Taiwan and is, to a considerable degree, a focus of Taiwan’s current sustained defensive operations. In September 2026, during the ROC Army’s annual large-scale Lu Sheng exercise, Maj. Gen. Lin Shih-wei, deputy commander of the Army Education, Training, and Doctrine Development Command, clearly stated at a press conference that this exercise was centered on the concept of successive resistance and sustained operations under Chief of the General Staff Admiral Mei Chia-shu’s erosion strategy. Most importantly, the exercise area was changed to northern Taiwan in order to conform with the focus on defensive operations and allow troops to become familiar with key terrain in the area of operations and the deployment and employment of troops and firepower.
Nearly One Month of Large-Scale Military Exercises
Another development deserving more attention is that in recent years the Taiwan military has begun extending the training duration of various live-force exercises. In addition to extending existing exercises such as the nationwide Han Kuang exercise and the brigade-level Lu Sheng exercise, it has also added several large-scale exercises.
The accumulated time of these military exercises has led the Taiwan military this year to spend almost an entire month participating in various live-force exercises, far more than in the past few years. This includes the five-day Immediate Combat Readiness Exercise in June, the five-day Joint Defense Exercise in July, the 10-day Han Kuang Exercise in August, and the 10-day Lu Sheng Exercise expected in October.
Besides allowing units to have more time to complete continuous training events that could not be conducted in the past, this also allows participating units to become familiar with scenarios related to long-duration sustained operations during a future Taiwan conflict. The longer training and exercise duration allows units to validate operations under prolonged combat scenarios, as well as the maintenance of combat capability and coordination with civilian sectors in the use of civilian resources, including manpower and material mobilization.
Taiwanese Navy’s Expanded Mission
Another aspect worth attention in recent years is that the ROC Navy has been playing more and more roles in Taiwan’s current defensive operations. In the past, the Taiwan government mainly planned naval units in wartime as fleet task forces. In recent years, there have been three notable changes.
First, the Marine Corps under the Navy has undergone a major transformation in recent years, shifting from a force responsible for offensive amphibious operations and power projection in the past to a defensive force for urban areas. In recent years, Taiwan’s Marine Corps has gradually given up its tanks and self-propelled artillery in favor of drones and anti-tank equipment. As the strategic reserve directly under the General Staff Headquarters, the Marine Corps has been deployed to the Taipei area, with its mission shifting to become a defensive force for the capital garrison area.
Second, the ROC Navy this year established a new Coastal Operations Command within the service. Its commander holds the same vice admiral rank as the Fleet Command commander, and it integrates units related to shore-based anti-ship missiles, shore-based radar, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR), and unmanned aerial systems, with the goal of establishing a coastal operations system across units and platforms.
Third, Taiwan’s Coast Guard this year added one new deputy director-general position, and in late September formally appointed a vice admiral from the Navy to the position. The purpose is to bring the Navy’s tactical thinking into the Coast Guard, inject key new momentum into the Coast Guard’s transition from peacetime to wartime, effectively connect communication channels between the military and Coast Guard, and deepen joint maritime-air defense and response mechanisms.
In addition, Taiwan’s Coast Guard has also begun, during the military’s annual exercises, to expand training events related to the transition from peacetime to wartime, allowing its Coast Guard vessels to undertake part of the sea-denial strike missions during wartime. Specifically, this year’s Han Kuang exercise had the Coast Guard conduct exercises under the control of the Navy’s Coastal Operations Command.
These changes all show that the ROC Navy is playing an increasingly important role in Taiwan’s current defensive operations. This includes sea denial and coastal operations, and also includes the capital garrison mission during the defense-in-depth phase.
Policy Implications
Taiwan’s current defense preparations are not only changes in concepts and efforts in equipment procurement, but have also seen quite significant developments in military training and deployment validation. More importantly, as the relatively weaker side in the cross-strait military balance, Taiwan must necessarily concentrate its resources to a greater degree and use them more efficiently. Therefore, we can also notice that there is now more Navy involvement in maritime and coastal denial operations, and even in the land-based attrition strategy and the defense-in-depth phase. The Coast Guard is also practicing the transition from peacetime to wartime,
But at the same time, these changes also point to a more critical area to observe in the future, which is whether Taiwan’s joint operations across the services, especially its command and control preparations, are in place. In the past, land operations were usually considered something for the Army to handle by itself. In a hypothetical scenario where the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) would be able to conduct an amphibious assault on Taiwan and then offload follow-on forces, it was typically assumed to mean that Taiwan’s air and naval combat power had already been largely paralyzed, while China had air and sea superiority. Now, this situation has changed to a considerable degree. Navy shore-based units and Air Force air defense units will also play important roles during the defense-in-depth phase, and therefore preparations for joint operations become quite important.
The first question mark is the joint command and control capability under the concentration of large numbers of forces, including Army and Navy forces concentrated in the northern region, as well as Air Force air defense assets. Efficient command and control of different units in conducting joint operations is quite critical.
Second, and even more critical, is whether Taiwan can increase the capacity of its joint operations training. The Taiwanese military’s only Joint Operations Training Base has limited training capacity. Because of geographic space limitations and the need to avoid disturbing nearby residents, it can usually only provide battalion-level training. The ROC Navy, Army Aviation, and Air Force also have difficulty participating together as formed units in exercises because of the limited airspace. Although annual large-scale exercises can validate and train service members’ ability to conduct joint operations, in practice they cannot fully replace basic joint operations training.
Taiwan has far fewer resources compared with China, so joint operations capability is key to allowing Taiwan’s combat power to be used more efficiently. This is also a key area of Taiwan-U.S. military cooperation. In January 2026, media reports stated that U.S. personnel had been stationed at Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defense Joint Firepower Coordination Center, which is responsible for cross-service fires deployment and coordination, and that joint staff work had reportedly already been conducted.
It is important to know that decentralization is a key capability when the command and control system is cut off, in order to maintain operational resilience. But for Taiwan, in the event of war, the best situation for resisting a Chinese invasion to the greatest extent should be to have a sound joint operations capability, so that resources can be converted into combat power to the greatest extent. Therefore, although experts in recent years have paid considerable attention to the Taiwan military’s efforts toward decentralization, joint operations capability is also critical.

Cabinet okays new body to bring roads, rail, ports, aviation under one planning framework
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:47:05 UTC
02:47:05 KST

The agency will prepare a comprehensive National Transport Master Plan with a planning horizon of 10 years or more (ANI Photo).
NEW DELHI: The Cabinet on Tuesday approved setting up India’s first integrated transport and logistics authority, giving the new body a mandate to plan, appraise and monitor projects worth over Rs 500 crore across roads, railways, ports, aviation, waterways, urban mobility and logistics.The Integrated Transport and Logistics Authority (ITLA) is aimed at ending fragmented planning across multiple transport ministries and agencies and driving greater coordination and multi-modal integration in infrastructure development. Announcing the decision, I&B minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said, “By fostering greater coordination and multi-modal integration, ITLA is a new institution responsible for prospective planning for infrastructure development in the country.”The new agency is modelled on similar institutions in the US, UK, Germany, Australia and Japan, and was first reported by TOI in April 2024.Govt said ITLA will also create a unified transport data repository by obtaining relevant transport and logistics datasets from multiple sources, including GSTN e-way bills, FASTag, Vahan, GPS-based systems, urban traffic management systems and other databases. It will undertake data analytics for planning, monitoring and impact assessment.
Each transport and logistics-related ministry will have an ITLA division to ensure better coordination and implementation of projects and schemes, officials said.The agency will prepare a comprehensive National Transport Master Plan with a planning horizon of 10 years or more. It will also evaluate five-year sectoral plans and annual plans of transport ministries to ensure consistency with the master plan and promote multi-modal infrastructure development.Vaishnaw said ITLA will coordinate the resolution of inter-ministerial issues and assess the impact of projects after their completion, making post-completion assessment an important part of its mandate.

Tuareg rebels withdraw from strategic town of Kidal in northern Mali
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:46:52 UTC
02:46:52 KST

Mali’s army says it has taken Kidal from Tuareg rebels, with Russia’s help
Announcement comes after Azawad Liberation Front said it was carrying out a ‘controlled withdrawal’ from strategic northern town.
Mali’s armed forces have entered the strategic northern city of Kidal, five months after separatist rebels seized it, following an air and ground campaign backed by Russia’s Africa Corps.
In a statement carried by state television on Tuesday, Mali’s transitional government said troops had “consolidated their positions” in the city, “supported by their Russian partners”.
It said the return followed “intense air-ground neutralization operations”.
But according to the armed groups that controlled the city, the Malian army entered Kidal on Tuesday without a fight.
The Tuareg separatist Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) movement announced earlier in the day that it had carried out a “strategic and controlled withdrawal” from Kidal. It cited the “disproportionate use of aerial assets by Russian mercenaries from Africa Corps”.
The group said the move was intended to “preserve human lives” and was a temporary measure.
The separatists seized Kidal, a Tuareg stronghold, in April, during coordinated attacks across the country with Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), the regional affiliate of al-Qaeda. The attacks, which also killed Mali’s defence minister, posed the biggest test yet for the military leaders who took power in coups in 2020 and 2021.
Mali has been racked by a security crisis since 2012, fuelled by fighters allied with various armed groups, including al-Qaeda, the ISIL (ISIS) group and Tuareg separatists. After the coups, the military government turned away from Western allies and towards Russia for help in combating the groups.
It first relied on the Wagner mercenary group, which was replaced in June 2025 by Africa Corps, a force under the direct control of Russia’s Defence Ministry.
Malian troops and Wagner fighters had retaken Kidal from armed groups in November 2023, only to lose it again in April.
“A successful recapture… affirms the military-led government’s authority and boosts the army’s morale, particularly after several high-profile setbacks, both in the north and the central regions in recent weeks,” said Beverly Ochieng, associate director of Control Risks.
“This is also an opportunity for Africa Corps to reprise its role as the Malian government’s security guarantor after appearing to lose significant ground, including in Kidal, since April,” she told the Reuters news agency.
But the change of control in Kidal is still largely “symbolic” and not “decisive” in Mali’s campaign against rebel groups, Ochieng added.

Chris Murphy, the Democratic senator from Connecticut, said the Pentagon denied him access to a US military base during a visit to the Middle East. Murphy had intended to visit the Al Udeid airbase, which has been repeatedly attacked during the US war in Iran.
“This trip confirmed for me that there is an active, unprecedented, unconstitutional effort underway to hide the costs of this war and the implications of this war from Congress and the American people,” Murphy told reporters during a stop in Saudi Arabia.
A senior Pentagon official told the Associated Press that Murphy’s office had been informed that it would not receive support to visit the base, per Pete Hegseth’s March directive restricting travel to the area.
“I’ve never encountered anything like this in my time in the Senate and it’s part of a deliberate campaign of obfuscation that my Republican colleagues in Congress should demand an end to,” Murphy said.
Speaking at a Maryland shipyard, Donald Trump said the biggest problem for him in negotiating with Iran is that no one knows who is running the country.
“Their second group of leaders are gone, and the biggest problem I have is nobody knows who the hell is running the country,” Trump said.
Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, spoke to the United Nations last month, and Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff has met with the country’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi.

5,236 amendments submitted to the 2027 State Budget draft — Parliament says it is a record
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
20:45:28 EEST

5,236 amendments submitted to the 2027 State Budget draft — Parliament says it is a record
Kyiv • UNN
5,236 amendments were submitted to the 2027 State Budget draft — 1.5 times more than last year. Two-thirds were called legislative spam.
A record 5,236 amendments were submitted to the draft law "On the State Budget of Ukraine for 2027," which is 1.5 times more than last year. This was reported by MP Roksolana Pidlasa, Chair of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Budgetary Matters, UNN reports.
Members of Parliament submitted 5,236 amendments to the 2027 budget bill. This is 1.5 times more than last year and a record for at least 24 years (statistics have generally been kept since the 2003 budget)
According to her, two-thirds of these amendments are so-called "legislative spam," submitted in order to speak for hours in the plenary hall or to demand that desired amendments be taken into account.
If at least 90 seconds are spent on each amendment, their consideration will take more than 16 full working days. Clearly, amendments to draft laws are necessary, but there must be common sense in everything. Alongside the budget, the Rada must also vote on other laws that are critical for receiving international funding
Additional information
On Tuesday, September 15, the Cabinet of Ministers submitted to the Verkhovna Rada the draft State Budget for 2027. This draft budget allocates UAH 4 trillion 885 billion for defense alone, amounting to almost 44% of GDP.
On September 16, the draft law was presented in the Verkhovna Rada chamber. In accordance with the procedure, by October 1, MPs, committees, and factions study the document and submit their proposals to the Committee on Budgetary Matters. The Accounting Chamber prepares its expert opinion.
The Accounting Chamber stated that the draft State Budget of Ukraine for 2027 includes more than UAH 1.5 trillion in external borrowing, but potential creditors have not yet been identified.
After that, the Verkhovna Rada considers the draft law on the State Budget of Ukraine for the following year in the first reading no later than October 20. However, according to MPs, consideration of the draft law is not planned for the nearest plenary session, which is to take place from October 12 to 16.
"It will be brought forward for October 26–30; Monday the 26th has already also been declared a plenary day to begin consideration of the amendments," MP Yaroslav Zhelezniak reported.
Adoption of the draft law in the first reading means approval of the Conclusions and Proposals concerning the draft law, which become binding for the Cabinet of Ministers to revise. Within 14 days after the draft law is adopted in the first reading, the government revises the draft budget, taking into account the Budget Conclusions of the Verkhovna Rada, and submits it to parliament for the second reading.
Consideration in the second reading must take place by November 20. The following are adopted in the second reading:
-  the maximum amount of the annual state budget deficit (surplus), the maximum amount of public debt, and the maximum amount of state guarantees to be provided; 
-  the total amount of state budget revenues, expenditures, and lending;  
-  the minimum wage for the relevant budget period, the subsistence minimum for the relevant budget period calculated per month per person, as well as separately for the main social and demographic groups of the population, and the level of subsistence minimum provision for the relevant budget period; 
-  budget allocations for intergovernmental transfers and other provisions necessary for the preparation of local budgets. 
By December 1, the Verkhovna Rada votes on the bill in the third reading and adopts the document as a whole.

France’s Mistral unveils ‘Le Chonk’, its latest model in sovereign AI push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:44:58 UTC
02:44:58 KST

France’s Mistral unveils ‘Le Chonk’, its latest model in sovereign AI push
- - Mistral launched “Le Chonk”, its biggest open-weight model, to give enterprises and governments more control over data, compute and AI operations.
- - The model can be downloaded or used on Mistral’s servers, and the company says it offers stronger security and lower costs than closed models.
- - Built on 4,000 Nvidia chips in Europe, Chonk is aimed at private, sovereign AI use and supports more than 160 languages.
AI generated
PARIS - French AI startup Mistral announced on Oct 6 its biggest open-weight model, dubbed “Le Chonk”, claiming enhanced performance and security capabilities for clients seeking to keep their data private instead of relying on closed models from the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI.
The new model lets users download and customise the parameters, or “weights”, that determine how it computes to their own servers.
It is Mistral’s first major product launch since it raised €3 billion (S$4.3 billion) in September in Europe’s biggest technology fund-raising ever.
The company is betting that companies and governments will increasingly want total control over their AI deployments, as opposed to using proprietary models that require handing over data to third parties and can be much more expensive.
“Enterprises across financial services, manufacturing and the public sector can govern the intelligence, data, compute and operations underpinning their critical infrastructure... without exposing their most valuable knowledge to anyone outside their own walls,” the company said in a statement.
“That one took some groundwork,” Mistral’s chief executive Arthur Mensch posted on X.
“Trained and served on our own compute, and RL shows no sign of saturation,” he wrote, referring to reinforcement learning to further develop AI models, and the possibility that adding further data starts to produce diminishing performance returns.
Open-weight models are also touted as more secure, a growing concern after several incidents of AI agents going rogue by hacking databases or otherwise doing things they were not supposed to do.
“The cyber defence capabilities will enable enterprises and governments to defend themselves against threat actors that are jailbreaking closed models to perform cyberattacks,” Mistral’s chief scientist Guillaume Lample said in the statement.
Data ‘under their control’
Mistral, considered Europe’s leading AI developer, was valued at over €21 billion in September’s funding round – far below the valuations for US giants like OpenAI or the AI operations of Google, Meta and SpaceX.
Anthropic is reportedly preparing an initial public share offering in the coming weeks that could see it valued at US$2 trillion.
But their so-called closed models that currently dominate the market are facing growing competition from open-weight models, largely from Chinese developers including DeepSeek and Moonshot.
These AI versions can be fine-tuned by clients for specific needs on in-house infrastructure, and used at a fraction of the cost.
Mistral’s new model also comes as a US open-weight rival, Reflection AI, announced its own widely anticipated Beam model on Oct 5, also promising cheaper operating costs.
Mistral said Chonk’s scores on performance benchmarks so far make it one of the best open-weight models available, and “by far the best in Europe and the US”.
It said the model, which is still being refined, was built on 4,000 Nvidia chips over two months at its own data centres in Europe.
Customers can either download the model to their own servers, or access it via Mistral’s infrastructure, including in “our European sovereign region where data stays under EU jurisdiction to ensure data remains under their control”.
Mistral said the model was trained on more than 160 languages, and can answer prompts and questions in each one natively. AFP

UN Human Rights Council adopts Poland's resolution on artificial intelligence in public administration
Poland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
19:44:30 CEST
02:44:30 KST

UN Human Rights Council adopts Poland's resolution on artificial intelligence in public administration
06.10.2026
On 6 October 2026, the UN Human Rights Council adopted without a vote the resolution on good governance prepared by Poland. For the first time in the Council's history, a document of this kind sets out principles for the responsible use of artificial intelligence by public institutions with full respect for human rights.
Artificial intelligence is increasingly used in public offices, the judiciary and public services around the world. These technologies make institutions more effective, but if used improperly they may lead to erroneous or discriminatory decisions.
The resolution calls on States to assess the impact of such systems before deploying them, to ensure transparency and human oversight of decisions, and to guarantee the right to challenge them. It also underlines the need to preserve access to public services for people who do not use digital channels.
The resolution provides for the UN to develop practical guidance for public administrations on the responsible use of artificial intelligence. It will support all countries, including those still developing their digital public services.
Poland initiated the resolution on good governance in 2008 and has led work on it in the Council ever since. This year’s text was prepared together with Australia, Chile, the Republic of Korea and South Africa, and co-sponsored by 58 countries from all regions of the world. Its adoption without a vote confirms the effectiveness of Polish diplomacy in building agreement across divides and Poland’s role in shaping international standards for new technologies.
The Human Rights Council, composed of 47 States elected by the UN General Assembly, is the foremost United Nations forum for the protection of human rights worldwide – and Poland is seeking a seat on it for the 2029–2031 term.
