Alleged Iranian spies planned ‘serious violence’ against UK journalists, court hears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:34:43 UTC
02:34:43 KST

Three alleged Iranian spies carried out surveillance and reconnaissance to target journalists in the UK as part of a plan to commit “serious violence”, a court heard on Tuesday.
Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, and Shapoor Qalehali Khani Noori, 57, are charged with offences under the National Security Act.
Their “subjects” included Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, journalists for London-based Persian broadcaster Iran International, as well as a founder member of UK Lawyers for Israel, Jonathan Turner, the court was told.
The prosecution alleges Sepahvand intended to physically carry out a “violent attack” against at least one of the targets, while Manesh and Noori assisted in planning.
Sepahvand claims he was threatened into conducting surveillance against his will, but the prosecution described this as an “entirely bogus claim”, telling jurors he did it to get paid and have his theft conviction in Iran “fixed”.
In a voice note read out to Woolwich crown court in London, Sepahvand told an associate he would “finish off” a target if he was paid £150,000.
“They made me a promise and said: ‘We’ll sort out your matter/court case, and we’ll give you £150,000 as well. Finish the job. We’ll show you him/her (the target),’” he said.
“This is an illegal job. It’s something that constitutes a criminal offence, and it carries a heavy prison sentence. At the absolute minimum, they should transfer £10,000 for now.
“Wherever they tell me, I’ll go there and stand there. If the person (the target) is inside, they pay the £150,000, and I’ll finish him/her off.”
The defendants were said to have visited addresses linked to their targets, taken photos and videos and used platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online between August 2024 and March last year.
There was no dispute that the three defendants conducted the surveillance and reconnaissance, the jury was told.
Sepahvand accepts he was doing so for the benefit of the Iranian regime but claims he was threatened or bullied into doing it, and that he “deliberately did a bad job of it”, the prosecution said.
The crown added that Manesh and Noori claimed they did not know they were carrying out the surveillance to assist the Iranian intelligence service.
The defendants are charged with engaging in conduct likely to assist a foreign intelligence service.
Sepahvand, of St John’s Wood, north London, is also charged with engaging in surveillance, reconnaissance and open-source research with the intention to commit serious violence against a person in the UK.
Manesh, of Brent, and Noori, of Ealing, are also charged with engaging in surveillance and reconnaissance, with the intention that serious violence against a person in the UK would be committed by others.
The three men, who deny all the charges, were assisted by interpreters in the dock. The trial continues.

Secret fee and nearly $18 million from the budget: in Georgia, they tried to calculate the cost of Kanye West’s concert
Kyiv • UNN
Starring Georgia received nearly $18 million in state support ahead of Ye’s concert. The show attracted more than 70,000 spectators and brought in $12.2 million.
Ahead of American rapper Kanye West’s (Ye) large-scale June show in Tbilisi, the state-owned company "Starring Georgia" received a subsidy of 42.6 million lari ($17.8 million) from the Georgian government. This follows from a document on the analysis of fiscal risks to the budget published by the Ministry of Finance, UNN reports, citing News Georgia and the bm.ge agency.
Details
The publication notes that the Starring Georgia project was created under the auspices of the Ministry of Culture to promote the country and develop tourism by inviting global music stars.
The 42.6 million lari was transferred to the company in 2025. This was Starring Georgia’s first state support since 2022, when the Black Sea Arena venue in Shekvetili received 73 million lari to launch the program. At the same time, throughout 2025 the company held no expensive concerts, while its main and most ambitious project in 2026 was Kanye West’s performance.

It remains unknown exactly how much of the budget funds received and the revenue from ticket sales went toward the performer’s fee.
Starring Georgia traditionally operates with limited transparency: key contracts and information about payments to artists are absent both from the company’s own website and from the unified public procurement registry. Moreover, in May 2026, the Georgian government officially exempted Starring Georgia from the mandatory market research requirement when concluding contracts.
Despite the lack of transparency regarding the budget, commercial ticket-sales figures for the show proved to be a record for the Georgian show business industry. The concert, held on June 12 at Tbilisi’s "Dinamo Arena" stadium, attracted more than 70,000 spectators. According to the company, gross ticket-sale revenue exceeded 31.8 million lari ($12.2 million).
Ye’s performance was the rapper’s first concert in Georgia and throughout the entire post-Soviet space, as well as the largest commercial show in the country’s history, surpassing Justin Timberlake’s record from last year (55,000 spectators).
Alongside the Georgian Finance Ministry’s document, it became known that the consolidation of cultural assets under the management of the Ministry of Culture had been completed. In January 2025, the Tbilisi State Concert Hall (Philharmonic) and the Black Sea Arena management company became part of Starring Georgia, while at the end of the same year, LLC "Service-7," the operator of the Tsitsinatela amusement park, joined the structure.

A quarter of a million demonstrators took to the streets across France on Tuesday as unions and teachers joined high school students demanding better learning conditions in protests that later descended into sporadic clashes with security forces.
Students have blocked the entrances to hundreds of high schools for 15- to 17-year-olds since late September, complaining of missing teachers, overloaded timetables, dilapidated classrooms and buildings that cannot cope with rising temperatures.
Rights groups, unions and the students have accused authorities of using disproportionate force. A teenager lost a hand on Monday after police fired a stun grenade, while another student reportedly lost several teeth last week after being struck by a police launcher round.
‘Neglected schools, sacrificed youth’
At Paris's Place de la Republique, protesters gathered beneath banners demanding better-funded schools, including one reading "Neglected schools, sacrificed youth".
"Gen Z has risen up and wants to be heard," 19-year-old Lilia told AFP at a massive march in central Paris, adding she hoped President Emmanuel Macron would listen.
The unrest comes ahead of a 2027 election to choose Macron's successor, with far-right candidate Marine Le Pen riding high in the polls despite a graft conviction.
An AFP reporter described the Paris march as largely peaceful, but tensions flared near its endpoint in the east of the capital as police fired tear gas and some demonstrators threw rocks at a line of officers carrying riot shields.
Police officials said that "300 hostile individuals" were attempting to confront officers.
Yanis, 16, said students felt ignored until the demonstrations turned violent. "It makes us feel like everything gets solved through violence," he said.
The interior ministry said 256,000 people had joined demonstrations nationwide, while union organisers put the figure at 450,000.
Macron addresses unrest
Macron is expected to meet with top officials including the interior and education ministers late Tuesday in response to the unrest, a government source said.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu condemned violence linked to the protests, telling lawmakers there was "no room for tolerance of violence".
"Burning down a high school does not improve the state of high school buildings," he told parliament, rejecting accusations the government had ordered "police repression" against protesters.
While many protests have been peaceful, some demonstrators have started fires, destroyed bus shelters or clashed with riot police.
Police have responded with batons, tear gas and riot-control rounds.
Police tactics face scrutiny
The government says 215 students and 715 police officers have been injured since the start of the movement.
A 15-year-old lost a hand to a sting-ball grenade fired by riot officers in the northern town of Lens on Monday.
A policeman was charged Tuesday over the firing of a tear gas grenade at close range that left a 14-year-old northwest of Paris without most of his teeth and with facial wounds.
In Metz, prosecutors requested a police inquiry after video footage circulated appearing to show a plainclothes officer inappropriately touching a detained female pupil younger than 15.
The government has sought to address the students' grievances, while accusing the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of encouraging the movement.
Veteran LFI presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon has strongly supported the protests, while calling for non-violent methods.
Thousands of arrests
Thomas, a 17-year-old student from the Paris suburb of Val-de-Marne, said some of the classrooms at his school were short of desks and chairs while the bathrooms lacked doors, toilet paper and soap. "We just want better conditions for studying," he told AFP.
Teachers and parents joined demonstrations across France.
In Lyon, parents organised to support the youngsters, while teacher Rindala Younes said she wanted to help students "convey their message peacefully".
"The high school students' demands are legitimate," she said.
Amnesty International on Monday said the French authorities should "put an end to the disproportionate police repression seen in recent days during student protests".
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said police had opened 10 internal investigations into allegations of misconduct.
Since the start of the movement, 24 schools have been burned or ransacked, according to the education ministry.
More than 5,000 people, 87 percent of them minors, have been arrested. The prime minister's office said 85 teaching staff have also been injured.

6 civilians killed, 4 injured in Houthi shelling south of Taiz, Yemen: State media

Mohammad Sio
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
At least six civilians were killed and four others injured, including women and children, in Houthi shelling of residential villages south of Yemen’s southwestern Taiz province on Tuesday, the state-run Saba news agency reported.
A woman was killed and four civilians, including a child and two women, were injured when Houthi shelling struck the villages of Al-Doum, Hujrah and Al-Manawid in the Bani Yusuf area of the Al-Mawasit district, the agency said, citing local sources.
In the Al-Misrakh district, a mortar shell fired by the Houthis struck a family home in the village of Al-Sarm, killing a man, his wife, and daughter, as well as his son’s wife and her children, according to the sources.
The sources also reported civilian casualties from continued Houthi shelling of residential villages in the Quds area amid ongoing fighting, without providing a separate casualty figure.
They said Houthi forces are surrounding several villages in the area and preventing residents and wounded civilians from leaving to seek medical treatment.
There has been no comment from the Houthis on the report.
The latest civilian casualties come amid a sharp escalation in fighting across Taiz.
On Monday, Yemeni Presidential Leadership Council Chair Rashad al-Alimi announced the launch of Operation Dawn of Yemen to restore state institutions, retake Sanaa, and end Houthi control. 
Government forces said the same day that they had retaken the strategic city of Mokha and the Bab el-Mandeb area in southwestern Yemen.
Government forces and their allies currently control the interim capital Aden in the south, the eastern provinces of Al-Mahra and Hadramout, the southern provinces of Shabwa and Abyan, most of Lahj, Taiz and Al-Dhale in the southwest, as well as parts of Marib in central Yemen and Al-Jawf, Hajjah and Saada in the north.
The developments are part of a military escalation that began in July, the broadest since a period of relative calm followed a UN-brokered truce that began in 2022.
Fighting intensified in September, when the Houthis seized key areas in the Al Hudaydah and Taiz provinces, including the strategic city of Mokha, before advancing as far as Mayun Island overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led Arab coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

OpenAI Is Pissing Off a Bunch of Mathematicians—Again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:28:33 UTC
02:28:33 KST

In August, OpenAI convened around 40 mathematicians to discuss what to do if AI outpaces human capabilities in the field. The company hinted that its powerful models had solved hundreds of long-standing math problems, say people who were in attendance, but company representatives assured attendees it would not release the solutions all at once—an assurance OpenAI spokesperson Lindsay McCallum says the company is “not aware of”—and, worried by how the community might react, sought advice on how to publish the findings.
Attendees responded with “a mixture of excitement and dread,” but the meeting was a promising first step, recalls Northwestern University mathematician Bryna Kra. The group, she tells WIRED, asked the firm not to just publish them in a blog or tweet, like they had done with 10 problems earlier that month. Instead, it would be important for OpenAI to publish papers explaining the work so that mathematicians could absorb, digest, and use the results, according to Kra. “Apparently, that input was ignored,” she says.
OpenAI has told people it plans to dump hundreds of results to unsolved problems on GitHub on Tuesday, people familiar with the plans tell WIRED. The release would be the latest of tens of thousands of mathematical solutions generated by AI this year, as frontier models become increasingly capable.
“On August 28, we began training a new internal model. In addition to resolving the Navier—Stokes Millennium Prize problem, this model has now resolved more than 100 long-standing open problems across most areas of mathematics,” says McCallum. “We are working to responsibly release the next math results from our model, drawing on advice and public recommendations from the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence at the Institute for Advanced Study to inform how we release these results. We have not set a release time.”
But for several leading mathematicians, the impending output is also a sign that the company has learned little from the controversies over previous releases.
In conversations with WIRED, the academics say they feel the field has become a playground for OpenAI and its rival Anthropic to show off their models as both prepare for blockbuster initial public offerings. In their rush to outdo each other, mathematicians say, traditional scientific processes for releasing and attributing results have been cast aside.
The most striking case so far came in September. OpenAI deployed thousands of agents to solve a legendary million-dollar Millennium Prize problem after hearing “rumors” that others were closing in on solutions. Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician and professor at New York University, accused the company of front-running the work he had done toward solving an element of the problem in a personal collaboration with Anthropic employee Levent Alpöge. The pair hadn’t published their work but had been using OpenAI’s tools to help them.
During an attempt to negotiate credit, Buckmaster claims, OpenAI researcher Sébastien Bubeck seemed to imply that Alpöge should be excluded from any paper, since that would make things complicated. (In response to a request for comment, Bubeck pointed to a previous public statement in which he denied asking for Alpöge to not be listed as an author.) Buckmaster said he refused. In a call, Bubeck claimed that there is some worry about what Anthropic is doing, according to meeting notes seen by WIRED. Levent must be talking to his leadership right now letting them know fucking OpenAI can get a Millennium Prize problem, he said, per the notes. What’s to stop Anthropic from giving all their compute to get a Millennium Prize problem?
According to the notes, Bubeck also seemed to suggest that Buckmaster would be ruining his career when Buckmaster threatened to tell the press about his belief that OpenAI had stolen his work. If you don't want me to be nice, then I don't have to be nice, Bubeck said, according to the meeting notes.
Nestor Guillen, a visiting math professor at NYU, tells WIRED that “there's a perception of mobster behavior” from the AI companies among mathematicians.
“We disagree with that characterization,” says McCallum.
“I feel a lot of angst, and I see this more and more in my colleagues in mathematics, not over AI, but over the AI companies,” Guillen says. “I think a lot of the angst is about the accumulation of power in one place.”
OpenAI assembled an advisory group in mid September to help determine how the company assesses and communicates new results, upholds academic and professional standards, and builds tools that support mathematical research and learning. But the company doesn’t seem to have made much progress, mathematicians say.
Many are frustrated that OpenAI and Anthropic continue to release results through blog posts, rather than scientific papers, which makes them harder to verify and often excludes prior work from other mathematicians. Piecemeal announcements aren’t limited to the labs: Alpöge himself announced he had disproved an 87-year-old conjecture through a tweet sent shortly after the World Cup final.
“Math by tweet and math by press release to me is not the way to nurture the ecosystem that created the fertile ground that they have trained on,” says Kra.
Some have set up new tools this year in reaction to the increase in machine-assisted proofs; the idea is to help the community both use new results and sort through what needs to be further digested. The tools include Hexagon, a repository for primarily AI-generated material, and Palomar, a registry of machine-verified mathematics.
While OpenAI has been directly encouraged to use these tools, “they haven't changed their behavior,” Kra notes. Nor does she feel the company’s actions are aligned with the Leiden declaration, a call by more than 4,000 mathematicians for AI companies to meet mathematicians’ standards that she helped write.
Several employees within OpenAI believe their technology has rendered math dead anyway, according to people who have spoken with them. (“We don’t believe the future of mathematics is set,” says McCallum. “We’re working with the math community to navigate the future collaboratively.”) While the scenario where AI capabilities outpace those of human researchers was framed as hypothetical during the August meeting, attendees who spoke to WIRED interpreted it as a warning about what was to come. The company has briefed mathematicians about its capabilities and breakthroughs in the same way “police might want to notify family before reporting a death in a car accident,” the person noted.
Bubeck appears to believe that his firm’s technology will swiftly end most mathematicians’ careers, according to a person familiar with his thinking. Bubeck tells WIRED he believes more capable AI could help mathematicians tackle more ambitious questions, better connect their work to solve real-world challenges, and make mathematics more accessible. “I see this as an opportunity to expand what mathematicians can do and the impact their work can have,” he says.
Mathematicians know they need to adapt, especially to equip younger generations, but they do not believe that their field is dead. “It changes how we're going to operate, but I think it's a moment that we can think bigger,” says Kra. She’s happy to have a new, powerful tool at her disposal to solve problems—she just wants companies’ disclosures to be better so that she can trust and build on the results.
“It's a scary time,” she says, “but it's also really a deeply exciting time.”
Update: 10/6/2026, 2:22 pm ET: WIRED updated the story to clarify a reference to a set of math problems OpenAI has told mathematicians it has solved.

Russia May Charge Air Travelers More to Keep Its Aircraft Industry Flying
Unknown

- Category
- World
Russia May Charge Air Travelers More to Keep Its Aircraft Industry Flying
Russia is considering a new surcharge on airline tickets to help finance the leasing and operation of domestically produced passenger aircraft.
This was reported by Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service (SZRU) on its official website on October 6.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The proposed charge would apply to both domestic and international flights, with the fee for international travel set substantially higher. Authorities intend to collect the additional revenue over several years to subsidize Russian-made passenger aircraft.
The agency added that the money would help cover the gap between aircraft production costs and discounted prices offered to Russian carriers. The program covers three major passenger aircraft families: the MC-21, SJ-100, and Tu-214.
The Foreign Intelligence Service described the measure as another attempt to transfer the financial burden of supporting Russian industries directly to consumers. It linked those pressures to Russia's war spending and broader strains on the federal budget.
The service also pointed to higher taxes, including VAT, and rising utility costs affecting Russian households. Utility tariffs are expected to increase for the second time this fall.
Russia's civil aviation sector has faced mounting difficulties since sanctions restricted access to Western aircraft components and spare parts. The proposed passenger surcharge would effectively enable travelers to contribute directly to efforts to sustain domestic aircraft production and operations.
The intelligence service also cited experts who expect higher ticket prices to reduce demand and overall passenger traffic, particularly as household incomes remain under pressure.
The push to subsidize domestic aircraft comes as Russian carriers struggle to keep their existing Sukhoi Superjet 100 fleets in the air.
Replacing the jet's foreign-made SaM-146 engines with domestic PD-8 units is estimated to cost $24.2 million to $26.5 million per aircraft.
Without state support, airlines face a gradual phase-out of the roughly 160 Superjets still in service. Between 2023 and 2025, Russian authorities also suspended operations of more than 480 aircraft, nearly half of the commercial fleet, due to technical defects and falsified maintenance records.

Online fashion giant Asos probes ‘unauthorised activity’ after hacking phone alerts
- - Asos is investigating “unauthorised activity” on third-party platforms after customers got a phone alert saying the retailer had been hacked.
- - The company said names and contact details may have been accessed, but payment card details and passwords do not seem affected.
- - The alert caused panic and sent Asos shares down nearly 10%; experts and UK cyber officials are helping as the probe continues.
AI generated
LONDON - UK online fashion giant Asos said on Oct 6 it was investigating “unauthorised activity involving third-party platforms” after its customers received a phone alert saying the retailer had been hacked.
Asos, which has 17 million active customers worldwide, said personal information like names and contact details “may have been accessed” but that it did not believe payment card information or account passwords were impacted.
The company noted its website and app were operating normally following the incident, which prompted its share price to slump initially by almost 15% in London.
Shares in the company had partially recovered by mid-afternoon but were still down on Oct 6 by nearly 10%.
“We are investigating unauthorised activity involving third-party platforms that we use to communicate with customers,” Asos said in a statement.
“We took immediate action to restrict access to the notification platforms and are working with our internal and external specialist advisers, as well as all relevant authorities.”
Customers had received a mobile app notification titled “Asos hacked” and directing them to a Telegram account.
“Dear Asos DPO and IT, we have fully compromised your Snowflake instance. Engage with us, or we will leak it,” read the notification, according to screenshots shared on social media and reported by British media.
DPO stands for data protection officer, while Snowflake is a US company that provides its clients with a cloud-based platform for data storage, management and analysis.
In a statement shared with AFP, a Snowflake spokesperson said the firm began an investigation as soon as it became aware of the reported notification.
“At this time, we can report that we have found no compromise of the Snowflake platform,” the statement added.
“We take customer privacy and security very seriously. The investigation is ongoing, and we will provide further updates as soon as more information becomes available.”
‘Panic’ aim
This kind of notification, which amounts to “psychological warfare”, is “designed to whip up panic”, said Marie Wilcox, market strategy analyst at cybersecurity firm Binalyze.
The attackers reasoned that “any panic piles on the pressure on Asos to think about paying up rather than taking time to develop a rational response,” she said.
Britain’s state-run National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has offered Asos assistance, according to sources.
A spokesperson for the country’s data watchdog, the Information Commission Office, said it did not appear “to have received a report on this matter at this stage”.
Asos told shareholders it has cyber security insurance with a large provider and that it was “too early” to quantify any potential impact on its trading, Britain’s Press Association news agency reported.
Founded in 2000, Asos generated £2.48 billion (S$3.1 billion) in revenue while posting net losses of £298 million in the 12 months to the end of August 2025.
Its own brands account for 40% of the value of goods sold on the platform, compared to 60% for partner brands.
In 2025, the UK was hit by a wave of cyberattacks targeting, among others, Jaguar Land Rover, Marks & Spencer, the department store Harrods and the Co-op food chain.
And three British airports belonging to the Manchester Airports Group were targeted by an attack in August that resulted in the theft of personal data belonging to 8.7 million customers. AFP

Lithuania Moves Closer Toward Scrapping Nuclear Weapons Ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:24:14 UTC
02:24:14 KST

Lithuania moved closer toward lifting its long-standing nuclear weapons ban on Tuesday, Oct. 6, after the amendment passed its first reading with 106-18 votes in favor.
The country’s Constitution currently prohibits weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases, including NATO’s, to be stationed on its territory. However, a final vote – scheduled for Jan. 12, 2027 – could remove that provision.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to Lithuanian news outlet LRT, Lithuania’s Constitution can only be changed through two votes held at least three months apart, each requiring a qualified majority of 94 in the 141-seat chamber.
“We will ensure stronger support that could be available to us,” Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas said. “By addressing the legal exceptions that Lithuania had compared with other EU and NATO countries, they will be gone and we will be equal.”
The resistance was led by a populist party Nemunas Dawn, with 14 of its members voting no and two abstaining.
The remaining opposition votes came from three members of the mixed parliamentary group and one lawmaker from the Farmers and Greens Union and Christian Families Alliance.
Moscow responds with escalation warning
The Kremlin promptly responded to the move.
Asked about the vote alongside reports that Washington is weighing a permanent US base in Lithuania, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow would treat either development as escalatory.
Ukraine Rejects Permanent EU Limits on Its Farm Exports After Accession
“A military base is part of military infrastructure. If someone’s military infrastructure – in fact, that of a major NATO member – is approaching our borders, of course, this can only be viewed as a step toward escalation,” he said, according to LRT.
“The same applies to the deployment of nuclear weapons on the territory of a neighboring country.”
Peskov’s remarks appeared to be milder than earlier warnings by Russian authorities, although he reiterated previous threats that Russia will have to take “all necessary measures to guarantee its security.”
Russia’s former President and current Deputy Chairman of the Russian Security Council, Dmitry Medvedev, previously threatened Lithuania by saying the country would “disappear from the map of the world” should it lift its nuclear weapons ban.
“If God forbid, something like this happens and we have to react to their actions, no one will step in for them,” Medvedev said, adding that NATO would not invoke Article 5 as this would mean “a global catastrophe.”
Medvedev made the remarks on Sept. 11, after Peskov had already threatened Vilnius with nuclear weapons earlier on that same day.
Why Vilnius wants the provision gone
Article 137, part of the Constitution approved by referendum in 1992, rules out both weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases on Lithuanian soil.
The lifting of the ban would essentially allow NATO, of which Lithuania has been a member of since 2004, to deploy nuclear forces on its territory.
Although Lithuanian authorities insist no nuclear weapons are headed to its territory for now, they point to the need to change the constitution due to uncertain geopolitical circumstances.
The discussions over the possible ban gained traction in July. “The geopolitical situation is getting worse… Our constitution was written when geopolitical circumstances were totally different,” Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda said.
Lithuania – among Ukraine’s strongest allies in Europe – borders both Russia’s exclave of Kaliningrad and the Kremlin’s ally Belarus.
Lithuanian Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas pointed to both countries on Tuesday again. “We are responding to Russia’s aggression,” he said. “If Russia had not started the war in Ukraine, we probably would not be having the discussions we are having today.”
In June 2023, Russia began deploying nuclear weapons to previously non-nuclear Belarus. Russia also deployed its nuclear-capable Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missile (IRBM) to the country, whose combat use in Ukraine marked the first combat use of its kind in history.
Russia and Belarus conducted a joint nuclear war drill in May, 2026.
On Oct. 3, Belarusian leader Alexander Lukashenko reaffirmed Minsk’s alignment with Moscow, pledging that his country will execute Kremlin decisions and preserve a unified fatherland from Brest to Vladivostok.
He also joked that he and Russian President Vladimir Putin often debate who is the greater “co-aggressor” in Ukraine, despite Belarus aiming to portray itself as neutral in the war.
Meanwhile, Russia deployed its Iskander tactical missiles to Kaliningrad – its only ice-free port on the Baltic, which happens to host the headquarters of the Russian Baltic Fleet.
NATO has long been concerned that Russia could station non-strategic nuclear weapons in the exclave, and the latest Kremlin’s escalatory rhetoric had raised additional fears that Moscow could be searching for a justification for a direct attack on the Baltic States.
Although NATO did not provoke Russia, the Kremlin said it was ready to use its entire arsenal of weapons to defend Kaliningrad should the alliance try to block the region.
Around the same time, Russia has also accused the alliance of a reckless course carrying a high risk of direct armed conflict and threatened to strike “decision-making centers” in member countries.

Safi was found guilty of two counts of rape, and Habibkheil of one. Both were convicted of arranging or facilitating the travel of a female with a view to exploitation. Ahmadzai was found guilty of one count of rape and one of sexual assault. The 17-year-old was convicted of one count of rape.

Immediately after they left, Safi began messaging the girl. He told her he loved her and asked her to send indecent images.
Four days later, Safi, in collaboration with Habibkheil, arranged for her to be collected by a taxi and brought into Bristol. She was taken to his house where she was raped over several hours.
The victim’s mother reported her missing and police found her and the 17-year-old boy at Safi’s house.
As officers arrived, the three men fled, eventually managing to make their way across the Channel in the back of lorry carrying frozen goods.
Footage from Safi’s mobile phone showed the men laughing and gesticulating in the back of the lorry, which the prosecution suggested showed they thought they had escaped. But they were swiftly arrested in France and returned to the UK.
The girl had been raped five times by the four offenders. In a victim personal statement, the girl said she felt like a different person now and could not leave her home alone. She had put on hold her dreams of going to college and working with children.
Bristol crown court was told the four were born in Afghanistan and displaced as young people by the “brutality” of the Taliban regime.
Habibkheil had lost his father to the Taliban and was instructed by relatives to travel to England. Ahmadzai had ambitions of being a mechanic when he arrived in the UK but was unable to as an asylum seeker. He is believed to have post-traumatic stress disorder and was terrified of being deported to Afghanistan.
The 17-year-old offender lost his parents in Afghanistan and fled to the UK aged 11. The court heard he suffered “horrendous abuse” en route to England, arriving aged 12. He had flashbacks and nightmares.
But Judge Cullum said their experiences did not excuse the serious psychological harm they had caused to a “vulnerable” girl who had been “groomed and trapped”.
DS Jo Babbage, of Avon and Somerset police, praised the girl’s bravery in telling police her story and being questioned in court. “It’s impossible to overstate the courage she has shown,” she said.
Babbage said: “We do understand there is going to be anxiety in communities, but we need to be clear that this is not about a culture, a community, any religious belief. This is about deep-rooted misogyny and criminal behaviour in individuals.”

====================================================================================================

His pregnant wife was murdered in front of him on Oct. 7. Three years later, he still talks to her
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:20:35 UTC
02:20:35 KST

Three years have passed since that Saturday, but for Hamid Abu Arar, the day never ended.
“Every day I live October 7, 2023,” he says. “You can’t ignore it or forget it. You have nine children at home who lost their mother, and they remind you of October 7 every day, every hour, every minute. They ask for their mother, ask why she isn’t coming back. I thought that as they grew older, they would understand, that maybe slowly it would leave their minds. But exactly the opposite happened.”
That morning, Abu Arar was driving to his agricultural job with his pregnant wife, Fatma, and their son Elias when Hamas terrorists who had invaded Israel opened fire on them. Fatma, who was four months pregnant, was murdered before his eyes. Hamid and Elias, then about six months old, were wounded.
Hamid hid with the baby for hours, listening as the terrorists spoke Arabic among themselves and discussed plans to attack civilians and Israeli security forces.
“I was in a state I had never experienced in my life,” he recalls. “I’m wounded in my shoulder and leg, my baby is wounded, my wife was murdered in front of me, and I don’t know where I am. The terrorists didn’t leave the area for a moment. They went to different places and came back to the junction, and I could hear them clearly. I heard their plans.”
At one point, he says, the terrorists prepared an ambush for an approaching IDF force. Hamid’s phone had already died after he spent hours passing information to Israeli security forces.
“I heard Hebrew from the other direction. I looked and saw the army,” he says. “The first thing that went through my head was: That’s it, our chance of surviving is over. They’ll start shooting at each other and we’re in the middle.”
“Then I told myself, ‘Hamid, you’re a strong man. You need to make a quick decision. You have to save the situation.’”
He removed his shirt, fearing that the soldiers might mistake him for a terrorist or believe he had kidnapped the baby, and walked toward them.
One soldier opened fire. “The bullets passed by my head, and some of the shrapnel went into my back. I was hit by 11 fragments. The officer shouted, ‘Cease fire, Israeli, Israeli.’”
Hamid continued toward the soldiers and warned them about the ambush. “The terrorists were waiting for them,” he says. “One wanted to open fire at the soldiers, and the other told him to wait, to let them come another seven or eight meters closer. They wanted to hit them at point-blank range. The soldiers were advancing without knowing. It was certain death.”
‘Mom blood, Mom blood’
After the soldiers fought the terrorists, Hamid and Elias were evacuated to Soroka Medical Center. But for Hamid, that was when the real battle began. Hamid and Fatma’s nine children, seven girls and two boys, were all young when they lost their mother. Their oldest is now only 11.
Elias is now 3, and his father says he is receiving treatment from an early-childhood psychiatrist for trauma. When Elias was around 2, Hamid began noticing changes.
“The child became angry, aggressive. At night you could see his hand shaking,” he says. “I took him for treatment and they told me he was experiencing trauma. I said to the doctor, ‘But he was six months old. What does he understand? What does he remember?’”
Then came a moment that changed Hamid’s own understanding. “Two or three months ago, Elias came to me while I was sitting in the living room and said, ‘Dad, I have a big gun.’ I asked him who he wanted to shoot. He couldn’t explain and said, ‘Mom blood, Mom blood.’ Like he meant the person who killed his mother.”
Hamid immediately got up, hugged him and told him his mother was in heaven. He then bathed him, changed his clothes, took him out to buy something and drove with him to the cemetery.
“He and I washed his mother’s grave,” Hamid says. “He calmed down. We went home and he slept.” It is only one moment, he says, in the daily reality of their home. “There is hardly a day without some crisis. If it isn’t this child, it’s that daughter. Every day, another one remembers Mom. Listen, I’m living a life that only Allah knows how I survive and how I cope with the children. There are nine of them. All I can say is that there is Allah in heaven.”
When Hamid speaks about Fatma, he is not talking only about the woman he lost, but about the life they almost had together. His voice breaks and he struggles to hold back tears. “We were a special couple. We met, we loved each other and built our life hand in hand. She was my right hand.”
‘Hamas destroyed everything’
Fatma was a beautician, and the couple had planned to open businesses of their own. They had already found a location in Rahat for her salon, which she planned to open with a partner.
“On the evening of October 7, I was supposed to sign the contract for her shop,” Hamid says. “We had already found the place, and then the Hamas terrorists came and destroyed everything. They left us no dream, nothing.”
The one dream that remains, he says, is the one they shared for their children: education. “Today I take care of the children. I even pay for private teachers for them and strengthen them,” he says. “I have very smart children. I promised them, and I am continuing Fatma’s dream.”
Hamid has not returned to work since October 7. His life revolves entirely around his nine children: driving them, picking them up, arranging schools, treatment and studies.
But he also needs treatment himself. “I live on five kinds of pills,” he says. “What can I do? Otherwise I can’t cope.”
Even with treatment, he cannot stay away from the place where his previous life ended. “There isn’t a week or 10 days that goes by without me going to the Gaza border area. I have to. I feel like I live there. My wife is there. My soul is there.”
He drives to the junction, sits there and sometimes stays for hours. “I just sit, smoke, talk to Fatma. I’m always telling her about the children.”
Elias, he says, looks exactly like Fatma. Perhaps that is also one reason the bond between father and son has become nearly inseparable. “If I go to Be’er Sheva to run errands, I do everything like a missile, fast, fast, so I can get back to Elias,” he says. “I can’t be without him. He is the air I breathe.”
Abu Arar’s story is also shaped by the identities that collided that morning. He was born in Gaza, grew up in Rafah and is a Muslim from a religious family. His Muslim wife was murdered by Hamas terrorists.
“What happened on October 7 has nothing to do with religion, unequivocally,” he says. “I know the Quran very well. To come to innocent people while they are sleeping, to babies, children and women and murder them in cold blood, where is that written? Our Islam is completely different.”
He says the terrorist who shot Fatma knew she was Arab. “He saw a religious Muslim woman wearing a head covering, there was a Quran in the car, he recognized that she was Arab and Muslim, and despite all that, he shot her.”
Abu Arar left Gaza in 1995. When he returned for a visit years later, after Hamas had seized control of the territory, he says he struggled to recognize the place where he grew up. “I was supposed to stay for three days and I didn’t stay six hours,” he says. “I said: This is not the Gaza I know. I felt like I was inside Iran, inside Tehran.”
Despite his fierce criticism of Hamas, Abu Arar insists on making another distinction. “You can’t say all of Gaza is Hamas,” he says, adding that there are also Gazans who oppose the terrorist organization and that he still receives updates from relatives living there.
A new life he cannot imagine
After October 7, Abu Arar received permanent residency and an Israeli identity card in recognition of his actions. He speaks with deep gratitude about Interior Minister Moshe Arbel, who helped arrange the status. “He stood by me like a man, an incredible man,” Abu Arar says. “I will never forget him, and I will never forget what he did.”
By contrast, he criticizes the policy of home demolitions promoted by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir. “It’s not good,” he says. “It creates division, it creates hatred. You can’t constantly talk about coexistence while at the same time playing with people’s emotions.”
Nearly three years after the massacre, relatives and in-laws tell Hamid that it is time to try to build a new life. He even tried. “But it isn’t it,” he says. “I can’t. It is very difficult to accept.”
“They tell me, ‘Hamid, you can’t live like this. Fatma is dead. You have to build a new life, get married.’ I tell them: It’s easy to talk. You can talk until tomorrow.”
Sometimes, he says, he sits alone and searches his memories of Fatma for “one small flaw,” something that might break the perfection with which she remains in his mind. “There isn’t one,” he says. “I’m telling you the truth, there isn’t. A woman like that is what I wish for anyone who wants to live with security, peace and hope.”
He knows Fatma herself would have wanted him to be happy. “But where is that happiness supposed to come from?” he asks. “Only from my children. For them to grow up and study, that is the only happiness I take.”
And that is the promise he intends to keep for her. “Their mother and I promised them they would be educated, and I will continue with that until the last minute of my life,” he says. “I am with them. I don’t leave them for a moment. I have nothing else. This is my family.”

Finland orders halt to work on two Google data centres
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:15:46 BST
02:15:46 KST

Finland orders halt to work on two Google data centres
- Published
Finnish authorities have ordered a halt to building work at two planned Google data centres amid concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.
The sites form part of Google's record €13bn (£11bn; $15bn) investment in Finland, announced less than a month ago and described by the company as its largest single investment in Europe.
The Finnish Supervisory Agency (LVV) said work at one site was carried out without a mandatory environmental impact assessment and ordered measures that would "significantly alter the environment" to be suspended by 23 October.
Google said it had "fallen short of our own high standards in this instance" and would follow the agency's guidance.
The orders relate to preparatory work carried out at the planned data centre sites in Muhos and Kajaani.
According to LVV's head of environment Tommi Muilu, work at the sites included the removal of trees and topsoil, the construction of site roads and storage areas, and changes to ditches.
Tuike Finland, the company behind Google's data centre projects, has been asked to provide an explanation and set out how it intends to proceed by 14 October. The agency said it could begin "enforcement proceedings" if the company failed to comply with its demand.
Hanna Halmeenpaa, chair of the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation, had previously told the AFP news agency that "nature sites which should be preserved" had been felled. The conservation group had previously called for work to be halted while the environmental requirements were examined.
In a statement to the BBC, Google said: "We understand the concerns and have fallen short of our own high standards in this instance."
It said it had "acted in good faith under the Forestry Act", carried out nature surveys and put measures in place to protect areas of high environmental value.
"As we continue our long-term work in the region, we are advancing our landscaping and biodiversity plans, which include tree planting across 130 hectares at Muhos," the company added.
Google announced last month that it would invest at least €13bn (£11bn; $15bn) in Finland over 2027 and 2028. Its plans included new data centres in Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala, alongside investment in its existing facility in Hamina.
The company said the infrastructure would help it meet growing demand for services including Search, Maps and its AI assistant Gemini.
Google said the construction phase in 2027 and 2028 would support more than 37,000 jobs and contribute an average of €3.6bn a year to Finland's economy.
As part of its expansion, Google also signed a 22-year power purchasing agreement with Finnish energy company Fortum covering up to half the capacity of the Loviisa nuclear power plant. Fortum said the agreement would help support the plant's continued operation until 2050.
Finland has attracted growing interest in data centres, with its cool climate and low-carbon electricity among the factors making it attractive to developers. Lower temperatures can also reduce the energy required to cool facilities filled with computer servers.

Putin clears UniCredit sale in Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:15:21 UTC
02:15:21 KST

Putin clears UniCredit sale in Russia
Russian President Vladimir Putin has cleared Italy’s UniCredit to restructure its Russian operations, paving the way for the banking giant to sell its business in the country.
UniCredit has operated in Russia since 1989 and is listed by the central bank as one of the country’s 13 key credit institutions. It is among a handful of EU-based lenders that have remained in the Russian market despite Western sanctions imposed following the 2022 escalation of the Ukraine conflict.
The presidential order, published on Monday, allows UniCredit Bank to split its Russian operations by creating a separate company. It also authorizes transactions involving all shares currently held by Italy’s UniCredit S.p.A., removing the need for additional approvals.
UniCredit said in May that it had signed a non-binding agreement with an unidentified UAE investor to split its Russian business in two. The Italian lender will retain a new entity handling international payments for non-sanctioned Western and Russian corporate clients, while selling the rest of the business to the investor.
The Italian lender expects the transaction to result in a loss of around €3-3.3 billion ($3.5-3.9 billion) and aims to complete the deal in the first half of 2027.
UniCredit has spent years reducing its exposure to Russia under pressure from European regulators. In 2024, the European Central Bank ordered it to further scale back operations, including by restricting new deposits and payments. By July of that year, the lender said it had reduced its cross-border exposure by 91% and domestic exposure by 65% compared with post-2022 levels.
Moscow has meanwhile tightened the rules governing corporate exits by companies from countries it considers “unfriendly.” Asset sales are generally subject to a minimum 60% discount and a budget contribution equivalent to 35% of market value, while certain transactions require presidential approval.
Putin’s decision on UniCredit comes as Moscow has taken temporary control of several other Western-owned businesses. In September, Russian assets belonging to Swiss food giant Nestle and French retailer Auchan were placed under temporary management.
Moscow has used the mechanism since 2023, when assets linked to Finland’s Fortum, Germany’s Uniper, France’s Danone, and Danish brewer Carlsberg were placed under temporary control. Russian officials have described the measures as a mirror response to Western actions against Russian assets abroad.
The measures are not necessarily permanent. Italian appliance maker Ariston regained control of its Russian subsidiary in March 2025 after Putin reversed its placement under temporary management.

The false passports said the pair, who have been reported to
prosecutors, were Israelis.
                                    
According to initial findings, neither of the couple has a
criminal record, although investigations are ongoing.
                                    
Security for flights to Israel is tight following the attempted
hijacking of the Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv last
week and Wednesday's third anniversary of the October 7 attacks.
                                    
After checks revealed no prior criminal records, the two
individuals—a man and a woman in their forties—were released and
boarded a flight to Albania, leaving the country. They appear to
be unknown to law enforcement.
                                    
They presented themselves at the document control point in the
boarding area, showing two passports indicating Israeli
nationality.
                                    
They were also carrying their genuine passports—documents from
their country of origin—which, according to the officers'
reconstruction, they had likely used for the first leg of their
journey, presumably to reach Italy.
                                    
The officers charged the travelers (without detaining them) with
document forgery, as they had booked their flight to Tel Aviv
using the details from the fake documents.

presence in the country was legal and they possessed valid
identification—and because initial checks revealed no suspicious
circumstances—the man and woman subsequently purchased two plane
tickets to Albania, the country to which they ultimately
traveled after being formally charged.

The pan-European Stoxx 600 rose 3.01 points, or 0.48%, to 636.63.
Germany’s DAX gained 194.98 points, or 0.77%, to 25,449.19, while Britain’s FTSE 100 added 43.75 points, or 0.42%, to 10,541.69.
France’s CAC 40 advanced 30.97 points, or 0.40%, to 7,865.07.
Italy’s FTSE MIB increased 443.02 points, or 0.87%, to 51,261.40, posting the strongest percentage gain among the five major national benchmarks. Spain’s IBEX 35 climbed 144.50 points, or 0.75%, to 19,444.20.
German manufacturing orders fell 10.6% month-on-month in August, following a revised 3.2% increase in July, according to the Federal Statistical Office. The decline largely reflected a reversal in large orders for aircraft, ships, trains and military vehicles. Excluding large-scale orders, new orders slipped 0.1%.
Eurozone retail trade volume increased 0.1% in August after falling 0.6% in July, said Eurostat. Sales rose 0.8% year-on-year. Non-food sales increased 0.5% month-on-month, while automotive fuel sales dropped 1.9%. Across the EU, retail trade rose 0.1% monthly and 1.2% annually.
In France, manufacturing output rebounded 0.3% in August after declining 0.8% in July. Overall industrial production, however, fell 0.3%, following a 0.6% contraction, according to the national statistics institute INSEE.
Meanwhile, Bank of Finland Governor Olli Rehn warned that a prolonged Middle East war would increase the risk of higher energy prices spreading to other prices and wages.
The European Central Bank (ECB) Council member said the spillovers had not yet emerged, while rising long-term interest rates were slowing growth and limiting the transmission of energy costs to broader inflation.
Rehn said the ECB would continue making interest rate decisions meeting by meeting, based on incoming information, amid heightened uncertainty.

Two meteor showers are lighting up the October sky—here’s how to see them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:14:22 UTC
02:14:22 KST

It’s fall, which means the nights are getting colder and longer—but they will also soon be speckled with shooting stars when a pair of meteor showers make their annual visit to Earth this month.
The first is the Draconid meteor shower, which is expected to peak on the night of October 8, followed by the Orionid meteor shower, which will peak on October 21, according to NASA.
The Draconids and Orionids are basically cosmic leftovers: As comets or asteroids orbit the sun, they leave a trail of debris, dust and ice. When Earth crosses paths with these trails, bits of that material burn up in the planet’s atmosphere—producing the stunning streaks of light we call meteors, or shooting stars.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The Draconids—which are named for the constellation Draco—owe themselves to Comet 21P/Giacobini-Zinner, a space rock that is just 1.24 miles (about two kilometers) in diameter. The Orionids—which are similarly named for the constellation Orion—originate from Halley’s Comet, which is about 9.3 miles (15 kilometers) in diameter at its widest.
The Draconids are the smaller shower, and NASA expects the display to only produce “a few meteors per hour” this year. On the upside, you don’t need to stay awake until the wee hours of the night to see it: “This is an ideal meteor shower for casual sky watchers, since it begins soon after darkness falls rather than in the early morning hours,” the agency says.
Sky gazers might have more luck spotting a meteor during the Orionids’ peak on October 21, but the “prime viewing window” will be before dawn, after the moon sets, according to NASA.
As with any meteor shower, you’ll have your best chance of catching shooting stars by viewing the sky from an area with limited light pollution and giving your eyes about 30 minutes to adjust to the dark.
If you miss these two showers, know that they aren’t all the sky has to offer this fall. As Scientific American previously reported, two other showers, the Southern and Northern Taurids, are set to peak on the nights of November 4–5 and 11–12, respectively. Happy viewing!

NATO nation decries drone strikes on merchant vessels off its coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:13:51 UTC
02:13:51 KST

NATO nation decries drone strikes on merchant vessels off its coast
Two commercial vessels were hit by unidentified drones on Tuesday off the Bulgarian coast in the Black Sea, Prime Minister Rumen Radev has confirmed.
The attack marks the first time when merchant vessels were attacked within the exclusive economic zone (EEZ) of a NATO member in the waterway. Such zones have a unique legal status and are adjacent to a country’s territorial waters, with the area being neither fully under its sovereignty or categorized as international open waters.
“This is an unacceptable attack in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. It is a blatant violation of international law and maritime law,” Radev said while speaking after an emergency government meeting to assess the incident.
The vessels, the Togo-flagged Alfa Watan and the Palau-flagged Able, were hit overnight around 80 miles (128 kilometers) off Bulgaria’s coast by unknown sea and aerial drones, according to the PM, who did not immediately assign the blame to any party.
The Alfa Watan, which was sailing to Romania from Egypt, sustained critical damage, sinking shortly after the attack with the status of its crew not immediately known, according to Radev. The second vessel, which sailed from Romania to Türkiye, caught fire, and its crew of 18 was rescued by a Bulgarian ferry. Two of the sailors suffered severe injuries and were flown to a hospital in the port city of Varna, Radev noted.
“As a state responsible within our exclusive economic zone for the health and lives of anyone navigating in this area, regardless of who is responsible, we are obliged to conduct emergency search and rescue operations,” the PM said.
“What is happening is seriously disrupting shipping in the Black Sea, driving up insurance costs even further and making shipping extremely difficult,” he added.
Neither of the likely suspects, Ukraine and Russia, made any remarks on the latest maritime incident in the Black Sea. While Kiev has been actively attacking shipping in the waterway heading to and from Russian ports, Moscow has recently begun retaliating in kind and striking vessels carrying military cargo and dual-use goods to Ukraine’s Black Sea ports. The retaliatory campaign has heavily damaged the Ukrainian shipping, effectively bringing the traffic to a halt.
The modus operandi described by Radev, with the attacks involving both sea and aerial drones, however, likely points at Ukraine. Kiev has repeatedly staged such combined attacks on commercial shipping, while Moscow has relied almost exclusively on aerial drones.
Once a key arms supplier of Kiev, Sofia has changed its stance on the Ukraine conflict under Radev’s government. Bulgaria withdrew from the so-called “coalition of the willing,” a European group of Kiev’s backers, and announced that it would no longer send weapons packages.

Les renforts d’Europol en IA suscitent des inquiétudes sur la protection de la vie privée
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:11:13 UTC
02:11:13 KST

BRUXELLES — Alors que l’UE prévoit de renforcer les moyens d’Europol à l’ère de l’intelligence artificielle, de hauts responsables européens mettent en garde que cela ne doit pas se faire au détriment de la protection de la vie privée des Européens.
Face aux cybercriminels, terroristes et espions qui se servent de l’intelligence artificielle pour faire des escroqueries, de l’extorsion et des cyberattaques, Bruxelles mise sur le renforcement des compétences en matière d’IA d’Europol — l’agence qui coordonne les renseignements policiers européens depuis 1998 — afin de lutter contre ces menaces.
“Europol est à un tournant”, a énoncé Fabienne Keller, députée européenne Renew membre de la commission des Libertés civiles. “Nous avons besoin d’un Europol plus fort, doté des ressources et des capacités nécessaires pour soutenir efficacement les forces de l’ordre nationales”, a-t-elle plaidé. Cela “doit aller de pair avec un fort contrôle démocratique et des garde-fous solides en matière de droits fondamentaux et de protection des données”.
Advertisement
L’UE a dévoilé cet été un projet visant à opérer une “évolution transformatrice” de l’agence basée à La Haye. Il est question de doubler son budget pour le porter à 3 milliards d’euros, et de lui conférer un rôle actif dans la lutte contre les nouvelles menaces, en lui donnant accès à davantage de données et à des technologies de pointe.
Mais ce projet soulève aussi des questions en matière de gouvernance et protection de la vie privée, suscitant un débat houleux sur l’étendue des pouvoirs dont devraient disposer les forces de l’ordre pour assurer la sécurité des citoyens face à l’IA et grâce à celle-ci.
Wojciech Wiewiórowski, le Contrôleur européen de la protection des données (CEPD), qui veille à ce que l’ensemble des agences et institutions de l’UE respectent les règles en la matière, s’est dit “tout à fait favorable” à l’idée de donner à Europol les moyens d’utiliser des données et de nouveaux outils basés sur l’intelligence artificielle. Mais il “faut qu’il y ait un contrôle”, a-t-il ajouté.
“Quand j’entends parler du renforcement d’Europol, de la modification de son champ d’action et d’investissements vraiment très importants dans l’agence elle-même, je m’en réjouis en tant que citoyen”, a-t-il poursuivi. “Mais je me dois de poser la question : pourquoi il n’y a rien dans la proposition sur la manière de superviser Europol ?”
Plus rapide et à grande échelle
Pour Jürgen Ebner, directeur général adjoint de l’agence, qui a été nommé le mois dernier à sa tête, la lutte contre la criminalité exige aujourd’hui de doter Europol de toutes les capacités offertes par l’intelligence artificielle.
Advertisement
“L’IA transforme la manière dont les crimes sont commis dans un large éventail d’activités criminelles”, a-t-il exposé une semaine après avoir été désigné par les représentants des Etats membres pour occuper ce poste, sous réserve de l’avis du Parlement européen. “L’IA rend les activités criminelles plus rapides, plus sophistiquées et plus faciles à mener à grande échelle. Cela représente un défi de taille pour les forces de l’ordre.”
Europol, qui emploie plus de 1 700 personnes, a été conçu comme une organisation de centralisation, collaborant avec les services de police européens afin de faciliter l’analyse et le partage d’éventuels éléments de preuve et d’autres informations liées aux enquêtes criminelles.
Dans le cadre du nouveau projet, l’UE compte désormais sur cette agence pour mettre au point de nouvelles façons d’utiliser l’IA afin de passer au crible les montagnes de données disponibles et d’aider les forces de police nationales à résoudre des affaires en temps réel.
Jürgen Ebner, directeur général adjoint d’Europol, qui a été nommé le mois dernier à la tête de l’agence, s’exprime lors d’une conférence de presse à Bruxelles, le 26 juin 2026. | Olivier Hoslet/EPA
Si les plus récentes avancées en matière d’intelligence artificielle peuvent être utiles aux criminels comme aux forces de l’ordre, ces dernières doivent en plus respecter les principes démocratiques. Alors qu’Europol pourra traiter un volume d’informations potentiellement colossal, la protection de la vie privée pourrait bien être le principe le plus menacé.
Cet enjeu est au cœur des préoccupations de Jürgen Ebner, qui est désormais pratiquement assuré de diriger Europol pendant les quatre prochaines années. Il a pointé les contrôles juridiques qui pèsent sur les forces de police lorsqu’elles tentent d’utiliser l’IA.
Pour lui, l’accès rapide aux preuves électroniques est essentiel pour tirer le meilleur parti des capacités émergentes de l’intelligence artificielle. “Elle peut aider les enquêteurs à filtrer de grands volumes de preuves numériques, à relier des informations entre elles et à identifier des renseignements exploitables”, a détaillé l’Allemand. “L’IA peut démultiplier les capacités des enquêteurs et des analystes, et leur donner davantage de temps pour interpréter les preuves.”
Advertisement
Vie privée versus sécurité
Les débats sur la manière dont la police collecte et traite les données des citoyens opposent souvent la sécurité à la vie privée. Toutefois, Jürgen Ebner a argué devant les policiers, lors d’une conférence à Lisbonne le mois dernier, qu’Europol ne devait pas basculer dans une situation où “la collecte de données devient une fin en soi, la technologie sert à justifier son propre usage, ou l’urgence sert de prétexte pour abandonner les garde-fous”.
S’également aux forces de police de toute l’Europe réunies à Lisbonne, Wojciech Wiewiórowski, le Contrôleur européen de la protection des données, a considéré que la proposition de l’UE “jette officiellement les bases d’une action policière en Europe fondée sur l’intelligence artificielle et les données”.
Le CEPD avait déjà épinglé Europol au sujet de ses pratiques en matière de collecte de données et s’était opposé à une proposition antérieure visant à élargir le champ de compétence de l’agence.
Il a averti que la proposition de réforme d’Europol comportait de graves risques en matière de vie privée, et permettrait à l’agence de conserver des données sur un “vaste” nombre de personnes n’ayant aucun lien avec des activités criminelles “pendant une période prolongée et indéterminée”.
La proposition préserve, certes, le rôle du CEPD dans la supervision d’Europol, mais Wojciech Wiewiórowski a pointé qu’elle ne prévoyait pas, parallèlement à l’expansion d’Europol, un renforcement équivalent des pouvoirs ou des ressources du CEPD. Il a également jugé qu’elle accordait “trop de pouvoirs aux organes internes d’Europol, sans contrôle extérieur”.
Pour le délégué à la protection des données d’Europol, Daniel Drewer, ces mesures accélérées sont nécessaires dans un monde marqué par “une évolution technologique rapide qui ne profite pas uniquement aux forces de police ou aux acteurs étatiques, mais également aux réseaux criminels”.
Advertisement
La réforme d’Europol intervient alors que le CEPD peine déjà à faire face à ses nouvelles responsabilités en matière de contrôle de l’utilisation de l’IA par les institutions européennes.
Par ailleurs, Stéphane Duguin, un ancien responsable de la lutte contre la cybercriminalité chez Europol et aujourd’hui à la tête de Protect.ngo, affirme que les forces de l’ordre ont également du mal à suivre le rythme des avancées technologiques et stratégiques de leurs adversaires. Au-delà des défis liés à leurs capacités techniques, il estime que le réseau policier européen doit également surmonter les obstacles liés à sa structure, mise en place il y a longtemps.
Les criminels ne commettent “pas seulement des cybercrimes, de s’ingérer dans les affaires étrangères ou de manipuler l’information, mais c’est ainsi que fonctionnent les forces de police. Et c’est là le problème”, souligne Stéphane Duguin. “Si l’on considère Europol hors de son contexte, cela n’a aucun sens, car c’est l’ensemble de la chaîne judiciaire qui doit évoluer. Si l’on dispose de moyens accrus pour enquêter sur les crimes en ligne mais qu’à la fin, les affaires ne sont pas portées devant les tribunaux en raison de la législation nationale, alors cela n’a aucun sens.”
Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Jean-Christophe Catalon.

AQRABA, Palestinian Territories - Israeli settlers on Oct 6 beat an AFP photographer, leaving him requiring hospital treatment, as he covered ongoing violence by settlers against West Bank olive farmers.
Jaafar Ashtiyeh, 58, a veteran photographer for the international news agency in the Palestinian territory, had tried to rush into a car for safety but two men tackled him down and clobbered him with their rifle butts, according to witnesses, his family and fellow journalists.
Ashtiyeh and another AFP photographer, John Wessels, were standing on a hill near the northern village of Aqraba watching the olive harvest from around 500m away when they saw an Israeli soldier detain a Palestinian.

One Palestinian dropped to the ground. He was also hospitalised, with a gunshot to the foot, according to the Palestine Red Crescent Society.
At least six other people then rushed towards the AFP journalists firing guns, with two of them beating Ashtiyeh as he tried to enter the car, which was clearly marked “Press”.
“I could hear his screams,” said Wessels, who was also threatened at gunpoint.
Ashtiyeh, who is Palestinian, was rushed by ambulance to a hospital in Nablus. He underwent X-rays which did not detect broken bones but he will remain in hospital for round-the-clock observation, said his son, Zain Jaafar.
The assailants stole Ashtiyeh’s camera equipment, Wessels said.
The violence took place despite the presence of at least a dozen fully equipped Israeli soldiers around 500m away, according to Wessels.
The man who first fired the gun was wearing a long white shirt as well as military fatigue trousers and boots, which are commonly worn by soldiers, Wessels said.
AFP has reached out to the Israeli military for comment.
‘Deeply alarmed’
“We strongly condemn yet another serious attack on journalists trying to report on events in the West Bank and demand a full investigation. It is unacceptable that journalists can be beaten and robbed by armed settlers in front of Israeli security forces who made no attempt to intervene,” said Phil Chetwynd, AFP’s global news director.
The Foreign Press Association, which represents international media in Israel and the Palestinian territories, said it was “deeply alarmed”.
“Israeli authorities must investigate why soldiers present in the area did not intervene in this attack against clearly identified journalists,” it said.
“This attack is a blatant attempt to intimidate the press and obstruct accurate reporting from the West Bank. International media have a responsibility to tell all sides of the story and will not be deterred by physical assaults or threats.”
Reporters Without Borders said it condemned the attack “in the strongest terms”.
“Israeli settlers’ attacks against journalists, carried out with complete impunity, are becoming more and more frequent in the West Bank,” said the advocacy group known by its French initials RSF.
Israeli authorities have detained 19 journalists in the West Bank, including one AFP contributor, in the three years since the Oct 7, 2023, attack on Israel by Gaza-based Hamas, according to Paris-based Reporters Without Borders.
Ashtiyeh was attacked almost exactly a year earlier during the olive harvest by settlers who threw stones at him and who then set his car ablaze.
In October, a settler hit another AFP journalist in the chin as he covered religious Jewish peace activists who seek to protect Palestinians from violence.
Violence has flared in recent months in the West Bank with near-daily attacks, thefts or vandalism by Israeli settlers against Palestinians.
There have also been attacks against Israelis, with a Palestinian shooting dead a settler in September.
Extremist Israeli settlers have been seizing olive groves owned by Palestinians, who see the trees as a cultural symbol.
Some 500,000 Israeli settlers live in the West Bank, which Israel captured in 1967, among three million Palestinians. Settlements in occupied territory are illegal under international law. AFP

Attacks on tankers in and around the Strait of Hormuz have underscored continuing risks to energy shipping, while publicly available Baltic Exchange figures show elevated earnings for vessels carrying crude from the Gulf to China.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) published alerts documenting at least eight attacks from Oct. 1 - 5 in and around the waterway, involving vessels struck by unidentified projectiles.
In an incident Monday, a tanker’s master reported a projectile strike that caused an engine-room fire. No casualties or environmental effect were reported at the time of the alert.
Separate reports described attacks on crude oil tankers and a liquefied petroleum gas carrier during the weekend.
UKMTO also reported that a tanker entering the strait Monday was contacted by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps 11 nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman.
The vessel was instructed to turn back or face being targeted, and its master confirmed complying with the instruction, said the agency.
UKMTO did not identify who carried out the projectile strikes in the reviewed alerts. It said authorities were investigating and advised vessels to transit cautiously and report suspicious activity.
The Baltic Exchange’s Oct. 2 tanker report assessed daily round-trip time-charter-equivalent earnings on its Middle East Gulf-China route at $1,221,893 for a standard very large crude carrier.
The benchmark covers shipments of 270,000 metric tons of crude. It measures estimated daily vessel earnings after voyage expenses.
The exchange said the market strengthened again after easing earlier in the week, although the route’s freight assessment remained slightly below the previous week’s level.

Rahul leads the march
Rahul Gandhi, along with several opposition leaders, began the march from Parliament towards the Election Commission headquarters, raising slogans of "Vote Chor, Gaddi Chhod" and carrying placards and cutouts of Gyanesh Kumar.

Two-state solution unpopular with majority of Israelis and Palestinians, poll finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:05:22 UTC
02:05:22 KST

A majority of Israelis and Palestinians oppose a two-state solution, according to a new poll released by Gallup on Tuesday, ahead of the three-year anniversary of the October 7 attacks on southern Israel.
Only 26 percent of polled Israelis said they would support the two-state solution, which entails the establishment of an independent Palestinian state alongside Israel. 65 percent of Israelis oppose two independent states, according to the poll.
Gallup noted that since 2023, it has been unable to include respondents from Gaza as it did in the past.
Among Palestinians who were polled from the West Bank and East Jerusalem, 32 percent said they support a two-state solution – while 58 percent oppose it.
The level of support for a permanent deal, which would establish an independent Palestinian state alongside an independent Israel, remained relatively low but stable since 2023, rising by 1 percent among Israelis and 6 percent among Palestinians.
However, these figures fall far from Gallup's 2012 poll, which found that two-thirds of Palestinians and 61 percent of Israelis voiced support for two states.
The poll also found widespread pessimism among both Israelis and Palestinians, with only 22 percent of Israelis and 21 percent of Palestinians indicating that they think a permanent peace will ever be achieved.
"Although optimism about the prospects for peace is marginally higher than the levels from 2023 around the time of the October 7 attacks, it is still a minority opinion for both Israelis and Palestinians," Gallup said in a press release.
On Wednesday, Israel will commemorate the three-year anniversary of Hamas' October 7 attack, during which roughly 1,200 people were killed and nearly 250 taken hostage to Gaza. While Gallup describes the attack as an "upheaval" that "ushered in a new era in the Middle East," it stressed that pessimism continues to characterize both sides.
"In Israel, the idea of an independent Palestinian state is deeply politicized, splitting clearly according to views on current leadership. Among Palestinians, views are less divided along political lines," Gallup said in the statement.
Gallup's survey is based on a random sample of 1,000 Israelis, as well as 1,000 Palestinians in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points.
