Lord Archer of Weston-super-Mare obituary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:05:18 UTC
02:05:18 KST

Jeffrey Archer, who has died aged 86, was irrepressible, though not necessarily in a good way. Ordinary humans would be sunk by the allegations of lies, thefts, frauds, gussied-up CVs, expenses fiddles, charity swindles, plagiarisms, insider trading deals, funding illicit coups and – perhaps most unforgivable of all – unpleasantness to underlings that dogged Archer’s life. But Lord Archer of Weston-super-Mare – bestselling novelist, disgraced politician, one-time athlete and convicted liar – was not ordinary: he was what the Titanic was designed to be, unsinkable.
One morning in September 2000, for instance, Archer emerged from Wimbledon police station. He had just been charged with perjury for persuading a friend to lie for him during his 1987 libel action against the Daily Star newspaper, which had claimed he had paid a sex worker to buy her silence.
That morning, Archer’s life had started to unravel: the following July he would be jailed at the Old Bailey for this crime. But instead of returning to his sumptuous Thameside apartment overlooking parliament to consult with lawyers or have a good cry, he smiled for the media, climbed into a chauffeur-driven BMW and went on to his next appointment. The Archer show had to go on. That evening he made his senior stage debut in a production of his own play at the Theatre Royal, Windsor.
The Accused was, if nothing else, strikingly topical. In it, Archer played Patrick Sherwood, a GP accused of poisoning his wife. Posters for the play read: “See You in Court”.
The stage was a simulacrum of the Old Bailey courtroom where he would later stand in the dock. Critics noted that it was a good job Agatha Christie was no longer alive to add the charge of plagiarism to the list he was soon to face. The Accused, they pointed out, bore a striking resemblance to her play Witness for the Prosecution. This was not the first time he faced allegations of plagiarism: Archer once judged a short story competition and duplicated many of the features of the winning entry in one of his own.
The theatre audience was the jury, giving their verdict on keypad. Most nights, Archer got off. In the real world, he was not so fortunate. But Archer’s comeuppance was not fatal. In jail, he wrote the three-volume memoir A Prison Diary and was regularly visited there by literary editors, eager to work up the raw copy of Britain’s most bankable novelist into publishable form in time to capitalise on the Christmas market.
Born in London, two weeks later Jeffrey moved with his family to Weston-super-Mare, in Somerset. He was the third child of Lola (nee Cook) and William Archer. The first two of Lola’s children, including another Jeffrey, were born outside marriage and given up for adoption. His father, a convicted fraudster and bigamist who was 64 when Archer was born, left the family home not long after and died in 1956, when his son was 15.
His doting mother spoiled him in compensation for that loss. She wrote a column for the local paper called Over the Teacups, about her scamp of a son who featured as “Tuppence”. He attended Wellington school, in Somerset – though he later implied he had attended the grander Wellington college, in Berkshire – where weedy Jeffrey was nicknamed The Pune, for his puny skin-and-bones physique, and bullied. He took up bodybuilding and athletics in response and was so successful at the latter that he became a blue at Oxford and later ran for Britain.
He left school with three O-levels (English literature, art and history), trained for the army and the police, and then found a niche at private schools as that rare thing, a popular PE teacher.
Then he went to Oxford, where he studied for three years at Brasenose College, though he was never registered there as an undergraduate. Rather, he studied for a teaching qualification on a course based at the college.
At Oxford, Archer also raised money for Oxfam, and succeeded in inviting the Beatles to visit Brasenose to sign a cheque and mingle with the dons in the senior common room. During that February 1963 soiree, undergraduate Sheridan Morley and Beatles drummer Ringo Starr found themselves at adjacent urinals. “[Ringo] asked if I knew this Jeffrey Archer bloke,” theatre critic Morley later told the Guardian. “I said everyone in Oxford was trying to work out who he was. Ringo said: ‘He strikes me as a nice enough fella, but he’s the kind of bloke who would bottle your piss and sell it.’”
While at Oxford, Archer wooed the student Mary Weeden, who in 1966 became his wife and later a chemistry lecturer at Cambridge University. Despite her husband’s shaming bankruptcies and his reported infidelities, Mary Archer justified standing by her man with more imaginative verve than, say, Tammy Wynette. She said much later: “I think I would find it a little monochrome, a little grey, to have a sort of a more conventional life with a more conventional husband.”
After leaving Oxford, he continued as a charity fundraiser, working for a medical charity and for the United Nations Association, whose chairman, the former Conservative MP Humphry Berkeley, alleged that Archer fiddled his expenses. He also served as a Conservative councillor on the Greater London council from 1967 to 1970, during which time he was accused of fiddling other councillors’ expenses. Despite these allegations, and despite Berkeley striving to convince Conservative central office that Archer was an unsuitable parliamentary candidate, he beat the future Tory minister Ian Gow to become Conservative candidate for Louth in Lincolnshire. He took the seat in a byelection on 4 December 1969, becoming – or so his book blurbs repeatedly claimed – the youngest MP in the House of Commons, aged 29. In fact, as Michael Crick points out in his biography, there were four younger MPs already in the Commons.
In 1974, he became one of the youngest MPs to relinquish his seat. That year, as a result of a complicated speculation he was involved in, Archer lost £500,000 in a fraudulent Canadian company called Aquablast. At the edge of bankruptcy, he resigned from parliament. In terms of fulfilling his ambitions, he may have been prudent: “I realised there would never be a career for me there,” he said of the Commons later.
Facing bankruptcy, he told his wife, then pregnant with their second child: “The only way I can get out of this is to write my way out of it.” Friends were sceptical that Archer could make capital from novel writing, having failed to do so from property deals. “Jeffrey, you can barely spell,” his friend Adrian Metcalfe told him, “let alone write.” “No, but I can tell stories,” Archer is said to have replied.
He was right. His first novel, Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less, published in 1976, became a bestseller, as did many of the more than 50 novels, prison journals, children’s books and short story collections that followed.
That fictional debut was something of a roman a clef, since it told the story of four men swindled out of $1m – roughly what Archer lost in business deals. The novel’s denouement though, in which the men revenge themselves on their swindlers, was part wish fulfilment and partly cribbed from the then popular movie, The Sting. His wife reportedly helped him edit it, correcting his spelling and grammar.
Later, teams of editors worked on making his novels publishable. They were impressed by his capacity for work: he would address the task in blocks of two hours at a time, then wrote as many as 17 further drafts at their behest.
Jonathan Coleman, one of four editors who worked on Archer’s international bestseller Kane and Abel (1979), said that, though the book was heavily edited, “he did the rewriting ... I mean, he wasn’t trying to write a literary masterpiece.”
He was, rather, trying to make money – and he did. Much came from TV adaptations, but he was a publishing phenomenon whose books were bought at the rate of 25,000 a month at the peak of his literary bankability, resulting in overall sales of around 300m copies.
By the mid-70s, then, the disgraced ex-MP was back. Yes, there was a report that he had stolen some suits from a Toronto store when he was giving evidence at the Aquablast trial in Canada in 1977, but that was never proved. And yes, some did complain that he trod on the little people as he rose again (“The sales people at HarperCollins loathed him – absolutely loathed him – because he was so awful to booksellers,” one company manager told Crick, referring to the sales rep as a “waste of space, being very abusive and unpleasant”), but none of this would stop him becoming rich and famous.
In 1979, Archer bought the Old Vicarage, Grantchester, a house associated with the poet Rupert Brooke. He also began to hold shepherd’s pie and Krug parties for politicians, business people and even journalists at his Thames-side apartment. He loved to give directions to the toilet: “Past the Picasso and left at the Matisse.”
He even returned to politics. Margaret Thatcher made him Conservative deputy chairman in 1985 – despite the misgivings of the senior Tories Norman Tebbit, Edward Heath and Willie Whitelaw – partly in gratitude for the sums he had funnelled into Tory party coffers.
The political return was shortlived. The following year he resigned because of newspaper allegations that he had paid Monica Coghlan, a sex worker, £2,000 through an intermediary at Victoria station to go abroad. In 1987, he sued the Daily Star for claiming he had slept with her.
In one of the case’s more memorable moments, Mr Justice Caulfield spoke to the jury: “Remember Mary Archer in the witness box. Your vision of her probably will never disappear. Has she elegance? Has she fragrance? Would she have, without the strain of this trial, radiance? How would she appeal? Has she had a happy married life? Has she been able to enjoy, rather than endure, her husband Jeffrey?” He said of Jeffrey Archer, “Is he in need of cold, unloving, rubber-insulated sex in a seedy hotel round about quarter to one on a Tuesday morning after an evening at the Caprice?” The judge’s questions, counterintuitively, were rhetorical. Archer won and was awarded £500,000 damages.
In 1992, thanks to the prime minister, John Major, Archer was politically rehabilitated again. Major made him a life peer, Lord Archer of Weston-super-Mare, chiefly because of his role in the previous year’s fundraising concert for Kurds. Archer, with the Red Cross, set up the charity Simple Truth.
But once more his philanthropy was questioned. Archer had claimed to have raised more than £57m for Kurdish refugees. Kurdish disaster relief groups claimed only £250,000 had been received by groups in Iraq. Years later, Scotland Yard investigated these discrepancies, but Archer was never prosecuted.
In 1994, Archer was back in trouble over alleged insider dealing involving shares in Anglian Television, of which his wife was a director. An inquiry by the Department of Trade and Industry concluded that Archer would not be prosecuted.
In 1999, aged 59, Archer was poised to fulfil one of his ambitions – to hold high political office – when he was selected as Conservative candidate for the London mayoral election of 2000. But that ambition was thwarted when the News of the World reported that he had perjured himself in the 1987 libel case.
His former friend, the TV producer Ted Francis, and his former personal assistant, Angela Peppiatt, decided to reveal that he fabricated an alibi at the trial because they thought he was an unsuitable mayoral candidate. He withdrew his candidacy the next day and was, in February 2000, expelled from the Conservative party for five years. The then party leader William Hague, who had hailed Archer’s “probity and integrity”, said: “This is the end of politics for Jeffrey Archer. I will not tolerate such behaviour in my party.”
Archer’s trial for perjury began in May 2001. Once more, his wife Mary gave evidence. Archer did not, though he had to hear his former secretary, Peppiatt, detail alleged marital infidelities with a former employee. During the judge’s summing up, his mother died. As a result, she missed seeing her son sentenced to four years’ imprisonment by Mr Justice Potts. He served only two years in jail and retained his life peerage.
Archer’s scandals were not over yet. A year after his release, he was accused by Equatorial Guinea’s government of co-financing the failed 2004 coup d’etat attempt.
He continued writing after his release. In 2007, he collaborated with the Catholic scholar Francis J Moloney in a book entitled The Gospel According to Judas. In this version of the story, Judas did not betray Jesus. The treatment of the story must have appealed to the disgraced peer, since in it he rehabilitated Judas. Perhaps in his mind, Archer – similarly maligned though more fairly – hoped for a similar rehabiliation.
Archer’s life was lived, if not told, in heroic denial of what he was. “He will dive over a cliff and then be amazed that he’s falling,” said his college friend Morley who, like many politicians in the party that Archer disgraced, remained supportive. “He thinks he’s Peter Pan, that he’ll never die. Everything he does he thinks is going to be all right in the end.”
In fiction, if not reality, Archer was rehabilitated. The maligned Judas became a national hero when in 2002 the writer Guy Jenkin wrote a TV comedy called Jeffrey Archer: The Truth. It told the version of the Archer story that never gets told (least of all in the newspapers) – about a misunderstood man who took the blame selflessly, suffered abuse, disgrace and imprisonment for the nation’s good.
“My Jeffrey Archer is the man who has frequently saved Britain over the last 30 years,” said Jenkin. “He’s beloved of all women he comes across, all men, all dogs – he’s a superhero.” If only the real Jeffrey Archer had been like that. But his life did not imitate art because it could not: it was rather, in the title of Crick’s biography, Stranger Than Fiction.
Archer retired from the Lords in 2024, and said that his final novel would be Adam and Eve. His death came unexpectedly, on the day before its publication.
He is survived by Mary, and his sons, William and James.

Russia denies anti-plague measures after pneumonia death
October 6, 2026
Russiadenied claims that it was imposing anti-plague measures following the death of a laboratory technician of pneumonic plague.
The woman worked at the anti-plague institute in Siberia's Irkutsk region.
The authorities in Russia, however, said the cause of death is yet to be confirmed, and Moscow's health authority Rospotrebnadzor has denied claims the country had put special measures in place.
Authorities deny reports of plague
According to Rospotrebnadzor, the information "does not originate from official sources" and is "untrue," with Irkutsk Governor Igor Kobzev adding that the inspection had found that the woman's death was a result of pneumonia.
"No microorganisms linked to the young woman's professional work were found in her biological samples," he said.
Plague is a disease that can occur in several forms, including pneumonic plague, known to be the most contagious and potentially fatal if not treated early.
Some reports in Russia suggested the woman could have caught the disease from a broken test tube, while others speculated on a potential link between her death and a lab accident at the institute.
The woman may have come into contact with up to 200 people, all of whom are under quarantine, according to one report.
World Health Organization monitoring situation
The World Health Organization (WHO) said the information it had received from Russia suggests that "no case" of the disease has so far been recorded in Irkutsk.
Russia has launched an epidemiological investigation into a case of pneumonia, labeled as "community acquired," in an employee at the Irkutsk Institute.
"Test results showed no presence of dangerous infectious disease pathogens" in the people who came into contact with the person, the WHO said, adding that the agency estimates the risk to be "moderate to low" for Irkutsk.
The WHO is still monitoring the situation closely, it said.
US President Donald Trump said he will discuss the case with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Trump also said the US intelligence is in "very deep discussions" on the matter, while also calling the disease "rough."
"That's a disease we used to be able to control, but somehow those microbes have gotten stronger and smarter. They’re like an army,” the US president told reporters at the White House.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington is monitoring the situation.
According to Rubio, Russia needs to "share more information with the world."

Kenya confirms first Ebola case as man dies in Nairobi after DRC return
More than 4,000 people have died in the worst outbreak in the DR Congo’s history, with confirmed cases surpassing 8,300.
Kenya has confirmed its first Ebola case after the death of a Kenyan national in Nairobi, who had returned from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).
The patient, who had lived in the DRC for seven years, had been ill for about a month before travelling by road from the DRC to Uganda’s capital, Kampala, and then flying to Nairobi on Saturday, Aden Duale, Kenya’s health secretary, told a news conference on Tuesday.
Seeking to halt local transmission, Kenya’s President William Ruto said at least eight family members of the victim and 21 healthcare workers have been quarantined, as he ordered an enhanced response to contain the virus in the country.
Earlier, Health Secretary Duale said 28 contacts, including family members and health workers who cared for the patient, had been identified. Another 23 passengers and four crew members who travelled on the same flight from Uganda were being traced.
Patrick Amoth, director-general of the Kenyan Ministry of Health, said the contacts will remain in isolation for 21 days and will be released if they test negative for the virus.
Uganda reported 20 cases and two deaths earlier in the year, but was declared Ebola-free in August.
The current outbreak, which is the DRC’s 17th, has spread rapidly since it was officially declared on May 15.
The outbreak has claimed more than 4,000 lives, according to figures released by the government on Friday, and confirmed cases have reached 8,300 across seven provinces, making it the worst Ebola epidemic in the country’s history.
The World Health Organization has warned that the epidemic is “far from over” and on track to surpass the regional 2014-2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak, which killed more than 11,000 people, primarily in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
At the same time, the United Nations organisation has advised against imposing travel and trade restrictions on Kenya, DRC and Uganda following the Ebola-related death in Kenya.

Herman Coliver Locus Architecture focuses California synagogue on mountain views
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:00:14 UTC
02:00:14 KST

Herman Coliver Locus Architecture focuses California synagogue on mountain views
San Francisco studio Herman Coliver Locus Architecture has completed a synagogue in San Rafael, California, with a second-floor sanctuary space that frames views of the surrounding mountains.
Herman Coliver Locus Architecture worked with congregants at the Congregatio Rodef Sholom synagogue to design an open and welcoming building to replace a previous brick structure on the site that they described as "weighty" and "opaque".
The synagogue, which was entirely clad in a light, sandy stone, has an L-shaped plan organised around a central courtyard on the lower floor.
Surrounding the courtyard are a kitchen, office spaces for staff, a social hall and youth lounge, while raised above are the sanctuary and Beit Midrash, or chapel, in two sculptural volumes.
"In our early design conversations with the congregation, what we heard from many, was that this edifice came to feel more closed than open to congregants and visitors as they approached the front door," said the studio.
"The exterior expression of the new building suggests Aliyah and transcendence. It invites one up and in."
Visitors enter the synagogue via the Community Entry Path – a slightly elevated pathway that "offers the time and space for one to shift one's frame of mind from the quotidian space of the parking lot".
From there, they move into a double-height lobby, which connects to a grand staircase that leads up to the main sanctuary or prayer spaces.
The upper level sanctuary is covered by a vaulted ceiling clad in slats and timber, which forms a giant window that overlooks the California forest. The studio raised this space to the building's upper level as, when asked, the congregation said they felt closest to God when in nature.
"Before placing and giving shape to the Sanctuary, we asked individuals in the congregation where in the world they felt closest to God, holiness, and the oneness of everything," said the studio.
"Most answered they felt this feeling most when standing in nature: on the beach, in the mountains, in the desert or forest," it continued.
"For this reason, we located the Sanctuary on the second floor to capture and frame a remarkable view of the forested hills to the east."
The sanctuary space was connected to a patio with the Beit Midrash, a building that serves as a gathering place for smaller services, on the other side. This space was designed with slightly curved roof that recall to the slopes of the surrounding hills. A youth space is affixed to the back of this volume.
Downstairs, the courtyard contains a fountain, a fire pit, young deciduous Pardes trees, a small amphitheatre and a turf area.
Glass folding walls lining the lower level open up into the space and connect the interior spaces to the outdoor area.
Details include hammered copper triangles populated with the words of the Jewish Golden Rule, Love Thy Neighbour as Thyself, that cover the central Torah ark in the main sanctuary and other prayers that are etched above doorways and laser-cut into door handles.
Herman Coliver Locus Architecture is based in San Francisco. Founded by architects Robert Herman and Susie Coliver in 1969, the studio specialises in affordable housing and sacred spaces.
Other recently completed synagogues include a design by Adjaye Associates in Abu Dhabi for an interfaith complex with a church and a mosque and one in Ukraine that opens like a pop-up book.
The photography is by Richard Barnes

Preparing for a wider European Union
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:59:49 UTC
01:59:49 KST

When more countries join the European Union, we need to be ready. This is why the European Commission has reviewed the actions needed to prepare the EU and countries seeking to join the EU for future enlargements.
The new measures will prepare the European Union's governance, policies and budget for enlargement, while strengthening the protection of EU values and the rule of law.
Adapting policies for a wider Union
The EU can take in more countries within the existing Treaty and budgetary framework. Some improvements would, however, be needed in terms of administrative capacity and implementation.
When it comes to budgetary arrangements, the Union budget can accommodate new Member States while continuing to finance the Union's existing priorities.
Strengthening governance for a larger Union
If more countries join the EU, the decision-making needs to be swifter and more effective. The Commission proposes making greater use of the possibilities under the Treaties to strengthen the Union’s capacity to act, including
- moving from unanimity to qualified majority voting in key areas, including for the opening of the negotiating clusters, helping to make the enlargement process more dynamic
- more effective handling of Article 7 procedures (i.e. the possibility to suspend certain rights of a Member State if it seriously violates the EU’s core values), including possible timeframes
The annual Enlargement and Rule of Law Reports will continue to serve as the main monitoring tools.
Gradually integrating candidate countries into the EU
The measures reinforce the gradual integration of candidate countries into the EU by
- identifying opportunities to deepen integration in strategic sectors such as energy, transport, digital and defence
- launching annual dialogues with enlargement partners to track progress, identify opportunities, and address gaps in gradual integration
Sectoral and institutional safeguards
The measures propose stronger safeguards for future accession treaties so that commitments made during negotiations continue to be respected after accession.
- A dedicated institutional safeguard would address serious breaches of the fundamental values enshrined in Article 2 of the Treaty on the European Union and the principle of sincere cooperation. In the most serious cases, measures could include the suspension of Council voting rights.
- Transitional arrangements could also be used where needed, including for the free movement of workers and services, agriculture, sensitive products, funding and participation in common EU systems.
Next steps
The Commission invites the European Council and the European Parliament to advance discussions and institutional preparations.
It will work with EU and candidate countries to align accession negotiations with the Union’s internal preparations and present roadmaps for Montenegro, Albania, Moldova, and Ukraine.
EU enlargement remains a key priority for the Commission and an important driver of long-term security, peace, stability and prosperity in Europe.

EU explains idea behind restrictions for Ukrainian farmers in Cluster 5 negotiating position
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
19:59:00 EEST
01:59:00 KST

EU explains idea behind restrictions for Ukrainian farmers in Cluster 5 negotiating position
A special regime of restrictions for Ukrainian agriculture after Ukraine's accession to the EU is planned to be included in the EU's negotiating position at the stage of opening Cluster 5: Resources, Agriculture and Cohesion.
Source: a European Pravda correspondent, citing EU officials familiar with the drafting of proposals for new approaches to EU enlargement, speaking on condition of anonymity
Details: The European Commission will propose that restrictions be established for Ukraine's agricultural sector in the EU's common negotiating position for Cluster 5.
"We will propose to the Council of the EU that the draft common position regarding the opening of Cluster 5 for Ukraine be amended. We believe this could actually help achieve unanimity in the Council of the EU," a source stated.
The official said the EU intends to finalise the conditions and restrictions for Ukrainian agricultural producers after Ukraine joins the EU following the relevant negotiations with the Ukrainian side, and will ultimately include the agreed wording when closing the agriculture chapter, which will take place closer to the end of the EU membership negotiations.
"This would define our position, which would then lead to the final agreement at the end of the negotiations," the European official added.
"The European Commission is already working on the assumption that after Ukraine's accession, its agricultural sector should not automatically receive the same access to agricultural subsidies and the EU market as the agricultural sectors of current member states, and that Ukrainian farmers should focus primarily on markets in non-EU countries," a second European Pravda source stated.
"Ukraine's agricultural sector is very different in terms of its productivity, in terms of unit costs, and in terms of its international markets. To treat them in the same way as any other sector that faces productivity challenges and might need financial support in the EU would mean conflating two objective situations that are very different," the first source explained.
The official stressed that before the war, almost all Ukrainian agricultural products were sold in North Africa and the Middle East.
"If we redirected those exports to the EU market, we would create serious, very serious problems for the countries that are currently buying – or used to buy before Russia started bombing grain shipments – Ukrainian meat and grain. This could actually potentially lead to famine in countries like Egypt and other North African countries, as we saw a few years ago when exports stopped. So from that point of view as well, there is a very important reason to avoid this situation," the official added.
Background:
- European Pravda recently reported that European Commissioner Marta Kos, who was presenting a draft of new approaches to enlargement on 6 October, also announced that the provisions agreed on for Ukraine in the agricultural sector may differ from those for other candidate countries.
- Kos noted that the new approaches to the EU accession process, which will also include the idea of "gradual integration", will only apply to countries that demonstrate progress in implementing reforms.
- It was also reported that the EU will present an accession roadmap for Ukraine on 28 October.

Turkey and Pakistan Preparing to Deploy Troops in Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:57:58 UTC
01:57:58 KST

Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan have agreed to move toward the practical implementation of their collective defense commitments and to prepare for the deployment of coordinated military forces and capabilities on Saudi Arabian territory.
This is stated in a joint statement following an emergency meeting of the Strategic Political and Defense Committee of the Mecca Defense Alliance.
The meeting was convened amid a deteriorating security situation around Saudi Arabia and a series of Houthi attacks on the kingdom’s territory.
Following the meeting, the parties decided to “immediately proceed with the practical implementation of collective defense commitments,” ensure the allocation of agreed-upon military forces and assets, and create the conditions for their rapid deployment in Saudi Arabia.
At this time, the specific number of troops, the composition of the units, their weaponry, or the timeline for their deployment have not been disclosed. It is noted only that the deployment will take place in accordance with agreed-upon mechanisms and the national legislation of the three states.
The parties separately reaffirmed the principle that the security of each of the three states is inseparable from the collective security of the entire alliance.
Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan signed the Mecca Agreement on Collective Defense on August 7, 2026. It stipulates that an armed attack on one of the participating states will be considered an attack on all of them.
Since signing the pact, the allies have not yet demonstrated an operational response to the first Houthi attacks — in particular, following the strike on the Saudi Aramco oil refinery in Jazan.
At a meeting on October 5, the allies also took another step toward establishing a permanent organizational structure. Retired Pakistani Lieutenant General Nauman Mahmood was appointed as the first secretary-general of the Mecca Defense Alliance; he will serve in this position for three years.
The establishment of the secretariat had already been planned following the results of the first meeting of the Strategic Political and Defense Committee, which took place on August 31 in Istanbul. At that time, the parties agreed to locate the permanent secretariat in Saudi Arabia and determined that the first secretary-general would be a representative of Pakistan.
They also announced their intention to develop joint military capabilities, defense industry cooperation, joint technology development, and weapons production.
On September 25, the foreign ministers of the three countries, on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, had already discussed the establishment of the alliance’s secretariat, committees, and working groups. At that time, they also agreed to hold urgent consultations among the chiefs of staff regarding possible assistance to Saudi Arabia.
In a joint statement on October 5, Turkey, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia condemned attempts to attack Mecca and Medina, as well as strikes on the kingdom’s cities, civilian targets, and economic infrastructure.
Amid an escalation of Houthi missile and drone strikes in September, Turkey announced its readiness to provide Saudi Arabia with military support in specific technical areas. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan emphasized at the time that the three countries already have allied obligations under the Mecca Agreement.
At the same time, Riyadh is receiving military aid from outside the trilateral alliance — the United Kingdom sent an RAF Voyager refueling aircraft to Saudi Arabia to refuel Saudi fighter jets during operations to repel Houthi attacks.
France has also announced the deployment of military personnel and air defense systems to Saudi Arabia to protect the area around the port of Yanbu.
In August, Saudi Arabia led a naval coalition of 14 countries formed to counter the Houthi blockade and protect shipping in the Red Sea and adjacent straits. The coalition included, among others, Turkey and Pakistan.

Why a PR voting system is the best bet for Britain | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:56:09 UTC
01:56:09 KST

It is common in the argument against proportional representation (PR) to reach for Italy as a cautionary tale, as Gian Lorenzo Spisso does in his letter (A proportional representation voting system could spell disaster for Labour, 30 September). The irony is that Italy does not actually have a proportional system: it has a mixed system. If we want to assess PR, we should look at countries that actually use it – Germany, Sweden, the Netherlands, Denmark – hardly synonymous with political instability.
Also, small parties or weak local representation are not unique to PR. The tiny Democratic Unionist party held the balance of power at Westminster less than a decade ago under first past the post (FPTP), while the Scottish National party and Plaid Cymru wield influence disproportionate to their UK-wide vote because their support is geographically concentrated.
Germany limits fragmentation with a minimum electoral threshold. And systems such as Germany’s combine PR with constituency MPs, while Ireland’s single transferable vote system retains a strong geographical link between voters and representatives.
Gian’s letter does raise a more interesting point: FPTP encourages major parties to contain competing tendencies within broad internal coalitions rather than allowing them to form separate parties. But is it preferable for those coalitions to be internal and opaque, forcing voters into tactical choices, rather than external and explicit, requiring parties to negotiate and find common ground?
The fundamental problem with FPTP is that millions of votes have little bearing on parliament. If your preferred candidate has no realistic chance of winning, voting for them does not translate into representation. In 2024, Labour won 33.7% of votes cast but 63.2% of the seats. That distortion is not a minor technical flaw. Who wields power depends heavily on where votes are cast rather than who people vote for. This disconnect is precisely why Britain needs electoral reform.
The question isn’t whether PR is perfect, but whether we can design a system in which parliament reflects the votes people actually cast. Other stable democracies do so. Britain can too.
Tom Walker
London
Re Gian Lorenzo Spisso’s letter and Zoe Williams’ article (Electoral reform could be a gamble too far for Burnham, 30 September), there are several reasons for the UK to adopt a more proportional voting system of which the most important is the moral one: it’s fairer.
In the last general election, the current system gave us a government that only about 20% of the electorate had voted for. No wonder the public has been hostile since the start of this administration: almost 80% of us didn’t vote for it.
There are other, more pragmatic reasons, particularly for those of us on the centre/soft left: if we are anxious to avoid having an extreme party in power, we need to ditch first past the post – and fast. Reform UK may be lagging a little in the polls at the moment, but with £76m behind them, they may be able to mount a campaign of mis- and disinformation that could persuade 30% of the electorate to vote for them – and they might win. If we don’t want an extreme right (or left) party in power, we need a way to elect MPs that reflects that view. We need proportional representation.
Of course, not all PR systems are the same. Italy uses a mixed system similar to the one used in Scotland for elections to Holyrood. However, as a report published by Make Votes Matter on possible future electoral systems points out, the Italian system “tilts the playing field rather than levelling it”. Its results do not reflect the views of the Italian population accurately.
The crucial effect of any proportional system that meets the criteria of the “good systems agreement” (which sets out the standards that a system should meet to be considered by the proposed national commission) is to encourage cross-party collaboration and cooperation. It undermines the tit-for-tat squabbling so typical of our House of Commons and reduces the policy flip-flop of right-left-right administrations that makes it so hard for businesses, and individuals, to plan long term. It is precisely that collaborative, creative approach to policy that would encourage the stability and prosperity our people are longing for.
Susanna Dammann 
London
Gian Lorenzo Spisso’s letter arguing against proportional representation voting in the UK is superficial and wrong-headed. Up and down the country there are huge numbers of voters like me whose entire lifetime has been spent thoroughly fed up with our unfair system. I am 79 now, and my vote has never elected an MP since I lived in an urban area private rental in my early 20s.
As a middle-class, left-leaning voter living in mainly middle-class towns and suburbs, my vote has been wasted in a succession of places. Of course PR could elect a rightwing government; it could also lock the right wing out of power for a long time, and as a democratic socialist I would be happy to live with the prospect of a long-term progressive coalition. PR would also give the Greens the scale of representation in parliament that their increasing national support deserves.
Steve Smart
Malvern, Worcestershire

Is regulation enough to stop AI systems killing us all? | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:56:04 UTC
01:56:04 KST

Once again a frontier AI model has been withdrawn because it fails safety tests (OpenAI scraps release of new model over safety concerns in internal testing, 28 September). There is the usual call for “independent oversight and regulation”, though never any explanation of how this would work or, most importantly, what evidence should persuade a regulator that an AI system is adequately safe.
There is a long engineering tradition of regulating safety-critical software systems, such as those controlling aircraft or nuclear power stations; international standards require “safety cases” – rigorous analyses that show that the possible hazards have been identified and controlled and that the probability of an accident is extremely low.
Typically, the safety case should show, with a probability of at least 99%, that an accident that could cause multiple fatalities will not occur more often than once in 1,000 years. It is extremely hard to provide evidence for such low probabilities, even for aircraft that at worst might kill 1,000 people in a single accident. The developers of frontier AI systems tell us that their systems might kill the whole of humanity, yet they have provided no detailed risk analyses, no safety cases that could be independently assessed, and no evidence that such safety cases could ever be produced for frontier AI systems.
How, then, can any rational person argue that independent oversight and regulation will be sufficient? Policy must be based on rigorous analysis of the facts, not on fantasy.
Martyn Thomas
Fellow and emeritus professor of IT, Gresham College

Unemployment and the rise of the Nazis | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:55:55 UTC
01:55:55 KST

Philipp Ruch believes that the impact of the 1929 Wall Street crash cannot explain the Nazi breakthrough at the 1930 Reichstag election, as the full effects of Black Thursday “didn’t fully arrive in Germany until July 1931” (‘Hitler was a lazy criminal who slept in until noon’: why most of what we think we know about the rise of the Nazis is wrong, 1 October). But unemployment more than doubled between 1928 and the 1930 election, and that fact alone might be thought sufficient to explain the change in Nazi fortunes. Not so, says Ruch, for “in regions where unemployment was high, the Nazi party performed relatively poorly. If anything, unemployment was a factor contributing to anti-fascist resilience.”
This, however, marks a failure to appreciate how rising unemployment was seen by most Germans at the time. Not only did they see it as signifying one aspect of the failure of the coalition parties in government to manage the economy competently, but they also rightly regarded it as fuelling the rise of the Communist party of Germany (KPD) – with it being the other great political beneficiary of the Wall Street crash along with the National Socialist German Workers’ party. As the KPD grew, so the Nazi party grew – as it was perceived as the only party with the resolve and the numbers (thanks to the brownshirts) to stop the communists seizing power on the streets.
The fact that the KPD proved a damp squib should not blind us to the fact that the party once inspired genuine, strong and very widespread fear.
John Plowright
Repton, Derbyshire

Syria's new rulers and Hezbollah: An unlikely détente?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:55:34 UTC
01:55:34 KST

Breadcrumb
Syria's new rulers and Hezbollah: An unlikely détente?
Lebanon’s Hezbollah and Syria’s post-Assad government have a contentious relationship formed in the bloody crucible of the Syrian civil war, when Hezbollah intervened against the Syrian opposition in 2013 in defence of the ailing regime of Bashar Al-Assad.
However, a recent Reuters report suggests that the two sides have held secret meetings in Turkey designed to defuse tensions between them, which may suggest a relative détente.
This follows sporadic clashes on stretches of the non-demarcated Syrian-Lebanese border since the fall of the regime, and accusations by the Syrian government that Hezbollah is operating cells inside the country.
According to the report, both sides agreed they held no hostility towards one another, and that Syria assured Hezbollah that it would not invade Lebanon.
Syrian officials also reportedly asked Hezbollah to help stop cross-border smuggling, and to dismantle its sleeper cells.
The Syrian government’s English-language platform quickly denied the report, stating “these claims are false. No such meeting took place”.
The Turkish Presidency’s communications directorate also denied the report, claiming it was "entirely unfounded". Hezbollah has not publicly commented on the report.
However, if these meetings did indeed occur, it would reflect a developing relationship between them from battlefield foes to pragmatic, albeit suspicious, partners.
A bitter history
After the 2006 war with Israel, Hezbollah and its former leader, Hassan Nasrallah, were once looked upon favourably by large parts of the Syrian population.
That changed in 2013 when the armed group intervened in Syria to bolster the Assad regime. “Hezbollah formed the elite troops fighting on behalf of the regime,” explains Issam Al-Reis, a senior researcher at ETANA, a Syrian research organisation, to The New Arab.
“By 2013, as the regime’s military weakened, they became the main force fighting the opposition,” he added.
“They often faced off against HTS [which formed Syria’s new government in 2024], and so they have both lost people fighting each other.”
Early on in its intervention, Hezbollah was implicated in the 2013 siege of Al-Qusayr, in which they restricted access to food, water, and medical supplies into the town, in a strategy that may have resulted in the deaths of hundreds of people according to the UN’s Commission of Inquiry.
Similar tactics were subsequently employed by the Shia group during the sieges of Homs and Aleppo.
HTS, in the guise of its previous iteration, the Al-Qaeda-affiliated Jabhat Al-Nusra, had claimed a number of bombings in Lebanon that killed dozens, many of them centred upon the largely Shia Dahiyeh in southern Beirut.
It is within this context that the relationship between Hezbollah and the forces that would become Syria’s new government became “one of extreme hostility,” Nicholas Blanford, a Beirut-based analyst at the Atlantic Council, tells The New Arab.
As Syria’s civil war developed, Blanford also acknowledges that their relationship developed an important “sectarian element”.
“It became an enmity not just between battlefield opponents but Shiite and Sunni Islamists.”
This enmity didn’t disappear following the fall of the Assad regime in 2024.
A new Syria
HTS launched its offensive the day after the ceasefire between Hezbollah and Israel began following the 2024 war. Over 11 days, it rolled back years of territory hard-won by the regime and its Lebanese ally.
Whilst Hezbollah’s leader Naim Qassem pledged to “thwart” the offensive, crippled by its recent confrontation with Israel, the armed group was able to do little to save Assad.
In the closing hours of Assad’s regime, tens of thousands of Syrian Shias, Hezbollah associates, and regime officials flooded into neighbouring Lebanon - many remain housed in Hezbollah funded refugee camps in north Bekaa.
Following the fall, relations between the two floundered. The Syrian government has repeatedly accused Hezbollah of running a network of cells within the country designed to destabilise the country’s fledgling post-war recovery or potentially incite conflict with Israel.
Last week, Syria’s Ministry of Interior announced the arrest of three individuals who they claim were part of a Hezbollah-affiliated cell, as they had been attempting to set up rocket launchers in the southern Syrian province of Deraa.
According to Al-Reis, following the 2018 reconciliation between the regime and the armed groups in southern Syria, Hezbollah recruited approximately 5,000 fighters from the factions.
“It has retained contacts in southern Syria and has been attempting to reconnect and recruit from that network,” he explains to The New Arab.
Hezbollah has repeatedly denied the accusations. In September, however, the intelligence branch of Lebanon’s Internal Security Forces carried out a series of raids, arresting five individuals, some with links to Hezbollah, who were allegedly training Syrian nationals in Lebanon for operations inside Syria.
Equally, the new Syrian government’s relations with Lebanon have been overshadowed by reports of US pressure on President Ahmed al-Sharaa to intervene militarily against Hezbollah.
Whilst al-Sharaa has repeatedly denied any intention to invade Lebanon, stating “we are looking for economic channels, not military ones,” in a June interview with Al Mashhad, it has nevertheless inflamed historical memories in Beirut.
Syria occupied large parts of Lebanon between 1976 and 2005.
“Since independence, some in Syria have continued to see Lebanon as an extension of ‘historical’ Syria,” says Blanford. “There are concerns that the new government may have this mentality, but so far they appear to be prioritising state-to-state relations.”
Syria has adopted a ‘no enemies’ approach to its post-Assad foreign policy. One element of it has been a rapprochement with Russia, which, in 2016, intervened in the Syrian civil war on behalf of the regime.
In October 2025, al-Sharaa visited Russia and met Vladimir Putin, a meeting which paved the way for Syria and Russia to agree on a deal in August which will hand over Russia’s bases on the Syrian coast to the Syrian military whilst allowing a small Russian contingent to remain on site.
However, Syria has not pursued a similar rapprochement with Iran. The countries still has no formal diplomatic relationship, and last week, Mohammed Al-Jafal, advisor for Afro-Asian Affairs at Syria’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, stated that any new relationship between the two “must respect Syria’s sovereignty”.
“The intensity of hostility to Hezbollah and Iran is much deeper than towards Russia,” says Blanford. “Russia is seen as a global player that will ultimately need to be accommodated with.”
The difficult relationship has also complicated Damascus’ engagement with the Lebanese state due to the “suspicion that Lebanon is controlled by Hezbollah,” Sam Heller, a Beirut-based Researcher with Center for International Policy, tells The New Arab.
“Bilateral engagement has been slow and incremental due to this, although the Syrians are slowly developing a feel for the make-up of Lebanon’s politics and the extent of Hezbollah’s real influence.”
Why now?
Before this recent meeting, there have been some signs of a potential softening of Hezbollah and Syria’s relationship. In July, Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Al-Shaibani said Damascus was open to meeting with Hezbollah. In August, Qassem said that “there is no impediment to a public meeting”.
The southern regions of both Syria and Lebanon are facing a sustained Israeli occupation, which may have influenced Ankara’s decision to facilitate talks.
“Turkey is playing a leading role regionally in opposing Israeli actions in Lebanon and Syria,” says Al-Reis. “For them, playing this intermediary role may be more about trying to balance Israel than anything.”
Hezbollah, meanwhile, is interested in “establishing a predictable relationship without recurring fears of border clashes and potential military escalation on a new front,” says Heller.
However, for Blanford, it seems that Hezbollah is operating a “dual policy,” of beginning to engage diplomatically with Syria’s rulers whilst still working to destabilise them in parallel.
Syria’s government may be more concerned about the risk of destabilisation posed by Hezbollah. Cells affiliated with the group have on several occasions been caught setting up rocket launchers in southern Syria - just one successful rocket launch against Israeli positions could invite a fierce Israeli response.
Yet analysts say that it remains politically difficult for the Syrian government to acknowledge talks between them due to the intensity of animosity from large parts of the Syrian population.
“Ultimately talks may just be driven by a sense that each side could undermine the other,” says Blanford.
“That despite the history of bloodshed between them, it is better for their own [respective] interests to reach some understanding.”
Cian Ward is a journalist based in Damascus, covering conflict, migration, and humanitarian issues
Follow him on X: @CP__Ward

Fallen fighter pilot Marat Mambetov is a Hero of Ukraine: what is known about the commander of the "Ghosts of Kyiv"
Kyiv • UNN
The commander of the "Ghosts of Kyiv," Marat Mambetov, was killed on October 1 during a combat mission in a MiG-29. He was 25 years old.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy posthumously awarded the title of Hero of Ukraine to Marat Mambetov, commander of the "Ghosts of Kyiv," who was killed on October 1. This is stated in Decree No. 1031/2026, UNN reports.
To award the title of Hero of Ukraine, with the Order of the "Golden Star," to Mambetov Marat Redvanovych, a major (posthumously)
The title was awarded for "personal courage and heroism demonstrated in defending the state sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine, and selfless service to the Ukrainian people."
Supplement
On October 1, pilot Marat Redvanovych Mambetov was killed in battle. He had been striking Russian occupiers in a MiG-29 fighter jet. His aircraft was hit by an enemy missile; the pilot ejected but did not survive.
The defender of Ukraine was born in 2001 into a serviceman's family in the Melitopol area (Zaporizhzhia). He had dreamed of the sky since childhood, which is why he enrolled at the Ivan Kozhedub Kharkiv National Air Force University. He mastered three types of aircraft: KhAZ, L-39, and MiG-29. In 2022, he successfully graduated from the institution and immediately joined the combat brigade—the "Ghosts of Kyiv."
Within the flight crew, he established himself as an intelligent, level-headed, and determined officer who did not shy away from the most difficult combat missions. In just the last two years of the war, he carried out nearly 200 combat sorties in MiG-29 fighter jets. He had dozens of enemy aerial targets destroyed to his credit. He also carried out intensive missile and bomb strikes against the occupiers' ground positions and provided cover for the operations of the Ukrainian Armed Forces' Ground Forces.
He was awarded state honors—the Orders "For Courage," 2nd and 3rd Class, and the President of Ukraine's distinction "For the Defense of Ukraine."
Major Marat Mambetov made his final flight on October 1, driving the invader out of the occupied Ukrainian lands. Unfortunately, after completing the mission, his aircraft was hit by an enemy missile. The Hero was 25 years old forever. He is survived by his parents and brother.
On Sunday, October 4, people in Kyiv said farewell to Mambetov. During the farewell ceremony for Marat Mambetov, Refat Chubarov, Chairman of the Mejlis of the Crimean Tatar People, delivered a speech.

Air Force Finalizes Decision to Put F-35s at Oregon Base Starting in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:54:02 UTC
01:54:02 KST

More than two dozen F-35 Lightning II fighters are officially heading to Kingsley Field, Ore., after Air Force Secretary Troy Meink signed the record of decision to base the jets there on Oct. 5, clearing the last bureaucratic hurdle for the Air National Guard base to host the service’s third F-35 formal training unit.
The 173rd Fighter Wing at Kingsley and Rep. Cliff Bentz (R-Ore.) announced the milestone in separate releases, capping a yearslong process to replace the base’s legacy F-15C and D fighters.
The very first aircraft are expected to arrive in summer 2027, but the entire transition will take “multiple years,” according to the 173rd Fighter Wing’s release. A recent environmental impact analysis report states that the final aircraft are expected to arrive in 2029.
Back in 2020, the Air Force announced plans to put an F-15EX Eagle II schoolhouse at Kingsley, which had long hosted F-15C/D training.
But within a few years, the service reconsidered that move, with officials citing the growing strategic focus on the Indo-Pacific and the need to field fifth-generation aircraft “as quickly as possible.” The Air Force was also scaling back its procurement plan for the F-15EX at the time.
In May 2023, the USAF announced its new plan to put an F-35 schoolhouse at Kingsley instead of an F-15EX one.
A lengthy environmental impact analysis process followed, and the Department of the Air Force issued its final report last month, clearing the way for the record of decision. The record is required to begin construction of new and existing facilities needed to accommodate the aircraft.
Originally, the 173rd said it expected to receive 20 F-35s with the switch and keep the same number of personnel. The environmental impact analysis report, however, states that Kingsley will receive 26 aircraft and add about 30 personnel.
This will be the third F-35 formal training unit in the Air Force—schoolhouses already exist at Luke Air Force Base, Ariz., and Eglin Air Force Base, Fla. As the service’s F-35 fleet grows, officials say they need to expand the training pipeline. FTUs are typically the last stop for a pilot to receive airframe-specific training before they move on to an operational unit.
“We are not simply receiving a new aircraft; we are taking on a mission that directly affects the Air Force’s ability to put combat-ready F-35 pilots into operational units,” Col. Adam Gaudinski, 173rd Fighter Wing commander, said in a statement. “Every pilot we graduate from Kingsley represents combat capability that can be delivered to an operational squadron. That is the responsibility we are accepting, and we are ready for it.”
Kingsley Field will be the 16th Air Force base to hose the F-35—Barnes Air National Guard Base, Mass., and Misawa Air Base, Japan, both welcomed their first F-35s in 2026.
Elsewhere in Oregon, the 142nd Wing at Portland Air National Guard Base has started receiving the F-15EX.

Ukrainian units hit record number of Russian air defense systems and radars in September, one of them 552 kilometers away
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:53:53 UTC
01:53:53 KST

In September, Ukraine struck more Russian air defense systems than in each month since 2024. Its Defense Ministry reports that Ukraine stepped up strikes on targets deep in the Russian rear, and this is how it hit this amount of protective systems, radars among them, in the history of the ePoints program.
ePoints are points that Ukrainian units earn for verified combat missions, from strikes to reconnaissance and evacuation, and spend on drones, ground robots, and electronic warfare systems on the state's Brave1 Market. In September, units confirmed hits on 33,087 Russian soldiers under the program, more than in any month this year except March and April.
Every result is recorded on video in the DELTA battlefield system and verified by the Brave1 defense innovation cluster, the ministry said. Russian losses are also growing far from the contact line, it added, and units are finding new and unconventional ways to inflict them.
The strikes are meant for "bleeding the Russian war machine," Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said on 4 October.
Deep strikes pass 11,000
In September, the number of hits more than 20 kilometers behind the front line exceeded 11,000 for the first time. Hits beyond 50 kilometers also set a record, most of them along the Russian logistics route between Mariupol and Crimea. One air defense system was hit 552 kilometers away.
Ukraine also now has a ballistic missile for such depths, not simply drones. It fired its first FP-7 in combat on 1 October, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced without naming a target. Its maker, Fire Point, plans an interceptor version that aims to achieve a first ballistic missile shoot down by mid-2027.
Troops down more propeller Shaheds
Even as Russia kept changing its air attack tactics and launched more jet-powered drones, Ukrainian troops shot down 28% more non-jet-powered Shahed drones in September than in August, the ministry said.
Jet drones remain the harder target. Ukraine shoots down 85 to 92% of propeller-driven Shaheds but only 50 to 60% of jet-powered ones, Zelensky said on 4 October, when he announced a new small missile called Nika for testing against them. Ukraine's military intelligence estimates that Russia builds about 3,000 jet-powered drones a month.

Outcry in Trinidad and Tobago after passing of police bill that could threaten press freedom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:53:21 UTC
01:53:21 KST

Journalists in Trinidad and Tobago have called for an urgent amendment to a sweeping new bill that increases police powers of search and seizure, which they argue threatens the country’s much-vaunted freedom of the press.
The government says the special operations bill 2026, passed on 24 September, is designed to tackle alarmingly high crime and murder rates in the Caribbean nation.
The country has spent more than a year in an almost perpetual state of emergency, with police empowered to bypass normal constitutional rights around arrest, detention, and search and seizure.
But journalists in Trinidad and Tobago have called for explicit exemptions in the new legislation to prevent police from searching and seizing their notebooks, phones and laptops.
In the past, journalists have been forced to challenge warrants empowering police to raid their homes and offices.
Although the country prides itself in honouring freedom of speech, ranking 19 out of 180 countries in the 2025 Reporters Without Borders press freedom index, this year it fell 13 places to 32, and journalists say they are deeply concerned about whether they can protect whistleblowers and vulnerable sources who share information on the understanding that they will be protected.
The president of the Media Association of Trinidad and Tobago (MATT), Prior Beharry, said the organisation had called for clause 15 of the bill to be urgently amended “to explicitly shield our devices and materials … and confidential source information from standard police seizure”.
Clause 15 prevents police from seizing “a tool of a lawful trade or business” or material protected by legal professional privilege. But MATT says journalism is not explicitly recognised as a protected trade, nor does the bill establish a procedure for handling confidential journalistic material discovered during searches. It wants the clause changed to “expressly name journalism as a protected lawful trade and safeguard journalists’ devices, materials and confidential sources”.
Beharry said the bill’s search‑and‑seizure powers were particularly worrying in a digital era where “the tools of a journalist is … usually [a] cell phone”. Though he said journalists had not been directly threatened under recent states of emergency, he warned that other restrictions were worsening.
“One of the issues we are having is the access to the government, the executive, including the prime minister, who has not had an official press conference for more than a year,” he said. “Ministries use state resources and we are not invited, but state media is invited.”
The independent journalist Pearce Robinson said the combination of surveillance capability, expanded search powers – without explicit protection for journalistic practice – and declining access to government ministers created a “concrete” threat to press freedom, with a particularly significant impact on investigative reporting.
“If your phone, your laptop and your notes can be searched or seized without explicit protection for journalistic material, that raises serious constitutional concerns,” he said. “Investigative journalism depends on people being able to speak confidentially.”
He also raised concerns about phone tapping and surveillance, pointing to an investigation by the Trinidad and Tobago Guardian which said that “judges approved 314 warrants to intercept communications in Trinidad and Tobago between 2020 and May 2026”.
“My concern is not that press freedom has disappeared,” he said. “It is that several of these pressures … are accumulating at the same time.”
Pedro Cárdenas, of the press freedom and human rights organisation Article 19, expressed concern about the clause in the new bill. “It empowers law enforcement officers to seize any vehicle, article or document deemed likely to be of substantial value. We find this clause particularly problematic because it is vague and opens up to discussion what is substantial value or not,” he said.
He added that it “might directly counter” existing international human rights laws.
The office of the prime minister did not respond to a request for comment.
Stuart Young, Trinidad and Tobago’s former prime minister, labelled the bill “unconstitutional and very dangerous”, adding that it “breaches fundamental and entrenched constitutional rights” and was passed “without a required constitutional majority in highly questionable circumstances”.
He said the government’s past use of emergency powers – including detaining citizens without charge – showed “the real likelihood of abuse” under the new legislation.

Ukrainian Velmart retail chain boosts direct manufacturer sourcing to 53%
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
19:52:53 EEST
01:52:53 KST

The Velmart chain of discount hypermarkets has restructured its supply chains and increased the share of direct deliveries from manufacturers to stores to 53%, its press service said.
"As of September, supplies to the chain cover more than 11,000 product items and are provided by more than 570 supplier partners. In September, the share of direct deliveries from manufacturers in the total value of goods received increased to about 53%, whereas in August this figure was 12%," the chain said in a press release.
According to the statement, local manufacturers supply products to their respective regions without routing them through a distribution center. This approach reduces the burden on interregional transportation routes and allows goods to be delivered to stores more quickly.
In addition, Velmart gives priority to supplies of everyday consumer goods, including dairy products, deli and prepared foods, meat, bakery products, groceries, vegetables, fruit, sugar, salt and flour. When Ukrainian-made products are unavailable, the chain looks for alternatives produced in Poland or Romania.
The Velmart chain is part of the multibrand Retail Group holding company. It operates 34 stores in 18 cities across Ukraine. It develops 10 private-label brands and has seven fully integrated production facilities for meat and fish products, both chilled and smoked, as well as culinary products, baked goods and confectionery.
The company is also developing the Graan Café chain of modern food courts at Velmart supermarkets and the Pukhnasti Spravy pet-products business.
According to the YouControl analytical system, in 2025 Foodcom LLC, which operates the Velmart chain, increased net revenue by 18.7%, to UAH 23.6 billion, while net profit rose 3.2-fold, to UAH 378.6 million.
Foodcom LLC's owner is listed as JSC Retail Group, with Roman Lunin as its ultimate beneficial owner.

Latvian president asks incumbent premier to begin forming next government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:51:06 UTC
01:51:06 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Latvian President Edgars Rinkevics on Tuesday tasked incumbent Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs with forming a new government after his United List party won the general election, public broadcaster LSM reported.
Rinkevics announced the decision following a meeting with Kulbergs, whose party secured 41 seats in the newly elected parliament, known as the Saeima.
The president said consultations with all parties elected to parliament showed that most supported United List and Kulbergs beginning talks on forming a government.
Negotiations will address the coalition’s composition, the division of responsibilities and the preparation of a draft government policy statement.
The announcement is political rather than a formal legal nomination. The president can officially nominate a prime minister after the new parliament convenes and the current government resigns.
The newly elected Saeima will hold its first sitting on Nov. 3.
United List has said it will first hold talks with its existing coalition partners, the National Alliance and New Unity, which won 10 and seven seats, respectively. The three parties would together control 58 seats in the 100-member parliament.
Kulbergs has ruled out cooperation with Latvia First, which placed second in the election with 17 seats, according to LSM.
A coalition comprising United List and the National Alliance alone would hold a slim 51-seat majority.
Analysts cited by the broadcaster consider a three-party coalition including New Unity to be the most likely scenario, although other arrangements remain possible.

Unknown

Poland to deploy Patriots near Ukrainian border, announces $26 billion civil defense plan
Poland will station Patriot air defense batteries in its Lublin region, bordering Ukraine, Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz announced on Oct. 5, according to Polish Radio. The same day, Prime Minister Donald Tusk announced his government will adopt a civil defense program worth 102.4 billion zlotys ($26.4 billion).
Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Patriot batteries are meant to reassure the residents of the Lublin region and protect Lublin airport and its air traffic, Polish Radio reported. Amid rising tensions between Russia and Poland, Russia has repeatedly violated Polish airspace.
The defense minister also announced that new military formations, including unmanned systems forces, will be created in the region, Polish Radio said.
Tusk announced his government will adopt a draft resolution for the Population Protection and Civil Defence Programme for 2027-2031, Polish state news agency Pap wrote.
"Five years of full funding for the program, we are talking about very large sums guaranteed for the protection of civilians and civil defense. It will be mainly investments," Tusk said.
While previous programs only paid for emergency purchases such as generators, local governments had pushed for a longer, better-funded program, Tusk said.
The money will be spent on shelters, equipment, rescue bases, stockpiles, and securing water and energy supplies during natural disasters and wartime, the prime minister said. Additionally, funding will go toward warning systems and ICT security, Tusk said. Of this money, 30 billion zlotys (about $7.7 billion) will be allocated to the regional authorities, according to him.
"Local governments will decide, so that they have a voice co-deciding what type of investment, whether it's a shelter, whether it's a firehouse, whether it's a matter of telecommunications - what is most needed," Tusk said.
On Sept. 13, Tusk warned that Russian escalation could increase in the upcoming months, following Russian strikes on a Polish-Ukrainian border crossing and a passenger train.
"The escalation of actions of the Russian Federation is becoming a fact and its examples are getting closer and closer to our borders," Tusk said in a briefing with defense officials. "What can be expected is that the next weeks and months will be a period of very intensive actions from the Russian side. Unfortunately, we cannot rule out that this escalation will also concern our territory."

EU offers 1-year flexibility on methane rules amid energy crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:50:49 UTC
01:50:49 KST

Melike Pala
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Tuesday that the European Union will give fossil fuel exporters an additional year of flexibility on methane requirements as the bloc seeks to ease energy costs amid a wider energy crisis.
Addressing the European Parliament in Strasbourg, von der Leyen said the measure would help reduce costs for exporters amid heightened pressure on Europe's energy markets.
"We will give flexibility to exporters for one more year on methane," she said, adding that the measure would "save additional costs at a moment of crisis."
The EU's methane regulation is designed to reduce methane emissions from the energy sector and covers fossil fuels produced within the bloc as well as imported oil, natural gas and coal.
Under the regulation's current implementation timeline, importers were due to begin demonstrating from Jan. 1, 2027 that methane emissions linked to the production of fossil fuels covered by relevant contracts had been monitored, reported and independently verified in line with standards equivalent to those applied under EU rules.
She said gas prices have risen 140% since the end of February, while diesel prices have doubled, adding that imported fossil fuels had cost Europe an additional €100 billion ($112 billion) without providing additional energy.
"Families and industries are paying the cost of a crisis far beyond our borders... Businesses are under high pressure. People struggle to pay their bills. And this could intensify as we head into winter," von der Leyen said.
The EU executive is also planning a strategic dialogue on European refineries and a new task force to aggregate energy demand and facilitate joint procurement, von der Leyen said.
She stressed, however, that the bloc's longer-term response must focus on reducing its dependence on fossil fuels.
"As long as Europe depends on oil and gas, our prosperity remains exposed to events beyond our control. When we import fossil fuels, we import the shocks and crisis that come with them," von der Leyen warned.
Von der Leyen said Europe should therefore replace fossil fuels with clean electricity generated within Europe.

Greek prime minister vows to ‘ramp up’ efforts to regain Parthenon marbles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:50:19 UTC
01:50:19 KST

The Greek prime minister has vowed to “ramp up” his country’s claims to get back the Parthenon marbles from the British Museum, emphasising that his UK counterpart, Andy Burnham, was hugely supportive of restitution efforts before he moved into Downing Street.
Kyriakos Mitsotakis said he would raise the issue in the strongest of terms when he met Burnham, who was culture secretary in a previous Labour government.
“Unfortunately they have not progressed,” he told a conference in Athens when asked about talks with London over a muted “hybrid” deal to repatriate the fifth-century BC marbles in return for a treasure trove of other antiquities.
“We will very clearly ramp up the intensity of our claims, not just with the British Museum, but also with the British government. I would also like to remind the audience that the new prime minister of the UK, unequivocally, was supportive of the return of the Parthenon sculptures before he became prime minister.”
It was the first time Mitsotakis had conceded that negotiations with the British Museum, under the aegis of its chair, George Osborne, had failed to make headway.
Upping the ante, he suggested the fate of the artworks was also connected to Burnham’s stated desire for the UK to have closer ties with the EU. Sculpted to adorn a monumental frieze that embellished the Parthenon, the carvings have been split between Athens and London since their controversial removal at the behest of Lord Elgin, Britain’s ambassador to the Ottoman empire, more than 200 years ago.
“For those of us who were saddened to see the United Kingdom leave the European family, we took great interest in the comments made by the UK PM,” said the Greek leader, citing the possibility of “a stronger relationship between the UK and Europe”.
“The Parthenon sculptures will be part of this debate, this is not just an issue for Greece. It’s an issue for Europe.”
The combative remarks come amid thinly disguised disdain in Athens for Burnham’s seeming about-turn on the sculptures. In private, Greek officials have voiced dismay that within days of assuming office, he should so publicly reverse his position, stating in one of his first interviews that the dispute was “an issue for the British Museum” to resolve.
Long seen as an advocate of repatriation, Burnham’s support for the antiquities to be returned to Athens dates back 25 years with Greek officials seeing his elevation as the best hope yet of finally ending the row.
In 2023, as mayor of Greater Manchester, he appeared to go further than ever before, posting on social media: “Send them back, no strings. And let’s use culture to change how Britain is seen around the world.”
“His change in stance caused great disappointment,” said one well-placed Greek heritage expert who has legally advised successive governments on the issue. “There was more than an element of perfidious Albion about it.”
The British Museum has been home to about 160 metres of the frieze since 1816, when a bankrupt Elgin was forced to sell the marbles in what, even then, was viewed as a controversial acquisition by the British government.
Mitsotakis, whose centre-right administration has sought to refocus the campaign on the idea of reunifying the masterpieces within view of the Acropolis, said on Tuesday that changing attitudes in Britain could not be dismissed.
There was, he said, still room for a “win-win” solution with the imminent closure and renovation of the National Archaeological Museum in Athens allowing gems that had never been seen outside Greece to be sent to the UK in exchange for the sculptures.
“[The marbles] reunification in Athens would also set a precedent for a unique cultural partnership between Greece and the UK, and in particular between Greece and the British Museum,” he said. “I will certainly make the case very forcibly to the British PM when I meet him. I think the time has come. British public opinion supports reunification of the sculptures and I do believe that now is the time to push in this direction.”
