Should NTHU’s president resign?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:38:23 UTC
01:38:23 KST

National Tsing Hua University (NTHU) president John Kao (高為元) was invited for a job interview in Hawaii just three days after being confirmed in May for a second term at NTHU.
Academic and industrial leaders requested his resignation.
In the US, university presidents serve at the pleasure of the university’s board of trustees or board of regents. Unless an employment contract explicitly protects them, they can be terminated at any time without cause under at-will employment doctrines. If the board finds out a president is interviewing elsewhere, it can legally terminate their presidency simply by citing a “loss of confidence” in their long-term commitment.
However, the internal academic affairs councils of universities in Taiwan generally do not have the direct, unilateral legal authority to fire a sitting president.
The University Act (大學法) stipulates that a president can only be removed for major misconduct if a high threshold — usually a one-third petition and a two-thirds majority vote by the council — is met. The case would be forwarded to the Ministry of Education to officially execute a dismissal.
There is legal precedent in Taiwan for the ministry to remove a president directly. In 2001, Peng Tso-kwei (彭作奎) of National Chung Hsing University was removed after the National Science Council confirmed that an article he coauthored had been plagiarized.
In 2005, Huang Kuan-tsae (黃光彩) of National Taiwan Normal University was removed only eight months after taking office due to inadequate credentials.
In 2018, the ministry refused to ratify the election of National Taiwan University (NTU) president-elect Kuan Chung-ming (管中閔) for 11 months due to conflict-of-interest allegations regarding his role as an independent board director of Taiwan Mobile.
Pro-Kuan alliances argued that delaying his appointment violated university autonomy, which was countered by the North America Taiwanese Professors’ Association in a public statement that true institutional autonomy is warranted only when universities rigorously follow baseline regulations and maintain transparency rather than bypassing them under the guise of independence.
The association compared a 2017 conference paper coauthored by Kuan and Chen to a 2016 master’s thesis by a graduate student of Chen’s, finding that Kuan and Chen’s paper copied from the student’s thesis, and that plagiarism was unequivocally committed.
The standoff grew so politically charged that three consecutive education ministers resigned over the issue before Kuan’s position was approved.
It is common for people to search for new jobs, so the only crime Kao committed was his naivety to accommodate a job interview, to which he was invited. Should that not be considered a badge of honor?
The University of Hawaii at Manoa generally has a lower academic ranking globally than NTHU. Moreover, even though Hawaii is a paradise, it faces fires, volcanic eruptions and flooding, and also has a high cost of living.
Kao cannot have been serious about moving to Hawaii and his explanation of simple curiosity appears to suffice.
NTU might have won the battle over Kuan’s appointment, but it lost the war by forever tarnishing its reputation.
Kuan’s alleged plagiarism should have disqualified him as a professor at NTU, let alone being promoted to president.
Justice will not be served if Kao is asked to resign while Kuan was approved.
Kao has in general been highly regarded in his running of NTHU. It is vitally important to retain capable and moral leaders to help Taiwan, instead of terminating their services over trivial matters.
Let naivety, forgiveness and kindness be still acceptable in academics.
James J.Y. Hsu is a retired professor of theoretical physics and a former president of the North America Taiwanese Professors’ Association.

“It is a very exciting time right now for all kinds of compute, and especially on the CPU [central processing unit] side,” Su said during a visit to Taiwan. “The overall market has increased a lot in 2026, and so we have also increased our own supply and capacity in 2026, but I can say that the demand is even higher than our supply, so we continue to ramp up supply.”

Photo: CNA
“We have been able to increase our supply as we have gone through 2026, and we’re going to substantially increase our supply in 2027,” Su said. “But we can definitely use more, and so that’s one of the reasons that I’m here is to make sure that our entire supply chain ramps up their capability on CPUs, GPUs [graphics processing units], and all of the AI demand.”
AMD used to plan for one or two years ahead, but now it must look to three, four or five years into the future to ensure “all of the capacity comes up at the same time,” Su said.

Can AI help students think harder?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:38:20 UTC
01:38:20 KST

Chen Chih-nung (陳啟濃), a former principal at Kuohsin Junior High School in Nantou County, wrote about writer Chu Yu-hsun’s (朱宥勳) frustration with artificial intelligence (AI) in creative writing (“Students losing their minds over AI,” Sept. 30, page 8). Chu said that he would refuse to judge any literary award that did not explicitly prohibit the use of AI.
A good story told powerfully and beautifully, one that resonates with readers and touches their hearts, is a good story regardless of how it is generated.
Literary competitions have always had to establish authorship. A 30-minute interview with shortlisted writers could provide conclusive evidence to show whether a piece was written by AI, with the help of technology or entirely by the author.
Writers know their work intimately: the plot, character arcs, structural decisions and evolution of the prose. Ask why they made choices, how earlier drafts differed or why a character changed halfway through the writing process.
Passing off an AI-generated manuscript as original work is difficult under such examination.
Clear rules should outline whether a competition prohibits AI entirely or allows it for editing. Announcing an interview requirement would itself discourage people from flooding competitions with prompt-generated manuscripts.
Rather than walking away from the judging table, experienced writers and critics such as Chu are needed more than ever to uphold artistic standards.
The question of how to respond to AI extends well beyond literary competitions.
Chen, like many educators, also worries that students will misuse AI “to the point that their intellectual and creative abilities stagnate.”
General solutions often involve restricting AI while returning to handwriting, reading aloud and other traditional methods.
The concern is legitimate. Students can produce an elegant essay on the causes of World War I without understanding the causes or a sophisticated analysis of Macbeth without reading the play. A finished product can no longer reliably demonstrate how much intellectual work occurred inside a student’s head.
Imagine a history examination beginning with a proposition: “The atomic bombing of Hiroshima was necessary to end World War II.”
Instead of writing an essay, the student gets five exchanges with an AI instructed to challenge whatever position they take. Each response the students give must be at least 200 words. The student might argue that the bombing ended the war quickly and avoided the casualties of sending ground troops to Japan.
The AI asks: How do you know Japan would not have surrendered without it?
Each answer determines the next question. A weak argument receives one kind of challenge; a sophisticated argument, a more sophisticated one.
Could a student earn high marks without knowing the history, framing arguments properly and writing clearly?
The teacher would grade the student’s prompts, writing and reasoning, as well as how well they know the subject, put forward arguments, respond to counterarguments and defend or revise their position when better evidence emerges.
That is what might be missing from much of the debate about AI and education. The ideal examination has arguably never been the written test. It is a conversation with a knowledgeable teacher.
A university professor can still do it with a handful of students around a seminar table. Mass education cannot provide that experience to every student. AI potentially can.
For the first time, every student could have something resembling an individual examiner, capable of listening to an answer, challenging it and adapting the next question accordingly.
When AI becomes part of the examination itself, it stops helping students avoid thinking and starts making it harder for them not to think.

Each layer normalizes daily coercion, narrows Taiwan’s freedom of movement and chips away at its maritime sovereignty — all while staying below the threshold of armed conflict. This is “gray zone” warfare at its most cost-effective — one of Beijing’s most promising

Ten indicted for smuggling chips, fraud
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:38:18 UTC
01:38:18 KST

The New Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office has indicted 10 people for allegedly using forged documents and bogus ties to National Chungshan Institute of Science and Technology (NCSIST) to procure controlled chips for military applications and smuggle them to China and Hong Kong.
The suspects were indicted on charges including aggravated fraud for potentially helping enhance China’s military capabilities, threatening national security and damaging Taiwan’s international reputation, prosecutors said.
They allegedly disguised the chips’ country of origin and their status as controlled products to smuggle them abroad, making about NT$360 million (US$11.33 million) in illicit profits, the indictment says.
Photo: Taipei Times
Beginning in 2017, ADWELL Technology Inc (優活創意科技) head Chen Chien-hsiung (陳建雄) and other codefendants allegedly imported semiconductors from abroad using forged NCSIST documents, while providing assurances that the products would not be exported or resold to entities subject to US sanctions, prosecutors said.
Once in Taiwan, they repackaged and relabeled the chips as made in Taiwan and used other methods to disguise their origin so they would not be subject to export restrictions before selling them to entities in China and Hong Kong, including shell companies they had established, prosecutors said.
That scheme generated about NT$120 million in illicit profits, they said.
The defendants illegally exported more than 10 types of controlled chips manufactured by Texas Instruments and Analog Devices from the US, the Philippines, Malaysia and South Korea, prosecutors said, adding that the chips could be used in military applications involving radar, electronics, ultrasound systems, antenna arrays and uncrewed military aircraft.
Under export-control regulations, buyers must provide an end-user statement verifying the ultimate recipient, intended use and destination of the products.
Manufacturers and authorized distributors will refuse transactions involving overseas customers, including those in China, prosecutors said.
Another group, allegedly led by Hygge Investment Ltd (享得投資) head Lai Chin-lan (賴金蘭), used similar methods, starting in 2019, to sell controlled chips certified for US military specifications to entities in Hong Kong, generating about NT$130 million in illicit profits, the indictment said.
A third person, Hui Chung Telecommunications (匯眾通信) and ZhanKai Technology Co (展開科技) head Yuan Tung-tai (袁同台), allegedly placed orders through the companies he controlled in Taiwan, and similarly submitted false declarations and disguised the products’ origins before shipping them to a company he had established in Hong Kong, prosecutors said.
The company then resold the chips to buyers in China and Hong Kong, they said.
One type of chip Yuan sold was intended for use in uncrewed military aircraft, they said, adding that he earned more than NT$100 million in illicit profits.
Prosecutors are seeking a 10-year prison sentence for Chen, eight years for Yuan and six years for Lai.
They are also seeking a six-year prison sentence for Zkey Technology Inc (華謚科技) head Chiang Kun-cheng (蔣昆成), and sentences ranging from one to three years for the remaining six defendants: Chen’s brother, Chen Chien-hui (陳建輝); former ADWELL head Chen Chien-wei (陳健偉); Stone Engine Technology Co (石擎科技) and WTG Technology Co (睿虎科技) head Wang We-feng (王維鋒); Kplus Technology Ltd (凱盟資通) head Tsen-Tien-chi (曾恬綺); EcoLumina Technologies Inc (晟明科技) head Tsai Yu-shu (蔡玉書); and HGT Application Inc (洪巨科技) head Hung Chun-min (洪俊民).
A source familiar with the investigation said the types of chips smuggled by Chen Chien-hsiung could be used in radar, missile guidance, uncrewed aerial vehicle flight-control and electronic warfare systems.
Despite the national security implications, the illegal trafficking of semiconductors and advanced electronic equipment, including artificial intelligence (AI) servers and dual-use chips, does not currently contravene the National Security Act (國家安全法), the source said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Authorities can deter entities only when they illegally transfer military or advanced technologies to hostile foreign powers or countries subject to export restrictions, they said.
Taiwan urgently needs more sophisticated mechanisms that emphasize prevention rather than relying on punishment after violations have occurred, the source said.

CDC announces the first local typhoid case of 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:38:17 UTC
01:38:17 KST

The Centers for Disease Control (CDC) yesterday announced this year’s first locally acquired case of typhoid fever, adding that although cases of flu-like illnesses, including COVID-19, declined slightly last week, the case numbers and deaths were still high.
CDC physician Lin Yung-ching (林詠青) said the typhoid fever case is a woman in her 30s who resides in central Taiwan.
The woman developed symptoms, including fever, vomiting and diarrhea, in late August, Lin said.
Photo: CNA
She sought treatment and took medicine to relieve her symptoms, but the fever, as well as headaches and general soreness developed early last month, Lin said.
The woman sought treatment again and was hospitalized, he said, adding that a blood culture test confirmed that she had contracted typhoid fever.
The woman recovered after about a week in hospital, he said, adding that she reported having eaten raw seafood — including sashimi and raw oysters — during the incubation period.
There are typically only about two or three locally acquired typhoid fever cases each year, Lin said.
The disease is an intestinal infection caused by the Salmonella typhi bacteria. It has an incubation period of about eight to 14 days.
Typhoid fever spreads through contaminated food and water, so sashimi, and raw oysters and clams are high-risk foods, Lin said, adding that people should practice good hand and food hygiene, such as only drinking boiled or bottled water when traveling in areas with poor public health and sanitation.
Common symptoms include persistent fever, headache, fatigue, loss of appetite, abdominal pain, diarrhea, relative bradycardia, and lower chest and abdomen rashes in some cases, he said.
As early symptoms of the disease are highly non-specific, it can often be misdiagnosed as gastroenteritis or other diseases, he added.
Meanwhile, CDC Epidemic Intelligence Center Director Guo Hung-wei (郭宏偉) said there were 139,060 medical visits for flu-like illnesses and 7,836 medical visits for COVID-19 last week, both slightly lower than a week earlier.
However, both are still in the epidemic period, Guo said.
There were 219 severe flu cases and 44 flu-related deaths, as well as 37 serious COVID-19 cases and 16 deaths confirmed last week, he said.
One of the COVID-19 deaths was a man in his 60s who had cirrhosis and received his last COVID-19 vaccine in 2022, Lin said.
The man developed a fever, coughing and general weakness in the middle of last month, and took medicine without consulting a doctor, Lin said.
He was hospitalized when his symptoms worsened, including difficulty breathing, and he died 10 days later, Lin said.
Contact tracing found people who lived with him had similar symptoms last month, but they had not been tested for COVID-19 and recovered, he added.
The CDC urged people with higher risk of developing severe illness or death from flu or COVID-19 to get vaccinated and to seek medical attention when they develop suspected symptoms.
Shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, cyanosis — a bluish or purplish discoloration of the skin, lips or mucous membranes — bloody sputum, chest pain, altered consciousness and low blood pressure can be signs of severe complications, it said.
CDC Deputy Director-General Lin Min-cheng (林明誠) said flu activity is expected to slightly fluctuate throughout this month, with the epidemic period possibly ending next month.
People should still practice good hand hygiene and cough etiquette to prevent infection and spreading the virus, he said.

Philippines strives to keep ube throne
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:38:16 UTC
01:38:16 KST

The Philippine ube has become a trendsetting sensation from Los Angeles to London to Seoul, with the humble yam’s bright purple hue drawing lines outside coffee shops and bakeries and millions of views on social media.
However, keeping pace with the international boom has proven tricky for the archipelago nation’s overwhelmingly smallholder farmers, with yields declining and some unable to commit to the plant’s nine-month growing time.
Fears that biopiracy might take a chunk out of the blossoming market have prompted the government to announce a ban on the export of the raw form of the yam.
Photo: AFP
Standing in his ube field south of Manila, farmer-exporter Al Bonifacio said he was in favor of doing whatever it took to protect the crop from any growers overseas trying to cash in on the craze.
“Purple is so royal and is very pleasing to the eye,” the 59-year-old said with a smile during a visit to his one hectare ube farm. “Our greatest fear is if we are not able to supply ube to the world, someone [else] will step in.”
Sold as powder, extract, paste or frozen puree, ube is easily mixed into coffee, pastries, ice cream, spreads and makeup.
At a Tokyo gelato shop, ube importer J.P. Mercado said the Japanese market was expanding rapidly after the craze first hit neighboring South Korea.
“It’s really taken off like wildfire,” he said as a batch of powder was slowly stirred into gelato, turning it a bright purple.
“I think social media has been hugely impactful,” he said, adding his client list ranged from small cafes to luxury hotels.
Ube was a staple of Philippine gardens as long as 5,000 years ago, boiled and eaten by families as a substitute to rice when provisions ran out.
Beloved for its mildly sweet, nutty flavor and velvety texture, it later evolved into a party food, consumed as a jam or stewed with sticky rice balls in coconut milk.
Demand exploded locally this decade, most memorably during a purple bread mania that swept the archipelago in the darkest days of the COVID-19 pandemic.
“I’m super-obsessed with ube,” university student Kym Trivino said as she sipped an ube-matcha concoction at one of Manila’s largest shopping malls.
Baker Diane Bustos said her company sells seven types of ube cookies.
“It took over matcha. That’s really something that we Filipinos should be really proud of,” she said.
However, as ube mania grows globally, clouds loom at home.
Bonifacio said the country’s small farmers widely lacked the facilities for postharvest storage and processing, while access to marketing and financing lagged.
Planting to harvest takes at least nine months, too long for most Filipino farmers who preferred the shorter growing period for beans, squash or bitter melon to feed their families, the farmer added.
Bonifacio said he had been forced to scour the rest of the country for raw ube to meet his growing export commitments, a process that can double his costs.
“We have the land, but quality planting materials are not always available,” local agriculturist Leonilyn Ladao said.
“Last year’s production was just 12,483 tonnes,” Philippine Bureau of Plant Industry official Jose Zalde Samson said of the five-year low.
Industry officials blamed typhoons, which hit key ube farming regions. For the first half of this year, production was up about 17 percent.
“The government has only started promoting ube in the past two to three years as demand spiked,” Samson said.
“Before the ube craze, it was a niche market,” he said, adding it had lagged behind high-value crops such as bananas, mangoes and coffee.
With the pressure on, the government is working on how it can boost supply.
“We are looking at how [the growing season] can be shortened to six months,” Samson said.
With neighbors like Thailand and Vietnam getting into the game, the Philippines is acting to protect its crown.
“We don’t want to export it to countries that could use Philippine ube varieties to compete with us,” Philippine Secretary of Agriculture Francisco Tiu Laurel said last month while revealing the ban on raw ube exports.
“We’ve had data that tubers were being [surreptitiously] exported,” Samson said, declining to provide further details.
Mercado said he backed the Philippine government’s move, which he believed would protect the country’s cultural heritage.
“Ube really is, I would say, very interlocked with the Filipino identity,” he said.
Bonifacio agreed.
We “are stewards of the ube industry,” he said, looking out over his crop. “We have a stake in this. We have to protect it.”

The Bureau of Consular Affairs has since April 7 had a “Level 4: Red” Travel Alert — meaning “evacuate, leave as soon as possible” — for the area, Lin said, adding that the representative office confirmed no Taiwanese were injured or killed in the airstrike.

Petsitters barred from administering shots, office warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:38:13 UTC
01:38:13 KST

The law does not permit petsitters to give medical injections to animals under their care, the New Taipei City Animal Protection and Health Inspection Office said yesterday.
Only qualified veterinarians and veterinary assistants are authorized to give medical injections to animals, with exceptions for veterinary students, graduates and certified animal medical assistants working under a veterinarian’s guidance, the office said in a statement.
The office issued the statement in response to a report that a petsitter had been giving shots to a cat with chronic kidney disease.
Photo courtesy of the New Taipei City Animal Protection and Health Inspection Office
The office said its investigation found the petsitter, who was not a licensed veterinarian, had provided medical treatment to someone else’s pet, potentially violating the Veterinarian Act (獸醫師法).
The offense carries a fine of up to NT$500,000, and the drugs and medical equipment involved are subject to confiscation, it said.
Administering subcutaneous fluids is a medical procedure and should not be treated as routine pet care, it said.
If an owner needs someone to give their pets medical injections, they should consult a veterinary clinic and make safe and legal arrangements, the office said.
The office cited an earlier official interpretation permitting owners, following veterinary diagnosis, prescription and instruction, to provide necessary care to their own pets.
Even petsitters who are trained to perform the procedure are not allowed to do so on a pet that belongs to another person, the office said.
Contravening the law is punishable by a NT$100,000 to NT$500,000 fine, it said.
There is a red line separating animal care and veterinary science that should not be crossed, New Taipei City Veterinary Medical Association head Luo Qing-bo (駱清波) said in the statement.
The appropriate type and dosage of the drug, injection site, method of injection and knowing the signs of adverse reactions are among the skills needed to give a shot to an animal, Luo said.
Giving shots is a medical procedure because, if performed incorrectly, it could result in infection, bleeding or other injury, he added.

====================================================================================================

From deer hides to semiconductors: Rethinking Taiwan’s economic miracle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:38:11 UTC
01:38:11 KST

Four centuries before Taiwan became a semiconductor powerhouse, its deer hides were finding buyers in Japan. The products could hardly be more different, but economist Wu Tsong-min (吳聰敏) sees a question connecting them: what enables a society to turn overseas demand into economic opportunity?
For governments hoping to emulate Taiwan’s chip industry, the answer matters. Taiwan is frequently cited as evidence of what industrial policy can achieve. Wu invites us to look beyond the factories and examine the institutions that made successive waves of development possible.
In a recent interview for the National Taiwan Normal University International Taiwan Studies Center Podcast, produced in collaboration with the International Journal of Taiwan Studies, the National Taiwan University professor emeritus argues that Taiwan’s transformation rests on institutions: the “rules of the game” that determine whether businesses and individuals can respond productively to economic opportunity. These rules govern investment, competition and access to markets. They can encourage enterprise, but they can also obstruct it.
Photo courtesy of Wikimedia Commons
Wu’s account challenges a familiar explanation of the “Taiwan miracle”. Wu places institutional reform at the center of the story, asking how changes to economic rules created conditions in which businesses could grow. To understand the economy of advanced chips, he begins with the economy of deer hides.
From the late sixteenth century, deer hides from Taiwan were exported to Japan and venison to China. In the seventeenth century, the Dutch incorporated Taiwan into the wider commercial networks of the Dutch East India Company. The island’s dependence on overseas markets thus long predates its electronics industry.
THREE INSTITUTIONAL TURNING POINTS
Trade, however, did not automatically bring sustained growth. Producers also needed conditions that allowed them to expand production and benefit from exchange. Wu’s history follows this relationship through three turning points: 1895, 1945 and the reforms around 1960.
The first came with Japanese colonial rule in 1895. Changes to land rights and administration, alongside investment in transportation and public health, helped establish foundations for a modern economy. Their effects extended beyond the end of colonial rule.
These changes formed part of a system of political domination and violence. Recognizing their economic consequences, of course, does not justify colonialism. It does, however, help explain the institutional inheritance with which postwar Taiwan began.
The second turning point came in 1945, when the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) government took control. Accounts of Taiwan’s economic success often move quickly to the export boom that began around 1960. For Wu, the intervening 15 years are essential to understanding why growth subsequently accelerated.
The government imposed extensive controls on foreign exchange, imports, investment and private business. Hyperinflation devastated the postwar economy. An overvalued currency and a complicated exchange-rate system also made it difficult for producers to compete internationally.
The textile industry illustrates the mixed consequences of state intervention. During the 1950s, tariffs, import restrictions and subsidized credit helped domestic producers expand. Yet protection weakened incentives to improve productivity, while foreign-exchange controls constrained their ability to compete abroad. Policies that helped establish an industry could also limit its development.
The third turning point came with reforms around 1960. Under pressure from US aid officials, Taiwan simplified the exchange-rate system, eased trade restrictions and improved conditions for private enterprise. KMT officials resisted dismantling controls. Changing the rules was a political struggle as well as an economic undertaking.
Businesses responded rapidly once those constraints eased. Exports expanded, private investment accelerated and Taiwan entered the sustained period of growth that became known as its economic miracle.
American assistance was crucial, Wu argues, for more than the money it supplied. Aid gave US officials leverage to press for reforms that the government had been reluctant to undertake. The significance of assistance lay partly in the institutional changes it helped bring about.
LIMITS OF INDUSTRIAL SUBSIDIES
This interpretation shifts the question from how much governments intervene to what their interventions enable. Wu’s argument does not require the state to retreat from economic life. Governments establish and enforce the rules within which markets operate. The issue is whether those rules support productive activity and allow businesses to respond when opportunities change.
The distinction is important as governments renew their emphasis on industrial policy. Governments want to secure supply chains and develop strategically important technologies. Semiconductor factories have become conspicuous symbols of these ambitions. Yet a factory is only one part of the economy that makes it viable.
Taiwan’s experience raises a difficult question for countries investing in chip production: can subsidies reproduce the conditions that allowed the industry to flourish? Financial support can help establish capacity. It cannot, by itself, recreate accumulated knowledge, skilled workers, competitive pressures or relationships with customers and suppliers.
Taiwan’s small domestic market made access to overseas buyers crucial. Its industries developed through networks of trade, investment, technology and knowledge extending far beyond the nation. International connections were part of the process through which productive capacity grew.
This dependence on international networks creates a tension for today’s policies of economic security. Governments are trying to reproduce aspects of Taiwan’s success while geopolitical rivalry is making some international connections more difficult to sustain. The pursuit of greater domestic capacity must contend with the cross-border relationships on which advanced industries depend.
TAIWAN IN A CHANGING WORLD
Taiwan faces its own version of that problem. Semiconductors are the latest expression of an economy repeatedly transformed by changing products and markets. Their success does not guarantee that the institutions supporting them will remain adequate as conditions change.
Geopolitics has long influenced Taiwan’s economic trajectory. Dutch expansion, Japanese colonialism, the Korean War and the Cold War reshaped its connections to the world. Artificial intelligence, supply-chain security and US-China competition now present another set of pressures. Meeting them will demand institutional adaptation as well as technological expertise.
Asked what a future historian writing Taiwan’s Economy: 500 Years might say about our era, Wu is cautious. Semiconductors would feature, and artificial intelligence might too. What remains uncertain is how Taiwan will respond to the changes still ahead.
Wu explored this history in his Chinese-language book Taiwanese Economy of Four Hundred Years (台灣經濟四百年) (2023). His English-language book, Institutions and Economic Growth in Taiwan: A Four-Century History is forthcoming next year from Cambridge University Press. Japanese and Korean translations of his work are also in prospect, opening further opportunities for readers beyond Taiwan to examine an economic history often compressed into the story of a miracle.
For countries seeking to emulate Taiwan, and for Taiwan itself, the value of this history lies in understanding how the conditions for growth were created. Institutions that supported one transformation may need to change before they can support another. Recognizing that need is easier than overcoming the political resistance reform can provoke.
From deer hides to semiconductors, Taiwan has repeatedly found new ways to participate in the world economy. Its next chapter will depend on whether it can sustain that capacity. As Wu puts it, “the ability to adapt is hard-earned.”
Ming-yeh T. Rawnsley is a research associate at SOAS University of London’s Centre for Taiwan Studies.

Belgian-American physicist wins Nobel for work on ‘ghostly messengers’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:38:10 UTC
01:38:10 KST

Belgian-American physicist Francis Halzen yesterday won the Nobel physics prize for groundbreaking work using South Pole ice to capture particles originating in the distant cosmos, providing insight into the far reaches of space.
“This year’s prize is about ghostly messengers from space,” Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences secretary-general Ellen Moons told a news conference.
Halzen was honored “for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin,” the jury said.
Photo: Reuters
Halzen’s work had been fundamental for the observatory, which consists of a cubic kilometer of ice that is equipped with light sensors, and had “paved the way for a new kind of astronomy,” the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said.
Using the observatory, researchers can capture neutrinos — rare subatomic particles — “from extremely energy-rich processes in the distant universe.”
Halzen, 82, was born in Tienen, Belgium, and is a professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison in the US.
“It was a great surprise, and I obviously didn’t expect it,” he told the news conference by telephone shortly after the prize was announced.
“But it’s a great pleasure to hear about this prize,” he added.
The academy said that high-energy neutrinos are created in the same environments as other particles.
“However, unlike other particles, neutrinos reach us without changing direction or losing energy. This means they can provide information that is not available in any other way,” it said in a statement.
Halzen first presented his idea for the observatory in 1988 and his idea quickly gained the support of other researchers.
Preliminary testing was conducted just a few years later, but the observatory was not completed until 2011.
“Cosmic neutrinos with extremely high energies are very rare, so an enormous volume of ice is needed to observe an adequate number of collisions,” the jury said.
“For me, the main pleasure of it, besides winning the Nobel Prize, is that I hope this reflects on the really courageous people who joined me in the beginning of this project,” Halzen said.
Asked whether neutrinos could even contain messages from potential distant civilizations, Halzen said that “it has been speculated that ... this would be an ideal way to communicate with aliens.”
“But I don’t think I will go there. I think we have enough realistic problems to deal with right now,” he said.

Novak Djokovic on Monday advanced to the China Open final after Daniil Medvedev was disqualified late in the second set, when a ball that came off the Russian’s racquet hit a spectator.
Taiwanese player Hsieh Su-wei and her partner, Latvia’s Jelena Ostapenko, yesterday defeated Chinese duo Wang Xiyu and Jiang Xinyu 6-1, 1-6 and 10-4 to reach women’s doubles round of 16. Hsieh was the only Taiwanese player to advance as compatriots Wu Fang-hsien, Chan Hao-ching and Liang En-shuo were eliminated in round of 32.
A man sitting in the stands behind Medvedev’s side of the court was seen holding his face and escorted from his seat after being hit, as Djokovic was serving for the match with the score at 7-5, 5-3.
Photo: AFP
Eleventh-ranked Djokovic was to play world No. 9 Alex de Minaur for the title last night after press time in Beijing.
The Australian had advanced over Hubert Hurkacz after the 29-year-old from Poland retired from their semi-final with an adductor muscle strain.
Medvedev’s disqualification arose from a moment deep in the match. When he failed to return a point, the ball bounced off the back wall, and Medvedev hit it with a backhand up into the stands, with the chair umpire stopping play.
“Terribly sorry to the spectator, first of all,” he told reporters afterward, adding that it was “100 percent an accident” and that he wished to apologize to the fan in person.
“The ball was bouncing back, so I tried to, like, just hit it anywhere, so it doesn’t go out from the court,” he said.
It had been a physical battle before Medvedev’s disqualification.
Djokovic was red-faced and hunched over between points, with both players forcing each other through grueling rallies, until the Serbian took control in the second set.
The 39-year-old put on a dazzling performance and saved 16 break points across the match, diving at the baseline and sprinting to the net.
“I didn’t see what happened, to be honest,” Djokovic told the crowd after the fan was hit.
“I’m sure that Daniil didn’t ... do it intentionally. It happened by accident. Sorry for the crowd,” he said, adding that it had been a tough contest.
“I know the feeling,” Djokovic told reporters later, recounting his own disqualification from the 2020 US Open after accidentally hitting a ball at a line judge.
“It’s horrible ... but it happens,” he said.

A separatist party on Monday night narrowly won Quebec’s election, a result that could make it tougher for Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney to maintain national unity against US President Donald Trump.
Provisional results showed the predominantly French-speaking province of 9 million people had opted for the Parti Quebecois (PQ) of Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, who is promising to hold a referendum on breaking from Canada once Trump leaves office.
At a jubilant victory party in Montreal, the 49-year-old former lawyer invoked “the courageous struggle” francophones have endured in a part of the world increasingly dominated by English speakers, adding that the “will find meaning when [francophones] obtain their own country.”
Photo: AFP
“A referendum is a chance to decide things for ourselves ... our national destiny will be achieved one day,” he told cheering supporters.
He still faces challenges, as the PQ only won 59 of the 127 seats in the Quebec National Assembly, or five short of a majority. The legislature must approve a referendum vote.
Plamondon conceded he would need support from opposition parliamentarians to proceed.
The widely expected result reflected voter fatigue with the Coalition Avenir Quebec (CAQ) government, in office since 2018, analysts said.
The CAQ lost all its 79 seats.
Carney, who has stressed the need for a united front to tackle Trump’s tariffs, must now work with a Quebec premier who is determined to break up Canada.
In addition, the energy-rich province of Alberta is to hold a nonbinding vote this month on whether its residents want independence.
Independence votes held by previous PQ governments in 1980 and 1995 failed, and polls indicate support for the idea of breaking with Canada is at 30 percent, near record lows.
Carney congratulated Plamondon, writing on X that “building a stronger Quebec is core to our mission of building a stronger Canada.”
The prime minister is popular in Quebec, and the separatist win was not seen as a repudiation of his stance toward Trump, whose confrontational policies have infuriated Canadians.
Plamondon, citing the political uncertainty and economic damage done by the tariffs, said he would not call another referendum until Trump is out of White House.
In remarks addressed to Carney, Plamondon said he would defend Quebec’s interests above all, but reiterated that he was happy to work with Ottawa whenever it suited Quebec.
Despite the unclear referendum prospects, some PQ policies look set to boost tension with Ottawa.
The party plans to resist any federal bid to boost immigration, cut Quebec’s ties to the British monarchy and block a proposed high-profile high-speed rail link with Ontario.
The PQ — which benefited significantly from vote-splitting between the five major parties in the fray — took just 27.9 percent of the vote, the lowest share of ballots ever captured by a winning party in Quebec electoral history.
The CAQ’s collapse reflects the fact that politics in Quebec is traditionally more volatile than elsewhere in Canada. The PQ jumped from seven seats to take power.
First-time voter Alexia Gomez, 19, invoked tensions with the US when she said she opposed an independence referendum.
“If Quebec becomes independent it would make us politically, economically and militarily vulnerable,” she said.
Lydie Periard, a 22-year-old student, said she was “very worried” by the PQ’s victory, condemning what she termed the party’s “populist” stance on immigration.
The PQ has backed immigration cuts, particularly for non-French speakers.

EDITORIAL: Tech expansion expands ‘shield’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:38:07 UTC
01:38:07 KST

Global expansion has evolved from an option into a dual-purpose strategic imperative for Taiwan’s semiconductor ecosystem amid demand for geographic diversification to hedge against geopolitical risks, as well as an insatiable appetite for artificial intelligence (AI) and high-performance computing devices.
Overseas expansion is expected to entrench Taiwan’s pivotal role in the global AI industry as long as the nation retains its lead in research, development and early deployment of cutting-edge manufacturing technologies.
The shift has been made evident by the global initiatives of industry leaders, including foundry companies Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC) and Vanguard International Semiconductor Corp, alongside premier silicon wafer supplier GlobalWafers Co.
Vanguard, which specializes in mature manufacturing nodes, last week inaugurated a new US$6.7 billion 12-inch fab in Singapore alongside NXP Semiconductors NV to manufacture mixed-signal, power management and analog chips, as well as interposers. The facility is fully booked and Vanguard is conducting preliminary evaluations for a second fab.
GlobalWafers in July announced plans to expand capacity in Texas under a proposed collaboration with Micron Technology Inc involving a 10-year supply agreement and US$500 million in support.
TSMC’s capacity expansion in particular has garnered significant strategic interest, making its fab announcements a focal point of industry analyses. In July, TSMC announced it would double down on its US presence, boosting its total investment in Arizona to a staggering US$265 billion to support the rapid adoption of agentic AI applications. The additional investment is expected to fund advanced wafer fabrication and packaging facilities, bringing the planned total to 12 facilities.
Reports last week said that TSMC is looking beyond Arizona, with local media saying the foundry giant is considering Texas for a second site to house six next-generation fabrication plants with potential investment surpassing the amount earmarked for Arizona.
Although TSMC did not confirm the reports, a move to Texas would further diversify its US manufacturing footprint. During TSMC’s initial 2020 site evaluation for its landmark US expansion, Texas was bypassed in favor of Arizona, industrial sources said.
On Saturday, Tesla Inc chief executive officer Elon Musk wrote on X: “Just discussions, but something may come of it,” in response to a report of a potential chipmaking collaboration between TSMC and Terafab, his semiconductor initiative in Texas. Musk had chosen Intel Corp as the major partner to build the facility with an initial investment of US$16.8 billion.
TSMC’s aggressive overseas expansion — including in Arizona, Japan’s Kumamoto, Germany and potentially other global hubs — has two effects for Taiwan: It could help preserve Taiwan’s pivotal position, and transform its geopolitical and economic leverage.
With TSMC also accelerating investments into new, advanced chip fabs and packaging plants from Hsinchu to Kaohsiung, it is apparent that rather than a “hollowing out” of domestic industry — which had been a concern in 2020 — the changes represent a strategic diversification driven by demand and geopolitical realities as TSMC seeks to maintain its competitive edge over rivals Intel and Samsung Electronics Co. This year alone, TSMC is building 25 fabs and advanced packaging facilities worldwide, including 13 plants in Taiwan.
For Taiwan’s semiconductor supply chain, it represents a good growth opportunity to expand overseas. Factory construction companies and clean room installment service operators such as Marketech International Corp, L&K Engineering Co, United Integrated Services Co and Acter Group Co are benefiting from the expansion.
Da Yi Cheng Technology Co, which specializes in electrical hook-up and secondary power distribution engineering for semiconductor fabs, reported revenue growth of about 130 percent for last year to NT$2.66 billion (US$83.7 million). During the first half of this year, its revenue jumped to NT$2.51 billion. With paid-in capital of only NT$259 million, the revenue growth is staggering for a company of its scale.
Da Yi Cheng has installed electrical hook-up and secondary power distribution engineering for numerous TSMC fabs, including its first Arizona fab. The Tainan-based firm has expanded its global footprint to Japan, Singapore and Dresden, Germany, following the moves of TSMC and other customers.
One downside of the global trend is that Taiwan’s “silicon shield” might be eroded.
However, if the nation can elevate its single-point defense to a global ecosystem of shared interests, Taiwan might be able to mitigate geopolitical risks.
In 40 years of watching politics, I have never seen anything quite like Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen’s (沈伯洋) breed of politician. He has a presence that commands attention, and a combination of qualities that appear to be the result of powerful political currents. What is it that makes Shen different? Throughout the past decades of local elections, I have not seen anyone seriously discuss a long-term vision for urban planning, let alone with the kind of clarity and insight that Shen possesses that compels people to keep listening. He is an exceptional storyteller, with an ability to present a vision
China prefers to win without firing a shot in its bid to strangle Taiwan’s strategic autonomy. Chinese military strategist Sun Tzu (孫子) would have approved. Its central tool at sea is the “cabbage strategy”: the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) layers fishing boats, maritime militia, coast guard cutters and warships around Taiwan’s contested waters in overlapping rings. Each layer normalizes daily coercion, narrows Taiwan’s freedom of movement and chips away at its maritime sovereignty — all while staying below the threshold of armed conflict. This is “gray zone” warfare at its most cost-effective — one of Beijing’s most promising
Taiwan’s energy security debate has been hyperfixated on fuel inventories, generation capacity and diversification of external supplies. While these measures are necessary, national endurance also depends on governance distribution and responsibility sharing. The rollout of the World Alliance for Disaster Management, in addition to this year’s Global Cooperation and Training Framework Energy Resilience Workshop and 921 Large-Scale Mobilization and Disaster Relief Exercise, proves Taiwan’s security narrative has expanded into civilian cooperation. The challenge Taiwan faces is one of sustainment through crisis and preservation through resilience, or how Taiwan can mobilize its communities, civil organizations and businesses to preserve essential services
During a tour of Taipei’s Wanhua District (萬華) on Sept. 22, Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) proposed a seemingly appealing urban-planning vision for the area: linking Xinfu Market (新富市場), East Sanshui Street Market (東三水街市場), Longshan Temple (龍山寺), Bopiliao Historical Block (剝皮寮歷史街區), Bangka Park (艋舺公園), the underground mall and surrounding commercial areas through neighborhood redevelopment and environmental improvements, while encouraging specialty and boutique business. It would create what Chiang called Taipei’s version of Omotesando — an upscale, tree-lined boulevard and shopping district in Tokyo — to attract young people and international tourists. The idea is not new. More than NT$200 million (US$6.28

As a kid, Richie Palacios was one of the biggest Yankees fans in Brooklyn, but on Monday night, he sent New York home in a huge playoff hole.
Palacios laced a two-run single to cap a four-run fifth inning that propelled the Tampa Bay Rays to a 5-2 victory and a 2-0 lead over the sloppy Yankees in their best-of-five American League Division Series.
“When I’m getting clutch hits, it doesn’t really matter who I’m playing against,” Palacios said. “But it’s very special to do this in a postseason against a team I grew up watching.”
Photo: AP
The 29-year-old second baseman, who also doubled off Gerrit Cole in the series opener, came to bat with two outs in the fifth against left-handed reliever Brent Headrick.
With his parents in the stands and runners on second and third, Palacios got a green light from manager Kevin Cash on a 3-0 count and fouled off a 145kph fastball. The left-handed hitter then fouled off three more pitches before lining a base hit to center field that gave Tampa Bay a 5-1 cushion.
“Probably the biggest hit in the game for us,” Cash said.
A fired-up Palacios gestured toward his teammates in the dugout as he celebrated at first base.
“If I got a green light with a 3-0 ... that means Cashy probably wants me swinging if it’s a pitch over the plate. Swung at one, missed it, and then just locked back in. Was able to relax myself and get a hit there,” Palacios said.
Game 3 is tomorrow morning Taipei time at Yankee Stadium, where the Rays will try for a series sweep.
It will be a homecoming of sorts for Palacios, who is playing in his first postseason. Palacios attended The Berkeley Carroll School in the New York City borough of Brooklyn and then Towson University in Maryland before getting selected by Cleveland in the third round of the 2018 amateur draft.
He was acquired by the St Louis Cardinals for cash in June 2023 and then traded to Tampa Bay for reliever Andrew Kittredge in January 2024.

DEFENSE
Bite-sized arms sales?
Minister of National Defense Wellington Koo (顧立雄) yesterday said he had not heard that the US was planning on carving up a potential US$14 billion arms sale into smaller chunks, but added that Washington’s commitments to Taipei’s defenses had not changed. US President Donald Trump has held back approval of the new package of arms sales to Taipei to maintain warm relations and a fragile trade truce with Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平). In December, Trump approved an US$11 billion package. Koo at the legislature yesterday said the US has repeatedly reaffirmed that its commitment to helping Taiwan strengthen its self-defense capabilities has not changed. The US Department of State did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
LABOR
Kuai Kuai strike ends
The union representing workers at snack maker Kuai Kuai Co’s only factory in Taiwan ended a five-day strike yesterday after reaching a deal with management on compensation for the company’s planned relocation. The deal was signed yesterday afternoon after two days of talks, with the company agreeing to provide more compensation than it had initially offered, according to a joint statement from the Taoyuan Confederation of Trade Unions and the Kuai Kuai union. Under the agreement, union members who resign within the next two years after being reassigned within the Jhongli factory in Taoyuan would receive statutory severance pay plus compensation equal to four months’ full wages, according to the statement.
Union members who resign by Sept. 30, 2028, due to required relocation would receive statutory severance plus eight months’ full wages. In addition, workers with at least 12 years of service under Taiwan’s new labor pension system would receive an additional NT$100,000, the statement said. The agreement contains a “no free rider clause,” meaning the negotiated benefits would apply only to union members. The strike began on Friday amid a dispute over the relocation of Kuai Kuai’s Jhongli factory.
CUSTOMS
Potato shipment intercepted
A shipment of potatoes imported from the US was intercepted after tests found excessive levels of potentially toxic glycoalkaloids, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) said yesterday.
The 339.58 tonne shipment contained 248mg/kg glycoalkaloids, exceeding the legal limit of 200mg/kg, even though the potatoes had not visibly sprouted, director of the FDA’s Northern Taiwan Management Center Liu Fang-ming (劉芳銘) said. The importer would have an increased sampling and inspection rate of 20 to 50 percent for future imports, Liu said. Meanwhile, a 133kg shipment of melamine soup spoons imported from China failed dissolution testing and must be returned or destroyed, Liu said. The importer would be subjected to enhanced sampling and testing rate of 20 to 50 percent, he said.
Other intercepted imports announced by the FDA yesterday included fresh melons and pickled ginger from Japan, fresh white radishes and Chinese yams from China, cod roe paste from France and fresh Chinese cabbage from Vietnam. The products were found to contain excessive levels of pesticides, preservatives or sweeteners.

====================================================================================================

Thomas Jefferson’s DNA punctures US’ slavery ‘amnesia’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:38:04 UTC
01:38:04 KST

New analysis using a strand of hair from former US president Thomas Jefferson has effectively settled a longstanding, acrimonious debate: He almost certainly fathered children with Sally Hemings, a young black woman he enslaved.
The scientific discovery, announced last week, is the result of a collaboration between the Smithsonian and researchers at the University of California Santa Cruz.
Many of Jefferson’s contemporaries were well aware of this relationship, along with the ubiquity of such interracial liaisons. So the fact that generations of historians and Jefferson defenders have struggled to accept this possibility is a testament to the US’ amnesiac relationship with slavery, and, no less important, the peculiar reordering of racial categories that followed its abolition.
Illustration: Mountain People
One cannot simply wish away written records. Consider the account of lawyer Josiah Quincy Jr of Boston. When he visited North and South Carolina in 1773, he came away stunned by what he saw.
Sex between masters and people who were enslaved, he confided to his journal, “is spoken of as quite a common thing: no reluctance, delicacy or shame is made about the matter. It is far from being uncommon to see a gentleman at dinner, and his reputed offspring a slave to the master of the table... The fathers neither of them blushed or seem[ed] disconcerted. They were called men of worth, politeness and humanity.”
Things began to change after the US broke away from Great Britain, its independence fueled by revolutionary ideas about equality and liberty. These ideals were not very compatible with the institution of slavery, to say nothing of the sexual abuses and coercion associated with it. As a consequence, many defenders of slavery preferred to adopt what historian Joshua Rothman has described as a “cultural code of public silence” on such matters, banning interracial marriage, but silently tolerating sexual relationships between white men and enslaved black women.
That agreed-upon silence made the public airing of Jefferson’s interracial affair so shocking. Accusations came from James Callender, a political pamphleteer who had spent much of the 1790s attacking elite Federalists. By 1802, Callender had fallen out with former allies such as Jefferson, and he turned on the president.
Callender wrote that Jefferson, “whom it delighteth the people to honour, keeps, and for many years past has kept, as his concubine, one of his own slaves. Her name is SALLY.” Callender went on to enumerate a now-familiar host of charges, the most notable of which was that Jefferson, the philosopher of equality, had fathered multiple children with Hemings, all of whom remained enslaved.
The charges stuck, and Jefferson’s Federalist opponents ran with the allegation, writing poems mocking the president, while others sketched unsubtle political cartoons that showed Jefferson as a rooster next to his hen, Hemings.
Jefferson’s domestic situation was well known in Virginia; his friend John Hartwell Cocke described the situation as typical, where “bachelor and widowed slave owners” took an enslaved woman as “a substitute for a wife.”
By 1850, the federal census added a new racial category that tacitly acknowledged the growing number of mixed-race people as “mulatto.” In Jefferson’s home state of Virginia, census takers tallied more than 44,000 people in this category, or 10 percent of the enslaved population. The rest of the South was not all that different, even if the numbers tended to be a little lower relative to the population.
The implications of so many enslaved, mixed-race people were obvious to anyone living in the antebellum era. Rebecca Ann Latimer, who was enslaved by a prominent planter family, described how “there were violations of the moral law that made mulattoes as common as blackberries.”
If the people who lived during that time could make such acknowledgments, why have Americans today struggled to accept what was?
One answer lies with how individual states policed racial categories after the Civil War. Some southern states initially repealed many of the laws forbidding sexual or marital relationships between the races, but the move was short-lived. The violent death of Reconstruction, the disenfranchisement of black people, and the rise of the Jim Crow South redrew boundaries.
This inevitably raised questions about the fate of mixed-race people. In Virginia, as in other states in the South, racial categories hardened, and the older system, which tolerated a degree of ambiguity in racial identity, was replaced by the infamous “one-drop” rule that effectively erased the possibility that anyone could be anything other than wholly black or white in the eyes of the law.
Virginia did so in stages, beginning with its “Racial Integrity Act” of 1924, which divided the population into two groups, “white” and “colored.” It was followed six years later by an act that specified: “Every person in whom there is ascertainable any negro blood shall be deemed and taken to be a colored person.” Other states — including those in the North — passed comparable laws, effectively banishing the racial ambiguity that was the legacy of sexual exploitation associated with slavery. The federal government removed the category “mulatto” in 1930.
The past few decades, by contrast, have been spent chipping away at the racial binaries put in place after the Civil War, with mixed-race people formally recognized by the federal census beginning in 2000.
Those resistant to reckoning with these parts of US history do the republic no favors. Conversations about slavery and the people who benefited from or suffered under its power dynamics are not supposed to be easy. They are an opportunity for us to do better in the present, and the threshold could hardly be lower than recognizing the truth of what happened between Jefferson and Sally Hemings — and between the thousands of other masters and the women they enslaved.
Stephen Mihm, associate dean and professor of history at the University of Georgia, is coauthor of “Crisis Economics: A Crash Course in the Future of Finance.” This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

He has a presence that commands attention, and a combination of qualities that appear to be the result of powerful political currents. What is it that makes Shen different? Throughout the past decades of local elections, I have not seen anyone seriously discuss a long-term vision for urban planning, let alone with the kind of clarity and insight that Shen possesses that compels people to keep listening. He is an exceptional storyteller, with an ability to present a vision
China prefers to win without firing a shot in its bid to strangle Taiwan’s strategic autonomy. Chinese military strategist Sun Tzu (孫子) would have approved. Its central tool at sea is the “cabbage strategy”: the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) layers fishing boats, maritime militia, coast guard cutters and warships around Taiwan’s contested waters in overlapping rings. Each layer normalizes daily coercion, narrows Taiwan’s freedom of movement and chips away at its maritime sovereignty — all while staying below the threshold of armed conflict. This is “gray zone” warfare at its most cost-effective — one of Beijing’s most promising
Taiwan’s energy security debate has been hyperfixated on fuel inventories, generation capacity and diversification of external supplies. While these measures are necessary, national endurance also depends on governance distribution and responsibility sharing. The rollout of the World Alliance for Disaster Management, in addition to this year’s Global Cooperation and Training Framework Energy Resilience Workshop and 921 Large-Scale Mobilization and Disaster Relief Exercise, proves Taiwan’s security narrative has expanded into civilian cooperation. The challenge Taiwan faces is one of sustainment through crisis and preservation through resilience, or how Taiwan can mobilize its communities, civil organizations and businesses to preserve essential services

Eclat Textile Co (儒鴻) yesterday said that its fourth-quarter revenue is expected to exceed the third-quarter level, driven mainly by higher shipments and steady average selling prices.
The garment and fabric supplier is highly confident in achieving record revenue and profit for the full year, Eclat chairman Richard Wang (王樹文) said on the sidelines of the Taipei Innovative Textile Application Show.
Third-quarter revenue was NT$10.57 billion (US$332.6 million), up 4.8 percent from the previous quarter and 9.7 percent from a year earlier, marking the highest quarterly figure since the third quarter of 2022, company data showed yesterday.
Photo: CNA
Cumulative revenue for the first three quarters totaled NT$30.28 billion, up 5.4 percent annually, the data showed.
The company reported record full-year revenue of NT$39.74 billion in 2022.
Eclat’s production facilities are operating at full capacity, an online report by the Chinese-language Liberty Times (the sister newspaper of the Taipei Times) yesterday quoted Wang as saying.
Photo: EPA/RITCHIE B. TONGO
The company is positive about its operating performance in the first quarter of next year, with order visibility extending to the second quarter, he said.
While the company’s product prices are expected to trend upward next year, the actual increase would depend on the price movements of oil and raw materials, he added.
Eclat’s major brand customers, such as Nike Inc and Lululemon Athletica Inc, have seen sharp declines in sales and share prices this year amid war-driven inflation, shifting market trends and fierce competition in the Chinese market.
Against this backdrop, orders from Nike and Lululemon have slowed, but Eclat still maintains close collaboration with them, and some urgent Nike orders are being shipped via air freight, Wang said.
Eclat, which also counts global brands such as Gap Inc, Target Corp and Under Armour Inc among its top customers, has added three new customers this year, and one of them started to place orders in the third quarter, he said.
The rapid growth of new customers has helped fill the gap left by large customers, he added.

Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) proposed a debate on drug policy yesterday, while Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan- an (蔣萬安) of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) said the issue could be discussed at a formal debate as controversy over Shen’s past writings continued.
Chiang, seeking re-election, said he and Shen have reached a preliminary agreement to take part in a TVBS-organized debate, with details to be negotiated by their aides.
Speaking while distributing campaign newspapers outside Zhongxiao Fuxing MRT station yesterday morning, Shen accused Chiang’s team of misrepresenting his drug policy positions and suggested making the issue the subject of their first debate.
Photo: Tien Yu-hua, Taipei Times
Chiang said all municipal issues, including drug policy, as well as the candidates’ positions on them, were open for discussion.
“This year will be no exception. I will definitely participate,” he said, referring to the tradition of debates in Taipei mayoral elections.
The dispute centers on a September 2014 article Shen wrote for Thinking Taiwan following actor Kai Ko’s (柯震東) arrested in China for taking marijuana.
Photo: Lo Pei-de, Taipei Times
The article criticized a New Taipei City proposal to add drug screening to school health examinations and argued that punishment-focused policies could reinforce inequalities and stigmatize disadvantaged students.
Shen discussed decriminalization, assistance for people with addiction and research into the social causes of drug use.
If decriminalization was considered too radical, he suggested Taiwan could follow other countries by establishing community centers that provided drugs and clean needles alongside social worker support.
In response to the criticism in recent days, Shen said his article discussed harm-reduction measures, citing methadone treatment and needle-exchange programs already implemented in Taipei. The 2014 article did not specifically mention methadone.
Methadone is classified as a Category 2 narcotic in Taiwan but also has lawful medical uses. It is administered orally under medical supervision to treat heroin dependence, while needle-exchange programs are a separate harm-reduction measure.
Chiang questioned Shen’s explanation that his 2014 proposals concerned policies already in place, asking why he had criticized measures that were being implemented at the time.
Chiang argued that Shen had either misunderstood those policies or was now reinterpreting his earlier position for electoral purposes.
The controversy widened yesterday afternoon when KMT lawmakers Lo Chih-chiang (羅智強) and Niu Hsu-ting (牛 煦庭) held a news conference questioning Shen’s past comments on the legalization of cannabis.
Lo cited a separate 2014 social media post in which, he said, Shen wrote that legalization was needed to address the underlying problems surrounding cannabis. He asked whether Shen still supported that position and the provision of drugs at community centers.
Responding later yesterday, Shen campaign spokesperson Tsai I-kae (蔡一愷) said studying a policy and advocating its implementation were different things.
Shen does not support cannabis legalization and opposes drugs entering schools, Tsai said, adding that a thesis Shen had supervised concluded Taiwan was not suited to legalizing cannabis.
Tsai accused the KMT of distorting academic research for electoral purposes, saying the attacks stigmatized higher education as well as Shen.

To support Nepal’s reconstruction, waive remittance fees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:38:01 UTC
01:38:01 KST

The flash floods that struck Nepal on Aug. 26 killed more than a thousand people and destroyed livelihoods, homes, farms and public infrastructure. With reconstruction and the economic recovery underway, support for the survivors can travel quickest through payment networks and family ties — as is often the case when disasters strike developing countries.
By waiving fees on these remittances for at least two months, money-transfer companies and banks could help Nepal move from rescue and relief toward reconstruction. Struggling Nepalese families would receive more than two and a half times the US$49.6 million that the UN is trying to raise through its emergency appeal.
Nepal is one of the world’s most remittance-dependent economies. Remittances exceeded US$16 billion in the last fiscal year, equivalent to more than a quarter of GDP. More than 3.5 million Nepalese work abroad, and the global Nepalese diaspora numbers more than 6 million — 20 percent of the country’s population. These expatriates are sending financial help to families in the affected districts, as are people and charitable organizations of many nationalities. These transfers could be worth more, and could bring greater relief, if they are allowed to move free of charge.
Remittances are a lifeline. Families use this income for groceries, medicines and healthcare. For a flood-displaced household, such transfers are what puts a meal on the table and pays for antibiotics that a relief camp cannot supply. Even in normal times, a share of remittance income goes directly into housing.
In the weeks ahead, remittances could help rebuild houses, school buildings, and village roads. They could keep children in the classroom, help businesses cope, and restore livelihoods by restocking destroyed shops, replacing lost livestock and replanting flooded fields.
The remittance industry has waived fees before in response to natural disasters, including after Haiti’s earthquake in January 2010, Pakistan’s floods in 2010, the Philippines’ typhoon in November 2013 and Nepal’s earthquake in April 2015. During the three months following the earthquake, remittances to Nepal increased by 18 to 26 percent from the previous quarter, and it is estimated that a fee waiver was worth US$40 million to US$50 million per month to Nepalese families.
Some of Nepal’s own money-transfer companies have already led the way, but only for a short period. What is needed is for the international money-transfer operators and banks that handle the bulk of Nepal’s inbound remittances to do the same.
A fee waiver would be worth even more this year than it was in 2015. According to Nepal Rastra Bank, remittances to Nepal averaged US$1.5 billion per month during the past two months, up almost 25 percent from a year earlier. If remittances continue at this pace and rise by another 20 percent over the next two months — in line with the 18 to 26 percent surge seen after the 2015 earthquake — it could reach about US$3.6 billion. A fee waiver would then amount to US$126 million to US$144 million, assuming an average fee of 3.5 to 4 percent for sending US$200. And since actual fees can rise to 6 to 12 percent on some remittance services, the savings could be even larger.
In addition to being several times greater than the UN’s appeal to raise almost US$50 million, such a contribution would be timely and targeted, because the money would be disbursed directly from overseas relatives to the households that know where it is needed. It is likely that a fee waiver would increase remittance volumes through formal payment networks.
The cost borne by money-transfer companies and banks that choose to help the Nepalese in their time of need is entirely manageable. In fact, the revenue forgone in the near term by waiving fees could bring new customers, increase transfers through formal channels, and earn lasting goodwill from families rebuilding homes, farms and livelihoods. After a disaster of this scale, keeping more of every remittance in the hands of Nepalese families is the right thing to do — and sound business.
Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, a former foreign and finance minister of Nigeria, is director-general of the WTO. Dilip Ratha is CEO of Ratha Global, an advisory and analytical services firm that specializes in remittances, cross-border payments, diaspora bonds and development finance.

He is an exceptional storyteller, with an ability to present a vision

Its central tool at sea is the “cabbage strategy”: the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) layers fishing boats, maritime militia, coast guard cutters and warships around Taiwan’s contested waters in overlapping rings. Each layer normalizes daily coercion, narrows Taiwan’s freedom of movement and chips away at its maritime sovereignty — all while staying below the threshold of armed conflict. This is “gray zone” warfare at its most cost-effective — one of Beijing’s most promising
Taiwan’s energy security debate has been hyperfixated on fuel inventories, generation capacity and diversification of external supplies. While these measures are necessary, national endurance also depends on governance distribution and responsibility sharing. The rollout of the World Alliance for Disaster Management, in addition to this year’s Global Cooperation and Training Framework Energy Resilience Workshop and 921 Large-Scale Mobilization and Disaster Relief Exercise, proves Taiwan’s security narrative has expanded into civilian cooperation. The challenge Taiwan faces is one of sustainment through crisis and preservation through resilience, or how Taiwan can mobilize its communities, civil organizations and businesses to preserve essential services

High-end office demand remains, JLL Taiwan says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:38:01 UTC
01:38:01 KST

Taipei’s high-end office market continued to attract solid demand in the third quarter as companies upgraded their workplaces, helping absorb new supply that pushed vacancies moderately higher, Jones Lang LaSalle Taiwan Ltd (JLL Taiwan, 仲量聯行) said yesterday.
Grade-A office transactions rose 8 percent from a year earlier to 12,279 ping (40,592m2) in the third quarter, with several large deals in the city’s Nangang District (南港) providing a major boost, it said.
Deals that had been under negotiation earlier this year were completed during the quarter, showing that companies remain willing to expand or move into newer, higher-quality offices, JLL Taiwan head of leasing advisory Christina Yu (游淑芬) said.
Photo: Hsu Yi-ping, Taipei Times
Demand helped support rents even as the vacancy rate in Taipei’s core business districts rose to 5.8 percent as new buildings entered the market, JLL Taiwan said.
Average rents reached NT$3,293 per ping a month, up 0.32 percent from the previous quarter and 2.3 percent from a year earlier, extending a moderate upward trend.
Xinyi District (信義) was the strongest-performing area, accounting for 55 percent of transactions in Taipei’s core business districts. Continued leasing at the Taipei Dome International Center was a major driver, with the largest deal covering 1,400 ping.
Companies are increasingly favoring newer offices, with buildings less than two years old accounting for 71 percent of leasing activity in the city’s core business districts, JLL said.
“Companies are increasingly looking beyond location and size when choosing offices, with smart-office features, employee experiences and ESG [environmental, social and governance] standards becoming more important,” Yu said.
The trend is also broadening the sources of demand beyond technology companies. Financial and insurance firms accounted for 26 percent of leasing activity last quarter, up sharply from 6 percent in the previous quarter, suggesting traditional businesses are also moving to modernize their workplaces, Yu said.
The market is expected to remain relatively stable in the near term. About 35,000 ping of new office space is due to be completed in this quarter, but much of it is expected to be occupied by the owners themselves, limiting the amount of space available for lease and cushioning the impact on vacancy rates, JLL said.
The bigger shift could come in the longer term as Taipei’s aging office stock puts increasing pressure on companies to relocate, Yu said.
About half of the office buildings in the city’s core business districts are older than 20 years, while a new wave of developments is scheduled to enter the market after 2028.
That could set off a new cycle of corporate relocations and workplace upgrades, keeping demand for high-quality offices relatively resilient even as Taipei faces a larger pipeline of new supply, JLL said.

Navigating challenges of teaching
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:37:59 UTC
01:37:59 KST

Accountant Lena Yin (尹崇恩) — daughter of Ruentex Group founder Samuel Yin (尹衍樑) — posted on social media on Teachers’ Day on Monday last week that after serving as a part-time university lecturer for seven years, she has decided to leave the profession, saying that being a teacher is exhausting.
The statement resonated with many teachers. Teaching should be a respected vocation, not one that comes with a high degree of legal jeopardy. Teachers need to practice three major techniques to protect the interests not only of themselves, but also of their students. If teachers cannot protect themselves in the classroom, how can they protect disadvantaged students?
Teachers should familiarize themselves with educational regulations directly relevant to their work, such as the Fundamental Act of Education (教育基本法), the Teachers’ Act (教師法), the Primary and Junior High School Act (國民教育法) and the Gender Equity Education Act (性別平等教育法).
When their teaching methods are questioned by parents, they can say that their methods are in accordance with the law.
Taiwan is governed by the rule of law. From the perspective of “systems theory,” schools are the “subsystems” of society.
So how could school campuses possibly become lawless?
Teachers should express themselves effectively, and develop the ability to convey their teaching philosophy clearly and persuasively with parents. During parent-teacher meetings, teachers should articulate their educational philosophy and its implementation.
They should also master how to manage interpersonal relationships and conflicts. Teachers should understand that parents have differing views and identify sources of conflict. They should act as a “buffer” to smooth conflicts.
Chiu Shih-chang is an
elementary-school teacher.
