Interview: More healthcare providers to adopt AI: Acer Medical
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:37:56 UTC
01:37:56 KST

Acer Medical Inc (宏碁智醫) expects Taiwan’s healthcare providers to accelerate artificial intelligence (AI) adoption in the coming years amid a growing consensus in the sector over the value of the technology, chairman Allen Lien (連加恩) said in an interview with the Taipei Times on Friday last week.
Over the past two years, healthcare providers in Taiwan have shifted from questioning AI’s capabilities to considering how to keep pace with other hospitals and overcome barriers to adoption, Lien said at the company’s office in New Taipei City’s Sijhih District (汐止).
However, such applications in Taiwan still lag behind Europe and the US, he said, adding that the company sees opportunities to help fill the gap.
Photo: Meryl Kao, Taipei Times
Acer Medical, a subsidiary of Acer Inc (宏碁), develops AI-powered medical software and platforms for disease screening, medical records and patient care management. The company’s products and services are used by about 600 to 700 healthcare institutions in Taiwan and more than 20 countries and regions abroad, Lien said.
Taiwan is the company’s largest market, while in Southeast Asia, Malaysia accounts for the largest number of healthcare institutions using its products and services, followed by Thailand, he said.
Aside from continuing to develop its AI transcription platform, Acer Medical plans to deepen its ophthalmology portfolio by codeveloping additional retinal imaging applications with partners in the Middle East, North America and Southeast Asia, he said.
The company late last year launched its VeriSee platform, integrating multiple ophthalmic screening functions and using a single retinal image to detect diabetic retinopathy, age-related macular degeneration and glaucoma.
Another product, VeriOsteo OP, launched in 2023, is osteoporosis screening software that can analyze chest X-rays taken for other purposes to identify previously undetected osteoporosis risks, Lien said.
Following broad adoption in local hospitals and demand in some Southeast Asian markets, Acer Medical is developing applications for other body parts, while also pursuing expansion and regulatory approvals in North America, he said.
The company is also working with wearable device providers on large language model (LLM) applications that integrate data such as blood pressure and blood glucose with hospital information systems and messaging apps, Lien said.
Initially focusing on post-stroke care, the system allows AI to flag issues for nurses to review before sending reminders to users, he said.
Acer Medical is discussing more than 20 projects with regional hospitals and medical centers, with some expected to be announced by the end of this year, he said.
As LLMs advance, Acer Medical is also expanding into data processing, system integration and model optimization, while using Acer Group’s (宏碁集團) hardware resources to provide on-premises computing capacity tailored to hospitals’ needs, Lien said.
The group’s subsidiaries include server products provider Altos Computing Inc (安圖斯) contributing to hardware and computing integration, Acer e-Enabling Service Business Inc (宏碁資訊) supporting system integration and Acer Biomedicals LLP (宏碁生醫) providing AI computing technology for cancer vaccine research, he said.
By taking advantage of the company’s healthcare expertise to connect Acer Group resources with hospitals’ needs, “we hope to become an important partner in helping Taiwan’s healthcare system become smarter, and then use the experience we gain here to help hospitals in other countries do the same,” Lien said.
In the first eight months of this year, Acer Medical’s revenue increased 50.1 percent year-on-year to NT$51.39 million (US$1.62 million), company data showed.
With support from government healthcare programs and expanding cooperation with local hospitals and overseas partners, the company’s revenue this year is expected to surpass last year’s NT$60.05 million, Lien said.
Acer Medical is optimistic that it can maintain a similar revenue growth rate next year to that of the past three years on the back of several new projects and more overseas expansions, he said.

Why bowl together when you can scroll alone?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:37:52 UTC
01:37:52 KST

Bowling has seen better days. Lucky Strike Entertainment Corp, the dominant player in the business, has lost almost half of its market value in the past year and had the rating on its debt cut further into junk territory.
Higher borrowing costs and iffy consumer sentiment are factors, but Americans just do not seem to want to bowl that much anymore. And it is not just bowling. Demand for other social forms of leisure is on the decline, too. Dave & Buster’s Entertainment Inc’s disappointing earnings and country clubs’ declining membership are cases in point. There might be a boom in exclusive members’ clubs in big cities. For most Americans, the places that provide outlets for in-person connection, such as recreation and senior centers or the grocery store, are closing.
It reflects a long-running trend in how we socialize, or do not socialize at all. Americans are spending much more time alone and on their screens. A less social nation not only portends big economic shifts, with “third spaces” closing and businesses running into trouble, but also impacts our mental health and well-being, while robbing us of the connections that in the past led to fresh interests and professional opportunities.
This is not a new lament. As far back as 2000, Harvard University political scientist Robert D. Putnam wrote in his famous book Bowling Alone that the decline of bowling leagues represented a degradation of community and social capital. After years of decline, leisure activities that involve neighbors, families and colleagues interacting seem at existential risk.
Bowling was once popular among all income groups because it offered a relatively low-cost and family-friendly way to socialize. People formed bowling leagues with friends or co-workers or just made the odd outing with other families.
League membership reached about 10 million people in its heyday in the 1970s. It has dwindled to about a million, with Lucky Strike saying that consumers prefer watching televised sporting events. Millions of Americans still bowl each year, more than play tennis or pickle ball. However, the share of the population that bowls in a day has been trending down since even before the pandemic. The US has lost one-third of its bowling alleys since 2001.
Leisure trends come and go as culture evolves and technology creates new interests and hobbies. Going to a Vaudeville show was a popular way to spend leisure time and budget in the 1880s. Movies and eventually television changed that. It could be that bowling has run its course and is soon to be about as relevant as a croquet tournament.
Consumers these days have limited budgets that are being squeezed by high energy prices and inflation, so they are more price sensitive to the marginal elements of their spending, and bowling is marginal. Companies such as Lucky Strike and Dave & Buster’s are land-intensive and carry lots of debt. The higher rate environment is forcing them to refinance at higher costs, cutting into their margins and hammering their ratings.
The underlying worry is Americans growing less willing to gather like they used to — bowling is, after all, a social activity. Not all forms of entertainment are losing ground. Americans across income groups still spend lots on discretionary services. We spend a fortune on concert tickets and travel. No doubt budgets are tighter, but consumers are making choices that cut out community engagement.
What has replaced bowling is not just concert going or watching a football game. We spend more time on video games and scrolling videos of other people with a more active social life. Even when we go to concerts or the theater, we might be alone.
This has led to a striking decline in all kinds of third spaces, places where people socialized away from home, including bowling alleys, recreation centers or shopping malls. People used to congregate, connect, build friendships and foster community in these places. We have become less likely to entertain people in our homes, too.
A more anti-social economy has implications beyond the business landscape. It can have wider negative externalities because isolation could contribute to worse mental health and loneliness that spills over to less productivity. Community in the past was often how people learned about new jobs. Sending in one of thousands of applications to an online posting has lower odds of success, can prolong the job search and frustrate us.
Trends in leisure are transient and even come back around. Movie theaters seem to be starting to make a comeback. And brands such as Tinder are launching new features designed to build community, in response to feedback from young people.
Perhaps an isolated Gen Alpha, hungry for more connection than Gen Z had, would shake things up and seek out social leisure again. We might find new third places, such as waiting in line for frozen yogurt. Or perhaps bowling would be discovered by influencers, and our new third place would be waiting in line for bowling shoes.
Allison Schrager is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering economics. A senior fellow at the Manhattan Institute, she is author of “Worth the Risk: The Seven Myths That Keep Us From Taking the Chances We Need to Take.” This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

Attack aircraft, military vehicles visible at China-Laos base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:37:49 UTC
01:37:49 KST

Light attack aircraft and military vehicles have arrived at a new China-Laos joint training facility announced on Tuesday last week, according to satellite images reviewed by Reuters.
The images, taken by commercial satellite provider Vantor, show what security analysts believe are eight K-8 light attack jets and more than two dozen support vehicles on a runway that is still being built — China’s latest expansion of its overseas military presence.
Taken on Wednesday last week — the day after the Chinese Ministry of National Defense announced it had set up the facility at Ban Keun outside the capital, Vientiane — the images show extensive construction work around the runway.
Photo: EPA
The swift development of the new facility is being closely watched by regional military attaches and security academics, some of whom say its construction potentially marks China’s first fully fledged overseas military base in Southeast Asia.
Despite more than 20 years of intense military modernization, China is widely perceived to lack a strong network of overseas facilities beyond the South China Sea, port access in Ream, Cambodia, and a logistics base in Djibouti.
Australian Strategic Policy Institute senior analyst Rachel Vandenbrink said the selection of Ban Keun for a facility that the Chinese People’s Liberation Army could access “is likely more about a target of opportunity than filling an obvious operational need.”
Photo: Vantor/Handout via Reuters
“Laos does have some geostrategic value as an accessible foothold in mainland Southeast Asia, given its shared border with China and infrastructure links, including [its] railway,” Vandenbrink said.
The Chinese defense ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The Laotian embassy in Bangkok and the Laotian Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Singapore-based security analysts Collin Koh (高瑞連) and Alexander Neill, as well as Vantor specialists, said the planes appeared to be Hongdu JL-8 aircraft, which the Chinese and Laotian air forces operate.
Also known as the K-8, the two-seater aircraft is extensively used for training as well as having light attack capabilities. It was jointly developed by China and Pakistan and is exported to other militaries.
Laos has four of the planes, according to the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies’ annual assessment of the world’s militaries.
Koh, a senior fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, described the Laotian planes as being of “questionable serviceability.”
As construction continues, diplomats and analysts are keeping watch for any sign of air defenses, ammunition and fuel storage as well as surveillance facilities — all of which could point to the base serving broader military functions beyond training.
Neill said that while the airfield looked relatively short and innocuous, it could later serve larger aircraft, including signals intelligence and electronic-surveillance planes to extend China’s reach into Southeast Asia.
“It looks like the airfield has been engineered to accommodate a runway extension allowing larger aircraft to operate,” said Neill, an adjunct fellow at Pacific Forum think tank in Hawaii.
In helping Laos build up Ban Keun, China is occupying a site the US used covertly at the height of the Vietnam War.
During the US war against communist forces in Laos in the 1970s, Ban Keun was an airfield known as “Lima Site 44” used by Air America, an airline discreetly owned by the CIA, according to records shared with Reuters by Ryan Wolfson-Ford, a Southeast Asia specialist at the Library of Congress.
The airline carried US-backed troops from the country’s Hmong highland minority as well as supplies into rough mountain airstrips known as “Lima Sites.”
As early as 1968, Ban Keun was used as a point from where Air America helicopters delivered Hmong troops to other combat zones, said Joachim Leeker, an academic who has written about the history of the airline.

ENGLISH DIGEST 實用美語(空中美語)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:37:49 UTC
01:37:49 KST

In a recent incident shared on social media, a troubling scene unfolded at a busy intersection. An ambulance, its siren blaring, attempted to pass through traffic, yet the vehicles ahead remained still. According to the original poster, the intersection was monitored by traffic enforcement cameras. Drivers, wary of automatic fines for crossing the stop line or running a red light, chose compliance over compassion and didn’t move. As a result, the ambulance was delayed for four crucial minutes, which could have meant the difference between life and death.
The intent of automated enforcement is both practical and necessary. These systems are designed to support police forces with limited resources and ensure safety in high-risk areas where on-site enforcement would be hazardous to officers. By deterring reckless behavior through consistent monitoring, technology theoretically creates a more disciplined driving environment.
However, the controversy lies not in the concept itself, but in the system’s shortcomings. While these cameras capture violations, the subsequent human review process often fails to account for emergency situations. For many drivers, the burden of proof has shifted unfairly. Those who yield to emergency vehicles frequently find themselves trapped in a bureaucratic nightmare, forced to take time off work to appeal unjust fines. Even with recorded footage, short retention often leads to a lack of evidence in these appeals, leaving drivers punished for doing the right thing. When the administrative cost of basic civic responsibility becomes too high, social cooperation inevitably weakens.
Photo: Freepik 照片：Freepik
The solution is not to abolish technology, but to refine its implementation. If the basic social virtue of yielding to an ambulance is replaced by the fear of an automatic fine, the system is fundamentally broken. More robust review mechanisms are needed, potentially including systems that compare ambulance GPS data with camera footage. Only then can technology truly serve both justice and humanity, rather than forcing people to choose between them.
近期在社群媒體上分享的一則事件中，一處繁忙的路口上演了令人憂心的一幕。一輛鳴笛的救護車試圖穿過車陣，然而前方的車輛卻紋絲不動。據原發文者稱，該路口被交通執法攝影機監控著。顧慮跨越停止線或闖紅燈會被自動開罰的駕駛們，選擇了遵守交通規則而非惻隱之心，並沒有移動。結果，救護車被延誤了關鍵的四分鐘，而這可能意味著生與死的差別。
科技執法的目的是既實用也必要的。這些系統被設計來支援資源有限的警力，並在那些現場執法對警員而言具危險性的高風險區域，確保交通安全。透過持續監測來阻嚇魯莽的行為，科技在理論上創造了一個更守紀律的駕駛環境。
然而，爭議不在於概念本身，而在於系統的缺陷。雖然這些攝影機捕捉到了違規行為，但後續的人工審核程序常常未能考量到緊急情況。對許多駕駛來說，舉證責任被不公平地轉嫁了。那些禮讓救援車輛的人經常發現自己陷入了官僚噩夢，被迫上班請假去申訴不公的罰單。即便有錄影畫面，短暫的保存期限往往導致這些申訴缺乏證據，讓駕駛反而因做正確的事情受到懲罰。當實踐基本公民責任的行政成本過高時，社會合作必然會削弱。
解決之道並非廢除科技，而是優化其執行方式。如果對科技執法罰單的恐懼，取代了禮讓救護車這項基本美德，那這個系統從根本上就是壞掉的。我們需要更完善的審查機制，可能包括將救護車的GPS數據與攝影機畫面進行比對的系統。唯有如此，科技才能真正兼顧公正與人性，而非強迫人們在兩者之間做選擇。

77-year-old former air force officer charged with spying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:37:47 UTC
01:37:47 KST

The Taoyuan District Prosecutors’ Office yesterday indicted a 77-year-old retired air force captain for allegedly spying for China and collecting personal information about Taiwanese intelligence personnel, including obtaining property records through his son, a real-estate agent.
The man, surnamed Fai (費), retired from the air force in 1976 and went on to serve as a township official in China’s Hebei Province in 2021, prosecutors said.
Prosecutors said Fai in January 2024 was instructed by a man named Gao Jinli (高金力) in China to collect information on an intelligence officer from a Taiwanese government agency in exchange for an undisclosed sum.
Photo: Yu Ruei-ren, Taipei Times
Gao allegedly asked Fai to find out the target’s occupation, vehicle information, home address and workplace, as well as other personal information, they said.
Fai allegedly hired a private investigator to look into the target, prosecutors said, adding the investigator was unaware of the purpose of the inquiry.
Fai allegedly used his 47-year-old son’s position at a real-estate company to access the company’s system and obtain records of properties registered to the target, prosecutors said.
He passed the information he had collected to Gao, they said.
In July 2024, Gao allegedly again instructed Fai to collect information on another officer.
On Aug. 17, investigators got a warrant to search Fai’s residence, subsequently detaining him.
After questioning Fai, a court granted prosecutors’ request to hold him incommunicado.
Fai denied the allegations, saying his personal information and telephone number had been misused, a source familiar with the case said.
Fai was charged under the National Intelligence Work Act (國家情報工作法) for alleged espionage and collecting, obtaining and disclosing information on the identities and movements of Taiwanese intelligence personnel to people in China.
He was also charged under the National Security Act (國家安全法) for allegedly collecting and providing documents and electronic records concerning classified matters, and under the Personal Data Protection Act (個人資料保護法) with illegally using personal information as a non-government entity.
His son was charged under the Personal Data Protection Act, prosecutors said.

Turnover, retention rates among public servants worsening
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:37:47 UTC
01:37:47 KST

For the past four years, more than 55 percent of civil servants quit after working less than five years, with the turnover rate reaching a new high last year, a report by the Legislative Yuan’s Budget Center said.
The center released the figures as part of the central government’s general budget for next year.
The turnover rate for civil servants remained high in the past few years, with 18,072 central and local civil servants quitting their jobs from 2022 to last year, the report said.
Photo: Chung Li-hua, Taipei Times
Of all those who quit during the period, 5,965 were first-time civil servants and had less than five years of service, accounting for 55 percent, it said.
The number of first-timers with less than five years of experience who quit rose from 1,341 people in 2022 to 1,652 last year, the report said.
They represented the bulk of resignations across the public sector over the period, at rates from 51.53 to 59.43 percent, surpassing 50 percent each year, it said.
The High Court and its subordinate courts had the highest number of new-hire resignations for employees with less than five years of experience at 419, the report said.
It was followed by the Ministry of Justice and its agencies’ 386 people, the Veterans Affairs Council and its agencies’ 343 people, the Ministry of Transportation and Communications and its agencies’ 264 people, and the Ministry of the Interior and its agencies’ 231 people, it said.
There were 3,323 resignations across local governments nationwide over the same period: 2,355 resignations in the six major municipalities, much higher than the other administrative areas’ total of 968 people, the report said.
The six special municipalities made up 71 percent of such short-tenure resignations across local governments, it said.
The budget center said that civil service retirements are increasing.
Fewer people are signing up for the national civil service examination, while shortfalls in recruitment are growing year by year, it said, adding the technical categories had the biggest shortfalls.
The authorities should identify the root cause of the shortfalls and enhance their employee assistance measures, the center said.
The goal is to develop strong public service workforces and friendly workspaces, increasing the government’s administrative efficiency, it said.

Lai lauds Taiwan athletes after lackluster Asian Games performance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:37:46 UTC
01:37:46 KST

President William Lai (賴清德) yesterday praised Taiwan’s athletes for their performances at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, saying their effort was a source of national pride regardless of the amount of medals won.
Meeting members of Taiwan’s delegation at the Presidential Office in Taipei, Lai congratulated the medalists in his remarks, saying that “regardless of the color, every medal is an honor for the country.”
Competing under the name Chinese Taipei, Taiwan won five golds, 17 silvers and 33 bronzes for a total of 55 medals, ranking 15th among 46 delegations based on the number of gold medals won.
Photo: CNA
It was Taiwan’s lowest gold medal haul and lowest overall ranking since the 1990 Asian Games in Beijing, when it ranked 16th in the medals table and did not win any gold medals, and the total medal haul of 55 was the second lowest in the last five Asian Games.
It had also won at least 10 gold medals in six of the previous seven Asian Games.
Lai also paid tribute to athletes who returned without medals.
“Your years of effort, enduring injuries and setbacks, and every step you have taken are equally significant to the country,” Lai said.
Lai highlighted the performances of several Taiwanese medalists, including high jumper Fu Chao-hsuan (傅兆玄), who cleared 2.25 meters to win Taiwan’s first Asian Games men’s track and field gold in 60 years, and swimmer Wang Kuan-hung (王冠閎), whose victory ended Taiwan’s 28- year wait for an Asian Games swimming gold.
Lai also applauded boxer Lin Yu-ting (林郁婷) for winning a second consecutive Asian Games gold after overcoming setbacks over the past two years and silver medalist Chen Nien-chin (陳念琴) for embracing her Indian opponent following their closely contested final.
Speaking on behalf of the athletes, Chen said her silver was her best Asian Games result, but stressed that individual achievements were built on the work of an entire support team.
“People see one person’s result, but what I want everyone to see is the group of people who made that result possible,” she said, thanking her coach, sparring partners and training team for their support.
Minister of Sports Lee Yang (李洋), a two-time Olympic badminton men’s doubles gold medalist, said he understood how strongly athletes wanted to win and make the most of the effort they had put into preparing for competition.
He said his ministry would continue improving logistical support, including transportation and meals, to ensure athletes were better cared for at future competitions.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:37:40 UTC
01:37:40 KST

In diligent, exhausted Japan, self-described elite “competitive sleepers” vied to lie down, relax and nap the fastest and deepest in a contest organized by a mattress company.
In the Tokyo competition, dubbed “Matt Race,” dozens of participants on Monday fitted with sleep tracking devices sprawled on comfy mattresses to slumber for up to 90 minutes, competing for the top prize of more than ￥2 million (US$12,645).
“Japan is often described as a country suffering from sleep deprivation, and people here are very diligent,” said Riichiro Nakama, creative director at organizer Koala Sleep Japan, the mattress company.
Photo: AFP
Inside a dimly lit room, participants slept with monitors attached to their heads, some cradling stuffed toys in their beds.
“By turning it into an event like this, I think we can get people to sleep together, raise interest in sleep,” Nakama said.
Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) data showed in 2021 that Japanese slept an average seven hours 24 minutes a day — the least of all OECD nations within the group — with experts citing long working and commuting hours and a busy nightlife economy as among contributing factors.
“It was over in an instant. I almost wish I could have slept a little longer,” participant Chisato Honda, 32, said.
“It was a happy competition,” he added.
The winner was chosen based on how quickly and soundly they slept.
“I want to live on my own, so I think I’ll use the money for the moving costs,” said Suimii, the contest winner who only gave her nickname.
“I also want a bed like a princess’, so I think I’ll buy that bed,” she added.

Nobel winner Deisseroth to visit in March next year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:37:39 UTC
01:37:39 KST

Karl Deisseroth, the Stanford University professor who on Monday won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, is scheduled to speak at Academia Sinica in March next year, the Science Media Center Taiwan said.
Peter Hegemann, a professor at Humboldt University of Berlin, Georg Nagel, a professor at the University of Wurzburg in Germany, and Deisseroth shared this year’s Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for “their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics,” the Nobel Assembly at the Karolinska Institutet said.
Deisseroth is to deliver a lecture as part of a series established by former Academia Sinica president Wong Chi-huey (翁啟惠), the Science Media Center Taiwan told a news conference later on Monday, at which four Taiwanese academics discussed the laureates’ research.
Photo: AFP
Lien Cheng-chang (連正章), a professor in National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University’s Institute of Neuroscience and dean of its College of Life Sciences who wrote the foreword to the Chinese edition of Deisseroth’s Projections: A Story of Human Emotions, said that despite Deisseroth’s quiet demeanor, his warmth and sensitivity are evident in the book.
Yao Hao-chieh (姚皓傑), an associate professor in National Taiwan University’s Institute of Brain and Mind Sciences, said that he collaborated with Deisseroth on a research paper that used optogenetic tools developed by Deisseroth to manipulate and regulate neural circuits with light and a high degree of specificity.
The technology enables researchers to better understand the relationship between the brain and behavior, and has become a widely used research tool, Yao said.
Deisseroth has patented the tools and platforms he developed, specifying that they are intended for research and treatment of neurological and psychiatric disorders and pain, Lien said.
The technology has been used in animal studies of drug addiction, mood disorders, depression and Alzheimer’s disease, he said.
Lin Wan-chen (林宛蓁), an assistant research fellow in Academia Sinica’s Institute of Biomedical Sciences, said that Deisseroth readily shares the tools and technologies he develops with other researchers.
It was Deisseroth’s willingness to share his work that helped optogenetics develop into a major field of research, Lin said.
In 2021, a research team used the technology on the retina of a blind person and, with specially designed glasses, restored some vision, Lin said.
Other researchers have also explored using the technology with cochlear implants and to suppress epileptic seizures, she said.
Kuo Hsiao-ying (郭曉縈), an assistant professor in National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University’s Institute of Anatomy and Cell Biology, warned that safety and other issues need to be addressed before the technology can be widely used to treat neurological and psychiatric disorders in humans.

Arizona Governor Katie Hobbs joined Taiwanese leaders at the opening of an economic and cultural office on Monday to aid Taiwanese businesses and citizens in the region, despite pressure from the Chinese government to block it.
The new Phoenix office, the 14th such office in the US, is meant to promote collaboration in technology, especially in semiconductor manufacturing, and better serve the growing number of Taiwanese in the city.
After the plans for the office were announced in July, Hobbs received two letters from China’s consulate general in Los Angeles asking her to object to the proposal, according to documents the governor’s office shared with The Associated Press.
Photo: AP
In a July 3 letter, the Chinese authority called on the governor to “refute such an attempt by the Taiwan authorities and stop any political gimmicks to harm the friendship and cooperation between China and the state of Arizona.”
The stance was reiterated in an Aug. 21 letter.
The letters were first reported by Phoenix radio station KJZZ.
Hobbs spoke about Arizona’s ties with Taiwan at Monday’s opening.
“Every Arizona elected official should show the courage necessary to support the partnership between Arizona and Taiwan,” Hobbs said. “As our economic partnership grows, we are mobilizing every available resource to support Taiwanese companies expanding here in Arizona.”
Academics say that local-level collaborations with the Chinese government and Taiwan have become more politicized as US-China relations have deteriorated over the years.
“China firmly opposes official interactions of any form between China’s Taiwan region and the US, including its federal and state governments,” Liu Chang (劉暢), a spokesperson for China’s embassy in the US, said in a statement on Monday.
Taiwan has been increasing its economic footprint in Arizona, with advanced chipmaker Taiwanese Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) pledging US$100 billion to expand its operation in northern Phoenix. That brings its investment in the city to US$265 billion, the largest foreign direct investment in US history.
About 500 Taiwanese engineers are working in Arizona to accelerate production at the TSMC facility, according to Jason Hsu (許毓仁), a former Taiwanese lawmaker and a senior fellow at the public policy think tank Hudson Institute.
Phoenix Mayor Kate Gallego said the city is seeing a sort of “baby boom” in its Taiwanese communities, with several labor and delivery rooms even launching Mandarin-language programs.
At the opening ceremony on Monday, Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) said the establishment of the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office in Phoenix is a milestone in the “symbiotic partnership” between Taiwan and the US.
The partnership is built on shared interests, mutual benefits and a commitment to working together to promote growth and prosperity, he said.
Lin said that Arizona is an important economic partner for Taiwan.
In the first quarter alone, TSMC’s US operations generated nearly US$600 million in profit, surpassing its full-year profit from last year, he said.
The strong growth demonstrated how Taiwan’s investments are creating value for both sides, he said.

Ukrainian military video shows reload vehicle for Russian Buk-M3 anti-aircraft system being destroyed by drones for first time
The Ukrainian military have used drones to destroy a Russian transport-loading vehicle for the Buk-M3 anti-aircraft missile system. The Third Separate Assault Brigade reported the strike.
Source: 3rd Assault Brigade; Ukrainska Pravda
Details: The brigade said the drones attacked a vehicle that was intended to reload the Buk T9243M. The strike was carried out by attack drone operators from the SkyFOM platoon in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Army Corps.

Footage of the Buk-M3 reload vehicle being destroyed. Video: 3rd Assault Brigade

What is 'Bibiwood'? The conspiracy theories around the FlyDubai incident
An alleged attempt by a FlyDubai co-pilot to crash a Tel Aviv-bound passenger plane has spawned conspiracy theories online, with sceptics branding the incident "Bibiwood" and questioning virtually every element of the official account.
The theories began circulating within hours of the incident aboard flight FZ1073 last Wednesday, ranging from claims that Israeli intelligence orchestrated the attack to suggestions that it never happened at all.
Others have focused on the timing ahead of Israel's 27 October election, the flight number, details in passenger videos and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's subsequent meeting with passengers involved.
Emirati authorities said the Omani co-pilot attacked the captain with an emergency axe and attempted to seize control of the aircraft before passengers and crew intervened.
Reuters reported on Monday, citing two Israeli officials with knowledge of the investigation, that the co-pilot told UAE interrogators he had planned the attack before joining FlyDubai.
What is 'Bibiwood'?
"Bibiwood" combines Benjamin Netanyahu's nickname, Bibi, with Hollywood, and is being used by sceptics who claim aspects of the incident were staged, manipulated or orchestrated by Israel.
The theories vary considerably.
Some allege the entire incident was a "false flag" orchestrated by Israel, with theories ranging from an attempt to generate international sympathy to claims it was staged ahead of Israel's 27 October election.
Netanyahu has been accused of capitalising politically on the incident after it occurred, publicly embracing returning passengers and linking the attack to earlier warnings he made about security threats
Opposition leader Yair Lapid accused Netanyahu's allies of playing "cheap politics", while a source close to the UAE government reportedly said Abu Dhabi believed "the election is driving the matter, not logic".
Israeli media have also questioned Netanyahu's handling of the incident, with the Times of Israel describing it as a "perfect campaign prop" as the prime minister sought to associate himself with the passengers' heroism
What are the theories based on?
Online sceptics have scrutinised videos filmed aboard the aircraft for apparent inconsistencies.
Some have questioned why oxygen masks were apparently not visible following reports that the aircraft rapidly lost altitude, while others have pointed to apparently calm passengers or objects remaining upright.
Passenger interviews have attracted similar scrutiny, particularly accounts from those who helped restrain the alleged attacker and regain control of the cockpit.
Early uncertainty also provided fertile ground for competing accounts.
While dramatic details emerged through Israeli media and officials, FlyDubai's initial statements were considerably more limited, describing an onboard incident while authorities investigated what had happened.
The UAE subsequently released a more detailed account confirming the attack and identifying the weapon allegedly used.
Sceptics have also questioned the fortuitous presence of two additional FlyDubai pilots aboard the aircraft, who were able to take control after the alleged attacker was subdued. The pair were reportedly "deadheading" crew - pilots travelling as passengers to be repositioned for operational duties.
Questions have also focused on how the cockpit door was opened. Captain Smit Machchhar has said crew outside were unable to gain access while the co-pilot controlled the cockpit, but that he eventually reached the door's internal release and opened it himself, allowing those outside to enter.
A fake video styled to resemble a BBC report has meanwhile circulated online alleging that Mossad and Indian intelligence were involved.
Questions about the official account have not been confined to anonymous social media users.
Ayoub Khan, the independent MP for Birmingham Perry Barr, publicly questioned the speed at which details of the investigation emerged.
Khan said he was "genuinely shocked" by how quickly Israeli authorities appeared to have established details about the alleged plot, adding: "I think I smell a rat."
The incident has also become entangled with broader opposition to Netanyahu and the Israeli government's ongoing genocide in Gaza, with social media users citing multiple instances of Israel lying about its activities.
The UAE investigation is continuing into the circumstances of the alleged attack, including the co-pilot's motives and possible connections.

Mudbrick houses: The heritage of traditional Iranian architecture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:35:29 UTC
01:35:29 KST

Mudbrick houses: The heritage of traditional Iranian architecture
TEHRAN - Across Iran’s deserts, dry plains and mountain valleys, houses built from earth form some of the country’s most distinctive architectural landscapes. Their rounded roofs, thick walls, shaded courtyards and, in places, tall windcatchers are more than picturesque features. They are the result of centuries of experience in building with local materials and adapting everyday life to a difficult climate.
Mudbrick, or adobe, is among the oldest building traditions in the ancient country. Archaeological evidence shows that sun-dried mud bricks were being used in the Iranian plateau as early as the late 9th or early 8th millennium BCE. At Tepe Ganj Dareh in present-day Kermanshah province, early walls were built with shaped, sun-dried mud bricks. This means that the history of earthen construction in Iran is far older than the Achaemenid, Sasanian or Islamic periods.
Over thousands of years, Iranian builders refined the use of earth into a sophisticated architectural tradition. Mud was readily available, relatively inexpensive and particularly suitable for many of Iran’s dry regions. It could be shaped into bricks, packed into walls or used in other forms of earthen construction. Straw and chaff were commonly mixed with the earth, while walls could be protected with mud, lime or other plasters.
For visitors, the appeal of these buildings lies not only in their age. Traditional earthen architecture offers a way to understand how Iranian communities once responded to heat, cold, limited water and scarce building materials without relying on modern mechanical systems.
Architecture shaped by climate
Much of central and southeastern Iran has hot, dry summers, strong sunlight and limited rainfall. Traditional houses developed in response to these conditions.
One of the most important features is the thick earthen wall. Such walls slow the transfer of heat, helping interiors remain relatively cooler during the day and retaining warmth when temperatures fall at night. The effect is reinforced by courtyards, shaded passages, underground spaces and carefully positioned openings.
In Yazd, perhaps the best-known surviving example of this approach, the relationship between architecture and climate can be seen throughout the historic city. UNESCO describes Yazd as a living example of the intelligent use of limited resources in a desert environment. Its traditional buildings use earth for walls and roofs, while courtyards, thick walls and windcatchers help create a more comfortable microclimate.
The result is an urban landscape that can appear almost monochromatic from a distance. Up close, however, its surfaces reveal different textures and shades of earth, plaster and brick. Narrow lanes often provide shade, while partially covered passages known as Sa’bats protect pedestrians from the intense sun.
For a traveler walking through Yazd’s old quarters, these details make the city feel less like an open-air museum and more like a functioning architectural system. The buildings, streets, water infrastructure and public spaces were designed as parts of the same environment.
The courtyard at the heart of the home
The traditional Iranian house was not simply a collection of rooms surrounded by walls. In many regions, the courtyard was the center of domestic life.
Rooms were arranged around an enclosed open space, creating privacy and providing a protected environment for family life. In desert cities such as Yazd, courtyards could also be positioned below street level. UNESCO notes that traditional houses in Yazd include sunken courtyards and underground areas, which helped improve the local microclimate.
This inward-looking design was also connected to cultural ideas about privacy. Unlike many modern houses, which open toward streets and public spaces, traditional Iranian homes often turned their main living spaces toward the courtyard.
The courtyard could contain trees, plants and sometimes a pool or water feature. These elements were not merely decorative. Shade and vegetation helped soften the heat, while water contributed to a sense of coolness and comfort.
The house therefore became a small climate-controlled world, achieved through architectural planning rather than machinery.
Windcatchers: an ingenious response to heat
Few elements of Iranian architecture are more recognizable than the Badgir, or windcatcher.
These tall towers rise above many traditional houses and other buildings in central Iran. Their function is simple but effective: they capture air and direct it into the building. Depending on their design and the prevailing conditions, windcatchers can help circulate air through rooms and other parts of a house.
Yazd’s skyline is particularly famous for them. UNESCO identifies windcatchers, courtyards and thick earthen walls as important elements of the city’s traditional climate-adapted architecture.
A Badgir also demonstrates an important characteristic of vernacular architecture: local builders did not necessarily need sophisticated modern technology to solve environmental problems. They observed wind, temperature, sunlight and seasonal changes, then incorporated that knowledge into the buildings themselves.
For tourists, climbing to a rooftop in the historic quarters of Yazd offers one of the best ways to appreciate this relationship. From above, windcatchers, domes and earthen roofs appear as a continuous architectural landscape, with modern development often disappearing behind the old city’s dense fabric.
From bricks to domes and vaults
Mudbrick was only one part of Iran’s earthen-building tradition. Builders also developed sophisticated methods for constructing arches, vaults and domes.
The advantage was both practical and structural. Curved roofs could span spaces without requiring the large quantities of timber that were difficult to obtain in many arid regions.
The technique can be seen on a monumental scale at Bam in Kerman province. The UNESCO-listed Bam and its Cultural Landscape contains the remains of a fortified settlement constructed with mud layers, known as Chineh, sun-dried mud bricks or Khesht, as well as vaulted and domed structures. The origins of Bam can be traced to the Achaemenid period, while the citadel reached its height between the seventh and 11th centuries.
Bam is particularly important because its architecture cannot be separated from the oasis that supported it. Underground irrigation channels, or Qanats, brought water into the settlement and allowed agriculture and urban life to develop in an otherwise arid environment. UNESCO considers the relationship between the earthen settlement and its water system an outstanding example of the interaction between people and their environment.
The earthquake of 2003 severely damaged the historic citadel, but conservation work has preserved and restored important parts of its traditional fabric. The site remains one of Iran’s most powerful places for understanding earthen architecture on a large scale.
An architectural tradition across Iran
Yazd and Bam are perhaps the best-known destinations, but earthen construction is not confined to these two places.
Traditional earth architecture can be encountered across large parts of central, eastern and southeastern Iran. Historic settlements and houses in areas around Kerman, Kashan, South Khorasan and Sistan reflect different versions of the same broad knowledge: use what the land provides and design buildings according to local climate and resources.
The materials and construction methods were not identical everywhere. Iran’s architectural traditions developed according to local soil, climate, available vegetation, water resources and building customs.
This regional diversity is one reason it is misleading to think of “mudbrick architecture” as a single architectural style. A house in Yazd may look quite different from an earthen building in Kerman or South Khorasan. What connects them is the use of earth and a long tradition of adapting architecture to place.
The archaeological record also shows that the use of mudbrick continued through different historical periods. Encyclopaedia Iranica notes that sun-dried mud bricks were predominant in Iran until the end of the Achaemenid period, while later periods saw increasing use of fired brick in important buildings.
This combination of continuity and change is visible across Iran’s historic towns. Earthen construction did not disappear when fired brick, stone and other materials became available. Instead, different materials were often used according to function, location and status.
Why mudbrick matters today
Traditional mudbrick houses are increasingly vulnerable to neglect, abandonment, urban expansion and the replacement of traditional materials with modern construction. Yet the knowledge embodied in them has gained new relevance at a time when architects around the world are looking for ways to reduce energy consumption and respond to climate change.
The historic city of Yazd has become an important reference point in this discussion. UNESCO describes its earthen architecture as a source of inspiration for contemporary architecture facing sustainability challenges.
The lesson is not that modern buildings should simply copy old houses. Rather, traditional architecture demonstrates how much can be achieved through passive design: orientation, shade, thermal mass, natural ventilation, compact urban form and the careful use of local resources.
One contemporary initiative is the Esfahk Mud Center in the historic village of Esfahk in South Khorasan province. Founded in 2015, the center focuses on education and the revival of traditional earthen construction techniques. Research on Esfahk has documented courses and practical work involving traditional building methods, including the construction of vaults.
For visitors interested in architecture, Esfahk offers a different experience from the major heritage cities. It provides an opportunity to see traditional techniques not simply as archaeological remains, but as knowledge that is still being studied, taught and tested.
A different way to experience Iran
The best way to understand Iran’s mudbrick heritage is to walk through it.
In Yazd, travelers can explore historic neighborhoods where earthen houses, windcatchers, domes, covered lanes and traditional water systems remain part of the urban landscape. UNESCO inscribed the Historic City of Yazd on the World Heritage List in 2017, recognizing its exceptional earthen architecture and its adaptation to the desert environment.
In Bam, the scale changes. The citadel reveals how earth could be used not only for individual houses but for an entire fortified settlement. Its walls, towers, courtyards, vaulted spaces and relationship with the oasis show how architecture, trade, water management and security were woven together.
Elsewhere, smaller villages and historic neighborhoods offer a quieter encounter with the same tradition. Their value often lies precisely in their simplicity: an earthen wall, a shaded alley, a courtyard, an arched roof or a weathered brick surface can reveal centuries of practical knowledge.
Iran’s mudbrick houses are therefore more than remnants of a pre-industrial past. They are evidence of how generations of builders learned to live with their environment. The earth beneath their feet became walls and roofs; scarce water shaped their settlements; the desert sun influenced the orientation of their homes; and the wind was turned into a natural source of ventilation.
For travelers, these buildings offer an architectural journey into that accumulated knowledge. For architects and conservationists, they offer lessons that remain relevant. And for local communities, preserving them means protecting not only old buildings but a part of the knowledge, identity and landscape that made life possible in some of Iran’s harshest environments.

Lithuania Moves to Lift Constitutional Ban on Nuclear Weapons on Its Territory
Lithuania’s parliament has backed a constitutional amendment that would remove the country’s ban on weapons of mass destruction, including nuclear weapons, being stationed on Lithuanian territory, LRT reported on October 6.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The proposed amendment would remove part of Article 137 of Lithuania’s Constitution, which currently prohibits weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases from being located on the country’s territory. The proposal under consideration concerns the provision on weapons of mass destruction.
Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas said removing the restriction would strengthen Lithuania’s resilience and deterrence capabilities while eliminating legal differences between Lithuania and other EU and NATO members.
Opposition Conservative leader Laurynas Kasčiūnas, who supported the amendment, said Lithuania’s existing restrictions prevent allied aircraft or ships carrying nuclear weapons from entering the country for deterrence purposes.
“With the current restriction, we cannot fully participate in NATO’s nuclear deterrence plans. Since nuclear deterrence is the queen of all deterrence, this decision is strategically important,” Kasčiūnas said.
Lithuanian Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas also supported the change, linking the initiative to the security environment created by Russia’s war against Ukraine and the presence of strategic weapons in Belarus and Russia’s Kaliningrad region.
“We are responding to Russia’s aggression. If Russia had not started the war in Ukraine, we probably would not be having the discussions that we are having today,” Kaunas said.
The debate over Lithuania’s constitutional restrictions also follows recent Russian nuclear threats involving Kaliningrad, the heavily militarized Russian exclave bordering Poland and Lithuania. On September 30, Reuters reported that Moscow had privately warned NATO it could resort to nuclear weapons if the alliance sought to isolate the region.
In a diplomatic note sent to NATO and reviewed by Reuters, Russia accused the alliance of pursuing a “dangerous and reckless course” that posed “high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict.”

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
InformNapalm examined Russian corporate and conformity records linked to NRTK KAPS LLC, a Moscow-based company headed and solely owned by Zorikto Gombozhapov, who is connected to the development of the Kurier military robot.
The investigation identified dozens of Russian declarations from 2025 and 2026 in which NRTK KAPS was listed as the applicant and Shenzhen-based HD LED TECHNOLOGY CO., LTD. as the manufacturer.
The equipment covered by the records included radio modules and modems, chargers, batteries, IP cameras, power supplies, and other electronics.
One declaration dated July 30, 2025, covered 4,200 WTX-2S6 batteries and 8,400 WTX-2A2DC batteries—a total of 12,600 units.
InformNapalm stressed that declarations of conformity are not customs records and do not prove that all of the listed equipment was actually imported into Russia or installed in Kurier systems. The documents instead demonstrate the scale of Chinese-origin equipment covered by declarations filed by a company directly linked to the robot’s developer.
The investigation also raised questions about the role of HD LED TECHNOLOGY. In one Russian declaration, the Chinese company was listed as the manufacturer of a JY-ME02-CAN encoder. However, an independent 2025 technical paper identified the same model as a product of Shenzhen-based WIT Motion.
InformNapalm said the available evidence does not establish the precise relationship between the companies, which could involve contract manufacturing, OEM production, consolidation, or resale.
Gombozhapov’s business links to China also predate the NRTK KAPS declarations. Another company he heads, Eychdi LLC, filed declarations in 2024 covering products from Chinese manufacturers SHENZHEN DICOLOR GROUP CO., LTD. and Unilumin Group Co., Ltd.
Corporate records examined by InformNapalm also showed that Gombozhapov previously co-owned Moscow-based NIHAO LLC with Chinese citizen Du Tianzhu, with each holding a 25% stake.
Kurier is a Russian remotely operated tracked UGV designed for logistics and combat missions, including ammunition transport, casualty evacuation, reconnaissance, mine-laying, and weapons carriage. Configurations have been shown carrying PKTM 7.62 mm machine guns, NSVT or Kord heavy machine guns, and AGS-17 and AGS-30 automatic grenade launchers.
On October 2, Russian Airborne Forces also conducted their first reported airdrop of Kurier UGVs from an Il-76 transport aircraft during the Center-2026 exercise. The systems were dropped from an altitude of roughly 600 meters before being used to support an assault unit.

Pezeshkian calls for broader engagement with EU, Asia
TEHRAN — Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has called for expanded political, economic, scientific, and cultural relations with countries across Europe and Asia, stressing Tehran’s commitment to peaceful engagement, multilateral cooperation, and stronger regional ties.
Pezeshkian made the remarks in separate meetings with the newly appointed ambassadors of Denmark, Thailand and India to Tehran, as well as during a ceremony to bid farewell to Iran’s new ambassadors to several countries.
Receiving the credentials of Denmark’s new ambassador, Pezeshkian said the Iranian nation had historically pursued peace, tranquility, constructive communication and healthy interaction with other countries.

Iran, Thailand seek wider cooperation

President urges new envoys to advance national interests
At a separate ceremony to bid farewell to Iran’s newly appointed ambassadors to the United Arab Emirates, Greece, Italy, Uganda and Senegal, Pezeshkian instructed the envoys to advance Iran’s national interests, expand multilateral relations and strengthen economic engagement with their host countries.

U.S. Army robot mule contest gets BLADE’s Hunter WOLF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:33:18 UTC
01:33:18 KST

- BLADE, formerly HDT, submitted its Hunter WOLF robotic vehicle for the U.S. Army's Infantry Last Tactical Mile resupply and casualty evacuation initiative.
- The U.S. Army selected six vendors in August and plans an operational assessment with an Army unit in early 2027 to inform production.
BLADE, the robotics company formerly known as HDT, said it has submitted its Hunter WOLF unmanned ground vehicle for the U.S. Army’s Infantry Last Tactical Mile initiative, a prototype effort to use robotic vehicles for resupply and casualty evacuation near the front line.
The company was one of six vendors the U.S. Army selected for the program in August. BLADE confirmed on Oct. 6 that the Hunter WOLF, a six-wheeled diesel-electric hybrid robot built for light and dismounted infantry, is the vehicle it will field. The company did not disclose the value of its agreement or how many vehicles it will provide.
The program, known as ILTM, focuses on the most exposed stretch of ground between rear support units and the forward line of own troops, where soldiers moving ammunition and supplies forward, or carrying wounded back, are most likely to come under fire. The U.S. Army chose the six vendors through prototype Other Transaction Agreements. The others are Maren-Go, Overland AI, Forterra, Hendrick’s Motorsports and American Rheinmetall.
According to the U.S. Army, the vendors will deliver production-ready prototypes that go through a series of demonstrations and assessments, ending with an operational assessment alongside an Army unit in early 2027. Feedback from that rotation is meant to inform a production decision on the Army’s next generation of autonomous infantry systems.
BLADE says the Hunter WOLF can carry 2,800 pounds (1,270 kg) autonomously, drive through dense forest, climb 60 percent grades and cross 40 percent side slopes. It can also supply electrical power to other equipment and accept different payloads depending on the mission, from cargo to casualty evacuation. The company describes the vehicle as production-ready and at Technology Readiness Level 9, the highest rating on the U.S. military’s scale, which indicates a system proven in actual operations.
“The Hunter WOLF is engineered, manufactured, field-proven and ready to support warfighters in challenging contested environments,” said Tom Van Doren, president of robotics at BLADE.
“It is battle-tested and field-proven to be the Army’s solution for the most dangerous and logistically complex segment of the battlefield,” Van Doren said.
The Hunter WOLF has been in service since 2017 and received upgrades in 2025. BLADE has run a string of evaluations with U.S. Army units this year, including the 10th Mountain Division and the 101st Airborne Division, and an August event with the 82nd Airborne Division at Fort Polk, Louisiana. The company has said the vehicle has supported the U.S. Marine Corps, Australian forces and the Ukrainian army and has been used in more than 60 field exercises.
In May, the company delivered Hunter WOLF vehicles to the 10th Mountain Division at Fort Polk under the U.S. Army’s Ground Optionally Autonomous Transport effort, training soldiers to operate and maintain them across several mission configurations.

INTERVIEW - 'We'll be up and operational' before ISS retires: Axiom Space CEO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:31:40 UTC
01:31:40 KST

- 'I believe there is a race to create a space economy,' Cirtain tells Anadolu
US firm Axiom Space will have its commercial space station operating before the International Space Station (ISS) is retired in 2030, the company's CEO said Tuesday.
"We're waiting on a solicitation from the US government, from NASA, for the procurement of the services for that replacement to the ISS. But meanwhile, we've been using our own capital to build our space station," Jonathan Cirtain told Anadolu on the sidelines of the 77th International Astronautical Congress in Antalya.
"We have two vehicles that we are in the process of completing the manufacture of, and we'll launch in 2028 and 2029 those first two modules," he said. "The International Space Station is not set to retire until 2030. So, we'll be up and operational in advance of the ISS being decommissioned."
Rather than build its own replacement for the ISS, NASA plans to buy services from privately owned and operated space stations. The agency put out a draft call for proposals in July. Its schedule targets contract awards in spring 2027.
Axiom, a Houston-based company, has flown four private astronaut missions to the ISS. It is also developing the spacesuits NASA astronauts are set to wear on the Moon. Cirtain, a physicist, became CEO in October 2025.
 
'Race to create a space economy'
Asked whether the world is entering a race to build the next space station, Cirtain said the competition is broader.
"I believe there is a race to create a space economy," he said. "Now that the ISS has done 25 years of research and development to demonstrate the uses of microgravity ... it's time to use those capabilities for the benefit of humans back here on Earth."
He also pointed to a separate competition over the Moon.
"I also think that there's a geopolitical race between the United States, Europe, and its allies, Japan, Canada, for exploration of the Moon and what resources are available there," he said.
Scientists believe the Moon's south pole contains water ice. That ice could one day supply astronauts with drinking water, oxygen and rocket fuel.
"The United States, its allies, and separately, China, are all seeking to explore and find out what those resources are," Cirtain said. "Whether it's a space race or something else ... what an exciting time it is to be in space."
As an example of what research in orbit can offer, he cited the cancer drug Keytruda. Its maker, Merck, has run crystal-growth experiments on the ISS since 2014. The research helped Merck develop an injectable version of the drug, which US regulators approved in 2025.
"There's a whole set of reasons why crystals grown in space are better than crystals grown on Earth," Cirtain said. He argued that commercial stations are now needed to turn such research into actual products.
 
Managing a more crowded orbit
Last month, US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said the US has weapons in orbit capable of defending its forces against hostile action. It was the most direct acknowledgment by a US official that such systems exist.
Asked how a commercial station could stay a neutral international laboratory amid such developments, Cirtain said: "I think the US government and what it might be doing for its defensive posture is kind of independent of how Axiom Station is meant to operate."
As for how he sees the future of the peaceful use of outer space, he said: "I think that is the purpose of Axiom Space. For the peaceful, purposeful use of space for the benefit of humans back here on Earth."
He said the ISS has gained extensive experience tracking and managing space debris and natural hazards such as micrometeorites. He warned, however, that growing traffic in low Earth orbit will demand more care.
"As more spacecraft are deployed, we're going to have to become more sophisticated about how we manage the use of low Earth orbit," he said. "I really hope that we are clever about the way in which we use that resource and don't saturate that resource."
Overcrowding, he added, could lead to more collisions and more maneuvers by spacecraft to avoid them.
On artificial intelligence, Cirtain acknowledged concerns over security. "I think there's a lot of interest in understanding how security around the use of AI should be considered," he said.
"But I also think that there's a lot of opportunity," he added. He said AI tools beyond the large frontier models could help operate spacecraft and make better use of data collected in orbit. "There are other types of artificial intelligence tools that I do believe benefit us."
 
Cooperation with Türkiye
Axiom Space and the Turkish Space Agency signed an agreement in January 2025 to explore how Türkiye's space industry could contribute to Axiom Station.
"This is an expansion of a relationship that's already existing," Cirtain said. He recalled that Axiom worked with Turkish industry and a university on a science payload for its Ax-3 mission in 2024. Alper Gezeravci, Türkiye's first astronaut, flew on that mission.
Axiom has since established a university alliance that includes Turkish institutions. Through the alliance, the company helps universities turn ground-based experiments into payloads that can fly in space.
"We see this as an ongoing relationship, and as the space ecosystem in Türkiye expands, we just see there even more opportunities for collaboration between Axiom Space and industry here in Türkiye," he said.
The congress runs through Friday.

BAE wins F-35 electronic warfare order for Lots 20-22
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:29:35 UTC
01:29:35 KST

- BAE Systems received a Lockheed Martin contract to deliver AN/ASQ-239 electronic warfare systems for F-35 Lots 20 through 22 and retrofits for older aircraft.
- The company has delivered more than 1,500 F-35 electronic warfare systems and did not disclose the new contract's value.
BAE Systems will build electronic warfare systems for three more production lots of the F-35 Lightning II under a new contract from Lockheed Martin, the company said on Oct. 6.
The contract covers AN/ASQ-239 systems for F-35 Lots 20 through 22, along with systems to retrofit and modernize older aircraft already in service. BAE Systems did not disclose the value of the contract or how many systems it will deliver.
The AN/ASQ-239, the F-35’s built-in electronic warfare suite, listens for radar and other signals around the aircraft, identifies threats and warns the pilot, and supports both self-protection and offensive electronic attack. BAE Systems says the system’s passive, long-range sensing lets pilots detect threats without giving away their own position, and that it is designed to help the jet operate against enemy fighters, missiles, drones and modern integrated air defense networks.
According to BAE Systems, much of that capability is software-based, so operators can update the system quickly to respond to new threats without waiting for hardware changes.
“We’ve been a trusted contributor since the origin of the Joint Strike Fighter program, and we’ve continuously evolved our EW hardware and software to maintain our warfighters’ decisive battlespace advantage,” said Amber Dolan, vice president of F-35 Solutions at BAE Systems. “We’re laser-focused on scaling production and delivering software-based capabilities to meet the rapid pace of conflict.”
BAE Systems, which has supplied the electronic warfare suite for every F-35 built, says it has now delivered more than 1,500 systems, up from the roughly 800 it had delivered in 2021, when it received its Lot 16 order. The systems are designed and built at BAE Systems facilities in Nashua, Manchester and Merrimack in New Hampshire, and in Austin, Texas.
To keep up with F-35 production, the company said it is using more automation, newer system designs and a broader supply chain, and has invested in its facilities to build and support more systems faster.
The new order follows years of work on an upgraded version of the suite. In December 2021, Lockheed Martin awarded BAE Systems a $493 million contract modification to develop new core hardware for the AN/ASQ-239 as part of the F-35’s Block 4 modernization, which is meant to improve the jet’s ability to detect hard-to-see threats and handle more threats at once.
The F-35 is flown by the U.S. Air Force, U.S. Navy and U.S. Marine Corps, as well as a growing list of allied air forces, and BAE Systems said the contract supports the global F-35 fleet.

Six-volume “1001 Questions on Resistance” unveiled in Tehran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:26:53 UTC
01:26:53 KST

Six-volume “1001 Questions on Resistance” unveiled in Tehran
TEHRAN- The six-volume book “1001 Questions on Resistance,” based on three decades of conversations with the late Hezbollah leader Sayyed Hassan Nasrallah, was unveiled Monday at the Sarcheshmeh Cultural Center in Tehran during a gathering examining his thought and legacy.
The ceremony was attended by Hojjatoleslam Mohammad Qomi, head of Iran's Islamic Ideology Dissemination Organization; Mohammad-Hossein Saffar-Harandi, a member of the Expediency Discernment Council; Hojjatoleslam Asad Qasir, a cleric and director of the Center for Authentic Islam; Hojatoleslam Ahmad Rahdar, a faculty member at Baqer al-Olum University; Abbas Khamehyar, a former Iranian cultural attaché in Lebanon; Mehdi Afraz, author of the book; and a number of religious, academic and cultural figures.
Speaking at the ceremony, Afraz described resistance as one of the most significant human ideas of the contemporary era, saying that important questions about its intellectual and social dimensions remain unanswered despite extensive discussion of the concept.
He said the six-volume collection was compiled to address some of the ambiguities surrounding resistance in public discourse and social life.
“After extensive research, we selected the personality and views of martyr Sayyed Hassan Nasrallah as the main source, because his entire life and actions were closely intertwined with the issue of resistance, while his words offer strategic guidance for Muslim societies,” Afraz said.
He described Nasrallah as a strategic architect of resistance, adding that the collection covers six major areas: the theology of resistance, political thought of resistance, resistance society, strategic equations of resistance, the resistance bloc, and resistance in Lebanon.
According to Afraz, the collection presents Nasrallah’s statements in the form of 1,001 questions and answers, with two principal objectives: fostering an emotional and spiritual connection with him that can contribute to media and artistic productions, and enabling readers to engage more directly with his ideas.
Addressing the ceremony, Qomi described “1001 Questions on Resistance” as an example of the effort to clarify and accurately narrate the history and ideas of resistance.
He said Nasrallah’s legacy should not be reduced to his military role, stressing that the late Hezbollah leader had presented resistance as a path toward progress and dignity for the oppressed, supported by rational, innate and religious arguments.
“We all feel a debt toward Sayyed Hassan, and there is much that needs to be done,” Qomi said, emphasizing that the task today is not merely to recall his character, conduct and courage, but to explain the path of resistance that he placed before humanity.
Khamehyar, a West Asia researcher and former Iranian cultural attaché in Lebanon, called for greater attention to the different dimensions of Nasrallah’s thought and the values he established in Lebanon.
He said Iranian media and public platforms had largely focused on Nasrallah’s military role over the past two years, arguing that this approach overlooks other aspects of his legacy.
“We must address the diverse values that Sayyed Hassan established in Lebanon and which later spread to other Arab and Islamic countries,” Khamehyar said.
Referring to the concept of the “School of Sayyed Hassan Nasrallah,” he called for its less-explored dimensions to be studied and highlighted.
He said understanding the resistance movement in Lebanon requires examining Nasrallah’s managerial abilities, rationality, realism, ethical conduct and emphasis on educating a new generation.
“Sayyed Hassan held classes more than he delivered speeches,” he said, noting that Nasrallah regularly held sessions for the families of martyrs and young people and devoted considerable attention to educating and developing cadres.
Saffar-Harandi said Nasrallah filled a vacuum for a hero in the Muslim world by establishing a new standard for political leadership.
He said Nasrallah represented a victorious model of resistance, creating expectations among his contemporaries and subsequent generations that would not easily be reversed.
Saffar-Harandi highlighted Nasrallah’s deep religious convictions, close connection with the people and courage in difficult circumstances. He also pointed to his understanding of Lebanon’s diverse social fabric, saying that despite leading a Shiite movement, he gained support among Sunnis, Maronites and other Christian communities.
He also described Nasrallah as a bridge between the Islamic Revolution in Iran and the Arab world, including Iraq, Yemen, Palestine and Syria.
Rahdar called for the compilation and publication of Nasrallah’s collected speeches in a volume similar to “Sahifeh-ye Nour,” the collection of the late Imam Khomeini’s speeches and writings.
He described Nasrallah as an “allameh” in the full sense of the word, saying it would take time for the different dimensions of his personality and thought to be fully understood.
He said the wisdom evident in Nasrallah’s speeches was not merely the product of theoretical study, but had developed through years of practical and ethical struggle.
“1001 Questions on Resistance” is published in six volumes covering the theology of resistance, political thought, society, strategic equations, the resistance bloc and the Lebanese resistance, offering a thematic presentation of Nasrallah’s views through 1,001 questions and answers.
Sayyed Hassan Nasrallah became secretary-general of Hezbollah in 1992, following the assassination of his predecessor, Sayyed Abbas al-Musawi. He led the movement for more than three decades, during a period that included the Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon in 2000 and the 2006 war between Hezbollah and Israel. Under his leadership, Hezbollah developed into a major political and military force in Lebanon and assumed a broader role in regional affairs.
Nasrallah was also widely known for his televised speeches, through which he addressed supporters and commented on major developments in Lebanon and the wider region. Born and raised in Beirut, he came from a family with roots in Bazouriyeh in southern Lebanon. While his public life was closely followed across the region, his personal and family life largely remained outside the spotlight.
He was tragically killed at the age of 64 during a series of intense Israeli airstrikes in southern Beirut on September 27, 2024.
The attack that claimed Nasrallah’s life was carried out by Israeli fighter jets targeting Hezbollah’s main headquarters, resulting in the martyrdom of several senior Hezbollah commanders and prominent Iranian Revolutionary Guards Lieutenant General Abbas Nilforoushan, who was present at the scene.
Under Nasrallah's leadership, whose name means "victory through God," Hezbollah evolved from a grassroots armed movement into the largest political party in Lebanon's recent history. Renowned for his captivating speeches, Nasrallah garnered attention throughout the West Asia and beyond, establishing himself as a significant figure within the Axis of Resistance, which includes Hezbollah, the Palestinian groups Hamas and Islamic Jihad, the Houthi movement in Yemen, and various Iraqi paramilitary factions.

Iceland ‘critical outpost’ for security, says US’ Rubio during visit

REYKJAVIK – US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Oct 6 during a visit to Iceland that the island had long been a “critical outpost” for security, as his country pushes for greater US influence in the Arctic region.
His trip came after US President Donald Trump stirred up the power balance in the region by making threats to buy or annex Greenland.
The US signed a security pact with Denmark and Greenland in late September that will allow Washington to establish two new military bases there, drawing the autonomous Danish territory further into US orbit.
Rubio said at a news conference that Iceland had long served as “a critical outpost for monitoring clandestine behaviour and deterring our adversaries”.
He arrived in Reykjavik on Oct 5 and has held talks with Icelandic Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir and top diplomat Thorgerdur Katrin Gunnarsdottir.
They covered topics including geothermal energy, data centres and the pharmaceutical industry.
With competition on the rise in the Arctic, Iceland has regained status as a strategic player, even as it continues to rely heavily on the US for security.
“For decades this nation, Iceland, has occupied a critical strategic position for our collective security and that remains true today more than ever before,” Rubio said.
At the start of September, Trump sparked new controversy by sharing an AI-generated map that appeared to show all of North America, the Caribbean, Greenland and Iceland as “the United States of America”.
In response, Reykjavik summoned the US ambassador and called the image “wholly inappropriate”.
Gunnarsdottir said on Oct 6 the issue had now been dealt with and she also welcomed the US deal with Greenland, adding that her country would continue strengthening ties with Washington.
EU rejected
Trump again signalled his obsession with Greenland on Oct 4, posting on his Truth Social platform an AI-generated image of his face looming over what appears to be its landscape, accompanied by the words “Hello, Greenland!”.
Icelanders voted in late August 52.8% to 47.2% against resuming negotiations on joining the EU, which have been frozen since 2013.
Since gaining independence in 1944, Iceland has never had a military. It relies on the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) for its security and on a bilateral defence pact signed with the US in 1951.
Washington does not have a permanent base in Iceland, but is looking to consolidate its control over Arctic access routes coveted by Russia and China.
Later on Oct 6, Rubio left Iceland for Athens, where he will participate in a “strategic dialogue” with NATO member Greece on regional and energy security, the US State Department said.
The wars in Iran and Ukraine have laid bare the fragility of energy supply chains, and Greece is positioning itself to become a key hub in south-eastern Europe for natural gas transport.
The visit follows media reports about possible conflicts of interest involving the US ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, a former fiancee of Donald Trump Jr and ex-wife of California governor Gavin Newsom.
In a letter addressed to Rubio, Congressman Gregory Meeks sought clarification of a Wall Street Journal report alleging that Guilfoyle had stated that the US could create “political change” in European countries.
Rubio will wrap up his European tour with a brief stop in Lisbon. AFP

Israel demolishes Jerusalem building, displacing 70 Palestinians
