Breadcrumb
Israel demolishes Jerusalem building, forcibly displacing dozens of Palestinians
Israeli bulldozers on Tuesday demolished a five-storey residential building in annexed East Jerusalem, displacing its 70 residents in a move the local Palestinian authority said was aimed at "forcible transfer".
Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who gleefully oversaw the demolition, claimed the building had been constructed without a permit.
"I love hearing this noise. We demolish what is illegal," Ben Gvir said in a video posted on X, which showed him inside the cab of one of the bulldozers.
Densely populated East Jerusalem faces a severe housing crisis, with thousands of homes built without permits, which its Palestinian residents say are near impossible to obtain from Israeli authorities.
The Jerusalem Governorate, the Palestinian local authority for the area, condemned Tuesday's demolition which it said was "a dangerous escalation in the policy of home demolitions and forcible transfer... and the imposition of a new demographic and urban reality".
Hanine Hreibat, a teacher and mother of four who was renting one of the 10 apartments in the building, said a large Israeli police force arrived in the At-Tur neighbourhood in the early hours of the morning, accompanied by three bulldozers.
They stormed the apartments and gave residents 10 minutes to leave, she said.
Hreibat told AFP she had woken up to the sound of her husband shouting at the police, asking them not to enter the bedroom where she was, adding she had endured "five minutes of terror, with weapons pointed at our heads".
She said police officers had allowed her to take only medicine, money, her handbag and ID card.
Among the rubble, residents collected gas cylinders and filled plastic bags with clothes they had managed to pull out from the huge mound of debris.
Hreibat said she had nowhere to go following the demolition.
"We'll look for a second home. Today we're at my in-laws' and tomorrow at my parents'," she said.
Residents confirmed to AFP that they had received a demolition notice on Monday, but did not know when it would be carried out.
Israel regularly carries out demolitions of what it says are illegal structures built by Palestinians in East Jerusalem and the occupied West Bank.
Israel captured East Jerusalem in 1967, later annexing it and declaring it part of its undivided capital, a move not recognised by the UN or most of the international community.
More than 360,000 Palestinians live in East Jerusalem as well as some 230,000 Israelis.
Palestinians aspire to make it the capital of a future Palestinian state, while Israel regards the entire city as its "unified and indivisible" capital.

'Our doors and hearts are always open to Iran': Malaysia's chargé d'affaires tells the Tehran Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:26:17 UTC
01:26:17 KST

'Our doors and hearts are always open to Iran': Malaysia's chargé d'affaires tells the Tehran Times
TEHRAN - Dato' Wan Aznainizam Yusri bin Wan Abdul Rashid arrived in Tehran in late August to take up the post of Chargé d'Affaires and Head of Mission at the Embassy of Malaysia. He will be elevated to Ambassador upon the formal presentation of his credentials.
In his first exclusive interview in Iran, granted to the Tehran Times, he talks about his first month in the country, Malaysia's firm stance on U.S.-Israeli aggression, the state of trade between the two countries, and the cultural and educational ties that keep Malaysians and Iranians connected.
He also shares what he hopes to achieve during his time here, and has a simple message for the people of Iran.
 
Below is the full text of the interview:
You have been in Tehran for a month now. What have your first impressions been of the country and its people?
My first impression of Iran is one of profound admiration and warmth. Upon arriving, one is immediately struck by the deep cultural heritage and historical ties that Malaysia and Iran have shared for centuries. Our nations are bound by a rich tapestry of mutual respect, intellectual exchange, and civilizational links that continue to strengthen our modern diplomatic relations.
What stands out most, however, is the remarkable resilience of the Iranian people. To witness how this nation has consistently overcome immense challenges, including decades of economic sanctions since 1980, is truly inspiring. The ingenuity, self-reliance, and strength they display in navigating these difficulties speak volumes about their character. And honestly, seeing how the country stood firm and successfully defended its capital during the onslaught of aerial attacks by Israel and the U.S. was truly remarkable. It showed the world a profound level of resolve and courage.
Above all, I have been deeply moved by the incredible warmth and hospitality of the Iranians. From my very first interactions, the generosity and welcoming nature of the people have made me feel entirely at home. I look forward to working closely with our Iranian friends to further deepen the bonds of friendship and cooperation between Malaysia and Iran.
The most important issue in Iran today is the U.S.-Israeli aggression, which has both a military and an economic dimension. Malaysia was one of the most outspoken countries in Southeast Asia in condemning the military phase of the war. What drove Malaysia to take that stance when many Muslim countries hesitated to explicitly condemn the U.S. and Israel?
Malaysia's strong stance against U.S.-Israeli military aggression is driven by a deeply ingrained, bipartisan foreign policy that prioritises international law, national sovereignty, and an absolute rejection of geopolitical double standards.
When people look at Malaysia's vocal position today, they shouldn't see it as a sudden political shift. It is actually the continuation of a long-standing, deeply rooted principle. For decades, Malaysia has held a firm, institutional stance against illegal warfare, unprovoked aggression, and the violation of any nation's sovereignty. We do not choose our principles based on political convenience or who the aggressor happens to be.
My Prime Minister, Dato' Seri Anwar Ibrahim, has been very clear on this at the global stage. Following the military strikes on Iran, Prime Minister Anwar immediately issued a statement condemning the attack. He had also made it clear to the world that we can no longer swallow lectures on human rights and democracy from Western powers when such double standards are playing out in real time. Under his leadership, Malaysia has consistently reaffirmed Iran's internationally recognized right to defend its own sovereignty under international law, while also calling for a peaceful resolution to the conflict.
This outspokenness is a legacy passed down through our leadership. Past Prime Ministers, including Tun Dr. Mahathir Mohamad, spent decades challenging Western hegemony and calling out global superpowers for using military and economic coercion against developing nations. Because this position is deeply embedded in our national identity, Malaysia's Parliament is entirely united on this issue, bridging all political parties to unanimously condemn these acts.
This is exactly why, at the recent UN General Assembly, our Foreign Minister, Datuk Seri Utama Mohamad Hasan, explicitly called out the global governance system. He stated plainly that Malaysia is sick of seeing the collective will of the General Assembly silenced by the Security Council's veto power. He demanded that to ensure true peace and global stability, the veto power must be challenged and ultimately abolished, especially when it paralyses action against crimes against humanity. Expanding membership is pointless if the veto remains an asymmetric tool for superpowers to shield aggression.
While other nations might hesitate due to pressure or strategic ties, Malaysia believes that staying silent makes one complicit. We speak out because true global stability cannot be built on deception, and a nation's right to exist in peace should never be compromised for another's tactical advantage.
How does Malaysia view Iran's role in regional security in West Asia?
Malaysia views Iran as an indispensable, sovereign pillar of regional security in West Asia, and our perspective is rooted in a clear recognition of interconnected global realities. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan have consistently underscored three fundamental parameters.
First, absolute support for sovereignty and stability. Malaysia respects Iran's territorial integrity and sovereign right to defend itself under international law. We have openly condemned external aggression against Iran, viewing unilateral attacks as grave violations of state sovereignty. For true peace to return to West Asia, all parties must decisively reduce tensions, halt escalations, and allow diplomacy to replace military hostility.
Second, an interconnected, self-reliant security architecture. Malaysia firmly believes that the security of West Asia is an interconnected whole. History has proven that the region cannot rely on external players, be it the United States or Israel, to engineer a manufactured or asymmetric stability. True, sustainable security can only be achieved when regional nations work together, manage their own borders, and determine their own future without foreign interference.
Lastly, deep appreciation for strategic cooperation. On a practical level, Malaysia deeply appreciates Iran's constructive role and cooperation in ensuring maritime safety. During periods of intense regional conflict and disruptions, Tehran actively facilitated the safe passage of Malaysian-owned merchant vessels through the critical chokepoint of the Strait of Hormuz. This concrete gesture is a testament to the trust between our nations and highlights Iran's capability to act as a responsible guardian of vital global trade routes.
Ultimately, Malaysia looks at Iran not through a lens of isolation, but as a key partner with whom we must engage to cultivate lasting, self-determined stability in the region.
How would you describe the current state of economic ties between Iran and Malaysia? Is it growing at all, given the difficulties caused by sanctions and the war?
The current state of economic ties between Malaysia and Iran is resilient and demonstrating growth, despite navigating a highly challenging landscape shaped by long-standing unilateral sanctions and recent regional volatility. While external geo-economic pressures and maritime instability present undeniable hurdles, both nations remain firmly committed to expanding their commercial relationship, driven by mutual economic interests and a shared vision of a self-reliant Islamic world.
Recent data demonstrates that commercial ties are not stagnant but are actively expanding where permitted. Total bilateral trade between Malaysia and Iran reached RM2.45 billion, with Malaysian exports driving the bulk of this volume at RM2.17 billion. Malaysia's exports are anchored heavily by palm oil and palm-based products, while primary imports from Iran consist of essential pharmaceutical products, edible fruits, and nuts, alongside permitted oil and gas derivatives. While this represents a fraction of Malaysia's total global trade, the baseline shows a clear upward trend. In historic periods of engagement, bilateral trade has scaled past RM3.68 billion. The institutional intent from both capitals is to use current frameworks to return to and exceed those levels.
The expansion of these economic links faces explicit operational constraints that both governments are actively trying to bypass. Malaysia strictly enforces United Nations-mandated sanctions. However, navigating unilateral secondary sanctions imposed by Western powers creates severe compliance and banking hurdles, making standard international trade settlements exceptionally difficult. Geopolitical tensions in West Asia, particularly conflict disruptions impacting shipping through critical maritime channels like the Strait of Hormuz, have also introduced high freight costs, logistical uncertainties, and supply chain bottlenecks for merchants on both sides.
During the recent BRICS Leaders' Summit in New Delhi, Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim engaged in vital bilateral talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. Malaysia reaffirmed its stance to pursue economic linkages guided by national interest and respect for state sovereignty. Among the high-potential sectors identified are food security and agriculture, where we can deepen the supply chain for Malaysian palm oil while collaborating on broad food security initiatives to counter global economic shocks. The halal economy also offers opportunities, leveraging Malaysia's global leadership in halal certification alongside Iran's robust domestic market to create a strong alternative trading network. We are also exploring permitted collaborative frameworks in energy distribution and technological exchange, as well as promoting joint academic ventures, research opportunities, and technical training between Malaysian and Iranian institutions to foster organic, long-term economic integration.
Our leaders also discussed how both nations can leverage the BRICS platform to bypass traditional geo-economic hurdles. The BRICS platform provides Malaysia and Iran with a powerful institutional framework to re-engineer our commercial relationship. For too long, developing nations have been vulnerable to unilateral secondary sanctions because the global financial architecture relies so heavily on a single currency. Through BRICS, we are actively working to change that.
At the global summit, Prime Minister Anwar advocated for a fairer global financing system that reduces our vulnerability to external economic pressures. For Malaysia and Iran, the most actionable path forward lies in Local Currency Settlement Mechanisms and de-dollarization. Malaysia has already successfully proven the value of local currency trading with regional neighbours like China and Indonesia; BRICS gives us the platform to expand that exact blueprint to a larger pool of Global South nations, including Iran.
Of course, we manage this path with clear institutional caution. Malaysia's trade strategy remains fiercely independent and balanced. We are not creating an anti-Western front, but rather building practical economic alternatives that protect our national interests. For Iran and Malaysia, the BRICS platform turns our shared desire for economic sovereignty into a technical, workable reality.
Ultimately, Malaysia views its trade relationship with Iran as a sovereign right. By utilizing joint commissions and exploring alternative investment channels, both nations are actively working to translate diplomatic goodwill into durable, practical economic partnerships.
Beyond politics and trade, how do you assess cultural and people-to-people ties between Iran and Malaysia?
While trade data and geopolitical alignments dominate headlines, the true heartbeat of the Malaysia-Iran relationship lies in our cultural and people-to-people ties. These connections are organic, deeply felt, and entirely insulated from external political pressures.
When we look beyond politics, what we find is a profound shared cultural heritage. Malaysia and Iran are bound by centuries of civilizational links and an overlapping tapestry of Islamic and Eastern values. At the core of both our societies are the sacred principles of hospitality, mutual respect, and genuine brotherhood. When a Malaysian visits Iran, or an Iranian arrives in Malaysia, I believe they do not feel like strangers in a foreign land. They instantly recognize a familiar warmth, a shared emphasis on family values, and a culture of welcoming the traveler with open arms.
A vital pillar of this contemporary relationship is our incredible alumni network. Over the past few decades, thousands of Iranian students have chosen Malaysia for their higher education. In my recent engagements with these Iranian alumni of Malaysian universities, I have been deeply inspired by how fondly they speak of their time in our country. Today, these individuals are professionals and entrepreneurs thriving right here in Iran. They serve as an irreplaceable human bridge between our nations, carrying a piece of Malaysian culture back with them and acting as organic ambassadors of our friendship. The same can also be said about the alumni of our very own Malaysian Technical Cooperation Programme, which has trained 419 Iranian officials in both the public and private sectors.
To harness this incredible energy, we are actively driving an initiative to establish the Malaysia-Iran Friendship Group. This group is designed to move beyond formal diplomacy, creating a lifelong network of collaboration. It will serve as a structured platform to deepen grassroots cultural ties, foster direct academic exchange between our universities, and create joint research initiatives. We want to ensure that the next generation of Malaysian and Iranian thinkers, artists, and professionals have a continuous, institutional framework to collaborate and innovate together.
Finally, we are aggressively building on this momentum through targeted tourism promotion. We want more Iranians to experience the multicultural beauty of our country firsthand. My team and I here in Tehran are focused on promoting Malaysia as the premier destination for leisure, family travel, and world-class higher education. This effort is perfectly timed with our global Tourism Malaysia push under the Visit Malaysia 2026-2027 campaign. We are showcasing Malaysia's renowned Muslim-friendly tourism offerings, diverse ecosystems, and modern infrastructure to the Iranian public.
Governments can sign treaties and businesses can exchange commodities, but it is the students, tourists, and cultural exchanges that weave the permanent fabric of our relationship. Malaysia and Iran will continue to nurture these bonds, ensuring our people remain closer than ever.
Are there concrete plans to expand exchanges in education, science, culture and tourism, for example scholarships, university partnerships, cultural weeks, or direct flight and tourism promotion?
Yes, there are concrete, active plans and freshly implemented initiatives to significantly expand our exchanges in education, science, culture, and tourism. Public statements and high-level diplomatic efforts from both Malaysian and Iranian leaders confirm that rather than just discussing potential frameworks, both nations have put definitive actions into motion to deepen grassroots connectivity.
Our academic cooperation has entered a highly practical phase, moving past generic agreements into targeted scientific collaboration. In high-level consultations, Malaysia's Minister of Higher Education, Datuk Seri Dr. Zambry Abdul Kadir, and Iran's Minister of Science, Research, and Technology, Hossein Simaei-Sarraf, explicitly committed to expanding university partnerships. They have underscored the need to bolster joint scientific research, share technologies, and establish specialized working groups. I have mentioned the MTCP earlier. Malaysia continues to leverage the flagship MTCP as a bridge to share our knowledge and expertise with our partners including Iran. This state-sponsored initiative by Malaysia had already provided direct training and knowledge-sharing for 419 Iranian professionals in tech, economics, and agriculture.
Cultural exchange is being institutionalized to create continuous, lifelong linkages between our thinkers and artists. During our official dialogue with the vibrant network of Iranian alumni who graduated from Malaysian institutions, we proposed a formal Malaysia-Iran Friendship Group. This group will serve as a permanent, non-political framework dedicated to fostering ongoing academic exchanges, cultural weeks, and continuous collaboration. On a broader civilizational level, both capitals have continuously supported the cross-pollination of our national identities. This includes establishing reciprocal language programs, such as Persian teaching courses in Malaysia and the promotion of Malay studies in Iran, alongside high-profile translations of classic Persian and Malay literature to deepen mutual understanding.
In a monumental boost to our people-to-people connectivity, direct flights between Tehran and Kuala Lumpur officially resumed following years of absence. We now have a weekly direct flight operated by Iran Air Tour since last August and soon Iran Air and Mahan Air. This direct aerial link drastically reduces travel hurdles and provides the necessary transport infrastructure to support a massive influx of tourists and students. To fully capitalize on this direct flight path, the Embassy of Malaysia in Tehran has launched the Malaysia Tourism Connect initiative. We are actively engaging with top Iranian tour operators and travel agencies to aggressively promote Malaysia's diverse, family-friendly, and world-class halal tourism environment. This forms a core component of our global Visit Malaysia 2026-2027 campaign, positioning Malaysia as the premier destination of choice for Iranian travelers.
By the end of your time here, what would you most like to have achieved in the Malaysia–Iran relationship, politically, economically, and in terms of people-to-people ties?
When my time here comes to an end, I want to look back and know that we didn't just maintain a diplomatic friendship. We built an unshakeable, self-reliant partnership that truly changes lives.
Politically, my goal is to leave our relationship completely integrated on the global stage. Based on the aspiration of both my Prime Minister and Foreign Minister, I want Malaysia and Iran to stand shoulder-to-shoulder as independent voices, defending state sovereignty, calling out international double standards, and pushing to reform a broken UN system. I also hope that there will be more exchanges of high-level visits from both Tehran and Putrajaya.
Economically, I want to turn our shared vision into everyday reality. By fully leveraging the BRICS platform, I hope that we will witness an increase in bilateral trade and investments between our two countries. We must find ways to bypass external financial pressures to comfortably push our bilateral trade past historic highs.
In terms of people-to-people ties, this is deeply personal to me. With direct flights finally restored, I want to see a massive surge in families, tourists, and students crossing borders under our Visit Malaysia campaign. By launching our formal Friendship Group, I want to ensure that our brilliant university alumni and researchers have a permanent, lifelong bridge to collaborate on the sciences of the future.
Ultimately, I want to leave behind a resilient network that protects our sovereignty and keeps the people of Malaysia and Iran permanently connected.
If you could say just one sentence to the people of Iran, what would that sentence be?
Choosing just one sentence is always difficult for a diplomat, because when you give a microphone to an ambassador, he will talk without being stopped. You know, we are just like singers. But if I were to have one simple sentence for the people of Iran, for my brothers and sisters in Iran, it would be this: please rest assured that our doors and hearts are always open to you all, because to know Malaysia is to love Malaysia, a country that is in every sense truly Asia.

Iran’s next move could leave the Middle East looking for the bomb
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:24:58 UTC
01:24:58 KST

Iran’s next move could leave the Middle East looking for the bomb
In Tehran, discussions about Iran’s potential withdrawal from the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) are growing increasingly urgent. Iranian Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Esmail Baghaei has recently acknowledged that the issue is being seriously considered by Iranian officials. His statements lend significant political weight to the discourse around Iran’s potential withdrawal from the NPT: One can no longer downplay it as something proposed by hardliners or fringe groups. While Baghaei also reaffirmed Iran’s commitment to its membership in the NPT and the associated obligations, he made it clear that the possibility of exiting the treaty is being considered.
This situation has been triggered by Tehran’s mounting frustration. Iran finds it increasingly difficult to justify why participation in the NPT demands constant concessions from it, while the country’s rights remain negotiable. Despite Iran’s regular affirmation of the peaceful nature of its nuclear program, disputes persist and external pressure continues to mount. This gives Iran reason to question the practical value of the agreement. The Iranian leadership is signaling that its willingness to remain a member of the NPT cannot be viewed as unconditional.
The NPT was designed to maintain balance: Non-nuclear states refrain from developing nuclear weapons and receive international guarantees, while their right to the peaceful use of nuclear energy is recognized by the treaty; nuclear powers, meanwhile, pursue negotiations toward nuclear disarmament. For Tehran, the critical issue lies in the balance of rights and responsibilities. Iran’s right to peaceful nuclear technology does not exclude the international monitoring of its nuclear program. But there is a difference between inspections and demands to relinquish nuclear technologies, and Iran believes that this line is increasingly being blurred.
A pivotal aspect of the NPT is the so-called ‘nuclear deal’ signed in 2015. Iran agreed to impose significant limitations on its nuclear program and accepted extensive international oversight in exchange for relief from sanctions. In 2016, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) confirmed that Iran had implemented the necessary measures to put the agreement into effect. However, in 2018, the US withdrew from the deal and reinstated sanctions. This unfortunate experience casts a shadow on how Tehran views any potential future compromises. Iran accepted the restrictions, but the change in Washington’s policy undermined many of the anticipated benefits of the deal.
Strikes against Iran and its nuclear facilities have further compounded the crisis of trust, raising concerns over physical security. The IAEA reported attacks on several Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025; this shows that even with international guarantees, the facilities remain vulnerable. It’s true that the NPT does not offer military protection or immunity from attacks. However, the main problem for Iranian political circles is that the international oversight of Iran’s nuclear program has failed to ensure a diplomatic settlement of disagreements.
This raises a poignant question for Tehran. If cooperation with international institutions does not prevent sanctions and strikes against Iran, then what argument can the supporters of the treaty bring up in favor of remaining a party to the NPT? The treaty’s supporters outline its theoretical benefits, but the country assesses its results. As the costs of external pressure rise, it becomes increasingly hard to convince anyone that further concessions will enhance security. Instead, there’s a growing perception that new compromises simply lead to new demands. This sense of injustice largely explains Iran’s current irritation.
Another factor is the unequal standing of the countries in the region. Israel is not a party to the NPT and does not face the same comprehensive oversight that Iran does. While Tehran is constantly questioned about its nuclear program, no one raises concerns about Israel. This situation strikes Tehran as fundamentally unfair; its participation in the treaty imposes restrictions that Israel does not have to deal with. From Iran’s perspective, Israel, which is not bound by the treaty, enjoys greater freedom, while Iran’s membership comes with constraints and threats. Consequently, the treaty’s opponents have a strong argument in favor of withdrawing.
One cannot dismiss the fact that the IAEA has grounds to question Iran’s compliance. The IAEA faces multiple restrictions in Iran when it comes to inspections, nuclear material tracking, access to facilities, and so on. The Iranian Foreign Ministry emphasizes that it remains committed to the NPT and expects respect for its rights under the treaty, noting that disagreements with the IAEA should be resolved through dialogue and inspections, not through threats or attacks on Iranian facilities.
The heightened public attention to Iran’s potential exit from the NPT is also tied to ongoing negotiations. The prospect of Iran’s withdrawal raises the stakes for the US and increases the cost of failing to reach an agreement. As long as Iran remains a party to the NPT, there are legal grounds for international oversight and the possibility of engaging in meaningful discussions about its nuclear program. Exiting the treaty would complicate this process and increase uncertainty. Tehran is signaling that maintaining the current negotiations framework requires political effort. If this framework is systematically undermined, there are no guarantees that it will exist indefinitely.
At the same time, Iran is raising the stakes. As long as Iran’s opponents believe that it will remain in the NPT despite pressure, the threat of withdrawal can be dismissed as mere rhetoric. Baghaei’s statements make it clear that the option of leaving the NPT is being seriously considered by Iranian officials. However, Tehran is in no rush to actually exit the treaty. The Foreign Ministry has reaffirmed Iran’s existing obligations while leaving the final decision to the country’s leadership and Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei.
By openly discussing the possibility of withdrawing from the NPT, Tehran can analyze the reaction of Russia, China, the EU, its neighbors in the region, and also its own populace. This will help assess the potential support for such a move and see whether other parties are willing to offer conditions that might persuade Iran to remain a party to the agreement. The Foreign Ministry’s statement is most likely driven by several factors, including a strategic calculation in negotiations, internal disagreements within the leadership, and a growing dissatisfaction with external pressure.
Moreover, Tehran understands that withdrawing from the NPT could further escalate tensions in the region. Türkiye and Saudi Arabia may believe that Iran is about to develop nuclear weapons, prompting them to consider their own nuclear capabilities. Their argument would be straightforward: If Iran no longer feels bound by the prohibition against acquiring nuclear weapons, why should its neighbors refrain from doing the same? Although withdrawing from the treaty doesn’t confer a legal right to nuclear arms, this detail could easily be overlooked in political debates. Tehran faces a serious risk: In its quest to enhance national security, it may inadvertently push its neighbors toward a nuclear arms race, and ultimately have to confront new threats. Therefore, we can neither be confident of Iran’s inevitable exit from the treaty nor reduce the situation to mere bluffing.
Iran’s reaction to Russia’s proposal regarding the export of its enriched uranium should be considered in this light. Baghaei confirmed that Tehran is considering Moscow’s offer and will act in accordance with its national interests. This keeps the door open for negotiations. Before taking such a step, Tehran seeks clarity on what it will gain in return and how this will affect its nuclear program moving forward. While Russia’s proposal could facilitate an agreement, Iran wants to be sure that the potential transfer of enriched uranium is accompanied by a genuine reduction in external pressure. Trust in Moscow plays an important part in this, but Iran needs assurances that all the other parties will uphold their end of the deal.
The main takeaway from the statement by the Iranian Foreign Ministry is that Iran no longer wishes to view its participation in the NPT as grounds for America’s endless, unfounded demands. Tehran insists on discussing its rights, the predictability of its partners’ commitments, and the potential for peaceful development. For now, this demand is articulated through diplomatic language, allowing room for negotiation. However, it is rooted in a profound crisis of trust. If the NPT continues to be perceived in Iran as a source of restrictions without practical benefits (an outlook that appears increasingly likely), then the arguments in favor of remaining a party to the treaty will become weaker. At some point, it may cease to be an issue that raises the stakes in negotiations and may become a matter requiring practical resolution.

Google ordered to halt data centre works in Finland over environmental concerns
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
19:24:52 EEST
01:24:52 KST

Finnish authorities have ordered Google subsidiary Tuike Finland to halt work affecting the environment at planned data centre sites in Muhos and Kajaani until environmental impact assessments are completed.
The Finnish Supervisory Agency, LVV, issued the request on Tuesday. Tuike Finland must stop the specified work immediately and no later than 23 October.
The order covers tree removal, excavation, blasting, crushing, soil removal, drainage work and the construction of site roads and storage areas.
Planning, measurements, soil surveys and work that has limited environmental effects and is easy to reverse remain permitted.
LVV said investigations available to the agency indicate that work has already changed both sites. This includes tree clearance, removal of topsoil, construction of roads and storage areas, changes to ditches and culverts and stormwater work.
“Our assessment is that these measures change the environment and cause impacts whose identification and assessment are among the central objectives of the environmental impact assessment procedure,” Tommi Muilu, head of LVV’s environmental department, said in the agency’s statement.
Environmental impact assessment procedures for both projects remain unfinished. They are expected to conclude during 2026.
Tuike Finland has until 14 October to submit a written response to LVV and state whether it intends to follow the request. Google has since said it will comply.
“We understand the concern caused by the situation. In this case, we did not meet the high standards we set ourselves,” Sondre Ronander, Google’s communications manager for Finland and Norway, said in a company statement.
Ronander said Google had acted in good faith under Finland’s Forest Act, conducted nature surveys and taken measures to protect sites with environmental value. He said Google plans to plant trees across 130 hectares in Muhos.
The dispute had already drawn scrutiny in September. The Finnish Association for Nature Conservation said more than 300 hectares of forest had been cleared at the planned data centre site in Leppiniemi, Muhos, while environmental impact assessment procedures were still incomplete.
The organisation argued that permanent land-use conversion on that scale should have been preceded by an environmental impact assessment. It also raised concerns about work at Google’s Otanmäki project in Kajaani.
The projects are a part of Google’s €13 billion data centre investment in Finland.
LVV said environmental assessments are intended to identify significant effects before decisions and major preparatory work take place. Large-scale changes made before the process ends risk limiting the assessment of alternatives and measures designed to reduce environmental harm.
If Tuike Finland fails to comply, LVV said it will consider administrative enforcement under environmental assessment legislation or other applicable laws. Such proceedings could include a conditional fine.
Google’s decision to comply means such enforcement is not required at this stage.

Paramount completed on Tuesday its takeover of Warner Bros Discovery, uniting two of Hollywood's most storied studios in a media empire spanning television, news and cinema under the control of David Ellison.
The combined company – renamed Skydance – brings together Paramount Pictures and Warner Bros Pictures, the CBS News and CNN networks, and the HBO and CBS television brands.
Ellison plans to eventually merge the Paramount+ and HBO Max streaming services over time.
"Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry," said Ellison, whose ultra-wealthy family has ties to US President Donald Trump.

Read moreParamount settles with US states, clearing path for Warner Bros. merger
The deal closed less than a week after a federal judge in California approved a settlement between Paramount and 12 US states that had sued to block the transaction on antitrust grounds.
Paramount won a bidding war against Netflix in February for Warner Bros Discovery, and the Trump administration approved the deal – one of the largest-ever media mergers – in June, without demanding a change to its business.

Background information

Its work has been highly regarded, and its continuity deemed necessary, so its mandate has been renewed in 2020, 2022, and 2024 for two-year periods. Israel mental health hotline gets nearly 1m calls since Gaza war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:20:35 UTC
01:20:35 KST

Breadcrumb
Israeli mental health hotline receives nearly one million calls since Gaza war began
An Israeli mental health support hotline has received nearly one million calls since October 2023, with data showing growing loneliness and an increase in calls involving suicidal thoughts among young Israelis.
The figures, published as Israel marks three years since the 7 October Hamas attack and the beginning of its genocidal war on Gaza, offer a picture of the prolonged psychological impact of years of conflict on Israeli society.
Israeli news site Walla reported that the ERAN emotional support organisation received around 929,000 requests for help over the past three years.
The contacts were made through telephone hotlines and online services, including WhatsApp, chat services, forums, email and text messages.
While the overall number of calls has fallen in recent months, demand for support remains high, according to the report.
One of the most significant changes has been a rise in loneliness, which has become the most commonly raised issue among those seeking help.
The proportion of calls relating to other issues such as anxiety, trauma and bereavement has meanwhile fallen, although ERAN cautioned that this did not necessarily mean psychological distress had eased.
Instead, the organisation said the nature of the difficulties being reported appeared to be changing after three years of war.
Family relationships, parenting and social relationships have increasingly featured in requests for help, while the proportion of contacts involving suicidal thoughts, intentions or behaviour has also risen.
The increase was particularly noticeable among teenagers and young adults, according to the data.
Mental health professionals cited by Walla said prolonged disruption to educational and social structures, uncertainty within families and the erosion of a sense of stability and belonging were among the factors contributing to distress.
Israeli soldiers struggle after prolonged war
Israeli soldiers and reservists accounted for a significant proportion of calls made by men during the three years of war.
Their requests for support centred on three broad areas: psychological pain, depression and acute distress; anxiety, trauma and bereavement; and loneliness.
The report said soldiers were struggling to discuss their experiences during military service and to navigate the transition between the battlefield and family life.
Repeated periods of military service and movement between the army and home could deepen feelings of isolation and make it harder for soldiers to resume relationships and roles they had left behind.
The proportion of enquiries from serving soldiers relating to violence and sexual assault had also increased, according to the report.
Israel has mobilised hundreds of thousands of reservists since October 2023 as its military operations expanded from Gaza to other fronts across the region.
'A difficult and prolonged reality'
ERAN chief executive David Koren said three years of war had subjected Israelis to a prolonged period of psychological strain.
"Behind every call is someone dealing with pain, loss, anxiety, loneliness or exhaustion, and sometimes several of these feelings at once," he said, adding that the organisation expected the coming year to remain challenging.
ERAN's professional director Shiri Daniels said the apparent return of aspects of everyday life should not be confused with psychological recovery.
The ability to carry out daily tasks "is not necessarily evidence of mental health", she said, pointing to continuing uncertainty and a sense of threat.
Psychological pressures can accumulate gradually and emerge through exhaustion, loneliness, relationship difficulties and a weakened sense of stability and security, Daniels added.
Israeli families have also faced prolonged military service, disruption to everyday life and continuing security fears, with the organisation reporting increased signs of distress during periods of heightened tension.
The findings come three years into Israel's genocidal war on Gaza, which has devastated the Palestinian enclave and killed tens of thousands of Palestinians.

Parliament and Council split on how non-EU countries get access to defense cash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:20:10 UTC
01:20:10 KST

BRUSSELS — Negotiations over the EU’s proposed €409 billion Competitiveness Fund are splitting capitals and Parliament over whether non-EU countries should be allowed to tap its defense money — and on what terms.
Fraught talks on those rules are expected to dominate negotiations on Tuesday night in the European Parliament, with officials saying the chances of a breakthrough are remote.
On Wednesday, EU ambassadors will discuss a compromise text put forward by the Irish presidency of the Council that would allow third countries to sign association agreements with the EU to take part in bloc-funded defense programs, according to a document seen by POLITICO.
Advertisement
France and a few other countries want to limit the outsiders' access, while most capitals want more room for companies from third countries, three diplomats told POLITICO. The EU money comes from the bloc’s taxpayers, and that creates pressure to keep the cash at home to benefit EU arms-makers. However, many countries want the EU to be open to allies, given their importance at a time of rapid geopolitical shifts.
EU institutions are haggling over the bloc’s next long-term budget, with make-or-break talks expected over the next months. The European Competitiveness Fund is the bloc’s main vehicle to boost strategic industrial competitiveness, the clean transition and security and defense. The Commission has proposed that €131 billion of the next ECF would be for defense and space.
It’s an enormous increase from about €25 billion for defense and space in the current budget, a sign of European reaction to the growing threat from Russia, the drive to continue supporting Ukraine and increasing uncertainty about the U.S. commitment to European security under Donald Trump.
Setting rules on whether companies and projects from outside the EU could qualify for ECF funding is already roiling relations with partners like Canada, which are pushing for closer ties with the bloc.
It is also annoying the United States, which is wary of a buy-European effort that could cut out its arms industry. NATO is concerned about fracturing the transatlantic alliance by encouraging European defense efforts.
Speaking recently in the European Parliament, NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe, U.S. Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, said that “a focus on where something is made rather than how well it performs in combat, how it performs on the battlefield, only benefits our adversaries.”
Advertisement
Outsiders looking in
In the Council, the original idea for how to access ECF defense cash had been for close allies like Ukraine and other EU partners such as Norway to automatically participate without having to sign an association agreement with the bloc and without needing to contribute to the program.
Now, the Irish Council presidency has put forward a draft proposal under which all non-EU countries wanting to participate would have to sign association agreements. That covers not only Canada and the U.K., but also countries like Ukraine and Norway. And all would also have to contribute, either with cash or, in the case of Ukraine, with defense technology, diplomats said.
Some officials said it is unlikely that EU ambassadors will reach a deal on the Irish proposal on Wednesday. The subject is being discussed “for the first time,” said a French EU official. “The aim, therefore, is not necessarily to reach a decision, but to gain a clear understanding of the various positions.”
Alexus Grynkewich speaks at the European Parliament in Brussels on Sept. 28, 2026. | Alain Rolland/EP
But many countries are pushing to get a deal done. “There is no point discussing it if we don’t move towards a decision,” said one diplomat, adding: “We’ve had 43 technical groups so far, the positions are known."
During the meeting, the explicit point of ‘Buy European’ — an effort to favor European weapons systems — is expected to be raised by France, two other diplomats said.
It’s not a new fight for member countries.
Advertisement
During negotiations over the European Defence Industry Programme — a €1.5 billion cash pot to boost the bloc’s defense industry — member countries clashed for months over whether EU money could finance foreign-licensed military equipment that was made in the bloc. They ended up reaching a deal that left some flexibility for missiles and ammunition. A similar discussion took place over the €150 billion Security Action for Europe loans-for-weapons scheme.
Parallel talks over the ECF in the European Parliament have also stalled.
“We still have time, as the Parliament is not yet ready,” said the French EU official.
The discussions in the industry committee are being led by MEPs Christian Ehler of the European People’s Party and Dan Nica with the Socialists and Democrats.
Nica and Ehler want countries with association agreements in defense to be eligible for EU funding with certain conditions attached. However, that view contradicts the opinion of the Parliament’s Committee on Security and Defence, which is more in favor of ensuring EU money stays in the bloc, said two of the people with knowledge of the issue.
Ehler confirmed that cooperation with third countries is the main sticking point in the negotiations. He called the opposition by some groups to opening the ECF’s defense funding to countries beyond Ukraine and the European Economic Area “entirely unacceptable and irresponsible.”

Nobel Prize in Medicine laureate Professor Karl Deisseroth nearly missed the call informing him of his victory from the committee. Associated Press writes, as reported by UNN.
Details
As the publication writes, Dr. Karl Deisseroth calls himself a "night owl" and often works until midnight. According to him, after reviewing scientific papers and corresponding with students, he had just gone to bed when he received a call from the Nobel Assembly in Stockholm.
"I almost felt as if I had lost the ability to formulate words, but after a minute or two I came to my senses," Deisseroth said.
While science correspondents spoke with Deisseroth by phone and via Zoom, the publication's photographer and videographer rushed to his home in Stanford. He feared that he had the wrong house before summoning the courage to knock on the door.
Dr. Michelle Monje-Deisseroth, the scientist's wife, opened the door and invited the photographer into the house, where the Nobel laureate was taking calls while sitting on the sofa.
Deisseroth admitted to the AP that he was surprised to learn that his work had been recognized with a Nobel Prize, but his wife was not surprised.
Recall
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine has been awarded to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel "for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics".

Land, memory and return explored in Rooted Movements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:19:18 UTC
01:19:18 KST

Breadcrumb
Amanda Batarseh's Rooted Movements: Land, memory and the possibility of return explored
In her forthcoming book Rooted Movements: The Radical Poetics of Palestinian Space (Syracuse University Press, 2026), Amanda Batarseh explores Palestinian rootedness amid colonialism, colonial violence, and exile through a discussion of various Palestinian literary works.
As a result of the 1948 Nakba, conceptualising Palestine within its own space becomes limiting and also exclusionary, given that the Palestinian diaspora constitutes a major proportion of what it means to be Palestinian.
Colonial displacement is therefore one factor. For Palestinians, rootedness, through a myriad of expressions all relating to land and culture, denotes a permanence that is embodied in the presence and existence of Palestinians themselves.
Amanda begins by exploring the Arabic language and symbolism to examine the connection between Palestinians and their land.
Roots, for example, connect to peoplehood and link directly to rootedness in land and trees, notably the olive tree.
This goes beyond the Zionist colonial erasure of Palestinians from their land, showing how Palestinian culture and literature preceded Zionism, while also possessing the potential to think and imagine beyond manifestations of colonial violence.
Memory, lived experiences, family history and cultural traditions all create a sense of belonging that transcends actual presence on the land, while creating ties to the land from which Palestinians have been displaced.
Within this reclaiming movement, Palestinians "rearticulate belonging, resistance and futurity."
As a result of displacement, land theft and death – all manifestations of colonial violence – Palestinian literature goes beyond the confines of geopolitical boundaries.
Land as resistance
Each chapter examines specific works by Palestinian authors and themes that bring indigenous narratives to the forefront.
From the geography of Palestine from the Ottoman era up to Zionist settler-colonialism, to narratives of land through storytelling, the imaginings of nationhood and how these disrupt boundaries, challenges to Zionist control over the Palestinian population, and future possibilities that are rooted in past and present resistance, Amanda offers an initial, profound glimpse into the Palestinian poetics of space.
For example, in Hussein Barghouti’s work, Amanda notes that the experience of Palestine is connected by movement that also happens in remembrance, as well as in how Palestinians relate to place.
Amanda notes, "Palestinian space has not only been occupied and remade by colonial domination over the past century, but also epistemologically reorganised – rendered intelligible through Western logics of progress and time."
Recovering Palestine from colonial redrawing of the territory meant that Palestinian literature would embody continuity.
Space becomes a protagonist in Palestinian literature, and a place where return is possible in imagination. As Barghouti writes, "even our most abstract thoughts are inseparable from spatial existence."
Tawfiq Canaan, whose work is discussed in the second chapter, deals with land narratives in which Zionist erasure is countered by "archiving and enacting the continuity of Palestinian territorial grounding and rooted presence."
Raja Shehadeh, whose work is also discussed and who penned a memoir titled Palestinian Walks, notes, "When I began hill walking in Palestine a quarter of a century ago, I was not aware that I was travelling through a vanished landscape."
For both Canaan and Shehadeh, Palestinian land narratives resist colonial dispossession, while their remembrance of land directly opposes colonial impositions. The Palestinian remembrance of and attachment to land is not bound by colonial narratives.
For Ghassan Kanafani, there is a distinction between literature written in Palestine and abroad in the diaspora, which generates a difference in expression. Palestinian literature written in Palestine expresses recovery of the land, while that written abroad is more tied to loss.
Similarly, in examining Ibtisam Azem’s novel The Book of Disappearance, in which Zionists are baffled and also scared by the complete disappearance of Palestinians, Amanda notes that "Zionist nation-building depends on Palestinian functional presence/absence as the precondition for the settler-colonial production and continuation of national space."
The Palestinian protagonist in the novel, on the other hand, experiences both presence and absence in terms of land. Palestine’s history does not disappear with colonialism.
Imagining return
Throughout the book, Amanda contextualises the literature discussed with detailed historical discussions of Palestinian history and colonial erasure, through which rootedness and exile are perceived as dynamic and full of possibility in the imaginings of Palestinian return.
Rather than cartography, the book examines rootedness within a space of movement where Palestinians can maintain their relationship with Palestine.
"The space that has been targeted for evacuation, or into which Palestinians have been expelled in an effort to render them homeless and rootless, is re-emplaced through radical Palestinian narrative practices," Amanda writes.
Ultimately, moving from loss as a result of the 1948 Nakba to the realm of possibilities of return, Amanda does not equate Palestinian identity solely with loss and erasure.
Rather, by examining various literary works and theories, the text argues that political borders do not impede thinking about and relating to Palestine.
Within the space of movement, rootedness is consolidated because the relationship to Palestine is cherished and expounded upon.
Ramona Wadi is a freelance journalist and book reviewer. Her writing covers a range of themes related to Palestine, Chile, and Latin America

Kyiv City Mayor Vitali Klitschko's September promise that the capital will receive "40 to 50" mobile shelters "within a month" is set to fall short after it was revealed on Oct. 6 that only 14 will arrive by the end of the year.
"We have already purchased shelters and within a month, the first batch, roughly, as far as I remember, 40 or 50 units, will be set up at transport stops where there are no stationary shelters nearby. And we are continuing this program," Klitschko said on Sept. 12.
But the Kyiv City State Administration (KMDA) told media portal Slidstvo.info on Oct. 6 that far fewer will arrive on a far longer timescale, despite Klitschko saying some had already been purchased.
Currently, only four mobile shelters operate in the city, installed by private organizations, according to Slidstvo.info. Meanwhile, KMDA's press service told the media portal that the city required at least 620 mobile shelters and 7,894 conventional ones.
The municipal transport company Kyivpastrans is supposed to buy the 14 mobile shelters after its new financial plan is approved, Slidstvo.info reports. The new shelters will be placed at Kyivpastrans branches and at the final stops of public transport lines.
The estimated costs are around Hr 54.2 million (about $1.2 million) in total, including VAT, while a single shelter for 50 people costs about Hr 4.8 million (about $107,000), Slidstvo.info said. The city's budget for public safety and civil protection for 2027 to 2029 sits at Hr 300 million.
According to the city administration, the capital's several district administrations did not request funding for mobile shelters when the city budget was drafted, and the city itself did not buy any shelters, Slidstvo.info said.
Kyiv's city government allocates funding for the capital's shelters, but the capital's 10 district state administrations are responsible for carrying out their share of shelter construction and repairs.
The district administrations, however, do not answer directly to the mayor. Their heads are appointed and dismissed by the president on the submission of the Cabinet of Ministers.
Individual owners and balance-holders are also responsible for maintaining some facilities in the network.
Kyiv's civil-protection shelter network currently includes 4,385 facilities, according to information provided by the KMDA to the Kyiv Independent.
Nearly nine out of every 10 shelters are classified as "basic shelters," which Ukrainian law does not consider protective civil-defense structures. These are usually basements, semi-basements, and other underground spaces adapted so people can take cover during an attack. They are not purpose-built protective structures and offer a low level of protection.
In a comment to the Kyiv Independent, KMDA said 397 facilities across the capital currently need work before they meet readiness requirements.

Paramount wraps up Warner Bros mega merger to create Hollywood powerhouse Skydance
Unknown

Paramount wraps up Warner Bros mega merger to create Hollywood powerhouse Skydance
- Paramount Skydance completed a US$110 billion takeover of Warner Bros Discovery, creating a Hollywood powerhouse under David Ellison and moving shares to the NYSE as “SKYD”.
- The merger joins major film, TV and news brands, including CBS, CNN, Paramount+ and HBO Max, after legal settlements cleared the main barriers.
- Ellison and Ynon Kreiz must integrate the firms, cut US$6 billion in costs and manage about US$80 billion in debt, with likely job losses and pressure on streaming growth.
AI generated
Paramount Skydance on Oct 6 completed its blockbuster US$110 billion (S$140.8 billion) takeover of Warner Bros Discovery, creating a Hollywood heavyweight that hands chief executive David Ellison control of one of the world’s largest entertainment and news businesses.
The deal brings together the studios behind Mission: Impossible, Harry Potter and DC Studios, alongside major television and streaming networks such as CBS, CNN, Paramount+ and HBO Max – forming an expansive entertainment company spanning film, TV and news.
Ellison laid out his vision for the new company in a memo to employees on Oct 6 in which he said the acquisition is “to build the next-generation media and entertainment company, powered by creativity and technology”.
The goal, he added, was not simply to get bigger but “to take on the biggest players in our industry”.
The new company, called Skydance, is the latest iteration of a conglomerate once controlled by the late Sumner Redstone that has precipitously shrunk over the years as audiences flock to news and entertainment delivered by a growing cadre of smaller publishers and creators chipping away at once-mighty Hollywood.
Skydance not only faces competition from Netflix, Disney and others, but also from tech giants Apple, Meta, and Amazon, as well as the growing threat of AI.
Shares of the combined company moved to the New York Stock Exchange from Nasdaq on Oct 6 to trade under the ticker “SKYD”.
Settlements with a coalition of US states and a Hollywood writers union removed the main legal barriers to the merger, one of the largest in media history. It comes as Hollywood faces falling cable-TV subscriptions, the high cost of competing for streaming audiences and persistent pressure from unions over jobs and creative workers’ rights.
Trump’s CNN problem
US President Donald Trump expressed approval when asked about the deal.
“It’s going to be a great company,” he told reporters. “That’s a great merger. I’m glad they let it go.”
Trump has attacked news organisations since his first term and recently took the unprecedented step of banning several news outlets from the White House, including CNN. The move came weeks ahead of the Nov 3 midterm elections, in which Trump’s fellow Republicans are defending narrow majorities in Congress.
CNN chief Mark Thompson and CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss will continue in their respective leadership roles in the new company and each will separately report to Ellison and Skydance co-chief executive officer Ynon Kreiz.
This would allay concerns from critics that Weiss, who took over as CBS News editor-in-chief in 2025, would have greater control over all of Skydance’s news operations.
The concerns are also fuelled by lawmakers’ criticism of Ellison for tailoring news coverage at Paramount-owned CBS News to favour Trump.
As part of the settlement, Ellison agreed to create an editorial independence board to oversee CNN and CBS. Experts warn that the board will be “toothless”.
Ellison said last week the Skydance name was chosen to retain the individual identities of Paramount and Warner Bros studios, rather than combining them under a new brand.
Wall Street analysts, however, said the name reinforces the extent of Ellison’s control, highlighting how some of Hollywood’s most iconic brands now answer to him and how he has a platform to impose his strategy and culture.
In just 16 years, Skydance has gone from an independent studio to the centre of one of Hollywood’s biggest power plays. Founded in 2010 by the son of Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, it built its reputation as a financial backer and producer of Paramount’s blockbuster Top Gun: Maverick.
After merging with Paramount in 2025, Skydance set its sights on Warner Bros, entering a heated bidding contest with Netflix while drawing interest from other potential suitors, including Comcast.
Warner Bros shareholders received an additional US$41.9 million in a “ticking fee”, based on the number of days between end-September and the deal-closing, according to a regulatory filing.
Broader Hollywood bet
Ellison named Kreiz, Mattel’s former chief executive officer, as Skydance co-chief executive officer to run day-to-day operations and lead the integration, while Ellison oversees creative direction and overall strategy.
Kreiz was also appointed to the company’s board on Oct 6, alongside former Activision Blizzard CEO Bobby Kotick. Former British prime minister Tony Blair will join the company as an adviser, it said.
In bringing on Kreiz, Ellison has signalled the need for a cost-cutter.
The duo face the task of combining two large companies while delivering US$6 billion in planned cost savings, a big part of which Paramount said would come from “non-labour sources”.
That includes combining technology and cloud providers of the two companies, but the scale of the cuts is expected to affect jobs across Hollywood.
Skydance plans to combine its streaming services, including HBO Max and Paramount+, into a single service and has pledged to release at least 30 films each in the first two years after closing, rising to 32 a year for the following three.
Skydance is also expected to carry about US$80 billion in debt, putting pressure on Ellison to grow streaming, preserve cash flow from cable networks and improve theatrical film performance.
Analysts at MoffettNathanson forecast profit, or EBITDA, of US$16 billion for 2028 and rising to US$19 billion in 2030. The research firm also predicted about US$67 billion in revenue in 2028, growing to roughly US$70 billion in 2030.
Ellison’s annual base salary will be US$5 million, with a target annual bonus of US$5 million, according to the filing. REUTERS

Russia drops war posts case against children’s hospice founder Moniava
Oct 6 - Russian investigators have dropped a criminal case against children's hospice founder Lida Moniava after finding her actions did not constitute a crime, her lawyer and a group of supporters said on Tuesday, a rare apparent reversal by authorities enforcing stringent wartime censorship laws.
Moniava was briefly detained in September and charged with deliberately spreading false information about the actions of Russian armed forces against Ukrainian civilians.
She denied the charge and was placed under pre-trial restrictions. Her Lighthouse charity continued its work supporting critically ill children and young people in Moscow region.
In a post on Telegram, a group set up to support her during the case announced what it called a miracle. "We have incredible news — the criminal case against Lida Moniava has been dropped."
It thanked those who had spoken up for Moniava. "Special thanks to the heroic patients from Lighthouse who came to support Lida at the court in wheelchairs and with ventilators," it added.
Her lawyer said investigators had informed him that they had dropped the case, Russian news agencies reported.
Moniava has publicly criticised the 4-1/2-year war in Ukraine on Telegram, calling it a crime that must end.
More than 1,380 people have faced criminal prosecution for expressing anti-war views since the full-scale war began, with around 350 currently in prison or pre-trial detention, according to Russian rights group OVD-Info. REUTERS

Commissioner Kos: EU enlargement now possible, in our interest, but issues need to be resolved
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
19:13:01 EEST
01:13:01 KST

European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos said that enlargement of the European Union was a long-term investment in peace, security and prosperity in Europe and was possible today, although certain issues still needed to be resolved.
She made the remarks on Tuesday in Strasbourg at a press conference where she presented a package of documents adopted by the European Commission concerning the European Union's preparations for future enlargement.
Kos said enlargement was in the EU's interest, as it was about protecting its interests and upholding its values. She said a larger Union represented a long-term investment in Europe's peace, security and prosperity, which was one of the reasons the European Union had been created. Enlargement also offered an opportunity to make Europe stronger, as a larger Union would increase its political and economic influence in a world marked by intense geopolitical competition.
According to Kos, enlargement would also bring tangible benefits to EU citizens by strengthening democracy, security and solidarity. She said it would benefit the European economy by strengthening the single market, creating more jobs and opening up more opportunities for people and businesses. She added that the package focused on what both candidate countries and EU member states needed to do to take the next steps in the enlargement process.
The commissioner outlined five groups of proposed measures. She said the first concerned practical solutions related to governance, the rule of law and policies. According to Kos, the EU could optimise the use of so-called passerelle clauses and expand the use of qualified majority voting where permitted by the treaties.
In particular, she said the proposal envisaged reducing the number of areas in which a single country could veto decisions supported by all other member states. She said this could apply, for example, to sanctions, the fight against tax fraud and the accession process, specifically the intermediate stages between the opening and closing of negotiations.
Kos said the second point concerned a more ambitious approach to gradual integration. She recalled that several months earlier the Commission had proposed possible changes to the enlargement methodology and presented three options: maintaining the status quo, enhanced gradual integration and a reverse membership model. She said member states had indicated that they did not support the reverse membership concept.
The commissioner said the current proposals on gradual integration were directly linked to that discussion and were aimed at substantially expanding opportunities to integrate candidate countries into specific areas of EU activity even before they obtained full membership.
At the same time, Kos stressed that gradual integration was not intended to replace full membership but rather to serve as a catalyst for the enlargement process. She said it would require two key components: progress on reforms by candidate countries and strategic alignment of positions, which she described as the novel element of the approach.
She said that once candidate countries met the required standards, they should be able to participate in strategic areas where cooperation brought mutual benefits to both current and future member states, including energy, transport, artificial intelligence, security and defence.
Kos identified the third point as the establishment of a common framework for accession and safeguards for the entire future enlargement process. She said countries seeking to join the EU had to meet very high rule-of-law standards and that the Union needed to be certain they would not deviate from those standards after accession, taking into account previous experience.
She said possible safeguard mechanisms included simplifying procedures for suspending financial support or restricting voting rights. She added that mechanisms were also being proposed to prevent new member states from blocking decisions on future enlargement because of bilateral disputes, describing this as another new element.
Kos identified the impact of accession on EU policies as the fourth point. She said the Commission's analysis showed that the EU was already prepared for enlargement in most policy areas, although certain sectors would require adjustments.
She said Ukraine's membership should not have a negative impact on EU farmers and that the Commission intended to support Ukraine in restoring access to its traditional export markets in third countries.
Kos said the fifth and final point concerned roadmaps for the four candidate countries that had made the greatest progress: Montenegro, Albania, Moldova and Ukraine.
She said the Commission planned to present indicative roadmaps for those countries in the enlargement reports due to be published on October 28. According to Kos, the aim was to help them maintain the pace of reforms, while the roadmaps would set out the next steps, preliminary timelines and clear expected outcomes, thereby increasing predictability in the accession process.
The commissioner stressed that no simplified procedures or shortcuts were envisaged.
The next step will be discussion of the proposed package in the European Parliament and the European Council.
Kos said the Commission's position was clear that EU enlargement was possible today, while acknowledging that a number of challenges still needed to be addressed.
She said one such challenge was the need to optimise EU institutions and ensure a more flexible and effective decision-making process. With regard to the rule of law and the principle of sincere cooperation, she said the Commission was proposing tools that would allow the EU to respond more decisively to serious violations, including by reducing funding or restricting voting rights.
On agriculture, Kos said the Commission proposed considering special mechanisms for Ukraine.
She added that the proposals would now be discussed with EU member states and that steps would be taken to ensure that an enlarged European Union would also become a stronger Union capable of determining its own future.
