Empowering a sustainable future: International Gas Union summit to be held in Hong Kong this October
[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]
Against a backdrop of persistent geopolitical uncertainties, global energy price trends and energy security have returned firmly to the spotlight. Taking place in Hong Kong late this month, the International Gas Union (IGU) Council 2026 and the “Empowering a Sustainable Future” Summit will offer an essential platform for cross-sector leaders to exchange perspectives on these pressing challenges.
Hosted by The Hong Kong and China Gas Company Limited (Towngas), the IGU Council 2026 and the “Empowering a Sustainable Future” Summit will run in the city from 26 to 29 October. The Council meeting will bring together around 70 international delegates, whilst the flagship summit will convene approximately 500 government officials, energy business executives, academics and industry experts from around the world for a series of in-depth panel discussions.
Held on 29 October at Hopewell Hotel, the “Empowering a Sustainable Future” Summit will centre on four pivotal themes: Asia Pacific: The Engine of Global Natural Gas Market Development, China Natural Gas Market Development, Strategic Roadmaps for Asia’s Energy Evolution, and Finance as a Driver: Strengthening Support for Energy Development. The agenda covers low-carbon energy, artificial intelligence (AI) and green finance.
Distinguished keynote speakers will include Mr Tse Chin-wan, Secretary for Environment and Ecology; Ir Arthur Li Hok-yin, Deputy Director of Electrical and Mechanical Services; and Ms Li Yalan, Vice President of the IGU. Representatives from prominent energy, financial and academic institutions across various countries and regions have also been invited to take part.
The summit has secured widespread cross-sector support and sponsorship. On the day of the event, an on-site exhibition showcase will feature leading energy enterprises presenting their latest breakthrough technologies and services to attendees.
The IGU is the world’s most influential and authoritative non-profit, member-based international organisation in the gas sector, with its membership representing more than 90% of global gas market share. As the corporate member representing Hong Kong, Towngas has long played an active role in supporting IGU initiatives, including the 29th World Gas Conference in Beijing and the Council Meeting in London last year.
Mr Peter Wong Wai-yee, Managing Director of Towngas, noted that bringing this edition of the IGU meetings to Hong Kong coincides with a pivotal moment when artificial intelligence presents both fresh opportunities and complex challenges for energy demand and applications. In response, the Hong Kong summit has specifically invited financial experts and scholars to share forward-looking perspectives on green financing and related topics.
During the event, host Towngas will organise technical site visits to give international delegates a firsthand look at Hong Kong’s diverse, real-world energy applications. Participants will inspect a pilot facility in Sai Kung that extracts hydrogen from the existing gas pipeline network for power generation. In addition to charging electric vehicles, the system supplies supplementary electricity and hot water through a combined heat and power (CHP) unit. Delegates will also tour a waste-to-energy project in Tseung Kwan O that converts landfill biogas into town gas. Furthermore, attendees will be treated to an evening cruise across Victoria Harbour, offering them a taste of Hong Kong’s vibrant cosmopolitan appeal whilst showcasing the city’s strengths on the global stage.
This year marks the start of the country’s 15th Five-Year Plan, which sets out a clear pathway for accelerating the green transition and advancing peak carbon and carbon neutrality targets. In tandem, the HKSAR Government has released the city’s first Five-Year Plan to align proactively with national development strategies. Convening the IGU Council meeting and Summit in Hong Kong at this juncture carries profound significance.
As host, Towngas looks forward to welcoming global industry leaders to Hong Kong to empower a sustainable future together. Through this premier international stage, Towngas seeks to showcase Hong Kong’s energy transition journey and contribute local expertise towards global energy security and high-quality, sustainable growth.

Britain’s Tories really, really don’t want to team up with Farage. They might still have to.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
16:00:06 UTC
01:00:06 KST

Britain’s Tories really, really don’t want to team up with Farage. They might still have to.
The Reform UK leader is the butt of mockery and vitriol at the Conservatives’ annual gathering in Birmingham. That could make a coalition near-impossible.
BIRMINGHAM, England — “Vile,” “horrible,” “betrayal,” “bastards.” For Conservative aides and politicians gathering at their annual conference this week, the hatred of Nigel Farage’s rival right-wing party Reform UK is real.
Since the opposition party’s last gathering, an already icy relationship with Reform’s national leadership has entered deep freeze. The defections of high-profile Tory politicians, including Robert Jenrick and Suella Braverman in January this year, added a personal animus to the battle for votes on the British right.
And yet, Tory Leader Kemi Badenoch has not categorically ruled out some kind of tie-up with Reform after a general election. Politically, she cannot afford to take it off the table.
Advertisement
Senior Conservatives at lunches and receptions this week were quick to aim invective and mockery at Reform — privately and sometimes in public, fueled by a row that Braverman triggered last week when she said that, as a British-born woman of British-Asian origin, she was “not an English person.”
“They’re just not our kind of people,” Conservative Leader Kemi Badenoch, the first black leader of a major political party, told the BBC about Reform on Tuesday.
Badenoch’s most senior aides put it even more bluntly. “They’re just nasty people,” said one top Conservative official, granted anonymity to speak frankly. “These people [Reform] have spent two years viciously attacking the exact people they would have to meet about any deal,” said another. “If Kemi and Rob go into a room, what are they going to fucking talk about?”
Badenoch told broadcasters Tuesday that she would rather force a second general election than strike a deal with Reform. That may be the only practical option left to her.
POLITICO spoke to more than a dozen senior Conservative politicians and aides at the party conference. Almost all indicated that a deal with Reform is not only undesirable, but the hostility is now so bad that it would fail if Badenoch ever tried to enact it.
A senior Reform official responded to this story by saying: “Two years of being hammered at the local elections has finally made the Tories crack. Quite clearly they’re obsessed with us whilst their own party crumbles around them. We look forward to consigning them to the dustbin of history.”
Advertisement
‘Cold day in hell’
If the U.K. held a general election now, almost all polling suggests Britain’s right-leaning vote would be deeply split between these two parties and further undercut by a third — the hard-right Restore Britain. That could allow Labour to squeeze through and win the most seats under the first-past-the-post electoral system, like it did in 2024.
If there was a real deadlock, even after a second election, Badenoch would be left with an unenviable choice: team up with Farage, or let Labour — perhaps with a rainbow coalition of Liberal Democrats, nationalists and Greens — run the show?
The relationship between the Conservatives and Farage, who left the party in 1992, has long been fractious and worsened after the 2019 election — when Farage stepped aside to aid a pro-Brexit majority for Boris Johnson, but received no thanks.
Since last year the defections (and the fighting talk they attracted) have sent the relationship nosediving further. Most of the opprobrium is saved for Jenrick. A year ago he was the guest speaker at a lunch with Tory donors and mayors, holding forth in private about the changes his party needed to make. Three months later he was gone. The defection of Danny Kruger, who was more respected by many on the Tory right, added hurt to insult.
The Conservatives produced an AI-assisted “tapestry” at this year’s conference that contained several mocking references to a crying Jenrick. Tory politicians repeatedly bring up the questions surrounding Reform’s finances.
Badenoch told broadcasters Tuesday that “the people in Reform are neck deep in scandal” and any tie-up “would just be one problem after another.” Her aides believe the public are no longer viewing Reform as a blank slate.
Advertisement
“I can’t imagine it being a nice coalition,” said a shadow cabinet minister. They added: “I think that Reform in power would go to pieces very quickly, they’re a very brittle top team. I wouldn’t want to be tied to that. I wouldn’t want to become responsible in any way for their mistakes or all the crazy ass money they’ve taken.”
Many of those most opposed to a Reform tie-up have been attending Tory conferences for decades. One center-right veteran of past Cabinets said: “It’ll be a cold day in hell when we get into bed with those bastards … The only way we could [enter government] is with a governing partner. If that’s the choice, I’d rather that we were a strong opposition.”
A second Conservative former Cabinet minister predicted: “There’s no way [Badenoch] will do a coalition. She just can’t trust them.” But they suggested Badenoch has other, less formal options that would still see a tie-up with Reform. “It depends how big the margin is,” they said. “If it’s anything, I think it would be a confidence and supply [agreement].”
‘Ethnicity is different’
Political tactics are one thing. Tory officials believe someone linked to Reform UK leaked a meeting 11 months ago between Katie Lam — a Conservative frontbencher — and Reform donor Nick Candy, to damage the Tories just as their conference was getting under way. (The meeting happened at a time of intense defection chatter.) A person with knowledge of the meeting insisted Lam had ignored a series of messages from Candy afterward.
But things have gone further in recent weeks. Braverman’s comments about Englishness, on an episode of the BBC’s Question Time debate program, struck a nerve for Badenoch personally while also providing her with a chance to differentiate herself from Reform.
Badenoch, who has campaigned for gender-specific toilets, told ITV’s Good Morning Britain on Tuesday: “Men and men and women are women, I’m very strict on that. But ethnicity is different. My children are half white and half black. We are a multiracial country. I think we should be proud of that.”
Advertisement
Hostility from Tory aides extends to Reform’s home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf and his pronouncements on social media. Yusuf said last month that Labour’s candidate in a special election was “born in Somalia. Do you understand what’s happening?” (The candidate, Sagal Abdi-Wali, moved to London as a child refugee in the 1990s.) Raheem Kassam, an ally of Farage in the U.S., posted on X last month calling Badenoch a “Nigerian scammer” (she was born in the U.K., moved to Nigeria and returned aged 16.)
A second shadow cabinet minister said: “We can’t allow the right to turn into this horrible, ugly thing. Let’s talk about the ideas.” James Cleverly, one of the Conservatives bidding to run for mayor of London in 2028, accused Braverman, Yusuf and other unnamed figures around Reform of amplifying “really quite vile positions” on race, ethnicity and nationality.
‘How it plays out … I don’t know’
The opprobrium is real — but so too is the Tories’ electoral plight.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has insisted he won’t call an early election, with the next not due until mid-2029. But it remains in his power to pull the plug when an opportunity arises.
All evidence points towards the Conservatives doing dismally if that happens any time soon. Kevin Hollinrake, the party chairman, admitted on Monday that it “doesn’t look winnable outright by anybody.”
A third shadow cabinet minister sounded softer in their opposition to a deal with Reform. They argued that while the Tories would not want to be shackled to Farage’s party, they did not want to see a “monster” coalition either between Labour and the Greens, Liberal Democrats and nationalist parties.
Advertisement
“How the world plays out when you actually live it, I don’t know,” they added. “We’ll just have to make whatever decision we think is in the best interests of the country at the time.”
Tiny changes to vote share would mean big changes to seat numbers in the multi-party world: “1% is the new 5%,” as a fourth shadow cabinet minister put it. A poll of 15,765 people by the firm More in Common suggests the balance of seats will be highly volatile depending on how badly the vote splits between parties of the right.
The self-funded survey, dated Aug. 21 to Sept. 21, projected Labour would be the largest party by far on 250 seats — ahead of Reform UK on 147 and the Tories on 125. A mere three- to four-point swing from the Conservatives to Reform or vice versa, however, would put either of those parties ahead of Labour.
The Conservatives and Reform attract different demographics of voter, though; a More in Common poll of 2,041 people on Sept. 25-29 found that those on the lowest incomes were more likely to back Reform than the Tories (23% to 20%), and for those on the highest incomes it was the other way round (23% to 13%).
This suggests there will be many seats where Labour comes through the middle and wins on a low vote share, like it did in 2024, said More in Common Executive Director Luke Tryl. Tryl added: “We’ll especially see this if Burnham manages to recreate Jeremy Corbyn’s 2017 coalition of Labour and Green supporters, tapping into that 40% of voters. It wasn’t enough for Corbyn to win a majority, but with a split right, it’d definitely be enough for Burnham.”
Hence both the Tories and Reform — wary of a tactical voting stampede — are arguing they are the best choice to win outright. Yusuf told GB News Tuesday: “It is clear the only party of the right that has a serious chance of a majority in parliament is Reform.”
Advertisement
But most of all, the Conservatives just don’t want to talk about it. A fifth shadow cabinet minister said “voters on the right really hate blue-on-blue” and want the Tories to focus on attacking the Labour government.
Here come the think tanks
This dilemma means some outriders are now caught in the middle, unable to choose firmly between the Tories and Reform.
Hosting its reception across the canal from the conference center on Monday night was the Centre for Government Reform think tank, run by former civil servant Ameer Kotecha. The group was at Reform’s conference too; it appears to have the blessing of senior figures in both parties.
Kotecha took a deliberate decision to have politicians from both parties on its board — the right-wing Tory peers Theodore Agnew and John Nash alongside Reform UK’s Scottish Leader Malcolm Offord. It is working on cuts to civil service headcount and getting more private sector expertise into government, which Kotecha calls the “plumbing” of the state.
“It’s important that we speak to both sides,” he told POLITICO. “We need to keep the hopper wide; if you’re talking about the really elite business talent for example, they’re quite often not yet willing to pin their colors to any one party mast.”
Others would prefer to see any sense of a deal closed off. Also hosting events on the conference fringe was Prosper UK, a center-right group led by figures including the former Scottish Conservative Leader Ruth Davidson. It will push for the party to win back liberal-minded voters who once backed the party and now support the Liberal Democrats in the south of England. It is a tricky electoral coalition.
Advertisement
‘We honestly believe now’
The mood at this week’s Birmingham jamboree can only be understood by looking to the political horizon.
The Conservatives are still trailing Reform in national polls, but unlike last year, members and aides have some confidence that — even if they cannot win an election now — the polls may be reaching an inflection point that would restore their status as the main challengers to the Labour Party.
The Tories hope to paint themselves as the voices of economic competence; a party that sees itself as having become more united as their rivals march further to the right, while facing pressure from the hard-right Restore.
“It’s not just bad blood, is it? I think we honestly believe now,” said a sixth shadow cabinet minister. “We do get a lot of support back from people who went to Lib Dems and if we did a deal with Reform, all that goes out the window.”
The first shadow cabinet minister quoted in this story said that local Conservative associations, which they visit regularly, used to ask constantly about a coalition. “And now nobody does,” they argued. “There are a lot of people who, having seen another year of Reform, don’t like what they see.”
The realities are still there, and grim for the Conservatives. But they are simply less stark than they were a year ago.
As the fifth shadow cabinet minister quoted in this story put it: “I’m not worried that we’re going to get wiped off the face of the map any more.”

An oil tanker is ablaze on a large scale near Russia’s Sochi

World Bank expects growth in Europe, Central Asia to slow to 2.2% in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:58:23 UTC
00:58:23 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Economic growth in Europe and Central Asia is expected to slow to 2.2% this year as higher energy prices, increased global uncertainty and weaker growth among trading partners weigh on activity, the World Bank said Tuesday.
The forecast compares with growth of 2.6% in 2025, according to the bank’s latest Europe and Central Asia Economic Update, titled “Making AI Work: Jobs, Firms, and Productivity.”
The slowdown is broad-based, reflecting weaker prospects across most countries in the region, although developing economies continue to demonstrate resilience.
Türkiye’s economy is projected to grow 2.8% in 2026, 3.8% in 2027 and 4.5% in 2028, according to the report.
Tight economic policies and higher imported energy costs are expected to slow Türkiye’s growth this year, while its expansion in 2027 and 2028 is forecast to make a significant contribution to the regional recovery.
The report said artificial intelligence could help reverse slowing productivity and revive economic growth, but shortcomings in skills, computing capacity and data readiness remain obstacles.
About one in five workers in the region holds a job meaningfully exposed to AI, while fewer than one in 10 firms currently uses the technology, primarily for basic tasks.
 
Middle East faces economic costs of conflict
In its separate update for the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, the World Bank projected a 2.1% contraction this year, following growth of 3.3% in 2025.
The conflict that began in February has imposed substantial economic costs, with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz hitting Gulf oil exporters the hardest.
Unlike previous energy shocks, which typically benefited oil exporters, reduced export volumes have cut output and government revenues. The repercussions also extend to tourism, aviation and logistics, while uncertainty weighs on financial markets and business confidence.
 
Growth strengthens in Africa, AI exports support East Asia
Sub-Saharan Africa’s growth is forecast to accelerate to 4.3% in 2026 from 4.1% last year, exceeding the bank’s April projection by 0.3 percentage points.
The region has remained resilient despite geopolitical tensions, climate shocks, declining development assistance and fiscal pressures.
East Asia and the Pacific is expected to grow 4.5% this year, supported in several economies by the production and export of high-tech goods linked to rising global AI investment.
The bank raised its 2026 growth forecasts for Vietnam to 7.4%, Malaysia to 5.1% and Thailand to 2%. Pacific Island economies, however, face weaker prospects because of their exposure to higher energy costs and limited buffers against external shocks.
Latin America and the Caribbean is projected to expand 2.2% this year, compared with 2.4% in 2025. The bank said stronger policy frameworks, private investment and improved confidence have helped several countries outperform the regional average.
 
Domestic demand supports South Asia
South Asia’s growth is expected to reach 6.9% this year, exceeding earlier projections, before easing to 6.7% in 2027.
Strong domestic demand, supported by remittance inflows and recent structural reforms, has helped the region withstand global shocks.
The bank warned that persistently high energy prices could increase inflation and tighten financial conditions, while a severe El Nino event could hurt agriculture and food security. A sharp reversal in global AI investment could also trigger financial strains.

Amelia Earhart investigators to study mysterious object in Pacific
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:54:29 UTC
00:54:29 KST

Amelia Earhart investigators begin expedition to study mysterious object in Pacific: "Follow the evidence"
A team searching for Amelia Earhart's lost plane has begun its expedition to the Pacific, where it plans to study a mysterious object that researchers say may be her aircraft.
The item, known as the Taraia Object, has been visible in photos dating back to 1938, the year after Earhart and navigator Fred Noonan disappeared over the Pacific Ocean during Earhart's attempt to become the first female pilot to circle the world. Earhart, Noonan and their Electra 10E plane were never found.
Researchers identified the "visual anomaly" in a lagoon on Nikumaroro, a small island in Kiribati about halfway between Australia and Hawaii. The island is about 400 miles southeast of Howland Island, where Earhart and Noonan were planning to travel.
Now, a team of researchers from Purdue University and the Oregon-based Archaeological Legacy Institute are traveling to Nikumaroro to examine the object. The research team previously said in a news release that there is "very strong" evidence that the object is Earhart's lost plane.
The team previously said they will take photos and videos of the lagoon and Taraia Object. Then, they will use magnetometers and sonar devices to scan the area before dredging the item from the water so researchers can attempt to identify it. The process will be documented by the Archealogy Channel, with short vlogs on their streaming platform, Heritage Broadcasting Service.
Richard Pettigrew, from the Archaeological Legacy Institute, said that he believes Earhart and Noonan landed on Nikumororo and camped there. He believes they survived on the island for some time, citing 1930s relics and human skeletal remains that were found there but lost over the decades.
"We owe it to Amelia's legacy at Purdue to follow the evidence," Steve Schultz, a senior vice president at Purdue University and field assistant on the expedition, told CBS News. Earhart lectured at the school before embarking on her final flight. Some of her belongings remain on display in the university's archives.
Some experts are skeptical. Ric Gillespie, the executive director of the International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery, told NBC News in 2025 that he does not think the Taraia Object is related to the Earhart expedition.
"We've looked there in that spot, and there's nothing there," he said.
For nearly a century, researchers have tried to find Earhart's missing plane, believing it will help them answer the question of what happened to the famed aviator. In 2024, another expedition team captured a sonar image that seemed to resemble a plane resting at the bottom of the sea. But the object was later determined to be a rock formation.
Wendy Rover of The Ninety Nines, an international organization for women pilots that Earhart helped establish, said she hopes the mystery of what happened to Earhart can someday be solved. Rover told CBS News that when she is flying and looking for safe places to land, she imagines Earhart doing the same while over the Pacific.
"Amelia Earhart was out there. She was going through that exact same thing," Rover said. "So yeah - what happened? What did happen? I would love to know."

EU plans 15-year probation period for new member states, gradual integration for candidates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:53:36 UTC
00:53:36 KST

Melike Pala
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
The European Commission on Tuesday proposed a new framework for future EU enlargement that would allow candidate countries to gradually integrate into selected EU policies before full membership, while subjecting new member states to stronger safeguards for up to 15 years after accession.
Under the proposed framework, new EU members could face an extended period of safeguards after accession, during which the bloc could take measures if a country seriously backslides on commitments made during accession negotiations, particularly on the rule of law, democracy, or fundamental rights.
European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos said the commission wants to ensure that countries joining the EU do not fall below the standards required for membership.
"We do not want a two-tier membership," Kos told a press conference in Brussels, stressing that both existing and new member states should enjoy equal rights.
She said the proposed safeguards would act as an "insurance policy" that could be activated if serious breaches occur.
The measures could include restricting financial support or, in the most serious cases, suspending a new member state's voting rights in the EU Council.
The commission is proposing safeguards covering a period of up to 15 years, while emphasizing that the specific transitional arrangements would have to be negotiated between the EU and each accession country and included in the relevant accession treaty or regulations.
 
Gradual integration before full membership
Alongside the safeguards, the commission is proposing a more ambitious approach to the gradual integration of candidate countries into the EU.
Kos described gradual integration as an "accelerator for enlargement and a bridge" between the EU's geopolitical objective of stabilizing Europe and its merit-based accession process.
Candidate countries that make sufficient progress on reforms and demonstrate strategic alignment with the EU could be allowed to participate in selected EU policies before becoming full members.
The commission plans to explore deeper integration in strategic sectors including energy, transport, artificial intelligence, security, and defense.
"Gradual integration is not a substitute for full membership," Kos stressed, adding that participation would remain "conditional, merit-based and reversible."
Kos identified Montenegro, Albania, Moldova, and Ukraine as the four most advanced candidates for EU membership and said it intends to publish indicative roadmaps for them.
 
Bloc seeks faster decision-making
The package also calls for changes to EU decision-making to prepare the bloc for a larger membership.
The commission said it would continue advocating the use of so-called passerelle clauses to move from unanimity to qualified majority voting in areas including sanctions, tax fraud, and certain fiscal measures in energy policy.
It also proposed using qualified majority voting for opening negotiating clusters and other intermediary decisions in accession negotiations.
The package will now feed into discussions among EU member states, the European Parliament, and the EU Council on the institutional and policy changes required for future enlargement.

The U.S. trade deficit widened sharply in August amid an influx of goods related to the artificial intelligence build-out and the vagaries of import tariffs, the Commerce Department reported Tuesday.
Imports swelled 4.3% for the month, pushing the total imbalance to $105.6 billion. That marked a 13.7% jump from July and was ahead of the Dow Jones consensus estimate for $102 billion.

Imports as a rule generally subtract from gross domestic product calculations. However, if the imports reflect stronger demand and consumption, they can be offset elsewhere.
Nevertheless, Goldman Sachs cut its tracking estimate for third-quarter economic growth to 3.1%, down 0.3 percentage point from its prior estimate. The Atlanta Federal Reserve's GDPNow tracker lowered its estimate to 3.7% following the trade report, down 0.1 percentage point from the last update.

Russia on Tuesday denied imposing anti-plague measures after the death of a worker at a biological research institute in Siberia, rejecting reports that she contracted pneumonic plague following a laboratory accident.
The 28-year-old researcher at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute died after developing pneumonia of an undetermined cause, according to Russian authorities.
Russian outlet People of Baikal identified the woman as Darya Shipilova and reported that she may have contracted pneumonic plague after a test tube broke at the laboratory. Other local media also reported a possible link between her death and an accident at the facility.
The outlet said as many as 200 people who may have had contact with Shipilova were placed under quarantine.
Russia’s consumer health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor, however, denied claims circulating online that special anti-plague measures had been introduced.
“We wish to clarify that the document and information in question do not originate from official sources and are untrue,” the agency said on Telegram.
WHO assesses risk as low
The World Health Organization said information provided by Russia indicated that no case of plague had been recorded in Irkutsk.
Russian authorities have launched an epidemiological investigation into what they described as a case of community-acquired pneumonia involving an employee of the institute, according to an update received by the WHO.
People who had been in contact with the researcher were identified and underwent medical monitoring and laboratory testing.
“Test results showed no presence of dangerous infectious disease pathogens in any of the contacts,” the Russian update said, according to the WHO.
Based on currently available information, the UN health agency assessed the risk as “moderate to low” for Irkutsk, low for Russia as a whole and very low for the rest of Europe.
WHO spokesperson Christian Lindmeier said the agency was continuing to monitor the situation and seeking to verify information surrounding the incident and laboratory tests.
Plague is a bacterial disease that can occur in several forms. Pneumonic plague affects the lungs and can spread through respiratory droplets. It can be fatal if not treated early.
US calls for transparency
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged Moscow on Tuesday to provide more information about the incident, saying Washington was monitoring developments closely.
“I think it’s incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world,” Rubio told reporters during a visit to Iceland.
Rubio cautioned against drawing conclusions about the nature of the incident without sufficient evidence, saying it would be “reckless” to speculate over whether an intentionally altered pathogen was involved.
US President Donald Trump said on Monday that Washington was closely following the situation and was prepared to offer assistance to Moscow.
Rospotrebnadzor later said Russia was prepared to help the United States tackle its own infectious disease outbreaks, citing measles cases and a fatal plague case reported in New Mexico in June.
An international conference on plague and other infectious diseases is scheduled to take place in Irkutsk on October 21-22. Organisers said the event was arranged in June and is unrelated to the researcher’s death.

"The final arbitral award is an obvious and important victory, which is the result of PrivatBank's 11-year legal battle to achieve justice and uphold the principle that illegal expropriation must have consequences," the bank's press release quoted Solvita Deglava, a member of PrivatBank's Management Board responsible for restructuring and distressed assets, as saying.

The final arbitral award is based on the tribunal's preliminary findings that it has jurisdiction to consider PrivatBank's claims and that those claims are admissible, as well as that the respondent violated the bilateral investment protection agreement. In the ruling, the tribunal rejected the respondent's objections concerning the illegality of the investments and ruled that they did not deprive the tribunal of jurisdiction or render the claims inadmissible, and therefore awarded the Ukrainian bank compensation and reimbursement of costs.
As reported, prior to April 2014, PrivatBank conducted significant operations and held valuable assets on the Crimean Peninsula, including loans, real estate and cash. Shortly after the illegal occupation of Crimea, Russia took a number of measures that resulted in the illegal expropriation of the bank's assets and the termination of its operations in Crimea.
Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan UK LLP and Asters Consult LLC assisted Ukraine in the proceedings.

64th Helicopter Wing in Germany Reorganized to Accommodate New Chinook Helicopters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:50:23 UTC
00:50:23 KST

The German Air Force has reorganized the 64th Helicopter Wing (HSG 64) and moved its command to Schönewalde/Holzdorf Air Base in Brandenburg.
The German media outlet Sicherheit & Verteidigung reported this.
As part of the reorganization, the wing’s headquarters, as well as its flight and technical units, moved from Laupheim to Brandenburg.
These changes are part of preparations to introduce the CH-47F Chinook Block II SR AAR heavy transport helicopters into service.
The German Air Force is restructuring its helicopter units ahead of the new helicopters’ first flights, scheduled for fall 2027.
The internal structure of HSG 64 Air Wing calls for three squadrons, two of which will handle air transport. The third squadron will conduct search-and-rescue missions for troops.
At the same time, construction is underway at the Holzdorf Air Base, where 47 ordered CH-47F helicopters are scheduled to be stationed.
The bulk of the construction work at the air base is expected to be completed by 2030, and the new hangars and infrastructure will be ready by the end of 2026.
The CH-47F Chinook Block II heavy-lift transport helicopter, in the SR AAR (Special Operations / Short Range Air-to-Air Refueling) configuration, is designed to provide high payload capacity and flight range in high-risk environments.
The updated Block II version features a reinforced airframe, more powerful Honeywell T55-GA-714A engines, and a modernized transmission. Adding an in-flight refueling boom and a fuel management system significantly extends the helicopter’s operational radius and mission duration without intermediate landings.
The SR AAR variant is designed to meet the specific needs of special operations units and provide logistical support in challenging environments. The helicopter is equipped with a state-of-the-art digital cockpit based on the CAAS (Common Avionics Architecture System) architecture, an enhanced onboard air defense system, and improved ACRB composite rotor blades.
In total, Germany is purchasing 60 Chinook helicopters to replace its aging fleet of CH-53s, and production has been underway at Boeing’s Philadelphia plant since May 2025.

Nearly two-thirds of Americans believe antisemitism has increased since the October 7, 2023, attacks, yet many continue to struggle with identifying and calling out common instances of anti-Jewish hatred in practice, according to a new national polling report.

Majority of Americans notice rise in antisemitism since Oct. 7
The first section of the report examined attitudes toward American Jews three years after October 7. The findings showed that 64% of Americans believe antisemitism or Jew-hatred has increased since October 7, 2023.
Among those who see antisemitism increasing, the top reasons cited included the spread of misinformation, Gaza protests, increased polarization, Jew-hatred becoming more socially acceptable, and a lack of condemnation.
The report found that 61% of Americans agree that criticism of Israel is often used as an excuse to express anti-Jewish views, a statistically significant increase from 53% in 2025.
The report noted that 30% of Americans remain unfamiliar with the term “antisemitism,” with that unfamiliarity rising to 39% among young adults aged 18 to 34.
The report said that 21% of Americans see antisemitism as a justified reaction to the Israel-Hamas War, a figure that jumps to 35% among young adults. Additionally, 15% of Americans believe American Jews are complicit in genocide.
Questions of loyalty also emerged. The report said that 22% of young adults believe American Jews support Israel more than the United States, and 25% of young adults state that an American who expresses strong support for Israel is less loyal to the US.
Among the respondents, 44% believe American Jews support the Netanyahu government, and 37% believe most American Jews support Israel’s war in Gaza.
Regarding overall public perception of Jewish people, 69% of Americans hold a favorable view. However, favorability drops to 61% among young adults aged 18 to 34, a cohort where unfavorable views climbed to 29%.
The data found that Americans who hold unfavorable views toward Israel are more than twice as likely to harbor unfavorable views of Jewish people compared to the general public (29% vs 12%).
Around 40% of US Jews have favorable view of Netanyahu
The second section of the report turned to Israel’s upcoming election and attitudes toward Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The survey found that 58% of Americans can correctly identify Israel’s prime minister. Overall, 40% of Americans view Netanyahu unfavorably, while 23% are unsure or have no opinion.
Favorability toward Netanyahu divided sharply by age and political affiliation, with younger Americans and Democrats viewing him most unfavorably.
The survey found that 19% of Americans reported that their views of Netanyahu shape how they view American Jews, and about one-third (35%) believed Netanyahu leaving office would improve their perceptions of Israel and Jewish people.
When examining what drives unfavorable views toward Israel, the report said that concerns stem primarily from the conflict, policies, and leadership rather than opposition to Israel’s existence as a Jewish state.
The polling highlighted limited public familiarity with Israeli democracy: only 30% of Americans know Israel is the only democracy in the Middle East, only 27% know Arab citizens of Israel can vote in Israeli elections, and only 21% know Arabs serve in Israel’s parliament.

Grassroots literary movement turns October 7 grief into books with new 'Bound in Memory' exhibition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:49:00 UTC
00:49:00 KST

When the scale of the October 7 massacre became clear, editor Dana Naomi Ben Shlomi watched news feeds flood with uniform, clinical digital boxes detailing the names and ranks of the fallen.
To her, these clinical notices felt like reducing a human life to a mere statistic.
“Every single one of them was an entire universe,” Ben Shlomi recalls. “I knew we had to rescue their personal stories from those uniform digital boxes.”
Ben Shlomi launched Kotvim Chaim (“writing life/living writers”), a grassroots initiative pairing bereaved families with writers, editors, and designers to preserve the legacies of those killed.
Today, the volunteer network has grown to over 500 literary professionals. The organization has shepherded 65 memorial books to publication, with another 135 currently in production.
National Library of Israel hosts archive
This profound literary archive is currently taking center stage at the National Library of Israel for an exhibition and commemorative event titled Bound in Memory, showcasing the hundreds of biographies deposited at the library since the outbreak of the war.
Among the newly published works is Hineni (“here I am”), a biography documenting the life of Supt. Dan Ganot.
Ganot was a 41-year-old deputy platoon commander in the Israel Police Directorate for Coordination of Enforcement Operations who rushed toward the unfolding massacre at Kibbutz Be’eri and never returned.
For his mother, Cheli Efrat Ganot, turning her son’s life into a tangible book was an act of profound resistance against the finality of death. “The book is a continuation of Dan’s path,” Ganot says. “The most important thing to me is the message within it – giving unconditional love and friendship.”
Angelica Agabayev, a volunteer writer who knew Dan through mutual friends, penned the book. Translating raw trauma into a cohesive narrative proved to be a grueling journey, requiring a rare hybrid of journalistic rigor and deep psychological sensitivity.
“It wasn’t simple,” Agabayev admits. “Not everyone is ready to open up. Some would start talking and break down. You have to walk on eggshells to preserve the story exactly as it was.”
Book's completion provides a structured anchor for bereaved families
For these families left behind, finishing the book has provided a structured anchor in a sea of grief. Despite the heavy loss, Ganot has used the book as a springboard to reclaim her life, choosing to lecture youth groups about Dan’s values.
“I chose life,” Ganot says. “Dan sowed the strength in me to keep choosing life.”
This is the exact transformation Ben Shlomi hoped to achieve.
“A bereaved family gets to choose the narrative of how their loved one will be remembered,” she says. “In doing so, they keep their light burning.”
The "Bound in Memory" exhibit is on level -2 at the National Library of Israel. For more information, visit: nli.org.il/en/discover/books/7-october-books

‘Raging desire for revenge’: How does the Arab world remember Hamas’s October 7 invasion?

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:48:49 UTC
00:48:49 KST

Three years after Hamas's October 7 invasion of Israel, Arab media coverage of the anniversary has focused heavily on the devastation in Gaza, often making little or no mention of the Israeli civilians killed in the attack that sparked the war and sometimes going as far as to celebrate it.
The Jerusalem Post has not identified a statement from an Arab leader expressing sympathy for Israeli victims of the October 7 attack as of Tuesday. However, Hamas shared a condemnation of the statement issued by UN Secretary-General António Guterres on the invasion.
Hamas has continued to deny targeting civilians, carrying out sexual assaults and mistreating hostages in captivity, claiming that investigations had disproved the allegations. However, a UN mission that visited Israel concluded that there were reasonable grounds to believe conflict-related sexual violence occurred during the October 7 massacre and that there was clear and convincing information that hostages had been subjected to sexual violence in captivity.
Former hostages have also repeatedly described the torture, starvation, and sexual violence they experienced while they were held against their will in Gaza.
Hamas demanded Guterres retract his statement, which acknowledged Hamas and other Palestinian terrorists “brutally” killed more than 1,200 Israelis and foreign nationals, deliberately targeted civilians and sexually assaulted and tortured hostages in captivity.
Articles from the Arab world support 'Al-Aqsa Flood' massacre
Though Guterres expressed sympathy for the victims of October 7, his statement also addressed the “untold suffering on Palestinians in Gaza” and insisted that both Hamas and Israel need to enter the next stage of the ceasefire agreement.
The Egyptian state-owned Maspero marked the anniversary of Hamas’s October 7 attack using the terrorist group’s name for the assault, publishing an article titled “New details emerge about the Al-Aqsa Flood... and the region’s involvement in a chaos plot” that featured exclusively Palestinian and Egyptian professors.
The article failed to share the number of Israelis killed during the “crushing blow,” instead reporting only that Hamas was able to “occupy the settlements located in the envelope” and kill “hundreds of soldiers and officers of the Zionist entity.”
Unmentioned in the report was that more than 800 of those killed on October 7 were civilians. The youngest known victim was Naama Abu Rashed, a Bedouin-Israeli newborn who died just 14 hours after she was delivered by emergency Cesarean section after her pregnant mother was shot in the stomach while being driven to hospital.
“Events did not end with the clashes of October 7th. As expected, they escalated into a war of extermination waged by the Zionist entity against the Gaza Strip, during which approximately 74,000 Palestinians were killed, and about 100,000 others were wounded,” the report continued.
“Around 90 percent of Gaza's buildings were destroyed, and its infrastructure was almost completely obliterated. The war did not stop at Gaza; it extended to wars against Lebanon and then against Iran, leading to subsequent changes in the map of the Middle East.”
The state media did not mention Hezbollah’s attacks on October 8, 2023, which led to the war on the northern front, instead focusing on the view of Dr. Emad Mohsen, who alleged Israel “unleashed the killing machine accompanied by intense hatred, loathing, and a raging desire for revenge,” which resulted in “genocide, famine, crimes against humanity, and the most heinous forms of violent behavior on a human level.”
'Thirst for Palestinian and Arab blood... genocide, murder, displacement'
“Above all, the true face of Zionist extremism, its expansionist desire, its thirst for Palestinian and Arab blood, its call for displacement, genocide, murder, settlement, and the undermining of the Palestinian dream of freedom and national independence, was revealed,” the paper published.
Al Ghad, the first independent daily Arabic newspaper in Jordan, also failed to mention the specific number of victims in its article on the massacre, instead focusing on Israel closing the crossing from Gaza and the West Bank for two days.
“On the morning of October 7, 2023, Hamas surprised Israel with an unprecedented attack on 11 military bases and 22 settlements along the Gaza Strip, resulting in the death, injury, and capture of hundreds of Israelis,” it reported on Sunday, adding that the explanation that Hamas argued it committed the attack "to end the unjust siege on Gaza and to thwart Israel's plans to liquidate the Palestinian cause and impose its sovereignty over the Al-Aqsa Mosque."
It also focused on the civilian deaths in Gaza, relying on figures by the Hamas-run Gaza Health Ministry, which doesn’t distinguish between combatant and civilian deaths.
The independent Lebanese news website Janoubia published a practical analysis of the threats facing Israel and its military successes since October 7 in an article titled “8 dangers threatening Israel on ‘October 7th!’”
Although the article referred to the attack as “Operation Al-Aqsa Flood” and did not mention its victims, it focused on Israel’s security situation and acknowledged several of the IDF’s achievements. It also mentioned the displacement of Israelis from communities near the northern and southern borders following the attacks, an aspect of the war that has received relatively little attention in much international media coverage.
Asharq Al-Awsat, a Saudi-owned media group headquartered in London, published an article stressing that assassinated Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar had warned Israel in 2022 that Hamas would respond if Israel continued “attacks” on Al-Aqsa Mosque and Jerusalem.
The article attributed the launch of “Operation Al-Aqsa Flood” on October 7, 2023, to Israeli actions and focused on whether Hamas had achieved its objectives. The article also acknowledged Israel’s “unprecedented” success in assassinating Hamas’s leadership, while accusing the IDF of conducting “an indiscriminate bombing campaign across the Gaza Strip” and, citing a UN committee, claiming that “Israel has sought to wipe out Gaza through a genocide operation.”
At the same time, Asharq Al-Awsat quoted Gaza-based Palestinian political analyst Mustafa Ibrahim criticizing Sinwar, saying that “popular criticism of Sinwar and anger over his ill-considered decision continue,” alongside the suffering of Gaza residents who lost their homes and property. Ibrahim added that Palestinians outside Gaza might support Sinwar’s actions because they had not experienced the same destruction, killing, and displacement.
Another recurring theme in Arab coverage was whether Netanyahu had received advance warnings of the attack from Arab states, shifting attention from Hamas’s actions to alleged Israeli intelligence and political failures. Haaretz first reported that Netanyahu denied receiving advance warning from the United Arab Emirates, while The Wall Street Journal later reported that Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel had warned Netanyahu of Hamas’s plans. Netanyahu has denied receiving such a warning.

Mamdani lit the fire. Now he’s handing us a squirt gun - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:48:48 UTC
00:48:48 KST

Rabbi Dr. Ari Berman, president of Yeshiva University, said it in five words. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is an “arsonist posing as a firefighter.”
The mayor’s defenders will call that unfair. So let’s be scrupulously fair. Set aside the atmosphere, the feelings, and anything Mamdani could pin on someone else. Judge him only on what he has said and done himself, on the record, much of it on camera. That record is more than enough.
What he said
In June 2025, a podcast host asked Mamdani about the chant “globalize the intifada.” He did not condemn it. He said what he heard in that language was a desperate desire for equality and Palestinian rights. Days later on NBC’s Meet the Press, Kristen Welker asked him three times to condemn the phrase. Three times he would not. He offered only that it was not language he used, and that a mayor should not police speech.
That was weeks after Jews were murdered in Washington and firebombed in Boulder, Colorado, attacks that New York’s Jewish federation tied directly to this kind of rhetoric. UJA-Federation of New York and other Jewish groups had publicly asked every mayoral candidate for exactly one thing: to condemn it. Only later, in a private meeting with business leaders, did he reportedly say he would “discourage” the phrase.
He has repeatedly accused Israel of genocide. He supports the boycott movement against Israel. And just last month, as Israel’s prime minister came to New York for the United Nations Security Council, the mayor of this city vowed to seek his arrest.
What he did
Last November, a crowd massed outside Park East Synagogue in Manhattan during an aliyah event, chanting “globalize the intifada.” The mayor-elect had a choice. His spokesperson’s statement faulted the synagogue, claiming the event violated international law. Jews were menaced at the door of their own house of worship, and the incoming mayor’s office scolded the Jews.
On January 1, within hours of taking the oath, Mamdani revoked the city’s adoption of the IHRA definition of antisemitism and its order barring city agencies from boycotting Israel. To his credit, he reissued an order on protests at houses of worship. The definition and the boycott protections stayed gone.
In April, he used his veto for the first time as mayor. He did not use it on a budget line or a zoning fight. He used it to kill a bill creating protest buffer zones around schools, over the objections of UJA-Federation of New York and a coalition of major Jewish organizations that called the veto a profound failure.
City Council’s own antisemitism task force has noted that roughly a quarter of antisemitic hate crimes in the city target children. A companion bill protecting houses of worship passed with a veto-proof majority. He let it become law without his signature and announced that he disagreed with its framing.
And this week, he unveiled an antisemitism strategy that refuses to define antisemitism and never mentions anti-Zionism.
What he is paying
Now look at what that plan puts on the table to physically protect houses of worship: $1 million, in a city budget of $126 billion. That is less than one penny out of every $1,000 the city spends.
And it is not even reserved for Jewish institutions. It covers vulnerable nonprofits and houses of worship of every kind. The same budget found $175m. for a new rental voucher program, 175 times as much.
The “more than $30m.” in the headlines is a magic trick. Most of it is a $26m. increase to the city’s general hate crimes office, which serves every community and was announced months ago.
Out of that pot come grants capped at $10,000 apiece. Another $4.5m. goes to a Holocaust memorial garden in Queens and a Jewish cultural center in Brooklyn. Worthy causes, but neither one stops a man with a knife at the door of a synagogue.
Meanwhile, Jews were the victims in 57% of all reported hate crimes in New York City through the first seven months of this year, according to NYPD figures. One community is absorbing more than half the hatred in the most diverse city on earth, and its mayor answered with a rounding error.
Put down the match
None of this is about feelings. Every word above is something Mamdani said, signed, vetoed, or chose not to say. That is what Berman means. You cannot spend years supplying the fuel, then show up with a squirt gun and ask Jewish New Yorkers to applaud.
If the mayor wants to be believed, the most important item in his plan would cost the city nothing. Condemn “globalize the intifada” by name, publicly, with no qualifiers. Stop calling Israel a genocidal state. Restore a definition of antisemitism that reflects what Jews are actually facing. Then fund security to match the threat, not the press release.
Until then, Jewish New Yorkers should take every dollar, apply for every grant, and never once mistake a gesture for protection. Call your council member. Demand that security funding be measured against the hate crime numbers, not last year’s budget line, and that City Council revisit the school buffer zone bill he vetoed.
We are not asking for special favors. We are asking for what every New Yorker deserves: to send our children to school and walk into our houses of worship without wondering who is waiting outside.
New York does not need a firefighter with a gas can in the truck. It needs a mayor who puts down the match.
The writer is an author and strategist whose work explores Jewish life, culture, and public affairs. She is the founder of 250Shabbat, a grassroots initiative strengthening Jewish identity through the shared experience of Shabbat, and host of The Silent Revolution podcast.

How a playwright transformed a sister’s loss into art for children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:48:29 UTC
00:48:29 KST

For Yuval Naim, the grief of losing her younger sister, Agam, in the Gaza conflict is not a static sorrow but a shifting landscape.
To process this new reality, the 28-year-old Jaffa resident has turned to the stage, channeling her family’s heartbreak into a children’s play titled Out of Three, One is Missing (Mishalosh Yotzet Achat), which premiered last week. Through a whimsical narrative about a hive of bees, Naim explores a heavy truth: There is no single, correct way to mourn.
“It was hard for me to cope with the grief. I told my psychologist I didn’t know what to do. She replied, ‘You’re a creator – so create,’” Naim said. “It made me realize that if I found it difficult to talk about Agam for the time being, I could express what I was going through through my art.”
Naim is the eldest of three sisters who grew up in the quiet settings of Pardes Hanna before moving to Kibbutz Mishmarot. Her sisters, Peleg and Agam, followed.
“Agam was driven to excel in everything she touched,” Naim recalled, sketching a portrait of a vibrant, deeply loved young woman. “She had so many different circles of friends – from her pre-military service year at the Edenim youth village to her intensive training as a combat paramedic. Even now, her friends still come to visit us. So many people loved her; she meant the world to so many.”
Agam Naim deployed in Gaza Strip for seven months
St.-Sgt. Agam Naim spent seven months deployed with combat forces in Gaza. She had fulfilled her frontline duties and was scheduled to transition to a safe, prestigious instructional role – commanding and training the next generation of paramedics. She was never supposed to re-enter the conflict zone. Yet, driven by fierce duty and loyalty to her peers, she insisted on going back one final time.
“Mom would tell her that the difference between a score of 90 and 95 didn’t really matter anymore,” Naim said, “but Agam would reply that she was going to be treating people, so it was important.
“She wasn’t supposed to go back into Gaza anymore, but she insisted on entering one last time just to say goodbye to her people and to be with them,” Naim said.
First female IDF soldier killed in Gaza during September 2024 operation
During this final entry, Agam fell. On September 17, 2024, at just 20 years old, Agam was killed alongside four other combat soldiers when an explosive device detonated in Rafah’s Tel Sultan neighborhood. She became the first female soldier killed in action during the ground operation in the Gaza Strip.
The tragedy in Out of Three, One is Missing is filtered through a metaphor children can understand. The story follows three busy bees. When the third bee suddenly disappears, the remaining two must navigate the hive alone.
“Each of the two remaining bees copes with the disappearance of the third bee in a completely different way,” the playwright explained, detailing the invisible friction that can fracture a grieving family.
“One desperately wants to hold a ceremony, while the other does not. One wants to speak about the missing bee, but the other isn’t ready to talk about her yet. One really wants to use laughter as a way to cope, while the other feels completely differently about it.”
Despite the underlying gravity, Naim deliberately keeps the texture of the play light and comedic. Much of the action centers on a competitive nectar-gathering tournament.
“While the play certainly deals with the different ways we cope with loss, for the most part, it is light and funny,” Naim said. “The bees are entirely caught up in a nectar-collecting competition that they are determined to win. They just aren’t used to being only two yet, and that brings its own set of challenges.”
The play ultimately serves as a lesson in empathy and radical patience. “The show demonstrates that you have to be patient with another person’s distinct way of coping,” Naim explained.
By translating her family’s private pain into a universal fable, she hopes to give children the tools to understand their own emotional worlds. “The play seeks to provide children with a safe space to see themselves, to recognize the ways they navigate different hardships, and to understand that all coping mechanisms are legitimate,” she explained.
As she moved through final rehearsals with her cast, Naim kept her eyes on the project's broader future.
“I want as many children as possible to see this play,” she said. “My aspiration is to bring it to one of the major children’s theaters and to take it on the road to regional councils and schools.”
In doing so, she ensures that while the family trio can never be whole again, Agam’s spirit continues to teach, protect, and heal. Yet away from the theater lights, the personal journey of grief remains a daily, quiet battle for the older sister left behind.
“Sometimes,” Naim reflected, “I still feel like my subconscious is just waiting for her to come back.”

The United Kingdom has reportedly warned Israel that it could expel 27 Israeli diplomats if Israel proceeds with plans to close the British Consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, according to Israeli media reports, in a diplomatic standoff that has pushed bilateral relations to a historic low.
The reported warning, first published by Israeli outlet Ynet on Monday, allegedly came from British Ambassador to Israel Simon Walters, who was said to have conveyed to Israeli officials that London would respond to the closure on a one-for-one basis.
According to the reports, such a move could effectively paralyze Israel’s diplomatic mission in London, which has already been operating without a permanent ambassador for more than a year.
The British Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), however, did not confirm the reported threat when approached by Anadolu.
“I would steer you away from rumours. We would not comment on speculation or live discussions,” a spokesperson said.
The reported dispute follows Israel’s decision to order the closure of the nearly 200-year-old British Consulate in East Jerusalem within 30 days.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar ordered the closure after Britain imposed economic sanctions and a trade ban on goods originating from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The Israeli government has described Britain’s measures as unjustified. Sa’ar called the UK’s trade restrictions a “moral distortion” and accused the Labour government of adopting a hostile approach toward Israel, according to Israeli media reports.
Ynet reported that Israeli diplomatic sources had indicated that Israel would respond to any British action against its diplomats.
The outlet quoted the sources as saying: “Israel has shown in the past that it will respond in kind to every step taken against it, and it will show it again.”
 
Quiet diplomatic efforts
The escalation has also prompted behind-the-scenes diplomatic efforts to prevent the closure of the British Consulate in East Jerusalem.
Reuters reported that UK National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell made a quiet visit to Israel last week in an effort to resolve the dispute and keep the consulate open.
According to the report, the diplomatic effort did not produce an agreement.
British officials have reportedly been particularly angered by Israel’s decision to give London only 30 days to close the consulate.
The British government has maintained that the consulate plays an important role in its engagement with Palestinians and that its closure would undermine longstanding diplomatic and humanitarian work.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said in September, referring to the Israeli government’s response to Britain’s sanctions measures: “I regret what the Israeli government has announced, but I’m proud of what we did and it was the right thing to do.”
He also previously rejected speculation about possible British retaliation over the consulate, saying: “I do not want to speculate on this, but we do not want this to happen. It would damage the very important work that we are doing, helping people in those communities. The consulate has been there for nearly 200 years. And this is a long-standing position that we have had. And so, you know, this is a conversation we continue to have, but we do not want this to happen.”
The confrontation marks a significant deterioration in relations between London and Israel, following Britain’s decision to impose measures targeting goods originating from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The British government has defended its sanctions policy as part of its response to developments in the occupied Palestinian territory and the broader conflict.
Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid has meanwhile criticized the government’s decision to close the British consulate, warning of the diplomatic consequences.
“Fighting with the world is not a policy. This effectively means closing our embassy in London. What benefit does this have for Israel?” Lapid said.
With the Oct. 8 deadline approaching for the reported closure of the British Consulate in East Jerusalem, the dispute remains focused on whether a diplomatic channel can prevent further escalation.

Zelenskyy: High Command sets tasks on electronic warfare, sanctions, supply of long-range drones to AFU
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
18:46:41 EEST
00:46:41 KST

Following a meeting of the High Command, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced the assignment of additional tasks for the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) and manufacturers in the field of electronic warfare, the preparation of new sanctions packages against Russia, and key objectives for supplying Ukrainian forces with long-range drones for the coming year.
According to him, detailed reports were presented during the meeting on the capabilities of electronic warfare systems and their use in protecting infrastructure. Zelenskyy said this component of defense accounts for a significant portion of the neutralization of Russian "suicide drones."
"Defense Intelligence of Ukraine also reported on Russia's technological priorities for this year and next, and on the supplies of critical components and equipment that Russia receives for weapons production to meet them," according to a post shared by the president on Facebook.
According to him, based on the findings of the Main Intelligence Agency's report, new sanctions packages will be prepared, and the intelligence agency will submit relevant proposals to the Cabinet of Ministers and the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine (NSDC).
"We are also working to synchronize our sanctions accross partners' jurisdictions," Zelenskyy said.
In addition, during the meeting, the High Command identified the main tasks for supplying Ukrainian forces with long-range drones for the coming year. The president emphasized that the main criterion in this regard must be Ukraine's ability to respond in kind to Russian strikes.
"The key criterion is that we must be able to respond to Russian strikes in kind," Zelenskyy said.

rotating octagonal forms marked with community voices shape queens landmark
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:45:55 UTC
00:45:55 KST

rotating octagonal forms marked with community voices shape queens landmark
developed in collaboration with astoria houses residents, revolving voices combines interactive structures with etched poetry to create a public space that shifts between everyday gathering and community storytelling.
Community voices inform waterfront Public landmark in Queens
Revolving Voices by The Urban Conga and local poet Tamra Cosby is a permanent public artwork and gathering space at Astoria Houses, a New York City public housing development in Queens. Located beside the Astoria waterfront and ferry dock, the installation brings community stories, memories, poetry, and imagery into a sculptural and interactive structure.
The project was developed through community engagement sessions with Cosby as part of From Roots to Arts: Celebrating NYCHA’s Cultural Heritage, an artist-in-residence program created by the Public Housing Community Fund and NYCHA. Residents shared memories, experiences, and ideas that informed both the physical design and the imagery and text embedded in the installation.
Revolving Voices features four rotating octagonal structures | all images ©Urban Conga
Rotating megaphone forms compose a changing public space
Taking the form of a megaphone, Revolving Voices by studio Urban Conga and poet Tamra Cosby consists of four large-scale octagonal structures arranged along the curve of a performance space and gradually decreasing in size. Their perforated metal exteriors depict people, activities, and stories from the Astoria Houses community, while the interiors feature etched messages, memories, and poetry by Cosby and other residents.
Each component can be manually rotated, changing the installation’s orientation and the views it frames. The structures can face outward toward the waterfront or turn inward toward Astoria Houses, creating different relationships between the artwork, its surroundings, and the community. The rotating forms also allow the installation to function as a set of portals, seating areas, and gathering spaces.
Revolving Voices serves not just as a visual work but as a functional gathering space for residents
Playable public artwork for everyday use and community events
Designed for both everyday use and community events, Revolving Voices supports sitting, climbing, exploring, performance, poetry, music, conversation, and reflection. By combining interactive structures with community-generated imagery and writing, the project turns a waterfront public space into a setting for gathering and storytelling.
inspired by the form of a megaphone, the octagonal structures metaphorically amplify and project the voices of the Astoria Houses community
‘By centering the voices, memories, and continued participation of residents, the work creates a place that feels rooted in the community and invites people to gather, engage, and connect,’ shares Ryan Swanson, Principal of Urban Conga.‘This piece reflects the idea that our voices may change over time, but they remain connected,’ adds artist Tamra Cosby.
the exterior perforated imagery celebrates the people, talents, and stories that make up the Astoria Houses community
‘The Connected Communities program places residents at the heart of the design process, ensuring that the art in our developments directly reflects the people who live there,’ says NYCHA Chief Executive Officer Lisa Bova-Hiatt. ‘Revolving Voices reflects the stories and lived experiences of residents living at Astoria Houses, and tells the history of the community in a fun, interactive way,’ comments Alex Zablocki, Executive Director of the Public Housing Community Fund.
the interior panels feature powerful messages, stories, and poetry from Tamra Cosby and other community members, created through community workshops
each unit rotates to be reoriented for different experiences within the space
a group of kids regulates and relaxes within the artwork
the movement of the artwork allows the community to make it theirs and adjust it as they want it to be set up
during community events, Revolving Voices creates as a backdrop for performance, music, conversation, and shared expression
the words in the artwork are cut out to create a textural moment, allowing people to literally feel the words within the work
Revolving Voices sits at Hallet’s Cove overlooking the Manhattan skyline
project info:
name: Revolving Voices
designer: The Urban Conga | @theurbanconga
poet: Tamra Cosby | @tamranottamara
location: Queens, New York
designboom has received this project from our DIY submissions feature, where we welcome our readers to submit their own work for publication. See more project submissions from our readers here.

56 Ukrainians Still Missing in Nepal After Flood as Search and Identification Efforts Continue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06

00:45:30 KST

- Category
- World
56 Ukrainians Still Missing in Nepal After Flood as Search and Identification Efforts Continue
The fate of 56 Ukrainian citizens missing after the devastating floods in Nepal remains unknown, even after the government formally ended its 40-day active search-and-rescue operation, Suspilne reported on October 6.
“Unfortunately, despite weeks of efforts by diplomats, consuls, and rescuers, they have still not been found among either the dead or the injured,” Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry stated.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“The Nepalese government’s announcement that the 40-day active search-and-rescue operation has ended does not mean that the search or efforts to establish the circumstances of people’s disappearances have stopped. Rescue services continue searching for and identifying remains,” the ministry continued.
According to data the ministry provided to Suspilne, 5,285 people are currently listed as missing in Nepal, including 261 foreign tourists. Of those, 56 are Ukrainian citizens.
Suspilne reported that the Ukrainian Embassy in India contacted Nepalese authorities again after the country began legally recognizing some missing people as deceased. Diplomats requested clarification on how deaths are officially documented when remains cannot be located or identified.
“The National Police of Ukraine continues the pretrial investigation and is completing the formation of a database of relatives’ DNA profiles for subsequent transfer to the foreign side,” Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry told Suspilne. “The case remains under special supervision of the Foreign Ministry, the Consular Service Department, and Ukraine’s embassies in India and China.”
Suspilne noted that Nepal formally ended the active search-and-rescue operation on October 5. Authorities reported that at least 1,455 people had died, while 13,795 people were rescued.
When the floods first struck Nepal in late August, Ukrainian authorities initially lost contact with an organized tour group of 46 citizens. The number of Ukrainians reported missing later rose to 53 as additional relatives contacted the Foreign Ministry’s emergency hotline.

MOSCOW, October 6. /TASS/. The new heavy truck market is expected at the level of 50,000 units as of the end of 2027, department director of Russian truck maker Kamaz Alexander Migal said at the CarX 26 forum.
"Our common vision of the next year is that we will see more or less the same volume within 50,000 vehicles," he said.
Macroeconomic factors continue influencing the market, including budgeting and the overall condition of the economy. The wear and tear in the heavy haulers segment is much higher than in the car market and the requirement for their renewal is more expressed. However, the desire of the business to change their vehicle fleets is not observed, the Kamaz spokesman said.
"So it follows the market will not move anywhere, we do not see growth thus far," he added.
According to the Russian Ministry of Industry and Trade, 4,100 trucks were sold in September 2026, down 5.4% in annual terms.

EU to present accession roadmap for Ukraine on 28 October
The College of Commissioners plans to approve EU accession roadmaps for the four leading candidate countries – Montenegro, Albania, Ukraine and Moldova – on 28 October, alongside the annual progress reports for candidate countries.
Source: European Pravda's correspondent in Brussels, citing an EU official familiar with the process, speaking on condition of anonymity
Details: The European Commission will present EU accession roadmaps for Ukraine, Moldova, Montenegro and Albania as part of the presentation of the 2026 Enlargement Package.
"Indicative EU membership roadmaps for Montenegro, Albania, Moldova and Ukraine will be presented within the framework of the 2026 Enlargement Package," the source said.
The official added that the roadmaps will be valid provided the candidate countries "maintain the pace of reforms".
Background:
- On 6 October, the College of Commissioners adopted a package on pre-enlargement policy reviews, which will enable new members, including Ukraine, to join the EU.
- European Pravda recently reported that the EU was also developing proposals under which the four countries considered the leading candidates for EU membership – Montenegro, Ukraine, Moldova and Albania – will receive accession roadmaps.
- European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos had previously announced plans to propose changes to the EU's internal operating mechanisms to introduce safeguards that will prevent new members from undermining key policy areas or going back on their commitments.
- Earlier, Kos outlined four areas for change in the EU's enlargement process: internal EU reforms, stronger democratic safeguards, gradual integration, and transitional measures.

Germany Arrests Former Intelligence Chief Accused of Passing Secrets to Foreign Spy Services

Unknown Publisher

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Germany Arrests Former Intelligence Chief Accused of Passing Secrets to Foreign Spy Services
Germany has arrested former Federal Intelligence Service (BND) chief August Hanning on suspicion of espionage and treason, accusing him of using classified information in contacts with foreign intelligence services.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Germany’s Federal Prosecutor’s Office on October 6, Hanning and former BND employee Manfred D. were detained under warrants issued by the Federal Court of Justice. Authorities also searched properties linked to the suspects in Bavaria, North Rhine-Westphalia, and Berlin.
Prosecutors allege that Manfred D. supplied Hanning with around 2,000 BND documents over several years in exchange for payment. Many contained classified information intended exclusively for internal intelligence use, including material prepared for briefings of senior German officials.
Hanning allegedly used some of the information in his private consulting work. Prosecutors said that on one occasion he used classified intelligence “to draft an analysis” for an officer of a foreign intelligence service. Authorities have not disclosed which foreign country was involved or whether the material reached its intended recipient.
Investigators also allege that Hanning maintained close contact for several years with a representative of another foreign intelligence service and passed political information partly based on material obtained from Manfred D.
Hanning headed the BND, Germany’s foreign intelligence agency, from 1998 to 2005. According to the BBC on October 6, the investigation emerged after authorities discovered classified BND documents on an electronic storage device during a separate investigation in 2025.
The arrest comes a day after current BND chief Martin Jäger warned that Germany has become an increasingly important target for foreign intelligence operations, sabotage, and political interference, particularly from Russia.
Speaking before the Bundestag on October 5, Jäger said Moscow was waging an undeclared “shadow war” against Germany and warned of further attempts at intimidation and interference.

Russian Tank Regiment Commander Goes to Inspect Front-Line Positions—Ukrainian Artillery Finds Him
