15:23:31 UTC
00:23:31 KST

Former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic is leaving the presidency in an attempt to remain in power. His resignation on Sept. 27, ahead of the early elections on Oct. 25, should be understood above all as an effort to continue leading the country as prime minister. Yet this maneuver is unfolding under circumstances he does not fully control, as sustained popular protests have now produced an electoral challenger.
Constitutional term limits explain why Vucic is seeking another office, but not why he stepped down seven months before his term expired. The timing appears intended to transform pressure on his administration into a contest for a new mandate. By taking the initiative in moving from the presidency to the premiership, he is trying to determine the terms of his own political continuity.
Moving from the presidency to the premiership is not a Serbian invention. Vladimir Putin took this route in 2008 before returning to the presidency in 2012. The analogy, however, has its limits. In Serbia, Vucic's success will depend on a parliamentary majority that must either be won outright or assembled with allies. A first-place finish for the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) would not automatically secure his election as prime minister.
The weakness of this strategy lies in the origins of the crisis. The collapse of the Novi Sad railway station canopy in November 2024, which killed 16 people, sparked a civil movement. Elections can determine who governs, but they do not establish responsibility for the disaster. Even a Vucic victory would not answer the demand for investigations and justice for the victims.
The most significant change in the political landscape is the student movement’s entry into the electoral contest. Its candidate list includes academics and professionals, giving the protest movement representation beyond the universities. The Democratic Party and the Kreni Promeni movement have chosen to support it without fielding candidates of their own. This shifts the confrontation from putting pressure on the government to potentially depriving the ruling party of its parliamentary majority.
The opposition, however, is not a single bloc. Other forces are competing alongside the student list, including the pro-European coalition European Serbia. The challenge is to unite voters who oppose Vucic but do not necessarily share the same political priorities. The trust earned through protest is an advantage; preserving it during negotiations over a program and alliances will be a further test.
The political atmosphere is characterized by a combination of civic mobilization, polarization, and distrust of institutions. The willingness to protest and organize shows that society has not resigned itself to the status quo. Yet the unsubstantiated accusations portraying opponents as foreign agents shift the focus away from citizen grievances, narrowing the space for constructive democratic dialogue. When political opponents are portrayed as enemies of the country, the legitimacy of political competition and the acceptance of electoral defeat are generally called into question.
Uncertainty about the outcome should therefore not be confused with a level electoral playing field. The OSCE/Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) report on the 2023 elections identified the structural advantages enjoyed by those in power. The mission deployed for this October’s vote will also assess media coverage, campaign financing, and electoral complaints. Observation matters, but the decisive test is whether institutions can remedy violations and ensure that the same rules apply to all contestants.
What can be expected from the elections? First, substantial parliamentary representation for the student list, which would reshape the opposition even if Vucic succeeds in forming a government. Second, the distribution of seats among smaller lists is likely to carry considerable weight in determining the majority. There are insufficient grounds to declare a winner at this stage. An NSPM poll narrowly favors the students, while Faktor Plus places Vucic's list ahead. These surveys were done at different times and should be interpreted cautiously. The elections are likely to institutionalize the challenge to the government but will not automatically resolve the crisis of trust between those in power, citizens, and opposition forces.
The significance of this confrontation, however, extends beyond domestic politics. The European Union is seeking to attract Serbia through the prospect of membership, investment, and economic integration, with the aim of drawing it away from Russia and towards Europe’s strategic orientation. The problem lies in the assumption that economic benefits will produce a lasting geopolitical alignment. Belgrade can benefit from its relations with Europe while maintaining its political ties with Moscow and using the competition between them to expand its maneuvering room. Within this relationship, treating Vucic as an indispensable guarantor of stability creates a contradiction because it risks supporting a policy that uses instability as a source of influence.
In Bosnia and Herzegovina, Belgrade’s support for former Republika Srpska President Milorad Dodik as well as Republika Srpska’s separatist policies fuels confrontation with state institutions. Vucic's condemnation of the judicial ruling against Dodik in February 2025 illustrates this political protection. Declarations of respect for the 1995 Dayton Agreement lose credibility when accompanied by support for actors who challenge Bosnia’s institutional order.
Vucic's political background helps explain this orientation. His longstanding collaboration with Vojislav Seselj and the Serbian Radical Party places his political formation within Serbian far-right. Seselj was convicted of crimes against humanity, while Vucic remained in his party until the split in 2008. This legacy is also evident in the public glorification of wartime figures. On Sept. 7, the late Ratko Mladic, convicted in 2017 of genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity, was buried in Belgrade with military honors and hailed by supporters as a national hero. Serbian government ministers attended the ceremony, although Vucic himself was absent. Honoring a figure convicted of such crimes demonstrates the absence of a political and symbolic break with the nationalism of the wars of the 1990s. Vucic's image as a pragmatic European partner must therefore also be judged against the way his government confronts this legacy.
Serbia’s geostrategic continuity, however, cannot be explained solely by one individual’s biography. Relations with Russia rest on historical ties, cultural and religious affinities, and state interests, particularly in energy and Moscow’s support for Serbia’s position on Kosovo. For this reason, fundamentally different behavior is not to be expected even if Vucic is removed from power. A majority united against corruption does not necessarily constitute a majority in favor of reassessing these interests.
Ultimately, the prospect of democratic change at home should therefore not encourage unfounded optimism about a geopolitical shift. Such a shift would require a change in policy towards neighboring states and respect for their sovereignty.

TOKYO, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- Japan's land ministry said Tuesday that its officials did not feel pressured by Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries Minister Kazuo Yana over road budgets for two municipalities whose mayors did not support him politically.
Yana is facing mounting criticism following reports last week that he told supporters in his constituency in May that fiscal 2026 road budgets had been sharply cut for Nasukarasuyama City and Nakagawa Town. The mayors of both municipalities supported his rival in the House of Representatives election in February.
The Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism, however, confirmed that Yana had contacted ministry officials to check fiscal 2026 road budgets for the two municipalities in Tochigi Prefecture, north of Tokyo.
The ministry said officials who responded to Yana's inquiries said they did not feel that he had attempted to influence or pressure them, although some could not clearly recall the matter and had kept no notes of their exchanges with him.
Yana on Monday largely acknowledged making the reported remarks, but retracted them and apologized, while saying he had not pressured the land ministry to cut the budgets and would not resign.
The planned government subsidies for road projects in fiscal 2026 have decreased from the previous year in three municipalities whose mayors supported Yana's rival, including Nasukarasuyama and Nakagawa, Kyodo News reported, citing municipal officials.
Meanwhile, the subsidies have increased in two municipalities in the same constituency whose leaders backed Yana, the report said.
While Yana's remarks have sparked widespread criticism, opposition lawmakers called for a full investigation and Yana's removal.
"The issue is whether political intervention or pressure distorted budget allocations that should be objective and neutral," Democratic Party for the People leader Yuichiro Tamaki told reporters, calling on Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi to order an investigation across all government ministries.
"To take budgets hostage in an attempt to expand one's local influence is conduct unbecoming of a politician," said Constitutional Democratic Party of Japan leader Shunichi Mizuoka.
Yana lost his single-seat district in Tochigi in the February election but retained his House of Representatives seat through proportional representation. He entered the Cabinet for the first time in the reshuffle in mid-September. ■

by sportswriters Li Chunyu and Wang Chunyan
BEIJING, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- China's 16-year-old Sun Xinran stepped into the spotlight at the China Open, showing maturity beyond her years in her WTA 1000 debut.
The girls' singles champion at this year's US Open and runner-up at both the French Open and Wimbledon, Sun advanced through the first two rounds in Beijing before her campaign ended with a 7-5, 6-1 loss to world No. 4 Coco Gauff of the United States on Monday.
Sun had previously beaten Germany's Eva Lys and 27th seed Cristina Bucsa of Spain, going further than many expected in her first China Open appearance.
"There were chances I could take, but there was some collapse in the second set," the teenager reflected after the match against Gauff. "Her rhythm is much faster than other players. She's able to mix it up and serves more powerful, much better than me. There are so many things I can learn from her."
Playing at the China Open for the first time, the Shenzhen native admitted she had been nervous but also proud to compete on Diamond Court during China's National Day holiday.
"I'm just so happy to play on that court. This is China, my home country. The crowd supported me a lot. I can hear them. They gave me energy," the wildcard player said.
Sun frequently clenched her fist after winning points, feeding off the support from the stands as she tested herself against higher-ranked opponents.
"This tournament gave me opportunity to play against top players. From the first round to the third round, my opponents are getting higher in their rankings. It just shows I have the ability to play against them. This really motivates me to improve myself."
Competing in a WTA 1000 main draw also required Sun to adjust to a level of intensity beyond the junior circuit, but her aggressive returning and composure off the court offered signs that she was becoming more comfortable at senior level.
"I just started playing professional matches. I don't want to give myself so big pressure. I want to focus on my tennis, move forward step by step, and we will see what is going to happen," she said.
Describing herself as an "all-round player," Sun said years of training and competition had given her confidence in her preparation.
"I've played many matches with great coaches and facilities. Our team has been working hard towards our goals," Sun said. "I have my interpretation of each game. I make full preparation before matches and focus on implementing the plan. I take my own pace."
This year has marked a breakthrough for Sun, who reached the girls' singles final at three Grand Slam tournaments.
"It gave me so many experience to play on the big court and also play with very good opponents. I think that really helps me to improve myself and play better in the profession," said Sun.
"Tennis is not only about the strategies and tactics in competitions. Off the court, it is also important to understand how to warm up and how to recover after matches," the teenager added.
Olympic champion Zheng Qinwen also offered encouragement to Sun during the China Open, saying, "She has achieved a lot as a teenager. I didn't manage to pull off what she has done when I was a junior, so I think she's incredible."
"I told her [Zheng] she is my idol. She had great milestones in her career, such as the Paris Olympics and the Australian Open," Sun noted. "I'm still a junior player. I will continue to learn from her. I will try to improve my serve and my energy on the court." ■

Clashes with police put ultra-Orthodox Haredi Jews draft issue at center of Israel’s election campaign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:20:50 UTC
00:20:50 KST

Abdel Ra'ouf Arnaout and Lina Altawell
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
- Opposition leaders pledge to end exemptions, cut funding for institutions whose students refuse military service if they win Oct. 27 election
- Lapid, Golan, Eisenkot and Bennett accuse Netanyahu government of allowing draft evasion to continue
Clashes between Israeli police and hundreds of ultra-Orthodox Haredi Jews in central Israel on Monday evening brought one of the country's most contentious issues to the forefront of campaigning ahead of the Oct. 27 election.
Israeli opposition leaders on Tuesday blamed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his government for allowing tens of thousands of Haredim to continue avoiding military service.
They pledged that if they form the next government, they would end widespread draft exemptions and halt funding for institutions whose students refuse to enlist.
The Haredim, represented mainly by the Shas and United Torah Judaism parties, have traditionally been key partners in Netanyahu-led governments, and he is expected to rely on their support in any potential coalition after the election.
The dispute has intensified as the Israeli army says it is facing troop shortages amid military operations on several fronts over the past three years.
The controversy escalated Monday after violent clashes between Haredi protesters and Israeli police, during which demonstrators called police officers “Nazis.”
Israeli public broadcaster KAN said hundreds of Haredim gathered outside the home of a man accused of evading military service in the city of Modi'in to protest his arrest.
Some demonstrators attempted to storm the building, triggering confrontations with police before the draft dodger was released, KAN said. Large police forces were deployed to the area.
The Israeli army said military police had conducted an operation in Modi'in as part of what it called efforts to enforce the Security Service Law against deserters and draft dodgers.
It said a large number of demonstrators gathered at the scene, obstructed military police and attempted to interfere with the arrest, prompting Israeli police to disperse them.
The army said enforcement operations against draft dodgers would continue.
 
Opposition targets Netanyahu
Opposition leader Yair Lapid said police had arrested a Haredi man accused of evading military service before hundreds gathered, confronted officers and called them “Nazis.”
“Is there no rule of law in this country?” Lapid wrote on US social media company X, while also criticizing National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir over the incident, calling him a “coward.”
Democrats party leader Yair Golan accused Netanyahu of continuing to finance draft evasion to preserve his governing coalition.
Golan said the upcoming election would provide an opportunity to end funding for draft evasion, introduce broader military conscription and restore what he called the rule of law.
Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot, a former Israeli army chief of staff, said the events in Modi'in were not isolated but reflected an effort to normalize the avoidance of military service.
He said a government under his leadership would enact what he described as a “real conscription law” aimed at increasing military manpower and ending a situation in which some Israelis serve while others do not.
Eisenkot said the Haredi draft issue had become central to the election, portraying the vote as a choice between another Netanyahu government that maintains the current system and a government that would enforce conscription.
Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, leader of the Together party, also blamed Netanyahu and his political partners for the situation.
Bennett pledged that under a government led by him, “no one who does not serve will receive a single shekel.”
Long-running draft dispute
Haredim account for around 13% of Israel’s population of more than 10 million.
Many refuse military service on religious grounds, arguing that they should devote themselves to Torah study and expressing concern that integration into secular society could undermine their religious way of life.
The dispute over Haredi conscription has intensified amid continued call-ups of reservists as Israeli military operations continue on several fronts, including Gaza, Lebanon, Iran and the occupied West Bank.
For decades, Haredi men received repeated military service deferments while studying at religious seminaries until they reached the age of exemption.
In June 2024, Israel’s Supreme Court ruled that ultra-Orthodox Haredi men were subject to military conscription and ordered an end to state funding for religious institutions whose students refused to enlist.

Two men in climbing gear scaled the nearby monument, where they unfurled a plastic banner reading “Neglected schools, sacrificed youth”.
“Gen Z has risen up and wants to be heard,” 19-year-old Lilia told AFP at a massive march in central Paris, adding she hoped the President would listen.
The unrest has erupted with just months to go before the 2027 election to choose a successor to centrist President Emmanuel Macron, with far-right veteran candidate Marine Le Pen riding high in the polls despite a graft conviction.
“I’m afraid for my future,” Selma, 15, told AFP without giving her surname, among the thousands marching in the country’s second-largest city of Marseille.
The Interior Ministry said 86,000 had already joined demonstrations across the rest of the country earlier on Oct 6. The CGT union put the figure at 260,000 people.
‘At war’
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu responded to the demonstrations, telling lawmakers in the National Assembly that there was “no room for tolerance of violence”.
“Burning down a high school does not improve the state of high school buildings,” he told Parliament, adding it was a “lie” to suggest the government had ordered “police repression” against protesters.
While many protests have been peaceful, some demonstrators have started fires, destroyed bus shelters or clashed with riot police.
Police have responded with batons, tear gas and riot-control rounds.
The government says 215 students and 715 police officers have been injured since the start of the movement.
A 15-year-old lost a hand to a sting-ball grenade fired by riot officers in the northern town of Lens on Oct 5.
The prosecutor’s office in the north-eastern town of Metz meanwhile said he called for a police inquiry over a possible sexual assault on a minor younger than 15, after video footage circulated of what appeared to be a plainclothes policeman groping a female pupil he had detained.
The government has sought to address the grievances, while accusing the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of being behind the movement.
Veteran LFI presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon has strongly supported the protests, while calling for non-violent methods.
Thousands of arrests
Thomas, a 17-year-old student from the Paris suburb of Val-de-Marne, said some of the classrooms at his school were short of desks and chairs while the bathrooms lacked doors, toilet paper and soap.
“We just want better conditions for studying,” he told AFP.
Adults turned out in droves on Oct 6 to support the young demonstrators.
Standing outside a school in Rennes, in western France, teacher Romain Dubourg told AFP he and colleagues had “talked about the police brutality we’ve witnessed” and decided to show up for the pupils.
In the eastern city of Lyon, Sandrine Buteau was among dozens of parents who organised to support the youngsters.
“As adults, we’re a bit like the security cordon,” she said.
Lyon teacher Rindala Younes said she was present to help the students “convey their message peacefully”.
“The high school students’ demands are legitimate,” she said.
Amnesty International late on Oct 5 said the French authorities should “put an end to the disproportionate police repression seen in recent days during student protests”.
The police have launched 10 internal investigations into allegations of brutality since the protests started, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said late on Oct 5.
Since the start of the movement, 24 schools have been burnt or ransacked, according to the Education Ministry.

Three Iranians face UK trial for allegedly spying for Tehran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:18:44 UTC
00:18:44 KST

Breadcrumb
Iranians charged with spying 'on behalf of' Tehran go on trial in UK
Three Iranian men went on trial in the United Kingdom Tuesday charged with spying for Iran, allegedly laying the groundwork for a violent attack against at least one London-based journalist.
The Iranian nationals visited addresses linked to people including two journalists working for the Farsi-language Iran International television news network, which Tehran has labelled a terror organisation.
Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, Farhad Manesh, 46, and Shapoor Noori, 57, who have all pleaded not guilty, appeared at a court in London accompanied by translators.
Prosecutor Bill Emlyn Jones told the jury the three were accused of conduct likely to assist a foreign intelligence service, "in other words ... they spied on people of interest to the Iranian regime".
The trio undertook surveillance and reconnaissance between August 2024 and February 2025, with Sepahvand allegedly earmarked to carry out any attack, he said.
The trial would focus on steps taken "on behalf of the Iranian regime to target journalists and others considered to be hostile to or even just critical" of it.
Iran International, which is based in London, had been critical of the Iranian government and supportive of opposition groups, he said.
Another of the men's targets was lawyer Jonathan Turner, a founder member of the group UK Lawyers for Israel.
The three accused do not deny visiting the addresses and taking photos and videos, but Sepahvand claimed he had been coerced and acted out of fear, the prosecution said.
Prosecutors labelled his claims "bogus" and alleged he was seeking payment and looking to have a criminal conviction for theft in Iran "fixed" in return for his actions.
Manesh and Noori said they were not aware that what they were doing was to assist the Iranian intelligence services, the prosecution added.
Emlyn Jones told the jury their intention was to "locate and target at least two journalists associated with ... Iran International and others".
'Retribution'
"Their ultimate objective was that one or more of their targets would be subjected to serious violence, no doubt as retribution for their criticism of the Iranian regime and to try to silence and deter others who might dare to voice their criticism," he added.
Those who attracted the attention of the trio included political satirist and Iran International journalist Kambiz Hosseini, who is long said to have been the subject of threats and intimidation from the Iranian intelligence services.
Mobile phone network data showed all three men visited the address where Hosseini was living.
Another target was Mojtaba Pourmohsen, also a journalist for Iran International and known as a poet and writer.
The three defendants, whom authorities said were Iranian-born but living in London at the time of their arrests, are all charged under the National Security Act.
Sepahvand is also charged with engaging in surveillance, reconnaissance and open-source research with the intention to commit serious violence.
Manesh and Noori are further charged with engaging in surveillance and reconnaissance, with the intention that serious violence would be committed by others.

Mucahithan Avcioglu
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
French AI company Mistral unveiled a new flagship model on Tuesday, saying it rivals the strongest Chinese open-weight models.
Mistral Large 4, also known as Le Chonk, is the company’s largest and most capable model to date, with strengths across coding, cybersecurity, finance, legal tasks and image understanding, according to a statement.
The model has approximately 1 trillion parameters, the learned values underlying its capabilities, with 49 billion active during processing. Its documentation lists a context window of 1 million tokens, allowing it to handle large volumes of information in a single request.
Developers can access a public preview through Mistral Studio, and the company plans to make it fully public by the end of October. Ahead of the release, Mistral is testing the system with cybersecurity specialists, vetted partners and state authorities.
Open-weight models allow organizations to deploy and customize AI on their own infrastructure, giving them greater control over data and access.
The company said the model was trained from scratch using 3,800 Nvidia Grace Blackwell graphics processors in its own European data centers. Training data covered more than 160 languages, including every official EU language.
Mistral raised €3 billion ($3.37 billion) in a Series D funding round in September, led by Samsung Electronics, which valued the company at more than €21 billion.

Israeli bulldozers on Tuesday demolished a five-storey residential building in occupied East Jerusalem which was home to about 70 people, in a move the local Palestinian authority said was aimed at "forcible transfer".
Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir, who gleefully oversaw the demolition, claimed the building had been constructed without a permit.
“I love hearing this noise,” Ben Gvir said in a video posted on X as he joined the demolition operation from inside one of the bulldozers.
Densely populated occupied East Jerusalem faces a severe housing crisis, with Israeli authorities using the lack of building permits as a pretext for demolitions, while Palestinians say such permits are nearly impossible to obtain.
‘Dangerous escalation’
The Jerusalem Governorate, the Palestinian local authority for the area, condemned Tuesday's demolition, which it said was "a dangerous escalation in the policy of home demolitions and forcible transfer... and the imposition of a new demographic and urban reality".
Hanine Hreibat, a teacher and mother of four who was renting one of the 10 apartments in the building, said a large Israeli police force arrived in the At-Tur neighbourhood in the early hours of the morning, accompanied by three bulldozers.
They stormed the apartments and gave residents 10 minutes to leave, she said.
Hreibat told AFP she had woken up to the sound of her husband shouting at the police, asking them not to enter the bedroom where she was, adding she had endured "five minutes of terror, with weapons pointed at our heads".
She said police officers had allowed her to take only medicine, money, her handbag and ID card.
Regular demolitions
Among the rubble, residents collected gas cylinders and filled plastic bags with clothes they had managed to pull out from the huge mound of debris.
Hreibat said she had nowhere to go following the demolition.
"We'll look for a second home. Today we're at my in-laws' and tomorrow at my parents'," she said.
Residents confirmed to AFP that they had received a demolition notice on Monday, but did not know when it would be carried out.
Israel regularly carries out demolitions of what it claims are illegal structures built by Palestinians in East Jerusalem and the occupied West Bank.
Israel occupied East Jerusalem in 1967 and later illegally annexed it, a move rejected by the UN and not recognised by the international community.
More than 360,000 Palestinians live in occupied East Jerusalem alongside some 230,000 illegal Israeli settlers. Palestinians see the city as the capital of their future state.

Birzeit University memorial destruction aims to crush Palestinian memory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:14:28 UTC
00:14:28 KST

Birzeit University memorial destruction aims to crush Palestinian memory
Israeli soldiers removed the monument to students and alumni killed by Israel and replaced it with a fig sapling.
After Israeli soldiers stormed Birzeit University near Ramallah to demolish a stone memorial dedicated to dead students, Rania Washaha, 47, felt the pain of bereavement again.
Her brother, Fadi, 34, was shot in the head by an Israeli soldier near the northern entrance to el-Bireh in the central West Bank in May 2021.
His name was among the 38 students from the university killed by Israel and listed on the stone pillar known as the Martyrs’ Monument.
Israeli soldiers raided the university campus at dawn on Monday, accompanied by 10 military vehicles. A bulldozer demolished the pillar, and soldiers took away the marble stone. In its place, the Israelis left a planter containing a fig sapling, bearing the inscription: “Water it twice.”
Targeting the University
This raid marks the fifth Israeli incursion into the campus since the beginning of 2026 and the 28th since 2002.
Birzeit University’s administration condemned the recent raid, describing the destruction of the Martyrs’ Monument as a violation of international law and an attack on education and national memory.
“Bulldozers won’t erase the memory of the martyrs, military vehicles won’t extinguish the light of knowledge, and these assaults won’t break the university’s resolve to pursue its academic and national mission,” a statement by the university pledged.
It came 10 days after another incursion by Israeli forces during the daytime, a day before the start of the new fall semester.
Nardeen al-Memi, the university’s public relations and media officer, told Al Jazeera in the brief minutes of their incursion, Israeli soldiers approached the monument for the first time and photographed it.
The Martyrs’ Monument was erected between 1994 and 1996, bearing the names of students and alumni at Birzeit killed by Israeli forces. The list starts with Sharaf al-Tayyibi, who was shot dead by Israeli forces on the campus in 1984. The names of other students and alumni were added during the years that followed.
“The last name inscribed on the monument was that of student Omar al-Naasan, whom soldiers killed in al-Mughayyir east of Ramallah on September 2 while he was confronting settler incursions,” said Nardeen. “Days after his death, his father came and personally wrote his son’s name on the monument.”
University students organised a protest at the site of the destroyed memorial on Tuesday afternoon, most viewing it as an Israeli attempt to intimidate them.
Sami Adel, a Birzeit student who wanted to use a pseudonym due to his fear of being detained, told Al Jazeera the memorial holds a place in the heart of everyone who has attended the university since the 1990s.
In recent years, Israel has tried to suppress any student activity dedicated to commemorating the martyrs, he said.
“Soldiers detained me for several hours three weeks ago and threatened that if I participated in any political student activity on campus, I would face a long and harsh detention,” he added.
Erasing memory
The removal of the memorial is part of a broader Israeli policy targeting memorials dedicated to Palestinians killed by Israel in the occupied West Bank.
The Israeli far-right has made the issue part of its campaign to erase markers of Palestinian identity.
Zvi Sukkot, a member of the Knesset from the Religious Zionism Party, destroyed one such memorial in the village of Madama, south of Nablus, with a sledgehammer in August. The Israeli military later said that it routinely removes “symbols of incitement”.
Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich submitted a list of approximately 40 Palestinian memorials, proposing their destruction, to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
There has been a wider targeting of civic and cultural symbols across the West Bank, particularly in Jenin, by Israeli authorities.
“Jenin Horse”, a monument constructed from the wreckage left behind by an Israeli incursion into the city, was removed. A memorial dedicated to Al Jazeera journalist Shireen Abu Akleh in Jenin was also targeted in 2023.
A cemetery containing the bodies of Iraqi soldiers killed during the 1948 war, also located in Jenin, has been raided by Israelis from illegal settlements.
Other landmarks embedded in the city’s collective memory, including the “Watermelon Roundabout”, have also been targeted.
Crushing resistance
Israel’s targeting of Palestine’s collective memory has coincided with a wider campaign of suppression in the occupied West Bank.
Palestinian universities have been a particular target in this pressure campaign, with campuses raided, students detained, and strict restrictions on activities and events within university grounds.
Israeli authorities are likely focusing on Palestinian universities because they hold a special significance for Palestinian resistance. They historically served as spaces for anti-occupation activism and have been an integral part of the Palestinian political landscape for decades.
Political analyst Mohammed al-Qeeq, who served as president of the Birzeit University Student Council between 2006 and 2007, told Al Jazeera that Israel has targeted writers, influencers, and activists, along with students, to deter any resistance to the occupation.
Universities have historically served as a “fundamental pillar” of Palestinian resilience and identity.
“Israel had also sought to weaken Palestinian political and social cohesion inside universities by deepening divisions between factions and creating chaos”, he said.
Remembering Fadi
For Rania, the memorial served to cement the names of the martyred students in the minds of the next generation of Berzeit students, including her brother’s.
“I cannot deny that I felt a pang of anguish when the memorial was demolished,” she told Al Jazeera. “I realised the goal wasn’t simply to uproot a physical object; I felt the suppressed violence Israel inflicts upon us.”
The memorial, constructed in 1996, stood on the campus when Fadi studied at Birzeit University. He had been arrested multiple times, spending a total of eight years in detention, and Israel denied Fadi the chance to wear a graduation gown.
“He didn’t even complete two years of study due to repeated arrests and injuries from soldiers’ gunfire,” Rania said. “Yet, he loved Birzeit University dearly and would stand by the memorial, contemplating the names of the student martyrs, never knowing that his own name would one day be added to theirs.”
This year, Rania’s son enrolled at Birzeit University as a first-year student. Shortly before classes started last September, an Israeli officer phoned him, threatening him if he participated in any student activities on campus. “Remember what we did to your uncle,” they warned him.

Russia’s Jet Drones Could Reach 900 Km/h, Air Force Warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:14:00 UTC
00:14:00 KST

Russia could eventually increase the speed of its jet-powered attack drones to 800-900 kilometers per hour (500-560 mph), posing a growing challenge to Ukraine’s air defenses, a senior Air Force official has warned.
Deputy Air Force Commander Col. Yurii Cherevashenko made the assessment during a meeting of the Ukrainian parliament’s Temporary Investigative Commission on Tuesday, Oct. 6, according to Suspilne.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Current Russian jet-powered drones are said too fly at around 600 kilometers per hour (370 mph).
“We have not seen such [speeds] yet, but we forecast them,” Cherevashenko said, referring to the projected 800-900-kilometer-per-hour range.
Jet drones could make up 80% of attacks
Cherevashenko said Russia had rapidly increased its use of jet-powered attack drones since July.
They currently account for around 40% of the drones used against Ukraine, while on some operational axes their share has reached 60%, he said.
“We forecast that around 80% of the drones used in strikes will be jet-powered,” Cherevashenko added.
Ukraine previously recorded an eightfold increase in Russian jet-drone launches between June and August. The faster aircraft are more difficult for mobile fire groups and conventional propeller-driven interceptor drones to pursue.
Jet-powered drones can also reach their targets more quickly, reducing the time available for Ukrainian air defenses and civilians to respond to warnings.
Ukrainian companies race to build faster interceptors
The Air Force is currently working with around 20 Ukrainian companies developing high-speed interceptor drones.
Rubio Calls on Russia to Clarify Suspected Plague Case
According to Cherevashenko, 14 companies have begun test flights, six have achieved results in destroying jet-powered drones, and three have produced systems the Air Force considers particularly promising.
Two models have already passed military codification, including an interceptor called Predator, or “Khyzhak” in Ukrainian.
Existing interceptor models reach around 460-500 kilometers per hour (285-310 mph), while some manufacturers claim speeds of up to 700 kilometers per hour (435 mph).
Ukraine is also testing five high-speed interceptor models, with one expected to reach production of approximately 400 units by the end of October.
Cherevashenko said interceptor drones in the quantities required by the Air Force were not expected before the end of November.
F-16s remain among the most effective defenses
Ukraine is also using F-16 fighter jets to engage Russia’s high-speed drones.
“F-16s are among the most effective means of countering jet-powered UAVs [unmanned aerial vehicles],” Cherevashenko said. “Any aircraft has a limited service life, and we are using that resource at an exceptionally high rate.”
Maintaining the aircraft in constant readiness is therefore difficult and requires continued assistance from Ukraine’s partners, he added.
Kyiv is seeking large quantities of 20-millimeter ammunition for the F-16’s onboard cannon, which offers a cheaper alternative to using scarce AIM-9 and AIM-120 air-to-air missiles against drones.
Cherevashenko said another key method was destroying the drones before launch by striking their bases, known as droneports.
Several such facilities have already been hit, he said, although many are heavily fortified with concrete and remain difficult to destroy.

Pedro Sánchez emphasises that the two Royal Decree-laws that have been approved "retain the essence" of those that lapsed, whilst incorporating "very positive additions"
Spain
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
17:13:00 CEST
00:13:00 KST

Pedro Sánchez emphasises that the two Royal Decree-laws that have been approved "retain the essence" of those that lapsed, whilst incorporating "very positive additions"
President's News - 2026.10.6
Moncloa Palace
Pedro Sánchez during his speech after the Council of Ministers (Pool Moncloa/Borja Puig de la Bellacasa y Sandra Armada)
The President of the Government of Spain, Pedro Sánchez, emphasised that two Royal Decree-laws approved by the Council of Ministers, containing 21 measures relating to housing, "retain the essence of those that were voted down in the plenary session of Parliament last Friday", "with some very positive additions". The Government has approved these measures, he explained, because the circumstances have not changed over the past few days.
During a press conference at Moncloa Palace, the head of the Executive once again called on the parliamentary groups to support the ratification of these decrees in the Permanent Deputation, "because this is not an ideological issue but one of humanity and pure common sense".
Pedro Sánchez emphasised that the measures set out in the decrees are not only "ambitious" but, above all, "reasonable and necessary", and are "the result of many months of technical analysis and dialogue with social organisations, the real estate sector, associations of property owners and tenants and parliamentary groups". "They are measures of pure common sense and humanity that unite small property owners and tenants, and put a stop to vulture funds", because they target only those seeking to speculate on housing. Furthermore, he emphasised, "they enjoy broad-based support that transcends ideologies".
The President of the Government of Spain, Pedro Sánchez, during the appearance to explain the agreements adopted by the Council of Ministers | Pool Moncloa/Borja Puig de la Bellacasa y Sandra Armada
Facilitating access to affordable rental accommodation and home ownership
The president explained that the 21 measures approved have four main objectives. The first is "to facilitate access to affordable rental accommodation and also to home ownership", by allowing tenants to claim tax relief on part of their rent in their tax return, which would amount to a deduction of nearly 1,000 euros a year for an average rent of 800 euros. It also provides a tax incentive for small landlords who let their properties at affordable prices.
He also highlighted a significant new development: the creation of a 10 billion euro ICO financing facility that will provide interest-free loans of up to 50,000 euros to individuals wishing to purchase their first home.
Increase the supply of housing
Secondly, the president pointed out that the decrees will also serve "to increase supply", with 280 million euros in guarantees to promote industrialised housing construction, and 400 million euros to support social housing providers. In addition, thousands of Social Security properties that can be used for housing will be transferred to CASA47, the public housing company.
Pedro Sánchez addresses the media during the press conference held at Moncloa Palace | Pool Moncloa/Borja Puig de la Bellacasa y Sandra Armada
Providing stability for landlords and tenants
Thirdly, the President of the Government of Spain pointed out that the decrees "will serve to provide people with peace of mind and stability". Specifically, they include the extension of tenancy agreements by up to two years for tenants who are up to date with their rent, and a cap on rent increases. They also include the establishment of "clear rules" on when tenancy agreements are renewed, when they end, and in which cases the landlord may reclaim their property. On this point, Sánchez clarified that the second Royal Decree-Law would come into force following its ratification by the Permanent Deputation.
Tackling speculation
Finally, the president explained that the measures approved today will also "help to combat speculation" by regulating seasonal and room-by-room lettings; limiting the purchase of property by vulture funds; linking the tax benefits of 'socimis' to affordable rent, and requiring tourist flats to "be taxed for what they are: a business", he said.
In any case, President Sánchez acknowledged that "these measures alone will not solve the housing problem", noting that "doing so requires driving a much firmer intervention in the housing market and continuing to build hundreds of thousands more homes - especially public housing and affordable rentals. That is the major challenge Spain will face in the coming years".
At this point, he conveyed the Government's "indignation" that these measures failed to pass last week during the plenary session of the Lower House of Parliament, because "behind them lie many hours, many months of dialogue, technical rigour and a commitment to reaching agreement between very different positions", and, "above all, many Spaniards waiting for a solution".

The Register that shatters the myth of Britain’s role in profiting from enslavement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:10:46 UTC
00:10:46 KST

Welcome to this month’s Cotton Capital newsletter. I’m Ahmed Reid, coming to you from Jamaica, where I am programme manager for the Guardian’s Legacies of Enslavement team.
The recently published Register of British Slave-Traders, reported exclusively in the Guardian, lists 13,000 men and women who invested in and profited from the trafficking of more than three million enslaved Africans between 1563 and 1807.
The Register captures a broad range of investors, from ordinary men and women in provincial towns to the monarchy. Queen Elizabeth I and many in her court invested in John Hawkins’s 1563 and subsequent missions. They provided Hawkins with money and ships, including the royal ship Jesus of Lübeck, which trafficked 359 Africans to the Americas in 1568. Elizabeth I’s successors – including James I, Charles I, Charles II, James II, William III, Queen Anne, George I, and George II – were major investors, shareholders, and directors in the state-sponsored Company of Royal Adventurers Trading in Africa, the Royal African Company, and the South Sea Company.
Other investors included famed philosopher John Locke (who ironically championed the concept of natural rights) and Tobias Rustat a University of Cambridge benefactor whose bust is still displayed in the Chapel at Jesus College despite the college’s attempts to seek permission from an ecclesiastical court to remove it). Forty-five vicars from the Church of England and 24 directors and governors of the Bank of England were also investors. As the project’s lead researcher, William Pettigrew, has stated, slavery was not a footnote in British history – it helped shape the country.
Some have expressed surprise at the extent of the involvement. The question worth asking is this: why, 193 years after emancipation, is the true scale of Britain’s role in chattel slavery still not fully understood in Britain?
Pre-existing evidence
The findings are not surprising to scholars in the Caribbean and the wider diaspora. Eighty-two years ago, Eric Williams, the Trinidadian scholar who later became prime minister, argued in Capitalism and Slavery that profits from chattel enslavement “financed the Industrial Revolution” in Britain. Williams, showed how manufacturing towns and industries, including banking, shipbuilding, insurance and warehousing, were integrated into colonial trade, as were some families.
The Nigerian scholar Joseph Inikori, in Africans and the Industrial Revolution in England, has shown that these linkages provided the scaffolding for Britain’s industrial advancement. During the 2007 Commons debate marking the Bicentenary of the Abolition of the Slave Trade, William Hague pointedly stated that: “William Pitt, when he was prime minister, said 80% of British overseas income was derived from our West Indian colonies.” Pitt should know.
Caribbean scholars, among them Williams, Sir Arthur Lewis, CLR James, Walter Rodney, Elsa Goveia, Kamau Brathwaite, Hilary Beckles, Orlando Patterson, George Beckford and Verene Shepherd, have spent their professional careers exposing the magnitude of Britain’s involvement in the trafficking of enslaved Africans and its impact across the Caribbean archipelago. Plantation ledgers, deeds, wills and probate inventories, whether in repositories in the Caribbean, Britain, or across Europe, show the accumulation and transfer of mind-numbing wealth to Britain.
Ship records document the names of ship captains and owners as well as the sadistic violence inflicted on enslaved men, women and children. Those of us who have worked in these archives have spent our careers seeing the names of these monarchs, merchants, vicars, bankers, absentee owners and institutions written alongside the names of the enslaved men, women, and children they owned as “property”. The evidence is not new.
Wall of silence
The reception of the Register reveals much about British attitudes towards chattel slavery and how it is taught in schools (pdf) as well as raising questions about why Britain’s role in chattel slavery has not been fully realised.
The reason, Catherine Hall has argued, is the conscious effort to occlude the archives. Hall argued that forgetting a nation’s violent past is an active process, not an accident, and Britain’s began as soon as the trafficking in enslaved people was outlawed in 1807.
Thomas Clarkson’s history of the abolition campaign celebrated white humanitarian men and omitted Black and women abolitionists and the horrors of trafficking in enslaved people. Abolition of the trafficking in 1807 and emancipation of chattel slavery in 1833 were recast as proof of British liberty and virtue. At the same time, the newly freed people were forced into an unpaid “apprenticeship” while the government paid £20m – or 40% of Britain’s public expenditure – in compensation to the owners of enslaved people. What emerged was an amalgamation of institutions and social and cultural forces to create a wall of silence around the period of chattel enslavement, colonialism and its harmful legacies.
The reaction to the Register shows that what Hall described 13 years ago remains true today. The real strength of the Register is that it will help break the wall of silence around Britain’s trafficking in enslaved Africans and “undo the forgetting”.

Regional spotlight
Manchester | Did you know that 7 October is World Cotton Day? Created in 2019 by representatives from Benin, Burkina Faso, Chad and Mali, it aims to address the issues facing the cotton industry today while acknowledging its history. This year, the Legacies programme is co-hosting an event at the Science and History Museum including talks, workshops and live textile demonstrations.
In the evening there will be a panel discussion featuring Duncan Ivison, the vice-chancellor of University of Manchester, Cleo Lake, the first black female lord mayor of Bristol, Adeola Adelakun, the co-founder of Black Creative Trailblazers, and artist Liam Hopkins, to discuss how World Cotton Day can help us work together to reflect on Manchester’s interwoven history. You can book free tickets for the evening event here. Across the city there will also be heritage trails looking at how Manchester’s history is woven into the streets. Keisha Thompson, Legacies of Enslavement programme manager
Sea Islands | October is Gullah Geechee Cultural Heritage Awareness Month, a time to honour the culture and history of the descendants of enslaved West Africans in the south-east US who retained their unique heritage. Started in 2014, the heritage month includes conferences, festivals, workshops, and film showings in the four states that encompass the Gullah Geechee Cultural Heritage Corridor: Georgia, Florida, North and South Carolina. Visitors come from all over the world to attend celebrations throughout the month.
The events kicked off with the Lowcountry Fish and Grits music festival on Hilton Head Island on 3 October with performers including Latrese Bush, a Gullah Geechee woman from Bluffton, who sung the jazz, soul and gospel music that defined her upbringing. The Georgia-based Gullah Geechee Ring Shouters also displayed the ring shout, a traditional ritual rooted in West African culture and Christianity. While moving counterclockwise in a circle, the performers stomp their feet, clap their hands and sing in call and response. The month will culminate with Charleston’s Grand Gullah-Geechee Hoodoo Ball in Mount Pleasant, South Carolina, on 31 October, where guests will be treated to Gullah Geechee cuisine, live music, spirituality and dance performances. Melissa Hellmann, US race and equity senior reporter
Jamaica | The global reparations movement has been gaining phenomenal pace, shifting from the fringes of international debate to the centre of diplomatic discussions. Caribbean governments have managed to push reparations on to the agendas of the Commonwealth, the UN, and in the parliaments and public domains of countries in the region, as well in the UK.
But within this broader push, one of the often overlooked elements is the call for repatriation – the right of people of African descent to return to the continent from which their ancestors were taken. For decades, repatriation was dismissed as symbolic or utopian. But African governments including Ghana, Sierra Leone and Liberia are now developing concrete pathways to residency and citizenship for diaspora Africans.
As the Commonwealth leaders summit approaches in November, repatriation is likely to become a prominent part of the conversation about what meaningful repair should look like, and how the Caribbean envisions its relationship with Africa. Natricia Duncan, Caribbean correspondent

The US House of Representatives have introduced a resolution honouring Indian flydubai pilot Smit Machchhar who was stabbed by his Omani co-pilot Hamam al-Hammami on September 30.
The resolution introduced as "Honoring Captain Smit Machchhar and the crew and passengers of Flydubai Flight 1073, and condemning the attempted terrorist attack on that flight" by Josh Gottheimer, Don Bacon and Michael McCaul, described the incident and hailed Machchhar.
"On September 30, 2026, Flydubai Flight 1073 departed Dubai International Airport for Ben Gurion Airport in Tel Aviv, Israel, carrying approximately 174 passengers, the majority of them Israeli citizens, including 4 United States citizens and 27 children," it stated.
"Whereas, midway through the flight, the first officer attacked the captain on the flight deck with the aircraft’s emergency crash axe and attempted to seize the flight controls, and the aircraft lost more than 14,000 feet of altitude in under 30 seconds," it desribed the incident. Whereas Captain Smit Machchhar, a citizen of India, fought off the attack and, despite grave injuries, used his remaining strength to unlock the cockpit door so that off-duty pilots could enter and land the aircraft and so that crew and passengers could restrain the first officer; Whereas the aircraft landed safely at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia with all passengers and crew accounted for; and Whereas, on October 3, 2026, the Attorney General of the United Arab Emirates announced that the Emirati investigation had determined that the first officer attempted to carry out a terrorist act," it added.
Then it went to resolve as follows:
- Resolved, That the House of Representatives—
- (1) honors Captain Smit Machchhar for extraordinary courage in protecting every soul aboard his aircraft;
- (2) commends the heroic actions of the off-duty pilots, cabin crew, and passengers who secured the flight deck and brought the aircraft safely down;
- (3) wishes Captain Machchhar and all who were injured a full recovery;
- (4) condemns the attack on Flydubai Flight 1073 as an act of terrorism and as an attack on the safety of international civil aviation; and
- (5) calls for a full and expeditious investigation by the Governments of Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, and for the United States and Israel to be kept fully informed.
On September 30, Flydubai Flight FZ1073, carrying more than 170 passengers and crew from Dubai to Tel Aviv, was forced into an emergency diversion after the co-pilot attacked Captain Smit Machchhar in the cockpit with a crash axe and attempted to take control of the aircraft.
The plane rapidly lost altitude before Machchhar, despite suffering serious injuries, managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to overpower the attacker; two off-duty pilots then helped land the aircraft safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
The UAE subsequently launched an investigation, and on October 3 its Attorney General said the probe had found that the co-pilot attempted to carry out a terrorist act. Investigators are continuing to examine the circumstances, motive, possible links and physical and digital evidence, with authorities in other countries also looking into the incident.

Breadcrumb
Israel was 'prepared to shoot down' flydubai plane before emergency landing
Israel was prepared to shoot down a flydubai plane with over 150 passengers onboard, a source has told CBS News.
The flight sent a distress signal after the copilot allegedly attacked the pilot in the cockpit and attempted to crash the aircraft. The passengers on the plane eventually wrestled control of the plane from the rogue copilot before the flight was redirected to Saudi Arabia.
Hamam al-Hammami, the Omani co-pilot accused of attacking the Indian captain of flydubai flight FZ1073 on 30 September, allegedly told investigators that he had planned to crash the aircraft into Israel's Ben Gurion Airport, according to Israeli reports.
Israel has a protocol in place to prevent an attack similar to 9/11, when hijackers took control of planes and crashed them into New York's World Trade Centre and the Pentagon in Washington.
The plan entailed sending fighter pilots as close to the plane as possible, hoping to visually inspect the cockpit and observe the situation in the plane. The fighter planes would then have attempted to observe the cabin to assess the status of passengers.
If they concluded that the plane had been hijacked, and the supposed hijackers could not be contacted via the plane's communication systems, Israel's prime minister and defence minister -- currently Benjamin Netanyahu and Israel Katz -- would be called.
The prime minister would the decide whether to authorise shooting the plane down.
In reality, these measures were not deemed necessary after passengers took control of the aircraft. Two off-duty pilots, who were flying as passengers, flew the plane safely to Saudi Arabia.
The incident has sparked questions about Israel's aviation security.
Haaretz reported that Israel's Shin Bet domestic security agency had repeatedly warned the transport ministry in recent years about weaknesses in the monitoring of foreign flight crews and passengers.
Netanyahu met some of the passengers who saved the plane shortly after its safe landing, while some were still covered in blood. This has led to opponents accusing him of attempting to claim political credit for the prevention of a disaster that they said exposed failures under his own government.
The security row comes as Israel prepares for elections which could see Netanyahu and his party, Likud, ousted from power.

What an Attack in Bulgaria’s EEZ Means Under International Law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:07:00 UTC
00:07:00 KST

What an Attack in Bulgaria’s EEZ Means Under International Law
Bulgaria’s Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) in the Black Sea extends to as much as 200 nautical miles, or about 370.4 kilometers, from the coastline or straight baselines, under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea and Bulgaria’s Law on the Maritime Spaces, Inland Waterways, and Ports.
Because the Black Sea is semi-enclosed and the distance between opposite shores is less than 400 nautical miles, the outer boundaries of Bulgaria’s EEZ have been determined through international delimitation agreements with neighboring coastal states, based on the median line principle.
Under the median line, or equidistance, method used in international maritime law, boundaries between states with opposite or adjacent coasts are drawn so that every point on the boundary is equally distant from the nearest points of the baselines from which each country measures its territorial sea.
The key difference between territorial waters and an EEZ concerns the scope of state sovereignty and jurisdiction. Bulgaria’s territorial sea extends up to 12 nautical miles, or about 22.2 kilometers, from the coast and forms part of the country’s state territory. Within those waters, Bulgaria exercises full jurisdictional, legislative and police control over the water column, seabed, subsoil and airspace, subject only to the right of innocent passage for foreign vessels.
The EEZ starts beyond the territorial sea and can extend to 200 nautical miles. It is not part of Bulgarian territory, but the country has sovereign rights over the exploration, exploitation, conservation and management of living and non-living natural resources there. These rights also cover energy production from water and wind, scientific research and the construction of artificial installations.
Special legal regime
The EEZ operates under a special legal regime. Bulgaria has jurisdiction in matters involving economic activities and the conservation of resources, while navigation and overflight retain the status of activities conducted on the high seas, effectively making the area international waters for those purposes. All states retain the freedom of navigation and overflight, as well as the right to lay submarine cables and pipelines in the zone.
An incident inside the EEZ does not by itself amount to a violation of Bulgaria’s maritime or airspace. Foreign ships have freedom of navigation there, so simply entering or passing through the zone does not breach the state border unless a vessel carries out unauthorized resource extraction, unauthorized scientific research or pollution.
Bulgaria’s sovereign airspace extends only to the outer boundary of its territorial sea, 12 nautical miles from the coast. The airspace above the EEZ is international airspace, meaning foreign aircraft entering or maneuvering there do not violate Bulgaria’s state border.
A drone attack on commercial vessels inside Bulgaria’s EEZ therefore requires a distinction between its legal characterization and its geopolitical consequences. From a strictly legal perspective under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, an incident beyond the 12-nautical-mile limit does not directly violate Bulgaria’s state border or sovereign territory because the waters and airspace there retain their international status.
At the same time, such an attack affects Bulgaria’s sovereign rights concerning protection of the marine environment and management of resources. Ships that are sunk or damaged create a direct danger of spills and pollution, potentially threatening the ecosystem and fishery resources within the Bulgarian zone. Bulgaria also has international responsibilities for maritime safety and for conducting search and rescue operations within its designated search and rescue region.
From the standpoint of national security, an incident of this kind represents a serious and immediate military-strategic and economic threat. Drone or missile attacks within the EEZ of a NATO and European Union member state increase security risks directly in the Black Sea. They can disrupt commercial routes serving Bulgarian ports, raise shipping insurance risks, endanger underwater infrastructure and put human lives at risk.
Because the EEZ is not sovereign territory, Article 5 of the Washington Treaty would not be legally applicable on the basis of an incident there. However, military activity in the immediate vicinity can provide direct grounds for NATO consultation under Article 4 concerning a threat to security and stability.
Background linked to the war in Ukraine
Since the start of the war in Ukraine, the formal use of Article 4 of the Washington Treaty has been requested twice by European Union and NATO member states.
The first and most significant request came on February 24, 2022, the day of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Eight Eastern European countries, including the six EU members Bulgaria, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and Romania, together with the Czech Republic and Slovakia, called for urgent consultations within the North Atlantic Council because of the direct threat to regional security and the territorial integrity of NATO’s Eastern Flank.
The second case occurred in September 2025, when Poland formally invoked Article 4 after an incident involving a breach of its airspace and the downing of Russian drones over Polish territory. Warsaw described the event as a major provocation and a threat to security.
Poland, Estonia and Romania have also considered or indicated readiness to use the same mechanism during other serious incidents. These included the November 2022 missile impact in the Polish village of Przewodów near the Ukrainian border, the hybrid migration crisis on the Belarus border, and repeated incursions by debris from Russian drones and military aircraft into Romanian and Estonian airspace.
The Black Sea has also seen a dangerous escalation in recent months, with repeated drone and missile attacks on civilian merchant ships. Several incidents have involved vessels flying the flags of Palau and Togo, including attacks on two general cargo ships in Bulgaria’s EEZ about 70 nautical miles east of Byala. One of those vessels sank, while a rescue operation was launched for the other. Similar incidents in the Odesa region have caused major fires, deaths and injuries among foreign crew members.
The attacks are carried out by Russian military drones and missiles as part of an effort to blockade Ukrainian maritime trade routes and discourage foreign operators from using ports in the region. Their consequences include deaths, destruction of ships and cargo, serious environmental dangers and a sharp increase in Black Sea shipping insurance premiums, leading many traditional shipowners to avoid the area.
Palau and Togo are examples of jurisdictions offering so-called "flags of convenience" through open registries. Shipowners use them because registration can be completed very quickly and cheaply through private agencies, while the jurisdictions offer no local taxation, limited bureaucracy and less restrictive rules on crew citizenship and qualifications.
The same systems can also make it possible to conceal the ultimate beneficial owner of a vessel through offshore structures. As established European and Western companies avoid sending ships into war zones because of strict regulations and insurers’ refusals to cover them, older vessels registered under "flags of convenience," including Palau and Togo, are used for high-risk voyages to and from Ukraine.
As attacks have become more frequent, Turkey has undertaken diplomatic efforts aimed at securing an agreement between Kyiv and Moscow to completely stop attacks on civilian merchant vessels and port infrastructure in the Black Sea. Those efforts have so far produced no tangible results.
Russia continues to use attacks on the merchant fleet as an instrument of economic pressure, while the lack of a control mechanism has allowed incidents to spread into the western Black Sea, including the EEZs of NATO member states.
Bulgaria’s EEZ in the Black Sea
Bulgaria’s EEZ is a maritime area located beyond and next to its territorial sea. The country does not exercise full sovereignty there but has specific sovereign rights and jurisdiction established by international maritime law.
Although the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea allows an EEZ to extend up to 200 nautical miles from the baselines used to measure the territorial sea, that distance cannot be applied mechanically in the Black Sea because of its limited size and the presence of other coastal states opposite Bulgaria. The boundaries of the Bulgarian EEZ have therefore been established through agreements with other countries in the region.
Unlike the EEZ, Bulgaria’s territorial sea is an area where the country exercises sovereignty. Other states retain freedoms inside the EEZ, including freedom of navigation.
Bulgaria nevertheless has exclusive rights to explore, exploit, conserve and manage natural resources within the zone. These include living marine resources and resources located on or beneath the seabed. Bulgarian jurisdiction also covers activities such as the construction and use of artificial islands, structures and installations, as well as protection of the marine environment.
The coexistence of freedom of navigation with the coastal state’s sovereign rights makes the EEZ particularly sensitive during military conflicts and other incidents.
A merchant ship traveling through the Bulgarian EEZ is not sailing through Bulgarian territorial waters, and the presence of a foreign vessel there alone does not violate Bulgarian sovereignty. Bulgarian institutions, however, retain certain responsibilities and powers concerning navigation safety, protection of the marine environment, prevention of violations and search and rescue for people in distress.
In the current incident involving the two vessels, the location of the attack is therefore significant. If the attack occurred within Bulgaria’s EEZ, it did not take place in Bulgarian territorial waters. However, attacks against civilian merchant vessels create serious challenges for international shipping security, compliance with international law and the ability of countries in the region to respond.
During the war in the Black Sea, the region’s significance extends beyond economic activity, bringing together trade routes, energy and resource interests, environmental risks and the security of civilian shipping.

Russian losses to Ukrainian drones surge in early October, Madyar says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:06:46 UTC
00:06:46 KST

Russian casualties attributed to Ukrainian drone strikes rose sharply during the first five days of October compared with the same period in August and September, Robert Brovdi, commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, known by his callsign "Madyar," said on Oct. 6.
Between Oct. 1 and Oct. 5, Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Forces recorded 2,699 Russian troops killed or wounded, compared with 1,931 during the same period in September, Brovdi said in a Telegram post. The figure represents a 39.7% increase, according to Brovdi.
Compared with the first five days of August, the reported number of Russian casualties was 76.5% higher, rising from 1,529 to 2,699.
The largest increase was recorded in the area of responsibility of the Ukrainian National Guard's 1st "Azov" Corps, covering the Dobropillia-Pokrovsk sector in Donetsk Oblast, according to Brovdi.
Ukrainian drone operators recorded 1,268 Russian troops killed or wounded in that area during the first five days of October, compared with 884 in the same period in September — a 43% increase. The figure was almost twice as high as the 664 casualties recorded during the first five days of August, representing a 91% increase, Brovdi said.
The figures cited by Brovdi cover only casualties attributed to Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces and do not include casualties from other Ukrainian military units.
Ukraine's General Staff said on Oct. 1 that Russian forces suffered an estimated 46,230 personnel losses in September, the highest monthly figure recorded by Ukraine so far in 2026.
Ukraine has increasingly relied on drones to inflict casualties and disrupt Russian operations along the front line.
Oleksiy Melnyk, co-director of the Kyiv-based Razumkov Center and a former Ukrainian Defense Ministry official, told the Kyiv Independent in May that drones now account for 70% to 80% of Russian casualties. FPV drones often carry enough explosives to kill a soldier outright, he said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said in July that Russia has lost more than 1.5 million troops killed or wounded since the beginning of the full-scale invasion. The figures cannot be independently verified, and Moscow does not publish comprehensive casualty data.
Russia has so far avoided announcing another nationwide mobilization, instead relying on an increasingly coercive recruitment system to replenish its forces.
Moscow uses financial incentives, regional recruitment quotas, pressure on businesses and public institutions, recruitment of students and reservists, as well as the enlistment of foreign nationals and residents of occupied Ukrainian territories to sustain its military manpower.
Ukrainian intelligence has also said Russia's General Staff is prepared to mobilize around 300,000 people in 2026 and another 300,000 in 2027 if needed.

Patria TRACKX Tracked Armored Vehicles to Be Equipped with RENK Transmissions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:06:06 UTC
00:06:06 KST

The German company RENK Group has received an order from Finland’s Patria for HSWL 076 transmissions for the new TRACKX family of tracked armored vehicles.
The company shared this with Militarnyi.
The value of the signed agreement is EUR 30 million.
Deliveries under the new contract are scheduled to begin in 2027. In early 2026, Patria had already ordered the first pre-production batch of these transmissions from RENK.
The HSWL 076 transmission gives the Patria TRACKX high mobility.
The vehicle has a combat weight of about 15 metric tons, a maximum speed of 80 km/h, and a range of up to 500 km. The TRACKX also has amphibious capabilities and can cross water obstacles at speeds of up to 4 km/h.
The HSWL 076, developed by the German company RENK, is designed for light tracked vehicles. The transmission transfers power from the engine to the tracks and handles steering and braking.
It has six forward gears and six reverse gears. The transmission weighs about 760 kg without lubricant, and its maximum power output is 300 kW.
The HSWL 076 is designed for vehicles weighing between 13 and 21 metric tons and can reach speeds over 80 km/h.
The transmission features digital control and supports drive-by-wire technology. This means that movement commands are transmitted electronically. As a result, the vehicle can be configured for remote control, autonomous convoy operation, and unmanned operation.
Militarnyi previously reported that Finland and Sweden had signed contracts to purchase the first Patria TRACKX tracked armored vehicles, which will undergo military testing before serial procurement begins.
The current procurement continues the agreement the Finnish Defense Forces and the Swedish Defense Materiel Administration (FMV) signed at the Eurosatory exhibition in June 2026. The document outlined the framework for cooperation between the two countries during the initial phase of TRACKX procurement and testing.

Proportion of people in Great Britain vaping who never smoked doubles in four years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:05:53 UTC
00:05:53 KST

More than 1 million people in Great Britain now vape despite never having been regular smokers, with rates nearly doubling in just four years, according to figures that health experts describe as concerning.
About 5.4 million people aged 16 and above in England, Scotland and Wales (9.9%) used e-cigarettes daily or occasionally in 2025, Office for National Statistics data showed. Vaping was highest among those aged 25-34 (16.4%).
However, the ONS also found about 2.9% (1.1 million) of Britons who had never smoked cigarettes reported using an e-cigarette daily or occasionally.
The proportion of never-smokers now vaping has increased sharply, almost doubling, since 2021, when 1.5% of people who had never smoked reported that they currently used e-cigarettes.
Estimates published in the Lancet Public Health journal in 2024 suggested there were 1,006,000 people in England who vaped despite never having smoked.
But the data published on Tuesday was the first time official ONS figures had confirmed that the figure for England, Scotland and Wales had topped 1 million. The 2025 figure for Great Britain (1.1 million) was up from 940,000 in 2024, the ONS said.
Justin Webb, an associate professor of physical activity and health at London Metropolitan University, said it was “somewhat concerning that 1.1 million people who have never smoked reported using an e-cigarette”.
He added: “Vapes can help adults stop smoking, but they are not risk-free and their full long-term effects remain unclear. We need to preserve their value as a quitting aid while strengthening protection against uptake among children and non-smokers.”
The ONS data showed 25-34 was the only age group in which there was a rise in e-cigarette use, increasing from 12.9% in 2024 to 16.4% in 2025.
That made the age group the most common users of e-cigarettes in the UK, overtaking 16- to 24-year-olds, who were the most common users between 2021 and 2024.
Meanwhile, separate ONS figures covering all four nations of the UK showed about 4.9 million people aged 18 and over (9.8% of the population) smoked cigarettes in 2025. This was a decrease from 2024 (10.6%) and continues a long-term downward trend.
David Mais, from the ONS, said: “Fewer than one in 10 adults now smoke. This is the lowest proportion on record and continues the long-term decline in smoking.
“At the same time, e-cigarette use remains more common than smoking and has followed an overall upward trend since 2020.
“E-cigarette users are also getting older, with those aged 25 to 34 now overtaking 16- to 24-year-olds as the age group most likely to use them. This may reflect existing users getting older, growing popularity among this age group or a combination of both.”
When it comes to smoking, men were more likely to smoke than women in the UK in 2025, continuing a trend observed in previous years. About 2.8 million men (11.3%) and 2.1m women (8.2%) were thought to be current smokers.
The largest reduction in smoking prevalence between 2011 and 2025 was among the 18-24 age group, from 25.7% to 7.2%, the ONS found.
Hazel Cheeseman, the chief executive of Action on Smoking and Health, said: “For the first time, fewer than one in 10 people in the UK smoke. This is really encouraging progress and shows what can be achieved through sustained action to reduce smoking.”
