00:05:19 KST

Fatih Erel and Halis Sunnetci
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Argentine football star Lionel Messi is set to make his final international appearance when Argentina face Benin in a friendly on Wednesday.
The 39-year-old will bid farewell to the national team at the Monumental Stadium in Buenos Aires, where River Plate play their home matches.
The stadium, the largest in South America with a capacity of around 85,000, will host the match, which is scheduled to kick off at 2 am Türkiye time (2300GMT Tuesday).
 
Unbeaten at Monumental Stadium
The Monumental Stadium is the venue in Argentina where Messi has scored the most goals for the national team.
Messi has made 28 appearances there for Argentina, recording 22 wins and six draws without a defeat while scoring 19 goals.
He scored his first goal at the stadium against Uruguay in a World Cup qualifier in 2008 and later registered hat-tricks against Bolivia in 2021 and 2024.
 
Farewell after 21 years
Messi is bringing an end to a 21-year international career marked by numerous records and trophies.
He holds Argentina’s all-time appearance record with 207 matches and has scored 125 goals, making him the highest-scoring South American player in international football.
Messi has won six international trophies at senior and youth levels: one FIFA World Cup, two Copa America titles, one Finalissima, one Olympic gold medal and one FIFA U-20 World Cup.
 
2026 World Cup his final tournament
Messi, who led Argentina to the World Cup title in 2022, again helped his country reach the final at the 2026 tournament, the last major competition of his international career.
Argentina, however, suffered a 1-0 extra-time defeat to Spain in the final to finish runners-up.
Messi scored eight goals during the tournament.
 
World Cup appearance record
Messi also holds the record for the most World Cup appearances with 34 matches.
He recorded 23 wins, five draws and six defeats across six World Cups in 2006, 2010, 2014, 2018, 2022 and 2026.
Messi scored seven goals during Argentina’s title-winning campaign in 2022 and eight at the 2026 tournament.
With 21 World Cup goals, he ranks second on the competition’s all-time scoring list behind France’s Kylian Mbappe, who has 22.

At ruined Donetsk’s airport, three Russians snap selfies and ready jet-powered Geran-4. Ukrainian drone slips in unseen and rams their launcher

00:04:50 KST

Russian troops were taking selfies beside a jet-powered Shahed launcher when a Ukrainian drone hit them. A Ukrainian drone attacked a pickup truck converted to launch Russian Shahed drones in the Donetsk airport area while its crew prepared to fire a jet-powered Geran-4, according to video from the Cursed Empire drone unit of the 100th Separate Mechanized Brigade that volunteer Serhii Sternenko published on 6 October.
Russia launches Shahed drones, including jet-powered ones, from pickup trucks and fixed launchers, and the ruined Donetsk airport, about 50 kilometers from the front line, is one of its drone bases. In September, Oboronka outlet counted that in general, Russia has at least 63 launchers at its drone bases, which are built to survive strikes.
The video shows three carefree Russian soldiers next to a pickup fitted with a launch frame.
"That was their last photo shoot," Sternenko noted, commenting on the hit on the soldiers.
The primary target
Earlier, an officer of the 1st Separate Center of the Unmanned Systems Forces, call sign “Falco,” explained that the primary goal of strikes on drone bases is to disrupt Russia's ability to launch drones.
This is done by destroying launchers and storage facilities, as well as creating an aerial threat over the drone base. Such attacks can delay drone launches indefinitely, while the destruction of infrastructure can reduce the overall number of drones launched.
But the "jewel" of anti-drone port operations is the military staff
Although these facilities are important targets, the Unmanned Systems Forces have another priority: drone operators.
“The most difficult and, at the same time, the most valuable target is the operator. They don’t stay near the launchers for long,” Falco said.
By taking out drone operators, Ukraine inflicts losses on a scarce resource. There are already relatively few of them, and Russia will have to spend additional money and time training new crews.

00:03:43 KST

MOSCOW, October 6. /TASS/. Moscow’s educational and scientific ties with partners in friendly countries are increasingly in demand as interest in such cooperation is growing, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said.
"On behalf of the Foreign Ministry, I can say that we can see a growing interest in direct educational and scientific ties with partners in friendly countries," she pointed out in a video address to participants in the International Tech Science Educational Forum with the participation of BRICS countries.
According to Zakharova, the instruments that for decades were viewed as universal are now used increasingly selectively, depending on the political situation. "Universities are excluded from cooperation programs, academic publications are retracted due to short-term factors and entire countries are cut off from research databases," she noted.
"In such a situation, the search for new ways of cooperation - direct, equal and independent of the political will of others - become a real practical goal and challenge. While the political framework for such cooperation is created at the inter-government level, it is the people - researchers, engineers, entrepreneurs and teachers - that give it content," the diplomat added.
Zakharova pointed out that discussions of cooperation between countries, including BRICS members, at the forum, was a positive factor. "A stable alliance is based on living professional connections, joint projects and mutual trust that take years to build. Diplomacy creates conditions for all this but it cannot replace it," she emphasized.

India opposition mounts protest after 130M deleted from voters list

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:02:00 UTC
00:02:00 KST

India's opposition leader Rahul Gandhi was briefly detained by police Tuesday during a protest march demanding the election chief's resignation over large-scale voter list revisions.
Gandhi, a senior leader of the main opposition Congress Party, was standing on a police barricade and waving the national flag, according to Agence France-Presse (AFP).
Officers detained him along with other lawmakers but released them soon after.
The revision of voter lists has drawn criticism over alleged irregularities in the decision-making process, with opposition politicians accusing the election commission of acting at the behest of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Critics also say the drive has disproportionately affected marginalized and minority communities, especially Muslims.
The Election Commission of India has rejected allegations of wrongdoing, saying the revision process is aimed at ensuring the accuracy and integrity of electoral rolls.
On Tuesday, opposition members began a march from parliament towards the commission's headquarters, but were stopped by a heavy police presence.
Gandhi and his lawmaker sister Priyanka Gandhi Vadra later camped inside the public radio's offices adjacent to the election commission.
"The country has been hijacked by Narendra Modi through vote theft," Gandhi told reporters from behind the iron gates of the public radio building.
"What has been done to our country is called treason. Nobody is going to escape."
Modi's party has defended the drive.
"Some opposition parties, particularly the Congress, are making a concerted effort to change the government and install Rahul Gandhi in power," party spokesman Sambit Patra told reporters Tuesday.
"They are deliberately attacking India's democracy and constitutional institutions."
The protest is part of a wider campaign against revision of electoral rolls, reignited by a report last month by The Indian Express newspaper.
The report said that two of the election commission's three members had formally objected at least 14 times to key decisions linked to the revision and that the names of 130 million citizens had been deleted since the exercise began in 2025.
Protests began Friday, demanding that commission chief Gyanesh Kumar step down.
"Gyanesh, it's done, bro," placards read at the protest Tuesday, alongside signs alleging electoral manipulation.
Opposition leaders pressed their demands for greater transparency, alleging that changes to the voter rolls could disenfranchise eligible voters.
Kumar has not commented publicly.
The election commission says the revision exercise is intended to identify fraudulently registered voters and prevent "foreign illegal immigrants" from voting.
The youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a satirical political movement that emerged online in May and succeeded in its campaign to oust the then education minister, has called for "mass mobilization" in the capital Saturday.
Major student groups aligned with left-wing parties have also said they would join Saturday's protest.
India's Supreme Court on Monday ordered the government and the election body to explain decisions linked to the revision exercise. Another hearing is expected to be held next week.

The European Commission proposes to establish a position right at the start of the negotiation cluster with Ukraine on the agro-industrial sector, under which Kyiv will continue its established practice of exporting Ukrainian grain to traditional markets – in particular, North Africa – rather than to European Union markets.
A high-ranking Commission official provided this clarification on Tuesday in Brussels while explaining the relevant proposal contained in the documents presented regarding the European Union's preparations for future enlargement.
Specifically, regarding Ukraine, the Commission said in the documents that "given the scale, structure and very high productivity of its agricultural sector, targeted arrangements should significantly limit financial support and market access for sensitive agricultural products, while helping Ukraine regain access to its traditional third-country export markets."

According to him, the aim is for Ukraine to continue supplying grain to traditional markets in North African countries, such as Egypt. At the same time, the official speaking with journalists emphasized that the absence of Ukrainian grain in these very markets could lead to serious consequences, such as food shortages.

Democrats see White House "pay for play" scheme with Balkan gas project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:00:31 UTC
00:00:31 KST

Democrats cry foul as U.S. lifts sanctions on Serb nationalist, MAGA-linked firm gets huge Bosnia energy contract
London — The involvement of a small American firm linked to associates of President Trump in an energy project in Bosnia and Herzegovina worth more than $1.5 billion has raised questions about how the White House could be using its leverage in the fragile Balkan state.
U.S. lawmakers accuse the Trump administration of lifting sanctions on Bosnian Serb separatist leader Milorad Dodik in an effort to enrich and empower allies of Mr. Trump, and of undermining longstanding U.S. foreign policy interests in the region in the process.
On Sunday, Mr. Trump was hailed by Dodik after his Serb nationalist party won one of Bosnia and Herzegovina's three presidency seats, which are split between Bosnia's Muslim minority, known as Bosniaks, as well as Serb and Croat ethnic groups under the country's complex power-sharing electoral system.
"If it had not been for Donald Trump's magnificent victory … we would probably be political corpses today," Dodik told supporters in a speech, in which he also thanked Russian President Vladimir Putin for his support.
Company with links to Trump poised to build gas pipeline
AAFS Infrastructure & Energy, a company incorporated in the U.S. last year and headed by President Trump's former personal attorney Jesse Binnall and Joseph Flynn, the brother of Trump ally General Michael Flynn, is close to securing a contract to develop the Southern Interconnection Gas Pipeline.
The pipeline project has been discussed by Bosnian officials for years, but long opposed by Dodik, who has close ties with the Kremlin. But Dodik, whose party has veto power in Bosnia's parliament, said he would not stand in the way of the proposal following the announcement of AAFS' involvement last April. Six months earlier, the Trump administration lifted sanctions against Dodik that were imposed by the U.S. Treasury almost a decade ago.
The pipeline would connect Bosnia and Herzegovina to Croatia's gas network, allowing Bosnia to import liquefied natural gas (LNG) from its neighbors. The project, which is valued at around $1.7 billion according to the Croatian government, would help make Bosnia and Herzegovina less reliant on Russian gas imports.
On its website, AAFS describes itself as a company focused on "energy security, project structuring, capital alignment, and long-term regional infrastructure development."
The company does not appear to have demonstrable experience in any similar energy projects.
The secessionist leader Dodik, who until recently served as the president of Bosnia's self-governing, Serb-run territory called Republika Srpska, has long been accused of undermining the U.S. brokered Dayton Accords, which ended the bloody sectarian violence between Bosnia, Croatia and Serbia in the 1990s.
The sanctions, which included asset freezes and visa bans, were imposed by the Obama administration in 2017. The Biden administration then imposed further sanctions in 2022, accusing Dodik of corruption, including the charge that he had handed government contracts to close business associates in Republika Srpska.
A congressional report published last month by House Democrats, titled "Pay for Play in the Balkans," alleges that those two decisions — the removal of sanctions on Dodik and his decision to not oppose the pipeline — are directly linked.
"The Trump administration has used its diplomatic influence and connections with shady characters like Michael Flynn … to facilitate the concession contract for the SIC [Southern Interconnection Gas pipeline] to AAFS Infrastructure and Energy LLC, a company owned and operated by Michael Flynn's brother Joseph Flynn and Trump-affiliated lawyer and political activist Jesse Binnall," the report alleges.
AAFS Infrastructure and Energy LLC did not respond to a CBS News request for comment.
Foreign agent registration filings (FARA) cited in the report and reviewed by CBS News show that Michael Flynn, President Trump's former national security adviser, last worked as a paid lobbyist for Republika Srpska in October 2025, the month during which the sanctions against Dodik were lifted.
Those same filings show that Flynn was paid $100,000 for that work by RRB Strategies, a lobbying firm run by Rod Blagojevich, the former Illinois governor who was convicted in 2011 of 18 counts of corruption and spent nearly eight years in a federal prison before being pardoned by President Trump last year.
Flynn provided strategic advice and counsel, analysis and information research, and introductions to the Republika Srpska government, according to the FARA filings.
Blagoyevich's firm originally signed a contract to "provide communications and public affairs support on behalf of the Republic of Srpska" in March 2025, separate FARA filings reviewed by CBS News show.
CBS News sought comment from email aliases associated with Flynn and Blagojevich, but did not receive any response by the time of publication.
On Nov. 13, 2025, the U.S. Embassy in Sarajevo said in a social media post that Chargé d'Affaires John Ginkel had met Bosnian Prime Minister Nermin Niksic to discuss the gas pipeline project and "to support the importation of U.S. gas through Croatia to consumers in Bosnia and Herzegovina."
One week later, the embassy announced a preliminary agreement for an "American company to develop, build, and manage the pipeline."
Four days after that, on Nov. 24, AAFS Infrastructure & Energy was incorporated in the state of Wyoming.
In January, the U.S Embassy in Sarajevo posted again confirming that a meeting had taken place between AAFS leadership, including Joseph Flynn and Binnall, and top Bosnian officials.
AAFS was then granted the status of lead investor and operator on the proposed natural gas pipeline in legislation passed by Bosnia's parliament in April.
Later that month, the Croatian and Bosnian governments signed a contract to construct the pipeline with U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright in attendance for the signing ceremony. At a news conference with Bosnia's energy minister on April 2, Binnall hailed the pipeline project as a "priority" for the Trump administration.
The White House declined to comment on the pipeline project last week, but an administration official said the sanctions against Dodik were lifted to prevent instability in the Balkans.
"This is yet another example of President Trump's pragmatic, farseeing foreign policy that has prevented disasters on perennial issues that his predecessors so often stumbled into," a White House official told CBS News on Friday, without elaborating on the type of disasters the Trump administration was preventing.
A State Department letter published as part of the House Democrat-authored congressional report said the decision to delist Dodik had helped ensure peace and stability in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The official who wrote the letter, Paul Guaglianone, said lifting sanctions against Dodik had led to Bosnian Serb separatists rolling back policies that would have destabilized Bosnia's government.
The lifting of sanctions "advanced U.S. interests in [Bosnia and Herzegovina] and the Western Balkans. On October 18, the Republika Srpska National Assembly (RSNA) withdrew most of the anti-Dayton legislation it had passed in recent years," the letter read. That legislation had included laws that would have blocked Bosnia's national police and judiciary from having any authority in Republika Srpska.
Political scientist and Balkans foreign policy expert Jasmin Mujanović told CBS News the legislation in question had already been struck down prior to the lifting of the sanctions against Dodik, and he was skeptical of the Trump administration's justifications for the move.
"This package of omnibus secessionist laws that the Serb nationalist authorities and the RS [Republika Srpska] entity in Bosnia had unlawfully voted through in the local assembly had already been struck down by the Constitutional Court of Bosnia Herzegovina," he said.
"If the argument is that the Trump administration nevertheless managed to get Dodik and his people to withdraw the laws, it's still unclear what the significance of that is, or for that matter, why, given that the laws are moot," he said, adding that it would "result in sanctions relief for an entire regime."

Rubio urges Russia to share more information on plague lab worker's death

Rubio urges Russia to share more information on plague lab worker's death
- Published
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has urged Russia to release more information about the death of a lab worker at a plague research centre in Siberia.
The incident has sparked a flurry of speculation about the circumstances in which the 28-year-old woman died.
Russian officials have said they are still investigating the cause of the death but those who came into contact with the victim all tested negative to pneumonic plague.
"I think it's incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world," Rubio told reporters. "We're watching it very closely, hour by hour."
Reports first emerged on Friday of almost 200 people being placed under observation in Siberia's Irkutsk region following the death.
The lab worker, named in Russian media as Darya Shipilova, had reportedly fallen ill a couple of days earlier.
Unconfirmed reports suggested that she had become ill after breaking a test tube containing the pathogen or following a field trip to a region where plague occurs naturally among wild rodents.
But Russian officials have played down those reports. The country's health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said the woman had died of "pneumonia of an undetermined etiology".
In a statement read out by World Health Organization spokesman Christian Lindmeier on Tuesday, Russia - which has a duty under global health rules to report outbreaks to the WHO - said: "No case of this dangerous disease has been recorded in the city of Irkutsk."
The statement added: "All of the patients' contacts have been reportedly been identified and are being monitored for illness, and none to date have shown symptoms of illness."
On Tuesday, the ongoing speculation sparked a back and forth between Russia and the United States, with questions about a possible spread outside of Russia.
Speaking during a trip to Iceland, Marco Rubio said the US had "measures" available to help Russia if the situation turned out to be more serious than claimed.
Rospotrebnadzor hit back with an offer of help to the the United States. "The Russian Federation is ready to assist the US in combating infectious disease outbreaks," it said in a statement.
Rubio's comments were echoed by US President Donald Trump, who said he was looking "very strongly" at the case, saying.
According to the Washington Post, external, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the state department, the Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response are working on the US response.
'Disease not detected'
Asked about the death following Rubio's remarks, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov cited the findings by Rospotrebnadzor.
Asked about the offer of help from the United States, he said it was a "good thing when mutual assistance is offered".
Also on Tuesday, Rospotrebnadzor issued a statement aimed at quelling speculation in a document circulating online about special anti-plague measures allegedly put in place.
"We wish to clarify that the document and information in question do not originate from official sources and are untrue," it said on Telegram.
The plague bacterium or Yersinia pestis, external, which killed up to half the population of Europe in the 14th Century when it was known as the Black Death, is found among rodents such as marmots in the area.
It was in response to an outbreak in the 1920s that the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, external was founded just more than 100 years ago.
Dr Simon Clarke, an associate professor in cellular microbiology at the University of Reading, told BBC Radio 4's PM programme that the pneumonic version of Yersinia pestis was nearly always fatal if left untreated, but could be overcome with antibiotics.
"Pneumonic plague can transmit from person to person and that is why there is the concern around this," he said.
He added: "But of course people's thought with any outbreak of infectious disease at all runs to... lockdowns and Covid and that is just not what's going to happen here."
"People think, 'Oh the plague, that's gone, that went hundreds of years ago,' but it hasn't," Clarke said.
"It's a threat to human health and that's why they need to study it."

Hoping for Better, 3 Years Since Oct. 7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:00:08 UTC
00:00:08 KST

My name is Rachel.
And I will always be the mother of Hersh Goldberg-Polin.
Hersh will always be my eldest child.
Hersh will always be my only son.
And Hersh will always be 23-years-old.
As one of the millions of parents around the world who have tragically and chokingly buried a child, I am stuck in time. I always will be.
Oct. 7 is approaching. That date upon which my son, Hersh, was stolen from a music festival advertised as being for peace, love, and unity. Hersh was held hostage for 328 sickening, agonizing, and starving days until his captors executed him with five other young and luminous people in a tunnel underneath Gaza.
His majestic body, that I carried in my body many moons ago, was returned to me in a bag, skeletal, bearing signs of torture, filthy, missing his left forearm that had been blown off during his abduction, and with six bullet wounds. I awake every day to the confusion of this truth. I am glued to time's flypaper of stickiness. I cannot move.
People care about us and want my family and me to improve—emotionally, psychologically, mentally, spiritually, and otherwise. They desperately want us to get... better. I am told this is similar to the way people who lost loved ones on 9/11 encounter well-meaning comforters, in the quarter century since they lost someone core to their identity, in this layered and puzzling place called life.
I remember waking up on Sept. 11, 2001, in our house in Berkeley, California. My husband Jon was already in the shower. It was around 6:30 in the morning, and I could hear baby Hersh, just 11 months old, cooing in his crib in the room adjacent to mine. The clock radio (remember those?) was on. In my fuzzy moments of waking, I shot up in bed when I heard the announcer say something about an airplane flying into the World Trade Center in New York.
I ran into the bathroom and said to Jon in the shower, “Hurry up and come quickly, something terrible is happening in New York.” Everyone in the United States has their tale of what happened that day.
My mother used to say that the day President John F. Kennedy was killed, everyone remembers where they were. She had gone into the dry cleaners to pick up a blouse, and the man at the register was crying. She asked what happened, and he said, “Oh dear, do you not know? The president was assassinated.” I also recall my grandmother remembering where she was when the attack at Pearl Harbor happened.
In our generation, we now have another day of “infamy.” Oct. 7, 2023. The day my “before” ended. On that morning, Jon and I were thrust into an odyssey of hardship I wish on no one. No one. We, and all of the families of the 251 treasured hostages abducted that day, ran in excruciating pain to the ends of the planet, trying desperately and agonizingly to save them.
We wanted everyone back, including the hostages whom we knew had been killed on Oct. 7, whose precious bodies had been savagely taken to be used as bargaining chips. And we were desperate to get back all of the live hostages while they were still living. But that was not to be. We failed them. Dozens of hostages went in alive, survived horrifying conditions and torture for hundreds of days, only to be murdered before they could be saved.
The hostages taken on Oct. 7 were from 39 different nations. They were Christians, Muslims, Jews, Hindus, and Buddhists. The youngest hostage was a nine-month-old redheaded baby and the oldest was a mustachioed grandpa. They kept themselves alive. Somehow. Those sacred and cherished souls. But we did not get to them in time.
Hostages killed in captivity, in different but heinous ways, were tricklingly returned to their families in bags. Even the little redheaded baby and his four-year-old brother. In smaller bags.
And now we approach three years of the day these people were taken from us. Taken from themselves and their lives. And so many ask, “Are you getting better?”
The question comes from a genuine place of curious benevolence, kindness even. I cannot imagine anyone means to cause harm. But the answer is “no.” No, we are not getting better.
Actually, I want to be careful and only speak for myself. Because pain and suffering are deeply personal and tailor-made for the one wearing it. My personal garment of affliction is not even similar to others in my family who are missing the same person. Our forever Hersh. Oh, my delightful sunny sun of son.
So, dear inquisitive asker, I am sorry; I am not getting better. I aspire and try to get different. To adapt to this bewildering truth. To breathe in this world without air. To wander the desert without water. But I am trapped in a cage of suffering. It is where I live. You see me and not the bars that keep me in this prison of pain. And I can fake it. Boy, can I act, pretend, and lie. When people want and demand our healing, I have learned that is called “toxic positivity.” It is emotional barbarism and emotional denial. I understand it comes from everyone being fiercely uncomfortable with misery. Who wants to think someone is always with an ache lodged in their throat? In their chest? In their spirit.
I grew up in Chicago, not far from the Lincoln Park Zoo. We went there with school every year. I didn’t like it. It felt unsettling to me. I don’t know why. I have seared into me the black panther that would pace rhythmically back and forth, back and forth, in what seemed like a jail. I feel like a kindred spirit to that sad and handsome cat from the late 1970’s.
I have blessings and laughter in my cage. And I strive and yearn to get out. One day. Even though the thousands of parents who have reached out to me, who all put their children in the ground before me, have explained that it will not get better. They reach out from all sorts of places, describing treasured innocent lives no longer here; and those who are here have their breathing constricted. Inhaling is an effort.
Hersh was a curious, radical listener who dreamt of quenching his wanderlust by traveling the world. He had planned and saved for many years. His ticket was purchased, and the flight date was Dec. 27, 2023. Alas, Hersh was to miss the flight because he was still being held hostage, starving, tortured, and surviving on that date in terrifying confinement.
And, fascinatingly, he was hopeful. I know it because he told us in a video his captors made of him that was given to my husband, Jon, and me. I know it because some hostages who did make it home told us that Hersh told them he was hopeful. What a gorgeous gift, to remain hopeful even when in the bowels of hell. I hope I can muster that kind of hope. I hope.
Hersh had many compasses. On his desk, clipped to his many backpacks, in his locker at school, and ubiquitous compasses on his phone (which he referred to as “cheating” compasses). And now what I dream of is finding the compass that will offer me the road to another word similar to compass, a word that encompasses compass. I long for directions to compassion. For me, my family, my people, all people. Compassion from me and to me.
We have all been taught that history is written by the ones with the power to hold the pen. I have no power. Just love. I am holding and wielding love. I have learned that love is stronger than death. My love for Hersh continues blooming and is more intricate than when he was right here.
Love does not die. It grows. Not in a cliché way, but in a flooding and abundant way. If you have felt it, you know it. Grief is a badge of love. But it is pinned to our skin so it hurts when we inhale. Or exhale.
On this approaching Oct. 7, I think of the 11-month-old Hersh from 25 years ago, on September 11th, 2001, who had big brown eyes like cookies and a furry white polar bear he slept with. That Hersh, who is now buried in the ground, in a grave overlooking a forest, five miles from where I am writing this. That Hersh, who will always be 23 years old.
My Hersh.
I pray for all of us in sorrow that some day, somehow and someway, we become different.
Godspeed.

‘A Mother’s Brain’ explores the neuroscience of motherhood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

A Mother’s Brain explores the neuroscience of motherhood
The book, by neuroscientist Susana Carmona, redefines ‘mommy brain’
A Mother’s Brain
Susana Carmona
MIT Press, $27.95
When it comes to new motherhood, the baby typically takes center stage, garnering most of people’s attention. But in a refreshing twist, neuroscientist Susana Carmona shifts the spotlight to the mom. In the opening pages of A Mother’s Brain, Carmona cheerfully tells us, “here, we’ll hardly discuss babies at all.” Mothers are her protagonists.
What follows is a captivating, passionate and well-grounded journey through the fascinating process of “matrescence.” A word coined to echo “adolescence,” another time of seismic changes, matrescence includes the intense reorganization a woman’s brain undergoes as she becomes a mom. So far, early studies have revealed a sculpting of brain circuits (and Carmona is quick to point out that less can be more), heightened social instincts and perhaps even a boost of resilience during old age.
This mom found the book to be a treasure trove of motherly delights. Scientific concepts are woven with social and cultural strands, from the poignant to the weird to the profound. Certain passages in the book allowed me the pleasure of relistening to the song “The Mother” by Brandi Carlile, in which she sings, “Welcome to the end of being alone inside your mind.” A Mother’s Brain also kindly pointed me to the viral video, “Mother Rat Saves Baby from Snake.”
As one of the foremost scientists studying matrescence, Carmona is an authoritative guide through the latest research, of which there is a dismayingly small amount. Still, the book covers scientific ground including hormones, evolution and brain networks. History, social constructs and the pressures of modern life come into the story, too.
If you prefer a light read, Carmona will occasionally warn you when a section is scientifically dense. Then she will invite you along anyway. “But if you do like hormones — well, we’re going to have fun,” Carmona writes at the beginning of a chapter. And it was fun. I was shocked to learn, for instance, just how massive the hormonal upheaval during pregnancy is. The amount of estrogen that floods a woman’s body, including her brain, during the 40 weeks of pregnancy is more than that of the amount that would otherwise accumulate over her entire fertile life, which lasts 35 years on average.
Along the way, Carmona thoughtfully addresses scientific puzzlers such as this: Mothers often report feeling less mentally sharp, yet laboratory studies show almost no neurological decline. Attributed to “mommy brain” or “momnesia,” mental slips might be due to a lack of sleep, or a shifting of attention, or even just an expectation.
This pervasive, negative stereotype of “mommy brain” can then build on itself, getting stronger as women buy into the incorrect idea that motherhood leaves them dumber. If a woman expects her memory to get worse, she’ll see signs of it in even normal mistakes. “I have watched brilliant women grow so insecure about their intelligence on becoming mothers that they abandon the projects that were once vital to them,” Carmona writes. Assumptions about their diminished brainpower can lead women to pull back from valuable parts of their lives. “It matters — a lot — how we talk to ourselves about these things.”
As a mother herself, Carmona brings her experiences into the narrative. It couldn’t be any other way. “Motherhood is lived,” she writes. “It happens in your gut, your identity, your core.”
At its heart, this book is a love letter to moms, who have been invisible to the scientific gaze for too long. It’s time to write a new tale of matrescence, Carmona argues. “A story that recognizes mothers as the essence of the human species, the carriers of knowledge about how we create bonds — and, through them, society and culture.”
By putting the intense and wild changes of motherhood into words, Carmona offers us a powerful and necessary story.

A New Neurotech Startup Launches to Rival Sam Altman’s Merge Labs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Sam Altman-backed Merge Labs has a new competitor in the race to build a brain-computer interface powered by ultrasound. Bridge Neurotech is launching with $13.5 million in funding, including from venture firm General Catalyst, which has also backed major tech companies such as Anduril, Anthropic, Airbnb, and Stripe.
The company is the latest in a growing field of startups that aim to translate signals from the brain into useful actions. Elon Musk’s Neuralink, plus Synchron, Paradromics, and Precision Neuroscience are all working on brain-computer interfaces to help people who have lost the ability to move or speak.
These approaches all require surgery of some kind, which is why Bridge founder and CEO Will Biederman says he struck out on his own. “It fundamentally comes down to a difference in vision,” he says.
Biederman developed the chip Neuralink licensed to use in its first devices as part of his PhD work, but his goal with Bridge is to build a wearable device that could be used by far more people than a brain implant. Only 100 or so people around the world have received an implanted brain-computer interface as part of clinical trials, including at least 21 volunteers who have gotten Neuralink’s device.
“The risks of neurosurgery really cannot be minimized or dismissed, and so the level of safety and benefit that these devices must deliver really is quite high,” Biederman says. “Nobody really wants a hole in their head.”
But wearable brain-computer interfaces have suffered from poor signal quality. Bone and skin weaken electrical signals before they reach external sensors, which affects the performance of a device. It’s why most companies are recording electrical impulses directly from neurons in the brain. Neuralink and others have shown that these electrical systems can allow paralyzed people the ability to control electronic devices, move robotic arms, and communicate in real time with just their thoughts.
Bridge Neurotech thinks ultrasound offers an alternative to current implants and external sensors. Ultrasound uses high-frequency sound waves to bounce off moving red blood cells and measure the speed and direction of blood flow. In the brain, fluctuations in blood flow closely follow neural activity.
Both Bridge Neurotech and Merge Labs have ties to Arbor Neuroscience, which was previously known as Forest Neurotech, a nonprofit founded in 2023 by Biederman and fellow researchers Sumner Norman and Tyson Aflalo to pursue “work that is too integrated and long-horizon for a single academic lab, and too early for a company.” The organization built an instrument that uses ultrasound to image brain function that is in trials in the UK.
Merge Labs spun out of Forest Neurotech in January, with Norman and Aflalo among the company’s cofounders, which also include Altman, researcher Mikhail Shapiro, and tech entrepreneurs Alex Blania and Sandro Herbig.
Maryam Shanechi, a neuroengineer at the University of Southern California, says because ultrasound measures brain activity indirectly from blood instead of directly from neurons, there is a natural delay of a few seconds between when neurons fire and the subsequent change in blood flow and volume.
“It captures a slower variation in neural activity,” Shanechi says. “That’s fine for a lot of applications, but it depends what you want to build.”
For real-time, fast-paced tasks such as moving a robotic limb instantly or rapid typing, this lag time could pose a challenge for ultrasound-based brain-computer interfaces. Bridge is planning to use predictive AI models to cut down on that lag time and boost the performance of its interface. Biederman says the company is interested in pursuing both consumer and medical applications but didn’t comment on specific plans.
The company is starting its first clinical study in volunteers in Redwood City, California. It’s an observational study, with no treatments or diagnoses involved, in which a small ultrasound probe will be placed on the side of the head of healthy adults, as well as those who have undergone skull surgery. Bridge’s probes, which use semiconductor silicon chips made by the portable ultrasound company Butterfly Network, will record brain activity while participants listen, watch, move, and speak.
Bridge isn’t releasing images of its device yet, but Biederman says it is “something close to headphones” that will sit on the temporal window, which is located slightly above the ear. As the thinnest part of the skull, “it's the easiest place to image through,” Biederman says. That’s relevant for ultrasound, because bone scatters and absorbs sound, which presents technical challenges for imaging noninvasively through the skull.
In a 2024 study, researchers from Caltech and the University of Southern California demonstrated that an ultrasound-based brain-computer interface could read and decode human brain activity, but it required a portion of the skull to be removed and replaced with a “window” through which ultrasound waves can pass. That is one of the biggest technical hurdles that Bridge will have to address.
“My vision is focused on noninvasive interfaces,” Biederman says. “I think that's where the biggest opportunity to help people is.”

Mexico arrests alleged cartel leader and fuel smuggler "The Tank"

Alleged Jalisco cartel leader and fuel smuggler dubbed "The Tank" is arrested in Mexico
Security forces in Mexico have arrested an alleged leader of a notorious cartel who is accused by the U.S. of drug trafficking and a large-scale fuel smuggling operation, authorities said Tuesday.
Ivan Cazarin Molina (a.k.a. "El Tanque"—meaning "The Tank"), was captured on Monday in the town of Zapopan in Jalisco state, security minister Omar Garcia Harfuch said in a social media post.
Mexican authorities say Molina, the alleged regional leader of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), runs a massive fuel theft network and is linked to homicides, kidnappings and drug trafficking. He is accused of being involved in the attack on a Mexican Army helicopter in Jalisco in 2015 that killed members of the Army and the Federal Police.
Harfuch posted several images of Molina being apprehended by National Guard members and being escorted in handcuffs.
The U.S. Treasury sanctioned Molina in September 2024, saying he was part of the inner circle of "El Mencho," the infamous Jalisco cartel leader who was later killed in a military operation.
"Although primarily involved in fuel theft, El Tanque has also engaged in drug trafficking, extortion, and homicide," the Treasury said at the time. "El Tanque's fuel theft generates tens of millions of dollars per year for himself and CJNG."
U.S. authorities allege Molina manages a network of ostensibly legitimate retail gas stations where he sells stolen fuel. He is also accused of selling stolen fuel to third parties in Mexico, who in turn sell it to the U.S. market, often in Texas.
Fuel theft — more commonly known as huachicol in Mexico — has risen to the second most profitable revenue stream for Mexican cartels behind drug trafficking, according to the U.S. Treasury.
"Fuel theft and crude oil smuggling are cash cows for CJNG's narco-terrorist enterprise, providing a lucrative revenue stream for the group and enabling it to wreak havoc in Mexico and the United States," Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent said in 2025.
One of Mexico's most powerful criminal organizations, CJNG is among eight cartels designated as foreign terrorist organizations by the U.S. government. In August, the State Department offered a $25 million reward for information leading to the capture of its new leader, Juan Carlos González, the California-born stepson of "El Mencho."

Russian Il-76s Flew 100+ Missions for UAE—and May Have Carried Weapons to Sudan
A sanctioned Russian cargo airline with a history of transporting military equipment has flown more than 100 missions linked to the United Arab Emirates since mid-2025, including flights that may have supported weapons deliveries connected to the war in Sudan, according to reporting cited by Defense Express on October 6.
Defense Express, referring to an investigation by Defense News, identified the operator as Aviacon Zitotrans, a Russian airline that operates at least four Il-76 heavy transport aircraft and has previously been linked to military cargo missions for Moscow.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The carrier has also reportedly transported supplies for units of Russia’s Africa Corps and previously moved various types of weapons, including missiles, to customers in Asia.
Against that background, Defense Express noted that its growing work on behalf of UAE interests stands out as another example of the airline’s role in sensitive international logistics.
Flight tracking reviewed in the investigation reportedly showed Aviacon Zitotrans aircraft departing from locations directly associated with the UAE military, including Al Ain and Sweihan air bases.
Other flights originated from the Chandana airstrip in Pakistan, a location associated with hunting grounds used by members of the Emirati ruling families.
The Sudan connection is harder to verify directly. According to the reporting cited by Defense Express, the aircraft’s transponders were repeatedly switched off over the Gulf of Aden and only appeared again during the return leg.
That pattern has fueled suspicions that the Il-76s continued toward Sudan while deliberately avoiding public flight tracking.
The aircraft identified in the reporting carried the registrations RA-76842, RA-76502, RA-76846 and RA-76834.
Aviacon Zitotrans has already been subjected to international sanctions over its role in transporting military cargo.
Defense Express suggested that this could make the airline particularly useful for operations that governments or commercial carriers may be reluctant to perform, since the company already faces significant restrictions and therefore has less exposure to additional reputational or financial penalties.
The relationship also fits into the broader economic ties between Moscow and the UAE that have deepened since Russia launched its full-scale war against Ukraine. The Emirates have become an important hub for Russian trade and financial activity as Moscow looks for alternative routes around Western restrictions, Defense Express noted.
Earlier, Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF) claimed responsibility for shooting down a Sudanese Air Force Il-76 Candid transport plane near the western town of Babanusa on November 4, reportedly killing everyone on board.
According to Russian military-linked Telegram channels, the aircraft was operated by a Russian civilian crew working under contract.

The Hague court awards PrivatBank $180.9 mln against claims exceeding $1 bln
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:58:36 UTC
23:58:36 KST

THE HAGUE, October 6. /TASS/. An arbitration in The Hague has awarded Ukraine’s PrivatBank a payment of nearly $180.9 million for its allegedly "expropriated" assets in Crimea, which, excluding interest, is over five times less than the bank's original claims. The Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA), which provides administrative support to the tribunal, announced the ruling.
The final award was issued on October 1. Interest accrues on the awarded $180.87 million from April 18, 2014, until the date of payment. The court also allocated the arbitration costs between the parties. The PCA did not disclose the interest rate or the cost-sharing ratio, and the text of the decision has not been made public.
PrivatBank previously stated that it was seeking more than $1 billion from Russia. The lawsuit was filed in April 2015, when oligarch Igor Kolomoisky (listed in Russia as a terrorist and extremist) was one of the bank's principal owners. PrivatBank was nationalized in December 2016 and is currently owned by the Kiev authorities.
Russia’s position
Russia did not recognize the jurisdiction of the Hague arbitration. In 2015, the Russian Justice Ministry stated that the 1998 intergovernmental agreement with Ukraine on the promotion and reciprocal protection of investments, cited by the bank, could not serve as a basis for resolving the dispute. Initially, the Russian side did not participate in the proceedings, and the arbitrator acting on its behalf was appointed by a competent authority rather than the defendant.
In 2019, Russia entered the proceedings and requested permission to present arguments regarding jurisdiction, the merits of the case, and the quantum of damages. The arbitration agreed to hear Russia only on the issue of the amount and on the objection that PrivatBank could not be considered a legitimate investor, as it had acquired its assets through corruption, fraud, and violence. In the final award, this objection was dismissed. Back in 2019, the arbitration had ruled that the claims of the second plaintiff, Finilon financial company, did not fall within its jurisdiction.
Russia’s interests in the proceedings are represented by the Prosecutor General’s Office of the Russian Federation and the International Centre for Legal Protection.
Russia challenged the 2017 and 2019 rulings — in which the tribunal affirmed its jurisdiction and found a breach of the agreement — in Dutch courts. The Hague Court of Appeal in 2022, and subsequently the Supreme Court of the Kingdom in December 2024, upheld those decisions. An application to set aside the final award may be filed with the same Court of Appeal within three months from the date the award is dispatched to the parties.
The bank’s exit from Crimea
PrivatBank ceased serving customers in Crimea in March 2014. On April 21, the Bank of Russia terminated the operations of the bank's branches on the peninsula, citing a failure to meet obligations to depositors. Compensation for residents of Crimea and Sevastopol — up to 700,000 rubles ($8,242) per person — was paid by Russia's Deposit Protection Fund. In September 2014, the State Council of Crimea nationalized assets located in the republic belonging to Kolomoisky and companies linked to him. Crimean authorities stated that proceeds from the sale of these assets were intended for PrivatBank depositors whose savings exceeded the compensation limit.
The bank itself also has outstanding claims against its former owners. In July 2025, the High Court of London found that they had misappropriated nearly $2 billion from PrivatBank, and in November, it ordered them to pay more than $3 billion, including interest and legal costs.
Crimea and Sevastopol became part of Russia following a referendum held on March 16, 2014 with a voter turnout exceeding 80%, 96.7% and 95.6% of participants voted for reunification with the Russian Federation, respectively. The treaty on the admission of the new constituent entities was signed on March 18 and ratified by the Federal Assembly on March 21. According to the arbitration’s findings, obligations under the agreement regarding Ukrainian investors in Crimea became binding on Russia as of that same date.

Pedro Sánchez is a master of the political comeback. But calling a snap election in Spain may be a gamble too far | Paolo Gerbaudo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:57:19 UTC
23:57:19 KST

To progressives across the west, Spain has been a rare glimmer of hope in a world where far-right parties are increasingly entering government. Under Pedro Sánchez, who became prime minister in 2018, the country has combined a post-Covid economic boom with a bold green energy transition programme, and a pro-immigration stance with a principled opposition to the war agenda of Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu. Yet, at the end of next month, this rare beacon of democratic progress could fall.
On Monday Sánchez called a snap general election, set for 29 November, after two decrees to address the country’s housing crisis were voted down in the lower chamber by politicians from rightwing parties. Speaking from the staircase of the Moncloa palace, Sánchez admitted that his government had not achieved all it had set out to do. “Many injustices remain to be corrected … particularly regarding inequality in public services and access to housing,” he said, adding: “To do more, we need to renew and expand public support.”
Sánchez attempted to pass the legislation after tens of thousands took to the streets to protest against the housing crisis, setting up camps reminiscent of the country’s 15-M anti-austerity movement and the global Occupy movement of 2011. But this explosion of popular anger has been long in the making. According to Spain’s national public opinion research institute Centro de Investigaciones Sociológicas (CIS), housing has been the country’s top preoccupation since the end of 2024, as a growing number of people struggle to pay rent.
In the latest gamble of his long career as master of the political comeback, Sánchez hopes to ride the wave of popular mobilisation to turn public attention away from the Ceuta immigration crisis of July, which rightwing opponents exploited as a demonstration of the government’s failures, and focus attention on the housing crisis, an issue where the left holds stronger political ground.
But this time it will be hard to convince Spaniards that with a new lease of life, the progressive coalition government will solve an issue it had promised to address a long time ago.
Sánchez’s troubles provide useful lessons for progressives all over the world about the difficulties of translating policy achievements into a solid base of political support. They are also a reminder that – as championed by New York’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani – addressing the affordability crisis rather than promising abstract economic growth is of more significance to voters.
In the US midterm election campaign, Republicans are struggling because of rising prices at the gas pump, while in Brazil, rightwing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro just rode to an impressive result in the first round of the presidential elections partly due to discontent with living conditions and household pressures. In Spain, Sánchez’s government is facing similar concerns about affordability, which are obfuscating an otherwise impressive macro-economic performance.
Indeed, seen from the outside, Sánchez’s Spain may appear to be a dazzling political success. The country, which in the 2010s was derided as part of the European Piigs – a term coined to mock Portugal, Ireland, Italy, Greece and Spain as the eurozone’s weakest economies – has become an economic powerhouse. In the years after the Covid pandemic, Spain’s GDP grew at a rate of around 3%, while France, Germany, the UK and Italy grew at a miserly 1% or less.
Spain is also held up as a model of successful green transition, with renewables now generating close to 60% of the country’s power, which has also kept energy bills low and helped insulate the country from the energy shocks caused by international crises. Spain, enabled by significant Chinese investment, is also surprisingly becoming the leading European hub for electric car production, to the dismay of some of the country’s traditional allies.
To these economic and environmental achievements add the significant social improvements achieved under Sánchez, exemplified by the rise in the minimum wage from €736 to €1,184 per month since 2018.
Yet despite these measurable successes, Sánchez’s centre-left coalition is now trailing the right by about 7 percentage points in national polling. That’s partly because while minimum wages have increased, median wages have remained relatively stagnant. But it is real estate that Sánchez’s government has been judged as failing to deliver: during its eight years in power, house prices have risen by an estimated 50%, with rents rising by over 40%.
As climbing the housing ladder becomes prohibitive, a growing number of young people in Spain are forced to pay extortionate rents. This is acutely felt in large urban areas, where the presence of tourists and digital nomads further increases rents, forcing out local residents; this is enabled by private equity firms, who purchase entire blocks to expel local inhabitants in order to create Airbnbs. Sánchez’s government has repeatedly promised to take action on these issues, but its measures have been thwarted by political gridlock or otherwise proven indecisive, partly due to fear of alienating homeowners and antagonising international finance.
If Spain’s centre-left coalition falls, the country could be left with an alliance of the mainstream conservative Partido Popular and the far-right party Vox. It would be the most rightwing Spanish government since Francisco Franco’s dictatorship. The lesson for progressives everywhere is clear: economic growth and ambitious reform will count for little unless working people feel the benefits in their daily lives.
- Paolo Gerbaudo is a senior researcher at the faculty of political science and sociology of Complutense University in Madrid and a lead researcher at the Alameda Institute

Will US President Donald Trump Visit Central Asia?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:57:00 UTC
23:57:00 KST

As U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s planned trip to Uzbekistan – at the head of a large delegation of American businesses – approaches, once again Central Asian governments and people are angling for a presidential visit. Both Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan have repeatedly invited Trump to make the trek; he’d be very welcome in the region and they’re hoping the novelty of being the “first” will get them on the presidential calendar.
In an interview with an Uzbek TV station, U.S. Special Representative for Global Partnerships Paolo Zampolli, said, “I know [Trump] wants to come to Uzbekistan. The president has an extremely busy schedule. But he told me about his intention to visit Uzbekistan. I myself am constantly promoting this issue. So, he will definitely visit Uzbekistan one day. We hope this visit will take place as soon as possible.”
That’s not exactly a firm commitment from a notoriously fickle administration, no matter the rabid headlines about the comments.
There has been no shortage of U.S. officials traveling to Central Asia since the dawn of the second Trump presidency. These include an October 2025 trip to Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan by Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau and Sergio Gor, concurrently the U.S. ambassador to India and also special envoy for South and Central Asian affairs. In February 2026, Gor returned to Central Asia, visiting Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan. In July 2026, Senator Steve Daines, a Republican from Montana – who co-founded the bipartisan Senate Central Asia Caucus in 2024 – traveled to Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan (and also Azerbaijan).
U.S. engagement with Central Asia has shifted from Afghanistan – an all-encompassing subject that dominated relations from 2001 to 2021 – to critical minerals, an especially hot topic for governments keen on dealmaking.
In November 2025, amid the fanfare of the C5+1 summit in Washington, in which all five Central Asian presidents were welcomed to the White House for the first time (although it was not the first presidential level C5+1 summit, as some have erroneously reported) – Rubio declared his intention to visit all five Central Asian states in the coming year.
“I personally intend to visit in the coming year,” he said during a reception after meeting with his Central Asian counterparts, as reported by Reuters. “All five,” Rubio added. “So I know it would probably be a week-long trip. So we’ve got to work on that and make that happen together.”
To date, the highest-ranking U.S. official to complete what I dubbed the “grand Stan slam” was then-Secretary of State John Kerry in 2015. It was during that trip that the C5+1, at the foreign ministers level, was launched in Samarkand, a month after a preview event on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly.
Rubio’s own envisioned “grand Stan slam” has been apparently whittled down to a trip to Samarkand, with a heavy business focus. According to a September 24 press release published by the U.S. embassy in India, and attributed to Gor, Rubio “will lead a historic business delegation of more than 100 American companies to Samarkand, Uzbekistan in mid-October to advance the U.S.-Central Asia strategic partnership and strengthen bilateral diplomatic and commercial cooperation.”
The Diplomat has heard rumored dates for the trip, but they have yet to be confirmed publicly. And that’s of little surprise. Not only is Rubio serving as secretary of state, but he’s also national security adviser – a role he took over on an interim basis in May 2025 after Michael Waltz flamed out by inviting a journalist into a high-level Signal chat. That role was made permanent on September 22. Rubio’s the second person to wear both hats simultaneously – the first was Henry Kissinger under Presidents Richard Nixon and Gerald Ford. All that to say: Rubio is a busy guy. The planned trip to Samarkand could, frankly speaking, be spoiled by any number of sudden crises.
Aside from Zampolli’s recent comment that Trump “wants” to come to Uzbekistan, there’s been no official word on that front. Trump is often discussed as disliking international travel. Of the three most recent presidents – Barack Obama (2009-2016) Trump 1.0 (2017-2020), and Joe Biden (2021-2024) he’s made the fewest international trips and visited the fewest foreign countries. Obama made a total of 25 foreign trips during his first term, Trump made 19, and Biden 21.
The statistics alone don’t tell the full story. Trump’s presidency ended with the COVID-19 outbreak, and Biden’s began with its lingering impact. So far in his second term, Trump has made 14 foreign trips – six in 2025 and eight so far in 2026. Trump is scheduled, officially, for one more international trip this year: from November 16 to 19, to attend the ASEAN Summit and the East Asia Summit in the Philippines and then to attend the APEC Summit in Shenzhen, China.
The year is drawing to a close, rapidly. The looming mid-term elections, scheduled for November 3 – and not looking good, per most polls, for the president’s party – might jerk Trump’s attention back to the domestic arena, making a late-year junket to Tashkent nearly impossible and potentially ruining future plans, too.
Trump does have two years left in his term, so a Central Asia visit may eventuate – he could also visit any of the more than 75 other countries a U.S. president has never traveled to while in office. Spoilers abound both internationally and domestically that could dash the highest of hopes for a U.S. president to finally step foot in Central Asia. But hope springs eternal.

Paris Police Prefect Patrice Faure, equivalent to the French capital's police chief, issued an order prohibiting a demonstration "against the genocide in Gaza and for respect of the ceasefire" slated to be held in Paris on Wednesday, the police confirmed on X/Twitter in a Tuesday post.
The order came at the request of French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, police said.
"In a context of heightened terrorist threat and while antisemitic acts remain at a historically high level in our country, such a demonstration on that day poses significant risks of disturbances to public order," Faure wrote.
"In the face of this, in particular, and in view of all the risks identified, my responsibility is to ensure the safety of all. I have therefore decided to prohibit this demonstration," he added.
October 7 "marks the third anniversary of the Hamas terrorist attack against Israel and will give rise to numerous commemorations," Faure noted.
French MP representing expats, including those in Israel, praises police's decision

"The march and rally is expected to start at Kings College London Strand and end at University College London via London School of Economics and SOAS. We have imposed strict conditions: Those taking part in the event must form up by 12:30hrs and remain in the shaded area (Lincoln’s Inn Field) of the first map below until the procession begins," the Met wrote.
"The procession must start by 12:30hrs with participants moving along the prescribed route. Anyone taking part in the procession must not deviate from this route as shown on the second map below – Remnant Street, Kingsway, Southampton Row and Russell Square," the Met added.
"The rally assembly must conclude by 14:00hrs when participants are required to disperse. No one taking part in the form-up assembly, procession or rally may wear a face covering that conceals their identity," the Met stated.
"We have imposed robust conditions on a student march due to take place on Wednesday, 7 October in central London to prevent serious disruption to communities," Met Deputy Assistant Commissioner James Harman said.
"The event is being held on the third anniversary of the October 7 terrorist attack on Israel and the start of the ensuing conflict in Gaza. This will be a day of mourning and reflection for many in London. We know how concerned Jewish communities are at the timing of this event," Harman added.
"The stringent conditions will help us manage this event and minimize disruption. Anyone who breaches the conditions or commits offenses faces arrest," he added.
"We hear the calls for this event to be banned - Police cannot ban protests and can only ask the home secretary to do so if the risk of serious disorder is so high that it can't be managed by conditions. That high bar is not met here," Harman explained.

"We are also aware of a planned student protest at Marble Arch on 7 October between 13:00hrs and 16:00hrs. We will impose conditions on this protest requiring it to take place away from Marble Arch and local synagogues that congregants may wish to attend on this significant day," he added.

IDF expected to resume draft evader operations as High Court deadline approaches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:55:07 UTC
23:55:07 KST

The IDF expects to resume proactive enforcement operations against military draft evaders and deserters in October after such operations generally did not take place during the recent period, according to a Justice Ministry summary dated Tuesday.
Deputy Attorney-General Dr. Gil Limon said the absence of proactive enforcement for a significant period did not meet the country’s security needs, particularly after senior military commanders described expanding the regular army as a strategic necessity.
He said it was also inconsistent with the principle of equality, the state’s commitments to the High Court of Justice and a court ruling striking down a law that had prevented the arrest of yeshiva students.
The four-page document summarizes a September 23 meeting led by Limon and attended by senior representatives of the IDF, Military Police, Israel Police and the Population and Immigration Authority.
IDF plans renewed October enforcement against haredi draft evaders
Military officials said proactive enforcement operations, including arrests, generally had not taken place during the recent period because authorities were concentrating their efforts at border crossings and making adjustments for the holiday season.
They said proactive enforcement was expected to resume in October, with Military Police and the relevant Israel Police stations coordinating operations in advance. The coordination is intended to allow the two forces to prepare jointly and provide a police response if exceptional incidents occur.
Overnight Monday, hundreds of haredi protesters surrounded Military Police officers attempting to arrest a draft evader in Modi’in and prevented them from taking him into custody. Israel Police officers were called to restore order and escort the soldiers from the building.
The IDF condemned what it described as an organized attempt to obstruct the arrest and endanger soldiers, saying enforcement would continue equally and within its authority.
During a concentrated enforcement operation from September 1 to 22, authorities arrested 212 draft evaders and deserters at Ben-Gurion Airport, the Allenby Bridge and the Begin crossing near Taba, the summary said. Military officials estimated that 163 of those arrested were haredi (ultra-Orthodox).
Authorities initiated proceedings against all 212, mostly through military disciplinary proceedings.
Of the 188 people arrested at Ben-Gurion Airport, 64 were caught only when they returned to Israel, raising concerns about gaps in enforcing restrictions intended to prevent them from leaving the country.
The Population and Immigration Authority said it quickly closed the gaps identified in border enforcement. Cases involving suspected illegal crossings were transferred to either Israel Police or the IDF, according to the document.
The summary also said prosecutors filed 360 indictments against draft evaders between January 1 and September 23. Military prosecutors estimated that 49 involved haredi draft evaders.
Only 16 indictments involving that group had been filed as of June, indicating an increase in the months that followed.
Military prosecutors said they were advancing measures to shorten the period of evasion required before criminal charges may be filed from 18 months to one year. They also plan to prosecute people who desert during the induction process after 30 days.
Those changes have not taken effect yet. Military prosecutors said they had completed their review of arguments raised by the Military Public Defender’s Office and expected to respond during October, after which the measures would be implemented.
The dispute follows a series of Supreme Court rulings requiring the state to enforce the military draft equally.
In June 2024, the court ruled that the government had no legal authority to refrain from drafting yeshiva students after the legal framework allowing their exemptions expired, and that the state must enforce the existing draft law.
In November 2025, a five-justice panel ordered the government to formulate an effective enforcement policy within 45 days, including significant criminal-law enforcement measures and broad complementary economic and civil steps.
Last month, the High Court unanimously struck down a law shielding qualifying haredi yeshiva students from arrest, investigation and other enforcement proceedings over draft evasion.
The state must submit its next update to the court by October 15. Limon requested that the relevant agencies provide updated arrest, indictment, disciplinary and enlistment figures by October 12.
The document also said a separate meeting would examine the gaps discovered in border controls and enforcement at Ben-Gurion Airport and the measures taken in response.
Keshet Neev contributed to this report.

JPR study finds 50% of British Jews emotionally attached to Israel, up sharply since Oct. 7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:55:07 UTC
23:55:07 KST

Half of British Jews now feel very emotionally attached to Israel, marking a sharp increase following the events of October 7, according to a major new empirical study by the Institute for Jewish Policy Research (JPR) released on Monday.
The report details how the post-October 7 landscape dramatically shifted emotional ties to the Jewish State and intensified concerns over antisemitism, even as core markers of domestic Jewish religious life and practice remained remarkably stable.
The study, called “October 8 Jews: The impact of October 7” on British Jewish identity, was conducted by Dr David Graham, a Senior Research Fellow at JPR.
Utilizing JPR’s longitudinal research panel, the study tracked the exact same group of 2,500 British Jews across multiple survey waves spanning a six-year period from July 2020 to June 2025. This allowed researchers to measure actual individual changes in attitudes and behaviors before and after October 7, 2023, rather than relying on retrospective accounts or single-snapshot polls.
The research aimed to examine whether widely discussed post-October 7 concepts applied to the UK, including the notion of the ‘October 8 Jew,’ describing individuals who experienced a renewed sense of Jewish consciousness and discovered that previously trusted progressive allies and spaces were no longer reliable, and the communal ‘Surge’, which refers to a broader rise in Jewish activity and engagement, particularly among previously unengaged Jews.
The report is organized into three core analytical sections that investigate how British Jews were impacted across different areas of life. The first section explores connections to Israel, the second shifts to experiences of antisemitism, and the third examines broader measures of Jewish identity, peoplehood, values, and religious observance.
UK Jews increasingly attached to Israel
The study first asked respondents about their connection to Israel through multiple indicators, revealing that overall emotional attachment rose from 72% in May 2023 to 76% in June 2024 and 78% by June 2025. Beyond that general rise, the report highlights a dramatic shift in intensity, with the proportion of those identifying as very attached surging from 38% prior to the attacks to 50% in June 2024 and holding steady at 51% in June 2025.
Analyzing these figures, the report explains that this represents an enduring change rather than a temporary spike, showing that Israel became far more central to personal identity.
Similarly, self-identification as a Zionist saw a statistically significant rise, climbing from 59% in November 2022 to 65% in June 2024, and holding at 66% in June 2025.
In contrast, the report notes that those identifying as anti-Zionist remained virtually unchanged at 9% to 10% across the same periods, while the proportion identifying as non-Zionist declined from 17% down to 14%, showing that people on the fence chose a side rather than shifting toward opposition.
The study also tracked the likelihood of making aliyah within five years, where the mean score on a scale from zero to ten increased from 1.38 in November 2022 to 1.95 in June 2024.
Analyzing these figures, the report notes that this post-October 7 rise in aliyah sentiment, while reflecting genuine increases in emotional attachment and Zionist sentiment, remained lower than the score of 2.29 recorded in July 2020 during the COVID-19 lockdown, explaining that such fluctuations likely reflect both a growing connection to Israel and changing perceptions of how comfortable and settled respondents felt living in the UK at different times.
Personal experiences with antisemitism rise in UK
The second section of the report evaluated personal experiences and perceptions of antisemitism, safety, and mental wellbeing. The survey found that personal experiences of antisemitism escalated drastically, with the proportion of respondents reporting that they had personally experienced at least one antisemitic incident jumping from between 17% and 20% in calendar years between 2020 and 2022 up to 29% in an 18-month tracking period spanning 2023 and the first half of 2024.
Public perception matched this reality; the proportion of respondents who viewed antisemitism as a very major problem in the UK nearly tripled from 17% in May 2023 to 47% in June 2024, reaching 50% by June 2025. This coincided with a sharp drop in average feelings of safety on a zero-to-10 scale, falling from 7.4 in May 2023 down to 6.2 in June 2024 and 5.8 by June 2025.
Consequently, the anxiety index mean score climbed from 2.99 in August 2021 to 3.76 in June 2024. Examining this sharp increase in anxiety, the analysis suggests that while rising antisemitism and declining safety certainly contributed, the elevated stress levels were likely driven primarily by concerns about antisemitism in the UK over and above concerns about Israel’s security, noting that anxiety increased uniformly across respondents regardless of their emotional attachment to Israel.
Furthermore, charitable giving priorities shifted notably, with the proportion of respondents prioritizing Israel charities nearly tripling from 6% before October 7 to 16% by June 2025. The report suggests that post-October 7 realities drove the Jewish population toward more particular Jewish causes at the expense of more universal general UK charities.
UK Jews report stronger ties to identity
The third section of the report investigated core dimensions of Jewish identity, peoplehood, and religious behavior. When respondents were asked to position themselves on a zero-to-10 scale regarding the strength of their Jewish identity, more than half chose nine or 10, with mean scores holding exceptionally steady at 8.29 in November 2022, 8.31 in June 2024, and 8.32 in June 2025.
When asked about the importance of feeling part of the Jewish People, 90% considered it important in May 2023, rising slightly to 92% in June 2024 before settling at 89% in June 2025, with those answering very important shifting marginally from 63% to 66% and 64% across those same waves. Similarly, when asked about participation in synagogue prayer services over the preceding 12 months, responses showed negligible movement, with 28% reporting no participation in November 2022 compared to 26% in June 2024 and 27% in June 2025, while regular attendees participating most or every Shabbat remained steady at 26%, 28%, and 27% respectively.
Self-described levels of religiosity also remained flat, with those placing themselves on the more strongly religious side resting at 49% in November 2022, 51% in June 2024, and 50% in June 2025. Taken together, these figures suggest that British Jews did not experience a broad-based transformation in religious observance or general identity strength following October 7.
The report concludes by emphasizing that October 7 acted as a profound watershed primarily regarding emotional connections to Israel and Jewish peoplehood rather than a total structural reinvention of British Jewish life. While solidarity, Zionist identification, and concerns over security heightened significantly, broader indicators of Jewish identity exhibited remarkable continuity with little to no measurable change.
In summary, the report noted that the “challenge facing Jewish leaders, educators and policymakers is how to translate these modest changes into deeper forms of participation, engagement and Jewish flourishing in the years ahead.”
