Escalation in Tigray raises risk of Ethopia-Eritrea war — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:13:27 UTC
23:13:27 KST

NAIROBI, October 6. /TASS/. The escalation of hostilities in Ethiopia’s Tigray region raises the risk of a direct armed conflict between Ethopia and Eritrea, Magnus Taylor, the Deputy Director of the Horn of Africa project at the International Crisis Group, was quoted as saying by the Africanews portal.
"The fact that Ethiopia and Eritrea are coming up against each other now suggests the regional picture is looking worse and you could see a kind of more broader escalation that goes beyond Tigray," Taylor said.
In his view, the escalation of the current standoff into a broader regional conflict would be "a worst-case scenario."
Taylor added that the retreat of the rebel Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) as a result of an offensive by Ethiopian federal forces may mean plans to shift from attempts to hold territory to insurgent warfare. In early October, Ethiopian troops established control over Tigray’s capital Mekelle.
Relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea deteriorated in recent months as Addis Ababa accused Asmara of supporting TPLF jointly with Sudan and Egypt - a claim that the three countries strongly rejected. In early October, Ethiopia closed its embassy in Asmara, with Eritrea subsequently announcing that diplomatic ties with its neighbor have been severed.
The Ethiopian government’s remarks about the need to secure reliable access to the Red Sea coast remain an additional source of tension. Earlier, Eritrea’s authorities accused Ethiopia of plotting to put these plans into practice by seizing the port of Assab. Addis Ababa maintains that it plans to resolve the issue peacefully.
Ethiopia lost access to the sea in 1993 after Eritrea declared independence following a referendum. Eritrea was formerly an Italian colony and later a British protectorate. In 1952, it was incorporated into Ethiopia as an autonomous region, but in 1962 Emperor Haile Selassie dissolved the federation and annexed the territory.

Staff reductions in government agencies to begin in Ukraine; the number of deputy ministers will decrease by 20%

The central government bodies plan to eliminate more than 4,000 vacant positions. The number of deputy ministers will be reduced by approximately 20%.
At the first stage, more than 4,000 vacant positions are planned to be cut in the central executive authorities. Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said this, reports UNN.
As part of optimizing and improving the efficiency of the state apparatus, more than 4,000 vacant positions are planned to be cut at the first stage in the central executive authorities
According to him, the most important thing is that we are conducting a functional diagnosis of the state apparatus. We will check what functions the authorities have and whether they correspond to the realities and priorities of the state, and only then determine the structure and final staffing level.
The number of deputy ministers will be tied to the volume of tasks and reduced by approximately 20%, while the number of deputy heads of other central executive authorities will be reduced by nearly 18%
According to the prime minister, a separate area is improving the training system, which should be tied to the tasks of a specific position. They plan to launch information initiatives and internships for young people. There is a separate program for veterans.
The Council for Public Administration has already resumed its work with the participation of government officials, parliamentarians, and experts. A detailed plan was presented at the meeting, and those responsible for each area were appointed. The goal of all these changes is a professional state apparatus capable of carrying out assigned tasks quickly and efficiently

Belgium’s transfer of three F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine will take place immediately after it signs an agreement with France to transfer the technology to a third party.
Belgian Defense Minister Theo Franken announced this in an interview with Ukrinform.
The need for additional approval arose because Belgium upgraded its F-16s with French radar warning systems. According to the defense minister, the approval process should not take long.
“We can do this fairly quickly. Our F-16s were modernized using French electronic warfare technology, so when we send them to Ukraine, we must have an agreement signed by France regarding transfer to a third party,” Theo Franken noted.
Immediately after receiving official permission from France, the Belgians will begin organizing logistics to ship the aircraft.
Belgian F-16 fighter jets are equipped with the French Carapace radar warning and threat detection system, developed by Dassault Electronique (now part of the Thales Group). The system is integrated into the aircraft’s fuselage and detects radiation from enemy radars, warns of missile launches, and automatically controls countermeasures, including the deployment of chaff and flares.
Belgium plans to transfer the first three F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by the end of the year.
On September 29, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced the delivery timeline.
In June, Theo Franken said the country expects to deliver seven aircraft by the end of the year: four as a source of spare parts and three for combat missions.
The overall plan calls for transferring 53 Belgian F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by the end of 2029.
According to the schedule, five aircraft are planned for delivery in 2027, 14 in 2028, and another 27 are expected to arrive in 2029.

Lithuania’s decision on nuke weapons poses threat to all of Europe — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:10:37 UTC
23:10:37 KST

MOSCOW, October 6. /TASS/. Lifting the ban on the deployment of nuclear weapons on Lithuanian territory could lead to anarchy and poses a threat to all of Europe, Alexander Stepanov, a military expert at the Institute of Law and National Security at the Russian Presidential Academy of National Economy and Public Administration (RANEPA), told TASS.
Earlier, the Seimas (parliament) of Lithuania voted to lift the ban on the deployment of nuclear weapons on the country’s territory. For the decision to take effect, a second vote is required in three months. During the plenary session, 106 deputies voted in favor of repealing the constitutional article prohibiting the deployment of nuclear weapons in the country, six abstained, and 18 voted against it.
"This leads to nuclear anarchy and opens the door to military nuclear technologies for countries that have no experience operating such complex systems, thereby creating additional threats for Europe as a whole. And if such decisions are adopted, as well as if plans to deploy nuclear weapons are implemented in practice, I believe that the Russian Federation will take all necessary steps to preemptively target such infrastructure facilities," Stepanov said.
The Seimas resolution provides for the removal of Article 137 from the constitution, which prohibits the deployment of weapons of mass destruction, including nuclear weapons, on Lithuanian territory. The same article prohibits the presence of foreign military bases. Vilnius is currently seeking to have the United States establish such a base in the country. As Seimas Speaker Juozas Olekas noted, the ban on the deployment of such weapons distinguished Lithuania from other EU and NATO countries.

Exhibition honours five Bulgarians who helped change America and the world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:07:54 UTC
23:07:54 KST

News
Exhibition honours five Bulgarians who helped change America and the world
Tuesday 6 October 2026 15:33
Tuesday, 6 October 2026, 15:33
Petya Ilieva
PHOTO Desislava Shapkarova
Font size
The portraits of five people with Bulgarian roots who made their mark in the United States and achieved worldwide recognition can now be seen at bus stops in Sofia, Plovdiv, Veliko Tarnovo and Burgas. Alongside their faces are short accounts of their lives and achievements.
The exhibition is the latest project by Bulgarian painter Petya Ilieva, whose Art for Diplomacy initiative brings art and culture out of galleries and museums and onto the streets, where everyone can enjoy them. Bus stops were chosen deliberately: the idea is to give people walking through the city or waiting for public transport a chance to discover something new and perhaps take an interest in history, culture or science.
“All five have inspiring stories. As children, they had particular interests, and through hard work they managed to make their dreams come true,” Petya Ilieva told Radio Bulgaria in an interview.
“What they have in common is that they knew from an early age what they wanted to do. They received an excellent education in their chosen fields and pursued their work with great passion. For most of them, their parents played an important role, encouraging their curiosity with books and taking them to exhibitions across Europe.
PHOTO Petya Ilieva
“We called the exhibition Bulgarian-American Angels. It was organised with financial support from the US Embassy in Bulgaria as part of the celebrations marking the 250th anniversary of American independence. We chose the name because these were Bulgarians who realised their full potential in America. They helped lay the foundations of engineering and space science, without which America would not be what it is today. None of the five ever lost touch with their homeland. Throughout their lives, whenever they had the chance, they made a point of mentioning their Bulgarian origins.”
Ilieva believes that the names of Assen Jordanoff, Peter Petroff, Viden Tabakoff, John Atanasoff and Viola Essen are probably unfamiliar to most Americans and many young Bulgarians. Yet in their respective fields, they remain pioneers whose work continues to inspire others.
Who are the five figures featured in the exhibition?
Assen “Jerry” Jordanoff (2 September 1896, Sofia – 19 October 1967, White Plains, USA)
From the skies over Sofia to the cockpits of American aircraft, Jordanoff was a Bulgarian aviation pioneer who helped shape modern flight.
An inventor, engineer and test pilot, he laid the foundations of aeronautical engineering in Bulgaria and wrote operating manuals for early American passenger aircraft. He is also credited with inventing the automotive airbag.
PHOTO Petya Ilieva
Viola Essen (stage name of Violeta Kolchagova)
A Bulgarian-American dancer who won over American audiences with her grace and freedom of movement, capturing the spirit of a new era in dance.
The daughter of Bulgarian immigrants, she became a dancer and choreographer with the renowned American Ballet Theatre and was among the pioneers of modern American ballet. She also had a romantic relationship with Marlon Brando.
PHOTO Petya Ilieva
Peter Petroff (21 October 1919, Brestovitsa – 27 February 2003, Huntsville, Alabama, USA)
Born in the Bulgarian village of Brestovitsa, Petroff went on to become an engineer whose ideas contributed to the early years of America's space programme.
He worked as an engineer at NASA and is credited with developing early satellite telemetry systems, the digital watch and wireless heart-monitoring technology.
PHOTO Petya Ilieva
Viden Tabakoff (14 December 1919, Stakevtsi – 6 June 2015, Cincinnati, USA)
From the small Bulgarian village of Stakevtsi to NASA's Apollo programme, Tabakoff devoted his career to engineering and scientific research.
An engineer, scientist, inventor and university lecturer, he helped advance jet propulsion technology, contributing to the developments that made space exploration possible.
PHOTO Petya Ilieva
John Vincent Atanasoff (4 October 1903, Hamilton – 15 June 1995, Frederick, USA)
An American physicist and mathematician of Bulgarian descent, John Atanasoff is widely regarded as the “father of the computer”.
Between 1939 and 1942, he and his student Clifford Berry developed the world's first electronic digital computer at Iowa State University, laying important groundwork for modern computing.
PHOTO Petya Ilieva
Five different lives, five different stories, all connected by their Bulgarian heritage. Through Bulgarian-American Angels, Petya Ilieva hopes to encourage more people to discover who these figures were and how their work contributed to progress around the world.
The printed panels will also travel to other locations, giving more people a chance to learn about their achievements.
“I hope that one day we can take the exhibition to the United States as well, so that the wider public there can get to know these people too,” Ilieva said.
Author: Desislava Semkovska
Supervising editor: E. Karkalanova
This publication was created by: Elizabeth Radkova

Metsola to take action after MEP Rima Hassan removes Israeli flag

2026-10-06

23:07:15 KST

French pro-Palestinian MEP Rima Hassan removed Israeli and EU flags from an exhibition commemorating the victims of Hamas’s 7 October terrorist attack, sparking outrage among fellow lawmakers. She could face a suspension of her daily allowance.
European Parliament President Roberta Metsola said she would take “all appropriate steps” against an MEP who sparked protests and criticism from fellow lawmakers in Strasbourg on Monday after throwing an Israeli flag to the floor.
Although Metsola did not name the MEP, the lawmaker was identified as Rima Hassan. Her office confirmed that she had removed an Israeli flag during an exhibition commemorating the victims of the 7 October 2023 terrorist attack in Israel.
According to parliamentary sources, she confronted Israeli artist Yaron Bob, who created the exhibition, accusing him of presenting a “one-sided account” of the attack.
"This house is a place where all of us must feel safe and secure and we reject in the strongest possible terms any action by any person that feels or makes anyone feel less protected," Metsola said in a statement in plenary session following the incident. "At a time of rising global antisemitism, we owe it to Europe's Jewish community to ensure that when they look at us, they see that this is their house too."
Metsola added that "all the appropriate steps" will be taken, "including the right of the person to be heard."
Born stateless in a Palestinian refugee camp in Syria, Hassan is one of France’s most prominent pro-Palestinian activists. She is currently on trial in France over alleged online remarks deemed to constitute an apology for terrorism, while Israeli authorities have accused her of being associated with Hamas.
Hassan could face a reprimand, a temporary suspension from Parliament’s activities, and/or a suspension of her daily allowance (€350 per day) for a period of up to sixty days.
An official in Metsola's office told Euronews that the Parliament’s presidency is now examining is now examining all available information to assess the incident and decide on the potential consequent penalty. The decision will not be taken during the current plenary session, the official added.
Hassan acknowledged in a statement from her office that she had removed the Israeli flag from its stand, but claimed the European Union flag, which was attached to the same base, fell as a result of the imbalance.
The statement said that “no flag was stepped on or damaged."
“Her gesture was directed exclusively at the holding, within the premises of the European Parliament, of an event organised in conjunction with the diplomatic representation of the State of Israel, during which objects presented as having been made from fragments of Israeli missiles were notably offered for sale,” the text said.
The gesture sparked reactions among MEPs and beyond the Parliament.
“Not even in the face of tragedy, her antisemitism can be put aside. Shame on her,” said Parliament’s vice-president Pina Picierno, from the Socialists and Democrats group.
Other lawmakers such as Renew Europe’s Nathalie Loiseau and European Conservatives and Reformists’ Nicola Procaccini also attacked her on social media and through statements in Parliament.
Israeli Foreign Affairs Minister Gideon Sa'ar described the incident as “shameful, outrageous, but sadly not surprising.”
Israel's ambassador to France Joshua Zarka told Euronews in an interview that Hassan "has been extremely active in her anti-Zionism and her anti-Semitism in support of terrorism," accusing her of "openly supporting what Hamas did on 7 October".
During an intervention at a plenary session, Hassan defended that the Parliament should "commemorate the victims of 7 October, without any association to the State of Israel," which she considers "a genocidal state" for the killings of civilians in Gaza.

EU Commission throws down the gauntlet to member states on reforming the bloc
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:07:10 UTC
23:07:10 KST

The European Commission is proposing fewer commissioners and less unanimity to prepare the EU for 30 or more members. However, EU diplomats say capitals are unlikely to agree.
The European Commission has put forward far-reaching proposals, including cutting the number of commissioners and moving away from unanimity, testing member states' appetite for internal reforms that stop short of treaty change.
The proposals are part of a broader package to make the EU's structures and decision-making fit for a membership of 30 or more countries. They are bound to be controversial among European capitals.
"The main question has been: is the EU fit for another enlargement? And there is a clear yes, a future enlargement is possible. Our assessment shows that in most policy areas, the EU is already fit for enlargement," Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos told reporters.
Unanimity
The Commission proposes identifying areas where so-called passerelle clauses could be activated, allowing the Council to move from unanimity to qualified majority. Activating those clauses, however, itself requires unanimity.
The idea of extending qualified majority voting is not new, particularly in foreign and security policy, where a veto can undermine the EU's ability to project geopolitical weight abroad.
Last month, 11 countries including France and Germany circulated a joint letter calling for the bloc to explore curbing obstructive foreign policy vetoes on the basis of sincere cooperation, notably through greater use of constructive abstention.
Asked whether member states back the move, Kos acknowledged that positions differ widely among EU countries. "It will not be easy, but it is worth trying," she said. A specific area she identified where less unanimity could be used is precisely during accession processes.
"Our proposal is to make our decision-making process more effective. We suggest using more QMV [qualified majority voting], which is nothing new. What is new is that we are suggesting that we will reduce the number of unanimity decisions in the accession process," Kos said.
Unanimity is required to grant a country candidate status and to close negotiations. In between, however, the current methodology gives any member state a veto over 150 steps.
The Commission also wants to make more use of enhanced cooperation, which lets at least nine member states pursue deeper integration on matters of crucial or strategic interest where blockages persist.
The most recent examples are the Ukraine Support Loan, from which Hungary, Czechia and Slovakia opted out, and the European Public Prosecutor's Office.
Here too, Brussels may meet resistance from some capitals, notably the so-called "Friends of the Western Balkans", a group that includes Italy and Austria. They have pushed back against differentiated membership and regulatory asymmetry.
Institutional changes
The Commission is also proposing to drop the principle that every EU country has a commissioner, which could prove problematic in a Union of 30 or more members.
Under the Lisbon Treaty, the Commission should have a number of members equal to two-thirds of the member states, chosen by "strictly equal rotation" that reflects the demographic and geographical range of all EU countries.
The system never took effect. In 2013, the European Council unanimously decided to keep one commissioner per member state, a concession to Ireland to secure a yes vote in its second referendum on the Lisbon Treaty.
Ireland was merely the most vocal opponent of losing a permanent presence in the Commission. Small member states widely fear their voice would be harder to hear in Brussels.
Rotation could also be hard to swallow for large countries such as France and Germany, which might find themselves left out of the College of Commissioners while the likes of Malta or Luxembourg are included.
"There are some candidates who say, no worries, this country can represent us. Other countries who say, yes, but not at the beginning. We would like to see how it [the Commission] works," Kos added.
The proposal for a leaner EU executive is well timed. The Commission is undergoing a so-called "large-scale review", and capitals are in intense talks on the bloc's next long-term budget, in which the EU administration is likely to face deep cuts.
Sceptical reception
Proposals that mainly affect candidate countries, such as safeguards against democratic backsliding and gradual integration, are likely to meet less resistance.
However, supporters of the reforms point out that, as candidates edge closer to joining the bloc, the question of how to keep an enlarged Union effective will be harder to dismiss.
Still, the suggestion is sure to raise eyebrows among European governments. Four EU diplomats who spoke to Euronews on condition of anonymity said these internal reforms are unlikely to fly.
The first test will come next week, when the enlargement reforms will land on the table of the EU leaders gathered for the European Council on 15-16 October.
"Some things are drafted to be killed," an EU diplomat said.

Everything you need to know about EU's first step to making Ukraine's membership real
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:06:40 UTC
23:06:40 KST

Everything you need to know about EU's first step to making Ukraine's membership real
European Council President António Costa (L) speaks with journalists alongside President Volodymyr Zelensky, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at the EU summit, the meeting of the heads of state and government of the European Union, in Brussels on June 18, 2026. (Michael Kappeler/picture alliance via Getty Images)
Editor's note: this article was updated with comments made at a press conference given by the EU's Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos.
BRUSSELS, Belgium — The European Commission published a document on Oct. 6 about the future of EU enlargement, a first step toward making Ukraine's eventual accession feel real, but also laying bare some of the work the bloc needs to do to be ready.
"As enlargement countries advance on their path of reform, the EU must be ready to welcome them," Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a press release.
The Commission was also asked by EU countries to propose ideas on how enlargement should work in the future, primarily in order to prevent backsliding on the rule of law by future EU members.
The 25-page communication is a first attempt to address both of these questions and to make enlargement feel like a real prospect for which the current 27 EU member states need to prepare.
It will be accompanied in October by a set of progress reports on how Ukraine and other candidate countries are faring with the reforms required of them, as well as concrete roadmaps for the four most advanced countries.
Those roadmaps will lay out specific milestones, with dates, between today and the eventual completion of the work required for Albania, Moldova, Montenegro, and Ukraine to become EU members.
The Commission's decision to focus on four countries is also considered an important "political signal," four different EU officials have told the Kyiv Independent.
"These countries have shown significant progress in terms of readiness over the last years," said Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos at a press conference to launch the document.
For Ukraine, that message is especially important, as its pace of reform has slowed in recent months, and given that it is much larger than the other three, its entry into the EU raises more challenging questions.
That decision to include Ukraine has also been coupled with a forceful defense by Kos of the reform work done so far, on the one hand, and a similarly strong push for Kyiv to keep passing reforms on the other.
Ukraine could break the bank
Just the financial cost of the EU's relationship with Ukraine puts it in a different league than the other three countries being discussed.
"For Montenegro, the bill is one euro per person, per year, so it was extremely cheap," a senior EU official told journalists ahead of the document's publication.
"Most of the accession candidates are very small countries, so we expect this enlargement grant to be relatively affordable … Ukraine is a very different animal," they said.
In the next EU budget, which spans 2028-2034, funding for candidate countries is set to come from a pot of money called "Global Europe," which the original Commission proposal for the budget set at 200 billion euros ($225 billion).
That proposal mentioned 15 billion euros ($17 billion) to be available for all candidate countries — not just the four most advanced — and a 100 billion euro ($113 billion) reserve for Ukraine, intended to address reconstruction.
But the cost of Ukraine's reconstruction was already estimated at $588 billion by the World Bank in February 2026.
"If you look at what has happened with funding of Ukraine, it's been completely driven by the war," the senior EU official explained in answer to a question from the Kyiv Independent.
"There is a massive uncertainty, no one is pussyfooting about that," they said.
read also
And farms strike at the EU's foundations
The EU's farmers have jealously guarded their subsidy program, the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), since its introduction in 1962.
In exchange for complying with EU rules, EU funding enables the bloc's farmers to continue operating in a food landscape where they would otherwise be unable to compete on price.
But the sheer size of Ukraine's agricultural sector puts it in a different league, prompting the Commission document to argue that "targeted arrangements should significantly limit financial support and market access for sensitive agricultural products."
The farming sectors of Montenegro, Moldova, and Albania are "a small stone you put in a pond, it doesn't create a lot of shocks and waves," a second EU official explained.
They explained that forcing Ukraine to fully integrate with all EU rules in the sector would raise their costs to the point that it could price them out of world food markets.
"Our budget can never compensate for gains that Ukraine's very competitive — the only real competitive agriculture sector in Europe — can gain in the world," a third EU official explained.
But equally, exempting Ukraine's agricultural sector from EU standards risks breaking the bloc's single market, which relies on all member countries' businesses operating on a level playing field.
Ukraine "will and can become a member of the CAP. Under which conditions, this will be discussed," Kos said.
"We also have to protect the farmers in the EU, and we are already discussing this subject with Ukraine," she added.
The Commission's document does not lay out a specific plan for addressing this already, arguing that it needs to be properly negotiated between Ukraine and EU countries.
However, two senior EU officials told journalists that they could see the discussion becoming very detailed, distinguishing between agricultural products. One rule for chickens, another for sunflower seeds, another for plant proteins, another for wheat, and so on.
More clear for them is that the EU needs to open the fifth enlargement cluster with Ukraine, and soon, where these questions can be fully grappled with.
The document commits the Commission to helping prepare the draft agreement for cluster five, to "reflect the targeted arrangements for Ukraine in the area of agriculture … at an appropriate moment."
Ukraine already unlocked two of the EU's six enlargement clusters in June and July, to-do lists of reforms required by the bloc in order for Kyiv to become fully aligned.
Another two are set to open on Oct. 13, if Kyiv passes a law expanding protections for the country's Hungarian-speaking minority the day before.
But the remaining two clusters cover sectoral issues such as agriculture and the trucking industry, where Ukraine has a competitive advantage, which intimidates some EU countries.
For the Commission, opening those two remaining clusters is important to do soon.
With a sweep of elections due to take place in EU countries in 2027, "if we do not make a step now politically, the discussion is going to get pretty complex," one EU official warned.
read also
Two-tier EU membership ruled out
To help make the prospect of Ukraine joining the EU more palatable over time, the Commission also makes several proposals on "gradual integration" of candidate countries into the EU.
Essentially, the plan would be to reward alignment with the EU by already unlocking some of the benefits that come with membership.
The idea is not entirely new, with Ukraine already included in the bloc's mobile roaming area, and Ukrainians being able to participate in the Erasmus youth exchange program.
But now the Commission wants to map every EU policy area, institution, agency, and program, for what could be offered to candidate countries, and when.
What gradual integration is not, however, is an alternative to EU enlargement, the document notes.
Likewise, the Commission is not proposing that new EU countries have fewer veto rights than existing members, except for a small voluntary commitment for countries not to use bilateral issues to stop other countries from joining.
And the plan to introduce safeguards to curtail voting rights if a country backslides on rule of law "will only be in place if there are breaches," Kos said.
Some other ideas pitched to include candidate countries more in the EU, such as observer seats in the European Parliament and Commission, as proposed by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, did not make it into the document.
"We don't want to open a new policy or political discussion," one senior EU official explained.
Instead, the plan is to show what is possible with the EU's existing framework, but if countries agree on other specific ideas, they can formally propose them.
One opportunity for EU countries to weigh such ideas will be when leaders are set to discuss the Commission's document as a whole on Oct. 15 in Brussels.
And it is expected that President Volodymyr Zelensky will be there with them.

The competing advances have intensified fighting across Kordofan, where government forces are seeking to consolidate their positions and expand control over key towns and routes.

The embassy said the practice of issuing student visas had not changed as of September 2026.
Russian citizens may apply for visas at the German embassy in Moscow, including for the purpose of studying at universities in Germany. Each such application is reviewed on an individual basis in accordance with established procedures, and decisions are made in line with the legal rules governing the presence of foreign nationals in Germany.
The German embassy refused last week to issue a visa to a graduate of HSE University’s design program who had been admitted to a German art university. Officials said she could use the knowledge gained at the German university for purposes other than intended, posing a threat to the country’s security.
In early September 2026, German authorities accused Russia of plotting sabotage at Leipzig Airport and pledged to tighten controls on entry for Russian citizens in response. German authorities want to reduce the number of visas issued to ensure that only Russians who do not pose a threat are allowed to enter, German Foreign Ministry spokesman Martin Giese explained. Officials did not specify exactly how this would work.

Spain court lifts Puigdemont arrest warrant, clearing way for his return home ahead of November elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:06:00 UTC
23:06:00 KST

Catalan separatist Puigdemont cleared to return to Spain
October 6, 2026
Spain's Supreme Court on Tuesday lifted an arrest warrant for Catalan separatist leader Carles Puigdemont, paving the way for him to return home ahead of a general election next month.
Puigdemont fled to Belgium in 2017 after leading a failed attempt for the wealthy northeastern Catalonia region to break away from Spain.
He had been wanted by authorities ever since, accused of embezzling public funds to hold an illegal independence referendum when he was head of Catalonia's regional government.
Judge Pablo Llarena lifted the arrest warrant shortly after Spain's Constitutional Court ruled that a 2024 amnesty for Catalan separatists also applied to embezzlement cases.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez welcomed the decision, saying it would allow Catalonia to "look to the future."
"We should celebrate that this also helps Catalan society, as it has been demanding throughout this time," he told journalists in Madrid.
How did the amnesty come about?
While Puigdemont and other members of his government fled abroad after the 2017 independence bid, several Catalan ministers who remained in Spain were sentenced to lengthy prison terms.
In 2024, in the face of strong opposition from Spain's conservative and right-wing parties, the Sanchez government passed an amnesty law. It intended to cover all offenses related to the secession attempt and ease tensions in the Catalonia region.
It also allowed Sanchez to secure the backing of Catalan separatist parties and stay in power after a 2023 election produced no clear majority.
But Puigdemont's Junts party withdrew its support last year, accusing Sanchez of failing to fulfill promises such as providing amnesty for its leader.
Around 400 separatists have benefited from the amnesty, but Puigdemont had been excluded because Spain's Supreme Court initially ruled the law did not apply to those accused of embezzlement. That changed after the Constitutional Court on Tuesday sided with one of Puigdemont's allies who had appealed against the top court's ruling.
Last week, Junts voted against housing relief measures proposed by Sanchez's government amid huge protests, prompting the prime minister on Monday to call a snap vote for November 29.

Two Spanish F-18s deployed in Romania under NATO command took off at dawn after two air targets were detected near the Ukrainian border. The objects did not ultimately enter Romanian airspace and were not intercepted.
Two Spanish F-18 fighter jets deployed in Romania under NATO command took off in the early hours of Tuesday after radar detected two aerial objects near the border between Romania and Ukraine, Romania's Ministry of Defence reported.
The Spanish aircraft were scrambled from the Mihail Kogălniceanu air base, near the city of Constanta in the south-east of the country, after surveillance systems detected the two objects in Ukrainian airspace, close to the river border with Romania.
The objects did not enter Romanian airspace, so the Spanish jets did not have to intercept or shoot them down, according to the Romanian authorities.
Alert for residents near the border
The incident prompted the Romanian authorities to activate protection measures for people living in the northern and eastern areas of Tulcea county, a region on the border with Ukraine and very close to some of the areas repeatedly targeted since the start of the Russian invasion.
At 2:20 local time, the authorities sent a message to residents via the national RO-Alert system because of the risk of falling objects from the air. The alert ended at 3:14.
The two Spanish F-18s are part of the detachment deployed in Romania to take part in NATO's enhanced Air Policing mission, which is intended to step up surveillance and protection of the Alliance's eastern flank.
The incident comes against a backdrop of repeated drone-related episodes near the border between Ukraine and Romania since the start of the Russian invasion in February 2022.

Russia on Tuesday proposed restoring cooperation with Afghanistan through the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) amid talks between the head of its Security Council and the Taliban administration's top diplomat
Russia’s Security Council head Sergey Shoygu told Afghan Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi during a meeting in Moscow that his country viewed Afghanistan’s integration into international relations, transport and energy projects, as a “key task in strengthening regional security and stability.”
“One step in this direction could be the resumption of engagement with Afghanistan within the framework of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, utilizing the previously established contact group,” Shoygu said at the meeting, according to Russian state news agency Tass.
Expressing Russia's interest in a “united, independent, and peaceful” Afghanistan, Shoygu was quoted as saying Moscow is ready to cooperate with Kabul in the fight against terrorism and drug-related crime.
Shoygu was further quoted as assessing Western statements about the possible return of US and NATO military infrastructure and facilities to Afghanistan as “absolutely unacceptable,” adding that Moscow hopes that other countries will follow Russia in recognizing Afghanistan’s Taliban-led government.
For his part, Muttaqi was quoted as thanking Russia's leadership for recognizing the current government in his country, stating that Kabul expects to strengthen cooperation with Moscow in areas such as the economy and security.
Muttaqi described the Moscow format of consultations on Afghanistan as an “important political initiative of the Russian Federation that has laid the groundwork for regular political consultations among the countries of the region.”
“We are convinced that this process must continue and be further developed,” he added.
Earlier Tuesday, Muttaqi held talks with Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexey Overchuk in Moscow, according to the Russian government's press service.
On Monday, Muttaqi took part in the eigth Moscow format consultations on Afghanistan held in Russia’s capital. That same day, he held bilateral talks with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.
The Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan in August 2021 after the withdrawal of US-led forces ended a two-decade war.
In July 2025, Russia recognized the Taliban administration as the official government of Afghanistan, making it the first country to do so.

Putin’s Family War Games Are Now in Full Swing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-06
14:04:14 UTC
23:04:14 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Putin’s Family War Games Are Now in Full Swing
What began as a Kremlin-backed “patriotic” family initiative has grown into nationwide military-style competitions where children as young as 11 train alongside their parents, handle weapons, practice battlefield skills, and are coached by veterans of Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Russia has expanded its military-style youth training into entire households, bringing parents and children together for nationwide war games that include shooting, grenade throwing, drone operations, and tactical exercises.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The Barents Observer on October 6, families from nearly every Russian region are taking part in the “Family Zarnitsa” competition, a Kremlin-backed initiative promoted as a way to strengthen “traditional values” and ties between generations.
Teams consist of two adults and two children aged 11 or older. Participants wear military-style uniforms and compete in exercises including grenade throwing, dismantling and reassembling Kalashnikov assault rifles, marksmanship, tactical field operations, first aid, and evacuating simulated casualties.
The training grounds are designed to resemble combat environments, while each family is assigned a coach who is a veteran of Russia’s war against Ukraine.
The project was formally presented in early 2025 by Russian Deputy Defense Minister Anna Tsivilova and was later backed by Vladimir Putin.
“Today, the ‘Family Zarnitsa’ project brings families together, strengthens the bond between generations, and integrates veterans of the Special Military Operation into a system of mentoring and patriotic education for young people,” Tsivilova said, using Russia’s official term for its war against Ukraine.
The competition is organized by several Kremlin-linked groups involved in the militarization of Russian youth, including Yunarmiya, VOIN, and Movement of the First, alongside the state-run Defenders of the Fatherland fund.
Russia has spent years expanding military and patriotic education among children and teenagers through organizations such as Yunarmiya and VOIN, whose combined membership now reaches hundreds of thousands of young Russians.
After regional qualification rounds, successful families advance to a national final. One of this year’s participants was the Maksimenko family from Zaozersk, a closed naval town on Russia’s Kola Peninsula.
The family defeated teams from Pechenga, Lovozero, and Murmansk before reaching the national final in Volgograd, where it finished 10th among 89 teams.
Yevgeniya Maksimenko, the family’s mother, said the competition included drones, mines, shooting, grenades, radio communications, and first aid, but described teamwork as its main lesson.
“We’ve become a REAL team. There are no ‘mums,’ ‘dads,’ or ‘kids’ here,” she wrote on social media.
Maksimenko has also been active in Russia’s ruling United Russia party. In 2025, she received an award from former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev for her work with the party’s women’s movement. Her eldest daughter, Liza, is a member of the VOIN military youth organization in Murmansk.
Earlier, in March 2025, Putin ordered the nationwide launch of “Family Zarnitsa,” a military-patriotic competition for parents and children proposed by Deputy Defense Minister Anna Tsivilyova. The initiative was designed to combine physical challenges with patriotic education and activities focused on Russian history and culture.

Italians and Czechs push Brussels to ease green rules as energy crisis hits industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:05:16 UTC
23:05:16 KST

Rome and Prague have joined forces to protect industry ahead of the EU leaders' summit in Brussels next week.
Italy and the Czech Republic have warned Brussels that the European Union's industrial base risks lasting damage unless the bloc eases the burden of its green rules, according to a letter seen by Euronews.
The joint warning, issued amid an unprecedented energy shock, reflects mounting pressure from EU capitals to protect domestic manufacturing as high energy and carbon costs collide with the bloc's decarbonisation targets.
"While security of supply remains the immediate priority, the combination of some of the world's highest energy prices, high carbon costs and exceptional fuel prices risks further weakening European manufacturing and accelerating the relocation of production and investment," reads the letter.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni visited her Czech counterpart Andrej Babiš in Prague last week to coordinate the plan of action between Rome and Prague ahead of next week's summit of EU leaders in Brussels.
Rome and Prague are targeting the bloc's carbon market, currently under political scrutiny, as well as its recently weakened methane rules, as they seek a broader coalition within the European Council.
The joint proposal outlines several targeted interventions designed to provide immediate economic oxygen to struggling European factories. Chief among them are the extension of free carbon allowances for heavy industry under the bloc's carbon market, the Emissions Trading System (ETS), and freezing the phasing out of free carbon allocations for sectors affected by the bloc's carbon border tax.
The push comes amid growing concern over European competitiveness, which is set to feature prominently on the agenda when EU leaders meet on October 15.
Italy and Czechia framed these measures as "temporary" interventions that "preserve long-term climate objectives". But several of their demands would amount to significant changes to the way the EU applies its climate rules to industry.
"A temporary suspension of the EU ETS would provide immediate relief to European industry from carbon costs. However, in the absence of sufficient support for such an option, it is worth considering a number of targeted and immediately actionable alternatives that the European Council could promote to alleviate the impact of the current shock and complement measures already announced at European level," reads the letter.
Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto recently went further, arguing that the ETS should be suspended until economic conditions improve.
"There would be better times" to reintroduce the carbon market in order to protect the environment, he said.
"A tax like the ETS today is unjust, absurd, unsustainable in international competition, and creates inequalities because it falls indiscriminately and equally on all European end consumers," Crosetto wrote on X.
The Meloni-Babiš initiative is the latest sign of a broader push among EU capitals to give greater weight to industrial competitiveness when implementing the bloc's climate policies.
Austria's Energy Minister Wolfgang Hattmannsdorfer made a similar case on the sidelines of a competitiveness ministers' meeting in Brussels on 24 September.
Hattmannsdorfer called for "economic patriotism" to keep industries and jobs in Europe, arguing that maintaining European production is crucial for regional wealth, welfare and environmental standards.

"The Strait of Hormuz is closed and the armed forces have full control over it, and this situation will continue until Iran's legitimate demands are met," Brigadier General Mohammad Reza Naqdi, a senior IRGC adviser, said in a media interview.

"They were the bully of the Middle East. They're not so much the bully anymore, but we have to finish up. And it's only a question of which way do we want to do it, the nice way or the not-so-nice way. And pretty soon you'll find out," he said.
Trump has repeatedly questioned its decision-makers, calling for "new leadership in Iran," and said the new Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei — who still has not made a single public appearance since he was appointed supreme leader in March — was "a sick man".
However, in a June podcast, Trump suggested the younger Khamenei is in charge. "They say he is giving approval, because that's the way it has been for a long, long time," the US president said.

23:00:00 KST

The risk of pneumonic plague spreading in Europe is very low, Lithuanian Health Minister Linas Kukuraitis said Wednesday, adding that the country’s hospitals have enough antibiotics to meet demand for about a month.
“Antibiotic reserves exist both at the national level, and hospitals should also have enough for up to a month to meet such a demand,” Kukuraitis told reporters.
Kukuraitis said Lithuania’s health system is better prepared to respond to infectious disease threats following the Covid-19 pandemic. The country has functioning infectious disease management infrastructure and established response procedures, he said.
He stressed that it has not been confirmed whether there was actually a case of pneumonic plague in Russia. Lithuania can currently assess the situation only on the basis of publicly available information, with a lack of reliable data presenting the main challenge, he said.
Kukuraitis said the strong reaction from the United States indicates that serious developments could be taking place in Russia, but that Lithuania currently has no independently verified information about the reported case.
The National Public Health Centre also said there is no increased risk of plague infection for people in Lithuania. Lithuanian institutions are monitoring the situation, but available information is limited and does not allow authorities to independently confirm that the woman who died in Russia had pneumonic plague.
Russian and local media previously reported that 28-year-old Daria Shipilova, who worked at a plague research institute in the Irkutsk region, may have died from pneumonic plague. Reports also said a possible laboratory incident had occurred and that her contacts had been isolated.
Russian officials, however, said post-mortem tests did not detect plague.
Kukuraitis previously said that if reports of plague in Russia were confirmed and the situation posed a threat to Lithuania, authorities could consider restricting the transit of Russian citizens through Lithuania. Any such measures would be coordinated with European Union partners.
Pneumonic plague is a rare bacterial infection caused by Yersinia pestis. It can be treated with antibiotics when diagnosed promptly, and antibiotics to treat the disease are available in Lithuania and elsewhere in Europe.

Woman from Rezekne sentenced to six years in prison for funding Russian military  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:10:30 UTC
23:10:30 KST

RIGA - The Riga City Court on Wednesday sentenced pro-Kremlin activist Polina Kamlova from Rezekne to six years in prison for funding the Russian military, LETA learned.
The woman was tried for transferring approximately EUR 43 for the purchase of drone-jamming equipment to be handed over to the Russian military.
In addition to the six-year prison sentence, she was placed on probation for three years. The court counted the time she spent in custody and detention in her sentence. Taking this into account, the remaining length of the sentence to be served is five years, one month, and 25 days.
The court left the imposed security measure - detention - unchanged until the ruling takes effect.
Kamlova may still appeal the ruling to the Riga Regional Court.
Without naming the individual, the prosecutor’s office previously told LETA that criminal charges were brought against an individual for committing a criminal offense under the section of the Criminal Law regarding the financing of an armed conflict.
The State Security Service (VDD) investigated the case before it was referred to the prosecutor’s office. VDD’s investigation revealed that in December 2024, Kamlova responded to a request from a contact person in Russia to provide funds for the purchase of drone-jamming equipment for Russian soldiers on the front lines in Ukraine.
Since it is not possible to make a transfer from a Latvian financial institution to a Russian financial institution, Kamlova turned to an acquaintance in Belarus. Thus, acting on the defendant’s request and unaware of the true purpose of the payment, she made a payment of 157 Belarusian rubles (approximately EUR 42.86) from her private bank account at a Belarusian financial institution to the bank account of Kamlova’s acquaintance at a Russian financial institution.
VDD initiated criminal proceedings against her on November 25, 2025.
The Criminal Law provides for punishment for the financing of an armed conflict with imprisonment for up to ten years and probation supervision for up to three years. Kamlova is currently in custody.
VDD detained Kamlova on December 2, 2025, and conducted searches at two locations associated with her in Rezekne and Preili Municipality.

TALLINN - The European Parliament has adopted a recommendation addressed to other EU institutions, expressing support for a world order based on multilateralism and stressing the need for dialogue with China on global challenges, peace and security, climate, and human rights.
At the same time, the report notes that EU-China relations have reached a difficult stage, as China employs unfair economic practices and holds a position on the war in Ukraine that is very different from the EU's, considering that the Chinese military has trained Russian soldiers to fight in Ukraine. The EU should therefore coordinate its actions with the US, G7 countries, and other like-minded partners, and China should use its influence on Russia to end the war in Ukraine.
The EU must urgently reduce its excessive economic dependence on China, as this can be used against the bloc. The EU must also de-risk in areas such as critical raw materials, pharmaceuticals, batteries, electric vehicles, information and communication technology, and semiconductors, as well as in other strategic sectors. China's industrial overcapacity, state subsidies, and access restrictions imposed on European companies are increasingly problematic for the EU economy. Investments into Europe must be screened more thoroughly, and the EU's vital technology, infrastructure, and supply chains must be more robustly protected.
Parliament demands a level playing field for the EU in trade and investment with China and wants the EU to respond proportionately when China fails to open its domestic markets. It also calls for strengthening the "Global Gateway" strategy partnerships, particularly in Africa and Latin America, as they offer an alternative to China's Belt and Road Initiative. Parliament stresses its continued support for the EU's One China policy but opposes any unilateral change to Taiwan's status quo by force or coercion.
The report also calls for the EU to more strongly combat cyberattacks, foreign interference, espionage, and hybrid threats, as well as to take a more robust stance on human rights. Parliament believes that more pressure should be put on China over its repression, use of forced labor, and policies in Tibet and Xinjiang. Additionally, Parliament expresses deep concern about the adoption of the so-called law on promoting ethnic unity and progress in China, as it further entrenches the country's assimilation policies. Parliament also demands that China unconditionally release all political prisoners.
In the plenary session, 454 MEPs voted in favor of the own-initiative report, with 86 against and 110 abstentions.
Rapporteur Hilde Vautmans from Belgium said that European policy towards China is changing and that a broad consensus is emerging in the EU on rebalancing economic relations. "I hope that Commissioner Šefčovič will address this tomorrow in Beijing. However, the Parliament's report goes even further. It calls for the EU to cooperate with China where possible but to remain firm on its security and values. As long as fundamental disagreements persist between the EU and China, our relationship will also be characterized by systemic rivalry."
Direct relations between the European Parliament and Chinese authorities were frozen from 2021 to 2025 after the Chinese government imposed sanctions on several MEPs in response to EU sanctions on Chinese officials and organizations for human rights violations. Relations were restored in 2025, and between March and June 2026, three parliamentary delegations visited China. A fourth visit is expected in October 2026.

RIGA - Public opinion on the Istanbul Convention could be gauged through a consultative referendum, the results of which would not be legally binding, Prime Minister and future candidate for the office, Andris Kulbergs (United List), said in a conversation with members of the press on Wednesday following a meeting with President Edgars Rinkevics.
Kulbergs stated that the United List had discussed the idea of a consultative referendum with the President. In his view, the Saeima could use such a referendum to pose a question to the public, receive an answer, and act accordingly.
The politician noted that the issue of the Istanbul Convention has generated significant public interest, making it a suitable topic for gauging public opinion in this way. Other questions could also be posed in consultative referendums. Although the results would not be legally binding, they would provide a clear signal to political forces and eliminate speculation, Kulbergs believes.
When asked whether postponing withdrawal from the Istanbul Convention is a condition for forming a new government, Kulbergs denied this. He emphasized that the public has given the United List a mandate for change, not for addressing ideological and divisive issues, so such matters are not on the United List’s agenda.
"Whether we will at some point hold a consultative poll or a referendum, and what politicians should do afterward, that is an open question," added Rinkevics, while noting that introducing a consultative referendum would first require changes to the law, which would take time.
The President added that there are differing opinions among legal experts regarding the possibility of putting international treaties to a referendum. While working on this issue last year, a large number of legal experts pointed to the possibility of putting a bill to denounce a convention to a referendum - rather than the treaty itself - while others held the opposite view.
Rinkevics emphasized that he currently sees no argument why Latvia should rush to withdraw from the Istanbul Convention, thereby becoming the first European Union (EU) country to take such a step.
The President reminded that, when submitting the bill to the Saeima for a second review, he had called for the issue to be left to the next parliamentary session and discussed in pre-election debates. The positions of the political parties have varied - some supported remaining in the convention, some strongly advocated for withdrawal, while others were willing to consider various options.
In his view, this is not an issue that needs to be rushed. Rinkevics noted that the new Saeima and government will face many pressing issues that require immediate attention. In consultations with most of the parties, he heard a willingness not to lower human rights standards or to raise issues that divide society.
As reported, last fall the United List, then in the opposition, together with other political forces, pushed for Latvia’s withdrawal from the Istanbul Convention, and the Saeima supported it, but the proposal sparked widespread public protests. President Edgars Rinkevics did not promulgate the law and referred it back to parliament for further review. The Saeima essentially agreed to entrust the final decision on the matter to the next parliamentary session, in which the United List has now gained a dominant role.
The United List's candidate for Prime Minister, current Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs - whom the President would like to see form the next government as well - has promised to focus his efforts on putting the country’s finances in order, ensuring security, and promoting economic growth.
The President expressed his view that, in his opinion, this issue should not be raised at this time. He would support the position of allowing the new Saeima and the Cabinet of Ministers to settle into their roles, while acknowledging that the issue of the convention might resolve itself.
Rinkevics also noted that the Saeima had adopted a resolution to draft a special law that would incorporate the positive aspects of the Istanbul Convention, but the government has yet to implement this resolution.
As another option under consideration, the President mentioned keeping the convention in force while simultaneously initiating discussions with Council of Europe (CoE) member states to clarify the provisions open to interpretation. He acknowledged that this would take a long time and emphasized that the issue should be resolved in a way that does not divide society.

EU's long-term budget: Parliament refuses to lower its ambitions  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:10:04 UTC
23:10:04 KST

TALLINN - The European Parliament debated the current state of negotiations on the EU's next Multiannual Financial Framework with representatives from the Commission and the Council in a plenary session. Parliament's rapporteur Siegfried Mureşan from Romania warned that Parliament will not agree to a smaller budget, as it would weaken Europe in the coming years and prevent the EU from achieving its goals, responding to crises, or dealing with unexpected events.
Mureșan reiterated that the Commission's initial budget proposal is at the same level as the outgoing budget period, despite growing challenges. The Commission's proposal for 2028-2034 amounts to 1.15 percent of the member states' Gross National Income (GNI), whereas the current Multiannual Financial Framework was 1.14 percent of GNI at the time of its presentation. "Reducing the budget would only weaken Europe," he stressed. Mureșan also emphasized that while member states' budgets have grown by 68 percent in absolute terms over the last seven years, the EU as a whole has not kept pace, meaning the perception of an ever-expanding EU budget is false.
Parliament's second rapporteur, Carla Tavares from Portugal, stated that Europe is no longer facing temporary crises but structural problems, and the EU's response must also be structural and far-sighted. Speaking on Parliament's position, she said: "We are not just demanding more money. We are demanding a budget that is consistent with the commitments assigned to the EU."
Tavares noted that while everyone generally agrees that Europe needs to spend more money to address priority issues in areas like competitiveness, energy independence, security, climate, education, and healthcare, some member states in the Council are still demanding a smaller budget and refusing new own resources. "It's as if we want a first-class Europe, but with a second-class budget! This isn't ambition; it's a contradiction. And it harms Europeans," she warned. "We don't have a choice between a cheap Europe or an expensive Europe. The choice is between an underfunded Europe mired in endless crises, or a Europe capable of anticipating problems, investing in its people and businesses, and shaping its own future," she concluded.
Most representatives of the political groups in the plenary also expressed support for Parliament's position, which was adopted in April 2026. In it, Parliament calls for a strong, realistic, and forward-looking budget that aligns with the EU's goals and is funded by new sources. The EU's long-term budget must serve the interests of its citizens, reduce inequality, and ensure sufficient funding for all key policy areas, including agriculture, regional development, cohesion, and social affairs. At the same time, the transparency and accountability of budget use must be improved.
Ireland's Minister for European Affairs, Thomas Byrne, confirmed that the Irish Presidency of the EU will present a new draft negotiating position for the Council on Saturday. "We want to move a step closer to an agreement, but a compromise will require difficult decisions," he said.
Piotr Serafin, the EU Commissioner for Budget, Anti-Fraud, and Public Administration, stressed that some countries continue to view the EU budget like an accountant's balance sheet: how much I put in versus how much I get out. "This approach was mistaken in the past, but with a modern budget, it doesn't work at all," Serafin said. He noted that the EU budget addresses common problems that member states cannot manage alone or that would cost everyone more if tackled separately.
Parliament adopted its position on the new Multiannual Financial Framework for 2028-2034 in April 2026. In it, Parliament called for an increase of approximately 10 percent to the budget originally proposed by the Commission to invest in key priorities such as defense and security, competitiveness, and cohesion and agricultural policies. Parliament also wanted to see new revenue streams to strengthen the EU budget, including a digital services tax, an online gambling tax, an extension of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), and a crypto-asset income tax. More than 93 percent of the EU budget goes directly to EU programs that support people and projects in all member states, with less than seven percent spent on administration.
Member states, however, according to the Council's initial position, want to reduce the Commission's proposed budget by two percent. The Irish Presidency of the Council plans to release its new negotiating package on Saturday, October 10. The EU's next long-term budget requires the approval of both the Council and the Parliament.

TALLINN – The Estonian Traders' Association recognized four outstanding retail projects of the year at its annual Trade Congress.
Category awards were given to The Club at the T1 center, the crisis store network established by the Estonian Stockpiling Agency and six retail chains, the acquisition of Prisma Peremarket and its merger with Coop, and the new intranet of Viru Keskus.
From the four category winners, the jury selected the nationwide crisis store network as the overall winner of the Trade Act of the Year 2026.
The nationwide crisis store network, created in cooperation between the Estonian Stockpiling Agency and six retail chains, was chosen as the Collaboration Project of the Year and the overall winner of the Trade Act of the Year 2026. The network's goal is to establish 110 crisis stores across Estonia by the end of 2026. The stores will be prepared to continue operating during long-term power outages, and it will be possible to pay by card even if the data connection with the bank is down.
According to Nele Peil, CEO of the Estonian Traders' Association, the project highlights the broader role of retail in society. "Retail plays a fundamental role in society. The crisis store network demonstrates this very concretely: traders help keep people's daily lives functioning even in difficult situations and contribute to Estonia's crisis preparedness together with the state," Peil said.
Ando Leppiman, Chairman of the Board of the Estonian Stockpiling Agency, stated that crisis preparedness is primarily born from cooperation. "Crisis preparedness does not arise from stockpiled supplies in warehouses or written plans alone, but is born from the joint action of people, companies, and the state. Interest has also been shown in the crisis store experience outside of Estonia, which shows that a functioning cooperation model can serve as an example for others," Leppiman said.
In the New Concept of the Year category, the T1 center was recognized for creating The Club. The concept, which combines training, working, and relaxation, expands the traditional role of a shopping center from a place to shop to a leisure environment. According to T1 data, the center was visited by an average of over 12,500 people per day in August, and the total turnover of tenants was approximately 10% higher than in the same month of the previous year.
The Development Project of the Year award was given to Coop Estonia for the acquisition of Prisma Peremarket and its merger with Coop. On September 1, Coop became the owner of Prisma Peremarket and its 13 stores, with nearly 700 employees joining the company.
All 13 stores will be integrated into Coop's systems between September and November. For the Roo Prisma store, the first to be transitioned, the technical and visual changes were completed in just over 16 hours.
The Technological Innovation of the Year category was won by Viru Keskus for launching its new intranet. The unified work and self-service environment connects 107 shops and nearly 1,200 users.
Among other things, the intranet consolidates employee training, user accounts, and access permissions into a single workflow. Previously, manually issuing an access card could take up to a week.
With the Trade Act of the Year competition, the Estonian Traders' Association recognizes projects that create significant value for customers, companies, or the broader development of Estonian trade.

Baltic states responded appropriately to threat to their underwater infrastructure - Atlantic Council expert  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:09:57 UTC
23:09:57 KST

RIGA - The Baltic states acted very appropriately by ensuring transparency regarding the threat to their undersea infrastructure and by cooperating closely with their allies to neutralize this threat, said Elisabeth Braw, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council and a member of the UK National Preparedness Commission, in an interview with LETA.
The author of the forthcoming book The Undersea War, which focuses on threats to undersea cables and pipelines, acknowledged that cable and pipeline infrastructure - especially cables - is an area where we remain vulnerable, as the cables lie on the seabed and have no protection whatsoever.
The only protection is the proper action of nations and maritime traffic participants - ships and all others. "We have now reached a point where we can no longer be certain that ships sailing in our waters will take care not to damage the cables, she said, acknowledging that we may never know whether, if a cable is snagged by an anchor, and if this was done intentionally or not," she said.
The expert assessed the Baltic states' response to incidents on the seabed of the Baltic Sea very positively. "In my opinion, the Baltic states are doing the right thing by ensuring transparency regarding these threats. It is essential to gain public support, and that is something all three Baltic states have done well. It is also necessary to cooperate closely with allies, but one's own public must definitely be involved in this process," said Braw.
The expert noted that in recent years, during several serious incidents involving undersea cables in the Gulf of Finland, the Estonians and Finns cooperated very closely to coordinate their responses, while the Latvians cooperated very closely with the Swedish government when a cable belonging to the Latvian Radio and Television Center was damaged, as it was a cable connecting Latvia and Sweden.
"It is precisely in such cases that radical openness and transparency are crucial. If the crew of the vessel that snagged the cable truly acted so carelessly that they severed the cable accidentally, then we should name that crew and ensure that everyone knows that these specific people caused the accident or incident, which could have significantly impacted, for example, Latvia's ability to function. After all, we need digital connectivity every day, every second," Braw said.
She specifically praised Latvia for implementing a national security education program in high schools, as Latvia is a step ahead of everyone else in this area.
"Latvia has the most comprehensive curriculum in this area; it is something other countries can learn from. This is also linked to transparency - teaching and educating young people about national security and how they can contribute to ensuring it," said Braw. Everyone has a role to play in helping to protect their country, even if it is something very small, such as verifying information before sharing it on social media.
