Physical attractiveness offers no protection for perpetrators of online misogyny
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:00:47 UTC
23:00:47 KST

People evaluating online misogyny judge the severity of the hateful content itself rather than giving attractive perpetrators a free pass. The findings suggest that when online harassment crosses an unambiguous moral line, users rely on message-based reasoning over heuristic shortcuts like physical appearance. The research was published in Computers in Human Behavior.
Social media users constantly encounter rapid streams of information and often rely on mental shortcuts to make quick judgments about what they see. This behavior is partly explained by the Elaboration Likelihood Model, a psychological framework describing how people process information through two distinct pathways. When individuals evaluate a message deeply, they use a central route of processing. When they lack the motivation or time, they tend to rely on a peripheral route, depending on accessible cues like a speaker’s visual appearance.
One well-documented mental shortcut is the attractiveness-leniency effect. This is a psychological bias where physically attractive people receive softer moral judgments after committing an offense. Because online environments are visually driven, a user’s profile picture can heavily influence how others interpret their intent and credibility. Yet research on online harassment has rarely examined whether this physical bias extends to perpetrators of digital misogyny.
Automated moderation systems often fail to capture the nuanced expressions of online hostility, shifting the responsibility of defining moral boundaries onto regular users. Rinat Meerson, Kevin Koban, and Jörg Matthes, researchers at the University of Vienna, sought to test whether an internet troll’s appearance alters how bystanders react to their posts. They also wanted to understand if the specific phrasing of the hostility changes those reactions.
Communication experts generally divide digital hostility into three categories: incivility, intolerance, and threats. Incivility involves rude or vulgar language that breaks social etiquette without necessarily targeting a demographic group. Intolerance communicates ideological exclusion or discrimination against a specific group, undermining democratic principles of equality. Threats involve explicit insinuations of physical or psychological harm, introducing an element of coercion and fear.
To test how these factors influence user reactions, the researchers designed an online experiment involving 884 adult participants in Austria. The participants first viewed three mock social media profiles featuring male faces. These faces had been scientifically validated in a prior database as having high, medium, or low physical attractiveness.
Next, the participants read three misogynistic comments that were ostensibly written by the men in the profiles. These comments were pre-selected by independent experts to represent either incivility, intolerance, or a direct threat. After viewing the material, the participants rated the comments on their acceptability and their level of sexism. They also reported their negative emotional reactions, their support for platform moderation, and their likelihood of intervening.
The researchers measured two types of behavioral responses: indirect and direct intervention. Indirect interventions involve low-risk actions like reporting a post or flagging it for community moderation. Direct interventions involve engaging in a social interaction, such as replying to the perpetrator or expressing public support for the victim.
The results showed that users categorized the hostility on a progressive scale. Participants rated both intolerance and threats as less acceptable and more sexist than mere incivility. The cognitive evaluations leveled off between the two more severe categories, indicating a ceiling effect. Once a comment crossed a certain boundary of unacceptability, users did not judge the direct threat to be much worse than the intolerant remark.
In contrast, emotional reactions continued to intensify across all three categories. Participants reported higher levels of anger and disgust as the comments escalated from incivility to intolerance. These emotional responses reached their absolute highest point when participants read direct threats.
When it came to taking action, the study revealed a split between private reporting and public confrontation. Participants expressed a higher intention to indirectly intervene as the severity of the hate increased. They also showed stronger support for platform moderation when viewing threats compared to uncivil or intolerant comments.
Yet their willingness to directly intervene remained consistently low across all types of comments. The researchers noted an asymmetry between moral condemnation and visible action. Users recognized the harm and felt negative emotions, but they remained hesitant to involve themselves in a public conflict. The authors suggest this reluctance stems from the reputational and emotional risks associated with public confrontation, such as the fear of retaliation.
Regarding physical appearance, the researchers found that perpetrator attractiveness had no effect on any of the outcomes. Participants evaluated the misogynistic comments with the same level of condemnation regardless of whether the profile picture showed a highly attractive or highly unattractive man. The researchers noted that these findings were not statistically significant for the attractiveness variable, meaning the pretty privilege bias failed to materialize.
The unambiguous nature of the misogynistic statements appeared to override any superficial mental shortcuts. The researchers propose that when a moral violation is highly explicit, users may engage in more systematic, central-route processing. In that case, the moral content of the message may dominate their evaluations, overriding any leniency typically associated with physical attractiveness.
The experiment relied on static text and images rather than a fully interactive social media environment. This limits how perfectly the study mirrors everyday scrolling, as real platforms feature moving elements and ongoing comment threads. The study also exclusively utilized male faces and focused solely on hostility directed at women.
Reactions to digital hate might shift if the comments were directed at a less uniformly protected social group. Different biases might also emerge if the perpetrator were female. Because attractiveness can sometimes work against women when it is seen as a sign of manipulativeness or deceptiveness, an attractive female troll might face harsher judgments for similar comments. Future research could explore how perpetrator gender interacts with physical appearance to shape bystander intervention.
The study, “Pretty privilege? Effects of perpetrators’ attractiveness and hate type on user responses against misogynist digital hate,” was authored by Rinat Meerson, Kevin Koban, and Jörg Matthes.

====================================================================================================

A love of intense sweetness shows a surprising link to financial choices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:00:45 UTC
23:00:45 KST

People who have a strong preference for intensely sweet tastes tend to grab a small reward available right now rather than wait for a larger one. New research published in Frontiers in Psychology suggests that this impatience may be partly explained by a general aversion to risk, rather than a stronger pull toward bigger rewards. The findings may help clarify the psychological and biological mechanisms connecting reward sensitivity to decision-making.
Reward sensitivity describes how strongly a person is motivated by the prospect of a reward. Scientists usually measure it with questionnaires or behavioral tasks, but one more physiological method is testing a person’s preference for sweet tastes. The sweet-liking phenotype, an observable biological marker, sorts people into two groups based on whether they strongly prefer highly concentrated sugar solutions or milder sweetness. Being a sweet-liker, a characteristic that is about half heritable and stable across life, is considered a physiological indicator of heightened sensitivity to a basic sensory reward.
A 2014 study found that people who intensely enjoy sweet tastes are more prone to choosing smaller, immediate rewards over delayed ones, a behavior known as delay discounting. Delay discounting is an economic and psychological measure of impatience. It captures how much less a reward seems worth to a person as the wait to receive it grows longer.
Separate neuroscience work, such as a 2009 study, demonstrated that the human brain relies on partly overlapping neural circuits to calculate the value of both delayed rewards and uncertain gambles. This physical overlap suggests that time preferences and risk preferences share common roots. Building on that idea, a 2018 study showed that a person’s tolerance for risk systematically alters how impatient they appear on delay-discounting tests, highlighting risk sensitivity as a potential hidden driver of impulsive choices.
The new study connects these threads by investigating whether biological sweet preference is linked to impulsive choices specifically through a heightened sensitivity to risk. The research was conducted by Anna Davidovich, senior research fellow Ksenia Panidi, and their colleagues at the Centre for Cognition and Decision Making at HSE University in Moscow. The team aimed to determine whether the link between sweet-liking and impulsivity could be explained by an increased desire for larger rewards, a heightened urge for immediate gratification, or a general avoidance of the uncertainty that comes with waiting.
“The study was motivated by the observation that sweet-taste preferences were linked to various kinds of addictions, such as alcoholism and other substance use disorders,” Panidi told PsyPost. “This observation suggests that sweet-taste preferences might be more broadly linked to impulsive decision making, due to the possible involvement of the opioid system in the valuation of rewards.” The opioid system refers to the brain’s own opioid chemicals, such as endorphins, which help regulate pleasure and pain.
“If this is the case, these differences in sweet-taste preference should then show up in other contexts (not linked to food rewards) that also imply value-based choices,” she explained. “This was the hypothesis that we decided to test using economic choices.”
To explore this, the researchers conducted two experiments. In the first experiment, 49 healthy adults completed a series of behavioral tasks. Participants took a standardized sweet-taste liking test, where they sampled five water solutions with varying concentrations of sucrose and rated their pleasantness. Those who rated the highest sucrose concentration as their favorite were classified as sweet-likers, while the rest were classified as sweet-dislikers.
It is important to distinguish this biological metric from everyday dietary habits. “The results of this study are very commonly misinterpreted as indicating that people who ‘like sweet food’ are more impulsive than those who don’t,” Panidi said. “In fact, sweet-taste preferences are very different from ‘sweet food preferences.’ Some studies even show that the correlation between the two is rather small.”
“The major difference is that the sweet-taste liking test only shows whether a person favors a sugar solution with the highest concentration of sucrose (i.e., 3 times higher than that of Coca-Cola),” she explained. “It does not necessarily mean that the same person would prefer sugary food, as food contains many more nutrients than just sugar (fats, proteins), which also affects food preferences.”
Participants also completed a lottery choice task to measure their risk preferences. In this task, they made 60 choices between a guaranteed payout of 100 monetary units and a risky lottery that offered up to 500 units at varying probabilities of winning (25, 50, or 75 percent).
After the lottery, they played a computerized balloon game, where they could earn real rubles by inflating a virtual balloon but would lose that balloon’s earnings if it popped. The taste test came first for 24 participants and last for the other 25, and the researchers controlled for this order, along with age and gender.
Twelve participants were classified as sweet-likers and 37 as sweet-dislikers. Sweet-likers did not rate the solutions as sweeter than sweet-dislikers did; they simply enjoyed the stronger ones more. The researchers found that sweet-likers were more risk-averse in the lottery choice task. They were less likely than sweet-dislikers to choose the lottery, and this gap held regardless of the prize size or the odds of winning.
However, the balloon task showed no differences between the two groups. The authors suggest this discrepancy might reflect that the lottery task involves explicit probabilities, while the balloon task requires people to learn about risk gradually through trial and error.
This aversion to risk ran counter to the researchers’ expectations. “Our initial hypothesis was that sweet-likers would be more prone to making impulsive choices which would also imply making risky choices, i.e., preferring an option where one can win bigger reward with some probability rather than taking a smaller amount of money for sure,” Panidi said. “However, we were surprised to see the opposite – sweet-likers showed higher preference for sure options compared to sweet-dislikers.”
“This might suggest that our common understanding of ‘impulsivity’ in risky contexts might be wrong,” she added. “In fact, making impulsive choices does not necessarily mean making risky choices. It might mean preference for more ‘tangible’ reward. If getting a small amount of money for sure feels more ‘tangible’ than playing a lottery, an impulsive person might prefer that small amount.”
In the second experiment, the research team recruited a new sample of 100 healthy adults to see how sweet-taste preferences relate to both risk and time delays. Because the task order had affected lottery choices in the first experiment, this time the taste test was always given last.
Alongside the same lottery choice task, participants completed a delay discounting task, which required them to choose between a smaller monetary reward available sooner and a larger reward available later. The two tasks were mixed together in blocks. Some of the delay choices offered the smaller reward immediately, while others enforced a delay for both the smaller and larger options.
Out of 100 participants, 28 were classified as sweet-likers. “I think an interesting observation is how stable the proportion of sweet-likers and sweet-dislikers in the population seems to be,” Panidi noted. “In our experiments, 25-30% of participants were classified as sweet-likers, which is pretty close to the proportions found in other countries where a similar method was used, such as South Korea or the UK.”
Sweet-likers again leaned toward the safe option, though in this larger sample the difference appeared only when the odds of winning were 50 percent, the point of greatest uncertainty. In the delay discounting task, the sweet-likers exhibited a specific pattern of impulsivity. When one of the rewards was available immediately, sweet-likers were more likely than sweet-dislikers to choose the immediate option.
But when both options required a waiting period, sweet-likers were actually more likely to choose the delayed, larger reward. Sweet-likers and sweet-dislikers did not differ in how strongly the size of the rewards or the length of the wait swayed their choices. Together, these patterns suggest that sweet-likers’ impatience is tied specifically to the availability of an immediate, certain outcome.
When the researchers accounted for each participant’s general risk aversion, the link between sweet-liking and choosing the immediate reward weakened by about 40 percent and fell just short of statistical significance. The authors interpret this as a sign that sweet-likers’ impatience may stem at least partly from a wariness of uncertainty: for someone who dislikes risk, a reward that arrives later can feel less certain than one in hand.
The two groups also looked alike on questionnaires. In the first experiment, sweet-likers and sweet-dislikers scored similarly on measures of sensation seeking and novelty seeking, and in the second they also did not differ on a standard impulsivity questionnaire or in how risky they rated themselves. The authors suggest that physiological and questionnaire-based measures of reward sensitivity may capture different things.
Panidi sees implications that reach beyond taste. “I think the main takeaway from this study is that the neurobiology of economic choice might have a much deeper physiological grounding than we might commonly think,” she told PsyPost. “At first, the link between sweet-taste preference and monetary choices might seem very indirect (how these two things might even be related?), but as we look deeper, we find that economic choices might be guided by our physiology just as much as our taste preferences.”
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost earlier this year, which relied on long-running household surveys of about 14,000 people in the United Kingdom rather than laboratory choice tasks. That study found that people who felt more dread about possible financial losses tended to be both less willing to take risks and less willing to wait for rewards.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study relied on laboratory tasks with small real-money stakes, which might not fully capture how people make high-stakes decisions in daily life. The effects were relatively small; in the first experiment, sweet-liking accounted for about 0.2 percent more of the variation in risky choices, and there were only 12 sweet-likers. The sample was limited as well: participants were young adults recruited in Moscow, and people with math, physics, economics, finance, or computer science backgrounds were excluded.
The delay discounting task offered only three sizes of sooner reward. This restricted range might have made it difficult to detect whether sweet-likers are more sensitive to the sheer size of a reward.
“I would not say practical significance is very important here,” Panidi said. “Rather, the results might be important for researchers as they suggest that we should further look into the mechanisms of opioid system involvement in economic or any other value-based choices. This might open the way to further investigation of addiction mechanisms.”
For instance, she suggested that “people who have preference for very sweet taste might be more prone to impulsive choices in various contexts, and knowing this might help them create the environment which discourages them from making unhealthy choices. But further studies are needed to make more solid conclusions.”
In addition, the lottery tasks in the study only involved positive gains, avoiding any scenarios where participants could lose money. Because the biological opioid systems linked to sweet-taste preferences may also be involved in evaluating threats, future studies could explore whether sweet-likers show a similar aversion to financial losses.
The research team also plans to observe these mechanisms more directly. “The next steps for this line of research would be in digging deeper into the neural differences between sweet-likers and sweet-dislikers, i.e., exploring what happens differently on the brain level when they make economic choices,” Panidi said.
The study, “Sweet-taste liking is associated with preference for less risky and immediate rewards in economic decision-making,” was authored by Anna Davidovich, Anna N. Shestakova, Nina Arzumanyan, and Ksenia Panidi.

Marine traffic not declining in southern part of Red Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:09:00 UTC
23:09:00 KST

MOSCOW, October 7. /TASS/. The number of vessel transits through the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait has not changed significantly following the escalation of the situation in Yemen and remains as 40-45 ships per day, according to TASS calculations based on vessel traffic data.
This volume of maritime traffic in the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait area has been recorded since July, when the Houthi rebels from the Ansar Allah movement first announced a de facto naval blockade of Saudi Arabia. Prior to that, an average of about 50-60 vessels crossed the strait daily.
The Bab-el-Mandeb Strait is a key maritime trade route that along with the Suez Canal provides ships with a shortcut from the Mediterranean Sea to the Arabian Sea and the Indian Ocean without having to circumnavigate the Cape of Good Hope at the southern tip of Africa.

TURKMENBASHI /Turkmenistan/, October 7. /TASS/. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov pointed to attempts by the Kiev regime to disrupt elections in Russia immediately after Moscow accepted a US proposal to hold a trilateral meeting on Ukraine.

Mayor of Turkish opposition stronghold Izmir defects to Erdoğan’s party
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:54:06 UTC
22:54:06 KST

The mayor of Izmir, Turkey’s third city and an opposition stronghold, has defected to the ruling AKP in a move hailed by Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, the Turkish president.
Turkey’s opposition is battling an increasingly intense crackdown, with a barrage of what observers say are politically motivated arrests and lawsuits targeting its mayors and elected officials.
Cemil Tugay’s decision to join the Islamic-rooted Justice and Development party (AKP) was announced by Erdoğan at a parliamentary group meeting in Ankara, where he welcomed the mayor amid a party-like atmosphere broadcast live on TV.
“I welcome Izmir mayor Cemil Tugay, who is today joining the AKP family,” Erdoğan said, presenting him with a party pin.
The scene caused anger and disgust on the streets of Izmir, a secular resort city of 4.5 million people on Turkey’s Aegean coast. Kadir Öztürk, 52, said of Tugay: “If I were his mother, I wouldn’t be able to show my face in public. His wife should divorce him. A person needs a backbone.” Tugay had vowed in January that he would never switch to the AKP and that if he did, his mother would disown him and his wife would leave him.
Taking control of the mayorship of Izmir, which has been governed by social democrats since 1999, is a big coup for Erdoğan, although opposition parties retain a majority on the city council.
The centre-left Republican People’s party (CHP) won a resounding victory in the local elections of March 2024, but it has since faced a growing intimidation campaign. Six of its provincial mayors have been arrested, including Ekrem İmamoğlu, the mayor of Istanbul, and 29 of its district mayors, according to figures published on Wednesday by the independent Diken news website.
There has been a growing number of defections to Erdoğan’s AKP, which had gained at least 17 opposition mayors before Tugay’s defection, the Medyascope news website said last week.
“This is a continuation of AKP’s strategy to reverse its major defeat in the 2024 local elections through force and repression,” said Berk Esen, a political analyst.
He said mayors were not changing sides because they had changed their ideology or been won over by the ruling party. Rather, many were doing it “out of fear”.
“This is a continuation of AKP’s strategy to reverse its major defeat in the 2024 local elections through force and repression,” added Esen.
Tugay took office as mayor in April 2024 just after CHP’s local election victory, but in June he resigned from the party after its leadership was replaced in a controversial court ruling.
The former CHP leader, Özgür Özel, went on to found the Yeni party, taking 90 lawmakers with him and becoming Turkey’s main opposition. Tugay said he would remain independent, leading to rumours he was planning to defect.
On Tuesday Özel spoke of the campaign of pressure, threats and blackmail faced by Izmir’s elected officials. “Those who do not bow to this pressure ... will remain our brothers until the day they die. But those who sell out and leave are traitors,” he said.

Raids on Overijssel livestock businesses over fraud and cruelty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:03:35 UTC
23:03:35 KST

Raids on Overijssel livestock businesses over fraud and cruelty
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Investigators from the food and product safety board NVWA have raided the homes and businesses of two livestock traders in Overijssel over suspected fraud and transporting sick animals.
The raids took place on September 30, the NVWA said on Wednesday. Investigators seized business records, phones, used ear tags and a pair of pliers for removing ear tags.
Every cow in the Netherlands must be registered and carry an ear tag with a unique number, so animals can be traced quickly if there is a disease outbreak or meat turns out to be contaminated.
Unregistered animals
At one trader’s premises, 88 animals were registered at a different address or not registered at all. At the other, 19 animals were incorrectly registered. Cattle without the mandatory ear tags were found at both sites.
With help from the police, investigators also stopped a lorry that had left one of the traders’ premises early in the morning. None of the 21 cattle on board were registered to his address. Another 32 cattle belonging to the same trader were found on a farm elsewhere in Overijssel. They had been imported but never registered in the Netherlands.
One trader’s business was registered on paper at the other’s address, keeping it out of sight. Cattle from the Netherlands and abroad were being kept there. Animals may only be gathered for sale or slaughter at approved collection centres, which have strict rules on cleaning and disinfecting livestock trucks to stop disease from spreading.
Sick cows
Inspectors also found a shed of cows in poor condition. Some could no longer stand and others had severe inflammation. One of the traders is suspected of transporting the animals even though they were too sick to be moved. The NVWA believes he then kept them because he could no longer sell them or have them slaughtered.
A vet put three cows down on the spot. The NVWA has taken administrative measures to make sure the rest get the care they need.
Neither trader has been arrested. The criminal investigation is being led by the public prosecution department’s specialist unit for environmental and fraud cases (Functioneel Parket). The NVWA told broadcaster NOS it could not say how it came across the pair.

US midterms could bring new wave of Israel critics to Congress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:02:21 UTC
23:02:21 KST

Breadcrumb
US midterms could bring new wave of Israel critics to Congress
Data and ratings from the Cook Political Report, an independent US election forecaster, and Decision Desk HQ, an election monitoring and forecasting platform, indicate that several districts in the US House midterm elections are likely to be won by Democrats.
The races include several new candidates who have been vocal opponents of Israeli policies in Palestine and the wider region.
With just weeks to go before voting day, forecasts point to Democrats having the advantage in the battle for the 435-seat House of Representatives.
The picture is more complicated in the 100-seat Senate, where 35 seats are being contested in the midterms.
The vote comes amid public dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump and Republican candidates over the war on Iran, as well as rising prices and inflation.
According to the latest estimates, Democrats are widely expected to take control of the House, while holding a relative advantage in the battle for the Senate.
The following is a summary of the key races.
Districts 'safe' for Democrats
The main districts classified as "safe" for Democrats by the Cook Political Report and not considered battlegrounds by Decision Desk HQ include:
- New Jersey's 12th District: Adam Hamawy (+13 points)
- Colorado's 1st District: Yemi Mobolade (+29 points)
- New York's 13th District: Yalinda Gonzalez (+32 points)
- New York's 7th District: Claire Valdez (+25 points)
- New York's 10th District: Brad Lander (+32 points)
- Michigan's 13th District: Donavan McKinney (+22 points)
All of these candidates would become new members of the US House if elected.
The candidates are progressives or socialists who have vocally opposed Israel's genocide in Gaza, with many making opposition to US arms shipments to Israel and funding from lobbying groups, particularly the pro-Israel lobby, prominent parts of their campaigns.
Several other districts where two Democrats are competing are also considered safely Democratic. These are in states with open-primary systems where candidates who advance from the primaries compete in the November election regardless of party.
The American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC, is spending millions of dollars in the general election to support pro-Israel candidates running against them.
- California's 34th District: progressive Angela Gonzalez Torres against incumbent Rep. Jimmy Gomez.
- California's 7th District: progressive Mai Phan against incumbent Democratic Rep. Doris Matsui.
- California's 14th District: progressive Aisha Wahab against Democrat Melissa Hernandez, who recently defeated her opponent in a special election to represent the seat for several months. The two are running against each other again in November.
The latest opinion polls indicate that candidates opposing US support for Israel could defeat candidates backed by AIPAC in several of these races, marking a potentially significant development in this year's elections.
'Swing districts'
Several districts where progressive Democrats are challenging Republicans remain competitive.
They include:
- California's 22nd District: progressive Randy Villegas against incumbent Republican Rep. David Valadao, with the Democratic candidate ahead by one point.
- Michigan's 7th District: progressive Democrat William Lawrence against incumbent Republican Rep. Tom Barrett.
The races are considered highly competitive, although Decision Desk HQ rates them as leaning Democratic.
Districts 'safe' for Republicans
The forecasts also classify several districts where progressive Democrats are challenging Republicans as safe for the Republican Party.
They include:
- Illinois' 11th District: Lebanese-American incumbent Rep. Darin LaHood against progressive Democrat Paul Nolley (+11 points).
- North Carolina's 10th District: incumbent Republican Rep. Pat Harrigan against progressive doctor Ashley Bell (+9 points).
- Arkansas' 3rd District: Republican Rep. Steve Womack against progressive Democrat Rob Wiers (+13 points).
- Indiana's 4th District: Republican Rep. Jim Baird against progressive Drew Cox (+15 points).
The US congressional midterm elections for the House and Senate, scheduled for 3 November, have now entered their decisive phase.
Trump, meanwhile, is relying heavily on his personal political appeal in an attempt to shift voter sentiment as Republicans grapple with domestic and foreign crises ahead of the vote.
Of the 435 seats in the House, a party needs 218 to secure a majority.
Republicans currently hold a narrow majority of 220 seats, compared with 215 for Democrats, meaning Democrats need a net gain of just three seats to take control of the chamber.
Republicans are also heading into the election facing the historical tendency for the president's party to lose congressional seats in midterm elections.
Trump's continued prosecution of the war on Iran has added to the challenges facing Republican candidates.
He has repeatedly insisted that the election will not force him to end the war, stressing that he was "not on the ballot".
